term_table.greek_sentence: ἀγρία δὲ σταφὶς οὐδὲν μὲν ἧττον τούτων δριμεῖά ἐστιν, εἰ μὴ ἄρα καὶ μᾶλλόν ἐστι πικρά· δριμεῖα γὰρ ἤδη καὶ μάλα καὶ θερμὴ σφοδρῶς, ὅθεν οὐδὲ τὸν ῥύπον ἀφαιρεῖ τῶν ἑλκῶν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὴν κατατήκειν πέφυκε τὴν σάρκα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Thus aristolochia and iris and panax do just this alone: they cleanse off and make clean the ulcers. But wild staphis is no less pungent than these, unless indeed it is even more bitter; for it is already pungent, and very much so, and vehemently hot, whence it not only removes the filth from ulcers but is also of a nature to melt down the flesh itself.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Thus birthwort, iris and panax do only this very thing: they cleanse away and make ulcers clean. But wild stavesacre is no less pungent than these, unless indeed it is even more bitter; for it is already pungent, and very much so, and vehemently hot, whence it not only removes the filth of ulcers but is by nature apt to melt away the flesh itself.

term_table.greek_sentence: τοιοῦτο δέ τι καὶ τοῦ σώματος εἴσω λαμβανόμενοι πεφύκασι δρᾷν οἱ πικροὶ χυμοὶ πάντες, οἷόν τι καὶ κατὰ τὰ ἕλκη· ῥύπτουσί τε γὰρ καὶ διακαθαίρουσιν αὐτὰ καὶ τὴν ἐν ταῖς φλεψὶ τῶν χυμῶν παχύτητα τέμνουσιν, ὅθεν ἐπιμήνιά τε κινοῦσι καὶ ταῖς ἐκ θώρακός τε καὶ πνεύμονος ἀναγωγαῖς τοῦ πύου συναίρονται, καὶ ὅλως, εἴτε παχὺ φλέγμα περιεχόμενον ἐν αὐτοῖς εἴτε πῦον εἴτ’ ἄλλο τοιοῦτο εἴη, διακαθαίρουσιν, ἐπιληψίαις τε κατὰ τοῦτο βοηθοῦσιν, ὅσοι γε μὴ δηλητήριοι τὴν φύσιν ὑπάρχουσιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And all the bitter juices are of a nature to do something of this sort also when taken inside the body, just as in the case of ulcers; for they cleanse and thoroughly purge them, and they cut the thickness of the humours in the veins, whence they both move the menses and assist in the bringing up of pus from the chest and lung, and in general, whether it be thick phlegm contained in them, or pus, or some other such thing, they purge it thoroughly, and in this respect they help in epilepsies—those of them, at least, that are not deleterious in their nature.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And all bitter flavours, when taken inside the body, are by nature apt to do something of the same kind as they do in the case of ulcers: for they cleanse and thoroughly clean them, and they cut the thickness of the humours in the veins, whence they both provoke the menses and assist in the bringing up of pus from the chest and lung; and in general, whether it be thick phlegm contained in them, or pus, or some other such thing, they thoroughly clean it out, and in this way they help in epilepsies, at least those of them that are not deleterious in nature; for those are contrary to nature in their whole kind.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: λεπτυν-τικός, ή, όν, of or for making thin, attenuating, Dsc. 5.88 , Gal. 6.572 , Diph.Siph. ap. Ath. 8.369d (also Comp. , ib.e): c.gen., χυλὸς λ. αἵματος Id. ap. Ath. 8.356d ; τὸ φῶς λ. τοῦ ἀέρος Stoic. 2.143 .
term_table.greek_sentence: Περὶ δὲ τῶν πικρῶν χυμῶν τῆς δυνάμεως ἀφορισάμενοι καὶ τμητικοὺς αὐτοὺς εἰπόντες εἶναι καὶ λεπτυντικοὺς καὶ ῥυπτικοὺς, καὶ δηλονότι θερμοὺς εἰς τοσοῦτον ὡς μήπω καίειν, ἐπὶ τοὺς δριμεῖς αὖθις ἴωμεν τῷ λόγῳ.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Having defined the power of the bitter juices, and having said that they are cutting and thinning and cleansing, and evidently hot to such a degree as not yet to burn, let us go on again in our discussion to the pungent ones.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: δια-βρωτικός, ή, όν, corrosive, Alex.Aphr. Pr. 1.99 , Gal. 1.280 ( Sup. ).
term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ πρῶτον μὲν θερμοὺς ἀκριβῶς αὐτοὺς εἴπωμεν, εἶτα διαβρωτικούς τε καὶ καυστικοὺς καὶ ἐσχαρωτικοὺς καὶ συντηκτικούς· ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ δέρματος ἐπιτιθεμένους ἅπαντας τοὺς τοιούτους εἶναι, εἴσω δὲ τοῦ σώματος λαμβανομένους, ὅσοι μὲν ὅλαις ταῖς οὐσίαις ἐναντιώτατα διάκεινται πρός τινα ζῶα, σηπτικούς τε πάντας εἶναι καὶ δηλητηρίους ἐκείνων τῶν ζώων.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And first let us say that they are precisely hot, then corrosive and caustic and eschar-producing and colliquative; that all such are of this kind when applied to the skin, but when taken inside the body, all those which in their whole substances are disposed most opposite to certain animals are putrefying and deleterious to those animals; but those which are so only in respect of the excess of their heat, if they are coarse-particled and earthy, are ulcerating to the internal parts, but if fine-particled, diuretic and sudorific, and, simply put, cutting and dispersing.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And first let us say that they are strictly hot, then that they are corrosive, caustic, eschar-forming and colliquative: all such are so when applied to the skin. When taken inside the body, however, those that are most opposite in their whole substances to certain animals are all putrefying and deleterious to those animals.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἐναντίος, α, ον, opposite, = ἀντίος (which is rare in Prose): of Place, on the opposite side, opposite, c.dat., ἀκταὶ ἐναντίαι ἀλλήλῃσιν Od. 10.89 ; Πάτροκλος δέ οἱ . . ἐ. ἧστο Il. 9.190 , cf. Od. 23.89 : hence, fronting, face to face, αὐτῳ οὔ πω φαίνετ' ἐναντίη 6.329 ; ὄττις ἐ. τοι ἰσδάνει Sapph. 2.2 ; δεῖξον . . τὸ σὸν πρόσωπον δεῦρ' ἐ. πατρί before him, E. Hipp. 947 ; τὰναντία τινί things open to one's sight, X. Cyr. 3.3.345 : abs., ἐ. στάνθ' E. Hipp. 1078 (but ἐ. κεῖσθαι look opposite ways, Pl. Smp. 190a ). with Verbs of motion, in the opposite direction, ἔνθα οἱ . . ἐναντίη ἤλυθε μήτηρ came to meet him, Il. 6.251 ; ἐναντίοι ἀλλήλοισιν ὄγμον ἐλαύνωσιν 11.67 ; δύο ἅμαξαι ἐ. ἀλλήλαις Th. 1.93 ; ἄνεμος ἐ. ἔπνει X. An. 4.5.3 . Astrol., in diametrical aspect, Vett.Val. 70.16 , Man. 3.360 . in hostile sense, opposing, facing in fight, c. gen., ἐναντίοι ἔσταν Ἀχαιῶν Il. 5.497 , cf. S. Aj. 1284 , X. An. 4.3.28 , etc.: c. dat., Il. 5.12 , E. Supp. 856 , IT 1415 ; οἱ ἐ. one's adversaries, A. Th. 375 , Gorg. Fr. 12 D. , etc.; the enemy, Hdt. 7.225 , Th. 4.64 , etc. generally, opposed to, τινί X. An. 3.2.10 ; τὸ ἐ. the opposite party, Id. Ath. 1.4 ; presenting obstacles, hindering, τινί S. Ph. 642 . ὁ δι ἐναντίας the opponent in a alawsuit, PFlor. 1.58.15 (iii A.D.), etc. of qualities, acts, etc., opposite, contrary, reverse, τἀναντί' εἰπεῖν A. Ag. 1373 ; δίκαια καὶ τἀναντία S. Ant. 667 : mostly c.gen., τὰ ἐ. τούτων the very reverse of these things, Hdt. 1.82 , cf. Th. 7.75 , etc.; δείξας . . ἄστρων τὴν ἐ. ὁδόν, i.e. τὴν τοῦ ἡλίου ὁδὸν ἐ. οὖσαν τοῖς ἄστροις E. Fr. 861 : also c. dat., Ὀρφεῖ δὲ γλῶσσαν τὴν ἐναντίαν ἔχεις A. Ag. 1629 ; τἀναντία πρήσσειν [τῇ ὑγιείῃ] Democr. 234 ; δύο τὰ -ώτατα εὐβουλίᾳ Th. 3.42 ; ἀγαθῷ κακὸν -ώτερον ἢ τῷ μὴ ἀγαθῷ Pl. R. 491d ; ἐναντία λέγει αὐτὸς αὑτῷ Id. Prt. 339b , cf. Ar. Ach. 493 ; τἀναντία τούτοις Pl. Prt 323d ; ἐναντία γνῶναι ταῖς πλείσταις [πόλεσιν] X. Lac. 1.2 ; τὴν ἐ. τινὶ ψῆφον θέσθαι D. 19.65 ; simply τὴν ἐ. θέσθαι τινί Pl. La. 184d : folld. by ἤ, τοὺς ἐ. λόγους ἢ ὡς αὐτὸς κατεδόκεε Hdt. 1.22 ; τοὐ. δρῶν ἢ προσῆκ' αὐτῷ ποιεῖν Ar. Pl. 14 ; τοὐ. ἔπαθεν ἢ τὸ προσδοκώμενον Pl. Lg. 966e , cf. R. 567c , etc.: freq. strengthd., πᾶν τοὐ., πάντα τἀ., quite the contrary, Lg. 967a , X. Mem. 3.12.4 ; πολὺ τοὐ. Stratt. 57 ; τὸ δὲ πολὺ ἐναντίον ἀποβήσεται Pl. Ap. 39c . τὰ ἐ. opposites in Philos., Pherecyd.Syr. 3 , Arist. Metaph. 986b3 , etc. in the Philos. of Arist. , τἀναντία (dist. fr. other ἀντικείμενα, Metaph. 1018a25 ) are contraries, esp. the two attributes within the same genus which differ most widely from each other (as hot and cold), Cat. 6a18 , al. ἐ. ἀποφάνσεις, προτάσεις, contrary propositions (All B is A, No B is A), opp. contradictory (v. ἀντιφατικῶς), Id. Int. 17b4 , APr. 63b28 . freq. in Adv. usages: from Hom. downwds., neut. ἐναντίον as Adv., opposite, facing, ἐ. ὧδε κάλεσσον here to my face, Od. 17.544 ; εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι ἐ. to look one in the face, 23.107 ; ἐ. προσβλέπειν τινά E. Hec. 968 , etc.; γυναῖκας ἀνδρῶν μὴ βλέπειν ἐ. ib. 975 : abs., D. 4.40 , etc.: hence, like a Prep. c. gen., in the presence of, τῆς βουλῆς IG 12.91 ; τῶνδ' ἐ. S. OC 1002 ; μαρτύρων ἐ. Ar. Ec. 448 ; ἐ. τοῦ παιδίου Id. Lys. 907 ; ἐ. ἁπάντων λέγειν Th. 6.25 ; ἐ. Διός Plb. 7.9.2 ; also neut. pl., IG 7.1779 (Thespiae). in hostile sense, against, c. gen., ἀνέσταν . . σφοῦ πατρὸς ἐ. Il. 1.534 ; ἐ. ἰέναι τινός 21.574 ; ἐ. μάχεσθαί τινος 20.97 ; ἐ. ἵστασ' ἐμεῖο 13.448 : abs., ἐ. μίμνειν stand one's ground against, ib. 106 : c. dat., νεικεῖν ἀλλήλοισιν ἐ. 20.252 ; ἐ. θεοῖς E. Or. 624 ; ἐ. τῷ ὅρκῳ πράττειν IG 22.1258.2 . contrariwise, in Att. also with the Art., τοὐναντίον on the other hand, τοὐ. δέ . . Antiph. 80.4 ; ἢ πάλιν τοὐ. Men. 460.5 ; conversely, Pl. Men. 89e . neut. pl. ἐναντία as Adv., c. dat., Hdt. 6.32 , Th. 1.29 , etc. with Preps., ἐκ τοῦ ἐ. over against, opposite, opp. ἐκ πλαγίου, X. HG 4.5.15 , etc.; ἐξ ἐναντίας, Ion. -ίης, Hdt. 7.225 , Th. 4.33 (οἱ ἐξ ἐ. the opposing parties, prob. in PGrenf. 2.78.26 (iv A. D.)); ἐκ τῶν ἐ. on the contrary, Plb. 5.9.9 ; ἀπ' ἐναντίας Ascl. Tact. 1.2 ; ἀπ' ἐ. Χωρεῖν Procop. Arc. 4 ; κατὰ τὰ ἐ. Pl. Ti. 39a : Geom., αἱ κατ' ἐναντίον τοῦ παραλληλογράμμου πλευραί the opposite sides of the parallelogram, Archim. Aequil. 1.9 ; αἱ κατ' ἐ. τομαί opposite sections (i. e. branches) of the hyperbola, Apollon.Perg. Con. 3.23 . regul.Adv. -ίως contrariwise, c. dat., τούτοις οὐκ ἐ. λέγεις A. Eu. 642 ; ἐ. διακεῖσθαί τινι Pl. R. 361c ; ἐ. ἀντικεῖσθαι Arist. Int. 17b20 ; πικρῶς καὶ ἐ. like an enemy, D. 19.339 ; ἐ. ἢ ὡς ἀνδραπόδοις τραφεῖσι Pl. Tht. 175d ; ἐ. ἔχειν to be exactly opposed, Id. Euthd. 278a ; πρός τι to be contrary in respect of . ., D. 1.4 ; in the Logic of Arist., Metaph. 1057b11 , al., cf. Procl. in Alc. p.268C.
term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ πρῶτον μὲν θερμοὺς ἀκριβῶς αὐτοὺς εἴπωμεν, εἶτα διαβρωτικούς τε καὶ καυστικοὺς καὶ ἐσχαρωτικοὺς καὶ συντηκτικούς· ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ δέρματος ἐπιτιθεμένους ἅπαντας τοὺς τοιούτους εἶναι, εἴσω δὲ τοῦ σώματος λαμβανομένους, ὅσοι μὲν ὅλαις ταῖς οὐσίαις ἐναντιώτατα διάκεινται πρός τινα ζῶα, σηπτικούς τε πάντας εἶναι καὶ δηλητηρίους ἐκείνων τῶν ζώων.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And first let us say that they are precisely hot, then corrosive and caustic and eschar-producing and colliquative; that all such are of this kind when applied to the skin, but when taken inside the body, all those which in their whole substances are disposed most opposite to certain animals are putrefying and deleterious to those animals; but those which are so only in respect of the excess of their heat, if they are coarse-particled and earthy, are ulcerating to the internal parts, but if fine-particled, diuretic and sudorific, and, simply put, cutting and dispersing.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And first let us say that they are strictly hot, then that they are corrosive, caustic, eschar-forming and colliquative: all such are so when applied to the skin. When taken inside the body, however, those that are most opposite in their whole substances to certain animals are all putrefying and deleterious to those animals.

term_table.english_sentence_A: And first let us say that they are precisely hot, then corrosive and caustic and eschar-producing and colliquative; that all such are of this kind when applied to the skin, but when taken inside the body, all those which in their whole substances are disposed most opposite to certain animals are putrefying and deleterious to those animals; but those which are so only in respect of the excess of their heat, if they are coarse-particled and earthy, are ulcerating to the internal parts, but if fine-particled, diuretic and sudorific, and, simply put, cutting and dispersing.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: δριμύς, εῖα, ύ, piercing, sharp, keen, βέλος Il. 11.270 : metaph., δριμεῖα μάχη 15.696 , Hes. Sc. 261 ; δ. χόλος Il. 18.322 ; μένος Od. 24.319 ; ἄχος Hes. Pl.Com. 154 ( Sup. ); χυμός Arist. de An. 422b13 ; ὀσμαί ib. 421a30 ; δριμέσιν ἰητρεύειν with pungent drugs, Hp. Fract. 27 ; δ. οἶνος Luc. Merc.Cond. 18 . Adv. -έως: Comp. δριμύτερον, ὄζειν Arist. Pr. 907a13 ; ῥεύματος δριμύτερον γενομένου Hp. VM 18 . metaph., of persons, bitter, fierce, ἀλάστωρ A. Ag. 1501 (lyr.); ἄγροικος Ar. Eq. 808 , etc.; also, keen, shrewd, κρόταλον E. Cyc. 104 ; ἔντονοι καὶ δ. Pl. Tht. 173a ; δ. καὶ δικανικός ib. 175d ; δ. ἐν τῷ ἀποκρίνεσθαι Arist. Top. 156b37 ; λόγος δριμύτατος Id. SE 182b37 (but λέξις and λόγος δ. of striking turns of phrase, Hermog. Id. 1.2 , 2.5 ): neut. as Adv., δριμὺ βλέπειν look bitter, Ar. Ra. 562 ; but also to look sharply, keenly, Pl. R. 519a , Luc. Symp. 16 ; ἐνορᾶν Id. Cat. 3 , Ael. VH 14.22 , D.C. 59.26 :—regul. Adv. δριμέως, Anaxandr. 15.3 ; ἐρασθῆναι Ael. NA 7.15 ; δριμύτατα ἀλγεῖν Id. VH 12.1 .
term_table.greek_sentence: ὑπὲρ ἁπάντων γὰρ τῶν τοιούτων ἐν τῇ θεραπευτικῇ μεθόδῳ λεχθήσεται, ὥστε καὶ περὶ τῶν δριμέων χυμῶν τῆς φύσεως ἤδη παύσομαι τὰ πλείω γράφων.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For about all such matters it will be spoken in the Therapeutic Method, so that I shall now cease writing more also about the nature of the pungent flavours.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For all such matters will be discussed in the Method of Healing, so that I shall now stop writing at greater length about the nature of the pungent flavours as well.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: διορ-ισμός, ὁ, division, distinction, Pl. Ti. 38c , Arist. EN 1134b33 , Porph. Abst. 3.20 . logical distinction, Pl. Plt. 282c ; definition, Arist. SE 168a23 , al. Math., particular enunciation of a problem, Procl. in Euc. p.203 F. statement of limits of possibility of a problem, Apollon.Perg. Con.Praef. , Archim. Sph.Cyl. 2.4 , Phld. Acad.Ind. p.17 M.
term_table.greek_sentence: ἀρκεῖ δὲ μόνον ἔτι διορισμοὺς ἀκριβεστέρους αὐτοῖς προσθεῖναι, καθ’ οὓς διαφέρουσι τῶν πικρῶν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: It suffices only to add to them still some more precise distinctions, according to which they differ from the bitter ones.
term_table.english_sentence_B: It is enough only to add to them, further, more precise distinctions, by which they differ from the bitter.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: τέφρ-α, Ep. and Ion. τέφρη, ἡ, ashes, as of the funeral pile, Il. 23.251 ; νεκταρέῳ δὲ χιτῶνι μέλαιν' ἀμφίζανε τέφρη 18.25 ; ὁ ἀὴρ ὁ ἐγκατακλειόμενος ἐν ταῖς θήκαις (coffins) . . διαλύει πάντ' εἰς τ. Thphr. Ign. 47 ; τ. πηγνυμένη νιφετὸν [σημαίνει] Id. Sign. 42 ; κἠπὶ τὴν τέφρην οἰχνεῖ (sc. τὸ πῦρ) Call. in PSI 11.1216.35 ; καταπάσας τέφραν, ἐμπάσαι τῆς τέφρας, Ar. Nu. 177 , Pl. Ly. 210a ; δόξαι τινὰ ψάμμον ἢ τ. ἐσθίειν Gal. 6.782 ; ἐκκρίνασα τὴν οἷον τ. τῶν ὑπεροπτηθέντων χυμῶν Id. 18(2).279 ; τέφρᾳ τιλθῆναι, prob. lime, Ar. Nu. 1083 (τίτανος is a form of τ. acc. to Gal. 12.140 ); ἡ τ. ἡ Φρυγία was used for eye-disease, Arist. Mir. 834b30 (cf. Pl. l.c.); so τ. κληματίνη Dsc. 5.117 ; τῆς τ. πλυθείσης ἡ κονία (cf. κονία 11 ) γίνεται Gal. 12.222 , cf. Thphr. HP 5.9.5 : prov., ὅρκους . . εἰς τέφραν γράφειν Philonid. 7 ; tefre, = nugacitas, Gloss. (With τεφ- [from θεφ-] cf. Skt. dáhati, Lith. degù 'burn', Lat. favilla, Gr. θέπτανος.)
term_table.greek_sentence: οὐ μόνον γὰρ ἰσχυρᾷ θερμότητι διαλλάττειν αὐτῶν πεφύκασιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ τοὺς πικροὺς μὲν ἅπαντας ὑπάρχειν οὐ θερμοὺς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ξηροὺς τὴν δύναμιν, ὡς ἄν τις μάλιστα σαφῶς εἰκάσειε, τέφρᾳ παραπλησίως, ἐν δὲ τοῖς δριμέσιν, ὅσοι γε οὐκ εἰσὶ πικροὶ, πολλὴν ἐνίοτε μεμίχθαι τὴν ὑγρότητα, καὶ διὰ τοῦτό γ’ ἐσθίειν ἡμᾶς οὐκ ὀλίγα τῶν τοιούτων σωμάτων.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For they are of a nature to differ from these not only by strong heat, but also in that the bitter ones are all not only hot but also dry in their power—as one might most clearly liken them, closely resembling ash—whereas in the pungent ones, those at least which are not bitter, much moisture is sometimes mixed in, and for this very reason we eat not a few of such bodies.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For not only are they by nature such as to differ from them in strong heat, but also in this: all the bitter are not only hot but also dry in power, as one might most clearly compare them, like ash; whereas in the pungent, at least those that are not bitter, much moisture is sometimes mixed in, and it is for this reason that we eat not a few bodies of this kind.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: σύστασις, εως, ἡ, (συνίστημι) bringing together, introduction, recommendation, πατρικὴν ἔχων ς. Plb. 1.78.1 ; ἡ πρός τινα ς. Id. 4.82.3 , cf. SIG 591.62 (Lampsacus. ii B.C.), D.H. Rh. 5.2 , Plu. Them. 27 ; ς. τῆς πρός τινα εὐνοίας J. AJ 15 .b. 7 ; care, guardianship, ἔτινηπίας οὔσας (ἀπέδωκεν[?]) εἰς σύστασιν Πτολεμαίῳ Γλαυκίου UPZ 20.23 (ii B.C.); power of attorney, PTeb. 317.14 (ii A.D.), etc. communication between a man and a god, ταῦτα σοῦ εἰπόντος τρίς, σημεῖον ἔσται τῆς συστάσεως τόδε PMag.Par. 1.209 , cf. 220 , 260 , al., PMag.Lond. 47.1 , 121.505 . protection, ἵνα διὰ τῆς σῆς δεξιᾶς ᾖ μοι ς. PSI 6.717.12 (ii A.D.). proof, Alex.Aphr. in Metaph. 12.3 , 409.16 ; confirmation, εἰς σύστασιν [τῶν ἀξιωμάτων] καὶ πίστιν ib. 271.14 ; ς. καὶ πίστεις τινός Hermog. Id. 1.10 ; πρὸς σύστασιν καὶ ἀσφάλειαν ἐπωμοσάμην PLond. 1.77.62 (vi A.D.), cf. BGU 1187.31 (i B.C.). (συνίσταμαι) standing together, close combat, conflict, ἐν τῇ ς. μάχεσθαι Hdt. 6.117 , cf. 7.167 ; ἡ ἐν ταῖς συμπλοκαῖς μάχη καὶ ς. Pl. Lg. 833a ; ἡ ἐκ ς. μάχη Hdn. 4.15.3 ; ὅταν . . σύστασιν ὁ ἀγὼν ἔχῃ Plu. Demetr. 16 , cf. Aem. 20 : metaph., disturbance in the human body, καθάρσεων καὶ συστάσεων τοῦ σώματος ἀρίστη ἡ διὰ τῶν γυμνασίων Pl. Ti. 89a ; καταστεῖλαι τὴν ς. τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ γυμνασίου Antyll. ap. Orib. 6.26.5 ; ς. ὅλου τοῦ σώματος (as a plague-symptom) Ruf. ap. eund. 44.17.2 ; ξ. τῆς γνώμης conflict of mind, intense anxiety, Th. 7.71 ; μένος μὲν ξ. τε σῶν φρενῶν δεινή E. Hipp. 983 ; so ἤν τις πόνος ἢ ς. γίνηται τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ Hp. Morb.Sacr. 17 vulg. ( f.l. for τάσις ). meeting, accumulation, e.g. of humours, ς. οὑγροῦ περὶ τὴν ὑπερῴην Id. Coac. 233 ; of water. Thphr. CP 5.14.5 (pl.), cf. D.S. 3.36 ; of winds, ib. 51 , POxy. 1768.9 (iii A.D., dub.): metaph., λόγων Pl. R. 457e ; combination, τραγῳδίαν . . εἶναι τὴν τούτων ς. πρέπουσαν ἀλλήλοις Id. Phdr. 268d . knot of men assembled, E. Andr. 1088 (pl.), Heracl. 415 (pl.); κατὰ ξυστάσεις γιγνόμενοι forming into knots, Th. 2.21 , cf. X. Eq. 7.19 . political union, more general than ἑταιρεία or σύνοδος, Isoc. 3.54 , cf. D. 45.67 ; ἐθνικαὶ ς. national unions, Plb. 23.1.3 ; κατὰ συστάσεις κωμάζειν D.C. Fr. 39.7 . contingent of four light-armed λόχοι ( 32 men), Ascl. Tact. 6.3 , Arr. Tact. 14.3 , Ael. Tact. 16.1 . friendship or alliance, Plb. 1.78.2 ; πρός τινας Id. 3.78.2 ; conspiracy, ἐπί τινα Plu. Pyrrh. 23 . composition, structure, constitution of a person or a thing, τῶ κόσμω Ti.Locr. 99d , cf. Pl. Ti. 32c ; τῶν ὡρῶν, τῆς ψυχῆς, Id. Smp. 188a , Ti. 36d ; of the parts of an animal, Arist. PA 646a20 , GA 744b28 , al.; σώματος Sor. 1.111 ; τῶν ἀτόμων Epicur. Nat. 35 G.; ἡ περὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ς. Pl. Ti. 75b ; φυσικὴ ς. Arist. Cat. 9b18 ; ἡ ς. τῆς πόλεως Id. Pol. 1295b28 , cf. 1332a30 ; τῶν πραγμάτων Id. Po. 1450a15 ; τοῦ μύθου ib. 1452a18 ; abs., plot of a drama, ib. 1453a31 ; τὴν ς. ἔχειν ἐκ τοῦ ψεύδους Phld. Rh. 1.361 S. ; περὶ τρόπων συστάσεως, title of work by Chrysipp.; προσώπου ς. expression of face, Plu. Per. 5 . abs., political constitution, Pl. R. 546a , Lg. 702d , etc. χωρίον ἀμπελικὸν ἐν συστάσει ἀρουρῶν ὅσων ἐστίν consisting of . . , PGiss. 56.7 (vi A.D.). coming into existence, formation, νόσων Pl. Ti. 89b , cf. c; πόλεων ς. καὶ φθοράς Id. Lg. 782a ; ἡ ἐξ ἀρχῆς τῶν ὅλων ς. D.S. 1.7 , cf. Plu. 2.427b ; τὴν ς. λαμβάνειν Arist. HA 547b14 , Plb. 6.4.13 , etc.; of a river, τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ς. λαμβάνειν Id. 9.43.1 ; ς. ἐπιβουλῆς Id. 6.7.8 . of bodies, density or consistency, πυκνότης καὶ ς., opp. ὑγρότης καὶ διάχυσις, Thphr. Vent. 58 ; ς. καὶ πῆξις Plu. 2.130b ; degree of solidity, consistency, σπέρμα . . τρυφερὰν ἔτι καὶ νεοπαγῆ τὴν ς. ἔχον Sor. 1.46 , cf. 58 ; solid knot or lump, [μαστοὶ] θρομβώδεις συστάσεις ἔχοντες ib. 88 ; μέχρι συστάσεως ἐμπλαστρώδους ἑψηθέν Gal. 11.134 , cf. 6.249 , Dsc. 3.7 ; τὰ ὑδατωδῶς ὑγρὰ πάχος καὶ ς. μηδεμίαν ἔχοντα Gal. 16.761 ; λεαίνεται μέχρι ς. Orib. Fr. 55 . a substance, πλάττειν ἐκ πηλοῦ ζῷον ἤ τινος ἄλλης ὑγρᾶς ς. Arist. PA 654b30 , cf. Plu. 2.696a ; ξηραὶ ς. Arist. HA 519b19 .
term_table.greek_sentence: εὐθὺς δὲ ταῦτα καὶ τῇ συστάσει μὲν ξηρότερα φαίνεται, καὶ τῷ δαπανᾶσθαι δ’ ἀεὶ καὶ ἀποῤῥεῖν αὐτῶν τὸ ὑγρὸν, ἐξατμιζόμενον ὑπὸ τῆς θερμότητος ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι τὸ καταλειπόμενον ἀποδείκνυσθαι γεωδέστερόν τε καὶ ξηρότερον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And straightaway these appear drier in their consistency, and, because their moisture is continually being consumed and flowing away, vaporised by the heat, it is necessary that what is left behind be rendered more earthy and drier.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And these at once appear drier in their consistency as well; and since their moisture is continually being consumed and flowing away, evaporated by the heat, what is left must necessarily turn out more earthy and drier.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἥσσων, ἧσσον, gen. ονος; Att. ἥττων, Ion. ἥσσων (not ἕσσων) Hdt. (v. infr.), Democr. 50 , Hp. VC 2 : formed from ἦκα (prop. ἠσσ-, cf. ἤκιστος), but in sense Comp. of κακός, μικρός: c. gen. pers., inferior; esp. in force, weaker, αἴθ' ὅσον ἥ. εἰμὶ τόσον σέο φέρτερος εἴην Il. 16.722 ; of horses, 23.322 , al.; ῥώμῃ ἥσσονες τῶν Περσέων Hdt. 8 113 , cf. 9.62 ; γυναικῶν ἥσσονες S. Ant. 680 ; Κύπριδος E. Andr. 631 ; ἔς τι in a thing, Hdt. 3.102 : c. inf. modi, ἥσς. τινὸς θέειν not so good at running, ib. 105 ; οὐδενὸς ἥσς. γνῶναι second to none in judging, Th. 2.60 ; ἱππεύειν ἥττ. τῶν ἡλίκων inferior to them in riding, X. Cyr. 1.3.15 . abs., οἱ ἥσς. the weaker party, A. Supp. 203 , 489 ; οὐχ ἥσσους γενέσθαι to have the best of it, Th. 4.72 ; τὸ λαμβάνειν τὰ τῶν ἡττ. X. An. 5.6.32 : c. dat. modi, ἥσσονες ναυμαχίῃ Hdt. 5.86 : c. acc. modi, τὸν νοῦν ἥσς. S. El. 1023 , cf. X. Cyr. 1.4.4 ; of things, τὸν ἥττω λόγον κρείττω ποιεῖν 'to make the worse appear the better cause', Pl. Ap. 18b , cf. Ar. Nu. 114 : pl., οἱ ἥττους λόγοι ib. 1042 , Isoc. 15.15 ; τὸ ἧσς. ἀδικία νέμεις E. Supp. 379 (lyr.). less, fewer, ἵνα πλείω μὲν ἀκούωμεν, ἥττονα δὲ λέγωμεν Zeno Stoic. 1.68 . c. gen. rei, giving way or yielding to a thing, a slave to . . , τοῦ τῆσδ' ἔρωτος εἰς ἅπανθ' ἥσς. S. Tr. 489 ; τῶν αἰσχρῶν Id. Ant. 747 ; ὀργῆς Id. Fr. 929 ; γάμων E. IA 1354 ; κέρδους Ar. Pl. 363 ; ἡδονῶν Pl. Prt. 353c ; γαστρὸς ἢ οἴνου ἢ ἀφροδισίων ἢ πόνου ἢ ὕπνου X. Mem. 1.5.1 ; χρημάτων Democr. l.c., Theopomp.Hist. 121 : generally, unable to resist, τοῦ πεπρωμένου E. Hel. 1660 ; νόσων καὶ γήρως Lys. 2.78 ; οἱ ἥττους τῶν πόνων [ἵπποι] X. Eq.Mag. 1.3 , 2.78 . neut. ἧσσον, ἧττον, as Adv., less, ὀλίγον δέ τί μ' ἧσς. ἐτίμα Od. 15.365 , cf. E. Hipp. 264 (anap.); ἧσσόν τι Th. 3.75 ; ἧσς. ἑτέρων Id. 1.84 ; ὁμοίως τε τρωθεὶς καὶ ἧσς. Hp.l.c.: mostly with Verbs, but also with Adjs., ἀριστοκρατίαι . . αἱ μὲν ἧττ., αἱ δὲ μᾶλλον μόνιμοι Arist. Pol. 1307a14 , cf. Mete. 340b8 : with a Comp. , ἧττ. ἀκριβέστερον Id. Pr. 957b8 ; ἧττ. εὐληπτοτέραν D.H. 3.43 codd.: with neg., οὐχ ἧσς., οὐδ' ἧσς., not a whit less, just as much, A. Ch. 181 , 708 , Th. 1.8 ; οὐδὲν ἧσς., μηδὲν ἧσς., S. Aj. 276 , 1329 ; for τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττ., v. μάλα .
term_table.greek_sentence: αὐτὸ μὲν γὰρ τὸ γλυκὺ πρὸς τῷ θερμὸν ὑπάρχειν ἢ μᾶλλον ἢ ἧττον, ἐξ ἀνάγκης δήπου καὶ ὑγρὸν ἢ μᾶλλον ἢ ἧττόν ἐστιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For the sweet itself, in addition to being hot to a greater or lesser degree, is surely of necessity also moist to a greater or lesser degree.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For the sweet itself, besides being hot to a greater or lesser degree, is of necessity, surely, also moist to a greater or lesser degree.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: θερμός, ή, όν (but θερμὸς ἀϋτμή h.Merc. 110 , Hes. Th. 696 ): (θέρω):— hot, θ. λοετρά Il. 14.6 , cf. Od. 8.249 ; θ. λουτρά Pi. O. 12.19 , S. Tr. 634 (lyr.), Pl. Lg. 761c , etc.; δάκρυα Od. 19.362 ; of water, ib. 388 ; of glowing wood, 9.388 ; θ. καύματα Hdt. 3.104 ( Sup. ); ἦν ἄρα πυρὸς ἕτερα -ότερα Ar. Eq. 382 : freq. in Att. , of hot meals or drinks, Telecl Id. 1.8 , 32 , Pherecr. 130.8 , etc.; of blood, S. OC 622 , Aj. 1411 (anap.); -οτάταν αἱμάδα Id. Ph. 696 ; of fever, θ. νόσοι Pi. P. 3.66 ; θ. σῶμα feverish, Th. 2.49 . metaph., hot-headed, hasty, freq. of persons, A. Th. 603 , Eu. 560 (lyr.), Ar. V. 918 , etc.; θ. καὶ ἀνδρεῖος Antipho 2.4.5 ; of actions, πολλὰ καὶ θ. μοχθήσας S. Tr. 1046 ; θ. ἔργον Ar. Pl. 415 ; δρᾶν τι νεανικὸν καὶ θ. Amphis 33.10 ; θ. ἐπὶ ψυχροῖσι καρδίαν ἔχεις S. Ant. 88 ; θ. πόθος AP 5.114 ( Phld. ); φάρμακον Alciphr. 1.37 ( Comp. ): c. inf., θερμότερος ἐπιχειρεῖν Antipho 2.1.7 : Sup. , ὦ θερμόταται γυναῖκες Ar. Th. 735 . still warm, fresh, ἴχνη AP 9.371 ; ἀτυχήματα Plu. 2.798f ; θ. κακά, opp. ἕωλα, ib. 517f ; γάμοι θ. καὶ ἴσως αὔριον Philostr. VA 4.25 . τὸ θ.,= θερμότης, heat, Hdt. 1.142 , Pl. Cra. 413c , etc. θ. (sc. ὕδωρ), τό, hot water, θερμῷ λοῦσθαι, βάπτειν, Ar. Nu. 1044 , Ec. 216 ; θερμῷ κεκραμένος οἶνος Gal. 11.56 ; also, hot drink, Arr. Epict. 1.13.2 . θερμόν, τό , grace, favour, θ. εὑρεῖν ἐν ἐρήμῳ LXX Je. 38(31).2 . τὰ θ. (sc. χωρία) Hdt. 4.29 ; but (sc. λουτρά), hot springs, X. HG 4.5.3 ; τὰ θ. τοῦ Ἡρακλέους Str. 9.4.2 . Adv. -μῶς Pl. Euthd. 284e : Comp. -ότερον, ἔχειν Eub. 7.1 : neut. pl. as Adv., θερμὰ θερμὰ πηδῶσαι Herod. 4.61 .
term_table.greek_sentence: εἰ δέ γε τῇ τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν φύσει μάλιστα οἰκεῖον ὑπάρχει, αὕτη δ’ ἦν εὔκρατος, ὑγρὰ καὶ θερμὴ, τὸ δ’ οἷον ὑπεροπτηθέντος τούτου γιγνόμενον ὅμοιον τιτάνῳ καὶ τέφρᾳ, ξηρὸν καὶ θερμὸν ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἀποτελεῖται.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And if indeed it is most akin to the nature of our body, and this was well-tempered, moist and hot, then that which comes to be, as it were, when this has been over-roasted, being like lime and ash, is of necessity rendered dry and hot.
term_table.english_sentence_B: If indeed it is most akin to the nature of our body, and this nature was well-tempered, moist and hot, then what comes into being when the sweet is, as it were, over-roasted, being similar to lime and ash, is of necessity rendered dry and hot.

term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ μέντοι καὶ δι’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ῥύπτειν τε πέφυκε καὶ καταθραύειν καὶ τέμνειν τοὺς γλίσχρους καὶ παχεῖς χυμοὺς, ὥσπερ ἡ τέφρα καὶ τὸ νίτρον.

term_table.greek_sentence: ὡς μὲν οὖν τοῖς στύφουσι [687] παραβαλεῖν, εἴη ἂν οὐκ ὀλίγῳ τινὶ λεπτομερέστερα τὰ πικρὰ τῶν φαρμάκων, ὡς δὲ τοῖς δριμέσι, παχυμερέστερα καὶ διὰ τοῦτ’ οὔτε διεξέρχεται ῥᾳδίως τῶν γλίσχρων τε καὶ παχέων χυμῶν, ὥσπερ ὅσα λεπτομερέστερα ταῖς οὐσίαις ἐστὶν, οὔτ’ ἀδυνατεῖ τέμνειν ὁμοίως τοῖς παχυμερέσιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: As compared, then, with the astringent things, [687] the bitter drugs would be not a little more fine-particled; but as compared with the pungent ones, more coarse-particled; and for this reason they neither pass easily through the viscous and thick humours, as do all those things that are more fine-particled in their substances, nor are they unable to cut, like the coarse-particled ones.
term_table.english_sentence_B: So, compared with astringent drugs, bitter drugs would be finer-particled by no small amount, but compared with pungent ones, [687] more coarse-particled. For this reason they neither pass easily through viscous and thick humours, as do the things that are finer-particled in their substances, nor are they unable to cut them, as the coarse-particled ones are.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἐν δὲ τῷ μέσῳ χρὴ τετάχθαι τὸ μέλλον τέμνειν ἑκατέρας τῶν ὑπερβολῶν, ἵνα μήθ’ ἑτοίμως ὡς αὐτὴ ἡ φλὸξ διεξέρχηται μήτ’ ἐν τῷ μέλλειν καὶ βραδύνειν ἀδυνατῇ διαιρεῖν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For that which is going to cut must be ranged in the middle between each of the two extremes, so that it neither passes through readily, like flame itself, nor, in delaying and being slow, is unable to divide.
term_table.english_sentence_B: What is to cut must be placed in the middle between each of the two excesses, so that it neither passes through readily, as flame itself does, nor, by lingering and being slow, is unable to divide.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ὑπερβολ-ή, ἡ, (ὑπερβάλλω) a throwing beyond others, δίσκων ὑπερβολαῖς Philostr. Im. 2.19 : in intr. sense, altitude of a star, Arist. Mete. 342b32 . overshooting, superiority, χερῶν ὑπερβολαῖς E. Fr. 434 ; στρατιᾶς Th. 6.31 . excess, τοῦ μεγέθεος Archyt. 1 ; opp. ἔλλειψις or ἔνδεια, Pl. Prt. 356a , 357a , 357b ; θερμασίης Hp. Vict. 2.65 ; ὑ. δισσὴ . . , τῷ ποσῷ καὶ τῷ ποιῷ Arist. PA 668b14 ; ὑπερβολὴν τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἔχειν c. acc. et inf., And. 3.33 , etc.: hence in various phrases, χρημάτων ὑπερβολῇ . . πρίασθαι at an extravagant price, E. Med. 232 ; ἐπέφερον τὴν ὑ. τοῦ καινοῦσθαι pushed on their extravagance in revolutionizing, Th. 3.82 ; οὐκ ἔχον ἐστὶν ὑπερβολήν it can go no further, D. 21.119 , cf. 25.54 ; ἃ μηδὲ πιθανὰς τὰς ὑ. ἔχει Men. Her. 62 ; so οὐδεμίαν or μηδεμίαν ὑ. λείπειν, Isoc. 4.5 , 110 , cf. D. 3.25 ; οὐδεμίαν ὑ. καταλείπων φιλοτιμίας SIG 545.13 (Delph., iii B. C.); εἴ τις ὑ. τούτου if there is aught beyond (worse than) this, D. 19.66 , cf. Isoc. 5.42 ; ταῦτ' οὐχ ὑ.; is not this the extreme, the last degree? D. 27.38 ; ὑπερβολὴν ποιήσομαι I will put an extreme case, Id. 19.332 ; τοσαύτην ὑ. ποιεῖσθαι ὥστε . . to go so far that . . , Id. 18.190 : folld. by a gen., ὑ. ποιεῖσθαι ἐκείνων τῆς αὑτοῦ βδελυρίας to carry his own rascality beyond theirs, Id. 22.52 , cf. 23.201 , And. 4.22 , Lys. 14.38 ; ὑ. ποιεῖν τῆς τιμῆς to raise the price, Arist. Pol. 1259a26 ; εἰς ὑ. εὐδαιμονίας ἥκειν Isoc. 11.14 ; τοσαύτας ὑ. δωρειῶν παρές χηται D. 20.141 ; ὑ. ἀνοίας ἔχειν Polystr. p.27 W. with Prep. in Adverbial phrases, = ὑπερβαλλόντως, εἰς ὑπερβολήν in excess, exceedingly; εἰς ὑ. ἄμεινον E. Fr. 494 ; ἀγαθὸς εἰς ὑ. Antiph. 80.11 ; ἐς ὑ. ἐκθερμαίνεσθαι Hp. Vict. 2.65 : c. gen., κτήσαιτ' ἂν ὄλβον εἰς ὑ. πατρός E. Fr. 282.6 ( v.l. εἰς ὑπεκτροφὴν πάτρας ); far beyond, τοῦ πρόσθεν εἰς ὑ. πανοῦργος, i. e. far more wicked, Id. Hipp. 939 , cf. D. 61.33 ; ἀναλίσκειν πάντα εἰς ὑπερβολάς Pl. Ep. 326d :— ἐξ ὑπερβολῆς Plb. 8.15.8 :—καθ' ὑπερβολὰν τοξεύσας with surpassing aim, S. OT 1196 (lyr.); καθ' ὑ. ἐπαινεῖν extravagantly, Isoc. 5.11 ; οἱ καθ' ὑ. ἐν ἐνδείᾳ ὄντες in extremity of need, Arist. Pol. 1295b18 ; αἱ καθ' ὑ. ἡδοναί Id. EN 1151a12 ; τὸ καθ' ὑ. τραχύ Phld. Po.Herc. 994.35 ; καθ' ὑ. ἁμαρτωλός Ep.Rom. 7.13 : c. gen., καθ' ὑ. φιλοδοξίας OGI 472.9 (Didyma, i A. D.):—so in dat., εὐτελὴς ὑπερβολῇ Men. 615 ; παχεῖ' ὑ. Philem. 41 ; ὑ. ἀγαθός Arist. HA 625a29 , etc. preeminence, perfection, without any notion of excess, δι' ἀρετῆς ὑπερβολήν Id. EN 1145a24 , cf. Rh. 1367b1 , Pol. 1284a4 ; ἡ ὑ. τῆς φιλίας the best and noblest kind of friendship, Id. EN 1166b1 ; but ἡ καθ' ὑ. φιλία, = ἡ καθ' ὑπεροχήν , Id. EE 1238b18 . overstrained phrase, hyperbole, ὑπερβολὰς εἰπεῖν Isoc. 4.88 ; οἱ πρὸς ὑπερβολὴν πεπονημένοι λόγοι ib. 11 ; ὑπερβολὰς εἰπεῖν make strong statements, Id. 3.35 , D. 27.64 ; as a figure of speech, Arist. Rh. 1413a29 , Demetr. Eloc. 52 , Str. 3.2.9 ; πρὸς -ὴν εἰρημένος Id. 1.2.33 . τὸ καθ' ὑπερβολήν the superlative degree, in Adjectives, Arist. Top. 134b24 ; τιθέναι ὑπερβολῇ ib. 139a9 ; καθ' ὑ. εἰπεῖν Id. Cael. 281a16 . overbid at auction, PPetr. 2p.44 (iii B. C.). crossing over, passage of mountains, etc., X. An. 1.2.25 , Plb. 3.34.6 , etc. in sg. or pl., place of passage, mountain-pass, with or without τοῦ ὄρους, τῶν ὀρέων, X. An. 3.5.18 , 4.1.21 , 4.4.18 ; ὑ. τοῦ Ταύρου Wilcken Chr. 1 ii 14 (iii B. C.); αἱ τῶν Ἄλπεων ὑ. Plb. 3.39.10 ; αἱ Ἄλπιαι ὑ. Str. 7.1.5 ; ἡ κατὰ τὸν Αἷμον ὑ. D.S. 19.73 . (from Med. ) delay, τοῦ κακοῦ Hdt. 8.112 , cf. Decr. ap. D. 18.29 , Plb. 14.9.8 ; [τῆς κρίσεωσ] ὑ. λαβούσης PEnteux. 65.3 (iii B. C.). the conic section called hyperbola, because the square of the ordinate is equal to a rectangle with height equal to the abscissa applied to the parameter (as base) but exceeding (ὑπερβάλλον), i. e. overlapping, that base, Apollon. Perg. Con. 1.12 , Procl. in Euc. p.419F.

term_table.greek_sentence: νυνὶ δ’ ἀρκεῖ γινώσκειν τό γε τοσοῦτον, ὡς ἡ πικρὰ ποιότης ἅπασα θερμαῖς τε ἅμᾳ καὶ ξηραῖς οὐσίαις συμβέβηκε, καὶ πρὸς τούτοις γ’ ἔτι λεπτομερέσι καὶ γεώδεσιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For now it suffices to know at least this much, that the bitter quality as a whole belongs to substances that are at once hot and dry, and in addition to these, moreover, fine-particled and earthy.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For now it is enough to know this much at least: every bitter quality belongs to substances that are at once hot and dry, and, in addition to these, fine-particled and earthy.

term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ γὰρ ἂν μάχεσθαι δόξειεν οὕτω γε τῷ γεώδει τὸ λεπτομερὲς, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ἁπλῶς λεπτομερὲς, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἐν γεώδει συστάσει τοιοῦτο εἶναί φημι τὸ πικρὸν, οἷον τίτανος καὶ τέφρα καὶ πᾶν ὅ τι περ ἂν ἀκριβῶς κατοπτηθῇ, καὶ γένηται σποδιὰ, μᾶλλον δ’ ἂν ἴσως ἀληθέστερον εἰκάζοιτο λιγνύϊ τινὶ καὶ αἰθάλῃ [688] φλογὸς, ἣ καὶ γευομένοις πικρὰ φαίνεται.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For in that way the fine-particled would seem to be in conflict with the earthy; but I say that the bitter is not fine-particled simply, but is such as it is within an earthy constitution, like lime and ash and everything whatever that has been thoroughly roasted and has become cinder-ash; or rather, perhaps, it might more truly be likened to a kind of smoky vapour and soot [688] of flame, which also appears bitter to those who taste it.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For taken in that way the fine-particled would seem to conflict with the earthy. But I say that the bitter is not simply fine-particled; rather, it is fine-particled as in an earthy consistency, such as lime and ash and everything that has been thoroughly roasted and has become cinders.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἀλλὰ διαπύρῳ μὲν σιδήρῳ καὶ λίθῳ τὰ πατὰ διάβρωσιν ἀναιροῦντα φάρμακα προσέοικεν ὑπὸ τῆς ἐν αὐτῷ σώματι θερμασίας, εἰς τοῦτ’ ἀγόμενα δηλονότι, καθάπερ ἥ τε χαλκῖτις καὶ τὸ μίσυ καὶ τὸ σῶρυ, καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ἀρσενικὸν, ὑδράργυρος, λιθάργυρος καὶ ἕτερα μυρία.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But the drugs that kill by corrosion resemble red-hot iron and stone, being brought to this state, evidently, by the warmth in the body itself, as for instance chalcitis, misy and sory, and besides these arsenic, quicksilver, litharge and countless others.
term_table.english_sentence_B: But the drugs that kill by corrosion resemble red-hot iron and stone, being brought to this state, evidently, by the warmth in the body itself, as chalcitis, misy and sory do, and in addition arsenikon, quicksilver, litharge and countless others. For all such things are coarse-particled and hot in potency.

term_table.english_sentence_A: Still more fine-particled than these, although earthy in their constitution, are lime, cantharis and the sea-hare; of these some ascend as far as the regions about the liver, and some even as far as the bladder and the thorax, acquiring the fiery quality in so great an interval [689] of their transport, while aristolochia and iris are more fine-particled even than these themselves; for they partake more than these of moist substance and of airy substance, and this is clear from their being neither so dry and brittle nor so heavy, and for this reason they have escaped the class of deleterious things.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Still more fine-particled than these, although earthy in their consistencies, are lime, cantharis and the sea hare. term_table.greek_sentence: τὸ δὲ τῆς ἐν Παλαιστίνῃ Συρίᾳ λίμνης ὕδωρ, ἣν ὀνομάζουσιν οἱ μὲν θάλασσαν νεκρὰν, οἱ δὲ λίμνην ἀσφαλτῖτιν, ἔστι μὲν καὶ γευομένοις οὐχ ἁλυκὸν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ πικρόν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But the water of the lake in Palestinian Syria, which some name the Dead Sea, others the Asphaltite Lake, is, to those who taste it, not only salty but also bitter.
term_table.english_sentence_B: But the water of the lake in Palestinian Syria, which some name the Dead Sea and others the Asphalt Lake, is, to those who taste it, not only salty but also bitter.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: λευκός, ή, όν, light, bright, clear (opp. μέλας in all senses), αἴγλη Od. 6.45 ; λευκὸν ( v.l. λαμπρόν ) . . ἠέλιος ὥς Il. 14.185 ; λ. φάος S. Aj. 708 (lyr.), cf. infr. 11.3 ; αἰθήρ E. Andr. 1228 (anap.); of metallic surfaces, λέβης Il. 23.268 ; λ. γαλήνη a glassy calm, Od. 10.94 ; of water, clear, limpid, Il. 23.282 , Od. 5.70 , A. Supp. 23 (anap.); λ. νᾶμα E. HF 573 ; - ότατος ποταμῶν Call. Jov. 19 . metaph., clear, distinct, of the voice, Arist. Top. 106a25 , S.E. M. 6.41 : in literary sense, clear, λ. στίχος AP 11.347 ( Phil. ): prov., λευκὸς Ἑρμῆς, when a rogue was detected, Macar. 5.53 . Adv. -κῶς, πάντα φαίνειν, of Hermes, Corn. ND 16 : Comp. -ότερον , διαλεχθῆναι Hld. 7.20 . of colour, white, freq. in Hom. , varying from the pure white of snow ([ ἵπποι] -ότεροι χιόνος Il. 10.437 ) to the grey of dust ( λευκοὶ ἐγένοντο κονισάλῳ 5.503 ); γάλα λ. 4.434 ; κρῖ 5.196 ; ἄλφιτα 18.560 ; ἡνία λεύκ' ἐλέφαντι 5.583 ; ὀδόντες 10.263 ; ὀστέα 16.347 ; ἱστία 1.480 ; φᾶρος 18.353 , etc.; λ. ἅρμα, = λεύκιππον , E. Ph. 172 ; of the white horses used by tyrants, λ. ζεῦγος D. 21.158 , cf. λεύκιππος; λ. λίθος marble, OGI 219.36 (Sigeum, iii B.C.), etc., cf. λευκόλιθος; λευκῷ<ʼν>λίθῳ λ. στάθμη a white line on a white stone, prov. of explanations which do not explain, S. Fr. 330 ; ἡ λ. ῥίζα white root (= ἡ τοῦ δρακοντίου, acc. to Gal. 19.118 ), Hp. Morb. 2.48 , Nat.Mul. 32 ; freq. of white or grey hair, λ. κάρη Tyrt. 10.23 ; θρίξ S. Ant. 1092 ; λ. γῆρας Id. Aj. 625 (lyr.); λευκὰ γήρᾳ σώματα E. HF 909 , etc. of the human skin, white, fair, sts. as a sign of youth and beauty, χρώς, πήχεε, Il. 11.573 , Od. 23.240 ; λ. παρειά, παρηΐς, S. Ant. 1239 , E. Med. 923 ; σάρξ, δέρη, ib. 1189 (v.l.), IA 875 (troch.); freq. with the notion of bare, κῶλον, πούς, Id. Ba. 665 , 863 (lyr.), Ion 221 (lyr.); cf. λευκόπους. of persons, white-skinned, Pl. R. 474e : hence, weakly, womanish, Ar. Th. 191 , Ec. 428 , X. HG 3.4.19 ; λευκῶν ἀνδρῶν οὐδὲν ὄφελος Macar. 5.55 ; cf. λευκόπρωκτος, λευκόχρως. λευκαὶ φρένες in Pi. P. 4.109 is expld. by Hsch. μαινόμεναι, frantic, passionate (cf. λευκῶν πραπίδων· κακῶν φρενῶν, Id.). λ. χρυσός, pale gold, i.e. gold alloyed with silver (prob. the same as ἤλεκτρον), opp. ἄπεφθος χρυσός, Hdt. 1.50 . metaph., bright, fortunate, happy, λευκὸν ἦμαρ νυκτὸς ἐκ μελαγχίμου A. Pers. 301 , cf. Ag. 668 ; a joyful day or holiday, Call. Aet. 1.1.2 ; λ. ἡμέρα a happy day, S. Fr. 6 , cf. Sch. Call. Iamb. in PSI 9.1094.39 ; variously expld. in Phylarch. 83 J. , Plu. Per. 27 ; ἡ λ. ψῆφος the vote of acquittal, Luc. Harm. 3 , cf. Hsch. λεύκη, ἡ, λευκόν, τό , as Subst., v. sub vocc. (Cogn. with Lat. lux, etc.)
term_table.greek_sentence: ἔχει δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ γεννωμένους ἅλας ὑποπίκρους ὁμοίως καὶ κατὰ τὴν ὄψιν εὐθὺς ἅμα πάσης θαλάσσης λευκότερόν τε καὶ παχύτερον φαίνεται, ἅλμῃ κατακορεῖ προσεοικὸς, εἰς ἣν οὐδ’ ἂν ἐμβάλῃς ἅλας, ἔτι τακήσονται, πλεῖστον γὰρ τούτων μετέχει.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And it has, likewise, the salts generated from it somewhat bitter; and to the sight it straightway appears at the same time both whiter and thicker than any sea, resembling a saturated brine, into which, not even if you throw in salts, will they still dissolve, for it partakes of a very great deal of them.
term_table.english_sentence_B: The salts generated from it are likewise somewhat bitter. To the sight too it appears at once whiter and thicker than any sea, resembling saturated brine, in which salts will no longer dissolve even if you throw them in, for it already contains a very great quantity of them.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἄχνη, Dor. ἄχνα, ἡ, anything that comes off the surface: of liquids, foam, froth, in Hom. of the sea, Od. 12.238 , al.; ἁλὸς ἄ. 5.403 , cf. Tim. Pers. 95 , A.R. 2.570 ; θοὴν ἀπερεύγεται ἄχνην, of a river, D.P. 693 : Medic., exudation, Hp. Int. 1 ; οἰνωπὸς ἄ. froth of wine, E. Or. 115 ; ἄχνα οὐρανία dew of heaven, S. OC 681 (lyr.); δακρύων ἄχνα dewy tears, Id. Tr. 848 (lyr.); also ἄχνη πυρός, i.e. smoke, A. Fr. 336 . of solids, chaff, in pl., ὡς δ' ἄνεμος ἄχνας φορέελ Il. 5.499 ; καρπόν τε καὶ ἄχνας ib. 501 ; down on the quince, μῆλον λεπτῇ πεποκωμένον ἄ. AP 6.102 ( Phil. ); ἄχνη ἡ ἀφ' ἡμιτυβίου fluff, shreds, used for lint, Hp. Art. 37 ; ὀθονίου Id. Mochl. 2 ; ἄ. Λυδῆς κερκίδος, of finespun fabrics, S. Fr. 45 ; ἄ. χαλκίτιδος metallic dust, Plu. 2.659c , cf. Orph. L. 455 ; ἄχναι wall-decorations, dub. in Aret. CA 1.1 (stramina Cael. Aur.). ἄχνην in acc., as Adv., morsel, the least bit, ἢν δ' οὖν καταμύσῃ κἂν ἄχνην Ar. V. 92 . πυρὸς ἄ., = χαμελαία , Dsc. 4.171 ; = θυμελαία , ib. 172 . ἄχναν· τὴν οἴκησιν, Hsch.
term_table.lsj_first_sense_gloss: anything that comes off the surface
term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ εἴ τις εἰς αὐτὴν καταδὺς ἀνακύψειεν, ἄχνην ἁλῶν ἂν εὐθέως κύκλῳ περὶ πᾶν ἴσχει τὸ σῶμα, καὶ διὰ τοῦτό τε βαρύτερόν ἐστι τῆς ἄλλης θαλάττης [691] τὸ ὕδωρ ἐκεῖνο τοσοῦτον ὅσον ἡ θάλαττα τῶν ποταμῶν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And if someone, having plunged into it, should come up again, he at once has a film of salt all round his whole body; and for this reason too that water is heavier than the rest of the sea [691] by as much as the sea is heavier than rivers.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And if someone dives down into it and then comes up again, he would at once have a crust of salt (ἄχνην ἁλῶν) all round his whole body. For this reason that water is heavier than the rest of the sea [691] by as much as sea-water is heavier than rivers.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: θάλασσα [θα], Att. θάλαμ-ττα IG 12.57 (but θάλασσα 22.236 ( 338 / 7 B.C.)), ἡ: —sea, Il. 2.294 , etc.: freq. of the Mediterranean sea, ἥδε ἡ θ. Hdt. 1.1 , 185 , 4.39 , etc.; ἡ παρ' ἡμῖν θ. Pl. Phd. 113a ; ἡ θ. ἡ καθ' ἡμᾶς Plb. 1.3.9 ; ἡ ἐντὸς καὶ κ. ἡ. λεγομένη θ. Str. 2.5.18 ; ἡ ἔσω θ. Arist. Mu. 393b29 ; ἡ ἔξω θ., of the Ocean, Id. Mete. 350a22 ; ἡ Ἀτλαντικὴ θ. Id. Mu. 392b22 ; ἡ μεγάλη θ. Plu. Alex. 73 ; of a salt lake, Arist. Mete. 351a9 ; ἐς θάλασσαν τὴν τοῦ Εὐξείνου πόντου Hdt. 2.33 ; πέλαγος θαλάσσης A.R. 2.608 ; κατὰ θάλασσαν by sea, opp. πεζῇ, Hdt. 5.63 ; opp. κατὰ γῆς, Th. 7.28 codd.; κατά τε γῆν καὶ κατὰ θ. Pl. Mx. 241a ; χέρσον καὶ θ. ἐκπερῶν A. Eu. 240 ; τῆς θ. ἀνθεκτέα ἐστί one must engage in maritime affairs, Th. 1.93 ; οἱ περὶ τὴν θ. sea-faring men, Arist. HA 598b24 , cf. term_table.lsj_entry_text: βαρύτης [υ], ητος, ἡ, (βαρύς) weight, heaviness, νεῶν Th. 7.62 , cf. Plb. 1.51.9 ; opp. κουφότης, Thphr. HP 5.3.1 ; heaviness of limb, β. ναρκώδης Plu. 2.978c ; of digestion, ἀπεψία καὶ β. ib. 128b . of men, troublesomeness, importunity, ἀηδίαι καὶ βαρύτητες Isoc. 12.31 ; disagreeableness, D. 18.35 , Plu. Cor. 30 , al.; β. φρονήματος Id. Cat.Mi. 57 . arrogance, Arist. Rh. 1391a28 ; gravity, τοῦ ἤθους Plu. Fab. I codd. of sound, depth, low pitch, opp. ὀξύτης, Pl. Prt. 316a , Arist. GA 778a19 , de An. 422b30 , Aristox. Harm. p.3M. , D.H. Comp. 11 , etc.; the grave accent, opp. ὀξύτης, Arist. Po. 1456b33 ; absence of accent, A.D. Pron. 38.15 , al. Rhet., adoption of an injured tone, Aps. p.331 H.
term_table.greek_sentence: ὥστ’ οὐδ’ εἰ βούλοιο κατὰ τοῦ βάθους καθεὶς ἑαυτὸν φέρεσθαι κάτω, δυνηθείης ἄν· οὕτως ἐξαίρει τε καὶ κουφίζει τὸ ὕδωρ, οὐχ ὡς φύσει κοῦφον ὑπάρχον, ὅπερ ἤδη τις εἷπε τῶν παλαιῶν σοφιστῶν, ἀλλ’ ὡς Ἀριστοτέλης ἔλεγε, διὰ βαρύτητα δίκην πηλοῦ βαστάζον τὰ κουφότερα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: So that not even if you wished, letting yourself down toward the depth, to be carried downwards, would you be able to: so much does the water raise and buoy one up, not because it is light by nature, which one of the ancient sophists once said, but, as Aristotle said, because through its heaviness it supports the lighter things, like mud.
term_table.english_sentence_B: So even if you wanted to let yourself down into the depth and be carried downwards, you would not be able to; so strongly does the water lift and buoy one up. This is not because it is light by nature, as one of the ancient sophists once said, but, as Aristotle said, because through its heaviness it carries lighter things, as mud does.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: πλοῖον, τό, (πλέω) prop. floating vessel: hence, generally, ship, A. Th. 602 , Ag. 625 , Hdt. 1.168 , IG 12.128.5 , etc.: more nearly defined, π. λεπτά small craft, Hdt. 7.36 , Th. 2.83 ; π. ἁλιευτικόν a fishing-boat, X. An. 7.1.20 ; ἱππαγωγὰ π. transports for horses, Hdt. 6.48 ; π. μακρά ships of war, Id. 5.30 , Th. 1.14 ; π. στρογγύλα or φορτηγικά ships of burden, merchantmen, X. HG 5.1.21 ; μεγάλα π. D.S. 13.78 ; ἱερὸν π. τοῦ Ὀσείριος OGI 56.51 (Canopus, iii B.C.): when distd. from ναῦς, without Adj., mostly merchant-ship or transport, as opp. ship of war, τοῖς π. καὶ ταῖς ναυσί Th. 4.116 , cf. 6.44 ; πλεῖν μὴ μακρᾷ νηΐ, ἄλλῳ δὲ κωπήρει πλοίῳ Foed. ap. eund. 4.118 ; πλοῖά τε καὶ τριήρεις Pl. Hp.Ma. 295d ; πλοῖα alone, = τριήρεις , X. HG 1.2.1 , Docum. ap. D. 18.106 .
term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ ὡς ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ πλείονα φορτία τῶν ἐν ταῖς λίμναις τε καὶ ποταμοῖς βαστάζει τὰ πλοῖα μὴ βυθιζόμενα, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἐν τῇ νεκρᾷ λίμνῃ πολλαπλάσια τῶν ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And moreover, just as in the sea boats carry greater cargoes without being sunk than those in lakes and rivers, in the same way in the Dead Lake they carry many times more than those in the sea.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Moreover, just as in the sea ships carry greater loads than in lakes and rivers without being sunk, in the same way in the Dead Lake they carry many times the loads they carry in the sea.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: θαλάσσ-ιος, later Att. θαλάσσ-ττιος, α, ον, also ος, ον E. IT 236 : (θάλασσα):— of, in, on, or from the sea, οὔ σφι θ. ἔργα μεμήγει Il. 2.614 ; κορῶναι εἰνάλιαι, τῇσίν τε θ. ἔργα μέμηλεν Od. 5.67 ; θ. βίος Archil. 51 ; χέλυς Alc. 51 ; θ. ἀνέμων ῥιπαί, κλύδων, Pi. N. 3.59 , E. Med. 28 ; Χάριτες Lyr.Adesp. 85.11 ; ὁ θ. [Ποσειδῶν] Ar. Pl. 396 ; of animals, opp. χερσαῖα, Hdt. 2.123 , cf. Pl. Euthd. 298d , Arist. HA 487a26 ; πεζοί τε καὶ θ. landsmen and seamen, A. Pers. 558 (lyr.); θ. ἐκρῖψαί τινα to thro wone into the sea, S. OT 1411 ; θ. νεκρός, of one drowned, Thgn. 1229 ; πλοῖον θ. sea-going vessel, POxy. 1288.6 (iv A.D.). skilled in the sea, nautical, Hdt. 7.144 ; γεωργοὶ καὶ οὐ θ. Th. 1.142 . like the sea, in colour, τῇ χρόᾳ Plu. 2.395b ; = ἁλουργής, στρώματα D.S. 34 / 5.2.35 . θαλάσσιαι, αἱ , name of certain priestesses at Cyzicus, CIG 3657.4 .
term_table.greek_sentence: τοσούτῳ γάρ ἐστιν τὸ κατ’ αὐτὴν ὕδωρ τοῦ θαλαττίου βαρύτερον ὅσον τὸ θαλάττιον τοῦ λιμναίου τε καὶ ποταμίου.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For the water in it is heavier than sea-water by as much as sea-water is heavier than lake-water and river-water.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For the water in it is heavier than sea-water by as much as sea-water is heavier than lake-water and river-water, since the substance of the salts, earthy and heavy, is added to it.

term_table.english_sentence_A: For the water in it is heavier than sea-water by as much as sea-water is heavier than lake-water and river-water.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For the water in it is heavier than sea-water by as much as sea-water is heavier than lake-water and river-water, since the substance of the salts, earthy and heavy, is added to it.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: πότιμος, ον, (πότος, πίνω) mostly of water, drinkable, fresh, Heraclit. 61 , Hdt. 8.22 , Hp. Medic. 2 , X. HG 3.2.19 ; κρήνη Plb. 34.9.5 : generally, τὰ π. Thphr. Od. 65 . metaph., fresh, sweet, pleasant, καρποὶ γλυκεῖς καὶ π. Id. CP 4.4.12 ; π. λόγος, opp. ἁλμυρὰ ἀκοή, Pl. Phdr. 243d ; of the writings of Isoc. , Phld. Rh. 1.200S. , cf. Lib. p.46O. ( Comp. ); π. δόγματα, ἔννοιαι, Ph. 2.275 , 1.72 ; τὰ χρηστὰ καὶ π., opp. τὰ δυσχερῆ καὶ μοχθηρά, Plu. 2.469c . of persons, pleasant, sociable, Theoc. 29.31 ( Comp. ); so also ποτιμώτερον συμπόσιον Hld. 3.10 . Adv., σοφῶς καὶ π. Philostr. VS 1.8.4 . porous, λίθος Pl. Lg. 947d . watered, irrigated, Apollon. Lex. s.v. πείσεα. = δευτερίας , Dsc. 5.6.15 .
term_table.greek_sentence: καί σοι καὶ αὐτῷ γεννῆσαι θάλατταν ἔξεστιν, ἅλας ὕδατι ποτίμῳ διατήξαντι καὶ γνῶναι πόσῳ βαρύτερον ἀποτελεῖται τὸ τοιοῦτο ὕδωρ τοῦ γλυκέος.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And it is possible for you yourself to generate sea-water, by dissolving salt in drinkable water, and to learn by how much heavier such water turns out to be than sweet water.
term_table.english_sentence_B: You yourself can also produce sea-water by dissolving salt in potable water, and so learn how much heavier such water turns out than sweet water.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: γλυκύς, εῖα ( -ῆα Herod. 4.2 ), ύ ( -ύν IG 14.1890 ), sweet to the taste or smell, νέκταρ Il. 1.598 ; οἶνος Epich. 124 , etc.; γλυκὺ ὄζειν Cratin.Jun. 1 , prob. in Crates Com. 2 ; opp. ὀξύς, Hp. term_table.greek_sentence: καί σοι καὶ αὐτῷ γεννῆσαι θάλατταν ἔξεστιν, ἅλας ὕδατι ποτίμῳ διατήξαντι καὶ γνῶναι πόσῳ βαρύτερον ἀποτελεῖται τὸ τοιοῦτο ὕδωρ τοῦ γλυκέος.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And it is possible for you yourself to generate sea-water, by dissolving salt in drinkable water, and to learn by how much heavier such water turns out to be than sweet water.
term_table.english_sentence_B: You yourself can also produce sea-water by dissolving salt in potable water, and so learn how much heavier such water turns out than sweet water.

term_table.greek_sentence: ὥστ’ ἔγωγέ ποτε μάταιον ἀπέδειξα τοῦ πλουσίου τὴν φιλοτιμίαν, ἐκ τῆς νεκρᾶς θαλάττης τοσοῦτο ὕδωρ κομίσαντος εἰς Ἰταλίαν, ὡς πληρῶσαι δεξαμενήν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: So that I myself once demonstrated as vain the ambition of a rich man who had conveyed so much water from the Dead Sea to Italy as to fill a pool.
term_table.english_sentence_B: So I once showed the ambition of the rich man to be vain, who had brought so much water from the Dead Sea to Italy as to fill a basin.

term_table.greek_sentence: μᾶλλον δ’ ἂν ἔτι βαρύτερον ἐργάσαιο τὸ τοιοῦτο ὕδωρ, εἰ τήξας τοὺς ἅλας ὡς πλείστους ὑπὸ κυνὸς ἐπιτολὴν, ἡνίκα μάλιστα θάλπος ἐστὶ σφοδρότατον, ἐάσαις ἐξοπτηθῆναι, παραπλησίως τῷ κατὰ τὴν ἀσφαλτῖτιν λίμνην.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And you would make such water heavier still if, having dissolved as much salt as possible at the rising of the Dog-star, when the heat is most intense, you should allow it to be baked out, in a manner similar to the water in the Asphalt Lake.
term_table.english_sentence_B: You could make such water heavier still if, after dissolving as much salt as possible at the rising of the Dog Star, when the heat is at its most intense, you let it be thoroughly baked, just like the water of the Asphalt Lake.

term_table.greek_sentence: φαίνεται γὰρ ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ ὕδατι μήτε ζῶον ἐγγιγνόμενόν τι μήτε φυτὸν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν εἰς αὐτὴν ἐμβαλόντων ποταμῶν ἀμφοτέρων, μεγίστους καὶ πλείστους ἐχόντων ἰχθύας, καὶ μάλιστα τοῦ πλησίον Ἰεριχοῦντος, ὃν Ἰορδάνην ὀνομάζουσιν, οὐδ’ εἷς τῶν ἰχθύων ὑπερβαίνει τὰ στόματα τῶν ποταμῶν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For it appears that in that water neither any animal nor any plant comes into being; but even of the two rivers that empty into it, which contain very large and very numerous fish, and especially of the one near Jericho, which they call the Jordan, not a single one of the fish passes beyond the mouths of the rivers.

term_table.greek_sentence: κἂν εἰ συλλαβὼν δέ τις αὐτοὺς ἐμβάλοι τῇ λίμνῃ, διαφθειρομένους ὄψεται ταχέως· οὕτως τ’ ﻿ [694] ἀκριβῶς πικρὸν ἅπασίν ἐστι καὶ ζώοις καὶ φυτοῖς πολέμιον, αὐχμῶδές τε καὶ ξηρὸν καὶ τὴν φύσιν οἷόν περ αἴθαλος ὑπὸ τῆς κατοπτήσεως γεγενημένον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And if someone were to catch them and throw them into the lake, he will see them quickly perishing; so [694] precisely bitter is it, and hostile to all things, both animals and plants, parched and dry and in its nature having become, as it were, soot through the roasting.

term_table.english_sentence_A: Their power is not only drying to a greater degree than that of the other salts, but also thinning, because they have been roasted more than the others.

term_table.greek_sentence: πᾶσι μὲν γὰρ τοῖς ἁλσὶν ὑπάρχει τι καὶ στυπτικὸν ἀμυδρὸν, ᾧ δὴ καὶ σφίγγουσι καὶ πιλοῦσι τὰ ταριχευόμενα τῶν κρεῶν καὶ μάλισθ’ ὅταν ὦσι χόνδροι τε καὶ δύσθραυστοι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For in all salts there is also something faintly astringent, by which indeed they bind and compact the meats that are being salted, and especially when they are in coarse lumps and hard to break.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For all salts possess something faintly astringent as well, by which they bind and compact meats that are being pickled, and especially when they are coarse-grained and hard to break.

term_table.greek_sentence: οὕτω δὲ δὴ καὶ τὸ νίτρον αὐτὸ καὶ ἀφρὸς αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ συνθέτῳ προσηγορίᾳ καλούμενον ἀφρόνιτρον ἔτι μᾶλλον τῶν ἄλλων πέφυκε ῥύπτειν, ὡς ἂν ἥκιστα μὲν στύφοντα, πικρὰ δ’ ἀκριβῶς ὑπάρχοντα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: So too nitre itself and its foam, and what is called by the composite name aphronitron, are by nature even more cleansing than the others, inasmuch as they are least astringent while being precisely bitter.
term_table.english_sentence_B: In the same way nitre itself, its foam, and what is called by a compound name aphronitre are by nature still more cleansing than the others, inasmuch as they are least astringent and thoroughly bitter.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: διαφορ-ά, ἡ, (διαφέρω) moving hither and thither, πεσσῶν διαφοραί moves, E. Fr. 360.9 . dislocation, τοῦ ὤμου Heliod. ap. Comp. 15 ; θεοῦ πρὸς ἄνθρωπον Plu. 2.1075c ; διαφορὰν ἔχειν to differ, Men. 426 . in Logic, the differentia of a species, ἐκ τοῦ γένους καὶ τῶν διαφορῶν τὰ εἴδη Arist. Metaph. 1057b7 , cf. term_table.greek_sentence: διαφέρουσι δ’ ὅμως οὐκ ἀσαφεῖ διαφορᾷ ἐν τῷ λεπτύνεσθαί τε καὶ κατειργάσθαι μᾶλλον ὑπὸ θερμότητος ξηρᾶς τὸν πικρόν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For the salty flavour is near to the bitter, since both are earthy and hot; yet they differ by no obscure difference, in that the bitter has been thinned and worked up more by dry heat.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Nevertheless they differ by no obscure difference, in that the bitter has been thinned and worked up more by dry heat.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: γεώδης, ες, earth-like, earthy, Pl. Phd. 81c , Hierocl. in CA Praef. p.417 M.; γ. καὶ ἄλιθον with deep soil, X. An. 6.4.5 , al.; τὸ γ. Arist. GA 753a25 , 782b22 ; τὸ -εστερον ib. 751b3 ; γ. φῦλον Aristid. Or. 43(1).14 ; ἄνθρακες -έστατοι Thphr. HP 5.9.1 . epith. of certain ζῴδια, Vett.Val. 10.11 .
term_table.greek_sentence: οὕτω δὲ δὴ καὶ αὐτῶν τῶν ἁλῶν ὅσοι σκληρότεροι καὶ πυκνότεροι καὶ γεωδέστεροι, τοιοῦτοι δ’ ὑπάρχουσιν ὀλίγου δεῖν οἱ ὀρυκτοὶ πάντες, ἧττον θερμοί τ’ εἰσὶ καὶ λεπτομερεῖς, ὅσοι δ’ εὔθρυπτοι καὶ χαῦνοι, λεπτομερέστεροί τε ἅμα καὶ θερμότεροι τὴν δύναμίν εἰσι, καί τινες ἐξ αὐτῶν ὑπόπικροι, μεταξύ πως ὑπάρχοντες ἁλῶν τε τῶν σκληρῶν καὶ ἀφρονίτρου.
term_table.english_sentence_A: So too, of the salts themselves, those that are harder and denser and more earthy—and such are almost all the mined salts—are less hot and fine-particled, whereas those that are friable and loose-textured are at once both more fine-particled and hotter in power, and some of them are somewhat bitter, being in a way intermediate between the hard salts and aphronitron.
term_table.english_sentence_B: In the same way, among the salts themselves, those that are harder, denser and more earthy (and almost all the mined salts are of this kind) are less hot and less fine-particled, whereas those that are easily crumbled and porous are at once more fine-particled and hotter in power, and some of them are slightly bitter, standing in a way between the hard salts and aphronitre.

term_table.english_sentence_A: There are indeed also some of the aphronitra themselves that are hard and coarse-particled, and do not even dissolve easily in water.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Now even among the aphronitres themselves there are some that are hard and coarse-particled, and they do not even dissolve readily in water.

term_table.english_sentence_A: But [696] my account now is not about the defective ones, but about those which, in accordance with their name, are naturally foam-like in their substance, such as is also the foam of nitre itself.

term_table.greek_sentence: λεπτομερέστατος γὰρ οὗτος ἁπάντων τῶν εἰρημένων, ὥσπερ γε καὶ τὸ τῆς Ἀσίας πέτρας ἄνθος.

term_table.english_sentence_B: For this is the most fine-particled of all those mentioned, just as is also the flower of the Asian stone.

term_table.greek_sentence: διὸ καὶ τὰς ὑπεραυξανομένας σάρκας ἀλυπότερον ἀποτήκει, δάκνει δ’ αὐτὰς ἤδη τὸ ἄνθος τοῦ νίτρου, δάκνει δὲ καὶ τὸ ἀφρόνιτρον, οὐδὲν δὲ ἧττον καὶ τὸ νίτρον αὐτὸ, καίτοι γε ἧττον ἐκείνων ὑπάρχον θερμόν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Wherefore it also melts away overgrowing flesh with less pain, whereas the flower of nitre already bites it, and aphronitron bites too, and no less nitre itself, even though it is less hot than those.

term_table.english_sentence_A: Wherefore it also melts away overgrowing flesh with less pain, whereas the flower of nitre already bites it, and aphronitron bites too, and no less nitre itself, even though it is less hot than those.

term_table.english_sentence_A: But it has been said before as well that the coarse-particled substance erodes more, when, that is to say, it partakes of some heat.

term_table.english_sentence_A: For no part of it passes through painlessly and quickly, as that of the fine-particled does, but being held back and always remaining and lingering, and sitting for a longer time upon one place of our body, it naturally becomes painful, like a thorn fixed in the flesh.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For no part of it passes through painlessly and quickly, as happens with fine-particled substance; instead, being held back, always remaining and lingering, and staying for a longer time at one place in our body, it reasonably becomes distressing, like a stake fixed in the flesh.

term_table.greek_sentence: οὕτω δὲ καὶ καθ’ ἕκαστον τῶν ἄλλων ὁμοία σχεδὸν ἡ τῆς ὀσμῆς αἴσθησίς ἐστι τῇ τῆς γεύσεως, ὥστε ἐνίων σωμάτων οὐδὲ γευσάμενοί ποτε, καθάπερ τῆς κόπρου, γιγνώσκομεν τὴν ποιότητα, καὶ κατὰ τοῦτό γε τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐδ’ ἐπιχειροῦμεν γεύεσθαι, τῷ πάνυ σφόδρα πιστεύειν τῇ ὀσφρήσει.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And so too in each of the other cases the sensation of smell is almost the same as that of taste, so that in the case of some bodies we recognise the quality without ever having tasted them, as with dung, and for this very reason we do not even attempt to taste them in the first place, because we trust the sense of smell so very strongly.
term_table.english_sentence_B: So too in each of the others the sensation of odour is nearly similar to that of taste, so that of some bodies, such as dung, we know the quality without ever having tasted them, and for this reason we do not even attempt to taste them in the first place, because we trust the sense of smell very strongly indeed.

term_table.english_sentence_A: [698] And yet the bitter was never fragrant, nor pleasant to us either as a drug or as food.

term_table.english_sentence_A: The generation of the bitter flavour appeared to arise from sweet things being thinned by heat, and bitter things are evidently hotter and more fine-particled in mixture than sweet things; but, further, the sensation of smell occurs in the very ventricles of the brain, as has also been demonstrated by me elsewhere concerning these matters, and the substance of odorous objects is vaporous.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: εἰσπνοή, ἡ, inspiration, inhalation, opp. ἐκπνοή, Arist. Resp. 471a8 , cf. Str. 3.5.7 ; μιᾷ ἐσπνοῇ θνῄσκουσι Aret. SA 1.7 .
term_table.greek_sentence: τὰ γὰρ ἀποῤῥέοντα τῶν σωμάτων ἀναμιγνύμενα τῷ περιέχοντι, κᾄπειτα διὰ τῆς κατὰ τὰς ῥῖνας εἰσπνοῆς εἰς τὸν ἐγκέφαλον ἐνεχθέντα, κινεῖ τὴν αἴσθησιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For the effluences from bodies, mingling with the surrounding air and then carried into the brain through the inhalation that takes place by way of the nostrils, stir the sensation.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For the things that flow off from bodies, mixing with the surrounding air and then being carried into the brain by inhalation through the nostrils, move the sense.

term_table.greek_sentence: εὐλόγως οὖν ὅσα μὲν ὀσμώδη πάντα καὶ θερμά· τὸ γὰρ τῶν ἀτμῶν πλῆθος ἐπὶ θερμότητι· οὐ μὴν εὐθὺς καὶ πᾶν ὀσμῶδες ἡδὺ, διότι μηδ’ οἰκεῖόν ἐστιν ἅπαν τοῦ κατὰ τὰς κοιλίας τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου πνεύματος.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Reasonably, then, all things that are odorous are also hot — for the abundance of vapours depends on heat; yet not everything odorous is thereby also pleasant, because not everything is akin to the pneuma in the ventricles of the brain.

term_table.greek_sentence: τὸ ῥόδον τοίνυν οὐ ταύτῃ μόνον ἀνομοιομερές ἐστιν, ᾗ τὸ μέν τι περιέχον ἐν αὐτῷ, τὸ δέ τι περιεχόμενόν ἐστι, περιέχον μὲν τὸ σκληρὸν καὶ γεῶδες, ἐν τούτῳ δὲ περιεχόμενος [701] ὑγρός τις χυλός.
term_table.english_sentence_A: The rose, then, is non-homoeomerous not only in this respect, that one thing in it is what contains and another what is contained — what contains being the hard and earthy part, and what is contained within this [701] being a certain moist juice — but also in that there must necessarily be, as we showed before, three residues of the juice itself: one earthy, just like the lees in wines; another airy, this one being analogous to the 'flower' in wines; and the third watery, which we said in all of them produces their boiling — and also their corruption, whenever it is not mastered and not completely altered during the time of the boiling.
term_table.english_sentence_B: The rose, then, is anhomoeomerous not only in this respect, that one part in it is containing and another contained, the containing part being the hard and earthy, and contained within this [701] a certain moist juice.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἐν δὲ τῇ τοῦ ῥόδου φύσει τὸ μέν ἐστι στρυφνὸν γευομένοις, ὅπερ ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι γεῶδές τε καὶ παχυμερὲς καὶ ψυχρὸν, ἕτερον δὲ πικρὸν, ὃ δὴ λεπτομερές τ’ ἐστὶ καὶ θερμὸν, καὶ τρίτον ἐπὶ τούτοις τὸ ὑδατῶδες, ψυχρὸν μὲν ἐξ ἀνάγκης, ἀλλ’ ἐν τῇ κατὰ τὸ λεπτομερές τε καὶ παχυμερὲς [702] ἀντιθέσει μέσον πως ὑπάρχον τῶν ἄκρων, οὗ τῇ μίξει καὶ τὸ στρυφνὸν καὶ τὸ πικρὸν οὐκ ἔστιν ἄκρως τοιοῦτον ἑκάτερον οἷόν περ λέγεται· πάσας γὰρ ἐκλύει τὰς ποιότητας ἡ τοῦ ὑδατώδους ἐπιμιξία.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But in the nature of the rose there is one part that is acerbic to those who taste it, which must necessarily be earthy, coarse-particled and cold; another that is bitter, which is in fact fine-particled and hot; and a third besides these, the watery, cold of necessity, but in the [702] opposition between fine-particled and coarse-particled standing somehow midway between the extremes; and by the mixture of this neither the acerbic nor the bitter is, either of them, such in the extreme degree as it is said to be, for the admixture of the watery relaxes all the qualities.
term_table.english_sentence_B: In the nature of the rose there is, to those who taste it, one component that is acerbic, which must necessarily be earthy, coarse-particled and cold; another that is bitter, which is fine-particled and hot; and a third besides these, the watery, which is of necessity cold, but in the opposition between fine-particled and coarse-particled [702] lies somehow midway between the extremes.

term_table.english_sentence_A: But in the nature of the rose there is one part that is acerbic to those who taste it, which must necessarily be earthy, coarse-particled and cold; another that is bitter, which is in fact fine-particled and hot; and a third besides these, the watery, cold of necessity, but in the [702] opposition between fine-particled and coarse-particled standing somehow midway between the extremes; and by the mixture of this neither the acerbic nor the bitter is, either of them, such in the extreme degree as it is said to be, for the admixture of the watery relaxes all the qualities.
term_table.english_sentence_B: In the nature of the rose there is, to those who taste it, one component that is acerbic, which must necessarily be earthy, coarse-particled and cold; another that is bitter, which is fine-particled and hot; and a third besides these, the watery, which is of necessity cold, but in the opposition between fine-particled and coarse-particled [702] lies somehow midway between the extremes.

term_table.english_sentence_A: This watery part itself, then, seems somehow already to have been worked up and made thin and heated, and on this account to be easily brought into vapours, and in this way the rose is both odorous and dries very quickly.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Because this is mixed in, neither the acerbic nor the bitter is in the extreme degree what it is called, for the admixture of the watery weakens all the qualities.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: γεῦσ-ις, εως, ἡ, sense of taste, Democr. 11 , Arist. EN 1118a26 , de An. 422a29 , etc. a tasting, LXX Da. 5.2 . food, LXX Wi. 16.2 , al. taste, flavour, Dsc. 1.12 , Gp. 5.7.3 . back of the tongue, Poll. 2.104 .
term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ ταῦθ’ ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ πάντα διὰ μὲν τῆς γεύσεως ἔνεστι τεκμήρασθαι, διὰ δὲ τῆς ὀσμῆς οὐχ οἷόν τε τῷ μήθ’ ὁμοίως ἀτμίζειν ἅπαντ’ αὐτοῦ τὰ μόρια μήθ’ ὁμοίως κινεῖν τὴν αἴσθησιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And all these things about it can be inferred through taste, but through smell it is not possible, because neither do all its parts give off vapour alike nor move the sense alike.
term_table.english_sentence_B: This watery component itself, then, seems somehow to have already been worked up, thinned and heated, and for this reason to be readily brought into vapours; and it is in this way that the rose is both odorous and dries out very quickly.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: γεύσ-της, ου, ὁ, taster, CIG 2214.8 (Chios).
term_table.greek_sentence: ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς γεύσεως ἅπανθ’ ὁμοίως τὰ μόρια τῶν γευστῶν σωμάτων προσπίπτει τῇ γλώττῃ καὶ κινεῖ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φύσιν, ὥστ’ οὐκ ἀσφαλὲς, ὡς εἴρηται, περὶ τῆς τῶν φαρμάκων δυνάμεως ἁπάσης ἐξ ὀσμῆς τεκμαίρεσθαι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: In the case of taste, on the other hand, all the parts of tastable bodies alike fall upon the tongue, and each of them moves the sense according to its own nature; so that it is not safe, as has been said, to make inferences from smell about the whole power of drugs.
term_table.english_sentence_B: All these things about it can be inferred through taste, but not through smell, because neither do all its parts give off vapour alike nor do they move the sense alike. In taste, by contrast, all the parts of tastable bodies alike fall upon the tongue, and each of them moves the sense according to its own nature.

term_table.english_sentence_A: And still more, it is not possible to conjecture anything from colours either about the power of drugs.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Still less is it possible to conjecture anything about the power of drugs from their colours.

term_table.greek_sentence: καθ’ ἕκαστον μέντοι γένος ἢ σπέρματος ἢ ῥίζης ἢ χυλοῦ δυνατόν ἐστι κᾀκ τῆς χρόας ἔνδειξίν τινα λαβεῖν τῆς κράσεως, οἷον αὐτίκα καὶ κρόμμυον καὶ σκίλλα καὶ οἶνος, εἰς ὅσον ἂν ᾖ λευκότερα καὶ ἧττόν ἐστι θερμά.

term_table.english_sentence_B: Within each kind, however, whether of seed or of root or of juice, it is possible to obtain from the colour as well some indication of the mixture. For example, onions and squill and wine: the whiter they are, the less hot they are, while the yellowish and tawny ones are hotter.

term_table.greek_sentence: τὰ δ’ ὑπόξανθά τε καὶ κιῤῥὰ θερμότερα, καὶ πυροὶ δὲ καὶ κέγχροι καὶ ὦχροι καὶ φάσηλοι καὶ ἐρέβινθοι καὶ ἡ τῆς ἴρεως ῥίζα καὶ ἡ τοῦ ἀσφοδέλου καὶ πολλῶν ἄλλων ὅμοιόν τι πεπόνθασιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For in each kind, for the most part, those that are tawny and yellow and red are hotter than the white ones; so that, if it is permissible to infer something from this source too about the power of drugs, let it be added to the account.

HP 1.10.7 , 7.13.2 , Crateuas Fr. 5 , Theoc. 7.68 , Dsc. 2.169 , etc.; cf. σφοδελός. oxyt., as Adj., ἀσφοδελὸς λειμών the asphodel mead which the shades of heroes haunted, Od. 11.539 , 24.13 : generally, flowery mead, h.Merc. 221 , 344 . (On the accent v. Hdn.Gr. 1.160 .)
term_table.greek_sentence: τὰ δ’ ὑπόξανθά τε καὶ κιῤῥὰ θερμότερα, καὶ πυροὶ δὲ καὶ κέγχροι καὶ ὦχροι καὶ φάσηλοι καὶ ἐρέβινθοι καὶ ἡ τῆς ἴρεως ῥίζα καὶ ἡ τοῦ ἀσφοδέλου καὶ πολλῶν ἄλλων ὅμοιόν τι πεπόνθασιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For in each kind, for the most part, those that are tawny and yellow and red are hotter than the white ones; so that, if it is permissible to infer something from this source too about the power of drugs, let it be added to the account.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Wheat, millet, ochroi, phaseloi, chickpeas, the root of the iris, that of the asphodel and those of many other plants are affected in a similar way. For in each kind, on the whole, those that are tawny, yellow and red are hotter than the white ones.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ὕδωρ [υ, v. fin.], τό, gen. ὕδατος: an Ep. dat. ὕδει in Hes. Op. 61 , Thgn. 961 ; later nom. ὕδος Call. Fr. 475 ; Boeot. οὕδωρ prob. in IG 7.3169 (Orchom.):—water, of any kind, but in Hom. rarely of seawater without an epith., ἄνεμός τε καὶ ὕ. Od. 3.300 , 7.277 ; but ἁλμυρὸν ὕ. 9.227 , al., cf. Th. 4.26 ; of rivers, ὕ. Αἰσήποιο, Στυγός, Il. 2.825 , 8.369 , al.; so in Lyr. and Trag., ὕ, Ἀσώπιον Pi. N. 3.3 ; ὕ. τὸ Νείλου A. Supp. 561 (lyr.): freq. in pl. (but only once in Hom. , ὕδατ' ἀενάοντα Od. 13.109 ), Καφίσια ὕδατα the waters of Cephisus, Pi. O. 14.1 ; ῥυτῶν ὑδάτων S. OC 1599 ; ὕδασιν τοίς Ἀχελῴου Id. Fr. 271 (anap.): spring-water, drinking-water, οἶνον ἔμισγον καὶ ὕ. Od. 1.110 ; ἀφυσσάμεθ' ὕδωρ 9.85 ; ὕδατα καὶ . . δῖτοι Pl. R. 404a ; πότιμον ὕ. X. HG 3.2.19 ; ὕ. πίνων a water-drinker, D. 6.30 , cf. 19.46 , Ar. Eq. 349 ; ὕ. δὲ πίνων οὐδὲν ἂν τέκοι σοφόν Cratin. 199 , cf. Aristopho 10.3 , Bato 2.9 , al.: ὕδωρ κατὰ χειρός water for washing the hands, v. χείρ; φέρτε χερσὶν ὕ. Il. 9.171 ; ὕ. ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἔχευαν 3.270 , Od. 1.146 , al.; λοέσσας ὕδατι λευκῷ Il. 23.282 :—on γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ αἰτεῖν and διδόναι, v. γῆ 1.2b :—a curse was invoked upon those who refused fire (i.e. the right to borrow burning embers) or water or to direct a traveller on his way, Diph. 62 , cf. X. Oec. 2.15 :—prov., ὅρκους ἐγὼ γυναικὸς εἰς ὕ. γράφω S. Fr. 811 , cf. Men. Mon. 25 ; ἐν ὕδατι γράφειν Pl. Phdr. 276c ; ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ πνίγῃ, τί δεῖ ἐπιπίνειν; if water chokes, what more can be done ? of a desperate case, Arist. EN 1146a35 , cf. ἐπιρροφέω 1 . rain-water, rain, ὅτε λαβρότατον χέει ὕ. Ζεύς Il. 16.385 ; ὗσαι ὕδατι λαβροτάτῳ Hdt. 1.87 ; ἐγίνετο ὕ. ἄπλετον Id. 8.12 ; πολύ Th. 6.70 , D. 59.99 ; ὕ. ἐπιγενόμενον πολύ X. HG 1.6.28 ; τὸ ὕ. τὸ γενόμενον τῆς νυκτός Th. 2.5 , cf. Hdt. 8.13 : more definitely, ὕδωρ ἐζ οὐρανοῦ X. An. 4.2.2 , Aristid. Or. 50(26).35 (but ἐζ οὐρανοῦ is a gloss in Th. 2.77 ): pl., ὕ. ὄμβρια Pi. O. 11(10).2 ; τὰ Διὸς, or παρὰ τοῦ Δ., ὕ. Pl. Lg. 761a , 761b ; τὸ ἐκ Διὸς ὕ. Thphr. HP 2.6.5 ; καινὸν ἀεὶ τὸν Δία ὕειν ὕδωρ, ὕδωρ τὸν θεὸν ποιῆσαι, Ar. Nu. 1280 , V. 261 (lyr.), cf. Thphr. Char. 3.4 : abs., ἐὰν πλείω ποιῇ ὕ. Id. CP 1.19.3 : κεραύνια ὕ. thunder-showers, Plu. 2.664f ; ὕ. πολλά, συνεχέα μαλθακῶς Hp. Epid. 1.1 . for ἐν ὕδατι βρέχεσθαι, Hdt. 3.104 , v. βρέχω. in the law-courts, τὸ ὕδωρ was the water of the water-clock (κλεψύδρ), and hence the time it took in running out, ἂν ἐγχωρῇ τὸ ὕδωρ D. 44.45 ; οὐχ ἱκανόν μοι τὸὕ. Id. 45.47 ; ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ ὕ., ἐπὶ τοῦ ἐμοῦ ὕ., in the time allowed me, Id. 18.139 , 57.61 ; οὐκ ἐνδέχεται πρὸς ταὐτὸ ὕ. εἰπεῖν one cannot say (all) in one speech, Id. 27.12 ; τὸ ὕ. ἀναλῶσαι Din. 2.6 ; πρὸς ὕ. σμικρὸν διδάζαι Pl. Tht. 201b ; ἐν μικρῷ μέρει τοῦ παντὸς ὕ. D. 29.9 ; ἐπίλαβε τὸ ὕ. stop the water (which was done while the speech was interrupted by the calling of evidence and reading of documents), Id. 45.8 ; ἐγχεῖται τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ὕ. τῷ κατηγόρῳ . . , τὸ δὲ δεύτερον ὕ. τῷ φεύγοντι Aeschin. 3.197 ; ἀποδιδόναι, παραδιδόναι τινὶ τὸ ὕ., to give him the turn of speaking, Id. 1.162 , Din. 1.114 . generally, liquid, ὕδατος εἴδη τὰ τοιάδε· οἶνος, οὖρον, ὀρός Arist. Mete. 382b13 , cf. Hp. Cord. 12 . part of the constellation Aquarius, Arat. 399 . a name for the winter solstice, Paul.Al. A. 4 . Ὕδατα, τά, as the name of places with hot or mineral waters, Ὕ. Σέζτια, Lat. Aquae Sextiae, Ὕ. Νεαπολιτανά, etc., Ptol. Geog. 2.10.8 , 3.3.7 , etc. [υ by nature, ὕδωρ Il. 18.347 , al. (usu. with ὕ when not at end of line), ὕδατος 16.229 , al., ὕδατι Od. 12.363 , al., ὕδατ' 13.109 , and so always in Att. (exc. sts. in dactylic verse, Ar. Ra. 1339 ); Hom. freq. has ὕδωρ (always at end of line exc. in phrase Στυγὸς ὕδωρ Il. 15.37 ), also ὕδατος Il. 21.300 , 312 , Od. 5.475 , ὕδατι Il. 23.282 , Od. 22.439 ; later Ep. admits ὕδωρ more freely, A.R. 4.601 , so that we find υ in the second half of the foot in h.Cer. 381 , Batr. 97 , A.R. 4.290 , etc.; also in Alc. Supp. 11.8 .] (Cf. Skt. udán-, gen. udn-ás 'water', O E. woeter, O Norse vatn; I.- E. u(e)d- with suffix r alternating with n (ὕδ-ṇ-τος): cogn. with Skt. u-ná-t-ti (root ud-), 3 pl. u-n-d-ánti 'moisten', cf. Lat. unda.)
term_table.greek_sentence: Πέμπτον τοῦτον ἐνστησάμενος λόγον ὑπὲρ τῆς τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων δυνάμεως, ἀναμνήσω πρῶτον ὧν ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν ἀπέδειξα χρησίμων εἰς τὰ παρόντα, ποιησάμενος τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀπὸ τῶν στοιχείων, ὕδατός τε καὶ πυρὸς, ἀέρος τε καὶ γῆς, ἅπερ ἔνιοι παρονομάζοντες ἀπὸ τῶν ποιοτήτων ὑγρὸν καὶ ξηρὸν καὶ θερμὸν καὶ ψυχρὸν εἶναί φασιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Having undertaken this fifth discourse on the power of simple drugs, I shall first recall those things demonstrated by me in the preceding books that are useful for the present matters, making my beginning from the elements, water and fire, air and earth, which some people, naming them derivatively from the qualities, say are moist and dry and hot and cold.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Having undertaken this fifth discourse on the power of simple drugs, I shall first recall those things I demonstrated in the preceding books that are useful for the present matters, making my beginning from the elements, water and fire, air and earth, which some people, naming them derivatively from the qualities, say are the moist and the dry and the hot and the cold.

Rh. 1405a36 : generally, τὰ ὁ. Epicur. Sent.Vat. 73 , cf. Metrod. Fr. 17 , etc. : c. dat., Polystr. Herc. 346p.86V. of like form, κρατῆρες Plb. 34.11.17 ; homogeneous, Arist. term_table.lsj_first_sense_gloss: of the same species or kind
term_table.greek_sentence: τὰ δ’ ἀπ’ αὐτῶν παρονομαζόμενα σώματα τά τε κοινὰ πάντων ἐστὶ στοιχεῖα καὶ τὰ κατ’ ἐπικράτησίν τινος τούτων, ὑγρὰ καὶ ξηρὰ καὶ ψυχρὰ καὶ θερμὰ προσαγορευόμενα, καὶ τὰ πρὸς τὸ σύμμετρον ὁμογενὲς, ἢ ὁμοειδὲς παραβαλλόμενα καὶ τὰ πρὸς ὁτιοῦν τὸ ἐπιτυχόν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: The bodies named after them are both the elements common to all things and those which are called wet and dry and cold and hot according to the predominance of one of these, and those which are compared with the well-proportioned member of the same genus or of the same species, and those compared with anything whatever that happens to be at hand.
term_table.english_sentence_B: The bodies named after them are, first, the elements common to all things; second, those called moist and dry and cold and hot according to the predominance of one of these qualities; third, those so called when compared with the well-balanced body of the same genus or of the same species; and fourth, those so called in comparison with anything whatever that happens to come along. Now the difference among these has been discussed many times.

term_table.greek_sentence: τὸ φάρμακον δὲ ἔμπαλιν αὐτὸ νικᾷ καὶ κρατεῖ τοῦ σώματος οὗπερ ἂν ὑπάρχῃ φάρμακον· ἐν τῷ πρός τι γὰρ ἑκατέρων εἶναι τὴν νόησιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Now concerning the difference among these it has been said many times, and no less has it also been said in what way nutriment differs from a drug, and that nutriment is mastered and overcome by the thing being nourished, whereas the drug, conversely, itself overcomes and masters the body of which it is a drug; for the conception of each of the two lies in the relative.
term_table.english_sentence_B: It was also shown that a drug naturally alters either according to some one quality, whichever it may be, heating or cooling or drying or moistening, or according to some pairing of those mentioned, or according to its whole substance.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἐδείχθη δὲ καὶ ὡς ἤτοι κατὰ μίαν ἡντιναοῦν ποιότητα τὸ φάρμακον ἀλλοιοῦν πέφυκεν, ἤ θερμαῖνον ἢ ψῦχον ἢ ξηραῖνον ἢ ὑγραῖνον ἢ κατὰ συζυγίαν τινὰ τῶν εἰρημένων, ἢ καθ’ ὅλην αὐτοῦ τὴν οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ τῶν τε δηλητηρίων ἔνια καὶ τῶν ἀλεξητηρίων οὐκ ὀλίγα καὶ τὰ καθαίροντα πάντα καὶ τῶν ἐπισπαστικῶν ὀνομαζομένων πολλά.
term_table.english_sentence_A: It was shown also that a drug is naturally such as to alter either in respect of some one quality, whichever it may be, heating or cooling or drying or moistening, or in respect of some conjugation of those mentioned, or in respect of its whole substance, as do some of the deleterious drugs and not a few of the alexipharmic ones and all the purgatives and many of those called epispastic.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Some of the deleterious drugs act in this last way, as do not a few of the protective remedies, all the purgatives, and many of those called attractive.

term_table.greek_sentence: τὰ δὲ κατὰ μίαν ἢ δύο ποιότητας ἐνεργοῦντα περὶ τὸ σύμπαν ἡμῶν σῶμα κατὰ τόδε τὸ γράμμα δίειμι, λαβὼν κᾀνταῦθα πάλιν ὑπόθεσιν ἀποδε δειγμένην ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν, ὡς τὰ πλεῖστα τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων ἀνομοιομερῆ τε καὶ σύνθετα κατά γε τὴν ἀλήθειάν ἐστιν, ὀνομάζεται δὲ ἁπλᾶ τῷ φύσει τοιαῦτα ὑπάρχειν οἷάπερ ἐστὶν, οὐδὲν ἐξ ἐπιτεχνήσεως ἡμετέρας προσειληφότα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Those drugs, however, which act upon our whole body according to one or two qualities I shall go through in this book, taking here again as an assumption what has been demonstrated in the preceding books: that most of the simple drugs are, in truth at least, non-uniform in their parts and composite, but are called simple because they are by nature such as they are, having received nothing in addition from our artifice.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Those that act upon our whole body by one or two qualities I shall go through in this book. Here again I take as a hypothesis what was demonstrated in the preceding books: most of the simple drugs are in truth anhomoeomerous and composite, but they are called simple because by nature they are such as they are, having taken on nothing further from our artificial treatment.
