Comp. ἀμείνων, ἀρείων<*> βελτίων, κρείσσων ʽκάρρωνʼ, λωΐων (λώʽωνʼ), Ep. βέλτερος, λωΐτερος, φέρτερος:— Sup. ἄριστος, βέλτιστος, κράτιστος, λώϊστος (λῷστος), Ep. βέλτατος, κάρτιστος, φέρτατος, φέριστος:— later, reg. Comp. ἀγαθώτερος LXX Jd. 11.25 , 15.2 , D.S. 8 Fr. 12 , Plot. 5.5.9 , Diod.Rh. p.53.9H. : Sup. ἀγαθώτατος D.S. 16.85 , Hld. 5.15 , etc. ( -ότατος POxy. 1757.26 (ii A.D.)). Adv. usually εὖ, q.v.: ἀγαθῶς Hp. Off. 9 , Arist. Rh. 1388b6 , LXX 1 Ki. 20.7 . (Etym. dub. ( ὅτι ἄγει ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ τὸν ὀρθὸν βίον Stoic. 3.49 ); perh. cognate with ἄγαμαι, hence admirable.)
term_table.greek_sentence: νῦν γὰρ οὐ πρόκειται τὴν ὕλην ἐπεξιέναι πᾶσαν, ἀλλὰ καθόλου μίαν ὑπὲρ ἁπασῶν τῶν τοιούτων δυνάμεων ποιήσασθαι διδασκαλίαν, τί δὴ τὸ καθόλου, ὃ περί τε τῶν ἐκπυϊσκόντων καὶ μαλαττόντων ἐστὶ γνῶναι βέλτιον, ὡς τὰ μὲν ἴσην ἀνάπτει θερμότητα τῇ τοῦ ζώου κατὰ φύσιν, ὅσα δὲ μαλάττει, πολὺ πλέονα, καὶ ὡς τὰ μὲν οὐ τῷ ποιῷ τῆς θερμότητος, ἀλλὰ τῷ ποσῷ μᾶλλον ἐνεργεῖν πέφυκεν, ὅσα δὲ τῶν σκιῤῥουμένων ﻿ [729] ἐστὶ μαλακτικὰ, τῷ ποιῷ μᾶλλον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For at present it is not my purpose to go through all the material, but to produce one general teaching concerning all such powers—namely, what the general point is which it is better to know about both the suppurating and the softening agents: that the former kindle a heat equal to that of the animal according to nature, whereas those that soften kindle much more; and that the former by nature act not by the quality of the heat but rather by its quantity, whereas those that are softening of indurated parts [729] act rather by the quality.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For it is not our present purpose to go through all the material, but to give a single general instruction covering all such powers. And what is the general point that it is better to know about those that bring to suppuration and those that soften?

term_table.greek_sentence: νῦν γὰρ οὐ πρόκειται τὴν ὕλην ἐπεξιέναι πᾶσαν, ἀλλὰ καθόλου μίαν ὑπὲρ ἁπασῶν τῶν τοιούτων δυνάμεων ποιήσασθαι διδασκαλίαν, τί δὴ τὸ καθόλου, ὃ περί τε τῶν ἐκπυϊσκόντων καὶ μαλαττόντων ἐστὶ γνῶναι βέλτιον, ὡς τὰ μὲν ἴσην ἀνάπτει θερμότητα τῇ τοῦ ζώου κατὰ φύσιν, ὅσα δὲ μαλάττει, πολὺ πλέονα, καὶ ὡς τὰ μὲν οὐ τῷ ποιῷ τῆς θερμότητος, ἀλλὰ τῷ ποσῷ μᾶλλον ἐνεργεῖν πέφυκεν, ὅσα δὲ τῶν σκιῤῥουμένων ﻿ [729] ἐστὶ μαλακτικὰ, τῷ ποιῷ μᾶλλον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For at present it is not my purpose to go through all the material, but to produce one general teaching concerning all such powers—namely, what the general point is which it is better to know about both the suppurating and the softening agents: that the former kindle a heat equal to that of the animal according to nature, whereas those that soften kindle much more; and that the former by nature act not by the quality of the heat but rather by its quantity, whereas those that are softening of indurated parts [729] act rather by the quality.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For it is not our present purpose to go through all the material, but to give a single general instruction covering all such powers. And what is the general point that it is better to know about those that bring to suppuration and those that soften?

term_table.greek_sentence: τῆς ἐμφύτου θερμότητος, οὐκ ἐπιθεῖναι προσήκει τὴν ποιότητα, πεφράχθαι χρὴ τοὺς πόρους τοῦ σώματος, ἵν’ ἔνδον ἀποστέγωσι τὰς ἀτμώδεις διαπνοάς.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For if it is fitting to increase the substance of the innate heat, and not to intensify (ἐπιθεῖναι) its quality, the pores of the body must be blocked, so that they may keep the vaporous exhalations shut in within; since those poultices at any rate which, either by cleansing or by heating more vehemently, allow the vapours to be dispersed, do indeed dry, but certainly do not produce pus.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For if what is fitting is to increase the substance of the innate heat, and not to add to (or intensify) its quality, the passages of the body must be blocked, so that they may keep the vaporous exhalations shut in within.

term_table.greek_sentence: ὑπό τε γὰρ τῶν ῥυπτόντων, εἰ καὶ μὴ θερμαίνει σφοδρῶς, ἐκφραττομένων τε καὶ ἀνοιγνυμένων τῶν πόρων συναπέρχεται καὶ τὸ τοῦ μορίου θερμὸν, ὥστε μὴ σώζεσθαι τὴν κατὰ φύσιν αὐτῷ συμμετρίαν· ὑπό τε τῶν σφοδρῶς θερμαινόντων ἐκκενοῦται μέντοι καὶ ταύτης οὐκ ὀλίγον, ὑποθερμαίνεται δὲ ἡ λοιπὴ, καὶ οὕτω συμβαίνει τὴν μὲν οὐσίαν τῆς ἐμφύτου θερμότητος ἐλάττονα γίγνεσθαι, τὴν ποιότητα δ’ ἐπιτείνεσθαι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For under the action of cleansing agents, even if they do not heat strongly, since the pores are unblocked and opened, the heat of the part also departs along with them, so that its natural due proportion is not preserved; and under the action of those that heat strongly, no small amount of this too is in fact evacuated, while what remains is somewhat heated, and thus it comes about that the substance of the innate heat becomes less, while its quality is intensified.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For under the action of the cleansing substances, even if they do not heat strongly, the pores are unblocked and opened, and the heat of the part departs together with what is carried off, so that its natural due proportion is not preserved. Under the action of the strongly heating substances, on the other hand, not a little of this heat is emptied out, while what remains is heated up further; and so it comes about that the substance of the innate heat becomes less, while its quality is intensified.

term_table.english_sentence_A: For under the action of cleansing agents, even if they do not heat strongly, since the pores are unblocked and opened, the heat of the part also departs along with them, so that its natural due proportion is not preserved; and under the action of those that heat strongly, no small amount of this too is in fact evacuated, while what remains is somewhat heated, and thus it comes about that the substance of the innate heat becomes less, while its quality is intensified.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For under the action of the cleansing substances, even if they do not heat strongly, the pores are unblocked and opened, and the heat of the part departs together with what is carried off, so that its natural due proportion is not preserved. Under the action of the strongly heating substances, on the other hand, not a little of this heat is emptied out, while what remains is heated up further; and so it comes about that the substance of the innate heat becomes less, while its quality is intensified.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀτμώδης, ες, = ἀτμιδώδης , Arist. Mu. 394a14 , Thphr. CP 3.16.4 . Adv. -δως Gal. Nat.Fac. 3.7 .
term_table.greek_sentence: χρὴ δὲ οὐδέτερον εἶναι τούτων, ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν ἀτμῶδες καὶ θερμὸν πνεῦμα περιέχεσθαι πλεῖστον, ἀκριβῶς δ’ εἶναι σύμμετρον τῇ θερμότητι, τοῦτο γάρ τοι κᾀν τοῖς παισὶν ὑπάρχον πλεῖστον ἅπαντα συναύξει τὰ φυσικὰ τῶν ἔργων.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But neither of these should occur; rather, the vaporous and hot pneuma should be contained in the greatest quantity, yet be precisely well-proportioned in its heat; for it is indeed this which, being present in greatest quantity in children too, helps to increase all the natural activities.
term_table.english_sentence_B: But neither of these ought to happen. Rather, the vaporous and hot pneuma ought to be contained in the greatest amount, and it ought to be exactly proportionate in its heat.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: αἱματικός, ή, όν, of the blood, θερμότης Arist. PA 697a29 ; ὑγρότης Id. GA 777a7 ; τροφή, ὕλη, Id. PA 652a21 , 665b6 ; χυμός Gal. 13.332 . = ἔναιμος , of animals which have blood, opp. ἄναιμος, Arist. PA 665b5 , cf. HA 489a25 ; τὸ ἧπαρ -κώτατον PA 673b27 .
term_table.greek_sentence: οὐδὲν δὲ κωλύει καὶ τὴν αἱματικὴν οὐσίαν καὶ ἀερώδη θερμὸν ἔμφυτον ἀκούειν ἅμα τῷ πνεύματι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And nothing prevents one from understanding by 'innate heat' also the blood-like and airy substance together with the pneuma.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Nothing, however, prevents us from also understanding by innate heat the sanguineous and airy substance together with the pneuma.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀερώδης, ες, like air, of the soul, Epicur. Fr. 314 ; Astrol., of signs, connected with the air, Vett.Val. 7.26 ; light of texture, Sch. E. Or. 1431 . = ἀέρινος 2 , τὴν χρόαν Dsc. 5.152 (dub.). τὸ ἀ. the airy nature, Placit. 2.11.2 , al., cf. Arist. Mu. 395a20 . full of air, Id. PA 669b2 .
term_table.greek_sentence: οὐδὲν δὲ κωλύει καὶ τὴν αἱματικὴν οὐσίαν καὶ ἀερώδη θερμὸν ἔμφυτον ἀκούειν ἅμα τῷ πνεύματι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And nothing prevents one from understanding by 'innate heat' also the blood-like and airy substance together with the pneuma.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Nothing, however, prevents us from also understanding by innate heat the sanguineous and airy substance together with the pneuma.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: στωϊκ-ός, ή, όν, (στοά) of a colonnade or porch: hence, Stoic (because Zeno taught in the στοὰ Ποικίλη) , οἱ τῆς Σ. αἱρέσεως ἡγεμόνες D.H. Comp. 2 , cf. Str. 13.1.57 , 14.6.3 ; ἡ Σ. Phld. Rh. 2.227S. , D.L. 6.14 ; οἱ Σ. the Stoics, Phld. Rh. 2.296S. , cf. IG 3.1359 , D.L. 7.5 ; οἱ Σ. φιλόσοφοι Act.Ap. 17.18 . (Στοϊκός in AP 9.496 (Athenaeus).)
term_table.greek_sentence: οἱ μὲν οὖν Στωϊκοὶ ταὐτὸν τοῦτο τὸ πνεῦμα τὴν οὐσίαν τῆς ψυχῆς εἶναι δοξάζουσιν· ἡμεῖς δὲ περὶ οὐσίας ψυχῆς οὔτε πάνυ τι τολμῶμεν ἀποφαίνεσθαι καὶ πρὸς τὰ παρόντα περιττὸν ὑπολαμβάνομεν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Now the Stoics hold that this very pneuma is the substance of the soul; but we neither venture at all to pronounce on the substance of the soul, and we consider it superfluous for the present purpose.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Now the Stoics hold that this very pneuma is the substance of the soul; we, however, do not venture to make any pronouncement at all about the substance of the soul, and for present purposes we consider it superfluous.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: σύμφυτ-ον, τό, comfrey, Symphytum bulbosum, Arist. HA 616a1 , Dsc. 4.10 , Ael. NA 4.47 . ς. πετραῖον, low pine, Coris monspeliensis, Dsc. 4.9 . = ἑλένιον , Id. 1.28 . = γλυκύρριζα , Id. 3.5 (versio Latina).
term_table.greek_sentence: ὅτι μέντοι τὸ σύμφυτον πνεῦμα, κᾂν εἰ μὴ τῆς ψυχῆς ἐστιν ἡ οὐσία, ἀλλὰ τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῆς ὄργανον ὑπάρχει, φθάνομεν ἐν τοῖς περὶ τῶν Ἱπποκράτους καὶ Πλάτωνος δογμάτων ὑπομνήμασιν ἀποδεδειχέναι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: That, however, the innate pneuma, even if it is not the substance of the soul, is at any rate its first instrument, we have already demonstrated in the commentaries On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato.
term_table.english_sentence_B: That the connate pneuma, even if it is not the substance of the soul, is nevertheless its first instrument, we have already demonstrated in the commentaries On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: μέλος, εος, τό, limb, in early writers always in pl., Il. 7.131 , Pi. N. 1.47 , etc. (κατὰ μέλος is corrupt for κατὰ μέρος in h.Merc. 419 ); μελέων ἔντοσθε within my bodily frame, A. Pers. 991 (lyr.), cf. Eu. 265 (lyr.); κατὰ μέλη (-εα) limb by limb, like μελεϊστί , Pi. O. 1.49 , Hdt. 1.119 ; τὰ τοῦ σώματος μέλη καὶ μέρη Pl. Lg. 795e ; μέλη ποιεῖν dismember, LXX 2 Ma. 1.16 : later in sg., AP 9.141 , Gal. UP 12.3 ,al.; ἡ κατὰ μέλος τομή Str. 2.1.30 . metaph., ἐσμὲν . . ἀλλήλων μέλη Ep.Rom. 12.5 , cf. 1 Ep.Cor. 6.15 . features, form, οὐκέτ' ἐγὼ . . γονέων μ. ὄψομαι BMus.Inscr. 1077 (Sudan). esp. musical member, phrase: hence, song, strain, first in h.Hom. 19.16 (pl.), of the nightingale (the Hom. word being μολπή), cf. Thgn. 761 , etc.; μέλη βοῶν ἄναυλα S. Fr. 699 ; esp. of lyric poetry, τὸ Ἀρχιλόχου μ. Pi. O. 9.1 ; ἐν μέλεϊ ποιέειν to write in lyric strain, Hdt. 5.95 , cf. 2.135 ; ἐν μέλει ἤ τινι ἄλλῳ μέτρῳ Pl. R. 607d , cf. D.H. Comp. 11 ; Ἀδμήτου μ. Cratin. 236 ; μέλη, τά , lyric poetry, choral songs, opp. Epic or Dramatic verse, Pl. R. 379a , 607a , al.; [μ.] ἐκ τριῶν συγκείμενον, λόγου τε καὶ ἁρμονίας καὶ ῥυθμοῦ ib. 398d . lyric portion of the Comic παράβασις, Heph. Poëm. 8.2 . music to which a song is set, tune, Arist. Po. 1450a14 ; opp. ῥυθμός, μέτρον, Pl. Grg. 502c ; opp. ῥυθμός, ῥῆμα, Id. Lg. 656c ; Κρητικόν, Καρικόν, Ἰωνικὸν μ., Cratin. 222 , Pl.Com. 69.12 , 14 : metaph., ἐν μέλει properly, correctly, ἐν μ. φθέγγεσθαι Pl. Sph. 227d ; παρὰ μέλος incorrectly, inopportunely, πὰρ μ. ἔρχομαι Pi. N. 7.69 ; παρὰ μ. φθέγξασθαι Pl. Phlb. 28b , Lg. 696d ; παρὰ μέλος λαμπρύνεσθαι Arist. EN 1123a22 , cf. EE 1233a39 . melody of an instrument, φόρμιγξ δ' αὖ φθέγγοιθ' ἱερὸν μ. ἠδὲ καὶ αὐλός Thgn. 761 ; αὐλῶν πάμφωνον μ. Pi. P. 12.19 ; πηκτίδων μέλη S. Fr. 241 : generally, tone, μ. βοῆς E. El. 756 . [In h.Merc. 502 θεὸς δ' ὑπὸ καλὸν ἄεισεν must be read for θεὸς δ' ὑπὸ μέλος ἄεισεν, and Ἕλλησιν δ' ᾄδων μέλεα καὶ ἐλέγους is corrupt in Epigr. ap. Paus. 10.7.6 .]
term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ δὴ καὶ περιέχεσθαι μὲν ἐν ἅπασι τοῖς τοῦ ζώου μέλεσι τουτὶ τὸ πνεῦμά φαμεν, οὐχ ὅμοιον δ’ εἶναι πανταχόθεν, καθάπερ οὐδὲ τὸ αἷμα ἀναγκαῖον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And indeed we say that this pneuma is contained in all the parts of the animal, but that it is not alike everywhere, just as it is not necessary that the blood be either.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Moreover, we say that this pneuma is contained in all the members of the animal, but that it is not alike everywhere, just as the blood need not be either; and that in the empty spaces too no small amount of its substance is contained, or rather a kind of material, as it were, which still needs a slight change for the generation of innate pneuma perfected in its proper qualities, but which already contributes sufficiently to the natural functions.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο, gen. τούτου, ταύτης, τούτου, etc.: the dual fem. never in Att. , v. ὁ, ἡ, τό, init.:—demonstr. Pron., this, common from Hom. downwds. ORIGIN and FORMS: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο prob. arose from a reduplication of the demonstr. ὁ, ἡ , τό with insertion of -υ- (= Skt. Particle u), e.g. ταῦτα fr. τα-υ-τα: Dor. gen. sg. fem. τούτας Philol. 11 ; nom. pl. τοῦτοι, ταῦται A.D. Synt. 111.23 : the former occurs Sophr. 24 , GDI 3045 B 6 (Selinus), SIG 339.16 (Rhodes, iii B. C.), etc., the latter is dub. in Sophr. 97 , certain in SIG 241 B 117 (Delph., iv B. C.): in Boeot. all forms begin with οὑτ-, as gen. sg. neut. οὕτω Supp.Epigr. 3.359.11 (iii B. C.); acc. sg. fem. οὕταν Corinn. Supp. 2.80 ; acc. pl. neut. οὗτα SIG 1185.20 (Tanagra, iii B. C.), etc.: gen. pl. fem. Att. τούτων, Cret. ταυτᾶν Leg.Gort. 5.19 ; neut. ταύτων Michel 1334.10 (Elis, iv B. C.).—In Ion. sts. written ταότην, ταο ͂τα, SIG 283.19 (Chios, iv B. C.), 46.7 (Halic., v B. C.), al.—In Att. οὗτος was freq. strengthd. by the demonstr. -ί, οὑτοσί, αὑτηί, τουτί, gen. τουτουί, dat. τουτῳί, acc. τουτονί; pl. nom. οὑτοιί, neut. ταυτί, etc., this man here: sts. a Particle is inserted between the Pron. and -ί, as αὑτηγί for αὑτηί γε, Ar. Ach. 784 ; τουτογί for τουτί γε, Id. V. 781 , Av. 894 , al.; ταυταγί for ταυτί γε, Id. Eq. 492 , Pax 1057 , al.; τουτοδί for τουτὶ δέ, Id. Pl. 227 ; τουτουμενί for τουτουὶ μέν, Id. Ra. 965 .—In codd. the ν ἐφελκυστικόν is sts. added in the forms οὑτοσίν, οὑτωσίν, and οὑτοσίν is said to be Att. by A.D. Pron. 59.24 , 82.11 . [This ι is always long, and a long vowel or diphthong before it becomes short, as αὑτηί, τουτῳί, οὑτοιί, Ar. Nu. 201 , Pl. 44 , Ach. 40 , etc.] USAGE in regard to CONCOR D. οὗτος is freq. used as a Pron. Subst.: hence neut. is folld. by gen., κατὰ τοῦτο τῆς ἀκροπόλιος Hdt. 1.84 ; εἰς τοῦθ' ὕβρεως ἐλήλυθεν D. 4.37 ; εἰς τοῦθ' ἥκεις μανίας Id. 36.48 ; ταῦτα τῶν μαθημάτων Pl. Euthd. 278b : but quite as freq. as Adj., in which case its Subst. commonly takes the Art., οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ or ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος.—But the Art. is absent, always in Ep. Poets (exc. Od. 18.114 ), οὗτος ἀνήρ Il. 14.471 , Od. 1.406 , etc.: sts. also in Trag., A. Pers. 122 (lyr.), 495 , S. Ph. 406 , OC 471 , 1177 : once in an Inscr., τοπεῖα: τούτων τὰ ἡμίσεα τοπείων IG 22.1622.135 (iv B. C.). sts. when the Noun is so specified that the Art. is not needed, ἐς γῆν ταύτην . . , ἥντινα νῦν Σκύθαι νέμονται Hdt. 4.8 ; ταύτας ἃς οἱ πατέρες παρέδοσαν μελέτας Th. 1.85 , cf. Pl. R. 449d , etc.; πατὴρ σὸς οὗτος, ὃν θρηνεῖς ἀεί S. El. 530 . when οὗτος is used in local sense, here, v. infr. c. 1.5 . when the Noun with which οὗτος agrees stands as its Predicate, αὕτη γὰρ ἦν σοι πρόφασις S. Ph. 1034 ; δικαστοῦ αὕτη ἀρετή [ἐστι] Pl. Ap. 18a : this exception extends to cases in which the Predicate is not so distinctly separated from the Subject, αἰτίαι μὲν αὗται προυγεγένηντο these were the grievances which already existed, Th. 1.66 ; ταύτην φήμην παρέδοσαν this was the report which . . , Pl. Phlb. 16c : freq. with a Sup. , κίνησις αὕτη μεγίστη δὴ . . ἐγένετο this was notably the greatest movement which . . , Th. 1.1 , cf. 3.113 : with πρῶτος Id. 1.55 , 98 , 6.31 , Ev.Luc. 2.2 . when 3rd pers. is used for 2nd to express contempt, οὗτος ἀνήρ, οὑτοσὶ ἀνήρ, Pl. Grg. 467b , 489b , etc. though οὗτος usu. agrees with the Noun that serves as Predicate, it is not rare to find it in the neut., μανία δὲ καὶ τοῦτ' ἐστί E. Ba. 305 ; τοῦτο γάρ εἰσι . . εὔθυναι D. 19.82 , etc.: and in pl., οὐκ ἔστι ταῦτα ἀρχή Aeschin. 3.13 ; ταῦτ' ἐστὶν ὁ προδότης Id. 2.166 : so with an explanatory clause added, τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν ὁ συκοφάντης, αἰτιᾶσθαι μὲν πάντα ἐξελέγξαι δὲ μηδέν D. 57.34 . so also with a Noun in apposition, τούτοισιν μὲν ταῦτα μέλει, κίθαρις καὶ ἀοιδή Od. 1.159 ; τούτου τιμῶμαι, ἐν πρυτανείῳ σιτήσεως Pl. Ap. 36e , cf. E. Fr. 323.3 , etc. the neut. also may refer to a masc. or fem. Noun, καρπὸν φορέει κυάμῳ ἴσον: τοῦτο ἐπεὰν γένηται πέπον κτλ. Hdt. 4.23 , cf. X. An. 1.5.10 , etc. the neut. is also used of classes of persons, μελιτοπῶλαι καὶ τυροπῶλαι: τοῦτο δ' εἰς ἕν ἐστι συγκεκυφός Ar. Eq. 854 , cf. Pl. Lg. 711a ; or of an abstract fact, οὐκ Ἰοφῶν ζῇ;—τοῦτο γάρ τοι καὶ μόνον ἔτ' ἐστὶ λοιπὸν ἀγαθόν Ar. Ra. 73 . with Prons., personal, οὗτος σύ, in local sense, v. infr. c. 1.5 . interrog., τί τοῦτ' ἔλεξας; what is this that . . ? S. Ph. 1173 (lyr.), cf. Ant. 7 ; ποίοισι τούτοις; for ποῖά ἐστι ταῦτα οἷς [ἔχεις ἐλπίδα]; Id. OC 388 , cf. Ant. 1049 ; Νέστορ' ἔρειο ὅν τινα τοῦτον ἄγει whom he brings here, Il. 11.612 . with οἷος, Od. 20.377 , Pl. Phd. 61c . possess., πατὴρ σὸς οὗτος this father of thine, S. El. 530 , cf. X. An. 7.3.30 . demonstr., οὗτος ἐκεῖνος, τὸν σὺ ζητέεις, where ἐκεῖνος is the Predicate, Hdt. 1.32 ; τοῦτ' ἔστ' ἐκεῖνο E. Hel. 622 , cf. Or. 804 ; αὐτὸ τοῦτο, v. αὐτός 1.7; τοῦτον τὸν αὐτὸν ἄνδρα this same man, S. Ph. 128 . exceptionally, Διφίλου οὗτος ὅδ' ἐστὶ τύπος IG 12(5).300 (Paros). ἄλλος τις οὗτος ἀνέστη another man here, Od. 20.380 . with Numerals, τέθνηκε ταῦτα τρία ἔτη these three years, Lys. 7.10c odd.; [στρατείαν] ἑνδέκατον μῆνα τουτονὶ ποιεῖται for these eleven months, D. 8.2 , cf. 3.4 ; τριακοστὴν ταύτην ἡμέραν Men. Epit. 27 ; ταύτας τριάκοντα μνᾶς D. 27.23 , cf. Pl. Grg. 463b , etc. SIGNIFICATION AND SPECIAL IDIOMS: this, to designate the nearer, opp. ἐκεῖνος, that, the more remote, ταῦτα, like τὰ ἐνταῦθα , things round and about us, earthly things, Pl. Phd. 75e (v. l.); cf. ὅδε init.: but οὗτος sts. indicates that which is not really nearest, but most important, δεῖ . . τὸ βέλτιστον ἀεί, μὴ τὸ ῥᾷστον λέγειν: ἐπὶ ἐκεῖνο μὲν γὰρ ἡ φύσις αὐτὴ βαδιεῖται, ἐπὶ τοῦτο δὲ κτλ. D. 8.72 , cf. 51.3 and 18 . when, of two things, one precedes and the other follows, ὅδε prop. refers to what follows, οὗτος to what precedes, οὐκ ἔστι σοι ταῦτ', ἀλλά σοι τάδ' ἔστι S. OC 787 , cf. ὅδε III. 2 : freq., however, where there are not two things, οὗτος refers to what follows, Il. 13.377 , Od. 2.306 , etc.; οὔκουν . . τοῦτο γιγνώσκεις, ὅτι . . ; A. Pr. 379 , etc. οὗτος is used emphat., generally in contempt, while ἐκεῖνος denotes praise, ὁ πάντ' ἄναλκις οὗτος, i.e. Aegisthus, S. El. 301 ; τούτους τοὺς συκοφάντας Pl. Cri. 45a ; so D. de Coron. uses οὗτος of Aeschines, ἐκεῖνος of Philip; but οὗτος is used of Philip, D. 2.15 , 4.3 . of what is familiar, τούτους τοὺς πολυτελεῖς χιτῶνας, of the Persians, X. An. 1.5.8 ; οἱ τὰς τελετὰς . . οὗτοι καταστήσαντες Pl. Phd. 69c , cf. Men. 80a ; τὸ θυλακῶδες τοῦτο the familiar bag-like thing, Thphr. HP 3.7.3 , cf. 3.18.11 , 4.7.1 ; οἱ τὰς κόρας ταύτας ὠνούμενοι τοῖς παισίν D.Chr. 31.153 . in Att. law-language, οὗτος is commonly applied to the opponent, whether plaintiff (as in Aeschin. 2.130 ) or defendant (as in Id. 1.1 ); so, in the political speeches of D. , οὗτοι are the opposite party, 4.1 , 8.7 , etc.; but in the forensic speeches, οὗτοι freq. means the judges, the court, 21.134 , 36.47 . much like an Adv., in local sense (cf. ὅδε init.), τίς δ' οὗτος κατὰ νῆας . . ἔρχεαι; who art thou here that comest . . ? Il. 10.82 ; freq. in Att. , τίς οὑτοσί; who's this here? Ar. Ach. 1048 ; πολλὰ ὁρῶ ταῦτα πρόβατα I see many sheep here, X. An. 3.5.9 (as v.l.): with Pron. of 2 pers., οὗτος σύ ho you! you there! S. OT 532 , 1121 , E. Hec. 1280 , etc.: and then οὗτος alone like a voc., οὗτος, τί ποιεῖς; A. Supp. 911 ,cf. S. Aj. 71 , E. Alc. 773 , Ar. Eq. 240 , Nu. 220 , al.: with a pr. n., ὦ οὗτος, Αἴας S. Aj. 89 ; ὦ οὗτος οὗτος, Οἰδίπους Id. OC 1627 , cf. Ar. V. 1364 : with voc., βέντισθ' οὗτος Theoc. 5.76 :—the fem. is rarer, αὕτη E. Med. 922 ; αὕτη σύ Ar. Th. 610 .—This phrase mostly implies anger, impatience, or scorn. simply as antec. to ὅς, Od. 2.40 , S. OT 1180 , etc.: freq. following relat. clause, ἅ γ' ἔλαβες, . . μεθεῖναι ταῦτα Id. Ph. 1247 , cf. 1319 , Ant. 183 , 203 , Pl. Grg. 469c . = τοιοῦτος, οὗτος ἐγὼ ταχυτᾶτι Pi. O. 4.26 ; σὺ τοίνυν οὗτος εὑρέθης D. 18.282 , cf. 173 . after a parenthesis, the Subject, though already named, is freq. emphat. repeated by οὗτος, οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ Ἀριστέης . . , οὐδὲ οὗτος προσωτέρω . . ἔφησε ἀπικέσθαι Hdt. 4.16 , cf. 81 (s. v. l.), 1.146 , Pl. Phd. 107d , etc. καὶ οὗτος is added to heighten the force of a previous word, ξυνεστῶτες . . ναυτικῷ ἀγῶνι, καὶ τούτῳ πρὸς Ἀθηναίους Th. 4.55 , cf. Hdt. 1.147 , 6.11 , etc.; so οὐδὲ τούτου Aeschin. 2.100 ; v. infr. VIII. 2 . repeated, where for the second we should merely say he or it, τοῖσιν τούτου τοῦτον μέλεσιν . . κελαδοῦντες Ar. Ra. 1526 , cf. Pl. La. 200d . ταῦτα is used in some special phrases, ταῦτ', ὦ δέσποτα yes Sir (i. e. ἔστι ταῦτα, ταῦτα δράσω, etc.), Ar. V. 142 , Pax 275 , cf. Eq.III; so ταῦτα δή Id. Ach. 815 ; ταῦτά νυν Id. V. 1008 ; so also ἦν ταῦτα even so, true, E. Ph. 417 . ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ὑπάρξει so it shall be, Pl. Phd. 78a . καὶ ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ταῦτα so much for that, freq. in Att. , as Pl. Smp. 220c . ταῦτα at end of a formula in epitaphs, etc., prob. short for ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει or ὁ βίος ταῦτά ἐστιν, e.g. οὐδὶς ( = -εὶς ) ἀθάνατος: ταῦτα IG 14.420 ; Προκόπι ταῦτα ib. 1824 ; χαίρεται ( = -τε ) ταῦτα ib. 1479 , etc.: similarly perh. in a letter, ἂμ μὴ πέμψῃς, οὐ μὴ φάγω, οὐ μὴ πείνω. ταῦτα POxy. 119.15 (ii/iii A. D.). Adverbial usages: ταῦταabs., therefore, that is why . . , Il. 11.694 ; ταῦτ' ἄρα Ar. Ach. 90 , Nu. 319 , 335 , 394 , al., X. Smp. 4.55 ; ταῦτα δή A. Pers. 159 , Pl. Smp. 174a ; ταῦτ' οὖν S. Tr. 550 , Ar. V. 1358 , etc.; αὐτὰ ταῦτα ἥκω, ἵνα . . Pl. Prt. 310e : τοῦτο is rare in this sense, τοῦτ' ἀφικόμην, ὅπως . . εὖ πράξαιμί τι S. OT 1005 ; αὐτὸ γὰρ τοῦτο just because of this, Pl. Smp. 204a . πρὸς ταῦτα so then, therefore, prop. used in indignant defiance, A. Pr. 992 , 1043 , S. Aj. 971 , 1115 , 1313 , OT 426 , OC 455 , etc. καὶ ταῦτα, adding a circumstance heightening the force of what has been said, and that, ἄνδρα γενναῖον θανεῖν, καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς γυναικός A. Eu. 627 : but mostly with a part., ὅς γ' ἐξέλυσας ἄστυ . . , καὶ ταῦθ' ὑφ' ἡμῶν οὐδὲν ἐξειδὼς πλέον S. OT 37 , cf. Ar. Ra. 704 , Pl. Phdr. 241e , etc.; or with a part. omitted, ἥτις . . τὴν τεκοῦσαν ὕβρισεν, καὶ ταῦτα τηλικοῦτος (sc. οὖσα) S. El. 614 ; so καὶ ταῦτα μέντοι Pl. Erx. 400b . καὶ ταῦτα anyhow, no matter what happens (or happened), ἐπεχείρησας, οὐδὲν ὢν καὶ ταῦτα you tried, but were no good anyhow, i.e. try as you might, Id. R. 341c , cf. term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ δὴ καὶ περιέχεσθαι μὲν ἐν ἅπασι τοῖς τοῦ ζώου μέλεσι τουτὶ τὸ πνεῦμά φαμεν, οὐχ ὅμοιον δ’ εἶναι πανταχόθεν, καθάπερ οὐδὲ τὸ αἷμα ἀναγκαῖον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And indeed we say that this pneuma is contained in all the parts of the animal, but that it is not alike everywhere, just as it is not necessary that the blood be either.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Moreover, we say that this pneuma is contained in all the members of the animal, but that it is not alike everywhere, just as the blood need not be either; and that in the empty spaces too no small amount of its substance is contained, or rather a kind of material, as it were, which still needs a slight change for the generation of innate pneuma perfected in its proper qualities, but which already contributes sufficiently to the natural functions.

term_table.english_sentence_A: But it is dispersed by cleansing things, such as the flour of barley and of beans; by drying things, such as Italian millet (ἔλυμος), common millet and lupines; by heating things, such as fenugreek is; and still more by things whose nature it is to heat and dry at the same time, such as darnel and bitter vetch, chickpeas and bitter vetchlings (ὦχροι).
term_table.english_sentence_B: It is dispersed by things that cleanse, such as barley meal and bean meal; by things that dry, such as panic, millet and lupins; by things that heat, such as fenugreek; and still more by things whose nature is to heat and dry at once, such as darnel, bitter vetches, chickpeas and ochroi.

EE 1238a3 ; ὅρκον μέγαν, ἅλας τε καὶ τράπεζαν Archil. 96 ; ποῦ ἅλες; ποῦ τράπεζαι; D. 19.189 ; τοὺς ἅλας παραβαίνειν ib. 191 ; τοὺς τῆς πόλεως ἅλας περὶ πλείονος ποιήσασθαι τῆς ξενικῆς τραπέζης Aeschin. 3.224 ; ἁλῶν δὲ φόρτος ἔνθεν ἦλθεν, ἔνθ' ἔβη 'light come, light go', Zen. 2.20 ; ἅλασιν ὕει, of great abundance, Suid. in pl. of medical preparations, Dsc. 5.109 . brine, Call. Fr. 50 . ἃ. ἀμμωνιακός rock-salt, PLond. 1.78.90 . ἃ. Ἰνδικός sugar, Archig. ap. Paul.Aeg. 2.53 . ἅλες, οἱ, metaph., like Lat. sales, wit, possible but unlikely in Pl. Smp. 177b , Ep.Col. 4.6 ; certain in Plu. 2.854c ; ἅλες called "χάριτες" ib. 685a . (Cf.sq.)
term_table.greek_sentence: ἔχει γάρ τοι καὶ ἁλῶν καὶ ζύμης ὁ ἄρτος.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And that which contains more oil is for the inflammations harder to concoct, [733] that with less for those that are seething; and indeed the plaster made from bread suits the inflammations harder to concoct, for bread in fact contains both salt and leaven, whereas that made from wheat flour suits the hotter ones.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Moreover, the poultice made from bread suits the inflammations that are harder to concoct, for bread contains both salt and leaven; that made from wheaten flour suits the hotter ones.

Adv. -μῶς Pl. Euthd. 284e : Comp. -ότερον, ἔχειν Eub. 7.1 : neut. pl. as Adv., θερμὰ θερμὰ πηδῶσαι Herod. 4.61 .
term_table.greek_sentence: τὸ δ’ ἐξ ἀλεύρου πυρίνου ταῖς θερμοτέραις.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Again, of wheat flour itself the pure sort brings to suppuration more, and of bread the pure sort more; for bran is both less hot and more dry, whereas the pure and nourishing flour is both moist and hot, and such things were shown to work together towards the generation of pus.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Moreover, the poultice made from bread suits the inflammations that are harder to concoct, for bread contains both salt and leaven; that made from wheaten flour suits the hotter ones.

term_table.greek_sentence: τὸ μὲν γὰρ πίτυρον ἧττόν τ’ ἐστὶ θερμὸν καὶ μᾶλλον ξηρόν· τὸ δὲ καθαρόν τε καὶ τρόφιμον ἄλευρον ὑγρόν τ’ ἐστὶ καὶ θερμόν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: So too, then, of the drugs applied to inflamed parts, those that are hot and moist, these also contribute to suppuration, such as pig's fat and calf's fat.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For the bran is both less hot and more dry, whereas the pure and nourishing flour is both moist and hot, and it has been shown that such things cooperate towards the generation of pus.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἐκπύ-ησις, εως, ἡ, suppuration, Id. Aph. 7.20 , etc.
term_table.greek_sentence: οὕτως οὖν καὶ τῶν φαρμάκων τῶν ἐπιτιθεμένων τοῖς φλεγμαίνουσι μέρεσιν, ὅσα θερμά τ’ ἐστὶ καὶ ὑγρὰ, συντελεῖ καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὴν ἐκπύησιν, οἷον τό τε χοίρειον στέαρ καὶ τὸ μόσχειον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For bull's fat and goat's fat were shown to be more pungent, and for this reason suitable for the colder and more scirrhous inflammations, whereas pig's and calf's fat is most appropriate to the inflammations properly so called themselves.
term_table.english_sentence_B: In the same way, then, of the drugs applied to inflamed parts, those that are hot and moist also contribute to suppuration, such as pig's fat and calf's fat.

term_table.english_sentence_B: For that of the bull and of the goat was shown to be more pungent, and for this reason suitable for the colder and more scirrhous inflammations, whereas pig's and calf's fat are most appropriate to the inflammations properly so called.

term_table.english_sentence_A: The fat of cocks is also most appropriate, and still more so that of the goose, which is already somewhat more dispersing.

term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ τὸ τῶν ἀγρίων ζώων πάντων στέαρ δριμύτερόν τέ ἐστι καὶ ξηραντικώτερον πολὺ τῶν ἡμέρων, καὶ μάλιστα τὸ τῶν παρδάλεών τε καὶ λεόντων, ὥστ’ οὐδὲν τούτων ἐκπυΐσκειν ἐπιτήδειον, ἀλλ’ ὡς εἴρηται, τὸ χοίρειόν τε καὶ μόσχειον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And indeed the fat of all wild animals is both more pungent and much more drying than that of tame ones, and most of all that of leopards and lions, so that none of these is suitable for producing pus, but, as has been said, pig's fat and calf's fat.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Moreover, the fat of all wild animals is both more pungent and much more drying than that of tame ones, and especially that of leopards and lions, so that none of these is suitable for promoting suppuration; rather, as has been said, pig's fat and calf's fat are.

term_table.english_sentence_A: And indeed the fat of all wild animals is both more pungent and much more drying than that of tame ones, and most of all that of leopards and lions, so that none of these is suitable for producing pus, but, as has been said, pig's fat and calf's fat.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Moreover, the fat of all wild animals is both more pungent and much more drying than that of tame ones, and especially that of leopards and lions, so that none of these is suitable for promoting suppuration; rather, as has been said, pig's fat and calf's fat are.

Supp. 8.5 , 25.10 :—a stronger form of τοῖος, bearing the same relation to τοιόσδε as οὗτος to ὅδε, such as this, in Hom. not so common as τοῖος, but in Att. the most common of the three forms; anteced. to οἷος, Od. 4.269 , Pl. Smp. 199d , etc.; to ὡς, Il. 21.428 ; to ὅς, ὅς, ὅσπερ, S. Ant. 691 , Th. 1.21 , Lys. 13.1 , 30.14 , X. Lac. 7.5 , Pl. R. 349d , etc.; to οἷόσπερ, v. l. in X. Cyr. 6.2.2 ; less freq. to a Conj., as ὥστε, A. Ag. 1075 , Pl. Smp. 175d : freq. also abs., Pi. O. 6.16 , Hdt. 2.2 , etc.; freq. with implications, so good, so noble, so bad, etc., Il. 7.242 , etc.; τοιοῦτον . . ἐστὶ τὸ . . τέλειον ἄνδρα εἶναι so great a thing is it . . , Pl. Hp.Ma. 281b ; τοιοῦτος ὤν being such a wretch, S. Aj. 1298 , cf. Ph. 1049 ; εἴς τι τοιοῦτον ἐμπίπτειν οὗ . . into such a condition in which . . , Pl. Grg. 511c ; freq. coupled with τοσοῦτος, Th. 5.63 , X. Cyr. 2.4.6 , etc.; with οὗτος, Pl. R. 461e , X. Cyr. 8.2.26 , etc. (so in the expression οὗτος τοιοῦτος, αὕτη τοιαύτη, just as he (she, it) is, of slaves or animals for sale, POxy. 95.19 (ii A. D.), etc.); εἰς σὲ τοιοῦτος ἐγένετο, τ. γίγνου περὶ τοὺς γονεῖς, so disposed towards . . , X. Cyr. 5.2.27 , Isoc. 1.14 : c. dat., τ. ἦσθα τοῖς λόγοισι such in thy words, S. Ph. 1271 : τ. ἕτερος such another, Hdt. 3.47 ; ἕτερα τοιαῦτα, ἕτερον τοιοῦτον, Id. 1.120 , 2.5 ; referring to what precedes, Id. 3.82 , Pl. Lg. 904d ; used instead of repeating an Adj., ἀθάνατος εἶναι καὶ στρατιῆς τ. ἄρχειν Hdt. 1.207 , cf. 3.82 , 7.10 . έ, Th. 3.58 : with the Art., οἱ τοιοῦτοι A. Pr. 952 , Ch. 291 , S. OC 642 , Hp. Art. 42 ; τὰ τ. Pi. O. 9.40 ; ὀνόματι ὁ τοιοῦτος ἐμὲ προσαγορεύων Antipho 6.40 cod. A. the sense is made more indef. in τοιοῦτός τις or τις τοιοῦτος such a one, Pi. O. 6.16 , Th. 1.132 , etc.; τοιαῦτ' ἄττα Pl. R. 386a ; in this case it may freq. be rendered by an Adv., ἡ διάρριψις τοιαύτη τις ἐγένετο took place in this wise, X. An. 5.8.7 ; ἐγένετο ἡ διακομιδὴ τοιαύτη τις Plb. 3.45.6 . τὸτ. such a proceeding, Th. 1.76 , etc.; διὰ τὸ τ. for such a reason, Id. 7.21 ; ἐκ τοῦ τ. Id. 3.37 ; ἐν τῷ τ. in such a case, ib. 81 , etc. (but also ἐν τῷ τ. in such a place, X. Ages. 6.7 ; ἐν τ. τῆς οἰκίας Id. Eq. 4.1 ); also ἐν τ. εἶναι τοῦ κινδύνου to be in such a state of peril, Id. An. 1.7.5 . in narrative, τοιαῦτα prop. refers to what goes before, τοιαῦτα μὲν δὴ ταῦτα A. Pr. 500 ; καὶ ταῦτα μὲν τ. S. El. 696 , cf. X. An. 2.5.12 , etc.; cf. τοιόσδε fin. after a question, τοιαῦτα affirms like ταῦτα (v. οὗτος c. VII. 1 ), just so, even so, E. Hec. 776 , El. 645 . τοιαῦτα abs., τἂ πλοῖα, τὰ τοιαῦτα ships and suchlike, D. 8.25 . τοιαῦτα as Adv., in such wise, S. OT 1327 : regul. Adv. τοιούτως only late, EM 650.42 .—Cf. τοσοῦτος. [τοι- freq. in Trag. and Com., e.g. A. Ag. 593 , Eu. 194 , 197 , 424 , S. OT 406 , Ar. Ra. 1399 , etc.; cf. τοιόσδε fin.]
term_table.greek_sentence: τὸ δ’ ὅτι δυνάμει μὲν τοιοῦτόν ἐστι τὸ διαπυΐσκον φάρμακον, ἐνεργείᾳ δὲ γίγνεται τοιοῦτον ἐν τῷ πλησιάζειν ἡμῖν, εἴρηται πολλάκις ἔμπροσθεν, ἀναμνήσομέν τε καὶ νῦν, ὥστε μνημονεύειν αὐτοῦ διὰ παντός.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And that the suppurating drug is of this kind in potentiality, but becomes such in actuality when it comes into contact with us, has been said many times before, and we shall recall it now too, so that it may be kept in mind throughout.
term_table.english_sentence_B: That the drug which brings to suppuration is such in potentiality, but becomes such in actuality on being brought into contact with us, has been said many times before. We shall recall it now as well, so that it may be remembered always.

term_table.english_sentence_A: There must indeed be something clogging in these too, just as in the suppurative drugs, but to the extent that it is fitting for them to be more evacuative, to that extent they also clog the pores less.
term_table.english_sentence_B: These too must have something clogging in them, as the suppurative drugs also do. But the more evacuant they ought to be, the less they ought to become plastered into the pores.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀεί-ζωον, τό, houseleek, Sempervivum, Thphr. HP 1.10.4 , Dsc. 4.88 ; ἀ. μέγα S. arboreum, ἀ. μικρόν S. tectorum, ib. 89 ; ἀ. λεπτόφυλλον stonecrop, Sedum stellatum, Ps.- Dsc. 4.90 .
term_table.greek_sentence: χρὴ τοίνυν εἶναι ταῦτα ψυχρὰ καὶ ὑγρὰ, καθάπερ ἀείζωόν τέ ἐστι καὶ ἀνδράχνη καὶ ψύλλιον ὅ τ’ ἐπὶ τῶν τελμάτων φακὸς, ἢ τὸ στρύχνον, ἢ τοῦτο μὲν οὐδὲ ὑγρόν ἐστι τὴν κρᾶσιν, ἀλλὰ μέσον ὑγραίνοντος ἁπλῶς καὶ ξηραίνοντος ἐξ ἐναντίων συγκείμενον δυνάμεων, ὑγραινούσης τε καὶ ξηραινούσης, ὅτι καὶ διττῆς οὐσίας μετέχει, γεώδους τε καὶ ὑδατώδους.
term_table.english_sentence_A: These, accordingly, must be cold and moist, as houseleek is, and purslane and fleawort and the lentil that grows on marshes, or strychnos—or rather this last is not even moist in its mixture, but intermediate between what simply moistens and what dries, being composed of opposite powers, a moistening and a drying one, because it also partakes of a twofold substance, earthy and watery.
term_table.english_sentence_B: These, then, must be cold and moist, as are houseleek, purslane, fleawort and the lentil found on standing waters, or strychnos. Or rather, this last is not even moist in its mixture, but is intermediate between what simply moistens and what dries, being composed of opposite powers, a moistening and a drying one, because it also partakes of a twofold substance, earthy and watery.

Op. 625 , Th. 869 ; ὑ. ἅλς, πέλαγος, θάλασσα, Pi. O. 7.69 . P. 4.40 , A. Supp. 259 ; ὑγρὰ νύξ a wet night, Pl. HA 617a1 . ὑ. σφυγμός a damp pulse, defined by Gal. 19.405 . soft, pliant, supple, of the eagle's back, Pi. P. 1.9 ; of the limbs and body, ὑγραῖς ἐν ἀγκάλαις E. Fr. 941 , cf. Babr. 34.7 ; ὑγρὸς τὸ εἶδος, of Ἔρως, Pl. Smp. 196a ; νεώτερος καὶ ὑγρότερος, opp. σκληρός, Id. Tht. 162b ; χορῷ . . ἔτερπον κέαρ ὑγροῖσι ποσσί B. 16.108 ; ὑ. ὀρχηστής Poll. 4.96 , cf. Arist. term_table.english_sentence_A: But if something has become hard from not retaining its innate moisture, we call this dry rather than hard, and its cure is a thorough wetting (διανσις) and a moistening, and not a softening, [741] just as the cure of what is tensed is relaxation, and of what is relaxed, tensing.
term_table.english_sentence_B: But if something has become hard from not retaining its innate moisture, we call it dry rather than hard, and its cure is soaking and moistening, not softening, [741] just as the cure of what is contracted is relaxation, and of what is relaxed, contraction. How these things stand is clearly seen in the skin, as Hippocrates too has said: 'of hard skin, mollification; of contracted skin, relaxation'.

term_table.greek_sentence: Ταῦτα δὲ ὁρᾶται σαφῶς πῶς ἐστι καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ δέρματος μὲν, ὥσπερ καὶ πρὸς Ἱπποκράτους εἴρηται, δέρματος σκληροῦ μάλθαξις, συντεταμένου δὲ χάλασις, οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ κᾀπὶ τῶν ἄρθρων πολλάκις.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And how these things are is clearly seen both in the case of the skin, as has also been said by Hippocrates, "of hard skin, softening; of tensed, relaxation", and indeed also, often, in the case of the joints.
term_table.english_sentence_B: It is also often seen in the joints. Relaxation is brought about when the ligaments around them and the tendons have been moistened beyond measure.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἡ μὲν οὖν χάλασις ὑγρανθέντων ἀμέτρως τῶν ἀμφ’ αὐτὰ συνδέσμων ἀποτελεῖται καὶ τῶν τενόντων, ἡ δὲ σύντασις οὐκέθ’ ἁπλῶς, ἀλλ’ εἴ τι ξηραινομένων ἐπιπλέον, ἢ ψυχομένων, ἢ φλεγμαινόντων, ἢ σκιῤῥουμένων.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Now relaxation is brought about when the ligaments around them and the tendons have been immoderately moistened, whereas tensing is no longer simple, but occurs whenever they are dried to excess, or chilled, or inflamed, or hardened into scirrhus.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Contraction, however, does not arise in one simple way: it arises if they are dried to some greater degree, or chilled, or inflamed, or become scirrhous. So it is at the joints.

term_table.greek_sentence: κατ’ ἄρθρα μὲν οὕτως· ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ δέρματος οὐχ οὕτω μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἐντὸς αὐτοῦ μυῶν καθ’ ὁντιναοῦν τρόπον εἰς ὄγκον αὐξανομένων, ὥστε καὶ διὰ πολυσαρκίαν τισὶν ἐκτείνεται πολλάκις.
term_table.english_sentence_A: In the joints it is so; but in the case of the skin not only so, but also when the muscles within it are increased in bulk in whatever manner, so that in some people it is often stretched even on account of corpulence.
term_table.english_sentence_B: In the skin it arises not only in this way but also when the muscles within it increase in bulk in any manner whatsoever, so that in some people it is often stretched even through excess of flesh. That it suffers this same thing in inflammations as well has been said before.

term_table.english_sentence_B: In the skin it arises not only in this way but also when the muscles within it increase in bulk in any manner whatsoever, so that in some people it is often stretched even through excess of flesh. That it suffers this same thing in inflammations as well has been said before.

term_table.greek_sentence: ὅτι δὲ κᾀν ταῖς φλεγμοναῖς ταὐτὸ τοῦτο πάσχει λέλεκται πρόσθεν, ὅθεν οὔθ’ ἁπλῶς ἕν τι τῶν χαλαστικῶν ἐστιν εἶδος βοηθημάτων, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ὑγραίνοντα χαλᾷ, τὰ δὲ θερμαίνοντα, τὰ δὲ μαλάττοντα, τὰ δὲ κενοῦντα, τὰ δὲ τοὺς παρὰ φύσιν ὄγκους καθαίροντα, τὰ δέ τινα τούτων κατὰ συζυγίαν ἐργαζόμενα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And that it suffers this same thing in inflammations as well has been said before; hence there is not simply one single kind of relaxing remedies, but some relax by moistening, some by heating, some by softening, some by evacuating, some by clearing away the swellings contrary to nature, and some by effecting certain of these in combination.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Hence there is not simply one single kind of relaxing remedies. Rather, some relax by moistening, others by warming, others by softening, others by evacuating, others by clearing away the swellings contrary to nature, and others by effecting some of these in combination.

term_table.greek_sentence: ὅσα μὲν γὰρ τὸν ἐπιπολῆς ἀφαιρεῖ ῥύπον, εἴτ’ οὖν ἑλκῶν εἴτε καὶ τοῦ δέρματος αὐτοῦ, ῥυπτικὰ προσαγορεύεται· τὰ δὲ καὶ τοὺς πόρους ἐκκαθαίροντα λεπτομερέστερά τέ ἐστιν τούτων καὶ τοῖς ἐμπλαστικοῖς ἐναντία, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐκφρακτικά τε καὶ καθαρτικὰ τῶν πόρων ὀνομάζεται.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For those which remove the surface dirt, whether of ulcers or of the skin itself, are called cleansing; but those which also clean out the pores are both finer-particled than these and opposite to the clogging ones, and for this reason are named unblocking and purifying of the pores.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For those that remove the dirt on the surface, whether of ulcers or of the skin itself, are called cleansing; but those that also clear out the pores are more fine-particled than these and opposite to the clogging drugs, and for this reason they are named unblocking and clearing of the pores.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἔστι δὲ ταῦτα νιτρώδη τε καὶ πικρὰ, καὶ κατὰ μὲν τοῦ δέρματος ἔξωθεν ἐπιτιθέμενα ﻿ [744] τὴν νιτρώδη ποιότητα μόνον ἀκριβῆ κεκτῆσθαι δεῖται πρὸς τὸ δύνασθαι δρᾷν ἅπερ εἴρηται, εἴσω δὲ τοῦ σώματος λαμβανόμενα, κᾂν εἰ στύψεώς τι μετέχῃ, δύναιτ’ ἂν εἶναι καὶ οὕτως ἔτι καθαρτικά τε καὶ διαῤῥυπτικὰ τῶν μειζόνων πόρων, οἷοίπερ κᾀν τοῖς ἀγγείοις εἰσίν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: These are nitrous and bitter; and when applied externally to the skin [744] they need to possess only the nitrous quality in an exact degree in order to be able to do what has been said, but when taken into the interior of the body, even if they share in some astringency, they could even so still be purgative and thoroughly cleansing of the larger pores, such as those in the vessels are.
term_table.english_sentence_B: These are nitrous and bitter. When they are applied to the skin from outside, [744] they need only possess the nitrous quality in its exact form to be able to do what has been stated.

(lyr.); περί τινος dub. in Ar. Ec. 653 ; πόροι πρὸς τὸ πολεμεῖν X. An. 2.5.20 . abs., providing, means of providing, opp. ἀπορία, Pl. term_table.greek_sentence: ἔστι δὲ ταῦτα νιτρώδη τε καὶ πικρὰ, καὶ κατὰ μὲν τοῦ δέρματος ἔξωθεν ἐπιτιθέμενα ﻿ [744] τὴν νιτρώδη ποιότητα μόνον ἀκριβῆ κεκτῆσθαι δεῖται πρὸς τὸ δύνασθαι δρᾷν ἅπερ εἴρηται, εἴσω δὲ τοῦ σώματος λαμβανόμενα, κᾂν εἰ στύψεώς τι μετέχῃ, δύναιτ’ ἂν εἶναι καὶ οὕτως ἔτι καθαρτικά τε καὶ διαῤῥυπτικὰ τῶν μειζόνων πόρων, οἷοίπερ κᾀν τοῖς ἀγγείοις εἰσίν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: These are nitrous and bitter; and when applied externally to the skin [744] they need to possess only the nitrous quality in an exact degree in order to be able to do what has been said, but when taken into the interior of the body, even if they share in some astringency, they could even so still be purgative and thoroughly cleansing of the larger pores, such as those in the vessels are.
term_table.english_sentence_B: These are nitrous and bitter. When they are applied to the skin from outside, [744] they need only possess the nitrous quality in its exact form to be able to do what has been stated.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: σμικρός, σμικρότης, σμικρόφθαλμος, v. μικρ- .
term_table.greek_sentence: ἔξωθεν μὲν γὰρ ἡ σμικρότης τῶν πόρων ὑπὸ τῆς στύψεως τυφλοῦσθαι φθάνουσα, πρὶν ἐκκαθαρθῆναι καλῶς, οὔτε παραδέχεται τοὐντεῦθεν ἔτι τὴν ῥυπτικὴν οὐσίαν εἰς τὸ βάθος οὔτ’ ἐκκαθαίρεται.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For externally the smallness of the pores, being closed up beforehand by the astringency before they have been properly cleaned out, neither thereafter admits the cleansing substance any further into the depth nor is cleaned out.
term_table.english_sentence_B: But when they are taken inside the body, even if they have some share of astringency, they can still, even so, be clearing and thoroughly cleansing of the larger pores, such as are also in the vessels. For on the outside the smallness of the pores is first closed up ('blinded') by the astringency before it has been properly cleaned out, and from then on it neither admits the cleansing substance any further into the depth nor is cleaned out.

term_table.english_sentence_A: And for this reason wormwood is naturally fitted to clean out thoroughly from within, but not from without; and it is compounded, as was said before, of a bitter and an acerbic power.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And for this reason wormwood is naturally fitted to clean out thoroughly from within, but not from without.

term_table.lsj_first_sense_gloss: sweet to the taste or smell
term_table.greek_sentence: ὅσα γὰρ ἂν εὑρίσκῃς νιτρώδη καὶ πικρὰ, ταῦτ’ ἐκκαθαίρειν ἴσθι δυνάμενα τοὺς πόρους πάντας· ῥύπον δὲ ἑλκῶν, ἢ καὶ τοῦ δέρματος, οὐ ταῦτα μόνον, ἀλλὰ [745] καὶ τὰ μετριώτερα ταῖς δυνάμεσιν ἀφαιρεῖν πέφυκεν, οἷάπερ ἐστι τὰ λεπτομερῆ γλυκέα, καθάπερ τὸ μέλι καὶ τῶν σιτηρῶν σπερμάτων ἔνια, καθάπερ ὄροβοι καὶ κύαμοι καὶ κριθαὶ καὶ θέρμοι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For whatever things you find to be nitrous and bitter, know that these are able to clear out all the pores; but the filth of ulcers, or indeed of the skin, not only these but [745] also those more moderate in their powers are of a nature to remove, such as the fine-particled sweet things, like honey and some of the cereal seeds, such as bitter vetch, beans, barley and lupins.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For whatever you find to be nitrous and bitter, know that these are able to cleanse out all the pores; but the filth of ulcers, or also that of the skin, not only these but [745] also things more moderate in their powers are by nature able to remove, such as are the fine-particled sweet things, like honey and some of the cereal seeds, like bitter vetch, beans, barley and lupins.

term_table.english_sentence_A: So that you could not find other drugs, in preference to these, more cutting and more thinning of the phlegmatic or viscous matters, or of pus, from the chest and lung, and more suitable for bringing them up.

term_table.english_sentence_A: Of such a kind are the seed of celery, of rock-parsley, of fennel, of daucus, of wild celery and of smyrnion, and indeed also seseli, ammi, phou and meon, asaron and acoron; by these the blood is not only thinned but also diffused and separated, in a manner similar to milk, the serous and thin part being set apart by itself, and the thicker part in turn consolidating with itself and being precisely unified.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Such are the seed of selinon, of petroselinon, of fennel, of daucus, of wild selinon and of smyrnion, and also seseli, ammi, phu and meon, as well as asaron and acoron. By these the blood is not only thinned but also liquefied and separated, in the same way as milk: the whey-like and thin part is separated off by itself, while the thicker part condenses upon itself and is closely united.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἔστι δὲ τοιαῦτα σελίνου σπέρμα καὶ πετροσελίνου καὶ μαράθρου καὶ δαύκου καὶ ἀγριοσελίνου καὶ σμυρνίου, καὶ δὴ καὶ τὸ σέσελι καὶ τὸ ἄμμι καὶ τὸ φοῦ καὶ τὸ μέον, ἄσαρόν τε καὶ ἄκορον, ὑφ’ ὧν οὐ λεπτύνεται μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ χεῖται καὶ διακρίνεται τὸ αἷμα παραπλησίως τῷ γάλακτι, τοῦ μὲν ὀῤῥώδους καὶ λεπτοῦ ἀποχωριζομένου καθ’ ἑαυτὸ, τοῦ δ’ αὖ παχυτέρου συνισταμένου τε πρὸς ἑαυτὸ καὶ ἀκριβῶς ἑνουμένου.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Of such a kind are the seed of celery, of rock-parsley, of fennel, of daucus, of wild celery and of smyrnion, and indeed also seseli, ammi, phou and meon, asaron and acoron; by these the blood is not only thinned but also diffused and separated, in a manner similar to milk, the serous and thin part being set apart by itself, and the thicker part in turn consolidating with itself and being precisely unified.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Such are the seed of selinon, of petroselinon, of fennel, of daucus, of wild selinon and of smyrnion, and also seseli, ammi, phu and meon, as well as asaron and acoron. By these the blood is not only thinned but also liquefied and separated, in the same way as milk: the whey-like and thin part is separated off by itself, while the thicker part condenses upon itself and is closely united.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: νεφρ-ός, ὁ, in pl., kidneys, Diog.Apoll. 6 , Hp. Aph. 4.78 , Pl. Ti. 91a , etc.: in dual, Ar. Ra. 475 : rarely in sg., Id. Lys. 962 , Euphro 1.25 : euphem. for ὄρχεις, Philippid. 5.4 : metaph., LXX Ps. 15(16).7 . (Cf. OHG. nioro 'kidney', Praenest. nefrones, Lanuv. nebrundines 'kidneys', 'testicles'.)
term_table.greek_sentence: πρὸς γὰρ δὴ τὸ ῥᾳδίως ἐπισπᾶσθαι τοὺς νεφροὺς ὅσον ὑδατῶδές τ’ ἐστὶ καὶ λεπτὸν καὶ ὀῤῥῶδες ἐν αἵματι ταῦτ’ ἄμφω συντελεῖ, χύσις μὲν αὐτοῦ τοῦ αἵματος ὅλου τὸ πρῶτον, ἐφεξῆς δ’ αὐτῇ διάκρισις, ὧν οὐδὲν ἄνευ θερμότητος ἰσχυρᾶς ἐνδέχεται γενέσθαι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For towards the kidneys' readily drawing to themselves whatever is watery and thin and serous in the blood, both of these contribute: first the diffusion of the whole blood itself, and following upon it the separation, none of which can come about without strong heat.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For both of these things contribute to the kidneys' easily drawing to themselves whatever in the blood is watery, thin and whey-like: first the liquefaction of the whole blood itself, and after it the separation. Neither of these can come about without strong heat.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀνάπτυσις, εως, ἡ, expectoration, Gal. 15.480 , Herod.Med. in Rh.Mus. 58.93 ; αἵματος Alex.Trall. 5.5 ; of fistulae, opening out, Antyll. ap. Orib. 44.23.6 .

term_table.greek_sentence: φύσις γὰρ [748] αὐτῶν, ὡς εἴρηται νυνὶ, θερμαντική τε καὶ ξηραντικὴ καὶ προσέτι συνακτική τε καὶ διακριτικὴ, συναγομένου μὲν εἰς ταὐτὸ τοῦ παχέος, ἀποκρινομένου δὲ καὶ διακρινομένου κατὰ τὴν τοῦδε σύνοδον ὅσον ἂν ὀῤῥῶδές τε καὶ λεπτὸν ἐμφέρηται τῷ αἵματι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For their nature, [748] as has just been said, is heating and drying, and moreover contracting and separating, the thick part being gathered together into one, while whatever serous and thin matter is carried in the blood is secreted and separated off in accordance with the coming-together of the former.

term_table.greek_sentence: ὅσα δὲ τὰς ἐν αὐτοῖς πωρώδεις συστάσεις ἐπιτήδεια τέμνειν ἐστὶν, τμητικὰ μὲν ἱκανῶς ὑπάρχει καὶ ταῦτα, θερμότητος δ’ ἥκιστα μετέχει· συνίστησι γὰρ ἀποξηραίνουσα τὸν πῶρον ἡ θερμότης, οὐ τέμνει καὶ διαιρεῖ.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And those which are suited to cut the stony concretions in them are themselves also sufficiently cutting, but partake least of heat; for heat, by drying out, consolidates the stone, and does not cut and divide it.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And those that are suitable for cutting the stony concretions in them are also sufficiently cutting, but share very little in heat; for heat, by drying out the stony matter, consolidates it, and does not cut and divide it.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀγαθός [αγ], ή, όν, Lacon. ἀγασός Ar. Lys. 1301 , Cypr. ἀζαθός GDI 57 :— good: of persons, well-born, gentle, opp. κακός, δειλός, οἷά τε τοῖς ἀγαθοῖσι παραδρώωσι χέρηες Od. 15.324 , cf. Il. 1.275 ; ἀφνειός τ' ἀ. τε Il. 13.664 , cf. Od. 18.276 ; πατρὸς δ' εἴμ' ἀγαθοῖο, θεὰ δέ με γείνατο μήτηρ Il. 21.109 , cf. Od. 4.611 ; κακὸς ἐξ ἀ. Thgn. 190 , cf. 57 sq.; πραῢς ἀστοῖς, οὐ φθονέων ἀγαθοῖς Pi. P. 3.71 , cf. 2.96 , 4.285 ; τίς ἂν εὔπατρις ὧδε βλάστοι; οὐδεὶς τῶν ἀ. κτλ. S. El. 1082 ; οἵ τ' ἀ. πρὸς τῶν ἀγενῶν κατανικῶνται Id. Fr. 84 ; τοὺς εὐγενεῖς γὰρ κἀγαθοὺς . . φιλεῖ Ἄρης ἐναίρειν ib. 649 , cf. E. Alc. 600 , al.: ἀγαθοὶ καὶ ἐξ ἀγαθῶν Pl. Phdr. 274a :—in political sense, aristocrats, esp. in the phrase καλοὶ κἀγαθοί (v. sub καλοκἀγαθός). brave, valiant, since courage was attributed to Chiefs and Nobles, Il. 1.131 , al.; τῷ κ' ἀγαθὸς μὲν ἔπεφν', ἀγαθὸν δέ κεν ἐξενάριξεν 21.280 ; cf. Hdt. 5.109 , etc. good, capable, in reference to ability, ἀ. βασιλεύς Il. 3.179 ; ἰητήρ 2.732 ; θεράπων 16.165 , 17.388 ; πύκτης Xenoph. 2.15 ; ἰητρός Hp. Prog. 1 ; προβατογνώμων A. Ag. 795 ; ἄρχοντες Democr. 266 : freq. with qualifying words, ἀ. ἐν ὑσμίνῃ Il. 13.314 ; βοὴν ἀ. 2.408 , 563 , al.; πύξ Od. 11.300 ; βίην Il. 6.478 ; γνώμην S. OT 687 ; πᾶσαν ἀρετήν Pl. Lg. 899b , cf. Alc. 1.124e ; τέχνην Id. Prt. 323b ; τὰ πολέμια, τὰ πολιτικά, Hdt. 9.122 , Pl. Grg. 516b , etc.: more rarely c. dat., ἀ. πολέμῳ X. Oec. 4.15 : with Preps., ἄνδρες ἀ. περὶ τὸ πλῆθος Lys. 13.2 ; εἴς τι Pl. Alc. 1.125a ; πρός τι Id. R. 407e : c. inf., ἀ. μάχεσθαι Hdt. 1.136 ; ἱππεύεσθαι 1.79 ; ἀ. ἱστάναι good at weighing, Pl. Prt. 356b . good, in moral sense, first in Thgn. 438 , cf. Heraclit. 104 , S. El. 1082 , X. Mem. 1.7.1 , Pl. Ap. 41d , etc.; ψυχῆς ἀγαθῆς πατρὶς ὁ ξύμπας κόσμος Democr. 247 : freq. with other Adjs., ὁ πιστὸς κἀ. S. Tr. 541 ; δικαίων κἀ. ib. 1050 :—ironical, τὸν ἀ. Κρέοντα Id. Ant. 31 . ὦ ἀγαθέ, my good friend, as a term of gentle remonstrance, Pl. Prt. 311a , etc. ἀ. δαίμων, v. sub δαίμων; ἀ. τύχη, v. sub τύχη; ἀ. θεός = Lat. bona dea, Plu. Caes. 9 , Cic. 19 . of things, good, serviceable, Ἰθάκη . . ἀ. κουροτρόφος Od. 9.27 , etc.; ἀ. τοῖς τοκεῦσι, τῇ πόλει X. Cyn. 13.17 : c. gen., εἴ τι οἶδα πυρετοῦ ἀ. good for it, Id. Mem. 3.8.3 ; ἑλκῶν Thphr. HP 9.11.1 . of outward circumstances, αἰδὼς οὐκ ἀ. κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ παρεῖναι Od. 17.347 ; εἰπεῖν εἰς ἀγαθόν to good purpose, Il. 9.102 ; ὁ δὲ πείσεται εἰς ἀ. περ for his own good end, 11.789 ; οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη 2.204 :—ἀγαθόν [ἐστι], c. inf., it is good to do so and so<*> Il. 7.282 , 24.130 , Od. 3.196 , etc. morally good, πρῆξις Democr. 177 ; ἔργα Emp. 112.2 , cf. Ep.Rom. 2.7 , etc. ἀγαθόν, τό, good, blessing, benefit, of persons or things, ὦ μέγα ἀ. σὺ τοῖς φίλοις X. Cyr. 5.3.20 ; φίλον, ὃ μέγιστον ἀ. εἶναί φασι Id. Mem. 2.4.2 , cf. Ar. Ra. 74 , etc; as term of endearment for a baby, blessing!, treasure!, Men. Sam. 28 :— ἀγαθόν τινα δεδρακέναι, πεποιηκέναι confer a benefit on . . , Th. 3.68 , Lys. 13.92 ; ἐπ' ἀγαθῷ τινος for one's good, Th. 5.27 , X. Cyr. 7.4.3 ; ἐπ' ἀ. τοῖς πολίταις Ar. Ra. 1487 ; οὐκ ἐπ' ἀ. for no good end, Th. 1.131 ; ἐπ' οὐδενὶ ἀ. τῆς Ἑλλάδος X. HG 5.2.35 :—in pl., ἡ ἐπ' ἀγαθοῖς γεναμένη (sic) κατασπορά PFlor. 21.10 (iii A.D.):—τὸ ἀ. or τἀ., the good, Epich. 171.5 , cf. Pl. R. 506b , 508e , Arist. Metaph. 1091a31 , etc.:—in pl., ἀγαθά, τά, goods of fortune, treasures, wealth, Hdt. 2.172 , Lys. 13.91 , X. Mem. 1.2.63 , etc.; ἀγαθὰ πράττειν fare well, Ar. Av. 1706 ; also, good things, dainties, Thgn. 1000 , Ar. Ach. 873 , etc.: good qualities, τοῖς ἀ., οἷς ἔχομεν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ Isoc. 8.32 , cf. Democr. 37 ; good points, of a horse, εἰ τἄλλα πάντα ἀ. ἔχοι, κακόπους δ' εἴη X. Eq. 1.2 . Comp. and Sup. are usu. supplied from other stems, viz. Comp. ἀμείνων, ἀρείων<*> βελτίων, κρείσσων ʽκάρρωνʼ, λωΐων (λώʽωνʼ), Ep. βέλτερος, λωΐτερος, φέρτερος:— Sup. ἄριστος, βέλτιστος, κράτιστος, λώϊστος (λῷστος), Ep. βέλτατος, κάρτιστος, φέρτατος, φέριστος:— later, reg. Comp. ἀγαθώτερος LXX Jd. 11.25 , 15.2 , D.S. 8 Fr. 12 , Plot. 5.5.9 , Diod.Rh. p.53.9H. : Sup. ἀγαθώτατος D.S. 16.85 , Hld. 5.15 , etc. ( -ότατος POxy. 1757.26 (ii A.D.)). Adv. usually εὖ, q.v.: ἀγαθῶς Hp. Off. 9 , Arist. Rh. 1388b6 , LXX 1 Ki. 20.7 . (Etym. dub. ( ὅτι ἄγει ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ τὸν ὀρθὸν βίον Stoic. 3.49 ); perh. cognate with ἄγαμαι, hence admirable.)
term_table.greek_sentence: τὰ δ’ ἧττον θερμὰ μετὰ τοῦ τέμνειν δύνασθαι βελτίω, καθάπερ αἵ τε ῥίζαι τῶν βασιλικῶν ὀνομαζομένων ἀσπαράγων, αἵ τε τοῦ βάτου, καὶ τὸ κέστρον καὶ τὸ πόλιον, ὦχρά τε καὶ ὕαλος ἡ ﻿ [749] κεκαυμένη, καὶ τὸ διὰ τῆς σκίλλης ὄξος, ὅσα τ’ ἄλλα τοιαῦτα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But those that are less hot, along with being able to cut, are better, such as the roots of the asparagus called 'royal', and those of the bramble, and kestron and polion, and ochre and burnt [749] glass, and the vinegar of squill, and all other such things.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: πυκν-ωτικός, ή, όν, serving to close the pores, δύναμις π. τῶν σωμάτων Dsc. 3.22 , cf. Sor. 1.50 , Aret. CA 2.1 ; ψυχροί τε καὶ π., of N. winds, bracing, Ptol. Tetr. 30 .
term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ δὴ καὶ τῶν ἐναντίων αὐτοῖς, εἰ μέν τι συνάγει τοὺς πόρους, πυκνωτικὸν ὀνομάζουσιν, εἰ δέ τι κλείει τὸ στόμιον, ἰδίῳ μὲν οὐκέτι προσαγορεύουσιν [750] ὀνόματι, γενικωτέροις δέ τισι συνάγον τε καὶ κλεῖον καὶ σφίγγον καὶ στεγνοῦν ὀνομάζοντες, ἡ δὲ φύσις ἑκατέρων ἐστὶν τῶν μὲν ἀραιωτικῶν μετρίως θερμὴ καὶ ἥκιστα ξηραίνουσα καὶ λεπτομερὴς, τῶν δ’ ἀναστομωτικῶν παχυμερὴς, δριμεῖα καὶ δηκτική· τῶν δ’ ἐναντίων αὐτοῖς ἡ μὲν πυκνωτικὴ ψυκτικὴ μὲν, οὐ μὴν οὔτε γεώδης οὔτε ἀερώδης, ἀλλ’ ὑδατώδης μᾶλλον, ἡ δὲ τὰς ἀναστομώσεις κλείουσα παχυμερὴς, ψυχρά.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And indeed, of their opposites too, if something draws the pores together, they call it condensing; but if something closes the mouth, they no longer address it by a name of its own, [750] naming it instead by certain more generic ones: contracting, closing, constricting and stopping up. The nature of each: that of the rarefying ones is moderately hot and least of all drying and fine-particled; that of the mouth-opening ones coarse-particled, pungent and biting.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And moreover, as for their opposites: if something draws the pores together, they name it condensing; but if something closes the orifice, they no longer address it by a proper [750] name, and instead call it by certain more generic ones: 'drawing together', 'closing', 'binding tight' and 'stopping up'. The nature of each is as follows.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: χαμαί-μηλον, τό, earth-apple, camomile, Orph. A. 921 . = ἀνθεμὶς λευκή , Dsc. 3.137 , Plin. HN 22.53 . = παρθένιον , Ps.- Dsc. 3.138 .
term_table.greek_sentence: παράδειγμα δὲ τούτων· ἀραιωτικῆς μὲν φύσεως χαμαίμηλόν τε καὶ ἀλθαία καὶ τὸ δι’ αὐτῶν ἔλαιον, οὐχ ἥκιστα δὲ καὶ τὸ διὰ τῶν ἀγρίων σικύων.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Of their opposites, the condensing nature is cooling, yet neither earthy nor airy, but rather watery; while that which closes the openings is coarse-particled and cold.
term_table.english_sentence_B: That of the rarefying ones is moderately hot, drying least of all, and fine-particled; that of the ones opening the mouths of vessels is coarse-particled, pungent and biting.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: κίκινος, η, ον, made from the κίκι-tree, ἔλαιον Dsc. 1.32 , Gal. 11.870 .
term_table.greek_sentence: ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ παλαιὸν καὶ τὸ κίκινον καὶ τὸ ῥαφάνινον ἔλαιον ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ἐστιν ἰδέας.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Examples of these: of rarefying nature are chamomile and marsh-mallow and the oil made from them, and not least also that made from wild cucumbers.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Of their opposites, the condensing nature is cooling, yet neither earthy nor airy but rather watery; the nature that closes the openings of the vessels is coarse-particled and cold.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἀναστομωτικῆς δὲ δυνάμεως ὅσα δριμέα τέ ἐστιν καὶ γεώδη πάντα, κυκλάμινος, σκόροδα, κρόμμυα, τῶν ταύρων αἱ χολαί.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But old oil too, and castor oil, and radish oil are of the same kind.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Examples of these: of rarefying nature are chamomile and marsh-mallow and the oil made from them, and not least also the oil made from wild cucumbers. Old oil, castor oil and radish oil are also of the same kind.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀναστομ-ωτικός, ή, όν, = foreg., Dsc. 1.4 , Antyll. ap. Orib. 10.25.2 .
term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ γὰρ καὶ ταῦτα φλεγμονῆς εἶναι λυτικὰ λέγοιντ’ ἂν, ἀναστομωτικὰ δ’ οὐδαμῶς ἁμαρτάνει δ’ ἐν αὐτοῖς ὁ Διοσκουρίδης, ἀναστομωτικῆς ἐνίοτε λέγων εἶναι δυνάμεως ἤτοι χαλαστικόν τι φάρμακον ἢ μαλακτικὸν ἢ ὑγραντικὸν ἢ φλεγμονῆς λυτικόν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For these too would be said to be resolvers of inflammation, but by no means mouth-opening. Dioscorides errs in these matters, sometimes saying that a relaxing drug, or a softening, or a moistening, or an inflammation-resolving one, is of mouth-opening power.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For these too might be called resolvent of inflammation, but in no way opening the mouths of vessels. Dioscorides errs in these matters, sometimes saying that a drug which is relaxing, or softening, or moistening, or resolvent of inflammation is of a power that opens the mouths of vessels.

term_table.english_sentence_A: Of those opposite to them, the substance of the condensing ones is that of cold water and of houseleek and of purslane and of green caltrop and of fleawort and of the herb which they call mouse-ears, and of the lentil from the marshes, and, to put it simply, of all things that cool without being astringent.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Of the drugs contrary to them, the substance of the condensing ones is that of cold water, houseleek, purslane, green caltrop, fleawort, the herb which they call mouse-ear, and the lentil from the pools; and, to put it simply, of whatever cools without being astringent.

term_table.english_sentence_A: Of those opposite to them, the substance of the condensing ones is that of cold water and of houseleek and of purslane and of green caltrop and of fleawort and of the herb which they call mouse-ears, and of the lentil from the marshes, and, to put it simply, of all things that cool without being astringent.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Of the drugs contrary to them, the substance of the condensing ones is that of cold water, houseleek, purslane, green caltrop, fleawort, the herb which they call mouse-ear, and the lentil from the pools; and, to put it simply, of whatever cools without being astringent.

term_table.greek_sentence: διὸ καὶ μανδραγόρας καὶ κώνειον, ὑοσκύαμός τε καὶ μήκων, αὐτὰς δὲ λέγω νῦν τὰς πόας, εἰ μὲν μετρίως τις χρήσαιτο, πυκνωτικαὶ [752] ταῖς δυνάμεσιν ὑπάρχουσιν· εἰ δ’ ἐπὶ πλέον, οὐ πυκνωτικαὶ μόνον, ἀλλ’ ἤδη καὶ ναρκωτικαί· εἰ δ’ ἐπὶ πλεῖστον, οὐκέτι ναρκωτικαὶ μόνον, ἀλλ’ ἤδη καὶ νεκρωτικαί.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Hence also mandrake and hemlock, henbane and poppy—I mean now the herbs themselves—if one uses them moderately, are condensing [752] in their powers; if more, they are not only condensing but already also numbing; and if to the greatest degree, they are no longer only numbing but already also mortifying.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For this reason mandrake and hemlock, henbane and poppy too (I mean now the herbs themselves), if one uses them moderately, are condensing [752] in their powers; if more liberally, not only condensing but by now numbing as well; and if most liberally, no longer only numbing but by now also deadening. The substance of the things contrary to the anastomotic [drugs], being coarse-particled and cold, is that of all the astringents that are without admixed pungency.

term_table.greek_sentence: οὐκοῦν ἔτι θαυμαστὸν οὐδὲν, εἰ μόνη συνάγειν καὶ κλείειν πέφυκε τὰ παρὰ φύσιν ἀναπεπταμένα τῶν ἀγγείων στόματα· μόνῃ γὰρ αὐτῇ πάνθ’ ὅσα δεῖται τὰ συναχθησόμενα πάρεστι, διὰ μὲν τὸ παχυμερὲς τῆς συστάσεως ἔξωθεν μὲν προσπιπτούσῃ, διεξέρχεσθαι δὲ τοὺς λεπτοὺς πόρους ἀδυνατούσῃ, διά τε τὴν ψύξιν εἴσω τε πιλούσῃ καὶ συναγούσῃ πανταχόθεν εἰς ἑαυτὰ τὰ πλησιάζοντα· διότι δὲ ξηραίνει, τοιοῦτον γὰρ ἐδείχθη πᾶν τὸ στῦφον, ἐκβοσκουμένη τε τὴν ἰκμάδα καὶ τονοῦσα τὸ μόριον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: So it is no longer any wonder if it alone is of a nature to draw together and close the mouths of the vessels that have been opened up contrary to nature; for in it alone are present all the things that what is to be drawn together requires: on account of the coarse-particled character of its consistency it falls upon the parts from outside and is unable to pass through the fine pores; on account of its cooling it compresses inward and draws together the neighbouring parts from every side into themselves; and because it dries—for every astringent was shown to be such—it feeds upon the moisture and tones the part.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Because of its cooling it compresses inwards and draws together from every side towards themselves the parts that lie near. And because it dries (for every astringent was shown to be of this kind), it consumes the moisture and gives tone to the part.

term_table.english_sentence_A: So it is no longer any wonder if it alone is of a nature to draw together and close the mouths of the vessels that have been opened up contrary to nature; for in it alone are present all the things that what is to be drawn together requires: on account of the coarse-particled character of its consistency it falls upon the parts from outside and is unable to pass through the fine pores; on account of its cooling it compresses inward and draws together the neighbouring parts from every side into themselves; and because it dries—for every astringent was shown to be such—it feeds upon the moisture and tones the part.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Because of its cooling it compresses inwards and draws together from every side towards themselves the parts that lie near. And because it dries (for every astringent was shown to be of this kind), it consumes the moisture and gives tone to the part.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἀλλ’ εἴπερ ἅπαντα συνέλθῃ ταῦτα, κλεισθήσεται τὸ στόμιον ὡς ὑπὸ δακτύλων τινῶν [753] ἔξωθεν τῶν μορίων τῆς στυφούσης οὐσίας συναγόμενον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But if all these things come together, the orifice will be closed, being drawn together from outside by the particles of the astringent substance as if by certain fingers [753].
term_table.english_sentence_B: But if all these things come together, the orifice will be closed, drawn together from outside by the particles of the astringent substance as if by fingers [753].

term_table.greek_sentence: ὅσα δὲ τῶν φαρμάκων ψυχρὰ μέν ἐστιν ἢ ὁμοίως ἢ μᾶλλον, ὑδατώδη δ’ ἐστὶ ταῖς οὐσίαις, ἀσθενῶς τὰ τοιαῦτα καὶ συνάγει τε καὶ σφίγγει διὰ μαλακότητα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But those drugs which are cold, either equally or more so, yet watery in their substances—such drugs both draw together and constrict only weakly, because of their softness.

term_table.greek_sentence: δεῖται γάρ τινος ἰσχύος ἀντιβατικῆς καὶ σκληρᾶς ἅπαν τὸ μέλλον πιλήσειν τε καὶ συνάξειν ὁτιοῦν ἰσχυρῶς, ἣν οὐκ ἔχοντα τὰ ὑδατωδέστερα ταῖς οὐσίαις φάρμακα τοὺς μὲν λεπτοὺς πόρους ἐν ἑκάστῳ σώματι συνάγει καὶ πυκνοῖ, τὸ δ’ ὅλον ὄργανον ἀδυνατεῖ σφίγξαι πανταχόθεν, ὥστ’ εὐλόγως τὰ τοιαῦτα πυκνωτικὰ μέν ἐστι, στεγνωτικὰ δὲ οὐκ ἔστιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For everything that is going to compress and draw together anything whatever strongly requires a certain resistant and hard strength; and since the drugs that are more watery in their substances do not possess this, they draw together and condense the fine pores in each body, but are unable to constrict the whole organ from every side, so that with good reason such drugs are condensing but are not stopping.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For everything that is to compress and draw together anything strongly needs a certain resistant and hard strength; and the drugs more watery in their substances, not having this, draw together and condense the fine pores in each body, but are unable to constrict the whole organ from every side, so that such drugs are reasonably condensing, but not binding (stegnotic).

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἔκ-κρισις, εως, ἡ, separation, Arist. Mete. 342a15 , Onos. 9.1 (pl.). secretion, of the animal functions, Arist. PA 689a16 , GA 727a2 ; τῶν ὑγρῶν Eun. Hist. p.263 D. = ἔκκριμα , of excrement, Hp. Aph. 2.15 ; of the menses, Arist. HA 583a2 , etc.

term_table.english_sentence_A: For indeed the stopping body—that which holds within itself and lets nothing out perceptibly—has been termed by the Greeks stegnon (stopped-up).

term_table.greek_sentence: ταυτὶ μὲν οὖν τοιαῦτα ταῖς κράσεσί τ’ ἐστὶ καὶ ταῖς δυνάμεσιν· τὰ δὲ ἀραιωτικὰ θερμαίνει μὲν πάντως· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν ἄλλως δύναιτο διαχέαι τε ἅμα καὶ χαλάσαι τὴν οὐσίαν, οἷς ἕπεται τὸ καὶ τοὺς πόρους εὐρυνθῆναι· χρὴ ﻿ [754] μέντοι μήτ’ ἄγαν αὐτὰ θερμὰ ταῖς κράσεσιν εἶναι, δριμέα γὰρ ἤδη ταῦτα καὶ φρίττειν ἀναγκάζει, μήτε ξηραντικά.
term_table.english_sentence_A: These, then, are of such a kind in their mixtures and powers; but the rarefying ones heat in every case, for otherwise they could not at once diffuse and relax the substance, upon which follows also the widening of the pores. term_table.greek_sentence: Ὅσα τοίνυν ἀλύπως θερμαίνει, ταῦτα ἀραιωτικὰ μόνον ὑπάρχει τῶν πάντων· εἰ δὲ μὴ θερμὰ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ παχυμερῆ ταῖς συστάσεσιν εἴη, σφοδρὰ μὲν ὑπάρχοντα καὶ καυστικὰ συντήκει τε τὰ σώματα δίκην πυρὸς, ἐσχάρας τε πολλάκις ὁμοίας ταῖς ἀπὸ τῶν καυστήρων ἐργάζεται.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But if they are not only hot but also coarse-particled in their consistencies, then, when they are vehement and caustic, they melt down the bodies in the manner of fire and often produce eschars similar to those from cauteries; but when they heat less than so as to burn, they belong to the mouth-opening power, so that the mouth-opening drug (reading the transmitted τῶν as uncertain) is in its substance at once earthy and fiery, but has arrived at such a degree of heat as not yet to burn.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Those, therefore, which heat without causing distress are, of all things, the only ones that are rarefying. But if they should be not only hot but also coarse-particled in their consistencies, then, being vehement and caustic, they melt down the bodies after the manner of fire, and often produce eschars like those from cauteries.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἐπουλ-ωτικός, ή, όν, promoting cicatrization, Id. 11.756 .
term_table.greek_sentence: ἔστι δὲ καὶ ταῦτα τῆς μὲν αὐτῆς τῷ γένει τῆς σηπτικῆς ὀνομαζομένης δυνάμεως, ἀσθενεστέρας δ’ εἰς τοσοῦτον ὡς τὸ μὲν ἐπιπολῆς μόνον ᾧ προσπίπτει καθαιρεῖν, εἰς βάθος δ’ ἀδυνατεῖν προσέρχεσθαι, καθάπερ καὶ τὸ τῆς Ἀσίας πέτρας ἄνθος, οὐ μὴν τῆς γε αὐτῆς τῆς ὄντως ἐπουλωτικῆς δυνάμεώς ἐστι τὰ τοιαῦτα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: These too are of the same power, in genus, as the one named putrefying, but weaker to such a degree that they reduce only the surface of that upon which they fall, and are unable to advance into the depth, like also the flower of the Asian stone; such things, however, are certainly not of the same power as the truly scarring one.
term_table.english_sentence_B: These too are of the same power in genus as the one named putrefying, but weaker to such a degree that they reduce only the surface of whatever they come into contact with and are unable to penetrate into depth, as is also the case with the flower of Asian stone.

term_table.english_sentence_B: Such are alum, the oak-gall which they call omphakitis, and burnt copper, especially when it has been washed.

term_table.english_sentence_A: For these too bring [wounds] to a scar accidentally, such a drug as myrrh is, and litharge; and oyster-shell, if it be burnt, and diphryges—for these too, sprinkled on dry, have often formed a scar.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ὄστρε-ον or ὄστρειον, τό, oyster; the proper Att. form is ὄστρειον ( ὄστρεια . . ἔλεγον οἱ ἀρχαῖοι Ath. 3.92e , cf. Moer. p.285 P. (who recommends ὀστρία [ι] wrongly), Phot. , etc.), and this is required by the metre in the earlier Poets, κόγχοι, μύες, κὤστρεια A. Fr. 34 ; ὄστρεια συμμεμυκότα Epich. 42 (ὄστρεα codd. Ath. ); πίννῃσι καὶ ὀστρείοισιν ὁμοίη Cratin. 8 ; πίνναι, λεπάδες, μύες, ὄστρεια Anaxandr. 41.61 (anap.); while ὄστρεον is used in late Ep. , Matro Conv. 16 , Nic. Fr. 83 , and is found in Pap., PCair.Zen. 82.13 (iii B. C.), POxy. 738.5 (i A. D.):—the readings vary in Pl. (v. infr. III), as in Arist. , cf. HA 490b10 , 525a20 : generally, of all bivalves, ib. 525a20 , 528a1 , Fr. 304 , Gal. 12.345 . oyster- or bivalve-shell, Arist. HA 531b5 , 590a32 . purple pigment, prob. that produced by the murex, cf. Arist. HA 548a12 ; ὄστρεον μόνον ἐπιφέρειν Pl. Cra. 424d ; ὀστρείῳ ἐναληλιμμένος Id. R. 420c ; τὰ σώματα ἐκέχριντο ὀστρείῳ Callix. 2 : ὄστρεα· τὰ κογχύλια, Αάκωνες ἄνθος, Hsch.
term_table.greek_sentence: καὶ εἰ καυθείη τό τε ὄστρεον καὶ τὸ διφρυγὲς, ἐπιπαττόμενα γὰρ καὶ ταῦτα ξηρὰ, πολλάκις ἐπούλωσεν.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ξηρός, ά, όν, dry, opp. ὑγρός, of a dried-up river, Hdt. 5.45 ; χειμάρρους ξηροὺς ὕδατος Arr. An. 4.3.2 ; ἠὴρ ξ. Hdt. 2.26 ; ξ. ἄνεμος Ar. Nu. 404 ; ξηροῖς ἀκλαύτοις ὄμμασιν A. Th. 696 ; ὀμμάτων ξ. κόραι E. Or. 389 ; μέτρα ξ. τε καὶ ὑγρά dry and liquid measures, Pl. Lg. 746d ; ὕλη αὔη καὶ ξ. ib. 761d ; ξ. γάλα, i.e. ripe cheese, Eust. 1001.51 (cf. περίξηρος) ; so τυρὸς ξ., opp. τυρὸς χλωρός, Antiph. 133.7 , cf. Philox. 3.8 ; ἐν ξηροῖσιν ἐκτρέφειν on solid food, i.e. cereals, E. Ba. 277 ; καρπὸς ξ., i.e. cereal, opp. κ. ξύλινος, produce of trees, i. e. fruit, wine, or oil, Pl. Criti. 115b ; ξ. χόρτος hay, PPetr. 3p.181 (iii B.C.) ; φοῖνιξ ξ. dried dates, PSI 1.33.14 (ii A.D.); ξ. καρποί, opp. οἶνος, ἔλαιον, Arr. Epict. 2.23.5 ; ξ. πυρίαι applications of dry heat, Hp. Acut. 21 , Archig. ap. Gal. 12.621 ; cf. ξηροπυρία. Adv. ξηρῶς by the use of dry powder, Hp. Epid. 6.3.13 (s.v.l.). of bodily condition, withered, lean, δέμας E. El. 239 ; ξηρὸς ὑπαὶ δείους Theoc. 24.61 ; ξ. κοιλίη costive, Hp. Aph. 2.20 . of the voice, cf. ξηρόφωνος. fasting: hence, generally, austere, τρόποι Ar. V. 1452 (lyr.); of persons, Antiph. 16 ; harsh, opp. ἡδύς, E. Andr. 784 (lyr.). metaph., of style, πραγματεία ἀτερπὴς καὶ ξ. Epicur. Fr. 505 ( p.358 U.); τὸ ξ. aridity, Demetr. Eloc. 238 ; of critics, ξηροὶ Καλλιμάχου πρόκυνες AP 11.322 ( Antiphan. ). as Subst. ἡ ξηρά (sc. γῆ), dry land, opp. ὑγρά, X. Oec. 19.7 (also Comp. ξηροτέρα γῆ ib. 6 ), cf. Ev.Matt. 23.15 , etc. ; τὸ ξηρόν Hdt. 2.68 ; ναῦς ἐπὶ τοῦ ξηροῦ ποιεῖν to leave the ships aground, Th. 1.109 ; ναῦς ἐς τὸ ξ. ἐξωθεῖν Id. 8.105 ; τὸ ξ. τοῦ ποταμοῦ the part of its bed left dry, X. Cyr. 7.5.18 : for Theoc. 1.51 v. ἀκράτιστος. ξηρά, ἡ, in a bath-house, room for dry heat, POxy. 2145.12 (ii A.D.).
