term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἔνιοι, αι, α, some; never in Ep. , Lyr., or Att. Poets before Men. , exc. Ar. Pl. 867 (cf. however ἐνίοτε); first used in Ion. Prose, as Hdt. 1.120 , 8.56 , Hp. Praec. 6 ; πολλοὶ μὲν . . ἔνιοι δὲ . . Lys. 25.19 ; ἔνιοι μὲν . . ἔνιοι δὲ . . Pl. Tht. 151a , X. Mem. 4.2.38 ; ἔνιοι μὲν . . οἱ δὲ . . Pl. Mx. 238e ; ἔνιοί τινες Isoc. 15.258 : later in sg., οὐ πᾶσα κίνησις θερμαίνει, ἀλλ' ἐνία ψύχει Arist. Pr. 884b13 , cf. Thphr. Vert. 1 ; περὶ ψυχῆς ἐνίας θεωρῆσαι Arist. Metaph. 1026a5 : neut. pl. as Adv., συμμανῆναι ἔνια δεῖ Men. 421 ; ἔστι καὶ ταὐτόματον ἔνια χρήσιμον Id. 486 .
term_table.greek_sentence: ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ πάντως ἀλεξιφάρμακον εἶναι θηρίου, καὶ μάλιστα τὴν κοιλίαν αὐτῆς.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Some also say that it is altogether an alexipharmic against a wild beast, and especially its belly.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Some people also say that it is in every way an antidote against a venomous creature, and especially its belly.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: θηρίον, τό (in form Dim. of θήρ), wild animal, esp. of such as are hunted, μάλα γὰρ μέγα θηρίον ἦεν, of a stag, Od. 10.171 , 180 (never in Il. ); in Trag. only in Satyric drama, S. Ichn. 147 (dub. in A. Fr. 26 ): used in Prose for θήρ, X. An. 1.2.7 , Isoc. 12.163 , etc.; of the spider's prey, Arist. HA 623a27 ; freq. of elephants, Plb. 11.1.12 , al.: pl., beasts, opp. men, birds, and fishes, h.Ven. 4 , Hdt. 3.108 . generally, animal, Id. 1.119 ; νενόμισται πῦρ θ. εἶναι ἔμψυχον Id. 3.16 ; of men, ἄνθρωπος πάντων θ. θεειδέστατον Antipho Soph. 48 ; εἰς θηρίου βίον ἀφικνεῖσθαι Pl. Phdr. 249b ; also θ. ὕειον Id. R. 535e ; of the dog, Theoc. 25.79 ; of fishes, Arist. HA 598b1 ; of eels, Antiph. 147.7 ; of leeches, IG 4.951.101 (Epid.); of other small creatures, Arist. HA 552b11 , 625b32 , Hp. ap. Gal. 19.103 , Theoc. 19.6 ; οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδὲν θ. τῶν ἰχθύων ἀτυχέστερον Antiph. 161.1 ; opp. plants, Pl. Smp. 188b : prov., ἢ θηρίον ἢ θεός, either above or below the nature of man, Arist. Pol. 1253a29 , cf. EN 1145a25 . beast, esp. as hostile and odious to man, θηρία τε καὶ βοτά carnivora and graminivora, Pl. Mx. 237d ; monster, creature, of sharks, etc., Hdt. 6.44 ; of Typhon, etc., Pl. Phdr. 230a , R. 588e ; of the Satyrs, S. Ichn. l.c.; ταυτὶ ποδαπὰ τὰ θ.; Ar. Nu. 184 , cf. Av. 93 . poisonous animal, Dsc. 1.75 , Act.Ap. 28.4 . Medic.,= θηρίωμα, Hp. Coac. 459 , Loc.Hom. 29 , cf. Gal. l.c. as a term of reproach, beast, creature, ὦ δειλότατον σὺ θηρίον Ar. Pl. 439 , cf. Eq. 273 ; κόλακι, δεινῷ θηρίῳ Pl. Phdr. 240b ; Κρῆτες, κακὰ θ. Epimenid. 1 ; δυσνουθέτητον θ., of poverty, Men. Georg. 78 ; ἡ μουσικὴ ἀεί τι καινὸν θηρίον τίκτει Anaxil. 27 , cf. Eup. 132 ; τί δέ, εἰ αὐτοῦ τοῦ θηρίου ἠκούσατε; said by Aeschines of Demosthenes, Plin. Ep. 2.3.10 ; θ. συνεστιώμενον, of woman, Secund. Sent. 8 . Astron., the constellation Lupus, Eudox. ap. Hipparch. 1.2.20 , Vett. Val. 6.13 .
term_table.greek_sentence: ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ πάντως ἀλεξιφάρμακον εἶναι θηρίου, καὶ μάλιστα τὴν κοιλίαν αὐτῆς.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Some also say that it is altogether an alexipharmic against a wild beast, and especially its belly.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Some people also say that it is in every way an antidote against a venomous creature, and especially its belly.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: βάτραχος [βα], ὁ, frog, Batr. 6 , 18 , 59 , al., Hdt. 4.131 , etc.: prov., ὕδωρ πίνειν βάτραχος a very frog to drink, Aristopho 10.3 ; βατράχοις οἰνοχοεῖν, of those who give what is not wanted, Pherecr. 70.5 ; μέλει μοι τῶν τοιούτων ἧττον τῶν ἐν τοῖς τέλμασι β. Jul. Mis. 358a ; χλωρὸς β., of the tree-frog, Thphr. Sign. 15 . = ἁλιεύς , a kind of fish, fishing-frog or sea-angler, Lophius piscatorius, Arist. GA 749a23 , Ael. NA 13.5 . frog of a horse's hoof, Gp. 16.1.9 , Hippiatr. 8 : hence Astron., of the star β Centauri, Ptol. Alm. 8.1 . ἐσχάρας εἶδος, Hsch. swelling under the tongue, Aët. 8.39 .—Dial. forms are cited by Gramm., Ion. βάθρακος, cited from Hdt. (prob. 4.131 ) by Sch. Il. 4.243 , Eust. 1570.11 , and found in PLond. 1.124.31 (iv/v A. D.); Ion. also βότραχος Hp. ap. Gal. 19 , βρόταχος Xenoph. 40 (as pr. n., GDI 5577 , 5592 ). βράταχος Hsch. (as pr. n., GDI 5727d29 ). Cypr. βρούχετος Hsch. Phoc. βριαγχόνη Id. Pontic βάβακος Id. Cf. βύρθακος, βρύτιχος.
term_table.greek_sentence: Περὶ κεκαυμένων βατράχων.] Τῶν γε μὴν κεκαυμένων βατράχων τὴν τέφραν αἱμοῤῥαγίας ἴαμά φασιν ὑπάρχειν ἐπιπαττομένην, ἀλωπεκίας δὲ ἰᾶσθαι μετὰ πίττης ὑγρᾶς.

term_table.english_sentence_A: On salted tellins.] And salted tellins too, when burnt, they say, produce an ash so caustic that, when it is mixed with cedar-oil and dripped onto the spot after we have pulled out the hairs of the eyelids from the roots, it prevents them from growing back again.
term_table.english_sentence_B: On salted tellins.] They say also that salted tellins, when burnt, produce an ash so caustic that, mixed with cedar-resin and dropped into the spot when we have pulled the hairs of the eyelids out from their roots, it prevents them from growing again.

term_table.greek_sentence: Χωρὶς δὲ καύσεως ἢ ἑψήσεως ὅλων τῶν ζώων ἐπιτιθεμένων τοῖς πεπονθόσι μορίοις ἢ εἴσω τοῦ σώματος λαμβανομένων ἐπειράθησαν, ἢ ὡς πεπειραμένοι γεγράφασιν ἔνιοι τῶν ἰατρῶν γῆς μὲν ἔντερα λειωθέντα, νεύροις διῃρημένοις ἐπιτιθέμενα, παραχρῆμα θαυμαστῶς ὀνινάναι, τὰ δ’ αὐτὰ ταῦτα πάντα σὺν γλυκεῖ πινόμενα φάρμακον οὐρητικὸν εἶναι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Without burning or boiling, people have made trial of whole animals, either applied to the affected parts or taken into the body—or some of the physicians have written as though they had made trial of them: earthworms, ground fine and applied to divided sinews, give immediate and marvellous help, and these same ones, all of them taken as a drink with sweet wine, are a diuretic drug.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Some of the physicians have made trial, or have written as though they had made trial, of whole animals applied to the affected parts, or taken into the body, without burning or boiling: that earthworms (literally 'intestines of the earth'), ground smooth and applied to severed nerves, help at once in a wonderful way, and that these same things, all of them, drunk with sweet wine, are a diuretic drug.

term_table.greek_sentence: Χωρὶς δὲ καύσεως ἢ ἑψήσεως ὅλων τῶν ζώων ἐπιτιθεμένων τοῖς πεπονθόσι μορίοις ἢ εἴσω τοῦ σώματος λαμβανομένων ἐπειράθησαν, ἢ ὡς πεπειραμένοι γεγράφασιν ἔνιοι τῶν ἰατρῶν γῆς μὲν ἔντερα λειωθέντα, νεύροις διῃρημένοις ἐπιτιθέμενα, παραχρῆμα θαυμαστῶς ὀνινάναι, τὰ δ’ αὐτὰ ταῦτα πάντα σὺν γλυκεῖ πινόμενα φάρμακον οὐρητικὸν εἶναι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Without burning or boiling, people have made trial of whole animals, either applied to the affected parts or taken into the body—or some of the physicians have written as though they had made trial of them: earthworms, ground fine and applied to divided sinews, give immediate and marvellous help, and these same ones, all of them taken as a drink with sweet wine, are a diuretic drug.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Some of the physicians have made trial, or have written as though they had made trial, of whole animals applied to the affected parts, or taken into the body, without burning or boiling: that earthworms (literally 'intestines of the earth'), ground smooth and applied to severed nerves, help at once in a wonderful way, and that these same things, all of them, drunk with sweet wine, are a diuretic drug.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἐπιτηδειότεραι δ’ εἰσὶ πρὸς ἅπερ ἔφην λέγων πεπειράσθαι τῶν κανθαρίδων ἐκ τῶν πυρῶν ὅσαι μηλίνας ἐγκαρσίας ζώνας ἔχουσιν ἐν τοῖς πτεροῖς, καὶ μᾶλλον, ἐὰν ἐμβαλὼν αὐτὰς εἰς ἀγγεῖον καινὸν κεράμιον, εἶτα περιτιθεὶς τῷ στόματι τοῦ ἀγγείου τῶν ἀραιῶν ὀθονίων τι κρατῇς οὕτω τὸ ἀγγεῖον, ὡς ἐστράφθαι τὴν ὀθόνην κάτω, δεχομένην τὸν ἀναφερόμενον ἀτμὸν τοῦ ὄξους ἄχρις ἂν ἀποθάνωσιν αἱ κανθαρίδες.
term_table.english_sentence_A: The more suitable among the cantharides, for the purposes for which I said I had made trial of them, are those from the wheat which have quince-yellow transverse bands on their wings, and more so if, having put them into a new earthenware vessel and then fastened one of the loose-woven linen cloths around the mouth of the vessel, you hold the vessel in such a way that the linen is turned downward, receiving the vapour of the vinegar rising up, until the cantharides die.
term_table.english_sentence_B: More suitable for the purposes for which I said I had tested cantharides are those from the wheat that have transverse yellow bands on their wings; and they are more so if you put them into a new earthenware vessel, then place some piece of loose-woven linen over the mouth of the vessel, and hold the vessel in such a way that the linen is turned downwards, receiving the vapour of the vinegar that rises up, until the cantharides die.

Alm. 1.10 , etc.: in pl., the senses, Democr. 9 , al.; δι' ἑπτὰ σχημάτων αἱ αἰ. Hp. Vict. 1.23 , cf. Pl. Tht. 156b , etc.: in sg. of the several senses, ἡ τοῦ ὁρᾶν αἴ. Id. R. 507e ; ἀπ' ὄψεως ἤ τινος ἄλλῃς αἰ. Id. Phlb. 39b ; organ or seat of sensation, X. Mem. 1.4.6 ; πάσα, τὰς αἰ. ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ εἶναι Arist. Fr. 95 , cf. Pr. 958b16 ; αἴ. πημάτων perception, sense of . . , E. El. 290 ; esp. of pain, Vett. Val. 113.10. al.; also of the mind, perception, knowledge of a thing, ἐν αἰ. γενέσθαι τινός Plu. Luc. 11 , etc.; αἴ. ἔχειν τινός, = αἰσθάνεσθαί τινος , have a perception of a thing, Pl. Ap. 40c ; περὶ ὑμῶν Tht. 192b ; πᾶσαν αἴσθησιν αἰσθάνεσθαι Phdr. 240d ; λαμβάνειν Isoc. 1.47 ; ἐν αἰ. εἶναι Plot. 4.7.15 :—also of things, αἴσθησιν ἔχειν give a perception, i.e. become perceptible, serving as Pass. to αἰσθάνομαι, Th. 2.61 ; more freq. αἴσθησιν παρέχειν Id. 3.22 , X. An. 4.6.13 , etc.; αἴ. ποιῆσαί τινι Antipho 5.44 , cf. D. 10.7 ; αἴ. παρέχειν τινός furnish the means of observing, Th. 2.50 ; αἴ. ἐγένετο περί τινος D. 48.16 . in object. sense, impressions of sense, Arist. Metaph. 980a22 ; stage-effects, Po. 1454b16 ; αἰσθήσεις θεῶν visible appearances of the gods, Pl. Phd. 111b . display of feeling, Arist. Rh. 1386a32 (v.l.). in hunting, scent, X. term_table.greek_sentence: ἐννοήσας οὖν αὐτὴν ἔτι ζῶσαν προστιθέναι τινὶ κεφαλὴν ὀδυνωμένῳ, δύνασθαι γὰρ ἀνώδυνον εἶναι φάρμακον, ὁμοίως τοῖς ἄλλοις ὅσα ναρκοῖ τὴν αἴσθησιν εὗρον οὕτως ἔχειν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: So, having conceived the idea of applying it, while still alive, to someone suffering pain in the head—for it could be a pain-stilling drug, like the other things that numb sensation—I found that this is so.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Then I conceived the idea of applying it, while still alive, to someone suffering pain in the head, reasoning that it could be an anodyne drug, like the other things that numb sensation, and I found that this was so.

term_table.english_sentence_A: On the sea-dragon and the red mullet.] They have written that the following animals, split open alive and applied at once to the affected parts, bring benefit: the sea-dragon placed upon its own wound, and likewise also the red mullet upon that of the dragon; house mice upon that of the scorpion, just as also the lizard; the shrew-mouse upon its own, and the Chalcidian lizard, which they also give to drink in wine, as curing its own bite.
term_table.english_sentence_B: On the sea dragon and the red mullet.] Some have written that the following animals, split open alive and applied at once to the affected parts, are beneficial: the sea dragon placed upon its own sting, and likewise the red mullet upon that of the sea dragon; house mice upon that of the scorpion, as also the lizard; the shrew-mouse upon its own bite, and the Chalcidian lizard, which they also give to drink in wine, as healing its own bite.

term_table.english_sentence_A: On the sea-dragon and the red mullet.] They have written that the following animals, split open alive and applied at once to the affected parts, bring benefit: the sea-dragon placed upon its own wound, and likewise also the red mullet upon that of the dragon; house mice upon that of the scorpion, just as also the lizard; the shrew-mouse upon its own, and the Chalcidian lizard, which they also give to drink in wine, as curing its own bite.
term_table.english_sentence_B: On the sea dragon and the red mullet.] Some have written that the following animals, split open alive and applied at once to the affected parts, are beneficial: the sea dragon placed upon its own sting, and likewise the red mullet upon that of the sea dragon; house mice upon that of the scorpion, as also the lizard; the shrew-mouse upon its own bite, and the Chalcidian lizard, which they also give to drink in wine, as healing its own bite.

term_table.greek_sentence: λέγουσι δὲ κᾀν τοῖς κατ’ Αἴγυπτον χωρίοις σκελετευθέντα τὸν καλούμενον ἀσείρακον τοῖς ὑπὸ σκορπίου πληγεῖσι δίδοσθαι καὶ τὸ καλούμενον κύβιον ἐπὶ κυνὸς δήγματος ὠφελίμως παραλαμβάνεσθαι κατὰ τοῦ τραύματος ἐπιτιθέμενον, ἄλλα τε πολλὰ τοιαῦτα, περὶ ὧν ἐπιπλέον ἐροῦμεν ἐν τοῖς κατὰ ἰδιότητα τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας ἐνεργοῦσιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: They say too that in the regions of Egypt the so-called aseirakos, dried, is given to those stung by a scorpion, and that the so-called kybion is employed with benefit for a dog's bite when placed upon the wound, and many other such things, about which we shall speak at greater length among the agents that act by the specific property of their whole substance.
term_table.english_sentence_B: They say also that in the districts of Egypt the so-called aseirakos, dried, is given to those stung by a scorpion, and that the so-called kybion is usefully employed for the bite of a dog, applied over the wound; and many other such things, about which we shall speak at greater length in the discussion of things that act by a peculiarity of the whole substance.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἔνιοι δὲ τῶν ἔμπροσθεν, ἕνεκα μὲν ψιλώσεως τριχῶν πιτυοκάμπαις τε καὶ ταῖς θαλαττίαις ἀκαλήφαις καὶ λαγωῷ τῷ θαλαττίῳ καὶ σκολοπένδρᾳ τῇ θαλαττίᾳ· πρὸς ὠταλγίαν δὲ σίλφαις ἐνεψηθείσαις τῷ ἐλαίῳ καὶ τοῖς καλουμένοις ὀνίσκοις.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And some of the earlier ones [did so], for the removal of hair, with pine-caterpillars, sea anemones, the sea hare and the sea scolopendra; and for earache, with silphai boiled in the oil and with the so-called oniskoi.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Some of the earlier ones, for stripping off hairs, used pine-caterpillars, sea nettles, the sea hare and the sea scolopendra; and for earache, silphai boiled in the oil, and the so-called oniskoi.

term_table.greek_sentence: Περὶ ἀλωπέκων καὶ ὑαινῶν.] Περὶ δὲ τῶν ὅλων ἐν ἐλαίῳ καθεψομένων ἀλωπέκων, οὕτως γάρ τινες ἀρθριτικοὺς θεραπεύουσιν, οἱ μὲν ζώσας ἐμβάλλοντες μεγίστῳ λέβητι τὰς ἀλώπεκας, οἱ δὲ καὶ τεθνεώσας, ἀναγκαῖον εἰπεῖν ἐπιπλέον, ἐπειδὴ πολλοὺς ἔδοξαν κατ’ ἀρχὰς μὲν ἀπηλλαχέναι τοῦ πάθους, οὐ μετὰ πολὺν δὲ χρόνον ὠφεληκέναι μόνον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: On foxes and hyenas.] Concerning whole foxes boiled down in oil—for some treat arthritics in this way, some throwing the foxes alive into a very large cauldron, others even dead ones—it is necessary to speak at greater length, since they seemed at the outset to have freed many from the affection, but not long afterwards only to have benefited them.
term_table.english_sentence_B: On foxes and hyenas.] Concerning foxes boiled whole in oil (for some treat arthritics in this way, some throwing the foxes alive into a very large cauldron, others dead), it is necessary to speak at greater length. They seemed at first to have freed many people from the affection, but after no long time to have only benefited them.

Pr. 251 , 606 (lyr.); βηχός Phryn.Com. 60 : κεφαλῆς for a head-ache, Pl. Chrm. 155b ; στραγγουρίας Arist. Th. 561 ; τοιαῦτα ἔχω φ. such charms have I, Hdt. 3.85 , cf. Apoc. 9.21 . poison, S. Tr. 685 , E. Med. 385 ; πιεῖν τὸ φ. Antipho 6.15 , Pl. Phd. 57a , 115a ; φάρμακα ἐσβεβληκέναι ἐς τὰ φρέατα Th. 2.48 ; φ. δηλητήρια SIG 37 A 1 (Teos, v B. C.); τοξικὸν φ. BGU 21 ii 14 (iv A. D.). lye for laundering, Stud.Pal. 22.56.12 (iii A. term_table.greek_sentence: εἴρηται δὲ πολλάκις ὡς τοῖς τοιούτοις φαρμάκοις ὑπάρχει τὰ διὰ βάθους ἐν τῷ σώματι περιεχόμενα πρὸς τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν ἕλκειν καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο τὰς ὀδύνας ἐνίοτε παύειν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: It has been said many times that it belongs to such drugs to draw toward the surface what is contained in the depth of the body, and for this reason sometimes to put a stop to pains.
term_table.english_sentence_B: It has been said many times that drugs of this kind have the property of drawing to the surface what is contained in the depth of the body, and in this way sometimes of stopping pains. For this does not follow from them in every case.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ποι-ητικός, ή, όν, capable of making, creative, productive, opp. πρακτικός (active, Arist. EN 1140a4 ), τινος Id. Top. 137a4 , Pl. Def. 411d ; ἡδονῶν Epicur. term_table.greek_sentence: οὐ γὰρ δὴ διὰ παντός γε τοῦτ’ αὐτοῖς ἕπεται μόνον, ἐκείνων τῶν ὀδυνῶν παυομένων ὑπὸ τῶν τοιούτων φαρμάκων, ἐφ’ ὧν ἐν τῷ βάθει περιέχεται χυμὸς ὀδύνης ποιητικὸς, ἢ διὰ τὸ πάχος τῆς οὐσίας ἢ διὰ ψύξιν ἢ δριμύτητα σφοδρὰν ἢ καὶ πνεῦμα φυσῶδες, οὐκ ἔχον διέξοδον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For it is certainly not in every case that this alone follows for them; those pains are stopped by such drugs in which a pain-producing humour is contained in the depth, either because of the thickness of its substance, or because of coldness or violent pungency, or even flatulent pneuma that has no way out.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Only those pains are stopped by such drugs in which a humour productive of pain is contained in the depth, whether because of the thickness of its substance, or because of coldness or violent pungency, or else a flatulent pneuma that has no outlet. Those, then, who used the foxes likewise made the oil dispersing.

term_table.greek_sentence: οἱ τοίνυν ταῖς ἀλώπεξι χρώμενοι καὶ αὐτοὶ διαφορητικὸν εἰργάζοντο τοὔλαιον, εἶτα πυέλους αὐτῷ πληροῦντες ἐνεβίβαζον αὐταῖς ὅλους τοὺς ἀρθριτικοὺς, ἐνδιατρίβειν χρόνῳ συχνῷ κελεύοντες, ἐκ τούτου τε συνέβαινεν οὐ μόνον τοὺς περὶ τοῖς ἄρθροις ὄγκους αὐτῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ σύμπαν σῶμα κενοῦσθαι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Those, then, who used the foxes themselves also made the oil dispersing; then, filling tubs with it, they set the arthritics whole into them, bidding them remain in them for a considerable time, and from this it came about that not only the swellings around their joints but also the whole body was emptied.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Then, filling tubs with it, they set the arthritics in them whole, bidding them remain in them for a long time. From this it came about that not only the swellings about their joints but also the whole body was evacuated.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ὕδωρ [υ, v. fin.], τό, gen. ὕδατος: an Ep. dat. ὕδει in Hes. Op. 61 , Thgn. 961 ; later nom. ὕδος Call. Fr. 475 ; Boeot. οὕδωρ prob. in IG 7.3169 (Orchom.):—water, of any kind, but in Hom. rarely of seawater without an epith., ἄνεμός τε καὶ ὕ. Od. 3.300 , 7.277 ; but ἁλμυρὸν ὕ. 9.227 , al., cf. Th. 4.26 ; of rivers, ὕ. Αἰσήποιο, Στυγός, Il. 2.825 , 8.369 , al.; so in Lyr. and Trag., ὕ, Ἀσώπιον Pi. N. 3.3 ; ὕ. τὸ Νείλου A. Supp. 561 (lyr.): freq. in pl. (but only once in Hom. , ὕδατ' ἀενάοντα Od. 13.109 ), Καφίσια ὕδατα the waters of Cephisus, Pi. O. 14.1 ; ῥυτῶν ὑδάτων S. OC 1599 ; ὕδασιν τοίς Ἀχελῴου Id. Fr. 271 (anap.): spring-water, drinking-water, οἶνον ἔμισγον καὶ ὕ. Od. 1.110 ; ἀφυσσάμεθ' ὕδωρ 9.85 ; ὕδατα καὶ . . δῖτοι Pl. R. 404a ; πότιμον ὕ. X. HG 3.2.19 ; ὕ. πίνων a water-drinker, D. 6.30 , cf. 19.46 , Ar. Eq. 349 ; ὕ. δὲ πίνων οὐδὲν ἂν τέκοι σοφόν Cratin. 199 , cf. Aristopho 10.3 , Bato 2.9 , al.: ὕδωρ κατὰ χειρός water for washing the hands, v. χείρ; φέρτε χερσὶν ὕ. Il. 9.171 ; ὕ. ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἔχευαν 3.270 , Od. 1.146 , al.; λοέσσας ὕδατι λευκῷ Il. 23.282 :—on γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ αἰτεῖν and διδόναι, v. γῆ 1.2b :—a curse was invoked upon those who refused fire (i.e. the right to borrow burning embers) or water or to direct a traveller on his way, Diph. 62 , cf. X. Oec. 2.15 :—prov., ὅρκους ἐγὼ γυναικὸς εἰς ὕ. γράφω S. Fr. 811 , cf. Men. Mon. 25 ; ἐν ὕδατι γράφειν Pl. Ζεύς Il. 16.385 ; ὗσαι ὕδατι λαβροτάτῳ Hdt. 1.87 ; ἐγίνετο ὕ. ἄπλετον Id. 8.12 ; πολύ Th. 6.70 , D. 59.99 ; ὕ. ἐπιγενόμενον πολύ X. HG 1.6.28 ; τὸ ὕ. τὸ γενόμενον τῆς νυκτός Th. 2.5 , cf. Hdt. 8.13 : more definitely, ὕδωρ ἐζ οὐρανοῦ X. An. 4.2.2 , Aristid. Or. 50(26).35 (but ἐζ οὐρανοῦ is a gloss in Th. 2.77 ): pl., ὕ. ὄμβρια Pi. O. 11(10).2 ; τὰ Διὸς, or παρὰ τοῦ Δ., ὕ. Pl. Lg. 761a , 761b ; τὸ ἐκ Διὸς ὕ. Thphr. HP 2.6.5 ; καινὸν ἀεὶ τὸν Δία ὕειν ὕδωρ, ὕδωρ τὸν θεὸν ποιῆσαι, Ar. Nu. 1280 , V. 261 (lyr.), cf. Thphr. Char. 3.4 : abs., ἐὰν πλείω ποιῇ ὕ. Id. term_table.greek_sentence: τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἐν θαλάττῃ τε καὶ ὕδατι γεννώμενα ζῶα κατὰ τὸν ἔμπροσθεν εἴρηται λόγον περὶ τῶν ζώων.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For the animals that are generated in the sea and in water have been discussed in the preceding account concerning animals; but those things which are generated in waters or from waters, yet are not animals, will now be discussed.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: θερμαν-τικός, ή, όν, capable of heating, calorific, τὸ πῦρ θ. Arist. Int. 22b38 ; ὁ οἶνος Epicur. Fr. 58 , cf. 60 ; τὸ θ. πρὸς τὸ -τὸν Arist. Metaph. 1020b29 , cf. Thphr. HP 6.3.6 : Sup. , Arist. Cael. 307a1 , Dsc. 1.19.4 : c. gen., τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς θ. οἶνος Pl. Ti. 60a .
term_table.greek_sentence: δριμύτατον δ’ ἐστὶ καὶ θερμαντικώτατον τοῦτο, διὸ καὶ καθ’ αὑτὸ μὲν ἄχρηστόν ἐστι, μίγνυται δὲ τοῖς ἀμβλύνουσι τὴν δύναμιν αὐτοῦ καὶ οὕτω γίγνεται πολύχρηστον ἐπὶ τῶν θερμανθῆναι δεομένων διαθέσεων ἔξωθεν προσαγόμενον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: This is most pungent and most heating, and for this reason by itself it is useless, but it is mixed with things that blunt its power and thus becomes of manifold use when applied externally for conditions that need to be heated.
term_table.english_sentence_B: It is extremely pungent and extremely heating. For this reason it is useless on its own, but it is mixed with things that blunt its power, and in this way it becomes of many uses, applied externally, in conditions that need to be heated.

OGI 331.11 (Pergam.); of the mind, Antipho Soph. 24a ; ἕξις ψυχῆς καὶ δ. Pl. Phlb. 11d ; distd. from ἕξις, Arist. Cat. 8b28 , de An. 417b15 , Zeno and Chrysipp.Stoic. 1.50 , 3.111 ; δ. ἁμαρτωλός Phld. Lib. p.560 ., al.; δ. σωματική, ψυχική, A.D. Synt. 278.10 : pl., Diotog. ap. Stob. 4.7.62 . disposition towards persons, Pl. R. 489a ; propensity, Cic. Att. 14.3.2 ; πρός τινα Sch. E. Hec. 8 . generally, state, condition, τὴν βασιγείαν εἰς τὴν ἀρχαίαν δ. κατέστησεν OGI 219.11 (Sigeum, iv/iii B.C.). Gramm., force, function, τοῦ ὀνόματος δ. εἰσὶ δύο, ἐνέργεια καὶ πάθος (e.g. κριτής, κριτός) D.T. 637.29 ; esp. of the voices of the verb, δ. εἰσὶ τρεῖς, ἐνέργεια, πάθος, μεσότης Id. 638.8 ; δ. παθητική, μέση, A.D. Synt. 210.19 , 226.10 ; also of tense, χρονικὴ δ. ib. 251.1 (s.v.l.); διαβατικὴ δ. transitive force, ib. 43.18 .
term_table.greek_sentence: δριμύτατον δ’ ἐστὶ καὶ θερμαντικώτατον τοῦτο, διὸ καὶ καθ’ αὑτὸ μὲν ἄχρηστόν ἐστι, μίγνυται δὲ τοῖς ἀμβλύνουσι τὴν δύναμιν αὐτοῦ καὶ οὕτω γίγνεται πολύχρηστον ἐπὶ τῶν θερμανθῆναι δεομένων διαθέσεων ἔξωθεν προσαγόμενον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: This is most pungent and most heating, and for this reason by itself it is useless, but it is mixed with things that blunt its power and thus becomes of manifold use when applied externally for conditions that need to be heated.
term_table.english_sentence_B: It is extremely pungent and extremely heating. For this reason it is useless on its own, but it is mixed with things that blunt its power, and in this way it becomes of many uses, applied externally, in conditions that need to be heated.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ποιότης, ητος, ἡ, quality, Pl. Tht. 182a (where he apologizes for the use of the word as ἀλλόκοτον ὄνομα), Arist. Cat. 8b26 , EN 1173a15 (pl.), Gal. Nat.Fac. 1.2 , POxy. 2113.16 (iv A.D.), etc.; of size, Babr. 28.10 , Aesop. 84 .
term_table.greek_sentence: Περὶ ἀλκυονίων.] Ἀλκυόνια ῥύπτει μὲν ἅπαντα καὶ διαφορεῖ, δριμεῖαν ἔχοντα ποιότητα καὶ θερμὴν δύναμιν, ἀλλὰ τὸ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττον ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐστιν οὐκ ὀλίγον, ἔν τε τούτοις αὐτοῖς οἷς εἴρηκα καὶ προσέτι κατὰ τὸ λεπτομερὲς τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας.
term_table.english_sentence_A: On alkyonia.] Alkyonia all cleanse and disperse, having a pungent quality and a hot power, but the more and the less among them is not slight, both in these very respects which I have mentioned and moreover in respect of the fine-particled character of the whole substance.
term_table.english_sentence_B: On alkyonia.] All alkyonia are cleansing and dispersing, having a pungent quality and a hot power. But the more and the less among them is not slight, both in the very respects I have mentioned and, further, in how fine-particled their whole substance is.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: σαπρός, ά, όν, (σήπω) rotten, putrid, Hippon. 23 , Hp. Oss. 13 ; of the lungs, diseased, Id. Morb. 1.13 ; of bone, carious, Id. Fract. 33 ; of wood, etc., rotten, ἱστίον Ar. Eq. 918 ; βύρσα Id. V. 38 ; πινακίσκος, φορμός, σχοινίον, Id. Pl. 813 , 542 , V. 1343 ; ἱμάς Men. 109.4 ; τοῦ διατειχίσματος ἀνελόντι τὰ ς. IG 22.1672.24 ; of a house, ς. καὶ ῥέουσα καὶ καταπίπτουσα Teles p.27 H.; ἐλαῖαι Thphr. HP 4.14.10 : prov., σαπροῦ πείσματος ἀντιλαβέσθαι Thgn. 1362 : esp., of fish that have been long in pickle, stale, rancid, τάριχος Ar. Ach. 1101 ; opp. πρόσφατος, Antiph. 218.4 , cf. 125.6 ; of withered flowers, D. 22.70 . Adv., -ρῶς λούει τὰ βαλανεῖα so as to leave one filthy, Arr. Epict. 2.21.14 . generally, stale, worn out, ἀρχαῖον καὶ σαπρόν Ar. Pl. 323 ; of clothes, PGiss. 26.6 (ii A.D.). Adv., -ῶς (perh. misspelt for -ός) περιπατῶ I am walking about in rags, BGU 846.9 (ii A.D.). of persons, γέρων ὢν καὶ ς. Ar. Pax 698 ; ὦ σαπρά, to an old woman, Id. Ec. 884 , Hermipp. 10 ; so εἶναι σαπρὸν κοὐδὲν δύνασθαι Ar. V. 1380 ; οὐδέν ἐσμεν οἱ ς. Eup. 221 ; ς. γυναῖκα . . ὁ τρόπος εὔμορφον ποιεῖ Philem. 170 . of wine, mellow (cf. σαπρίας), Eup. 442 , cf. Philyll. 24 ; τρὺξ παλαιὰ καὶ σαπρά Ar. Pl. 1086 ; of old wine, ὀδόντας οὐκ ἔχων, ἤδη σαπρὸς . ., γέρων γε δαιμονίως Alex. 167.4 . εἰρήνη σαπρά, a joke παρὰ προσδοκίαν, Ar. Pax 554 . metaph., unsound, bad, λόγος Ep.Eph. 4.29 ; opp. καλός, Vett.Val. 36.30 , cf. PSI 4.312.13 (iv A.D.); ἄρουραι PGiss. 13.22 (ii A.D.); τὰ ς. ταῦτα Arr. Epict. 3.16.7 ; ὡς ς. καὶ κίβδηλος ὁ λέγων . . M.Ant. 11.15 , cf. Sammelb. 5761.23 (i A.D.), PSI 6.717.4 (ii A.D.); τὴν ς. εἱμαρμένην the evil fate, PMag.Leid.W. 14.38 . of sound, αὐλεῖ γὰρ σαπρὰ . . κρουμάτια Theopomp.Com. 50 (perh. f.l. for σαθρά , v. σαθρός 2 ).
term_table.greek_sentence: ἔστι δ’ αὐτῶν ἓν μὲν πυκνὸν καὶ βαρὺ καὶ μοχθηρὸν κατὰ τὴν ὀσμὴν, ὄζει γὰρ ἰχθύων σαπρῶν, ἐοικὸς κατὰ σχῆμα σπόγγῳ.
term_table.english_sentence_A: One of them is dense and heavy and bad in smell, for it smells of rotten fish, and resembles a sponge in shape.
term_table.english_sentence_B: One of them is dense and heavy and foul in smell, for it smells of rotten fish, and in shape it resembles a sponge.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: προμήκης, ες, (μῆκος) prolonged, elongated, βέλεα Hp. VC 11 , cf. S. Ichn. 294 ; π. ἡ τῶν ὄφεων φύσις Arist. GA 718a20 ; σφῆκες -έστεροι τὴν μορφήν Id. HA 627b25 , etc.; of Pericles, π. τὴν κεφαλήν Plu. Per. 3 . protruding, γλῶσσα Aret. SA 1.5 . oblong, σχῆμα Pl. Tht. 148a ; φύλλον προμηκέστερον ἀπίου Thphr. HP 3.10.1 ; of rightangled triangles, having the sides which contain the right angle unequal, Pl. Ti. 54a . of numbers, made up of two unequal factors (as 8 = 2 X 4 , 32 = 4 X 8 ), opp. τετράγωνος or ἰσόπλευρος, Id.Tht.l.c., D.L. 3.24 ; also of solid numbers, having not more than two out of three factors equal, Anon. in Tht. 42.45 .
term_table.greek_sentence: δεύτερον δ’ ἄλλο προμηκέστερον τῷ σχήματι κοῦφον καὶ ἀραιὸν, ὀσμὴν φυκίοις ὁμοίαν ἔχον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: A second, different one is more elongated in shape, light and loose-textured, having a smell like seaweed.
term_table.english_sentence_B: A second is more elongated in shape, light and porous, with a smell like that of seaweeds.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: κοῦφος, η, ον, light, nimble, Hom. only in neut. pl. as Adv., κοῦφα ποσὶ προβιβάς stepping lightly on, Il. 13.158 , cf. Hes. Sc. 323 ; κοῦφα βιβῶν Pi. O. 14.16 ; κ. ποσὶν ἄγ' ἐς κύκλον Ar. Th. 954 (lyr.); also κούφοις ποσί Pi. O. 13.114 ; κουφοτάταις πτερύγων ἀκμαῖς Ar. Ra. 1353 ; πήδημα κ. ἐκ νεὼς ἀφήλατο A. Pers. 305 ; κ. ἐξᾶραι πόδα S. Ant. 224 ; κ. ἅλμα E. El. 439 (lyr.); κ. αἴρειν βῆμα Id. Tr. 343 ; οὐ τοῖς κούφοις ὁ δρόμος LXX Ec. 9.11 : metaph., κουφότεραι . . ἀπειράτων φρένες too buoyant, Pi. O. 8.61 . metaph., easy, light, τελεῖν . . κούφαν κτίσιν to make achievement easy, ib. 13.83 ; κ. εἰ δοίης τέλος A. Th. 260 ; κ. νύξ an easier night, of a sick person, Jul. Mis. 342a ( Comp. ); περίπατος Sor. 1.46 ; τὸ ὅσιον ἅπαν κ. ἔργον OGI 383.120 (Nemrud Dagh, i B. C.); of government, light, κουφοτέραν βασιλείαν less oppressive, Isoc. 9.51 ; ἡ εὔκλεια κουφοτέρα φέρειν X. Cyr. 8.2.22 ; of an antagonist, easy-going, κουφότατος ἦν κρατήσας Id. Ages. 11.12 ; δεσπότην ἀπράγμονα καὶ κ. ἐξαπατᾷ θεράπων Men. Per.Fr. 1 . unsubstantial, airy, vain, τὸ νέον . . κούφας ἀφροσύνας φέρον S. OC 1230 (lyr.); οὐδὲν ἄλλο πλὴν . . κούφην σκιάν Id. Aj. 126 ; ἐλπίδος τι εἶχον κούφης Th. 2.51 ; κ. καὶ πτηνοὶ λόγοι Pl. Lg. 717c ; κ. πρᾶγμα a trifle, ib. 935a ; κ. γράμματα a small letter, E. IT 594 ; of persons, = κουφόνους , Hdn. 5.7.1 ; τὸ κοῦφον τοῦ νοῦ levity, Paus. 5.21.14 , cf. Hdn. 7.8.6 . light in point of weight, opp. βαρύς, Pl. Phlb. 14d , R. 438c ( Comp. ), etc.; κούφα σοι χθὼν ἐπάνωθε πέσοι may earth lie lightly on thee, E. Alc. 462 (lyr.), cf. Hel. 853 ; κούφη σοι κόνις ἥδε πέλοι IG 14.1942.4 ; κούφη σεῖο γαῖ' ὀστέα κεύθοι ib. 329 (Himera); κ. πνεύματα light airs, S. Aj. 558 ; ὀστᾶ τε καὶ κ. κόνις Men. 538.3 ; τὸ κουφότατον . . τῶν κακῶν . . πενία Id. Kith.Fr. 2 . Medic. in various uses, σικύαι κοῦφαι dry cuppings, Philum. ap. Orib. 45.29.17 , cf. Sor. 2.11 , etc.; also κούφου μένοντος τοῦ ἰοῦ on the surface, Philum. Ven. 7.3 ; μὴν κ. the eighth month of pregnancy, Sor. 1.56 ; of food, easy to digest, light, Arist. EN 1141b18 , etc. of troops, light-armed, οἱ κ. τῶν στρατιωτῶν Hell.Oxy. 6.4 ; ὡπλισμένοι κουφοτέροις ὅπλοις X. Mem. 3.5.27 ; κούφη στρατιά Plu. Fab. 11 ; τὰ κ. τῆς δυνάμεως Plb. 10.25.2 . of ships, lightly-laden, Th. 6.37 , 8.27 . light, slight, ἁμαρτήματα Pl. Lg. 863c ; κουφότερα γυμνάσια, opp. ἀναγκαῖα, Arist. Pol. 1338b40 ; κ. ἐργασίαι ib. 1321a25 . empty, κεράμια Gp. 7.24.2 , cf. PLond. 5.1656.6 (iv A. D.), PFlor. 314.8 (v. A. D. ): hence as Subst., κοῦφον (sc. κεράμιον), τό, jar, in pl., POxy. 1631.16 (iii A. D.), PFay. 133.6 (iv A. D.), PStrassb. 1.10 (vi A. D.). Act. , relieving, assisting, χερὶ κούφᾳ Pi. P. 9.11 : prob. to be taken in this sense in Theoc. 11.3 . Adv. -φως lightly, nimbly, κ. ὀροῦσαι A. Eu. 112 ; κ. ἐσκευασμένοι, of soldiers, Th. 4.33 ; ὡπλισμένοι X. Mem. 3.5.26 , etc.; κ. ἔχειν to be relieved, Arist. Pr. 873a16 . metaph., lightly, with light heart, κουφότερον μετεφώνεε Od. 8.201 ; κ. νοῆσαι Sapph. Supp. 5.14 ; κ. φέρειν, opp. δεινῶς φ., E. Med. 449 , 1018 ; ὡς κουφότατα φέρειν Hdt. 1.35 ; διάγουσα κούφως doing well, of a patient, Hp. Epid. 1.26 .δ ́. lightly, with ease, A. Pr. 701 .
term_table.greek_sentence: ἐφ’ οἷς ἄλλο τέταρτον, ὁμοίως μὲν τῷ δευτέρῳ λελεγμένῳ κοῦφόν τε καὶ ἀραιὸν, ἐοικὸς δὲ ἐρίοις οἰσυπηροῖς.
term_table.english_sentence_A: In addition to these there is another, a fourth, light and loose-textured like the one mentioned second, but resembling greasy, unwashed wool.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Besides these there is a fourth, which is light and porous like the second one mentioned, but resembles greasy unwashed wool.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: λεία (B), Ion. ληΐη, Dor. λᾴα ( Pi. O. 10(11).44 ), ἡ, booty, plunder, freq. in Hdt. (v. infr.), etc. ( Hom. and Hes. always use ληΐς); esp. of cattle, opp. ἄνθρωποι, Pi.l.c., Th. 2.94 (v. infr. 4 ); λείας ἀπαρχὴν βοῦς S. Tr. 761 , cf. Aj. 54 , 145 (anap.): pl., ἐφθαρμένας εὑρίσκομεν λείας ἁπάσας ib. 26 ; rarely of persons, ἀγόμεθα λεία E. Tr. 614 ; prey of hunters, Id. Rh. 326 : generally, booty, Th. 8.3 , X. HG 1.2.4 , 1.3.2 ; τοὺς λοιποὺς ληΐην θέσθαι give them up as plunder, Hdt. 4.202 ; λείαν ποιεῖσθαι τὴν χώραν, = λεηλατεῖν τὴν χώραν , Th. 8.41 ; λείαν ἄγειν X. HG 1.2.5 : prov., Μυσῶν λεία, of anything that may be plundered with impunity, Stratt. 35 , D. 18.72 , Arist. Rh. 1372b33 . plunder (as an act), ζῶσι ἀπὸ ληΐης καὶ πολέμου Hdt. 4.103 . stolen property, τὴν λ. ἀποδοῦναι PCair.Zen. 145.16 (iii B.C.), cf. PSI 4.438.10 - 13 (iii B.C.). flocks and herds, cattle, ἀπογραφὴ λείας PHib. 1.33.2 (iii B.C.), cf. PPetr. 3p.279 (iii B.C.), BGU 1012 (ii B.C.), D.S. 19.21 , 97 ; ἀτέλεια τῆς λ. OGI 748.9 (Cyzic., iii B.C.). (Lit. the people's property, cf. Lat. populari 'plunder'.)
term_table.greek_sentence: τὸ δὲ πέμπτον ἔξωθεν μὲν ἐπιφανείᾳ λείᾳ περιγράφεται, τὴν δ’ ἐντὸς οὐσίαν ἔχει τραχεῖαν, οὐδεμίαν μὲν ἔχον ὀσμὴν, ἐν τῇ γεύσει δὲ δριμὺ φαινόμενον· ἔστι γὰρ δήπου καὶ θερμότατον ἁπάντων τῶν ἀλκυονίων, ὡς τρίχας ἀποκάειν δύνασθαι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: The fifth is bounded on the outside by a smooth surface, but has its inner substance rough, having no smell, but appearing pungent to the taste; for it is indeed also the hottest of all the alkyonia, so that it is able to burn off hairs.
term_table.english_sentence_B: The fifth is bounded on the outside by a smooth surface but has a rough substance within. It has no smell at all but is perceived as pungent to the taste; for it is, of course, also the hottest of all the alkyonia, so that it can burn off hair.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: λειχήν, ῆνος, ὁ, tree-moss, lichen, implied in Thphr. (cf. λειχηνιάω). a kind of liver-wort, that grows on damp rocks, Dsc. 4.53 ; but ἵππειος λ., = ἱππολειχήν , Nic. Th. 945 . a lichen-like eruption on the skin of animals, esp. on the chin, mentagra, A. Ch. 281 (pl.), Hp. Aph. 3.20 (pl.), Thphr. Sud. 14 (pl.), LXX Le. 21.20 , Gal. 14.75 , Aët. 8.16 ; also, of the ground, blight, canker, A. Eu. 785 (lyr.). in horses, the normal callosity on foreleg, chestnut, Dsc. 2.43 (pl.), Cael.Aur. TP 1.138 (pl.).—In codd. freq. written λιχήν.
term_table.greek_sentence: διὸ τῶν μὲν πρώτων δύο λειχῆνας καὶ ἀλφοὺς καὶ μέντοι καὶ ψώρας καὶ λέπρας ὠφελούντων, ἔτι τε λαμπρυνόντων τὸ δέρμα διὰ τὸ σύμμετρον τῆς δυνάμεως, δύναται ταὐτὸ ποιεῖν τουτὶ τὸ ἔσχατον εἰρημένον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Therefore, while the first two benefit lichens and alphoi and indeed also psorai and lepra, and further brighten the skin owing to the due measure of their power, this last-mentioned one can do the same thing.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Therefore, while the first two benefit leichenes and alphoi, and indeed also psorai and leprai, and moreover make the skin bright because of the moderateness of their power, this last-mentioned one is able to do the same.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ὀρυκ-τός, ή, όν, dug, formed by digging, τάφρον ὑπερθορέονται ὀρυκτήν Il. 8.179 , al., cf. X. term_table.greek_sentence: Περὶ ἁλῶν.] Ἅλες τῆς αὐτῆς κατὰ γένος δυνάμεως οἴ τ’ ὀρυκτοὶ καὶ οἱ θαλάττιοι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: On salts.] Salts, both the mined and the sea salts, are of the same power in kind.
term_table.english_sentence_B: On salts.] Salts, both the dug and the sea salts, are of the same power in kind.

Pers. 558 (lyr.); θ. ἐκρῖψαί τινα to thro wone into the sea, S. OT 1411 ; θ. νεκρός, of one drowned, Thgn. 1229 ; πλοῖον θ. sea-going vessel, POxy. 1288.6 (iv A.D.). skilled in the sea, nautical, Hdt. 7.144 ; γεωργοὶ καὶ οὐ θ. Th. 1.142 . like the sea, in colour, τῇ χρόᾳ Plu. 2.395b ; = ἁλουργής, στρώματα D.S. 34 / 5.2.35 . θαλάσσιαι, αἱ , name of certain priestesses at Cyzicus, CIG 3657.4 .
term_table.greek_sentence: Περὶ ἁλῶν.] Ἅλες τῆς αὐτῆς κατὰ γένος δυνάμεως οἴ τ’ ὀρυκτοὶ καὶ οἱ θαλάττιοι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: On salts.] Salts, both the mined and the sea salts, are of the same power in kind.
term_table.english_sentence_B: On salts.] Salts, both the dug and the sea salts, are of the same power in kind.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: στύφ-ω, Hp. Int. 14 , etc.: aor. inf. στύψαι Hsch. :— Pass. (v.infr.):—contract, draw together, τὴν κοιλίην στύφεσθαι becomes costive, Hp. Aër. 7 ; στῦψαι πλάδον Aret. CA 1.1 ; esp. of an astringent taste, χείλεα στυφθείς having his lips drawn up by the taste, AP 9.375 ; δέρμα ἐστυμμένον, i.e. made watertight, Gal. 12.846 ; mix with στυπτηρία, PMag.Leid.V. 6.18 ; aor. 2 part. Pass. στυφέντα in this last sense, PHolm. 24.13 (στυφόεντα cj. Lagercrantz): metaph. of sounds, φωναὶ στύφουσαι τὴν ἀκοήν, opp. διαχέουσαι, D.H. Comp. 15 . in dyeing, treat fabrics, etc., with a mordant, Lysis ap. Iamb. VP 17.76 ; στῦψον τῇ ἰσάτι prepare it by a preliminary dyeing with woad, PHolm. 21.42 ; στύφει [τὴν ἄγχουσαν] fixes alkanet, ib. 15.18 . intr. in Act. , στύφει κατ' ὀλίγον τὸ οὖρον gradually diminishes, Hp. Int. 14 . intr., to be astringent, Arist. Pr. 863b17 , Philonid. ap. Ath. 15.675e , Dsc. 1.116 , 118 , Sor. 1.81 , Gal. 6.68 , Hices. ap. Ath. 7.321a . metaph., to be harsh, austere, gloomy, Them. Or. 27.339a , cf. Hsch. s.v. στύψαι. [υ , Nic. Al. 278 , cf. 375 (ἐν-); υ to be assumed in στυφέντα (s.v.l.).]
term_table.greek_sentence: διαφέρουσι δὲ τῷ μᾶλλον πεπιλῆσθαι τὴν οὐσίαν τῶν ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἁλῶν, διὸ καὶ τὸ παχυμερές τε καὶ στῦφον ἐν τούτοις μᾶλλόν ἐστιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: They differ, however, in that the substance of the salts from the earth is more compacted, for which reason the coarse-particled and astringent element is greater in these.
term_table.english_sentence_B: They differ in that the substance of the salts from the earth is more compacted, which is why the coarse-particled and the astringent are present to a greater degree in these.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ποιότης, ητος, ἡ, quality, Pl. Tht. 182a (where he apologizes for the use of the word as ἀλλόκοτον ὄνομα), Arist. Cat. 8b26 , EN 1173a15 (pl.), Gal. Nat.Fac. 1.2 , POxy. 2113.16 (iv A.D.), etc.; of size, Babr. 28.10 , Aesop. 84 .
term_table.greek_sentence: λέλεκται δὲ καὶ περὶ τῶν Σοδομηνῶν τῶν ἐν τῇ νεκρᾷ θαλάσσῃ καλουμένῃ γεννωμένων ἐν τῷ τετάρτῳ γράμματι, καὶ εἴ τις ἐκεῖνο τὸ βιβλίον ἀνέγνωκεν ἐπιμελῶς, ἀναμνήσεως αὐτῷ μόνον δεήσει νῦν, ὥστε ῥηθείσης τῆς γευστῆς ποιότητος αὐτὸν ἐπίστασθαι τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ φαρμάκου.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Something has also been said in the fourth book about the Sodomene salts, those produced in the so-called Dead Sea, and if anyone has read that book carefully, he will now need only a reminder, so that, once the gustatory quality has been stated, he may know the power of the drug.
term_table.english_sentence_B: The Sodomene salts, produced in what is called the Dead Sea, have also been discussed in the fourth book, and if anyone has read that book carefully, he will now need only to be reminded, so that, once the quality perceived by taste has been stated, he will know the power of the drug.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἁλυκ-ός, ή, όν, salt, Hp. Acut. 42 , Aër. 1 , Ar. Lys. 403 , LXX Ge. 14.3 ; brackish, Thphr. HP 4.3.5 .
term_table.greek_sentence: τῆς οὖν ἁλυκῆς ποιότητος διαφορούσης τε ἅμα καὶ συναγούσης τὴν πλησιάζουσαν οὐσίαν, τὸ καλούμενον ἀφρόνιτρον ἐν τούτῳ τὴν διαφορὰν ἔχει, καθόσον ἕνα μόνον ἐν τούτῳ τὸν ἐπικρατοῦντα χυμὸν ἐναργῶς ἔστιν ἰδεῖν, ὃν ὀνομάζουσι πικρὸν, διαφορητικὴν ἔχοντα δύναμιν, συνακτικὴν δ’ οὐκ ἔχοντα, καθάπερ οἱ ἅλες.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Since, then, the salty quality at once disperses and draws together the substance that comes near it, the so-called aphronitron has its difference in this, insofar as in it one can clearly see only one prevailing flavour, which they call bitter, which has a dispersing power but does not have a contracting one, as salts do.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Since, then, the salty quality both disperses and at the same time draws together the substance it comes near, what is called aphronitron differs in this respect, inasmuch as in it one can clearly see only one prevailing flavour, which they call bitter, having a dispersing power but not having a drawing-together power, as salts do.

term_table.english_sentence_B: Since, then, the salty quality both disperses and at the same time draws together the substance it comes near, what is called aphronitron differs in this respect, inasmuch as in it one can clearly see only one prevailing flavour, which they call bitter, having a dispersing power but not having a drawing-together power, as salts do.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: περισσ-ωματικός, Att. περιττ-, ή, όν, of the nature of περιττώματα, excretive, excrementitious, ἀπόκρισις Arist. PA 681b36 ; ὑγρότης Plu. 2.130b ; π. [μόριον] for excretion, Arist. HA 531a29 , etc. of persons, abounding in περιττώματα, ib. 584a6 , Pr. 873a18 ; σώματα Id. GA 766b35 ( Comp. ); βρέφη Alex.Aphr. Pr. 1.2 ; π. καὶ παχὺς τὴν σάρκα, of a pig, Jul. Or. 5.177c .
term_table.greek_sentence: οὗτοι γὰρ ὅσον μὲν ὑγρόν ἐστιν ἐν τοῖς σώμασι, τοῦτο πᾶν ἐκβόσκονται· τὸ δ’ ὑπόλοιπον τῆς στερεᾶς οὐσίας συνάγουσι τῇ στύψει, διὸ καὶ ταριχεύουσι καὶ ἄσηπτα φυλάσσουσι τὰ σώματα τῶν σηπομένων, ὑγρότητα περιττωματικὴν ἐχόντων ἀδιάλυτόν τε καὶ ἄσφιγκτον τὴν οὐσίαν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For salts consume all that is moist in bodies; and the remainder of the solid substance they draw together by their astringency, for which reason they also pickle, and keep free of putrefaction, the bodies of things that putrefy, which have a superfluous moisture and a substance that is loose (ἀδιάλυτον) and not compacted.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For salts consume all the moisture that is in bodies, while the remainder of the solid substance they draw together by their astringency; for this reason they also pickle, and keep unputrefied, the bodies of things that putrefy, which have residual moisture that is undissipated and a substance that is not tightly bound.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: περισσός, Att. περιττός, ή, όν, (from περί, as ἔπισσαι from ἐπί, μέτασσαι from μετά) beyond the regular number or size, prodigious, δῶρα Hes. Th. 399 (never in Hom. ); ῶʼμος Trag.Adesp. 458.3 ; στάθμα, dub.sens., v. ἕλκω B. 3 . out of the common, extraordinary, strange, ἔ τι περισσὸν εἰδείη if he has any signal knowledge, Thgn. 769 ; εἴ τι φρονεῖς καί τι περισσὸν ἔχεις Philisc.( PLG 2.327 ); π. λόγος S. OT 841 ; ἄγρα E. Ba. 1197 (lyr.); πάθος Id. Supp. 791 (lyr.); βίος οὐδὲν ἔχων π. ἀλλὰ πάντα σμικρά Antipho Soph. 51 ; οὐ γὰρ π. οὐδὲν οὐδ' ἔξω λόγου πέπονθας E. Hipp. 437 ; περισσότερα παθήματα Antipho 3.4.5 ; τὰ π. τῶν ἔργων καὶ τερατώδη Isoc. 12.77 ; ἴδια καὶ π. Id. 15.145 ; π. καὶ θαυμαστά Arist. EN 1141b6 ; πρᾶξις π. Id. Pol. 1312a27 ; οὐθὲν δὴ λέγοντες π. φαίνονταί τι λέγειν Id. Metaph. 1053b3 ; τί π. ποιεῖτε; Ev.Matt. 5.47 ; περιττοτάτη φύσις Arist. HA 531a9 ; συνανθρωπίζον . . πάντων περισσότατον, of the dog, Ath. 13.611c , cf. Clearch. 24 ; in Literature, striking, τὸ περιττόν, as a quality of οἱ τοῦ Σωκράτους λόγοι, Arist. Pol. 1265a11 ; τὰ σοφὰ καὶ τὰ π. refinements, Epicur. Fr. 409 ; opp. κοινὸς καὶ δημώδης, Longin. 40.2 (but also, elaborate, π. καὶ πεποιημένος Id. 3.4 ; in bad sense, far-fetched, D.H. Pomp. 2 , Dem. 56 ). of persons, extraordinary, remarkable, esp. for great learning, π. ὢν ἀνήρ E. Hipp. 948 ; τοὺς . . π. καί τι πράσσοντας πλέον Id. Fr. 788 ; δυστυχεῖς εἶναι τοὺς π. Arist. Metaph. 983a2 ; π. γένος τῶν μελιττῶν Id. GA 760a4 : freq. with the manner added, π. κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν Id. Pr. 953a10 ; περὶ τὸν ἄλλον βίον περιττότερος somewhat extravagant or eccentric, Id. Pol. 1267 b24 ; τῇ φύσει π. Id. HA 622b6 ; κάλλει Plu. Demetr. 2 ; ἐν ἅπασι Id. Dem. 3 ; τὴν ὥραν Alciphr. 1.12 : c. inf., D.H. Comp. 18 . c. gen., περισσὸς ἄλλων πρός τι beyond others in . . , S. El. 155 ; θύσει τοῦδε περισσότερα greater things than this, AP 6.321 (Leon. Alex. ); περιττότερος προφήτου one greater than . . , Ev.Matt. 11.9 . more than sufficient, superfluous, αἱ π. δαπάναι X. Mem. 3.6.6 ; περιττὸν ἔχειν to have a surplus, Id. An. 7.6.31 ; οἱ μὲν . . περιττὰ ἔχουσιν, οἱ δὲ οὐδὲ τὰ ἀναγκαῖα . . Id. Oec. 20.1 : c. gen., τῶν ἀρκούντων περιττά more than sufficient, Id. Cyr. 8.2.21 ; τὰ π. τῶν ἱκανῶν Id. Hier. 1.19 : freq. in military sense, οἱ π. ἱππεῖς the reserve horse, Id. Eq.Mag. 8.14 ; οἱ π. τῆς φυλακῆς ib. 7.7 ; π. σκηναί spare tents, Id. Cyr. 4.6.12 (but τοῖς περιττοῖς χρήσεσθαι their superior numbers, Id. An. 4.8.11 , cf. Cyr. 6.3.20 ); τὸ π. the surplus, residue, Inscr. ap. eund. An. 5.3.13 (but τὸ π. τοῦ Ἰουδαίου the advantage of the Jew, Ep.Rom. 3.1 ); Ἁρπυιῶν τὰ π. their leavings, AP 11.239 ( Lucill. ); τὸ π. τῆς ἡμέρας the remainder of the day, X.Eph. 1.3 ; π. γράμματα supplementary provisions in a will, BGU 326ii9 (ii A.D.). in bad sense, superfluous, useless, οὐδέ τι τοῦ παντὸς κενεὸν πέλει οὐδὲ π. Emp. 13 ; μόχθος π. A. Pr. 385 , cf. S. Ant. 780 ; π. κἀνόνητα σώματα Id. Aj. 758 ; βάρος π. γῆς ἀναστρωφώμενοι Id. Fr. 945 ; ἄχθος Id. El. 1241 (lyr.); τὰ γὰρ π. πανταχοῦ λυπήρ' ἔπη Id. Fr. 82 ; αὐδῶ σε μὴ περισσὰ κηρύσσειν A. Th. 1048 ; π. πάντες οὑν μέσῳ λόγοι E. Med. 819 ; π. φωνῶν Id. Supp. 459 . excessive, extravagant, μηχανᾶσθαι περισσά commit extravagances, Hdt. 2.32 ; περισσὰ δρᾶν, πράσσειν, to be over-busy, S. Tr. 617 , Ant. 68 ; π. φρονεῖν to be over-wise, E. Fr. 924 (anap.); ἡ π. αὕτη ἐπιμέλεια τοῦ σώματος Pl. R. 407b ; μῆκος πολὺ λόγων π. Id. Lg. 645c ; redundant, overdone, οἱ καρτεροὶ καὶ π. λόγοι Id. Ax. 365c , etc.; of dress, ἐσθὴς π. Plu. 2.615d ; περισσοτέρα λύπη 2 Ep.Cor. 2.7 ; τοῦ τὰ δέοντ' ἔχειν περιττὰ μισῶ I hate extravagance in comparison with moderation, Alex. 254 , etc. of persons, over-wise, over-curious, περισσὸς καὶ φρονῶν μέγα E. Hipp. 445 , cf. Ba. 429 (lyr.); ὁ πολυπράγμων καὶ π. Plb. 9.1.4 ; τὴν περὶ τὸ σῶμα θεραπείαν ἀκριβὴς καὶ π. Plu. Cic. 8 ; so, of speakers, π. ἐν τοῖς λόγοις Δημοσθένης Aeschin. 1.119 . as a term of praise, subtle, acute, ἀκριβὴς καὶ π. διάνοια Arist. Top. 141b13 . Arith., ἀριθμὸς π. an odd, uneven number, opp. ἄρτιος, Epich. 170.7 , Philol. 5 , Pl. Prt. 356e , etc.; π. ἡμέραι Hp. Aph. 4.61 ; τὸ π. καὶ τὸ ἄρτιον the nature of odd and even, Pl. Grg. 451c , etc.; π. χῶραι the odd places in a verse, Heph. 5.1 ; ἀρτιάκις π. ἀριθμός a number divisible by an odd number an even number of times, as 2 , 6 , 10 , Euc. 7 Def. 9 . περισσότεροι more in number, extra, Carnead. ap. S.E. M. 9.140 . περιττόν, τό, = στρύχνος μανικός, θρύον 11 , Thphr. HP 9.11.6 ; περισσόν Dsc. 4.73 ; περίσκον Orib. 12.8.56 . Adv. περισσῶς extraordinarily, exceedingly, θεοσεβέεες π. ἐόντες Hdt. 2.37 ; ἐπαινέσεται π. E. Ba. 1197 (lyr.); π. παῖδας ἐκδιδάσκεσθαι to have them educated overmuch, Id. Med. 295 ; περιττοτέρως τῶν ἄλλων far above all others, Isoc. 3.44 ; περισσότερον τοῦ ἑνός Luc. Pr.Im. 14 ; also περισσά Pi. N. 7.43 , E. Hec. 579 , etc. remarkably, περισσότερον τῶν ἄλλων θάψαι τινά more sumptuously, Hdt. 2.129 ; οἴκησις π. ἐσκευασμένη Plb. 1.29.7 ; περιττότατα ἔχειν to be most remarkable, Arist. HA 589a31 ; κοσμουμένη π. καὶ σεμνῶς Plu. 2.145e ; περισσότατα ἀνθρώπων θρησκεύειν in the most singular way, D.C. 37.17 ; ἡδέως καὶ π. in an uncommon manner, D.H. Comp. 3 ; εἰπεῖν στρογγύλως καὶ π. Id. Is. 20 ; ἰδίως καὶ π. Plu. Thes. 19 ; τὰ καινῶς ἱστορούμενα καὶ π. Id. 2.30d . abundantly, ἐχέτω π. τῆς κρόκης Alciphr. 3.41 . with a neg., οὐδὲν περισσὸν τούτων nothing more than or beyond these, Antipho 3.4.6 ; οὐδὲν τῶν ἄλλων περιττότερον πραγματεύεσθαι Pl. Ap. 20c ; οὐδὲν π. ἢ εἰ . . no otherwise than if . . , Id. Smp. 219c ; περισσόν alone, furthermore, LXX Ec. 12.12 ,al. τὰ περισσά in vain, AP 12.182 ( Strat. ). ἐκ περιττοῦ superfluously, uselessly, Pl. Prt. 338c , Sph. 265e ; but ὑπερέχειν ἐκ π. to be far superior, Id. Lg. 734d , cf. 802d ; ἡ κάμινος ἐκαύθη ἐκ π. Thd. Da. 3.22 ; ἐκ π. χρησάμενος τῇ παρρησίᾳ Luc. Pro Merc.Cond. 13 ; cf. ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ.
term_table.lsj_first_sense_gloss: beyond the regular number or size
term_table.greek_sentence: οἷς τοίνυν σώμασι μηδ’ ὅλως ἐστὶν ὑγρότης περιττὴ, καθάπερ τῷ καλλίστῳ μέλιτι, καὶ πεπίληται τὸ στερεὸν σῶμα, καθάπερ τοῖς λίθοις, ἀδύνατον τούτοις σαπῆναι, διόπερ καὶ ἡ τῶν ἁλῶν χρῆσις οὐκ ἐπὶ τούτων εὐδόκιμος, ἀλλ’ ὑφ’ ὧν ὕποπτος ἡ σῆψις.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Accordingly, bodies in which there is no superfluous moisture at all, as in the finest honey, and whose solid body is compacted, as in stones, cannot putrefy; wherefore the use of salts is not well regarded in the case of these, but in those cases where putrefaction is suspected.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Those bodies, then, in which there is no superfluous moisture at all, as in the finest honey, and whose solid body is compacted, as in stones, cannot putrefy; for this reason the use of salts is not esteemed in their case, but in those in which putrefaction is to be suspected.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἅλς (A), ἁλός [α], ὁ: dat. pl. ἅλασιν (v. infr.):— salt, πάσσε δ' ἁλὸς θείοιο Il. 9.214 , cf. Od. 17.455 ; ἁλὸς μέταλλον a salt-mine, Hdt. 4.185 ; ἁλὸς χόνδροι lumps of rock-salt, ib. 181 : sg. also Ar. Ach. 835 , Philyll. 28 , Axionic. 8 : more freq. in pl., Od. 11.123 , Hdt. 4.53 , al., etc.:—prov. phrases: οὐ σύ γ' ἂν . . σῷ ἐπιστάτη οὐδ' ἅλα δοίης Od. 17.455 ; φῄς μοι πάντα δόμεν· τάχα δ' . . οὐδ' ἅλα δοίης Theoc. 27.61 ; ἅλας συναναλῶσαι, i.e. to be bound by ties of hospitality, Arist. EN 1156b27 ; τῶν ἁλῶν συγκατεδηδοκέναι μέδιμνον to have eaten a bushel of salt together, i.e. to be old friends, Com.Adesp. 176 ; οἱ περὶ ἅλα καὶ κύαμον, of friends, Plu. 2.684e , cf. Arist. EE 1238a3 ; ὅρκον μέγαν, ἅλας τε καὶ τράπεζαν Archil. 96 ; ποῦ ἅλες; ποῦ τράπεζαι; D. 19.189 ; τοὺς ἅλας παραβαίνειν ib. 191 ; τοὺς τῆς πόλεως ἅλας περὶ πλείονος ποιήσασθαι τῆς ξενικῆς τραπέζης Aeschin. 3.224 ; ἁλῶν δὲ φόρτος ἔνθεν ἦλθεν, ἔνθ' ἔβη 'light come, light go', Zen. 2.20 ; ἅλασιν ὕει, of great abundance, Suid. in pl. of medical preparations, Dsc. 5.109 . brine, Call. Fr. 50 . ἃ. ἀμμωνιακός rock-salt, PLond. 1.78.90 . ἃ. Ἰνδικός sugar, Archig. ap. Paul.Aeg. 2.53 . ἅλες, οἱ, metaph., like Lat. sales, wit, possible but unlikely in Pl. Smp. 177b , Ep.Col. 4.6 ; certain in Plu. 2.854c ; ἅλες called "χάριτες" ib. 685a . (Cf.sq.)
term_table.greek_sentence: Περὶ ἁλῶν κεκαυμένων.] Ἅλες κεκαυμένοι τὸ μὲν διαφορητικὸν μᾶλλον ἔχουσι τῶν ἀκαύστων, εἰς ὅσον αὐτῶν λεπτομερέστερον γίγνεται τὸ σῶμα, τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς λαμβάνον δύναμιν, ὡς κᾀπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐδείχθη τῶν κεκαυμένων συμβαίνειν, οὐ μὴν ὁμοίως γε τοῖς ἀκαύστοις συνάγειν καὶ πιλοῦν τὴν στερεὰν οὐσίαν ἔτι δύνανται.
term_table.english_sentence_A: On burnt salt.] Burnt salt has the dispersing property more than unburnt salt, to the extent that its body becomes more fine-particled, taking on its power from the fire, as was shown to happen in the case of the other burnt substances too; yet it is no longer able, in the same way as unburnt salt, to draw together and compact the solid substance.
term_table.english_sentence_B: On burnt salt.] Burnt salt has the dispersing [property] to a greater degree than unburnt salt, in proportion as its body becomes more fine-particled, taking on a power from the fire, as was shown to happen also in the case of the other burnt [substances]; it is not, however, still able to draw together and compact the solid substance in the same way as unburnt salt.

term_table.english_sentence_A: On froth of salt.] Froth of salt is a foam-like efflorescence of salt, being of a nature much more fine-particled than salt itself, so that it is able both to thin and to disperse much more than salt does, whereas it cannot contract the remainder of the substance as salt does.

term_table.english_sentence_A: This too is one of the things generated in sea-water and in certain other waters resembling the sea, as for instance at Apollonia in Epirus and in other such places; upon many naturally occurring waters this drug is found floating like a foam, being soft while it floats on the surface, but afterwards drying out so as to become harder than dry pitch.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Thus at Apollonia in Epirus and in other such places this drug is found riding like foam upon many naturally occurring waters. It is soft while it floats on the surface, but afterwards it dries, so that it becomes harder than dry pitch.

term_table.english_sentence_B: The power of the drug is drying and heating, somewhere about the second order.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἔναιμ-ος, ον, with blood in one, θεοὶ ἔ. καὶ σαρκώδεις of flesh and blood, Hdt. 3.29 ; charged with blood, opp. ἄναιμος, ἔναιμον καὶ πυκνόν, οἷον ἧπαρ Hp. HA 489a30 , PA 690b11 , al. Χρῶμα ἔ. blood-colour, Pl. Ti. 68b . metaph., full of blood, vigorous, Χλωρὰ καὶ ἔ. τὰ πράγματα Gorg. ap. Arist. Rh. 1406b9 (nisi leg. ἄναιμα). ἔναιμα (sc. φάρμακα) medicaments for stanching blood, Hp. Art. 63 : sg., Fract. 24 ; φάρμακον ἔ. Thphr. HP 4.7.2 . ἔ. ἀγωγή treatment of bleeding wounds, Orib. 46.8.15 , cf. 45.18.31 . Adv. -μως ibid., Antyll.ib. 44.23.46 .
term_table.greek_sentence: εἰκότως οὖν αὐτῷ χρῶνται πρός γε τὰς κολλήσεις τῶν ἐναίμων τραυμάτων πρὸς τἄλλα, ὅσα ξηραίνειν δεόμενα μετὰ τοῦ θερμῆναι μετρίως.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Reasonably, then, they use it for the agglutination of bloody wounds, and for the other conditions, all those that require to be dried together with a moderate heating.

term_table.greek_sentence: Περὶ σπόγγου.] Σπόγγος ὁ μὲν κεκαυμένος δριμείας ἐστὶ καὶ διαφορητικῆς δυνάμεως.
term_table.english_sentence_A: On sponge.] Sponge, when burnt, is of a pungent and dispersing power.
term_table.english_sentence_B: On sponge.] Sponge, when burnt, is of a pungent and dispersing power. One of our teachers also used it against the haemorrhages that occur in surgical operations.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: αἱμο-ρραγία, ἡ, haemorrhage, Hp. Art. 69 , Aph. 7.21 ; any violent bleeding, ib. 5.16 ; nose-bleeding, Gal. 17(1).50 , etc.
term_table.greek_sentence: ἐχρῆτο δ’ αὐτῷ τις τῶν ἡμετέρων διδασκάλων καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐν ταῖς χειρουργίαις αἱμοῤῥαγίας, ἕτοιμον ἔχων ξηρὸν μὲν καὶ ἄνικμον, δεδευμένον δὲ μάλιστα μὲν ἀσφάλτῳ, μὴ παρούσης δὲ ταύτης πίττῃ, προσετίθει δ’ αὐτὸν τοῖς αἱμοῤῥαγοῦσι χωρίοις, ἔτι καιόμενον, ὡς ἐσχαροῦσθαί τε ἅμα τὸ μόριον καὶ οἷον πῶμά τι λαμβάνειν αὐτὸ τὸ σῶμα τοῦ καυθέντος σπόγγου.
term_table.english_sentence_A: One of our teachers used it also for the haemorrhages that occur in surgical operations, keeping it ready, dry and devoid of moisture, soaked preferably in asphalt, or, if this was not at hand, in pitch; and he applied it to the bleeding places while it was still burning, so that the part was at once made to form an eschar and the body of the burnt sponge itself was received as a kind of stopper.
term_table.english_sentence_B: He kept it ready, dry and without moisture, but soaked, preferably in asphalt, or in pitch if asphalt was not available. He applied it, still burning, to the haemorrhaging places, so that the part was at the same moment turned into an eschar and received the very body of the burnt sponge as a kind of lid.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἔριον, τό, Ion. εἴριον GDIiv p.876 (Chios, iv B. C., also written ἔρια ibid.), Hdt. , Hp. , and always in Hom. term_table.greek_sentence: καινὸς δ’ ὁ σπόγγος αὐτὸς καθ’ ἑαυτὸν οὐχ ὡς ἔριον ἢ μοτὸς τιλτὸς, ὕλη μόνον ἐστὶ τῶν ἐπιβρεχομένων ὑγρῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ξηραίνει σαφῶς.
term_table.english_sentence_A: New sponge, in and of itself, is not, like wool or a plucked lint-pledget (μοτὸς τιλτός), merely a material for the liquids poured upon it, but also dries manifestly.
term_table.english_sentence_B: A new sponge by itself is not, like wool or plucked lint, merely material for the liquids with which it is moistened; it also clearly dries.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ὀξύ-κρατον, Ion. ὀξύ-κρητον, τό, (κεράννυμι) sour wine mixed with water, Dsc. 2.105 , Aret. CA 1.1 , Antyll. ap. Orib. 45.18.31 , 4.11.14 , Erot. s.v. μᾶζα , Gal. 11.439 , al., Aët. 15.1 .
term_table.greek_sentence: εἴσῃ δὲ χρησάμενος ἐπὶ τραύματος αὐτῷ μόνῳ μεθ’ ὕδατος ἢ ὀξυκράτου ἢ οἴνου κατὰ τὰς τῶν σωμάτων διαφορὰς, ὡς προείρηται, κολλήσει γὰρ αὐτὰ παραπλησίως τοῖς ἐναίμοις ὀνομαζομένοις φαρμάκοις.
term_table.english_sentence_A: You will know this if you use it on a wound by itself with water or oxykraton (vinegar-and-water) or wine, according to the differences of bodies, as has been said before; for it will glue them together much like the drugs called enaima (those for bloody wounds).
term_table.english_sentence_B: You will know this if you use it on its own on a wound, with water or oxycrate or wine according to the differences of the bodies, as was said before. For it will agglutinate them in a way similar to the drugs called enhaemous.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: φάρμακον [v. sub fin.], τό, drug, whether healing or noxious: in Hom. the sense is freq. determined by an epith., φάρμακα, πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ . . , πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά Od. 4.230 ; τόδε φ. ἐσθλόν 10.287 , cf. 292 ; φ. ἤπια, ὀδυνήφατα (v. infr. 2 ); κακὰ φ. ib. 213 ; φ. λυγρά ib. 236 ; φ. οὐλόμενον ib. 394 ; ἀνδροφόνον 1.261 ; θυμοφθόρα φ. 2.329 ; so, after Hom. , προσανέα φ. Pi. P. 3.52 ; παιώνια A. Ag. 848 ; χρήσιμον Pl. R. 382c ; θανάσιμα Ph. Bel. 103.31 ; ὀλέθριον Luc. Herm. 62 . healing remedy, medicine, in Hom. mostly of those applied outwardly, ἐπιθήσει φάρμαχ' ἅ κεν παύσῃσι μελαινάων ὀδυνάων Il. 4.191 ; ἐπ' ἄρ' ἤπια φάρμακα πάσσε ib. 218 ; ὀδυνήφατα φ. πάσσων 5.401 , 900 , cf. 11.515 , 830 , 15.394 ; προσάλειφεν ἑκάστῳ φ. Od. 10.392 ; φ. περιαλείφειν Ar. Eq. 906 ; also of potions, πιὼν φάρμακ' Od. 10.326 ; φ. πεπωκώς Hdt. 4.160 , cf. Pi. l. c.; παρὰ τοῦ ἰατροῦ Pl. R. 406d , cf. Grg. 467c ; φ. χριστόν E. Hipp. 516 ; ἔγχριστον Theoc. 11.1 ; ἐπίχριστον Str. 17.1.10 ; ἐπίπαστον Theoc. l. c.; καταπλαστόν Ar. Pl. 716 ; ποτόν E. Hipp. l.c.; freq. in Medic. writers, Sor. 1.4 , Gal. 6.265 , etc.; of medicines for cattle, PFlor. 222.11 (iii A. D.). c. gen. (v. infr. 11 ), φ. νόσου a medicine for it, remedy against it, A. Pr. 251 , 606 (lyr.); βηχός Phryn.Com. 60 : κεφαλῆς for a head-ache, Pl. Chrm. 155b ; στραγγουρίας Arist. HA 612b16 , cf. 624a16 ; μέθης Amphis 37 ; δίψης AP 6.170 ( Thyill. ); but ὑγιείας φ. a medicine to restore or maintain health, Aristid. Or. 37(2).11 . enchanted potion, philtre: hence, charm, spell, Od. 4.220 sq., Ar. Pl. 302 , Theoc. 2.15 , PSI 1.64.20 (i B. C.); φαρμάκοις τὸν ἄνδρ' ἔμηνεν Ar. Th. 561 ; τοιαῦτα ἔχω φ. such charms have I, Hdt. 3.85 , cf. Apoc. 9.21 . poison, S. Tr. 685 , E. Med. 385 ; πιεῖν τὸ φ. Antipho 6.15 , Pl. Phd. 57a , 115a ; φάρμακα ἐσβεβληκέναι ἐς τὰ φρέατα Th. 2.48 ; φ. δηλητήρια SIG 37 A 1 (Teos, v B. C.); τοξικὸν φ. BGU 21 ii 14 (iv A. D.). lye for laundering, Stud.Pal. 22.56.12 (iii A. D.). generally, remedy, cure, Hes. Op. 485 , Alc. 35 , etc.; μεῖζον . . τῆς νόσου τὸ φ. the cure too strong for, i. e. worse than, the disease, S. Fr. 589.4 , cf. Com.Adesp. 455 ; φ. πραΰ, of a bridle, Pi. O. 13.85 ; φ. τινι for a thing, Thgn. 1134 (pl.), Archil. 9 ; πρός τι Arist. Pol. 1321a16 ; ποττὸν ἔρωτα Theoc. 11.1 ; but most freq. φ. τινός remedy against . . χλαῖνα . . φ. ῥίγευς Hippon. 19 ; Ζεὺς πάντων φ. μοῦνος ἔχει Simon. 87 ; τὸ σιγᾶν φ. βλάβης ἔχω A. Ag. 548 ; φ. πόνων, λύπης, E. Ba. 283 , Fr. 1079 ; δόλοι . . χρείας ἀνάνδρου φ. ib. 288 ; φόβου Pl. Lg. 647e ; λήθης φάρμακα (of γράμματα) E. Fr. 578.1 ; v. εὐδιανός. c. gen. also, a means of producing something, φ. σωτηρίας Id. Ph. 893 ; μνήμης καὶ σοφίας φ. Pl. Phdr. 274e ; ὑπομνήσεως ib. 275a , cf. 230d ; ἀθανασίας Antiph. 86.6 ; ἡσυχίας Arist. Pol. 1273b23 ; φ. μανίας, of the oil applied to wrestlers, D.L. 1.104 . ἐπὶ θανάτῳ φ. ἑᾶς ἀρετᾶς εὑρέσθαι a remedy or consolation in his own virtue, Pi. term_table.greek_sentence: Περὶ γάρου.] Γάρος δυνάμεώς ἐστι θερμῆς ἱκανῶς καὶ ξηρᾶς, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πρὸς τὰ σηπεδονώδη τῶν ἑλκῶν ἐχρήσαντό τινες αὐτῷ τῶν ἰατρῶν, ἐνιᾶσί τε τοῖς δυσεντερικοῖς τε καὶ ἰσχιαδικοῖς.
term_table.english_sentence_A: On garum.] Garum is of a sufficiently hot and dry power, and for this reason some of the physicians have used it for the putrefactive sorts of ulcers, and they inject it both into dysenterics and into those with sciatica.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: δύναμις [υ], ἡ , gen. εως, Ion. ιος, Ion. dat. δυνάμι : (δύναμαι):— power, might, in Hom. , esp. of bodily strength, εἴ μοι δ. γε παρείη Od. 2.62 , cf. A.translation: These, then, are the qualities: wetness and dryness, [705] heat and cold. The bodies named after them are both the elements common to all things and those which are called wet and dry and cold and hot according to the predominance of one of these, and those which are compared with the well-proportioned member of the same genus or of the same species, and those compared with anything whatever that happens to be at hand. Now concerning the difference among these it has been said many times, and no less has it also been said in what way nutriment differs from a drug, and that nutriment is mastered and overcome by the thing being nourished, whereas the drug, conversely, itself overcomes and masters the body of which it is a drug; for the conception of each of the two lies in the relative. It was shown also that a drug is naturally such as to alter either in respect of some one quality, whichever it may be, heating or cooling or drying or moistening, or in respect of some conjugation of those mentioned, or in respect of its whole substance, as do some of the deleterious drugs and not a few of the alexipharmic ones and all the purgatives and many of those called epispastic.

But concerning these matters I think I shall still [706] add what is lacking in what follows. Those drugs, however, which act upon our whole body according to one or two qualities I shall go through in this book, taking here again as an assumption what has been demonstrated in the preceding books: that most of the simple drugs are, in truth at least, non-uniform in their parts and composite, but are called simple because they are by nature such as they are, having received nothing in addition from our artifice. And indeed also that some are coarse-particled and earthy in their substances, others fine-particled and airy, and others as it were watery and intermediate between those mentioned—these points too, having been demonstrated in the preceding discourses, let them stand for me as assumptions with a view to what is going to be said. These things, then, being laid down, one must now begin the discourse.

The need for drugs arises for human beings often simply as this alone, namely of drugs that either heat or cool or moisten or dry, or that act according to some conjunction of these; but sometimes as of drugs that tighten and draw together what has already been relaxed beyond the limit of the moderate, [707] or relax what is tensed, or rarefy what has been condensed or condense what is loose, or soften what is hard or harden immoderate softnesses, or empty what is full or fill what is empty, or that accomplish some other such thing. For one who has been chilled—not only a physician, but any layman whatever—led by the very nature of the matter, desires to find a heating drug, and likewise one who is being burnt up by a burning fever desires a cooling one. So too any layman whatever who has a sodden ulcer bids the physician to dry it, and, if it should be dry and moistureless, to moisten it. And indeed, when they perceive dryness together with heat throughout the whole body, as do both those who have been scorched by the sun and those who have been worn out by fatigue, they long to bathe and they drink cold water, and whatever may be capable of moistening and cooling at once, this they contrive to find out; and many of the laymen, led by nature itself, often procure for themselves the remedies for these conditions.

Of phlegmone, however, and of scirrhus and oedema, of erysipelas and putrefaction, of herpes and gangrene, no longer does any one [708] of them attempt to seek the cure for himself, since each of such conditions is already greater than the understanding of a layman and requires some more august science; and they name such a science medicine, and the one who practises it a physician. And they themselves advance thus far, as to know that a hollow ulcer needs flesh-production, a foul one cleansing, and a level one cicatrization; yet they do not know the drug that produces flesh or cleanses or cicatrizes. In the same way too, if they should have a muscle or tendon that is hard or tense or slack, they know precisely that the hard one has need of softening agents, the tense one of relaxing agents, and the slack one of tightening agents; yet they do not know the drug that softens or relaxes or tightens, but to discover such things is the work of the physician alone. For as far as heating and cooling, moistening and drying agents are concerned, one can find some of the laymen sharing with the physicians in the discovery of drugs; but in the matters now stated, all are already without experience.

Now, as was also shown earlier, even in the case of [709] the heating and cooling, moistening and drying agents themselves, the discovery of them all is not equally ready. For that mustard and pellitory heat, and that purslane and strychnos cool, and that water and olive oil moisten while vinegar and sea-water dry, is agreed by nearly everyone, not only by physicians but also by laymen. Rose oil, however, whether one must say that it heats or that it cools, and likewise vinegar and olive oil too, and many other such things, have been the subject of considerable dispute.

Concerning such matters of power, then, I have gone through in the four treatises before this one: in the first and second, refuting the arguments of the sophists and showing the true method by using which one might find the powers of drugs; in the third, having taken leave of the sophists, I went through from the beginning all the logical inquiries, by going through which especially, and being, as one might say, trained by them, one will be capable of finding the powers of all drugs; and in the fourth I made my discourse about the objects of sense proper to the [710] tongue, which indeed they name flavours (χυμοί), demonstrating how one, setting out from there, might find the primary qualities and powers. I also touched, to the extent that need called for it, on the odorous qualities at the end of that book, showing how much it is possible to take from there too for the discovery of the primary powers. But in this present discourse, the fifth, another kind of powers is set before me to expound—second, as one might say, and third, after the primary ones that are common to all. For since each of the particular drugs is not mixed in the same manner out of those, one of them, I think, has become relaxing, another tensing or softening or hardening or rarefying or condensing.

Further, on the basis of the actions which they are naturally fitted to perform, they were said to have in them powers that are rarefying and condensing, softening and hardening, clogging and cleansing, drawing and repelling, and in addition to these relaxing, tensing, mouth-opening, contracting, thickening, thinning, pain-relieving, pain-producing, concocting, suppurating, dispersing, [711] sweat-producing, stupefying, numbing, sleep-inducing, deranging, putrefying, burning, corroding, eschar-forming, liquefying, compacting, productive of bad humours, tempering, purging, checking, roughening, smoothing, blocking and unblocking. And as people proceed still further and name them, as it were, individually according to each of the effects: diuretic, emetic, gently evacuating, laxative, errhine, phlegm-expelling, promoting or checking the menses. And likewise, of milk and of seed, either generative or extinguishing, either provoking or checking. And still more, when they name certain powers hepatic or splenic or otic or ophthalmic or dental or sciatic or nephritic or podagric or arthritic or pleuritic or cough-relieving or stone-crushing, they arrive at the particular ones. In the same manner it has also been said that there is a certain flesh-forming power for an ulcer, and a scarring one, and an agglutinating one, and a reducing one; and it is almost not even possible to count all the particular powers, if we attempt to name them after each of the effects produced.

But it is also, [712] I think, both finer and more methodical, having withdrawn from the long and disorderly account, to define the composite powers of drugs by useful kinds, not saying that in the poultice made with wheat flour there is a suppurating or soothing or pain-relieving or dispersing or relaxing power, but that it is moderately moist and hot. For it was stated in what preceded under what signification we apply such an expression. So too, that iris is not a drug that moves urine or menses, nor a cough-drug, nor one that is suited to pleuritics or peripneumonics or those with empyema, nor that it brings aid in epilepsies and spasms and palpitations and tremors and ruptures and strains, nor that it fills ulcers with flesh and cleanses them, and sinuses too, and stops pains of the side and of the liver and spleen, nor that it disperses scrofulous swellings or draws flesh away from bones.

And in the same way, nor that it is suited for gonorrhoea, or that it is usefully mixed into fomentations of the womb, as softening and opening the mouths of vessels; nor indeed that it cleanses away lentil-spots or freckles [713] and cures chronic headache, or that it is naturally disposed to destroy embryos and draw them down. Rather, it suffices, having said that its mixture is hot to such a degree, and dry to such a degree, and fine-particled up to such a degree, to have indicated thereby all the things now mentioned and many others besides these. And in another way again, it suffices to say of it that it is bitter, yet not extremely so, but such that some sweetness seems to be mixed in. The first manner of teaching, then, is peculiar to the Empiricists, whereas the second befits above all a rational man, and it is this one that we now propose to go through. All the other matters discussed previously throughout the four commentaries are proper to the theory of drugs itself, except where, by way of community, the discussion touched upon the therapeutic method. But the matter now at hand belongs rather to that discipline, so that I often deliberated whether to pass over it entirely.

But because it seemed good to me to train in advance those who are going to follow the reasonings of the therapeutic method, and because most of my companions, and especially [714] those to gratify whom I came to this treatise, asked me to carry it through in this way, for this reason I shall take up the discussion in this book, making my beginning from the suppurating and the softening drugs; since both are hot and moist, yet each in a different manner. For the former are so inasmuch as they generate a heat most similar to the body that is being brought to suppuration, in addition to neither removing anything of the moisture that is present in it nor adding to it; the latter inasmuch as they kindle a heat even greater than the natural one and draw together some of the moisture. Now the notion of the suppurating drugs is at once clear and familiar to everyone; for suppuration is a change into pus. But concerning the softening drugs and softening itself it is no longer possible to speak so simply, because it is not possible to do so concerning the hard and the soft body either.

since indeed one thing is called hard simply, as earth is; another by predominance, as nail and spur and horn; another in relation to the well-proportioned member of the same genus or of the same species, when one makes the comparison in the manner of this particular animal, such as an elephant, or this particular man, such as Heracles; [715] and another as compared with anything whatever, as Diogenes compared with Aristotle. In the same way the soft too is spoken of either as being such in the extreme degree, or by predominance, or in relation to the well-proportioned member of the same genus or of the same species, or in relation to anything whatever that happens to come to hand. And that it is also possible to speak of all such things in three ways—some as possessing unmixed and extreme the qualities from which they derive their names, some as relative to the well-proportioned member of the same genus or of the same species, and some as compared with anything whatever that happens to come to hand—and that it makes no difference whether one speaks in the former way or in the latter, has already been demonstrated by me many times.

Leaving aside, then, all the remaining significations, let us examine the soft and hard things [as spoken of] in relation to the best-constituted human being, whom indeed we have made the rule and measure of all things so called—and not [in relation to] any chance part of him, such as bone or soft fat, but the part that is intermediate in mixture, the skin, and of this above all the part on the hands, where precisely the tactile faculty is at its most exact. And it comes to the same thing that something is named soft or hard according to predominance, with reference to the whole substance, [716] since our touch is a kind of mean, as Aristotle too taught. And Plato too seems to hold roughly this view when he said: "hard are those things to which our flesh yields, soft those which yield to the flesh." For in this very treatise, the Timaeus, he showed the skin of the human being to be flesh in kind. And indeed Aristotle too, when he said that the soft is what yields into itself and the hard what does not yield, seems to declare the same as Plato, especially in that he says such things are judged with reference to touch, as with reference to a mean. But the hard or soft in the comparison with anything whatever appears to be judged by yielding or not yielding more or less. And indeed when we say that our own skin itself, or a muscle, or some other part has been hardened, we name it thus by comparing its acquired condition with its natural state. And surely, for bodies in such a state, the return to the natural condition is softening.

But since each thing becomes harder in many ways — either being dried, or being congealed, or being overfilled [717] so as to be violently distended, or being affected according to some conjunction of these — the softening too, in the case of each of them, will be specific to it. Let us then draw distinctions concerning all of them in order, first recalling that an easy-going attitude about nouns and verbs is for the most part not ignoble, but rather its opposite is illiberal, whenever it is not necessary to make distinctions about them. For so Plato said, and for us now, for the present occasion, it is necessary to make distinctions about the meanings of 'hard', beginning again from the same points which we stated just now. For what yields into itself is soft, provided that it is a simple body; but what is composed of several things, either touching one another, like a heap of wheat-grains, or somehow interwoven, like a fleece or plaits (πλόκαμα), could yield and at the same time not be soft.

Conversely, in the case of things that have been completely filled, such as wineskins or bladders, the two together do not yield into themselves, yet neither is what is contained hard; nor, for that matter, has the container, once it has been filled, become harder than it was or taken on some other acquired condition, [718] except only that it has become stretched from having previously been slack. Such a thing, then, I for my part call resistant and not hard, whenever I choose to speak with precision. I concede, however, if anyone should wish to name it hard as well, and I myself often call it so, reminding only of this: that there is neither one nature of things that have been hardened nor one remedy. For what has been hardened by dryness needs to be moistened, what by congealing to be heated, what by filling to be evacuated, what by dryness together with congealing to be both moistened and heated, and what by congealing together with filling to be both heated and evacuated. Bodies, then, are dried without congealing in immoderate exercises, in strong sun, in severe deprivations, in burning fever, and by certain drugs, namely those that dry without cooling. They are congealed by strong cooling alone, just as they are also filled through an influx of abundant moisture. And they are dried and congealed at the same time when causes capable of coexisting concur in the same thing, as for instance if someone should overexert himself in the cold.

So too it is both filled and congealed through a flux [719] that is cold, or through some chilling of the part. And of the chilling, in turn, the cause is threefold: one from the things that impinge from outside, such as air, water, or a drug, as they often bring it about in cases of erysipelas; another, the proper mixture of the affected part; and another, third, in addition to these, arising from the humour that has flowed into it. For often that humour has already become hotter than it was, either because it is putrefying or because it is altered by the parts in contact with it that are hot by nature; but the chilling which it imparted to some part of those that are colder by nature persists for a long time. In so many ways, then, are bodies hardened and softened. The softening drug, however, seems not to bear upon all these ways, but especially upon those that have been hardened through congelation, and still more if there is also some moisture contained in them contrary to nature, as in the case of parts that have become scirrhous. For if a thing has become hard through dryness, they bid one moisten, not soften, such a thing, just as also they bid one evacuate, not soften, what has been filled.

But concerning names it is neither fine to quarrel [720] nor necessary to be exact. It is better to proceed to the differences in the things themselves, in which error also brings great harm to the sick. What has been dried out, then, needs moistening drugs, about which I have already spoken sufficiently earlier; what has been congealed by cooling needs heating ones. Nor are these things unknown either; but what has been filled needs either cooling drugs or heating ones or those properly called drying. For all of these evacuate the surplus moisture, each according to its own principle. Those that cool do so in a twofold manner, at once repelling and at the same time drawing out, together with the heat, much moisture, as Aristotle taught. Those that heat, by dissolving into vapours the moisture contained in the bodies that are being heated; and those that dry, like those called dispersing, these too in a twofold manner, either drinking up the moistures when they are present in certain pores, or altering the whole part. But what the right moment for the use of each is belongs not to the present treatise but to the therapeutic method.

But those [721] that have been hardened by cooling together with dryness, it is fitting to heat and at the same time to moisten, not in the way that suppurating parts are treated, with heat and moisture that are moderate according to nature; rather, the drug must be hotter to the extent that the cooling has prevailed, and moister to the extent that the dryness has; and to define the measure of these too belongs to the therapeutic method. Here it will suffice to go through a certain outline of the form of the drugs by means of a few examples. Hot water, then, moistens and heats, and so does oil.
