And if both are mixed together into the same thing, the mixture made from them will be much more moistening and at the same time heating, just as are also baths of drinkable waters with abundant oil. This same thing is produced also by the quality of foods when it is of the same sort; for this reason too the remedies for attacks of boulimos happen to be of this kind. For the affection involves cooling together with dryness, and their cure is through the opposites.

The poultice made with wheat flour, however, which brings well-tempered natures to suppuration, neither removes anything worth mentioning of the natural moisture in the parts [722], and much less does it add any; just as it is also of a nature neither to intensify nor to blunt the warmth, but only to increase it in respect of its substance. And it is not the same thing to intensify the quality and to increase the substance. These matters too will be shown more precisely a little later. Such drugs, then, we call moist and hot, not as being moister and hotter than our substance, but as being of a mixture similar to ours, which is moist and hot according to the ancient account, as we said in the work On Mixtures. It is not in this way, however, that we say that water is moist or galbanum hot, but the former as wetting and soaking our flesh, the latter as heating it. For even if the water be hot, so that it is sometimes able to empty the parts that have been raised into a swelling through an influx of humours, it nonetheless in every case moistens the homoeomerous parts, as has also been shown by me in the first book.

The drugs that bring about suppuration, then, by their heating, like hot water, disperse the surplus [723] moisture, that which is contained in the empty spaces, as has been demonstrated in the treatise On Uneven Dyscrasia. To bodies in their natural state, however, in the homoeomerous parts themselves, it adds no moisture, just as it does not remove anything clear or perceptible. For being equal to them in their mixtures, they are preservative of their substance, so as to alter it in no respect. At any rate, in suppurations the moisture is altered, and also if somewhere there is bruised flesh, but all the other parts which are in their natural state preserve their own substance. For since three alterations occur in the bodies of animals, one is precisely according to nature, when the food is concocted in the stomach, or when the juice generated there is concocted in the viscera and vessels, so that from this in turn each member is nourished; another is precisely contrary to nature, in all things that are putrefying. These, then, are in a way opposite to each other. The third is mixed from both and intermediate, having something of the first, the one according to nature, and something of its opposite, the one contrary to nature.

For the one according to nature has these two features: [724] both that the alteration comes about from matter proper to the animal, and that it is completely mastered by the innate heat. The one contrary to nature, by contrast, has its change brought about by an alien heat, and to nothing useful; while the one intermediate between them, the one that follows in suppurations, is brought about by the innate heat, though not by one that masters completely; for neither is it accomplished out of matter that is completely useful, just as not out of matter that is altogether alien either. As, then, the alterations according to nature, being brought about by the innate heat, are assisted by a similar heat from outside, in the same way also is the alteration in suppurations. At any rate, we know of nothing that contributes so much to concoction in the belly as a human body touching it. And some people, applying children to themselves at night while resting, perceive a most evident benefit. For this heat is more akin and far more proper than that which comes through fomentations. And some people even apply small puppies to the belly while resting for the sake of the same benefit, increasing the quantity of the heat that concocts the foods, not its quality.

Such, then, must also be the drug that is going to assist [725] suppuration, of the very same kind as the innate heat itself is in well-tempered natures; but if the nature is hotter than it ought to be, the suppurating drug in that body will need to be hotter, and hotter than the moderate one by just so much as the nature too is hotter than the well-tempered one, so that this, for its part, is already evident from the therapeutic method, namely that the suppurating drug is peculiar to each individual human being. And not least is what has often been demonstrated by us also attested by these considerations, namely that all the powers of drugs must be examined with reference to the best-mixed human being; for no art whatsoever can be constituted, unless one first sets up, as it were, a certain rule and target for the kind of material in which it is engaged, and then directs all the particulars toward that.

Again, then, positing in our account the best-mixed human being as a kind of target, and referring to him, we say that a suppurative drug is something different from the one that softens parts that are becoming scirrhous, and that their mixtures are such as we said earlier [726] they were: that of the one which assists nature toward the generation of pus being well-proportioned and similar to the body to which it is applied; and, because our nature is moist and warm, such drugs are often called moist and warm; whereas that of the one which softens the scirrhous part is much warmer than the well-mixed nature, yet certainly not already strongly warm. For the condition of parts becoming scirrhous begins from a viscous and thick flux that has been wedged in the small pores of the part. When the fine-particled moisture in it has been dispersed, and then the remainder has been cooled and has taken on, as it were, a kind of congelation, what is called scirrhosis follows; and for this reason they say both that the affection is cold and that its cure is through warming agents. But since the surplus moisture was present together with the cooling, the remedy too will be composite: because of the cooling the condition needs warming agents, and because of the alien and surplus moisture, evacuating agents.

Hence none of the scirrhous conditions is cured either by agents that dry vehemently, or by those that heat strongly, [727] or by those that are capable of both of these. For those that heat vehemently, having dispersed by force the moisture lying beside and contained within the parts, dry out the remainder, so that it becomes incurable; while those that dry vehemently, even if they do not heat, bring the flux wedged in the scirrhous parts to the extreme of dryness, not through the intermediate step of evacuating the fine-particled portion, but directly and in accordance with their own nature. Therefore only those which heat, yet not vehemently, together with not drying strongly, cure such conditions; and such drugs are called softening, since at one and the same time they do both things, melting what is congealed and little by little dispersing it. All such drugs, then, are hot and not very dry, differing from the pus-producing ones in that they are hotter and drier than these.

For the former have a heat that is akin and most similar to that of our bodies, whereas the softening ones are more vehement, yet not [728] so much so as to dry up the remainder by the violence of their attraction. Further, the suppurative ones preserve the moisture already present in the parts affected by scirrhus, whereas the softening ones consume some small portion of it. And for this reason, though the heating and drying drugs are countless, those which partake at once of a moderate heat and have had the good fortune to possess a dryness proportionate to it—these alone are softening of parts affected by scirrhus, such as bdellium, storax, galbanum, ammoniac incense, deer's and calf's marrow, goat's and bull's fat, and whatever others are of this kind.

For at present it is not my purpose to go through all the material, but to produce one general teaching concerning all such powers—namely, what the general point is which it is better to know about both the suppurating and the softening agents: that the former kindle a heat equal to that of the animal according to nature, whereas those that soften kindle much more; and that the former by nature act not by the quality of the heat but rather by its quantity, whereas those that are softening of indurated parts [729] act rather by the quality. For just as, if it were possible to keep one's hands or some other limb constantly laid upon the part that needs suppuration, it would in this way suppurate most quickly, in the same manner, if the drug too were most similar to the mixture of the human being, it will most quickly concoct what needs to be changed into pus. And what needs this is sometimes the flesh, when it has been bruised, and sometimes the humour that produces the inflammation. And indeed, that such a drug must be clogging, in order to be precisely suppurative, this too now seems to me to appear clearly. For if it is fitting to increase the substance of the innate heat, and not to intensify (ἐπιθεῖναι) its quality, the pores of the body must be blocked, so that they may keep the vaporous exhalations shut in within; since those poultices at any rate which, either by cleansing or by heating more vehemently, allow the vapours to be dispersed, do indeed dry, but certainly do not produce pus.

Such are the meal of barley, of chickpeas, of fenugreek and of beans, [730] and still more that of darnel, bitter vetch, Italian millet (elymos), lupines, millet, and of all drying things. For under the action of cleansing agents, even if they do not heat strongly, since the pores are unblocked and opened, the heat of the part also departs along with them, so that its natural due proportion is not preserved; and under the action of those that heat strongly, no small amount of this too is in fact evacuated, while what remains is somewhat heated, and thus it comes about that the substance of the innate heat becomes less, while its quality is intensified. But neither of these should occur; rather, the vaporous and hot pneuma should be contained in the greatest quantity, yet be precisely well-proportioned in its heat; for it is indeed this which, being present in greatest quantity in children too, helps to increase all the natural activities. There are, then, some who do not recognise even this very point, and, besides not recognising it, bring a charge against Hippocrates for saying that growing things have the greatest amount of innate heat.

But we must not misunderstand him, and must recognize that 'innate heat' has been said of that which we also call pneuma in each of the animals, about [731] which Aristotle too wrote. And nothing prevents one from understanding by 'innate heat' also the blood-like and airy substance together with the pneuma. Now the Stoics hold that this very pneuma is the substance of the soul; but we neither venture at all to pronounce on the substance of the soul, and we consider it superfluous for the present purpose. That, however, the innate pneuma, even if it is not the substance of the soul, is at any rate its first instrument, we have already demonstrated in the commentaries On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato. And indeed we say that this pneuma is contained in all the parts of the animal, but that it is not alike everywhere, just as it is not necessary that the blood be either. And that no small substance of it is contained also in the empty spaces, or rather, as it were, a kind of matter which still needs a slight change for the generation of innate pneuma perfected in its proper qualities, yet already contributes sufficiently, at least to the natural activities.

And surely one of the natural works is also the change into pus [732]; for in this respect too it is a kind of concoction. One must, I think, keep the pneuma within as much as possible whenever something is to be concocted. But it is dispersed by cleansing things, such as the flour of barley and of beans; by drying things, such as Italian millet (ἔλυμος), common millet and lupines; by heating things, such as fenugreek is; and still more by things whose nature it is to heat and dry at the same time, such as darnel and bitter vetch, chickpeas and bitter vetchlings (ὦχροι). Most suitable for the generation of pus are, among things poured over as affusions, well-tempered water or water-and-oil; among things used for moistening, well-tempered oil; and among poultices, wheat flour prepared with water-and-oil and bread itself—and this too must be boiled in due measure. For what has been boiled for a very long time is somewhat more drying and suits the inflammations that are harder to concoct, whereas what has been boiled less suits those that are very hot and, as one might say, seething.

And that which contains more oil is for the inflammations harder to concoct, [733] that with less for those that are seething; and indeed the plaster made from bread suits the inflammations harder to concoct, for bread in fact contains both salt and leaven, whereas that made from wheat flour suits the hotter ones. Again, of wheat flour itself the pure sort brings to suppuration more, and of bread the pure sort more; for bran is both less hot and more dry, whereas the pure and nourishing flour is both moist and hot, and such things were shown to work together towards the generation of pus. So too, then, of the drugs applied to inflamed parts, those that are hot and moist, these also contribute to suppuration, such as pig's fat and calf's fat. For bull's fat and goat's fat were shown to be more pungent, and for this reason suitable for the colder and more scirrhous inflammations, whereas pig's and calf's fat is most appropriate to the inflammations properly so called themselves. The fat of cocks is also most appropriate, and still more so that of the goose, which is already somewhat more dispersing.

[734] For they are finer-particled in their substances, just as that of oxen and goats is coarser-particled and more earthy. And indeed the fat of all wild animals is both more pungent and much more drying than that of tame ones, and most of all that of leopards and lions, so that none of these is suitable for producing pus, but, as has been said, pig's fat and calf's fat. Pitch and resin also produce pus, when, that is, they have been strained through (διηθεῖσαι) with some oil or with rose oil. And here too, for boiling inflammations one must melt them with rose oil, but for the colder ones with one of the heating oils, such as castor oil, radish oil, old oil and Sicyonian oil. And if at some time you use wax alone for the sake of suppuration, the others not being at hand, melt this too in one of the heating oils. For by itself it is less hot than would suffice to produce suppuration, although it does possess the property of plastering over. It is therefore suitable only for boiling inflammations, strained through in one of the heating oils.

But just as this (wax) falls short of the due measure, relative to inflammations that are intermediate in mixture and to the natures both of human beings and of parts, so resin and pitch exceed it by a little [735]. And for this reason all the things just now mentioned, when mixed together, bring to suppuration in due measure. But these matters already belong to the treatise on the composition of drugs, which the sequence of the inquiry has compelled us to touch upon in some way. I return again to what lies before us. What lies before us is to define the general nature of suppurating agents, what sort it is. It was said that it must be heating and moistening in due measure, which, expressed otherwise, is neither to exceed nor to fall short of the mixture of the body that alters it, but to be as nearly similar to it as possible. And that the suppurating drug is of this kind in potentiality, but becomes such in actuality when it comes into contact with us, has been said many times before, and we shall recall it now too, so that it may be kept in mind throughout. The mixture of the suppurating agent, then, is of some such kind; the consistency of its body, however, is a clogging one. This belongs most of all to viscous things, as to pig's fat, butter, frankincense, and the poultice made from wheat flour.

[736] For these are moderately hot and moderately moist and viscous, and for this reason they are suitable for suppurations. Groats (chondros), however, are more drying than wheat flour, but no less viscous, if not indeed even more so; hence in the case of inflammations of the middle sort they are less suitable for suppuration, but in the case of the moister ones they are better than wheat flour. But these matters too now already go further beyond the present treatise; let us therefore return again to the drugs that are softening of parts that are becoming indurated (skirrhous), touching here again upon the therapeutic treatise only so far as will contribute to making clear what is going to be said. Now, they call skirrhos the tumour contrary to nature that is painless and hard. Some of these, when they have grown and hardened to the greatest degree, become not only painless but also hard to perceive and devoid of sensation. Their generation is from a thick and cold humour. And of such there are in the bodies of animals only two, black bile and phlegm that has been excessively dried.

And for this reason the scirrhous swellings too are in every case either phlegmatic [737] in their substance, or melancholic, or mixed from both. Now, it is not the occasion at present to go through their diagnosis; but it is now time for me to speak about the softening drugs, since they specifically name "softening" those that are curative of the scirrhous swellings that have arisen from dried-out phlegm and thick juice (χυλός). These form especially around the heads of the muscles and the tendons that grow out from them. For all those that become scirrhous from melancholic juice are cancerous and are exacerbated by the softening drugs. But how one ought to be mindful of these will be stated in the books of the Therapeutic Method; whereas those that have become scirrhous from a viscous and thick humour that has congealed require heating and drying drugs, yet not strong and violent ones; rather, it suffices for them to be of the second, or sometimes even the third, order of heating drugs, and of the first order of drying ones.

And since there is a not inconsiderable latitude of more and less in bodies that have been hardened, it is necessary, surely, that [738] the latitude of the drugs that cure them also be not small; so, for instance, even goat's fat has sometimes benefited bodies hardened in this way, and so has hen's fat. But these are weaker and soften only moderate hardnesses; goose fat, however, is stronger than that of hens and cocks, and he-goat's fat is stronger than that of goats, as is bull's fat, though less so than he-goat's. Moreover, deer's marrow also softens sufficiently, and after it calf's. For all such drugs are hot and moderately dry, and by nature they heat far more than they dry. Hence, if someone should at some point call them hot and moist in their powers, one must concede the point; for they stand only a little apart from things that neither dry nor moisten. Of the same genus as those just mentioned, but stronger, are ammoniac incense, storax, galbanum, and Scythian bdellium. Among these, the fresh ones are better for softening; for when they grow old they dry more strongly than they should. Marrow and fat, too, have this property.

For these too, as they age, [739] become more pungent than they were and drier. And indeed Sicyonian oil also belongs to this class, and old oil not least, and among the prepared oils the lily oil (sousinon). But it is not my purpose here to speak about compound drugs. Then also the root of marsh-mallow and of wild cucumber and certain other plants, when boiled down, some in oil, others in water, come to have the power of the softening drugs, just as do the leaves of wild mallow, both raw and boiled. This, then, is a simple drug, like pig's fat that has been aged. And this too must not contain any salt, just as none of the other things that soften may; for salts dry vehemently. All the other drugs, both simple and compound, that are naturally such as to soften—for those too will be spoken of again—are hot, of the second or sometimes the third order, but gently dry. There must indeed be something clogging in these too, just as in the suppurative drugs, but to the extent that it is fitting for them to be more evacuative, to that extent they also clog the pores less.

[740] The power of the softening drugs, then, has been sufficiently shown by me; next I shall go through the hardening ones. These, accordingly, must be cold and moist, as houseleek is, and purslane and fleawort and the lentil that grows on marshes, or strychnos—or rather this last is not even moist in its mixture, but intermediate between what simply moistens and what dries, being composed of opposite powers, a moistening and a drying one, because it also partakes of a twofold substance, earthy and watery. But it is not my purpose now to lead the discussion off into the particular materials, but only to define the generic powers. If, then, something both cools and dries, this too certainly hardens, but it does not belong to the hardening drugs properly so called. For a body becomes hard by congealing rather than by evacuation, as we also said before.

But if something has become hard from not retaining its innate moisture, we call this dry rather than hard, and its cure is a thorough wetting (διανσις) and a moistening, and not a softening, [741] just as the cure of what is tensed is relaxation, and of what is relaxed, tensing. And how these things are is clearly seen both in the case of the skin, as has also been said by Hippocrates, "of hard skin, softening; of tensed, relaxation", and indeed also, often, in the case of the joints. Now relaxation is brought about when the ligaments around them and the tendons have been immoderately moistened, whereas tensing is no longer simple, but occurs whenever they are dried to excess, or chilled, or inflamed, or hardened into scirrhus. In the joints it is so; but in the case of the skin not only so, but also when the muscles within it are increased in bulk in whatever manner, so that in some people it is often stretched even on account of corpulence. And that it suffers this same thing in inflammations as well has been said before; hence there is not simply one single kind of relaxing remedies, but some relax by moistening, some by heating, some by softening, some by evacuating, some by clearing away the swellings contrary to nature, and some by effecting certain of these in combination.

[742] But Thessalus and nearly all his followers, as in many other matters, so too in these confuse both the names and the things, writing down whatever occurs to them without testing it; whence it will perhaps be necessary for us also, once we have completed the matters at hand, to write at some point against them. For the present, however, let us go through what is continuous with what has been said, making our beginning once more from the drugs called clogging, since they too have been spoken of frequently. To put it briefly, then, a clogging drug is one which is plastered into the pores in the human body in a way that is hard to loosen. I have spoken sufficiently about the nature of the pores which we posit in the treatises On Mixtures. And it was demonstrated in the book before this one that the clogging drug must also be entirely non-biting. For if anything biting were present in it, it will not be able to remain in the pores, but will easily be expelled, either having melted away something of the parts, or in any case having drawn moisture from the depth.

And it is clear [743] that the clogging drug must also be earthy in its consistency, or at any rate viscous. But about these matters enough has been said earlier too. The opposite to it would be called cleansing-out, or unblocking of the pores, just as the clogging drug itself is not only clogging but also obstructing. And it would be, just as it is opposite in its effects, so also in the nature of its body neither viscous nor non-biting, but nitrous and fine-particled. For indeed it is in the more and the less that they differ from one another, not differing in the genus of their substance—the clogging drugs from those that foster dirt, and those that clean out the pores from the cleansing ones. For those which remove the surface dirt, whether of ulcers or of the skin itself, are called cleansing; but those which also clean out the pores are both finer-particled than these and opposite to the clogging ones, and for this reason are named unblocking and purifying of the pores.

These are nitrous and bitter; and when applied externally to the skin [744] they need to possess only the nitrous quality in an exact degree in order to be able to do what has been said, but when taken into the interior of the body, even if they share in some astringency, they could even so still be purgative and thoroughly cleansing of the larger pores, such as those in the vessels are. For externally the smallness of the pores, being closed up beforehand by the astringency before they have been properly cleaned out, neither thereafter admits the cleansing substance any further into the depth nor is cleaned out. But all the parts about the belly and those about the liver and spleen and all the other viscera, having very large pores in themselves, are benefited with respect to the strength of the vessels more than they are harmed with respect to the smallness of the orifices. And for this reason wormwood is naturally fitted to clean out thoroughly from within, but not from without; and it is compounded, as was said before, of a bitter and an acerbic power. Accordingly I have no need to write out in addition the particular instances of any such drugs either.

For whatever things you find to be nitrous and bitter, know that these are able to clear out all the pores; but the filth of ulcers, or indeed of the skin, not only these but [745] also those more moderate in their powers are of a nature to remove, such as the fine-particled sweet things, like honey and some of the cereal seeds, such as bitter vetch, beans, barley and lupins. And yet even among these themselves the flour of beans and of barley only cleanses, but does not unblock the pores; whereas that of bitter vetch and of lupins, and especially when they are bitter, has, in addition to cleansing, already something also clearing of the pores. Something similar also holds for almonds. For of these too, those that are bitter both cleanse and clear out the pores, whereas those that are edible cleanse but do not unblock. The seed of the nettle, however, clears the pores in the same way as bitter vetch and bitter almonds. And of the same kind, evidently, are also squill and iris, and all the others which, as has been said, have the bitter quality predominant in themselves. For nitre itself by itself, and aphronitron, and the foam of nitre, and seriphon, and southernwood, and all other such things, when taken with foods and drinks, are of the same power.

And straightaway it belongs to all of these also to be thinning of thick and viscous humours, just as it belongs to all the clogging ones [746] to make the humours in the body of the human being thick and viscous. So that you could not find other drugs, in preference to these, more cutting and more thinning of the phlegmatic or viscous matters, or of pus, from the chest and lung, and more suitable for bringing them up. And it belongs to these same ones also to clear out the obstructions in the liver and the moderate ones in the spleen; but the stronger obstructions require more vehement drugs: bark of caper and roots of tamarisk, scolopendrion and squill, and the herb called, for this very reason, asplenon. And these same ones too must be used differently for each of the viscera: in the case of the liver, by themselves alone; in the case of the spleen, mixing them with vinegar or boiling them in it; in the case of the affections in the chest and lung, with honey-water and ptisan and oxymel and the sweet among wines. But these matters already belong to the therapeutic method; and therefore I pass over, for the present, the reasonings concerning them. For they will be stated both in that treatise and in the one on the composition of drugs.

[747] What it is still necessary for me to note in addition to what has been said will alone be stated: that whenever we wish to stimulate a more copious urination, one should not make much use of the drugs that have been mentioned, but of those that are both more pungent and at the same time more heating. For it was said earlier that everything pungent is hot. Of such a kind are the seed of celery, of rock-parsley, of fennel, of daucus, of wild celery and of smyrnion, and indeed also seseli, ammi, phou and meon, asaron and acoron; by these the blood is not only thinned but also diffused and separated, in a manner similar to milk, the serous and thin part being set apart by itself, and the thicker part in turn consolidating with itself and being precisely unified. For towards the kidneys' readily drawing to themselves whatever is watery and thin and serous in the blood, both of these contribute: first the diffusion of the whole blood itself, and following upon it the separation, none of which can come about without strong heat. And for this reason all such drugs work against the expectorations of pus from the chest.

For their nature, [748] as has just been said, is heating and drying, and moreover contracting and separating, the thick part being gathered together into one, while whatever serous and thin matter is carried in the blood is secreted and separated off in accordance with the coming-together of the former. Now this the kidneys are the first to draw to themselves, but what is being condensed and dried out is no longer easily expectorated. And for this reason, as was said just now, such a drug must be cutting, yet not conspicuously hot, so that it may not dry strongly, and it must be given together with moistening gruels and drinks for the sake of the same use. Those which cleanse the kidneys, however, are likewise cutting, but there is no need at all of abundant moisture. And those which are suited to cut the stony concretions in them are themselves also sufficiently cutting, but partake least of heat; for heat, by drying out, consolidates the stone, and does not cut and divide it.

But those that are less hot, along with being able to cut, are better, such as the roots of the asparagus called 'royal', and those of the bramble, and kestron and polion, and ochre and burnt [749] glass, and the vinegar of squill, and all other such things. But Thessalus, that most clumsy fellow, just as he insolently abuses the other parts of the art with gross errors, so also attempts to disparage these, thinking that there is no drug that is specifically hepatic, or nephritic, or pleuritic. But his errors we have demonstrated in other writings; in the present discourse we shall expound the remaining powers of the simple drugs, beginning once more from the rarefying and the mouth-opening ones. For these too seem in some way to come close to those mentioned before, which we said cleanse and cut and unblock and divide, yet not to be altogether alike. First, then, the notions of these too must be defined, and then in this way their substances must be investigated. Those that open the pores in the skin they call rarefying, and those that open the mouths of the vessels, mouth-opening.

And indeed, of their opposites too, if something draws the pores together, they call it condensing; but if something closes the mouth, they no longer address it by a name of its own, [750] naming it instead by certain more generic ones: contracting, closing, constricting and stopping up. The nature of each: that of the rarefying ones is moderately hot and least of all drying and fine-particled; that of the mouth-opening ones coarse-particled, pungent and biting. Of their opposites, the condensing nature is cooling, yet neither earthy nor airy, but rather watery; while that which closes the openings is coarse-particled and cold. Examples of these: of rarefying nature are chamomile and marsh-mallow and the oil made from them, and not least also that made from wild cucumbers. But old oil too, and castor oil, and radish oil are of the same kind. Of mouth-opening power are all things that are both pungent and earthy: cyclamen, garlic, onions, the biles of bulls, the sediments of all the unguents that are at once coarse-particled and hot, such as the iris unguent and the marjoram unguent, which indeed also open up haemorrhoids that have become blind.

But those drugs said to open the mouth of the womb when it has closed because of some inflammation or dryness or scirrhus [751] would be of such a power accidentally, not primarily nor in themselves—just as neither are those which, when lips or eyelids or nostrils or pharynx or foreskin or seat or some other such mouth of an organ have closed because of inflammation, have cured the inflammation and thereby also corrected the closure. For these too would be said to be resolvers of inflammation, but by no means mouth-opening. Dioscorides errs in these matters, sometimes saying that a relaxing drug, or a softening, or a moistening, or an inflammation-resolving one, is of mouth-opening power. Such, then, are the substances of the rarefying and of the mouth-opening drugs. Of those opposite to them, the substance of the condensing ones is that of cold water and of houseleek and of purslane and of green caltrop and of fleawort and of the herb which they call mouse-ears, and of the lentil from the marshes, and, to put it simply, of all things that cool without being astringent.

Hence also mandrake and hemlock, henbane and poppy—I mean now the herbs themselves—if one uses them moderately, are condensing [752] in their powers; if more, they are not only condensing but already also numbing; and if to the greatest degree, they are no longer only numbing but already also mortifying. The substance of the drugs contrary to the opening ones, being coarse-particled and cold, belongs to all astringents, without any admixture (ἐπὶ μίκτον) of pungency. Sufficient examples of their material have been given in the fourth book, in which I have also explained the substance of such drugs, which is earthy and cold. So it is no longer any wonder if it alone is of a nature to draw together and close the mouths of the vessels that have been opened up contrary to nature; for in it alone are present all the things that what is to be drawn together requires: on account of the coarse-particled character of its consistency it falls upon the parts from outside and is unable to pass through the fine pores; on account of its cooling it compresses inward and draws together the neighbouring parts from every side into themselves; and because it dries—for every astringent was shown to be such—it feeds upon the moisture and tones the part.

But if all these things come together, the orifice will be closed, being drawn together from outside by the particles of the astringent substance as if by certain fingers [753]. But those drugs which are cold, either equally or more so, yet watery in their substances—such drugs both draw together and constrict only weakly, because of their softness. For everything that is going to compress and draw together anything whatever strongly requires a certain resistant and hard strength; and since the drugs that are more watery in their substances do not possess this, they draw together and condense the fine pores in each body, but are unable to constrict the whole organ from every side, so that with good reason such drugs are condensing but are not stopping. And understand me now as calling 'stopping' all those that hold back the perceptible excretions. For indeed the stopping body—that which holds within itself and lets nothing out perceptibly—has been termed by the Greeks stegnon (stopped-up).

These, then, are of such a kind in their mixtures and powers; but the rarefying ones heat in every case, for otherwise they could not at once diffuse and relax the substance, upon which follows also the widening of the pores. It is necessary, [754] however, that they be neither excessively hot in their mixtures — for such are by that point pungent and compel shivering — nor drying; for these too are both colliquative and painful to the sensitive bodies. Those, therefore, which heat without distress are the only ones of all that are rarefying. But if they are not only hot but also coarse-particled in their consistencies, then, when they are vehement and caustic, they melt down the bodies in the manner of fire and often produce eschars similar to those from cauteries; but when they heat less than so as to burn, they belong to the mouth-opening power, so that the mouth-opening drug (reading the transmitted τῶν as uncertain) is in its substance at once earthy and fiery, but has arrived at such a degree of heat as not yet to burn. But if it should be caustic and yet not vehemently so, and moreover fine-particled, such a thing will either be altogether non-biting, or with little biting and pain will melt away some of the fleshy parts.

For, by neither altering all at once, as the strongly hot things do, nor passing through with difficulty, as the coarse-particled things do, [755] it has an activity that escapes notice, if indeed, among alterations, it is the sudden changes that are most perceptible, and, among passages, the violent ones. For the coarse-particled caustic, in whatever part it settles, causes distress, being fixed in it like a splinter. But that kind is eschar-producing, in the same way as the caustics; whereas the drugs about which the argument is now concerned produce no eschar, and are called putrefying, though they have not obtained a name that is properly their own. For the truly putrefying things are those that moisten together with heating. Nevertheless we call them so because of the similarity of the symptom, for a painless destruction is brought about by both. Now the modes in which things are destroyed are several: for things that have been excessively cooled, excessively heated, excessively moistened and excessively dried are destroyed; but we do not say that all things that are destroyed putrefy, but only those that undergo this together with a foul smell. About the names, then, one should not be greatly concerned.

But one must know that the drugs called septic and putrefying, such as arsenic and sandarach and chrysocolla, [756] and dryopteris and pine-caterpillar and aconite, all melt and melt away, and especially the soft flesh, without pain. Some of them they specifically name 'reducing' (kathairetika), and they use them for the scarring-over of ulcers that have excess flesh. These too are of the same power, in genus, as the one named putrefying, but weaker to such a degree that they reduce only the surface of that upon which they fall, and are unable to advance into the depth, like also the flower of the Asian stone; such things, however, are certainly not of the same power as the truly scarring one. For those are of such a nature as neither to reduce nor to melt away anything of the flesh, but to harden and to dry: alum, and the gall-nut which they call omphakitis, and burnt copper, and especially the washed. For the unwashed has something reducing in it, as does copper scale too; but the washed is the finest of the scarring drugs. For that which is going to produce a scar well must both be moderately astringent and dry.

[757] Hence also the fruit of the Egyptian thorn, and the dry rinds of the pomegranate, and all such things are among the scarring drugs. But among the majority of physicians not only the appellation but also the knowledge of the power of all such drugs has been confused. For they sometimes name 'scarring' also the drugs that reduce and are colliquative of the flesh, because when we use these too the ulcers often arrive at a scar; but this happens neither primarily nor in accordance with their own proper power, nor with every use. For such drugs, when precisely dust-like, with the pestle of the mortar being rolled over the flesh, bring the ulcers to a scar. But if you should use a little more, it both bites and colliquates the flesh and makes the ulcer hollow, the opposite of the truly scarring drugs. For unless you apply a considerable amount of those, it will accomplish nothing. For in the scarring-over of level ulcers the task set before us is to alter the flesh and to make it skin.

This comes about through those [drugs] that are able to contract it and bind it [758] and compact and condense and dry and callus it; for the skin is, as it were, a kind of callused flesh. The drugs able to act in this way, then, are called scarring drugs primarily and properly; the others, the reducing ones, secondarily and accidentally, as also all those that dry without biting and without being astringent. For these too bring [wounds] to a scar accidentally, such a drug as myrrh is, and litharge; and oyster-shell, if it be burnt, and diphryges—for these too, sprinkled on dry, have often formed a scar. One must know, both in these discussions and in all the others, that where I add the word "often", I wish to indicate this: that such [drugs] sometimes also fail of what they promise, because they do not produce it primarily nor in accordance with their own power. The scarring drugs, however, are able in some measure to bring to a scar every level wound, just as the moderately and non-bitingly cleansing drugs are fillers of hollow ones.

But there will be a very full discussion concerning the power of such things in [759] the writings on the Therapeutic Method, with which this book has shared in many places, as was also stated earlier at its beginning. Therefore I think that, having now brought to a close the account concerning these, I shall pass to another kind of powers, those named drawing and repelling. Drawing, then, are all those that attract more vehemently the things lying in the depth; repelling, all those that drive away toward the depth the humours that approach in them. The substance of the former is hot and fine-particled, that of the latter, conversely, cold and coarse-particled. For the hot always draws, and the cold repels; but the fine-particled hot draws more vehemently, and the coarse-particled cold, such as the astringent, pushes more violently. So it is from the vehemence of the activity that each has its name.

The matter of the astringents, then, is evident; but as for that of the drawing drugs, one kind is self-grown, while another has its origin from a putrefaction that turns sour: self-grown is that of dittany, and that of propolis and thapsia, and that of sagapenum, and that of the juices, [760] the Cyrenaic and the Median, and whatever other there may be that is similar to these. From putrefaction, on the other hand, is that of leaven and that of the so-called psoricum. And now dung too, being from putrefaction—all kinds would thus indeed be of drawing power, but the difference among them is not small. For that of the pigeon is sufficiently drawing, and at an equal distance from this on either side stand that of the goose, toward the hotter, and that of the cock, toward the colder. That of humans and of pigs falls still further short of this. That of dogs is like the cleansing drugs, and more so when they eat bones. And that of the land crocodiles achieves this still more precisely. There is also another kind of drawing drugs, which attracts by affinity of quality, which is nothing other than by similarity of the whole substance, just as also things that are nourished draw to themselves their proper nourishment. Among such drugs are all the purgatives and some of the protective ones. And all such drugs must be hot.

For among things that are similar in their substances, the hotter is more drawing, [761] inasmuch as it has taken on heat as an ally to the similarity. For such a thing, drawing by two causes, will have the advantage over that which attracts by only one of them. And it will make no difference whether one speaks of an attractive (epispastikē), a drawing (helktikē) or a drawing-in (helkystikē) power. But since enough has been said about these too, let us pass on to the powers named alexeterial and alexipharmic. The nature of these too is twofold: some alter, while others evacuate from the affected body either the destructive venom or the deleterious drug. Now it alters either in respect of some single quality, or a conjugation of two, or in respect of the whole substances; and it evacuates by similarity of whole substance and by fine-particled heat. So the differences of the benefit derived from them will be four in all, two alterative and two evacuative. And the one that helps by the opposition of quality is obvious.

For if the deleterious drug, or the venom of the animal, should be cold, they will be helped by heating drugs; [762] but if hot, by cooling ones; and if dry, by moistening ones, but if moist, by drying ones; and so too, if it is at once cold and moist, by drying and heating ones, but if hot and dry, by moistening and cooling ones, and analogously in the remaining two conjugations. Nor is the alteration brought about through the powers that act according to the whole substance unclear to those who remember what has been demonstrated before in the commentaries On the Natural Faculties and, in addition, in those On Mixtures. For the powers that alter the deleterious drugs are in their nature midway between the bodies that are affected and the drugs that injure them, so that there is a proportion: as the body is to the alexipharmic power, so is that power to the deleterious drug; and likewise, as the deleterious is to the alexipharmic, so too is the alexipharmic to the body. And for this reason nearly all the things that are opposed to deleterious drugs, when taken in larger quantity, greatly injure the body of the animal.

It is necessary, therefore, that all such [763] powers be given in such a due proportion of quantity that they neither harm the body by their abundance nor, through smallness of amount, are overcome by the deleterious things. But this already belongs to the therapeutic method; for now let us hold to what comes next in order. Every deleterious venom is evacuated by drugs applied from without, such as those that effect the attraction either by heat or by the similarity of the whole substance. Here too the alexipharmic must be, as far as is at all possible, intermediate in its nature between the body which it treats and the venom which does the harm. For if it is most opposite to the body, it will rather act upon it like some deleterious thing, and will not evacuate the venom. For, to take up the whole matter once again for the sake of clarity, one must know that all deleterious powers are most opposite in mixture to the bodies harmed by them. If, then, they are evacuated by drugs similar in mixture, these too would surely be opposite to the natures of bodies.

And indeed they are in a way contrary, yet not to such a degree as to destroy, but rather they are of a double character, being established in the middle between those things that outright harm the body of the animal and [764] those that benefit it. Whether you wish to call them deleterious powers, or destructive, or corruption-producing, or anything else whatsoever, it will make no difference; and in the same way whether (you call the others) protective or alexipharmic. Nor indeed, if someone should wish to name those that are curative of venomous beasts 'protective', and those that are curative of deleterious drugs 'alexipharmic', as some have already thought fit, should one dispute with these people either over the names. For curing diseases in the appropriate manner comes not from these, but from the knowledge of the things themselves. Since about these matters too as much has been said as is proportionate to the present purpose, let us now pass on in order to the account of the pain-relieving and soothing or mitigating powers, or however one might wish to name them. A pain-relieving power, then, is in one case really such, in another only so called, as if someone were to say that even a dead man is free of pain. The really pain-relieving power, then, is that of the things that heat in the first order, whenever it is contained in a fine-particled substance.

But that of the things called cold [is anodyne only in name], when, employing an unmixed cooling, they numb [765] the part; and numbness is all but insensibility. Those things, however, which stop pains by curing the condition would not reasonably be called anodyne; for this belongs in common to all things that treat. The truly anodyne drugs, then, must be fine-particled and not much hotter than the moderate ones, for the sake of evacuating, dispersing, rarefying, thinning, concocting and evening out everything that, in the pained parts, has been caught and shut in—whether of pungent or viscous or thick humours, or of many such blocked up in fine pores, or indeed of some vaporous and thick, or sufficiently cold, pneuma—having no suitable way out.

So they must have no astringent power whatsoever attached to them, not even if the place or the affection should additionally require it; from which it is clear that sometimes [such a drug] will not benefit the condition at all but will only soothe the pain, in which case indeed it will truly be called pain-relieving, while sometimes it will also be of some benefit to the condition itself and will have a twofold power, being a drug at once pain-relieving [766] and curative. But about such matters too more will be said in the books of the Therapeutic Method. For the present it suffices to go through the point that, of these drugs specifically named pain-relieving, some, as has been said, belong to the first order of heating drugs—and these are indeed truly pain-relieving, like dill oil—while some are nearly the same [in mixture] as our own body, like those called suppuratives, about whose material it has been spoken earlier. Distinctions concerning their use will be drawn in the books of the Therapeutic Method. But those which, when drunk, produce lethargic sleep (καταφορά), and which for this reason are called by most people pain-relieving and soporific, are of the mixture most opposite to the truly pain-relieving ones. For they all cool the body and numb the sensation to such a degree that, if a little more should be drunk, they bring on death. The best of them for the use at hand are those that dry.

And those which contain an abundance of cold moisture, as hemlock does, are not good when drunk; such too is mandrake, [767] except for the dry bark of its root, and henbane, except for its seed. Among these the white seed is better than the black. Some, however, are contrary to us in their whole substances, and for this reason, even if the smallest amount is taken, they harm in every case, such as dryopteris and the pine-caterpillar and thapsia and the mad strychnos and quicksilver, and some of the mushrooms, and the saliva and the biles of venomous animals. For all such things are deleterious by their kind, not by their quantity. And for this reason none of them is put into the protective antidotes, as are the juice of the poppy and myrrh and storax and saffron. For these, if they are drunk in too large a quantity, some drive one mad and others bring on death; but when mixed with the other ingredients in a certain due proportion they give help. Those of them which harm the understanding are, straightaway, for the most part productive of heaviness of the head, filling the head with a multitude of bad vapours. Some also attack the mouth of the stomach, so that the parts about the head are affected in sympathy.

And in common, all of them harm the brain in a twofold way, either [768] being opposed to it in their whole substances, or altering the mixture in respect of one or two qualities. But since these matters too have been discussed sufficiently, at least for present purposes, it would be timely to take up again the heads of what has been said and to add what seems to be lacking to the account. For in strict truth nothing remains, since all the secondary powers have already been discussed, as to what sort they are according to genus, and not a few of those according to species have also been set beside them as examples, starting from which one could go through the remaining ones. But for the sake of clarity it would be no worse to recapitulate them in brief heads.

To take an example at once: everyone speaks of a certain purgative power, yet not everyone grasps alike that the name signifies two things: one, something common to all things that in any way whatever clear out the superfluities of the animal; the other, something in the pre-eminent sense, applied to those which do so through vomitings or through evacuation of the belly; nor [do they grasp] that the purging which takes place either through the nostrils and [769] the mouth is of the same genus as such purgations. They call the drugs poured in through the nostrils for the sake of purging the head errhines, while all those that are gargled and chewed they gather under one name and call apophlegmatizing, and they name their powers apophlegmatic. Of the same genus as these are also all those which, when applied to the womb, purge. For all those which I have listed as purging possess a drawing power, some of some one humour, others of two or even more, and this is common to them. Whereas all those which, by thinning the thick and viscous humours, are naturally fitted either to move urine or to assist the expectorations from the chest and lung do indeed clear out as well, but are not named in the same way as the aforementioned; rather, some are called diuretic and cough-drugs, others promoters of the menses, differing from the aforementioned in that they do not possess a drawing power of humours proper to them, as those do. Accordingly, in these cases too the account requires a further distinction, of the following sort.

Those which are applied to the womb in pessaries, or fomentations, or in some such manner, [770] act by a twofold cause: some provoking [the flow] by heating alone, others by the so-called drawing and purgative powers, which we have shown to produce the evacuations by affinity with the things drawn. But those which are drunk produce the evacuations by thinning the blood and by unblocking and opening up the pores, not, however, by any drawing power. The former, then, are of the same kind as purgatives, the latter as those which generate milk and seed, about which we shall speak a little later, after we have first gone through the cough-drugs, since these too are named in a twofold way, some from producing coughs, others only from stopping them. Their powers are most opposite to one another. For some are of a thinning nature, others of a thickening one. The thinning power, then, arises in hot and fine-particled substances, the thickening in cold and coarse-particled ones. Let this discussion, then, end here. It is fitting to pass on to the one deferred a little earlier.

For there is a certain community and likeness of actions and powers both [771] in the things that promote and in those that stop menses, milk and seed. And somehow adjacent to these lie the diuretics and the cough-remedies (βηχικά), wherefore one must speak about each of them in turn. The powers productive of milk and seed are some of them in drugs only, others also in foods. In drugs, whenever by thoroughly heating the phlegmatic humours we change them into blood; in foods, according to the likeness of the whole substance, and whenever they are of good humour and moderately moist and of a lukewarm heat, of just such a kind as milk also is. For the blood partakes of a heat commensurate for the animal, while the yellow bile partakes of a heat greater than the measure, just as phlegm partakes of coldness. Milk, so far as concerns heat, stands in the middle between phlegm and blood, yet it does not stand at an equal distance from each, but is farther from phlegm and nearer to blood. So whenever milk is collected insufficiently in the breasts and you wish more to be produced, examine the matter of the blood: for either it is less than is fitting or more faulty.

The [772] lesser, then, requires that the whole regimen be moistening and warming; the more faulty, if it is bilious, requires first purgation, and then the kind of regimen that has been described; but if it is phlegmatic, it requires drugs that warm, either in the first or in the second order, yet do not dry. Better among these are those which are not only drugs but also foods: rocket and fennel and dill. And I mean the herbs themselves while still green and moist; for when dry they both dry and warm more than is needed. Of this kind too are smyrnion and celery and sion and polion, these too green, before they have been dried. For indeed all drying things, feeding upon the moisture of the blood, render it at once thicker and less, and hotter than it should be, if they are hot by nature, but colder, if cold.

And surely it needs to be moderately hot and in no way thick for the generation of milk; whence all things of that sort extinguish milk rather than generate it, whereas those that heat, as has been said, but share in no evident dryness, were reasonably said to have [773] powers generative of milk. These, then, are few in number; for it is not at all easy to hit upon the aforesaid due proportion in the mixture. But infinite, as one might so put it, and beyond enumeration are those that harm milk; for both those that heat more than they should, and those that dry, and those that cool—the former damaging the quality of the blood, the latter making its whole substance less—prevent milk from coming to be. Similar in power to those just mentioned are those things which are naturally such as to provoke or to stop the menses. For the matter common to both is the blood in the veins. This, then, whenever it is at once free-flowing and moderate in quantity, furnishes an abundant supply to each of the two. And indeed, that there are not small veins common to the breasts and the womb, and which these happen to be, has been stated in other works. For this reason, whenever the blood is carried to the one of the two parts, the other is dried up.

And for this reason, those women in whom the menses flow in due measure do not collect milk in the breasts, and those in whom [774] this is abundant have their menses completely held back. It is therefore no wonder if the regimens and the drugs that generate and those that stop the purgation from the womb in each month and the generation of milk in the breasts are similar. They differ, however, to this extent: insofar as the conditions of the uterus sometimes require hotter and more cutting ones. For the veins there need to have their mouths opened more than those in the breasts, and they require blood that flows more freely, since the uterus itself contributes nothing to its passage. For the menses are sent into the veins in it, not drawn; but into the breasts [the blood] is not only sent but also drawn, and for this reason the blood that does not arrive in sufficient quantity at the breasts needs in addition less assistance from drugs. And whatever promotes the blood's passing downward (ὑπέρχεσθαι), these things also help deficient purgations.

But those [purgations] that have been impaired to a greater degree, or are even entirely held back, none of such things any longer cures; rather savin [775] and meum, iris and calamint, pennyroyal and dittany, asarum and costus, cassia and cinnamon, amomum and aristolochia, and bounion, and whatever others are of this kind, cure the complete suppressions of the purgations of the womb. For such things also lead the way for the urine. But in this one respect alone do they differ from those same drugs that are named diuretic, in that they do not dry strongly. For heating is common to the three classes of drugs, both those that cooperate with the generation of milk and those that cooperate with the flows of the menses and of urine. They differ, however, in the amount of heat and in the fact that some dry and others do not; for those that do not dry and heat moderately are useful for the generation of milk, whereas those that heat to a greater degree, yet do not dry strongly, are good for the flows of the menses. And urination both of these promote, and for this no less also those that heat while drying.

And for this reason such drugs have been called diuretic par excellence, not because they alone set urination in motion, but because they set it in motion alone, without menses and [776] milk. For, in addition to everything else, the drying drugs are not even suitable for expectorations from the chest and lung. For those too need to be cut, but not dried, just as indeed the stones in the kidneys and bladder do. But such drugs have been discussed earlier. Just as in the case of milk, so too in the case of seed, people are accustomed to name some drugs generative, and those opposed to these quenching, others provocative, and those opposed to these checking. Generative, then, are those that generate what did not previously exist, and quenching those that destroy it; provocative are those that bring what has been gathered in the depth to the surface, and those opposed to these are the checking ones. Generative of seed, then, are those foods that are at once nourishing and flatulent and akin to the whole substances; and those drugs that are pneumatic and hot; quenching are all those that dry and all those that cool and are opposed to the substances; and furthermore provocative are those that are flatulent and hot without drying, while checking are their opposites.

For since the substance of the seed [777] has its generation from a useful residue, and is also pneumatic, all those things that are able to generate and to provoke seed must be at once nutritive and pneumatic. Bulbs, then, and chickpeas and beans and octopuses and pine-nut are called, and are, foods rich in seed; skink and satyrion are drugs. Nourishments and at the same time drugs rich in seed are the seed of flax and rocket. But all those foods and drugs whose nature is to cool, which thicken and congeal and render the seed stagnant, have the power of things that restrain it, not of things that destroy it. For lettuces and blites and oraches and gourd and mulberries and melons and cucumbers, whether they be ripe or whether they be not ripe. But those which dry do not permit the seed to come into being at all, even if they are hot in nature, like rue; and if they do not heat either, much more so, like the water-lily. These, at any rate, it is reasonable to suppose are contrary to seed also in respect of the specific property of their substance.

And the same analogy of foods and [778] drugs can be found in the case of milk and of the menses. In another way, there fall under the same genus as these all those things that assist the expectorations from the respiratory organs and all those that are naturally such as to move urination. For all these are of thinning power, just as their opposites are of thickening power. But concerning the thinning diet a separate work has been written, in which, in the same book, the thickening things are no less made clear. As for the thinning and thickening drugs, select them from the three books that follow these, taking as your aim, in the case of the thinning ones, those that have heat and fineness of parts, and in the case of the thickening ones, the opposites. For it has been shown by us in what precedes that the nature of fine-particled drugs is a distinct one, belonging not only to those that heat; and in the same way also that of coarse-particled ones belongs not only to those that cool. And just as in the case of such things there is a certain analogy in their powers, in the same way one must seek it in the case of all, even if no established name happens to exist.

At any rate, certain powers are called 'sharp-sighting' (oxydorkic), namely those which set the eyes right when, though having no perceptible affection, they function badly. [779] And clearly there must also exist, in the case of the ears and the nostrils and each of the other senses, analogously, some such power; yet no 'sharp-hearing' power has in fact received a name, just as none has in the case of smell or taste or touch, even though in the perceptible things themselves it exists analogously. And if one were to extend the similarity still further, there would necessarily be, in the case of each of our parts as well, some such power of drugs, by which, evidently, the function of the part becomes better—as, for instance, that of the stomach. For here too one can often find a certain atony of it of such a kind as dim-sightedness is in the case of the eyes, when they are neither inflamed nor afflicted with flux nor ulcerated nor have any other manifest evil.

And indeed the drugs that correct such a condition of the stomach have been called peptic (digestive), not having, in the form of their appellation, anything [780] analogous to the sharp-sight-producing drugs, but being closely similar in their action and power. Since we also said that certain powers have been named from parts of the body, it would be no bad thing to go through these too. For they are suited neither, as one might suppose, to all the affections of the part, nor to some one affection in such a way as to benefit no other; rather, they have received their appellation from the part either because they are used most often, or because they act most effectively, upon this particular part. Ophthalmic powers, because we use them both most effectively and most often upon the eyes, as for instance the collyrium of roses and that of pompholyx and the one called knikos and the libanium and all the others, which one may also use when the ears are affected, and the mouth, and the nostrils, and the genitals and the seat, yet neither so often nor so beneficially. And again hepatic, splenic, pleuritic and stomachic powers, since we see these too benefiting each of the parts mentioned both most effectively and most often.

But what the cause of the benefit [781] is will be stated in the treatise on the Therapeutic Method, in which we shall also go through all the other matters concerning the use of drugs, so that there is no need to prolong things further here, except perhaps to remark briefly on the use of names which certain other physicians among the more recent ones introduced in their innovating, and not least those called Methodics. For that certain powers are said by them to be checking, or constricting, or contracting, or repelling, or something else of that sort, is neither absurd nor obscure. But when they say that certain materials or powers are metasyncritic, what is said is neither clear nor true nor proper to their sect, seeing that they claim to shun the indication derived from dogmatic suppositions, since the manifest communities (καινότητας) suffice for them. But that, when the pores of the body are turned aside from the state according to nature into the state contrary to nature, certain affections are constituted in the peculiar character of their alteration, is a dogmatic supposition.

And it follows upon this also that there are, for such affections, [782] certain metasyncritic powers, namely ones that alter the pore-formation of our composite that is contrary to nature. For this is indeed how Thessalus and his followers use the names, and then in the case of those who are chronically afflicted with fluxes they employ such powers, having neither demonstrated that an alteration of the pores occurs in such affections nor being able to show that these particular drugs are by nature such as to metasyncrise the faulty pore-formation. For why, in the gods' name, do mustard and thapsia and pellitory, and the root of the caper, and in general all things whose nature is to burn, if they remain for a long time in contact with the body, metasyncrise the pore-formation? For that the rheumatic parts are benefited by such drugs is clearly evident; but why they are benefited is a problem of natural theory. We, then, say that their mixture is moist and cold, and that for this reason they need things that heat and dry; but others will state a different cause, according as they happen to hold views about the elements of the body.

It is not, however, fitting for anyone who is led by another sect to utter [783] the name of 'metasyncrisis', except for those who both consider and name the bodies of animals 'compounds' (synkrimata), composed of masses that are atomic, or minimal, or partless, or homoeomerous; and not even for all of these, but for those who, like Thessalus, refer such diseases to the rule of the alteration of the pores—for Thessalus does not say this insofar as he is a Methodist. For whenever he discourses with us as a Methodist, he withdraws from the indication drawn from hidden things; rather, [he says it] insofar as he is a dogmatist, beginning from the same elements as Asclepiades, though certainly not following him in every respect. But this is not the occasion to go through such matters at greater length. For some of them are more proper to the Therapeutic Method, and others will be stated more precisely in the [books] on the sect of Themison and Thessalus.

It is therefore now time to bring this book too to a close here, after adding to it two further heads: the one falling among the matters deferred earlier, concerning the contrary powers; the other necessary for the book that follows, and defining the [784] order of each of the drugs that heat and cool, moisten and dry. The contrary powers, then, are to be judged from their effects, as we have shown many times throughout this whole treatise, when we said that certain powers are clogging, contrary to the cleansing ones, unblocking contrary to the obstructing ones, softening contrary to the hardening ones, and relaxing contrary to the tensing ones. For astringent, or pungent or bitter or sweet or sour, we showed to be not powers of drugs but gustatory qualities, so that either the contrariety is not to be sought in these at all, or it is not to be sought as in powers. And the point of reference even in these is twofold: their activities and their mixtures. The activities consist in condensing and rarefying, or drawing something from the depth or repelling it, and thickening the materials or thinning them, or blocking the pores or unblocking them.

The mixtures, on the other hand, [are to be judged] according to hot and cold, moist and dry, concerning all of which a sufficient determination has been made in the fourth book, [785] where we showed that the astringent is earthy and cold, the sour fine-particled and cold, the bitter earthy and fine-particled, and that which is cold without any notable quality watery. So too the pungent was shown to be fiery, and the salty earthy and hot, though not yet fiery. Likewise also the sweet is hot, but not yet caustic. And all oily things are both watery and airy. And their actions, surely, followed upon their mixtures. For the astringent is of such a nature as to contract, compress, condense, repel and thicken, and, before all these, to cool and dry; the sour to cut, divide and thin, to unblock and cleanse thoroughly without heating; and the pungent acts similarly to the sour, at least as regards thinning thoroughly and cleansing thoroughly. But it differs in that the sour cools while the pungent heats, and further in that the former repels while the latter draws and disperses.

So too the bitter thoroughly cleanses the pores and scours and thins and [786] cuts the thickness of the humours without evident heat. The watery cold thickens and congeals and contracts and compacts and deadens and numbs. The pungent thins, thoroughly cleanses, disperses, and bursts open and draws and forms an eschar. The salty contracts and binds tight, preserves as in pickling, dries without notable heat or cooling. The sweet concocts, relaxes, rarefies. The oil-like moistens, softens, relaxes. It is therefore now easy, measuring by what has been said, to discover which of the flavours are opposite in their mixtures and which in their actions. For me it would be a fitting moment, once I have defined the orders of the mixtures and powers in drugs, to bring the discourse to a close here. Now the well-proportioned drug, such that it is of a mixture like that of the body to which it is applied, inasmuch as it neither dries nor moistens, nor cools nor heats, it is appropriate to call neither dry nor moist, nor cold nor hot.

But that which is either drier or moister, or hotter [787] or colder, is named from the predominating power. And it suffices, under each predominance, to establish four orders with a view to practical use, calling hot in the first order whatever heats us, yet not manifestly, but with the additional need of some rational demonstration. So too cold and moist and dry, whatever requires demonstration, not yet having acquired a strong or manifest activity. Those things, however, that are already of such a nature as to heat or cool or dry or moisten clearly will be said to be of the second order. Those that do so already vehemently, yet not to the extreme, of the third. And those that are of such a nature as to heat so as both to form an eschar and to burn, of the fourth. So likewise those that are of such a nature as to cool more vehemently, so as already to mortify, these too are of the fourth. But it is not possible to find anything that dries in the fourth order without burning; for whatever dries to the extreme, this in every case also burns.

Of the third order of drying things, however, something can also be non-burning, as for instance all those things which are strongly astringent, [788] among which are omphacium and sumach and alum and balaustion and the unripe oak-gall (omphakitis). Among these very things, some are close to those which burn, such as scale of copper and burnt copper, so that they lie somewhere in the indistinct region between the third and the fourth order; others are in the middle, such as burnt copper if it has been washed; and others at the beginning, such as hypocistis. In the same way, in the second and the fourth order too, one can make threefold distinctions; for the cautery surely does not dry in the same way as mustard, even though both belong to the fourth order. Concerning all these matters distinctions will be drawn in what follows, under each simple drug separately.

But since something is also called softening and relaxing, rarefying and condensing, clogging and dispersing, and very many others similar to these, it would be better to go through such things too; and together with them, or even before them, also the [620] substance and at the same time the power of all the flavours, about which something has been said at the end of the first of these commentaries, when I also set out the passage of Plato from the Timaeus; but there it was for the sake of recalling the perceptible affections which the tongue is naturally disposed to undergo in the case of each of them, whereas here my account will be about their substance and power. For surely the other parts of the animal too are affected similarly to the tongue, yet they do not perceive the affections accurately; whereas the tongue, possessing, in addition to being affected, also accuracy of sensation, is capable of discerning the nature of all these. For indeed it is not the case (οὐ καὶ δὴ τότε) that what is hot or cold or dry or wet is naturally such as either to cool or heat or dry or moisten the tongue, but not also each of the other parts; rather, just as it disposes and alters this one, so too it disposes and alters the others, the difference among them arising in respect of more and less, not in respect of being affected or not being affected.

For that the tongue is by nature capable of discerning a dry and a wet and a hot and a cold body no less than all the other parts of the animal [621] is obvious to everyone; but bitternesses and sweetnesses, saltinesses and sournesses, harshnesses and acerbities and pungencies, it alone is believed to distinguish, although the similarity of the affections can be found in all the other parts as well, and especially in those that are ulcerated. For indeed the hardness and density of the skin shuts out and resists and prevents the powers of the things falling upon it from outside from passing through to the flesh. For thus too that saying was spoken by Hippocrates, that 'to ulcers the cold is biting', although to the skin, before it was ulcerated, it was not biting. And the cold is biting also to the eyes and to the nostrils and to the parts of the animal in the mouth.

and not least to the inner parts of the stomach and intestines, so that it is often even difficult to discriminate whether someone is chilled or is being bitten on account of the pungency of a humour; and these things come about with good reason. For since the cold, whatever it touches, draws together the substance of those things and condenses and constricts it, first it is necessary in this process that the thin moistures be excreted, [622] just as the tear from the eyes and the coryza from the nostrils; and then it also appears biting to them, though in a different manner from the hot. For it is not by eroding what is continuous but by tearing it apart that the cold is at once painful and biting; whence it does not appear such to hard bodies either. For when soft bodies are drawn together and compressed, it happens both that their moisture is squeezed out and that their parts are torn apart: the moisture, as in a sponge that is drawn together and compressed by our hands; the being torn apart, as in things that are divided and pulled apart, whether by us dragging with our hands or by something else. For it is necessary that rare and soft bodies too undergo something of this sort from the cold, since the rarity readily admits the cooling within, and the soft parts in the depth are still more readily congealed by it.

Accordingly the cold, entering through each of the pores in rare bodies—such as all ulcerated parts are, and the eyes and nostrils and mouth and the parts about the belly—takes hold of all the parts of the bodies being cooled and, in a certain manner drawing them together and compacting them with many [623] holds all round, tears them away from the parts continuous with them. It is necessary, then, that in this affection not a few empty spaces come to be, not only because the thin moistures, being squeezed, are excreted, but also because the soft substance is drawn together into a smaller place. But an empty space cannot come into being in continuous bodies while their continuity is preserved.
