If, therefore, one does come into being, it is clear that the continuity is destroyed and the continuous body is torn apart, and in this there arises the affection of sensation that is at once painful and biting. Yet the quality of the two is not the same—of those things that bite by cooling and of those that bite by heating—but in the case of the former we at once also have a sensation of the substance being drawn together and constricted, whereas in the case of the latter one of its being dissolved and diffused. And indeed the speed too is not alike in the two affections; rather, in the case of cooling things the biting is somewhat slower, whereas in the case of heating things it runs through most swiftly.

Since, then, it has now been sufficiently distinguished, both by the nature of the things themselves and by our perception of them, and it has been clearly stated [624] in what way the hot and in what way the cold appear biting, one ought surely to reason, even before hearing it from us, that of the biting drugs some must necessarily be hot in their powers, others cold. And from us one may further learn the distinctions among them precisely, having first recalled that we call both a drink and a bath, when they are well-tempered, hot, sometimes using the term loosely; for they ought rather to be called well-tempered and moderate than hot. Things that are hot in this way, then, are gentle and friendly; for what is condensed and congealed in our bodies is diffused, and it is in this affection above all that pleasure lies for living beings. But when they persist for a long time, even these gradually become painful; for it passes over into such an excess of diffusion that our substance is dispersed, dissolved and scattered. But even in this case they cause distress without biting, producing faintness and a collapse of the power, so that death too follows.

But those that are still hotter than these cut and divide and separate the substance, so that of necessity they appear biting, just as [625] boiling water does and fire itself. And of cold things, in the same way, those that contract but do not yet tear apart the continuity of the body that comes near them are merely cold, but not yet in any way biting. But those that, in addition to contracting, tear apart — and plainly all such things employ compression violently — present themselves as biting. Now contracting and congealing the underlying matter is always the property of the cold, while diffusing and melting is that of the hot; but common to both, when they have been increased beyond measure, is biting. Those, then, that are precisely cold and hot, in addition to all the other rare and soft parts of which we spoke earlier, now take hold of our skin as well. And I myself remember once travelling through snow so deep that no part of the ground appeared bare; the air appeared perfectly clear, and a certain breath was blowing off from the snow, so extremely cold that it bit not only the eyes, or indeed the nostrils, but the whole face as well. And if someone put out a hand, it took hold of this too in the same way.

But all those that fall short of extreme cooling or heat do not bite the [626] skin: the cooling ones, because they are able neither to tear apart anything of its continuity, on account of its hardness, nor to succeed in penetrating into the depth, because of the condensation of the surface; the heating ones, both because they do not corrode but only diffuse, and because they sometimes pass readily through the pores. And what contributes most to affections of this kind is the coarse-particled or fine-particled character of the substance of the drugs. For among the cooling ones the fine-particled reach the depth more, and for this reason bite more vehemently; while among the heating ones the coarse-particled ulcerate more, and for this reason cause distress more violently. Now air is more fine-particled, earth more coarse-particled, and water is between both. But air, when set on fire, becomes flame, and earth live coal, whereas water receives strong warmth but becomes neither flame nor live coal, because of its innate moisture. For flame and live coal are forms of fire.

And all fire is hot and dry, but it is not possible for water to become dry, and for this reason it does not receive the quality of fire exactly, as earth and air do. No drug, then, [627] is as hot as flame or live coal or boiling water; but even if it is extremely hot, it certainly, at any rate, falls very far short of these. Nevertheless their heat does advance as far as burning, whenever it is contained in a coarse-particled substance. But those [heats] contained in fine-particled substances sometimes do not bite at all, but only heat; and there are times when it is biting, yet does not thereby also burn. One must keep in mind the notion of fine-particled and coarse-particled things, namely that we call fine-particled those which are quickly dissolved into fine parts, and coarse-particled those which cannot undergo this. Now that which dissolves them is the heat in the body of the animal, in whatever manner they happen to be applied on each occasion; but their being broken up into fine or coarse parts they have from their own nature, so that, among cooling drugs too, those which are coarse-particled cannot bite, since they do not get so far as to penetrate the outer surface of the skin.

But those that are fine-particled both penetrate easily and reach to the [628] depth and bite the soft parts of the animal; and still more biting are those that are at once fine-particled and uneven in their mixtures. And it has been shown in what precedes that nearly all are uneven. For it is either impossible or very difficult to find any substance whatsoever that is precisely homoeomerous. At any rate, we said that wine has in itself one coarse-particled residue, from which, as it is separated out and carried down over time, the lees are formed; and another, which is called the 'flower', which floats on the surface during the time of boiling, but later is carried down into the lees; and a third, watery one, mixed through the whole of the wine, to which also the boiling belongs first and foremost. And a fourth, in addition to these, is the real wine itself. And it has been shown that in oil too and in milk and in all the other juices there is a similar nature of residues, and still more in all mined substances taken as wholes.

Having recalled these things, we must now investigate concerning all drugs, and first of all guard against suffering what most of those who have inquired into such matters [629] have suffered. For they construct their argument as though all of them were homoeomerous, not conceding that either wine or oil or any of the others is composed of parts differing in their powers; and still more than in these cases, with regard to vinegar they are amazed if we dare to say that it has lost the innate heat of the wine but possesses the heat that comes from putrefaction—which is indeed also the view of Aristotle and Theophrastus. For the vinous parts of the wine are chilled in the change into vinegar, while the watery residue, as it putrefies, comes to possess a certain acquired heat, just as do all other things that have putrefied. And vinegar becomes something composite, made up of parts most opposite in their powers, some of them chilled, others hot, just like all the ashes of burnt wood. For in those too what is, as it were, an ember-like residue (empyreuma) is scattered about in small particles, and this is quite hot, while all the rest is earthy and cold.

And for this reason, whenever ash that has been steeped in water is strained in due measure through certain rare bodies, the hot and [630] pungent parts are carried off together with it in this process, while what is left over is no longer hot, since it has deposited its fiery parts in the water. People call such water lye, which is analogous to sea-water and brine in respect of its condition, its generation, and its power. For those are composed of water and salts, while the water that washes through the ash, having become composite out of itself and the parts it has carried along, in this way produces what is named lye; and if we did not already know beforehand that it came into being from water and the sooty parts of the ash, we would perhaps suppose it to be a simple and uncompounded body.

For we have experienced something of this sort also in the case of vinegar: being unable to see its generation through sense-perception, we disbelieve the argument. But, if nothing else, having at least observed the difference of the unripe grape from it, we shall be right to believe that not only a sour flavour but also some other, pungent flavour has been mixed into it; and for this reason the juice of the unripe grape cools completely, so that it is also supremely suited for causus, when applied over the mouth of the stomach or the whole of the hypochondria, and for everything whatsoever that we may wish to cool, [631] whereas vinegar is not so in like manner. For it is not strictly one thing, nor sour only, but also pungent. So then, whatever is sour only is in every case cold, whether it be pear, or apple, or sumach, or the fruit from brambles, or that from the mulberry, or that from the pomegranate, or whatever other fruit, or juice, or plant, such as oxylapathon and oxalis, which indeed they also call oxys. For if, when you taste it, the sourness in it appears to you strong and clear, but nothing of pungency shows itself, you will in every case find this flavour to be cooling; and use it with confidence, whether you wish to use it against causus, applying it on the hypochondria, or against erysipelas, or against some other hot affection. And in the same way you will clearly find all cold diseases harmed by it. But when the quality appears to you mixed, then along with pungency one must also suspect heat, while along with astringency one must suspect another kind of coldness. For sour coldness is fine-particled, whereas astringent coldness is coarse-particled.

[632] But the proofs of these matters we shall state a little later. What it is necessary first to advise those who investigate such things, without sophistical imposture, for the sake of truth itself, it is now time for me to say: that one must not only be trained in reasoning, by means of the logical methods which I constantly recommend, and which I set out in my commentaries on demonstrations, but must also carefully exercise the sense of taste upon the humours (flavours), beginning from those that possess some single quality whatsoever in the most evident manner.

If you wish to understand pungency clearly, [do so] in the case of garlic and onion and the things similar to them, tasting continually and chewing for a very long time and trying to store accurately in your memory the perception of the affection that arises; if astringency, in the case of gall-nut and sumach and the like; if bitterness, by tasting nitre and bile; if sweetness, boiled-down must and honey; and further, in addition to these, whether you wish to take water as being without quality or as intermediate in quality with respect to taste, I ask you, having tasted this [633] water too, to hold it accurately in memory, and most of all that water which displays none of the qualities I have now mentioned, neither sweetness nor pungency nor sourness nor bitterness, and in addition to these, moreover, which is neither considerably hot nor excessively cold. For setting out from here you will arrive more readily both at the discrimination of all the other faint flavours and at that of those which, as I for my part say, are sweet, but as certain others say, watery, such as is the flavour of green reeds and of dog's-tooth grass and, in addition, of wheat and barley and emmer and many others, which Theophrastus too mentions, inquiring whether several species of sweet flavours are to be posited, or whether they are to be supposed to differ from one another by the more and the less. But concerning these matters I shall make the distinctions again later.

Whatever sensation the most qualityless water affords you, whenever you find such a sensation in one of the dry things, such a thing is clearly outside all manifest heat and cold, having a condition [634] as nearly as possible in the middle, or even inclining a little toward the cold. But if, being so disposed in respect of the difference according to heat and cold, it should be dry in its consistency, it must necessarily be earthy and dry without biting. All such drugs are called by the physicians "clogging", just as most of those that have been thoroughly washed; starch, pompholyx and white lead and lime and cadmia and Cretan earth and Cimolian earth and chondros and Samian star and fullers' earth are among the clogging drugs. Some of them are not only earthy but also watery in nature, and some also contain in themselves not a little air; all these, however, are viscous, and for this reason clogging. For the nature of the clogging drugs is twofold: the one precisely earthy and dry, the other in every case viscous, but mixed from water and earth and for the most part also air, as sweet oil also is. It has been said earlier what kind of thing I mean by "sweet".

This, then, is mixed from airy and earthy and watery substance together; the white of the egg [635] is composed in some way from the same things, but is earthier than oil; and indeed the cheesy part of milk is clogging too, as is the soft fat of the pig. For the soft fat of a bull and of a he-goat has much pungency, and fiery pungency at that; that of an ox and a she-goat less so, yet the hard fat of these too is already somewhat pungent. For indeed the soft fat of such animals is called hard fat (stear), on account of its thickness; for in addition it is not only hotter but also earthier than that of pigs. That of a goose and of a cock is both hotter and drier than that of pigs, but it is also fine-particled and least earthy. So too is that of all winged creatures, because the substance of their body too has no small share of the airy. But about these there is another discussion. At any rate, all soft fats that do not yet have any pungency are clogging of the pores, and the drier and earthier ones more so. Such too is washed wax; for it too lays aside the pungency that comes from the honey. It is evident that these things are not said about wax that is bitter by nature, as the Pontic is.

For that one has its bitterness from wormwood, and even if you were to wash it ten thousand times, you would not wash the bitterness out completely. One must also beware of the wax derived from pungent and thyme-flavoured honey, whenever you wish to prepare a drug that is entirely non-biting. Suitable for washing, therefore, is the wax from a more watery and least pungent honey. Such, then, are the clogging drugs. Concerning the astringent and the sour ones I return once more. The astringent ones are earthy and coarse-particled in the consistency of their masses, and cold in their quality; the sour ones are fine-particled in their bodies, but cold in the same way as the astringent ones. The proof concerning both is twofold: according to sense-perception, by way of inference (ἐξ ἀπαγωγῆς), and according to reason, from their substance. Of the proofs there will be stated first the one that is clearer to most people, but weaker with regard to scientific demonstration.

All the fruits from trees, as many as appear sweet to us when they have ripened, are, when just coming into being, both acerbic and dry in their consistency, each according to the nature of the [637] tree that generates it, as Theophrastus too said somewhere—olives, grapes, apples, pomegranates, mulberries, dates, pears. But as they advance in time they become moister, and they take on sourness in addition to the acerbity, and, laying this aside little by little, they become sweet in turn as they are brought to completion. Some, however, do not acquire the sweetness even on the trees, but only after they have been removed, with time. Others again do not pass through sourness as an intermediate stage, but arrive directly from acerbity at sweetness, as does also that of the olive. And indeed, that all are concocted by the hot is clear, and that this is of two kinds—the one the proper innate heat of each, the other from without, from the sun, yet connate and proper to them—we surely know plainly, if we remember the elements that always underlie our account. But if they are more acerbic at the beginning, and become sweet as they ripen, then their sweetness arose for them from warmth, and their sourness and acerbity from cooling.

And since, at [638] the beginning, while they are still woody, as Theophrastus too said, they are at once dry and acerbic, whereas the abundance of the moisture flowing into them renders them sour, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is earthier, the sour one moister; so that Plato too spoke correctly when he defined them: 'all such earthy particles as are carried in the juices, which, being dissolved (κατατηκόμενα) and contracting and drying up the moist portions of the sensitive parts of the tongue, appear acerbic when they are rougher, and harsh when they roughen less.' And we, in addition to this, shall correctly say that such a flavour is also cold in its mixture. For if it were earthy only, it would be clogging, not acerbic; and in a way the argument, having now passed over to the very substance of the flavours, lays hold of scientific demonstration.

For if it clearly belongs to the acerbic juice to contract and dry and roughen the tongue, and it was shown in the preceding discussions that bodies are contracted and constricted and compacted by cold alone, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is in every case cold; and since it also dries unevenly [639] — for this was what does the roughening — it would in every case also be earthy. For the watery [flavour] passes through everything evenly. For it is inseparable from it, even if it is torn apart, to be united again; whereas for the earthy body that is carried along in the juices both being torn apart is already present, and no longer coming together easily belongs to it as well. And moreover, the peculiar character of the sensation of each of the two affections, if you recall it, will bear witness to the same things. For the passage of sour flavours through the sentient bodies appears to take place quickly, but that of acerbic ones slowly. And sour things appear to act rather in depth, acerbic things on the surface. All these things, then, indicate that acerbic bodies are coarse-particled, while sour ones are fine-particled.

These points, then, are sufficiently in agreement with one another — both what has been said on the basis of the very substance of the things and what has been said by way of induction from what is discovered by perception. But it would be no worse to add these points too, recalling here again the usage of the names: that both are said to be astringent, the harsh and the acerbic, but they differ in the more [640] and the less. And indeed, that drugs possess many qualities, not only different but also in conflict with one another, and sometimes even wholly opposed, has been sufficiently shown before; but it is necessary now too to begin from this point. For if, when you taste it, the same thing appears to you to be at once both acerbic and biting, I shall bid you leave this drug aside and go on to the one that is acerbic without being biting. And if it appears neither sour nor sweet nor bitter, but, as far as is at all possible, having a single unmixed quality, that of astringency, then at that point to test it by experience in the manner I have often laid down for you before. For if it has at once both the astringent and the biting, or some other evident quality and power mingled with the astringency, it is superfluous and vain to bring such a drug to the test when you are examining the activity of astringency. For it is unclear whether it was because of the astringency, or because of one of the qualities mixed in with it, or indeed because of both, that it acted in this or that way upon the body that came into contact with it.

Chalkitis, then, and misy [641] and chalkanthos and scale of copper and sory, being at once astringent and biting, act according to both qualities upon each of the bodies with which they come into contact, yet they cannot teach us clearly whether they have their burning on account of the astringency or on account of the pungency. It is better, therefore, to leave these aside and to taste many others in succession, looking for a pure astringency, separately and by itself as far as is at all possible, and when you have found such a one, then at that point to judge the drug by the methods you have often heard before: for instance, if on tasting balaustion, or oak-gall, or kytinos, or hypokistis, or strychnos, or glaukion, or acacia, or juice of sumach, or some other such thing, it should appear to you to be precisely acerbic, while having no other manifest quality, then on such things to examine and test precisely the activity of astringency. And let the examination, as has often been said, be made by you both on bodies in the best constitution that are precisely healthy, and on the simple affections, whether hot, or cold, or dry, or moist.

For if the healthy [642] body itself should appear to be clearly cooled, and it is suited to hot affections, and it imparts a manifest cold quality to the patient himself, then one may at that point venture to declare something about astringency as cooling. But if it should be found to be the opposite, with healthy bodies being heated by it, hot diseases being exacerbated and cold ones benefited, one must consider such a drug not to cool but to heat. In the same way one should also make the test of pungent things themselves by themselves, turning to onion and garlic and pepper and pellitory and ginger and soapwort, elecampane and lime. For just as one who has mixed pepper with juice of strychnos is not competent to test either of them, so neither is one who tests things that have been mixed by nature. And in the same manner I require you to investigate also the sour quality and the bitter and the sweet, bringing them to the test as intense and as isolated as is possible, and discovering their powers by experience.

But to bring to trial everything whatsoever that is acerbic, or harsh, or bitter, as though one were going to obtain in it a test of acerbity, or harshness, [643] or bitterness, is dreadfully absurd. For if it partakes of one quality only, you will have the same trial of the drug and of the quality; but if of several, the drug will then clearly perform an activity mixed from all of them, so that the activity of the single quality under judgment still remains unclear. If, then, one must judge as has been stated before, both those who supposed that it is not possible at all to declare anything about the power of the flavours, and those who made the judgment in another way, supposed incorrectly. For it is both possible to declare something about them, and it is fitting to make the judgment in no other way than as has now been stated. Now if they had said that there is no need at all of the examination concerning the flavours when we investigate the powers of drugs—for it is possible even without these to discover their power by experience—I would have praised rather than blamed them. But since they treat of it as something necessary, yet unknowable, it is just to blame these men on two counts: both because they took what is not necessary to be necessary, and because they despaired in advance of its discovery.

For indeed the judgment of the power of each of the [644] drugs is found sufficiently, without the discrimination of the flavours, by experience alone, when it is tested in the manner I have already stated countless times. And I myself have now come to the discussion concerning the flavours, not on the grounds that it is impossible to discover what is sought otherwise, but both on account of consistency with the first principles, so that I might show that everything follows upon the reasonings about the elements and that nothing anywhere conflicts with them, and so that I might refute those who said that all astringent things heat. Some use of it, too, might be found for the treatise now before us. But these things I shall try to show later; for now I return to the matter at hand, and I urge those who desire the truth, tasting for themselves all astringent things, just as we did, whenever they find astringency precisely in some body, unmixed as far as possible with the other qualities, then to examine through experience whether such a body is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist. This, then, each person, if he is sensible, will do by himself on his own.

But for me it is perhaps necessary [645] to make some declaration about my own experience, in general terms in the present discourse, and in particular through the treatises that follow. The general account concerning all of them would be as follows. Every astringent body, at least one that is pure of the other qualities, so far as regards perception, I have always found, upon testing, to be cold. Indeed, even some of those that are mixed in their qualities, namely those that are moderately sweet and bitter and pungent, were clearly found to be cooling, since evidently the power of being astringent and of cooling prevails in them, so that the other powers are obscured. By the same reasoning, all sour things too, both those that are simply sour, such as oxalis and oxylapathon, and some of those mixed with other qualities, whether sweet or pungent or bitter, are found no less to be cooling: pomegranates and apples and plums and grapes and figs and mulberries and cherries and vinegar itself. But with this last, as was said before, a certain pungency is mixed in, while with the fruits sweetnesses and acerbities, and in some of them also faint bitternesses.

And indeed, [646] all those things too that are astringent and at the same time sour in their qualities were, as I found on trial, all of them clearly cooling; whereas all those that are merely sweet [I found] to partake straightaway of heat too, in proportion to the amount of their sweetness, so that none of the very sweet things is cold; yet something moderately sweet might also be cold, whenever the greater part of the substance of its body is watery—not, however, cold to such a degree as that which is strongly acerbic or sour, but in the way that has been stated somewhere earlier concerning the things that partake of a lukewarm warmth. And all bitter things are hot, as for instance bile and nitre and the very old wines and countless seeds. For the seed of rue, and especially that of the wild kind, and that of tordylium and that of spondylium and that of melanthium, and lupins, and more so the wild ones, and bitter vetch, and of these too the wild ones more so, and the so-called pelekinos (it is found among wheat), and certain almonds, which are indeed for this very reason called bitter, and certain seeds of gourds (συκίων), and that of the Median apple, and in addition to these countless other things appear bitter to those who taste them.

[647] But concerning bitter things more will be said in what follows. Taking up once more the account of astringent and sour things, let us now set upon it the conclusion that befits it. As for the harsh, then, that it is a slackened acerbic one must recall from sensation; but what its genesis is will now be stated. Since the acerbic body was earthy and cold, it will necessarily be slackened in three ways: either by being heated, or by being moistened, or by undergoing both together at the same time. If, then, it is heated only, it is neither moister nor softer, but, remaining hard, it will acquire sweetness in addition, as do the acorns of oaks and especially those called chestnuts. But if it is moistened only, then if the moisture is coarse-particled and watery, it will be rendered harsh; for watery moisture blunts the power of every flavour. But if the moisture is fine-particled and airy, it makes it sour; for it has been shown that what is fine-particled and cold produces a sour quality.

But if it is moistened and heated at the same time, with a watery moisture it will have its transition into sweetness, but with an airy one [648] into oiliness. And it has now become quite evident how fruits that are acerbic at the beginning, as time goes on, some become exactly sweet, some sour, some harsh, some remain acerbic always, and some turn out oily; and indeed, in accordance with the admixtures of the aforesaid qualities, they have a very great variety. Acerbic to the end, then, is the fruit of the holm-oak and of the strawberry-tree and of the Valonia oak and of the cornel, because it remains cold and dry, just such as it was from the beginning, only growing in size and acquiring no other great alteration. For these very trees themselves too are at once denser and drier and colder. Acerbic and at the same time sweet is the fruit of the myrtle and that of the wild pear and that of the oak, and more sweet than acerbic is the one called the chestnut; harsh only is both the fruit and the wine of the Aminaean vines, and all those that are similar to these. Harsh and at the same time sweet is the fruit of the date-palm and, among wines, the Surrentine and the Sabine and the one called Albates (Alban), and all the others of this kind.

Sweet alone is the Theraean and the Scybellite [649] and the boiled-down must, and all the others that resemble these. Oily, both as fruit and as juice at once, is in the strict sense that of the olive, and indeed also all the others from which oil is prepared, such as that of the castor-plant (kiki) and that of the radish, and the sesame seeds themselves and the nuts and the almonds. For all such things, as they age, become completely oily, since the watery and superfluous moisture in them evaporates away, while the proper moisture is worked up by the innate heat and thoroughly concocted. Those fruits, then, which become oil-like only are both edible and sweet; but those to which some bitterness accrues in the course of the change become inedible. For everything bitter is inedible, and it comes about through an excess of warmth, as we shall demonstrate next.

But everything sweet is hot, and yet does not immoderately exceed the heat that is in us; rather, just as hot water, which we take pleasure in touching, and especially when we have been chilled, is most pleasant and most beneficial so long as it warms us [650] to the point of diffusing the parts of the body that have been congealed by the cold, yet without dissolving or cutting and separating their continuity, so too every sweet food is in every case hot, yet does not reach so great a degree of heat as to cause distress, but remains within the limits of what diffuses, smooths and softens. Recall here again what has often been said by us before, that some things act upon and are acted upon by one another in respect of one or two qualities, others in respect of their whole substances; and among these latter we said there are not a few drugs and all nutriments. The genus of these seems to be twofold, as Theophrastus too indicated. For some are oily, like soft fat, others sweet to a greater or lesser degree, like all the fruits that we eat and the flesh of animals, and indeed also many herbs and roots and flowers and shoots. For even if some such thing is acerbic, like wild pears and cornel-berries,

Nevertheless, it too certainly partakes of sweetness, provided at least that they are not precisely acerbic, like the oak-gall and the sumach; yet even so, for these very reasons the use of them is now rather as drugs [651] than as food. At any rate, women with the cravings of pregnancy, those who are full, and those whose stomach is relaxed are seen to desire to taste such things, whereas when hungry, on the contrary, people turn away from both the acerbic and the sour, and admit the sweet and the oily and long to be filled with these. And surely the oily itself is also sweet, and everything that nourishes is from the class of sweet things. And this belongs to them with good reason and, so far as is possible, in accordance with the very essence of nourishment. For nutrition is the replenishment of what has been emptied. But what was emptied was proper to the body, so that what nourishes must necessarily also be proper. And if proper, it is of necessity pleasant and friendly, and immediately also moderately hot in relation to what is nourished. But in this there is no small degree of more and less, because we do not arrive at our foods while being precisely in accordance with nature.

For the body of those who need nourishment must only have been emptied, if they are going to be accurate and discerning judges of its proper quality. [652] But if in addition to this they become hotter than they should be, or colder, either in the whole body or in the regions around the tongue or the stomach, they will need not only things that will nourish, but also things that either cool or heat. And for this reason, among foods too, now one, now another appears more pleasant to such people. For since what is pleasant is of two kinds in genus, one being that which fills up what has been emptied, which was nourishment, the other that which heals what has been altered, and this is now a drug, it comes about for foods, when they are administered to bodies that are not only emptied but also changed in quality, that they are now found pleasant in a twofold manner, as nourishments and drugs at the same time. But as drugs, certain ones that cool and heat and dry and moisten will reasonably both profit and benefit at once; whereas as nourishments, only those that are akin and proper to the whole substances of the things nourished. It belongs to these straightway, evidently, to be moderately hot in relation to the things nourished.

And for this reason too there is not one single kind both of foods [653] and of drugs for all animals; for each of them takes pleasure in, and is benefited by, both in accordance with its own proper substance and, at the same time, its disposition. But if these things are so, the less sweet among foods will also be less hot, while the more sweet will be hotter by just as much as it is sweeter. And if it should fall into an excess of heat, such a thing is no longer even sweet, but already appears bitter, as honey does when it becomes old and when it is boiled down, and so too each of the other sweet things. For just as, from a due proportion of heat, sweetness arises in each of the bodies in a twofold manner—for some are sweet by their proper and innate heat, others by acquired heat—in the same way the bitter things too: some undergo this by being heated beyond measure by themselves through the changes that take place over time, while some suffer it by being burnt up by acquired warmth. Concerning the bitter things, then, we shall speak next.

But all sweet things come close, in their heat, to the bodies to which they appear sweet, and they become [654] such in a twofold manner, as has been said: some by their own proper heat, as honey, others by an acquired heat, as all things prepared by means of fire. And for this very reason, as long as they are hot, so long do they also appear more pleasant to those who stand in need of restorative nourishment. And it seems that must, too, appears sweet not only by its own proper warmth but also by an acquired one. For, as both Theophrastus and Aristotle said, there is present in grapes and in the other fruits a great deal of what is, as it were, a kind of ember-like residue (empyreuma) from the sun's warmth, by which that which is still watery in them and, as it were, half-concocted is brought to concoction and worked up, being assimilated to that which changes it; so that if you press out the juice of whatever fruit you please, you will find it at once fermenting (ζέοντα) just like must, though the fermentation (ζέσις) differs in degree of more and less to the extent that one fruit differs from another in heat. But when the watery and half-concocted part has been changed and worked up, and the warmth that produces the fermentation has been dissipated by transpiration, the proper qualities of the juices appear unmixed, so that it is then also that we discern what sort the wines are according to their own proper nature.

And here [655] it is precisely this to which I ask you to pay the closest attention: that all the harsh wines gradually cease to be such. For as they age they always acquire a certain pungency and sweetness, and with time they cast off the astringency that previously belonged to them. There is indeed, after the boiling, in some of the wines a pure sweetness, at once pleasant and proper to the nature of the juice itself, not like the earlier one, which was a kind of mixture of the proper sweetness and of that arising from the boiling of the half-concocted and watery residue; so that, if it is agreed that all wines become hotter as they grow old, and it happens to the harsh ones among them, in aging, first to take on a certain sweetness and pungency as they lay aside their astringency, next to increase in pungency while gradually ceasing from sweetness, and then again, over a longer time, to become quite pungent and to take on bitterness continually, and finally, when they thicken, to turn entirely bitter—then it is evident that the sweet is hotter than the acerbic, and the bitter hotter than the sweet.

But if sweetness arises from [656] a due proportion of heat, it is clear that acerbity will be produced by the cold prevailing. That sourness, too, is brought about by cooling has been shown by us also earlier. But since in the present discussion we have set forth the change of wines over time that is according to nature, let us say something also about that which is contrary to nature. Just as, then, acerbic wine over time becomes first sweeter, then more pungent and more bitter, and finally turns wholly bitter, so in the same way the wine that has been chilled at once becomes sourer, and if it is completely cooled off it turns completely sour; and the wine that straightaway at the gathering of the fruits, when rain has set in, has been filled with foreign moisture, and the one that has otherwise taken on water—all such wines readily become sour on slight occasions. Contrary to these, those that are brought near fire become sweet both immediately and, later on, ever more so.

But when they run on to a very long time, these too change over into bitterness no less than the others, [657] and in a way this seems to be consistent with itself also according to the account of nature. For if the unripe grape is sour, but the ripe grape sweet, and ripening comes about in all fruits from the solar heat, it is quite clear that what is less perfect and colder is sour, while what is more perfect and hotter is sweet. So when wine, in being cooled, turns sour again, it is evident that it returns again to the same juice from which it came. Nevertheless, the juice of the unripe grape differs in power from vinegar to this extent, that to vinegar there accrues a certain pungency from a putrefactive heat. And for this reason Aristotle rightly said of it that the heat proper to the wine is cold, while the acquired heat is hot. But the juice of the unripe grape does not have this heat, and therefore not the pungency either. Moreover, there accrues to them a certain difference also from the more and the less in the fine-particled character of their substance. For vinegar is more fine-particled than the juice of the unripe grape, and indeed perception too bears witness to the argument. For the cooling from vinegar differs from that from the juice of unripe grapes in its vehemence and its mixed character.

[658] For the cooling from the unripe grape is weaker, yet it does not partake of foreign heat even in the least; whereas that from vinegar is stronger to just the extent that it is also more fine-particled. And vinegar has a share also of a warming pungency, not sufficient to overcome the cooling from the sourness, but serving towards the swiftness of the passage. For to the extent that the hot is more capable of finding a way through than the cold, to that extent also the pungent juice passes more readily than the sour through the pores of the sentient bodies, so that the one, arriving first, as it were makes a road, and the other follows not long after; and in this the mixed and hard-to-interpret character of the sensation is brought about, since sensation can neither declare vinegar simply cold—for it perceives in it a certain fiery pungency—nor simply hot. For the cooling from the sourness that follows, always overtaking the warmth from the pungency that leads the way, dims it and extinguishes it on the spot. And for this reason the sensation and the disposition arising from the cooling are much greater than those arising from the heat.

[659] But if you mix a little vinegar with a larger quantity of honey, you will at once clearly perceive both cooling and heat. For if you blend a little honey with much vinegar, the mixture will appear to you cold in greater measure than hot; but if a little vinegar with much honey, more heating than cold; and even if you mix equal amounts in bulk, you will still find the vinegar prevailing, at any rate in power. But if, as has been said, the honey is greater by much, you will in turn find in such a blend the cooling equal to the heat. For vinegar has departed from the things that are moderately hot toward coldness by some many-times-greater amount than honey has toward heat. At any rate, it has been shown previously too that it is not possible for violent heat to coexist with sweetness. And it was well said long ago that all true things agree with one another. And so indeed, in the case of hypochondria that are burning inwardly, the juice of the unripe grape is better than vinegar itself, because it has a cooling that is neither violent and striking nor mixed with biting heat.

Those who suffer in this way need, on the one hand, to be soothed without violence, as has been said, and, on the other, to acquire from outside no [660] biting heat or pungency. These matters, then, already in some way touch upon the therapeutic method, which shares at many points with the treatise now in hand; and for this reason, leaving them aside, let us return again to what lies before us. The juice of the unripe grape, then, is not only sour but also acerbic. For, as was said earlier too, nearly all the fruits of trees, at their first generation, as Theophrastus also said, are acerbic to those who taste them; then, when they become filled with moisture, they take on sourness and lose some of their acerbity. But neither what is added nor what is taken away is equal in all fruits, neither according to their species nor according to their genus at all. To take an immediate example, among unripe grapes some partake more of acerbity, some more of sourness, and some of both in equal measure. But for cooling burning fevers all of them are, with good reason, suitable. For not only is the sour cold, but the acerbic too, as we also said earlier. Here again, then, the argument departs toward the therapeutic method.

So let us bring it back again to the subject [661] before us. It was, as I think, the subject proposed from the beginning in this book to go through all the flavours, and nearly all of the most important have already been discussed, since through the interconnection of the argument we were compelled to touch upon the others as well. For it is not only the acerbic, the harsh and the sour that have been discussed, but already many times also the sweet, the bitter and the pungent. It is necessary, however, to add what is lacking for the completeness of the whole account. In the case of astringent things nothing great or noteworthy is lacking that will not be clear from what has already been said. But in the case of sour things something might perhaps seem to someone to be lacking, a point which has deceived even some of the reputable physicians: for because weak wines change and turn sour in spring and in summer, but in winter are preserved in their proper qualities, it seemed to some that sourness is generated by heat. And their supposition is further strengthened by wine that has been agitated rather violently, and by wine that has been transported rather far in ships.

For indeed all such wines, when they are weak, [662] turn sour very quickly. And moreover some of those who have written on agricultural matters recommend that the storage jars be buried in rooms turned toward the north, on the grounds that cooling preserves their quality, whereas heat alters it. And indeed this is also seen to happen in many places, having been put to the test by experience itself. For some wines readily turn sour when they are stored away in southern and sun-exposed places; and it seems to me that one should make the beginning of the solution of the points stated from here. For the fact that not all wines turn sour when heated, but only those which are colder right from the start, and that this does not befall any of those that have been aged, will find for us the road to the truth. For the argument will seek the cause on account of which the wine that is by nature cold and weak is shown up by the external heat—and yet this very word, 'is shown up', once uttered, resolves all the difficulties that have been stated. For something closely similar happens to wines, all those which happen to be by nature colder and more watery, as happens also to small and weak flames.

For if you set these too in a strong sun, [663] you will see them becoming utterly faint, or even being extinguished altogether. So too a burning lamp, if you should place it beside some other vehement and large flame, or set it in a strong sun, you will at once behold it withering away and being dispersed. And indeed, even if you were to fan a weak and small flame strongly, you will extinguish it sooner than increase it. For a weak nature withstands neither strong motion nor strong warmth, but is dispersed by it rather than increased; since in fact in many regions they deliberately move and transport the wines, just as they also expose them to the sun and heat them, so that some of them become unpleasant, taking on the quality from the smoke. And among us in Asia, when the season of summer comes, nearly all of them, poured into flagons, are set upon the roof-tiles of the houses, and after this, taking them down, they store them in upper rooms beneath which, in the ground-floor rooms, a large fire is going to be burned; and in general they always turn the storerooms toward the south and toward the sun, those for whom this is to concoct them more quickly and make them drinkable.

For what comes about in the others over a long time, [664] this comes about in the shortest time for wines heated in this way. And it is no wonder that some of those who have written on agricultural matters, on the basis of the experience gained in their own regions, have pronounced rather rashly about all wines. But Theophrastus and Aristotle and their followers, who extended their experience further and, through their training in natural philosophy, articulated everything more accurately, taught us many other things of this kind and also, concerning wines, that they undergo something similar to our own bodies. For do we not observe that these too, according to how they stand in point of weakness or strength, are benefited and harmed by the same things? For indeed vigorous exercises and the sun make hot and robust bodies stronger, but cast down, disperse and chill those that are not of this kind; and of wines, those that are hot by nature are ripened more quickly both by motion that fans them and by the sun that heats them through and by flames burning nearby.

But those that are colder and more watery, all such things expose and compel to suffer more quickly what they were going to suffer a little [665] later. For each of the things that exist is preserved in its own proper nature by its own proper heat, but is destroyed by immoderation from without, whether by a foreign excess of heat or by a preponderance of cooling. And what is brought about by both is one thing, but the manner of its coming-to-be is not one. Hence this manner of the difference is not equally easy to detect for all laymen. When the particular heat of each of the things that exist is overcome by the cold, it is quite clear even to ordinary people. But when it is dispersed by a more vehement heat surrounding it from outside, it escapes the notice of those unexercised in the study of nature, who do not know that the moderate heat is beneficial to all things, whereas the immoderate is no less harmful than the cold. But in general it is good to know this, that the sourness in juices seems to arise most of all in their being changed by the heat yet not completely mastered by it.

One might infer this not least also from acid eructations, since these at any rate do not follow upon foods that are not changed at all in the stomach, just as they do not follow upon those that have been thoroughly concocted, [666] but only upon those that are half-concocted, as one might put it. I call half-concocted those which, having received the alteration from the heat in the stomach, were nevertheless not mastered by it to the end. So too milk and the juice of barley-gruel and all other such things turn sour more quickly in the summer season than in winter and require cold rooms in which they are to be stored so as to last for a longer time. From all of which it is clear that the generation of the sour quality lies in being changed by the hot, while not yet, however, having been completely mastered. For this reason too it belongs to most fruits before they are ripened. And this too seems somehow to agree with what was said at the beginning about the sour flavours. For if indeed they have undergone something similar to the northerly conditions of the weather, so as to be fine-particled and at the same time cold, it is evident that their generation does not occur without heat, just as it does not for the air either.

And for this reason the things that chill us completely and deaden us, such as hemlock and poppy-juice (meconium), henbane and mandrake, are least of all [667] sour. All the sour flavours are indeed cold, yet they do not cool to such a degree as to kill. For neither would they be fine-particled, if they were cold in the extreme; so that it has now been shown not only that the sour flavour is cold, but also to what extent it is cold. One tests it, as to what sort of thing it is in its nature, in the case of oxylapathon and oxalis, which indeed they also call oxys. This is a wild pot-herb; for in these it appeared to me to be, in some way, most unadulterated and alone, sharing in no acerbity, as the fruits of trees do. For these manifestly have their sourness mixed with some acerbity, just as vinegar has it mixed with pungency. Now what is properly named sour among the flavours is perceptible to the tongue alone, as is also the pungent. But what is common to both, the biting, is already perceptible also to touch. And the tongue is capable of discerning both: the common ones, as any other of the sentient bodies is too; the proper ones, as the organ of taste. And it seems to me that this special property belongs to it in accordance with the kinship and the alienness of whole substances.

For it has already been stated and demonstrated many times, [668] and none the less it will be stated again, what it is to act or to be affected according to whole substances. But it seems fitting that I now too make mention of it, so far as suffices for the present purposes, beginning from somewhere about here. From the four elements the generations of all the particular bodies derive, being unequal and differing in their mixtures. For some have more of fire than of the other elements, some more of water, others, as it may happen, of earth, and some of air. From such inequality, then, the peculiar characters of the particular bodies were brought to completion: from the elements themselves those of plants, and from these those of animals, as has been shown in the discourses on the elements. And some things change directly into one another, others through other things as intermediates; as, for instance, earth changes into wheat and barley and the other such things, and each of these in turn into the flesh of a human being, yet it is not possible for earth itself to become flesh, passing over the change that lies in between.

And indeed, among the things that change into one another, some have a ready and swift alteration, others a difficult and protracted [669] one. Those that are close in their similarities have a swift one, those that are further removed, a slower one. It was necessary, therefore, I think, that there come to be in animals, by the agency of nature, some organ capable of discriminating the similarity and dissimilarity of substances, which, by diagnosing their natures, will choose what is akin and shun what is alien. This, then, is the tongue, which, through the surplus of its sensation, possesses a diagnosis not only of things cold, or hot, or dry, or moist, but also of things akin and not akin. For into this part alone six nerves are implanted, whereas each of the other parts has a share of either one or two, and not even of these themselves so large. And since some things are more akin to the nature of our body and others less, and some are in this conjugation of mixture and others in that, the gustatory qualities have of necessity turned out to be more numerous.

But common to all things that nourish is the sweet; for everything that nourishes is sweet, either to a greater or to a lesser degree; whereas common to the things that do not nourish is what is named by negation of the sweet, or privatively, [670] such as 'not sweet' and 'salty' (ἁλυκόν). The particular differences, however, came to be more numerous, and reasonably so, by the fact that what is proper to each of the things that exist is one, since its own nature too is one, whereas the things foreign to it are very many, some more removed from its substance, others less. Accordingly, all those things that are exactly sour and acerbic and bitter, and in general that have any other quality whatever apart from the sweet, are all non-nourishing, just as all those that are only sweet are all nourishing; and of those that are mixed in their qualities, those which are at once both sweet and acerbic are more coarse-particled in their substances and cold in their mixtures, as we also showed a little earlier; while those which are at once both sour and sweet are more fine-particled than the acerbic ones, but they too, in their turn, cool. And indeed the bitter ones are hot, and the pungent ones hotter still than these. All such things, then, nourish together with sweetness; but by itself none of the things mentioned is capable of nourishing.

Things become mixed in a twofold manner: either by being non-homoeomerous in their substances and having qualities that differ [671] according to their parts, or by being simple and homoeomerous, but coming to be mixed in the course of the change of things that differ greatly into one another. For neither does honey become bitter all at once, but whether it is boiled for too long or grows old, it changes into bitterness little by little as it undergoes this; nor do those fruits that end up sweet, as some of the cucumbers and melons, themselves cast off all at once the quality they had from the beginning. For in all things that are altered by nature the changes occur little by little, and especially when their alteration and transition is accomplished into qualities that differ greatly, or are even entirely contrary. Just as, then, what is exactly sweet is nutritive and what is purely bitter non-nutritive, so what lies between nourishes, but less than the sweet. And it is the same also with the other qualities; for all of them except the sweet are non-nutritive. And indeed the elements themselves are far more non-nutritive and without quality in respect of taste.

And for this reason earth and water too — for both of these also are without quality to the taste and non-nourishing, just as air and fire — so that also in accordance with the [672] admixture of the qualities the quality of sweet things is often slackened, a watery substance predominating in the fruits of nearly all plants growing on the ground. For wheat, barley, beans, chickpeas and all the others of this kind, being at the beginning, because of their moisture, nearly without quality in taste, become sweeter in time as they ripen and dry out; while an earthy and dry substance predominates in chaff, hay, dog's-tooth grass, dry reeds and wood, some of which, before they have been dried out, are sweet to us and sometimes give nourishment to the body, such as the 'brain' of the date-palm — for so they name its uppermost part — and the soft roots of dog's-tooth grass and of reeds, and especially of those in Egypt, and indeed also the shoots of most trees. For it is always by similarity to what is nourished that what nourishes appears sweet, and by dissimilarity not sweet.

And since there are many dissimilarities, it is necessary that in this matter the non-sweet qualities too be many; these it is impossible to explain in words, but it is possible to recall them to mind, since all men know precisely that the sensation and condition arising in the tongue from acerbic [673] things is one, that from sour things another, and that from salty things different, that from bitter things different again. Just as, then, those foods which are most similar to the natures of the things being nourished display sweetness and require no preparation, in the same way those which are further removed in their mixture require, some of them, seasonings, and others both together; and it is indeed no wonder that, although none of the seasonings themselves is edible, it contributes to the pleasure of what has been prepared by means of it. For when two immoderate things come together it is possible for the mixture from both to be rendered well-proportioned and for this reason to appear sweet, though the immoderate things are not themselves such. And when indeed the preparation of foods takes place through boiling or roasting or in general by something hot, there is nothing either puzzling or unreasonable in things which previously were not pleasant now becoming most pleasant.

For the nature of the hot evidently alters quickly whatever it comes into contact with and changes it [674] into another form, so that this too is no longer a puzzle, if some things become more pleasant and others less pleasant when they are brought near the fire, and some need to be boiled for the shortest time, others for a very long time. For those which are most similar to the mixtures of the bodies being nourished already appear sweet without boiling and preparation, whereas the dissimilar ones are all unpleasant before they have been prepared. The excessively hot ones need to be tempered by the cold, the considerably cold ones by admixtures of hot foods and by fire. In the same way, those that are earthy and dry need moisture, while those that are watery and moist more than is fitting need dryness. Thus the drynesses are corrected by the admixtures of moist things, and the moistnesses by the admixtures of dry things and by fire. The greatest proof of what is being said is the change that takes place in the mouth. At any rate, in those who have gone without food for a rather long time the spittle appears salty, and if for a very long time, not only salty but by then bitter as well.

And so too the whole body is turned to bile; and if it were all sensitive in the same way as the tongue, it would, I think, easily perceive the saltiness [675] within itself and the bitterness, and in addition to this the sweetness itself as well, which always belongs to blood in its natural state. But as it is, whenever, some vessel having been ruptured or opened up, blood is poured out over the tongue all at once and hot, it appears sweetest, when, as has been said, it is in its natural state. For blood that has become diseased is bitter or salty, or displays some other quality of that kind; yet throughout the whole body of the animal it goes unperceived, just as the biles and the phlegm do. And yet of the biles the one always appears bitter, even if it touches a small part of the tongue, while the black one appears sour. And of phlegm too, when it comes near the tongue, the one kind has often clearly appeared sweet, another sour, another salty, this too being undetected throughout the whole animal. It is therefore no wonder either why honey, the sweetest of all things, generates the bitterest humour, and why it does so especially in those in their prime, in those who are hot by nature, and in those with fever.

For just as, outside the body too, when it has been exposed for a longer time to [676] fire it becomes bitter, in the same way also in the bodies of animals, when it comes into contact with an unmixed heat, it generates the bilious humour. But in colder mixtures, whether on account of age, or on account of the nature of the body, or on account of disease, it readily changes into good and well-proportioned blood. For in such bodies, being neither overheated nor altered to excess, but undergoing something similar to what has been moderately boiled, it is completely assimilated to them and preserves its sweetness. And what wonder is it that honey departs from its original sweetness under the more vehement heat in animals or under more prolonged boiling, seeing that even apart from these it becomes bitter over a longer time through the heat within itself? For the difference lies only in the speed of the change, not in its undergoing a different affection from a different cause.

For indeed both the affection itself and the changing agent, which is the cause, [are the same in both cases]: the affection is bitterness, and the cause is the immoderateness of the heat; and since the immoderateness that leads to alteration is of two kinds in genus, either strength of what comes near, [677] or length of time, honey receives the one from us and from fire, the other from itself. And rightly this comes about over a longer time in the case of the one from itself, because the changing agent is also weaker. So that which comes about from a lesser cause in a longer time—what is surprising if this comes about from a greater cause in a shorter time? But milk (χάλα), although it is sweet to the taste, never becomes bitter from itself. For in it the hot is overcome by the cold rather than overcoming it, and for this reason it turns sour when left standing. For it is composed of three substances differing in their qualities, as I said earlier as well: the first the thick one, from which cheese comes; the second the oily one, from which butter comes; and the third the watery one, which we call whey. But of these the oily one is especially well-tempered, and the thick one falls a little short of it; whereas the whey-like residue is cold and moist, so that milk as a whole falls considerably short of the body that is moderate in heat, and for this reason it changes from itself into sourness rather than bitterness.

[678] And if it were possible to taste it once it has been concocted both in the stomach and in the veins, it would be found, I think, sweeter than honey. For what honey has from outside and from itself, this milk acquires in the course of being concocted. And when the body of the animal is sufficiently hot, milk gains as much in sweetness as honey loses. And this happens with good reason. For that which is sweet in the highest degree, and for this reason no longer admits any addition of sweetness, must necessarily change into the next quality in sequence; whereas for that which is deficient, what completes it accrues from concoction. For these reasons, then, milk, when it goes unconcocted in the stomach, admits twofold alterations: in the colder belly it turns sour, while in the hotter it is rendered nidorous and bitter. Honey, however, never admits the change into sourness in the course of being concocted; for it is too hot for it to turn sour, not being overpowered. For both are biting to the tongue, the sour and the bitter; yet sensation does not possess this as something proper to the tongue.

For indeed, even if you were to apply them to any other flesh whatever that is bare of skin, they bite [679] that too, from which it is clear that the biting is a perceptible proper to touch, not to taste. And moreover, the things called pungent, such as pellitory and garlic and onion, also possess the property of biting, not the tongue alone but also all the rest of our flesh. So this biting, then, is common to three flavours, the sour, the bitter, the pungent — but to the sour as being at once cold and fine-particled (for this was shown earlier), and to the bitter and the pungent as being hot. That the bitter flavour is hot, then, has just now been demonstrated by me. But concerning the one properly called pungent there is, to begin with, no need even of demonstration. For the activity that comes from sense-perception anticipates the conviction that comes from reasoning, so that no one has even disputed about it; rather Plato declares it to be the hottest of all, as do Aristotle and Theophrastus, and there is no physician, either among the ancients or among the more recent, who holds any other view.

For heating belongs to it according to the very account of its substance, so that even if you were to ask any layman whatsoever what he calls a pungent [680] food, he would say, I think, that which heats strongly in being tasted, such as pepper and pellitory and cress and garlic and onions and all things of this sort. And it seems to me that this genus of flavours alone, lacking a proper name of its own, makes use of the common one by way of pre-eminence. For although both the bitter flavour and the sour are pungent, both of them, in whatever body we find the pungency to be vehement, even if it is neither bitter nor sour, we are accustomed to call it pungent, although such bodies are many in species. For some of them are edible, others not. Now the edible ones necessarily have some faint sweet quality mixed in. And for this reason we use many of them as relish, and many only as seasoning; but as foodstuffs we use none of them, because of the vehemence of their power. Of those that are not eaten, some are deadly, others simply drugs; but all of them at any rate, when applied upon our skin, readily produce an ulcer.

Some of these too display [681] a bitter quality, just as not a few of the edible ones display a sweet one; yet they are not named bitter, because this quality is slight and weak in them, whereas that of pungency is strong. And some we do not even dare to taste, such as thapsia, or cantharides, or any other of those that kill by corrosion or putrefaction; but even in the case of these it is possible to conjecture that the taste is pungent from what they effect upon the whole body. Many, too, are at once strange in their odours and clearly indicate their contrariety to man, as these very ones just mentioned, and the juice of hemlock and that of poppy, and further that of mandrake and henbane. For indeed we have just now, recently, seen the juice of a plant which a certain centurion brought from the barbarian country bordering on Egypt. It was so heavy and unpleasant in smell that one did not even dare to taste it, but conjectured it to be deadly; he used it for arthritic pains at their height, and it clearly seemed, even to the patients themselves, to have a cooling power.

It is yellowish in colour, and as heavy in smell as [682] that of hemlock, except insofar as it also gives off a slight fragrance of a somewhat aromatic kind. The name of the plant from which the juice is produced, he said, was lycopersion. But about the deleterious drugs we shall speak again later. All the pungent flavours, however—for it was about these that the discussion was—one must recognise as being hot in the highest degree; next after them the bitter ones, and then after these the sweet. And since in all of them there is a considerable latitude, the one that is more pungent and bitter and sweet is obviously also hotter, while the one that is less so falls short in heat by just as much as it also falls short of the exact quality in respect of taste.

The defining mark of the bitter juice is cleansing, of the pungent burning, and of the sweet nourishing, at least when each of them is complete according to its own nature, that is, when they are, as far as is at all possible, unmixed with other qualities. For instance, the bitter is in every case hot; but the one that has just come into being from the transformation of the sweet is both less bitter and less hot, whereas the one that has been altered to the greatest extent is extremely bitter [683] and has already come close to the pungent, so that it no longer only cleanses but also erodes and bites. Thus aristolochia and iris and panax do just this alone: they cleanse off and make clean the ulcers. But wild staphis is no less pungent than these, unless indeed it is even more bitter; for it is already pungent, and very much so, and vehemently hot, whence it not only removes the filth from ulcers but is also of a nature to melt down the flesh itself. And all the bitter juices are of a nature to do something of this sort also when taken inside the body, just as in the case of ulcers; for they cleanse and thoroughly purge them, and they cut the thickness of the humours in the veins, whence they both move the menses and assist in the bringing up of pus from the chest and lung, and in general, whether it be thick phlegm contained in them, or pus, or some other such thing, they purge it thoroughly, and in this respect they help in epilepsies—those of them, at least, that are not deleterious in their nature. For those are contrary to nature in their whole kind. And in this way too they are of a nature to harm those who spit blood.

[684] For those patients need astringent and viscous things, not cutting and dividing ones. These matters, then, already in some way touch upon the therapeutic method. Having defined the power of the bitter juices, and having said that they are cutting and thinning and cleansing, and evidently hot to such a degree as not yet to burn, let us go on again in our discussion to the pungent ones. And first let us say that they are precisely hot, then corrosive and caustic and eschar-producing and colliquative; that all such are of this kind when applied to the skin, but when taken inside the body, all those which in their whole substances are disposed most opposite to certain animals are putrefying and deleterious to those animals; but those which are so only in respect of the excess of their heat, if they are coarse-particled and earthy, are ulcerating to the internal parts, but if fine-particled, diuretic and sudorific, and, simply put, cutting and dispersing.

Some of them also assist the expectorations from the chest [685] and the flows of the menses; but when and how and with what method they are to be used, it is not the business of the present treatise to go through. For about all such matters it will be spoken in the Therapeutic Method, so that I shall now cease writing more also about the nature of the pungent flavours. It suffices only to add to them still some more precise distinctions, according to which they differ from the bitter ones. For they are of a nature to differ from these not only by strong heat, but also in that the bitter ones are all not only hot but also dry in their power—as one might most clearly liken them, closely resembling ash—whereas in the pungent ones, those at least which are not bitter, much moisture is sometimes mixed in, and for this very reason we eat not a few of such bodies. That every bitter flavour is not only hot but also dry in its mixture, the determinate experience first and foremost teaches, about which I have spoken often before, and furthermore, in addition to experience, the same result follows for those who examine the matter by reason.

At any rate, when sweet things are heated further, whether [686] by fire or by the innate heat, the generation of bitter bodies was shown to take place. And straightaway these appear drier in their consistency, and, because their moisture is continually being consumed and flowing away, vaporised by the heat, it is necessary that what is left behind be rendered more earthy and drier. For the sweet itself, in addition to being hot to a greater or lesser degree, is surely of necessity also moist to a greater or lesser degree. And if indeed it is most akin to the nature of our body, and this was well-tempered, moist and hot, then that which comes to be, as it were, when this has been over-roasted, being like lime and ash, is of necessity rendered dry and hot. And indeed for this very reason it is of a nature to cleanse and to break up and to cut the viscous and thick humours, just like ash and nitre. For their consistency is neither airy nor fine-particled, nor indeed watery, but, as was also said a little earlier, more earthy, thoroughly worked over by the heat, their substance being, as it were, over-roasted.

As compared, then, with the astringent things, [687] the bitter drugs would be not a little more fine-particled; but as compared with the pungent ones, more coarse-particled; and for this reason they neither pass easily through the viscous and thick humours, as do all those things that are more fine-particled in their substances, nor are they unable to cut, like the coarse-particled ones. For that which is going to cut must be ranged in the middle between each of the two extremes, so that it neither passes through readily, like flame itself, nor, in delaying and being slow, is unable to divide. But about these matters something will also be said in the discourse after this, the fifth. For now it suffices to know at least this much, that the bitter quality as a whole belongs to substances that are at once hot and dry, and in addition to these, moreover, fine-particled and earthy. And one must understand what is said as a whole, joining it together into one, and not reading each part by itself.

For in that way the fine-particled would seem to be in conflict with the earthy; but I say that the bitter is not fine-particled simply, but is such as it is within an earthy constitution, like lime and ash and everything whatever that has been thoroughly roasted and has become cinder-ash; or rather, perhaps, it might more truly be likened to a kind of smoky vapour and soot [688] of flame, which also appears bitter to those who taste it. Now iron and stone are a coarse-particled earthy body, whereas soot and ash are fine-particled. A red-hot stone or iron, however, is more coarse-particled than lime and ash, and much more so than soot, and in addition to this hotter. But the drugs that kill by corrosion resemble red-hot iron and stone, being brought to this state, evidently, by the warmth in the body itself, as for instance chalcitis, misy and sory, and besides these arsenic, quicksilver, litharge and countless others. For all such things are coarse-particled and hot in potentiality, and for this reason, being set on fire in the course of time through the change that takes place in the animal, like red-hot stones or iron they ulcerate and burn the parts about the belly, being unable even to be distributed because of their heaviness.

Still more fine-particled than these, although earthy in their constitution, are lime, cantharis and the sea-hare; of these some ascend as far as the regions about the liver, and some even as far as the bladder and the thorax, acquiring the fiery quality in so great an interval [689] of their transport, while aristolochia and iris are more fine-particled even than these themselves; for they partake more than these of moist substance and of airy substance, and this is clear from their being neither so dry and brittle nor so heavy, and for this reason they have escaped the class of deleterious things. And indeed cantharis too, when taken on occasion in small quantity and mixed with the things with which it ought to be, besides doing no harm to the bladder, further also thoroughly cleanses the kidneys, and the more active of the diuretic drugs contain something of cantharis as well. But about such things there is another discussion. That the bitter flavour coexists with bodies that are dry in mixture it is possible to infer also from the fact that bitter things are of all things the most difficult to putrefy and least of all generate worms and certain other animals, such as are naturally produced in roots and herbs and fruits as they putrefy. For we see worms and putrefactions arising most of all in moist bodies.

But the things that are exactly bitter—and I so call those which partake of no other perceptible quality—are inedible to almost [690] all animals, not to human beings alone, because every animal is moist, to a greater or lesser degree, whereas bitter things are dry, similar to ash and lye. Accordingly no animal eats ash or lye or soot or lime, nor any of the exactly bitter things. For wormwood is not only bitter but also acerbic, and the sea is salty rather than bitter, and partakes of a very great deal of the potable, just as this was long ago sufficiently demonstrated by Aristotle. But the water of the lake in Palestinian Syria, which some name the Dead Sea, others the Asphaltite Lake, is, to those who taste it, not only salty but also bitter. And it has, likewise, the salts generated from it somewhat bitter; and to the sight it straightway appears at the same time both whiter and thicker than any sea, resembling a saturated brine, into which, not even if you throw in salts, will they still dissolve, for it partakes of a very great deal of them.

And if someone, having plunged into it, should come up again, he at once has a film of salt all round his whole body; and for this reason too that water is heavier than the rest of the sea [691] by as much as the sea is heavier than rivers. So that not even if you wished, letting yourself down toward the depth, to be carried downwards, would you be able to: so much does the water raise and buoy one up, not because it is light by nature, which one of the ancient sophists once said, but, as Aristotle said, because through its heaviness it supports the lighter things, like mud. And in accordance with this, indeed, even if you bound a man's hands and feet together and let him go into the water of that lake, he will not go down. And moreover, just as in the sea boats carry greater cargoes without being sunk than those in lakes and rivers, in the same way in the Dead Lake they carry many times more than those in the sea. For the water in it is heavier than sea-water by as much as sea-water is heavier than lake-water and river-water. For there is added the substance of the salts, earthy and heavy.
