And it is possible for you yourself to generate sea-water, by dissolving salt in drinkable water, and to learn by how much heavier such water turns out to be than sweet water.

But they have also already established a certain measure for the brine being well-mixed for saltings: if an egg should appear floating upon it—since, so long as it is still sinking and not yet swimming about the surface of the [692] brine, the brine is rather watery and sweet. And it becomes terribly salty when so much salt has been thrown in that it is no longer possible for the salt subsequently added to dissolve. And if you weigh this water, it will be found heavier than all waters. So that I myself once demonstrated as vain the ambition of a rich man who had conveyed so much water from the Dead Sea to Italy as to fill a pool. For I readily produced the same thing by throwing a very great quantity of salt into drinkable water. And you would make such water heavier still if, having dissolved as much salt as possible at the rising of the Dog-star, when the heat is most intense, you should allow it to be baked out, in a manner similar to the water in the Asphalt Lake. For in this way this water too will be as heavy as that one. And if you should bind a man, or throw any other animal whatsoever into it, it will be borne up on the water just like boats.

And indeed such water will at once also be more bitter, [693] just as if you should also wish to boil it down over a fire; for whatever salty thing you heat to excess will become bitter for you. So, at any rate, the water of the Asphaltite Lake itself, being enclosed in a hollow and hot place and baked by the sun, becomes bitter. For this reason, indeed, it is more bitter in summer than in winter. And if you draw some of it and set it down in a vessel in a hollow place exposed to the sun, just as we ourselves did in the summer season, it very soon appears to you to have become more bitter than it was. But all these things bear sufficient witness to what was said a little earlier concerning the generation of the bitter. However, the reason for which the discussion turned aside to the Asphaltite Lake has not yet been fully stated by me. For it appears that in that water neither any animal nor any plant comes into being; but even of the two rivers that empty into it, which contain very large and very numerous fish, and especially of the one near Jericho, which they call the Jordan, not a single one of the fish passes beyond the mouths of the rivers.

And if someone were to catch them and throw them into the lake, he will see them quickly perishing; so [694] precisely bitter is it, and hostile to all things, both animals and plants, parched and dry and in its nature having become, as it were, soot through the roasting. And yet not even the water of that lake is precisely bitter, since not even the salts themselves are—they call them Sodomene, from the mountains surrounding the lake, which are called Sodoma—and many of the people who dwell round about use them for all the purposes for which we use the other salts. Their power is not only drying to a greater degree than that of the other salts, but also thinning, because they have been roasted more than the others. For in all salts there is also something faintly astringent, by which indeed they bind and compact the meats that are being salted, and especially when they are in coarse lumps and hard to break. Such, most precisely, are the majority of the mined salts, and less so than these are those generated from the sea and, in many places of the earth, from light waters that have been dried up. Third after these are the mined salts, which are by nature such as to cleanse rather than to be astringent and to contract.

Close to these in power are the Sodomene salts, [695] being in lumps like the sea salts, but on account of the bitterness mixed in with them being more cleansing and more dispersing than those from the sea. So too nitre itself and its foam, and what is called by the composite name aphronitron, are by nature even more cleansing than the others, inasmuch as they are least astringent while being precisely bitter. For the salty flavour is near to the bitter, since both are earthy and hot; yet they differ by no obscure difference, in that the bitter has been thinned and worked up more by dry heat. So too, of the salts themselves, those that are harder and denser and more earthy—and such are almost all the mined salts—are less hot and fine-particled, whereas those that are friable and loose-textured are at once both more fine-particled and hotter in power, and some of them are somewhat bitter, being in a way intermediate between the hard salts and aphronitron. There are indeed also some of the aphronitra themselves that are hard and coarse-particled, and do not even dissolve easily in water.

But [696] my account now is not about the defective ones, but about those which, in accordance with their name, are naturally foam-like in their substance, such as is also the foam of nitre itself. For this is the most fine-particled of all those mentioned, just as is also the flower of the Assian stone. For this too is sufficiently fine-particled, but less hot than aphronitron. Wherefore it also melts away overgrowing flesh with less pain, whereas the flower of nitre already bites it, and aphronitron bites too, and no less nitre itself, even though it is less hot than those. But it has been said before as well that the coarse-particled substance erodes more, when, that is to say, it partakes of some heat. For no part of it passes through painlessly and quickly, as that of the fine-particled does, but being held back and always remaining and lingering, and sitting for a longer time upon one place of our body, it naturally becomes painful, like a thorn fixed in the flesh. Since what is fitting has been said about all the flavours, it would remain still to speak also about the vapours.

For it is for this class [697] of sensible things (αἰσθητικῶν) that nature fashioned the sense of smell. Now most of them affect us in the same way as the flavours themselves. For all sour things, and before these vinegar itself, stir the sense of smell and the sense of taste alike; and the pungent ones, such as garlic and onions, these too distress and bite the sense of smell no less than the sense of taste. And so too in each of the other cases the sensation of smell is almost the same as that of taste, so that in the case of some bodies we recognise the quality without ever having tasted them, as with dung, and for this very reason we do not even attempt to taste them in the first place, because we trust the sense of smell so very strongly. And indeed, those fragrant foods which, having putrefied, distress us by their smell, these too we at once throw away without even attempting to taste them; and in almost all cases smell and taste agree with one another. In the case of the most pleasant things, however, such as roses, they differ and stand very far apart.

For not only are they not pleasant to those who taste them, but they even display no small degree of bitterness. [698] And yet the bitter was never fragrant, nor pleasant to us either as a drug or as food. What, then, is the cause of this disagreement — a question which Theophrastus too investigated; but perhaps it is better that we also say what we know about it. The generation of the bitter flavour appeared to arise from sweet things being thinned by heat, and bitter things are evidently hotter and more fine-particled in mixture than sweet things; but, further, the sensation of smell occurs in the very ventricles of the brain, as has also been demonstrated by me elsewhere concerning these matters, and the substance of odorous objects is vaporous. For the effluences from bodies, mingling with the surrounding air and then carried into the brain through the inhalation that takes place by way of the nostrils, stir the sensation. Reasonably, then, all things that are odorous are also hot — for the abundance of vapours depends on heat; yet not everything odorous is thereby also pleasant, because not everything is akin to the pneuma in the ventricles of the brain.

For just as, among the flavours that fall upon the [699] tongue, the most proper were the sweet ones, while those that are not proper possessed many differences, so too among the vapours those proper to the pneuma in the brain are friendly and pleasant, whereas those not proper differ from one another by not a few differences, but names are not assigned to all of these, as they are in the case of the flavours. For we say that this or that thing has a certain sour and pungent odour, but we no longer say a harsh or acerbic or salty or bitter one; rather we refer most of the objects of smell to these two appellations, calling them fragrant and foul-smelling: fragrant by analogy with the things that are sweet to the tongue, foul-smelling by analogy with those that are not sweet. For the genus of these latter, so far at least as the flavours are concerned, has no name under a single designation. And it seems that from bodies which are not odorous either altogether little flows off, or what flows off is incommensurate in its particles, as in the case of the precisely salty and the acerbic. And whenever I say that something is precisely such or such, I mean that it is pure and unmixed, so far as is possible, with any other quality.

For the substance of both is coarse-particled, and in addition that of the acerbic ones is cold, [700] so that it is likely that what flows off from them is both scanty and thick and, as it were, earthy in its masses, and for this reason does not even enter the brain in the acts of breathing. Hence it is not safe to draw inferences from smell about the mixture of perceptible things, as it is from taste. For odourless things are coarse-particled in their substances, but it is not yet clear how they stand in respect of heat and cold; whereas odorous things are in some way fine-particled and hot. Yet the amount of the fineness of particles or of the heat is no longer indicated. But indeed the greatest factor, for all odorous things, in their indicating nothing clear about the mixture is the unevenness of their substance, about which I have already spoken many times, showing that most bodies are non-homoeomerous in their constitution. And now too, for the sake of clarity, one example will be stated.

The rose, then, is non-homoeomerous not only in this respect, that one thing in it is what contains and another what is contained — what contains being the hard and earthy part, and what is contained within this [701] being a certain moist juice — but also in that there must necessarily be, as we showed before, three residues of the juice itself: one earthy, just like the lees in wines; another airy, this one being analogous to the 'flower' in wines; and the third watery, which we said in all of them produces their boiling — and also their corruption, whenever it is not mastered and not completely altered during the time of the boiling. It is on account of this kind of residue that some people store away the juices after boiling them, others after first drying them in a strong sun. For on account of the earthy and the airy residue they are not at all afraid that the juices will be corrupted, seeing that these both separate out and are resistant to putrefaction in their substances, because they are also dry in their mixtures. But about these matters enough has been said before.

But in the nature of the rose there is one part that is acerbic to those who taste it, which must necessarily be earthy, coarse-particled and cold; another that is bitter, which is in fact fine-particled and hot; and a third besides these, the watery, cold of necessity, but in the [702] opposition between fine-particled and coarse-particled standing somehow midway between the extremes; and by the mixture of this neither the acerbic nor the bitter is, either of them, such in the extreme degree as it is said to be, for the admixture of the watery relaxes all the qualities. This watery part itself, then, seems somehow already to have been worked up and made thin and heated, and on this account to be easily brought into vapours, and in this way the rose is both odorous and dries very quickly. And all these things about it can be inferred through taste, but through smell it is not possible, because neither do all its parts give off vapour alike nor move the sense alike. In the case of taste, on the other hand, all the parts of tastable bodies alike fall upon the tongue, and each of them moves the sense according to its own nature; so that it is not safe, as has been said, to make inferences from smell about the whole power of drugs. For only these things can be discerned, as many as have just now been stated. And still more, it is not possible to conjecture anything from colours either about the power of drugs.

For in each colour there are found both hot and cold and dry and moist things, as has been demonstrated by me also in the first books [703] of this treatise. Within each kind, however, whether of seed or of root or of juice, it is possible to obtain from the colour too some indication of the mixture; for example, straightaway, onion and squill and wine, to the extent that they are whiter, are also less hot, while the yellowish and tawny ones are hotter; and wheat and millet and ochri and phaseli and chickpeas and the root of iris and that of asphodel and of many others are affected in a similar way. For in each kind, for the most part, those that are tawny and yellow and red are hotter than the white ones; so that, if it is permissible to infer something from this source too about the power of drugs, let it be added to the account. But the best course, as has been said and stated many times, is to discover the powers from qualified experience; for you would not go wrong in this either. Before, however, one has discerned the power by experience, taste displays most things, with smell too, as has been said, bearing some small additional witness.

[704] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 5. Having undertaken this fifth discourse on the power of simple drugs, I shall first recall those things demonstrated by me in the preceding books that are useful for the present matters, making my beginning from the elements, water and fire, air and earth, which some people, naming them derivatively from the qualities, say are moist and dry and hot and cold.

But if anyone is vexed by the length of the discussions, he ought not to blame us for this, but rather the physicians who have written things [541] that are plausible but not true. For I myself even now still fear that, because of the brevity of the refutation directed against them, some of the sophisms may lead astray the young men who associate with them. For if they came to the reading of the books trained in the logical methods and knowing how one ought to resolve sophisms, neither would those who commit some fallacy in their demonstrations escape their notice, nor would we, when we teach the truth itself concisely. But since the majority of the physicians themselves are unexercised in these matters, and some, in addition to this, are also by nature rather sluggish in their reasoning, if these men should not obtain the assistance from us of refuting the sophisms, they will easily be persuaded by the sophists; so that, as far as these men are concerned, the treatise might even seem to be lacking in something.

But since it is not possible to aim at all the readers, who are dissimilar not only in their natures but also in their ages and their conditions, the kind of discourse which seemed likely to be most useful to the greatest number I adopted in the two commentaries before this one [542]: in the first I examined the power of vinegar and of water, while in the second I went through for the most part the subject of oil, adding also a few remarks about rose oil. In this third one, however, we shall make the discourse of the kind which I had resolved right from the beginning to undertake, first distinguishing the meanings of each of the names; next going through the elements, as it were, of the whole treatise, and then in this way arriving at the syllables, as it were, from which the very end of the treatise, towards which we are hastening, will now readily follow. Now the division of the names teaches nothing further beyond what was said in the third book On Mixture and in the first of these commentaries, but I shall recall it now as well. Each of the bodies is called, and appears, either hot or cold or dry or wet, sometimes being so in accordance with its own nature, sometimes having taken on some acquired quality.

It is our custom to say that what is such according to its own nature is, and appears, such primarily and in itself and through itself, [543] potentially (δυνάμει); whereas what has taken on an acquired quality is, and appears, such according to some accident. And of those things themselves which are said to be hot, or cold, or dry, or wet according to their proper nature, some are such in actuality, others potentially — this 'potentially' now spoken of differing from the one said a little before; for that one was set in contrast with 'accidentally', whereas this one with 'in actuality'. And of those which are such in actuality, one is called hot, or cold, or wet, or dry simply, like the elements; another by predominance, like a man and a horse and an ox and a dog and all the animals as wholes; another in some respect relative to the well-proportioned thing of the same genus or of the same species, as, for instance, a lion compared with a man, or a man in his prime with a child; and another relative to anything whatever one happens upon, as Dion relative to Theon.

And indeed, of the bodies that are said to be potentially of such or such a kind, we said that each is necessarily so called with reference to what is such in actuality: the one, because it is easily set ablaze, with reference to what is simply hot in [544] actuality; the other, because it heats animals, with reference to what is hot by predominance. So too, what heats a human being is potentially hot in relation to a human being, and what heats an ox or a horse, in relation to an ox or a horse. And similarly, one thing is so in relation to this particular human being, another being hot or cold or moist when compared only with the nature of that one. From this distinction of the names we derived benefit for the recognition of their mixture: if something were said to be hot, or cold, or dry, or moist in relation to a human being, we deemed it right to leave aside all the other animals and to make the trial and the test on the human being alone; but if in relation to an ox, or a horse, or a deer, or any one of the other animals, that the trial should again in turn be made on that one alone. And in these matters we also censured those who try to discover the powers of the drugs from the consistency, or colour, or heaviness, or lightness, or the quality presented to taste or to smell by each of them.

All these things, then, appear to have followed upon the correct division of the names; [545] and the elements, as it were, of the inquiry before us we showed to lie in the knowledge of the primary qualities, which we demonstrated in the work On the Elements according to Hippocrates—moistness and dryness, hotness and coldness; and the discovery of these too came to us, one may almost say, from correctly distinguishing the things signified by the names. For by marking off a drug from nourishment in that the former alters in respect of quality, whereas the latter is assimilated to the substance of the body, we were guided from there, in the course of the argument, to the discovery of the qualities that alter us. And since alterations are twofold in genus—some being species-producing, which indeed are properly and primarily named alterations, others breaking apart and drawing together the parts of our body, which people call alterations by a misuse of the term rather than by proper naming—we say that the powers of drugs are contained in the first of these.

For nothing, [we say,] is able to change from one species into another species without being heated and cooled and dried and [546] moistened. And I mean "from species into species" when, out of bread and ptisane and lentil-soup, blood and phlegm and bile, both yellow and black, come to be, and out of these in turn bone and soft fat and sinew and flesh, artery and vein, and each of the other parts of the animal. But if something, by cutting us, as glass or a sword does, or by bruising, as stone and lead do, or by drawing together the parts that have been separated, as bandaging does, alters these parts in some way, [we say] that such things are not drugs; for an alteration of this kind does not remove each of the things that exist from its own proper nature. For whether you break bread into many pieces and cut it up, or whether you gather it together into one out of many small pieces, it does not depart from its proper form, nor does bread become flesh when it is broken down, nor bone if it should happen to be brought together in this way; but when, in the course of being concocted in the belly and the veins, it changes into blood and phlegm, and then out of these into bone and flesh and the other parts of the body, it is altered in its whole substance and departs from its original nature, passing over into another species.

Yet all the affections of the body were shown to receive their alterations and changes of substance into another form from nothing other than the hot, the cold, the dry [547] and the moist. And accordingly we said that the primary and elemental form-producing qualities are four—moistness, dryness, heat, coldness—and we inquire, for each of the drugs, which of these it possesses as predominant in its mixture. Straightaway, then, on this first point most of those who have investigated them seem to me to have gone wrong, in that they examine the predominant quality simply, as certain natural philosophers do; and indeed many of them, reading the writings of Theophrastus and Aristotle unmethodically, reason fallaciously. And yet the difference is very great between making distinctions concerning hot and cold and dry and moist with a view to the whole of nature, and doing so with a view to human beings only. For when one looks to the whole of nature, each of these is said in two ways: in one sense simply, in the other by predominance.

each of the elements simply, but a human being and [548] a horse and an ox by predominance. But when the examination is carried out in relation to something, one must consider only that in relation to which it is said. And what we are inquiring is not whether the moist is simply greater than the dry in sea-water—for this we see plainly—but whether it is so in relation to a human being. Nor indeed even in relation to him when compared simply in this way, as if you were to compare a lion with him as well; for even so sea-water is moister than a human being. How, then, do we still inquire whether sea-water is dry in its power? How else than in the sense equivalent to its being drying of the human body? To this alone, then, must one look, leaving the rest aside. But most physicians do the opposite, for they look at everything else rather than at this. How, then, having turned toward the human being and withdrawn from the rest, shall we come to know how sea-water stands in respect of activity toward him?

Clearly, by applying it to the body and taking trial of what happens, both in bathing in sea-water and in drenching or fomenting with it, and in frequently placing upon parts wool and sponges soaked in sea-water, and in mixing it with plasters and cerates, [549] and in all these cases distinguishing from what sometimes results per accidens that which is accomplished in accordance with the proper power of the drug itself? For in this lies the whole decisive force of the discovery, and this alone almost none of them touches upon. But the assertions of the philosophers deceive them, since they are unable to perceive the homonymy. For not only, as was said just now, is one thing said by them to be so simply and another by predominance — for fire is hot simply, but a human being by predominance — but they also hold that 'by predominance' itself is said in two ways: the one according to the bulks of the substance, as we too distinguished in the treatises On Mixtures, as for instance if you were to mix two choes of water boiling to the utmost degree with one chous of altogether cold water; the other according to the activity of the qualities. But this latter they state as something already dependent upon a doctrine, no longer taking it from what evidently appears.

For having assumed that the cold draws together and condenses the substance and renders it immobile, whereas the hot rarefies and diffuses and concocts and [550] moves it, they reasonably declare that the hot prevails in all plants. For neither, they say, would the distribution of nutriment from the earth to the greatest extent otherwise come about, nor its alteration, nor its concoction, nor indeed the growth of plants at all, or their sprouting, or the generation of fruits, if the hot did not prevail; and so then again among the plants themselves they declare one to be hotter, another colder. On this assumption, then, depends also their account concerning roses, that they are hot: for the hot prevails to a greater degree in them than in certain other plants. And from another assumption again, in turn, the account concerning oil and soft fat: for because they burst into flame very quickly, on this account they say that they are hot in power. And in yet another way again, all things that are sweet: for because they are most akin and most similar to our mixtures, we being hot by nature, on this account they say that these too are hot.

For the philosophers, then, inasmuch as they are making pronouncements about the whole of nature, such matters are rightly investigated and stated; but for physicians, who have a different [551] aim, not rightly. For neither because the hot predominates in the activities in roses, nor in general because it is by genus a plant, is it thereby hot on account of any of these things. For we were not inquiring into the hot in that way, but as relative to man; since, by the criterion of the hot's predominating in the activities, every plant will be hot, and still more all the animals. So then let them say that poppy and mandrake and hemlock and salamander are hot; but they do not say so; rather, as if from one mouth, they all declare that all these are cold. And yet the salamander is an animal, one that is surely nourished and grows and moves—things which, they say, come about when the hot predominates in the mixture. How then is it that in these cases they look to the relation to man, but in others to the whole of nature, or to the activities of the primary qualities? I for my part say that one ought not to declare only the salamander or hemlock to be cold in their powers, as relative to man, but to judge all the other things in the same way as well.

since hemlock not only does not cool starlings, nor kill them [552] as it does us, but even nourishes them and, evidently, warms them; for everything that nourishes a hot substance surely increases its heat and preserves it. And the substance of the body of starlings is hot not only insofar as they are animals, but also insofar as they are blooded creatures. It has, then, been demonstrated by me many times, in many treatises already, that there are certain affinities and conflicts of qualities in all existing things, and that what is akin is readily assimilated, whereas what is contrary sometimes changes both plants and animals towards destruction. And indeed, that their affinities come about in accordance with the peculiar character of the whole substance—this too has been stated and demonstrated by me many times. But they are unable to discern this, and for that reason they make pronouncements about most drugs carelessly and at the same time falsely. For there is only one safe criterion in their case, the test in relation to a human being, provided that we distinguish in it what is per accidens from what is per se.

And one who attends to this will call neither vinegar nor rose oil hot; for both cool us primarily and in themselves, vinegar strongly, [553] rose oil to a slight degree. What sort of thing this 'to a slight degree' is, I shall explain. For together with it there will also come into view the account concerning the middle mixture of all drugs, of which I made mention in the book before this one as well, when discussing olive oil. If, then, any of the bodies or drugs that come into contact with us is in actuality hot in the same way as we are, or on approaching us becomes hot in like manner to us, such a thing is of the middle mixture, so far as comparing it with us is concerned, since in itself it could be called hot by predominance, just as we too are. But if something is neither already hot in the way we are nor becomes such in approaching us, this is colder than the mixture of a human being, even if in some way or other the hot predominates in it. And indeed, in approaching us, it will take away and diminish something of the heat present in us.

For just as, if of two waters, both hot, but the one more and the other less, you were to mix the less hot into the more hot, you would slacken its warmth, so if into the heat from rose oil, which is lukewarm even in relation to the mixture of a human being, you were to mix in human heat, you would in every case take away something of it and cool it down. One should not, then, be surprised if something that is hot in its own right and in itself, when brought to another hotter thing, is able to cool it. For this is a nature common to all alterable bodies, that when they come near one another they act and are acted upon to an inapparent degree (εἰς ἄδηλα), the less hot becoming hotter by the agency of the more hot, and the more hot being disposed in the opposite way by the less hot. For you may learn this clearly through touch itself. For to it the same things often appear now hot, now cold: cold when it has become hotter, and hot when it has become colder. And someone recently put to us the problem why we urinate cold in the baths but hot outside, not following that the urine itself is lukewarm in the same way both in the baths and outside, whereas we are not in the same condition with respect to the surface of the body while bathing and before it.

For while we are bathing we have it [the surface of the body] [555] hotter than the urine, but outside colder; so that with good reason the urine appears to it hot outside the bath, but cold inside. For it has the sensation of what is less hot than itself as of something cooling it down, and of what is hotter than itself as of something heating it up. And it is open to you, for the sake of testing what has been said, when you are already sufficiently warmed while bathing, to order a small pail of moderately lukewarm water to be brought in and to put your hands or your feet into it. For the water will appear to you not lukewarm, but quite cold. But if, immediately upon entering the bath, you were to touch the water in the pail, it will appear less cold to you. For always, to the extent that you have been warmed beforehand, to that extent will it appear cold. And there is nothing surprising in this, if indeed also most well waters, those that have deep springs, appear lukewarm when touched in winter. But if, having bathed, you were to touch them with warm hands, they would not appear lukewarm to you, and much more so if you were still bathing.

Since, then, we have touch as our criterion in the discriminations of hot and cold things, and refer our judgments of them to the condition of that [faculty], [556] we are, reasonably enough, often misled, so as even to call cold what is not cold in itself, and hot what is not hot in itself. And for this reason, when bathing we think the urine cold, but when we have been shivering in the frost we think the well water hot. And if we should forget the conditions in which we were when we touched both, remembering only the sensation that came to us, we might perhaps at some point declare that the water is simply hot and the urine simply cold. But neither of them is simply either hot or cold, but only in relation to us; and not even in relation to us simply, again, but to us as being in a certain condition. What each of them is simply in relation to us would be stated when it is examined in relation to our middle and best mixture, just as, if it were being tested in relation to man simply, the examination would surely in any case be made in relation to the well-mixed man. All these errors too, then, depend on the division of names, which almost everyone despises.

[557] For since 'cold' and 'hot' are said in one sense simply, in another by predominance, in another by comparison with the well-proportioned thing of the same genus, and in another in relation to anything whatever that happens to be at hand, we reasonably go wrong often amid the homonymies, forgetting what sort of hot thing we are judging and passing over to another. But it has already been said countless times, and will be said again, that one must investigate the power of drugs according to the fourth and last of the significations just mentioned. For neither is each of them hot simply, as fire is—for that would indeed be impossible—nor is it proposed to examine whether it is hot by predominance, as blood is; nor yet whether it is called hot in relation to the well-proportioned thing of the same genus or of the same species, as a lion is among animals, and as that which is in its prime, within each of the species, is in relation to that which has grown old. Rather, the inquiry is whether each of the drugs is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist in relation to a human being.

and not even in relation to him as something compared in the manner of a relative, but whether it is so in power — that [558] is, whether, when brought near to him, it renders the part which it touches hotter, or colder, or moister, or drier. So that both the matter of judgement and that of discrimination will lie in experience, which most physicians abandon, inquiring instead whether the rose is red or fragrant, and neglecting, when they have been overheated in the head, to put on it garlands of roses, or their juice, or rose oil, and so to learn by experience what happens. For if they are heated up, it would rather be hot; but if they are cooled, cold — which is the same as saying that it is cooling in relation to human nature; for one must always keep this in mind, although I never cease saying it countless times, while most people mishear it, and one must pardon them, perverted as they are by sophists who talk nonsense at length. The matters of experience, then, are thus easy, both concerning the power of roses and concerning all the other drugs.

For it is surely possible both to crown oneself with roses, and, having at some time pounded them, to apply them as a plaster to the mouth of the stomach of a person burning with fever, and [559] having pressed out their juice, to gulp it down, and having mixed it with water or with oil, to rub some one of the parts of the body with it. And yet why do I say this to these people, when in fact some people, mixing rose juice with opobalsam, rub their bodies with it in the burning heats under the Dog-star for the sake of cooling, having learned by experience itself that they cool sufficiently? But out of excessive wisdom Herodotus the physician does not even admit that rose oil with vinegar, which they specifically call oxyrhodinon, cools us; then, having recalled at least this much, that he himself uses it in the beginnings of phrenitic diseases, and being aware of the contradiction—for it is agreed by almost all physicians, even down to the followers of the most senseless Thessalus, that at the beginning one must repel and cool rather than warm and relax—he says that it does not cool but is astringent. And yet there was nothing difficult in his too, when he himself was at some time overheated by the sun—for he was a human being subject to the same affections as we are—moistening his head with oxyrhodinon and coming to know by experience the activity of the drug.

[560] And it would have been very easy, I think, also when chilled to use it at some time, pouring it over the head, instilling it into the ears, pouring it into the nostrils, and rubbing the whole forehead with it, just as we use marjoram-oil and iris-oil and the other warming unguents. For indeed, according to him, oxyrhodinon heats not even moderately, being composed of two very hot drugs. But if Herodotus did not dare to use it, it is right, I think, that those of the present day should make trial of the power of the drug on themselves, whenever they have either been chilled or been scorched by the sun, just as I have often made trial of it on myself and on not a few others who had been scorched, having moistened the head with it. For it is better that they should first themselves have made trial of what they say, and so advise us and record it in their books. But indeed, I know not how, although guarding against engaging in controversy, I have been compelled to it by their shamelessness.

So I return once more to what I set out from the beginning, namely that the powers of drugs [561] must be judged by experience, using them both on those who are in blameless health and on those suffering diseases as simple as possible, whether hot, or cold, or dry, or moist. For if you judge in this way, olive oil will be found neither hot nor cold relative to a well-tempered human being, while rose oil will be found already somewhat colder, yet certainly not strongly cold, but, as I am accustomed to name it, of the first distance and order of the cooling things. For just as water, for instance, is in one case precisely well-tempered, in another either warmer or colder, yet not thereby in any way hot or cold, to speak absolutely, so too among drugs olive oil belongs to the middle mixture, whereas the juice of roses belongs to the colder one, though not by any great amount, being, as I have also said before, at lukewarm warmth. And of the same order as it is what is called linseed, so far as concerns the lukewarmness of its warmth, but by being coarse-particled it differs to no small degree.

For the juice of roses is precisely fine-particled, as is shown [562] by its drying easily, by its partaking of no viscosity, and by its dissolving the odours of the other perfumes. For it appears to do this too by nothing other than by being the first to fill up the olfactory passages; for when the others are about to pass through and penetrate, it occupies them beforehand and fills them. Chamomile too is, as regards fineness of parts, similar to the rose, but as regards heat it is rather of the power of olive oil, which is proper to the animal and well-proportioned; wherefore it is also a help against fatigue, if anything is, and soothing of pains, and it relaxes and slackens what is tense, softens what is moderately hard, and rarefies what has been condensed. And it is resolvent of fevers, as many as cause trouble without inflammation of a viscus, and of these especially those which arise from bilious humours or from condensation of the skin. For this reason, indeed, among the wisest of the Egyptians it has been consecrated to the sun and held to be a remedy for all fevers. But in this they do not speak the truth; for it is a remedy only for the fevers I have mentioned, and of these when they are already being concocted.

It does, however, benefit well also all the [563] others, both those that are melancholic and those that are phlegmatic and the offspring of inflammation of a viscus. For chamomile is a most noble remedy of these too, whenever it is applied to them once they are already being concocted, and on this account it is also kindly to the hypochondria if anything is. And linseed too, at any rate, the ancient account says is of this sort. And indeed that too is really kindly to the viscera in the hypochondria, but less so than chamomile. For it is both less hot, as has been said, and in addition to this it is coarse-particled; the rose, however, does not come close to them in these respects, although, as far as concerns the lukewarmness of its heat and its fine-particled quality, this too would have been sufficiently useful for inflammations in the hypochondria; but the astringency that accompanies it does harm in many ways, and especially in those cases in which chamomile is of good repute, either rarefying the condensed parts of bodies, or softening the hardened, or relaxing the tense. For astringency is hostile to all such things.

For the onsets and increases of inflammations, however, and especially [564] of superficial ones, rose oil is better than chamomile, because these require both a lukewarm warmth and a slight astringency. For at the beginning cooling and astringent things are useful, during the increases those which are lukewarm and moderately astringent, and at the peaks of inflammations those which warm more, in due measure, and disperse strongly. All these matters will be discussed at greater length in the books of the Therapeutic Method. For now I return again to the subject at hand. For indeed the drugs of the middle mixture, and those which deviate slightly toward either side, may seem at one time to warm and at another in turn to cool, and sometimes neither to warm nor to cool but to preserve the bodies in the condition in which they received them; and this happens to them with good reason, if indeed lukewarm water and urine appear cold in the baths, but warm to those who have been chilled.

If, then, in accordance with the condition of the things being affected, the agent too appears not to act in the same way, it is clear that neither the rose nor the oil nor chamomile [565] nor linseed, nor indeed dill nor fenugreek flour, nor wheat flour either, nor countless others—both those that are exactly intermediate in their mixtures and those that depart slightly from it—will display the same activity throughout. For neither are we all mixed alike when we are healthy, nor do we fall ill with the same diseases. To take an immediate example, rose oil is, in its mixture, mixed intermediately between oil and the juice of roses; for it is less hot than the one and more so than the other. For it cools those who are burning, obviously by the lukewarmness of its heat, while it also warms a little those who have been chilled, since this too is a work of lukewarm warmth, just as baths too both warm those who are shivering and cool those who are burning. And for this reason, even if you mix rose oil into drugs whose nature it is to cool or to heat, you will do no great harm, just as you will do no notable good either. For lukewarm warmth is not capable of harming parts that have been chilled, but neither is it able to cure them.

For everything that is being treated, [566] inasmuch as it is being brought from some excess into due proportion, needs not what is itself moderate in its mixture, but the opposite excess. At any rate, if you should wish to make cold water well-tempered, you must not mix in what is already well-tempered; for in that way the mixture of both will be lukewarm. Rather, it is fitting to go to boiling water and to mix this with the cold. And indeed what is mixed with the cold must be hotter than the moderate by just as much as the cold itself was colder than the moderate. For neither will what is slightly colder than the moderate recover the middle mixture by means of what is much hotter, nor will what is much colder do so by means of what is slightly hotter. But if what needs treatment is much colder, it is necessary that what is to treat it also be much hotter; and if it is slightly colder, what treats it must also be slightly hotter. In a word, what is to treat must stand as far from the middle as what is to be treated, the distance of each lying, obviously, in opposite directions.

For that which stands at a similar distance in the same direction, being similar in mixture to what is being treated, is capable of bringing about no alteration, so that it will neither harm anything affected nor benefit it. That which is less [distant] will indeed benefit, yet it will certainly not cure. If, then, the affection should be cold, while the heat of the drug is lukewarm, it will certainly help the affection somewhat, yet it will not in every case bring it back to the natural proportion, so that it will not cure it at all. Again, if the affection should be small, such that it has shifted from the moderate warmth that is according to nature to, as it were, a kind of lukewarm warmth, while the drug is cold, the affection must necessarily be chilled and harmed by the cold. The same holds even if the affection is hotter than the proportionate state: by drugs similar to it, it will be kept in the same state, but it will be harmed by those less hot than themselves (ὑπὸ τῶν ἧττον ἑαυτῶν θερμῶν), yet it will certainly not be fully cured. Here too, then, there arrives once again a certain homonymy, extended over the whole of life and leading astray in many places.

For indeed we sometimes call what is mixed in due proportion [568] "hot", as for instance a bath of that sort and a drink, and also what falls short of this by not much, and in addition to these everything hotter still. But if we were using the names precisely, we would call the well-proportioned not "hot" but "well-tempered"; and whatever is more immoderate than this, that which is immoderate in the direction of the hotter we would call hot to a lesser and to a greater degree, and that which is in the direction of the colder cold to a lesser and to a greater degree. And so too, I think, in the case of drugs, if we were naming precisely, we would have called something well-tempered and intermediate, like olive oil; and if something is hotter than it, hot, like fenugreek; and if something is colder than it, cold, like the rose. But the reason we do not use the names in this way is that not all bodies are cooled by such drugs as rose-oil is. For those bodies that are cold in like degree to it and those that are colder still, in the one case it does not alter at all, and in the other it even heats.

It would seem, then, to be unreasonable if, while agreeing that something heats, we then call it cold, [569] just as if one were also to call well-water in winter cold, the water which appears lukewarm to chilled hands. From these occasions, then, the use of the names, having been thrown into disorder, disorders in turn the knowledge of the things as well. In the same way too, concerning dry and moist, once the names were confounded, the knowledge of the things was confounded along with them. And yet, although distinguishing properly the things signified by the names seems a small matter, it is found to have the greatest power for the knowledge of the things. But about moist and dry we shall speak a little later, when we have brought to a conclusion the account concerning hot and cold. For indeed not much of the distinctions belonging to it seems still to be lacking, once at least it has clearly been shown that it is nothing to wonder at that, under the action of a single drug, differing bodies are some of them heated, others cooled, and others undergo neither of these.

For in the relative sense it is very easy, when one comes to the particular cases, to say that rose oil, when applied to such-and-such a body, is of a nature to preserve it in the mixture in which it found it, whereas when brought to another body of such-and-such a kind it heats [570] and another it cools. But to make a universal pronouncement about its power is difficult without first drawing distinctions and reaching an agreement about the names. The distinction and the agreement would be as follows: since the bodies of human beings differ very greatly both in their mixtures from the beginning and in those that accrue to them according to their ages and in those according to the habits of their way of life, it is surely necessary that they be altered in different ways by the same drugs. At any rate, if you compare a young man, hot by nature, a labourer by way of life, with an old woman who is also colder by nature, you would find the excess no smaller than that of one of the drugs that heat considerably in relation to those that cool. Conceive for me, then, someone intermediate between these, both well-mixed in nature right from the beginning and preserving this good mixture by appropriate habits.

And having set these three before your mind as, so to speak, the targets of temperament, consider the drug that is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist in general, and ask with reference to which temperament among these it is [571] better to look in naming it. Is it to the best-tempered one, which is indeed one single thing and the mean of all the others, or to those that are immoderate and ill-tempered and undefined and almost infinite in number? For to me the question of this division does not even seem to admit of comparison, nor to stand in need of any inquiry; rather it appears plainly, to anyone possessed of even a little sense, that one should take the body that is rightly constituted and simple and one, laying it down as a kind of rule and target, and steer straight by it, and so judge the others too with reference to it. Let such a body, then, be laid down by us as the rule of the power of drugs. And let that drug which kindles a warmth similar to the temperament of this body be named well-tempered, even if it seems ever so manifestly to heat an old man who is chilled. But as for that which either heats or cools such a body, let the one that heats be called hot, and the one that cools cold.

And let there be made, for the sake of clear teaching, an ordering of the degrees of distance of these very things: on the side of the cold, the first being that in which one would place rose oil, the second that in which the rose itself will be, and a third after this and a fourth, until we arrive in our account at the [572] coldest things, hemlock and poppy-juice and mandrake and henbane. On the side of the hot, in turn, dill and fenugreek first, and next in order as second whatever appear to be second, and then third and fourth, until we arrive at those which burn. And in the same manner, in the case of the moistening drugs too, beginning again from the well-proportioned [mean], let us make orders in succession as far as the extremes. For the use of such knowledge for the therapeutic method is no small one. Or rather, if one must tell the truth, if someone does not draw the distinctions in this way, he will harm rather than benefit those who read him. As it is now, in addition to the other errors which the majority of physicians commit when expounding the powers of the simple drugs, one can also find this, which is the more harmful: among the heating drugs, for instance, there may be written dill and fenugreek and misy and lime, and among the cooling ones rose oil and mandrake and hemlock, as though fenugreek were close to lime, or rose oil to hemlock, and not separated by the many orders of drugs lying between them.

But [573] we, at any rate, shall try, so far as we are able, to bring so great and difficult a task into some order and to write down both those drugs that are near one another in their powers and those that are far apart. And let us do this not by entrusting the judgment of them to plausible arguments, but to determinate experience, just as this too has often been said in what precedes. It is surely evident that such a judgment is safe, but at the same time long and involving much labour for us who are going to arrive through it at the end of what is proposed; yet for those who wish to read through these writings it alone is capable of making them skilled in the art and of providing, as it were, a certain eye that discerns the truth. Accordingly, having added in this book whatever is still lacking for the whole elementary exposition, we shall speak in the fourth about the power of the flavours (χυλοί), since this too seemed good to our companions; and in the fifth about the secondary and composite powers in all simple drugs in general; and then in this way we shall pass over to the particulars in the subsequent treatises.

[574] There remains, then, first, a point which the discussion has often already been compelled to mention even before, but did not go through completely. This is that nearly all drugs, even if they appear simple to sense-perception, are at any rate compound in their nature, and often indeed have within themselves even the most opposite powers, such as an excretory and a checking one, a thickening and a thinning one, a rarefying and a condensing one, a clogging and a cleansing one, a tensing and a relaxing one, and all the other oppositions, as we shall show in the discussion after this. And it is nothing remarkable if, in the case of such powers, in one and the same drug a heating and a cooling power should appear, or a drying and a moistening one, a fine-particled and a coarse-particled one. For if the first and most active powers did not have such a combination, neither would those that come after them have been similarly combined.

But if we ourselves mix, as it may happen, juice of sumach with honey, we concede that what is mixed from both has not only an astringent but also a cleansing power, and not only a power retentive of the belly [575] but also an evacuating one. But that in milk the two powers are contained, one excretory and at the same time one that checks the belly, we no longer concede in the same way. And yet this is even easily separated into whey and curd, and it is agreed by all that the one loosens the belly, the other restrains it. This we still do not readily concede in the case of cabbage too. For when we press out its juice and gulp it down either alone or with honey, we see that it is purgative, but, not being able to eat the remainder, we disbelieve that it is checking. But if someone, having boiled the whole of it, pours off the first water, in which it deposited its juice, and then, having thrown it again into other clean water and boiled it again, pours off this too, he will find the juice purging, but the cabbage itself restraining the belly—and much more so if one pours off the water not twice but three or four times.

For the more thoroughly it deposits its juice in it, the more purgative it will make that [water], while it will show the remaining substance of the cabbage, the flesh as it were of the vegetable, to be checking [576]. And so it is also with beets and with nearly all the others whose juice is either pungent or nitrous or salty; since indeed even in lentils, although they have considerable astringency to the taste, there is nevertheless something of this kind. For the decoction of these too is laxative of the belly; but this juice is clearly mixed to the taste, as if you were also to mix something nitrous with a harsh one. But the juice of sea-shellfish and of all the other oysters is simply salty and laxative. Yet the flesh itself of these too holds back the belly, and you will find what is said to be true if you prepare them in the same way as the cabbages. For indeed the broth of older cocks too loosens the belly, although the flesh is checking. And in the scale of copper too there is a twofold power, just as also a twofold quality; for it is both astringent and biting; and on this account, by its being astringent it cicatrizes the dry ones among ulcerated fleshes, while by its biting it melts down the flabby ones.

But if it should be taken into the body, [577] it purges, and does not check the belly. For the astringent power is overcome by the pungent and purgative one, just as if you were also to mix juice of sumach with scammony. For what results from both will be purgative, not checking of the belly, even though to the taste the harsh juice will rather predominate. So too not a few of the purgatives, when given with the flesh of a quince-apple, escape notice in taste and are manifest only in their activity. Some are also given by means of the flesh of the date, others by means of myrtle-berries or with Chian mastic, or with some other of the things that are good for the stomach and astringent, so as both to escape the taste and to upset the stomach less. But even if the astringent things prevail over the purgatives in the quality relative to taste, in the other power at least they are overcome. For often the tongue is overcome in accordance with the preponderating part of the substance, whereas the activity comes about in accordance with the strength of the power.

When, therefore, a small substance possessing a vehement power, having been mixed with another substance, large in quantity and possessing a weak power, arrives inside the body, it escapes the taste, but accomplishes its work [578] more effectively than that other. These things too are wondered at by the many, and they consider it a puzzle if some astringent body is by nature such as to purge, as for example aloe and scale of copper and burnt copper; for, they say, these ought on the contrary rather to check the belly, not to stimulate it. But that the apple, if it so happens, which together with the scammony is astringent, purges — this at any rate no one wonders at; and yet, setting out from this point, it would have been very easy, I think, to infer in the case of aloe as well that a certain mixed power exists. And if it were possible to separate the purging part in it from the non-purging, as we do in the case of milk and cabbage and very many others, it would no longer be wondered at. And indeed it is even possible, in a way, to do this. For aloe that has been carefully washed moves the belly altogether weakly or not at all. This same thing happens also to scale of copper and to burnt copper itself, as we too have found by trial after washing them thoroughly, their purging being faint. But in any case, the drug-like character of the quality, too, immediately upon tasting, displays the mixed nature of the power.

[579] For if there were always a single quality in each of the drugs that are astringent to the taste, it would never be the case that some of them are edible and others drug-like; rather, they would differ from one another only in being more or less astringent. But as things are, this is not so. For one kind of astringency appears pleasant and agreeable, another unpleasant and drug-like: that of pear, apple and pomegranate pleasant, that of scale of copper and aloe unpleasant and drug-like. And yet scale of copper is less astringent than a quince-apple, so that one could not even refer the strangeness of its quality to the vehemence of its astringency. Similarly, other edible things too are more astringent than aloe, scale of copper and burnt copper itself. In such cases, then, the mixed character of the substance is manifestly apparent; in others, even if it is not apparent, one must infer it, and not suppose that astringency effects one thing in the case of aloe and something else in the case of the apple. For it is reasonable that, in all cases, not only astringency but also each of the other qualities does one and the same thing, at least according to its own nature.

But because nothing is found that is exactly pure or unmixed [580] with other qualities, the differences of the activities are different in one astringent thing and in another. For the action of the medlar is one thing, that of scale of copper another, that of aloe another, and different again that of mulberries, if it should so happen, or of oak-gall, or of pomegranate rind, or of alum, or of sumach; and it would have been better for those who ventured to make some pronouncement about the activity of astringent drugs to have spoken in general about astringency itself rather than about the astringent things. For the astringent thing is not only astringent, but, in addition to being astringent, is either pungent, or oily, or sweet, or bitter, or salty, or sour. Astringency, however, is this one thing only, throughout, exactly what it is, just as sweetness and saltiness and each of the other qualities also are. And if, just as astringency is one, the astringent thing too were one, its action would throughout be one. But since, in addition to being astringent, it has been shown to possess yet other qualities, not a few, it will always act in accordance with all of them, but conspicuously now according to one, now according to another, namely the one that prevails, in relation to the condition of the body that comes into contact with it.

At any rate milk, lentil and cabbage [581] plainly loosen the belly in some people and hold it back in others. Now the cause why any one quality and power whatsoever of a drug does not always act manifestly, and in each individual body, I shall state in the following book. For the present my purpose is only to recall what happens, so that no one may disbelieve that in most drugs there are opposite qualities and powers. But even this very point involves much examination and not a few distinctions, even though it has seemed to everyone an easy matter to discover the qualities and powers that are opposite to one another. At any rate nearly all readily lay it down that being astringent is opposite to purging. But it is in no way opposite, as I shall demonstrate as the discourse proceeds. For the present, however, my argument has been brought to its conclusion by way of surplus, in showing that even if someone posits that these are opposite, nothing absurd follows, since it is indeed possible for the most opposite qualities and powers sometimes to come together in a single substance.

In the case of juices, at any rate, it was said also earlier [582] that the heaviest part in them is one thing, the lightest part another, and a third something else, mixed through the whole juice. And it is no wonder if in the juice of the rose too there is one part that is heaviest, analogous to the olive-lees (amorge) and the lees of wine, another that is lightest, this too analogous to the "flowers" that float upon each of the juices; and a third, like the part that ferments in must; and in addition to these a fourth, the most unmixed and purest part itself, of which these three are the residues. But it happens that all the other juices turn sour and putrefy as they undergo corruption, and only oil, honey and wine last for a long time. Consequently it is not possible, by means of the fermentation and separation of the other juices, to discover clearly the form of each of the residues; rather, right from the beginning they require some boiling and mixture with some other one of the juices that persist. So then we also store the juice of the rose by mixing it with honey, or boiling it together with oil, or steeping whole roses in it.

But that it is plausible that in this too the four kinds are present — that which [583] is proper to the juice itself and the three residues — is evident to see, and especially because what pertains to their quality is not simple; rather, the rose will seem to you to have some astringency too, if you should wish to chew it thoroughly. It has also a certain sweetness and, as it were, a slight biting. And even if none of these appeared to those tasting it, it would have sufficed, from the fact that it is not completely astringent, to grasp the mixtures of the other juices. For if the harsh one were alone, it would be extreme; so that if it is not extreme, neither is it alone. For whatever genesis of astringency you might posit, if you should conceive that it alone, apart from the others, comes to be in a thing, it is necessary that this be produced at its extreme — just as, if heat alone should come to be in some body, such a thing will be completely fire. For the admixtures of contraries break the extremes.

In the homoeomerous bodies, then, it is heat and coldness, moistness and dryness that produce all the particular differences; but in the non-homoeomerous bodies there are pungencies and sournesses, harshnesses [584] and acerbities and sweetnesses and oilinesses, so that each of the homoeomerous bodies, in the parts themselves, has not many qualities but one, whereas the whole non-homoeomerous body has very many. For if, say, a thousand homoeomerous bodies are contained in the cyathus of some particular juice, it is possible that a hundred of them are astringent, sixty biting, six hundred are the sweet ones, two hundred the bitter, forty the salty, and that all these are mixed through one another, and that one cannot take any perceptible portion so small that it does not have a share in all of them.

so that, in the contact with the tongue, all of them act, each part of them according to its own distinct character, upon whatever part it happens to have come into contact with, and the disposition is transmitted from the part first affected to the whole tongue—just as when, in severe cold, we plunge a single finger all at once into cold water and shiver with the whole hand, and often with the entire body as well. For the transmission in sensitive bodies from the part first affected to the whole animal takes place swiftly, so that when a part is heated the whole is heated along with it, when it is cooled the whole is cooled along with it, when it is dried [585] the whole is dried along with it, and when it is moistened the whole is moistened along with it, and often the whole undergoes contrary affections at one and the same time. But in order that you may come to a better notion of what is being said, it is perhaps better to direct your mind to another example as well. You have seen, I think, at some time, when a stone has been thrown into still water, that the water begins to move from that point and extends the movement in a circle, with the thing that struck it as if at a centre. So when, at one and the same time, two stones thrown into different places in still water generate two circles passing through one another, you will see contrary movements in every part of the water; whence this phenomenon has presented a difficulty even to the natural philosophers themselves, whether it is different parts that move in respect of each of the two movements, or the same parts that are moved by both. For that the one circle does not stop the other, nor prevent it from travelling onward, is plainly seen. Conceive, then, the same thing as this for me, when at one and the same time we plunge our feet into cold water and our hands into hot. For the movement of each of the two affections passes through to the whole body, and they meet one another as contrary movements.

[586] And perhaps it makes no difference even if they did not travel in opposite directions, but the one, having taken its impulse from one of the feet, and the other from the other, were to advance. For in that case it is possible neither to say that the whole body is affected by nothing, nor that it is affected by only one of the two. For it is clearly affected, and it is affected by both, being heated and cooled at the same time, just as, I think, happens also in the leipyriai and the epialos fevers, except that in those the condition of cooling and that of heat does not set out from outside, but from the body itself. But if even now someone does not follow what is being said, still from what is about to be said it is very easy for him to obtain the test. For indeed it is not even far from the matters under investigation, but is itself one of the affections of the tongue. For if, having thoroughly mixed an equal bulk of wormwood and of honey, you apply it to the tongue, the mixture of both will appear to you sweet-bitter, as the poets call love, the tongue not perceiving honey at one time and wormwood at another, nor only one of the two, but throughout perceiving both, mixed in a certain unaccustomed mixture.

Something of this kind [587] also comes about when a harsh and a nitrous power come together into a single juice, whether nature herself has mixed them or some physician has compounded them. For the tongue perceives the quality of each of the two juices at one and the same time, and if it perceives them, clearly it is also disposed according to their proper powers; and each of the other parts of the body must necessarily be affected in the same way, even if it does not perceive the qualities. For one must not suppose that the tongue differs from the other parts in being affected or not, but in the fact that none of its proper affections escapes its notice, owing to the precision of its perceptive power. Its looseness of texture also contributes to this; for the juices, descending more easily into the depth and acting upon the soft parts, produce a disposition that is strong and a perception of it that is more evident. But the greater power lies rather in the precision of the perception, not in the strength of the disposition; for the strength of the disposition arises no less in ulcerated parts too, but because precision of perception is absent, the qualities of the juices escape notice.

[588] Yet it is possible, both in those parts and even before them, while the skin is not yet ulcerated, to infer by reasoning the mixed activity that arises in bodies from the opposite powers at the same time. For if you apply the juice of strychnos to an inflamed part, you will see it being condensed and compacted and the transpirations being held back; so that, if you were to do this for a longer time, you would no longer even preserve the part red, but you would make it either livid or black, just the sort of thing that most physicians continually do in cases of erysipelas as well; for these too they blacken and harden in the course of time by chilling them immoderately. If, then, you were to apply not strychnos but anthemis upon the inflamed part, you will see it undergo all the opposite effects: for it will be rare and diffused and soft and slack, and much of the superfluity in it will be transpired away, and it will never become livid or black, even if you use the chamomile for many days in succession; for this is of a nature to diffuse and to disperse, not to contract or condense or shut off the transpirations.

That chamomile, then, is of a power contrary to that of strychnos is clear from these [589] considerations; and that, if you should also mix the two, you will clearly observe the powers of each, I tell you from having made the trial myself, though I should wish that you too arrive at knowledge of what happens through the trial itself rather than trust me as I describe it. This, indeed, I know that everyone will do who is a lover of truth. But I must bring the ensuing argument to its conclusion as though these things had already been shown. For if, when strychnos and chamomile are applied together, the part is seen to become neither so dense and hard and tightly stretched and livid as if one had used strychnos alone, nor so loose-textured and soft and slack and red as if one had used chamomile alone, but to take on the condition intermediate between the two that have been described, it is reasonable that both drugs have acted in accordance with their own power. For if neither had acted, but both had remained inert, the part would have kept the condition it had from the beginning, as if we had applied nothing at all; and if one of them had acted while the other had been completely overcome, the part would have been affected not with the intermediate condition but with one or the other of the extremes.

And indeed, if each of them [590] acted, and these were opposite in their powers, then the body was affected in opposite ways at the same time. For surely they did not act by dividing up the times between them, so that, say, when both had been applied for a whole day, one of the drugs acted during the first six hours and the other during the remaining six. For this hypothesis is nonsensical and destitute not only of all demonstration but also of all plausibility. Therefore the underlying substance did not come to be diffused and contracted in the way that happens to those who have washed in a bath and afterwards stepped into cold water, but rather as if you were to sprinkle cold water on someone while he is bathing. For in this way he will undergo the opposite affections not at different times but at one and the same time. As, then, in the case of compound drugs it is nothing to wonder at that opposite dispositions arise simultaneously in bodies, so neither is it in the case of simple ones, when these too appear simple with respect to sensation in general and diagnosis, but are in respect of their very nature compound.

And indeed, just as in the cases where we ourselves compound and mix something, sometimes, as it may happen, putting in more of the [591] astringent juice, sometimes the sweet, or bitter, or salty, or pungent, or some other of the opposites, and sometimes both in equal amounts, so it is possible also for nature, in trees and shrubs and herbs and animals and in the earth itself, to mix the opposite juices either in their bulks or in their powers, and sometimes also one of the two as predominant, so that their activities are alike in the equal mixtures, but different in the unequal ones. Let no one, then, as was said before, straightaway suppose that to discourse about an astringent juice and about astringency itself is the same thing. For astringency is conceived as one simple thing, whereas the astringent body is of two kinds, just as the heating body also is: the one simple and extreme, such as fire, the other heating by predominance of heat, such as blood.

And so too the astringent: one kind is extreme, as for instance alum and melanteria and gall-nut and sumach, while the other is so by partaking to some degree also of the astringent quality, such as pear and wine and apple [592] and rose. For in the rose a very small amount of what is astringent is mixed with a many-times-greater amount of what is not of that kind, so that the effects of its astringency too are proportionately slight, extending only so far that the tone of the bodies which come into contact with it is not dissolved by the relaxing power in the rose. It is therefore no wonder that it is a remedy for inflammations, and especially those in their increase and growth, or rather also those still beginning. And rose oil, inasmuch as it is in its nature intermediate between oil and rose, is the best drug in the increases of inflammations. For oil itself is useful at the peaks of inflammations, as experience shows, and we shall state the cause in the books of the Therapeutic Method; but rose oil, having been blended into a state intermediate between the simples from which it came to be, displays its benefit at the intermediate time.

For at the beginnings one must rather repel and check the influxes; at the peaks, disperse without biting; and in the increases, repel and disperse at the same time—a thing which someone hearing it apart from the aforesaid reasonings would perhaps [593] disbelieve. But as things now stand, I do not know whether anyone is so dull as not yet to be persuaded by the argument. For indeed the indications in the ascents of inflammations must necessarily be opposite. For to pass all at once from things that are astringent and contract the substance to those that relax and diffuse it is absurd, and in the interval between the peak and the beginning, when the diseases are still increasing, it is right neither simply to repel, as at the beginnings, nor yet to disperse, as at the peaks; but just as the condition of the affection is intermediate between the opposites, so too the cure must be intermediate, neither astringent, as at the beginnings, nor dispersing, as at the peaks. And indeed everything intermediate is mixed from the opposites, either by their being blended with one another throughout, or in small particles, the parts lying side by side also escaping perception. Whether, then, you wish rose oil to have been blended from the opposites in this way or in that, to me it makes no difference, for the point at issue is demonstrated either way.

But I know that, once you have spent more time with all the arguments about these matters, both those which Theophrastus [594] wrote and those which we set forth throughout this whole treatise, you will find the second mode of mixture. And indeed it also belongs to rose oil to penetrate into the depth and to moisten dry bodies more than olive oil does. And I think you have often seen people rubbing the dense sort of leather cloaks with rose oil. For olive oil and water-and-oil do not soak them well, being too coarse-grained to be able to penetrate inside; whereas in the case of rose oil it happens that, in addition to the other properties it has, its astringency too, slight though it is, contributes in no small measure to this. For things that are strongly harsh and acerbic, condensing the outer surface immediately upon falling on it, prevent the moistures from being carried inward. But things that are astringent to a slight degree, while having in themselves for the most part a substance that is at once fine-particled and lukewarm, so far from being prevented by the astringency from descending into the depth of the bodies they come into contact with, are rather even assisted, being pushed onward by it.

For those which are simply fine-particled and hot rather disperse [595] the moistures out of the bodies which they come near to, and do not add others. Those which are at once coarse-particled and cold are by nature not able to introduce any moisture at all in the first place. But those in which there is a moisture that is at once lukewarm and fine-particled — nothing prevents these, on account of the fine-particled and at the same time lukewarm character of their substance, from being readily set in motion and passing through the pores of the bodies that are moved (κινουμένων). That they do not heat sufficiently is clear from the fact that they do not disperse the moisture present in them. And if, in addition to happening to be such, they also partake of some slight astringency, of such a kind as both to push on toward the depth whatever fine-particled part has already entered the pores, and in some way to constrict and condense the outer surface, these are the most effective of all moistening agents. For astringency, when it closes off the pores beforehand, drawing together into itself and compacting the substance it comes near to, stands as an obstacle to those things whose nature is to soak.

But the astringency that is so weak that, in rose oil, it is overcome rather than overcoming, is not able to get ahead of the [596] fine-particled and fine parts of the rose oil; but as those sink into the depth, it begins to act about the outer surface, felting and drawing together and condensing it as far as it is able.
