From this it necessarily follows that the small-particled bodies which have already got in by the pores are pushed forward inward, and are prevented from running back outward, since the pores have been closed off. And indeed toward works of this kind the innate heat of our bodies also contributes in no small measure. For it both draws inward toward itself and thins by breaking down; and for this reason even the drugs that are cold by nature, the so-called deleterious ones—hemlock and poppy and henbane seed and mandrake and all the others of this kind—act more quickly and more strongly in hot natures. And this too, though it has been supposed to be one of the insoluble problems, will readily have its solution for you, if you attend to what is being said not carelessly.

For if indeed it is impossible for such drugs to kill unless they also chill the heart itself, then surely they must travel inward, [597] being broken up and thinned. But this they do not have from their own nature — for they are coarse-grained and hard to move, and would never of themselves have obtained division into fine parts and forward motion — and they need some acquired heat that cuts and thins and breaks them up into small pieces and, as it were, guides and conducts them into the fine pores of all the parts. So as long as they lack such heat, they delay and are slow, being held up in the large pores and, as it were, swimming about in the veins and arteries, and presumably also, in the course of time and amid their long wandering, being themselves affected in turn by the humors contained in these vessels.

For it has already been shown many times that all the qualities act upon one another in some respect, and that a stone has been affected by the continuous striking of a drip of water, and a sword has been blunted while cutting wax; and it has further been demonstrated that the activities in animals come about through the solid bodies within them, so that so long as these have not yet been chilled by the cooling drugs, it is necessary [598] that the animal survive; but they are not chilled before the drugs have penetrated into their proper pores. And this does not belong of themselves to the coarse-grained and cold drugs, unless they happen upon something to guide them. What guides them, as the first cause, is the attraction of the arteries, for these were shown, in dilating, to draw everything that lies near; and, as the second and material cause, the fineness of parts of the substance, which the colder and more coarse-particled drugs, not possessing it of themselves, need others to supply. Accordingly, all bodies that are cold in their mixtures both have the attraction of the arteries weaker than hot ones—for this too was shown—and are unable quickly to break down the substances of the drugs into small parts. And in consequence the drug, delaying, is itself likely to undergo something in the course of time, so that sometimes it is even concocted; just as the juice of lettuce also is. For in time this too is concocted; but if it manages to reach the heart unimpaired, it kills much like hemlock. And all the other strongly cooling juices undergo this as well.

For [599] if they should not be able to destroy quickly, from that point on they become altogether ineffective. But those that kill by erosion and putrefaction have it in them to become strong as they linger. For all things putrefy in time, and still more in a moist and warm place. Fittingly, then, for those whose harm comes from cooling, the speed of their action contributes to destruction; for being warmed in time they lose the power by which they had their action. But for those whose action comes from putrefying, time increases the action, since it also increases the putrefaction. For no animal can perish without the heart ceasing its activity, and it is not possible for this to cease without some very great dyscrasia. For surely it will not cease moving simply because it has become hotter than is proper, to whatever degree it happens, or colder. And in the same way, neither if it should become moderately dry or moist. For it will act worse on account of such dyscrasias, but it will not be motionless until it has received some extraordinary warmth, or cooling, or one of the other active qualities.

Something similar happens to the drugs that kill by cooling, whenever they are slow in coming to the heart, to what often happens in the case of moist and green pieces of wood. [600] For these too, when many of them are placed on the fire all at once, quickly extinguish it; but when they are all set around it in a circle and dried beforehand and warmed beforehand, and then placed on it little by little, not only do they not extinguish it, but they even become nourishment for the fire. So too, then, hemlock kills a human being, arriving at the heart still strong, because of the width of the pores, the abundance of heat, and the strength of the attraction exerted by the arteries; but it does not kill starlings, since, owing to the opposite causes, it is held back and delayed and, in the course of that time, is first concocted beforehand and prepared beforehand, being warmed in advance by the heart as by a kind of hearth, just as the wood is outside [the fire]. So that this too is neither wonderful nor puzzling, but is something of the kind that belongs also to lettuces. For these nourish human beings when eaten in moderate quantity.

But if someone were also to press out their juice and gulp it down in abundance, he will die in the same way as those who have taken hemlock [601] or poppy-juice. So just as lettuce, when it gets ahead and chills the heart, kills, but when it has been concocted becomes nourishment for the animal, in the same way, I think, hemlock too kills a human being by arriving first, but nourishes starlings by being slow. And it will not kill even a human being, if it is taken in a small amount. This too the Attic old woman showed, whom everyone mentions, who began from a very small quantity of hemlock and advanced without harm to a considerable quantity. For at the beginning the small amount was overcome because of its very smallness, and through habituation it became connatural. And it is not now the occasion to render the cause of the fact that habits have very great power and are, as indeed has been said by the ancients, acquired natures. For in that way the digression would become greater for me than the main work, in addition to the fact that a separate treatise has been written on this subject. Rather, one must draw together and bring to its conclusion the present account.

Of the drugs, then, that kill by cooling, none is deleterious in its kind, but [602] only in its quantity. In the case of those that corrode and putrefy and heat, however, it is not the same; but about these we shall speak a little later. Those that kill by cooling, however, will not kill when taken small in amount, just as neither will it if you pour a little water on a large flame, or lay upon it a single piece of wood, moist and green. For just as, if it does not have abundant warmth breaking it up and conducting it as far as the heart, it is impossible for it to kill, so, if that which breaks it up and conducts it is far stronger, it will completely overcome and transform the drug and make it nourishment for itself. At once, then, at this point one must also bear in mind that other fact, that the drugs cold by nature too were rightly said by the ancients to be cold in power. For these too in some way take their cooling from us, just as the hot ones take their heating. And if those do so in one manner and these in another, it makes no difference; for what is universal and common in both is the same: the beginning of the alteration proceeds from the body that is going to be affected to the drug that is going to act.

But the things that are hot in power are altered [603] only by being heated by us, whereas those that are cold by nature are altered by being broken down and by taking on an acquired motion in addition. Since, therefore, it does not belong to them, qua cold, to act without the body that is acted upon, they have rightly been called cold in power. For they do not have the cooling of us in actuality completely from themselves, but they must first be acted upon by us in order that they may cool. For both being broken down into small pieces and taking on an acquired motion in addition are affections of the drugs. Nevertheless, one must concede to anyone who wishes to call such things too cold in actuality, since the disagreement will then remain merely one of name, provided that the matter itself is agreed upon. For, as I have just shown, all such things require a hot body in order to act. And for this reason both poppy-juice (meconium) and hemlock, when mixed with wine, naturally kill more quickly—but not in every proportion. For a very small quantity, if mixed with a very great quantity, would even be completely overcome; but a large quantity mixed with a little is conducted to the heart, yet cannot be overcome.

But if someone should already have drunk the juice of the poppy, which is of such a nature as to kill, and yet still be alive, then reasonably [604] this person too is cured by old wine drunk in quantity, and the more so if it should be one of the noble wines; for it also heats more. For that the heart has not yet been violently chilled is clear from the fact that the man is still alive; and that in the slowness of its journey the drug has in any case already been in some way altered beforehand by the body, just as green wood is when it lies near the fire, this too is not unclear. So warm wine drunk in this condition is the best remedy, and we ourselves once restored a man who had been chilled to the extreme with Lesbian wine. And Falernian and Surrentine, Ariusian and the harsh Tmolite, and all the other wines that are hot and strictly vinous, would be able to display the same activity as the Lesbian. For in general, whatever wine is thin and transparent in consistency, tawny or yellow in colour, fragrant in smell, and in being mixed requires a very great deal of water, is of such a nature as to heat sufficiently and to be carried easily to every part of the body.

Such a wine, then, in its nature, and old in age, when mixed rather strong [605] cures also those who have already been chilled, not only by poppy juice or by some other of such cooling drugs, but also those who in diseases fall into syncope either stomachically or cardiacally. But the wine that is drunk together with the cooling drugs themselves in order to kill more quickly—this is neither much nor of noble quality, but only so much as suffices to break them up and to convey them to the heart by the impetus of the distribution. And concerning these matters let this suffice. But since I also promised to speak about the drugs that kill by putrefaction and erosion—that they become worse with time, and that they are destructive of our nature in their kind, not, like the cooling drugs, merely by their quantity—it would now be the time for me to speak about these as well. For indeed the account of them is also in some way connected, in a certain respect, with the discussion of the drugs that heat in potentiality.

For it is likely that most of such things are already hot in actuality too, but that they escape our notice, [606] either because we ourselves partake of more warmth, or because their substance is coarse-particled. For let us again recall the same things, that in the bath urine appears cold to us. And let us recall also that, when sometimes we were unable to go down into a hot pool, having first gone down into another less hot than it, we then used without discomfort the one that had until then seemed unbearable. And indeed spring water too in winter appears lukewarm to those who have cold hands, but to the others it does not appear so. For in general, as was said before too, each of the bodies perceives the things that come into contact with it according to its own disposition. Thus, at any rate, if with your hand cold you thrust it down into a heap of wheat, you will clearly perceive heat, but if it is hot, you will not perceive it; yet into a heap of pigeon dung, and especially that of wild pigeons, even if you put your hand in hot, you will perceive a clear warmth. So too misy and chalcitis, verdigris and lime and countless others of such things, if you plunge your hand into them when they are heaped up, will at once appear hot to you.

If, however, you take some lump from among them, its outer surface having been chilled by the external and surrounding air, you will reasonably perceive no heat at all. [607] For you are touching its chilled parts, and that before breaking it up into fine pieces. In the same way, in winter, well water, or otherwise spring water, has often appeared warm to those touching it; but if someone were to touch it after first warming his hands, it will appear cold. And it is possible to call to mind countless other such instances, from which no one would disbelieve that those among drugs which are hot in potentiality relative to us are hot in actuality for another kind of animals. Let this, then, have been said as a sort of by-work along the way. But those things which, on coming into contact with us, destroy either by erosion or by putrefaction — for it was about these that the discussion was — have reasonably been supposed to be deleterious to the constitution of a human being in their kind, not, like the cooling agents, in quantity only.

For these latter are also sometimes overcome and become nourishment for the animal, whereas the putrefying ones, even if they are taken in the smallest bulk, in every case undergo corruption, because all putrescible things putrefy [608] when they are heated and moistened, and the blood is hot and moist. Putrefactive drugs, therefore, can never cease being putrefied and putrefying in turn. And for this reason some of them kill a very long time after they have been taken, and especially those that are coarse-particled and earthy in their substances. For these settle in our bodies, then in the course of time putrefy, and erode and destroy along with themselves the neighbouring parts of the animal. For the more fine-particled ones might sometimes even be excreted together with the residues; and it is for roughly these two causes that some of those which kill by putrefaction and erosion have on occasion failed to kill: one, which I have just now finished stating, when they happen to be excreted together with the residues before they have harmed the body; the other, when the one who has taken them has somehow had the good fortune to make use of foods, or of things that would otherwise have been of benefit, or of some physician, if it so chanced, in attendance.

For when the harm from them is great, it is not possible [609] to be restored by regimen and by the use of powerful drugs and a physician giving help. But if the poison were altogether small in quantity, it is possible that this too accomplishes nothing, by reason of its being excreted along with the residues and the person's using the requisite regimen—as, for example, if it were a hundredth part of a drachm of cantharis. For this will be excreted together with the urine before it injures the animal. Indeed, cantharis is actually mixed into diuretic drugs, just as very many other deadly things are mixed into the alexipharmaka. And such compound drugs, when they are suitably mixed, become most efficacious, as for instance the diuretic made with cantharis. For in any case the impulse of cantharides is somehow, even otherwise, toward the bladder by way of the urine; at least that is how they ulcerate it, eating it away. But when a little of them is mixed with many beneficial ingredients, it guides those along, but is unable to eat through.

For everything that is to act, I think, even if it be most powerful, requires some quantity of magnitude, seeing that even fire, if it be altogether minimal, [610] besides not burning, cannot even heat. At any rate, the hundredth part of a spark is imperceptible to us. From all of which it is quite clear that those things which kill by cooling, when taken in small amounts, would be able to nourish the body, as indeed the juice of lettuce does, whereas those which kill by eroding or putrefying are not able to nourish, not even if on account of their smallness they pass through the body without harm. For such things are in kind contrary to the constitution of a human being. Just as we said earlier in the case of the juices, that almost none of them is unmixed with a foreign quality, but both in trees and in herbs and in fruits they are mingled with those of a different kind, so one must conceive that in drugs too the substances of many heterogeneous things are mixed in. For you would find, if you reckoned it out, that the Cnidian berry differs from safflower in partaking of a very great amount of heat. For the similarity of the substances of both it is possible for you to learn both through touch and through sight; and third, in addition to these, that both are evacuants of phlegm.

For it has been shown [611] by us in the commentaries On the Natural Faculties that attractions are brought about through affinity of the qualities present in the substances. For a considerable heat is mixed into the Cnidian berry, and in this respect it differs from safflower. And for this reason, among the purgative drugs, when they fail to purge, some, besides doing no harm to the body, even become nourishment for the animal, while others turn into what is destructive and deleterious. For in every case the purging drug has some likeness to at least one of the humours in us, but not in every case is some deleterious power mixed into it, so that neither will it in every case do harm when it has not purged, but it will be concocted and will generate such a humour as that of which it was drawing. I am not unaware, however, that it is not possible to follow such arguments adequately for those who have not been previously trained in the commentaries On the Natural Faculties.

For it was shown in those writings that very many attractions come about in virtue of an affinity of qualities, and that for this reason each of the parts of the animal too [612] draws to itself its own proper nourishment. And it follows from this doctrine that the purging drugs too are akin to the humours that are drawn, but that those which draw are in some way more active, just as the Magnesian stone too is more active than iron. For it too is iron-like and is found in the iron mines and resembles iron remarkably in appearance, but it is in some way stronger, so that it draws rather than is drawn. And indeed one must not despair of safflower's being phlegmatic, as it shows in its colour, but it is, owing to its heat, stronger than phlegm, so that it draws rather than is drawn. And in the same way also the Cnidian berry; but if it should ever be overcome by our body—and this happens continually to safflower, but not very much to the berry, because of its strength—instead of purging it becomes nourishment, just as hellebore always is for quails. And since I have come upon this argument, I wish also to recall a certain logical theorem, demonstrated also in the commentaries On Demonstrations, which is useful for the present matters. The theorem is as follows.

Of demonstrations, [613] some conclude that this belongs to that of necessity, others that it may possibly belong. And of these latter, some pass over into belonging of necessity, whenever they follow from necessary principles, just as in this very point which has now been demonstrated by us. For in the Cnidian berry and in safflower it is not possible to show with evident clarity the phlegmatic humour contained in them; but what is possible, likely and contingent does belong to the argument. But since we have also shown that attractions come about through the similarities of substances—for it has been demonstrated many times that in purgations there is an attraction of what is akin to the purging drugs, not an alteration of all the humours together—it is necessary that a certain similarity belong to both substances, that of what purges and that of what is purged. Since, then, what is purged is phlegm, assuredly the attracting agent too must of necessity be phlegmatic. But I said that the attracting agent must be phlegmatic, not outright phlegm itself. For we said that similarity belongs to the substances, not identity.

For it is entirely the opposite: neither does iron attract iron nor [614] flesh flesh, but the iron-stone attracts iron, and flesh attracts blood. For the same and the similar differ, I think. For phlegm is the same as phlegm, and safflower as safflower, but safflower is similar to phlegm, yet certainly not the same. For neither, in the case of those foods which we call bilious or phlegmatic, do we so name them on the grounds that they already contain bile or phlegm. For the absurdity of this opinion too has been demonstrated both in the treatises On the Natural Faculties and in many other places. These matters, then, and all such things must be set aside; but that point must be taken up again, namely that of the purging drugs themselves some already possess the similarity suitable for attraction, whereas some do not yet have it completely.

but acquire it in the body of the animal, in the same way as the caustic drugs; so that in their case too the likeness is twofold, the one in actuality, the other in potentiality, just as in the case of all the others; and indeed that with the similar humours in [615] each there are mixed other dissimilar ones, some drug-like, others not. And thus, in the failures of purgations, some of the purgatives do us some harm, while others become harmless nourishment. Since I have once come to the discussion of purgative drugs, it is perhaps not worse to say something also about the so-called over-purgations. These, then, come about when the purgative drug, having gained sufficient strength, produces at the mouths of the vessels that extend down to the belly both a biting and at the same time an opening of the mouths that is greater, and, by continuously irritating and tearing the bodies, breaks down the power in the vessels. For the very sort of thing that is seen to happen in the case of the belly, when its power collapses into extreme weakness, must be supposed to happen also in the veins. What, then, is it that happens in the case of the belly? Vomitings of everything that has been swallowed, when the weakness befalls its upper parts, and lienteries, when it befalls the lower.

And these matters too are demonstrated at [616] greater length in the Causes of the Things Evacuated. An affection of this kind must be supposed to occur in the veins in the excessive purgations. While at the beginning both the opening of the mouths (anastomosis) and the weakness are still moderate, what is thinnest and less proper is excreted; but when both have advanced further, now even the thick humours and those most proper to the animal are evacuated. For this reason, then, yellow bile is excreted first, phlegm second, black bile third, and last of all these, in the excessive purgations, the blood: this, as the humour most proper to nature; while, before it, the thinnest comes first and the thickest last. Now the order of their evacuation has been spoken of also by Hippocrates in the book On the Nature of Man, but it will be stated now as well, so that nothing be lacking to the account. For if you give a drug evacuative of phlegm, in the excessive purgations yellow bile is evacuated first, black bile second, and the blood last. But if the drug is evacuative of yellow bile, phlegm will follow, black bile third, and the blood fourth.

And indeed, [617] if it is purgative of black bile, it will evacuate that first, and after it the yellow, then in the same way the phlegm, and last of all the blood will follow, as though flowing out from vessels that are by now lifeless, since great weakness has seized them and their mouths have arrived at extreme distension. From this it is clear that in over-purgations the humour most proper to human beings is evacuated last, and each of the others according as thinness or thickness happens to belong to it. The cause of the fact that the humours not proper to the purging drug are excreted at all lies in these three things: the weakness of the vessels, the width of the mouths, and the biting of the purgative. For when the vessels can no longer retain the humours within themselves, and their mouths are laid open, and the drug persists in irritating, and no longer has the proper humour to draw, it is altogether necessary that the others be excreted in the order stated.

For perhaps even the biting, by persisting, would of itself have sufficed to rouse the organs to excretion, but much more so when [618] opening of the mouths and weakness of the vessels concur together. The opening of the mouths comes about, as has been said, through the strength of the drug, through which the biting also comes about; the weakness of the vessels, on the other hand, comes about both through the violent fatigue which happens to arise in their being bitten and, as it were, milked by the purging drug, and in addition through the dyscrasia that seizes them in excessive purgings. For whichever of the humours you evacuate entirely, dyscrasia must of all necessity follow. These, then, are the causes of the humours not proper to the purgative also being evacuated; while of their being evacuated in the aforesaid order the cause is the thinness and thickness of the evacuated humours themselves, and in addition the greater or lesser affinity of each of the humours to the constitution of the animal.

[619] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 4. How, then, a drug is said to be cold, or hot, or dry, or moist in power, and in what manner one must test it, has been determined earlier.

And they do this, most of them being ignorant not only of natural theory [460] but also of the logical methods which anyone who demonstrates anything whatsoever must necessarily employ, so that, knowing neither what has been well discovered by the natural philosophers nor the matters about which those same men have reasonably been in doubt, they often dare to declare the opposite of both. Come now, by the gods: if I, beginning now to speak somewhat as follows—that, there being four elements, air and earth and water and fire, the white and bright colour is inherent by nature in nothing else except radiance and fire—and then, having called Empedocles and certain others of the natural philosophers as witnesses to the argument, were to declare that all bright bodies partake of the greatest amount of fire, having neglected to look at snow and white lead and ice and countless other things that are at once the brightest and the coldest, and then, when someone brought these forward, were to run away from the refutation that comes from sense-perception and demand that one go to reason and by this investigate the matters concerning nature, and not entrust the whole to irrational senses—would I not seem to those who have intelligence to be mad, not even knowing the things from which I begin my argument?

For it is from sensation, [461] I think, and through sensation that we learned all axioms of this kind, that the sun is bright, that flames are yellowish, and that most live coals are yellow. If, then, we must renounce the senses, we shall have no demonstration, neither we of what we have just said, nor Empedocles when he writes thus: "the sun, hot to behold and bright in every direction." But if these things are true, it is clear that sensation must be trustworthy long before them. But they say that it is indeed necessary, for beings who are at any rate human, to begin from the senses; yet it is not fitting to remain at sensation throughout, but to proceed to what is more divine, reason. For in sensation even the irrational animals have a share, but in reason only the gods. And starting from this point, they stretch out a long discourse. And some of them even call upon Anaxagoras as a witness, who declared concerning snow that it is not white.

This man, then, they say, being a natural philosopher, stands above sense-perception and despises [462] its appearances, but ascends to reason, and by this hunts out the nature of the things that are. But if I must say what occurs to me, as a free man and one who throughout his whole life has been zealous for the truth, I think that those who babble such things have advanced beyond melancholy. For if they overturn the things that appear clearly through the senses, they will have no starting point from which to begin their demonstrations. But if they begin from them as from things trustworthy, how will they afterwards reasonably distrust them? For the principles of demonstrations are more trustworthy than the things demonstrated, which require credibility from other things. But the principles of demonstrations are trustworthy not only in themselves, by themselves, but also with a view to the discovery of the things under investigation. And I for my part would pray that all things fell clearly under our senses and that there were nothing that escaped them, since in that way nothing would be either insoluble or disputed.

But since some things do escape them, one must try to bring reasoning to bear upon these, yet neither from afar, as those men do, nor syllogising inconclusively, but first [463] dividing precisely the significations of the names, so that no deception arises from homonymy in what follows; and second, distinguishing what acts in itself from what acts incidentally. Both of these have been discussed precisely in what precedes, and the significations of things said to be hot in potentiality, or cold, or dry, or moist, or anything else whatever, have been divided. And how one may discover the proper power of each drug, marking it off from those that are incidental (τοῖς κατὰ συμβεβηκός), we have gone through in general in the third book of On Mixtures, and in the treatise now in hand we go through it by means of the particulars, as we have already done in the first book in the case of water and vinegar; and here again we shall do so in the case of olive oil and rose oil, having first shown how great an error is committed by those physicians who begin their demonstrations from afar. For what need was there to examine the colour of oil, or of roses, when one is able to use the things themselves in many ways, not only on healthy bodies but also on diseased ones?

For it is possible, taking roses themselves by themselves and their juice, to apply them [464] to the body, both when healthy and when sick with a simple disease, as was said before, and, mixing them with sweet oil, to apply them to bodies that are strongly cooled or heated, rubbing them in and fomenting and bathing them, and to take them into the interior of the body either from above through the mouth or from below through the seat, and then to observe what happens in each use. For indeed it is for this very purpose that we investigate the power of all drugs, in order that we may have those that one must use when the hypochondria and the head are burning hot, or chilled, or ulcerated, or inflamed, or suffering some other such affection—both these parts themselves and all the other members of the body. Then, having in this way a road at once evident and short to what we are seeking, shall we still examine the colours, or odours, or consistencies, or sounds of each of the drugs, doing something like those who wish to recognise some man from a likeness, whether sculpted or painted, when it is possible to look upon the very person who is to be recognised?

[465] In this respect, then, they seem to me to err in no small way, and still more than this in those matters where they babble inconclusive and undemonstrated things, being ignorant of demonstrative method. For let fire be assumed to be either yellow or red, or however they wish, for it makes no difference to me. What, then, has this to do with everything red being hot? For it must be said, if it so happens, that all fire is red; but to assert that everything red is fire is ridiculous, and still more so if someone were to say that everything red is hot. If it had been assumed from the outset in the argument that everything hot is red, it would perhaps have been possible, by twisting the proposition, to declare everything red to be hot—though erring manifestly in this too; for it is the propositions that convert, not those that are inverted, that are true together with one another; but nonetheless the fallacy would, I think, have been close at hand. But since not even this itself has been assumed at the start—I mean that everything hot is red—it is not possible, even by inverting it, to say that everything red is hot.

In three ways, then, those who assert that roses are hot in their mixture, [466] because they are also red, go wrong in their argument. First, because, without having shown that all fire is red, they attempt to convert with it another statement, that everything red is fire, as if it were true; second, because they do not know that it is the propositions that convert with (ἀντιστρέφοντας) true propositions, not those that reverse them (ἀναστρέφοντας), that are themselves also true; and third, because even if they do convert, what will be concluded from the conversion is not that everything red in colour is hot, but a different proposition of the same kind, that everything red is fire. And that such a proposition is not only useless for the present purpose but also manifestly false is clear to everyone. For what we need to have demonstrated is not whether everything red is fire, but that it is hot. Since if indeed everything red is fire, then clearly the rose too will be fire for us. But physicians who, I think, do not know the logical methods go most seriously astray first of all in this very point, that they overstep their proper boundaries.

For experience, together with brief epilogisms, is sufficient to discover the powers of drugs; and then, in their arguments too, they err in ways similar to children who have just learned [467] logical theory. Those too are caught in the same fault who infer something about the power of drugs from their odours. For neither is everything fragrant hot, as some say, not knowing how one must understand what has been said by Aristotle and Theophrastus on these matters—which we shall define in the fourth of these commentaries—nor is everything hot fragrant; nor indeed is everything foul-smelling hot, nor, if something is hot, is it foul-smelling. So too, if someone should say that everything foul-smelling is cold, or that what is cold is foul-smelling, he does not speak the truth. For indeed among hot things countless ones are fragrant, others foul-smelling, and others neither; and likewise among cold things. And yet why do I say "cold" and "hot", when we ought to say "heating" and "cooling", which are in fact what we are investigating? For it is certainly not what is hot without qualification, or what is examined in relation to this, that it is proposed to investigate now, but what heats the human body. And likewise cold not without qualification, but whatever cools a human being.

So here again, not having distinguished the significations of the names, [468] they go wrong because of the homonymy, just as if someone, while discoursing about the land dog, should pass over in his argument to the sea dog, thinking that, just as the name of both animals is one, so also their nature is one. But it has been shown clearly by us in the commentaries On Mixture, which we said right at the beginning should precede this treatise, that what is hot in potentiality is one thing, and what is hot in actuality another; and that, of this hot in actuality, one kind is said to be hot simply, another by predominance, another in relation to the well-proportioned thing of the same kind, and another in relation to anything whatever that happens to be at hand. And indeed we said that man is hot not simply, as fire is, but hot by predominance; for there is in him a greater portion of the hot than of the cold. Accordingly, all the things that are said by these people to be hot in potentiality will be so called in virtue of their heating him. And the judgment of them is both very easy and will be tested through experience, requiring, as was also said before, brief epilogisms.

The sophists, then, passing over these matters, both waste the time of the young [469] and, leading astray by sophisms men unexercised in the solution of sophisms, fill them with false doctrines. For they ought to have made mention neither of colour nor of odour, nor indeed of consistency, or smoothness, or roughness, or anything else of the kind. For what does it matter that oil is viscous, or that it is smooth, or that it is glistening, or wet, or pale-yellow, or oily, or slippery, or hard to dry when smeared upon bodies? For from none of such things is it possible to infer whether it is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist in its power. For indeed, among viscous things and smooth things and glistening things, some manifestly heat us, others cool, and some dry, others moisten. And in respect of each of the accidents belonging not to oil alone but to all the other things as well, there is nothing to be found fixed or constant, such that one could establish upon it some universal premise.

For I pass over saying that in all such arguments the sophists do not even employ scientific [methods] [470] for the discovery of the premises, but [argue] from induction; and, what is worst of all, that they have never even inquired into the nature of induction, nor, should anyone challenge them to this, do they dare to follow, but they even censure those who occupy themselves at all with demonstration. And still worse, that they sometimes reason not even from induction alone, but from examples, just as the orators do. For the one who asserts that oil is cold because it is also viscous, just as phlegm is, reasons by means of an example, furnishing an equal strength of demonstration, in the same way as the one who says that it is hot because it is viscous, like birdlime; and the one who asserts that it is hot because it readily bursts into flame, like asphalt, [furnishes a demonstration of equal strength] to the one who says that it is cold because it readily congeals, like water.

For establishing something from an example or from examples differs from what is established through induction in this respect: the one who establishes from examples mentions one or two of the things of the same kind, or at any rate few, omitting the majority, whereas the one who proceeds from induction attempts to encompass everything that is known through experience, and [471] to omit, so far as possible, nothing that is obvious and clear to the many, but also what is hidden and known to few. Hence the induction that proceeds through all the things known from experience is forcible and persuades strongly, and the imposture becomes detectable only to those who have been trained in demonstrative methods. And for this reason we have gone through it at greater length in the commentaries On Demonstration; and perhaps one day we may also compose a single separate book on it by itself. But even now the nature of induction itself will appear no less, and that of the example much more so. For I have resolved to go through, under heads, everything that has been said by physicians about the power of oil, plausibly in appearance, but not truly. And first, what has been said by Diocles in the Archidamus, that Archidamus supposed the skin to be hardened and scorched in those who are rubbed with oil, and for this reason preferred dry rubbing.

For he thought, he says, that the oil, being heated by the rubbing, [472] is set ablaze together with the skin and burns it, and that in this way it draws out the moisture and dries it considerably, just as, among things that are roasted, those that have been anointed. For these too become harder than if one roasted them without oil. But perhaps it is better to copy out Diocles' statement itself in full. It runs as follows: "Rubbing with oil he did not approve of in the same way. For first he thought that such rubbing becomes uneven, because the hands slip and cannot take hold of the flesh in the same way on account of the grease. Further, he said that the skin is hardened and burnt more in those rubbed in this manner than in those rubbed dry. For the oil, being heated by the rubbing, is set ablaze together with it and burns, just as, among things that are roasted, those that have been anointed more than those not anointed, since, as the oil is set ablaze, they are heated and have their moisture drawn out excessively and are hardened the more. In the same way too things boiled in oil become brittle and crisp for the same cause. In addition to this, just as wood and hides and the other things that are rubbed with oil let the oil pass through into the interior, so he thought bodies do as well."

And when this happens, [473] many of the things that are accustomed to flow through the flesh together with the pneuma and to pass out are held back, just as also through strainers and linen cloths and wools and all the things through which something is strained, when oil is poured on and smeared over them, the liquids cannot flow in the same way. And when such excretion is intercepted, some of them flow back inward, and, gathering together, fill up the pores, being entangled with one another and enclosed by the oil because the oil has something glutinous in it, just as in other cases the oily substance is seen to catch up dust and chaff and other such things. And as the pores are continually and little by little obstructed, it is necessary that many of the things accustomed to come about according to nature are accomplished worse. He also supposed that it has something biting in it, on account of which it both makes the eyes water and makes the throat rasp and scrapes the belly and produces bloody evacuations when it is drunk.

Those, then, who anoint themselves without rubbing it does not trouble at all; for the biting is too weak to produce any sensation; but with rubbing, [474] as it penetrates into the flesh, it does more harm by its biting, just as many drugs, when merely smeared on in this way, are less strong, but when pressed in and penetrating inward act more powerfully. And indeed with nettles and many other things, those who touch them gently are not troubled at all, but those who strike against them and press on them are pained. These, then, are the things that Diocles says in the Archidamus. And it is possible to consider at once both what is plausible in them and what is faulty. For that anything whatever that is boiled in oil loses its own proper moisture and quickly becomes friable and brittle, while it suffers nothing of the kind in water, we have been taught by experience, so that in this respect Archidamus stated nothing false. But whereas he ought, just as Aristotle and Theophrastus and certain other philosophers propound and solve such problems in their physical inquiries, himself also, if indeed he wished to seek the causes of everything that comes about, to propound and solve them in the same way as they do; since he does not appear to be doing this, it is in this above all that he seems to me to go wrong.

For what appears evidently must always [475] be posited first, and next, if one wishes, its cause must be examined, composing natural problems in some such manner as this. Why does olive oil make the things boiled down in it dry and crumbly and brittle, whereas water makes them moist and soft? Or why do things boiled in oil dry out, whereas things otherwise steeped in it preserve their own proper moisture more than if they had not been steeped at all? And why does it cure the bitings from squill and nettle? And why is it curative of these, while it itself bites the eyes? Why does it not bite all the rest of the body, but bites the eyes? Why does it roughen the pharynx, but soothe ulcers? Why is it laxative of the belly? Why is it curative of fatigues? Why does it keep those who anoint themselves from being chilled? Why is it destructive of insect animals? Why is it softening of straps and hides, but hardening of almost all things that are boiled in it? This is one kind of problems for you, belonging to the natural philosopher alone. The other, which is now common also to those from the arts, is as follows.

For what reason do cooks, when roasting fish and meat, first smear them [476] with oil? Why do the gymnastic trainers rub athletes with oil? And why do the physical instructors also rub the boys? For it is possible to give an empirical cause for each of such problems: the cooks would say that they smear the fish and the meat for this reason, that their outer parts become dry and scorched round about when they are roasted without fat; the gymnastic trainers would say that they rub the athletes in oil because this both dissolves the fatigues already present and mitigates those to come, and makes the rubbing itself perfectly even and gentle, and prepares the body for the movements to come. And for these same reasons the physical instructors too will say that they anoint the boys both before the exercises and after the exercises. Why, however, oil is a remedy for fatigues, neither a gymnastic trainer nor a physical instructor nor an Empiricist physician knows any longer. Yet it is not the case that, because they do not know, they abandon what evidently appears.

For not even knowing why white hellebore purges upward and black downward, [477] nor knowing why cnecus is evacuative of phlegm and epithymum of black humours, they nevertheless use the drugs for those purposes which experience has taught, and they treat those in need, and they trust what is evidently apparent, and they laugh at those who establish the contrary by reasoning. But Archidamus, in addition to his disdaining, in many matters, what is evidently apparent, seems to me to deserve justly to be censured in this respect as well. For he says that dry rubbing is better than that with oil, because it renders the body harder and drier in those who are anointed, whereas it becomes softer in those who are rubbed dry. Yet no less, in this same discourse, after proceeding a little further, he says that wood and hides and the other things that are rubbed with oil let it pass through as far as their depth, and that this is the greatest testimony that in our bodies too, passing inward, it plasters up the pores and prevents the outflows of the moist humours. And I for my part do not know how these things agree.

For if oil prevents the outflows of the fluids, it would surely not be said to dry, so that [478] it is in vain that it is guarded against, as something drying, in the rubbings. And he seems to me to err also in thinking that those who are rubbed in oil are disposed in a similar way to things boiled in it. For he surely does not say that hot, or cold, or well-tempered, or lukewarm, or boiling oil does the same things, just as water itself does not either. For this too evidently, if it is applied cold, condenses and compacts and contracts and constricts what is being excreted, just as, if it is boiling to the extreme, it burns; but if it is applied well-tempered and moderately hot, it relaxes and rarefies and liquefies and disperses. But if it is neither markedly cold nor hot, but such as what is called by most people spring-water, then it does none of the things mentioned, but displays its own proper power. So too, then, if anyone wishes to examine oil, let him first render it free of all acquired coldness and heat, and in this way make the test.

For that which is extremely cold will no longer act upon the things that come near it according to its own power alone, but also through the predominance of the foreign quality; [479] and so too that which is sufficiently hot. But if you are willing to set it outside both of these and then test it, only thus would you discover the proper power of oil. So that when someone is rubbed with oil in the customary way, as all those devoted to gymnastics are, he is rubbed in oil alone, with every quality from without kept away from the outset. But when someone, having made it either boiling or sufficiently hot, or even extremely cold, then uses it, the action must necessarily become composite, from both the proper power of oil and the acquired quality. And often it is necessary that the proper power of each of the drugs be completely hidden, when it has taken on a very strong quality from without. What similarity, then, is there between boiling herbs in boiling oil and rubbing down the bodies of those who exercise? For above all, as has also been shown before, one must avoid proofs drawn from external things, when one is in a position to apply to each thing its own proper test. But if ever someone should wish to do even this, let him at least try to compare similar things, as he did in the case of the hides and the straps.

For no one, having first warmed the oil or [480] first cooled it in snow, but each taking whatever oil comes to hand, rubs down straps and hides, just as, I think, the physical instructors also rub down the boys with whatever oil comes to hand, neither having first warmed it on a fire nor first cooled it on snow. Since indeed we ourselves, not infrequently, have cooled a burning head by pouring very cold oil over it. And if the oil should contain no salt, it will cool still more. And if it should also be pressed from unripe olives (ὠμοτριβές), much more so still. We prepare this too in much the same way as water: for having first warmed it, we then set it in unmixed cold water. And if there should also be a spout set above it, dashing down upon it—the vessel containing the oil having obviously been stopped tight beforehand—it would in this way be made colder still. And it becomes sufficiently cold also when, having first been warmed, it is hung in a well touching the water. For even that which does not touch the water becomes cold, but less so. Such preparations, then, render the oil cold, and the opposite ones render it hot.

And we use the latter too, in the case of bodies that have been chilled, [481] putting into a tank of warm oil those who have become numb in some part, or are tremulous, or spasmodic, or subject to palpitation, or immobile, or insensible, or of impaired sensation, or suffering some other such thing. If, then, someone were to make pronouncements about the power of drugs on the basis of every use, he would straightway come to think that oil is for us both heating and cooling, both moistening and drying, just as Diocles' Archidamus does too, even if he does not follow out his own contradictions. For when he says that things boiled in oil are dried out and become brittle, he shows its power to be a drying and dispersing one; but when he says that it sinks into hides and plasters up our pores and prevents the natural outflows of the moist humours, from these he surely shows in turn that its power is most contrary to those things that disperse and dry. But in these matters, while at least still stating the phenomena, he does not reason correctly about them; whereas in his account of its biting quality he does not even go through all of these phenomena.

For its biting the eyes and making the throat rough, [482] and scraping the belly and bringing on bloody evacuations, are sufficient testimonies that a biting power belongs to it. But that it is also painless for ulcers, and that it entirely cures the bitings of the belly when poured on and injected, and soothes the irritations arising from itchings—these too, in turn, being no small signs of its opposite power—has been completely left out. And if, once both have been stated in succession, someone should wish to draw a conclusion, one of two things follows: either, as an empiricist, he will say that he knows the power of each of the drugs from experience in relation to something, but is ignorant of its proper nature in itself; or, as a rationalist, that contrary powers, both biting and soothing, belong to the same drug—and then, I think, he will have the greatest difficulty in rendering the cause of why sometimes the one of them acts perceptibly and sometimes the other, the other being either destroyed or at any rate not clearly apparent.

The solutions of all such puzzles, if they are posed as physical problems, are exceedingly difficult; but if they are referred to the use of the art, they require much experience [483], and epilogisms not many in number, but accurate and well-defined. For first, whether every oil is biting to the eyes or not, it is better to determine by experience, not to improvise, like orators arguing for either side. Then next, whether every oil is likewise throat-roughening, or laxative to the belly, or scrapes it so as sometimes to stir up bloody excretions, or whether one of the oils does these things and another does not, and one more and another less. By differences of oil I mean now not, as one might suppose, those of different kinds, such as castor oil and radish oil and walnut oil and balanos oil and the like. For the physician must indeed know the powers of these too; but it is not fitting at present to mention them. For it suffices, I think, in the first instance to examine that oil itself which is most properly and especially named 'oil' by all men. For indeed the fruit from which this is produced, alone among the rest, is called elaia (olive), and the tree too is called elaia.

And this [484] is called oil simply and in the primary sense, whereas all the others are so called by a kind of metaphor and catachresis. Of this oil itself, then, the one properly so named, about which we are conducting our entire discourse at present, I say that there are several differences: in respect of age, when it is either fresh and as it were must, or in its prime, or old; in respect of the manner of its preparation, when it is either bare and simple and on its own, or has been made with salt; in respect of the difference in the fruit itself, when the fruit is either ripe or unripe; and in respect of alteration brought about by artificial treatment, when it is either kept such as it happened to be prepared from the beginning, or has been whitened. Concerning its whitening not a few others have written, and it will also be discussed by us in what follows. Of all these oils I myself took pains to make trial of the power. And what I discovered in the case of each I shall relate after this; but now I wish first to bring to a conclusion the matters I set out upon.

For most physicians [485] seem neither to test drugs correctly nor to reason correctly about their power. For one must test only those that are unmixed and free of every acquired quality: first on the best constitution of the body, next also on ill-tempered bodies, and then in this way on simple diseases, as has been distinguished both in the book before this one and in the third book On Mixture; and one must reason, always distinguishing what is accidental from what is primary and per se. But some physicians go astray not only in these matters but also in their opinions about affections. Take olive oil, for example: that it is a remedy for fatigues nearly all agree; but what sort of affection fatigue is, they no longer agree. For one says it is a dryness of the joints, which have been drained of moisture in the movements; another adds also the muscles; and yet another, contrary to these, says it is much moisture and tension and warmth, a flux having come upon the parts that have been vigorously moved.

Another, however, blames not an abundance of moistures but [486] quality alone, saying that in the more immoderate movements certain colliquations occur of fat together with soft flesh, of which one part is transpired outward, while another part is retained in the body, and this, being pungent and biting, produces the, as it were, oil-like condition. So that even if it is agreed that fatigues are cured by oil, the fact that the condition of the body is disputed allows nothing certain to be inferred about the power of oil. And this happens not only in the case of fatigue, but also whenever, on account of pain, or biting, or inflammation, we give oil to drink, or pour it in through the seat, or foment with it. For in the case of inflamed wounds we pour it over not by itself, but together with moderately warm water, just as in fatigues together with baths of sweet waters. And not even in the case of inflammation is there agreement as to what sort of thing the condition is. And when we inject it through the seat or give it to drink, not even then, indeed, do we know clearly to what sort of body we are applying it, whether to one full of phlegm, or of bile, or of certain other residues.

For it is clear that it will not affect the person in the same way when it finds the whole intestine together with the stomach full of viscous phlegm, and when [it finds them full] of bilious residues, or of some other pungent humours, or of much excrement, or when it meets with none of these but with the whole stomach and the intestines perfectly clean, or when, in addition to being clean, this [belly] is also roughened. Most physicians, then, reason very carelessly and negligently about all these matters, not having said in what condition the person is to whom the oil is given, nor even what sort of oil it is; and then some of them assert that it bites and scrapes the inner parts in every case, while others assert that even if there is some biting already present beforehand, it soothes this too. For surely it makes no small difference whether one introduces into a phlegmatic belly the oil which is called, and really is, entirely without salt, or into a clean one that which partakes of a great deal of salt. For both will empty the belly, but by different powers.

For the unsalted oil in a phlegmatic belly works through its slipperiness, in the same way as [488] mallows, blites and mulberries; whereas the salted oil in a clean belly works through its pungency, much as brine and sea-water do. And indeed the latter will scrape, while the former will not scrape. Let us therefore say neither, simply, that oil in every case scrapes the inside, or produces bloody stools, nor that it soothes bitings, but rather that the salty oil scrapes in a clean belly, while the unsalted oil in a phlegmatic belly does not scrape. Sometimes, however, the salty oil may cure bitings accidentally, just as melikraton and brine and whey of milk do. For these sometimes carry out together with themselves the humour that produces the biting, and they become remedies for biting in the same way as all the other things that wash away and cleanse. But after the injection such drugs, so far from stopping the biting at once, actually exacerbate it. For they bring about the cure by reason of evacuation, not by reason of tempering. A cerate, however, injected many times, made with rose oil and suet or soft fat, has at once cured the bitings by reason of tempering.

And indeed oil [489] by itself alone, the sweetest, has often accomplished this, as likewise has goat's suet, or the juice of chondros-gruel, or a cerate made with sweet oil. We ourselves, too, by injecting warm oil into those who have pain in the internal parts because of some chilling, have often rendered them free of pain immediately. And if we conjecture the chilling to be greater, we add dill as well, heating the oil; and if greater still, rue and bitumen too. All such things, then, [are unknown] to the majority of physicians, who do not know either how to distinguish the pain arising from dyscrasia from that arising from cacochymia, nor that, among the drugs injected on account of pain, one cures by heating the chilled part, another by evacuating the biting humour, and another by tempering it.

Often, too, mixed conditions arise from dyscrasia together with biting, in which we are accustomed to inject oil of dill or oil of rue, having melted goose fat into it; if this is not available, then at least [490] that of hens; and if not this either, one of the others. And if none of these is at hand, we mix in some non-biting wax—this is what I call the washed wax—or indeed, by Zeus, the oil itself, whitened, injected on its own; for this too is analogous to non-biting wax. Rash, then, and undiscriminating is the assertion both of those who have declared every oil to be biting on every occasion and of those who have declared it soothing. For the briny kind is biting, while the saltless and sweet kind is soothing, as far as depends on itself; for even this might sometimes seem, owing to the conditions to which it is applied, no longer to be such. For each of the tempering drugs, when it becomes stronger than the biting humours, blunts their biting; but if a small amount of it is mixed with humours stronger in their powers or greater in quantity, it is corrupted along with them and nourishes the cacochymia, whence one must also evacuate at once those who are exacerbated by the tempering remedies, as being filled with much corruption that is hard to move.

[491] Thus, then, milk too often, as soon as it has been taken, turns sour in some people and nidorous in others, before, having been well concocted, it can temper the corruption. And in these people one must first evacuate the greater part of the cacochymia and only then administer both groats and ptisane and milk and all the other things which, when well concocted, contribute to euchymia; one must not, however, suppose, so far as this is concerned, that all of them possess either worse or contrary powers, nor deliberately pass over in one's discussions one of the two things that happen, just as Archidamus, in the case of oil, mentioned the eyes that are bitten and the rasping throat and the belly that is scraped, but that sweet oil, when drunk, has often at once cured even a stomach that was being strongly bitten, and when injected has soothed the bitings throughout the whole belly, and when smeared on has stopped those arising on the skin from thapsia and nettle and squill—this he no longer mentioned.

I myself do not dispute it either, nor do I disbelieve those who assert that in nearly all existing things many and differing powers are contained; indeed I promise to demonstrate [492] this in the discourse that follows. Yet not on this account do I say that the power which prevails in each thing is unknowable. If you distinguish what is per se from what is per accidens, everything will be clearly recognized. For consider each case in some such way as this by means of examples, positing in the argument as an illustration two persons who are bitten alike at the mouth of the stomach and who take the juice of ptisane or spelt-groats or washed bread, and then for the one the biting ceases, while for the other it increases. Is it, then, that so far as depends on itself the juice of ptisane, or the spelt-groats, or the bread, is biting, but by some accident in the case of one of the two men it not only did not increase but even soothed the biting? Or did it soothe so far as depends on itself, but by some accident in the case of the other man exacerbate it? For my part, I say that the juice of ptisane, or the spelt-groats, or the bread, or, by Zeus, milk, being tempering in its own nature, the biting is exacerbated in the other of the two men because it has first been overcome by the corruption.

And thus I know that nearly all the [493] ancient physicians too held, just as also the best of the more recent ones; though there might perhaps be someone who escapes my notice. For nothing is beyond the daring of some of the more recent physicians, so that they would declare that groats, or bread, or ptisan by their own nature increase the corruptions, but in some cases soothe them by some accident. But he who says these things has no demonstration to offer for his assertion. We, however, say that if ptisan were by nature of bad humour, it would never have soothed bitings. But in fact it is often seen to soothe, both when taken from above and when injected through the seat; from which it is clear that in its own nature it is of good humour, but when at times it is corrupted together with the humours that produce the bitings, it increases the symptom. Perhaps, then, someone might ask us whether none of the things of bad humour has ever cured a biting. I for my part know that this happens not infrequently; but I say that such drugs cure the bitings not by tempering, but by carrying out along with themselves that which bites.

And for this reason [I say that they] both immediately and until [494] such time as they have been evacuated bite the person and leave behind a certain rough sensation in the parts, one that needs another drug — not so, however, the well-humoured and sweet-humoured ones. For these soothe both immediately and without producing any evacuation, and they bring on no rough sensation; quite the contrary, they are curative of rough sensations. At any rate, chondros and milk and ptisane we both give to eat in such conditions and inject through the seat, once we have washed away the troubling matter either by means of honey or some other such thing. And at this juncture fat too becomes useful to us, and sweet cerate and sweet oil. Consider that both now and throughout the following discussion I mean all sweet things, both those prepared without salt and those that have been washed. Having, then, four signs by which to distinguish what is soothing in itself from what is soothing incidentally, you will easily discover the power of each of such drugs. The four signs are these.

First, whether it soothes immediately or not; second, whether the distressing matters are evacuated along with it or not; [495] third, whether it leaves behind some roughness in the bodies or not; and fourth, whether it would not appear beneficial to those who are in such a condition. For that which neither soothes the bitings immediately, but is rather excreted with greater vehemence, nor remains within and heals, and which leaves behind some painful roughness in the bodies and exacerbates this if it is applied a second time, is erosive and biting by nature, though it sometimes heals bitings by accident; whereas that which is soothing even immediately and provokes no excretion, nor roughens while it remains, and becomes a remedy for the parts that have been roughened, is itself beneficial by nature, but there are times when it becomes biting through the cacochymia which alters and corrupts it.

These things have been said by me, and the argument has taught at once the occasion or the manner of use of each of the two kinds of drugs and at once the discovery of their power, and it has also demonstrated that the juice of ptisane, and chondros, and tragos, and milk, and washed bread belong to the things of good humour, and indeed also that soft fat and hard fat, and sweet oil [496] and sweet wax, are of the nature of the soothing agents. And sweet wax would be both that which is such by nature—since some, at least, are bitter to those who taste them—and that which, in addition to being such, has also been washed in good water. One must wash not only wax but also pitch and resin, and oil and anything else whatsoever of this kind that does not mix with water, first warming it moderately, then pouring it down into a broad and large vessel containing in itself a quantity of water that is at once most pure and most devoid of quality. For in this the thing being washed, whatever it may be, deposits its own pungency. And one must also rub it up and beat and crush and knead it with the hands sufficiently, so that every part of the drug being washed may come into contact with the water; and having done this, one must pour off the first water, and, warming the thing being washed once more, throw it into other water, likewise pure; and one must beat it up again for as long as possible, until it deposits its own quality in the water.

And it is possible for you to discern this also by tasting; then to do this a third and [497] fourth time and many times in succession, until the water no longer receives any quality at all from the drug being washed. In this way, then, one should wash all things that can be heated and melted. But if something is stony and hard, like cadmia and scale of copper and burnt copper, one should break those down thoroughly into fine pieces and grind them for a very long time in spring water that is as pure as possible, pouring off the previous water many times, until nothing settles on top when the water stands still and it becomes without any quality of the drug being ground; but so long as either something of its quality is perceptible to those tasting, or something settles on top, up to that point one should continue both grinding and pouring off. For if one washes in this way any of the things that can be washed, it becomes non-biting. And indeed oil appears in this process to become not only non-biting but also whiter. But one must not beat it up vigorously in the same way as pitch and wax and resin, so that its mixture with the water does not become hard to separate; rather, having let it stand still, one should easily take it up as it floats on top.

There are also other methods of whitening oil among those who have written the books [498] on preparations and those on materia medica, as also the ones in Dioscorides, in the first book. But the majority of those methods, by consuming the watery and the yellowish-red part of the oil, render what remains white, whereas the method by washing does so by, as it were, scouring it clean and wiping it off. Concerning the condition of washed drugs and of those that are whitened, more will be said again later; but I return to the matter at hand. Oil, if it is neither the so-called omphacine (for that at any rate is astringent), nor prepared with salt, nor yet fresh and, as it were, still seething, and if in addition to all these it has been carefully washed, will produce no biting either when drunk or when injected. And if it is roughening to the pharynx, this at least would be nothing towards its being biting. For everything that is biting and pungent is also roughening, but certainly not everything roughening is biting and pungent. For only in this way would oil have been demonstrated to be biting, namely if everything roughening had been agreed to be biting.

So here too there comes in again [499] the fallacy arising from the inversion of the conditional, this a small and paltry sort of error. For it is agreed that everything biting is throat-roughening; and it is agreed also that oil is throat-roughening. But from these assumptions it is not concluded that oil is biting, whether we make the premises categorical or hypothetical, because neither is anything concluded from two universal affirmatives in the second figure, nor is the conditional necessarily true. In the categorical syllogism the two premises will be these: everything biting is throat-roughening, all oil is throat-roughening; and from these, once granted, nothing will be concluded. As for the hypothetical premise, which Chrysippus and his school call a conditional proposition, we have no way of taking it as true either from perception or from logical consequence.

For it is not the case that, either through perception or from perception, or however one may wish to name it, axioms of the following sort have been obtained—'everything biting is also throat-roughening', and 'if something is biting, this is also throat-roughening'—nor, if everything biting is also throat-roughening, is everything throat-roughening [500] thereby also biting; nor from 'everything, if it is biting, is also throat-roughening' does it follow that 'everything, if it is throat-roughening, is also biting'. Rather, the proposition 'if not throat-roughening, then not biting either' is true, for it converts; but not 'if something is throat-roughening, it is forthwith also biting', for this inverts. And it has been shown in the logical methods that arguments which convert with true arguments are true, whereas those which invert are no longer in every case true. If, then, it is not necessarily true that, if something is throat-roughening, this is forthwith also biting, neither would oil be shown to be biting from its being throat-roughening. For only if it had been agreed that everything throat-roughening is biting would such a conditional have been found true—'if oil is throat-roughening, it is also biting'—so that, when a co-assumption of the following kind has been added to this argument, 'but indeed oil is throat-roughening', the conclusion follows, according to the first indemonstrable, as follows: 'therefore oil is biting'.

But in fact they ought not to have argued [501] in this way, that if something is biting, this is straightaway also throat-roughening, but rather that only biting things are throat-roughening; for in that way all throat-roughening things would be biting. But this very claim, that only biting things appear throat-roughening, is both stated contrary to sense-perception—for oily things too appear throat-roughening—and the point at issue has been readily assumed, confirmed neither from perception nor from demonstration. And further, in addition to these things, it is the mark of men who are ignorant of what sort of condition that of throat-roughness (κέρχνειν) is, which it is perhaps better to explain to them. Throat-roughness comes about when some unevenness contrary to nature is formed in the throat. For the pneuma, being accustomed always to be carried along a clean and smooth path, when it strikes against certain protrusions along it, produces a certain agitation and, as it were, an uneven shaking in the throat, and in this way the animal is provoked to cough. For just as nature has also implanted in animals many other innate affections for the sake of preservation, in the same way it has also implanted sneezing and cough.

sneezing in order to thrust out the things that irritate and distress in the [502] nostrils, and cough in order to thrust out those in the throat. Such a condition is twofold: either the membrane itself along the artery is dried out and roughened, or some uneven body is carried within it, whether liquid in its nature or even solid. For this reason, even if some small particle of bread, or of some other of our foods, should at some time slip, against our will, into the passage of the breath, we are compelled to cough; and if, while we are drinking, some of the drink flows aside all at once, it is similarly irritated and calls forth a cough. For some portion of what is drunk is always filtered through along the rough artery into the lung, but so small that it is at once snatched up by the organs and readily distributed in every direction. It does not, however, by any means lodge in a mass (διΐσταται) anywhere in the passages of the breath, nor is the animal irritated to cough. But whenever either more of this, or some other such liquid, or a solid body is carried into the rough artery, from then on it is necessary to cough, until what distresses is cast out by the vehemence of the breath.

Something analogous to this occurs also when the breath strikes against the very membrane lining the inside of the windpipe once it has become roughened, [503] except that this condition is different from the one mentioned before. For this one takes away and scrapes off something of the membrane of the windpipe, whereas in the former condition something falls upon it on the inside. What is common to both is the unevenness of the passage of the breath. These matters have been discussed at greater length in the books on the Causes of Symptoms. But for the present it suffices to know that all biting things produce the unevenness and the hoarseness (kerchnos) by roughening the throat, while oil-like and oily things do so by being plastered around it. For whatever falls upon the coat of the windpipe contrary to nature and is plastered on so as to be hard to detach becomes unfamiliar to the organs and to the breath carried through them, and distressing to the animal. And I am not now saying this as though most oils were not also biting in their quality.

For those that contain salt and those that are altogether new are in every case biting, not because of their own proper substance, but because in all the juices derived from plants there is carried along a twofold residue, as Theophrastus has sufficiently demonstrated and as we too shall demonstrate in what follows: the one the thicker [504] and, as it were, more earthy, the other the thinner and more watery. In oil too both of these are present, requiring time for concoction and separation; but in the course of time the one settles as sediment, the other is consumed away. And first the earthy and thicker part settles, what is called amorge; the other, the thinner and, as it were, more watery part, is itself also in a way composite, consisting of a certain airy substance and a thin serous one. This serous part is tawny in colour, and has taken on by impression the quality of the thick and earthy part that settles. The oil itself, however, is non-biting and white according to its own nature; whence, when this thin residue has been separated off, it becomes whiter and sweeter than it was. It is separated off in many ways. For either, having set a wide-mouthed vessel full of oil in the hot sun, they repeatedly lift it out of it with shells and dash it down from above, or they place hot ash beneath the vessels that contain the oil, imitating as far as possible a sun-like warmth.

[505] For they guard against the greater heat, which alters it in quality and readily gives it a burnt, greasy smell; or they set olive-stones or grain around it in a circle, or they add certain drugs to the vessels themselves; in a word, they draw out and consume the watery part and preserve what remains. If, then, you take oil that is sweet and white in this way, which from the beginning had no share of salt at all, and in addition also wash it, as was said before, this is for you the least biting of all drugs. And indeed we have often given oil of this kind to certain people to drink, and have ourselves taken it for the sake of trial, and it was entirely non-biting in the intestine and least roughening to the throat, and when poured into the eyes it brought on a slight sensation, troubling them by its strangeness and unfamiliarity alone rather than by its pungency. Oil of this sort, then, being oil in the strict sense, moistens and softens everything, being neither extremely cold, as has been said, nor hot when applied.

But that oil which also has a share of salt necessarily has something of biting as well; yet I should be surprised if anyone [506] puts in so much salt that it becomes stronger than the oil-like and oily substance, and that merely in order that someone may prove Archidamus right when he says that the skin is scorched in those who are rubbed with oil—since indeed I know that this too is often done, both for certain other purposes and for podagra and arthritis.
