For some people rub the affected parts with finely ground salt together with a little oil, in the intervals obviously and not during the paroxysms, in order to dry up and disperse all the superfluity and to instil a certain good condition and strength into the weak parts. But in this case the salt predominates, whereas in oil it is predominated over. And one ought to compare the person who is anointed and rubbed with things that are soaked in oil rather than with things that are boiled in it, since we are surely not going to boil the man down in boiling oil, but to anoint him with well-tempered oil. For it would have been better, as I have often said before as well, to look at the thing itself as it happens, since it is perceptible and perfectly clear. For there is surely no need of examples from outside in matters that can be known in this way.

But if indeed [507] at some time the matter under investigation should also be unclear, so as to require proof from other things, not even then should one set down as testimony of the power of the thing under investigation things that are most remote and most dissimilar, passing over what lies near at hand. It is surely evident and clear to all that rubbing with oil is far less fatiguing than dry rubbing and softens bodies, rather holding together and keeping in whatever is of a nature to flow off from us outward, not dispersing and drying it. And this Diocles himself also conceded, when he declared oil to be clogging of the pores, restraining of what flows off, and softening of hides. But if what is apparent did not suffice for him, and for this reason he thought it better to adduce to his argument some piece of external evidence, he ought to have mentioned things that are soaked in cold oil, not things that are boiled down in boiling oil. Just as in such matters he passes over what is apparent, so too does he in asserting that rubbing in oil becomes uneven because the hands slip.

For we all clearly perceive the very opposite: rubbing with [508] oil is even, while dry rubbing is uneven. For in dry rubbings the hands drag the skin along with them and, as it were, double it and fold it over upon itself, firmly and contrary to nature. Then, when the former fold, so to speak, can no longer follow the hands as they pass over it, this fold runs back and is drawn back toward the continuous part, while the hands pass all at once to another part of the skin, skipping over the under part of the fold; and for this reason we perceive such rubbing as hard, uneven, and fatiguing: hard, because the skin is forcibly stretched and bruised, and for the same reasons also fatiguing; uneven, because the rubbing hands do not fall upon every part of the skin, but always skip over the under part of the fold. And this happens both because of the natural roughnesses of the skin, especially in bodies past their prime, and because it is slack in almost all other people, and most of all in the lean and in old men.

For if the skin were smooth and uniform throughout and precisely stretched, it would not be folded over [509] easily, nor would it make the movements of the hands over it uneven; rather, I think, they would run easily forward, slipping readily from the first parts to others, because they would drag along with themselves no part of the skin. But since it is slack and rough, it needs some drug from outside that will fill up its wrinkles and supply slipperiness to the rubbing hands; and for these purposes you would find nothing more suitable than oil. And one might wonder at Archidamus, who neither showed respect for what is evidently apparent nor discovered the account of it, but declared the opposite on both points. For dry rubbing appears uneven, and that with oil even, and reason bears witness to these things not least by explaining the cause. But concerning Archidamus and Diocles, enough for the present purposes. For I wish, since I have once come to demonstrating the faulty road of the discovery of the powers, using oil as an example, to go through the whole argument as quickly as possible.

So when the philosophers say that olive oil is [510] hot, and set down as no small evidence of this, as they think, the speed of its change into flame, some people object and say that this indeed belongs to it because it is thin and airy, but that from its congealing quickly in winter it clearly displays its coldness; for it is more readily overcome by the cold not only than wine and vinegar, but even than water itself. Others, objecting to these claims, concede that it is airy, and say that this appears clearly from its lightness, yet they do not also agree that it is cold in its power. For all air is hot in its nature, as its generation also shows: for water, having been thinned and dissolved by heat, becomes air. And it is clear that from this point a very great question takes them over, one disputed even among the most reputable philosophers, Aristotle and his followers supposing that air is hot, while those from the Stoa suppose it cold.

But also concerning the oil's congealing quickly, which seemed to those who declare it cold [to be a proof], those who assert that it is hot counter-propose the fact that it does not congeal violently, as water does. [511] For they say that what happens in its case is not even congealing at all, if we examine the matter precisely, but a kind of setting and thickening, and they say that this comes about because it is thick and viscous, not because it is cold; so that here too the argument from either side again arrives at an impasse, the one party establishing opposite conclusions from the fact that oil is overcome by cooling sooner than water, the other from the fact that water congeals more than oil. In addition, then, to disputing about these matters, not even all agree that it is airy. For its lightness, they say, is a sign of this, but its thickness is no small evidence that it is earthy. And some, combining both, say that it is at once airy and earthy. There are also those who laugh at these people, on the grounds that by their account they completely remove what belongs most of all to oil, namely its moistness. In addition to these points, then, from its being viscous some demonstrate that it is cold, others that it is hot, and some that it is dry, others that it is moist.

For if the parts had not been drawn together and condensed and held closely to one another, it would not have become viscous; [512] and these are all works of the cold. For it is the nature of the hot to diffuse and loosen and thin the parts and to separate them from one another. Others, conversely, say that nothing would become viscous without heat prevailing, as is shown also in the boiling of all juices, both those that are pressed out of herbs and those from fruits. For being at first watery and thin in their consistency and running, once they have been boiled they become thick and viscous. And indeed from particular examples too each side plausibly establishes the opposite conclusions: the one proposing bird-lime and honey and liquid pitch and resin and other such things among those agreed to be at once both viscous and hot; the other mentioning the juice of hemlock and fleawort and orach and blite, and in addition to these bringing forward phlegm as a kind of colophon to their argument, for this clearly seems to them to be both viscous and cold. But also from the fact that oil dripped onto those who are being phlebotomized makes the blood flow freely one can see each side establishing opposite conclusions.

For the one party say that it produces the free flow by diffusing [the blood] through its heat, the other that it does so by furnishing slipperiness through its coldness, [513] like ice. And then, turning aside from this point, they discourse about the nature of all slippery things, ascending in their argument to the furthest extremity of learned disquisition. But others, condemning the wandering of these men, as they call it, bring forward soft fat for the argument, which is closest to olive oil in its nature but can be clearly discovered as to what sort it is in its mixture; for since it is formed within ourselves it could not escape notice. To begin with, at any rate, they say that in healthy and well-nourished bodies much soft fat is generated, bodies which no one, not even if mad, would call cold; for such bodies come about when nature is strong, and nature all the natural philosophers have agreed to be a hot thing. But some, contradicting these, say that soft fat is generated in colder mixtures, as women and those who live an idle life show.

And further, among the nations too, they say that where cold prevails men become fatty, and where heat prevails, lean; and they put forward as an example for their argument the Celts, Thracians, [514] Bithynians, Pontics and Galatians, who are at once inhabitants of a cold country and straightway also fatty for the most part; whereas the Arabs, Libyans, Egyptians and Ethiopians, and all others who dwell in a hot land, are all lean and dry. There are also some who, even apart from particular examples, dispute with one another by means of the general argument itself: the one side holding that the oily humour would not even come to be in us unless the nutriments were well worked up by nature, the other that this humour is contained in the nutriments but is consumed by the warmth in us, just as oil is by the flame, and that when this warmth becomes weak it is accumulated throughout the body. Some of them also adduce the animals for the argument, those which are colder by nature being all fattier, such as bears, sheep and pigs, and those in turn which are hotter being drier and without fat, such as lions, leopards and dogs. Further, then, from the fact that bees, flies, wasps and ants are destroyed when wetted with oil, some try to demonstrate that oil is cold, others that it is hot, and some that it is moist, others that it is dry.

For since the animals mentioned are bloodless and for this reason cold, [515] some say that they are readily chilled by the oil and die on that account; others, that, being thoroughly heated, they do not endure the change to the opposite. And further, others say that they are dried immoderately, because they have already been dried out by nature, and are harmed by reason of the excess; while yet others say that they are moistened, by the contrariety to their nature. Now that they should argue in opposite directions from one another in the case of the insects would perhaps be nothing to wonder at; but that they also argue for either side from what happens to us ourselves is indeed worthy of wonder. For some say that one sweats more, others less, if one anoints oneself while bathing; and neither do those who say 'more' agree with one another about the general power, nor those who say 'less'.

But of those who say that we sweat more, some refer the cause to heat, others to viscosity, the former asserting that what is hot is by nature provocative of sweats, the latter that what is viscous, becoming a thing that catches and collects what previously flowed off quickly and for that reason escaped perception, thus makes the [516] quantity of the sweats evident. Those, on the other hand, who say that persons who have anointed themselves in baths and exercises sweat less attribute to it, some a clogging power, others a cooling one. And indeed, also from the phenomena, some say that it dries, others that it moistens: that it moistens, those who suppose that the anointed sweat more; that it dries, others in turn. And moreover, that it keeps those who have anointed themselves from being chilled, some saying that by its thickness and viscosity it keeps off the cold in the manner of a garment or a screen, others that by its natural heat it also warms up together with itself the things near it. Further, then, from the fact that it does not harm or wipe out what is written with ink in books, although all the other liquids do wipe it out, some say that its nature is dry and, as it were, moistureless, like sand and ash, while some say that it is also rather coarse-particled and unwrought. So too its not mixing with the other liquids some refer to lightness and fineness of parts, others to viscosity and thickness, since it does mix with juices that are similar, as for instance with the decoction of mallow.

And the same things are said also [517] about the fact that earth is not properly soaked by oil, although it is wetted by the other liquids, such as water, wine and vinegar. Here too some blame the dryness of its substance, some its fine-particled nature, and there are those who blame its coarse-particled nature: those who blame the fineness of parts say that it passes through the pores of the earth without touching them, while those who blame the coarseness of parts say that it does not enter them at all. And it is not possible to refute either party, since on either cause certain things can also fail to mix with what is adjacent to them, if indeed to some of the natural philosophers too the commensurability of the pores seems to be the cause of mixture. I for my part am now going through these matters under heads, recalling only the starting-points of the arguments. But if someone wished to extend each of them and to establish it from both sides, in that way he would, I think, fill not one book but very many. And it is already possible to observe that such wandering of the arguments is not only long—for that would be tolerable—but also ascends to the summit of natural philosophy, and sometimes is also hard to decide.

But if one should also know that it is altogether [518] useless to physicians, one will, I think, avoid such a path of arguments still more. For we inquire neither simply whether each of the drugs is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist, nor whether it is moistening, or drying, or heating, or cooling for ants, or wasps, or bees, or any other of the animals, but how it stands in relation to the human body. Since, then, it is possible to make the test on human beings, they do not do well to turn aside to other things. The correct test is first that on well-tempered bodies, next that on ill-tempered ones, and then, as has often been said by us before as well, that on hot and cold and dry and moist diseases. In these we required that one pay attention, and also that one distinguish that which acts in itself from that which acts incidentally.

And this will come about, first, if it is applied to affections that are as simple as possible; second, if it displays its own power perceptibly right from the beginning, or after a time, or even once it has been completely removed, as cold water does which produces a recall of warmth [519]; and further, in addition to these, if it is unmixed with any other quality, insofar as it is possible to produce such a thing. How, then, one might produce oil of this kind has been stated before; but how one might apply it to a simple disease will now be stated, after we have first recalled this much, that, as was shown in the treatise on the differences of diseases, some bodies have been turned toward the hotter without any cacochymia or inflammation of the chest or of a viscus, as is wont to happen in severe cases of heat-stroke (ἐγκαύσεις), while others have been turned toward the colder, as in what are now customarily called by all people 'chills' (ψυγμοί). In such conditions, then, by applying oil you will discover clearly whether it is by nature such as to heat us or rather to cool. Let it, obviously, be free of every strong acquired quality; for one must always bear this in mind in the case of every drug. This, then, is the main point of the account; but the actual outcome is shown by experience. Those who have suffered heat-stroke, in addition to not ceasing from the heat, become also more nauseous and, as time goes on, hotter.

[520] But for those who have been chilled, clearly nothing results from anointing with oil, whether toward benefit or harm. From which it is also clear that, even if it is by nature such as to heat us, yet certainly it is not so vehemently or manifestly, as resin and pitch and asphalt are. And you must understand now neither dry resin or pitch or asphalt—for no one would even anoint himself with these—nor indeed those melted in the sun, for such a thing would no longer be a simple or naturally occurring drug; but, in the case of resin, either the one called 'self-flowing', or the terebinth and mastic resin while still liquid and fresh, or, of the pine resin, the oil-like part that stands on top in the jars; and, in the case of pitch, the liquid kind, and still more the oil-like part floating upon it, which indeed they call pissanthos, for it really is like a sort of flower of pitch. And likewise asphalt, the liquid kind, and further that from Media.

For all these are oily and have a very great share of the oil-like nature, yet they heat manifestly, just as stacte myrrh and pine oil, or juniper oil, or cedar and laurel oil, and other such things, clearly heat through those who have been chilled, [521] but in the extreme distress those who have been burned by heat. These, then, are agreed from both sides to heat. But oil is agreed from neither side either strongly to heat through those who have been chilled or to harm those who have been burned by heat. Yet it is not obscurely, either, that it becomes a cause of a certain nausea (ἄση) for those who have fallen into fever as a result of heat-burning (ἔγκαυσις), and it appears to augment the heat, just as also in pure erysipelas. These are surely bilious fluxes; for surely in these very cases too it is clearly seen to increase the warmth, even if you apply it extremely cold. For in cases of heat-burning, if it be without salt, and in addition whitened, it affords some relief when poured over cold. But in cases of erysipelas, however cold it may be, it benefits nothing, but is even of a nature to harm: those that arise purely from a bilious flux, all of them, with the greatest harms, and those from blood mixed with it, with smaller ones, though not even these are trivial. And less than these, but still manifestly, it also distresses seething inflammations; from all of which, as I inferred, it seemed to me to kindle a heat closely similar to that of whatever bodies it happens to have come into contact with.

At any rate it [522] appears, when applied to moderately warm bodies, to warm them moderately, while in strongly warm ones it kindles a strong warmth. Now it has already been stated in the third book On Mixtures, and it will be stated now as well, that each of the drugs applied to the body—those, that is, which we said are hot in their powers—receiving from us the starting-point of their being heated, some heat us back in the same measure, others more vehemently. Olive oil, then, appeared to me, when I examined its powers in particular cases, to be among those that heat back to an equal degree. For I always found it producing a lukewarm heat in moderately warm bodies, and a seething heat in those that are seething. And for this reason it appeared to me neither to help in any noteworthy way nor to harm in cases of spasms and tremors, of insensibility and impaired sensibility.

For it could not benefit, because it does not heat strongly, nor was it capable of harming, since it does not cool at all; whereas, once it had taken on a strong acquired heat, it benefited sufficiently—whenever we set those so affected into tubs [523] of hot oil containing certain roots, or heating herbs, boiled down in it. Hence it is with good reason, as it were, a kind of matter for the other drugs. For if you mix cold things with it, the mixture will be cold, and if hot things, hot. For whatever belongs to the middle mixture serves both of the extremes, so that it is able neither, if it should be mixed with a hot thing, to render what is mixed from both cold, since it is not itself cold, nor, if with a cold thing, hot, for neither is it hot. And on this account it is with good reason that some say it heats us, others that it does not heat. For it would seem to heat in that it arrives at a warmth equal to that of the body heating it; at any rate it is able in this way to heat back in return. But because it does not augment the heat which it found, it would not seem to heat; for (they say) the work of what heats is not to preserve the heat it found, but to increase it.

The sources of this kind of dispute are three: the failure to distinguish the kinds of things that are said to heat [524] us, the confused use of homonymies, and the failure to leave room for any mean. Now things are said to heat us both when they are hot in actuality, like fire itself, and when hot in potentiality; and of the things hot in potentiality, some do so as foods, others as drugs, others as coverings. And as for 'the hot' itself, we are accustomed to name thus both what is already such in actuality and what is so in potentiality, as has often been said before as well. But that which is hot in actuality includes both what is hot simply, like fire, and what is hot by predominance, like the animal, and what is hot when compared with the well-proportioned member of the same genus, and what is hot relative to anything whatever that happens to be at hand. What is hot in potentiality, on the other hand, is first distinguished by opposition from what is hot accidentally, and then in turn has as many differences of signification as what is hot in actuality has. For being, as it were, a kind of matter suitable for what is hot in actuality, one part of it is suited to the things called hot simply, another to those hot by predominance; and another would be the proper matter for things compared with the well-proportioned member of the same genus or of the same species, or with anything whatever that happens to be at hand.

For this reason too, when considering things in relation to man, [525] we thought it right to withdraw from all the others. In all these respects, then, those who have inquired into the power of drugs go wrong, and in addition to these they further pass over the intermediate states, both in our natural mixtures, as we showed in the treatises On Mixtures, and in the examinations of drugs. For they frame their arguments as if the drug under examination had of necessity to be either hot, or dry, or moist, or cold, as though it were not possible for something to be placed in the middle between the things that heat and those that cool us, and some other thing in the middle between those that dry and those that moisten. And some are so foolish that not even upon hearing the truth are they able to follow it. At any rate I know some who even attempt to argue against it, claiming that nothing is intermediate in its mixture. But against these persons the appropriate things have been said in the work On Mixtures, and in what follows they will be said no less.

But, hastening to put an end to the present [526] discourse, I return once more to olive oil. For it happens to it, as a nutriment, perhaps to heat us, whenever it is taken into the interior of the body; for it seems to certain physicians and philosophers of no mean repute that, just as from foods, so also from olive oil there comes about a certain addition to the body. And it also happens to it, as a drug, to be in some way intermediate between the things that heat and those that cool us; and it belongs to it, moreover, as a covering, to warm us—and this, indeed, seems to me to be the most proper likeness, above all others, of its nature. For just as each of our garments, being warmed by us ourselves, is naturally disposed to warm us in return, so too is olive oil. But just as none of those becomes hotter than the very body that warms it, so neither does olive oil.

The whole matter would be well understood by you — and it will prove useful not only for the present but also for everything that is to come — if you were to call to mind the very air that surrounds us, which sometimes becomes colder than the heat within us, to such a degree that we need certain screens and coverings against it, and at other times becomes hotter again, to such a degree that we cannot bear it but flee for refuge into [527] some shelter and shade. And there are times when it is in such a moderate state that we desire neither the things that would warm us nor the things that cool us, but our contact with it is painless and imperceptible. This third mixture, then, the one just described, I call moderate, and I say that it is intermediate between the others and neither heats our body nor cools it; of the other two, the one heats us and the other cools us. And I say that both the warmth that comes from garments and the warmth that comes from oil resemble the intermediate and moderate mixture of the air that surrounds us. But if even so what I wish to indicate is not clear, I think you will understand it better in the following way. Conceive for me two human beings, similarly mixed in body, touching one another either with the chest and belly alone, or also with the hands and legs. If, then, the air surrounding them should have the same mixture as these two human beings, so that the warmth in the three bodies is equal, then in such a case nothing could be said to be heated by anything.

For bodies that are alike in every respect undergo [528] no alteration from one another. But if the surrounding air is cold, the men would be said to warm each other, although they are not in fact warming, but keeping off the cold. Accordingly the many, being accustomed to use names loosely, call that which prevents one from being cooled "warming", not correctly. Now one must allow them to name things as they wish, but that the same thing is signified by the verb "to warm" in each of the two expressions must in no way be further allowed. For it is certainly not the same thing to supply warmth to something from oneself, or to keep off the cold. This being so, whatever things fall upon us from outside and have the same warmth as the body, whether they have taken it from themselves or from other things or indeed from ourselves, these, according to the strict account, must be said neither to warm us nor to cool us; but if anyone wishes to use the term loosely, it must be allowed, provided only that in the expression he recalls the difference of the meanings. For it is in one way that the warmer air is said to warm us, and in another way the well-tempered air.

Analogous to the hotter [air] are pellitory and mustard and [529] pepper, and to the moderate [air] soft fat and oil. For the airs are hot in actuality, the drugs in potentiality. For we ourselves do not make the air hot, but [we are heated] because we come close to air of such a kind; whereas the drugs, as we showed also in the third book On Mixtures, taking from us the beginning of the change toward being heated, are of such a nature as to heat us back in return, some to an equal degree, some more, some less. Now oil belongs among those that heat back equally. And it also belongs to it, from its being viscous and hard to run off and obstructive of the pores, to augment the warmth, as it seems, in a twofold way: on the one hand from its being plastered around in the manner of a garment or a screen, and on the other, from its blocking up the pores, the preventing of the greater part of the vaporous heat from flowing out from within. For these reasons, then, it does not even allow our bodies to be dried, unless it is applied warm and over a longer time; and all men, having learned this power of it by experience —

those whom they wish to sweat more abundantly, whether bathed or unbathed, they do not apply oil to them straight away at the beginning, [530] but in the case of those who have been ill, once they have begun to sweat, they warm it and pour it over them; in the case of those who are ill, once they have sweated sufficiently; and in the case of the healthy, those who come from a long journey on foot and from rather many exercises, or who have had their body dried out in any other way whatsoever, these they allow to anoint themselves even before sweating; but those who have failed to digest, or who have a plethoric body, these they do not permit to use oil even when they bathe. And it seems to me that here too oil is in the middle between the things that moisten us and those that dry us, just as a little earlier it was shown to be between those that heat and those that cool. For water moistens, while laurel oil and cedar oil dry.

At any rate, olive oil applied simply, just as it is, without having been warmed beforehand by ourselves through artifice, or cooled — for this one must always bear in mind in every case — preserves our mixture such as it found it, restraining as far as possible and preventing all the vaporous transpirations from being evacuated from the body. But if you rub the [531] limbs with oil for a longer time, you will both generate a certain acquired heat from the rubbing, and you will benefit those suffering from fatigue in this way: partly because the fat penetrates inside the body into the fine pores so as to soften what has been hardened, partly because by its heat it disperses whatever pungent and thin moisture, generated in fatigues from colliquation, was being held in beneath the skin. For sweats are seen flowing off outwardly in those who exercise, and not a few residues and, as it were, colliquative products are seen flowing together inwardly into the belly. And from these one must reckon that, even if it is not evident, many such things in need of evacuation are also left behind throughout the whole body. For in fatigues a twofold condition arises, as has been demonstrated elsewhere: the homoeomerous parts of the animal are dried, while the empty spaces are moistened, not with a useful moisture in accordance with nature — for that would be plethora — but with one that is thin, pungent and biting; and for this reason they also require remedies of two kinds, those that moisten the dryness and those that evacuate the pungent moisture.

And for this reason, against both of these, the baths in [532] sweet waters happen to be most useful, since by their moisture they correct the dryness of the organs, and by their heat in turn they also disperse the thin humour. And if indeed water were able to remain in bodies and not easily flow away, it alone would be sufficient. But since what is poured over from outside flows off easily, and what enters into the pores of the body flows out again, having no hold, for this very purpose oil is usefully mixed in, and the more so if one is rubbed down at length with both together, which the ancients called chytlousthai, and they set over against it xēraleiphein (dry anointing). This too is in some way, in and of itself, curative of fatigues, but it falls very far short of chytlōsasthai. For, apart from everything else, whenever the water is beaten up and rubbed together with oil, it has a mixture that is quite hard to dissolve, so that on whatever bodies the oil is smeared and plastered around, the water too is compelled to remain in contact with these for a longer time. So here too, then, oil is as it were a kind of material of moistening and drying agents, just as it was shown earlier to be of heating and cooling ones.

For if it is mixed with a drying thing, it renders the whole drying, and if with a moistening thing, it makes this too moistening; and often the mixture of both has been rendered even more moistening than the very thing that moistens primarily, as is the case with water. For water moistens primarily, but, because it does not remain for any length of time, having an activity of short duration, it benefits only weakly. Oil, therefore, becoming a bond for it, since it compels it to remain in contact for the longest possible time with those who need the help that comes from it, has been rendered the best of all remedies for bodies that are dried out and parched. In the same way, if you mix a drying drug with oil, such as chalcitis, or pellitory, or oak-gall, or soapwort, the mixture of both will be drying. Oil, then, since it serves all the things that are mixed with it, is reasonably, as it were, a kind of material of all of them. It necessarily diminishes their proper activity, but not indeed their benefit; rather, there are times when it even increases it. For it is certainly not the same thing, even if it will seem so to some, to increase the activity of something and to increase its benefit.

For the activity is in accordance with the proper power of each thing, whereas the benefit [534] is sometimes also by accident. Now, more will be said at greater length in what follows about benefit by accident; but it will be stated now too, to the extent that is required for the present matters. For water beaten up with oil, so as to produce what is called hydrelaion, helps those who are fatigued more than if it were present alone, not because its proper power is intensified, but because it remains for a long time on those who need it. And that, if the binding agent is not intermediate in its mixture, it will often oppose, in their activities, the things that primarily help those who need them — this you can be taught in general from the very nature of drugs, and also from the record of drugs according to species. From the general consideration, because the thing admixed, if it draws the power of the drug blended with it toward the opposite, can sometimes even prevail and completely transfer the mixture of both into another kind.

For that which has the role of matter in the mixture ought to display neither any notable form nor any power [535]. And from the experience drawn from particulars you would learn as follows that what has the role of matter ought neither to heat nor to cool nor to dry nor to moisten: if, first, you were to recall what I mentioned a little earlier concerning liquid pitch and resin and myrrh, bitumen and cedar-oil and laurel-oil and all the other things that heat. For all of these, when rubbed up with water in the same manner as oil, heat rather than cool and dry rather than moisten, and for this reason they are not by nature very apt to relieve the sensations of fatigue. For they are neither of the same power as water, so as to cooperate with it in some way rather than to act against it, nor of the power midway between the extremes, so that they might serve, like a kind of matter, that which acts primarily. For they dry and heat rather; they do not moisten and cool as water does. But if you were to mix water with one of the things that strongly dry and heat, you will see not only none of the things it naturally does coming about, but even water itself completely obscured, as if it had not been mixed in at all in the first place.

Chalcitis, then, and sandarach and misy [536] and all the others that heat and dry us vehemently still preserve their own power strong when mixed with water. From every side, then, it is clear that whatever is going to serve each of the two extremes, like a kind of matter, must be intermediate in its mixture; and so, in placing oil too in this position, you would not go wrong. For all the particular effects will agree with you, and you will blame for the length of the argument not us, but all those who, stepping beyond the straight road, turn aside onto a bad and long one. For this reason I too have been compelled to lengthen this discussion, since the truth itself admits of a very swift discovery, inasmuch as it sets out from the very things that evidently appear. Yet I have not lengthened the discussion to such an extent as is possible for one who has chosen to write down all the things badly said by them and to teach thoroughly the causes of their errors. And yet to state the causes is perhaps necessary, in order both to guard against the fallacies arising from them in the whole judgement of particular drugs and to hold to the true teaching in a more scientific manner.

[537] For our convictions about matters are increased when we not only know the truth itself but also learn thoroughly the causes of all the fallacies. This, then, we shall work out in what follows. But now, having added a few things about rose oil to what was said at the beginning, I shall bring the discussion to a close at this point. It has been said, then, that it is not reasonable to attend to smells or colours or any other of the accidents in the examinations of powers, but rather to what is clearly apparent in both healthy and diseased bodies. And it has also been demonstrated that olive oil, when it is unsalted and entirely pure, belongs to the middle material. So that rose oil too—the precise and simple and truly rose oil—must be prepared from this oil and have nothing more drug-like in itself, as the perfumers are accustomed to prepare it, astringing the oil beforehand with aromatics before putting in the roses, so that it may become lasting and more fragrant.

But it is perhaps better to distinguish them by their names as well, [538] just as I know the ancients also did. For they call 'rose oil' that which has been prepared without the aromatics; but that to which something of these too has been added they no longer call oil, but by now 'unguent' (μύρον). And so, since oil is as it were a kind of matter for heating and cooling drugs, being itself of the middle mixture, and rose oil is composed of oil and the juices of roses, it too is surely of such a mixture as the juice of roses is. And it is surely very easy to make the test of its power—not only of the juice of roses alone by itself, but also, having compounded rose oil, on both healthy and diseased bodies, as has already often been said. You will find, then, that those who are still burning are cooled by it and immediately perceive some benefit, while all those who have been chilled are manifestly harmed, so that from both sides you clearly understand that its power is cooling rather than heating.

Nevertheless, the cooling produced by rose oil does not appear to you strong, but it will seem to be, in a way, very close [539] to the middle mixture. For the sake of clear teaching I name such drugs as belonging to the first nature and order of cooling agents, just as, again, I name those which have departed a little from the middle mixture toward the hotter as belonging to the first remove and order of heating agents. These, then, are the things one must know at present about rose oil. For it will be necessary for me, in the discourse that follows as well, to make mention of the drug once more and to add what is lacking in what we have said.

[540] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 3. That I had resolved to write in the treatise now in hand only what is useful for cures, I have as witnesses first and above all the gods, and then also the companions who urged me to make mention, so far as is possible, of those who have pronounced incorrectly concerning the power of simple drugs.

[379] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK I. How great a benefit it is to know accurately the powers of simple drugs, both for the composition of compound ones and for the timely use of those already discovered, I do not need to show at present. For the one point will be demonstrated in the writings on the composition of drugs, the other in the writings on the therapeutic method.

But what comes next in order after the treatise On Mixtures, this will be stated here, [380] once we have first distinguished the meanings of the expressions and the names that we shall use in the course of this discourse. We call a drug, then, anything whatever that is capable of altering our nature, just as, I think, we also call nourishment anything whatever that is capable of increasing our substance; for both belong to the category of the relative. The simple drug has itself also been so named by antithesis to the compound, and it is that which is purely in accordance with its own nature. The power is a certain active cause. Of this, one kind is in actuality, the other consists in being about to act (ἐν τῷ μέλλειν). In actuality, the power of heating is in fire and that of cooling in ice; in prospect, the power of heating is in pyrethrum and castoreum and the like, that of cooling in henbane and mandrake and similar things. Now, that there is a certain power—in purgative drugs a purgative one, in emetics an emetic one, in sternutatories a sternutatory one, in cough-remedies a cough-remedial one—and, in the case of each of the other actions, one named derivatively from what is brought about by them, almost no one will dispute.

But what the substance of this power is, [381] some have supposed to be unknowable, as for instance the Sceptic philosophers and those among the physicians who are called Empiricists. And those who declared it to be knowable have also differed among themselves. For some refer it to the sizes and the shapes and the positions of the corpuscles and the pores, while others refer it to heat and cold and moisture and dryness, each group according to its own doctrine of the elements; so that we too, since we have shown through the writing(s) On the Elements according to Hippocrates that the bodies both of all other things and of animals have come to be from hot and cold and dry and moist, shall posit these as the substances of the active powers both in all other things and in drugs. For so it had been shown also in the third book On Mixtures; and indeed anyone who wishes to follow what is now being said must have been exercised in that treatise; for in fact everything that one needs to know in general about drugs has been stated in that work. And now we shall say nothing newer with respect to the genus as a whole; but whatever has been written there generically, this we shall work out specifically in these commentaries.

[382] First, then, and above all, one must make the test of the power under judgement on the basis of the very thing in relation to which it is predicated. For it does not follow, if hemlock is cooling for a human being, that it is thereby so also for a starling, nor, if it is nourishing for a starling (ἀνθρώπων), that it is thereby so also for a human being. In the same way, it does not follow, if hellebore is purgative, that it is thereby so also for quails, nor, if it is nourishing for them, that it is thereby so also for human beings. Next, one must distinguish what is so per accidens from what is so primarily and in virtue of itself. For cold water sometimes produces a recalling of heat by cooling the skin and contracting and condensing it; for a recalling of heat follows upon this, as was shown in the third book On Mixtures. Hot, in turn, often cools by dispersing the humour that is doing the heating. For if someone, having made these distinctions precisely, should come to the examination of the power under inquiry, he does not seem to me likely to go astray easily.

But to make the judgement from nothing other than that in relation to which the power is predicated is actually quite easy: we are to examine neither whether oil is destructive of insects, nor whether it is [383] oily or viscous or light, when what we are inquiring into is whether it is of a nature to heat, or to cool, or to dry, or to moisten the human body. In the same way, we are to examine neither whether the rose is red in colour, nor whether white lead is white. For neither is what is red necessarily hot nor what is white necessarily cold; rather, the question is whether, when applied to our bodies, they heat them primarily and in themselves, and neither through some other intermediary nor incidentally; and if this be so (εἴη), then they are hot in power, just as, if they cool, they are cold. For from where, by the gods, are we able to say whether white pepper and the Cnidian berry and safflower and lime and white hellebore are hot in power? Or from where that Samian star and Selinusian earth and white lead and snow and milk are cold? For all the things mentioned are white in colour, yet in respect of their powers they are most opposite. Snow and lime, then, are most alike in colour, but most opposite in their powers; and it is sense-perception that judges the opposition.

For when snow is applied, we perceive it as cold immediately, at the [384] first contact, and, for as long as it touches us, as cooling ever more and more. And we see that it neither persists any longer nor is preserved, if it meets with even a slight warmth. Quicklime, on the other hand, does not appear to cool even at the first contact, and for as long as it is in proximity to us it manifestly heats ever more and more. From this it is also clear that the proper power of a drug will be judged by its doing one and the same thing throughout, for as long as the drug touches us. For that which, from beginning to end, so long as it is in contact, heats ever more and more, is such not in virtue of some accident but in virtue of its own nature. So too, that which cools from beginning to end is cold in virtue of its own power, not in virtue of an accident. But if you examine its power without having waited a period of time, and subsequently after the washing, you will go astray on many counts. And perhaps at some point you will even say that cold water is not only cold in power, but also hot.

when it appears to cool, continuously, for as long as it is in contact with us, [you will call it] cold; but when it has often brought about a recall of heat, [385] hot. One must not, therefore, leave these matters undetermined; and each of the drugs being tested, as was said also in the books On Mixture, must partake of no acquired cooling or heat, lest the acquired quality adulterate its natural power. And further, in addition to these things, as this too was said there, let nutriment and drug be distinguished by you, and let it be remembered that both are spoken of in relation to something, and that in many cases they are constituted in one and the same substance, in the manner in which we demonstrated this too. And no less that some things act upon and are affected by one another with their whole substances, others in respect of one or two qualities; and in addition to these, that some are fine-particled, others coarse-particled: fine-particled being all those that are easily broken down into fine parts, coarse-particled the opposite. In a word, one must bear in mind all the distinctions stated in the third book On Mixtures, so that the power of drugs of every kind may be examined according to them.

Let water, then, first be set before us for examination, because it is both the most common thing for all human beings, [386] healthy and sick alike, and the most necessary for life. And first let it be administered to a well-tempered body, being neither conspicuously cold nor hot; next also to those that are ill-tempered by nature, and third to those that are so by way of an affection; for in this way we would examine accurately, in all cases, its proper power. Administered, then, to the well-tempered body, over a longer time it will in every case cool it; administered to the ill-tempered body, it will cool the colder one more quickly and the hotter one more slowly. And it will always cool them all, even if someone should use it not on many successive days but on one, or for several hours; for water of this sort will not produce a recall of heat in any of them. For it is unmixed cold water that, when it has been in contact (ὁμιλῆσαι) for a short time with a well-fleshed and young nature of body, recalls warmth; but when people use it otherwise, it will always cool.

And indeed, even if such water were applied to those who are ill with some simple disease, whether hot or cold in mixture, it will clearly cool these too; for the affection must be simple, as was also determined in the third book On Mixtures, so that what is applied may cool not accidentally [387] but through its own nature. Since indeed, often, when the condition is composite, one thing comes about primarily from the drug and another accidentally, as in inflammations. For the affection is the offspring of a hot and abundant flux; and such drugs as warm moderately, by evacuating the superfluity, at once, I think, also make the affected part colder. But when the condition is simple and single, what is accidental cannot come about in its case. So at any rate, when you examine the matter in this way, drinkable water will appear cold from every point of view. Yet the other naturally occurring waters, those that are sulphurous, bituminous and nitrous in their qualities, do not have the same power; for none of them, when it is applied separated from acquired heat or coldness, appears to cool. And indeed the sea too, even by itself, before it takes on an unmixed acquired cooling, does not appear to cool very much at all.

For in the case of drinkable water, if someone were to swim in it through a whole day, even though it is not very cold but lukewarm as from the sun, he will necessarily [388] be chilled. But very many of the young men have endured the sea without distress, not only through a whole day but sometimes even through the night. From which it is clear that water—at any rate drinkable and sweet water—is always cold according to its own nature, whereas the sea is not similarly so. And if at some point in the discussion one does not add "drinkable", but we say simply that water, so far as depends on itself, is cold, one must not quibble as though we had spoken deficiently or without due distinction. For whatever is precisely and purely water, unmixed with any other substance, that is necessarily cold according to its own power; but if, being filtered through a bituminous, or sulphurous, or nitrous, or aluminous place, it should cleanse off something of the substance of that place and sweep it along together with itself, such water is already mixed and not precisely water—just as if you yourself should wish to mix a good quantity of salt, or alum, or some other such thing with drinkable water, as indeed we often do when, being without sea-water, we wish to prepare brine.

For in that case we throw some salt into the water; and so great, [389] then, is the difference in power, that water itself—the sweet kind, that is, which is neither manifestly cold nor hot, but such as what is called sun-warmed—if you apply it to an erysipelas, you will produce no harm at all to the person's body; but if you apply sea-water, or brine, or some such mixed water, bituminous or sulphurous, you would harm the person so much as to burn the part. Water, then, in and by itself is cold in power; but if, having attached to it an acquired heat, you should wish to foment a person's body with it, you will perhaps suppose that you have applied something simple and natural, whereas it is in fact somehow composite, having taken on either some portion of the substance of fire, or at all events its quality. For just as, if you had also mixed some salt into it, it would admittedly have been composite, so too, and all the more, since you have mixed in fire—whether its quality or its substance—you have now too in some way made it composite. And muddy water too is surely composite, as for instance that of the Nile and that in Egypt; but when filtered through earthenware vessels it becomes precisely pure.

But one must filter it not once but [390] twice or three times, although even so it is perhaps impossible to make it perfectly pure; yet when the mud carried along in the waters escapes all perception, it suffices, for such a use at least, to call such waters pure and unmixed. These are judged by three senses, taste, sight and smell. Pure to the taste, if it should take on no quality but appear entirely without quality; pure to the sight, when it is unmixed and perfectly transparent. So too with respect to smell it must display no quality, in the way that some of the extremely bad waters present a smell of sourness, or of pungency, or of brine, or of putrefaction, or of some other unnameable badness. Accordingly, the water that is free of all these is not itself, with respect to its nature at least, perfectly unmixed, just as no other of the four perceptible elements is either; yet in relation to perception and to use it is unmixed.

At any rate, water of this sort is also cold, as has been said, in its own nature; since indeed, if you were to heat strongly not only water, [391] but also mandrake and henbane and hemlock and poppy-juice, you would not only thoroughly heat a human body by applying them, but even burn it. Let all the drugs that are being tested, then, be free of every acquired and strong heat and cooling, and not only water. That all sweet water manifestly cools you may learn also from the following. If you soften a moist cerate with cold water and, having soaked it carefully, apply it to some hot affection, you will cool it down at once. One should mix in as much of the water as possible, and the mixing would best come about in roughly this way. One must melt wax, as pure as possible, in oil and make a moist cerate; then, having cooled and scraped it, knead it in a mortar with the hands while pouring on cold water, to the extent that the cerate is able to take it up and the water does not at all run off.

This also cools those who are burning with fever, if it is applied over the hypochondria, and every phlegmonē (inflammation), and likewise herpetes and carbuncles, erysipelas and phygethla and, to put it simply, all the [392] hot diseases. Do not, then, use sweet water alone, but, having mixed sea-water or brine with it as well, use it on whichever of the aforesaid conditions you wish; for you will at once observe no small difference, since the drug that results no longer cools any of the aforesaid conditions, but actually burns them up still further. So great, then, is the difference between drinkable waters and brine and sea-water. And no less than brine and sea-water, the sulphurous and bituminous waters, the nitrous ones, and those that display to the taste something of chalcanthum or misy or chalcitis, or, simply, of any of the drugs that are hot by nature, are all hostile to the hot conditions of our body. From which it is clear that all these are hot in their powers, whereas drinkable water alone is cold. And that this alone of the waters mentioned is also precisely moist you will recognise by the same method.

For if you moisten with this the ulcers that are parched and dry beyond what is needful, you will very quickly make them moist and flabby, whereas all the other waters dry ulcers; and the ulcers of fishermen [393] appear dry and as it were pickled, while those of bath-attendants appear moist and flabby. And if you should wish to apply a soaked lint (μότον) to ulcers, you will find them becoming moist from drinkable water, but dry from brine and sea-water. The aluminous waters, however, such as those in Italy called Albula, are both suitable for the other ulcers and also easily dry all the rheumatic ones. Thus, then, none of the other waters is of a nature to moisten, because it is not even water in the strict sense, but mixed and bastard, having taken on an admixture either of alum and chalcitis, or of salts, or of some other such thing. Whence some of them are exacerbating to ulcers, namely all those that are sufficiently pungent and biting.

And indeed, for one who is thirsty water is a soothing remedy, while all the other waters are provocative; and for the dropsical sweet water, both as drink and as bath, is most contrary, whereas the salty, nitrous, sulphurous and bituminous waters are all beneficial. And you could imitate, just as [394] sea-water, so also each of the others, by an admixture of the substance which appears to predominate in each. For by casting sulphur into sweet water you will produce sulphurous water, and by casting in alum, aluminous water, and so with each of the others. This, then, is the proper nature of water: it is moist and cold. But when it takes on an acquired heat, it heats and moistens the things that come near it, except that it is not of a nature to do both alike at the same time; rather, it moistens in the highest degree, whether it be lukewarm or well-tempered or even hotter, but it does not heat in the highest degree, at least so long as it is not boiling to the utmost. Let the account be examined first in the case of the well-tempered nature. If, then, you apply to this water that is temperately hot, whether bathing or affusing any part whatsoever, you will render it moister than itself and hotter during the very time of the affusion.

But if you were to stop at this point, without having contracted, compacted and condensed the body by the use of cold, a little later you will find that it has become colder than it was; for the body, when it is somewhat rarefied, becomes colder, since the innate [395] warmth is dispersed through it more immoderately. Yet the use of hot water does not render the body drier afterwards in the same way as it renders it colder. And yet this too might seem to happen, on account of the rarefaction of the pores, the softness of the body and the diffusion of the substance; for in such conditions it must necessarily give off more vapour, and vapour is moisture that has been thinned. But the truth is not so. For the softness which bodies acquire upon hot baths is a proper and inseparable sign of moisture alone in the body of an animal, as we showed in the books On Mixtures; and the flesh in ulcerated parts clearly displays such a thing, being rendered flabby and moss-like upon these affusions with hot water. The body is, however, emptied in such conditions, so that it now holds less moisture within itself than before. And one might forgive those who think that the body is dried by hot baths and by affusions of moderately hot water.

For they go wrong in a way closely similar to those who suppose that old men [396] are moister than young men. For old men have more moist residues, but the naturally constituted and organic parts themselves are moister in young men, as has been shown also in the second book On Mixtures. And so it is also in the case of affusions and baths and, simply, of every moistening by means of hot water. For the moistures in the vessels and in the other empty spaces are all evacuated, but the very bodies of the vessels and the whole fleshy kind become moister than they were. And this power alone, as it seems, water never casts off—sweet water, obviously. For not even when, boiling, it burns bodies do the burnt parts become dry, as happens in things roasted by fire. Likewise, neither when, having become extremely cold, it is poured over some part through a whole day or even for a longer time, does it render that part drier, although indeed it appears wrinkled and very small.

But these things happen to it because the moisture from the vessels and the other spaces has been emptied out, whereas the natural parts themselves become in no respect drier than they were; and one must [397] remember this too and always, throughout the whole discussion, preserve the principle of inferring the power of each of the drugs from what clearly appears, and of always testing it in relation to that with respect to which it is said to be hot or cold or moist or dry. If, by way of supplement, someone should wish to adduce proofs from external things, I do not forbid this either, but I advise him to apply his mind to it with precision. For it involves numerous fallacies; but these I shall state in what follows. The only thing, however, that one might take from external things as evidence that the drug being judged heats or cools is what concerns its contact with fire. For it is not unreasonable to suppose that what is easily set ablaze is hot in potentiality. For we remember, I think, all the significations of "in potentiality" that were distinguished in the third book On Mixtures. One of them, then, was also the sense according to the proper matter of that which is said to be some particular thing in potentiality. And if something changes easily into fire, this is fire in potentiality, clearly not in actuality.

For this [398] sense of 'potentially' is set in opposition to 'in actuality', whereas the other, 'in itself', is opposed to 'in virtue of an accident'. In this manner of judging, then, one ought to investigate and draw distinctions. And one who wishes to pass safely from external things to the bodies of animals must consider first whether the drug being tested is fine-particled or coarse-particled, and second whether it is continuous with itself and dense throughout, or has gaps and is rare. And for this reason one must give a fuller account of this matter too. For this too seems to be a kind of principle and, as it were, an element, requiring a very great deal of theoretical inquiry. Now it is evident that none of the things agreed to be hot in their powers heats us before it has been broken down into fine parts. If, then, one were to sprinkle coarse-grained pepper on the skin, one would perceive no heat at all. And in the same way, even if one were to place it on the tongue, or swallow it, or use it coarse-grained in any other way whatsoever, without having ground it thoroughly and sifted it and ground it very finely, so that it becomes dust-like.

For what is fine as [399] dust, when sprinkled upon the skin, heats, and more so if you rub it in, and likewise when applied to the tongue and when swallowed down into the belly; but when applied whole and coarse-grained it does not heat the skin at all, and to the tongue and to the belly it brings only a slight sensation of heat. Since, then, that which is easily broken down into fine parts is called fine-particled, and the opposite coarse-grained, and since it belongs to things that are hard and viscous to be broken down into fine parts either with difficulty and hardly or not at all, whereas things that are brittle and soft, without viscosity, are readily dissolved into the finest parts, it is clear from this, I think, that many things are hot in potentiality and are easily set on fire, yet do not easily heat us.

For fire, being of all things at once the most fine-particled and the hottest, both penetrates easily into the very depth and breaks up and thins and changes and overcomes and converts to its own nature, consorting in every way with what comes near it and prevailing over it; but our warmth, in addition to being coarse-particled and vaporous, is moreover also weak, so that it does not easily [400] change what comes near it. And it was shown in the third book On Mixtures—without which it is impossible to follow what is said in the present work—that none of the things that appear to heat us is of such a nature as to heat in the same way as fire, but rather as easily-kindled material does. For taking the beginning of their change from the heat in us, just as dry reeds do from the fire, they heat us in return and become, as it were, certain parts of the innate warmth, as those reeds become parts of the fire. For what was previously reed now becomes fire, so that it even increases the whole substance of the fire that changes it. And it was also shown that some things, having received a slight change from outside, then proceed by their own nature to the greatest degree of alteration. So it is no wonder if some drug has the beginning of its first change from the warmth in us, but from there proceeds further than even the very thing that changes it. For the peculiar character of each of the bodies, being in the one case well-disposed and in the other ill-disposed toward warmth, does not have an equal increase following from equal beginnings.

[401] And indeed, the fact that a very small body is easily altered and changed by what is brought near it, whereas a larger one acquires a perceptible alteration only over time and with difficulty, is not only demonstrated by the natural philosophers but also believed by all men from the very experience of what happens, and it bears sufficient witness to what is now being said. For if the particles of pepper need to receive some beginning of change from us, and receive it the more easily the smaller they are, it is no wonder that we perceive them heating the more quickly, the more carefully we have broken them down into the smallest pieces. But further, that the outer boundary of the skin is callous-like and hard and cold, whereas the whole depth beneath it is warmer in proportion as we proceed inward, no one disputes. Having added to this argument two further principles, demonstrated by us in other treatises, you will then be able to draw the whole conclusion as follows.

The one of the principles — or lemmas, or [402] axioms, or premises, or however you may wish to name them — that go into the demonstration has been demonstrated in the commentaries On Mixtures: that the whole skin is continuous with itself in its original generation, but in time becomes perforated and has very many pores, in the same way as sieves. The other of the premises useful for the syllogism is that the whole body breathes out and breathes in, as Hippocrates said. About this too more has been said in the work On the Use of Pulses, where we show that, whenever the arteries, in being dilated, draw into themselves from every side and attract through all the pores, they draw not air only or vapour, but also everything which, being readily drawn and fine-particled, promptly follows the rush of the pneumatic substance. These things being so, many veins and arteries open by their mouths into the pores of the skin and into its inner surface, and one must suppose that not a few mouths of arteries and of veins reach into the perforations of the pores, and no less toward the outer surface, so as to terminate there with their mouths.

But whatever part of the pepper [403] has become exactly dust, the arteries draw in along with the surrounding air, and this too is at once also transformed by the innate heat, on account of both its smallness and its connate aptitude for the alteration brought about by warmth. For to be hot potentially was nothing else for it than being so constituted as to be heated easily. And if once this belongs to it, it is nothing to wonder at that, being carried in the course of time to every part of the body, it heats the body in return, and that for this reason the parts that first touched such drugs are heated first and most of all, and second those continuous with these, and so in succession now the third and the fourth, according to the nearness of their position, are heated along with the part that was heated first. These things have a scientific demonstration, yet not one that is convincing to those unexercised in first principles. For one must have been exercised both in the reasonings concerning the elements and in the treatises on mixtures and on the use of the pulses, and before all these one must have been trained in the demonstrative methods. Few, however, are those who are able to go through all of these.

[404] Nevertheless, for these too it will suffice, at least in my opinion, to occupy themselves with the evident things themselves, touching on brief epilogisms, so that they may consider the cause on account of which coarse-particled things, when applied, do not heat the bodies of human beings, even if they are hot by nature, to have been stated only for those able to follow it, while they themselves are content with what appears clearly through the senses. And it appears clearly that none of the coarse-particled things, before it has been thoroughly broken down and thinned, is either itself affected by our body or able to act back upon it in any way. For this holds not only in the case of pepper, or mustard, or cachrys, or all the other things that heat us, but likewise also in the case of things cold in their powers. At any rate, if someone, having broken the bark of mandrake root into large pieces, should lay it upon the skin, or apply it as a plaster, or swallow it whole, he will accomplish nothing; but when it has been worked sufficiently fine it is of such a nature as to cool.

So too the seed of the poppy and that of hemlock—and yet this latter is the most violent of cooling agents—before it has been thoroughly crushed, when brought near [405] our skin, is altogether weak. Do not then be surprised if dry reeds and hairs, though easily burnt up, nevertheless do not warm us when brought near. For to begin with, they are not even altered by the warmth in us so as to warm in return, because they cannot be crushed to a dust-like fineness; since the reed from India, which they also call the aromatic reed (aromatites), by being pounded and sifted and in general by being broken up, evidently appears to warm more than the one found among us, as has also been agreed by all the physicians older than ourselves. One must consider, as has been said, not only whether the substance of the drugs under examination is coarse-particled or fine-particled, but also whether it is rare or dense. I call rare that whose parts are interspersed with empty spaces—we of course knowing and always remembering how 'empty space' is spoken of by those who assert that substance is unified: namely, not as it seems to Epicurus and Asclepiades, but rather the empty space in all rare bodies is full of air.

So when a body is interspersed with many such [406] open spaces, it is set on fire more easily than dense bodies, even if it is similar to them in its mixture with respect to hot and cold. For the air in the open spaces, being most readily affected, itself bursts into flame immediately at the first contact of the fire, and burns up the whole body along with itself, taking hold of each part of it from every side. If, then, small bodies, when flame surrounds them in a circle, are readily kindled — for this is manifestly evident — it is reasonable that the rare body is quickly set on fire, since the flame touches all the parts in its depth. So too, then, fire burns up dry reeds quickly, even if they are less hot than some other substance, because of the multitude of the pores, which previously air had occupied, but which, once fire has touched them, the flame spreads through. For air set on fire is flame, earth set on fire is live coal. And that the dry reed has very many airy pores, its lightness is the strongest evidence.

For a body that is dry by nature cannot otherwise become [407] light, unless it has emptiness within it. In the same way pumice too, and dry sponge, and all things that are cavernous and full of empty spaces, are light in weight. Thus the reed also readily bursts into flame, not only by being dry but also by partaking of a very great amount of air; yet for our body it is hard to heat, because of the coarse-particled character of its substance. When, therefore, judging the mixture of one of the drugs from its contact with fire, we wish to find out whether it also appears such in relation to us, we must look to the constitution of its substance. For if it is fine-particled and continuous with itself, it will display toward us the same nature that it displays toward fire; but if it is rare and coarse-particled, it is possible for it to be altered easily by fire, yet not by the warmth within us, and for this reason not to heat us in return either. Now that these matters have been thus defined, let us return again to the account of water. For that it is fine-particled one can infer from its flowing most readily through both locks of hair and woven fabrics.

For on account of its moistness [408] and softness and its having nothing viscous, it possesses parts that are easily broken and are readily divided even down to the smallest size; yet, being such, it nonetheless neither heats us according to its own nature nor is it a proper nutriment of fire, but, quite the contrary, it is set against it and at variance with it and extinguishes it, being most opposite to it. And it is no wonder if water, being cold and moist, is arrayed in opposition to fire, which is hottest and driest in its nature. One conjectures, then, as has been said, also from the contact with fire how each of the drugs stands with regard to heat or cooling. Yet one must not immediately suppose that it appears such to us as well, if it should not also be fine-particled and dense. Thus, at any rate, oil too, although it is readily set ablaze, does not heat us very quickly or manifestly, because of the viscous and coarse-particled character of its substance, being plastered, in a manner hard to release, upon whatever it first comes into contact with. And for this reason it persists for a very long time upon all the things on which it is smeared, being able neither to be readily thinned and dispersed by the surrounding air, nor indeed to be readily taken up into the interior of the body.

Water, [409] on the contrary, being very quickly dissolved into vapours, is readily dispersed. And for this reason, even if you boil, putting oil together with water into the same vessel, the water is dispersed and used up first. So too, even if, having thoroughly mixed in litharge or white lead or anything else whatever, you wish to boil both, you will see the water being dispersed first. It is not the case, then, that simply whatever is set aflame more quickly straightway appears hotter in relation to us as well. For it was shown earlier too that, of the things which heat in actuality, one kind was hot simply, like fire, and the other hot by predominance, like the heat in us. So too, of the things hot in potentiality, one kind is such in relation to what is primarily and simply hot, the other in relation to what is called hot by predominance. Consequently, it is not fitting to pass simply from the relation to fire of the drugs being judged over to ourselves, but only after one has drawn the distinction that has been stated.

And this same distinction is necessary also whenever we infer that something is cold from its congealing easily. [410] For among things that are in the same condition as regards the fine-particled or coarse-particled character of their consistency, that which is congealed more quickly by the cold is colder in its mixture. But where the one is more fine-particled, as wine, say, and the other more coarse-particled, as oil, it is not necessary that the colder one congeal more quickly or to a greater degree. Rather, if by as much as the one is colder, by so much the other is more coarse-particled, both will congeal at the same time, but the more coarse-particled would seem to have congealed more, owing to the hardness of its consistency. For it is reasonable, I think, that among things that have congealed to a like degree the more coarse-particled also becomes harder. But if either the one is colder by more than the other is more coarse-particled, or, conversely, one of them is colder by less while the other is more coarse-particled, it is no longer possible for these to congeal in an equal time; rather, that which is colder by more than the other is more coarse-particled congeals in a shorter time, and that which is colder by less than the other is more coarse-particled, in a longer one.

And in the same way, too, whichever of them appears more or less [411] hard, this must necessarily turn out in proportion to the magnitude of the excess. One must therefore bear these things in mind, and also that being cooled is not the same thing as being congealed, even if the latter comes about most of all through being cooled. For being cooled is receiving a cold quality, whereas being congealed is being hardened through cooling. Accordingly, all bodies that are fine-particled, because they are easily affected, are readily both heated and cooled, but are no longer readily congealed, as air and fire: for the one is not congealed at all, and the other is not congealed in the same way as glass and pitch and wax and resin and asphalt—although asphalt, at any rate, is very hot; but its coarse-particled and earthy part contributes to the thickness of its congealing. And on touching it you would find it still hot when already completely congealed, just as, I think, lead and tin likewise are congealed while still boiling. Thus indeed Hippocrates also said of water that that which is quickly heated and quickly cooled is always the lightest; for the more fine-particled it is, the more easily it is affected.

[412] And finer-particled is that which partakes least of earthy mud. One must not, therefore, infer simply or at random the power of the material in relation to us from its affections in relation to fire, but only together with the distinctions that have been stated. Hence the judgement is not equally safe as the one made in relation to ourselves. And the transition that goes still further beyond this one is altogether precarious; and yet very many physicians use it, some saying that everything viscous is hot, others everything astringent, others everything sweet, and still others the harsh or the acerbic; and some posit the opposites in the case of each of these. About the errors in these matters I shall speak next. But now I wish to complete the present discussion, namely that if one should wish to judge the material also from its association with fire, it is not fitting to judge simply or indeterminately, nor to suppose that each of the things judged stands in the same way in relation to a human being and to fire. Water, then, is most opposite to fire, being cold and moist in its power.

[413] But brine and sea-water and bituminous water and sulphurous water are no longer so; for all such waters have departed from water in the direction of the hotter. But concerning the naturally occurring waters these remarks too are sufficient; for when we make our discussion of each of the drugs whose qualities the water itself has taken on, we shall add whatever has now been said about them rather obscurely or deficiently. Let us now pass on to the remaining liquid drugs, among which the dispute has been greatest concerning vinegar, some saying that it is cold, others hot, and some granting it a certain heat while taking away another, like those who say that vinegar is wine that has died and is a corpse; for these say that it has lost the heat proper to wine but has acquired in addition a certain putrefactive heat.

And I for my part would have praised their opinion, and readily accepted it and shared the risk with them concerning both the assertion and the doctrine, if I had been able to discover some device, as in milk for the separation of the [414] opposite parts, so here too. But as things stand, that milk is not wholly homoeomerous, nor the same as itself in every respect, its splitting clearly demonstrates, many methods having been discovered by human beings for the separation of the cheesy parts from the whey-like parts. In the case of vinegar, however, nothing of this kind has been discovered, nor is it possible to demonstrate clearly that whatever of it is precisely thin and liquid cools, while that which is carried in it in the manner of the substance of lees, just as also in wines, heats; for only in this way could one clearly demonstrate that it is composed of parts opposite in their powers, as milk is. Now in all the liquids that come from fruits that are pressed out there is carried something coarse-particled, which indeed also settles down with time, called lees in the case of wines, and amurca in the case of oil.
