And analogously in all the others too there exists in them the lees, as it were, even if it has not obtained proper names. There is, then, something of this sort in vinegar too, and perhaps this is the part that partakes of heat, while the thin part is that which partakes of cooling.

And perhaps even in the thin part itself [415] there is carried along some small amount, distributed within a large quantity, which is of the other nature than the whole is. For that it is cold in a greater proportion than it is hot is, I think, evidently apparent to those who truly examine its power. And I am amazed how some have declared vinegar to be hot to such a degree as to resemble a cautery. At any rate, they say that it is in this way that it also checks haemorrhages. For, in the first place, so great a heat would not escape our perception. And secondly, in keeping with the very likeness of those hot things themselves, if it were such, it would surely in some way produce an eschar, just like the hot drugs. For in the case of these we see clearly, whenever we wish to check blood by means of them, that no small eschar is produced, so that if you do not make an eschar, you do not check the blood either. For this becomes, as it were, a kind of lid over the haemorrhaging bodies. And for this reason we also apply the cauteries to them thoroughly heated through, knowing, I think, that those which are not such, besides accomplishing nothing, actually even harm and exacerbate the haemorrhages.

For indeed it is not [416] in virtue of its own nature, nor by heating, that fire checks them; rather, having burned up whatever it falls upon, it makes the residue, as it were, of the burning into a lid for the underlying parts, which the Greeks are accustomed to call an eschar. But vinegar [checks them] in a way like none of the eschar-producing drugs, but rather as astringent things check haemorrhages without an eschar, so that in this respect, then, it would be supposed not to heat in the extreme but to cool. It is better, however, as has also been said before, to withdraw from such pieces of evidence; for he does not refer the judgment to sensation, nor does he reason from what lies adjacent, nor from close at hand, but from afar and through lengthy premises. And I shall show his absurdity more fully in the discussions that follow. We, then, in accordance with the method [laid down] from the beginning, shall make trial of its power on those who are faultlessly healthy, and then in succession on those of bad temperament, and then also on the sick.

So, having soaked a sponge or wool in vinegar, we shall apply it to whatever part of healthy bodies we like, and then, [417] as has been said before, at the very first moment we shall ask the laymen—for they will judge such matters impartially, because they are not enslaved to any doctrine—whether they perceive cooling or warmth. It is clear that we shall apply it neither extremely cold nor hot; for this too has already been said before. If, then, the vinegar being applied is of this sort, and especially if it is not very old nor extremely pungent, they will perceive a clear cooling, from the very first moment and after one hour and two and three and four; later on, however, they will also have some impression of a certain warmth already being generated little by little in the part. But if the vinegar is strongly pungent, at the beginning they will say that they are being cooled with this one too, yet they will quickly perceive the warmth that comes back upon it, and not after a long time, as in the case of the younger and not very pungent vinegar.

From these things it is clear that it is cold in every case, but already also partakes of some small warmth, which, by reason of its pungency, through some accident, in time moderately warms the [418] bodies somewhat; and yet not even this does it do always, but it is of a nature to do so in some cases. Accordingly, those oedemata that are loose and painless have no sensation of warmth either at once or later when vinegar is applied. An itching, however, arises in them, on account of which also, in those who use it to the extreme, a slight redness often runs over the surface, so that it would seem to warm slightly neither primarily nor according to its own proper order, but rather to irritate by the biting of its pungency. But since we have once passed over from healthy bodies to the affections, let us recall what it is of a nature to do in the hottest and the coldest conditions. So when someone is burned up by thapsia that has been smeared on, vinegar quenches the burning heat.

And this anyone who wishes may learn by trial, just as we too did upon ourselves, in order to obtain an exact test of the drug's power: having smeared the shins in many places, when after four or five hours they began to burn and to become inflamed, on one spot we sprinkled some vinegar, on another water, another we anointed with oil, another with rose-oil, and another with some other one of the things believed either to blunt pungencies [419] or to cool heats; and of all of them vinegar was found to be the most effective. It is clear, then, that it is not by blunting the pungencies and bitings, in the same way as oil and rose-oil—for indeed that too is naturally capable of doing these things—but by cooling. For if it is not possible for it to cure the inflammations arising from thapsia in any other way except either by cooling or by blunting the bitings and pungencies, and one of the two does not belong to it, then it must of necessity cure by the remaining one. And of all the other hot affections as well it is cooling—of some more, of others less: inflammations, herpetes, phygethla, erysipelata, carbuncles. So that, if the vehemence and roughness of its power were not distressing, we would not use anything else for cooling. And yet some set down this very thing as the greatest indication of its heat. For it would not, they say, be either pungent or biting or corrosive or roughening, if it did not possess a share of abundant heat.

For just as contracting and condensing is the property of the cold, so cutting and dividing is the property of the hot [420], and this belongs not least to vinegar. For it cuts and eats through not only the bodies of animals, but also clots and calluses and stones and pottery and bronze and iron and lead, and, almost as for fire, so too for it all things are passable and traversable, no substance withstanding it or being able to resist or hold out against the violence of its passage. For it is, indeed, also fine-particled, closely resembling fire, and of this touch too is no small testimony, but it also appears such to those who taste it, and it percolates through the finest woven fabrics more readily than water, and eats through everything, as was said a little before. And indeed what else than fire do they make vinegar out to be by their argument? Just as, to be sure, do those who assert that it dissolves clots by its cooling, from pressing and compacting and squeezing everything from every side, as if someone had taken them in his own fingers and crushed them. But these too in turn fall out into the opposite extreme to such a degree as to declare it colder even than snow.

But it is just to censure both parties for their [421] lack of measure. For neither, if it is cold, is one thereby to declare it colder than snow; nor, if it is hot, hottest. For there would not even be any dispute about its power, were it not ranked somehow near the middle and far removed from each of the extremes. For no one has disputed about the power of hemlock or mandrake, nor about cardamom and cachrys, but the former are agreed by all physicians to be cold, the latter hot. In the same way henbane and poppy-juice are cold, pepper and mustard hot. And besides these countless others, some hot in power, others cold, are agreed upon by all physicians. But that vinegar, just as rose oil too, is neither extremely cold nor extremely hot is evident from the very fact that it is a matter of doubt. And each of them must in some way be neuter.

Now since 'neutral' things are spoken of in three ways, as Herophilus too divided them — some by participating equally in both of the extremes, others by participating in neither, and others by participating now in this one, now in that — these too are surely of the nature of the neutral things, either according to one of the significations [422] or according to several of them. To me, at any rate, it seems rather to be by participating in each of the extremes, and by seeming now perceptibly to heat, and again to cool. In this way, then, both vinegar and rose oil might be called neutral. But if someone should attempt to show them neutral also on the ground that they participate in neither of the extremes, he too will perhaps be well supplied with certain persuasive arguments, yet not with demonstrative and scientific ones. This I think I know precisely, and most of all concerning vinegar. For the fact that both parties are well supplied with persuasive arguments, both those who prove it coldest and those who prove it hottest, is no small evidence that it participates in both. Yet it is difficult to establish sufficiently by argument its participation in the contraries, when we are unable to dissolve and split its substance, as we do in the case of milk and very many other things, all of which the discourse will exhibit as it proceeds. And for this reason we long to lay hold of a more evident and less hazardous starting-point.

That principle, as it seems to me, must be hunted down from the fine-particled [423] and coarse-particled nature, about which I have indeed spoken before, but it is better now too to go through it at greater length, since Plato also says that concerning principles the most discussion ought to take place. Now there is no one who has not called air fine-particled, evidently because it is easily broken up into fine parts and readily passes through the densest bodies; or, if they apply the name 'fine-particled' to it on some other ground, let them teach us clearly. For we, for our part, shall certainly not say that air is composed of fine corpuscles, as the leaders of the other sect would say. For it is continuous and one as a whole, nowhere containing any void within itself. In a body of such a nature, fineness of parts is conceived solely by the speed of its division into small parts. But if air is fine-particled for this reason, not all fire will be fine-particled. For bronze and iron and stone and wood and everything that has been turned to glowing coal is surely fire, yet it is not more fine-particled now than before.

Flames, however, [424] which are a different kind of fire, are truly fine-particled. So neither is all fire fine-particled, nor is everything fine-particled fire. For since the live coal is fire but not fine-particled, and air is fine-particled but not fire, why ever do nearly all physicians and philosophers readily take for granted all the premises, both the one that declares all fire fine-particled and the one that declares everything fine-particled fiery? For if one were to consider the matter carefully and apply one's mind to the facts, one would not say that the live coal is more fine-particled than air. For let us recall, in a severe frost and a northerly condition of the weather, the purity of the air that surrounds us, and let us compare it, if you will, with red-hot iron; for we shall recognise from such examples that there is something that is cold and precisely fine-particled, and something that is hot and coarse-particled.

So that whenever some people reason, from vinegar's being biting, that it is fine-particled and hot, [425] one must not concede the point to them. For not everything fine-particled is hot; indeed, perhaps not even everything biting is fine-particled. But for the present let it be conceded, although we could say that both snow and the north wind and cold water are biting, not only to the eyes but also to ulcers and to all rare bodies; just as Hippocrates too said, 'the cold is biting'. But even if someone, as I said, should concede this, that everything biting is also fine-particled, he will not straightaway concede that it is also hot. Vinegar, then, is not hot because it is biting, but it is fine-particled, like northerly air, yet certainly not hot. Whence, then, does a sensation of faint heat arise in some people? Perhaps, as I also said earlier, because it is composed of opposite powers, in the same way as milk; and perhaps also because it brings about a recall of heat. It could also be that what has a rough and painful passage through produces pain and draws a hot flux to the place. For this too is evident, that something flows in to parts that are in pain.

But [426] not much would flow in, because the vinegar is cold and repels what is being brought to the part. But as much of it as is exactly thin, this, escaping the grasp of the drug, slips past and becomes fixed in the part, no longer running back, as the thicker portion does. For indeed the redness that blooms on the surface of the parts irritated by vinegar appears to be exactly thin. Perhaps, however, there is also some other cause that cannot be known. For it was for this very reason that I forbade beginning the examination of the powers from too far back, namely that one must inevitably fall in with problems of natural philosophy that involve no small difficulties; and our present task is not, as if we were natural philosophers, to discover the causes of all things, but to recognise the powers of drugs, with a view both to using them skilfully and to becoming good makers of compound drugs.

For that it is not possible to compound a drug well oneself, nor to use one compounded by another, before knowing the powers of the simple drugs, is sufficiently demonstrated both in the Therapeutic Method and in the work on the [427] composition of drugs. Since, then, the present treatise has this aim, once we have first found what is useful from them, one must withdraw from physical problems, which contain numerous difficulties. For from what mixture, in general, do sourness and sweetness and bitterness, saltiness and harshness and pungency, and each of the other qualities, naturally arise? Even for the natural philosophers themselves, when they investigate, the greatest and very many difficulties come to light in the course of the arguments. These, then, I advise one to guard against like a precipice, since we have a highway by which it is possible to judge drugs: and first, as has already been said by me a little earlier, to reckon that no power of the drugs that strongly heat or cool is disputed, but that those to which this has happened belong to neither class; and next, that many of the things that are simple with respect to perception are composed of opposite powers.

For not only milk, but also the sulphurous, the bituminous, and the nitrous waters, and all such of the naturally occurring [428] waters as there are, have come about from an admixture of the opposite powers, if indeed water is cold and moist according to its own nature, whereas bitumen, sulphur, misy, chalcitis and the other things of this kind are hot. One must also bear in mind that many of the hot things are coarse-particled and many of the cold things fine-particled, and in accordance with these principles pronounce securely about the power of drugs. For, to take an immediate example, it suffices to say that vinegar is fine-particled and cooling and drying, having withdrawn from the more physical reasonings about it. For from knowing these things one will know how it ought to be mixed with the other drugs.

These, then, are the things for which I reproach those who have prated at length about its power, and still more than these I reproach very nearly all physicians, because they did not distinguish all the simple drugs according to the more and the less; it sufficed them to say that these, as it may happen, heat and those cool, and that these dry and those moisten. For this is not useful when known simply in such a manner, [429] but rather up to what degree fleawort cools, up to what degree also strychnos or scandix or white lead, purslane and lettuce, and up to what degree cassia heats, and up to what degree cinnamon, or amomum or amaracus. So too in the case of drugs that dry and moisten by their powers, one must know not only the universal, but what has first departed from the well-tempered mean between the contraries in their powers, what comes next after that, and so to distinguish a third and indeed a fourth and a fifth remove, if possible, defining them by clear boundaries. For in such a recognition of the powers there will be available to us both the use of the simples themselves with art and the ability to compound them by method, and, in addition to these, the correct use of those already compounded.

This, then, is a most difficult matter and one requiring much precision and practice; for in all such cases it is necessary to begin from experience, as has already been said, and to reason securely, guarding against [430] entangling oneself in insoluble inquiries. And at this one might well wonder at those who have investigated such things, seeing them fall by their own hands in most of the matters they investigate and write about, like Herodotus. For beginning from the whole most ancient record of compound drugs, they proceed to the examination of the simples contained in them: since vinegar, say, has been mixed into these particular heating drugs, on that basis they straightway declare that it too is hot. For neither is it clear to anyone, before he has discovered its power on its own, whether it has been mixed in correctly; nor, even if that were conceded, do we yet know the method of the composition of drugs, judging by which we shall discover on what principle a single cooling drug has been mixed with many heating drugs, or indeed a heating one with cooling ones.

But when they also make mention of non-evident conditions to which it seems to be suited, and then attach to dogmatic assumptions further fallacies, inferring things under inquiry from things under inquiry and non-evident things from non-evident things [431] by means of one another, then above all one may observe their idle talk. For as to the statement that they also furnish the Empiricists with a starting-point for counter-argument, on the ground that they readily put their trust in all the composite powers (δυνάμεσιν), as though it were not possible that many of them, at any rate, have been made in error and are badly composed—for they will say, I think, just as indeed they do say, that the primary and active powers of each of the drugs are sought by us in vain, since experience has already got hold of an innumerable multitude of simple and compound drugs, which are trusted even by those very people who vainly seek the primary powers. For if all their particular uses are known and agreed upon by everyone, whereas the causes in virtue of which each acts have not yet been agreed upon, it is clear that neither the composition nor the use of the drugs has been discovered from knowledge of the primary powers; rather it is experience that put these together, while reason advances only as far as the plausible.

These things, then, and many others of this kind, the physicians from the school of experience will seem to say [432] rightly against those who trust all drugs that have been written down in whatever manner, and who choose to fit plausible causes to the claims made for them.

And I, in addition to these points, would say this too: that Herodotus, who supposes all the other sects to be bad except the Pneumatic, and Metrodorus except that of Asclepiades, and Zeno except that of Herophilus, and Hermogenes except that of Erasistratus, and one man after another all except his own—yet concerning compound drugs alone they trust without scrutiny all the writings, whether they be those of men of the same opinion or even of just anybody, and often indeed they try to supply plausible causes for drugs most badly composed; and what is more astonishing than this, that they do so while having no experience whatever of the things they praise, but having put their trust in others—just as someone recently was going through many and great praises of a drug for podagra, and while he was still speaking there came upon the scene a podagric man who was in so moderate a condition as to be able to walk, and when we bade him furnish a trial of it on that man first, [433] he applied the drug to the foot, and the man was sleepless the whole night and on the following day was not only unable to walk as before, but was not even able to be carried about. So without scrutiny and so rashly do some trust others, while others willingly deceive others. But even if all the compositions of the drugs which they mention were in good order, still they overturn the use of the theory of them by what they do. For they say that it is for the sake of the preparation and use of compound drugs that they investigate the powers of the simples, and as witnesses of this they call upon almost all the ancients, Erasistratus, Herophilus, Philotimus, Diocles, Praxagoras and Hippocrates himself. But when they come to the examination of these, they discourse with us as if we already knew all the composite powers.

And how is it that you are not investigating the powers of the simple drugs in vain, someone, I think, might say to [434] them, if you already know those of the compound drugs? For if you already know those powers for the sake of which you instituted the inquiry into the simples, it is superfluous to investigate the latter. And even if someone were to concede this to them, yet as for what has already been said before as well, I do not know how anyone could tolerate it, when they attempt by means of lengthy arguments to establish things contrary to what manifestly appears. For I have already had experience of a man who had come to such a degree of stupefaction that he thought fit to despise the senses. Someone straightaway asked him whether white pepper seemed to him to be hot. He, as was to be expected, agreed; then, being asked again, 'From where do you know this?', and having said that it appears to be such, he was deservedly laughed at by those present, since he did not understand what he was uttering. For this very 'appearing' declared sensation to be trustworthy for him, the very sensation which a little before he had condemned as untrustworthy. For from where, by the gods, do we know that fire is hot, having learned it from what syllogism?

[435] or by what demonstration have we been assured of it? And whence did we learn that ice is cold, other than from sensation? Then someone, leaving this aside, fills his books with natural problems. Or is it not also one of those problems, for what cause vinegar makes earth ferment up? For it is open to us, I think, to say that we do not know, just as with many other problems of this kind. But if someone takes it offhand that it is because it is hot, or because it is cold—for they say both—he throws himself into disputed and obscure arguments. I for my part would be content if I could accurately discover even the things that lie adjacent to what appears through the senses, delimiting among them and distinguishing what is in itself from what is incidental: for instance, to take an immediate case, some people, having drunk oxykraton in the summer season, are clearly cooled and remain free of thirst; but it is not yet clear whether this is on account of the vinegar, for they mix a little of it with much water, and they take it not even warm, but as cold as possible.

Perhaps, then, someone might say that, because water is slower and remains for a very long time in the hypochondria, [436] neither being passed downward nor being distributed, for this reason vinegar is mixed with it, to become as it were a sort of vehicle for its transport in every direction. And in this way, even if water is drunk with wine, it is more thirst-quenching than by itself, since the wine guides it toward distribution. So the cooling and the cure of thirst come about on account of the water, which is cold and moist in nature; whereas wine and vinegar become an aid to it and, as it were, a wing for its transport to all the parts of the animal, not themselves cooling and moistening. For in that case they would rather be given alone than with water, since by reason of their fineness they are readily distributed and depart from the hypochondria. But since we have once come to this argument, it is not amiss to go through the whole of it carefully. For that it is possible both that vinegar guides the water and does not cool it, and that it does not merely guide but also cools, is plainly obvious. But which of the two is true requires examination.

This point, at any rate, would be decided if one were to give [437] to someone both wine and vinegar, each separately by itself. For upon wine the man is seen always to become thirstier, whereas upon the drinking of vinegar he is sometimes thirstier and sometimes less thirsty, because thirst itself also arises in two ways, the one through deficiency of moisture, the other through excess of heat; so that it is nothing to wonder at if it does not cure the former but does cure the latter. For it cannot moisten, but it cools in no feeble way. Therefore vinegar, when drunk, could never cure either the thirst that arises upon a dry condition or that upon a hot and dry one. But if ever moisture concurs together with heat in the same place, vinegar will be the best remedy for thirst of this kind. Such a condition is indeed rare, occurring sometimes in dropsical effusions, when a quantity of brackish fluid has gathered in the belly, and in those in whom salty phlegm has been plastered within it.

But for those who are thirsty in other ways—in burning fevers and in all the scorching ones, and in those that occur in summer and in violent heat—[438] the condition is composite, made up of heat and dryness, so that reasonably their remedy too is composite: the vinegar cooling in no feeble manner and passing through easily in every direction, and the water, besides cooling, being moreover the moistest of all things; for nothing is moister than water. Just as, therefore, the reasoning that stands far removed from sense-perception of the drug being tested is not safe, so neither is the use of it when mixed with something else. For the thing being judged must be examined itself, by itself alone, both on healthy bodies, well-tempered and ill-tempered, and on diseased ones. On well-tempered ones, then, as has also been said before; on ill-tempered ones, as Hippocrates said, vinegar is most beneficial for bitter-bilious natures, but is most contrary to those melancholic in mixture. And again, in the case of the diseased, if a simple drug should be examined on the basis of a simple condition.

But if it should ever be mixed with something else, what is mixed with it must be intermediate in its mixture, as the preceding [439] account demonstrated in the case of water and cerate. For it is reasonable, I think, that what has been combined with something that is in its mixture neither of the extremes but, as far as possible, intermediate should itself be the cause of the effects produced. At any rate, cold water, when mixed with simple cerate, which neither heats nor cools, cooled because it was cold in its mixture. But if you had mixed one of the heating substances with such a cerate, the drug would have become heating for you, just as we have often added euphorbium or castoreum for many conditions. So then, if you mix vinegar thoroughly with simple cerate, you will make the drug much colder than the cerate, inasmuch as what was mixed in is cold. And this will be a good drug for you against erysipelas and phlegmonai, herpetes and anthrakes; but if you examine the mixed thing as if it were simple—for indeed they do this too—you will go wrong in the greatest matters.

For one must not call vinegar agglutinating of wounds, but rather oxykraton, which is something very different in its nature [440] from vinegar. For just as verdigris is not flesh-forming for wounds either, but the cerate that has taken on a small portion of verdigris, in the same way neither is vinegar agglutinating, but water that has taken on a very small amount of vinegar; vinegar itself, by itself alone and bare, considerably irritates those wounds that need agglutination, inasmuch as, by its fineness of parts, it is both corrosive and painful. So neither do they speak properly in such matters, nor when they join unknowns to unknowns. For having demonstrated nothing separately about the wounds that are to be agglutinated, or filled with flesh, or cicatrized, they reason by induction, asserting that all astringent things are agglutinating of wounds. But such things must be grasped in the universal not by induction but through demonstration, as we shall do in the commentaries on the therapeutic method; but anything of this sort stated simply in this way is not only undemonstrated but also false.

For neither chalcitis, nor gall-nut, nor the very rinds of pomegranates, [441] nor omphacion, nor alum, and far less burnt copper, nor scale, nor misy is of such a nature as to agglutinate wounds, and countless other astringent things are unable to agglutinate. And if indeed someone should say not this, but that all agglutinating things are astringent, here too many things will be shown to agglutinate without being astringent. Neither statement, then, is true when stated simply and without distinction, neither when they assert that all astringent things agglutinate a wound, nor when they assert that all wounds which are agglutinated are agglutinated by means of astringent things. But far more absurd and false even than these are the things they say also concerning sensation, when they say that biting things and pungent things and bitter things and salty things, and in addition to these even the things softest and most pleasant in their qualities, are astringent, as though the astringent were not something perceptible by taste, but something taken over from their own legislation. For the pomegranate and the apple, if it so happens, and the medlar, and certain kinds of pears, and myrtle-berries and sorb-apples, and Aminaean and Marsian wine are manifestly astringent to us.

But wheat and spelt (ζειαί) and millet perhaps [442] were astringent to Herodotus, though to no other human being. For I myself have inquired of countless people both about these and, still much more, about starch (ἄμυλον), for Herodotus says that this too is astringent, just as he also says of pepper, which is itself astringent to none of the other human beings, all those who examine the qualities purely and without being bribed. But Herodotus confounded everything into one and the same thing: both the things most pungent in their powers and the things that are corrosive in the extreme, and the softest and the gentlest—he said that all of them are astringent, as though for some people victory lay in giving the lie to sense-perception. But not so: this very thing will be the greatest proof of the badness of his arguments. And as if wishing to outdo him in falsehoods against the senses, Metrodorus the Asclepiadean, among other things, does not admit that resin and asphalt heat us, and says that all astringent things also cool, even though, if nothing else, chalcitis and chalcanthum and misy are sufficiently astringent and yet arrive at such a degree of heat that they burn us.

So it is no longer in any way surprising if [443] these men talk a great deal of nonsense and lead themselves astray by false reasoning, not daring to admit the truth even about things that appear plainly. Then some of them, like Herodotus and Dioscurides, from the fact that certain drugs benefit diarrhoeas and dysenteries, infer that these are astringent, although they share in not even the slightest astringency, but on the contrary are, in their powers, more rarefying and relaxing than the astringents, which draw together, compact, condense and constrict bodies. For having once despised sense-perception, they overturned and confounded everything, seeking to establish by faulty reasoning things that can be clearly discerned by perception. At any rate goat's fat is most opposite to all astringents both in taste and in power, just as is also wheat flour, starch and countless other things among those which plaster over, soothe and blunt pungencies, and in this way help those who pass biting and pungent stools.

And if it is astringent on these grounds, then let olive oil too be counted by us among the astringents, [444] since indeed it too has often benefited those who are violently bitten, when injected. And so will wax, and pig's fat, and that of hens and of geese, and the juice of spelt-groats and of tragos. For we inject these too, and sometimes cerate, into those who are strongly bitten, just as we do goat's fat. But goat's fat displays a more evident benefit because it readily congeals, is smeared over the intestines, and remains there for a very long time. Whether it congeals quickly because of its thickness or because of some other cause, I have no need to investigate these matters now, since the fact is evidently apparent. But just as the fact that it both congeals very quickly and blunts the bitings of the intestines is more credible because it is apparent, so too is the fact that it has no share in any cooling or astringency. These men, then, reason from non-evident things about things that are apparent; or rather, if the truth must be told, they deceive themselves by false reasoning, whereas it is fitting for us to go back up to sense-perception, and to attend to it carefully throughout, all the more insofar as all the sophists tell not a few lies against it.

So then, having once more reminded [445] them that the things which are evident to laymen were evident to them too, when they did not yet, out of contentiousness, look down on the senses, but were later lost through excessive wisdom, I shall pass on to the continuation of the argument. Each nature of the sensible objects is subject to its own particular sense: heat and cold and hardness and softness to touch; whiteness and blackness and yellowness and redness, and, to speak summarily, the whole genus of colours, to sight; bitterness and sweetness, harshness and acerbity, sourness and saltiness and pungency, to taste; and a man will plainly seem to be mad if he should attempt either to judge colours by taste or flavours by sight. In the same way one must also understand concerning touch and concerning the other senses, that the tangible differences are to be judged by touch, the audible ones by hearing, and those in vapours by smell. These things being so, let us hear, if you wish, Plato too expounding the differences of tastable things. One must not, however, direct one's mind to his natural philosophy.

For it would not be timely for me now [446] to recall it, nor do I call the man as a witness for that purpose, but only for the sake of showing to what kind of thing the Greeks are accustomed to apply each of the names. Listen, then, to Plato speaking: 'For all those earthy parts which, entering in around the small vessels, which are as it were testing-instruments of the tongue, and which are stretched toward the heart, and falling into the moist and soft parts of the flesh, being melted down, contract the small vessels and dry them up—those which are rougher are called acerbic, those which roughen less, harsh. And those things which are cleansing of these and wash away everything about the tongue, when they do this beyond the measure and lay hold further, so as to melt away something of its very nature, as does the power of nitres, have all in this way been named bitter. But those which fall short of the nitrous condition and employ their cleansing to a moderate degree appear to us salty, without rough bitterness, and rather agreeable to us.'

But those which have shared in the heat of the mouth and, being smoothed by it, are kindled together with it and in turn themselves burn back that which has heated them through, and which are carried, by reason of lightness, upward toward the senses of the head, [447] and which cut everything that falls in their way because of these powers — all such things have been called pungent. But when these same things have been thinned beforehand by putrefaction, and enter into the narrow veins, and possess a commensurability with the earthy parts present there and with such as are of air, so that, setting them in motion around one another, they make them be stirred together, and being stirred they fall upon one another and, entering into others, produce other hollows, being stretched around those that enter — which, when a hollow moisture has been stretched around air, sometimes earthy, sometimes also pure, become moist vessels of air, hollow and rounded waters; and those of the pure moisture settle into transparent ones, called by the name 'bubbles', while those of the earthy moisture, being moved and raised up together, are named 'boiling' and 'fermentation': the cause of these affections has been termed acid.

But to all the things that have been said about these matters there is a contrary affection, arising from a contrary cause, whenever the composition of the things that enter, in moist bodies, being by nature akin to the condition of the tongue, smooths by anointing the parts that have been roughened, and, as for the parts that have been contracted or dissolved contrary to nature, [448] draws together the former and relaxes the latter, and settles everything as far as possible according to nature: everything of this sort, which becomes a pleasant and welcome remedy for everyone against the violent affections, has been called sweet. Throughout this whole passage Plato explained which things it is customary to call harsh, which acerbic, which salty and nitrous, which bitter, which pungent, which sour, and which sweet; evidently calling what we call astringent 'harsh', for so it was named among the ancient Greeks. Yet he does not confound everything into one and the same thing, as these people do, who assert that even pepper is astringent, though it belongs to the nature of the pungent things, and vinegar, which belongs to that of the sour things, and who are not ashamed even to assign some of the sweetest things to the astringents. Since, then, everything has been confounded by them, right from the very beginning not even powers can be discovered. For the starting-points of every discovery and demonstration are the things evident to sense-perception and to thought.

But these people throw both of these into confusion and confound everything together into one, both the activities and affections of the senses and, much more still, those of the intellect, [449] inasmuch as these have not been exercised in logical theory; so that it is a task to guard oneself against their idle talk and not to partake in some measure of their so abundant and vain prattle; and it is no small task either to re-educate and convert those who have been perverted by them to such a degree as to despise the senses, to be unexercised in logical theory, and to be uninstructed also in the reasonings about nature which the philosophers examine. For in any case they would surely have recognised at least this much, that one must fear and guard against the difficulties contained in these, and entrust oneself to the senses rather than to spurious arguments concerning the power of simple drugs. But such people it is not possible to re-educate; for the sake of the others, however, those who are able to be benefited, the account of the sense-objects proper to the tongue must be taken up again and distinguished precisely.

Now, by Theophrastus, Aristotle and Mnesitheus the physician and their followers, the gustatory power is named chymos, with the second syllable [450] beginning from the letter mu; whereas the composition out of moist and dry, concocted by heat, is named chylos, with the second syllable beginning from lambda. Among those older than they, however, not only the Attic writers but the Ionians too, both are written with the mu. For indeed in Plato the philosopher, in Hippocrates and in the ancient comic poets it is found so written. But in the present discourse let it be stated by us, for the sake of clear teaching, that the gustatory power, or quality, or whatever one may wish to call it, is chymos, with the letter mu, while the thickened moisture in animals and plants is chylos, with the second syllable beginning from lambda. One must know, then, that the chymoi found in each plant and animal, and indeed also those found in the earth, are very many and not easy to number in their kinds; but the gustatory differences among them have seemed to some to be eight in number, to others seven, and to others fewer still than these.

Plato, then, in the Timaeus, in the passage written out above, first mentions two flavours which are of the same kind but differ in respect of the more and the less [451]. He names one of them harsh, the other acerbic. The harsh would be the one which is called astringent by us, while the acerbic comes to be by an intensification of this, as indeed Plato himself has shown. These, then, are to be counted as one kind; another is that of those opposed to them, the nitrous, the salty and the bitter. And among these too the bitter is what comes about from an intensification of the nitrous, while the salty is either weaker than the nitrous, or else takes on something of astringency as well. Next, the pungent is spoken of by Plato, and after it the acid, and last the sweet. By Theophrastus the oily is also added, having been omitted by Plato in his account of the objects of sense proper to the tongue, but written just before in his account of the juices of plants, where he distinguished the wine-like from the oil-like and the honey-like. But in that account, in addition to the three which I have just mentioned, he posited a fourth genus of juice, embracing it under a single name and calling it sap. But in the passage where he passed over to the things perceptible by taste, he mentioned the sweet immediately among them.

For it surely makes no difference whether one says "sweet" or [452] "honey-like," just as it makes none whether one says "oily" or "oil-like." But he has left out the oily, as having nothing to do with taste. To explain it precisely is not possible, since neither is any other of the perceptible affections; yet it is possible to remind someone who has shared in the same sensation. For if anyone has ever tasted quinces, or apples, or myrtle-berries, or medlars, he knows clearly that the sensation arising in us on the tongue from these is one thing, and that from astringent bodies another. For astringent or cooling things appear to press inward the part of us that touches them, evenly from every side, as it were pushing and compacting and drawing it together; whereas harsh things seem to penetrate into the depth and to bring on a certain rough and uneven sensation, as if drying up and consuming all the moisture of the sentient bodies, so that the specific character of the affections produced by the bodies that act astringently upon us and by the harsh flavours is different in each case, and cannot even be stated clearly in words.

But any man who has sense knows [453] what I mean. And when the body that comes into contact with the tongue strongly dries and contracts and roughens it to a greater depth, as unripe wild pears and cornel-berries do, everything of this kind is named acerbic (στυφνόν, so Kühn, presumably for στρυφνόν), differing from the harsh things by intensity. But what we call astringent is not at all readily to be found stated by Theophrastus and his followers. It seems, in fact, to signify something the same as the harsh, or to be some genus common to this and to the acerbic. And all those things which, in touching the tongue, do not contract it nor constrict it, as the astringent things do, but appear to do entirely the opposite, cleansing and washing away, even if something astringent should lie alongside them—all these we call salty. Those that cleanse even more than these, to the point of actually roughening painfully, are called bitter. Those that bite and eat through together with strong heat, pungent. And those that bite without it are called sour, and there belongs to them also the property of causing fermentation.

But those things which, as it were, smear over and fill up and settle the roughened and, as it were, eroded parts of the [454] tongue, these, when they touch it with manifest pleasure, are called sweet, and without this pleasure, oily. I, then, have attempted to go through in discourse, as far as was at all possible for me, matters that are hard to explain. But I marvel at those who readily call everything astringent, both the pungent and the bitter and the sweet and the oily and the sour. For indeed different names have been laid down for the things from of old, and of the perceptible affections too the difference, for us, is no small one. It would perhaps have been better, if they wished to do natural philosophy, not to overturn the phenomena and confound the appellations, but to inquire of what mixture or disposition or constitution of body, or however they may wish to name it, astringency comes to be the offspring, and of what saltiness and bitterness and sourness and pungency and sweetness and oiliness, the very things which Plato and Aristotle and Theophrastus and their followers attempted to define.

For it is clear that, if all things have been mixed from hot and cold and dry and moist coming together, then each of the qualities mentioned too is from the mixture [455] of these. If, then, they were to attempt to explain how each of the flavours mentioned comes to be, I would gladly listen and would feel no small gratitude towards them. But if they do not even do this, and moreover confound all the perceptible differences into one and the same thing, so as to run the risk of calling all bodies astringent, I would neither wish to listen to them, and I would pray that they cease from vain contentiousness. But we shall attempt, in what follows, to show of what mixture each of the flavours is the offspring. For the present I wish only to accustom learners, as they proceed to trial, to select beforehand just that which is useful for the art, whenever they wish to judge how each of the drugs disposes us. For we are certainly not investigating what sort of thing it is in itself and in relation to the whole of nature. For it is clear that in that way neither vinegar nor sea-water would be said to dry us, or to be dry in its power.

For each of them is in actuality moist; but if it appears to dry us [456], it will be called dry in relation to us, evidently, and to our nature, which is the same as saying "drying". And indeed hot and cold and moist, in the same manner, whenever they heat and cool and moisten us, will be so called in relation to us, not in relation to the whole substance, nor in themselves. And indeed, if we keep only this in mind, experience alone will be the most secure criterion of all things, so that those who abandon it and attempt their arguments from some other starting-point not only speak falsely, but also overturn what is useful in the inquiry. For it is not set before us to investigate what sort of thing each of the drugs is according to its own nature, but what sort of thing it is naturally disposed to do to us. So let my first book end here. In the next one, the second, taking up olive oil and rose oil as an example for the argument, I shall show there too the faulty paths of the arguments by the use of which the majority of physicians mislead first themselves, and then, together with themselves, many others as well.

And when this has been completed, passing on to the third of these treatises, I shall try to go through all the logical questions that precede the whole exposition concerning simple drugs, so that in the fourth I may now define the powers themselves of all of them—which I would have taken up straightaway from the beginning, had not nearly all the books of the more recent physicians been full of fallacies. These, then, must first be cleaned out and cleared away from the soul of the learner, so that they may in no way stand in the way of what is true. For as Hippocrates says, so Plato too used to say: not only, in the case of bodies that are not clean, the more you nourish them the more you will harm them, but also with unclean souls, if you offer them nourishing arguments, not only would you do no good at all, but you will even do no small harm.

For these very reasons, then, and because many of my companions wished that the fallacies of the more recent physicians be refuted, not only in the gatherings which we hold on each occasion when spending time together with them, but also through these commentaries, I was compelled to linger at greater length over the first two books, so that in the third, having by then a hearer pure in soul and able to follow true arguments, I may go through all that one must know about the principles of the [458] inquiry set before us, and after that go through all the powers of each of the drugs. This will be accomplished, I think, in eleven books in all, each of roughly the same size as this one, which is the first of them all. Since it now has its due measure, I set this sentence upon it as its conclusion.

[459] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 2. The sophists who overstep their proper bounds make our account of the power of simple drugs a long one. For beginning from far off, and holding sense-perception in dishonour, and throwing themselves into matters that are in doubt even among the philosophers, they lose, along with the things they do not know, even those that are clearly known.

[11.1.1] [1. On the flesh of the viper.] Not all the fleshes of animals nourish a human being; those of some are even deadly, no less than the drug-like substances which they call deleterious; and of the fleshes that do nourish us some are this alone, nutriments, while some, in addition to nourishing, also possess the power proper to a drug, since by drying or moistening and heating or cooling they alter the body. At any rate, one can clearly see that those of vipers heat and dry when they are dressed, like eels, with oil and salt and dill and leek and, obviously, water in due measure. That they purge the whole body through the skin you may learn also from what I myself experienced while still a young man in our Asia, each instance of which I shall now go through in order. A man sick with the affection called elephas for a while shared the life of his familiars; but when, from association and intercourse with him, some came to share in the affection, and he himself was by now foul-smelling and hideous to look upon, they built a hut for him near the village on a low part of the hill beside a spring and settled the man in it, bringing him food for as many days as sufficed for him to live on. About the rising of the Dog-star a wine, very fragrant, in an earthenware jar was brought to reapers who were reaping near him. The one who brought it set it down near the reapers and went away; and when the time for drinking came for them, their custom was to pour out a krater and mix the wine with water in due measure, but when a young man had taken up the jar and was pouring the wine out into the krater, a dead viper fell out along with it. So the reapers, fearing lest they suffer some harm from the drink, themselves drank water, and as they were departing they bestowed, out of humanity forsooth, the whole of the wine upon the man sick with elephas, judging it better for him to die than to live in such a state. But he, drinking from it, became healthy in a marvellous manner. For the whole mound-like roughness of his skin fell away, like the covering of the soft-shelled animals; and what remained appeared quite soft, like that of crayfish and crabs when the surrounding shell has fallen off. Another such case came about from a similar chance event in Mysia in Asia, not far from our city. A man suffering with elephas set out to make use of naturally hot waters in hope of benefit. He had a concubine, a slave, young and beautiful, who had many lovers; to her the sick man entrusted certain other matters of the household and indeed also the affairs of the storeroom. When they had lodged, while he was using the waters, in a house that had adjoining to it a parched plot full of vipers, one of these fell into a wine-jar lying carelessly about and died in it; the concubine, considering what had chanced to happen a godsend, offered her master his drink from this jar. And he, drinking it, was healed in the same way as the man in the hut. These, then, are now two lessons for you of experience by chance; and a third in addition to them from our own imitation. For when a certain man sick with this disease, more philosophical than the common run, was terribly distressed and kept saying that it was better to die than to live, to him in so wretched a condition I disclosed the two aforementioned chance occurrences. And he—for he was himself experienced in augury and had the use of a friend who excelled marvellously in that study—sat watching the birds together with him and was prompted to imitate what had been learned through experience, and by drinking wine drugged in this way he became leprous. Some time later we cured his lepra too with the customary drugs. A fourth after this man, who had made it his craft to catch live vipers, was in the beginning of that affection, and it was our concern that he be healed as quickly as possible. So having cut a vein of his and purged him with a drug that evacuates black [bile], we advised him to use the vipers he caught, preparing them in a dish, just like eels. This man, then, was treated in this way, the affection dispersing from him by transpiration. Another man, a wealthy one—this man not a countryman of ours, but he came from the middle of Thrace, a dream having urged him to Pergamon—then, the god having ordered him in a dream both to drink of the drug made from vipers every day and to anoint his body externally with it, the affection changed after not many days into lepra, and this disease too was in turn cured by the drugs the god commanded. So the flesh of vipers reaches this degree of drying power; but since some of those who ate it were seized by a most violent thirst, on this account they also call the vipers dipsades. There are those who say, too, that those bitten by them are not filled when they drink, but burst before they cease to be thirsty. For this reason I inquired of those who hunt vipers in Rome, whom they call Marsi, whether they had any sign to teach me distinguishing each of the two kinds of vipers; but they said there was no kind at all of dipsad vipers, but that those living by the sea and in places having much saline soil have salty flesh, and that for this reason many such arise in Libya, while in Italy there are none because of the moistness of the country. These things, then, I heard the Marsi say, yet I cannot state with certainty whether they tell the truth in the whole or also lie in some respect. For that in the places they mentioned some vipers arise having salty flesh seems to me most plausible, since I know that the fleshes of animals change along with their foods; yet I cannot declare that there is no kind of dipsad vipers. The safest course, therefore, is to guard against hunting the vipers in such places for eating or for the preparation of a drug, such as is this famous one which almost all physicians call theriac. And since it is our custom, when we prepare the so-called theriac troches, to remove not only their head but also the tail, I have often reflected that the whole head is perhaps removed reasonably, on account of the venom contained in the mouth, but the tail unreasonably. For one cannot even say this, that it must be done so on account of the residues of the food, both the moist and the dry. For having killed them, and then skinned and opened them up, we take out and throw away all the inner parts, so that only the substance of the flesh is left along with the arteries and veins that grow through it, which have a very small bulk in relation to the whole flesh and are not even visible unless one examines very carefully. The troches, then, which they indeed also call theriac, we prepare as follows. Taking them cleaned, we then boil them in water until they seem to us thoroughly boiled. We throw in dill along with them into the water right from the start, and after the boiling we separate the spines from the flesh, then mix the flesh with bread ground fine. This bread we take not any chance one, but as far as possible the purest and well baked in a klibanos, having salt and leaven in due measure. We dry it beforehand in a dry room free of damp, until it becomes so dry as to be able to be pounded in a mortar. Yet we do not mix it by pounding, but by soaking it in the water in which we boiled the vipers. The flesh itself, before mixing it with the bread, we grind in a cooks' mortar until it becomes thoroughly smooth. And after this, having moulded small thin troches and then dried them in a warm and dry room, we keep them, putting them away again in such a room. These, then, we prepare at the onset of summer, when the flesh of vipers is at its very best. We use them later, pounding and sifting them, then grinding them smooth again and mixing them with the salts prepared for pleasure, and we also put some of them into the theriac. The salts made from roasted vipers are also made at the same season, we throwing the live vipers into a new pot together with the drugs strewn beneath and placed around them, all of which it is not the business of the present treatise to tell now. For perhaps someone will reasonably reproach us also regarding the preparation of the troches, as having gone through it out of season. But since these things have already been said, let them be kept, even if they seem not very properly to belong to the treatise before us. Let what follows be said in the fitting measure. It is fitting to recall the general power of the flesh of vipers, saying that it is strongly drying and dispersing, together with heating moderately. Its power hastens, as it seems, to the skin, moving through it the residues in the body. So a not small multitude of lice is generated in those who have abundant kakochymia in their bodies, and what is called the epidermis separates from the skin and falls away like a scale, in which the thick and earthy of the humours carried to the skin are retained more, by which psorai and leprai and elephantes come about. These things, then, I had to say to you about the fleshes of the viper; next I shall take up the argument again. The fleshes of animals hotter by nature not only nourish us but also heat, those of colder ones cool. In the same way those of drier ones dry, and those of moister ones moisten. Remembering, then, what you learned in the books On Mixtures, when you recognise some animal to be drier in mixture, as for instance the wild boar than the domestic pig, know that its flesh too is more drying, and likewise for the other differences of mixtures, for example that the sheep is drier than the pig, the goat than this, the ox than this, and the lion than this. So too in heat the lion is hotter than the dog, the dog than the bull, the bull than the ox whose testicles have been cut out. In proportion, then, to the superiority in mixture of the other animals their fleshes too will differ. And on this account, wishing to dry the body you will give the flesh of animals drier in mixture, wishing to heat it, that of hotter ones, attempting to make it colder, that of colder ones, and moister, that of moister ones. Not small, too, is the difference of fleshes in some of them having been salted. For they differ altogether, so that often the salted flesh of an animal moistest in mixture is by far more drying than the unsalted flesh of one dry by nature. And roasted flesh is drier than that boiled in water. Some have also written that the fleshes of other animals help both when eaten and when applied on affected parts, for example that of the land hedgehog dried, if drunk, for sufferers from elephantiasis and cachectics and those subject to spasm and nephritics, and further those who have the dropsy called anasarca. If it is by nature able to do these things, its power would be strongly dispersing and drying, like also that of the dried weasel, which indeed benefits epileptics when drunk. The flesh of salted cats, ground smooth and applied, they say draws out splinters, as evidently having a drawing power, and that of mussels suits wounds that have come about from a biting dog. But I find no special power that such wounds require, as do those arising from the bite of a rabid dog. And the flesh of snails, first pounded in a mortar and afterwards ground smooth, becomes most drying of all parts that have excessive moisture, so that it suits even the dropsical. The moisture from them, taken alone by itself without the flesh, is called by most people snail's slime, and mixed with frankincense or aloe or myrrh or some of these or all, until it has the thickness of a cerate, it becomes a glue-holding drug and dries well the suppurating slimy discharges (ὑποπύους μύξους) of the ears. It is also a drying anakollema for fluxes into the eyes, applied on the forehead. Some use it also for splinters, grinding them whole together with their shells, and there are some who use it also for the checking of the menses. The fleshes alone by themselves I too once in the country applied, having ground them smooth, upon a wound that had come about together with a wounding and crushing of a sinew, and the wound was well glued together and the sinew did not become inflamed. He was a hard and rustic man; I did however mix with them, as they were being ground, flour-dust taken from the wall adjoining the mill. Some of the physicians before us have written that myrrh or frankincense must be mixed with them for such use, but I had neither of these outside the city on the farm. One could also mix in smooth roasted (φρικτῆς) resin, if it were at hand. When, however, you wish to take much of the slime of the snails alone, prick their flesh with a stylus. They must not have been caught many days before, for they dry up with time. When fresh they have much of the viscous moisture, which they emit when pricked with the stylus. This moisture also becomes an anakollema for the hairs in the eyelids that are contrary to nature.

[11.1.2] [2. On soft fat and hard fat.] Soft fat and hard fat. These too are among the most common of the parts in animals. For all well-nourished animals have soft fat or hard fat, whereas the lean and ill-nourished often appear to have none at all, and often so little and so dry that it is difficult to use. Hard fat differs from soft fat in thickness; and hence hard fat arises in animals whose whole nature is more earthy, just as soft fat arises in those whose nature is moister. For this reason, accordingly, soft fat melts easily under fire but, once melted, does not easily congeal; hard fat, on the other hand, neither melts easily, and if it is melted it congeals very quickly and appears much harder than soft fat. A well-nourished pig, then, has the most soft fat, owing to the natural moistness of its mixture, whereas cattle and goats and all the other horned animals, owing to their dryness, produce the most hard fat. But you, if you wish, may call the whole oily and fatty substance in animals hard fat, as most physicians do; and you are also permitted to name this whole genus soft fat. What you are not permitted to do, if you wish not to speak falsely, is to say that the fat of goats is moister than that of pigs. For this latter is nearly the moistest of all the others, and for this reason it is in its activity close to oil in power, though it is more softening than oil and more concocting. And for this reason it is mixed into the poultices suited to inflammations. But for those who suffer biting in the region of the rectum or the colon we inject goat's rather than pig's fat, not because it is more blunting of acridity (for so far as nature is concerned pig's fat blunts more, and for this reason it is mixed also into the drugs that treat ulcers, such as the one called parhygron), but because goat's fat congeals easily on account of its thickness, whereas pig's fat flows away like oil; for this reason we inject the former rather in cases of dysentery and tenesmus, when we wish to soothe their biting. And some, through fineness of particles, blunt acridities more, when the painful agent is in the depth of the bodies that are being bitten. For the coarse-particled passes through whole bodies less, the fine-particled more, and it is mingled with all the biting ichors. In this respect, accordingly, goose fat too blunts more what bites in the depth of bodies. It is also hotter than pig's fat. Between them, indeed, is that of cocks; and that of male animals is always hotter and drier. And among these themselves, that of those whose testicles have been excised is less hot and dry; for the castrated male is always assimilated to the females of the same kind. The common head of the argument, which must be kept in mind, is this: that the differences of the soft fat or hard fat in animals, or however you wish to name this whole genus of the oily and fatty part of the body in animals, always arise according to the mixture of the animals. Since, then, the pig falls short in heat and dryness of nearly all four-footed animals, for this reason it also has soft fat that is less hot and more moist. Now the power of all soft fat is moistening and heating of human bodies; for this must be kept in mind throughout, having been stated at the beginning of this treatise; but the differences among each of them are according to more and less. For the soft fat of the pig, relative to us, possesses moistening abundantly, but heating not in the same way as oil does; rather, the fat of pigs too is at the level of the heat in us. That of bulls is much hotter and drier than that of pigs, we remembering again here too that the male is always drier and hotter than the female, and that the castrated male is assimilated to the female, as indeed is everything young; and that among the young themselves the female is moister and less hot than the male. Thus, then, calf's fat also falls short of that of bulls in heat and dryness, and that of kids of that of goats; and that of she-goats falls short of that of he-goats, and among these again that of bulls of that of lions; for the latter is the most dispersing of nearly all the fats in four-footed animals. For it is also the hottest of them and the most fine-particled, so that if you were to mix it into the drugs suited to ulcers and inflammations, not only will you do no good but you will also do harm, having made the drug more pungent than is fitting. But for chronic hardened swellings and contractures of sinews and, in general, all scirrhous conditions it is most serviceable, cases in which pig's fat appears most ineffective. That of bulls stands roughly equally distant from each: by as much as it is hotter and drier than that of pigs, by so much it falls short of that of lions. Since, then, it is set in the middle, it is reasonably mixed into both kinds of drugs, both those that treat scirrhous conditions and those that concoct inflamed parts, such as the so-called tetrapharmakon, composed of wax and resin and pitch and fat. For into this, whether you put bull's or calf's or he-goat's or she-goat's or pig's fat, you will make a drug that brings to suppuration and concocts. But pig's fat, when put in, is suitable for children and women and, in a word, the soft-fleshed, while that of the bull is useful for diggers and reapers and all who have hard flesh either through natural mixture or through the kind of life they lead. All fat, as it ages, becomes hotter than it was and more fine-particled, and so also more dispersing. This holds for nearly all things that age, those at least that do not first putrefy. For wine and honey and vinegar and cheese and butter and oisypos and every oil, whether mastic oil or castor oil or radish-seed oil or the oil from olives itself, when aged become thinner and more fine-particled, and for this reason appear more pungent to those who taste them and more dispersing to those who use them, in all conditions that are hardening and difficult to dissolve. Now I have said that it appears more pungent to those who taste it. But some of those who corrupt the meanings of words call all such things not pungent but astringent, as far as pepper, as though it made no difference to say astringent or pungent. And if you were to ask them again about oak-galls and myrtle-berries and medlars and pomegranate rind, and omphakion and sumac, they say that these too are astringent, although we have in their case a sensation most opposite to that which arises in us from pepper and pyrethron and mustard, and euphorbion and onion and garlic and adarke. If, then, just as they apply the name of astringency in common to both of the affections that arise in us in tasting, so they also think that the affections themselves have a single nature, then one must suppose them to be something other than human beings, alone possessing senses of their own. But if they agree that the unripe grape and sumac and oak-gall and balaustion and hypokistis draw together and constrict our substance, whereas pepper and mustard and pyrethron separate and bite and pass through, then they name improperly as astringent the things that bite and heat, yet in the knowledge of the drugs themselves they have not gone wrong. And if one must say by conjecture whether they go wrong in names or in things, I for my part would say that the men have gone wrong rather in names, and especially those unaccustomed to the Greek language, such as Dioscorides of Anazarbus, who has said many things well among the matters recorded concerning medical material, but is ignorant of the meanings of Greek words. This man, then, when he says that the fat of goats is more astringent than that of pigs: if by more astringent he wishes to indicate more pungent, we shall accept the statement as true; but if he means that which has such a quality and power as sumac and rhubarb and hypokistis and balaustion, we shall say that the statement is not true. And since they say that the fat of vipers, too, when someone has plucked out from the roots the hairs in the armpits and smears it on, prevents these too from growing, it seemed to me better to test this as well, and having done as they bade I found them to be lying, just as also in their claim that it cures the beginnings of cataracts. That bear's fat is suited to alopecia they wrote truly, but we have drugs more approved than it for the condition. But when they say that fox's fat cures ear-aches, without distinguishing which ear-aches they mean, since they do not even know in an articulated way what they are saying, one must not pay attention at all. Others praise the fat of fishes, as for cataracts or whatever condition they wish to name. Others write not simply of fishes but of river fish, others rather of sea fish, so that they may seem to know something more than the many.

[11.1.3] [3. On marrow.] Marrow is of a softening power for bodies that are becoming hardened and scirrhous, whether it be muscles, tendons or ligaments that suffer this, or even viscera. I have always found that of deer the best, and next after it that of young cattle, which indeed they also call calves (moschoi), and for this reason they also name their marrow 'calf-marrow' (moscheion). That of he-goats and of bulls is more pungent than these and more drying, so that it cannot dissolve scirrhous hardnesses, if we remember at all what was said about these matters in the fifth book. From calf and deer marrow, then, softening pessaries are compounded for the affections of the womb, and medicines prepared with marrow, having a softening power, are applied externally over the womb itself. And not only the marrow from the bones is taken, which indeed is truly marrow, but also that from the spine, which they also call spinal marrow, being harder and drier (αὐχμηρότερον) than the other. For the latter is softer and oilier, and for this reason I store the marrow from the spine separately, by itself, without the other. I take care that neither of the two marrows should either rot or acquire mould. So I first take them in winter, just as the fat too, and then, drying them in a room that is upstairs and free of moisture, I store them away with dry bay leaves. For moist and fresh leaves impart much of their own quality, so that the marrows become more pungent. But if ever, when the surrounding air is hot and humid, you should wish to store away marrows or fat, let a room be prepared for you that is neither hot—such as those facing south especially are, for in such rooms they rot—nor underground and damp, for in such rooms they grow mouldy, but one that is upstairs and facing north, with small windows thrown open so as to receive the northerly winds by day and by night.

[11.1.4] [4. On the heads of maenides.] A certain man used the heads of salted maenides, by burning them, for fissures in the seat (anus); and this same man used them also for a uvula that had become chronically hardened (scirrhous). Their power, then, seems to be a drying one, not very pungent. For this latter property belongs to some of the burnt substances, whereas drying at least is common to them all.

[11.1.5] [5. On the head of hares.] Another, burning a whole head of a hare, used it for alopecia together with bear's fat. [11.1.6] [6. On the head of lizards.] Some people write that the head of the lizard, ground fine, draws out splinters and myrmeciae and acrochordons and callus-warts.

[11.1.7] [7. On the brain of a hare.] We have learned that the brain of a hare, both rubbed on and eaten, is beneficial in the case of children who are teething, the whole head having, of course, been boiled, as I am accustomed to do; its power, however, is not at all exceptional, but similar to honey and butter and the other things which are suitable for the teeth of growing children. Some have also written that this brain, when eaten, helps against fears.

[11.1.8] [8. On the horns of deer and goats.] Horns of deer and of goat are used above all when burnt, just as we too have often used them both for whitening the teeth and for firming up flabby gums. Some of those who have written on such matters particularly commend that of the deer, claiming that, if after being burnt it is washed, it also thoroughly cures dysentery and spitting of blood, and further the so-called coeliac conditions, and that given to those suffering from jaundice it is beneficial; and in all these cases they prescribe giving two spoonfuls. Some have also mixed it, as has been said, burnt and washed, into the drying collyria for the fluxes in the eyes. For evidently the power of all such things is drying, as has also been said.
[11.1.9] [9. On the lung of lamb, of pig, and of fox.] The lung of lamb and of pig is believed to cure the chafings caused by shoes. That of the fox, if dried and drunk, benefits asthmatics.

[11.1.10] [10. On the liver of a rabid dog.] As for the liver, some have written that the liver of a rabid dog, if roasted and eaten, becomes a remedy for those bitten by it; and I know some of those who took it who are alive, but not by that alone, for they used in succession the other drugs as well, of which we have experience in the case of those bitten by rabid dogs. I have heard, however, of some who trusted in it alone and later died.

[11.1.11] [11. On the liver of a goat and of a he-goat.] Some roast the liver of a goat and then, taking the ichor that flows out of it, use it for nyctalopes; and they also direct that its vapour, while it is being boiled, be received with the eyes open. And moreover they say that, eaten roasted, it is suitable for these same affections, and that it exposes epileptics, if it is eaten. And they say that the liver of a he-goat has the same power.

[11.1.12] [12. On the liver of the lizard.] Some have written that the liver of a lizard, inserted into decayed teeth, produces freedom from pain. [11.1.13] [13. On the stomach of the shearwater.] Some commend the stomach of the shearwater as a concocting drug, if one either takes it straightaway boiled or administers it dried. But when we put it to the test we found the promise empty, just as also that of the inner coat of hens, which too some people say, when they have dried it, benefits those with stomach complaints if it is drunk.

[11.1.14] [14. On the liver of a wolf.] As for the liver of the wolf, I have often thrown it into the hepatic drug made with eupatorium, yet I have not found by experience any noteworthy preeminence in it, when comparing it with the preparation made without it.

[11.1.15] [15. On castoreum.] They call the testicles of the beaver castoreum. It is a renowned and much-used drug, so much so that a whole book was written by Archigenes on the use of castoreum. He, then, went through its particular powers; but I, just as with the other drugs, so also with this one shall state its general power, by looking to which one will be able to discover the particular ones for oneself. That it heats is evident. For if you should wish, having worked it perfectly smooth and moistened it with oil, to anoint and rub some part with it, you will clearly perceive that part being heated. Now all heating things, dispersing something of the adjacent substance, immediately also dry it, unless the thing be moist by nature, like oil and water, and take on an acquired hot quality, not a power, just as these very things do when brought near fire and the summer sun. Accordingly castoreum, its consistency being dry and having in addition the heating [property], reasonably dries. This, then, is common to it and to very many other drugs; but it is sufficiently fine-particled, and in this respect it is more powerful than others which heat and dry similarly to it. For fine-particled drugs are more active than coarse-particled ones, even if they have equal power, from their passing through and going into the depth of the bodies with which they come into contact, and especially when these are dense, like the sinewy parts. Clearly, at any rate, such parts are greatly benefited by castoreum for the reason stated. But most physicians are ignorant, in the use of castoreum attending in their minds only to the fact that some part trembles or is convulsed, or is without sensation or without motion, or has impaired sensation or impaired motion, not knowing that such symptoms follow upon dissimilar conditions of the body.
