But you, having learned from Hippocrates that spasm occurs upon repletion and upon evacuation, where it is necessary to evacuate what is contained contrary to nature in the nerves, both give castoreum to drink and apply it externally upon the skin; but where spasm occurs through excessive dryness, know that this drug is most contrary. By the same reasoning it is also most beneficial to those who tremble because of plethora, but most contrary to those who fall into such an affection through evacuation. Analogously to the affections mentioned I have found also the condition of the hiccuping that arises in the stomach, having made the distinction: if the patients suffer this from plethora, come to the use of castoreum; but if it should arise through dryness and evacuation or through the biting of pungent humours, avoid the drug. One might indeed suspect, attending to its smell and taste, that it has a substance most alien to the human body. In use, however, it appears to do none of the things which such substances do, some harming the stomach, some the belly, some the head, some something else. But this drug, whether you administer it to a moist body needing dryness, or to a cold one [needing] heat, or to a moist and cold one requiring heat and dryness, displays great benefit and inflicts no harm upon any part, and especially when the person is without fever, and, among those with fever, when the fever is not very hot but what one might call a lukewarm fever, such as arises especially in comatose states (kataphorai) and lethargies. To very many we have given castoreum, giving to drink together with white pepper a spoonful of each in honey-water (melikraton), and no one was harmed in any way; rather, when the menses were retained, having first evacuated moderately from the ankle, then giving castoreum with pennyroyal (glechon) or kalaminthe (calamint), I have always found the drug moving a purgation, without the woman being harmed in anything. It also expels retained afterbirths (choria). All these things, then, it does when drunk in honey-water (melikraton). Those whose belly is intractably filled with wind, or who suffer colic or hiccup, in consequence of cold and viscous humours or of thick and flatulent pneuma, it helps when drunk in oxykraton (vinegar-and-water); and whatever it benefits when taken inside the body, these it benefits also when applied upon the skin together with Sicyonian oil or old oil. For the conditions needing more heat it is appropriate also to rub [the part] with it by itself. It helps too if someone, burning it on coals as a fumigation, draws it in through inhalation, and especially the moist and cold affections of the lung and the brain. The lethargic and comatose affections, however, all those with fevers, it is better to treat not by moistening it with any of the oils mentioned, but rather to apply it in rose oil to the head and the neck.

[11.1.16] [16. On the kidneys of skinks.] The parts around the kidneys of skinks are drunk as being productive of tension in the genital member, and what seems to act antagonistically to them is above all lettuce seed drunk with water. Some people also say that a decoction of lentils drunk with honey stops the tensions.

[11.1.17] [17. On the hooves of goats and asses.] Some people burn the hooves of goats, then, moistening the ash with vinegar, smear it on cases of alopecia, so that such ash too would be of a thinning power. Some say that the hooves of asses, when burnt, cure epileptics if they are drunk continuously, and that, kneaded with oil, they disperse scrofulous swellings; and that the same ash, sprinkled on dry, heals chilblains.

[11.1.18] [18. On burnt bones.] Burnt bones are of a sufficiently dispersing and drying power, and some people say that those of human beings are most of all capable of this. The astragalos of a pig, at any rate, when burnt and then drunk, they said cures flatulent distensions and colics. And I have known some of the men of our own time who, giving burnt human bones to drink, without those drinking knowing what they were drinking, so that they should not feel disgust, completely cured many of epilepsy and arthritis.

[11.1.19] [19. On the slough of a snake.] Some have written that the slough of a snake, boiled up in vinegar, cures toothaches. [11.1.20] [20. On the skin of a sheep.] The skin of a sheep freshly flayed, wrapped around those who have been scourged in whatever manner, manifestly helps more than anything else, so as to cure them in a single day and night; for it both concocts and disperses the blood that has gathered under the skin.

[11.1.21] [21. On the lichens of horses.] Some have written that the lichens of horses, ground fine with vinegar, cure epilepsies, and some people also advise using them against the bite of any wild beast. [11.1.22] [22. On spider's web.] Some write that spider's web keeps superficial wounds free from inflammation.

[11.1.23] [23. On old hides.] Old hides from shoe-soles, when burnt, they have written to be suitable for the pressure-sores caused by shoes, as though, forsooth, they did this by some antipathy. Now while these are inflamed they are not helped, but once the inflammation has ceased they are reasonably helped by being dried; for such ash is drying. And we ourselves once used it in the country for such an ulcer arising from chafing. And such ash reasonably treats also the burns among ulcers and the so-called chafings that occur on the thighs.

[11.1.24] [24. On ostreia (shellfish).] Some people call 'ostreia' all the testaceous animals (ostrakoderma), as they were named by Aristotle. But what is called by most people 'ostreon', pronounced without the iota in the second syllable, they posit as one particular species of the ostreia, including in the whole genus both the whelks (kērykes) and the purple-shells (porphyrai) and the clams (chēmai) and the pinnas and all the similar creatures, about which I shall speak in what follows.

[11.1.25] [25. On whelks (kerykes) and purple-shells (porphyrai).] The shell of whelks and purple-shells, since it is extremely hard, I have never used without burning. When burnt, however, it is of a drying power, and it must be ground finely, so as to become dust-like, having of course first pounded it somewhat and sifted it. Let this be a common rule for you in the case of all things that have a stony and shell-like substance. For if it is not finely ground, they are like sands. And the meal that results from grinding them is, in itself and on its own, suitable for malignant ulcers. This very point too is common to all things that dry strongly without biting noticeably; for those that bite, by irritating, become causes of fluxes. And there is yet another thing common to all such things: with oxykraton (vinegar-and-water) or vinegar or honeyed wine or oxymel they become suitable for putrefactive ulcers. For this reason all stones too, when brought to such a use, some more and some less, but all in turn, are of benefit.

[11.1.26] [26. On oysters.] The shell of oysters, when burnt, is of a power similar to the shell of the trumpet-shells, and still more fine-particled, or, to put it more safely, less coarse-particled. For all things whose body has an earthy and hard consistency and solidification are considerably coarse-particled, and for this reason it is also fitting to pulverize them carefully. So whenever we say that one of these is more fine-particled than another, one must understand the expression in this way: as if we were to say that Odysseus is bigger than Thersites, both of them being small, or that Ajax is smaller than Achilles, both of these too being big. All such things have in themselves, as has also been said before, something of the contracting power, through which, their substance having been compacted, they have become hard and earthy; and when they cast this off through burning they acquire in addition the opposite power, which we call dispersing. If you wash them and burn them, the whole of what is, as it were, the fiery residue (ἐμπύρευμα) is deposited in the water, and this it accomplishes by heating in a fine-particled way, so as sometimes even to putrefy. The remainder becomes earthy and non-biting, and this is especially useful for moist ulcers, for filling and for cicatrization. So I use the burnt shell of what are specifically called oysters for the chronic cavities arising from fluxes that are hard to fill with flesh, those that are fistulous and deep, applying it around on the outside together with old pig's fat. This is called by most people axoungion. And into the sinus itself I insert one of the things that make flesh grow in such cases, such as burnt diphryges, which they call spekarion. Of similar power in kind are also the burnt shells of the other shell-skinned animals, but most of all, as I said, that of oysters, then that of trumpet-shells and purple-shells. Such ash, then, is mixed into clogging, dispersing powers, and together with every kind of fat it disperses. But since old fat is more dispersing, it is mixed rather with that. The drug becomes more pungent than is fitting if you mix with it one of the pungent fats, about which I drew distinctions earlier. But the ash of all such things also brightens the teeth, not only by the cleansing element of its power but also by the roughness of its substance, just like pumice and the potsherd of ovens. In such a use, then, it is not necessary to pulverize very finely the things so burnt, but for malignant ulcers you will in all cases pulverize them finely beforehand. And it also moderately reduces and represses excess growths of flesh. With salt, indeed, all such things when burnt make the dentifrice more effective, so as to dry flabby gums, but they also help putrid ulcers.

[11.1.27] [27. On the cuttlefish.] The shell of the cuttlefish is quite loose-textured, not stony like those of oysters. Now cleansing, as with the other shells of the shell-skinned animals, is common to it along with them, just as drying is too. But the fine-particled quality of its substance belongs to it as something exceptional compared with the others, which is why we also use it, when burnt, for alphoi, ephelis, lentigines and scabies. Moreover, mixed with mined salt it melts away the pterygia that form in the eyes. And even before being burnt, when roasted and finely ground, it both brightens the teeth and dries wounds. On account of the moderate degree of its roughness we are also accustomed to use it for the great roughnesses in the eyes which they call sycoses, carving out of it something resembling a collyrium in shape and rubbing them with it so as to draw blood. For when this has been done, the reducing collyria too act better upon them.

[11.1.28] [28. On the lids of purple-shells.] Some have written that the lids (opercula) of purple-shells (porphyrai), drunk with vinegar, cure swollen spleens, and that, used as a fumigation, they benefit women who are being suffocated hysterically and expel retained afterbirth (choria).

[11.1.29] [29. On oesypum-bearing wool.] Wool that is still dirty, and for this reason called by some "oesypum-bearing", usefully receives the affusions applied to parts that have been bruised or struck in any way whatever, contributing to the benefit derived from them by means of the oesypum. Wool that has been washed and no longer contains the oesypum becomes a kind of material suitable for receiving the moistures that are poured on. When burnt, it has a power that is pungent and hot together with fineness of particles, so that it melts away even the flabby flesh upon ulcers very quickly. It is also put into a drying drug; and burn it just as also most of the others, filling a new earthen pot and then covering it with a lid that has several holes.

[11.1.30] [30. On burnt hair.] Burnt hair, much like burnt wool, is of a sufficiently heating and drying power. [11.1.31] [31. On the power of eggs.] It would be in keeping with the teaching about the parts to speak also about eggs, for I have nowhere else to mention them. Eggs, then, are not parts of animals, just as the fruit is not a part of trees, nor the embryos of pregnant females; rather they stand in analogy to the things that grow upon them. Of the things that grow upon, some appear to be wholly proper to the natures of the plants or animals, others not wholly so, like the mistletoe that grows upon oaks, nor, simply, anything of a different kind that grows upon trees, whether tree or shrub or fruit or herb or in general some shoot, like mushrooms. Among the proper ones, then, is the wool on sheep and the hair on the other animals; and the horns too, those that fall off and grow again, as on male deer, belong to this class. But the things conceived stand in analogy to fruits, being produced by nature for the sake of the succession of the kind. One of these is also the egg, which has come into being for the sake of the continuance of the kind. It is also useful as food, but it is not now proposed to speak about food. Whatever, therefore, it effects as a drug, these things will be stated in this account, as we discover its power, both in respect of its parts and of its whole substance, from a few of the particular uses; for we have learned how, once the general power of each of the things that exist has been discovered, we are able to carry it over to many particular uses. And we have also learned beforehand how from one or a second trial it is possible to reason out the general power. Now the white and thin part of eggs, which we also use for ophthalmias, is among the least biting of drugs, nor have I met with failure from such a dyskrasia as milk often has, as we showed earlier in the case of animals that have failed to digest or have been excessively hungry or excessively thirsty or have used bad foods, things which indeed tend to occur more in women on account of faultiness of regimen. Eggs admit only one single badness, that from age, which is very easy to guard against by using fresh ones. The most customary for us and most easily procured is that of hens, and for this reason we use it, having no need of the others, although they have the same nature. In its mixture it is colder than the well-tempered. One must therefore use the white of eggs not only for the eyes but also for all the other conditions that need the least biting drugs, such as all the malignant ulcers at the seat and the genitals. It is also usefully mixed with the drugs that check hemorrhages from the meninges, which are drugs that plaster over without biting and are astringent. And for the malignant kinds of ulcers it is mixed with those that are naturally fitted to dry them without biting, such a drug as washed pompholyx and some of the metallic substances when washed, about which an account has been given earlier in their own section. The yolk of eggs too is of similar nature, and for this reason it is mixed into non-biting cerates, the eggs having been boiled or roasted. It is clear, however, that these will differ from one another by a slight difference, because roasting makes them gently more drying, and in so far as it has acquired this power, to that extent it loses of the soothing quality. It is also mixed into non-inflammatory poultices, as, for the seat, with those made with melilot. We use the whole raw egg, mixing in rose-oil, for inflammations about the eyelids and ears and breasts, both those that occur when these have been struck and otherwise, and for the sinewy bodies, such as the elbow and the tendons at the fingers, or the joints in feet and hands. An egg boiled in vinegar, if eaten, dries the fluxes of the belly. And if you were to mix with it one of the things suitable for dysentery or a coeliac condition, and, having fried it on a smokeless and moderate fire, such as that from charcoal, were to give it to eat, you will benefit the sufferers not in the least degree. Most suitable for such a mixture are omphakion and sumach, both the kind sprinkled on dishes, called the red, and its juice, as well as oak-gall and pomegranate rind and the ash of whole roasted snails. Suitable too are grape-stones and myrtle-berries and medlars and cornel-berries. More drug-like than these are balaustion and hypocistis and kytinoi. And for burns too it is beneficial applied raw at once, whether one takes up its white alone in soft wool, or soaks the whole together with the yolk and applies it. For it cools moderately and dries without biting. Being such, we use it also for the so-called anakollemata applied to the forehead, and we glue back the hairs of the eyelids, mixing in one of the suitable substances, such as frankincense is, especially when it is oily and not old and dry. But in cases of this kind it is the viscosity of the white of eggs that is useful, not its mixture, unless one were to say it is useful in so far as it in no way opposes the drug being applied. For some of the viscous substances do oppose, like mistletoe, which, being pungent and hot, is opposed to things that do not need to be heated. And it has often been said that drugs having no strong power are mixed as matter with those that have such powers, and for this reason are of manifold use, serving those that act strongly. The egg, being such, and at the same time acquiring in addition no small difference according to the degree of boiling or roasting, becomes of manifold use. For boiled and roasted and fried it is mixed with the drugs that dry moistures, while with those that cut what is in the chest and lung is mixed the so-called rhophēton, which ought to be boiled in water only so far as to become warm. In accordance with the same nature it is employed for those whose throat has been roughened through shouting or through the pungency of a humor, plastering itself around the affected parts and remaining there like a poultice, and by the non-biting quality of its substance both soothing them and curing them thoroughly. By the same reasoning it also heals the roughnesses in the stomach and belly and intestines and bladder.

[11.1.32] [32. On burnt hedgehogs.] Of both hedgehogs, the sea and the land kind, the whole body when burnt produces an ash of cleansing, dispersing and reducing power. Some people, at any rate, have used it for both overgrown flesh and the foul kinds of ulcers.

[11.1.33] [33. On snails.] Snails, whole, burnt together with their shells, with omphakitis gall-nut and white pepper mixed in with them, are of great benefit in dysenteries in which the ulcers are not yet putrid. The proportion should be one part of the pepper, two of the gall-nut, and four of the ash of the snails. Having made these thoroughly smooth, sprinkle them on the foods and give them to drink in water or in wine that is white and harsh. Without being mixed with gall-nut, the ash of snails is of a sufficiently drying power, which also has, on account of the burning, something of heat. Unburnt, the snails, pounded smooth together with their shells, are applied over the whole belly in the case of the dropsical, and over the swellings in the joints in the case of the arthritic. And their application becomes hard to remove, but it dries sufficiently. And indeed one ought to allow them to remain applied throughout, until they fall off of their own accord. This is also to be done in the case of swellings from a blow that are hard to resolve, and in the case of a contusion that has occurred in the ears. For they dry all of these sufficiently, even if a viscous and thick fluid is contained in the depth.

[11.1.34] [34. On burnt crabs.] The ash of river crabs, for its part, is drying in the same way as the things mentioned before, but by the peculiarity of its whole substance it acts wonderfully in the case of those bitten by rabid dogs, both on its own, but also much more together with gentian and frankincense. There should be one part of frankincense, five of gentian, and ten of the crabs. Now we have on occasion, though rarely, used them burnt in another manner, but for the most part in the manner in which Aeschrion the Empiricist used them, an old man most experienced in drugs, a fellow citizen and teacher of ours. There was a dish of red copper, upon which he set the crabs alive and burnt them until they were reduced to ash, so as to be ground fine easily. This Aeschrion always had the drug prepared and ready in his house, burning the crabs in the season of summer, after the rising of the Dog-star, when the sun was in Leo and the moon was eighteen days old. And he gave this drug to those bitten by rabid dogs to drink every day up to the fortieth, sprinkling a good-sized spoonful into water. But if he was taking care of the bitten person not from the beginning but some days after the bite, he sprinkled in two spoonfuls each day. He also used upon the wound itself the clogging drug made from Bruttian pitch, opopanax and vinegar, which takes one litra of pitch, one Italian xestes of the most pungent vinegar, and three ounces of opopanax. These things, although they do not belong to the present treatise, I have written because of my confidence in the drug, since no one who has used it as described has ever died. I shall also compose separately another treatise on the things that act by the peculiarity of their whole substance, among which are all such things as these. One must therefore pardon the untimeliness of the writing, both now and where it has sometimes occurred in other places of this treatise, because of the benefit from what is said, which is very great and which I wish to be preserved for the people who come after us, even if death intervening should prevent me from writing the treatises that follow this one. Our teacher Pelops, wishing to state the causes of all such things, said plausibly that the crab, being an aquatic animal, benefits those bitten by rabid dogs, who are in fear of being seized by a most dry affection, rabies, on account of which they also fear water. And he said that river crabs, not sea crabs, are suitable, since, because of the admixture of salts, which are most drying, sea animals would not preserve exactly their opposition to rabies. And when someone said to him, why then do not all the animals living in drinkable water help in like manner to the crabs?, he said: because they cannot receive the same preparation as the crabs. For when these are burnt their ash, becoming drying, both consumes and at the same time disperses the venom of the biting dogs. These things, then, Pelops used to say, professing and priding himself on knowing the causes of all of them. But I, unless I have first persuaded myself that I know something accurately, do not attempt to persuade my neighbours. Accordingly I have not accepted Pelops' account as true either, since it admits of numerous counter-arguments, but I hold that the crabs too help by the peculiarity of their whole substance. But because none of those who used them has died, with their whole bodies at any rate [τοῖς γε μὴν σώμασιν ὅλοις], I wished this to have been made clear by me already, even if it is not proper to the present treatise. For this was not what was proposed.

[11.1.35] [35. On burnt swallows.] Not in the case of those animals alone which I have mentioned, but of swallows too many have made use, burning them and mixing honey with the ash, then smearing it on those suffering from synanche, and in general on all the affections that arise in the pharynx and uvula together with swellings. Some people also use this ash for sharpness of sight. Others dry them out like mummies and give them to drink in the quantity of a drachm.

[11.1.36] [36. On cicadas.] Some also make use of dried cicadas for colic conditions, together with an equal number of grains of pepper, and they give either three or five or seven, both during the intermissions and during the paroxysms. Others roast them and give them to be eaten by those who are affected in the bladder.

[11.1.37] [37. On larks.] The lark, this small winged animal which we often see also along the roads, when boiled in broth benefits colic patients. One must eat it continually and often together with the broth. This animal has on its head a sort of crest, as it were, of naturally grown hairs, on account of which the fable which Aristophanes the comic poet wrote was also fashioned. He speaks about it in the following manner: "For you are by nature ignorant and meddlesome, and you have not learned your Aesop, who said in his tale that the lark came into being first of all birds, before the earth, and that then her father died of a disease, but there was no earth, and he lay exposed for five days; and she, at a loss for want of any means, buried her father in her own head." This they say Theocritus too hints at when he says, "Nor do the tomb-bearing crested larks roam about"; for he means those that have the tomb upon their head. I have added these things to my account because I wish to indicate clearly the animal the lark, what sort of upstanding crest of hairs it has upon its head, since I have made trial of its benefit for colic patients, and I wish to make it well known to those who do not know it, since it resembles the birds called pyrgitai, but is distinguished by its crest and is a little larger than that bird. And indeed the plant called korydalis too is suitable for these same colic patients. And let this too be known to you as a by-the-way.

[11.1.38] [38. On hens.] The plain broth of hens is of a tempering power, just as that of old cocks is of a laxative power. One must boil them with salt for a very long time. But of these things we ourselves have experience.

[11.1.39] [39. On the weasel.] A weasel, however, we have never burnt, though they have written of it that its ash, smeared on with vinegar, benefits gouty and arthritic patients, since it is by nature capable of dispersing sufficiently, and that, dried out and drunk, it benefits epileptics, evidently in virtue of the same power. Some also say that it is altogether an alexipharmic against a wild beast, and especially its belly.

[11.1.40] [40. On burnt frogs.] The ash of burnt frogs, at any rate, they say is a remedy for haemorrhages when sprinkled on, and that it cures alopecia with liquid pitch. [11.1.41] [41. On the hippocampus.] And the hippocampus too, the sea creature, when burnt whole, some have written benefits alopecia, it too evidently being of a drying and fine-particled power—or rather its ash. Some mix it with amaracine unguent, some with liquid pitch, and some with old swine's fat.

[11.1.42] [42. On salted tellins.] And salted tellins too, when burnt, they say, produce an ash so caustic that, when it is mixed with cedar-oil and dripped onto the spot after we have pulled out the hairs of the eyelids from the roots, it prevents them from growing back again. On earthworms. Without burning or boiling, people have made trial of whole animals, either applied to the affected parts or taken into the body—or some of the physicians have written as though they had made trial of them: earthworms, ground fine and applied to divided sinews, give immediate and marvellous help, and these same ones, all of them taken as a drink with sweet wine, are a diuretic drug.

[11.1.43] [43. On bedbugs.] They have also written about bedbugs, that if they are drunk with vinegar they expel leeches that have been swallowed down. But we, for our part, since we always expel them by means of the eating of garlic, have had no need of bedbugs.

[11.1.44] [44. On cantharides.] Of cantharides, however, we have sufficient experience in the case of scabby (psora-like) nails, to which, when applied together with the suitable cerates or plaster-drugs, they draw the nails out, so that they fall off whole. We have also mixed them into the compositions suited to psorai and lepra, and into some of the putrefying drugs, and sometimes also into those that expel the so-called corns (heloi). One of our teachers used to put a little of them into a diuretic drug. Some people put in only the wings and the feet, which indeed they say are also protective remedies for those who have drunk their bodies (tōmata); others do the opposite, but we put them in whole. The more suitable among the cantharides, for the purposes for which I said I had made trial of them, are those from the wheat which have quince-yellow transverse bands on their wings, and more so if, having put them into a new earthenware vessel and then fastened one of the loose-woven linen cloths around the mouth of the vessel, you hold the vessel in such a way that the linen is turned downward, receiving the vapour of the vinegar rising up, until the cantharides die.
[11.1.45] [45. On the bouprestis.] In the same way it is fitting also to store the buprestes. These too are a kind of animal, resembling the cantharides in appearance and in power.

[11.1.46] [46. On the pine-caterpillar.] And indeed the caterpillars found on pines, fittingly called pine-caterpillars (pityokampai), are of such a power as well. [11.1.47] [47. On the salamander.] And some people also mix the ash of the burnt salamander into putrefying, leprotic and psoric powers.

[11.1.48] [48. On the torpedo.] And some people have written that the torpedo too, whole—I mean, obviously, the sea animal—cures headaches when applied to the head, and turns back a prolapsed anus. But I, having made trial of both, found that it brings about neither. So, having conceived the idea of applying it, while still alive, to someone suffering pain in the head—for it could be a pain-stilling drug, like the other things that numb sensation—I found that this is so. And I think that the first person to use it also set out to use it prompted by some such notion.

[11.1.49] [49. On the sea-dragon and the red mullet.] They have written that the following animals, split open alive and applied at once to the affected parts, bring benefit: the sea-dragon placed upon its own wound, and likewise also the red mullet upon that of the dragon; house mice upon that of the scorpion, just as also the lizard; the shrew-mouse upon its own, and the Chalcidian lizard, which they also give to drink in wine, as curing its own bite. And the scorpion, too, [they say,] thoroughly cures its own sting when applied pounded smooth; and likewise also when eaten roasted. They say that it is suitable also for those bitten by a viper, and the gecko for those [stung] by a scorpion. They say too that in the regions of Egypt the so-called aseirakos, dried, is given to those stung by a scorpion, and that the so-called kybion is employed with benefit for a dog's bite when placed upon the wound, and many other such things, about which we shall speak at greater length among the agents that act by the specific property of their whole substance. Some of the physicians of our own time have used the oil in which whole animals have been boiled. And some of the earlier ones [did so], for the removal of hair, with pine-caterpillars, sea anemones, the sea hare and the sea scolopendra; and for earache, with silphai boiled in the oil and with the so-called oniskoi. These are animals that make themselves into a ball by drawing together upon themselves, which some among us call 'beans', since they are similar to edible beans when they have rolled themselves into a ball, being grey in colour. In the countryside one may see these in very great numbers being produced under the water-jars in which the country people carry the water from the springs, and they set these down near the hearth; and I have seen some of those who practise medicine in the country always using the oil from them for all pains of the ears, without distinguishing according to what condition the pain has arisen; whence, reasonably, they sometimes succeed, but sometimes also do harm. And what wonder, when even some of the renowned physicians have written about such things without distinction? Such, at any rate, are also the books of Apollonius on easily procurable drugs. This man, then, has also written that the 'entrails of the earth' (earthworms) boiled down in oil soothe pains of the ears; but some think it right to mix them with goose fat and use them thus.

[11.1.50] [50. On foxes and hyenas.] Concerning whole foxes boiled down in oil—for some treat arthritics in this way, some throwing the foxes alive into a very large cauldron, others even dead ones—it is necessary to speak at greater length, since they seemed at the outset to have freed many from the affection, but not long afterwards only to have benefited them. For the affection returned to them, though indeed not so violent as it had been before. Now what belongs to the foxes is in no way more dispersing than what belongs to the hyena, which, when boiled in oil in the same way, makes the oil most dispersing. It has been said many times that it belongs to such drugs to draw toward the surface what is contained in the depth of the body, and for this reason sometimes to put a stop to pains. For it is certainly not in every case that this alone follows for them; those pains are stopped by such drugs in which a pain-producing humour is contained in the depth, either because of the thickness of its substance, or because of coldness or violent pungency, or even flatulent pneuma that has no way out. Those, then, who used the foxes themselves also made the oil dispersing; then, filling tubs with it, they set the arthritics whole into them, bidding them remain in them for a considerable time, and from this it came about that not only the swellings around their joints but also the whole body was emptied. Since, then, their whole body had previously been disposed plethorically, it was no wonder that benefit arose from the emptying, since nothing flowed in to the affected parts because the whole body was being emptied, as the humours contained in them were dispersed. But just as before, when their body was unaffected, a bad regimen produced the affection, in the same way or even still more it was likely that through a similar regimen they would again be disposed in the same way in the joints that had suffered.

[11.2.1] [1. On the things generated in the sea and in salty waters.] These alone, which still remain for the whole treatise, have as their suitable occasion the present one. For the animals that are generated in the sea and in water have been discussed in the preceding account concerning animals; but those things which are generated in waters or from waters, yet are not animals, will now be discussed.

[11.2.2] [2. On adarkion.] Adarkion—some people call it, in the masculine, adarkos, others, in the feminine, adarke—is in its substance like a kind of congealed foam, formed by salty water congealing around rubbish and reeds. This is most pungent and most heating, and for this reason by itself it is useless, but it is mixed with things that blunt its power and thus becomes of manifold use when applied externally for conditions that need to be heated. For it is not possible to take it inside the body, because of the vehemence of its power.

[11.2.3] [3. On alkyonia.] Alkyonia all cleanse and disperse, having a pungent quality and a hot power, but the more and the less among them is not slight, both in these very respects which I have mentioned and moreover in respect of the fine-particled character of the whole substance. One of them is dense and heavy and bad in smell, for it smells of rotten fish, and resembles a sponge in shape. A second, different one is more elongated in shape, light and loose-textured, having a smell like seaweed. Another, a third, is in shape similar to a worm, but is purplish in colour and soft in consistency; they call it Milesian. In addition to these there is another, a fourth, light and loose-textured like the one mentioned second, but resembling greasy, unwashed wool. The fifth is bounded on the outside by a smooth surface, but has its inner substance rough, having no smell, but appearing pungent to the taste; for it is indeed also the hottest of all the alkyonia, so that it is able to burn off hairs. Therefore, while the first two benefit lichens and alphoi and indeed also psorai and lepra, and further brighten the skin owing to the due measure of their power, this last-mentioned one can do the same thing. For it does not merely cleanse those off, as it were the outer surface, but it also skins and excoriates, advancing into the depth of the skin so as to produce ulcers. The one mentioned third is the most fine-particled of all, wherefore also, when burnt, it cures alopekiai when smeared on with wine that is tawny in colour and thin in consistency. The fourth is of the same kind as these in power, but not a little weaker.

[11.2.4] [4. On salts.] Salts, both the mined and the sea salts, are of the same power in kind. They differ, however, in that the substance of the salts from the earth is more compacted, for which reason the coarse-particled and astringent element is greater in these. Now the sea salts melt at once when water is poured over them, whereas those from the earth do not undergo this. Of the same kind as the sea salts are also those produced in certain lakes that possess saltiness, in the summer, when the water is baked out of them, as for instance the Tragasian salts near Sminthium. For there, from the naturally occurring waters, which are quite hot, abundant water collects and forms a pool in no great space, and this is wholly used up during the summer, being dried by the sun; and since the place has an innate saltiness, all that is left of it becomes salt, taking its name both from the place and from the waters. For indeed the naturally occurring waters themselves in that place are called Tragasian, being of a most drying power, and the physicians in that place use them for this purpose. Something has also been said in the fourth book about the Sodomene salts, those produced in the so-called Dead Sea, and if anyone has read that book carefully, he will now need only a reminder, so that, once the gustatory quality has been stated, he may know the power of the drug. Since, then, the salty quality at once disperses and draws together the substance that comes near it, the so-called aphronitron has its difference in this, insofar as in it one can clearly see only one prevailing flavour, which they call bitter, which has a dispersing power but does not have a contracting one, as salts do. For salts consume all that is moist in bodies; and the remainder of the solid substance they draw together by their astringency, for which reason they also pickle, and keep free of putrefaction, the bodies of things that putrefy, which have a superfluous moisture and a substance that is loose (ἀδιάλυτον) and not compacted. Accordingly, bodies in which there is no superfluous moisture at all, as in the finest honey, and whose solid body is compacted, as in stones, cannot putrefy; wherefore the use of salts is not well regarded in the case of these, but in those cases where putrefaction is suspected.

[11.2.5] [5. On burnt salt.] Burnt salt has the dispersing property more than unburnt salt, to the extent that its body becomes more fine-particled, taking on its power from the fire, as was shown to happen in the case of the other burnt substances too; yet it is no longer able, in the same way as unburnt salt, to draw together and compact the solid substance.

[11.2.6] [6. On nitron.] Nitron. This drug too was shown to have a power intermediate between salt and aphronitron. [11.2.7] [7. On flower of salt.] Flower of salt: some people name it as a single word, halosanthon, while others divide it and call it flower of salt (halos anthos). This drug is moist, more fine-particled even than burnt salt, pungent in quality and sufficiently dispersing in power.

[11.2.8] [8. On froth of salt.] Froth of salt is a foam-like efflorescence of salt, being of a nature much more fine-particled than salt itself, so that it is able both to thin and to disperse much more than salt does, whereas it cannot contract the remainder of the substance as salt does.

[11.2.9] [9. On asphalt.] Asphalt. This too is one of the things generated in sea-water and in certain other waters resembling the sea, as for instance at Apollonia in Epirus and in other such places; upon many naturally occurring waters this drug is found floating like a foam, being soft while it floats on the surface, but afterwards drying out so as to become harder than dry pitch.

[11.2.10] [10. On the asphalt generated in the Dead Sea.] The finest asphalt is generated in the sea called Dead. This is itself a certain salt lake in Coele Syria. The power of the drug is drying and heating, in roughly the second order. Reasonably, then, they use it for the agglutination of bloody wounds, and for the other conditions, all those that require to be dried together with a moderate heating.

[11.2.11] [11. On sponge.] Sponge, when burnt, is of a pungent and dispersing power. One of our teachers used it also for the haemorrhages that occur in surgical operations, keeping it ready, dry and devoid of moisture, soaked preferably in asphalt, or, if this was not at hand, in pitch; and he applied it to the bleeding places while it was still burning, so that the part was at once made to form an eschar and the body of the burnt sponge itself was received as a kind of stopper. New sponge, in and of itself, is not, like wool or a plucked lint-pledget (μοτὸς τιλτός), merely a material for the liquids poured upon it, but also dries manifestly. You will know this if you use it on a wound by itself with water or oxykraton (vinegar-and-water) or wine, according to the differences of bodies, as has been said before; for it will glue them together much like the drugs called enaima (those for bloody wounds). But if it is not new but has been in use, you will clearly recognise how far it falls short of the new one when applied to wounds, whether soaked in water or in wine or in oxykraton (vinegar-and-water). And there is nothing surprising in the fact that, in the case of new sponge, while the power it had from the sea is still preserved, bodies are moderately dried. It is able to do these things so long as it still preserves the smell from the sea, since with time, even if it has not yet been brought into use, it loses its smell and is likewise unable to dry.

[11.2.12] [12. On garum.] Garum is of a sufficiently hot and dry power, and for this reason some of the physicians have used it for the putrefactive sorts of ulcers, and they inject it both into dysenterics and into those with sciatica.

[11.2.13] [13. On brine.] The brine of salted fish, like garum, is suitable both for putrefactions and, when injected, for cases of sciatica and dysentery; by its pungency it draws out the humours troubling the hip-joint and empties them out through the intestines, while in dysentery it washes around and dries the putrefactive ulcers. Some physicians have used especially the brine of salted silouroi and that of maenides for such conditions, and we too have used it on putrefactive ulcers in the mouth.

[10.2.1] On the fluids in animals. [a. On blood.] Blood: one must evidently understand in addition "of an animal in its natural condition", for this is what is truly blood. Melancholic or bitter-bilious or phlegmatic or serous or putrefactive blood is mixed from the blood that is blood in truth and from the humour and ichor that has been mingled with it. And of the natural blood itself, in each animal one kind is moister, another drier, and one more, another less hot; for no blood is cold.

[10.2.2] [2. On pig's blood.] Pig's blood, then, is moist and less hot, resembling human blood most closely in its mixture, if indeed the flesh of pigs also resembles that of humans. At any rate we already know of many innkeepers and cooks who have been caught selling human meat as pork, and yet none of those who ate it perceived any difference whatever. But I have also heard certain trustworthy men relating that they had eaten in a certain inn an abundant broth with most delicious meat, and that, when they were already filled, they found in it the forward part of a finger at the very nail; and, fearing the people in the inn lest they too be eaten, as being accustomed to the practice, they immediately went out, and, having vomited what they had eaten, continued on their journey. And indeed they said that not long afterwards those at the inn were detected in the fact that they had been slaughtering men; so that one might reasonably suppose that the blood of pigs too is most similar to that of humans. For from such blood comes both the first generation of the flesh and its nourishment thereafter, so that whoever says that human blood is useful for some disease, let him first demonstrate in pig's blood, if not the same, at least a similar activity. For even if it should fall somewhat short of human blood in power, it will at any rate do something comparable, and once this is recognised we shall expect the benefit from human blood to be more complete. Just as, if it appears to preserve not even a small part of what is promised, there is no reason to make trial on human blood either. For we have found by experience that like things are productive of like effects. At any rate, among us at Pergamum, and almost throughout the whole of Asia, those who have trephined fractured bones of the head are accustomed to apply pigeon's blood to the thick meninx. Then someone who happened to have a wood-pigeon but had no pigeon used the blood of the wood-pigeon, and nevertheless the man was saved. And another, using the blood of a turtle-dove on another patient, did the man no harm. For to use similar things for the same affections when those previously tested are not available is one of the things agreed upon and attested by experience. And indeed the greater part of human life is carried through in this manner.

[10.2.3] [3. On the blood of the pigeon.] Since I mentioned the blood of pigeons by way of example, it would be no worse to take this up now as well in the discussion. For some also use it for hyposphagmata that occur in the eyes, obviously taking at once what flows out of the animal as it is being slaughtered. For one man, pouring it hot upon the hyposphagmata, used to divide the veins at the outgrowth of the wings, so that the animal itself might suffice for many uses. Another, plucking out the feathers of tender nestlings—these are soft and have their quills full of fluid—squeezed out this very fluid and instilled it into the eyes. Among other physicians a dispute arose whether one ought to drip onto the meninx the blood of a nestling or of a full-grown pigeon, and whether that of a male or of a female. But I know in Rome countless persons whose skull-bones had been trepanned who were in no way harmed by the use of rose-oil, without pigeon's blood; it must, however, be warm, just as the pigeon's blood is. And perhaps indeed it is beneficial by the moderateness of its warmth to the touch, not by some special and unknown power. There also coexists in it the good temperament with respect to its power; but what of this? For rose-oil too has this, together with partaking also of a slight astringency, so that you will have nothing greater, at least in the case of a trepanned head, when using good rose-oil. I showed earlier how the faultless rose-oil ought to be prepared. There are also very many collyria curative of hyposphagmata, and especially those containing much myrrh, such as the one of Democrates called diasmyrnon. Next after these are those made with much frankincense, and after these those made with saffron; and the juice of fenugreek is better than pigeon's blood for such things. Why, then, should one need to wait for pigeons or wood-pigeons or turtle-doves, when one has fenugreek, the most easily procured drug of all, and the collyria mentioned are ready to hand? In the same way we shall not need the blood of an owl either for those who breathe with difficulty. Some, indeed, do not give the blood to drink, but, having boiled the bird itself, order it to be eaten in plain broth. The blood, at any rate, some give dripped into water, others into wine; and a certain man was praising this blood excessively in the presence of a woman who continually suffered from dyspnoea, but when I inquired what kind of dyspnoea he knew to have been cured by it, he did not even know that there are several kinds.

And so he did indeed use it on the woman, but it did no good at all, [10.2.4] [4. On the blood of the bat, the hare, hens, goats, lambs and kids, bears, bulls and he-goats.] just as neither does that of the bat, which some have written, when smeared on the breasts of maidens, keep them contracted for a very long time. This too is false, just as is the claim that hair does not grow in the armpits, which Xenocrates, doing well, discredited as untrue. He himself, however, recommends that after the use of that blood one sprinkle on either chalcanthon or hemlock seed; and he says that when this is done the hairs either do not grow at all or grow downy, as if he were bringing in the seed of hemlock as some trifling drug, and not one sufficient by itself to cool vigorously whatever parts it is applied to. Some also smear the blood of the bat on the genitals of boys, thinking that by this they will keep the parts without pubic hair for a very long time. And yet they ought to have thought not 'for a very long time', but that they would remain such for ever, just as they suppose about the armpits too. Now from the part being strongly cooled it is reasonable that something of this kind should come about; but the blood of the bat is not cold in power to so great a degree, for no blood at all is cold. As food, however, many often use blood, that of the hare and of hens and of goats; but that of the hare and of hens not a few even of those in the cities, while that of goats those in the countryside, filling the goats' stomachs with it together with the fat, as Homer said the suitors did. But our discourse now is not about things taken in the role of food, but about those taken as drugs. Some things, as has also been said before, are at once both foods and drugs; of these [we treat] in this treatise insofar as they are drugs, not insofar as they are foods. For indeed those who have given the blood of the goat with honey to those suffering from dropsy administer it as a drug, not as a food, as do those who have used it roasted against dysentery or against a flux of the belly. And it seems to me that someone came to this use having supposed that its coarse-particled and earthy quality together with heat is drying. For hemorrhages of the meninges, finding the blood of cock and hen written up by them, I neither hoped that it would do anything great, and I was, on the one hand, ashamed to judge it by experience, lest I should seem meddlesome or foolish if, passing over so many and such approved drugs, I hoped that the blood of these birds would accomplish more; and on the other hand, since such a hemorrhage is perilous, it did not seem to me right to resort to any of the untried things. For such an experiment is thus dangerous, and is reasonably undertaken only by kings upon wicked men. I condemned in advance also the blood of lambs, which some say cures epilepsy when drunk; so I was not going to judge this by experience either. But if anyone wishes to make the test, I know clearly that the very writers of such things will be condemned. For all drugs which, when drunk, benefit epileptics are of the cutting power, and the blood of lambs is least of all of such a kind. As for what is said by Xenocrates about the blood of kids, thinking it possible that it might accomplish something because of the admixture of vinegar, I referred it to one of those living in the countryside to carry out, a man fond of farming but educated in the primary education; and he says that, having used it on two who spat blood, he found some benefit. But it seemed to me, from what he related, that neither of them had spat it either from an artery or from the larynx or the lung. Xenocrates, at any rate, writes in the first book On the Benefit from Animals, where he discusses kids, word for word as follows: 'Very useful for those who spit blood. One must, while it has not yet congealed, mix with about half a kotyle an equal amount of pungent vinegar, then, having boiled it up, divide it into three and give one part to be gulped down each day.' So it is possible for you, at some time in the countryside, when you lack the other things, to use this too, since the trial is without danger. The blood of the bear, applied hot to abscesses, may possibly ripen them. I shall add to the account also that of the goat and of the he-goat and of the bull. And it is open to you, if you wish, passing over countless of the readily available drugs by which we ripen abscesses, to slaughter bears and bulls and he-goats, evidently at each use. For certainly no one who has applied it once to the affected part will demand what the drug promises, nor indeed when it has already become cold so as to have congealed.

[10.2.5] [5. On the blood of green frogs.] As for the blood of the small green frogs, which some call brexantes, since someone affirmed that, once you have plucked out the hairs of the eyelids and smeared it on, they no longer grow back, I found it to be false when I subjected it to trial. Afterwards I also found this written by certain authors, just as also that of the krotones (ticks), which the ancients rather call kynoraistai. But neither did this one, when brought to trial, make good its promise.

[10.2.6] [6. On the blood of the crocodile and of the rest.] Whether that of the land crocodile is productive of sharpness of sight, I was not going to test either, since I have approved drugs that sharpen the sight, just as I was not going to test whether that of stallions covering mares is escharotic and putrefying, nor whether that of house mice makes acrochordons fall off. For I had many other remedies for this affection too, just as also for the one harder to cure than it, the so-called myrmecia; and I was on my guard against carrying off a reputation for sorcery, since the envious physicians were already getting ahead of me in saying that I make my predictions concerning the sick on the basis of some divinatory art, not of medical theory.

[10.2.7] [7. On milk.] Milk. This has a twofold use, the one as nourishment, the other as a drug. But what it can do as nourishment has been shown both through the Therapeutic Method and in the other works. Its power as a drug I shall now state, having first recalled, in this case too, as a little earlier in the case of blood, that what is going to be said must be understood not of diseased milk but of that which is according to nature in each of the animals. Now the healthiest milk, just like blood, is pure and unmixed, partaking neither of bitterness nor of acidity nor of pungency nor of saltiness nor of foul smell, but, as one might say, fragrant or odourless, or, if anything, partaking of some slight fragrance. It is evident that it is also pleasant when tasted, having a slight sweetness, just like healthy blood, from which also the generation of milk takes place. Such milk is most advantageous against pungent and biting fluxes, not only washing them away from the troubled parts—for this it has in common with water—but also plastering itself around the bodies, so that what flows in does not fall upon them bare. And not only in this does it have the advantage over water, but also in its washing them round, because it contains in itself a cleansing moisture, the one called whey, which is first washed away and in addition washes the bodies. With all the rest, which is thick and oily, it plasters itself around them in the very manner in which fat and suet do, and the white of an egg, and the cerate made from washed wax and oil; for these too soothe the bitings from pungent ichors, by being plastered around the bodies, having a non-biting nature. But all milk, being most easily altered, and especially when the surrounding air is hot, loses much of the power described, unless one uses it immediately, warm, as poured out from the breasts. Most of all, then, one should use the milk of a woman who is in good bodily condition and well regulated in her diet, for this is most akin to the human body; second, that of the other animals, such as have not departed far from the nature of man. You will know this easily from the smell of their flesh, which is unpleasant in those which stand far off in their mixtures, such as dog, wolf, lion, leopard, fox, hyena, bear and the like, but not unpleasant in those not far off, such as pig, goat, horse, ox, ass, sheep. And accordingly all men, taught by experience, use goat's, sheep's, cow's and ass's milk, and make cheeses from them, except from ass's milk. For this is very thin and full of serous moisture, just as cow's milk is thick. The goat's is intermediate in consistency, while the sow has milk that is unconcocted and watery. All milk is composed of three substances, the cheesy, the serous, and the oily, which cow's milk appears to have in the greatest quantity, from which also they make what is called butter, which is of concocting and relaxing power, wherefore they also use it especially for parotid swellings and buboes.

[10.2.8] [8. On whey of milk.] Whey, as has been said, has a cleansing power, and it is taken for the purpose of evacuating the bowel and is injected by means of clysters, cleansing round about and washing away without biting the pungencies in the intestines. And one would do best to wash out ulcers that contain pungent ichors with whey instead of water. And as for the drugs that are dispersing of ecchymoses and black discolorations, these too it is better to wash round with whey, not with water. In this way, then, we use it also for bruises beneath the eyes and for hyposphagmata, mixing it with the drugs proper to these conditions. The cheesy and thick part of the milk is rather plastered on, and in this respect it blunts the pungencies. But when it takes on in addition some other drying power, it becomes an excellent drug for dysenterics and for all the pungent fluxes in the bowel; and it takes this on by means of red-hot stones, previously heated through, that are thrown into it. These must be the ones they call pebbles (kachlekes), and the milk must be boiled until the greater part of the whey-like moisture in it has been used up. We, however, produce the same or even a better power by means of red-hot iron cylinders thrown into it. For iron, as has been said, partakes of an astringent power, and for this reason I myself had several cylinders prepared, attached to the ends of spits, so that one may easily lift the iron by the handle once it has been heated. And just as with cauteries, so too I wrap the handles of these in rags. Whole milk is useful against the pungent fluxes of the eyes, both by itself and together with the simple collyria, and further against hyposphagmata and bruises beneath the eyes; and indeed, applied on the outside upon the eyelids, together with rose-oil and egg, when those suffering from ophthalmia are about to sleep, it ripens their inflammations; but let this milk be a woman's, fresh, dripped from the breasts. We inject it also into ulcerated wombs, both by itself and also mixing it with the drugs that treat without biting, with which it is mixed, and whenever we soothe the ulcers in the seat that are painful because of pungent ichors or inflammations or folds that have risen up. In this way too we use it for the affections of the genitals and, simply, for all that need soothing because of inflammation or biting or malignancy. For this reason, then, it is also applied to cancerous ulcers, mixed with anodyne drugs, such as especially those made with pompholyx. And what need is there to say that, as a mouthwash and as a thing held in the mouth for inflamed parts in the mouth, it is most anodyne when gargled? And it adequately soothes inflamed paristhmia about the uvula and the antiades, and on this account also synanche; and to speak simply, as I said, it is a soothing drug, having even its whole substance unbiting, but much more so when we have used up by moderate boiling the greater part of its whey-like moisture. So at any rate physicians seem to me to have been prompted to give milk also against the deadly drugs that kill by erosion, as the sea hare kills and the cantharis. Some give it also to those who have taken aconite or thapsia. But these things they devised with good reason, whereas in other matters they have manifestly spoken falsely, as in the matter of the bitch's milk, that it prevents hair from coming up from the eyelids, if, after they have been plucked out, it is smeared on the place from which the roots of the hairs were drawn out. By the same reasoning those who wrote that it keeps the hairs from sprouting quickly on the genitals, if it is smeared around before puberty, and that it expels dead embryos when drunk, do not speak the truth. And they write certain other things savouring of sorcery about the milk of these and of certain other animals, which at the very outset I myself refused to tell, even if I had had experience of them as being truly said.

[10.2.9] [9. On cheese.] Cheese. To the account of milk it is fitting to add also one on cheese, because it is milk that has set. Yet not the whole substance of the milk sets in cheeses, but only the thick part, the thin and whey-like part being separated out and parted off. And milk was said to have in itself also a certain fatty and, as it were, oil-like nature, and I said that this is present in greatest quantity in cow's milk, and that when it has been parted from the rest of the milk, this oily part, having come to be by itself, is called butter, whereas when it has set together with the whole milk—the whey-like moisture obviously having been separated off in the setting—it makes the cheese oily. And some of the cow's-milk cheeses become so oily that something oil-like flows out of them. With time, both these and all the others will appear more pungent to you when you taste and smell them. And once, when a cow's-milk cheese had been brought to me, judging from its smell that it was pungent, I threw it aside; and I for my part supposed it had been used up by the household servants, but the one accustomed to keep such things, after a long time, bringing it out from the storeroom, asked what indeed I ordered concerning it. And since it appeared inedible on account of its pungency, it became a problem, by way of amusement, how one might dispose of it usefully. Just then, when a certain arthritic was brought to me on a chair, having chalk-stones (pōroi) in his joints, it occurred to me to boil a salted leg of pork, which was in the house, to soak the cheese in the decoction, and, having unified it well in a mortar, to apply it upon the chalk-stones. And indeed the arthritic was benefited very greatly by this drug. For as his skin burst open spontaneously without incision, portions of the chalk-stones flowed out painlessly every day. And when the cheese at my house had been entirely used up, the arthritic, having procured another such for himself, kept it for a later occasion, and later used it again when it had aged; and since then too I found by trial the same benefit, he continued thereafter to use it often, and taught certain others of his friends who suffered in like manner. This, then, became known from our own devising, confirmed by experience; but fresh cheese, which is of a mixture opposite to the old, I once applied to a man in the country who had a wound moderate in size, having of course first ground it smooth. And over it, on the outside, I applied leaves of dock. If these were not at hand, leaves of vine, of plane, of beet and of lettuce could also be applied. The cheese itself, then, being soft, glued the wound together. And another, the one called in Pergamum, where I live, and in the Asia lying above it 'oxygalaktinos' (sour-milk cheese), when applied in like manner glued together a large wound that a countryman had. For the soft and newly-set cheese has a repelling power, cooling gently. And the oxygalaktinos, in addition to these, acquires also a slight dispersing power.

[10.2.10] [10. On butter.] Boutyros or boutyron, however you wish to name it, in the masculine or in the neuter. It is produced, then, from the oiliest part in milk, as has been said before. I am surprised, however, how Dioscorides says that it has its origin from sheep's and goat's [αὐγείου] milk. For I know this drug to be produced from cow's milk, and for this reason I think it is also called boutyron; and it is of a concocting power, having a little of the dispersing power too, in bodies that are intermediate in respect of softness and hardness. For one must always bear in mind that simple statements, made without any addition or qualification, are said with reference to bodies intermediate in mixture. For this drug is unable to disperse the swellings contrary to nature in bodies that are completely hard, whereas soft bodies that are inflamed it both concocts and disperses easily, so that we have completely cured parotid swellings and buboes and the inflammations in the mouth and a great many other things with it alone, in the bodies of children and of women when they are affected. But also in children who are growing their teeth, when smeared on continually, it thins the gums no less than honey does, the gums through which the passage out comes about for the teeth. And all the other inflammatory affections in the mouth, after the influx has ceased, it disperses and concocts. Hence it is also mixed into the plasters applied externally over parotid swellings, hypochondria and buboes. And indeed, when swallowed into the stomach and distributed through it, it contributes greatly to the expectorations from the lung in pleuritic and peripneumonic affections, along with concocting them as well. Licked up on its own, then, it concocts more but brings up less, whereas together with honey and bitter almonds it brings up more but concocts less.

[10.2.11] [11. On rennet.] All rennet is of a pungent and dispersing power, and evidently also of a drying one; for this follows of necessity from what has been said. But they have written that the rennet of hares cures epileptics if drunk with vinegar, and that it heals the female flux and dissolves milk that has clotted in the belly, which we too have put to the test, not only with hare's rennet alone but also with the rennet of the other animals; the hare's, however, is better than all of them. In the same way, when drunk, it also dissolves blood that is clotting in the belly, the hare's perhaps more than the others, yet not it alone, as some have written; rather, this too is common to all rennet. Some people say that hare's rennet, when drunk, checks the spittings of blood from the chest, but I have neither seen anyone else use it nor have I myself ventured to use a pungent drug for an affection that requires astringency. Horse's rennet they have written to be especially suitable for dysenterics and coeliac patients.

[10.2.12] [12. On the rennet of the seal.] That of the seal they praise as being exceptionally suitable, on the ground that it possesses a power like that of castoreum. But as for what they have written that each of the rennets effects through the special property of its whole substance, this is not the occasion to speak of it.

[10.2.13] [13. On bile.] This humour has been demonstrated to be the hottest of the humours in each animal. Just as, then, animals have blood and flesh of unlike mixture, so by the same reasoning they have bile too. For in the hottest animals the bile too must necessarily exceed the biles of the other animals, while in those less hot than these this humour too must fall short proportionately, by as much as it falls short in the others as well. For you have learned that the humours in each of the blooded animals are in all four: blood, phlegm, and bile both yellow and black. You have also learned that it is the custom not only of physicians but of all Greeks to name yellow bile simply 'bile', on the assumption that those who hear it will supply the name of the colour, but not to name black bile simply 'bile', but with the addition of this whole phrase, 'black bile'. But you also know that they sometimes call yellow bile 'pale yellow', and that in the bladder upon the liver we sometimes see it pale yellow and sometimes yellow in the dissections of animals. You have heard too that the yellow is hotter than the pale yellow by just as much as it is also thicker. For when a serous moisture is mixed with yellow bile the result is that the pale yellow comes about, just as, conversely, the pale yellow, when heated further, is rendered thick in consistency and yellow in colour. And so indeed among animals too it appears yellow in the hotter ones and pale yellow in the less hot. And when the hot animals happen to have gone hungry and thirsty, it turns toward a black colour, having this sometimes verdigris-like, sometimes dark blue, and sometimes the colour of woad, which is duskier than that of cabbage. So you too must attend to the colour of the biles when you prepare a drug in which some bile is also contained. They mix the bile of the bull into the so-called cycliscs and trochiscs, such as that of Andron and of Polyeides and of Pasion and the one of Bitinus. But when they prepare any of the drugs useful for the eyes, [they use that] of hyena and cock and partridge and certain other animals. The bull's bile is obviously hotter and more drying than that of castrated oxen. For the castrated animal is always assimilated to the female and the young. Just as, then, these exceed the mature in moisture but fall short in heat, in the same way the castrated ox falls short of bulls. And in certain bulls I have seen the bile dark blue, the yellow having been over-roasted; this I did not think fit to throw into the drug being prepared, but chose the moderately yellow bile of another bull. For that bull had been excessively distressed, being dragged with violent bonds, so that it is quite clear that, having also become enraged in this struggle, it had acquired a hotter mixture. It is likely too that it was both thirsty and hungry while being violently hauled along. To put it in sum: just as urine appears moderately pale yellow on moderate drinking, but yellow in those who have been thirsty and have abstained from food and have laboured much, and white in those who have been filled and made drunk, so too bile changes its colours, toward the yellower in exercises and fasting and thirst, and toward the whiter in the opposite conditions. Know, then, that if you put into the drug being prepared a bile that is sufficiently yellow, you will make it hotter; if a pale yellow one, moderately hot; and if one that is slack and watery, falling short of the appropriate mixture by as much as the bile too has turned toward the whiter. So too, then, for those who open closed haemorrhoids by means of bull's bile, it has appeared sometimes weak and sometimes pungent beyond what is appropriate. Now some difference arises also from the body that is being treated with the bile, which may be of acute or dull sensation, and readily or hardly affected. But from the bile itself, as I said, the variation is no small one. At any rate the same man is bitten more by yellow bile and less by pale yellow. It is quite clear, then, even from its opening the haemorrhoids, how pungent this humour is; but it also appears biting to those who use it themselves, and for this reason we are wary of using yellow bile alone by itself for any other disease or symptom. For indeed the aforementioned cycliscs take only a little of the bile, and the drugs compounded for sharpness of sight, which take some of them hyena's bile, others that of partridge or cock or some other animal, have honey mixed in, and juice of fennel or opobalsam. The bile of some animals has been especially praised among physicians as both sharpening the sight and at the same time dispersing the beginnings of cataracts, as that of the fish—they call it callionymus—and of the hyena and the sea scorpion and the hen and the partridge. The weakest is that of pigs, to such a degree that it is not unbearable even to ulcers; indeed it appears the most watery of all biles, except for that of wild pigs that live in the mountains. For just as the whole flesh of these is hotter and drier, so too is the bile. Some use the bile of domestic pigs for ulcers in the ears, not a disreputable drug, and you too may use it when none of the compound drugs is at hand, for there are countless of them. According to the magnitude of the condition some other bile of another animal might also be fitting. For when the ulcer is both chronic and contains much ichor and pus, it will tolerate even the more drying biles, such as that of sheep, slightly more pungent than that of pigs, and more than this that of goats, to which that of bears and of oxen is somewhat similar. That of bulls is stronger than these, but falls short of that of hyenas. And this in turn is itself [compared] to that of the callionymus and the sea scorpion and the sea tortoise. Some have written that the bile of the wild goat helps those suffering from night-blindness. The biles of all the winged animals too are more pungent and more drying than those in the quadrupeds, and among the winged ones themselves those of hens and partridges are the better for medical use. Those of hawks and eagles are sufficiently pungent, and are also corrosive, for which reason they also appear verdigris-like in colour, and sometimes even black. Knowing, then, these differences among them, and knowing also which of the affections need to be dried more and which less, if you have tested any one bile whatsoever by its works, you will be able from those to pass over to the others by method, so as always to take up the one fitting the affection. For since the intensity belonging to each power lies in the realm of conjecture, you must pass from some determinate starting-point to the untested material, having learned from what has been tested before the degrees of superiority among them. And I have set out for you clear signs from the colour of the biles and the mixture of the animals.

[10.2.14] [14. On sweat.] Sweat. This too is one of the fluids generated in the body of the animal, having the same matter and the same mode of generation as urine. For the generation of both is from the liquid that is drunk, when it is heated in the body and at the same time takes on something of a bilious substance. But sweat has been worked up to a greater degree, having passed through all the intervening parts as far as the skin. Sweats and urines must, however, necessarily differ from one another in accordance with the mixtures of the animals, which vary from one another both by nature and according to age, and not a little also according to the preceding regimen. It is clear too, even if it is sometimes left unmentioned, that what pertains to the seasons of the year and the present condition of the weather, and further the regions, produces no small difference in the bodies of animals. But for the sake of brevity in the account I am accustomed to embrace all such things under one heading, saying that they vary in accordance with the mixture of the air that surrounds us. For this embraces the differences among regions in respect of heat and cold, just as it does the seasons of the year and the present or the preceding condition. So whenever the discussion is about urines or sweats or blood or fat or suet or any other of the things in the body, when we distinguish the differences among animals, one must understand the discussion as referring to healthy bodies that have the mean condition of their own proper mixture. So too with sweat: that it partakes of the quality called salty and briny, taste bears witness. For sweat, often flowing into the mouth against our will, displays the said quality, and often it also shows along with it a clear bitterness. Its colour too reveals its nature. For just as urine according to nature is moderately pale yellow, so too is sweat. You will readily recognize this in those who bathe, when they are scraped with the strigil without oil. For it collects in the hollow of the strigil, displaying both the colour such as I have described and the taste, having the salty clearly, but the bitter faintly. But about urine the physicians have written even more than is fitting, because it is collected abundantly every day by all men, privately and publicly. About sweats, however, either nothing, or rather some of those over-curious things that border on sorcery. And apart from such things, some have recorded superfluous things that can be accomplished by other medical material. In the wrestling-schools the sweat of those exercising is mixed with the floor-dust (πάτος) — some of those who affect Attic diction over-curiously call it κονίσαλος — and it contributes something to the bare floor-dust toward the dispersing of swellings contrary to nature. For that bare dust has more of the repelling power, but a very faint dispersing one. But after receiving the sweat of those exercising it acquires in addition much of the dispersing power. At any rate, in inflammations of the breasts such floor-dust applied by itself is a quite effective remedy. If it seems to you too dry, smear on henna-oil, and if it is very dry indeed, also soften it up with the henna-oil. It is better, however, to choose not the dry but the soft. If henna-oil is not available, it suffices to mix in good rose-oil. This drug is also quite useful for women who after childbirth choose to quench their milk, when it has, so to speak, curdled in the breasts. Starting from it you can also use it for other similar affections. I myself, at any rate, once used it on a bubo and saw the swelling quickly subside.

[10.2.15] [15. On urine.] Urine. Its whole nature has already been spoken of in the account of sweats. It will be said now too that as great a difference as there is among the biles across the animals, so great a difference is there also among the urines. All are hot in their powers, but more so the urine of the hotter animals, less so that of the colder. On human urine. The urine of a human being is nearly the weakest of all the other urines, except that of domestic swine whose testicles they excise; for the mixture of the whole body of those animals is similar to that of human beings, and their urine is likewise weak. Strong, on the other hand, is that of the boars in the mountains, as is evident also from its smell, which is most pungent. And in the case of all the other animals as well you can recognise its power through the smell; for to taste those urines is most loathsome, seeing that even the urine of boys a man of noteworthy character and life could not bring himself to drink when he fell ill of a pestilential disease in Syria, during which many persons who had drunk urine, some of boys and some of men, seemed to have been saved by this. Human urine, then, is of cleansing power if anything else is, as many show, and the fullers in particular, who clean and wash the dirt from our soiled garments with it.
