The physicians too, having observed this power of it, scour psora and lepra with it and pour it over those ulcers that are full of much moisture and dirt and uncleanness, and much more so when they have something putrefactive about them. They also inject urine into the genitals, when these are so affected, and into ears that run with pus. And they treat achores and pityra (bran-like scales) with it, pouring it over the head. We, however, have felt repugnance at doing these things, being well supplied with other drugs for them. But the ulcers on the toes, and especially those from stumbling, once they have become free of inflammation, I myself have often cured with urine in slaves and rustic men who were setting out on a journey without a physician. For placing a lint-plug upon the ulcer, then wrapping it on the outside with a linen cloth and binding it, I ordered them, whenever they felt the urge to urinate, to let the urine run over the toe and not to undo the bandage until it was completely healed. For I also gave my consent if I learned of anyone else in the country, without a physician, pouring urine over ulcers, when they are in the lower parts from the thorax down to the tips of the feet; but as for the ulcers that arise about the head or on the face, I felt repugnance at allowing anyone to pour urine over these. The drug, however, which is prepared by means of a boy's urine, and which some call chrysocolla, since they use it for the soldering of gold, I say is excellent for ulcers that are hard to heal. It is made with a mortar fashioned in the shape of a bowl out of red copper, having a pestle of the same material, into which, as the boy urinates, the pestle is turned round many times, so as to rub off something not only from the mortar but also from itself; and this is done over several days, until the urine takes on a honey-like consistency. This must be done in the sun; for it is rubbed off from the copper more easily in such air, or, if there is no sun, the room should otherwise be warm. This drug, mixed with the things suitable for the healing of malignant ulcers, we use, as I said, as the best. For it has no loathsomeness, in much the same way as urine poured over the head and about certain other parts. As for actually drinking urine, what could one even say? Some of the physicians, indeed, have written about the thick and white sediment that settles in urine, saying that it cures erysipelas. Now those cases that are still fiery and truly erysipelas no drug among the hot and pungent ones can benefit; but those already cooled by means of cooling agents both this and many other dispersing drugs can help. So it is possible to use this when the erysipelas has formed not about the face or near it, but either on one of the limbs or on the back or the belly. To drink a boy's urine for the sake of the so-called orthopnoea is not necessary, since there are other drugs too which help this affection. And indeed one person who drank it was not freed from the affection, so that it has nothing exceptional compared with the others.

[10.2.16] [16. On saliva.] Saliva, whether one wishes to call it sielon or sialon or ptyelon (spittle), makes no difference to me. But one must know that its power differs both among the species of animals and, in each one of them, according to whether it is healthy or ill, has eaten or drunk, or is without drink and has fasted. For just as the urines and the biles and sweat, so too spittle is weak in those who have eaten, but strong and pungent in those who are excessively thirsty and excessively hungry. Between both lies that of those who have digested well but have not yet eaten or drunk. With this saliva, accordingly, children's nurses also cure lichens, wetting the little finger and then rubbing the affected skin; and they do this frequently, so that in the time between the applications the power from the saliva is preserved in the lichen. But many country people also chew grains of wheat and apply them to boils; for it disperses them and brings them to maturation quickly. And yet if they were moistened with water, they do not help in the same way. It is quite clear, therefore, that the saliva itself furnishes the strength of the benefit. On soft and childish bodies, however, they apply chewed bread, not grains of wheat. All things chewed in this way disperse both bruises beneath the eyes and the other ecchymoses, and more so when the bread is chewed together with a small radish. In its whole substance spittle is most opposed to the beasts that kill human beings, as Nicander the poet also says somewhere. And someone who had promised to show me an incantation that kills scorpions, having said it once, spat upon the scorpion; then, having said it a second time in succession, spat upon it again; then, when he had said it a third time and spat down upon it, the scorpion died. Later, however, without the incantation, I observed the scorpion dying from the saliva alone, and suffering this very thing quickly in the case of the spittle of those who are hungry and thirsty, slowly in the case of those who are filled with foods and drinks, and in the case of the others in proportion.

[10.2.17] [17. On the things generated in the body.] Other things, too, are generated in the body contrary to nature, which it is not seemly to mention; but there is also generated the stone in the bladder, about which some have written, going so far as to say that it breaks up the stones in the bladder. This, then, is false, as has been judged by experience. But whether it breaks up the stones in the kidneys at all, I have not even tested, since I have other approved drugs for this symptom. As for pus and all things of that kind, I leave it to those who are clever at such matters, along with certain sorceries, to speak of them. Dung, however, is one of the things generated in the body when animals are in their natural condition, just as is also the filth in the ears; about each of the two, then, I shall go on to speak in order.

[10.2.18] [18. On dung.] Dung—whether you wish to call it dung (kopros) or excrement (apopatēma) will make no difference. Know that this substance has a most dispersing power. That of human beings is loathsome because of its foul smell. But that of oxen and goats and land crocodiles and dogs, when they have eaten bones, is not foul-smelling, and it has afforded sufficient trial not only to us but also to the others among the physicians before us. Asclepiades, at any rate, the one surnamed Pharmakion, collected all the other compound drugs too, so as to fill many books; and he frequently uses dung for many affections, mixing it not only into the drugs applied from outside, but also into those taken inside by the mouth.

[10.2.19] [19. On dog's dung.] I myself, at any rate, know this too, having made trial of the wondrous power both of human dung and of dog's dung. I shall speak to you first about dog's dung, which one of our teachers used continually, giving a dog nothing but bones to eat for two days in succession, as a result of which the dung becomes hard, white and least of all foul-smelling. Taking this, then, he dried it, so that later, whenever he wished to use it, it could easily be ground fine. He used it for synanche, dysentery and the most long-standing of ulcers. For synanche, then, mixing it with the drugs that are in other respects suitable for this affection; in the case of dysenterics, with milk that had been boiled down, the so-called pebbles (κάχληκες) having been thrown into it red-hot—or, as I later came to use iron because it is easy to procure, throwing this red-hot into milk that had first been well boiled. Some of the physicians, I know not how, call such milk 'split' (σχιστόν); for it was not this that ought to be so called, but those cases in which we separate and split off the whey from the curd-like part. But the physician, having ground the dry dog's dung fine, threw it secretly into the milk which had the pebbles quenched in it, and taught this only to his most genuine pupils. Of these two uses of dog's dung, then, I have very extensive experience, as of a wondrous drug, just as also of its use in the most malignant ulcers. For in those cases too he mixed a little dog's dung with the approved drugs, and the drug plainly became stronger than it had been by itself; and wherever there was need to disperse and dry something, he mixed it with those drugs as well.

[10.2.20] [20. On human dung.] Of human dung I have an experience of the following kind. A certain man was continually and violently troubled by inflammations in the region of the pharynx, so as to be in danger of being suffocated, and indeed on account of this danger he was compelled to be phlebotomised. Someone who met him promised to give him a trial of a drug, and asked that he himself be called before the phlebotomy whenever at some time again one of the parts about his pharynx became inflamed. And so, being called, and then having smeared on a drug, he quickly cured the man. When it had already worked a second time as well, not on him alone but also on others suffering in the same way, the man who was continually in danger of being choked asked, offering a fee, to learn the drug; he was at once wealthy and liberal with regard to the expenditure of money. When they had come to an agreement about the fee, the man who was selling the recipe said that the drug had its benefit by a certain antipathy, and that the antipathy consisted in the patient's not knowing what it was composed of. He therefore bade another learn it in his stead, whoever seemed to him most trustworthy, and that this man, if he was willing, should swear to give the recipe of the drug to no one so long as he himself, the seller, lived. In accordance with this, after the death of the one who revealed it, the one who had learned it cures not only his own man but others also, and to me, though I had not even asked for the recipe of the drug, this man gave it willingly. It was the dry dung of a child, triturated with Attic honey. The child whose dung they were going to take was dieted, just as the man who gave the drug himself showed, on the eating of lupins—these being eaten in the customary way with well-baked oven-bread (klibanites) containing a moderate amount of salt and leaven. He also gave old wine to drink. All these things were moderate in bulk, so that the child digested them exactly well. Having used such a diet on the first day, he did not yet take up the dung on the following day; but on that day, having again dieted the child in the same way, he took what was excreted on the third day, and drying it he used it in a manner similar to dog's dung, as has been said before. He said that the one who had taught him, avoiding the stench arising from other foods, chose lupins, but that he himself, for the sake of trial, had many times fed the child on the flesh of fowl and of partridge well boiled in water or in plain broth, and the drug had worked no less. These things, then, I am able to tell you about dog's and human dung.

[10.2.21] [21. On wolf's dung.] The dung of wolves someone used to give as a drink to colic patients, not only during the paroxysms but also in the intervals—at least those who suffered without inflammation. And I saw some of them no longer seized by the affection, and those who were seized never again strongly affected, not even after a short time. That man too took in preference the whiter dung of wolves, which is excreted when they have eaten bones. I marvelled at him because, even when hung on as an amulet, it often manifestly helped. So this man took dung that had not even fallen upon the ground; and this is not difficult to come by, for that animal has the nature, like the dog, of raising one of its hind legs and urinating and defecating against something projecting from the ground. Thus wolf's dung is often found in the summer season on thorns and on certain shrubs and on bars (κλείθροις) and on well-grown herbs. There is also found in their dung some of the very bones of the devoured animal that have escaped digestion just as they escaped chewing, and this too he pounded and ground fine and gave to the colic patients to drink. And if the person were a man of fastidious cleanliness, he mixed in salt and pepper or some such thing. He gave it for the most part in wine thin in consistency, but sometimes also in water. As for the dung hung on as an amulet, he ordered the sufferer to have on his flanks a pendant, preferably made of wool, and not from just any sheep; for it is much better from one torn apart by a wolf, so as to be suitable for such a use. But if such wool were not at hand, he ordered that the strap wound round the flanks, and the thing itself containing the dung, be of deer's hide. We too, putting some of the dung into a little pot as big as the largest bean, hung it on some people for the sake of trial, and marvelled when we saw most of them manifestly benefited. We made on the little pot two things like ears, through which the strap was passed. This, then, by way of digression, if one is going to put trust also in things hung on in this way—I mean in such a way that what is hung on is a substance, not barbarian names, as some of the sorcerers are accustomed to use—since indeed I have tried other substances too that act similarly in other affections. But now is not the time to speak about them; so let us return again to the matter before us.

[10.2.22] [22. On goat's dung.] For I have mentioned human, dog's and wolf's dung, but not yet that of the other animals, although still more than those mentioned remain, some of them affording a very frequent use, others a rarer one. Most frequently, then, we use the dung of goats—these are specifically called spyrathoi—which is of a pungent and dispersing power, so as to be suitable even for indurating swellings, not of the spleen only, for which many physicians most frequently use such dung, but also of other parts. I myself, then, in the case of a knee that had a chronic swelling hard to resolve, used it in oxykraton (vinegar-and-water), ordering that barley-meal be applied as a plaster with the dung added to it, and the man benefited marvellously. It was one of the country people on whom this was done. And so now another country person too, who used it in the same way for similar swellings, not only at the knee but also at other parts, was benefited. For the drug is too pungent to treat city women or children, or in general the soft-fleshed. But the particular use of all drugs will be spoken of in the work on their composition. And in the case of the dropsical and the splenetic we use goat's dung in many ways. And indeed when burnt it becomes finer-particled, though clearly not more pungent. Hence it is also suitable for alopecia and for everything that requires cleansing drugs, such as lepra and psora and lichens, and all other such things. It is mixed also with dispersing plasters, such as those for parotid swellings and for buboes that have become chronic. For its power, both unburnt and burnt, is cleansing and dispersing, and the dispersing element it has is by no means small. At any rate, for the bites of vipers, and far more still for those of the other venomous creatures, a certain physician, one of those practising in the fields and villages, used it with vinegar and saved a great many. This same physician also gave the spyrathoi to the jaundiced to drink in wine, and used them for the female flux, applying them as a pessary together with frankincense. The best physician ought to know all such things, but to choose the better ones, and especially in the case of city people and men of standing, on whom I would never have used such a drug, having an abundance of very many better ones. Nevertheless, there does arise at times a need even for such things, on journeys and hunts and during a stay in the country, when none of the better ones is at hand, or when the country man is hard-fleshed, like an ass. For many such people in the country are fit to drink spyratha. And what was said also in the preceding about urines and biles and saliva, remember this now too: that the general and common power is the same for all of them, but that it is altered according to the mixtures of the animals. For of animals drier in mixture the dung too is more drying, just as that of hotter ones is more heating; but none cools, just as none moistens. The difference would also be great according to the nature of the things they have eaten, and for this reason it is greater in humans than in the other animals, because this animal uses the most varied food. For what likeness is there between those who have eaten garlic and onions, or gourd, as it may happen? But a goat's spyrathoi would differ a little from one another according to the pastures, yet not so much as those of humans.

[10.2.23] [23. On ox dung.] In the same way the dung of oxen too shows little variation, being itself likewise of a drying power. It also possesses the drawing power, as is shown by its benefiting the bites of bees and wasps. These, however, may also be benefited by virtue of the peculiarity of the whole substance. A certain physician experienced in drugs, in the Mysia on the Hellespont, used to smear the dropsical with ox-dung (βόλβιτον) and lay them down in the sun. This same man also applied it to the inflamed parts of country people, taking it moist in spring, when the oxen graze on the grass. It is quite clear that this kind is much more moderate in its power than the other. By the other I mean that which results from the eating of chaff; for this is intermediate between the one just mentioned and that which results from the feeding on bitter vetch. It is evident, then, that just as the dung from grassy pasture is suitable for inflammations, so this one is suitable for the dropsical. One must know, however, that all such drugs are appropriate for the hard bodies of country people, diggers and reapers and those who perform such heavy labour, on whom the physician in Mysia also used it against scrofulous swellings (χοιράδες) and all scirrhous tumours, applying it as a plaster with vinegar.

[10.2.24] [24. On sheep's dung.] This same man also used the dung of sheep for acrochordons, myrmeciae and thymi, and the hard boils (dothienes) that are called corns (heloi), soaking it in vinegar. But he also brought burn-ulcers to scar, mixing some of this dung with a rose-oil cerate. And indeed by means of that of goats he likewise treated those who had been burned, mixing these too, a very small quantity, with a many-times greater bulk of the cerate. And in general it was his earnest pursuit to treat everything by means of the things readily available in the fields, among which, evidently, are also the herbs and the shrubs and the young shoots of trees and the sprouts and the soft leaves and the fruits and the barks, concerning which more will be said in the work on readily available remedies.

[10.2.25] [25. On the dung of the pigeon.] At any rate, the dung of the pasturing pigeons—for so some people call them, distinguishing them from the domestic ones—I myself too use very constantly for many purposes as a heating drug, applying it, pounded and sifted dry together with kardamon (cress) seed, in place of mustard in those cases that require a phoinigmos (reddening). It is quite clear that I mean all those who have become chronic in such affections as sciatica, hemicrania, skotomata (darkenings of vision) and skotodinoi (dizzy vertigo), kephalaiai (chronic headaches), and the chronic pains in the sides or shoulder-blades or tendon or loins, and in addition to these also nephritic and coeliac conditions and podagric arthritides, whenever there is not yet a formation of poroi (chalk-stones) in their joints. This dung, then, has nothing foul-smelling about it, and especially when it has been dried. For this reason we use it in the cities too in many ways, mixing it now with one drug, now with another.

[10.2.26] [26. On the dung of hens.] As for the dung of hens, having seen the physician in Mysia using it on those being choked by the eating of mushrooms, I too used it on certain persons in the city who had partaken of them, in all cases ground fine in three or four cyathi of oxykraton and oxymel, and it manifestly helped them quickly. For a little later those being choked vomited a very thick phlegmatic humour, upon which they were completely freed of the symptom. This dung is less hot than that of pigeons. The physician in Mysia also gave the dung of hens to chronic colic patients to drink in honeyed wine; and if this was not available, in vinegar or in wine mixed with water. You must bear in mind the general account concerning all animals, that both in respect of what is contained in their bodies, liquids and solids alike, and in respect of their parts, there is a very great difference between those called mountain animals and those in plains and marshes and lakes and in the house. For always those that take exercise are drier than those that take no exercise, and those that use drier and hotter foods than those that use moister and colder ones. In the case of pigeons, at any rate, because of my continual use of the dung, I always found that of those reared in houses falling very far short of that of the mountain, free-ranging ones. I found too that of hens much weaker—namely that of those shut up and fed on bran—but stronger by no small degree in those in the fields, feeding in the farmyards and outside them.

[10.2.27] [27. On the dung of geese and storks.] The dung of geese is useless because of its great pungency; and I reckon that of hawks and eagles is also. But the difficulty of procuring all such material is in itself something to be avoided. Taking their start precisely from this, some people testify all the more to strong powers in materials of this kind, since they will not easily be refuted, like those who have written that the dung of storks cures epileptics. But this, although it happens to be far easier to procure than many of the other things they write about, is nevertheless superfluous, in addition to the fact that what has been written about it is not even true. At any rate, someone who was persuaded by those who write such things and drank some of this dung gained no benefit. Indeed, even before trial, those who write these things reveal the worthlessness of what they promise. For since people have difficulty in breathing in many ways, they add in their account neither what suits all of them nor what suits these particular ones or this one. Some, to be sure, of those who have written say that such things are remedies not for difficulty of breathing simply, but for orthopnoea—stork's dung and owl's blood and human urine and other things more absurd than these—not knowing that a phlegmatic and viscous humour blocking the bronchia of the lung becomes the cause of this affection, and that the cure lies in evacuating it, and that its evacuation comes about with its being coughed up along with a cough, and that this cannot happen unless a rather pungent drug has been drunk many times. But these people are so full of nonsense, or are charlatans, or I know not what to call them, that they say that each of these absurd drinks, once drunk, frees the sufferers from their difficulty of breathing—a thing which, not even if someone were able to insert a probe into the lung and through it remove the humour plastered on, would have been accomplished at a single attempt. It would therefore have been better for them to say not that this particular blood or urine cures difficulty of breathing if it be drunk [once], but if it be drunk [habitually]; and better still, that it will not cure wholly and in every case, not even if it be drunk continuously, but that it has cured many, and many it has benefited, yet without completely freeing them from the disease. But let us now leave these people and go on to the continuation of the argument. For since every dung has the pungent and dispersing quality, it is according to the more and the less in one's having this power than another that the particular differences among them arise, and for this reason some treat this particular affection more, others that one.

[10.2.28] [28. On the dung of mice.] Thus, at any rate, they have also written that the droppings of mice cure alopecia, and there was a certain physician who used, for this affection, the compound drug prepared with the dung of mice. And another ordered a suppository to be prepared with the dung of mice, to be applied to a child in need of its natural evacuation (τῶν οἰκείων), at which all who heard laughed, that, when there are so many things which, applied to the seat, rouse the bowel to excretion, that man passed over all of them and came to the dung of mice. For one may truly be ashamed of such things, and of bringing them to the test, since everyone condemns as a meddler and a charlatan whoever does and says these things. Concerning the dung of mice, then, these remarks too are sufficient.

[10.2.29] [29. On the dung of land crocodiles and of starlings.] The dung of these land crocodiles, the small ones that creep along the ground, luxurious women have made a thing of high esteem, women for whom it will not suffice to render the skin about the face bright and taut with the other drugs, numerous as they are, but they add to these also the dung of crocodiles. Similar to it becomes also that of starlings, when they eat rice alone. It is quite clear, then, that such dungs have a cleansing and a drying power, each of them moderate, and those of starlings are far more moderate and fainter. The dung of crocodiles, however, just as it is of a nature to remove the ephelis of the face, so also is able to take away alphoi and lichens.

[10.2.30] [30. On the dirt of human beings.] Dirt is generated not only over the whole skin of the body, but also in the ears; yet because of its small quantity it is hard to procure, and for this reason they have written nothing about it, except that the dirt from the ear suits paronychiae—which is indeed the only kind that can be taken by itself. For the dirt that accumulates on the whole skin is scoured off in the baths and the wrestling-schools, itself too contributing something to what is called patos, about which we have spoken before. Its generation also reveals its nature. For if dirt is the coarse-particled and earthy residue of what is evacuated through the imperceptible transpiration, it is of a drying power, having also something of heat. The dirt, however, that accumulates on the wool of sheep, from which they make what is called oesypum, is of a concocting power, similar to butter; and it has also something slightly dispersing. Galen, On the Mixture and Power of Simple Drugs, Book 11. Proem. Most of the parts in animals are common to all of them, but none is so common as flesh; for every animal has this: blooded flesh in the case of man and all quadrupeds and birds, snakes and lizards and tortoises and other such creatures, and without blood all the shellfish and not a few of the water-dwelling animals, just as also of those in the earth itself. And what is eaten of animals is chiefly the flesh; for indeed the greater bulk of the viscera too is made up of the flesh in them. Some physicians call the flesh in these parenchyma, because the blood poured out from the veins congeals around all the vessels, as they suppose, and they give the name flesh only to that in the muscles. About names, as we always say, one should not quarrel, but one must practise the knowledge of the things themselves; and since we lay claim to this throughout, all that we know about the parts, both peculiar and common, of each animal—some things taught by experience, others by reason—we shall state in order, making our beginning from what is properly called flesh.

[9.1.1] On earths. [1. On the differences of earth.] Since two things are signified by the name 'earth', it is necessary first to distinguish them for the sake of clarity in what is to be said. One of them is familiar to all the Greeks. For both when they sow wheat or barley or any of the other seeds which are called Demetrian, they say the earth must be moderately moist; and when they plant vines or fig-trees or olives or any of the other trees, they bid one guard against both the earth that is extremely devoid of moisture and dry, and that which is moist and muddy. For indeed they call earth that has been kneaded with liquid 'mud', and those who have written on agriculture, in the differences of lands, speak of black-soiled, clayey and sandy as distinguished. They also call 'oily' the earth from which the mud becomes viscous, and another, disposed in the opposite way to this, non-oily and producing, as one might say, a crumbly mud. This, then, is one signification of the name 'earth', familiar to all. The other belongs to the philosophers alone, since they say that the elements of bodies are earth and water and air and fire. For they call the body that is extremely dry and cold 'earth'. According to them, then, none of these composite bodies is the elemental earth, yet they say that they have the greatest share of earth, such as adamant and rocks, and the harder they are in body, the more earthy they say they are — the reverse of the farmers. For the latter do not call the harder consistency of bodies more earthy, but call such things stones and rocks, most unsuitable for farming; and they say that the most exact earth is that which is furthest in consistency from rock, seeing that they even find fault with the clayey and the sandy for most purposes. According to the signification among the philosophers, then, the differences of earth will be defined by three genera: for one part of it is stone, another a mined body, and the third the cultivated earth — a disagreement having arisen among them concerning the mined bodies that are poured (fusible), such as copper and tin and lead; for some people say that these have the greater share not of earth but of water. All other men, however, call 'earth' only that substance which, when kneaded with liquid, becomes mud. It is about this that I too have now resolved to state the differences, adding only this further, that the aforesaid division of earthy bodies into stones, mined things and cultivated earth has been stated apart from the bodies that are properly called 'natural'. If these are added, all woods too, and many parts of fruits, as also of animals, will be named earthy in substance: parts of fruits — the stones of olives and the pips of grapes and the shells of nuts and of pine-cones, and many others of this kind; of animals, the bones and the horns and the teeth. But concerning the parts in plants that are earthy and hard, something has been said before, and something may be said now as well; concerning those in animals it will be said next in order, after I have first gone through the kinds of earth. For you may call them both differences and kinds and genera. I mean by these stones and the mined bodies and the earth that dissolves into mud; and first I shall state the differences of the earth so named by all the Greeks, which has in common that, on coming near water, it dissolves immediately and becomes mud. For that which is so called among the philosophers has its signification not common to all, but familiar to those alone.

[9.1.2] [2. On the differences of the earth that is customarily so named.] I said that all Greeks customarily give the name "earth" to that which, when it is thrown into liquid, is at once dissolved and becomes mud. Of this, then, one kind is that which men cultivate, having certain differences in its own right (κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον λόγον), in being oily and viscous—a kind which is in every case also black in colour—while the other is more crumbly and non-oily, which they call argil, this too being in some degree whiter. These differences are the most opposed; the others lie between these, either approaching more nearly to the one or to the other, and some seem to be exactly in the middle, standing at an equal distance from both. There are also differences of earth that arise from admixture of bodies of a different kind, insofar as they are stony and sandy; and they separate the mixed-in substance from such earths by soaking and kneading them with much water, until they make the whole liquid. For when this settles, all the stony and sandy matter carried in it sinks to the bottom, while the exact earth floats above. For something of this sort happens also in the case of the Lemnian earth, which some call Lemnian miltos and certain others Lemnian seal, because of the seal sacred to Artemis which is impressed upon it. For the priestess, taking this earth with a certain local honour—not with animals being sacrificed, but with wheat and barley given in return to the place—conveys it to the city, and having kneaded it with water and made a liquid mud and stirred this violently, then having let it settle, she first removes the water on the surface, then, taking the oily part of the earth beneath it and leaving behind only the stony and sandy matter that has settled, which is indeed useless, she dries the oily mud to such a degree until it comes to the consistency of soft wax, and taking small portions of this she impresses upon them the sacred seal of Artemis, and then again dries them in the shade until it is rendered exactly free of moisture, and this becomes the drug known to all physicians, the Lemnian seal. For so some name it, as I said, because of the seal impressed upon it, just as some also, because of its colour, call it Lemnian miltos. It has, then, the same colour as miltos, but differs from it in not staining when it is touched, as that one does, and also in respect of the hill in Lemnos, which is wholly tawny in colour, on which there is neither tree nor rock nor plant, but only earth of this sort. Three differences of it are found: one, the aforesaid, of the sacred earth, which no one else touches except the priestess; a second, different one, of the true miltos, which the carpenters especially use; and a third, of the cleansing (ῥυπούσης) kind, which those of the washers of linens and garments who so wish use. Having read in Dioscorides and certain others that goat's blood is mixed with the Lemnian earth, and that from the mud produced by this mixture the priestess moulds and seals what they call Lemnian seals, I desired myself to investigate the proportion of the mixture. Just as, then, I travelled to Cyprus for the sake of the mines in it, and to Coele Syria, which is a part of Palestine, for the sake of asphalt and certain other things in it worth investigating, so too I did not hesitate to sail to Lemnos, intending to see how much of the blood is mixed with the earth. And on the second occasion of coming from Asia to Rome, travelling on foot through Thrace and Macedonia, I sailed first from Alexandria Troas to Lemnos, having found a ship putting out for Thessalonica, the ship-master having agreed to put in first at Lemnos; and he did put in, but not at the city where he should have. For at the start I did not even know that there were two cities on the island, but supposed that, like Samos and Chios and Cos and Andros and Tenos and all the islands in the Aegean, so too Lemnos had a single city bearing the same name as the whole island. But when I disembarked from the ship, I learned that the city was called Myrina, and that the hill was neither in connection with Philoctetes nor in connection with the temple of Hephaestus in the territory of that city, but in the other, called Hephaestias, and that that city was not even near Myrina; and since the ship-master could not wait for me, I deferred to a later time, when I should come from Rome to Asia, the viewing of Hephaestias. And this was accomplished for me, just as I hoped and proposed. For when, having crossed from Italy to Macedonia and having travelled through almost the whole of it, I arrived at Philippi, which is a city bordering on Thrace, going down from there to the nearby sea, which is a hundred and twenty stades distant, I sailed first to Thasos, somewhere near two hundred stades, from there to Lemnos seven hundred, then again from Lemnos the same seven hundred to Alexandria Troas. And for this reason I have deliberately written about the voyage and the stades, so that if anyone wishes to see Hephaestias himself just as I did, knowing its position, he may thus prepare for the voyage. For in the whole island of Lemnos, Hephaestias lies in the part toward the east and Myrina in the part toward the west. And what is said by the poet about Hephaestus, "he fell in Lemnos," seems to me to have set up (ἐπίστασθαι) the myth because of the nature of the hill. For it appears most like something burnt, both in colour and because nothing grows on it. To this hill, then, the priestess came, at the time when I set foot on the island, and casting a certain number of grains of wheat and barley onto the earth and performing certain other acts in accordance with the local reverence, she filled a whole wagon with the earth. And having conveyed it to the city, as I said just now, she prepared the much-talked-of Lemnian seals. It seemed good to me, then, to inquire whether they had ever before received in their tradition any account of goat's or she-goat's blood being mixed with this earth. At this inquiry all who heard laughed, being not ordinary men but very well educated both in other matters and in the whole local history. But I also received a book from one of them, written earlier by one of the local men, in which he taught the whole use of the Lemnian earth, whence I too did not hesitate to make trial of the drug, taking twenty thousand seals. And the man himself who gave the book, being counted among the first men of Hephaestias, used the drug for many purposes. For both on wounds, old ones and those hard to cicatrize, and on viper-bites and in general bites of venomous animals, and in cases of deadly drugs, giving it not only beforehand but also afterwards, he used the seal. He said also that he had experience of the drug made with juniper berries, into which Lemnian earth also is put, which provokes vomiting, if someone drinks the protective remedy while the deadly drug is still in the belly. But of this we too have experience in the case of the sea-hare and cantharides, when people suspected that they had taken something of this sort, and immediately vomited everything upon the drug made with the Lemnian seal, and afterwards suffered none of the symptoms that follow sea-hare and cantharides, even though the administration of the deadly drugs was proved. But whether against the other deadly drugs, those called deleterious, the drug made with juniper berries and Lemnian earth has the same power, is unclear to me. The man from Hephaestias went so far as to declare that it even cures the bite of a mad dog, when drunk in diluted wine and applied to the ulcer in very pungent vinegar. But with vinegar he said it cures also the bites of the other venomous creatures, with leaves of herbs applied externally, which we have learned to be opposed to putrefactions. He praised most of all scordium, then the slender centaury, then horehound. On malignant and putrefactive ulcers at any rate, whenever I used the Lemnian earth, it helped greatly. The use is in accordance with the magnitude of the badness of the ulcer. For the foul-smelling and very flabby and dirty ulcer admits the Lemnian earth dissolved in very pungent vinegar to a muddy consistency, in the same way as the troches, of which different people use different ones—I mean those of Polyeides and Pasion and Andron, and this one now mentioned, called Betinos. For all these, drying strongly, benefit the malignant ulcers, being diluted sometimes with sweet wine, sometimes with boiled-down must, sometimes with honeyed wine, sometimes with some of the white wines or the tawny or the yellow, as the need may command. For these matters will be distinguished elsewhere. Likewise they are also sometimes diluted with vinegar, and with wine or water or oxymel, or with vinegar-and-water and honey-and-water. And the Lemnian earth, diluted with each of the things mentioned, is a suitable drug both for the agglutination of fresh wounds and for the cure of chronic or hard-to-cicatrize or malignant ulcers. And likewise all the other medicinal earth. For it will be necessary to distinguish, just as earlier we distinguished from the elemental earth—in which stones too were included—the earth that is dissolved into mud, so now from the cultivated earth the medicinal. For it is no worse to name thus that which we use for treatments, although even of the cultivated earth the oily kind is useful for the treatment of all parts that need to be dried; whence in Alexandria and Egypt many use it by their own choice, many as a result of dreams. At any rate I saw at Alexandria some dropsical and splenetic people using the mud of Egyptian earth. And many, anointing their shins and thighs and forearms and upper arms and backs and sides and chests with the mud of this earth, were clearly benefited. In the same way this mud benefits old inflammations and the loose kinds of oedema, so that I know some who had become swollen in their whole habit as a result of immoderate evacuation from haemorrhoids who were manifestly benefited. And some completely cured chronic pains fixed in some part with this mud; for all earth has a drying power, since by nature its body is dry, and when it is exactly unmixed with fiery substance, it dries without the least biting; and its having been washed contributes to this.

[9.1.3] [3. On the washing of earth.] All earth is washed in the same manner as that previously described for the Lemnian: first it is kneaded up with water that has no indication of any medicinal quality; then, when the mud has settled and the water has been removed from above, next that which lies beneath it is separated from the stony and sandy matter settling at the bottom. And if you have a trained gustatory sense, you yourself will be an accurate judge of which earth needs to be washed and which does not. For some do not need washing, while some need to be washed twice or three times. The Lemnian, then, you receive ready, washed once by the priestess, and not needing to be washed a second time.

[9.1.4] [4. On Samian earth.] Samian earth does not even need to be washed. We use rather the one of its two kinds which they also call the Samian star, for spittings of blood, from whatever source they happen to arise, just as we use the Lemnian seal. By the same power they also help haemorrhages from the womb and the so-called female flux, and indeed also dysenteric ulcerations before the ulcers become putrefactive; it is the custom of physicians to call such conditions nomai, from the putrefaction 'grazing' (nemesthai) upon the neighbouring parts, destroying them along with the part first damaged. I have sometimes used the Lemnian earth too in such cases, and it clearly did good both when injected through the seat and when drunk, the ulcers having first been washed out, as we are accustomed to do, first with a fairly undiluted melikraton, and second with brine. It was injected, then, in juice of plantain, and it was drunk in watery oxykraton (vinegar-and-water). The Lemnian earth appears to have a power not a little more active than the Samian, which is why parts that have already become inflamed do not tolerate its power, but are plainly made rough, and most of all when the person is soft-fleshed. Whereas by the Samian earth not only is none of the parts in such a state exacerbated, but it is actually soothed, and most of all the hotter and more flaccid parts, such as the breasts and the testicles and the glands. In such a case you would use this sort of earth suitably if, after grinding it fine in water, you mix in as much good rose oil as will, once mixed in, not allow the drug to dry out. What is prepared in this way is good also for the other inflammations that are hot, and for incipient buboes and gouty fluxes, and in general wherever we wish to cool moderately while soothing, so that the power of the Samian earth is manifestly shown to be moderately cooling. Its substance is also somewhat more airy when compared with the Lemnian, as its lightness shows. By these marks, then, test every other medicinal earth as well. By marks I mean the lightness and heaviness in its consistency, and the roughness and smoothness in its taste, and in addition the glutinous and the cleansing quality. For the Samian star is glue-holding and viscous, the Lemnian seal also having a little of this sort of quality. Both Selinusian and Chian earth have a cleansing power, and a moderate one, which is why some women use them on the face. It has been shown in the third book of the Method of Healing that everything that is slightly cleansing is suited to the fleshing-over of ulcers, and if it dries, it is also good for cicatrization; and the most suitable of these for superficial ulcers and burns are those which, in addition to drying without biting, neither heat nor cool perceptibly. Hence Selinusian and Chian earth are the finest drugs for burn ulcers; for these require drugs that cleanse most moderately without conspicuous warming or cooling, which is the case with Selinusian and Chian and Samian earth. It has been said that the so-called star is also a kind of the latter, surpassing the other earth in having something viscous and glutinous, which is why neither for other ulcers nor for burns is it a match for the others, those at least which do not have the glutinous quality. For the glutinous quality makes the substance more clogging, so that it does not cleanse, at least whenever no other pungency is present in addition to the viscous and glutinous body, as there is in bird-lime. Chian and Selinusian earth, however, fall short of the Samian for incipient inflammations about the breasts and testicles and groins. Nevertheless they are not unsuitable, when nothing else of those that act perfectly is at hand. Cimolian earth, being of mixed power, has something cooling, but also something slightly dispersing; hence when washed it lays this aside, while without being washed it acts by both powers, just as many other compound drugs do which both disperse and repel. And according to the nature of the liquids mixed with it, it manifestly displays each of its two powers. For mixed with repellent and cooling liquids it renders the mud produced from itself and them cooling and repellent, and with dispersing ones it renders it dispersing as well. In this way, at any rate, it also suits burns, and some laymen smear it on, having kneaded it on the spot with vinegar. In such use the vinegar should not be too pungent; and if it should be so, it is better to mix water with it. Remember, however, that this is common to every light earth: for all of them benefit burns when smeared on at once with vinegar or oxykraton, preventing them from blistering. In this one must look also to the nature of the body being treated, whether it is soft or hard, always knowing this as a general principle, that soft bodies do not tolerate the power of strong drugs, whereas hard bodies tolerate it. These matters, however, are not proper to the present treatise; for they will be spoken of at greater length both in the books on the composition of drugs and in those on readily available remedies. The present exposition has from the beginning striven to discover the general powers of drugs, attending to which a person will have very ample resources for their particular use, provided of course he has learnt in addition the method of using them; so that it is no longer fitting to prolong matters, but, as was said before, to recall now too that earth itself, unmixed with any other substance of a different kind, is of a drying power without biting. But since it is impossible to find any body that is exactly unmixed, it is fitting to examine in addition the admixture of what has come to be attached to it, according to the differences in lightness and heaviness and those in taste. For if it has some suggestion of astringency, it has taken on as much coldness as astringency; and if some pungency should appear, it has as much heat as pungency. One must consider in the same way in the case of light and heavy earth: the light earth becoming such whenever it partakes of abundant airy substance in the mixture throughout its whole self, while the heavy, the more it is such, by so much the more is a purer earth. It is a property of earth not to melt when it comes near fire, which lead and tin, silver and gold do have; so that when you hear of a silver-earth or gold-earth or iron-earth—for some so name those taken from the mines—do not suppose that the silver or the gold or the iron is blended through and through with the earth, but that small particles lie near small particles of the earth, mixed in with them, of gold in the gold-earth, of silver in the silver-earth, of iron in the iron-earth, and that these, being melted by the fire in the furnaces, come together with one another. In the same way the earth that contains glass is sandy, for it is in sand especially that small grains of this kind of substance are often found. And those experienced in these matters, on seeing such sands, recognize how much glass they can gather from them; and many small grains of gold are found in certain sands, but those who occupy themselves with these things do not extract the gold and the glass from every sand, choosing, of course, those which yield the most at little expense, since to spend a great deal in the furnaces and obtain a trifle of the substance collected seems to them unprofitable. For this reason, then, although many sands contain grains of gold and glass, those skilled in these matters do not go to all of them. By the same reasoning they do not pick out copper or silver or iron or tin or lead from every earth. Nor indeed, when they separate each of the things mentioned from the earth mixed with it, is the residue like the other earths, which I said are customarily so named by all Greeks, having as a common mark that they are soaked through and easily dissolve into mud. For the residue of the earth in the mines becomes stony, unmeltable and not to be soaked through. By 'being soaked through' I mean being moistened through the whole substance, and by 'being wetted' being moistened on the outer surface alone, the moisture not penetrating to its depth. Thus too the mined cadmia is produced, being stony and not to be soaked through. But about such bodies we shall speak in due course; now I shall return again to medicinal earth, which, because it readily dissolves into mud when soaked in water, is for this reason named earth, and because we have need of it as of other drugs, for this reason might reasonably be called pharmakitis. And yet some call only the so-called ampelitis earth pharmakitis, either as being the only one of this kind or as having the medicinal power more effectively, which is indeed true. It is named ampelitis not because it is better to plant vines in it, but because, smeared around the vines, it destroys the worms that breed on them, which the vine-dressers in our country call sknipes. These are bred when spring sets in, when the vines sprout, and especially the swelling part of them from which the shoot grows, which they call the eye. By eating through these eyes, then, the sknipes do no small harm to the vines, which is why those skilled in these matters smear the roots of these eyes. On this account, then, such earth is called both ampelitis and pharmakitis, showing from its destruction of the sknipes too how much medicinal power it possesses. It stands far apart also from the other kinds of earth which we use for cures, coming already near to the stony. Hence you will find it mixed in the prescriptions of drugs where it is fitting to dry and disperse something. For it does not have the non-biting, moderate and soothing quality like the Chian and Samian and Selinusian. Of the Cimolian also it has been said before that it is slightly stronger than these, but still non-biting itself too, and especially if it has been washed. The Cretan earth too is somewhat like these, but it is quite weak, having much of the airy, yet it has the cleansing quality, which is why people brighten dirty silverware with it; so that you might have this too for the purpose for which we have said before that the others which cleanse without biting are suitable. Of all these the Lemnian has a stronger power, for there is present in it also something of astringency, and the Eretrian a still stronger one than this, though not so as actually to bite. And if it is washed too, it becomes quite moderate, like those mentioned before. It is possible for this earth to be washed not once but even two or three times, as also the Cimolian. And indeed some also burn it, making it evidently more fine-particled and more pungent, so that it passes over into the dispersing power. And if, having been burnt, it is washed, leaving the pungency behind in the water but keeping the fine-particled quality from the roasting, it becomes more drying. Hence, whereas unburnt earth of every kind is, by the common account, useful for ulcers, that which has been washed after being burnt is even more so, and is useful also for ulcers that are hard to flesh over and hard to cicatrize. There being two kinds of it, the one ash-coloured in hue is better than the very white. There is also another earth called pnigitis, resembling the Cimolian in its whole power but differing in colour, for it is black, like the ampelitis, and it has the viscous and glutinous quality no less than Samian earth, but sometimes even more. There was also given to us, in this great plague, another earth from the part of Armenia bordering on Cappadocia, more drying, yellowish-ochre in colour; the one who gave it called it a stone, not an earth, and it is extremely smooth, like lime too—I so name, obviously, burnt rock. But just as nothing sandy is carried along in that, so neither in the Armenian; for after being broken up with the pestle in the mortar it is as smooth and stone-free as lime and the Samian star, though not equally light with the star. Hence it is also more compact than it and less airy, and for this reason gives those who look at it more carelessly the impression of being a stone. It makes no difference for present purposes whether one calls it a stone or an earth, knowing that it dries in the highest degree. For in dysenteries and fluxes of the belly, and spitting of blood and catarrh, and in addition putrefactive ulcers in the mouth, it is most suitable. And indeed it greatly benefits those who suffer fluxes from the head into the chest, so that it also strongly helps those who are continually short of breath for such a cause. And indeed those who labour under consumption—these too it benefits. For it dries their ulcer, so that they no longer even cough, unless they should err considerably in their regimen or the surrounding air should suddenly fall into a bad mixture. And it seems to me that, just as we have often observed in the case of fistulas, not only in other parts but also at the seat, that without inserting a collyrium that removes the filth or the callus from the fistula, by the drying drug alone they are brought together and closed, so it happens also in the case of the ulcer in the lung. For this too appears to be benefited in like manner by drying drugs, whenever it is moderate and not very large; so that some of those who had them thought they had been completely rid of them, and of those who travelled from Rome to Libya for such a cause some were completely persuaded that they were healthy, and for some years passed their lives without complaint, and then at some later time, when they had lived a less guarded regimen, a relapse of the disease occurred. These, then, as I said, the bole from Armenia manifestly helped, even though they were living in Rome, and still more those continually short of breath. And in this great plague, which is similar in form to the one that occurred in Thucydides' time, all who drank this drug were cured quickly, while all those whom it did not benefit died, nor were they helped by anything else; from which it is clear that it failed to help only those who were in an incurable state. It is drunk with wine thin in consistency, moderately mixed if the person is entirely free of fever or feverish only slightly, but quite watery if he is more strongly feverish. Nor indeed are the pestilential fevers violent in their heat. As for ulcers that need to be dried, what need is there even to say how great a power this Armenian bole has? You may call it, as I said, both a stone, as the one who gave it named it, and an earth, as I would say, since it is also soaked through by liquids.

[9.2.1] On stones. [1. On the active qualities of stones.] Among the naturally occurring bodies are also the stones, which differ from what is customarily called earth in that they are not soaked through. They have powers, some in virtue of the peculiar character of their whole substance, others in virtue of their active qualities; how these differ from one another has been stated earlier. Now, then, let our account be of those which act in virtue of their active qualities, in which there also lies the method of their actual use. For the powers in virtue of the peculiar character of the whole substance were shown to be without method and without reason, and to be known by experience alone. For why this stone, on touching a haemorrhaging wound, checks the flow we do not know; but why they put the stone called haematites into ophthalmic remedies we do know, for such a thing is a discovery of reason. If, at any rate, having rubbed it down on an ophthalmic whetstone with water to the thickness of honey, you choose to taste it, you will perceive an astringent power. And you have learned that inflammations that are still increasing, and especially those in sinewy parts, must be repelled with astringent drugs; but when the blood no longer flows into the part, one should mix the discutient drugs with the astringent ones, and little by little pass over to the former alone. We shall speak, then, about such powers in stones, having first recalled what we went through at greatest length in the writings against those who censure people who commit solecisms in speech. For some of these do not permit one to say lithos in the masculine, but if you say "throw ton lithon at the dog", they shriek as though they themselves had been struck on the head with a stone; just as, if someone says ton dryn ("the oak") in the masculine, they cry out as though he had struck them with a piece of wood. If, then, someone, obeying them, remodels the names customary among physicians, saying hē lithos hē haimatitis and hē pyritis and hē galaktitis and hē schistē, he will be condemned as fussy and as using counterfeit terms, since all, from a custom already of long standing, name their varieties in the masculine: haematites, pyrites, galactites, melitites, gagates, schistos, Phrygian, Arabian, Memphite. Conversely they say hē petra ("rock") in the feminine, not ho petros in the masculine. Thus they name it Asian petra, not Asios petros, but Asian lithos (ton lithon Asion). So too "flower of Asian petra", and they say that lime comes from burnt petra. Heraclides of Tarentum, however, and certain others say that lime comes not from every stone but only from petra, naming in this way, par excellence, one of the stones, the hardest. I, at any rate, am accustomed deliberately, varying the names, to say all such things in both ways—things about which some people dispute uselessly—showing in practice that the clarity of the expression is in no way harmed, whichever way one says it. And it is no wonder that those who do not know that clarity must be posited as either the one and only virtue of natural expression, or at any rate the first and best of all the others, turn aside into such nonsense. I shall speak, then, first about those stones which, when rubbed on mortars or whetstones, dissolve into a juice.

[9.2.2] [2. On haematites, galactites and melitites.] One among stones of this kind is also the one called haematites, so named from its resemblance in colour, just as also the galactites, since that one too, when dissolved into a juice, appears similar to milk. And the melitites, which produces a juice resembling it in colour, has been so named from its resemblance in taste. Now it has been shown in the fourth of these commentaries that every sweet juice becomes such through a moderate heat, while the astringent one does so through cooling. Accordingly the haematites stone will have as much of coldness as it has of astringency, the melitites a moderate heat, and the galactites a mixture intermediate between both. Reasonably, then, physicians have ventured to mix the haematites stone into ophthalmic medicaments. And you may use it by itself as well when the eyelids have become rough: if they have become so together with inflammation, making the dilution with egg, or better still with a decoction of fenugreek; if without inflammation, with water. Always begin from a moderately liquid form, pouring it in by means of the probe; but when you see that it tolerates its power, make it ever thicker and more so. And in the end you will make it so thick as to anoint with the tip of a probe, with the eyelid turned under or turned out. This same stone, rubbed down in the same way on a whetstone, is suited to spittings of blood and to all ulcers. Ground dry so as to become powdery, it reduces overgrowths of flesh. No one, however, uses it alone by itself. But I have used it in the cases I have mentioned, having discovered its power from its quality in respect of taste, and then wishing to test by experience whether I had inferred rightly. And the very ulcers on the eyes it alone brings to cicatrization, being rubbed down, as I said a little before, and either instilled or applied beneath the lid as a salve. For I tested this too by experience.

[9.2.3] [3. On schistos and many other stones.] The stone called schistos has a power similar to this stone but weaker, and after it the galactites. The melitites, as I said, has already taken on something of heat as well. Each of them, then, departing little by little from the power of the haematites, is brought into use for the eyes in the same way, but is milder; and milder drugs are always gentler for parts that are still inflamed, but weaker, for parts whose inflammation has subsided, with respect to healing them completely. Since drying is common to all stones, those of them which, whether dissolved into a juice or otherwise ground fine, have at the outset no quality upon tasting, these one must consider to be the weakest, the gentlest and the least biting. But those which appear to display some distinct quality upon tasting have a strength proportionate to the quality: if they are astringent, toward repressing, constricting, compacting and drawing together; if biting, toward heating, dispersing and melting; and intermediate between these are those which only cleanse, without being astringent or biting. Now the haematites and the schistos, the galactites and the melitites are dissolved into a juice when rubbed, as I said, on whetstones and in mortars, there being also other stones that are dissolved into a juice, such as this one produced in Egypt, which they use for glossing linen cloths. It is more devoid of quality than those mentioned, exhibiting neither astringency nor cleansing nor biting. Hence this alone belongs to this stone, namely drying, and for this reason, mixing it with cerate, they use it for the cicatrization of ulcers on soft bodies. It is also mixed into ophthalmic preparations in the same way as those mentioned before. But to the degree that it is more softening than they, because it has no active quality, to that degree it is more moderate and less perceptible. Some people call this stone moroxos, others graphis.

[9.2.4] [4. On the thyites of Dioscorides.] Of all the stones that have been mentioned, the one brought from Ethiopia has a stronger power; it is somewhat greenish, being named as though it were iaspis. This stone, when dissolved into a juice milky in colour, is biting to those who taste it, and for this reason no one has mixed it into ophthalmic preparations, neither those repelling fluxes nor those curative of ulcers, but only for the purging and cleansing of the things that, without inflammation, cast a shadow over the pupils, among which are also the fresh scars, which it is of a nature to thin. It also cleanses away those of the pterygia that are not very hard.

[9.2.5] [5. On the Judaic stone.] There is also another stone, stronger in its power, which occurs in Palestinian Syria, white in colour, well-proportioned in its shape and having lines as though made by a lathe. They name it, after the country in which it is naturally produced, Judaic, and they use it against the stones in the bladder, dissolving it on a whetstone and giving it to drink in three cyathi of hot water. For our part, in the cases in which we tried it, it accomplished nothing as regards the stones in the bladder, but against those that form in the kidneys it is active.

[9.2.6] [6. On pyrites.] One of those possessing a strong power is also the stone called pyrites, which we use by mixing it into a dispersing plaster. The schistos is also added to it. By this drug pus (πτύον) has often been dispersed, but also a clotted mass that had formed in the spaces between the muscles. All stones must be pounded and ground very fine indeed whenever they are brought into use, in the same way as those mixed into ophthalmic powers. For if they are not rendered dust-fine, so as to sink into the depth of the bodies to which they are applied, they will remain similar to these sea and river sands, which themselves too possess the power common to all stones. At any rate they dry the somewhat swollen and dropsical flesh, when the sick lie down in them after they have been heated. We do not, however, use them for anything else, as we use the aforementioned stones for ophthalmic powers and for those that staunch blood and the female flux, and further as an agglutinating remedy for ulcers, and as a scarring and flesh-forming one. For those of them that are not pungent are all useful for these purposes, just as the pungent ones, which I mentioned later, are useful for cleansing and scouring and removing, for thinning and dispersing and strongly drying and melting.

[9.2.7] [7. On phrygios.] The stone called phrygios also partakes of this power. I have always used it burnt, and against the putrefactive sort of ulcers either by itself or with vinegar or with honeyed wine or with oxykraton (vinegar-and-water); and for the eyes, making from it a dry drug, which many have already received from me and have in their possession. I also mix certain other things with it. It will be spoken of in the treatise on the composition of drugs; for now it suffices to have set out its power in general. For it dries strongly, having something of astringency together with biting. And I have said also in what precedes that the best and most widely useful drugs are all those of mixed character, having in themselves the two powers, the repelling and the dispersing.

[9.2.8] [8. On agēratos.] There is also the stone called agēratos, which we see the leather-workers using; it is of a mixed power, both astringent and dispersing, but only the astringent one needs to be considered. It manifestly benefits inflamed uvulas, yet to those who taste it it does not appear to have any clear astringency or pungency.

[9.2.9] [9. On the Assian stone.] There is also another stone generated at Assos, which for this very reason they call Assian; it is not hard like rocks, for it is porous-looking (πωροειδής) in both colour and consistency, friable and loose, and there grows upon it something resembling the finest flour, the kind that settles on the walls of the mills when flour is being sifted. They call this drug, then, flower of Asian stone. It is fine-particled, so as to melt away flabby flesh without biting. The rock on which it is generated, though it has a power similar to it, falls short of it in the vehemence of its activity; for the flower surpasses it not only in melting away, dispersing and desiccating (ταριχεύειν) more, but also in doing these things strongly without biting. This flower of Asian stone also has something salty in its taste, so that one may conjecture that it gets its generation from a kind of dew from the sea settling on the rock and then being dried by the sun.

[9.2.10] [10. On gagates and the Thracian stone.] There is also another stone, black in colour, which, when it comes into contact with fire, produces a smell similar to that of bitumen; Dioscorides and certain others say that it is found in Lycia, by the river named Gagates, from which indeed we say the stone itself has its appellation. I, however, did not see that river, although I sailed along the whole of Lycia in a small boat for the sake of inquiry into the things in it. But I did bring many plate-like black stones, which generate a weak flame if they are placed on fire, from Coele Syria, stones generated in the hill that surrounds the sea named the Dead Sea, in its eastern parts, where bitumen also comes into being. And the smell of the stones was similar to bitumen. I used them for chronic emphysemata occurring at the knee that are hard to treat, mixing them with the preparations that have been tested against this symptom, and it clearly seemed to us to have made their power more manifest. I also mixed it with the so-called barbaros, and the drug clearly became more drying, so as even to close up sinuses, and not only to glue together bloody wounds, for which it has been believed to be especially suited. There is also another stone, which Nicander too mentions, writing thus: "Or you might burn the Thracian one in fire exceedingly; then, sprinkled with water, it will be set going, but a little oil sprinkled on quenched it, when it smells it—the stone which herdsmen bring from the Thracian river, which they call Pontos." But not even Nicander writes of any benefit from it for medicine, apart from the foul smell, which, when it is burned as a fumigation, drives away venomous creatures.
[9.2.11] [11. On magnetite and the Heraclean stone.] Among the stones there is also one called both magnetite and Heraclean, which has a power similar to that of haematites.

[9.2.12] [12. On the Arabian stone.] The stone called Arabian, which resembles ivory, is of a drying and cleansing power. [9.2.13] [13. On alabastrites.] And the onyx called alabastrites also comes into medical use when it has been burnt. Some people also give it in a drink to those with stomach complaints.

[9.2.14] [14. On smyris (emery).] And the so-called smyris: that it is of a sufficiently cleansing power is clear even from the gem-engravers who use it for this very purpose; but that it also renders the teeth clean, we have ascertained by experience.

[9.2.15] [15. On pumice.] And if pumice too is counted among the stones, it too is of the same power so far as concerns cleansing, just as is also the potsherd from roof-tiles, and still more than that the one from ovens; but emery at any rate has something pungent in it, and for this reason some mix it with caustic and drying powers and with those that treat flabby gums. Pumice, however, when burnt does not fall short of emery for the same uses.

[9.2.16] [16. On the stones found in sponges.] The stones found in sponges are also of a stone-breaking power, not however one so strong as to break up the stones in the bladder; rather, those who wrote this have told a falsehood. But they do break up those in the kidneys, as do also those from Cappadocia, which they say are generated on Mount Argaeus. These dissolve into a juice milky in colour, so that it is quite clear that they are of a thinning power without heating perceptibly.

[9.2.17] [17. On ostracites.] As for the stone called ostracites, I hear some people praising it as having a sufficiently drying power, compounded of astringency and pungency, just as they also praise the one called the earthy stone: they say that these both cleanse the pupils and heal inflammations of the breasts and of the testicles, when introduced in water. Indeed, the scrapings of the Naxian whetstone also prevent the breasts of maidens from swelling up at the season of maturity, and likewise the testicles of boys, as evidently partaking also of a cooling power.

[9.2.18] [18. On ophites.] The stone called ophites, too, when burnt, is of a cleansing and stone-breaking power, just as glass also is; for it too, when drunk with white, thin wine, breaks up quite effectively the stones in the bladder, but no one would count it among the stones.

[9.2.19] [18. On green jasper, omphatites, hierakites and the Indian stone.] Some people attest for certain stones a special property of the sort that the green jasper does in fact possess, benefiting both the oesophagus and the mouth of the stomach when it is worn as an amulet. Some also set it in a ring and engrave upon it the serpent that has the rays, just as King Nechepsos wrote in his fourteenth book. Of this stone, then, I too have sufficient experience: having made a kind of string of small stones of this sort, I hung it from the neck, so proportioned that the stones touched the mouth of the stomach. And they appeared to be no less beneficial even though they did not have the engraving which Nechepsos prescribed. As for the omphatites stone, a truly trustworthy man said that it benefits those bitten by vipers when worn as an amulet. But such powers lie outside the use that proceeds by method, as do also those of the hierakites and of the Indian stone, which stops the blood from haemorrhoids.

[9.2.20] [20. On sapphire.] For indeed the sapphire too is believed, when drunk, to benefit those struck by a scorpion. [9.2.21] [21. On aphroselinon.] And the so-called aphroselinon likewise [is believed to benefit] epileptics, though we ourselves have not put it to the test. There are also certain other stones which are hung as amulets by some people, and some of them even bearing certain characters engraved upon them and letters, just as the hieracites, which has proved suitable for haemorrhoids, and which we ourselves have tested. But now is not the occasion to speak about such things, which have their credibility from experience alone and have not been brought into use according to any rational method. There will, then, be another occasion and place for these matters. For now let us return once more to what has been set before us from the beginning in the whole treatise.

[9.3.1] On the metallic drugs. [1. On the common accounts, constitutions and powers of the metallic substances.] It is the custom among physicians to call 'metallic' those drugs whose generation takes place in the mines, whether it is self-produced or comes about through a furnace. And there is a third class besides these, namely all those which humans in turn prepare from these same substances in whatever manner, such as white lead (psimythion), psorikon, sandyx, phykos. They will all be spoken of in order, then, according to the sequence of the letters with which each of the names begins, after we have first stated in common about all of them that point which we made a little earlier in the case of the stones and, above these, higher up, in the case of medicinal earth. For just as those do, in the same way all the metallic drugs too have in common the property of drying. For their substance is earthy, in the sense of elemental earth, as I am now using the term. But just as, by us, from potter's clay the storage-jars and the roof-tiles and the pots and the other things of this kind are produced, hardened through fire once their moisture has been roasted out, in the same way, in the earth, when long-lasting heat unites and blends the mixed substance of earth and water, and sometimes also of air, and then dries it, the constitutions of the metallic drugs come about. And the nature of the places in which these are formed, according as they are more or less cold, congeals some of them more and others less. Just as, then, among the varieties of earth the substance of elemental earth is greatest while that of the airy is small, so in the mined substances much of the fiery is blended in. And the stones are intermediate between them; wherefore also most of the metallic drugs, when washed, some once or twice, others many times, become useful for the powers that dry without biting. Such, then, are the common accounts which it is necessary to know in advance concerning all of them; and next will be stated the particular ones for each individually, according to the order of the letters with which the names of the drugs begin.

[9.3.2] [2. On salt.] Salt. There is both the kind that comes to be from the sea in the so-called salt-works, which we shall also mention among the marine drugs, and there is also the kind called mined salt, which is included in the genus of metallic drugs. All of them have a power similar to one another, both the mined kinds and those from the sea, about which an account has been given earlier, in the fourth book, in that discussion when we were distinguishing the salty and the brine-like flavour from the bitter. It will be said now too that the flavour in aphronitron is both bitter and cleansing, whereas that in salt falls short in cleansing by as much as it has the advantage in astringency. For it is mixed from two qualities, a cleansing and an astringent one. That both dry sufficiently was demonstrated earlier as well. In between both of them is that of litron.

[9.3.3] [3. On Armenian stone.] Armenian stone (armeniakon) has a cleansing power together with a slight pungency and a very slight astringency. Accordingly, being of such a kind, it is also mixed into the ophthalmic preparations; and on its own as well, having ground it fine and worked it into a dust-like powder, they use it dry for the growth of the hairs on the eyelids, whenever, owing to pungency of humours, some of them fall out and others become stunted and ill-nourished. For, having consumed these pungencies, it [is said] to bring the part back to its natural good condition, to which belong, among other things, the growing, increasing and strengthening of the hairs of the eyelids. For some of these are directly the works of the drugs, while others come about through the mediation of the nature that governs the bodies of animals, just as is also the case with what they call the kalliblephara (eyelid-beautifiers) made from these same substances: for these themselves moderately dry the moderately damaged parts, consuming the moisture that destroys the hairs; and once this has been destroyed, nature arrives at its own proper activities, since the things that until then were hindering it are no longer present.

[9.3.4] [4. On arsenikon.] Arrhenikē or arrhenikon—for it is named in both ways—is of caustic power, both unburnt and burnt. It is quite clear that it also becomes more fine-particled when burnt.
