They use it also for the depilation of hairs, as burning them away; and if indeed it is left on for some time, it attacks the skin itself as well.

[9.3.5] [5. On aphrolitron.] Aphrolitron differs from aphronitron. For foam of nitron is a drying drug, resembling wheat flour to look at; for it is also white, not ash-coloured like the flower of the Asian stone. Aphronitron, however, is not floury nor loose, but set and compacted; it is what all those who are dirty use every day in the baths, since it has a cleansing power, so as not only to scour away dirt but also to cure itching, the ichors that produce it being dispersed by it. Reasonably, therefore, physicians prepare with it many of the dispersing drugs. The foam of nitron is of the same nature and power as nitron, but has a more fine-particled substance. It was said, however, a little earlier that aphrolitron is intermediate in power between aphronitron and salts. For aphrolitron possesses the cleansing power alone, whereas salts possess the astringent power as well, though the cleansing power is much greater.

[9.3.6] [6. On gypsum.] Gypsum too, in addition to the power common to all earthy and stony bodies, in virtue of which it was said to dry, has further acquired this as well, that it is of a clogging power. For it unites with itself and sets and turns to stone when it has been moistened, and for this reason it is also usefully mixed with the dry drugs suited to haemorrhage. For it alone, by itself, becomes stony and hard as it sets, and on this account I devised the practice of moistening it with the thin and white part of an egg, the part useful for ophthalmias, mixing in the finest, dust-like part of wheat flour, that which settles on the walls in mills. One must take up what has been kneaded in this way on soft hairs of a hare, or indeed on some of the similarly soft materials.

[9.3.7] [7. On burnt gypsum.] Gypsum that has been burnt does not possess the clogging property to the same degree, but becomes more fine-particled and more drying, and moreover also repelling, and especially when it is soaked in oxykraton (vinegar-and-water).

[9.3.8] [8. On diphryges.] Diphryges is of mixed quality and power. For it has in itself something moderately astringent and also moderately pungent, and for this reason it is a good drug for malignant ulcers. I brought back a considerable quantity of this drug too from Soli in Cyprus, where the mine is, about thirty stades from the city. For it had been thrown out in the place between the building situated at the mine and the village lying below it. The overseer in charge of the mine said that what is found after the cadmia was useless, and that it was therefore thrown away just like the ash of burning logs on hearths. This drug proved quite serviceable to me for many purposes: both for the putrefactive ulcers in the mouth, both by itself and with skimmed honey, and for synanche, when the influx has already been checked beforehand by means of astringents. And having cut off a uvula I used it alone, both immediately and up to cicatrization, since it often produces a precisely sealed scar both of this part and of all parts that have been ulcerated. So too for all ulcers in the genitals and in the seat; and the use is similar to that for those in the mouth. For indeed parts that are similarly hot and moist in some way delight in the same drugs. But such a discussion already touches upon the treatise on the composition of drugs. Leaving it aside, then, let us go on to what lies before us, stating the general power itself of each drug, just as we have also stated that of diphryges. I shall add, however, to the account of it something useful to know not only about diphryges but also about the Lemnian seal and pompholyx and opobalsam and Indian lycium. For I learned the preparations of these while still a youth, producing a prepared product indistinguishable from the genuine ones. The man who taught them, for a large fee, was most meticulous not only in these matters but also in other similar ones. For this reason, therefore, I made it my concern to travel to Lemnos and Cyprus and Palestinian Syria and to lay up for my whole life a great quantity of each of these drugs; but I was also fortunate to obtain, at that time, the Indian lycium that had just been brought to Phoenicia together with the Indian aloe, when I was returning on the road from Palestine, being persuaded that it was Indian both by the very fact that it had been conveyed by camels together with the whole cargo, and by the fact that the adulterated product could not be recognised by those conveying it, since the material from which it is prepared is not produced in those regions. It seemed to me by no means better to write down the compositions of the counterfeit ones, since wicked men regard learning such things as a godsend. For it is not necessary, along with the means of distinguishing the true and genuine ones, also to know the compositions of the counterfeit ones, since these contribute nothing to the diagnosis of them. And I would have wished, had it been possible for me, also to erase the preparations of counterfeited drugs found in those who were my elders.

[9.3.9] [9. On sulphur.] All sulphur is of drawing power, being hot in mixture and fine-particled in substance, so that it also withstands many of the venomous creatures. I myself, at any rate, have used it often in cases of the sea-stingray and the dragon-fish, and having taught certain fishermen, I heard after a time that they praised the drug greatly. The use is made both with the drug dry, sprinkled upon the puncture, and with it mixed with saliva. For having thought of this too, I found it attested by experience; and I conceived also that it would be effective moistened with urine. For I was teaching the fishermen drugs that were altogether easily procurable, and I said that they would do well to use it also with old oil, with honey, and with terebinth resin. And indeed experience passed judgment on all of these. And I have not seldom cured psora, lichens and lepra with this drug, together with terebinth resin. For it cleanses away all such affections without repelling toward the depth, whereas many other drugs that cure them have a mixed power so as both to disperse and to repel.

[9.3.10] [10. On verdigris.] Verdigris has a pungent quality for those who taste it, being dispersing, reducing and melting not only of soft but also of hard flesh. It has been said in what precedes that some people call many drugs of this kind scarring, because, having ground it fine and made it dust-like, they touch ulcers overgrown with flesh with the olive-shaped tip of a probe. Then on the following day they find them drawn back, even though they know that if they were to apply a little more, they will find the ulcer not drawn back but actually eaten away; for it melts and disperses the flesh, whereas scarring drugs draw it together, compact it, bind it tight and make it callous. And verdigris is biting to the taste as well, not only to ulcers. But if one mixes a little of it with a great deal of cerate, the mixture of both becomes cleansing without biting. It has been said before concerning the nature of such drugs, and how some people deceive themselves on the basis of such compositions, attributing either a flesh-forming or a scarring power to drugs to which one ought not, since it is not these themselves that are by nature able to do this, but the compounds composed from them that bring it about.

[9.3.11] [11. On cadmia.] Cadmia is produced, for one thing, in the course of the generation of copper in the furnaces, since the whole of that earth from which the copper is generated during the smelting sends up on high a kind of soot or smut—or soot and smut, however one wishes to call it. If you wish to call it not an earth but a stone, from which, when it is separated out in the furnaces, one part becomes copper, another cadmia, another diphryges, let that make no difference. It is produced also in the silver mines by a similar separation or generation, or however you wish to name it. But cadmia is also produced when pyrites stone is smelted. And cadmia is also found in Cyprus without a furnace, and one would rightly name such a kind a stone. At any rate, at Soli there was still very little of the cadmia produced in the smelting-works at the time when I visited the island. But having received from the man in charge of the mines stones that are found on the mountains and in the torrent-beds, when I brought them to Asia and Italy my friends thought they were receiving a very great gift, since that is better than the other cadmia. Such a kind, then, one would reasonably name stony cadmia; whereas of the furnace-made kind, one sort is called by physicians botryitis, the other placitis: botryitis is that which collects in the higher parts of the buildings during the smelting, placitis that which collects in the lower parts. And it is evident that the botryitis is finer-particled, the placitis coarser-particled, but both are of a drying power, like the other substances also that are mined and stony and earthy. Besides the drying power it also has the cleansing power to a moderate degree. The kind from the furnaces, at all events, necessarily has something also of the power of fire. Reasonably, then, by washing it they make a drug that dries and cleanses moderately without biting, so as to be useful for ulcers requiring filling, both in the eyes and in the whole body. As for the excessively moist or putrefactive ulcers, in bodies that are very soft, such as those of eunuchs and children and women, such cadmia is beneficial; but in those that are hard and firm there is need of drugs that dry more vigorously. One must therefore always remember that in all statements made simply the account is to be referred to the well-tempered nature, intermediate between the extremes—as when we say that a drug is either filling for ulcers or scarring, or does anything else whatever; referring to this nature now we too say that cadmia has a drying and slightly cleansing power, whereas in the distinction according to heat and cold it is in a way balanced, producing neither effect conspicuously.

[9.3.12] [12. On cinnabar.] Cinnabar is of a moderately pungent power, and it also has something of astringency. [9.3.13] [13. On pumice.] Pumice: if you rank it among the mined substances, the fault-finders will object; and if among the stones, they will not concede that it is a stone, and much more still not that it is an earth, nor one of the things from the sea. And yet one must at some point speak about it, since it is put into the flesh-forming drugs and the cleansing drugs for the teeth—the former unburnt, the latter burnt, at which time it also becomes more fine-particled, in like manner to all the other burnt substances; but in the burning it takes on something pungent, and it lays this aside again when washed. It would seem to brighten the teeth not by its power alone but also by its roughness, just as if you were to triturate and apply emery or potsherd or some such thing, which themselves too perhaps brighten in both respects, both because they have something cleansing and by their roughness. By the same reasoning burnt horns too are brightening agents for the teeth.

[9.3.14] [14. On lye made from ash.] Lye. Lye comes into being when ash is washed; and the Greeks give the name "ash" to the residue of bodies that have been burnt, whether these be stony in nature or parts of trees or of animals. Accordingly the lye too comes to be in conformity with the nature of what is washed: from that which has a most pungent fiery residue it is most pungent, from that which is not of this kind it is more moderate. For this reason it is also mixed into the so-called putrefying powers, since it has a caustic heat, burning without pain by reason of the fine-particled character of its substance.

[9.3.15] [15. On kyanos.] Kyanos (blue copper carbonate, azurite) — whether you wish to name this drug in the masculine or in the feminine — is of a pungent power, both reducing and dispersing, to a greater degree than cinnabar; and it also partakes of astringency.

[9.3.16] [16. On the scale from copper, iron and steel.] Of scale, one kind is that of copper, a drug of manifold use, another that of iron and of steel (stomoma). Some also name a nail-scale (helitis). All of them, then, dry strongly, but they differ from one another both in the very fact of drying less or more, and in being of coarser-particled or finer-particled substance, and in partaking of astringency less or more. Now the nail-scale holds first place in drying; for it is also more fine-particled than the others, having also taken on something of verdigris; whereas the scale of iron partakes of greater astringency, and that of steel still more so, for which reason they are also better than that of copper for the malignant kinds of ulcers. But the scale of copper takes down and melts away flesh more, and the nail-scale still more than this. All scales, however, are biting not feebly, by which it is also clear that the constitution of their substance is not altogether fine-particled, but rather coarse-particled. For among things that have the same power, the more fine-particled is always the less biting, as was shown in the preceding discussions.

[9.3.17] [17. On litharge.] Litharge dries, just as do all the other metallic, earthy and stony drugs, yet it does this most moderately. And in respect of the other qualities and powers too it is somehow in the middle, neither clearly heating nor cooling, and it partakes moderately of the astringent and of the cleansing. For this reason it falls short both of the flesh-forming drugs, which were shown to be moderately cleansing, and of those that draw together and are astringent. But for chafings on the thighs it is a useful drug, since it partakes to a slight degree of both the powers mentioned. It would therefore reasonably be reckoned of the middle rank among the metallic drugs. Hence we also often use it as a material, mixing it with those that have a strong power, whether biting or astringent or producing some other effect, just as among the meltable substances we use wax for most drugs as a kind of material, because it too is in a way placed in the middle of those that have a strong power.

[9.3.18] [18. On nitron.] Nitron has been said already before to be intermediate in power between aphronitron and salts; but when burnt it comes nearer to aphronitron, being rendered more fine-particled as a result of the burning. Accordingly it dries and disperses and, if it is taken into the body, it cuts and thins the thick and viscous humours much more than salts do. Aphronitron, however, unless there is great necessity, no one even swallows, since it is bad for the stomach, although indeed it is more cutting than nitron. At any rate, in cases of choking from mushrooms a certain countryman used it and was always held in good repute. We too use nitron, both burnt and unburnt, and still more its foam, in such cases.

[9.3.19] [19. On melanteria.] Melanteria is among the sufficiently astringent drugs, in addition to being fine-particled almost most of all the astringents. [9.3.20] [20. On writing-ink.] The black with which we write: this too dries sufficiently when dissolved in water. And applied as a smear straightaway, it also benefits burn-wounds. And if it also contains vinegar, much more so.

[9.3.21] [21. On misy.] Misy. At the mine in Cyprus mentioned before, in the mountains of Soli, there was a certain large house, where along the right-hand wall—though on the left relative to us who were entering—there was an entrance into the mine itself, in which I saw certain belts, as it were, extended to a very great length, three of them one upon another: the lowest that of sory, upon it that of chalcitis, then that of misy. The man who at that time was overseer of the mine, showing me these things, said: "Just as you have now come when we are in poverty of the cadmia that is smelted in the furnaces, so you see these three established in wondrous wealth." And so, taking a very great quantity of it, I brought it first to Asia and from there to Rome, and I have kept it until now, about thirty years having passed in between. And by some chance the present treatise had advanced as far as the eighth book, about twenty years ago, without this ninth being added to it, because I had not yet seen some of the stones, and moreover because of the occupations that intervened on account of other matters. But now, as I am adding this ninth book, in the meantime there occurred by chance a most beautiful sight, such as someone might himself have contrived on purpose. For, needing misy for a certain drug that was being prepared, I picked up a lump about a handful in size, although misy does not generally have such a consistency, but breaks apart into small coherent pieces. Wondering, then, at its unusual compactness, and having crushed the lump, I found on the surface, all round, the misy, like a kind of efflorescence of what was within; and upon it, between chalcitis and misy, a sort of half-completed change from chalcitis into misy—for the lump was originally of chalcitis; and what was in the depth was exact chalcitis, having as yet undergone no alteration. Having seen this, then, and having reflected that in the mine too the misy is generated upon the chalcitis in this way, as verdigris upon copper, I examined the sory still preserved in my possession, to see whether it was taking on any change into chalcitis, and a slight hint of it appeared, which perhaps itself too would be able, over a long time, to attain the change into chalcitis; so that it is no wonder that the three drugs—I mean sory, chalcitis and misy—are of a power of the same kind, differing in fineness of particles and coarseness of particles. For the most coarse-particled among them is sory, the most fine-particled misy, and chalcitis has a power midway between both. All three burn and produce the so-called eschars, yet even though they burn they share in astringency. But misy bites less than chalcitis when applied to hard flesh, although it is not less hot than it; rather it has this from the fine-particled nature of its substance. And whereas both are fusible in boilings, and chalcitis more so than misy, sory does not melt, because it has a more stony and more vehement coagulation, just as in turn misy, through having been worked up by its innate heat, being drier than chalcitis, is reasonably also harder to melt.

[9.3.22] [22. On molybdaena.] Molybdaena has a power closely resembling that of litharge, having departed a little from the middle mixture toward the colder; but neither does it partake of a cleansing power. Both drugs are fusible, and not, like stones and cadmia and sand, infusible. Their melting takes place most quickly when the oil has received vinegar in addition. It melts, however, even if you mix in water and boil it for a very long time. And just as in Cyprus I took the cadmia that is generated in the mountains and in the torrent-beds, which is, as I said, a kind of stone, in the same way I also saw molybdaena lying cast down in very great quantity together with the other stones along the road that leads from Pergamum to Ergasteria. Ergasteria is the name of a certain village, in which there are also mines, between Pergamum and Cyzicus, four hundred and forty stades distant from Pergamum.

[9.3.23] [23. On lead.] Lead is of a cooling power. For it has not only much moist substance congealed by cooling, but also airy substance, partaking of little of the earthy. That, then, it has a very great deal of moist substance congealed by cooling, let the melting and flowing that happen to it quickly, once it comes into contact with fire, be your evidence. That it has airy substance too, this is the sign: lead alone of the things we know increases both in bulk and in weight when stored in underground rooms that have turbid air, such that the things lying in them are quickly filled with mould; and the leads that bind the feet of statues to the stones have often been seen to have increased; and some have risen to such a bulk as to hang down from the stones like ice. These, then, are plausible indications, prior to experience, of something of its moistness and coldness; the scientific and secure ones are known through experience. At any rate, if you prepare a mortar from lead and, with a leaden pestle, putting into it whatever liquid you wish, you grind in such a way that both the pestle and the lead give off a certain juice, you will find what is generated from the two of them much colder in power than the liquid happened to be. You may put in water, and thin watery wine, and oil, and anything whatever of this kind. And if you wish to make the juice still more cooling, let the oil be omphacine, or rose-oil, or quince-oil, or myrtle-oil. Using the juice generated for the inflammations in the seat that arise together with ulcers or folds, and for those in the genitals and testicles and breasts, you will have an excellent drug. Likewise also against all the other fluxes at their onset, those which fall upon the groins or the feet or the other joints, and indeed also for malignant ulcers, so that, having used it also against the cancerous ones, you will marvel at the drug. If you wish to gather quickly a very great deal of the juice of lead, try grinding in the sun or in air that has in any way become warm. The drug will be of manifold use to you if you also grind it with the cooling juices put in, such as of houseleek, cotyledon, endive, lettuce, chondrile, psyllion (fleawort), unripe grape and purslane. And whichever of these do not readily give off juice, like purslane, one should mix with them some of the other liquids, such as that of the unripe grape, which even on its own, when put into the aforementioned mortar, produces a very fine cooling drug. But lead when flattened out, without any of the other things, itself alone by itself, becomes a bedding under the loins of athletes in training when they have nocturnal emissions, manifestly cooling them. And somewhere a thin plate made from lead, well bandaged over a ganglion, made it disappear completely. Everyone will bandage well who has learned from Hippocrates to press upon the lesion rather than on this side and that. It is therefore no wonder that burnt lead too, when it has been washed, comes to be of cooling power; before being washed it is evidently of mixed power. And this very drug, burnt lead, is good for ulcers that are turning malignant; but when it has been washed, it becomes much more an excellent drug for both filling them up and cicatrising them. It suits also the so-called Chironian ulcers and all cancerous ones, both by itself and mixed with some of the cicatrising drugs, such as the one made with cadmia. One should undo the dressing at the beginning every day, if the ichor is abundant; if not, every third or even every fourth day. And let a sponge from cold water be laid on from outside, which, whenever it dries, should be moistened. These things, then, have been said at greater length than befits the present treatise, as I was carried forward by the kinship of the subject. But it is now time to pass on to what follows.

[9.3.24] [24. On potsherd.] Potsherd is of a drying and cleansing power, and most of all the potsherd from ovens, because of its having been thoroughly baked. For this reason too, among the plasters, the one which they call Hephaestias, being prepared with this, becomes an excellent scarring drug.

[9.3.25] [25. On pompholyx and spodion.] Pompholyx is produced also in the smelting of copper, just as cadmia is too. But it is produced also from cadmia itself when it is smelted; and in Cyprus, since the procurator did not have the equipment for the smelting of copper, he ordered pompholyx to be prepared from cadmia itself, while I was present and watching, the cadmia being thrown onto the fire in small fragments, with, evidently, something of the smith's kind (χαλκευτικῆς φύσεως, perhaps a smith's bellows) applied to it. And there was a kind of covered roof which received the soot that was carried upward as the cadmia was smelted; this I collected and had as pompholyx. But what is carried down in the opposite direction and falls onto the floor is what is called spodos, which is collected in greater quantity in the smeltings of copper. Some people name it in the neuter, spodion, and the so-called antispodion seems to have a power similar to it. I myself have never used the latter, because one always has pompholyx in abundance. For anyone who has this would not even use spodion, let alone antispodion. Pompholyx is a drug which, if it has been washed, is nearly the most excellent of all those which are by nature such as to dry without biting; hence it is suitable for the cancerous kinds of ulcers and all the other malignant ones. It is accordingly mixed into the collyria compounded for the fluxes of the eyes and into all those that treat the phlyctaenae in them or ulcers, and for the ulcers at the seat and the genitals. And it is the finest drug for drying without biting, as I said. But it is not the business of the present treatise to linger on these matters.

[9.3.26] [26. On sandarach.] Sandarach is of caustic power, like what is called arsenikon. Reasonably, therefore, they mix it into the dispersing powers and the cleansing ones. [9.3.27] [27. On sandyx.] Of what sort of power sandyx is will be stated in the account concerning psimythion (white lead).

[9.3.28] [28. On slag.] All slag is a drug that is sufficiently drying, but that of iron most of all. And indeed, having made it very fine in the most pungent vinegar, and after this boiling it, I use it for ears that have been discharging pus for a long time as a most drying drug, so that those who see it being prepared marvel and disbelieve it before the trial, whether the ears can tolerate such a drug. The slag of silver they specifically call helkysma, and it is also mixed into certain plasters which are evidently of drying power.

[9.3.29] [29. On stimmi.] Stimmi. In addition to its drying power this drug also has astringency, which is why it is also mixed into the ophthalmic drugs, both those that are moulded into the so-called collyria and the dry ones, which indeed they call dry collyria.

[9.3.30] [30. On alum, the fissile, the round and the liquid.] Alum. The very name of this drug is derived from astringency, for it possesses this in the most vehement degree. Though it is coarse-particled, the kind called fissile is somewhat more fine-particled than the other alums; after it comes the round and the knuckle-shaped (astragalus-like). Quite coarse-particled are the liquid kind and those named plate-alum (plakitis) and brick-alum (plinthitis).

[9.3.31] [31. On lime.] Lime: the unslaked kind burns violently, so as to produce an eschar; the slaked kind also produces an eschar itself at once, but after one or two days it burns less and produces an eschar less, and after a time it does not produce eschars at all. It still heats, however, and melts away the flesh. If it is washed, it deposits its biting in the water and makes what is called lye, while it itself dries without biting. And if it is washed two or three times or more often, it becomes completely free of biting and dries nobly without biting.

[9.3.32] [32. On mercury.] Mercury is not one of the naturally occurring drugs but one of those that are prepared, like white lead and verdigris and psoricon and litharge. I have no experience of it, either as destroying life if swallowed, or when applied externally.

[9.3.33] [33. On phykos.] Of what sort of power phykos is will be stated in the account concerning psimythion. [9.3.34] [34. On chalkanthos.] Chalkanthos. I have also made observation concerning chalkanthos, which by chance changes into chalkitis. For I brought this drug too from Cyprus in very great quantity. And the whole of its outer part, after nearly twenty years, became chalkitis, while the inner part was still chalkanthos. For this reason I still keep up to now the piece that is changing in this way, watching how far the change advances toward the depth in each year, just as that of chalkitis into misy, as has been said before. One may marvel, in the case of this drug, how a not ignoble heat is mixed with the strongest astringency. It is clear, then, that it is able most of all things to cure moist flesh as by salting, consuming the moisture by its heat, and by its astringency drawing together and compacting the substance. For in this very action it also squeezes out something of the moisture itself, and it binds and dries and draws together toward itself the substance of the whole flesh. In Cyprus, then, at the time when I was there, I saw this drug being collected in the following manner. There was a house, large but not high, lying before the entrance to the mine. And along the left wall of this house, which was on the right hand for those entering, a tunnel had been hollowed out into the adjoining hill, in breadth such that three men could touch one another, in height such that the tallest man could walk upright. This tunnel sloped downward, but was not steep or precipitous. At its end, it being about a stade long, there was a pit full of water, greenish and thick and lukewarm. Throughout the whole descent there was a warmth similar to that in the first rooms of the baths, which they are accustomed to call promalakteria. The water collected each day was a quantity of about eight Roman amphorae, falling in small drops, in the twenty-four hours of the whole day and night, out of the hill which had been bored through. Certain fettered men, then, carrying up this water, threw it into square basins in the house lying in front, made of pottery, in which, congealing in a few days, it became chalkanthos. To me, when I went down to the end of the excavation, where the lukewarm and greenish water was collected, the smell of the air appeared stifling and hard to bear, smelling of chalkitis and ios. And the water itself, when tasted, had the same quality. For these reasons the fettered men carried up the amphorae both naked and with haste, and did not endure to remain for a longer time, but quickly ran back up, lamps burning on either side in the walls of the excavation at a measured interval, which did not themselves last for a long time either, but were extinguished very quickly. This excavation, then, I heard from them had been dug little by little over many years. For this, they said, which you now see carried down from the hill into the pit, the greenish water, is accustomed to become less than itself little by little, and when it is near to ceasing, the fettered men again dig under the adjoining part of the hill. And once before, what was being dug through collapsed all at once, so as to kill all of them and to destroy the whole passage. Whenever, then, this happens, they again make another opening and dig through, until the water answers. These things I was able to tell you about chalkanthos, perhaps indeed not necessary, yet better to be known than to be unknown. And remember that I said the mine of sory and chalkitis and misy had been seen by me on the left hand of those entering, so that from these things I was able to conceive that the rainwater percolating in the hill washes around and rinses all that earth, from which sory and misy and chalkitis came into being spontaneously, and, by smelting, copper and kadmeia and pompholyx and spodion and diphryges.

[9.3.35] [35. On chalcitis.] Chalcitis: it has been spoken of in the account of misy, so for now it will suffice to say this much, that it possesses the astringent and the pungent power mixed together. The pungent one predominates, being so vehement as to go as far as burning the flesh and producing what is called an eschar. When this drug has been burnt it bites less, but dries no less, and it also lays aside no small part of its astringency, so that burnt chalcitis is in every way better than the unburnt, becoming more fine-particled, like the other burnt substances too, but not taking on pungency in addition, as many others do. And you have learned also that all burnt substances, when washed, become more moderate and less biting.

[9.3.36] [36. On burnt copper.] Burnt copper has something pungent as well, and it also partakes of astringency, and for this reason, if it is washed, it is an excellent drug for the cicatrization of ulcers; it is able to effect this even before being washed, and especially in the case of harder flesh. For tender flesh, however, the washed kind is more useful.

[9.3.37] [37. On flower of copper.] Flower of copper: this is of a more fine-particled power than both burnt copper and the scale. Reasonably, then, those who prepare collyria with it cleanse and remove the great roughnesses of the eyelids, which they call sycoses.

[9.3.38] [38. On chrysocolla.] Chrysocolla. This drug too belongs to those that melt flesh, yet it does not bite strongly; it is, however, sufficiently dispersing and drying. Some people, then, give this name only to the mined kind, while others give it to the kind prepared in a copper mortar with a copper pestle by means of a boy's urine, which some people count among the different kinds of ios (verdigris). It is better to prepare it in summer, or at any rate in warm air, grinding the urine in the mortar. It is better, too, that the copper from which you make both the mortar itself and the pestle be red; for more is rubbed off as the pestle is turned round when the copper is softer. This drug is most suitable for malignant ulcers, both by itself and mixed with others, as will be stated in the books on the composition of drugs. For now it suffices to know this much: by as much as it dries more and bites less than the mined chrysocolla, by so much does it surpass it in fineness of particles. And indeed, if you burn that mined chrysocolla itself, you will make it much more fine-particled.

[9.3.39] [39. On psimythion.] Psimythion (white lead). This drug too bears witness to the power described before it. At any rate, although it is itself dissolved by pungent vinegar, when tasted it is nevertheless neither pungent nor biting nor dispersing, but clogging and cooling, being of a power most opposed to that of verdigris; and yet that too comes into being when vinegar dissolves the copper. When psimythion is burnt and has changed into what is called sandyx, it becomes a drug more fine-particled than itself, though not yet, however, a heating one. The phykos, for its part, while preserving the coldness of psimythion, has acquired fineness of particles, so that by means of it its power is able to sink down into the depth of the bodies it comes into contact with.

[9.3.40] [40. On psoricon.] Psoricon. The drug is produced when a double quantity of chalcitis is mixed with litharge, both being first ground fine in the most pungent vinegar, then put into a new pot, which you will bury for forty days in midsummer in a dung-heap. This drug becomes at once more drying and less biting than chalcitis, and evidently also more fine-particled. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 10. None of what is now to be said will bring great benefit to those ignorant of what was said at the beginning of the treatise in the first five books, and some of it will perhaps even harm the man who uses the drugs written in it without possessing a method. I shall therefore address you as one who has learned those things, having first recalled the chief point of the whole treatise. It was shown that drugs act, in respect of the qualities called active, by heat and cold and dryness and moistness, and that by the mixture of these they become acerbic and harsh and saline and salty and bitter and pungent and sweet, and some cleansing, some repelling, some drawing, some softening, some caustic, some putrefying, some escharotic, and further, in addition to these, in respect of other more specific activities, flesh-forming and cicatrizing and agglutinating of fistulas or ulcers, or reducing of overgrowing flesh. It was also shown that the universal power may be discovered by indication from a single trial—and not any chance trial, but one made together with the distinctions stated; and that once the universal power has been discovered there is no longer any need of trial as regards the particular activities, except solely for the confirmation of what reason has discovered. In this way, then, let us now too make our judgment of the material before us, and this is the material derived from animals. For in the three books following in order after the fifth, the sixth, seventh and eighth, we went through the material concerning plants—not, evidently, all that exists throughout the whole inhabited world, but as much as we ourselves have experience of. In the book before this one, the ninth of the whole treatise, the material concerning earthy and stony bodies. It remains for us still to go through the material concerning animals; then there is still left over that of the things generated in the sea and in lakes, or in general in water, which are neither plants nor earth nor stone nor animal. Such things are altogether very few and will be written last, after we have gone through what pertains to the bodies of animals. The order of teaching for these too will follow the order of the first letters in their names. And just as in the material of plants I also gave an account of the juices produced from them, so too now the teaching of the power will be not only of the solid parts in animals but also of what is contained in them: phlegm, bile, blood, urine, dung and the like. Now in what was said before, not many of the particular items in the materia written by physicians were unknown to me, but I myself took pains to know their powers through experience; and if there was any whose power I did not know, I did not write about it at all, not thinking it right to trust others even about a single thing of this kind, because I had found that some of them lie about many things. But with the material now before us it is not so. I confess that there are very many parts and fluids contained in the bodies of animals of which I myself have had no such experience as some have written of; for some of them are lewd and disgusting, and some are even forbidden by the laws—about which I do not know how Xenocrates came to write, a man who lived not long ago but in the time of our grandfathers, when the Roman empire had forbidden the eating of human beings; yet he, as though having made trial himself, writes with full confidence what affections human brain, when eaten, or flesh or liver is naturally fitted to cure, and what the bones of the head or shin or fingers cure, some burnt, some unburnt, when drunk, and what blood itself cures. These things, then, even if contrary to the laws, are at least not lewd. But the drinking of sweat and urine and a woman's menstrual blood is lewd and disgusting, and no less than these dung, of which Xenocrates wrote what it is able to do when smeared on the parts about the mouth and the throat and swallowed down into the belly; he has written also about the filth in the ears being swallowed. I for my part would not have endured to swallow even this, on condition of never falling ill; and I consider dung far more disgusting than it. And it is a greater reproach for a man of sound mind to be called a dung-eater than a performer of shameful acts or a catamite; indeed even among performers of shameful acts we loathe those who phoenicize more than those who lesbianize, and the man who drinks menstrual blood seems to me to suffer something similar to the former. Neither, then, would any human being in his natural condition endure to come to the trial of these, nor of those things which are more moderate than these yet still lewd—to smear some part of the body with dung on account of the affection in it, or with human semen. Xenocrates is accustomed to call it gonos, and he distinguishes with all care what the gonos by itself alone is naturally fitted to help when smeared on, and what it helps after the intercourse of man and woman, when it has fallen out of the woman's vagina. For there must have arisen some great poverty of remedies, for someone to treat chilblains with a man's semen that did not remain inside but flowed out of the woman upon intercourse. Indeed much of this kind of material is in what he has written about the benefit derived from animals. For it is not only of man, evidently, that he recounts what power urine has when drunk, or dung when swallowed and smeared on the parts in the mouth, but of each of the other animals as well, and much else besides of things hard to procure, as when he mentions the elephant or the Nile horse. As for the basilisk, I have never even seen the beast, and if what is said about it is true, it is dangerous even to come near this animal. Others too wrote things similar to Xenocrates about animals, from whom Xenocrates himself also copied out the most part. For whence could he have had the means himself to make trial of so many things and of such a kind? At any rate our own Attalus, who was once king, appears to write less, although he was most ambitious concerning the trial of such things. And someone, praising the same kind of treatise by Ateuristus, gave me that too to read through—a work produced, as it seems to me at least, without the personal observation of its author. I therefore shall mention neither basilisks nor elephants nor Nile horses nor anything else of which I have no experience myself; and as for the so-called philtres, attracting-charms, dream-senders and hate-charms—for I deliberately use their own names for them—I would not have mentioned them in writing at all, even if I had sufficient experience, just as I would not deadly drugs or those which, as they themselves call them, are affection-producing. For some of those are even ridiculous: to bind one's opponents at law so that they can utter nothing in the court, or to make the pregnant woman miscarry, or never conceive, and all other such things. Most of these are indeed also impossible by the test of experience, and some, even if possible, are at any rate harmful to the life of men; so that I, by the gods, wonder with what thought some men came to write them. For things which bring disrepute to the living when known—how did they hope that these would bring them good repute after death? If, being kings among men, they made trial of them on those condemned to death, they did nothing terrible. But since private persons, having had no such authority in their whole life, came to write them, one of two things follows: either, not having made trial themselves, they write about what they do not know, or, if they did make trial, they are the most impious of all men, having given destructive drugs for the sake of trial to those who had done no wrong, and sometimes even to fine and good men. For instance, someone, seeing two physicians standing by the dealers in petty wares, brought them honey, pretending to sell it. They tasted it and were discussing the price, and as they offered little, he hastened off and withdrew, and neither of the physicians survived. For all such things, then, it is right to hate those who wrote them no less than those who did them, but even more, in proportion as it is a lesser wrong to do some evil alone than together with many. And with the doer his acquaintance with evil theorems died too, but that of all who wrote is immortal, furnishing weapons of wrongdoing to the wicked. Let us then now speak about the things useful to men, as many as we have experience of.

[8.13.1] [1. On spike of nard.] Spike of nard heats in the third degree, and dries in the second degree when it is complete. It is composed of a sufficiently astringent substance, of a pungent, hot substance that is not abundant, and of a certain slightly bitter one in small measure. Being composed of such powers, the root is reasonably suited both to the liver and to the stomach. Both when drunk and when applied externally it moves urine, heals bitings of the stomach, dries the fluxes in the belly and the intestines and, in addition to these, those in the head and the chest. The kind called Indian is stronger, being blacker than the kind called Syrian.

[8.13.2] [2. On Celtic nard.] Celtic nard is in some way similar in power, as to its kind, to those mentioned before, but weaker for all purposes except for urine. For it is hotter than they are, but less astringent.

[8.13.3] [3. On mountain nard.] Mountain nard, which is also called thylakitis and pyritis, grows most abundantly in Cilicia, and is weaker than those mentioned before. [8.13.4] [4. On narthex (giant fennel).] The seed of narthex (giant fennel) heats and thins, while the inner part, when still green, the so-called pith (enteriōnē), partakes of a certain astringent quality, on account of which it is suited to those who spit blood and to those with bowel complaints.

[8.13.5] [5. On mustard.] Mustard heats and dries in the fourth order. [8.13.6] [6. On narcissus.] The root of narcissus is of a drying power to such a degree that it glues together the largest wounds, even as far as cuts in the region of the tendons. It also has something cleansing and attractive about it.

[8.13.7] [7. On neuras.] Neuras, which some call poterion, is of a drying power that does not bite, so that it is even believed to glue together severed sinews. Its roots especially are of this sort. And indeed some also give the decoction of them to those who suffer in the sinews.

[8.13.8] [8. On nerion.] Nerion, or rhododaphne, is a shrub familiar to everyone. If it is applied as a plaster on the outside of the body, it is of a dispersing power; but taken internally it is destructive and deleterious, not only to human beings but also to most grazing animals.

[8.13.9] [9. On nymphaia.] Of nymphaia both the root and the seed have a drying power that does not bite. Accordingly it checks both the fluxes of the belly and seed that is carried off in nocturnal emissions and otherwise too immoderately, and it also benefits dysenterics. The nymphaia that has the white root is of a more vigorous power, so as to cure the female flux. Both this one and the one that has the black root are drunk in harsh black wine. They also partake somewhat of a cleansing power, so that they cure alphoi too, and alopeciai. They are soaked, for alphoi in water, for alopeciai in liquid pitch. The one that has the black root is better for these purposes, just as the one with the white root is for the other.

[8.14.1] [1. On xanthion.] Xanthion. It is also called phasganion; the fruit is of a dispersing power. [8.14.2] [2. On xyris.] Xyris, though some [call it] xyrida, is of a fine-particled, drawing and dispersing and evidently also drying power, both the root and, much more than it, the fruit, which indeed is both diuretic and curative of spleens that are becoming hardened (scirrhous).

[8.14.3] [3. On xiphion.] The root of xiphion, and especially the second one, the upper, is of a drawing and dispersing and, evidently, also drying power. [8.15.1] [1. On the oē.] The oē is the tree, whose fruit is called oa, though by most people oua, with the u; it partakes of an astringent quality, but one much weaker than that of the medlar. For this very reason it is both pleasant to eat and less constricting of the belly than the medlar.

[8.15.2] [2. On wine.] Wine is of the second order of heating things, but that which is sufficiently old is of the third, just as the kind called must is of the first order. And its drynesses are proportional to its degrees of heat.

[8.15.3] [3. On wild figs.] Wild figs (olynthoi) are of a pungent and dispersing power, on account of the juice carried in them, which is common to the whole tree. Boiled, therefore, they disperse hard swellings, while raw they also expel myrmecia and thymi.

[8.15.4] [4. On holostion.] Holostion is of a drying power together with being astringent, whence they also give it to drink for ruptures. [8.15.5] [5. On olyra.] Olyra is intermediate in nature between wheat and barley, both as a food and as a drug. Reason, therefore, about this one too from those.

[8.15.6] [6. On onagros.] Onagros, or onothēra, or onothouris. The root of this, when dried, gives off a certain wine-like smell. And in its power too it is most like wine. [8.15.7] [7. On onosma.] Onosma, or osmas, or phlonitis, or onōnis, is composed of a pungent and bitter substance. For this reason it is also believed both to kill and to expel embryos, when its leaves are drunk with wine.

[8.15.8] [8. On onobrychis.] Onobrychis is of a rarefying and dispersing power. For this very reason the leaves of the green plant, applied as a plaster, disperse phymata; and those of the dry plant, drunk with wine, cure strangury. Moreover it also calls forth sweats when it is smeared on with oil.

[8.15.9] [9. On ononis.] Ononis has a root that is heating, already somewhere about the third order. Its bark is especially useful, having also something cleansing and cutting, whence it is not only diuretic but also breaks up stones. By the same power it also quickly detaches eschars. They also use it for pains of the teeth, boiling it down in oxykraton (vinegar-and-water) and ordering the patient to rinse the mouth with it.

[8.15.10] [10. On vinegar.] Vinegar has been shown in the first of these commentaries to be of a mixed substance, cold and hot, both fine-particled; but the cold prevails over the hot. The drug is sufficiently drying as to belong already to the third order at its completion, whenever, that is, it is strong.

[8.15.11] [11. On oxyakanthos.] Oxyakanthos. For this tree, just as it is closely similar to the wild pear in appearance, so too is it in its power. And indeed the fruits as well: that of the wild pear is simply acerbic, whereas that of the oxyakanthē is also fine-particled and has a little that is cutting. The fruit of the tree, however, does not resemble that of the wild pear, but is similar to myrtle berries, being red and loose-textured. It also has stones. And not only when eaten but also when drunk it is checking of all fluxive affections.

[8.15.12] [12. On juice.] Juice: the Cyrenaic is of all the hottest and the most fine-particled, and for this reason also the most dispersing. Nonetheless the others too are sufficiently hot and pneumatic; for the greater part in them is of airy and fiery substance. Juices are indeed very many in number: for when any root whatsoever or a stalk is cut, what flows from the incision, thick and viscous, is juice. But in a more specific sense, as it were by virtue of a certain preeminence, they give this name to the Cyrenaic, the Median and the Syrian.

[8.15.13] [13. On origanum.] Origanum: the Heracleotic kind is more active than the onitis, and more active than both is the wild kind, which some call Heraclean panax, others konyle. All of them are of a cutting, thinning and heating power, possessing these in the third degree. But the kind called tragoriganos has in addition taken on something of astringency as well.

[8.15.14] [14. On bitter vetch (orobos).] Bitter vetch dries in the second degree, intensified, and heats in the first; and in so far as it partakes of bitterness, to that extent it cuts and cleanses and clears obstructions. Taken in a larger quantity, it draws blood through the urine.
[8.15.15] [15. On orobanche.] Orobanche is of a dry and cold mixture in the first order. [8.15.16] [16. On rice.] Rice has something astringent, wherefore it also checks the belly moderately.

[8.15.17] [17. On dog's orchis.] Orchis. The same plant is also called dog's orchis (kynos orchis). The power of its root, which is bulb-like and double, is moist and hot; for this reason also it appears rather sweet to those who taste it. But the larger root seems to contain much moisture that is superfluous and flatulent, and on account of this, when drunk, it also incites to sexual intercourse (aphrodisia). The other, the smaller one, is on the contrary sufficiently worked up, so that its mixture inclines toward the hotter and drier; whence this root not only does not incite the impulses toward intercourse, but, entirely to the contrary, both checks and suppresses them. They are eaten roasted, in the manner of bulbs.

[8.15.18] [18. On the orchis called serapias.] Orchis, which they also call serapias, is of a drier power than the former one, whence it is not similarly suitable for sexual intercourse. Applied as a plaster it disperses oedemas and cleanses filthy ulcers and heals herpetes. When dried it dries much more still, so that it heals both the putrefactive and the malignant among ulcers. For it also has something somewhat astringent, and on account of this it restrains the belly when drunk with wine.
[8.15.19] [19. On osiris.] Of osiris, the herb from which brooms too are made, the quality is bitter, and the power unblocking, whence it also benefits the obstructions in the region of the liver.

[8.16.1] [1. On pankration.] Pankration. The root of this resembles squill both in taste and in power, so that some even use it when squill is not available. For it effects everything in the same way as regards kind, but it is by far weaker.

[8.16.2] [2. On paliouros.] The leaves and the root of paliouros have a share, not obscurely, in an astringent power, so as even to check a flowing belly, and in a dispersing power to such a degree as even to treat phymata, at least those that are not excessively inflammatory and hot. The fruit partakes of a cutting power to such a degree as even to break up stones in the bladder and to assist expectorations from the chest and lung.

[8.16.3] [3. On papyrus.] Papyrus by itself does not come into medical use at all. But when soaked or burnt it becomes useful. Soaked, then, in oxykraton (vinegar-and-water) or in wine, it glues together fresh wounds, and especially when it is laid around them in a circle. But here it is, as it were, a kind of material receptive of the healing drugs. When, however, it has been burnt, it now becomes a drying drug, just as the ash of burnt paper also does, except in so far as that of papyrus is weaker.

[8.16.4] [4. On the Heraclean panakes.] Heraclean panakes: from this is also produced what is called opopanax, when its roots and stalks are cut. The opopanax itself is of very manifold use, being heating, softening and dispersing. One would place it, as regards heating, in the third rank, and as regards drying, in the second. The bark of the root is a drying and at the same time heating drug, but less so than the juice; and indeed it also has something cleansing. For this reason we use it both for bones laid bare and for ulcers that are becoming malignant. For such things are sufficiently flesh-producing, in that they cleanse and at the same time dry and do not heat very violently, all of which are required of what is to produce flesh, as we demonstrate in the books of the Therapeutic Method. Its fruit, being itself also hot, is a drug promotive of the menses. It has become customary, I know not how, for almost everyone now to call this herb not panakes but panax.

[8.16.5] [5. On the Asklepian panakes.] Asklepian panakes. This is less hot than the panakes described before, whence they use it, together with its flowers and its fruit, for ulcers and phymata and phagedaenae, mixing them with honey.

[8.16.6] [6. On Chironian panakes.] Chironian panakes. This too is of a power similar to the one written before. [8.16.7] [7. On paronychia.] Paronychia has been named from its action, for it cures paronychias; and, as Dioscorides says, also kēria. Its power is fine-particled and drying and does not bite. For such too must the drugs for paronychia be. And it is clear that a drug of this kind is also capable of dispersing all the affections that need to be dispersed. For such are all those that belong to the third rank in heating and drying, provided that, like this one, they are of a fine-particled substance.

[8.16.8] [8. On pentaphyllon.] Pentaphyllon (cinquefoil). The root dries strongly, but is least of all pungent. For this reason too it is of manifold use, just as are all the other things which, being of fine-particled substance, dry without biting. For this root too is drying already, as it were, in the third order, while partaking least of all in any manifest heat.

[8.16.9] [9. On peplos.] Peplos; some, however, call it foam-like poppy. This shrublet too has a juice similar to that of the spurges (tithymalloi), both in its other respects and in that it purges, just as they do.

[8.16.10] [10. On peplion.] Peplion. This shrublet too has a juice, as do the tithymalli, and it grows for the most part beside the sea, having a root that is useless, just as the peplos also does; and a juice that is strong, which is itself likewise not very useful, but the seed at any rate is useful, and flatulent, purging in a manner similar to the seed of peplos.

[8.16.11] [11. On pepper.] Of pepper, the root resembles costus most closely in its power. As for the fruit, that of the plant when it has only just sprouted is long pepper, and for this reason it is also moister than the ripe fruit. A sign of its moistness is both that, when stored away, it is easily bored through, and that it does not bite immediately, but begins after a short while and then persists for a longer time. The fruit that is, as it were, in its unripe-grape stage is white pepper, which is more pungent than the black; for the latter is already, so to speak, over-roasted and over-dried. Both heat and dry strongly.

[8.16.12] [12. On persea.] The leaves of persea partake moderately of an astringent power, so that they can at times also be applied beneficially to parts that are haemorrhaging. [8.16.13] [13. On periclymenon.] Of periclymenon both the fruit and the leaves are useful, being of a cutting and at the same time heating power to such a degree that they even render the urine bloody when drunk for a longer period. At the beginning, however, it is only diuretic, while applied externally in an ointment with oil it heats. It also benefits those suffering from the spleen and those with difficulty in breathing. The proper measure of the draught is the quantity of one drachm with wine. It also dries up the seed, and some say that, if it is drunk for a longer time, those who drink it become altogether infertile. Some also fix an appointed term of days for such a draught, as Dioscorides too does, saying that these are recorded as thirty-seven. He also says that the urine becomes bloody from the sixth of the days.

[8.16.14] [14. On peristereon.] Peristereon (vervain) has received its name from the fact that pigeons (peristerai) spend their time in it. It has a drying power to such a degree as to glue wounds together. [8.16.15] [15. On petasites.] Petasites is of the third order of drying agents, whence they use it for malignant and phagedaenic ulcers.

[8.16.16] [16. On parsley.] Of parsley the seed is the most useful part, the whole herb together with the roots being of a similar but weaker power. And just as in taste it is pungent with bitterness, so also in its actions it is heating together with cutting, and for these reasons it promotes the menses and urine abundantly. It also dispels flatulence. It too, then, would be of the third order of things that heat and dry. Those in Cilicia call parsley only that which grows on Amanus; but this is smyrnion rather than parsley, though it certainly does not depart much from the power of parsley.

[8.16.17] [17. On peucedanum.] Of peucedanum we use chiefly the root, but we use also the juice and the expressed juice. All of these are of the same power in kind; but the strongest of them is the juice, which heats and disperses considerably, whence it has also been believed to be suitable for all the affections of the sinews, and for the diseases of the lung and chest that arise through thickness or viscosity of humours. It benefits both when taken into the body and also when smelled. And by its thinning and cutting it has sometimes stopped at once the pains of hollowed teeth, when inserted into the cavity, because it is fine-particled and heating. And indeed it also benefits indurated spleens by cutting and dispersing and thinning the thick humours. The root may be used for these same purposes; and it also detaches scales of bones very quickly, because it dries vigorously, though it heats less than the juice. For malignant ulcers it is an excellent drug when plastered on dry; for it both cleanses and produces flesh and brings them as far as cicatrization, heating in the second order, already more or less completed, and drying in the third, at its beginning.

[8.16.18] [18. On rue.] Rue: the wild kind is already of the fourth order of heating agents, the cultivated kind of the third. It is not only pungent to the taste but also bitter, by which it also has the power of cutting and dispersing thick and viscous humours. By the same power it also moves through the urine. Moreover, it is also fine-particled and dispels flatulence, and for this reason it is suited to flatulent distensions, and it checks the urges towards sexual intercourse, and it disperses and dries vigorously; for it is among the drugs that dry strongly. And what in the preceding discussions we said is called moly and besasa would itself also be wild rue.

[8.16.19] [19. On pitch.] Pitch: the dry kind dries and heats at the second degree of removal from the moderate, and it is by nature more apt to dry than to heat; the liquid kind, conversely, heats more than it dries. It also has something fine-particled, by which it benefits both asthmatics and those suffering from empyema. As to quantity, it suffices to take a cyathus, mixing it with honey. But they also have something cleansing and concocting and dispersing, just as to the taste too they are slightly bitter and pungent. Thus indeed they also remove leprous nails when mixed with wax, and they cleanse away lichens. They also concoct all hard and unconcocted swellings when added to plasters, and for all such purposes the liquid kind is stronger. Dry pitch is inferior for these things, but more suitable for the gluing together of wounds. It is clear, then, from these things that a considerable amount of hot moisture is mixed into liquid pitch.

[8.16.20] [20. On pitch-oil.] Pitch-oil is produced from liquid pitch, being similar to it in kind, but more fine-particled in its substance. [8.16.21] [21. On pistachio.] Pistachio. This plant grows most abundantly in Syria. Its fruit is of a somewhat more fine-particled substance, one that has something slightly bitter and aromatic in it. Accordingly it clears obstructions and thoroughly cleanses, above all the parts about the liver, but also indeed those about the thorax and lung.

[8.16.22] [22. On pine-cone seeds (pityides).] Pityides. This is the name given to the fruit of the pine (pitys); but some, using the word loosely, call that of the fir (peuke) likewise by the same name. They are of a mixed power, inasmuch as they are both astringent and possess a certain pungency together with bitterness. Hence they also assist expectorations from the chest and lung.

[8.16.23] [23. On the pine (pitys).] The bark of the pine (pitys) has the astringent power prevailing in it, to such a degree that, applied as a plaster, it cures chafings (paratrimmata) excellently and checks the bowels, if it is drunk. It also cicatrizes burns. And the bark of the fir (peukē) is similar to it, but more moderate in power. In the leaves of both trees, since they are much moister than the bark, there is a power agglutinating of wounds. In the kōnos-pine, however, even if the power is similar to these, it is nevertheless stronger, both in the bark and in the leaves, so that it can no longer do well any of the things mentioned before, but already has something biting and distressing. The soot (lignys) from the aforesaid is useful for eyelids affected with ptilosis (ptila), for corners of the eyes that are running (mydrōntes), eroded around and weeping.

[8.16.24] [24. On pityousa.] Pityousa. Some consider this too to be a species of spurge (tithymallos), because it has the juice just as those do, and because it purges in a manner similar to them, and in all other respects it resembles them in its power.

[8.16.25] [25. On the plane tree.] The plane tree is of a moister and colder substance, not by any great margin, than the moderate ones. For this reason its green leaves, when pounded fine and applied as a plaster, give manifest benefit to inflammations in their beginning. Its bark and its little globes, however, are already of a more drying power, so that the former, boiled down in vinegar, is employed for pains of the teeth, and the little globes, with fat, for ulcers caused by burning. There are also some who, by burning the bark, produce a drying and cleansing drug, so that with water it cures lepra, and applied by itself as a plaster it cures old and foul ulcers which arise from much moisture. One should guard, however, against the down on the leaves of the tree; for when breathed in it injures the windpipe, drying and roughening it violently, and it damages the voice, just as it also damages the sight and the hearing when it falls into the eyes and ears.

[8.16.26] [26. On polygonon (knotgrass).] Polygonon has something astringent in it too, but what prevails in it is the watery cold, so that it is in the second order among cooling drugs, or perhaps somewhere at the beginning of the third. At any rate it benefits those who suffer a burning heat of the stomach when applied cold from outside as a plaster, as it does also erysipelas and hot inflammations. And being of such a nature it also repels fluxes, and in this way it seems to be drying. For this reason it is also a good drug for herpetic sores (herpetes), and for ulcers, both the other kinds and most manifestly those that are inflamed and fluxional. It is also agglutinating for bleeding wounds. It benefits too the ulcers in the ears, and even if there is a considerable amount of pus in them, it dries this up as well. Through the same powers it also stops the female flux and dysentery and the bringing up of blood, and immoderate discharges from any other source whatever. Dioscorides says that it also provokes urine when given to those suffering from strangury, yet he does not define precisely the condition in which it ought to be given. For all the purposes mentioned the male is stronger than the female.

[8.16.27] [27. On polygalon.] Polygalon has leaves that are moderately harsh. When drunk they are thought to generate milk, so that the hot and the moist would predominate in it. [8.16.28] [28. On polygonaton.] Polygonaton is of a mixed power and quality; for it has something both of astringency and of pungency and of bitterness and of a certain indescribable unpleasantness. For these reasons, then, it is not even of manifold use, except only that some apply the root as a plaster to wounds. And there are those who cleanse away the spots on the face by means of it.

[8.16.29] [29. On polemonion.] Polemonion—others call it philetairion, and some, like the Cappadocians, chiliodynamis—is of a fine-particled and drying power, whence some give its root to drink with wine for cases of sciatica and dysentery and a spleen that is becoming scirrhous.

[8.16.30] [30. On polion.] Polion is bitter to those who taste it and moderately pungent. Accordingly it clears obstructions from all the viscera and moves urine and the menses, and while it is still green it glues together large wounds, and especially the shrub-like species of it does so; but once it has become dry it heals the malignant ulcers when sprinkled on, and the smaller kind does this more.

[8.16.31] [31. On the small polion.] The small polion, which we also use in the antidotes; for this one is both more pungent and more bitter than the larger, so that it is of the third order of drying things, and of the second order, fully completed, of heating things.

[8.16.32] [32. On polyknemon.] Polyknemon dries and heats at the second remove (ἀπόστασις), so that for this reason too it is agglutinating of wounds. [8.16.33] [33. On potamogeiton.] Potamogeiton is astringent and cooling in a manner closely resembling polygonon; but its substance is more coarse-particled than that of polygonon.

[8.16.34] [34. On polypody.] Polypody has a quality that is at once sweet and harsh predominating, so that it is of a drying power that is sufficiently non-biting. [8.16.35] [35. On horehound.] Horehound, just as it is bitter to the taste, so also for those who use it has an activity that agrees with such a flavour, unblocking both the liver and the spleen, and thoroughly cleansing the parts about the chest and the lung, and provoking the menses. But also, when applied as a plaster, it both cleanses and disperses. And one might place it, in respect of heat, somewhere in the second rank already being completed, and in respect of dryness, in the third, either at its middle or being completed. Its juice they also use, with honey, for sharpness of sight; and moreover they also purge jaundice through the nostrils with it, and they also take it up for pains of the ears that have already become chronic, in so far as there is need to unblock and thoroughly cleanse both the passage itself and the outgrowths of the meninges.

[8.16.36] [36. On propolis.] Propolis is of a cleansing power that is not strong, but of a drawing power that is sufficiently strong; for it is fine-particled in its substance. It heats in the second degree, already being completed, and the third beginning.

[8.16.37] [37. On ptarmike (sneezewort).] Of ptarmike the flowers are of sternutatory power, whence indeed the herb also has its name. The whole little shrub disperses bruises under the eyes (hypopia) and the other extravasations of fluid (ecchymoses). For its mixture is hot and dry, while still green in the second rank, but if it should be dried, in the third.

[8.16.38] [38. On elm.] With the leaves of elm we once glued together a fresh wound, trusting in the fact that an astringent and at the same time cleansing power is contained in them. The bark is still more slightly bitter and astringent, so that it even cures lepra with vinegar; and while it is still green and fresh, if it is wound around wounds like a bandage, it is able to glue them together. The roots too are of the same power, so that some also foment with the decoction those fractures which require the formation of a callus.

[8.16.39] [39. On pteris (male fern) and thelypteris (female fern).] Pteris has a root that is especially useful. For it destroys the broad worm, if one takes a weight of four drachms of it in honey-water (melikraton). And in the same way it is nothing to be wondered at that it destroys living embryos and expels dead ones. For it is bitter, partaking of a small degree of astringency. On this account, too, when applied to ulcers it is of a strongly drying power, yet not biting. And the so-called thelypteris has a power similar to it.

[8.16.40] [40. On pyknokomon.] Of pyknokomon the root, the fruit and the leaves alike are of a dispersing and drawing power, being also pungent to the taste. The leaves, then, disperse phymata and boils, while the fruit is stronger; and it is of a nature to effect these things when mixed into some one of the dispersing plasters, such as is the one made with barley-meal; and it also draws splinters and all such things to the outer surface. The root is inferior and weaker for the purposes just mentioned, yet it is purgative of yellow bile.

[8.16.41] [41. On pyrethron.] Of pyrethron we use the root, which has a markedly caustic power, in virtue of which it soothes the pains of chilled teeth, is rubbed on with oil before periodic rigors, and benefits those who are numb and paralysed.

[8.16.42] [42. On wheat.] Wheat, of what sort of nature it is as food, does not belong to the present treatise; but as a drug applied externally it is of the first order of heating things, yet it is not by nature either drying or moistening in any evident way. It also has something viscous and obstructive. The starch prepared from it becomes colder and more drying than wheat itself. And the plaster made from bread is of a more dispersing power than that made from grains of wheat, inasmuch as the bread has previously received both salt and leaven; for leaven is of a power that attracts and disperses what lies in the depth.

[8.17.1] [1. On rhamnos.] Rhamnos dries and disperses in the second degree, and cools in the first degree at its completion or the second at its beginning. For this reason it also cures herpetes and cases of erysipelas that are not very hot. One should use its tender leaves for these purposes.

[8.17.2] [2. On radish.] Radish heats in the third degree, and dries in the second. The wild kind is more active in both respects; and indeed the seed too is more active than the plant itself. The power in it is dispersing, so that it has in fact proved beneficial also for bruises beneath the eyes and the other livid affections, on account of such a power.

[8.17.3] [3. On rheon.] Rheon — some call it rha — is of a mixed mixture and power. For it has something earthy and cold, as its astringency shows; but there is also present in it a certain heat, for when chewed for a longer time it appears somewhat pungent. And indeed, that it partakes of a certain airy, fine-particled substance is shown both by its looseness and its lightness, and not least also by its effects. For on this very account, although it is astringent, it nonetheless benefits not only strains but also ruptures and orthopnoea. So too it cures livid marks and lichens when smeared on with vinegar. And that the effects of its astringency too are vigorous one may learn from the fact that it helps those who spit blood, coeliacs and dysenterics. For the fine-particled airy part does not work against the earthy cold; rather, by guiding it and leading it into the depth, it becomes the cause of a stronger activity.

[8.17.4] [4. On resins.] All resins dry and heat. They differ from one another in having more or less of what is pungent in taste and heating in power, and in that some of them are less fine-particled and others more so, and in that some partake of astringency and others do not. Reasonably, the one from the lentisk has been preferred out of all of them; they call it mastic. For in addition to its partaking of a little astringency, so that it is suited to the weaknesses (atonies) and inflammations about the stomach (stomachos), the belly and the liver, it also possesses the power of drying, and that without distress. For it is least pungent and most fine-particled. Of the others the terebinth resin holds first place, not having its astringency as manifest as mastic does, but possessing a certain bitterness, on account of which it is also more dispersing than mastic. Through this same quality it also possesses a cleansing power, to such a degree that it even cures psora (scabby itch). And indeed it also draws up things from the depth more than the other resins, because it is more fine-particled than they. The pine resin (peukine), and still more than this the stone-pine resin (strobiline), are more pungent than it, yet they neither disperse more nor draw more. Intermediate among them are the pitys-pine resin and the fir resin, being more pungent than the terebinth resin, but less pungent than the pine and stone-pine resins. The terebinth resin also has a softening power. Second in softening is the lentisk resin, just as the cypress resin is pungent.

[8.17.5] [5. On the rose.] The power of roses has been stated in what precedes at greater length, namely that it is composed of a warm watery substance mixed together with two other qualities, the astringent and the bitter. And indeed of what sort each of the two is in its nature, both the bitter and the astringent, has been stated by me in the fourth of these commentaries. Their flower is still more astringent than the roses themselves, and evidently for this reason drying.

[8.17.6] [6. On rose-root.] Rose-root (rhodia rhiza), the kind that grows in Macedonia, is of a fine-particled and dispersing power. In heating, one should place it somewhere in the second degree of departure, or even in the third at its beginning.

[8.17.7] [7. On rhododaphne (rose-laurel).] Rhododaphne, in respect of its whole substance, is deleterious not only to human beings but also to most grazing animals; in respect of its mixture, it belongs to the third mixture of heating things at its beginning, and to the first of drying things.

[8.17.8] [8. On pomegranates.] Every pomegranate partakes of the astringent quality, yet it does not predominate in all of them. For some of them are sour, and some are sweet more than harsh. And indeed the benefits of each of them must necessarily come about in accordance with the predominating quality. It has been stated in the fourth of these treatises concerning the sweet, the harsh and the sour flavour, so that from those discussions it is possible for you to reason out also the difference among pomegranates. The seeds are more astringent and more drying than the juice; and still more so than these are the rinds, which are called sidia. Of a similar power to these are the kytinoi (pomegranate flowers).

[8.17.9] [9. On rhous (sumach).] Rhous, the shrub-like plant, is astringent and drying, just as the tanners too use the plant for drying and making the hides astringent, and for this reason it is called by the physicians the tanners' plant (byrsodepsike). It is chiefly its fruit and its juice that come into use, being of a sufficiently harsh quality. And the whole of its use in particular cases agrees with the perception by taste. This drug too, then, would be drying in the third rank, and cooling in the second.

[8.17.10] [10. On dirt.] Dirt: that from the statues in the gymnasia, on which abundant oil lies, is both dispersing and softening. That in the wrestling-schools differs from it to the extent that it has taken up a share of the dust. They call this dirt patos. The former, then, is dispersing of unconcocted swellings, while the second is the best remedy for inflammation of the breasts; for it both quenches their fiery quality and represses the influx and disperses what is contained in them. For it is composed of dust and oil and human dirt and sweat. The dust, then, is emplastic and cooling and repelling, the oil softening, and the sweat and the dirt dispersing. But that from the statues, since it does not have the dust and has taken on some verdigris from the bronze, is reasonably more pungent. We have mentioned it here too, because the greatest part of it consists of the oil-like substance, which has its origin from a plant. But it will be necessary to mention it also among the things derived from animals, on account of the sweat.

[8.18.1] [1. On sagapenon.] Sagapenon is a juice, hot and fine-particled, in the same way as the other juices. It also has something cleansing, by which it both cleans away and thins the scars in the eyes. Moreover, it is also a good drug for suffusions and for dimnesses of sight that arise through thickness of the humours.
