The plant itself from which it comes, being similar to the narthex, is weak and useless; and clearly it is that which is called sagapenon in the first place. For its juice is so termed by those who use the word loosely, just as we also name many other things by catachresis through an elliptical expression. For it would have been more complete to call it not sagapenon but juice of sagapenon.

[8.18.2] [2. On sampsychon.] Sampsychon is of a fine-particled and dispersing power; for it both dries and heats in the third rank. [8.18.3] [3. On the rottenness of woods.] Rottenness of woods, and especially of those which partake of astringency together with a cleansing quality, as does the elm, cleanses and fills up moist ulcers.

[8.18.4] [4. On sarcocolla.] Sarcocolla is the tear of a Persian tree, having a mixed power from a certain clogging substance and a slight bitter one, whence it dries without biting and for this reason is able to glue wounds together.

[8.18.5] [5. On satyrion.] Satyrion or trefoil (triphyllon) is moist and hot in its mixture, and for this reason it also appears sweet when tasted. It possesses, however, a moisture that is superfluous and flatulent, and on this account it incites to sexual intercourse. The root of the plant too is of a nature to do these things. And, as some write, it also cures opisthotonos, when drunk with harsh dark wine.

[8.18.6] [6. On celery.] Celery is hot to such a degree as to move urine and the menses. It also dispels flatulence, and the seed more than the herb. The power of mountain-celery and of horse-celery is similar; but horse-celery is weaker, just as mountain-celery is stronger.

[8.18.7] [7. On seris.] Seris is a somewhat bitter vegetable, and the wild kind more so; and for this very reason some call it pikris, while others name it kichorion. It is of a dry and cold mixture, having both qualities at the first degree of departure. The cultivated kind cools more than the wild, but through admixture of much foreign moisture it loses its drying power. Both share in the astringent quality, just as chondrile does too; for this also is a species of seris.

[8.18.8] [8. On seriphon.] Seriphon. This has been discussed in the sixth book, in the account of apsinthion. For it is similar to apsinthion in appearance and taste, yet it nonetheless differs: in taste, in that it is not astringent in the same way as that one, and heats and is bitter to a greater degree, with a certain saltiness; and in power, in that it is bad for the stomach and kills worms more than apsinthion does, both when applied externally and when taken into the body. And indeed one must place it in the second order, at its intense degree, as regards heating, and in the third as regards drying.

[8.18.9] [9. On seseli.] Seseli. Both the root and, further, the fruit as well are among the heating things to such a degree as to be a sufficiently diuretic drug. It is also fine-particled, so that it is suitable also against epilepsies and orthopnoea.

[8.18.10] [10. On sesame.] Sesame has in itself not a little of the viscous and the oily, whence it is clogging and at the same time softening and moderately hot. Of the same power is also the oil derived from it. And the decoction of the herb too is of a similar power.

[8.18.11] [11. On sesamoides.] The large sesamoides, which has also been named Anticyran hellebore because its seed purges in a manner similar to hellebore. This is also similar to hellebore in its other power; and indeed in cleansing, heating and drying as well it is like that plant in its power.

[8.18.12] [12. On the white sesamoides.] The seed of the white sesamoides partakes also of a certain pungent quality, but it is bitter to a considerable degree. Accordingly it heats, breaks up and cleanses.

[8.18.13] [13. On sideritis.] Sideritis has indeed also something cleansing, but the greater part of it is moist and moderately cold, and it has partaken of some slight astringency, whence it is both non-inflammatory and agglutinating. Some also call the Achilleios sideritis; it is similar to the aforementioned in its power, at least as regards the properties just mentioned, but surpasses it in astringency. For this reason it is also suitable for haemorrhages and dysentery and the female fluxes.

[8.18.14] [14. On the edible cucumber.] The edible cucumber, when already ripe, is of a more fine-particled substance, but when not such, of a more coarse-particled one. Nonetheless they also partake of a cleansing and cutting power, whence they are diuretic and brighten the body, and more so if one dries the seed and then, having pounded and sifted it, uses it as a cleansing wash. A moist and cold mixture prevails in them, yet not strongly, but such that it is placed somewhere in the second rank. If, however, one were to dry the seed or the root, it is no longer even of the moist nature, but already of the drying nature in about the first rank, or even the beginning of the second. The cleansing quality, too, is greater in these than in the flesh of the fruit.

[8.18.15] [15. On wild cucumber.] Of the wild cucumber both the juice of the fruit, which they call elaterion, and no less also that of the root and of the leaves, happen to be suitable for cures. Elaterion, then, provokes the menses and destroys the foetus when applied as a pessary, just as do the other things that are at once bitter and fine-particled, especially if they also partake of some heat, as indeed elaterion does. For it is bitter in the highest degree, but hot to a small extent, so as to be of the second order in respect of heat. Such a thing is also at once of dispersing power; thus, at any rate, some anoint with it those suffering from synanche, together with honey or old oil. It is good also for those suffering from jaundice when poured into the nostrils with milk; and used in this way it also cures headaches. Such, then, is elaterion; but the juice of the root, as also that of the leaves, is similar to elaterion in power, though weaker. And the root itself is of a closely similar power; for it cleanses and disperses and softens, but its bark is more drying than it.

[8.18.16] [16. On silphium.] Of silphium the juice is the hottest, but nonetheless the leaves too, and the stalk and the root, heat vigorously. All of them are of a rather flatulent substance and on that account hard to digest. When applied externally, however, upon the body they are more active, and most of all the juice, which possesses a considerable drawing power. And indeed it also has something reducing and melting-away in it, on account of its aforesaid mixture.
[8.18.17] [17. On sison.] Sison is hot and somewhat bitter to the taste. Hence it is diuretic and digestive, provocative of the menses and unblocking of all the obstructions in the viscera.

[8.18.18] [18. On sion.] Sion, to the extent that it is in some way aromatic in taste, to that extent has also partaken of a power that is in some way heating. It is dispersing and diuretic, breaks up the stones in the kidneys, and is promotive of the menses.

[8.18.19] [19. On the root of sisaron.] The root of sisaron, when boiled, is both good for the stomach and diuretic, heating in the second order, but having also something of bitterness and something of slight astringency.

[8.18.20] [20. On sisymbrion.] Sisymbrion is of a fine-particled, dispersing power and mixture, heating and drying in the third rank. And its seed too is fine-particled and hot, whence some give it (αὐτήν) with wine to those who hiccup and to those suffering from gripes.

[8.18.21] [21. On sisymbrion.] Sisymbrion, which some call kardamine, since it has something resembling kardamomon in taste, when it is dry belongs to the third rank of things that dry and at the same time heat, but when it is moist and green, to the second.

[8.18.22] [22. On skandix (shepherd's needle).] Skandix is one of the wild vegetables, somewhat acrid and bitter, so that in drying and in heating it belongs either to the second order at its height or to the third at its beginning. It is sufficiently diuretic and unblocking of the viscera, being composed of the qualities mentioned.

[8.18.23] [23. On squill] Squill is of a sufficiently cutting power, though not indeed strongly hot; rather, in this respect one would place it in the second order of heating things. It is better to take it roasted or boiled, for in this way the vehemence of its power is relaxed.

[8.18.24] [24. On the root of skolymos.] The root of skolymos brings on a great quantity of foul-smelling urine, if one boils it down in wine and drinks it. And for this reason it also cures the foul smells both of the armpits and of the whole body. This, then, belongs to the drug in its entire substance, as being purgative of such a humour. But its activity in respect of the qualities shows the drug to be hot in the second order already being completed or the third beginning, and dry in the second.

[8.18.25] [25. On skordion.] Skordion. This is compounded of manifold humours and powers. For it has in it something bitter, something acerbic and something pungent, and its pungency most of all resembles garlic (skorodon), whence, I think, it also derived its name. Accordingly it at once thoroughly cleanses and warms the viscera, moves the menses and the urine, and cures strains and ruptures and pains of the sides arising from obstruction and chilling when drunk; it glues together large wounds when plastered on green, and it cleanses foul ones and brings malignant ones to a scar when sprinkled on dry.

[8.18.26] [26. On garlic.] Garlic dries and heats in the fourth degree of departure. What is called ophioscorodon (snake-garlic) is a wild garlic, stronger than the cultivated kind, just as the other wild plants are.
[8.18.27] [27. On skordoprason.] Skordoprason, just as in taste and in smell it possesses a quality mixed of garlic and leek, in the same manner also [does so] in its power.
[8.18.28] [28. On scorpioides.] Scorpioides heats in the third rank, and dries in the second. [8.18.29] [29. On smilax.] Smilax, or taxos (yew), is a tree of deleterious power.

[8.18.30] [30. On myrrh.] Myrrh belongs to the second order of things that heat and dry. At any rate, when plastered upon wounds in the head it is able to glue them together. It also partakes of no small bitterness, on account of which it both kills and expels embryos and worms. And from this source it also possesses the cleansing property. So at any rate it is also mixed into the ophthalmic preparations, those which are compounded for ulcers and thick scars. For the same reason it is also mixed into the drugs given for chronic cough and asthma; yet it does not roughen the windpipe as some of the cleansing agents do, but has its cleansing so moderate that some mix it even into the drugs called arteriacs, as a drug that heats and dries sufficiently, taking no precaution at all against the cleansing that comes from its bitterness.

[8.18.31] [31. On bovine myrrh.] Bovine myrrh has a heating, diffusing, softening power. [8.18.32] [32. On smyrnion.] Smyrnion, which some call wild hipposelinon (horse-celery), is also of the same genus as celery and parsley. And it would be stronger than celery, but weaker than parsley. It is therefore a drawer-down of the menses and a diuretic, and hot and dry in the third order. Those in Cilicia give the name parsley (petroselinon) to that which grows on Mount Amanus. It too, however, is a smyrnion, but it is less pungent than parsley and smyrnion, and for this reason it can also be applied to wounds, since it dries without causing distress. But it is also dispersing of hardened parts. Its other power is similar to celery and parsley, wherefore we also use its seed for the menses and urine and asthmas.

[8.18.33] [33. On sonchos.] Sonchos, when it has reached maturity, is one of the thorny plants, but while still green and tender it is eaten in the same way as the other wild vegetables. Its mixture is in a way mixed, for it is composed of a watery and an earthy substance, both of them slightly cold. For indeed it partakes of some astringency and manifestly cools, both when applied as a plaster and when eaten. But when it has been completely dried, its mixture becomes earthy, possessing a moderate degree of heat.

[8.18.34] [34. On sparganion.] Sparganion too is of a drying power. [8.18.35] [35. On sparte (Spanish broom).] Sparte, with which in our country they bind the vines: both its fruit and the juice of its rods are of a drawing power, and not feebly so.

[8.18.36] [36. On staphylinos.] Staphylinos: the cultivated kind is weaker, the wild kind stronger in every respect. It moves urine and promotes the menses—the whole herb does so, but especially the seed and the root. It also has something cleansing in it, which is why some people apply its fresh leaves with honey as a plaster to phagedaenic ulcers in order to make them clean.

[8.18.37] [37. On stachys.] Stachys, the shrub resembling horehound, is pungent to the taste and bitter, belonging to the third order of heating agents, so that with good reason it not only moves the menses but is also an abortifacient drug, and it expels the afterbirth (choria).

[8.18.38] [38. On stoibe.] Of stoibe the fruit and the leaves are especially useful, having an astringent power that does not bite. It is also, in drying, evidently somewhere at the beginning of the third rank, whence their decoction is injected both for dysenterics and for ears discharging pus, and is agglutinating of large wounds. It does these things more evidently with harsh black wine, for it dries strongly all the moistures that are contrary to nature. Further, the leaves while still green, applied as a plaster, have a power of checking haemorrhage, and it also benefits the bruisings of the eyes that result from a blow when applied as a plaster.

[8.18.39] [39. On stoechas.] Of stoechas the quality in relation to taste is both bitter and moderately sub-astringent. Its mixture is composite, from a small amount of cold earthy substance, from which it is astringent, and from another, larger amount of thinned earthy substance, from which it is bitter. And because of the conjunction of both, it is naturally suited to unblock, thin, cleanse and strengthen both all the viscera and the condition of the whole animal. For it was shown in what precedes that all the drugs which are composed of such substances perform the said activities.

[8.18.40] [40. On stratiotes.] Stratiotes: the aquatic kind is moist and cold in its power, while the land kind has also something of astringency, so that for this reason it is able both to glue together wounds and to be useful for ulcers. Some people also use it for haemorrhage and for fistulas.

[8.18.41] [41. On strouthion.] Of strouthion we use chiefly the root, which is pungent in taste, and hot and dry in mixture, being of course from the fourth order. It is also cleansing and irritant, and for this reason it also provokes sneezing, in the same way as the other things which are pungent when tasted and hot in their mixtures.

[8.18.42] [42. On storax.] Storax warms, softens, and concocts; for this reason it also benefits coughs, catarrhs, coryzas and hoarseness, and it promotes the menses, both when drunk and when applied as a pessary; and the soot (lignys) of it when burnt is in some way similar to that of frankincense.

[8.18.43] Figs, the dry ones, are hot in power, somewhere about the first order already being completed, or the second beginning; and they also have something fine-particled. From both of these they are capable of concocting the hard sort of swellings, and they at once disperse them. And so applied by themselves as a plaster they are of such a power; and their decoction too is of a similar nature. But where you wish rather to concoct, one should mix in wheat flour, and where to disperse, barley-meal. Bread stands midway between these. But such matters belong more properly to the composition of drugs and to the therapeutic method. For the present it suffices to know these things also about dried figs. One should know too that the dirtier ones are more apt to concoct, while those more pungent in taste are by nature cleansing and dispersing; and what results when they have been boiled in water for a very long time is similar to honey, not only in consistency but also in power. Green figs, when eaten, because of the admixture of moisture, are of weaker power; both kinds, however, the moist and the dry, move the bowel. The figs of wild fig-trees are of pungent and dispersing power. So too the unripe figs of cultivated trees, for they still partake of the juice of the fig-tree.

[8.18.44] [44. On the fig-tree.] The fig-tree is of a hot and fine-particled mixture, as both its juice and the sap of its leaves show. For each of them is strongly hot, so that it not only bites or cleanses vigorously, but also ulcerates and opens up the orifices and casts out myrmecia. It is also purgative. The juice and the sap of the wild fig-tree, which they call erineos, are stronger for all purposes than those of the cultivated one. And their young branches (kradai) too are so hot and fine-particled in mixture that, when thrown in with tough beef as it is being boiled, they make it tender.

[8.18.45] [45. On rock comfrey.] Rock comfrey is composed of opposite powers. For it has something cutting, by which it is naturally fitted to clear out the pus contained in the thorax and lung; and it has something contracting, by which it also helps against bringings-up of blood; and, third in addition to these, a certain moisture that is warm, not immoderately so, on account of which it also appears sweet to those who taste it and pleasant to the sense of smell. Chewed, it allays thirst, and it cures the roughnesses in the windpipe. In accordance with the mixture of all the powers mentioned, it is capable at once both of dispersing and of contracting and binding bodies. And for this reason it is both applied to intestinal hernias and drunk with oxymel for sprains and ruptures. Those who give it also for dysentery and red flux, boiling it in wine, use it as a drying and contracting agent, and those who give it for kidney disease, as a cleansing and cutting one.

[8.18.46] [46. On the great comfrey.] The other comfrey, the great one, is of a power similar to that of the one mentioned before, yet it does not appear sweet to those who taste it nor fragrant to those who smell it; in these respects, then, it departs from the one described above, but insofar as it has something viscous and biting, it is similar to squill. They use it for all the same purposes as the one mentioned before.

[8.18.47] [47. On sphondylion.] Of sphondylion the fruit is of a pungent and cutting power, so that it is a good drug both for asthma and for epilepsy. It also benefits those suffering from jaundice. And the root too, being of a similar power, is suitable for the same conditions, and in addition it also removes the calluses arising from fistulas; one must scrape it around and insert it. And the juice of the flower too is stored away, being suitable for the more chronic ulcers in the ears.

[8.18.48] [48. On schinos (mastic tree).] Schinos (mastic tree): this shrub is composed of a watery substance gently warm in its power and of an earthy cold one, not in large quantity, on account of which it is also moderately astringent. It dries, then, in the second order when already being completed, or in the third when beginning. In the difference according to heat and cold, it is somewhat intermediate and well-balanced. It has a similar astringency in all its own parts: in roots, in branches, in young shoots, in sprouts, in leaves, and further in fruit and bark. And if you should squeeze out juice from its green leaves, this too is of a similar order, moderately astringent, whence it is also drunk both by itself and together with the other drugs, as many as heal dysentery and coeliac conditions. And indeed it is also suitable for spittings of blood and haemorrhages from the womb and prolapses of the seat and of the uterus, being something close to hypocistis.

[8.18.49] [49. On the flower of schinos (mastic tree).] The flower of schinos heats moderately and is moderately astringent, and furthermore it is not devoid of the fine-particled nature. Accordingly, for these reasons the drug is also diuretic and promotive of the menses, being employed both in fomentations and in draughts. It also benefits the inflammations in the liver, the stomach and the belly. Of it the root is more astringent, while what is called the flower is hotter. In all its parts, in some more, in others less, something of astringency shows itself on tasting, on account of which it is also mixed with the drugs given to those who spit blood.

[8.18.50] [50. On smooth rush, sharp rush and whole rush.] Of rush, one kind is called smooth, another sharp rush, another whole rush. The sharp rush is thinner and harder, the whole rush thicker and more spongy. The fruit of the whole rush is sleep-inducing; of the sharp rush there are two kinds: the one fruitless, of which there is no use for cures, the other fruit-bearing; and the fruit of this too is soporific, but less so than that of the whole rush. This one, indeed, is also productive of headache. Both, if roasted and drunk with wine, dry up the fluxes in the belly and check the red flux. From which it is clear that their mixture is composed of an earthy substance that is gently cold and a watery one that is gently hot, so that they are able both to dry the lower parts and to send up to the head vapours that are mildly cold, by which they also render people soporific.

[8.19.1] [1. On the terebinth.] Of the terebinth both the bark and the leaves and the fruit have something astringent. But they also heat in the second order, so that it is already clear that they also dry: while they are still fresh and moist, moderately, but once they have been dried, in the second order. The dried fruit is close even to the third order of drying agents. For it is so hot that its heat becomes quite clear at once even to those who chew it. For these reasons, then, they are also diuretic and benefit the spleen.

[8.19.2] [2. On beet.] Beet partakes of a certain nitrous power, by which it both cleanses and disperses and purges through the nostrils. When boiled, however, it lays aside all that is nitrous and pungent, and comes to have a power that is free of inflammation and gently dispersing. The white beet is stronger for cleansing and dispersing, since the black beet has also something of astringency, and more in the root than in the other parts.

[8.19.3] [3. On teukrion.] Teukrion is of a cutting and fine-particled power, whence it also cures spleens. And one might place it in the third rank of drying things, and in the second of heating things.

[8.19.4] [4. On ash.] Ash. The residue of burnt wood is so called, being compounded out of opposite substances and qualities. For it has in itself on the one hand something earthy, on the other something as it were sooty or smoke-like, or whatever one wishes to call it. Now these parts are fine-particled, and when the ash is soaked in water and filtered through they are carried off along with it. But what earthy part is left behind becomes weak and non-biting, having deposited its hot power in the lye. Not all ash, however, has exactly the same mixture, but it varies according to the difference of the material that has been burnt. Dioscorides, though, says—I do not know how—that it has an astringent power. And yet fig-wood ash is free of every such quality, because the tree itself too, unlike oak and holm-oak and strawberry-tree and valonia oak and mastic-tree and ivy and all other such trees, displays the acerbic quality in no part of itself, but is wholly full of a strong, hot and pungent juice. From acerbic woods, then, the ash has no small astringent element, and I myself know that I once checked haemorrhages by means of it, when no other drug was at hand. But fig-wood ash no one would ever use for this purpose, for this one has much of the pungent and the caustic mixed with the cleansing, and in both respects it differs from the ash from oak woods, both because the sooty element in it is far more pungent and because the earthy element, as it were, is in those somewhat sub-astringent, whereas in this it is cleansing, as it is in the ash of the spurges (tithymalloi). Lime too is a kind of ash, being more fine-particled than that from woods, inasmuch as stones need to be roasted more thoroughly in order to become ash, yet nevertheless it too has much of the fiery residue (empyreuma), as it were. And for this reason, when washed, it becomes a drying drug without biting, and the more so if it is washed twice or even three times. It becomes sufficiently dispersing when washed with sea-water. It will be spoken of also when our discussion comes to deal with the minerals.

[8.19.5] [5. On telephion.] Telephion is of a drying and cleansing power, not however of a manifestly hot one; rather, in this respect one might perhaps place it in the first order. It dries, however, in the second order at its intensified degree, or at the beginning of the third. And for this reason it is suited to putrefactive ulcers, and it cures leukai and alphoi with vinegar.

[8.19.6] [6. On fenugreek.] Fenugreek is hot in the second order, but dry in the first, and for this reason it exacerbates inflammations that are seething, whereas those that are less hot and all that are more scirrhous it cures by dispersing them.

[8.19.7] [7. On spurges (tithymalloi).] All spurges (tithymalloi) have as their predominant power the pungent and hot one; but there belongs to them also a bitterness. The strongest in this is the juice, and next come the fruit and the leaves. The root too shares in the powers mentioned, but not equally. Now the root itself, boiled with vinegar, cures pains of the teeth, and especially those that arise when the teeth are eaten away. The juices, which have a more vigorous power, are inserted into the hole of the teeth; but if they touch the other parts of the body they at once burn and ulcerate them, which is why wax is plastered around them on the outside. For they belong to the fourth order of heating things, which indeed we said is that of the caustics. In this way too the juice, smeared around, removes the hairs; but since it is more vigorous, it is mixed with oil, and if this is done many times, the roots of the hairs are completely destroyed by being burnt and the body becomes bare of them. By the same power they remove acrochordons, myrmecia, pterygia and thymoi. They also cleanse away lichens and psorai, because they share in the cleansing power too on account of their bitterness; and phagedaenic ulcers, and those of the anthrax kind and the gangrenous, because they heat vigorously and cleanse, they are naturally fitted to benefit, if one happens to use them at the right time and in due measure. For indeed they also remove the calluses of fistulas by the same power. All these things both the leaves and the fruit are naturally fitted to do, similarly in kind but more weakly; and these people are accustomed to use also against the fish in standing waters, for very quickly, stupefied by them and rendered half-dead, they are brought up to the surface of the water. There being seven of them, the strongest are the one named charakias, which indeed some people also call the male, and the female, called myrsinites, and the tree-like one that grows among the rocks; next the one resembling phlomos (mullein) and the kyparissias, then in this order the paralios, then the helioskopos. In proportion to the power of theirs that has been described are the ash and the lye made from it.

[8.19.8] [8. On tragacanth.] Tragacanth has a power similar to that of gum, a certain clogging quality and a rather blunted pungency. And indeed it also dries in much the same way as that does. [8.19.9] [9. On tragion.] Of tragion, the leaves, the fruit and the tear (gum) are of a drawing and dispersing power. It is also fine-particled and hot in power, already somewhere at the beginning of the third rank. It draws out splinters, breaks up stones, and moves the menses when drunk in the weight of one drachm. This tragion, which resembles the schinos (mastic tree), grows only in Crete. The other tragion, the one smaller than this, whose leaves resemble those of scolopendrion, appears in many places, and it partakes of no small astringent power, so that it is suitable also for the fluxional affections.

[8.19.10] [10. On tragoriganon.] Tragoriganon: it has been discussed earlier, in the account of Origanum. [8.19.11] [11. On tribolos.] Tribolos is composed of a moist substance that is moderately cold and of a dry one that is, for its part, not moderately cold. In the land kind the earthy cold element prevails, which we have also shown to be astringent, while in the water kind the watery element prevails; and for this reason both are suitable both against the beginnings of inflammations and, in general, against all fluxes. The fruit of the land kind, being fine-particled, breaks up stones in the kidneys when drunk.

[8.19.12] [12. On tripolion.] Tripolion. The root is pungent to the taste and hot in its power to the third degree of remove. [8.19.13] [13. On trefoil (triphyllon).] Trefoil (triphyllon); some call it asphaltion, others oxyphyllon, some people minyanthes, and there are those who name it knikion. The first three names derive from attributes of the shrub; as for the remaining two, I do not know from where they come. The power of the plant is hot and dry, after the manner of asphalt, to which it is similar in smell, being of the third order in both respects. And for this reason, when drunk, it also relieves pains of the sides arising from obstructions, and it moves the urine and the menses.

[8.19.14] [14. On trichomanes.] Trichomanes has the same powers as adianton. [8.19.15] [15. On trychnon or strychnon.] Trychnon: some people name it with the sigma, strychnon. The edible kind, which grows in gardens, everyone knows and uses for all conditions that need to be cooled and made astringent; for it has both these powers in the second order. Of the others, which are not edible, one is called halikakabon, having a red fruit resembling a grape-berry in shape and size, which they also use for garlands; the other is the shrub-like, sleep-inducing kind; and third after these is the madness-inducing kind. Now the halikakabon is similar in the power of its leaves to the garden-grown trychnon, and has a diuretic fruit; and for this reason it is also mixed into many of the compound remedies that are suited to the liver or bladder or kidneys. Of the sleep-inducing strychnon, the bark of the root, drunk with wine, is sleep-inducing, taken in the weight of one drachm. In other respects too it is similar to the juice of the poppy, but weaker to such a degree that it belongs to the third order of cooling things, whereas that one is placed in the fourth. The seed of this trychnon has a diuretic power; but it is madness-producing when more than twelve clusters are drunk. The remaining one of the trychna mentioned is useless for the cures of internal parts. For if four drachms of them are taken, they bring on death; if fewer, madness. A single drachm is harmless, except that even this has nothing useful in it. But when it is plastered on the body externally, it cures malignant and spreading ulcers. Best for this purpose is the bark of the root, drying at about the second order already being completed and the third beginning, and cooling at the second order beginning.

[8.20.1] [1. On hyacinth.] Of hyacinth the root, which is bulb-like, is of the first order in drying, and in cooling of the second order already nearly completed or even of the third beginning. At any rate it is believed to keep boys beardless for a very long time when applied as a plaster in wine. The fruit cleanses gently and is astringent, and for this reason it too is given to those suffering from jaundice with wine, drying already somewhere about the third order, while with respect to heat and cooling it stands in the middle.

[8.20.2] [2. On truffle.] Truffles, familiar to all, possess in their composition a predominating, more earthy substance, with some small portion of the fine-particled mixed into it. [8.20.3] [3. On water-pepper.] Water-pepper has been so named from the places in which it grows and from its similarity in taste to pepper. It is hot, but not to the degree that pepper is; and moreover the little plant, while still green, applied as a plaster together with its fruit, disperses bruises under the eyes and swellings that are becoming hardened (scirrhous).

[8.20.4] [4. On henbane.] Henbane: the one with black seed is productive of madness and stupefying. Close to it in power is also the one whose seed is moderately yellow; both are to be avoided as useless and deleterious. Most suitable for cures is the one whose seed and flower are both white, belonging roughly to the third order of cooling things. The flower of the one with black seed is moderately purplish, while that of the one with yellowish seed is faintly quince-yellow.

[8.20.5] [5. On hyperikon.] Hyperikon (St John's wort) heats and dries, being of fine-particled substance, so as to provoke both the menses and urine. For these purposes one should take the whole fruit, not the seed alone, but together with the leaves; applied as a plaster while green, it is able to bring to a scar other lesions and in particular burns. And if, once it has been dried, you pound it and sprinkle it on, you will heal the flabby and putrefactive kinds of ulcers. Some people also give it to drink to those suffering from sciatica.

[8.20.6] [6. On hypecoon.] Hypecoon is of cooling power, from roughly the third rank of cooling things, so as to fall a little short of poppy. [8.20.7] [7. On hypoglosson.] Hypoglosson has been so named because it produces, beneath the tips of the clusters, outgrowths like little tongues. The root and the juice of the shrublet are of softening power.

[8.20.8] [8. On hyssop.] Hyssop heats and dries in the third order, and it is also fine-particled. [8.21.1] [1. On lentils.] Lentils are strongly astringent, but as regards heat and cold they stand in the middle. Moreover, they also dry in the second order. Now their body itself dries and stops the belly, whereas the decoction drives it forward; for which reason also the first water is poured off whenever they are taken for the sake of retention.

[8.21.2] [2. On phakos (duckweed).] Phakos (duckweed), the kind on the marshes, is of a moist and cold mixture, being of roughly the second order in both respects. [8.21.3] [3. On phaleris.] Of the herb phaleris both the juice and the seed and the leaves, when drunk, are believed to help against the pains of the bladder, as it has in it something fine-particled and hot.

[8.21.4] [4. On phalangites.] Phalangites. It has been so named from its helping those bitten by phalangia. It is of a fine-particled, drying power, whence it is also thought to be of help to those suffering from colic.

[8.21.5] [5. On phlomos.] Phlomos (mullein) — some people both write and pronounce it with a p. One kind is white in its leaves, the other black. And of the white kind one is the male, whose leaves are narrower, the other the female, whose leaves are larger. And in addition to these there is another phlomos, called wild, which is golden and quince-yellow in its flowers. And yet another besides these, which they specifically call phlomis and thryallis. Now the root of the first two, being acerbic to the taste, helps in conditions of flux. Some people also rinse the mouth with it for pains of the teeth. The leaves, however, are of dispersing power. So too are the leaves of the others, and especially those of the one that is golden in its flowers, with which they also make the hair yellow. For the leaves of all of them are of a drying and moderately cleansing power.

[8.21.6] [6. On the date palm.] The date palm, the tree, partakes of astringent power in all its parts. Thus the juice of the branches is harsh, being composed of a watery substance that is lukewarm and an earthy substance that is cold. Of a similar nature to this is also what is called the "brain," which is edible. Its fruit, and especially the sweet kind, has partaken of no small heat. Being edible, it comes into much use, not only when applied externally, where we need to tone something and to dry and to draw together and to compact and to condense, but also when taken as food, both together with other things and by itself. What they call elate, the tender shoot of the date palm, has the same power as the brain within it. Its covering, as it were, also itself possesses an astringent quality, but it dries more than all the things mentioned, inasmuch as in the consistency of its substance it is drier than they and partakes least of moisture, so that they rightly use it on putrefactive ulcers. And they mix it into the drugs that draw together relaxed joints and into the hepatic and stomachic preparations, both external and internal. The root of the plant too is of a drying power without biting, having itself also something of astringency.

[8.21.7] [7. On phorbion.] The seed of phorbion is used, with honey, against leukomata; but it is also believed to draw out splinters. And the herb too seems to be capable of the same as this, from which it is clear that it partakes of a fine-particled, drawing and cleansing power.

[8.21.8] [8. On phou.] Phou. The root of this herb is somewhat aromatic, similar in power to nard, but in most respects weaker; it promotes urine more than Indian and Syrian nard, and similarly to Celtic nard.
[8.21.9] [9. On phykos (seaweed).] Phykos, taken out of the sea while still moist and green, both cools and dries in the second order, for it also has something moderately acerbic.

[8.21.10] [10. On phyllitis.] Phyllitis, being of an acerbic quality, not unreasonably benefits diarrhoea and dysentery when drunk. [8.21.11] [11. On the leaf of malabathron.] The leaf of malabathron is similar to nard in its power.

[8.22.1] [1. On galbanum.] Galbanum is the juice of a plant of the fennel-stalk kind, being of a softening and dispersing power. And it would be, in heating, somewhere around the beginning of the third order or the completion of the second, while in drying it is at the beginning of the second order.

[8.22.2] [2. On chamaedrys.] Chamaedrys has the bitter quality predominant, but it is also somewhat pungent. From these, evidently, it fittingly dissolves the spleen, moves urine and menses, cuts the thickness of humours, and clears out the obstructions in the viscera. And one would place it in the third order with respect to drying and heating, and indeed more with respect to drying than to heating.

[8.22.3] [3. On chamaikissos.] The flower of chamaikissos, being sufficiently bitter, clears the obstructions in the liver. Some people also give it to those with sciatica. [8.22.4] [4. On chamelaia.] Chamelaia has the bitter quality predominant. Hence it is able, with honey, to cleanse thoroughly the exceedingly foul ulcers and those that have the largest eschars.

[8.22.5] [5. On chamaileuke.] Chamaileuke is hot in power at about the third rank and dry at the first. [8.22.6] [6. On chamaileon.] The root of chamaileon, that of the black kind, has something poisonous in it, whence its use is external, against psorai and lichens and alphoi and in general whatever needs cleansing, and it is mixed with softening and dispersing drugs. And it heals the phagedaenic ulcers when applied as a plaster. For it is dry at about the third rank already, but in heating it is of the second rank at its completion. The root of the white chamaileon is given against flat worms, in the quantity of an oxybaphon, with harsh wine. They administer it also to the dropsical, since it too is similar in mixture to the root of the black kind, except insofar as it is more bitter than that one.

[8.22.7] [7. On chamaepitys.] Chamaepitys, in respect of taste, has the bitter flavour stronger than the pungent, while in respect of its action it thoroughly purges and cleanses the viscera more than it heats. For this reason it is a good drug both for those suffering from jaundice and in general for those whose liver is readily obstructed. It also draws down the menses, both when drunk and when applied as a pessary with honey. It is also a diuretic drug. Some people also give it to those suffering from sciatica, boiling it down in honey-water (melikraton). When green, the herb is also able to glue together even large wounds, and it heals putrefactive ulcers, and it disperses the hardnesses in the breasts. For in drying it belongs to the third order, and in heating to the second.

[8.22.8] [8. On chamaisykē.] Chamaisykē has a power that is at once cleansing and pungent, so that both its shoots applied as a plaster and the juice from them remove acrochordons and myrmecia. With honey they also cleanse away the thick scars in the eyes. They also benefit the dimnesses of sight that arise through thickness, as indeed also the beginnings of cataracts.

[8.22.9] [9. On chelidonion.] Chelidonion is of a strongly cleansing and hot power; and indeed its juice too is useful for sharpness of sight in those cases in which something thick collects at the pupil and needs to be dispersed. Some people have also used the root for those suffering from jaundice as a result of an obstruction of the liver, giving it to drink in white wine with anise. Chewed, it is useful for pains of the teeth. The smaller chelidonion, being more pungent than the greater, quickly ulcerates the skin when applied as a plaster, and casts out scaly (leprous) nails. Its juice purges through the nostrils, being strongly pungent, so that this herb too would belong by now, more or less, to the fourth order, as that order is already being completed, both in respect of heating and of drying.

[8.22.10] [10. On chondrile.] Chondrile. Some people call this too seris. For it is in some degree of the same power as that one, except insofar as it has more of the slightly bitter in its taste, and for this reason it is drier in its power.

[8.22.11] [11. On chondros.] Chondros is, to be sure, also an excellent food, just as wheat is too, but it is not the business of the present treatise to draw distinctions concerning food; as a drug, however, it is of clogging power. In its mixture it is similar to wheat, having more of the viscous quality than that, by which it is both more nourishing than it and becomes, as it were, a kind of material suitable for the reception of vinegar, sea-water and brine, and whatever other such things dry vigorously; and for this reason some have supposed that this seed too is among the things that dry sufficiently. But chondros itself belongs rather among the things capable of concocting, just as wheat does, and these dry least of all. It is because of the admixture of drying drugs that the compound made from them, becoming drying, deceives most physicians, so that they attribute the cause of the drying to chondros itself, disregarding the things mixed in.

[8.22.12] [12. On chrysokome.] Chrysokome, which is also called chrysites: its root has the pungent together with the astringent quality as the predominant ones, for which reason it is not of manifold use either. Its use, at any rate, when it has been boiled down in honey-water (melikraton), is in cases of peripneumonia and in hepatic diseases. It also has something that promotes the purgation of the menses.

[8.23.1] [1. On pseudodictamnon.] Pseudodictamnon (false dittany) has the power of a weak dittany. [8.23.2] [2. On psyllion.] Of psyllion (fleawort) the seed is especially useful, being of the second order of cooling things; with respect to the pairing of drying and moistening it is somehow intermediate and well-balanced.

[8.24.1] [1. On basil.] Basil is of the second order of heating things, but it has a superfluous moisture. Hence it is not useful taken inside the body, but applied externally as a plaster it is useful for dispersing and concocting.

[8.24.2] [2. On okimoeides.] Okimoeides—some call it philetairion—: the root is useless, but the seed is of a fine-particled and drying power, without biting. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 9. Proem. Those drugs that are parts of plants, and fruits, and juices, and saps have been spoken of before; now it is proposed to go through, of the remaining drugs, those that are mined and those that are kinds of earth itself. Following upon this, something will also be said about the parts in animals which we use in the capacity of drugs for cures. It seems to me better to set out first a certain general account concerning all of them, both for the sake of clarity and so that what has been said may be heard in an articulated manner. For if anyone were to follow in all things those who have written either treatises on drugs or on materia medica or on their preparation, he will go greatly wrong in many matters and will misunderstand what is said by me with precise distinction. The general account that is about to be given has two chief heads: the one is whether, among self-grown drugs, those that have been burnt should be considered hotter or colder; the other concerns astringent drugs, of which the harsh and the acerbic were earlier shown to be species. Now these matters have already been discussed in the fourth of these books, but it is better to recall now too that the quality and power of astringent drugs appears to be most opposite to pungent ones. For acacia is astringent, and balaustion, and hypokistis and kytinoi and oak-gall and rheon and sumach, and omphakion and medlars, and cornels and pomegranate rinds and myrtle-berries. Pungent are euphorbion and garlic and onions and leeks and mustard and pepper and ginger and smyrnion, and origanon and pennyroyal, and calamint and thyme. We need, then, only recall what sort of sensation we have of each of the things mentioned. For the difference of their quality will follow immediately—the difference which I went through in the fourth book together with all the other gustatory differences. Astringents, then, contract and bind and compact our substance, and for this reason, when applied externally to whatever part you wish, they immediately show it wrinkled and drawn in. Conversely to these, pungent things applied to the skin clearly heat it and raise it into a swelling together with a red colour, and if they remain long, they ulcerate it. These, then, manifestly appear to cut and to heat, and for this reason to draw towards themselves the blood from the neighbouring parts. Astringents, on the other hand, are of a nature to repel what is contained within them by cooling and contracting and compacting. The power of astringents, then, is most opposite to pungent things, and the quality according to taste has nothing similar. How, then, some say that both pepper and garlic and all pungent things are astringent, it is not even possible to conceive. For if, just as they say these are astringent, so they also called sumach and balaustion and omphakion and medlar and all other such things pungent, altering the usage of the Greeks in their names, we would suppose them ignorant of the words of the Greeks together with the things signified by them, but not, at any rate, insensible with respect to the gustatory faculty or the olfactory; but since they call by one name two things which, both in the sensation of smell and in that of taste, and in what they are seen to do, have a nature most opposite to one another, it is fitting to marvel at the men, whether for their insensibility or for their folly or for both at once. For they do something very like the man who says that snow produces the same sensation as fire; and indeed someone, out of habituation to so bizarre a use of names, once told me that nothing prevented one from saying that snow has the same quality and power as fire; for it too has often been seen to burn off the feet of those who have walked through it for a long way. For such men, then, no short time is needed to cleanse away the filth from the soul. But for those who have not been so unfortunate as to live out their lives in complete ignorance, having read beforehand the fourth of these treatises, what has been said up to this point suffices by way of reminder, for the sake of hearing in an articulated manner the names as applied to each of the things proper to them, as all Greeks are accustomed to use them. I shall now pass on to the second inquiry, which is no longer about a name and what is signified by it, but about the nature of a thing. For most people believe that all things that have been burnt become colder than they themselves were, while some, on the contrary, think that the heat of all burnt things is increased—both sides being in error. For some things manifestly appear to become hotter, both to taste and to touch and in the power observed in use, as I said earlier regarding pungent and astringent things, while others on the contrary appear less hot after being burnt; and this we recognize clearly both by sensation and by use. I mean by 'use', just as I said regarding the earlier cases, when things applied to the skin make it in some cases redder and hotter, in others bloodless and cold, and some raise it into a swelling, while others draw it in. Pungent things, then, lose much of their heat when burnt, while those not of this kind acquire heat; but none of the things burnt is completely cold. For there is left behind in them a kind of empyreuma, as it were; for so Aristotle named it, and this is what is washed off in washings. It is the most fine-particled part of the substance of burnt things, and when this has gone off together with the water, the remainder of the burnt thing is an earthy substance. For the burning consumes all the moisture, and what is left behind is earthy, together with what was called by Aristotle the empyreuma. When, then, someone takes this away and separates it by washing, the water in which the drug was washed acquires a fine-particled hot power, while the remainder becomes earthy and cold, able to dry without biting. I have spoken about these matters before as well, but it is no worse to recall them now too, so that anyone who has a fresh recollection of them may follow more accurately what is to be said.

[7.10.1] [1. On kalaminthe (calamint).] Kalaminthe (calamint) is fine-particled in its substance and hot and dry in its mixture, from roughly the third order in respect of both qualities. The indications of these are clear, both those that appear to the taste and those that are recognised through experience. For to the taste it is pungent and manifestly hot, and it has some altogether slight slightly-bitter quality. For those who test it and apply it to the body, first, when applied externally, it heats greatly and bites and lacerates the skin and in the end produces an ulcer. Taken into the body, both by itself dry and in honey-water (melikraton), it manifestly heats and stirs up sweats and disperses and dries the whole body. For this reason, at any rate, some have used it also against periodic rigors, externally boiling it down in olive oil and anointing the whole body with it together with vigorous rubbing, and internally taking it, as has been said. And indeed some also apply it as a plaster over the hips in sciatic ailments as a noble remedy; for it draws what lies in the depth to the outer surface and heats the entire joint, and manifestly scorches the skin, and, both drunk and applied as a pessary, it very effectively summons the menses. It is also a good drug for those suffering from elephantiasis, not only by nobly dispersing the thin humours, but also by strongly thinning and cutting the thick ones, such as are those that generate this disease; so too it brightens black scars and disperses bruises beneath the eyes. It is better in such cases to apply it as a plaster fresh, boiled in wine, rather than dry. For when dried it becomes stronger and more ready to burn. Because it is of such a kind it is also employed against the bites of venomous beasts, just like cauteries and all those drugs that are hot and pungent and fine-particled and readily draw to themselves from the depth all the adjacent moisture. The bitterness that accompanies it is altogether slight; but it does, with respect to some things, what the strongest bitterness does, because it is combined with vehement heat together with a fine-particled substance. Thus at any rate its juice, both injected and drunk, is of a nature to destroy ascarides and intestinal worms. By the same reasoning also the worms in the ears, or if somewhere else in the body such a condition should arise in a putrefying ulcer. So too, both drunk and applied as a pessary, it destroys and expels the foetus. The cutting power, then, belongs to it on account of its heat and fine-particledness and bitterness, the cleansing power on account of the bitterness alone. And accordingly it benefits asthmatics on account of all that has been said, and the jaundiced chiefly on account of its bitterness, just as nearly all the other bitter things also do, by cleansing and purging the obstructions in the liver. For all the aforesaid uses the mountain variety is the more effective.

[7.10.2] [2. On aromatic reed.] Aromatic reed partakes both of a slight astringency and of a very small degree of pungency. The greater part of it, however, is of earthy and airy substance, well-tempered in the pairing of hot and cold. Hence it is moderately diuretic, and it is mixed into the remedies applied to the liver and the stomach, and it is usefully mixed into the fomentations for the uterus, as many as are employed on account of inflammation or for the provoking of the menses. Let it therefore be placed in the second rank of things that heat and dry, and indeed drying more strongly than it heats. It also has something fine-particled in it, as do all the other aromatics as well; but in most of those the fine-particled element is very abundant, whereas in the reed it is not much.

[7.10.3] [3. On the fence-reed (phragmites).] Some have written that the root of the fence-reed, together with bulbs, draws out barbed points and splinters from the depth, as though some drawing power belonged to it. We ourselves, however, have not put this to the test; but so far as one may judge by taste, it partakes of a cleansing power that is not small, and one that is hardly at all pungent. The green leaves, however, cool moderately, these too partaking of the cleansing power. Its bark, when burnt, comes to be of a sufficiently fine-particled and dispersing power, having also something cleansing, so that it both dries and heats at roughly the third rank, and dries more than it heats. One ought to guard against its so-called anthēlē (the plume); for when it falls into the ears it becomes plastered on so as not to be removable, and it harms the hearing, so that it often produces deafness.

[7.10.4] [4. On kankanon.] The root of kankanon is of a power that does not bite and is moderately drying, and of a coarse-particled, clogging substance. Hence, when steeped in wine, like tragacanth, and licked up, it heals the roughnesses of the windpipe; and no less, if one also chews it thoroughly, the juice that flows off benefits the windpipe in the same way as that of liquorice.

[7.10.5] [5. On hemp.] The fruit of hemp is both non-flatulent and drying to such a degree that, if it is eaten in larger quantity, it dries up the semen. Some, however, express its juice while it is green and use it for pains of the ears, those that arise, as it seems to me, through obstruction.

[7.10.6] [6. On kapnios (fumitory).] Kapnios—others call it kapnos—partakes of a pungent and at the same time bitter quality, and is not entirely free of the acerbic one either; hence it provokes copious bilious urine and cures obstructions and weaknesses (atonies) in the liver, and its juice is sharpening to the sight and draws forth no little tear, just as smoke does, whence also its name. A certain layman also used it as strengthening the stomach together with loosening the bowels. For he first dried the herb and stored it, and then sprinkled it on—for the sake of evacuation, in honey-water (melikraton), but when he wished to strengthen the stomach, in mixed wine [evidently].

[7.10.7] [7. On caper.] Of caper, the bark of the root has the bitter quality predominant, the pungent second, and after this the acerbic. From which it is also clear that it is composed of different and conflicting powers. For it is able to cleanse and to purge and to cut by the bitterness that accompanies it, to heat and to cut and to disperse by the pungency, and to draw together and to condense and to bind by the acerbity. And for this reason this drug too, if indeed anything does, benefits scirrhous spleens, being mixed externally with the suitable plasters, and taken inside the body, either boiled down in vinegar and oxymel and the like, or dry, pounded, and mixed with these. For indeed, taken in this way, it manifestly empties the viscous and thick humours, not through the urine only, but also by way of the belly. And often they pass bloody stools as well, upon which both the spleens are benefited and the pains in the hip. And indeed it also moves the menses and draws off phlegm and helps ruptures and spasms. But with what drink one should mix it in each of the affections is not a matter for the present treatise, but either for that on the composition of drugs or for the therapeutic method. And the bark of the root, applied as a plaster to malignant ulcers, is a good drug, inasmuch as it is able both to cleanse them off and to dry them strongly; and it helps pains of the teeth in accordance with the aforementioned qualities, sometimes boiled together with vinegar, sometimes with wine, and often by itself alone, being bitten upon. Nor does it belong to the present treatise to determine the occasions for these things either. For this is not what is set before us now, but rather to take from each of the particular actions some indication of its powers, carrying the account back to the principles laid down from the beginning. It is evident, then, from what has been said that there is in it a certain cutting power, and a cleansing, and a dispersing, and a contracting one. For indeed it also removes alphos with vinegar, and disperses scrofulous swellings and hard tumours, when mixed with the drugs suitable for these. The fruit has power analogous to the bark of the root, except insofar as it is weaker in all respects. And indeed the leaves and their stalk also are of similar power, and I myself know that I once dispersed with the leaves, in a few days, a scrofulous hardness. We mix with them, of course, something of the agents that blunt the vehemence of the power. Nor is it anything surprising if the juice also destroys the worms in the ears on account of its bitterness. But the caper that grows in very hot regions, as for instance that in Arabia, is much more pungent than ours, so that it also partakes to a greater degree of the caustic power.

[7.10.8] [8. On kardamon.] The seed of kardamon (cress) partakes of a caustic power, like mustard, and for this reason people heat through with it sciaticas, headaches and anything else that requires rubefaction (phoinixis), just as with mustard. It is also mixed into the drugs given for asthmatics, as being evidently able to cut thick humours strongly, just like mustard too; for it resembles that in all respects. And the herb, when it has become dry, is of a power similar to that of the seed, but while still moist and green, on account of the admixture of watery moisture, it falls very far short, and in this state is so moderate in its biting that it is even possible to use it with bread as a relish.

[7.10.9] [9. On kardamomon.] Kardamomon (cardamom) too is, to be sure, of a sufficiently hot power, though not so strongly as kardamon (cress); rather, to the degree that it is more pleasant and more aromatic than kardamon, to that degree it has also received a share of a weaker hot power. It is not, however, capable of ulcerating, even when applied by itself as a plaster, but it also has something of bitterness carried along within it, on account of which it both destroys worms and strongly scours away scabby eruptions (psorai), also when used with vinegar.

[7.10.10] [10. On caraway.] The seed of caraway heats and dries in roughly the third order, having a moderately pungent quality. For this very reason it both dispels flatulence and is diuretic—not the seed only, but the plant as well.

[7.10.11] [11. On cassia.] Cassia dries and heats in roughly the third rank. It is also fine-particled to a sufficient degree, and in taste the pungent is most abundant in it, but there is also something slightly astringent, so that on account of all these properties it both cuts and at the same time disperses the superfluities in the body, and in addition to these it further instils strength into the organs. It is also suitable for retentions of the menses, whenever, on account of both the quantity and at the same time the thickness of the residues, they are prevented from being evacuated adequately.

[7.10.12] [12. On nuts.] Nuts. The tree has something astringent both in its shoots and in its leaves, but it is evident and most abundant in the husk of the nut, both fresh and dry. It is for this reason, at any rate, that the dyers also use it. We, for our part, press them out and, boiling the juice with honey in the same way as that of mulberries and of brambles, use it as a stomatic drug, and for all the other purposes for which the previously mentioned juices are suitable. Of the nut itself, the edible part is oily and fine-particled, so that for this reason it also yields its juice readily, and the longer it lies stored away, the more it becomes so. Indeed, it is possible to press oil out of it when it has aged. At that time it also becomes quite dispersing, so that some cure even gangrenes and anthraxes and aegilopes with it, and some use it also for wounds of the sinews. When fresh, it also has something of the astringent quality. The part that is still unripe and not yet dry, like the other fruits that are green, is full of half-digested moisture. Its dry shell, however, when burnt, becomes a fine-particled, drying and non-biting drug. There is also another kind of nuts, smaller ones, which are called Pontic, having a larger share of the cold earthy substance, so that both the plant itself and the fruit and the bark appear harsher to one tasting them; in other respects it is similar to the large nut which is called by some the royal nut. This small nut is called by most people leptokaryon.

[7.10.13] [13. On caucalis.] Caucalis. Some call this wild daucus; for it is similar to it both in taste and in power. For it heats, like that one, and dries, and is diuretic, and it is indeed also pickled for keeping.

[7.10.14] [14. On karpesion.] Karpesion is similar to the plant called phou both in taste and in power, but it is fine-particled to a greater degree, and for this reason it cleanses the obstructions of the viscera more than that one does, and moves urine, and purges kidneys that are forming stones. It is not, however, fine-particled to such a degree that one may use it in place of cinnamon when the latter is not available, as Quintus used to do. Now the Pontic karpesion is better than the Laertic, yet not even it comes near cinnamon in power, but falls short of the best cassia by no small margin. Each of the two is named after certain mountains of Pamphylia, in which it grows; and you could obtain very great quantities of them in Syria.

[7.10.15] [15. On millet.] Millet cools in the first order, but dries either in the third order relaxed or the second order intensified. It is also, to a slight degree, fine-particled. Hence, from such a consistency and mixture, when eaten as a food it is altogether the least nourishing of nearly all the cereal foods. Moreover, it also dries the belly; applied externally in bags it is suitable as a fomentation for those who need to be dried without biting, and when applied as a plaster it is of a nature to dry; however, the plaster made from it becomes quite crumbly and for this reason awkward to use.

[7.10.16] [16. On cedar.] Cedar is twofold in kind: the one is shrub-like, similar to the junipers (ἄρκευθοι), the other a tree of no small size. Both are of a hot and dry mixture, from roughly the third rank in both respects. Kedrea, however—for so the oil from the cedar is called—might already seem to touch upon the fourth rank, being considerably hot and at the same time fine-particled. Soft flesh, then, it putrefies readily and at the same time painlessly, just as do the other things which are of the same rank in respect of heating but fine-particled in their substances; but on hard flesh it acts over a longer time and with difficulty. All such drugs, then, are called both putrefying and septic (σηπτά). They differ from one another in the more and the less. And among such drugs themselves kedrea is from the first and weakest rank; for most of them are considerably active. Such ones, then, destroy even the flesh of dead bodies; kedrea, however, dries dead bodies and preserves them unputrefied, feeding upon their superfluous moistures but not touching the solid bodies. In living beings, however, the heat in the bodies, augmenting together with it the power of the kedrea, becomes the cause of the soft flesh being burned through by it. And it is no wonder if, being so great in power, it is naturally able to destroy lice and nits and ascarids and the worms in the ears, and when applied kills living embryos and expels dead ones; just as it does also the semen itself from intercourse, when smeared around the genital. And for these reasons it is a contraceptive drug second to none for those who use it thus, and it performs many other such things in particular. A proof, at any rate, of its heating strongly, as also when it is instilled into the holes of the teeth: for it soothes the pain, but breaks them. It also thins the scars of the eyes and cures the dimnesses of sight that arise through thickness of humours. The oiliest part of it and most precisely oil-like, which is collected by means of wool suspended above it while it is being boiled, becomes more fine-particled than the whole kedrea, but less pungent, although heating no less. For it has, in relation to the coarser-particled remainder of the kedrea, the same ratio that oil has to amurca. Whence that one, inasmuch as it is coarse-particled, is biting and mouth-opening, and for this reason at once irritating to ulcers and productive of inflammation. The oil-like kedrea, on the other hand, is mild in power to such an extent that laymen, having learned by experience, treat the wounds inflicted on sheep being shorn by the shears by smearing it on, as they do also liquid pitch. They also use it against the scabs of sheep and against ticks. The kedrides—for so they name the fruit of the cedar—have a more moderate power, so that they can even be eaten. If, however, someone takes too many even of these, he has pain in the head and is heated and is bitten in the belly.

[7.10.17] [17. On the great centaury.] The root of the great centaury, just as it displays opposite qualities in taste, so too displays opposite activities in use. In taste it appears pungent and at the same time astringent, together with a certain slight sweetness; but in its activities the pungency shows forth the works of heat, promoting the menses and drawing down dead embryos and destroying and expelling living ones, while the astringency shows forth the works of coarse-particled and earthy coldness, in gluing together wounds and in benefiting those who spit blood. Two drachms of it are given to these, to those with fever with water, to those without fever with wine; and in respect of the activity arising from all its qualities together it is suitable for ruptures and spasms and dyspnoea and coughs that have become chronic. For in these cases one must not only evacuate what is contrary to nature, but also strengthen and give tone to the parts that have been cleansed. For the evacuating, then, the pungency is useful, when it is not alone nor unmixed, but is mingled either with some sweetness, or at all events not with bitterness. For in this way it will not have the strong and the violent character, since some well-tempered substance is mixed with it; for such is the sweet quality. And for strengthening and drawing together what has been evacuated there is the use of the astringency. Its juice produces the same effects as the root, and some use the drug in place of lycium.

[7.10.18] [18. On the small centaury.] Of the small centaury the root is altogether ineffective, but the shoots, and still more the leaves upon them and the flowers, are most useful. The bitter quality predominates in them, partaking also a little of astringency, and on account of such a mixture the drug is strongly drying, without biting. That all such drugs are more useful has both been said before, and now it is no less a fitting moment to recall it, once we have gone through all its activities in particular. Thus large wounds are agglutinated when it is applied as a plaster, the herb itself being still fresh, and old ulcers and those hard to cicatrize are brought to scar when it is used in the same way; and when dried it is mixed into the agglutinating and drying compounds, as many as are of a nature to heal sinuses and fistulas, and to soften old hardnesses and to heal malignant ulcers. It is mixed also with the drugs that heal fluxional conditions, for which the best drugs are those that dry vehemently, together with some astringency, and have no biting. Some inject the decoction of the herb into those suffering from sciatica, as bringing away bilious and thick matters, for indeed it purges such things; and moreover, when it acts vehemently so as to evacuate bloody matter, it helps all the more. Its juice, being of a closely similar power, that is, a drying and cleansing one, is of a nature to accomplish well the other things aforesaid, and is smeared with honey upon the eyes, and applied as a pessary it draws down the menses and embryos. Some also give it to drink to those whose nerves are affected, as evacuating and drying painlessly the matter that has been impacted. And indeed it is also an excellent drug for obstructions in the liver, and good too for a spleen becoming scirrhous, both when applied externally and no less if one wishes also to drink it.

[7.10.19] [19. On the cherry.] The cherry tree bears a fruit that does not partake of astringency equally in all the individual plants; for in these too, just as in pomegranates and apples, in some the harsh quality prevails, in some the sweet, and in some the sour. And indeed, even among the sweet ones themselves, those that are not yet ripe are in some cases quite acerbic, in others sour, in the same way as mulberries. But in unripe mulberries the sour quality prevails over the acerbic, whereas in cherries this is not always so. The sweeter ones, then, loosen the contents of the intestine more, but are less good for the stomach, while the harsh ones are the reverse. Those that are sour suit phlegmatic stomachs and stomachs full of superfluities; for they dry more than the harsh ones and also have something cutting in them. The gum of the tree has one power in common with all drugs that are viscous and at the same time non-biting, a power which also suits roughened windpipes, and another peculiar to it, if indeed what some write is true, that when drunk with wine it benefits those suffering from stone. For in that case it would possess some fine-particled power.

[7.10.20] [20. On the carob-tree.] The carob-tree is of a drying and astringent power, as is also its fruit, the so-called carob-pods (keratia), which obviously partakes also of a certain sweetness. These too have undergone something similar to cherries: for when moist they rather loosen the belly, but when dry they rather check it, inasmuch as they have given off their moisture by evaporation and retain the more earthy part of their substance as the remainder.

[7.10.21] [21. On kestron.] Kestron, or psychotrophon, in Latin betonica (betony), has a cutting power, as its taste shows; for the herb is rather bitter and somewhat pungent, as its action in individual cases also shows. For it breaks up the stones in the kidneys, and purges and cleanses the lung, the chest and the liver, and moves the menses, and benefits epileptics, and treats ruptures and strains, and when plastered on the wound it helps against all bites of wild beasts, and when drunk it is of use to those suffering from acid eructation and to those with sciatica.

[7.10.22] [22. On oak-gall.] Oak-gall: the one called omphakitis is a sufficiently acerbic drug, partaking for the most part of a cold earthy substance, on account of which it dries and repels fluxes and draws together and binds tight the slack and weak parts, and nobly withstands all the fluxional affections. And let it be placed in the third order in drying, but in the second in cooling. The other gall, the yellow, loose and large one, dries also itself, but to the degree less to which it has also partaken less of the acerbic quality. Boiled, accordingly, by itself, and then ground fine, it is a not ignoble poultice for inflammations and prolapses in the seat. One must boil it in water when a moderate astringency is required, but in wine when a more vehement one; and if there should be need to augment the astringency still more, let the wine also be harsher for you. The country people among us call this "wine-gall". When burnt, the galls become of a blood-staunching power and clearly take on heat and pungency from the burning, and they are more fine-particled than the unburnt ones and more drying. But whenever you wish to make them blood-staunching, one must, having made them red-hot upon charcoal, quench them in wine or vinegar.

[7.10.23] [23. On wax.] Wax is in a way in the middle between the heating and the cooling, the moistening and the drying things. It has, however, also something coarse-particled and clogging, on account of which it might perhaps seem not only not to dry but even, incidentally, to moisten, since it hinders the transpirations; whence it is also the material of the other drugs, both the heating and the cooling ones, while by itself it would be among the weak concoctive drugs, not as taken inside the body but as one of those applied from outside. For it has some small share of a dispersing and warm power, of which honey has partaken in the greatest degree.

[7.10.24] [24. On the castor plant (kikis).] Just as the fruit of the castor plant both purges and has a cleansing and dispersing power, so too does the leaf, but in every respect weaker. The oil from the fruit is hotter and more fine-particled than ordinary oil, and for this reason it is also dispersing.

[7.10.25] [25. On cinnamon.] Cinnamon is fine-particled in the extreme, yet not hot in the extreme, but of the third order; nothing, however, among the things that heat equally with it dries so much, on account of the fine-particled nature of its substance. Cinnamomis, for its part, is as it were a kind of weak cinnamon, and some call it pseudo-cinnamon.

[7.10.26] [26. On kirkaia.] Of the herb kirkaia, Dioscorides says that the root, drunk with sweet wine, purges the womb, being fragrant and heating, while the fruit, given in a gruel, assists in the generation of milk.

[7.10.27] [27. On kistos.] Kistos, or kistharos, is a shrub astringent in taste and in all its particular actions. Its leaves and small shoots, however, when ground fine, dry and are astringent to such a degree as to glue together wounds. The flowers are more active, so that when drunk with wine they cure dysentery, atony of the stomach, fluxes and moistures. Applied as a plaster they benefit the putrefactive kind of ulcers, for their power is drying in no feeble way, roughly at about the second degree of distance from the balanced, by now in some measure complete. The shrub is cold to such a degree as to share in only a tepid warmth. The so-called hypokistis is very considerably more astringent even than the leaves, a sufficiently active drug for all fluxional affections, such as bringings-up of blood, female fluxes, and coeliac and dysenteric conditions. But also, if you should wish to strengthen some part that has become slack through excess moisture, it instils tone into it in no feeble way. So indeed it is mixed into stomachic and hepatic plasters, and it is put into the antidote made from vipers for the sake of strengthening and giving tone to the bodies.

[7.10.28] [28. On kisthos.] Kisthos or ladanon. This kisthos, growing in the hotter regions, though not different in kind from the one among us, has acquired on account of the region a distinctive heat of its own, a dispersing heat, and it differs from the one among us in both respects, in having laid aside its coldness and in having taken on heat. In other respects, then, the properties of this kisthos are similar to those of the one among us; but what is called ladanon is produced from it, a drug hot in the first degree of departure, and that already more or less completed, so as even to touch upon the second, partaking also of some slight astringency; and it is also fine-particled in its substance, and for these reasons it is moderately softening and likewise dispersing, and evidently also concocting. It is therefore no wonder that it is especially suited to conditions of the womb, since in addition to what has been said it also has something slightly astringent, for which reason it also strengthens hair that is falling out. For it consumes whatever bad moistures there are at their roots, and by its astringency it draws together and tightens the pores in which they are fixed. Alopecia and ophiasis, however, it is unable to cure, these being affections that require a more dispersing power than that of ladanon. For these arise through bad humours, viscous and thick, which the cutting and dispersing drugs most of all draw out and evacuate. And these must be of a fine-particled power and one that is least astringent, yet not so fine-particled and drying as to over-dry and to consume, together with the humours gathered there contrary to nature, the natural moisture that makes the hair grow. For in that way it will not so much cure alopecia as produce baldness; but these matters already belong to the therapeutic method.

[7.10.29] [29. On ivy.] Ivy is compounded of opposite powers: for it has something also of an astringent substance, which indeed we showed to be earthy and cold, and it has something also of a pungent one, which taste too testifies to be hot; and a third, in addition to these, it partakes of a watery, lukewarm substance—the green one, at any rate. For in the process of drying this must necessarily be dispersed first, while the earthier remains behind, both the cold and astringent and the hot and pungent. But the green one, when its leaves have been boiled with wine, is agglutinating of large wounds and curative of those that are turning malignant. It also cicatrizes the ulcerations from fire.
