The leaves boiled with vinegar benefit splenetics. Its flowers are somewhat stronger, so that, triturated with cerate, they suit burns. The juice is also an errhine drug, and it cures the chronic fluxes of the ears and the old ulcers in the ears and the nostrils. Should it appear too pungent, it is mixed with rose-oil or sweet oil. Its tear kills lice and strips away hair, being of a hot power to such a degree as to burn faintly. For it is, as it were, a sort of watery sap, like other tears too.

[7.10.30] [30. On clinopodium.] Clinopodium is of a heating power, but not yet of a caustic one. It is also fine-particled in its substance, and one might place it in the third order both in heating and in drying.

[7.10.31] [31. On klematis.] The leaves of klematis are of a pungent and caustic power, so that they even strip away lepra. It would therefore be of the fourth order of heating things, at its beginning. The daphnoides is also called klematis, which some call myrsinoides and some polygonoides. But this is not ulcerating nor pungent, like the one mentioned before; rather it benefits diarrhoea and dysentery when drunk with wine. It soothes pains of the teeth when chewed, and it benefits pains of the womb when applied in a pessary, so far does it fall short of burning or ulcerating, as the former does. But the most admirable Pamphilus, just as he talks nonsense about everything else, writing about things he does not know, so too has run both of these together into one and the same. Dioscorides, however, mentions both in the fourth book, the one simply named klematoeides at the end of the book, the other at the beginning. Hence there is no need for me either to write out further the forms of both, just as I have not done so in the case of the others.
[7.10.32] [32. On knēkos.] Of knēkos we use the seed only for purgations; for it belongs to the third order of heating things, if anyone should wish to use it externally.

[7.10.33] [33. On the Cnidian grain.] The Cnidian grain also purges itself, but it is of a pungent and caustic power. [7.10.34] [34. On the dyer's grain.] The dyer's grain has an astringent and at the same time a bitter quality, and it dries by means of both without biting, and for this reason it is suitable both for the large wounds and for woundings of the sinews. Some grind it fine with vinegar on such occasions, others with oxymel.

[7.10.35] [35. On the plum tree.] The fruit of the plum tree loosens the belly, and more so when it is fresh, less when it has been dried. Dioscorides, however, says—I do not know how—that Damascene plums, when dried, check the belly. For these too plainly loosen it, though less than those from Iberia. The Damascene ones are more astringent, those from Iberia sweeter, and indeed the trees too correspond to their fruits: those in Iberia are less astringent, those around Damascus more so. To speak generally, those in whose leaves or shoots some clear astringency is apparent, these, when boiled down, become a mouth-rinse for inflammations about the uvula and tonsils. The fruit of the wild kinds is manifestly astringent and checking of the belly. This plant is called in Asia proumnon. Some say that the gum of the tree, drunk with wine, is capable of breaking up stones, and with vinegar cures the lichen-eruptions of children; and if it does this, it is clear that it partakes of a cutting and fine-particled power.

[7.10.36] [36. On glue.] Glue, which they prepare for books out of fine wheat flour (semidalis) and finest flour (gyris), is of a clogging and concocting power for whatever parts it is applied to as a plaster.

[7.10.37] [37. On the gourd.] The gourd is of a moist and cold mixture, in the second rank in both respects; whence also the juice of its scrapings is suitable for earaches that arise from inflammation, when it is used together with rose-oil. So too the whole of it, applied as a plaster, moderately cools hot inflammations. When eaten, moreover, it is watery and allays thirst.

[7.10.38] [38. On colocynth.] Colocynth is bitter to the taste, but those effects of bitterness which attach to a drug when it is drunk it is unable to perform manifestly, because of the purgative power which it possesses in itself in strong measure, since it is excreted through the belly beforehand together with the things that it purges. The juice of it when green, rubbed in, benefits cases of sciatica.

[7.10.39] [39. On komaros.] Komaros. The tree is acerbic in quality, together with its fruit, and this they call memekylon. This fruit is also bad for the stomach and productive of headache. [7.10.40] [40. On gum.] Gum is a tear that congeals upon the trunks of the trees that produce it, just as resin too does on many trees, those which are of a nature to produce resin. It is of a drying and clogging power, and clearly it is also curative of roughnesses.

[7.10.41] [41. On lye.] Lye. What is, as it were, the washing-off of ash is so called. The most cleansing and most drying of all is that from fig-wood ash and from the spurges (tithymalloi), and it is almost already of the so-called putrefying power, the nature of which I set out in the fifth book.

[7.10.42] [42. On konyza.] Konyza, both the larger and the small, are of similar mixture and power; appearing pungent and bitter to the taste, they heat quite plainly, whether one, having pounded the leaves together with the tender twigs (for the plant is shrub-like), plasters them on some part, or whether, having boiled them down in oil, one uses this. At any rate such an oil seems also to be a protective remedy against the rigors that come by periods. And their flowers too are of similar power, so that some, having ground these as well together with the leaves, give them to drink with wine for the purpose of moving the menses forcibly and expelling embryos. There is also a third kind of konyza, growing in moister places, more foul-smelling and weaker than both. But those mentioned first are of the third order in drying and heating.

[7.10.43] [43. On coriander.] Coriander (korianon), or korion, or however you wish to name it — for the ancient Greeks call it korianon, whereas all the more recent physicians name it korion, as does Dioscorides, who says, not correctly, that the herb is cooling. For it is composed of opposite powers, having much bitter substance, which was shown to be fine-particled and earthy, and also not a little watery moisture that is lukewarm in power; and it also has something of a slight astringency. From all of these it acts in the various ways that Dioscorides wrote of, but certainly not by cooling alone. But I shall set out the cause of each of its particular actions, even though I had proposed in the present treatise to go through my own opinion only. Yet perhaps nothing will prevent it — rather, if the truth must be told, what is said in this manner about a few drugs will both be of some benefit and will recall to mind the methods set out earlier. First, then, not only Dioscorides but many other physicians too make pronouncements about diseases without drawing distinctions, just as indeed among those of the present day one can find not a few physicians of good repute who, beyond all else, go most gravely astray in this respect. For sometimes, when the part that has had the erysipelas has become black and livid and cold and no longer needs the cooling drugs as before, but now those that evacuate the humour lodged contrary to nature in the region, these men still cool it; and sometimes they pass over to the dispersing drugs, and yet say they are curing erysipelas. And indeed they write some drugs for cases of erysipelas that are still beginning and increasing, and others for those in decline. But this is not how it is. For it must no longer be called erysipelas when its fiery, boiling and bilious character has departed, nor must the remedies for such conditions be considered cold in their powers; but just as, if right at the beginning, whether from a blow or in any other way whatever, a livid or black swelling had arisen in some part, it would have been considered a cold affection and one needing dispersing and heating drugs, in the same way, if a hot condition should ever change into a cold one, one should forget the former and name the second by another name; or, if you should not wish to change the name but, as some do, to write some remedies for the beginning and others for the decline, you should by no means consider the drugs of the decline to be cold: it must be granted that one may name such a condition erysipelas, if one wishes, but it must not be granted that one still call it hot, once it has been cooled down. Let us not, then, consider what helps it at that stage to be cooling, as Dioscorides does coriander, because, applied as a plaster, as he himself says, with bread or barley meal it cures erysipelas. For coriander with bread would never cure a strict erysipelas, that is, one which is fiery and yellow, but only one that is already cooling off. For this reason we, in the preceding books, when we required that the power of each of the drugs be tested by discriminated experience, advised choosing an affection as simple as possible. But the majority of physicians do not know even that most diseases attack as composite right from the start, nor that strict erysipelas is one affection and another is what is now habitually called by all of us, or at any rate by the ancients, phlegmone. And in between there are very many others, some, as one might say, phlegmonous erysipelases, others as it were erysipelatous phlegmonai. You might sometimes also find neither predominating but the two exactly balanced; and indeed erysipelas sometimes appears to become oedematous, as another becomes scirrhous, so that no small number of composite diseases is accumulated. About these more has been said both in certain other works and in the writings of the Therapeutic Method, and it will be said now too, since it is necessary to mention them at least to this extent: that the aforesaid plaster would never cure a strict erysipelas. I call it strict when the part has been filled with a bilious flux. And that coriander is far from cooling, you can learn even from the very things Dioscorides wrote. For he says that it dissolves scrofulous swellings (choirades) with bean meal. But that none of the cooling drugs is capable of dissolving scrofulous swellings, I think not even Dioscorides himself would dispute, having recorded countless drugs curative of scrofulous swellings, all of which he agrees are both hot in their mixtures and dispersing in their actions.

[7.10.44] [44. On korōnopous.] The root of korōnopous is believed to benefit those with coeliac affections when eaten. [7.10.45] [45. On kostos.] Kostos partakes very slightly of the bitter quality and power, but very largely of the pungent and hot one, so that it even ulcerates; for which reason they rub the body with it, together with oil, before the onset of the attack in those who shiver periodically. In the same way they also resort to kostos in cases of sciatica and paralysis, and in general wherever the aim is either to heat some part or to draw some humour from the depth to the surface. For the same reason it is also diuretic and draws the menses, and is suitable for ruptures and sprains and pains of the sides. Through the bitterness that accompanies it, it also destroys flat worms, and on account of this they also use it for epheleis with water or honey. There is also present in its mixture a certain flatulent moisture, on account of which it also incites to sexual intercourse when taken with honeyed wine.

[7.10.46] [46. On kotyledon.] Kotyledon is of a mixed power—moist, somewhat cold, and with a certain faintly astringent quality, and together with this a slight bitter one—whence it cools and repels and is cleansing and dispersing. It therefore treats erysipelatous inflammations and inflammatory erysipelas, and it is an especially and quite useful plaster for a stomach that is burning. The leaves eaten together with the root are believed to break up stones and to move urine.

[7.10.47] [47. On the cornel.] Of the cornel tree, the fruit too is quite acerbic, although it is edible, so that it is not at all surprising that it draws together and strongly checks the belly, just as medlars do too. And the leaves and the shoots too are acerbic to the taste and dry strongly, so that they are able to glue together even the largest wounds, and especially those of hard bodies. But for small wounds or soft bodies they are rather adverse, for they put these under strain, drying them to a greater degree than is required.

[7.10.48] [48. On cabbage.] Edible cabbage is of a drying power, both when eaten and when applied externally. It is not, however, as yet in any way sufficiently pungent, but is such that it both glues wounds together and heals the malignant kind of ulcers, and inflammations that are already becoming scirrhous and hard to resolve, and those erysipelata that are of this sort. By the same power it heals epinyctides and herpetes. It also has something cleansing in it, by virtue of which it also treats leprai. The seed, when drunk, destroys worms, and most of all that of the Egyptian cabbage, inasmuch as it is also drier in its mixture; and it is clear that the seed partakes of a bitter quality, just like all the other drugs that are suited against worms. By the same power it benefits ephelides and lentigines (phakoi) and whatever else requires moderate cleansing. The stalks of the cabbage, when burned, produce a strongly drying ash, so that it even partakes already to some degree of the caustic power. In accordance with this, then, they also mix old fat with it and use it for chronic pains of the sides and for anything else of this kind, if there should be such; for the drug is rendered strongly dispersing.

[7.10.49] [49. On wild cabbage.] Wild cabbage is hotter and drier in mixture than the cultivated, just as practically all other wild plants too are stronger in both powers than the cultivated plants of the same kind. Hence it is not even taken within the body without distress, since it has departed further from the human mixture. For this very reason it is also more bitter to those who taste it than the cultivated kind. For the cultivated kind too has something slightly bitter and pungent, but the wild has each of these in a strong form, and for this reason it both disperses and cleanses more vigorously than the cultivated.

[7.10.50] [50. On sea cabbage.] Sea cabbage, besides evacuating the belly, being slightly salty and slightly bitter to the taste, would also be suitable for the uses external to the body, for all those things to which such qualities are fitting.

[7.10.51] [51. On krataiogonon.] The seed of the herb krataiogonon is pungent to those who taste it and vehement for those who use it, being similar to millet. [7.10.52] [52. On samphire (krethmon).] Samphire is somewhat salty to those who taste it, together with a slight bitterness, and for this reason its power is cleansing and at the same time drying. But it is weaker in both respects than bitter things.

[7.10.53] [53. On barley.] Barley is of the first order in drying and cooling, and it also has some slight cleansing property. It is by some small degree more drying than bean-flour from which the husk has been removed. In all other respects it is similar for those who use it externally. When eaten, however, it has the advantage over beans in this respect, that it puts off its flatulent quality; whereas in the bean, however it is boiled, the flatulent quality persists. For it is of a more coarse-particled substance than barley, and for this reason it is also more nourishing than barley. And since both have departed only a little from the mean, for this reason they are of manifold use. For drugs of this kind are mixed to a great extent with others, like certain materials, and for this reason wax and oil too are combined with not a few drugs. But barley-groats are much more drying even than barley itself.

[7.10.54] [54. On krimnon.] Krimnon. This is the name given to the coarse-particled part both of wheat flour and of the flour from zeia. It is more nourishing than barley meal, but harder to digest. The gruel made from it is called poltos, and the one from zeia is gently binding to the belly, and more so if it has been roasted.

[7.10.55] [55. On lily.] Of the lily, the flower is mixed in its temperament, from a certain fine-particled and earthy substance, from which it also has its bitterness in taste, and from a certain well-tempered watery substance. Hence both the oil made from it and the perfume are of a non-biting dispersing and softening power, as a result of which it is also most suitable for hardnesses in the womb; and the root and the leaves, ground fine by themselves, dry and cleanse and disperse moderately. So at any rate it is also fitting for burns; for these too require a power that is moderately drying and at the same time cleansing. Accordingly, having roasted the root and then ground it fine together with rose-oil, they apply it to burns until cicatrization. For it is also in other respects a good drug for bringing all ulcers to cicatrization. Moreover, it also softens the womb and draws forth the menses. The leaves they boil beforehand and apply, these too, until cicatrization, not only to burns but also to the other ulcers. And some also preserve them in vinegar and use them as wound-remedies. There is more of the cleansing power in the root than in the leaves, yet not much even in this, as has been said before; for they belong to the first rank of cleansing drugs, which is why, when we wish to cleanse away alphos or psora or lepra or achores or anything of that kind, we mix in with it one of the other, stronger drugs, such as honey is. And when this is mixed with it in due proportion it is also fitting for divisions of the sinews and for all the other things that need to be dried vigorously without biting. We once also stored away the juice of the leaves, having boiled it with vinegar and honey; the juice was five times the amount of each of the two, and the drug was well esteemed for everything that needs to be dried vigorously without being bitten, such as those large wounds that occur especially at the heads of the muscles, and those ulcers that are flabby and chronic and hard to cicatrize. These matters, however, already belong to the treatise on the composition of drugs, from which I try to keep away as far as possible for the present, but the nature of the subject often compels one to touch upon it, and one must quickly withdraw from these things again and return to what now lies before us.

[7.10.56] [56. On krokodeilion.] The seed of krokodeilion is pungent and aromatic, diuretic and a mover of the menses, so that it would be of a hot power, both dispersing and drying. The juice, too, of the stalk and of the seed, being of a similar power, benefits those suffering from kidney disease. The root strongly assists the expectorations from the chest, being less pungent than the seed, but no less bitter. It also draws blood through the nostrils.

[7.10.57] [57. On saffron.] Saffron has indeed also something slightly astringent, which was shown to be earthy and cold; but what predominates in it is a heating quality and power, so that its whole substance is of the second order of heating things and of the first of drying things, and for this reason it also has something concocting, the slight astringency too contributing to this. For in drugs that do not heat vehemently, when a small astringency is present in addition, it has the same power as the substances called clogging, which, when they coexist with heat, we showed to be not vehemently concocting.

[7.10.58] [58. On onion.] Onion is of the fourth order of heating things. Its substance, moreover, is rather coarse-particled, whence also, when applied, it opens the mouths of haemorrhoids, and, smeared on with vinegar in the sun, it cleanses away alphoi, and, rubbed on alopecias, it stimulates the hairs more quickly than alcyonium. But if one separates its juice from it, what remains is to a considerable degree of a hot earthy substance, while the juice itself is of a watery and airy heat. Thus, then, when smeared on beneath the eyelids it also benefits those with hypochyma (suffusion) and those whose sight is dulled on account of thickness of humours. And from the mixture of this, the whole onion is flatulent when eaten, and for this reason those that are drier in mixture are less flatulent.

[7.10.59] [59. On the bean.] The bean lies on either side of the middle mixture, very close to it both in respect of drying and in respect of cooling. Its flesh also participates to a slight degree in a certain cleansing power, just as the husk does in an astringent one, and for this reason some physicians, having boiled the whole bean with oxykraton, have given it to dysenteric patients, to those with coeliac affections and to those prone to vomiting. As a food it is flatulent and hard to digest if ever anything was, though it is suitable for expectorations from the chest and lung. As a drug applied externally it dries without causing distress. Indeed we have often used it on gouty patients, boiling it in water and then mixing in pig's fat. On contusions and wounds in the region of the sinews we have applied the flour with oxymel; and on parts already inflamed from a blow, with barley-meal. It is also a good plaster for the testicles and the breasts, for these parts, when inflamed, like to be cooled moderately, and especially when the breasts are inflamed because the milk has curdled within them. Accordingly the milk too is quenched by such a plaster, just as the pubic region of children, when plastered over with bean flour, remains without pubic hair for a longer time.

[7.10.60] [60. On cyclamen.] Cyclamen is varied in its power; for it both cleanses and cuts and opens up and draws out and disperses. This is clear from its particular effects. For its juice opens up haemorrhoids and forcibly provokes evacuation of the bowel when applied on a tuft of wool. So too it is mixed with the powers that disperse phymata and scrofulous swellings and all the other hardnesses, and it is suited to those suffering from cataract, being smeared on beneath the lids with honey, and in addition to these it also purges through the nostrils. So violent is its power that even when the epigastrium is anointed with it, it draws down the belly and destroys embryos; and indeed in other ways too it is a strong abortifacient when applied in a pessary. The whole root is weaker than the juice, but it too is violent. For it moves the menses, both when drunk and when applied, and it benefits those suffering from jaundice, not only cleansing out the viscus but also excreting the bile in the whole body through sweats. Hence after the draught one must assist in every way the production of sweats. The quantity of it that is drunk should be up to three drachms, either with sweet wine or with melikraton. It also cleanses the skin, both in other respects and in treating the alopecias and the ephelides and all the exanthemata. It also benefits hard spleens when plastered on, both fresh and dry. Some give the dry root also to asthmatics. The other cyclamen, which some call kissanthemon because it resembles ivy in its flower, while it has a useless root has a fruit sufficiently active that, when drunk with two kyathoi of white wine for several days, it heals spleens, moving urine and drawing down the belly; and it also expels the afterbirth and helps asthmatics. Its quality to one tasting it is pungent and somewhat viscous.

[7.10.61] [61. On cumin.] Of cumin we use chiefly the seed, just as with anise and lovage and caraway and parsley. It is also of a heating power, like each of those, and of a diuretic and flatulence-dispelling one, being in the third rank of things that heat.

[7.10.62] [62. On kynosbatos (dog-rose).] Kynosbatos. Of this shrub the fruit is not feebly astringent, while the leaves are moderately so, so that the use of each part of them is also evident. But the woolly matter in the fruit is to be guarded against, as being injurious to the windpipe.

[7.10.63] [63. On cypress.] Of cypress, the leaves and the shoots and the little globes, when young and soft, are agglutinating of large wounds in hard bodies. From this it is clear that it is of a drying power, one having nothing conspicuously pungent and hot, as indeed the taste also bears witness; for there appears in it some small amount of the pungent, a very great amount of the bitter, and still much more of the acerbic throughout the whole plant. And there is only so much of the pungent and the hot in it as to guide the acerbity toward the depth, while itself producing no heat and biting in bodies. For this reason it feeds upon the moistures lying in the depth in flabby and putrefactive conditions painlessly and at the same time safely, whereas the heating and drying powers do indeed consume the moistures that are contained there, but draw in others by their pungency and heat. In this way too it benefits those suffering from enterocele. For it both dries and imparts tone to bodies that are slack through moisture, inasmuch as the astringency sinks down into the depth by being guided by the heat mixed with it, which has come to such a measure as to be able to guide, but not yet to be able to bite. Some also use it for carbuncles and for herpes, mixing it with barley-meal, so that it may consume, without heating, the moistures that produce such diseases. And some use it also against erysipelas, mixing it with barley-meal together with water or watery oxykraton.

[7.10.64] [64. On kypeiros (galingale).] Of kypeiros the roots are especially useful, being heating and drying without biting. Hence they are wonderfully beneficial for ulcers that are hard to cicatrize on account of much moisture. For they also have something astringent, and for this reason they are also suitable for ulcers in the mouth; and indeed one must also attest to them a certain cutting power, by which they are also fitting for those suffering from stone and move urine and menses.

[7.10.65] [65. On kypros.] Kypros. Of this tree the leaves and the young shoots come into use, being for the most part of a mixed power and mixture. For it has something dispersing, derived from a watery substance that is moderately hot, and it has something astringent, derived from the cooling (ψυχώσεως) of the earthy [part]; whence, boiling them down, people foment burns with the water. They use them also against fiery inflammations and carbuncles; for they are drying without distress and without biting. And moreover, when chewed, they are suitable for the ulcers that arise spontaneously in the mouth, and especially for the aphthous ones and for the aphthae of children themselves.

[7.10.66] [66. On kytisos.] The leaves of kytisos are of a dispersing power mixed with a lukewarm watery one, just as those of mallow are too. [7.10.67] [67. On hemlock.] That hemlock is of a power that is cooling in the extreme, everyone knows.

[7.10.68] [68. On the pine (kōnos).] Of the pine (kōnos), the fruit — which indeed they also call kokalos and strobilos — when it is green as a whole has, together with moisture, something bitter and pungent, and for this reason it is suitable for those with internal suppuration (the empyic), and for all the others who need to cough up and expectorate easily the matter in the chest and lung. But the edible fruit from it is, on the one hand, a nourishment hard to digest and strong, and, on the other, as a drug it is suitable for smoothing roughnesses, and especially when, having been soaked in water, it has deposited in that water all the pungency it contains. For all the remainder becomes less biting and more clogging, standing in the middle between hot and cold quality, blended from watery and earthy substance, and partaking least of airy substance.

[7.11.1] [1. On hare's-foot.] Hare's-foot is of a drying power, so that it dries up well the fluxes in the belly. [7.11.2] [2. On lathyris.] Lathyris. Some say that this too is a species of tithymallos, both because, in like manner to them, it has a juice and because it purges in the same way as they do, and it is similar to them in its power as a whole, except in so far as the seed appears sweet to those who taste it, and it is this indeed that most of all possesses the purgative power.

[7.11.3] [3. On lampsane.] Lampsane (charlock), when eaten, is productive of bad humour, but applied as a plaster it has something cleansing and dispersing. [7.11.4] [4. On dock (lapathon).] Dock (lapathon) is of a moderately dispersing power, but sorrel (oxylapathon) is of a mixed one; for together with the dispersing power it also partakes of something repelling. Their seed also has something clearly astringent, so that it cures both dysentery and diarrhoea, and especially that of sorrel (oxylapathon). The horse-dock (hippolapathon) grows for the most part in marshes; it is of the same power as those mentioned, but weaker.

[7.11.5] [5. On leimonion.] The fruit of leimonion, which is harsh, they give with wine to those with bowel complaints, to dysenteric patients, and to those who spit blood. It also benefits the female flux. The quantity of an oxybaphon is sufficient.

[7.11.6] [6. On lichen.] Lichen, the one on rocks, is indeed a sort of bryon (tree-moss), but it would correctly be named as belonging to the genus of plants. It seems to have been so named because it cures lichens. It is of a cleansing and at the same time moderately cooling power, yet drying in both respects. The cleansing and drying quality it has from the rock, the cooling from the watery; for it grows on moist and dewy rocks. And that what is composed of substances of this kind should be anti-inflammatory is nothing to wonder at. But whether it also stops haemorrhages, as Dioscorides says, I am not able to say.

[7.11.7] [7. On leontopetalon.] Of leontopetalon we use chiefly the root, which is dispersing and drying and heating, being in the third order. [7.11.8] [8. On lepidion.] Lepidion is of the fourth order of things that heat, being similar to kardamon in smell and in taste and in power, but it dries less than it.

[7.11.9] [9. On leukas.] Leukas is of a predominantly pungent quality, and of a hot and dry mixture, somewhere in the third order. [7.11.10] [10. On leukakanthon.] Leukakanthon, which some call polygonaton and others ischias: the root of this is bitter, and for this reason it both cuts and dries in the third order; but in heating it is of the first order.

[7.11.11] [11. On leukoion.] Of the leukoion the whole bush, too, is of a cleansing and fine-particled power, but the flowers partake of it more, and of these the drier ones more than the fresh, so that it also thins the thick scars on the eyes, and their decoction promotes the menses and calls forth the chorion and dead embryos, and if it be drunk, it is an abortifacient drug. For indeed it is also bitter, if anything is, and if one should soften the vehemence of its power by admixture of much water, or by one of such things, one will have a good drug against inflammation as well. Thus at any rate its decoction too, if it be not undiluted, cures inflammations in the womb when applied as a fomentation, and especially those that have become chronic in a scirrhous manner. Thus also with a cerate it treats ulcers hard to cicatrize. Some use it with honey also against aphthae. The fruit, being of the same power, is most suitable when drunk in the amount of two drachms or applied as a pessary with honey; it is believed to move the menses and to destroy living embryos and to expel dead ones. The roots, being of a similar power, except insofar as they are more coarse-particled and more earthy, with vinegar cure spleens that are becoming scirrhous. Some also cure scirrhous inflammations by means of it.

[7.11.12] [12. On the white poplar.] The white poplar, the tree, is somehow mixed in its mixture, from a watery, lukewarm substance and an earthy one that has been made fine, whence it also partakes of the cleansing power.

[7.11.13] [13. On frankincense.] Frankincense is heating in the second rank, and drying in the first. It also has something slightly astringent, but the astringency is least evident in that which is white in colour. Its bark, however, clearly possesses the astringent power, and for this reason it also dries vigorously, since it stands in the second rank of drying agents at its full extent. It is also more coarse-particled than frankincense and partakes least of pungency. On account of these qualities and powers of it, then, there is considerable use of it among physicians, in the case of those who spit blood and of stomach patients, coeliac patients and dysenterics, who mix it not only into the remedies applied externally but also into those taken into the interior of the body. Its shoot is of a drier and hotter power than frankincense itself, so as to reach the third degree. It also has something cleansing, so that for this reason it seems both to clean out and to fill up the ulcers in the eyes, just as do that from myrrh and that from storax.

[7.11.14] [14. On libanotides.] There are three libanotides: one is fruitless, while the two others bear fruit, and all are of similar power, softening and dispersing. The juice both of the root and of the herb, mixed with honey, cures the dimnesses of sight that arise from thickness of the humours. Of the libanotis useful for garlands, which the Romans call rusmarinum, the decoction, when drunk, benefits those suffering from jaundice. For all the libanotides share in a cleansing and cutting power.

[7.11.15] [15. On soot.] All soot is drying, for which reason it is also earthy in substance, having also some remnant of the fire that burned up the material, but this is small. Its whole nature, however, is earthy and fine-particled. The differences in kind within it arise according to the material that has been burned: from the more pungent and hotter material the soot too turns out of that same kind, while from the sweeter material the soot here likewise becomes similar to it. For instance, people use the soot of frankincense, mixing it into the ophthalmic remedies, even those which are suitable while the eyes are still inflamed and suffering from flux and having ulcers; for these are cleansed and made to grow flesh by them. They also use it, further, in the remedies called kalliblephara (eyelid-beautifiers). That of terebinth and that of myrrh are harmless, much like that of frankincense; that of storax is stronger than these, still more so that of liquid pitch, and still more than this that of cedar. They use the more pungent ones for the eyelids called ptila (lashless), for corroded canthi, and for moist eyes without inflammation; the milder ones both for these and also for the conditions for which, a little earlier, the soot of frankincense was said to be suitable.
[7.11.16] [16. On lovage.] Of lovage both the root and the seed are among heating things to such a degree as to move the menses and promote urine, and moreover they are also dispellers of flatulence.

[7.11.17] [17. On linseed.] Linseed, when eaten, is flatulent, even if it has been roasted; so full, then, is it of superfluous moisture. It is also hot, in roughly the first order, and in respect of moisture and dryness it is placed roughly in the middle.

[7.11.18] [18. On mercury (linozostis).] Linozostis is used by everyone only for purgations of the belly. Nevertheless, if someone should also wish to make trial of it by applying it as a plaster, he will find it to be of a sufficiently dispersing power.

[7.11.19] [19. On lonchitis.] Of lonchitis, the kind that has the triangular seed resembling a lance-head in shape, the root happens to be most of all similar in some way to that of daucus, and for this reason it is also a diuretic drug. Of the kind that is similar to scolopendrium, the leaves, when green, are suitable for the gluing together of a wound, and when dry, drunk with vinegar, they cure spleens that are becoming indurated.

[7.11.20] [20. On lykion.] Lykion or pyxakanthon is a thorny tree, from which also the so-called lykion is produced. This, then, is the liquid drug which they use for bruises under the eyes (ὑπώπια) and for the inflammations and ulcerations in the seat and the mouth, and for herpetes and putrefactions and the malignant kinds of ulcers, and ears running with pus, and chafings and paronychiae. For it is of a drying power, composed of substances of different kinds, the one fine-particled and dispersing and hot, the other earthy and cold, from which it has its astringency. But this quality is present in the drug only to a very slight degree altogether, whereas its dispersing and drying is not slight, but of the second rank (ἀπόστασις), while in heat it is placed somewhere about the middle and the well-balanced. Hence they also use the drug for differing affections, as a cleansing agent for the things that darken the pupils, and as a contracting agent, applying it to coeliac and dysenteric patients and to female flux. This lykion, then, is produced in greatest quantity in Lycia and Cappadocia. The other, the Indian, is stronger in every respect.

[7.11.21] [21. On lysimachios.] Lysimachios has the astringent quality predominant, on account of which it both glues wounds together and, applied as a plaster, stops haemorrhages from the nostrils; and it is also a styptic drug for the other haemorrhages, both the plant itself and its juice, the latter still more; and when drunk it cures dysentery, bringing up of blood, and female flux.
[7.11.22] [22. On lychnis.] The seed of the lychnis used for garlands is hot in about the second order, or indeed already the third, and likewise dry in the same manner.

[7.11.23] [23. On cultivated lotus.] The cultivated lotus, which some call trefoil (triphyllon), is of moderately concocting power, and likewise also of drying power. In the pairing according to heat and cooling it is somehow in the middle and well-tempered. The wild lotus is produced most abundantly in Libya. Its seed is of the second order of heating things, and it also has something cleansing. The seed of the Egyptian one is even made into bread.

[7.11.24] [24. On the lotus tree.] The lotus tree partakes of an astringent quality, though not a strong one, and it is also fine-particled and drying. At any rate the filings of its wood are suitable for female flux, for dysentery and for coeliac conditions. It is boiled down sometimes in water, sometimes in wine, as the need may dictate, and it is not only injected but also drunk. Moreover, the fact that it checks hair that is falling out is no small indication that it possesses a certain astringent power together with a moderately drying one; for it was said also in the discussion of ladanon that whatever is going to check falling hair must be of such a power as this.

[7.12.1] [1. On macer.] Macer is a bark brought from India, in taste quite acerbic, with a certain slight aromatic pungency; when smelled it is pleasant, like most of the Indian aromatics. It seems, then, that it too is composed of a mixed substance, the greatest part of it earthy and cold, but some small part hot and fine-particled, whence it dries and is astringent strongly, and for this reason it is mixed into the medicinal powers for coeliac and dysenteric patients, being in the third rank of drying agents, while in the distinction according to heat and cold it produces neither effect conspicuously.

[7.12.2] [2. On malabathron.] The leaf of malabathron is similar in its power to spikenard (the spike of nard). [7.12.3] [3. On mallow and althaea.] Mallow: the wild kind has a share in a gently dispersing and, to a slight degree, softening power. The cultivated kind, in so far as it has taken on a share of watery moisture, is to that extent also weaker in its power. Its fruit is stronger to the same degree as it is also drier. The so-called tree-mallow also belongs to this genus, but it is the most dispersing of those mentioned; it is also named althaea.

[7.12.4] [4. On mandrake.] Mandrake has the cooling power predominant, so as to be of the third order of cooling agents. Nevertheless it also partakes of a certain heat, and, in the apples at least, of moisture as well, whence these too are comatose-inducing in their power. The bark of the root, being strongest, not only cools but also dries, whereas the rest, the inner part, is weak.

[7.12.5] [5. On fennel] Fennel heats strongly, so that it can already be of the third order; but it does not dry to a like degree, rather in this respect one would place it in the first order, and for this reason it is generative of milk—which it would not generate if it dried strongly—and by the same reasoning it helps those suffering from cataract. It is also diuretic and promotive of the menses. There is also another, wild fennel, which on account of its size they call hippomarathron (horse-fennel), whose root and seed are of a more drying power than in the cultivated kind; so that they seem to me also on this account to stop the belly. For they certainly have no share in any clear astringency. Of this plant, then, not only the root but also, much more, the seed is similar to cachrys, and is able both to break up stones and to cure those suffering from jaundice and to move the menses and to promote urination, though not to collect milk as the former does. There is another hippomarathron, whose seed is round and pungent, similar to that of coriander, like in power to that of the hippomarathron, but weaker.

[7.12.6] [6. On mastic.] Mastic, the white kind customarily called Chian, is in a way composed of opposite powers, an astringent and a softening one. For this reason it is suitable for inflammations of the stomach, the belly, the intestines and the liver, heating and drying in the second degree of remove. The black kind, which is called Egyptian, dries more than the former and has a smaller share of the astringent power, whence it is in a way better suited to conditions that require a stronger dispersing. In this respect, at any rate, it is also a good drug for boils. However, the mastic oil and mastic unguent are prepared from the Chian kind, and hardly at all from the Egyptian; and this too is clearly of a power similar to that of mastic.

[7.12.7] [7. On melanthion.] Melanthion heats and dries in the third rank. It seems also to be fine-particled; at any rate it is in this way that it also cures catarrhs, being applied warm in a linen cloth so that it is smelled continuously. And indeed it is also most free from flatulence when taken inside the body, from which it is clear that it is of a fine-particled substance and one thoroughly worked up by heat. For this reason, at any rate, it is also bitter. It was shown in the fourth of these commentaries that the bitter quality is generated when the earthy substance arrives at the extreme of fineness and elaboration. It is therefore no wonder that it is also of a nature to destroy worms, not only when eaten but also when applied externally over the belly; for it was shown that the bitter humour is of a nature to do this too. Nor indeed is it surprising, to one who remembers what was said in the preceding books, that it expels lepra and corns (heloi) and myrmecia. So too it benefits orthopnoea and promotes the menses that have been held back on account of thickness or viscosity of the humours, and in general, wherever we need to cut and cleanse and dry and heat, the drug is most useful.
[7.12.8] [8. On melilot.] Melilot is of mixed power. For it has something astringent too, but it also disperses and concocts; for the share of hot substance in it is greater than that of the cold.

[7.12.9] [9. On honey.] Honey both dries and heats in the second order. It is of a power and mixture that is simple to the greatest degree possible, belonging to the kind of drugs customarily named by us cleansing; but when boiled it becomes less pungent and cleansing, which is why they use it for the agglutination of sinuses. If, however, some honey is bitter, as is also that in Sardinia, it is evident that this too is of a mixed power, just as if one of us had mixed apsinthion into it. And what is called sakchar, which is brought from India and Arabia Felix, solidifies, as they say, around reeds, and it too is a kind of honey. It is, then, less sweet than that among us, but similar to it in power, insofar as it cleanses and dries and disperses; insofar as it is neither bad for the stomach, like that among us, nor thirst-provoking, it has departed from its substance.

[7.12.10] [10. On melissophyllon.] Melissophyllon is similar to horehound in its power, but falls far short of it. For this reason no one even uses it; for it is superfluous, when horehound is present in such abundance everywhere on earth, to use melissophyllon. If, however, horehound should at some time not be available, one may use it for all the same purposes as that, provided one recognises the deficiency of its action.

[7.12.11] [11. On medlar.] The medlar they sometimes call trikokkon ("three-stoned"), because it has three stones in all inside itself, and each of these is a seed of the tree, just as those found in apples are of the apple-tree, and the grape-seeds of the vine, and the kenchramides of the fig-tree. The fruit of the tree is quite acerbic and scarcely edible, and quite checking of the bowel. The acerbic quality is present in no small measure also in its shoots and in its leaves.

[7.12.12] Medion. In the case of medion it happens that the root is mixed in a manner opposite to the fruit. For the root is harsh and checking of fluxes, both the others and in particular the so-called female flux. The seed, on the other hand, is so far from doing anything of the kind that it actually provokes the menses, being of a fine-particled and cutting power.

[7.12.13] [13. On poppy.] Of poppy, one kind is called rhoias, because its flower quickly falls away (flows off), another cultivated, since it is grown in gardens. And indeed, besides these there are two other wild poppies, the one having its head (capsule), as it were, squat and sunk down, the other having one more elongated than this, but as a whole larger-grown and drier. From this poppy the juice flows out, and for this reason some also call it rhoias. The power of all of them is cooling. But of the garden-grown kind, which they also call thylakitis, the seed, which is white to look at, is moderately soporific. This is why they also sprinkle their seeds on loaves of bread and eat them soaked with honey. Of the kind mentioned first, whose flower we say falls away quickly, the seed cools more strongly, so that one could not use it on its own without harm, as one does with that of the garden-grown kind when mixing it with honey. It is sufficiently soporific when taken in this way, but they sprinkle a little of it on honey-cakes and itria (sesame-and-honey wafers) and loaves of bread. Of the kind mentioned third, the seed, being black, is already drug-like, cooling considerably. The kind mentioned fourth is the most drug-like of all, both in its seed and in its heads and in its leaves and in its juice; for it cools strongly, leading as far as numbness and mortification, whence it is the physician's task to use it well, mixing it with drugs that blunt the strength of its cooling. For it belongs to the fourth and last order of cooling things. But how one might best make the mixture according to method is not proper to the present treatise but to that on the composition of drugs, which we are writing next after this one.

[7.12.14] [14. On horned poppy.] Horned poppy is so named from its fruit, which has a slight curve, as fenugreek too does, so as to resemble an ox's horn. It is called by some the seaside poppy, since for the most part it grows near the sea. It has a cutting and cleansing power, so that the root of the herb, boiled down in water to the half, benefits hepatic conditions, while the leaves and the flowers help those ulcers that are very foul and malignant. One must, however, desist from them once the ulcers have become clean; for it is of a nature to cleanse to such a degree that it even melts away something of the clean flesh itself. It is indeed on account of this strength that it removes not only the filth but also the eschars of ulcers.
[7.12.15] [15. On Heraclean poppy.] Heraclean poppy is also called foam-like (aphrodes), because, being small, it is entirely white and foam-like. Its seed is purgative of phlegm.

[7.12.16] [16. On the apple tree.] The apple tree is not all of one nature, just as the fruit is not either. For some of the apples are sweet, some harsh, some acerbic, some sour, and some altogether slack and watery. And indeed the watery element prevails in these last, so that their mixture is both moister and colder; the cold earthy element in the acerbic ones; in the harsh ones both this and the cold watery element, just as in the sweet ones the watery element is well-tempered. In the same way the leaves, the juices and the barks of the trees also differ from one another, so that with those that are harsher and sourer you could glue wounds together and check the influx in inflammations that are coming into being, and strengthen a slack stomach and belly, while with the more watery ones you could relieve moderate inflammations both when they are beginning and when they are increasing. But these matters belong already to the therapeutic method, and so they must be left aside all the sooner. That a very great quantity of superfluous and cold moisture is contained in all apples is clear also from the fact that the juice of none of them keeps, but all turn sour and spoil. For only the juice of quinces and sparrow-apples, which indeed on account of the prevailing astringency are less moist than the others, is able to keep when boiled with honey; by itself, however, it is not even thus lasting.

[7.12.17] [17. On the Persian apple-tree.] The Persian apple-tree is now customarily called by everyone simply 'Persian', the word 'apple' itself being omitted. The tree has the bitter quality predominant in both its shoots and its leaves, and for this reason its leaves, when ground fine and applied over the navel, kill worms. In other respects too it is a dispersing drug. Its fruit, that is, the edible 'Persian', is moister and colder in mixture.

[7.12.18] [18. On the Armenian apple-tree.] Armenian apple-tree. The ancient name of this tree has fallen out of use; for everyone calls both the fruit and the tree prekokkion. The fruit is both moist and cold, being affected in both respects roughly in the second degree of departure (from the balanced state).

[7.12.19] [19. On the Median apple-tree.] Median apple-tree. The fruit of this is no longer called the Median apple, but is named citron by everyone. In respect of its seed it has the sour quality and the drying power prevailing, so that it is of the third order among the things that dry and cool; in respect of its rind it here too has a share of a drying mixture, but one that possesses no small amount of the pungent, and for this reason this part dries in the second degree. It is not, however, cold, but either balanced or a little below. Its flesh is of thick humour, phlegmatic and cold; for this part is eaten, just as the rind is too. But the seed is entirely inedible, both the moist and sourish part, about which I spoke first, and the stone found within it, which is really the seed; and this is bitter and clearly dispersing and drying, standing apart from the balanced things in about the second order. And the leaves too are of a drying and dispersing power.

[7.12.20] [20. On meon.] Meon (spignel). The roots of this are useful, being hot in the third remove and dry in the second. For this reason, at any rate, those wishing to move urine and to call forth the menses use the drug. It is also productive of headache when taken in greater quantity, inasmuch as it is hot to a greater degree than it is dry. For the heat in it carries up to the head a moisture that is still rather undigested and flatulent, and in this way harms it.

[7.12.21] [21. On rough smilax.] Rough smilax is vine-like, so that it winds around trees in many ways, upward and downward. Its leaves both have something pungent when tasted and, when used in other ways as well, heat.

[7.12.22] [22. On smooth smilax.] The smooth smilax is in some way similar to the one previously mentioned in its power. [7.12.23] [23. On the mulberry tree.] The fruit of the mulberry tree, when ripe, loosens the belly, but the unripe fruit, when dried, becomes a sufficiently constricting drug, so that it is suited both for dysenteries and coeliac conditions and the others that are characterised by flux. It is pounded and mixed with cooked dishes, just as the fruit of the sumach is, or, if one wishes, it is drunk in water or wine. That the juice of the ripe fruits is useful for stomatic drugs on account of the astringency that is present in it, no one is unaware. And it is evidently also suited for many other particular conditions, as many as require a moderate astringency. The unripe fruits, in addition to acerbity, also partake of sourness. And the whole tree, in all its parts, seems to have a certain mixed power, composed of a checking and a cleansing power. In the bark of the root the cleansing power predominates, together with a certain bitterness, so that it also kills the broad worm; but in the other parts, the checking power. In the leaves and the shoots the mixture is in some way intermediate between both.

[7.12.24] [24. On myagros.] The seed of myagros is oily, so that if it is crushed it also gives off something oil-like, which is of a clogging power. [7.12.25] [25. On mushrooms.] The mushroom is a plant cold and moist to a considerable degree, whence it also comes close to a deleterious power. And some of them actually kill, and especially those that have a nature mixed with some putrefactive quality.

[7.12.26] [26. On mylē.] The root of mylē, being similar to a small bulb, is of a contracting power, so that Dioscorides says that, when it is applied together with darnel flour, it also heals a womb whose mouth has been opened.

[7.12.27] [27. On mouse-ear.] Mouse-ear (myos ōtis); some, however, say "mouse's ears" (myos ōta). It dries in the second order, but possesses no evident heat. [7.12.28] [28. On tamarisk.] Tamarisk is of a cleansing and cutting power, without drying evidently, but it also has some astringency. And on account of these qualities and powers it considerably benefits a scirrhous spleen, when the roots, or the twigs, or the leaves are boiled down in vinegar or in wine. It also cures toothaches. The fruit and the bark have taken on no slight astringency, so as even to come near to omphakitis oak-gall, except that, insofar as the acerbity is clear in the oak-gall, in the fruit of tamarisk the mixture is uneven. For much that is cleansing and fine-particled is mixed into its nature, which does not belong to the oak-gall. One can nevertheless use it, when oak-gall is not available, for all the same purposes as that, and likewise the bark too. And the ash of tamarisk when it has been burnt becomes of a sufficiently drying power, having the cleansing and cutting element in greatest measure, and the astringent element in small measure.

[7.12.29] [29. On myriophyllon.] Myriophyllon is of a drying power to such a degree as to glue together wounds. [7.12.30] [30. On myrrhis.] Myrrhis—some, however, call it myrrha—has a fragrant and sweet root; it is moving of the menses and purgative upward of what comes from the chest and the lung, so that it would be of the second rank of heating things, having also something fine-particled.

[7.12.31] [31. On myrtle.] Myrtle. This plant too is composed of opposite substances. Nevertheless the cold earthy substance predominates in it, though it also has a fine-particled hot one, whence it dries strongly. The leaves, the shoots, the fruit and the juice do not differ much from one another in respect of astringency. The knob-like outgrowth, however, upon the trunk and the branches themselves, which some call myrtas, to the degree that it is drier than the parts just mentioned, to that degree also both dries and is astringent more vehemently. Some store it by pounding it, then taking it up in wine and forming it into troches. The dry leaves are also more drying than the green ones, for clearly some moisture is mixed into the green. The juice is pressed out not only from the green leaves but also from the fruit. All of these are of a constricting power, both when applied externally to the body and when taken internally, because they have no substance mixed in that is at all poisonous or purgative.

[7.12.32] [32. On moly.] Moly. Some call this wild rue, some harmala, the Syrians besasa, just as indeed the Cappadocians also call it moly, because at the root it is black but has a milky flower. Its power is fine-particled and hot in the third degree of distance, whence it also cuts thick and viscous humours and is dispersing and urges on to urination. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK Θ. Proem. Whatever, then, remains of the power in plants will be stated in this book—and not even all of this, but only the activities of the active qualities. For the works of the whole substance of plants we shall go through later, by themselves. Having, then, reminded those who have read the earlier parts, once more at this very point, that for each simple power we made the division according to more and less into four orders, and that we marked off the breadth of each order by clear boundaries, and taught a certain method for the very discovery of the powers, and gave demonstrations of all these things and set up aims and criteria for each power, both particular and common, we shall thus now add what is lacking, having urged anyone who has not become acquainted with the earlier parts either to keep away from these altogether too, or, if he is industrious, first to read through the treatise from the beginning. For everything that will be said will appear to him at once both obscure and undemonstrated, before he has exercised himself in those.

[6.1.1] [1. On abrotonon (southernwood) and apsinthion (wormwood) and the species of each.] Of abrotonon, this herb, there is no need to write either its form, after so many and such men, or its particular actions, as those men, even if not with distinctions, at any rate clearly set them forth. More will be said by us too about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs and in that on readily available remedies, and sometimes also in the books of the Therapeutic Method, whenever the need calls. Only, what has been set out from the beginning, to examine the general powers of all drugs, this follows in the case of the others as well, and now already it must be done and it must be stated that abrotonon is hot and dry in power, ranked somewhere in the third rank and degree of removal after the well-balanced states, having a certain dispersing and cutting power. Of the same power too is its rubbing (τρίψις), having taken it on, just as the flesh-forming and the biting. That such a rank is assessed in relation to the well-tempered nature has been said often before. And we discovered its mixture not least by judging from taste too, for it is sufficiently bitter. And such a flavour was shown to be earthy in substance, but to be thinned by abundant heat, so that it both heats and dries not ignobly. Nevertheless, also by the distinguished experience, about which much has been said before, having tested it accurately, we found this drug to be of the same mixture. For whether, having pounded the foliage together with the flowers—for the rest of it, the stalk, is useless—you sprinkle it on a clean ulcer, it appears biting and irritating; or whether, having steeped it in oil, you wish to foment either the head or the belly, it will be found to heat vigorously. And indeed those who are seized periodically by rigors, if you rub these too before the onset, they shiver less, and it does not escape the perception, immediately upon being applied, that it heats. That it is likely to kill worms, being bitter, is quite clear even before experience, if we remember what was said in the fourth of these commentaries about the nature of the bitter flavour. And you will know at once that it also has a certain dispersing and cutting power. But also that this must necessarily belong to it more than to apsinthion you will be able to reason out, first from the taste. For abrotonon partakes of some very slight acerbity, but apsinthion of not a little; and then also from the fact that abrotonon is bad for the stomach, as indeed seriphon is too, while apsinthion is good for the stomach. For it was shown about these too before that the bitter in and of itself would be entirely bad for the stomach, but the harsh or the acerbic or in general the astringent good for the stomach. And when the qualities are mixed with one another, the more vigorous would prevail. These things, then, suffice for you to know in this treatise. For it will be shown in the books of the Therapeutic Method how one might best use such a drug. And for this reason no longer seek to hear either that, applied as a plaster with boiled quince or with bread, it cures inflammations of the eyes, or that it disperses tumours (φύματα) when boiled smooth with raw barley meal. For neither of these two nor any of the others is proper to the present treatise, but for those who produce an empirical teaching it is written among the readily available drugs, whereas those who wish to practise the art rationally have need of the Therapeutic Method. For, among other things, one might be harmed rather than helped by such a history. To Hippocrates, then, writing in the Aphorisms, 'pains of the eyes drinking of unmixed wine, or a bath, or fomentation, or phlebotomy, or purging resolves', and yet not adding which pains, then, drinking of unmixed wine resolves, which a bath, and which fomentation, which phlebotomy, which purging, one would, I think, grant pardon for three reasons. For he was producing an aphoristic teaching, in which, on account of its conciseness, he has allowed many things to be said thus, and he wrote all the remedies of pains, even if he did not distinguish for which sort of pain which of them is fitting; and also in many places in his other writings he gave us starting-points for the distinctions in what was said in this way. But those who have written neither in other books about such aphorisms nor in a detailed and long treatise, write aphoristically and briefly, and if in addition to these they indicate one thing out of many, they harm us in more respects than they help. For since there are many differences among ophthalmias, and one of them needs the aforementioned plaster while the others are harmed, he who uses it in all cases without distinction will harm many more than he helps. In this manner, then, we must write not only about abrotonon but also about all the others, discovering the powers in respect of heating and cooling or moistening or drying from the methods I have often stated, but whatever is accomplished according to the peculiarity of the whole substance by experience alone. It has been shown about such things too that they are deleterious, and antidotes to deleterious things, and cathartic. For of these it is not possible to make the discovery rational, but only to find a certain plausible suspicion in some cases—not indeed in all, as this very thing too has been shown through the foregoing. But about the powers discovered in this way I shall make my discussion separately in what follows, once I have first gone through, for each species of drug, those concerning heating and cooling, moistening and drying, and whatever follows upon these. Having added, however, just so much more about abrotonon, I shall bring the discussion to an end: that the most admirable Pamphilus, although writing this herb first and perhaps, if of none of those following, at least of this one having wished to become an eyewitness, has nonetheless erred very greatly in thinking that the plant is called santonicum by the Romans. For abrotonon differs from santonicum, as Dioscorides too wrote most accurately in the third book On Materials, and all physicians and dealers in sundries know this at least. For of abrotonon there are two species, the one considered male, the other female, as this too has been distinguished in Dioscorides and Pamphilus and countless others. Different from it is apsinthion, of which again one must posit species, themselves three, of which the one is called homonymously with the genus apsinthion, of which kind the Pontic especially is, another seriphon, another santonicum. But if one should say that apsinthion is one thing, seriphon another, and santonicum another, it makes no difference for the present purposes. For we have not come to divide a name, but we are concerned about the things themselves. Since, then, these too are clearly different from one another in their forms and their tastes and their powers, let anyone, if he wishes, name them all by a single appellation, but let him teach the powers accurately. We, then, said that the forms have been sufficiently stated by Dioscorides and not a few others, so that one need not write again what has been correctly said by one's predecessors. But if those men left anything undistinguished in the powers of this plant, for the sake of which indeed I have come to this digression, I shall try to add it. Apsinthion is less hot than those mentioned, as partaking of the most astringency. And if this too is less fine-particled than they, it is also thinning, in the same manner, less than they, yet not indeed less drying. Of the others, santonicum, having its name from the Santonian country in which it grows, is nearest in power to seriphon, falling short by some little in thinning and heating and drying. Seriphon itself is less hot than abrotonon, but hotter than apsinthion, sufficiently bad for the stomach and as displaying a certain saltiness together with bitterness, and further partaking of a little acerbity. So too abrotonon and santonicum are sufficiently bad for the stomach. For alone among them apsinthion, and especially the Pontic, is good for the stomach, because it partakes of the most astringency. Burnt abrotonon is hot and dry in power, still more than burnt dry gourd and root of dill. For those are fitting for ulcers that are moist and at the same time callused without inflammation, and for this reason especially they seem to agree with those on the foreskins of the genitals. But the ash of abrotonon is biting to all ulcers. And for this reason it is fitting also against alopecia with fine-particled oil, namely castor-oil or radish-oil or Sicyonian or old oil, and especially Sabine. And it brings forth beards that come up slowly with whichever of the oils mentioned, and no less than those when moistened with mastic-oil. For it is rarefying, in addition to being fine-particled and biting and hot, which powers of it indeed one must especially know, and no longer need anything of the particulars in this treatise.

[6.1.2] [2. On agnos or lygos.] Agnos or lygos, the shrubby plant, is hot and drying at about the third degree of departure, fine-particled to a considerable extent, and to the taste pungent and at the same time astringent — agnos, or lygos. The withies (lygoi) themselves which it bears are useless for medicine, but the leaves and the seed are dry and hot in power and fine-particled in substance. For so it appears to those who use it, and to those who taste it the leaf, the flower and the fruit are at once pungent and somewhat astringent. The fruit is also edible, and it heats manifestly, besides being productive of headache. If it is roasted — for it is eaten in this way too among the dessert-nuts — it affects the head less. It is non-flatulent in the belly, both the unroasted and, still more, the roasted. Both the roasted and the unroasted fruit also check the impulses toward sexual intercourse, and the leaves and flowers of the shrub are able to do this same thing, so that not only when eaten and drunk are they believed to contribute to chastity, but also when strewn beneath. For this reason, too, at the Thesmophoria the women at Athens strew the whole shrub beneath themselves, and from this comes its name. From all this it is clear, if we remember what was said in the preceding commentaries, that agnos heats and at the same time dries and is most non-flatulent. And there is a proof that its power is precisely fine-particled: for its affecting the head comes about, on good reasoning, not through an abundance of vaporous pneuma generated by it, but rather through heat and fineness of particles. For if it were generative of flatulent pneuma, it would have inflated the belly and would have sharpened the impulses toward sexual intercourse, like rocket. But since it not only does not sharpen them but is by nature apt to suppress them, it would be most of all of the power of rue in heating and drying; yet it is not equal to it. For it falls short a little in both; for rue is both more heating and more drying than it. It differs also in the admixture of quality and power. For the seed of agnos and the shoots bring in a certain moderate astringency, whereas rue, when it is dry, is precisely bitter and pungent, and when moist, slightly bitter. Yet nothing harsh or acerbic is attached to it, or if it should seem to someone to be attached, I know it will seem altogether faint, and in no way equal to that of agnos. For this reason, too, the seed of agnos is more suitable than rue for liver and spleen when they are hardened and obstructed. But these matters already belong to the therapeutic method, from which to refrain altogether while pronouncing on the power of drugs is impossible, whereas to leave it quickly and return again to what is set before us would be the work of a prudent man. Still more in the case of the drugs that follow I shall try to do just this, I mean to reckon out the general power from some few evident facts and then withdraw from the particular actions. For it suffices for the present purposes to know only this, that agnos is hot and dry in power, not moderately but at about the third of the degrees of departure, and fine-particled to a considerable extent. For he who knows these things, and then learns in addition the therapeutic method, will himself discover how he will move the menses by means of it, how he will disperse hardened parts, and how he will prepare by means of it an anointment against fatigue or a heating one.

[6.1.3] [3. On agrostis.] Of agrostis the root is moderately cold and dry, having something slightly biting and fine-particled. The herb itself cools in the first degree of distance, but is balanced in respect of moisture and dryness. The seed of the other kind is weak, but that of the kind on Parnassus is drying, fine-particled and somewhat astringent. Agrostis has an edible root, so long as it is soft, sweet and watery, yet having something pungent and a little that is somewhat astringent. The herb itself is entirely watery to those who taste it. From which it is clear that the root is moderately cold and dry, and for this reason agglutinating of bleeding wounds. The herb itself, applied as a plaster, cools, though not strongly, and stands in the middle between moisture and dryness. The biting and fine-particled element in the root is indeed small, yet it is nonetheless wont at times even to break up stones, if one boils it down and drinks it. The seed of the other kind is weak, but that of the kind on Parnassus is diuretic and dries fluxes of the belly and of the stomach. For its power is drying, fine-particled and somewhat astringent.

[6.1.4] [4. On anchousa and the four kinds of anchousa.] Of anchousa there is a fourth kind (τέταρτόν ἐστιν εἶδος; the sense intended is that there are four species), of which the onokleia has a root that cools considerably and dries, being at once astringent and slightly bitter, and capable also of thinning and scouring away the bilious humours and of condensing the bodies. Its leaves it has weaker than the root, yet they too are astringent and dry. And the one called lykopsis cools and dries, and has a root more astringent than that of the onokleia. The onocheilos is both hotter and more drug-like; for it has more of the pungent, and that immediately to the taste. Hotter still than this is the one which is small and more bitter and happens to be still more drug-like. The anchousai, then, are not all of the same power. For the one called onokleia has a root at once astringent and slightly bitter, capable both of condensing the bodies and of moderately thinning and scouring away and washing off the bilious and salty humours. For it was said in what precedes that the acerbic quality, when mixed with the bitter, is by nature such as to produce these effects. Thus indeed it is also beneficial to those suffering from jaundice, from the spleen and from the kidneys. It is also capable of cooling, and when applied as a plaster with barley-meal it helps erysipelas; and it scours not only when drunk but also when applied externally, and for this reason it cures alphos and lepra with vinegar. These are the works of the root, and the powers behind the works are those stated. The leaves of the plant are weaker than the root, but are not free of drying and of being astringent, so that they also cure diarrhoea when drunk with wine. And the one called lykopsis is likewise suited to cases of erysipelas and has a root more astringent than that of the onokleia. Of the onocheilos, also called Alcibiadeion, the power is more drug-like; at any rate it has more of the pungent, and that immediately to the taste, and it is quite suitable for those bitten by vipers, applied as a plaster, worn as an amulet, and eaten. The remaining fourth one, small and alone among them almost nameless, is similar to the Alcibiadeion, but is more bitter and still more drug-like, and for this reason is suited against the broad worms, drunk in the quantity of an oxybaphon with hyssop and cress.

[6.1.5] [5. On the root of agaric.] Agaric is a root, that is to say, one growing upon a trunk; at the first taste it is somewhat sweet, but a little later it shows itself slightly bitter, and in time it brings on the impression of a certain pungency, and of a slight astringency. It is also loose in consistency. From all of which it is quite clear, if indeed we remember what was said in the earlier commentaries, that the drug is composed of an airy and an earthy substance, thinned by heat, and that it participates least of all in the watery. For these reasons, then, it has a dispersing and heating power, and one cutting of thickness, and it cleanses out the obstructions in the viscera, and on this account heals those suffering from jaundice, those who are so afflicted because of an obstruction of the parts in the region of the liver. It benefits epileptics too through the same power, and periodic rigors, such as are the offspring of thick or viscous juices—these also it heals. It also helps those bitten or stung by beasts that do harm by chilling, both applied externally over the affected part and taken into the body in a weight of one drachm with diluted wine. It is also purgative.

[6.1.6] [6. On ageraton.] Ageraton is of a dispersing power, and in a somewhat gentle way one that is free from inflammation (ἀφλεγμάντου). [6.1.7] [7. On adianton (maidenhair).] Adianton, as regards heat and cold, is balanced, but it dries, thins and disperses. For indeed it makes alopecia grow hair again, it disperses scrofulous swellings and abscesses, it breaks up stones when drunk, and it contributes in no small measure to the bringing up of viscous and thick humours from the chest and the lung, and it checks a flux of the belly. Yet it does not impart any clear heat, just as it does not impart cooling either. Rather, one would place it, with respect to the opposition and mixture in these qualities, in the middle rank.

[6.1.8] [8. On aeizoon.] Aeizoon of either sort, both the small and the large, dries to a slight degree, because it is also moderately astringent, being free of every other strong quality, so that the watery substance rather predominates in it; but it cools not moderately, for it belongs to the third remove and order of cooling things. For these reasons, then, it is suitable against erysipelas, but also against herpetes and against the inflammations arising from fluxes.

[6.1.9] [9. On aigilops.] Aigilops has a dispersing power, and this is clear from its taste, for it is in some degree mildly pungent. Not only this, however, but it is clear also from the fact that it cures inflammations that are becoming hardened and the aigilopes.

[6.1.10] [10. On darnel.] Darnel dries and heats effectively, so that it comes nearer to the pungent drugs than iris does. It is not, however, fine-particled as that one is, but falls far short in this respect; and one might place it at the beginning of the third rank of heating drugs, and at the end of the second of drying ones.

[6.1.11] [11. On black poplar.] Of the black poplar, the flowers are hot in power, at the first remove from the well-tempered things; but in the distinction according to drying and moistening it has departed only a little from the well-tempered and middle things toward the drier side. It is also fine-particled rather than coarse-particled. And its leaves are in a way similar to the flowers, except that they are in every respect weaker and less active; and its resin is similar in power to the flowers and even hotter. But the seed is more fine-particled and more drying than the resin and the flowers, though not very much hotter.

[6.1.12] [12. On akakia (acacia).] Of akakia both the plant itself is acerbic, and its fruit and its juice, which, when it has also been washed, becomes at once both weaker and less biting, as though laying aside a certain pungency in the washing. If, indeed, it is smeared on some healthy part, it at once renders this drier and contracted, and it never produces a sensation of heat, but has a cooling that is not very strong. It is clear, then, that the drug is cold and earthy, with a certain watery substance also mixed in with it. One might conjecture, too, that it is not homoeomerous, but has certain scattered parts that are fine-particled and hot, which depart in the washing. And let this too be placed in the third order of drying agents, and in the second of cooling agents, when it has been washed; the unwashed, however, in the first.

[6.1.13] [13. On akalyphe.] Akalyphe. Of this herb too, both the fruit and the leaves—for it is these especially that come into use—are of a sufficiently dispersing power, so that it heals both phymata and parotid swellings. It also has something flatulent in it, by which it also arouses the impulses toward sexual intercourse, and especially when the seed is drunk with sweet wine. That it does not heat violently, but is sufficiently fine-particled, is attested both by the bringing-up of the thick and viscous humours in the chest and lung, and by the fact that the parts of the body which it touches itch.
