But the pneumatic quality, in which it has been said to share, is generated as it is being digested; for it is not pneumatic in actuality, but in potentiality. It moves the bowels moderately by the mere fact of cleansing and, as it were, tickling, not by purging. And gangrenous and cancerous conditions, and in general whatever needs to be dried without being bitten, it heals appropriately, being fine-particled and dry in its mixture, yet not sharing in heat to such a degree as actually to bite.
[6.1.14] [14. On akanthos.] Akanthos. Some call it melamphyllon, others paiderōs. The leaves have a moderately dispersing power, while the root is drying and gently cutting and fine-particled.

[6.1.15] [15. On akanthion.] Akanthion. The root of this plant and its leaves are of a fine-particled and hot power, so that they also help those suffering from spasms. [6.1.16] [16. On white akanthos.] White akanthos. Some call this leukakanthos. Its root is drying and moderately astringent, for which reason it benefits those with bowel and stomach complaints, checks fluxes of blood, reduces oedemas when applied as a plaster, and relieves aching teeth, if the mouth is rinsed with its decoction. The seed is of a fine-particled and hot power, so that it is also suitable, taken in drink, for those suffering from spasms.

[6.1.17] [17. On the Egyptian akanthos.] Egyptian akanthos: some call it Arabian. It also resembles the white akanthos found among us, but it is more astringent and more drying in its power, so that its root helps even the female flux. And against all the other things for which the one found among us helps, both its root and its fruit help more vigorously. The latter also [helps] the inflated swellings about the uvula and about the seat, and it brings ulcers to a scar, having a moderate and not unpleasant astringency.

[6.1.18] [18. On akoron.] Akoron. Of this we use the root, which is pungent and moderately somewhat bitter to the taste, and not unpleasant in its smell. From this it is clear that it is hot in its power and fine-particled in its constitution. In agreement with this is also the fact that it moves urine, benefits spleens that are becoming indurated, and cleanses and thins the thicknesses of the cornea. Its juice is better for this purpose. It is clear too that it is in every way drying. And indeed let it be placed in the third order in both respects, both in heating and in drying.

[6.1.19] [19. On aconite or pardalianches.] Aconite or pardalianches. This is of a putrefying and deleterious power, wherefore one must guard against taking it in food or drink. For causing some part to rot away from the body, however, or at the seat, it is suitable. The root of the herb is useful for these purposes.

[6.1.20] [20. On aconite or wolf's-bane.] Aconite or wolf's-bane (lykoktonon). This too is of a power similar to the other, but it is more particularly its nature to destroy wolves, just as that one destroys leopards. [6.1.21] [21. On elder and dwarf elder.] Elder, both the large, tree-like kind and the more herbaceous kind, which indeed they also call dwarf elder (chamaiakte): both are of a drying power, and of an agglutinating and moderately dispersing one.

[6.1.22] [22. On halimon.] Halimon. This plant is a shrub, growing most abundantly in Cilicia above all, where they also eat its shoots both fresh and by storing them up for keeping. The plant is also generative of seed and of milk, and in taste it is salty and has something slightly astringent. From all of which it is clear that it is non-uniform in its parts, but the greater part of its substance is warm in a well-tempered degree, with a moisture that is unworked and gently flatulent.

[6.1.23] [23. On aloe.] Aloe. This herb does not grow much at all in our country, and that which grows in Greater Syria is more watery and weaker in its power. Nevertheless it is of such a nature as to dry to the extent of agglutinating wounds. But in the hotter regions, among which are Coele Syria and Arabia, it is much better. Best of all, too, is that in India, whose juice is this drug that is imported here, called aloe, which furnishes very great usefulness through drying without biting. It is not of a simple nature, but, as the taste also bears witness, it is astringent and at the same time bitter. It is, then, moderately astringent, but strongly bitter. It also loosens the belly, being one of the drugs called evacuant of excrement, so that from what has been said it is clear, if we remember at all what was demonstrated in the fourth book, that among drying drugs it is of the third degree, and among heating drugs either of the first degree in its intense form or of the second in its relaxed form. The particular actions also bear witness to the mixed character of its power. For the drug is good for the stomach, if any other is, and agglutinating of sinuses. It heals those ulcers which are hard to cicatrize, and especially those about the seat and the genitals. It also benefits inflammations of these when dissolved in water, and agglutinates wounds in the same manner. It is likewise suited, for one who uses it in the same way, to inflammations in the mouth and nostrils and eyes. And in general it is of a nature both to repel and to disperse at the same time, together with cleansing to a slight degree, to the extent that it is harmless to clean ulcers.

[6.1.24] [24. On alysson.] Alysson. The herb has been named alysson because it wonderfully benefits those who have been bitten by a rabid dog. But given even to one already rabid it has often cured him completely. This it is able to do from the similarity in respect of its whole substance, and it has been said earlier that a power of this kind is grasped from experience alone and is altogether without method. But if one were to use it also for many purposes, one will recognize that it is of a moderately drying and dispersing power, in addition to having something cleansing as well. By this, at any rate, it also cleans away alphos and ephelis.

[6.1.25] [25. On alsine.] Alsine or mouse-ear. This too has a power similar to that of helxine, cooling and moistening; for it is of a watery, cold substance, and hence it cools even without astringency. For these reasons, then, it is suited to boiling inflammations and to moderate cases of erysipelas.
[6.1.26] [26. On amarakon.] Amarakon heats not ignobly, but dries not violently. Rather, in heating it is of the third order, while in drying it is of the second.

[6.1.27] [27. On ambrosia.] Ambrosia, applied as a plaster, has a power that is astringent and repelling. [6.1.28] [28. On ami.] Ami. Of the herb which they call ami, the seed is the most useful part; it is of a heating, drying and fine-particled power. To those tasting it, it is also somewhat bitter and pungent, and clearly also diuretic and dispersing. Its heating and drying would follow from the third order at its height.

[6.1.29] [29. On amaranth.] Amaranth is of a cutting and thinning power. Accordingly its tuft, drunk with wine, draws the menses, and it is believed to dissolve clots of blood themselves, not only those in the belly but also those in the bladder. At that time, however, one ought rather to drink it with honeyed wine; and, when drunk, it is simply drying of all fluxes, though it is bad for the stomach.

[6.1.30] [30. On amorge (olive-lees).] Amorge is of an earthy, hot substance; yet it does not partake of heat to such a degree as to be manifestly biting. And if it is also boiled down, it becomes much more coarse-particled still, and dry. And it would belong to the second order of things that heat and dry, somewhat more intensified. Thus indeed it heals the ulcers of bodies that are dry in mixture, but it exacerbates those in all the others. For it is tensing, like resin and dry pitch and asphalt, which themselves too are agglutinating of bodies that are very hard, whether they have a wound or sinuses; but all the others they tense and exacerbate.

[6.1.31] [31. On ampeloprason.] Ampeloprason: if you were to conceive of something intermediate between garlic and leek, you would find the power of ampeloprason. For it is, as one might say, a wild leek, whence it is also more pungent and drier than the latter, just as all other wild things are compared with the cultivated, and for this reason it is both worse for the stomach and more cutting of thick and viscous humours, and more unblocking of obstructed organs. In this way indeed it has often set in motion both urine and menses, whenever they are held back by a thick and viscous humour. It is hot to such a degree that it is already able to ulcerate when applied as a plaster. And it was said earlier that all things that are hot to this degree belong to the last order.

[6.1.32] [32. On the wild vine.] The grape-clusters of the wild vine are of a cleansing power, so as to treat epheleis and spots and whatever such things arise on the surface of the skin. They also have something astringent, both the clusters themselves and the young shoots, which indeed are also preserved in brine.

[6.1.33] [33. On the cultivated vine.] Of the cultivated vine the power is similar to that of the wild one, but weaker in every respect. [6.1.34] [34. On the white vine.] Of the white vine, which indeed they call bryonia and psilothron, the first shoots are customarily eaten by everyone in the spring, as a food good for the stomach because it is astringent, and because it has an astringency that is also slightly bitter and gently pungent; for this reason they also move urination moderately. The root has a certain cleansing and drying and fine-particled power, and one moderately hot. For this reason it also dissolves spleens that are becoming scirrhous, both when drunk and when applied externally with figs, and it cures psora and lepra. Its cluster-like fruit is useful to the leather-tanners.

[6.1.35] [35. On black vine.] Black vine. This one is properly called bryonia; it is in all respects similar to the one previously mentioned, except that it is weaker. [6.1.36] [36. On almonds.] Almonds. The bitter ones are manifestly of an altogether thinning power, both for one who infers from their quality and for one who judges by experience. Concerning the bitter quality, then, it has been spoken of in the fourth of these commentaries; and as for the evidence of experience, it suffices, when one has put forward these two instances, to be taught from these very facts about their power. For they clear away ephelis, and they contribute considerably to the expectoration from the chest and lung of viscous and thick humours. These effects, we showed, belong in genus to the thinning power, in species to the cleansing power. And indeed, that it would also be of the unblocking power incidentally, this too has been demonstrated previously. But experience bears witness. At any rate it adequately clears out the impactions of thick and viscous humours in the liver, in the extremities of the vessels. And indeed it also cures pains of the sides that arise from such a cause, and those in the spleen, colon and kidneys. And the tree itself as a whole has a similar power, so that people clear away ephelides by sprinkling on its roots boiled. As for those almonds that are sweet, these too partake of a slight bitterness; but since the sweetness prevails, it is concealed, though it becomes plainly evident when they age. It has been demonstrated in what precedes that the sweet quality is moderately hot.

[6.1.37] [37. On ammoniac.] Ammoniac is the juice of a certain narthex (giant fennel). It is of an intensified softening power, so that it both dissolves the hard concretions around the joints and cures spleens that are becoming scirrhous and disperses scrofulous swellings.

[6.1.38] [38. On amomon.] Amomon is similar in its power to akoron, except that akoron is drier, whereas amomon is more concoctive. [6.1.39] [39. On anagallis.] Anagallis, both kinds, the one having the blue flower and the one having the red, are of a sufficiently cleansing power, having also something gently warming and drawing, so that they even draw out splinters. Their juice purges through the nostrils for the same reason, and, speaking generally, they have a drying power that does not bite, whence they both glue together wounds and help putrefying parts.

[6.1.40] [40. On anagyros.] Anagyros is a foul-smelling and pungent shrub, of a dispersing and heating power. But the green leaves, being less pungent because of the admixture of moisture, are reducing of swellings (oedematous parts), whereas when dried they are of a cutting and strongly drying power. Of a somewhat similar nature is also the bark of their root. The seed is still more fine-particled, but it is also emetic.

[6.1.41] [41. On androsaimon.] Androsaimon is a shrub-like plant of twofold nature: the one is called askyron or askyroeides, being a species of hyperikon (St John's wort); the other is that which is called by some dionysias. The fruit of them is purgative, while the power of the leaves is drying and moderately cleansing, so that it is believed also to cure burns. Boiled down in harsh wine, they render the wine agglutinating for large wounds.

[6.1.42] [42. On androsakes.] Androsakes is a bitter and pungent herb. When dried and drunk, both the plant itself and its fruit are able to move urine sufficiently, and evidently also to disperse and to dry.

[6.1.43] [43. On andrachne.] Andrachne is cold and watery in its mixture, but it partakes of some small harsh element. Hence it also repels fluxes, and especially bilious and hot ones, together with changing them and altering them in quality by cooling sufficiently. And it would be, in its power of cooling, of the third degree of removal from the well-balanced and middle ones, and in that of moistening, of the second. For these reasons, indeed, it benefits those burning with fever as much as anything else, when applied over the mouth of the stomach and the whole of the hypochondria, and especially in the case of hectic fevers; and it is a remedy for haimodia, itself smoothing and filling up [the teeth] that have been quickly dried out by contact with acid juices, through having its moisture viscous. And its juice likewise, so that it cools not only when applied externally but also when drunk. This indeed also holds of the herb itself when eaten whole. And because of its being mildly astringent it is also a suitable food for dysenterics and for the female flux and for bringings-up of blood. For these purposes, however, the juice is much more effective than the herb itself.

[6.1.44] [44. On anemone.] All anemones are of a pungent and cleansing power, and one that is attractive and opens up the mouths of vessels. Hence the root, when chewed, draws forth phlegm, and the juice purges through the nostrils and thins the scars in the eyes. The anemones also cleanse the foul ulcers and remove lepra, and when applied as a pessary they bring on the menses and draw up milk.

[6.1.45] [45. On dill.] Dill heats to such a degree that one would suppose it to be either of the second order at its intensified degree or of the third at its relaxed degree. Among drying agents it is of the second order at its beginning, or of the first at its intensified degree, so that, reasonably enough, when boiled down in oil it is dispersing, pain-relieving, sleep-inducing, and concoctive of raw and unconcocted swellings. For the oil made from it comes somewhere near in mixture to the drugs called pus-producing and concoctive, except that it is a little hotter than they and fine-particled, and for this reason also dispersing. When burnt it becomes of the third order of heating and drying agents, and on this account, plastered upon flabby ulcers, it benefits them, and especially those on the genital member. The chronic ones on the prepuce it also cicatrizes well. The dill that is still green and full of juice is evidently moister and less hot, so that it will be more concoctive and more sleep-inducing than the dry, but less dispersing. For this reason the ancients too seem to me to have used garlands made from it at their drinking-parties.

[6.1.46] [46. On anthyllis.] Anthyllis is twofold, but both kinds dry moderately, so that they even glue wounds together. The one of them that resembles chamaepitys is somewhat more fine-particled than the other, so that it is suitable also for epileptics. This same one is also more cleansing than the other.

[6.1.47] [47. On anthemis.] Anthemis or chamaemelon (chamomile). This herb has been discussed also in the third book at greater length; but it will be stated now too, in summary, that it dries and heats in the first order. It is also fine-particled, and for these reasons it is dispersing and rarefying and relaxing in its power.

[6.1.48] [48. On anise.] Of anise the seed is most useful, being pungent and slightly bitter, so that it comes near to the heat of the caustic drugs. It is also of the third rank in drying, just as in heating. For these reasons it is both diuretic and dispersing, and it settles the flatulent distensions in the belly.

[6.1.49] [49. On antirrhinon.] Antirrhinon, or anarrhinon, has a fruit resembling the nostrils of a calf, useless for cures. The plant itself is of a power closely similar to that of boubonion, but much inferior, so that from what was said about that one you will learn about this one as well.

[6.1.50] [50. On aparine.] Aparine: some call it philanthropon, others omphakokarpon; it cleanses and dries moderately. It also has something fine-particled. [6.1.51] [51. On the pear-tree.] Of the pear-tree the leaves and the young shoots are harsh, while the fruit also has something of a watery sweetness; from which it is clear also that its mixture is somewhat uneven in respect of its parts, having one part earthy and another watery, and under each head one part cold and another well-tempered. And for this reason, when eaten, pears are both good for the stomach and allay thirst; and when applied as a plaster they both dry and moderately cool, as I myself know, having closed a wound with them when no other drug was at hand.

[6.1.52] [52. On wild pears.] The so-called achrades (wild pears) are both more astringent than the other pears and more drying, and for this reason, evidently, they also glue together larger wounds and avert fluxes.

[6.1.53] [53. On apokynon.] Apokynon, or dog's-cabbage (kynokrambe). Some also call it kynomoron, since it destroys dogs very quickly, just as lykoktonon (wolf-killer) destroys wolves. It is a poison for human beings, a quite foul-smelling herb, and on this account it is also in every way hot to no small degree, though not proportionately dry; for this reason, then, when applied as a plaster it is also of a quite dispersing power.

[6.1.54] [54. On argemone.] Argemone. The power of this herb too is both cleansing and dispersing. [6.1.55] [55. On arisaron.] Arisaron. This is also much smaller than arum, and has a root the size of an olive. But it is much more pungent than it.

[6.1.56] [56. On aristolochia (birthwort).] Aristolochia: its root is most useful for cures, being bitter and slightly pungent. Of these the round kind is more fine-particled and in every respect more active. Of the other two, the clematitis kind is more fragrant, so that the perfumers also use it for perfumes, but it is weaker for cures. The long kind is less fine-particled than the round, yet it too is not inactive, but is of a cleansing and heating power; and compared with the round it cleanses and disperses less, but heats no less, and perhaps even more. Hence in those cases where there is need of moderate cleansing the long kind is more useful, as in the fleshing-up of ulcers and in fomentations of the womb; but where a thick humour must be thinned more strongly, the round is what is needed. For this reason the round also treats better the pains that arise through obstruction or some thickness of unconcocted pneumata, and it draws out splinters and cures putrefactions and cleanses the foul kind of ulcers and brightens the teeth and gums. It also helps asthmatics and those suffering from hiccup, as well as epileptics and the gouty, when drunk with water; and for ruptures and spasms it is suitable, if indeed any other drug is.

[6.1.57] [57. On juniper.] Juniper is hot and dry, of the third order in both respects. Its fruit is hot in like manner, but it does not dry in like manner; rather, in this respect it would be of the first order.

[6.1.58] [58. On arction.] Arction—the one resembling phlomos, which has a tender, white and sweet root, a long and soft stalk, and a fruit like cumin—is of a sufficiently fine-particled power, and for this very reason is also drying, though moderately, and cleansing; whence both its root and its fruit, boiled down with wine, somehow soothe pains of the teeth. And for burns and chilblains both the decoction of these, poured over as a fomentation, and also the young shoots are remedies.

[6.1.59] [59. On the other arction.] The other arction, which they also call prosopis, whose leaves are most similar to those of the gourd (kolokynthe), except in so far as they are larger and harder, is dispersing and drying. It also has something moderately astringent, and for this reason its leaves too are curative of old ulcers.

[6.1.60] [60. On arnoglosson.] Arnoglosson (plantain). This too is of a mixed mixture. For it has something watery and cold, and it also has something harsh, which is earthy, dry and cold, so that it cools and at the same time dries, and in both respects it is of the second degree of distance from the mean. Now all drugs that are dry together with coldness are suitable also for malignant ulcers, for fluxes and for putrefactions. And for this reason also for dysenteries; for indeed it also stops haemorrhages and, if anything is burning hot, it cools it, and it is agglutinating of sinuses and of other wounds, both fresh and old alike. And among almost all drugs of this kind arnoglosson is either first or second to none in the balanced proportion of its mixture. For it partakes of a dryness that does not bite and of a coldness that does not yet numb; and its seed and its roots are of a similar power, except that it is drier and less cold. But the seed is more fine-particled, while the roots are more coarse-particled. And the leaves themselves of the herb, when dried, become of a more fine-particled and less cold power, since their watery superfluity has evaporated and been dispersed. For this reason, then, they use the roots also for pains of the teeth, both chewed and boiled in mouth-rinses; and for obstructions in the liver and kidneys they use these too, but also the leaves, and still much more the seed. For all these partake of a certain cleansing power, which it is likely is present also in the green herb, but is overcome by the abundance of moisture.

[6.1.61] [61. On arum.] Arum. This too has come to be from an earthy, hot substance, and for this reason it is of a cleansing power, though not a strong one, as dracontium is. It is therefore, both in drying and in heating, of the first order in both respects. Its roots are the most useful part. And indeed, when eaten, they cut the thickness of humours moderately, so that they are also suitable for expectorations from the chest. Dracontium, however, is more suitable for these purposes.

[6.1.62] [62. On artemisia.] Artemisia. The herb artemisia too is twofold. Both kinds heat and dry moderately, and let them be placed, in heating, in the second degree, and in drying, either at the end of the first or the beginning of the second. They are also moderately fine-particled, so that they are moderately suitable both for stones in the kidneys and for fomentations of the womb.

[6.1.63] [63. On asaron.] Asaron. Of this herb the roots are useful; they are similar in power to those of akoron, but more intense, so that from what has been said above about that one, one must form one's knowledge about this one as well.

[6.1.64] [64. On asclepias.] Asclepias. Dioscorides wrote about this herb in his third book. We, however, have as yet no experience of it. [6.1.65] [65. On aspalathos.] Aspalathos is, to the taste, pungent and at the same time astringent, and in its power it is evidently composed of dissimilar parts, heating by those parts of itself which are pungent, and cooling by the other, harsh parts, so that it dries in both respects and cools, and for this reason it is useful against putrefactions and fluxes.

[6.1.66] [66. On asparagus.] Asparagus, the rock variety or the myacanthine, is of a cleansing power, yet it neither heats nor cools perceptibly. For this reason it is also unblocking for the kidneys and the liver, and especially the roots of the plant and the seed. And indeed it also cures toothaches by drying, which is precisely what the teeth most need. The Athenians pronounce it with a phi, aspharagos.

[6.1.67] [67. On asplenon.] Asplenon. The herb is fine-particled, yet not hot in its power. For this reason it both breaks up stones and dissolves spleens. [6.1.68] [68. On astragalos.] Astragalos is a small shrublet, having astringent roots, on account of which it is also among the drying agents in no mean degree. At any rate it cicatrizes old ulcers and arrests the belly when it is in flux, if one boils the root down in wine and drinks it. The shrub grows most abundantly in Pheneos in Arcadia.

[6.1.69] [69. On aster Atticus.] Aster Atticus. Some name it bubonion, because it is believed to cure buboes not only when applied as a plaster but also when worn as an amulet. It has indeed something dispersing too, but not least also something cooling and repelling, so that it is of mixed power, just like the rose as well—but this one, at any rate, is not astringent.

[6.1.70] [70. On the raisin (astaphis).] Astaphis: the cultivated kind partakes gently of a digestive (concocting) power together with an astringent and a dispersing one. The wild kind partakes of a strongly pungent power, so as to draw off phlegm and to cleanse vigorously, so that it is also suitable against psora. It partakes also of a certain caustic power.

[6.1.71] [71. On asphodel.] Asphodel. Of this too the root is useful, as with arum and asaron and dracontion, being of a cleansing and dispersing power; and when it has been burned, its ash becomes hotter and more drying and more fine-particled and more dispersing, and for this reason it also cures alopecia.

[6.1.72] [72. On atraktylis.] Atraktylis, or wild knēkos, is one of the thorny plants. This plant is of a drying and moderately hot power. [6.1.73] [73. On atraphaxis.] Atraphaxis is moist and cold in its mixture: moist in the second rank from the middle ones, and cold in the first, which indeed we said to be a tepid heat, such as the roses too possess, except that it has no share in astringency. But it is watery and least of all earthy, like mallow, and indeed it passes through the belly quickly, as that one does, on account of its viscosity. There is also some altogether slight dispersing quality in it. The cultivated mallows and atraphaxeis are much moister and colder than the wild ones. Hence for inflammations and phygethla, the cultivated ones are more serviceable for those that are beginning and increasing and still soft and as it were seething, while the wild ones are for those at their peak and declining and hardening. Its fruit is of a cleansing power, whence it is also useful against jaundices arising from obstructions of the liver.

[6.1.74] [74. On aphake.] Aphake is of astringent power, just as the lentil also is. But it is also eaten in the same way as lentils. And it is harder to digest than they are, but it dries more strongly, and it partakes of a moderate degree of heat.

[6.1.75] [75. On apsinthion.] Apsinthion possesses an astringent, a bitter and a pungent quality all at once, heating and at the same time cleansing, toning and drying. For this reason it both leads the bilious humours in the stomach away toward the downward evacuation and empties them out through the urine. And still more does it purge out through the urine what is bilious in the veins. For these reasons, when administered, it is of no benefit at all to phlegms contained in the stomach; and so likewise if they should happen to be in the chest and lung. For the astringent power in it is stronger than the bitter. But by virtue of partaking also of a certain pungency, it is hot in greater measure than it is cold. And if one had to define its mixture, taking it as a whole, according to the primary powers, even though it is non-uniform in its parts, we would say that it is hot of the first degree, but dry of the third. Its juice, however, is much hotter than the herb.

[6.2.1] [1. On the balanos myrepsike (ben-nut).] The balanos myrepsike (ben-nut) is brought from the barbarian land, and the perfumers use the juice of its flesh, which is hot in its power. The remaining pressed residue, the earthy and hard part, has the bitter quality predominating; but some astringency too is mixed in it, and for this reason it has an activity that is at once cleansing and cutting, and also contracting and compacting, so that it is suitable both for ionthoi and phakoi, ephelis and itching, and indeed also for psora and lepra; moreover, it also dissolves spleens and a liver that is becoming scirrhous. If someone were to drink a drachma's weight of its flesh with melikraton, he will experience the drug as an emetic; and often it also evacuates abundantly through the lower bowel. Hence, when we use the drug for the purpose of thoroughly cleansing one of the viscera, and especially the liver or the spleen, we give it with oxykraton. And for the other, external activities too it rejoices especially in vinegar; for in this way it becomes so effective as to cleanse away even psora and lepra, and much more still the conditions lesser than these—phakoi, alphoi, ionthoi, ephelis, achores, ulcerous eruptions and all those of thick humour. It also brightens scars. That, when plastering the spleen with it, it is better to mix in one of the drying meals, such as bitter-vetch and darnel meal, would belong rather to the treatise on the composition of drugs, not to the one now in hand; and it will be stated also in the Euporista. For the present it suffices, having said that the power of the aforementioned drug is cleansing and cutting together with a certain astringency, to pass on to another. Its bark, however, is very astringent, so that one could use this too for all those purposes for which there is need of strong astringency.

[6.2.2] [2. On balsam.] Balsam dries and heats in the second degree. It is also fine-particled, so as to be aromatic. Its juice is of a more fine-particled power than even the plant itself, yet not hot to such a degree as some suppose, deceived by its fineness of parts. Its fruit is of a similar power in kind, but falls far short in respect of being fine-particled.

[6.2.3] [3. On balaustion.] Balaustion is the flower of the wild pomegranate, just as kytinos is that of the cultivated ones. It is strongly astringent to the taste. And indeed it is of a drying and astringent power, and evidently also of a coarse-particled one, if we remember at all what was said in the fourth of these commentaries, when we showed that everything astringent is earthy and cold. It has no appearance of any other quality, and for this reason one would hold that it dries and cools in no mean degree, if indeed it was not wrongly demonstrated by us in the fourth of these commentaries that the astringent quality belongs to earthy cold bodies. And moreover the phenomena also bear witness. For if you sprinkle it upon chafings and upon other ulcers, you would very quickly see them proceeding to a scar. For these reasons, too, in the case of dysenteric patients who bring up blood, and further of fluxes in the belly and the womb, there is no one among the physicians who have written therapeutic treatises who does not use this drug.

[6.2.4] [4. On bramble.] Of the bramble, the leaves, the shoots, the flower, the fruit and the root all partake of an astringent quality, and not obscurely. But they differ from one another in this: the leaves, and especially the soft and young ones, since they partake of a very large amount of water, are only slightly astringent. By the same reasoning the shoots too, so that when chewed they cure aphthae and the other ulcers in the mouth, and indeed are also able to glue together other wounds. For their mixture is composed of a cold earthy substance and a lukewarm watery one. The fruit, if it is ripe, partakes in no small measure also of the moderately hot juice, which is sweet, as we have shown, so that both for this reason and because of its moderate astringency it is edible and not unpleasant. The unripe fruit, however, is dominated by a cold earthy substance, and for this reason it is both acerbic and strongly drying. And indeed each of the two is also dried and stored away, being more drying than the fresh. The flower too is of the same power as the unripe fruit, (both being) drugs suitable for dysenteries and fluxes of the belly and atonies and spittings of blood. The root, in addition to being astringent, has further taken a share of no small amount of fine-particled substance, on account of which it also breaks up the stones in the kidneys.

[6.2.5] [5. On batrachion.] Batrachion has four differences according to species. All of them are of a strongly pungent power, so as to ulcerate with pain. Accordingly, for one who uses it in due measure, it strips off psora and lepra, detaches leprous nails, disperses tattoo-marks, and removes acrochordons and myrmecia. And indeed it also helps alopecia, when applied for a short time; for if they are left on long, the skin is not only flayed but even forms an eschar. All these, then, are the works of the stalk and the leaves, applied green as a plaster. The root, when dried, is a sternutatory drug, like all the others that dry strongly. It also helps pains of the teeth, along with breaking them, evidently by drying strongly. And, to speak summarily, both the root and the whole herb are vehemently hot and dry.

[6.2.6] [6. On bdellium.] Bdellium: the kind called Scythian, which is also blacker and more resinous, is of a sufficiently softening and active power. The other, the Arabian, which is also more translucent, dries more than the softening agents do. So as much of it as is fresh is both moist and, when pounded, is softened easily, and is suitable for all the same purposes as the Scythian. But as much of it as is older and sufficiently bitter in taste and pungent and dry has already fallen out of the due proportion of those agents that soften indurated parts. Some use them, and especially the Arabian, for bronchoceles and hydroceles, moistening it with fasting spittle so that it has a plaster-like consistency. The Arabian also seems, when drunk, to break up the stones in the kidneys, to promote urine, and to cure the passages of unconcocted winds and pains of the sides and ruptures.

[6.2.7] [7. On bechion.] Bechion has been so named from its being believed to help coughs and orthopnoeas, if one takes either the dried leaves, or the root, burns it as a fumigation upon charcoal and inhales the smoke that is carried upward. It is moderately pungent, so that it is also believed to break painlessly all the abscesses in the region of the thorax. The green leaves, indeed, also benefit the inflamed parts, albeit with difficulty of concoction, when applied externally as a plaster, because of the admixture of watery moisture, in which all green and tender things share, some more and some less. For the already dried leaves of bechion are of a power more pungent than is suited to inflamed parts.

[6.2.8] [8. On blite.] Blite is an edible vegetable, moist and cold in its mixture, at about the second degree of departure from the well-mixed. [6.2.9] [9. On the cultivated bulb.] Bulb, when eaten, is colder and thicker and generative of a viscous humour; for it is also hard to digest, flatulent and aphrodisiac. But when applied as a plaster, because it partakes of bitterness and astringency at the same time, it becomes astringent and agglutinating, and obviously drying. For it was shown that bitterness is found in the cleansing substances, astringency in the agglutinating ones, and dryness follows upon both.

[6.2.10] [10. On emetic bulb.] Emetic bulb is much hotter than the mixture of the bulb previously mentioned. [6.2.11] [11. On boubonion.] Boubonion, or Attic aster, has been so named from the belief that it heals buboes when applied as a plaster and when worn as an amulet. It is of moderately dispersing power, because it is both moderately hot and dries neither violently nor in a contracting manner, and especially when it is still soft and young.

[6.2.12] [12. On bugloss.] Bugloss is moist and hot in its mixture, whence also, when thrown into wines, it has been believed to be a cause of good cheer. It is suitable also for those who cough on account of roughness of the pharynx, when boiled down in honey-water (melikraton).

[6.2.13] [13. On bounion.] Bounion, which some call arktikon, is among the heating things to such a degree that it is both diuretic and promotive of the menses. And the false bounion (pseudobounion) too is hot in a manner similar to it.

[6.2.14] [14. On buphthalmon.] Buphthalmon has been so named from its flowers, which seem to resemble in shape the eye of an ox; and in colour, at any rate, they are most similar to those of anthemis. They are, however, considerably larger than these and more pungent, and for this reason also more dispersing, to the point of curing even hardnesses when mixed with cerate.

[6.2.15] [15. On brathy (savin).] Brathy is among the things that dry strongly, in respect at least of the three qualities which it also displays to the taste, in a manner similar to cypress, except that it is more pungent than it and, as one might say, more aromatic. It therefore partakes both of this very quality which I have just mentioned, the pungent, which is established upon a hot mixture, and further of a bitterness and an astringency fainter than in cypress. For in so far as it surpasses cypress in pungency, by so much also, for this reason, is it more dispersing. It is therefore not able to glue wounds together, because of the strength of its dryness and heat; for it has partaken of both of these to such a degree as to be already tensing and inflaming. But for putrefactions it is suitable in the same way as cypress, and especially for those that are more malignant and more chronic; for these bear without distress the strength of the drug. And accordingly it also cleanses, with honey, the parts that have turned black and those that are very foul, and detaches carbuncles. On account of its fineness of particles it is also a drawer-down of the menses, if anything is, and it moves blood through the urine, and it destroys living embryos and expels dead ones. Let this drug too, then, be placed in the third of the degrees of removal (ἀποστάσεων) in respect both of heating and of drying, being among the most fine-particled. For these reasons it is also mixed into unguents, and especially into the gleucine, and it is put into a very great number of antidotes. Some even put in double its amount in place of cinnamon, for it is of thinning and dispersing power if it is drunk.

[6.2.16] [16. On britannica.] Of the herb britannica the leaves too are astringent and agglutinating of wounds, being similar to those of wild dock (lapathon), except in so far as they appear darker and hairier. The juice from them is likewise astringent, so that some even boil it down and store it away as the most efficacious of the stomatic drugs; for it seems to heal even parts that are already putrefying.

[6.2.17] [17. On oats.] The oat is one of the pulses, but as a drug it has a power similar to barley. For applied as a plaster it dries and disperses moderately and without biting. It is also slightly colder in its mixture and has something of astringency as well, so that it also benefits the diarrhoeas of the belly.

[6.2.18] [18. On bryon (seaweed).] Sea bryon is composed of an earthy and at the same time a watery substance, both of them cold. For it is astringent when tasted, and when applied as a plaster to all things that are hot it manifestly cools and benefits them.

[6.2.19] [19. On bryon or also splanchnon.] Bryon (tree-moss), which some call splanchnon. It is found on oaks, pines and white poplars. It has also an astringent power, though not a strong one; for it is not sufficiently cold, but somewhere near the middle, because it has also partaken of a dispersing and a softening power, and especially that which is found on cedar wood.

[6.3.1] [1. On gallion.] Gallion is so named from its curdling milk. It is similar to aparine (cleavers), having a drying and somewhat acrid power. Its flower is thought to be suitable for haemorrhages and to heal burns. It is both fragrant and quince-yellow in colour.

[6.3.2] [2. On gentian.] Gentian. The root of this herb is sufficiently active where there is need to thin and to purify thoroughly, and to cleanse away and to clear obstructions; and it is no wonder that it is capable of these things, being intensely bitter.

[6.3.3] [3. On grape-seeds.] Grape-seeds are dry in the second order, and cold in the first. Their substance is coarse-particled and earthy, as is shown by the taste, for they appear acerbic; and experience teaches it too, for they are quite suitable for all the fluxional affections of the belly.

[6.3.4] [4. On gingidion.] Gingidion, just as in taste it partakes of both bitterness and astringency, so too in its mixture it partakes of both heat and cooling. It is drying in respect of both qualities, and moreover it is also good for the stomach, because it has a share of no small astringency. Its heat, then, it possesses not altogether distinctly; but it dries in the second degree.

[6.3.5] [5. On glaucium.] Glaucium is astringent with a certain unpleasantness, but it also cools so manifestly that it often cures erysipelas on its own, at least such cases as are not severe. And its mixture is compounded of a watery and an earthy substance, both of them cold, not however to the extreme degree, but in the way that spring water is.
[6.3.6] [6. On glaux.] Glaux, the herb: this too seems to be generative of milk. And if this is indeed so, it would be in some way hot and moist in its mixture.

[6.3.7] [7. On pennyroyal.] Pennyroyal. This herb too, inasmuch as it is pungent and slightly bitter, both heats and thins strongly. A sufficient proof of its heating is that, applied as a plaster, it reddens the skin, and if it is left on, it goes further and ulcerates; of its thinning, that it makes the thick and viscous humours from the chest and lung easy to expectorate and provokes the menses.

[6.3.8] [8. On gloios.] Gloios is moderate and also softening. [6.3.9] [9. On glycyrrhiza.] Glycyrrhiza (liquorice). Of this shrub the juice of the roots is most useful, being sweet in the same way as its roots, together with a certain slight astringency. For this reason it is also naturally fitted to smooth roughnesses, not only in the windpipe but also in a scabby bladder, by the moderateness of its mixture; its nature, then, would be akin to our mixture, for the sweet was shown to be of this kind. But since a certain astringency is also present in it, its mixture as a whole, so far as concerns heat and astringency, would lie most of all in the region of lukewarm heat, very close to the well-proportioned. And since what is moderately sweet is also moist in its mixture, the drug is fittingly thirst-allaying, being at once moderately moist and colder than the nature of man. Dioscorides says that the root, when dry and finely ground, becomes a suitable drug to be sprinkled on for pterygia.

[6.3.10] [10. On glycyside.] Glycyside, which they also call pentorobon and paeonia, has a root that is gently astringent with a certain sweetness, and, when chewed for longer, also with a slightly bitter pungency. Accordingly it both moves the menses, when drunk in the quantity of an almond with melikraton — one must, of course, pound it and sift it and so sprinkle it in; and it also clears out an obstructed liver and the kidneys. But these things it is naturally fitted to accomplish insofar as it is pungent and slightly bitter, whereas insofar as it also has something astringent, it stops the fluxes in the belly. In that case one must boil it down in one of the harsh wines and drink it. In general it is strongly drying in its power, so that I would not despair that it has with good reason been believed to cure the epilepsies of children even when hung about the neck. And indeed I once knew a child who for eight months was not seized at all from the time when he wore the root, but when the amulet somehow slipped off from his neck, he was at once seized, and when another was hung about him again, he was once more without complaint. It seemed to me better to remove it yet again for the sake of a test, and when we had done so, since he was convulsed again, we suspended a large and fresh piece of the root from his very neck, and from that point on, for the rest of the time, the boy became completely healthy and was no longer seized. It was reasonable, then, either that certain particles flowing off from the root, and then drawn in through inspiration, thus treat the affected places, or else that the air itself is turned and altered by the root. For in this way, too, the Cyrenaic juice benefits an inflamed uvula, and roasted melanthion manifestly dries catarrhs and coryzas, if someone, having tied it hot into a loose-woven linen cloth, continuously draws the heat from it through inspiration by the nostrils. And indeed, if you put several threads, and especially ones from marine purple, around a viper's neck and strangle the viper with them, and then hang each of the threads about the neck, it marvellously benefits the tonsils and whatever grows out around the neck. About such matters, then, I may perhaps go through separately at some time. But as for the mixture of peony, one must know that it is fine-particled and drying, yet not manifestly hot, but either well-balanced or hotter by some small degree.

[6.3.11] [11. On gnaphalion.] Gnaphalion. It is so named from the fact that its leaves, being soft, are used in place of gnaphala (wool-flock stuffing). They are white and moderately astringent, and for this reason some give it to dysenterics with one of the harsh wines.
[6.3.12] [12. On turnip.] The seed of turnip provokes to sexual intercourse, being generative of flatulent pneuma. So too the root is both hard to digest and flatulent, and generative of seed.

[6.4.1] [1. On damasonion.] Damasonion, or also alisma. Concerning this herb Dioscorides says in the third book that the root, if drunk, cures dysenteries and checks the bowels and soothes oedemas. We ourselves have not put these to the test; but that the water in which it happens to have been boiled, when drunk, breaks up the stones forming in the kidneys, we have tested by experience. It is clear, then, that it possesses a certain cleansing power.

[6.4.2] [2. On daucus.] Daucus, which some indeed call staphylinos. The wild kind is less edible than the cultivated, but more vigorous in all respects; the cultivated kind is edible, but weaker. It is of a pungent and heating power, and for this reason also of a thinning one. The root, then, in addition to what has been said, also possesses something flatulent and aphrodisiac. As for the seed, that of the cultivated kind also has in itself something that stimulates towards sexual intercourse, whereas that of the wild kind is completely non-flatulent, and for this reason it is both diuretic and provocative of the menses.

[6.4.3] [3. On the seed of daucus.] The seed of the herb daucus is sufficiently heating as to be among the most active of diuretic drugs, and to be a mover of the menses. It is also sufficiently dispersing when applied externally. And the herb itself is of a similar power, but weaker than in the case of the seed, on account of the admixture of watery moisture. Yet this too is hot in its mixture.

[6.4.4] [4. On the laurel, the tree.] Of the laurel tree both the leaves and the fruit dry and heat strongly, and its fruit more so than the leaves. The bark of the root is less pungent and hot, but more bitter, and it also has something of astringency. For these reasons, then, it also breaks stones and benefits the liver. It is drunk with fragrant wine, in a weight of three obols.

[6.4.5] [5. On laurel, the herb.] Of laurel the herb, which they also call Alexandrian, the mixture is manifestly hot, and to those who taste it it is pungent and slightly bitter, and in those who drink it it promotes the menses and urine. Of the ground-laurel (chamaidaphne) the tender shoots are also eaten. This too is similar in its power to the Alexandrian laurel, just as is also what is called daphnoeides (laurel-like).
[6.4.6] [6. On dittany.] Dittany is of a more fine-particled substance than pennyroyal; in other respects it is similar to it. The so-called pseudo-dittany is weaker in every respect than dittany.

[6.4.7] 7. On dipsakos. Of dipsakos, the thistle, the root is drying of the second order, and it also has something cleansing. [6.4.8] 8. On dorykniion. Dorykniion is similar in mixture to poppy and mandrake and to the cooling agents of that kind, being dominated by a watery coldness that is very active; for in a small amount it stupefies, but taken in a greater amount it kills.

[6.4.9] [9. On dracontion.] Dracontion has something closely resembling aron both in its leaves and in its root. But it is more pungent than it and more bitter, and for this reason also both more heating and more fine-particled. It also has a certain slight astringency, and when this combines with the two qualities already mentioned, the pungent and the bitter, the drug becomes active in the highest degree. For indeed the root thoroughly cleanses all the viscera, thinning especially the thick and viscous humours, and it is the best drug for malignant ulcers; and it cleanses away and scours off, in general, both the other things that need cleansing and, with vinegar, alphoi. The leaves, having a similar power, are suitable for ulcers and for fresh wounds, and the less dry they are, the more they agglutinate; for the drier ones are more pungent in their power than is fitting for wounds. It is also believed to keep moist cheese free from putrefaction when placed around it on the outside, on account of the dryness of its mixture. The fruit is stronger not only than the leaves but also than the root, so that it is believed to melt away even cancers and polyps. And its juice cleanses away the things in the eyes.

[6.4.10] [10. On dryopteris.] Dryopteris is, to one tasting it, of a mixed quality: sweet, pungent, somewhat bitter, and in its root also acerbic. It has a putrefying power, whence it also strips away hairs.

[6.4.11] [11. On the oak.] All the parts of the oak share in an astringent quality, but to a greater degree the membranous part in the bark of the trunk, and that beneath the shell of the acorn, which lies upon the flesh of the fruit. Hence it has been believed to be useful for female flux, spittings of blood, dysenteries and chronic fluxes of the belly; and they use it chiefly by boiling it down. Still more vigorously astringent are the phegos and the prinos, whether one wishes to call them species of oak or to hold that they differ in their whole genus. And indeed the leaves of these plants, when tender and applied as a plaster, are by nature able to dry in no mean fashion, while those of the other oak less so, in proportion as it has partaken less of astringency. I myself, at any rate, know that I once glued together a wound made by a sickle, when no other drug at all was at hand, with the leaves of the oak. I ground them on a smooth stone and plastered the wound together with the whole surrounding region. The fruit of the oak too is of the same power as the leaves. And some of the physicians have used it for inflammations that are still beginning and increasing; for those that are already vigorous have no need of astringents. Such matters, however, belong to the therapeutic treatise rather than to the present one. For the present purposes it suffices to know that the oak has partaken of astringent power to the extent stated, and on this account of a drying and astringent power, but that in respect of heat it is a little below the middle things, among those which one might, so to speak, call tepid.

[6.5.1] [1. On ebiskos.] Ebiskos, or althaia. It is the wild mallow, dispersing, relaxing, allaying inflammation, soothing, and ripening tumours (phymata) that are hard to bring to maturation. Its root and its seed act in other respects in the same way as the green herb, but they display a power that is more fine-particled than it, more drying, and in addition more cleansing, so that they even cleanse away alphoi (white leprous patches), and the seed breaks up the stones in the kidneys. The decoction of the root is beneficial also against dysentery and diarrhoea and against the bringing-up of blood, since it has a certain astringent power.

[6.5.2] [2. On ebony.] Ebony is one of the woods that dissolve into a juice if it is rubbed with water, just as some of the stones do. Its power is heating, cleansing and fine-particled, whence it is also believed to cleanse the things that darken the pupils. It is also mixed with the other ophthalmic powers, those which are suitable for old ulcers, fluxes and phlyctaenae.

[6.5.3] [3. On the olive.] Of the olive, the young shoots partake of cooling to just the same degree as of astringency. As for the fruit, the perfectly ripe is moderately hot, whereas the unripe is more astringent and colder.

[6.5.4] [4. On olive oil.] Oil: that from the olive, which we also call oil in the most proper sense, has had the nature of its mixture determined in the preceding books; for it was shown to be moistening and moderately hot. Such is the sweetest oil, produced especially from tree-ripened fruit. But the oil called raw-pressed and omphacine (from unripe olives), to the degree that it partakes of astringency, to that same degree partakes also of coldness. As for old oil, that which comes from sweet oil grown old is hotter and more dispersing, whereas that from raw-pressed oil, so long as it preserves something of its astringency, is of mixed power, but when it has completely cast this off, it becomes like the other. And indeed those who in the preparation throw in olive-shoots also produce an oil resembling the omphacine. One ought not to inquire how it has been prepared, but rather taste it oneself: if it shows any astringency, one should suppose that to the degree it partakes of this, to that same degree it partakes also of coldness, as does the oil brought from Iberia, which they call Spanish; but if on tasting it shows no astringency at all, but is perfectly sweet, one should consider this to be moderately hot. And if it also appears fine-particled—such is the oil that is pure and translucent to the eye, and when a small quantity, once taken up, spreads over the greatest extent of the body and remains continuous with itself, and is drunk up by the skin—one should consider this the finest and the oil that most fully possesses the excellence of oil, of the kind that the Sabine oil is. That washed oil is the least biting has been stated earlier too; and how one may best wash it I shall say in the following treatise, that on the composition of drugs, where there will also be a discussion of the Sicyonian oil and of any other such oil. For now I am going through the simple drugs, and I shall now add the account of the other oils. For there is named also a castor oil (kikinon), produced especially in Egypt, from the fruit of the kiki, and radish-seed oil, and sesame oil, almond oil and walnut oil, and further mustard oil, mastic-tree (schinos) oil, laurel oil, melanthion (black cumin) oil, terebinth oil, mastic oil, myrtle oil, ben-nut (balanos) oil, henbane oil, and not a few others besides these, all pressed out from fruits or seeds. These differ from one another by the same differences as the fruits themselves. For castor oil is more fine-particled and more dispersing, most like old oil from the olive; hence, wherever castor oil is prescribed in some composition of a drug, if it is not available one should use the common oil, and especially if it be Sabine. Radish-seed oil is in other respects like this one, but hotter, and mustard oil hotter still than this; like the latter is the oil from melanthion. Contrary to these are myrtle oil and sesame oil, the former by being astringent, the latter because they are coarse-particled. Of mixed power are mastic-tree oil, terebinth oil and mastic oil, for they not only soften but are also astringent. Almond oil has bitterness predominating, but partakes also of some astringency; not so walnut oil, however, which is of a single, simple power, the dispersing. Hotter and more dispersing than it is laurel oil, and cedar oil more so still than this; near to the latter is the oil from liquid pitch, pine-resin oil (dadinon), less hot than laurel oil but more drying. Henbane oil is of mixed power, at once softening and cooling. Castor oil loosens the belly, and the oil from the Cnidian berry still more than this, and so much the more as its berry is more purgative than the kiki itself. The oil from the wild olive, too, is not of a simple mixture, but at once cleansing and astringent. This is the driest, as oils go, and after it the Istrian, and next to these the Spanish. The oiliest are the Libyan and the Cilician, while the Sabine is at once oily and fine-particled; in the middle of all those mentioned lies the oil of the Cycladic islands, Greece and Asia. Oily oil is judged by its viscosity, fine-particled oil by its translucency and purity, by the greatest extent of the body being anointed by the smallest quantity, and by its being readily drunk up by the skin. From what has been said you can now also know about the other oils, as many as are called by the same names as the perfumes—I mean rose oil, quince oil, lily oil, and all such as are made by steeping fruits or flowers or shoots or leaves in oil. For each of these, when prepared together with aromatics, is made into a perfume. More will be said about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs; having said what is useful for the present purpose, I shall take my leave. The oil will be altered according to the nature of each of the things thrown into it. From what you learn about each of the things thrown in, throughout this whole work in general, from these you would be able to know also about the oil of each of them individually.

[6.5.5] [5. On elatine.] Elatine is moderately cooling and astringent. [6.5.6] [6. On elaphoboskos.] Elaphoboskos is of a hot and fine-particled power, and for this reason also of a drying one, roughly at the second degree at most of the gradations.

[6.5.7] [7. On elenion.] Of the herb elenion the root is the most useful part; it does not heat immediately at the first contact, and for this reason one must say that it is not precisely hot and dry, like black and white pepper, but hot together with a superfluous moisture; and for this reason it is also suitably mixed into the linctuses used for the bringing up of viscous and thick humours in the chest and lung, and with it people redden the parts that are troubled by cold and chronic affections, such as certain cases of sciatica and hemicrania and continual dislocations of certain joints on account of moisture.

[6.5.8] [8. On elelisphakos.] Elelisphakos is manifestly of a heating mixture, gently and slightly astringent. [6.5.9] [9. On hellebore.] Hellebore, each kind, both the white and the black, is of a cleansing and at the same time heating power. For this reason they are also suitable for alphos, lichen, psora and lepra; and indeed the black, inserted into a callused fistula, in some two or three days detaches its callus from it, and, used as a mouth-rinse with vinegar, it benefits the teeth. And let them be placed in the third rank of things that heat and dry. To the taste the black is the hotter, while the white is slightly bitter.

[6.5.10] [10. On helxine.] Helxine, which some call perdikion, others parthenion, others sideritis, and there are those who call it Herakleia. Its power is cleansing and gently astringent, together with a somewhat cold moisture. Hence it heals all inflammations both at their beginning and in their increase up to the peak, and especially the hot ones. And indeed it is also applied as a plaster to incipient phygethla. Its juice, too, with rose-oil, is moderately suited to inflammatory pains of the ears. Some also gargle with it for affections of the tonsils, and certain physicians have given it to those with chronic coughs. Of its cleansing power it gives clear evidence also in the case of glass vessels.

[6.5.11] [11. On black helxine.] Helxine, the one also called kissampelos, is of a dispersing power. [6.5.12] [12. On elymos.] Elymos, which is also called meline. It belongs to the pulses, being similar to millet both in form and in power, little nourishing and drying. It also checks to some extent the fluxes in the belly, just as millet does too. And if it is applied externally as a plaster, it both dries and cools.

[6.5.13] [13. On empetron.] Empetron seems to be useful for purgations only, drawing off phlegm and bile. It is salty to the taste, so that one might use it also for other purposes, for those for which we showed that the salty substance too has power; it is also called prasoeides (leek-like).

[6.5.14] [14. On epithymon.] Epithymon is stronger than the power of thyme, which is in all respects drying and heating in the third degree. [6.5.15] [15. On epimedion.] The power of epimedion is moderately cooling, with a watery moisture. At any rate it has no notable quality, but it is able, when applied as a plaster, to keep the breasts firm and upright; and they say that it is also a contraceptive when drunk.

[6.5.16] [16. On epimelis.] Epimelis: this plant is acerbic and, as one might say, a wild apple-tree. It is called by the country people of Italy ounedon (unedo). It grows most abundantly in Calabria. Its fruit is acerbic, but bad for the stomach and productive of headache; for some strange quality is mixed in with it.

[6.5.17] [17. On the chickpea.] Chickpea: a flatulent pulse, nourishing, good for the bowels, diuretic, generative of milk and seed, and it also promotes the menses. Those called "rams" (krioi) are more diuretic than the others. Their decoction breaks up the stones in the kidneys. The other kind of chickpeas are called orobiai, and it is of the same power, attractive, dispersing, cutting, cleansing. For they are hot and moderately dry, but they also partake somewhat of bitterness, on account of which they purge the spleen and liver and kidneys, and clean off scabies (psora) and lichen, and disperse parotid swellings and testicles that are becoming indurated, and with honey they heal the malignant kinds of ulcers.

[6.5.18] [18. On wild chickpea.] The wild chickpea is stronger in every respect than the cultivated one, that is, both hotter and more drying, to the very degree that it is also both more pungent and more bitter.

[6.5.19] [19. On heath.] Heath is of dispersing power. One should use above all its flower and its leaves. [6.5.20] [20. On creeping thyme.] Creeping thyme is of heating power to such a degree as to move the menses and the urine. It is also quite pungent to the taste.

[6.5.21] [21. On erysimon.] The seed of erysimon, just as in taste it appears closely similar to kardamon (cress), so too in its power is fiery and heating. But whenever one must use it in a linctus, it is better to roast it after first soaking it in water, or to tie it up in a linen cloth, then wrap it round with dough and bake it. It is useful, together with lincti, for the expectoration of viscous and thick humours in the region of the thorax and lung. But it also benefits parotid swellings that are becoming scirrhous and old hardnesses in the breasts and testicles. Dioscorides says that applied as a plaster with water or with honey it helps hidden cancers.

[6.5.22] [22. On erythrodanon.] Erythrodanon. It is the red root of the dyers, acerbic and bitter to the taste; hence all the things which were said in the book before this one to be done by such powers when they come together into one with each other, all of these you will clearly observe in this root. For it thoroughly cleanses both spleen and liver, and evacuates urine that is thick and copious and sometimes even bloody; and moreover it draws forth the menses and moderately cleanses whatever things require cleansing. At any rate it helps white alphoi when smeared on with vinegar. Some also give it to those suffering from sciatica and to the paralysed to drink with melikraton.

[6.5.23] [23. On eupatorion.] Eupatorion, the herb, is of a fine-particled, cutting and cleansing power, without any manifest heat, which is why it also clears out the obstructions in the liver. It also partakes of a slight astringency, on account of which it also imparts tone to the viscus.

[6.5.24] [24. On euphorbion.] Euphorbion is of a caustic and fine-particled power, like the other juices. [6.5.25] [25. On ephemeron.] Ephemeron—not the poisonous one, which they also name Colchicon, but the other one, which indeed is also called wild iris. It has leaves and a stalk like the lily, but a long root, not a round one, as the Colchicon has. It is for the most part a finger in thickness, and is astringent and fragrant. From these it is clear that it is of a mixed power and mixture, both repelling and dispersing. The particular effects also bear witness to this. For indeed the root, at least, is not ineffective for toothaches as a mouth-rinse, and the leaves are suitable for the risings and peaks of phymata. One must boil them in wine and apply them as a plaster before suppuration occurs.
[6.5.26] [26. On echinos.] The fruit of the herb echinos is acerbic and for this reason repelling and drying. They use it both for the fluxes of the eyes and for the ears.

[6.6.1] [1. On zeia.] Zeia is somehow intermediate in its whole power between wheat and barley, so let it be known from those. [6.6.2] [2. On ginger.] Of ginger the root is what is useful, which indeed they bring to us from the barbarian land. It heats, then, strongly, but not at the first contact, as pepper does. For this very reason one must also suppose it to be less fine-particled than pepper. For otherwise it would be dissolved into fine parts and would quickly become hot in actuality, as that one does. At any rate it appears to partake of some substance that is still unworked and coarser-particled, and this not dry and earthy but rather moist and watery. For this reason, indeed, it is also easily bored through, because it has a share of superfluous moisture. At any rate none of the things that are either precisely dry, or moist but possessing a moisture that is worked up and proper to them, suffers this. Long pepper too has undergone the same thing as this, and for this reason the heat from ginger and long pepper persists for longer than that from white and black pepper. For just as the flame from dry reeds is kindled all at once and is scattered in every direction most quickly, in the same way too is the flame from drugs that are dry in their power. But that from the moister ones, by analogy with green wood, is both kindled more slowly and persists for longer; whence also the use of each of the two kinds of drugs is different. For when we wish to heat the whole body quickly, one must give those which heat quickly on coming near the heat of the animal and are quickly carried in every direction. But when we wish to heat some chilled part, one must act the opposite way: those which, heating slowly, persist for the longest, these are applied. Now ginger and long pepper, even if they differ in this respect from black pepper, yet differ only slightly. But kardamon and mustard and thapsia and the dung of wild pigeons both become fully ignited over a longer time and persist for the longest.

[6.6.3] [3. On zythos (beer).] Zythos is more pungent than barley by no small degree, and productive of bad humour, as having been generated from putrefaction. It is also flatulent, and has on the one hand something pungent and heating, but for the most part it is cold, watery and sour.

[6.6.4] [4. On leaven.] Leaven is fine-particled and moderately hot. For this reason, then, it both draws up what lies in the depth and disperses it, painlessly and without biting. This substance too is compounded of opposite powers, as are many others. For it partakes of a cold acidity and of a putrefactive heat, and in addition of the heat deriving from the salt and of that deriving naturally from the flour.

[6.7.1] [1. On hedyosmon (mint).] Hedyosmon (mint), which some call minthe. For there is another, non-fragrant minthe, which they also call kalaminthe (calamint). Both are pungent to those who taste them and hot in their power, from roughly the third rank of heating things. Yet the fragrant minthe is weaker than kalaminthe and less heating. For, to speak generally, the one is, as it were, wild, the other cultivated, so that, owing to the moisture that accrues to it from being grown in gardens, it also moderately stimulates towards sexual intercourse. This is common to all things that partake of a half-digested and flatulent moisture. On account of such a mixture of the herb, some also apply it with barley meal upon abscesses, which kalaminthe cannot do, because it heats and dries more violently than such things require. It also has in itself something bitter and acerbic, and by the bitter it destroys worms, while by the acerbic, when drunk with oxykraton (vinegar-and-water), it checks recent bringings-up of blood. It is fine-particled in substance, if any other herb is.

[6.7.2] [2. On hedysaron.] Hedysaron, or pelekinos. The seed of this shrub is reddish-yellow in colour and two-edged like axes; it appears bitter and somewhat astringent, whence it is good for the stomach when drunk, and it clears out the obstructions in the viscera. The twigs of the whole shrub act in the same way.

[6.7.3] [3. On hemerocalles.] The root of hemerocalles, being similar to that of the lily both in appearance and in power, benefits burns in a similar way to it. For it is of a gently dispersing power, together with having also something repelling.

[6.7.4] [4. On hemionitis.] Hemionitis partakes of astringency together with bitterness, and for this reason it also benefits those suffering in the spleen when drunk with vinegar. [6.7.5] [5. On erigeron (groundsel).] Erigeron has a mixed power, at once cooling and moderately dispersing.

[6.7.6] [6. On eryngo.] Eryngo exceeds the moderate in heat either by little or not at all, but it partakes of no small fine-particled dryness. [6.8.1] [1. On thalietrum (meadow-rue).] Thalietrum has leaves resembling those of coriander, and a stalk of the thickness of rue's. Its power is drying without biting; at any rate it cicatrises the chronic among ulcers.

[6.8.2] [2. On thapsia.] Thapsia is of a pungent and strongly heating power together with moisture. For this reason, then, it draws forcibly from the depth and itself disperses what has been drawn. But it accomplishes these things over a longer time, because it is filled with abundant superfluous moisture, on account of which it also quickly spoils.

[6.8.3] [3. On the lupin.] The lupin is eaten after it has been boiled and has, over many days, deposited its bitterness in water, and at that point it becomes a food of thick humour. As a drug, however, the lupin of this kind belongs among the clogging agents, whereas the one which retains its innate bitterness is cleansing and dispersing. It also destroys worms, both when applied as a plaster and when licked up with honey or drunk with oxykraton (diluted vinegar); and indeed its decoction too is of a nature to expel worms. And moreover, when poured over externally it benefits alphoi, achores, eruptions, psorai, gangrenes and malignant ulcers, some by cleansing, others by dispersing and drying without biting. It also cleanses out the liver and the spleen, when taken with rue and pepper for the sake of pleasantness. It also draws down the menses and embryos, when applied as a pessary with myrrh and honey. The flour of lupins is likewise dispersing without biting. For it treats not only livid parts but also scrofulous swellings (choirades) and hard tumours (phymata); in that case, however, one must boil it in vinegar, or in oxymel, or in oxykraton, finding out, evidently, what is required according to the mixtures of the patients and the difference of the affection. But it is not the task of the treatise now before us to make such distinctions. It also disperses livid parts; and all the other things which the decoction was said above to do, the flour too is of a nature to accomplish. Some also apply it as a cataplasm to those suffering from sciatica.

[6.8.4] [4. On wild lupine.] The wild lupine is more bitter and stronger for all purposes than the cultivated one, being of the same power as it in kind. [6.8.5] [5. On thlaspi.] Thlaspi, the seed. This too is pungent in its power, so that when drunk it also bursts the internal abscesses, and it moves the menses and kills embryos, and when injected through the seat it helps cases of sciatica by evacuating bloody matter. For in other respects too it is purgative, upward and downward, of bilious humours, when drunk in the quantity of an oxybaphon.

[6.8.6] [6. On lettuce.] Lettuce is a moist and cold vegetable, though not in the extreme degree—for then it would not have been edible—but more or less, as one might say, to the degree of the power, or rather the coldness, of spring waters. For this reason it is suitable for hot inflammations and for the small and slight cases of erysipelas, though it is not capable of sufficing against the greater ones. It is also a food that allays thirst. Its seed, taken in drink, checks gonorrhoeas (seminal fluxes), whence it is also given to those who have nocturnal emissions. So too the seed of the wild lettuce, whose juice they also collect: it cleanses away argema and mistiness (achlys) of the eye, and it is also applied, smeared on with woman's milk, against epikaumata (burn-like ulcers of the eye).

[6.8.7] [7. On thyme.] Thyme cuts and heats manifestly; for this reason it also moves urine and menses, draws down embryos, and thoroughly cleanses the viscera when drunk, and it assists the bringing up of matter from the chest and lung. And so it must be placed in the third rank both in drying and in heating.

[6.9.1] [1. On Idaean root.] Idaean root, when tasted, is extremely acerbic, and to one who tests it by its works it displays the same power, curing haemorrhages and fluxes of the belly and dysentery and the female flux and all other such things, both when drunk and when applied externally.

[6.9.2] [2. On mistletoe.] Mistletoe is composed for the most part of airy and watery substance that is hot, and to the least degree of earthy substance. At any rate the pungent in it is greater than the bitter, and accordingly its actions too are in keeping with its substance. For it draws moistures forcefully out of the depth, not only the thin ones but also the thicker ones, and these it melts down and disperses. It is one of those drugs that do not heat immediately after the first application, but require time, like thapsia. This too has been said earlier, that it is a property of drugs that are hot in power, whenever they have abundant superfluous moisture.

[6.9.3] [3. On the violet.] The leaves of the violet possess a predominant watery and somewhat cold substance, and for this reason, applied as a plaster both by themselves and with barley meal, they soothe hot inflammations. They are also applied over the mouth of the stomach when it is burning, and over the eyes.

[6.9.4] [4. On hippouris (horsetail).] Horsetail has an astringent quality together with bitterness, and for this reason a drying one that is strong and at the same time non-biting. Therefore, applied as a plaster, it glues together even the largest wounds, even if sinews happen to have been cut through, and also the so-called enteroceles; but also against the bringing up of blood, and against the female flux, and especially the red one, and further against dysentery and the other fluxes in the belly, the herb is a noble drug when drunk in water or in wine. Some write about it that its juice once healed wounds of the bladder and of the small intestines. It also helps haemorrhages from the nostrils and flux-like affections in the belly, when drunk with one of the harsh wines, or in water if they happen to be feverish.

[6.9.5] [5. On hippomarathron.] Hippomarathron (horse-fennel): this will be spoken of together with fennel. [6.9.6] [6. On woad.] Woad (isatis): the cultivated kind, which the dyers use, is of a strongly drying power, yet not at all biting; for it is at once bitter and astringent. For these reasons it also glues together even the large wounds of hard bodies, even if they are in the heads of the muscles, and it is beneficially plastered upon haemorrhaging parts, and it wonderfully disperses and at the same time represses oedematous swellings, and it wonderfully withstands all malignant ulcers, whether they are putrefying or being eroded. But if at any time it should appear stronger than the nature of the patient, one must mix with its leaves, finely ground, either bread or barley meal or wheat meal or barley groats, according to the predominant condition in each case. The wild woad, however, has something pungent, already clearly perceptible both in taste and in action, and on this account, being more drying than the cultivated kind, it withstands moist putrefactions more strongly, but in the other respects mentioned above it is worse, for it now dries more immoderately and with biting; and such parts become irritated and inflamed. But because of the strength of its power it is also useful for those suffering in the spleen, where the other kind is not yet of any help.

[6.9.7] [7. On isopyron.] Isopyron, or phasiolon, has a seed that is bitter and somewhat astringent. Accordingly it cleanses and cuts the thick humours, while at the same time drawing together and binding the bodies, and for this reason it also assists expectoration from the chest, and it clears out the liver, and it is believed not to work against those who spit blood but even to be of additional benefit to them. For on account of the mixed character of its mixture it seems to be suited even to opposite conditions.

[6.9.8] [8. On willow.] One might indeed use the leaves of the willow too for the gluing together of bloody wounds; nevertheless it is its flower above all that almost all physicians use for the preparation of a drying plaster. For their power is drying and non-biting, and it also has astringency. Some, moreover, by making a juice from them, obtain a non-biting and drying drug useful for many purposes.
