For nothing is of more manifold use than a non-biting and drying drug that is slightly astringent, as will be shown more precisely in the books on the composition of drugs. The bark of the tree, too, is closely similar in power to that of the flowers and of the leaves, except insofar as it is drier in mixture, as of course are all barks. But some burn this and use the ash for whatever they need to dry strongly. At any rate they remove the so-called corns and calluses, and myrmekiai as well, by soaking it with pungent vinegar. Others, incising the bark at the season of flowering, collect a certain sap and use it against the things that darken the pupils, it being a drug at once cleansing and fine-particled. And one might use it, being of such a nature, for many other things as well. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK Η. Preface. In writing this seventh treatise on the power of simple drugs, we think it necessary to say in advance that it will be clear only to those who have engaged with the preceding ones not in a cursory way; the others, I think, will misunderstand rather than learn anything of what is to be said in it, and will both go astray themselves and perhaps slander us, as if we were writing some things incorrectly. Now those who are sensible, I know, will be persuaded, and if they have any concern at all for the theory before us, will read through the whole treatise from the beginning; but those who are meddlesome rather than fond of learning will disobey the admonition, and perhaps that is nothing surprising, if indeed some of the uninitiated have even dared to read books of the mysteries. But neither did those who wrote those books write them for the profane, nor do I write these things for those not yet exercised in the first principles. In this book and the one after it there will be set out the primary powers of the remaining plants, we having here too arranged the order of instruction according to the order of the letters with which they begin. In the book before this one, then, we proceeded as far as iota; here we shall make our beginning from kappa, after first recalling only this much further, that we shall refer everything to the principles previously demonstrated. For it is by each of the drugs being hot or cold, or wet or dry, or fine-particled or coarse-particled to such-and-such a degree that the differences of their particular activities arise; but the advancing to such-and-such a degree in each of the aforesaid is inexpressible, at least with respect to the most exact truth. Yet we have attempted to encompass this too within clear boundaries, sufficient for the use of the art, by showing that one class of drugs is that which arrives at a mixture similar to our bodies, once it has received from the heat in them some beginning of change and alteration; another is that which becomes hotter than what is in us, of which we thought fit to make four orders: the first, that which is unclear to sense, so as to require reasoning to detect it; another after it, the second, already in some way clear to sense; another, the third, heating strongly but not yet in any way burning; and after it the fourth and last, the caustic. So too of cooling drugs: the first order is that of those requiring reasoning for the demonstration that they cool; the second, of those cooling perceptibly; the third, of those cooling strongly; and the fourth, of those that deaden. And analogously to these also with regard to moistening and drying drugs.

B.translation: These, then, are the qualities: moistness and dryness, [705] heat and coldness. The bodies named after them are, first, the elements common to all things; second, those called moist and dry and cold and hot according to the predominance of one of these qualities; third, those so called when compared with the well-balanced body of the same genus or of the same species; and fourth, those so called in comparison with anything whatever that happens to come along. Now the difference among these has been discussed many times. No less has it been said in what way nourishment differs from a drug: nourishment is mastered and overcome by that which is nourished, whereas the drug, on the contrary, itself overcomes and masters the body of which it is a drug; for the conception of each lies in the category of relation. It was also shown that a drug naturally alters either according to some one quality, whichever it may be, heating or cooling or drying or moistening, or according to some pairing of those mentioned, or according to its whole substance. Some of the deleterious drugs act in this last way, as do not a few of the protective remedies, all the purgatives, and many of those called attractive.

Concerning these, however, I think I shall [706] add what is still lacking in what follows. Those that act upon our whole body by one or two qualities I shall go through in this book. Here again I take as a hypothesis what was demonstrated in the preceding books: most of the simple drugs are in truth anhomoeomerous and composite, but they are called simple because by nature they are such as they are, having taken on nothing further from our artificial treatment. Moreover, some are coarse-particled and earthy in their substances, others fine-particled and airy, and others as it were watery and intermediate between those mentioned; since these things too were shown in the preceding discussions, let them stand as hypotheses for me with respect to what is going to be said. These things, then, being laid down, the discussion must now be begun.

The use of drugs for human beings often arises simply for this alone, namely their heating or cooling or moistening or drying, or their acting according to some combination of these; but sometimes it arises for their tightening and drawing together what has already been relaxed beyond the limit of the moderate, [707] or relaxing what has been tensed, or rarefying what has been condensed, or condensing what is porous, or softening what is hard, or hardening immoderate softnesses, or emptying what is full, or filling what is empty, or effecting some other such thing. For a person who has been chilled, not only the physician but any layman whatever, led by the very nature of the matter, desires to find a heating drug, and likewise one parched by a fever of the ardent (causus) kind desires a cooling one. So too any layman whatever who has a sodden ulcer bids the physician dry it, and if it is dry and without moisture, moisten it. And indeed, when they perceive dryness together with heat throughout the whole body, as those who have been scorched by the sun and those who have been fatigued long to bathe and drink cold water, they contrive to find whatever is capable of moistening and cooling at once; and many of the laymen, led by nature itself, do often provide themselves with the remedies for these conditions.

Yet for inflammation and scirrhus and oedema, for erysipelas and putrefaction, for herpes and gangrene, none [708] of them any longer attempts to seek the cure for himself, since each such condition is by now too great a matter for a layman's judgement and requires some more august knowledge; and they call such knowledge medicine, and the one who practises it a physician. They themselves advance only so far as to know that the hollow ulcer needs filling with flesh, the foul ulcer cleansing, and the level ulcer cicatrization; but they do not know the drug that fills with flesh, or cleanses, or cicatrizes. In the same way, if they have a muscle or a tendon that is hard or tense or slack, they know precisely that the hard one has need of softening drugs, the tense one of relaxing drugs, and the slack one of tightening drugs; but they do not know the drug that softens or relaxes or tightens. Finding such things is the work of the physician alone. For as far as heating and cooling, moistening and drying drugs go, one can find some of the laymen sharing with the physicians in the discovery of drugs; but in the matters just mentioned, all of them are entirely without experience.

Now, as was also shown earlier, even [709] in the case of the heating and cooling, moistening and drying drugs themselves, the discovery is not equally readily achieved for all of them. For that mustard and pellitory heat, and that purslane and strychnos cool, and that water and oil moisten, while vinegar and the sea dry, is agreed by almost everyone, not by physicians alone but also by laymen. Rose oil, however, whether one ought to say that it heats or that it cools, and likewise also vinegar and oil, and many other such things, have occasioned considerable dispute.

Concerning the power of such things I have treated in the four commentaries preceding this one: in the first and second, refuting the arguments of the sophists and showing the true method, by using which one might discover the powers of drugs; in the third, having left the sophists aside, I went through from the beginning all the logical questions, by going through which most thoroughly and, as one might say, by being made skilled in the art (technōtheis), one will be competent to discover the powers of all drugs; and in the fourth I made my discourse concerning the sensibles proper to the [710] tongue, which they call flavours (chymoi), showing how someone setting out from there might discover the primary qualities and powers. I also touched, so far as need called for it, on the olfactory qualities at the end of the book, showing how much it is possible to obtain from that source too towards the discovery of the primary powers. But in this present fifth book I propose to expound another class of powers, secondary, as one might say, and tertiary, in addition to the primary ones that are common to all things. For since each of the particular things is not mixed from those in the same way, one of them, I think, has become relaxing, another tightening or softening or hardening or rarefying or condensing.

Further, on the basis of the effects (ἔργα) which they are naturally disposed to produce, they have been said to have in them powers that are rarefying and condensing, softening and hardening, clogging and cleansing, drawing and repelling, and besides these relaxing, tightening, opening the mouths of vessels, contracting, thickening, thinning, anodyne, pain-causing, concocting, bringing to suppuration, dispersing, [711] sweat-inducing, stupefying, numbing, sleep-inducing, causing derangement, putrefying, burning, corroding, eschar-forming, liquefying, compacting, producing bad humours, tempering, purgative, checking, roughening, smoothing, obstructing and unblocking. And when they proceed still further and name them, as it were, individually after each of the effects, they call them diuretic, emetic, evacuant downward, laxative, errhine, phlegm-expelling, bringing on the menses or checking them. Likewise also either generative or extinguishing or provocative or retentive of milk and of semen. And still more, when they name certain powers hepatic or splenic or aural or ophthalmic or dental or sciatic or nephritic or podagric or arthritic or pleuritic or for cough or stone-breaking, they arrive at the particular powers. In the same way it has also been said that there is a flesh-forming power for an ulcer, and a scarring one, and an agglutinating and a removing one. Indeed, it is scarcely even possible to enumerate all the particular powers if we attempt to name them after each of the things they bring about.

But indeed [712] I think it finer and more methodical to withdraw from the long and disorderly account and to define the composite powers of drugs by useful classes: not saying that in the poultice made with wheaten meal there is a suppurating, or soothing, or anodyne, or dispersing, or relaxing power, but that it is moderately moist and warm. For it was said in the preceding books in what signification we apply an expression of this kind. So too one should not say of iris that it is a drug that moves urine or moves the menses, or that it is a cough drug, or that it suits those with pleurisy or with peripneumonia or with empyema, or that it helps against epilepsies and convulsions and palpitations and tremors and ruptures and strains; nor that it fills ulcers with flesh and cleans them, and stops pains of the sinuses and of the sides and of the liver and spleen; nor that it disperses scrofulous swellings or brings flesh up out of bones.

And in the same way [one should not say] that it is suited to seminal flux, or is usefully mixed into fomentations of the uterus, softening and opening up the mouths [of the vessels]; nor indeed that it cleans away lentigines or ephelides [713] and cures chronic headache, or that it is naturally apt to destroy embryos and draw them down. Rather, it is enough to say that its mixture is hot to such a degree, dry to such a degree, and fine-particled up to such a point, and thereby to have indicated all the things just mentioned and many others besides. In another way, again, it is enough to say of it that it is bitter, though not extremely so, but so as to seem to have some sweetness mixed in. The first mode of teaching is peculiar to the Empiricists, while the second befits above all a rational man, and it is this that we now propose to go through. All the other things said earlier in the four books belong properly to the theory of drugs itself, except where the account touched, by way of overlap, on the therapeutic method. The present topic, however, belongs more to that method, so that I often considered passing over it entirely.

But since it seemed good to me to give a preliminary training to those who are going to follow the reasonings of the therapeutic method, and since most of my companions, and especially [714] those as a favour to whom I came to this treatise, asked me to do so, for this reason I shall take up the account in this book, making the beginning from the drugs that bring to suppuration and those that soften. For both are hot and moist, but each in a different way. The former generate a heat most similar to that of the body being brought to suppuration, and besides neither take away any of the moisture present in it nor add any. The latter kindle even more heat than the natural and gather together some of the moisture. Now the conception of the drugs that bring to suppuration is at once clear and familiar to all, for suppuration is a change into pus. About softening drugs and about softening itself, however, it is no longer possible to speak so simply, because neither is it possible about the hard and the soft body.

if indeed one thing is called hard simply, as earth is; another by predominance, as a nail and a spur and a horn; another in relation to the well-proportioned of the same genus or of the same species, as when one compares some particular animal, for instance an elephant, or some particular man, for instance Heracles; [715] and another when compared with anything whatever, as Diogenes in relation to Aristotle. In the same way the soft too is spoken of, either as being such in the extreme, or by predominance, or in relation to the well-proportioned of the same genus or of the same species, or in relation to anything whatever that one happens upon. That all such things may also be spoken of in three ways, some as having unmixed and extreme the qualities from which they are derivatively named, others as compared with the well-proportioned of the same genus or of the same species, others as compared with anything whatever that one happens upon; and that it made no difference whether one speaks in that way or in this, has been shown by me many times already.

Leaving aside, then, all the other meanings, let us examine the things that are soft and hard relative to the best-constituted human being, whom we have made the canon and measure of all things so called. And we do not measure relative to any chance part of him, such as bone or fat, but relative to the part intermediate in its mixture, the skin, and of this especially the skin of the hands, where the tactile faculty is brought to its greatest precision. It also turns out that what is so named soft or hard by predominance, as relative to the whole substance, comes to the same thing, [716] since our touch is a kind of mean, as Aristotle also taught. Plato too seems to have held much the same view when he said: 'hard are those things to which our flesh yields, soft those that yield to the flesh.' For in this very treatise, the Timaeus, he showed that the skin of the human being is flesh in kind. And indeed Aristotle too, when he said that soft is what yields into itself and hard what does not yield, seems to declare the same as Plato, especially since he says that such things are judged relative to touch, as relative to a mean. But what is hard or soft in comparison with anything whatever appears to be judged by its yielding or not yielding more or less. And indeed when we say that our skin itself, or a muscle, or some other part, has become hardened, we name it so by comparing the acquired condition with its natural state. And the return of bodies in this condition to their natural state is, of course, softening.

Since each thing becomes harder in many ways, being either dried, or congealed, or overfilled, [717] so as to be violently distended, or suffering these in some combination, the softening will also be specific to each of them. Let us therefore draw distinctions about all of them in order, first recalling that a free and easy use of nouns and verbs is for the most part not ignoble; rather, its opposite is illiberal, when it is not necessary to draw distinctions about them. So Plato said; and for us now, for the present [purpose], it is necessary to distinguish the meanings of 'hard', beginning again from the same points we have just stated. For that which yields into itself is soft, if indeed it is a simple body. But what is composed of several things, either touching one another, like the heap of wheat, or in some way interwoven, like fleece or braids, could both yield and at the same time not be soft.

Conversely, in things that are filled completely, such as wineskins or bladders, the two together do not yield into themselves; yet the contents are certainly not hard, nor has the container, when it has been filled, become harder than it was, or taken on any other acquired condition, [718] except that it has merely been stretched from its previously slack state. Such a thing, then, I call resistant and not hard, whenever I choose to speak with precision. I concede, however, that if anyone wishes he may call it hard too, and I myself often call it so, reminding only of this: that there is neither one nature of hardened things nor one remedy. For what has been hardened by dryness needs to be moistened; what by congelation, to be warmed; what by filling, to be emptied; what by dryness and congelation together, to be both moistened and warmed; and what by congelation and filling together, to be both warmed and emptied. Bodies, then, are dried without congelation in immoderate exercises, in intense sun, in severe deprivations, in a causus-like fever, and by certain drugs, namely those that dry without cooling. They are congealed by strong cooling alone, just as they are also filled through an influx of abundant moisture. They are dried and congealed at the same time when causes that are able to coexist converge upon the same thing, as for instance if someone were to overexert himself in frost.

In the same way, bodies are both filled and congealed through a cold flux [719] or some chilling of the part. Of the chilling, in turn, the cause is threefold: one from the things that fall upon it from outside, such as air, water or a drug, as they often bring it about in the case of erysipelases; another, the proper mixture of the affected part; and a third besides these, arising from the humour that has flowed into it. For often that humour has itself already become hotter than it was, either by putrefying or by being changed by the parts touching it that are hot by nature; but the chilling which it has imparted to some one of the parts that are colder by nature persists for a long time. In so many ways, then, bodies are both hardened and softened. The softening drug, however, does not seem to apply to all of these ways, but specifically to those hardened through congelation, and still more if some moisture contrary to nature is also contained in them, as in the case of things that have become scirrhous. For if something has become hard through dryness, they bid one rather to moisten such a case, not to soften it, just as also to empty, not to soften, things that are filled.

But about names it is neither good to quarrel [720] nor necessary to be precise. It is better to go on to the differences in the things themselves, in which an error also brings great harm to the sick. Now what has been dried out requires moistening drugs, about which I have already spoken sufficiently before, and what has been congealed by cooling requires heating ones. Nor are these things unknown. What has been filled, however, requires either cooling drugs, or heating ones, or those properly called drying. For all of these evacuate the superfluous wetness, each by its own principle. Those that cool do so in two ways, at once repelling and also drawing out, together with the heat, much moisture, as Aristotle taught. Those that heat do so by dissolving into vapours the moist matter contained in the bodies being heated. Those that dry, such as the so-called dispersing drugs, these too act in two ways, either by drinking up the wetnesses, when they are present in certain pores, or by altering the whole part. But what the right time for the use of each is belongs not to the present treatise but to the therapeutic method.

But those parts that [721] have been hardened by cold and dryness together ought to be warmed and moistened at the same time; not in the way that parts that have suppurated are treated, with heat and moisture together that are moderate and in accordance with nature, but the drug must be warmer by as much as the cold has prevailed, and moister by as much as the dryness has; and defining the measure of these too belongs to the therapeutic method. Here it will be enough to go through a sort of outline of the kind of drugs, using a few examples. Hot water and oil, then, moisten and warm. And if both are mixed together into one, the mixture made from them will be much more moistening and warming at once, just as baths of potable waters with abundant oil are. The quality of foods, when it is in the same condition, also produces this very same effect; for this reason the remedies for cases of boulimia have also turned out to be of this sort. For the affection involves cold together with dryness, and their cure is through contraries.

The poultice made from wheaten meal, however, which brings well-tempered natures to suppuration, neither draws off from the natural moisture in the parts [722] anything worth mentioning, nor, still less, adds any. In the same way it does nothing to the warmth either: it is by nature disposed neither to intensify it nor to blunt it, but to increase it in respect of substance alone. Yet to intensify the quality and to increase the substance are not the same thing. This too will be shown more precisely a little later. Drugs of this kind, then, we call moist and warm. We do not mean that they are moister and warmer than our own substance, but that they are of a mixture closely similar to ours, which is moist and warm according to the ancient account, as we said in the work On Mixtures. It is not, however, in this sense that we say water is moist or galbanum warm. We call the former moist as wetting and soaking through our flesh, and the latter warm as warming it. For even if the water be warm, so that it is sometimes able to empty parts raised into a swelling through an influx of fluids, it at any rate certainly moistens the homoeomerous parts, as has been shown by me in the first book as well.

Drugs that bring to suppuration, then, by heating in the same way as hot water, disperse the superfluous [723] moisture, the moisture contained in the empty spaces, as has been demonstrated in the treatise On Uneven Bad Mixture. To bodies that are in their natural state, however, to the homoeomerous bodies themselves, they add nothing of moisture, just as they also take away nothing evident or perceptible. For since they are equal to them in their mixtures, they are preservative of their substance, so as to alter it in no respect. In suppurations, at any rate, the moisture is altered, and also any crushed flesh there may be, but all the other things that are in their natural state preserve their own substance. For of the three alterations that occur in the bodies of animals, one is strictly in accordance with nature: when food is concocted in the stomach, or when the juice (chylos) generated there is concocted in the viscera and vessels, so that from it in turn each member may be nourished. Another is strictly contrary to nature, in all things that putrefy. These, then, are in a way opposite to one another. The third is admixed from both and intermediate, having something of the first, the one in accordance with nature, and something of its opposite, the one contrary to nature.

For the natural one has these two features: [724] that the alteration takes place out of material proper to the animal, and that it is exactly mastered by the innate heat. In the unnatural one, the change is brought about by foreign heat and leads to nothing useful. The one intermediate between them, which accompanies suppurations (empyēseis), comes about through the innate heat, but a heat that does not exactly master it. For it is not accomplished out of material that is exactly useful, just as it is not accomplished out of material that is wholly foreign either. So, just as the natural alterations, which come about through the innate heat, are assisted by a similar heat from outside, in the same way the alteration in suppurations (diapyēseis) is assisted too. We know, at any rate, that nothing contributes so much to concoction in the stomach as a human body touching it. And some people, placing children against it at night while they rest, perceive a most evident benefit. For this heat is much more akin and more proper than that which comes through fomentations. Some people also, for the sake of the same benefit, place small puppies against the stomach while they rest, increasing the quantity of the heat that concocts the foods, not its quality.

Such, then, must also be the drug that is to assist suppuration [725], namely of the same kind as the innate heat itself is in well-tempered natures. But if the nature is hotter than it should be, the suppurating drug will have to be hotter in that body, and hotter than the moderate one by just as much as the nature too is hotter than the well-tempered one. So this much is already evident from the therapeutic method: the suppurating drug is peculiar to each individual human being. And these things bear witness, not least, to what we have often demonstrated, that all the powers of drugs must be examined with reference to the best-tempered human being. For no art can be established at all unless one first sets up a kind of canon and target for the class of material with which it is occupied, and then directs all the particulars by reference to that.

Once more, then, positing in our account the best-mixed human being as a kind of target, and referring to him, we say that a suppurative drug is something different from one that softens indurated parts, and that their mixtures are such as we said [726] earlier: that of the drug which contributes to the generation of pus is moderate and similar to the body to which it is applied by nature; and because our nature is moist and hot, such drugs are often called moist and hot. The mixture of the drug that softens what is indurated, on the other hand, is much hotter than the well-mixed nature, yet not already strongly hot. For the condition of indurated parts begins from a viscous and thick flux that has become wedged in the small pores of the part. When the fine-particled moisture in it has been dispersed, and the remainder has then been chilled and has undergone a sort of congealing, what is called induration follows. For this reason they also say that the affection is cold, and that its cure is through warming agents. But since there was superfluous moisture together with the chilling, the remedy too will be compound: the condition requires warming agents because of the chilling, and evacuating agents because of the foreign and superfluous moisture.

Hence none of the parts undergoing scirrhous hardening is cured either by the drugs that dry vehemently, or by those that heat strongly, [727] or by those capable of both. For the drugs that heat vehemently, having violently dispersed the moisture lying alongside and contained in the parts, dry out what remains, so that it becomes incurable. The drugs that dry vehemently, even if they do not heat, and not through the intermediate step of evacuating the fine-particled part, nevertheless bring the flux wedged in the scirrhous parts to the extreme of dryness, directly and in accordance with their own nature. Only those drugs, then, which heat, but not vehemently, and at the same time do not dry strongly either, cure such conditions. Such drugs are called softening, since they do both things at one and the same time: they liquefy what has been congealed and disperse it little by little. All such drugs, then, are hot and not very dry. They differ from the suppurative drugs in being hotter and drier than these.

For the former possess a heat that is akin and most similar to our bodies, whereas the softening ones are more intense, though not [728] so much as to dry out the remainder by the violence of their drawing. Further, the suppurating ones preserve the moisture already present in the parts undergoing skirrhos, whereas the softening ones consume some small part of it. And for this reason, though heating and drying drugs are countless, only those which share in a moderate heat and have also happened to have a dryness proportionate to it are softening of parts undergoing skirrhos: for example bdellium, storax, galbanum, ammoniac incense, the marrow of deer and of calf, the fat of goat and of bull, and all other such things.

For it is not our present purpose to go through all the material, but to give a single general instruction covering all such powers. And what is the general point that it is better to know about those that bring to suppuration and those that soften? That the former kindle a heat equal to the natural heat of the animal, whereas those that soften kindle a much greater one; and that the former are naturally disposed to act not by the quality of the heat but rather by its quantity, whereas those that are [729] softening of indurated parts act rather by its quality. For just as, if it were possible to keep the hands, or some other limb, always laid upon the part that needs suppuration, it would in this way come to suppuration very quickly, in the same way, if the drug too is most similar to the mixture of the human being, it will very quickly concoct what needs to be changed into pus. What needs this is sometimes the flesh, when it has been bruised, and sometimes the humour that produces the inflammation. And indeed, that such a drug must be clogging if it is to be strictly suppurative, this too, I think, is already clearly apparent. For if what is fitting is to increase the substance of the innate heat, and not to add to (or intensify) its quality, the passages of the body must be blocked, so that they may keep the vaporous exhalations shut in within. For those poultices that, either by cleansing or by heating more strongly, allow the vapours to be dispersed, do dry, but they do not bring to suppuration.

Of this kind are the meal of barley and of chickpeas, and that of fenugreek and that of beans, [730] and still more that of darnel, bitter vetches, elymos, lupins, millet, and of all the drying substances. For under the action of the cleansing substances, even if they do not heat strongly, the pores are unblocked and opened, and the heat of the part departs together with what is carried off, so that its natural due proportion is not preserved. Under the action of the strongly heating substances, on the other hand, not a little of this heat is emptied out, while what remains is heated up further; and so it comes about that the substance of the innate heat becomes less, while its quality is intensified. But neither of these ought to happen. Rather, the vaporous and hot pneuma ought to be contained in the greatest amount, and it ought to be exactly proportionate in its heat. For it is this, present in the greatest amount in children, that helps increase all the natural functions. There are, then, some who do not know even this very thing, and who, besides not knowing it, find fault with Hippocrates for saying that growing bodies have the most innate heat.

But we must not mishear him; we must recognise that what has been called innate heat is that which we also name pneuma in each of the animals, about [731] which Aristotle too wrote. Nothing, however, prevents us from also understanding by innate heat the sanguineous and airy substance together with the pneuma. Now the Stoics hold that this very pneuma is the substance of the soul; we, however, do not venture to make any pronouncement at all about the substance of the soul, and for present purposes we consider it superfluous. That the connate pneuma, even if it is not the substance of the soul, is nevertheless its first instrument, we have already demonstrated in the commentaries On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato. Moreover, we say that this pneuma is contained in all the members of the animal, but that it is not alike everywhere, just as the blood need not be either; and that in the empty spaces too no small amount of its substance is contained, or rather a kind of material, as it were, which still needs a slight change for the generation of innate pneuma perfected in its proper qualities, but which already contributes sufficiently to the natural functions.

Now one of the natural works, surely, [732] is also the change into pus, for in this respect too it is a kind of concoction. And one must, I think, keep the pneuma inside as much as possible whenever it is proposed to concoct something. It is dispersed by things that cleanse, such as barley meal and bean meal; by things that dry, such as panic, millet and lupins; by things that heat, such as fenugreek; and still more by things whose nature is to heat and dry at once, such as darnel, bitter vetches, chickpeas and ochroi. Most suitable for the generation of pus are, among things poured over the part, temperate water or water-and-oil; among things used to moisten it, temperate oil; and among poultices, wheaten meal made up with water-and-oil, and bread itself. This too must be boiled in due measure. For what has been boiled for a very long time is somewhat more drying and suits the inflammations that are harder to concoct, while what has been boiled less suits those that are very hot and, as one might say, seething.

And the one containing more oil is for those harder to concoct, [733] the one containing less for the seething ones. Moreover, the poultice made from bread suits the inflammations that are harder to concoct, for bread contains both salt and leaven; that made from wheaten flour suits the hotter ones. And again, of wheaten flour itself the pure flour brings to suppuration more, and of bread the pure bread more. For the bran is both less hot and more dry, whereas the pure and nourishing flour is both moist and hot, and it has been shown that such things cooperate towards the generation of pus. In the same way, then, of the drugs applied to inflamed parts, those that are hot and moist also contribute to suppuration, such as pig's fat and calf's fat. For that of the bull and of the goat was shown to be more pungent, and for this reason suitable for the colder and more scirrhous inflammations, whereas pig's and calf's fat are most appropriate to the inflammations properly so called. The fat of cocks is also most appropriate, and still more that of the goose, which is already somewhat more dispersing.

[734] For they are more fine-particled in their substances, just as that of oxen and goats is both more coarse-particled and more earthy. Moreover, the fat of all wild animals is both more pungent and much more drying than that of tame ones, and especially that of leopards and lions, so that none of these is suitable for promoting suppuration; rather, as has been said, pig's fat and calf's fat are. Pitch and resin also promote suppuration, when strained, evidently, with some oil or with rose oil. Here too one must melt them with rose oil for seething inflammations, and for colder ones with one of the heating oils, such as castor oil, radish oil, old oil and Sicyonian oil. And if you ever use wax alone for the sake of bringing to suppuration, the others not being available, melt this too in one of the heating oils. For by itself it is too little hot to bring to suppuration, though it does have the property of clogging. It is therefore suitable only for seething inflammations, when strained in one of the heating oils.

And just as this [wax] falls short of due proportion with respect to inflammations that are intermediate in their mixture, and to the natures both of men and of parts, so resin and pitch exceed it by a little [735]. For this reason all these things just mentioned, when mixed together, bring to suppuration in due proportion. But these matters already belong to the treatise on the composition of drugs, which the sequence of the theory has in a way compelled us to touch upon. I return again to the matter proposed. What is proposed is to define the universal nature of the things that bring to suppuration, of what kind it is. It was said that this nature must heat and moisten in due proportion. Expressed otherwise, it must neither exceed nor fall short of the mixture of the body that alters it, but must be as nearly similar to it as possible. That the drug which brings to suppuration is such in potentiality, but becomes such in actuality on being brought into contact with us, has been said many times before. We shall recall it now as well, so that it may be remembered always. Such, then, is the mixture of what brings to suppuration; the consistency of its body is something clogging. This belongs above all to viscous things, such as pig's fat, butter, frankincense, and the poultice made with wheaten meal.

[736] For these are moderately hot and moderately moist and viscous, and for this reason they are suitable for suppurations. Groats (chondros), however, are more drying than wheaten meal, but no less viscous, if not indeed even more so; hence in middling inflammations it is less suitable for suppuration, but in the moister ones it is better than wheaten meal. Since these matters, too, already go further beyond the present treatise, let us return once more to the drugs that are softening of indurated parts, touching here too upon the therapeutic treatise only so far as will help to make what is going to be said clear. Now, they call skirrhos the swelling contrary to nature that is both painless and hard. Some of them, when they have grown and hardened to the greatest extent, become not only painless but also of dulled sensation and insensible. Their generation is from a thick and cold humour. In the bodies of animals there are only two such humours: black bile and phlegm that has been dried to excess.

And for this reason the scirrhous swellings too are without exception either phlegmatic [737] in their substance, or melancholic, or mixed from both. Now, concerning their diagnosis, this is not the occasion to go through it; but concerning the softening drugs, it is now time for me to speak, since people call 'softening' specifically those drugs that are remedial for scirrhous swellings arisen from phlegm that has been dried out and from thick juice. These form chiefly around the heads of the muscles and the tendons that grow out from them. For whatever becomes scirrhous from melancholic juice is all cancerous, and is exacerbated by the softening drugs. But how one ought to bear these in mind will be stated in the books of the Therapeutic Method. Whatever, on the other hand, has become scirrhous from viscous and thick humour that has congealed requires warming and drying drugs, not, however, strong and violent ones. It suffices for them to be of the second, or sometimes even of the third, order of warming drugs, and of the first order of drying drugs.

Since there is no small latitude, in respect of the more and the less, in hardened bodies, there must surely also be [738] no small latitude in the drugs that cure them. For instance, goat's fat has sometimes benefited parts hardened in this way, and so has that of the hen. But these are weaker and soften moderate hardnesses. Stronger, however, than that of hens and cocks is goose fat; and stronger than that of she-goats is that of the he-goat, and also that of the bull, though less so than that of the he-goat. Moreover, the marrow of deer softens sufficiently, and after it that of calf. For all such drugs are hot and moderately dry, and are by nature disposed to heat much more than to dry. Hence, if someone should at times call them hot and moist in their powers, this must be conceded, for they stand only a little removed from the drugs that neither dry nor moisten. Of the same genus as those mentioned, but stronger, are ammoniac incense, storax, galbanum, and Scythian bdellium. Of these the fresh ones are better for softening, for as they grow old they dry more strongly than they should. This, indeed, marrow and fat also have.

For these too, when they grow old, [739] become more pungent and drier than they themselves were. Moreover, Sicyonian oil also belongs to this class, and old oil not least, and among the prepared oils, oil of lilies (sousinon). But it is not my purpose here to speak about compound drugs. Next, the root of althaea and of wild cucumber, and certain other plants, when boiled down, some in oil and others in water, come to have the power of the softening drugs, as do the leaves of wild mallow, both raw and boiled. This, then, is a simple drug, as is pig's fat that has been aged. But this too must contain no salt, just as none of the other things that soften may; for salts dry strongly. All the other drugs whose nature is to soften, both simple and compound (for those too will be discussed later), are hot, of the second or sometimes the third order, but only mildly dry. These too must have something clogging in them, as the suppurative drugs also do. But the more evacuant they ought to be, the less they ought to become plastered into the pores.

[740] The power of softening drugs, then, has been sufficiently set out by me; I shall next go through those that harden. These, then, must be cold and moist, as are houseleek, purslane, fleawort and the lentil found on standing waters, or strychnos. Or rather, this last is not even moist in its mixture, but is intermediate between what simply moistens and what dries, being composed of opposite powers, a moistening and a drying one, because it also partakes of a twofold substance, earthy and watery. But it is not my purpose now to bring the discussion down to the particular material, but only to define the generic powers. If, then, something both cools and dries, this too certainly hardens, but it is not among the hardening drugs proper. For the body becomes hard by congelation rather than by evacuation, as we were also saying earlier.

But if something has become hard from not retaining its innate moisture, we call it dry rather than hard, and its cure is soaking and moistening, not softening, [741] just as the cure of what is contracted is relaxation, and of what is relaxed, contraction. How these things stand is clearly seen in the skin, as Hippocrates too has said: 'of hard skin, mollification; of contracted skin, relaxation'. It is also often seen in the joints. Relaxation is brought about when the ligaments around them and the tendons have been moistened beyond measure. Contraction, however, does not arise in one simple way: it arises if they are dried to some greater degree, or chilled, or inflamed, or become scirrhous. So it is at the joints. In the skin it arises not only in this way but also when the muscles within it increase in bulk in any manner whatsoever, so that in some people it is often stretched even through excess of flesh. That it suffers this same thing in inflammations as well has been said before. Hence there is not simply one single kind of relaxing remedies. Rather, some relax by moistening, others by warming, others by softening, others by evacuating, others by clearing away the swellings contrary to nature, and others by effecting some of these in combination.

[742] Thessalus, however, and nearly all his followers, as in many other matters, so in these too confound both the names and the things themselves, writing down without examination whatever comes into their heads; hence it will perhaps be necessary for us too, once we have completed the task before us, to write against them at some time. For the present, let us go through what follows on from what has been said, making a fresh start from the drugs called clogging, since they too have frequently been discussed. To put it briefly, then, a clogging drug is one that becomes plastered into the pores throughout the human body in such a way that it is hard to release. I have spoken sufficiently about the nature of the pores that we posit in my commentaries On Mixtures. And it was demonstrated in the book before this one that the clogging drug must also be wholly non-biting. For if anything biting were present in it, it will not be able to remain in the pores, but will be readily excreted, either after melting away some of the parts around it, or at any rate after drawing moisture to itself from the depth.

And it is clear [743] that the clogging drug must also be earthy in consistency, or at any rate viscous. But enough has been said about these things earlier as well. Its opposite might be called clearing out, or unblocking of the pores, just as the clogging drug itself is called not only clogging but also blocking. And just as it is opposite in its effects, so too in the nature of its body it would be neither viscous nor non-biting, but nitrous and fine-particled. For it is by the more and the less, not in the genus of their substance, that clogging drugs differ from those that foster the growth of dirt, and drugs that thoroughly clear the pores differ from cleansing ones. For those that remove the dirt on the surface, whether of ulcers or of the skin itself, are called cleansing; but those that also clear out the pores are more fine-particled than these and opposite to the clogging drugs, and for this reason they are named unblocking and clearing of the pores.

These are nitrous and bitter. When they are applied to the skin from outside, [744] they need only possess the nitrous quality in its exact form to be able to do what has been stated. But when they are taken inside the body, even if they have some share of astringency, they can still, even so, be clearing and thoroughly cleansing of the larger pores, such as are also in the vessels. For on the outside the smallness of the pores is first closed up ('blinded') by the astringency before it has been properly cleaned out, and from then on it neither admits the cleansing substance any further into the depth nor is cleaned out. But all the parts about the belly, and those of the liver and spleen and all the other viscera, since they have very large pores within them, are benefited with respect to the strength of the vessels more than they are harmed with respect to the smallness of the openings. And for this reason wormwood is naturally fitted to clean out thoroughly from within, but not from without. It is compound, as was said before, of a bitter and an acerbic power. So I need not add in writing any of the particulars of such drugs.

For whatever you find to be nitrous and bitter, know that these are able to cleanse out all the pores; but the filth of ulcers, or also that of the skin, not only these but [745] also things more moderate in their powers are by nature able to remove, such as are the fine-particled sweet things, like honey and some of the cereal seeds, like bitter vetch, beans, barley and lupins. And yet even among these very things, the meal of beans and of barley only cleanses away, but does not clear the obstructions out of the pores, whereas that of bitter vetch and of lupins, and especially when they are bitter, has, in addition to cleansing, already something capable of cleansing out the pores as well. Something similar holds also for almonds. For of these too, those that are bitter both cleanse and thoroughly cleanse out the pores, while those that are edible cleanse but do not clear obstructions. The seed of the nettle, however, cleanses the pores in the same way as bitter vetch and bitter almonds. Of the same class, evidently, are also the squill and the iris, and all other things which, as has been said, have the bitter quality dominant in themselves. For indeed nitre itself on its own, and aphronitre, and foam of nitre, and seriphon, and southernwood, and all other such things, when taken with foods and drinks, are of the same power.

And all these at once also have the property of being thinning of thick and viscous humours, just as all clogging drugs [746] have the property of making the humours in the human body thick and viscous. So you could not find any other drugs in preference to these that are more cutting, more thinning and better suited to bringing up whatever comes from the chest and lung, whether phlegmatic matters, viscous matters or pus. These same drugs also have the property of clearing out obstructions in the liver, and the moderate ones in the spleen; but the stronger ones need more vehement drugs besides: caper bark and tamarisk roots, scolopendrion and squill, and the herb called asplenos for this very reason. These very drugs, too, must be used differently for each of the viscera: for the liver, by themselves alone; for the spleen, mixing them with vinegar or boiling them in it; and for conditions of the chest and lung, with melikraton, ptisane, oxymel and the sweet wines. But these matters already belong to the therapeutic method; therefore for the present I pass over the reasonings about them. For they will be set out both in that treatise and in the one on the composition of drugs.

[747] What I must still point out in addition to what has been said will simply be stated: that whenever we wish to provoke a more copious urination, we should not use the drugs mentioned at all, but rather those that are both more pungent and more heating. For it was said earlier that everything pungent is hot. Such are the seed of selinon, of petroselinon, of fennel, of daucus, of wild selinon and of smyrnion, and also seseli, ammi, phu and meon, as well as asaron and acoron. By these the blood is not only thinned but also liquefied and separated, in the same way as milk: the whey-like and thin part is separated off by itself, while the thicker part condenses upon itself and is closely united. For both of these things contribute to the kidneys' easily drawing to themselves whatever in the blood is watery, thin and whey-like: first the liquefaction of the whole blood itself, and after it the separation. Neither of these can come about without strong heat. And for this reason all such things work against the expectoration of pus from the chest.

For their [748] nature, as has just been said, is heating and drying, and besides this gathering-together and separating: the thick is gathered together into one, while whatever serous and thin matter is carried along in the blood is excreted and separated off in the course of the thick's coming together. The kidneys, then, draw this to themselves first, while what is condensed and dried out is no longer easily coughed up. And for this reason, as was said just now, such a drug must be cutting, yet not manifestly hot, so that it does not dry violently, and it must be given together with moistening gruels and drinks for the same purpose. Those, however, that cleanse the kidneys are likewise cutting, but they have no need at all of abundant moisture. And those that are suitable for cutting the stony concretions in them are also sufficiently cutting, but share very little in heat; for heat, by drying out the stony matter, consolidates it, and does not cut and divide it.

But those that are less hot, while still able to cut, are better, such as the roots of the so-called royal asparagus, and those of the bramble, and kestron and polium, and ochre and glass that has been [749] burnt, and the vinegar made with squill, and all other such things. Thessalus, that most inept of men, just as he wantonly and faultily abuses the other parts of the art, so too attempts to disparage these, holding that there is no drug specifically hepatic, or nephritic, or pleuritic. But his errors we have demonstrated in other writings; in the present discourse we shall expound the remaining powers of the simple drugs, beginning again from the rarefying and the anastomotic. For these too seem in a certain way to come close to those mentioned before, which we said cleanse and cut, clear obstructions and divide, yet not to be wholly alike to them. First, then, we must define the conceptions of these too, and only then investigate their substances. Those that open the pores in the skin they call rarefying; those that open the mouths of the vessels, anastomotic.

And moreover, as for their opposites: if something draws the pores together, they name it condensing; but if something closes the orifice, they no longer address it by a proper [750] name, and instead call it by certain more generic ones: 'drawing together', 'closing', 'binding tight' and 'stopping up'. The nature of each is as follows. That of the rarefying ones is moderately hot, drying least of all, and fine-particled; that of the ones opening the mouths of vessels is coarse-particled, pungent and biting. Of their opposites, the condensing nature is cooling, yet neither earthy nor airy but rather watery; the nature that closes the openings of the vessels is coarse-particled and cold. Examples of these: of rarefying nature are chamomile and marsh-mallow and the oil made from them, and not least also the oil made from wild cucumbers. Old oil, castor oil and radish oil are also of the same kind. Of the power that opens the mouths of vessels are all things that are pungent and earthy: cyclamen, garlic, onions, the bile of bulls. Also the sediments of all unguents that are at once coarse-particled and hot, such as the iris unguent and the marjoram unguent, which indeed open haemorrhoids that have become blinded.

But the drugs said to open the mouth of the uterus when it has closed up through some inflammation, or dryness, or scirrhus [751] would be of such a power accidentally, not primarily nor in themselves. In the same way, when the lips, eyelids, nostrils, pharynx, foreskin, anus or some other such organ with a mouth have closed up through inflammation, the drugs that cured the inflammation and so also corrected the closure are not of such a power either. For these too might be called resolvent of inflammation, but in no way opening the mouths of vessels. Dioscorides errs in these matters, sometimes saying that a drug which is relaxing, or softening, or moistening, or resolvent of inflammation is of a power that opens the mouths of vessels. Such, then, are the substances of the rarefying drugs and of those opening the mouths of vessels. Of the drugs contrary to them, the substance of the condensing ones is that of cold water, houseleek, purslane, green caltrop, fleawort, the herb which they call mouse-ear, and the lentil from the pools; and, to put it simply, of whatever cools without being astringent.

For this reason mandrake and hemlock, henbane and poppy too (I mean now the herbs themselves), if one uses them moderately, are condensing [752] in their powers; if more liberally, not only condensing but by now numbing as well; and if most liberally, no longer only numbing but by now also deadening. The substance of the things contrary to the anastomotic [drugs], being coarse-particled and cold, is that of all the astringents that are without admixed pungency. Sufficient examples of their material have been given in the fourth book, in which I also explained the substance of such drugs as being earthy and cold. It is therefore no longer anything to wonder at if this substance alone is naturally able to draw together and close the mouths of the vessels that have opened contrary to nature. For to it alone is present everything that the things to be drawn together require. Because of the coarse-particled character of its consistency it falls upon them from outside but is unable to pass through the fine passages. Because of its cooling it compresses inwards and draws together from every side towards themselves the parts that lie near. And because it dries (for every astringent was shown to be of this kind), it consumes the moisture and gives tone to the part.

But if all these things come together, the orifice will be closed, drawn together from outside by the particles of the astringent substance as if by fingers [753]. Those drugs, however, which are cold, either to the same degree or more, but watery in their substances, both draw together and constrict weakly, because of their softness. For everything that is to compress and draw together anything strongly needs a certain resistant and hard strength; and the drugs more watery in their substances, not having this, draw together and condense the fine pores in each body, but are unable to constrict the whole organ from every side, so that such drugs are reasonably condensing, but not binding (stegnotic). Understand me now as calling 'binding' those that check the perceptible excretions. For the binding body, the one that holds in (stegon) within itself and lets nothing go out perceptibly, has been called by the Greeks stegnon, 'tight'.

These, then, are of this kind in their mixtures and in their powers. Rarefying drugs, on the other hand, in every case heat; for otherwise they could not at once diffuse and relax the substance, upon which there follows also the widening of the pores. [754] They must, however, be neither excessively hot in their mixtures (for such drugs are by then pungent and compel shivering) nor drying; for these too are colliquative and painful to the sentient bodies. Those, therefore, which heat without causing distress are, of all things, the only ones that are rarefying. But if they should be not only hot but also coarse-particled in their consistencies, then, being vehement and caustic, they melt down the bodies after the manner of fire, and often produce eschars like those from cauteries. Those that heat less than is required to burn belong to the power of opening the mouths of vessels, so that the drug that opens the mouths of vessels is in its substance at once earthy and fiery, but has come to such a degree of heat as not yet to burn. If, however, it should be caustic, yet not vehemently so, and moreover fine-particled, such a drug will either be entirely free from biting, or, with slight biting and pain, will melt away some part of the fleshy parts.

For because it neither alters all at once, as the intensely hot things do, nor passes through with difficulty, as the coarse-particled things do, [755] it has an activity that goes unnoticed, since among alterations it is the sudden changes that are most perceptible, and among passages through it is the forcible ones. For the coarse-particled caustic, in whatever part it settles, distresses it, being stuck in like a splinter. But that one is eschar-forming, in the same way as the caustics. The things with which the present discussion is concerned neither produce an eschar and [yet] are called putrefying, though they have not obtained an appropriate designation. For the truly putrefying things are those that moisten together with heating. Nevertheless we do call them so on account of the similarity of the symptom, for a painless destruction comes about from both. There are, to be sure, several modes of things being destroyed: for things that have been excessively chilled, excessively heated, excessively moistened and excessively dried are all destroyed; but we do not say that all things that are destroyed putrefy, only those that undergo this with a foul smell. About names, however, one need not be very earnest.

One must know that the drugs called putrefactive and putrefying, such as arsenikon, sandarake and chrysocolla, [756] dryopteris, the pine caterpillar and aconite, all melt and colliquate, and above all soft flesh, without pain. Some of them are specifically called reducing (kathairetika), and people use them for the scarring over of ulcers with excess flesh. These too are of the same power in genus as the one named putrefying, but weaker to such a degree that they reduce only the surface of whatever they come into contact with and are unable to penetrate into depth, as is also the case with the flower of Asian stone. Such things, however, are not of the same power as the truly scarring one. For those do not reduce or melt away any of the flesh; they are by nature apt to harden and to dry. Such are alum, the oak-gall which they call omphakitis, and burnt copper, especially when it has been washed. For the unwashed has something reducing about it, as does the scale of copper, whereas the washed is the finest of the scarring drugs. For what is going to scar well must be both moderately astringent and drying.

[757] Hence the fruit of the Egyptian thorn, the dry rinds of the pomegranate, and everything of this kind also belong among the scarring drugs. Most physicians have confused not only the name but also the knowledge of the power of all such drugs. For they sometimes also call scarring those drugs that are catheretic and colliquative of the flesh, because ulcers often come to a scar when we use these as well. But this happens neither primarily, nor by their own proper power, nor with every use. For such drugs, made exactly like fine dust and applied by means of the knob of the probe (μύλης, apparently for μήλης) rolled over the flesh, bring ulcers to a scar. But if you use a little more, they both bite and colliquate the flesh and make the ulcer hollow, the opposite of the truly scarring drugs. With those, unless you apply a considerable amount, it will accomplish nothing. For in the scarring of level ulcers the aim is to alter the flesh and make it skin.

This is brought about by those [drugs] that are able to draw it together, constrict [758] and compact it, condense and dry it, and make it callous. For skin is, as it were, a kind of callused flesh. Drugs able to act in this way are therefore called scarring primarily and in the strict sense; the others, the reducing ones, are so called secondarily and accidentally, as are also those that dry without biting and without being astringent. For these too bring [ulcers] to a scar accidentally; such a drug is myrrh, and also litharge. And if oyster-shell and diphryges are burnt, then these too, sprinkled on dry, have often scarred [ulcers] over. One must understand, both in these discussions and in all the others, that wherever I add 'often' I mean to indicate that such drugs sometimes fail to deliver what they promise, because they do not bring it about primarily, nor by their own power. Scarring drugs, however, are able to scar over every level ulcer, just as drugs that cleanse moderately and without biting are able to fill up hollow ones.

The power of such drugs will be discussed at greatest length in [759] the books of the Therapeutic Method, with which this book shares common ground in many places, as was also stated earlier at its beginning. For this reason I think that I shall now bring the discussion of these to a close and pass on to another class of powers, those named drawing and repelling. Drawing powers, then, are those that draw up more vehemently what lies in the depth; repelling powers are those that drive toward the depth the humours that come close to them. The substance of the former is hot and fine-particled, that of the latter, conversely, cold and coarse-particled. For the hot always draws, and the cold repels. But the fine-particled hot draws more vehemently, and the coarse-particled cold, such as the astringent, thrusts more forcibly. Each, then, takes its name from the vehemence of its activity.

The material of astringent [drugs] is obvious. Of the drawing [drugs], however, some material is natural (self-grown), while some has its origin from a putrefaction that turns things acid. Natural is that of dittany, of propolis and thapsia, of sagapenum, and of the juices [760] of the Cyrenaic and the Median [silphium], and of anything else, if there is any, similar to these. From putrefaction come that of leaven and that of what is called psoricum. Further, there is also dung, which arises from putrefaction. All [kinds of dung] would in this way at least be of the drawing power, but the difference among them is not small. For that of the pigeon is sufficiently drawing; and equally distant from it on either side stand that of the goose, toward the hotter, and that of the cock, toward the colder. Falling still further short of this [i.e. the cock's] are that of human beings and that of pigs. That of dogs is like the cleansing drugs, and the more so when they eat bones. And that of land crocodiles achieves this still more exactly. There is also another kind of drawing drugs, which attract by affinity of quality, which is nothing other than by similarity of the whole substance, just as things that are nourished also attract their proper nourishment. To such drugs belong all the purgative ones and some of the protective remedies. All such [drugs] must be hot.

For among things similar in their substances, the hotter is the more drawing [761], having, as it were, taken on heat as an ally to the similarity. For such a thing, drawing by two causes, will have the advantage over that which attracts by one of them alone. It will make no difference whether one speaks of an attractive, a drawing, or a tractive power. But since enough has been said about these too, let us pass on to the powers named protective and antidotal. The nature of these too is twofold: some alter, others evacuate from the affected body either the destructive venom or the deleterious drug. They alter, then, either by some single quality, or by a pairing of two, or by their whole substances; they evacuate by the similarity of the whole substance and by fine-particled heat. In all, therefore, there will be four differences of the benefit coming from them, two alterative and two evacuative. And the one that helps by the opposition of the quality is plain.

For if the deleterious drug, or the venom of the animal, should be cold, they will be benefited by heating drugs; [762] if hot, by cooling ones; and if dry, by moistening ones, if moist, by drying ones; and so too, if it is at once cold and moist, by drying and heating ones, if hot and dry, by moistening and cooling ones; and analogously in the case of the remaining two pairings. Nor is the alteration that comes about through [the action] of the powers in respect of the whole substance obscure to those who remember what was demonstrated earlier, both in the commentaries On the Natural Faculties and, in addition, in those On Mixtures. For the powers that alter deleterious drugs are by nature intermediate between the bodies that are affected and the drugs that harm them, so that there is a proportion: as the body is to the protective power, so is that power to the deleterious; and likewise, as the deleterious is to the protective, so also is the protective to the body. And for this reason nearly all the things that oppose deleterious drugs, if taken in larger quantity, greatly harm the body of the living creature.

It is necessary, then, that all such [763] powers be given in such a due proportion of quantity that they neither harm the body by their abundance nor, through their smallness, are overcome by the deleterious drugs. But this already belongs to the therapeutic method; for now let us keep to what comes next. Every deleterious venom is evacuated by drugs applied from outside, namely by those that effect the drawing either by heat or by the likeness of their whole substance. And here too the protective remedy must be, as far as is possible, intermediate in its nature between the body which it treats and the harmful venom. For if it is most opposite to the body, it will rather act upon the body like some deleterious drug, and will not evacuate the venom. For, to take up the whole matter again for the sake of clarity, one must know that all deleterious powers are most opposite in mixture to the bodies harmed by them. If, then, they are evacuated by drugs similar to them in mixture, these drugs too would surely be opposite to the natures of the bodies.

And indeed they are contrary in a way, yet not to such a degree as to destroy it; rather they incline both ways, being set in the middle between the things that directly harm the body of the animal and [764] those that benefit it. Whether you choose to call the powers deleterious, or destructive, or corruptive, or whatever else you like, it will make no difference; and in the same way, whether you call the others alexeteric or alexipharmic. Nor, if someone should wish to name those remedial for venomous beasts alexeteric and those remedial for deleterious drugs alexipharmic, as some have already thought fit to do, must one dispute with these people either about the names. For the proper healing of diseases comes not from these, but from knowledge of the things themselves. Since enough has been said about these matters too, in due measure for present purposes, let us now pass next to the account of the anodyne and soothing or mitigating powers, or however one might wish to name them. Now, of anodyne power, one kind is truly so, while another is only called so, as if someone were to call even a dead human being anodyne. The truly anodyne power, then, is that of things that warm in the first order, when it is contained in a fine-particled substance.

The other is that of the so-called cold drugs, when, employing unmixed cooling, they numb [765] the part; and numbness is very nearly an absence of sensation. Those drugs that stop pains by healing the condition could not reasonably be called anodyne, for this belongs in common to all things that treat. Truly anodyne drugs, then, must be fine-particled and not much hotter than the moderate ones, so as to evacuate, disperse, rarefy, thin, concoct and even out whatever has been caught and shut up within the parts in pain: pungent, viscous or thick juices; many juices obstructed in narrow pores; or also some vaporous and thick, or considerably cold, pneuma that has no suitable outlet.

There must therefore be absolutely no astringent power at all in them, not even if the place or the affection should additionally require it. From this it is clear that sometimes they will in no way benefit the condition but will only soothe the pain, in which case they will also be called truly anodyne; but sometimes they will also give some additional benefit to the condition itself and will have a twofold power, being at the same time an anodyne [766] and a healing drug. These matters too will be discussed more fully in the books of the Therapeutic Method. For the present it is enough to explain that, of these drugs specifically named anodyne, some, as has been said, belong to the first rank of the heating drugs, and these are indeed truly anodyne, such as dill oil; others are [hot] to a degree close to that of our own body itself, such as those called suppurative, whose materials have been discussed earlier. Their use will be determined in the books of the Therapeutic Method. Those, however, that produce torpor when drunk, and for this reason are called anodyne and soporific by most people, are of a mixture most opposite to the truly anodyne drugs. For they all cool the body and numb sensation to such an extent that, if a little more is drunk, it brings on death. The best of them for the use in question are those that dry.

And those that contain a quantity of cold moisture, as hemlock does, are not good when drunk. Such too is mandrake, [767] except for the dry bark of its root, and henbane, except for its seed; and among these the white seed is better than the black. Some, however, are contrary to us in their whole substances, and for this reason, even if they are taken in the smallest amount, they do harm in every case: for instance dryopteris, the pine caterpillar, thapsia, the maddening strychnos, quicksilver, some of the mushrooms, and the saliva and biles of venomous animals. For all such things are deleterious by their kind, not by their quantity. And for this reason none of them is put into the protective antidotes, as are the juice of the poppy, myrrh, storax and saffron. For if these are drunk in larger quantity, some of them drive one mad and others bring death; but when mixed in with the other ingredients in a certain due proportion they are of help. Of these, those that harm the intellect are, most of them, at once productive of heaviness of the head, filling the head with a quantity of noxious vapours. Some also lay hold of the mouth of the stomach, so that the parts in the head suffer in sympathy.

In general, all of them harm the brain in a twofold way: either by being [768] contrary in their whole substances, or by altering its mixture through one or two qualities. And since these matters too have been discussed sufficiently, at least for present purposes, it would be time to take up again the main headings of what has been said and to add what seems to be lacking in the account. For in actual truth nothing remains: all the secondary powers have already been stated, of what sort they are according to genus, and not a few of the powers according to species have also been set beside them as examples, starting from which one could go through the remaining ones. But for the sake of clarity it would be no worse to go over them again under brief headings.

For instance, everyone names a certain purgative power, but not all of them equally grasp that the name signifies two things: the one a common sense, applied to all things that in any way whatever clear out the residues of the animal; the other a sense by pre-eminence, applied to those that do so through vomitings or the drawing down of the belly. Nor do they grasp that the [purgation] which takes place through the nostrils and [769] mouth is of the same kind as such purgations. The drugs that are poured in through the nostrils for the sake of purging the head they call errhines; those that are gargled and those that are chewed they take together under one name and call apophlegmatizing, and they name their powers apophlegmatic. Of the same kind as these are also those that purge when applied to the uterus. For all the things that I have listed as purging have a drawing power, some of a single humour, others of two or even more, and this is common to them. For those that are of a nature, by thinning the thick and viscous humours, to provoke urine or to assist the expectorations from the thorax and lung, clear out as well, but they are not named in the same way as the aforementioned. Rather, some are called diuretic and cough drugs, others drugs that bring on the menses. They differ from the aforementioned in that they do not, as those do, have a drawing power of humours proper to them. In these cases too, however, the account needs a further distinction, as follows.

Those that are applied to the uterus in pessaries, or in vapour-baths, or in some other such way [770] act for a twofold cause: some provoke [the flow] by heating alone, others by the so-called drawing and purging powers, which we have shown to produce the evacuations through their affinity with the things drawn. But those that are drunk produce the evacuations by thinning the blood and by clearing the obstructions from the pores and opening their mouths, not by any drawing power. The former, then, are of the same kind as the purging drugs, the latter as those that generate milk and semen, about which we shall speak a little later, after we have first gone through the cough drugs, since these too are named in two ways: some from producing coughs, others merely from stopping them. Their powers are most opposite. For some are of a thinning nature, the others of a thickening one. The thinning power, then, arises in hot and fine-particled substances, the thickening power in cold and coarse-particled ones. Let this discussion end here. It is proper to pass on to the one postponed a little earlier.

For there is a certain community and likeness of actions and powers among [771] the things that provoke and that stop menses, milk and semen. Lying somehow alongside them are the diuretics and the cough remedies, so each of these must also be discussed in turn. The powers productive of milk and semen are found some in drugs only, others in foods as well. In drugs, when by heating the phlegmatic humours we change them into blood; in foods, according to the likeness of the whole substance, and when they are of good juice, moderately moist, and of a lukewarm heat, such as milk itself also has. For blood partakes of a heat commensurate with the animal, yellow bile of more than is in measure, just as phlegm partakes of more coldness. Milk is midway between phlegm and blood as far as heat is concerned, yet it does not stand equally distant from each, but is farther from phlegm and nearer to blood. Whenever, then, milk collects deficiently in the breasts and you wish more of it to be produced, examine the blood; for it is either less than is proper or more depraved.

The [772] deficient blood, then, requires the whole regimen to be moistening and warming; blood of worse quality, if it is bilious, requires first purging and then a regimen of the kind described; if it is phlegmatic, it requires drugs that warm, either in the first or in the second order, but that do not dry. Better than these are those that are not drugs only but also foods: rocket, fennel and dill. I mean the herbs themselves while they are still green and moist, for when dry they both dry and warm more than is needed. To this class belong also smyrnium, celery, sion and polium, these too green, before they have been dried. For all drying things, consuming the moisture of the blood, render it at once thicker and less in quantity, and hotter than it should be if they are hot in nature, colder if they are cold.

The blood, I suppose, needs to be moderately hot and in no way thick for the generation of milk.
