Hence all things of this kind quench milk rather than generate it, whereas those that heat, as has been said, but have no share in any evident dryness, have reasonably been said to possess powers generative of milk [773]. These, then, are few in number, for it is not easy to hit upon the due proportion in the mixture described above. But the things that harm milk are, as one might put it, countless and beyond enumeration. Those that heat more than is needed, those that dry, and those that cool all prevent milk from being generated: some by damaging the quality of the blood, others by making its whole substance less. A power closely similar to those just mentioned belongs to the things that by nature promote or stop the menses. For the material common to both is the blood in the veins. When this is at once free-flowing and moderate in quantity, it furnishes an abundant supply to each. It has, moreover, been stated elsewhere that there are veins, and not small ones, common to the breasts and the uterus, and which these happen to be. For this reason, whenever the blood is carried to one of the two sets of parts, the other is dried up.

And for this reason women whose menses flow in due measure do not collect milk in their breasts, and in those in whom [774] this is abundant the menses are completely held back. It is therefore no wonder if the regimens and the drugs that produce and those that stop the monthly purgation from the uterus are similar to those that produce and stop the generation of milk in the breasts. They differ, however, to this extent: the things concerning the womb sometimes require hotter and more cutting drugs. For the veins there need to be opened at their mouths more than those at the breasts, and they require the blood to be more free-flowing, since the womb itself contributes nothing to its conveyance. For the menses are sent into the veins in it; they are not drawn. Into the breasts, however, the blood is not only sent but also drawn, and for this reason blood that does not arrive in sufficient quantity at the breasts needs slighter assistance from drugs. And whatever things prompt the blood to pass downward also benefit deficient purgations.

But those [purgations] that have been impaired to a greater degree, or are even entirely suppressed, none of such things any longer cures; rather savin [775] and meum, iris and calamint, pennyroyal and dittany, asarum and costus, cassia and cinnamon, amomum and birthwort, and bunium, and all other such things, cure the complete suppressions of the purgations by way of the uterus. For such things also lead on the urine. But they differ from those same drugs that are called diuretic in this one respect only: that they do not dry strongly. For heating is common to three kinds of drugs: to those that assist the generation of milk, and to those that assist the flows of the menses and of the urine. They differ, however, both in the quantity of their heat and in that some dry and others do not. For those that do not dry and that heat moderately are useful for the generation of milk; those that heat to a greater degree, yet do not dry strongly, are good for the flows of the menses. Both of these, indeed, also promote urination; but no less effective for this are those that heat while drying.

And for this reason such drugs have been called diuretic in a special sense: not because they alone stimulate urination, but because they stimulate urination alone, without menses and [776] milk. For, besides the other points, drying drugs are not suitable for expectorations from the thorax and lung either. Those too need to be cut but not dried, just as the stones in the kidneys and bladder do. Such drugs have been discussed earlier. Just as with milk, so too with semen, they are accustomed to call some drugs generative, and the ones opposite to these extinguishing; others provocative, and the ones opposite to these checking. Generative, then, are those that generate what did not exist before, and extinguishing those that destroy it. Provocative are those that bring what has been collected in the depth to the surface, and the ones opposite to these are checking. Generative of semen, then, among foods are those that are at once nourishing and flatulent and akin in their whole substances; among drugs, those that are pneumatic and hot. Extinguishing are all drying ones, all cooling ones, and those contrary in their substances. And moreover provocative are those that are flatulent and hot without drying, and checking are the opposite ones.

For since the substance of the semen [777] has its generation from a useful residue, and is moreover pneumatic, all things that are able to generate and to call forth semen must be at once nourishing and pneumatic. Now bulbs, chickpeas, broad beans, octopuses and pine-cone are said to be, and are, foods productive of much semen; skink and satyrion are drugs that do so. Things that are at once nourishments and drugs productive of much semen are the seed of flax and rocket. But all foods and drugs that are by nature cooling, and that thicken and congeal the semen and make it stationary, have the power of those that check it, not of those that destroy it. Such are lettuces, blite, oraches, gourd, mulberries, melons, and cucumbers, whether they are ripe or not ripe. Those things that dry do not even allow the semen to be generated in the first place, even if they are hot in nature, as rue is. And if they do not heat as well, they do so much more, as the water-lily does. These, at any rate, may reasonably be held to be opposed to semen also through the peculiar property of their substance.

The same analogy of foods and [778] drugs is also to be found in the case of milk and of the menses. In another way, there fall under the same genus with them those things that assist expectorations from the respiratory organs and those that naturally provoke urination. For all of these are of thinning power, just as their opposites are of thickening power. But on the thinning diet I have written separately, and in the same book the thickening things are set out no less. The thinning and thickening drugs, however, you should select from the three books that follow these, taking as your mark, for the thinning ones, those that have heat and fine-particledness, and, for the thickening ones, the opposite. For we have shown in the foregoing that the nature of fine-particled drugs is a distinct one, belonging not only to heating drugs; and in the same way the nature of coarse-particled drugs belongs not only to cooling ones. And just as in such cases there exists a certain analogy among the powers, in the same way one should search in all cases, even if there happens to be no established name.

At any rate, certain powers are called 'oxydorcic' (sight-sharpening): those which correct the eyes when, having no [779] perceptible affection, they nonetheless function poorly. And clearly there must also be some such power, analogously, for the ears and the nostrils and for each of the other senses. Yet no 'sharp-hearing' power has been given a name, just as none has for the sense of smell or taste or touch, even though such a power exists analogously in the very matters of sense themselves. And if one were to extend the similarity further, there must also be, for each of our parts, some such power of drugs, by which, evidently, the function of the part becomes better: as, for example, the function of the stomach. For here too one can often find a certain atony of it, of the same kind as dimness of sight is in the eyes, when they are neither inflamed nor suffering a flux nor ulcerated nor have any other evident ill.

And indeed the drugs that correct such a condition of the stomach have been called 'digestive' (πεπτικά). In the form of their designation they are not [780] analogous to the 'sharp-sighting' ones, but in their effect and in their power they are closely similar. Since we said that some powers have also been named from parts of the body, it would not be amiss to go through these as well. For they are neither suited, as one might suppose, to all the affections of the part, nor to a single one in such a way as to benefit nothing else. Rather, they got their designation from the part either because [they are used for it] most often, or because they act most of all upon that particular part. They are called ophthalmic because we use them both most of all and most often on the eyes. Such are the collyrium made from roses, the one made from pompholyx, the one called Cnicus, the Libanium, and all the others. It is possible to use these also when the ears are affected, and the mouth, the nose, the genitals and the seat, though neither so often nor so beneficially. Again, [we call powers] hepatic, splenic, pleuritic and stomachic because we see these, too, benefiting each of those mentioned most of all and most often.

What the cause of the benefit is [781] will be stated in the treatise on the Therapeutic Method, in which we also go through everything else concerning the use of drugs, so that there is no need to lengthen the discussion here any further, except perhaps to remark briefly on the use of names which certain others of the more recent physicians introduced as innovators, and not least the so-called Methodists. For that they speak of certain 'checking' (stalticai) powers, that is, constricting, or drawing together, or repelling, or something else of that kind, is neither absurd nor obscure. But when they say that certain materials or powers are 'metasyncritic', what is said is neither clear nor true nor proper to their sect, since they claim to avoid the indication taken from dogmatic suppositions, for, they say, the apparent novelties suffice them. But that, when the pores of the body are turned aside from the natural state into the unnatural, certain affections arise according to the particular character of their alteration, is a dogmatic supposition.

And from this assumption there follows also the claim that for such affections [782] there are certain metasyncritic powers, namely powers that alter the unnatural pore-formation of our compound. For it is precisely in this way that Thessalus and his followers use these terms, and then they apply such powers to those who suffer chronically from flux, without having demonstrated either that an alteration of the pores occurs in such affections or that these drugs are by nature such as to effect metasyncrisis, nor being able to point out the faulty pore-formation. For why, in the name of the gods, do mustard, thapsia and pellitory, and the root of the caper, and in short all things whose nature is to burn, if they remain in contact with the body for a long time, effect a metasyncrisis of the pore-formation? That the fluxional parts are benefited by such drugs is plainly evident; but why they are benefited is a problem for natural inquiry. We, then, say that their mixture is moist and cold, and that for this reason they need things that heat and dry; but others will give other causes, according to whatever assumptions they happen to hold about the elements of the body.

It is not, however, fitting for anyone of those who are led by another sect to utter [783] the name 'metasyncrisis', except for those who both consider and name the bodies of animals 'syncrimata', made out of masses that are atomic, or least, or partless, or homoeomerous; and not even for all of these, but only for those who, like Thessalus, refer such diseases to the canon of the alteration of the pores. For Thessalus does not say this insofar as he is a Methodist, since, whenever he discourses with us as a Methodist, he departs from the indication taken from things non-evident; he says it insofar as he is a dogmatist, starting from the same elements as Asclepiades, though not following him in every respect. But now is not the time to go through such matters at greater length. For some of them are more proper to the therapeutic Method, while others will be stated more precisely in the books on the sect of Themison and Thessalus.

It is time, then, to bring this discussion too to a close here, after adding to it two further main headings. The one belongs among the matters deferred earlier and concerns contrary powers. The other is necessary for the discussion that follows, and defines the [784] order of each of the heating and cooling, moistening and drying drugs. Contrary powers, then, must be judged from their effects, as we have often shown in this whole treatise. We said that certain clogging powers are contrary to the cleansing ones, unblocking ones to blocking ones, softening ones to hardening ones, and relaxing ones to tensing ones. For astringent, pungent, bitter, sweet or sour we showed to be not powers of drugs but gustatory qualities. So either one must not seek contrariety in these at all, or one must not seek it as one does among powers. Yet even in these the aim is twofold: their activities and their mixtures. The activities lie in condensing and rarefying; or in drawing out something from the depth, or repelling it; and in thickening the materials or thinning them; or in blocking the pores or unblocking them.

The mixtures, on the other hand, concern the hot and the cold, the wet and the dry; all of these were sufficiently distinguished in the fourth book [785], where we showed that the astringent is earthy and cold, the sour fine-particled and cold, the bitter earthy and fine-particled, and that which is without any distinctive quality cold and watery. In the same way the pungent too was shown to be fiery, and the salty earthy and hot, yet not, however, already fiery. Likewise the sweet too is hot, but not yet caustic. And whatever is oily is all both watery and airy. And their works, of course, followed upon their mixtures. For the astringent is by nature such as to draw together, compress, condense, repel and thicken, and, before all these, to cool and dry; the sour to cut, divide and thin, to unblock and cleanse thoroughly without heating; and the pungent acts similarly to the sour, at least in thinning out and cleansing thoroughly. But it differs in that the sour cools while the pungent heats, and further in that the one repels, while the other draws and disperses.

In the same way, the bitter cleanses the pores, scours them, thins, and [786] cuts the thickness of the humours, without evident heat. The cold watery thickens, condenses, contracts, compacts, deadens and numbs. The pungent thins, cleanses, disperses, breaks open, draws, and forms an eschar. The salty contracts and binds tight, preserves as in pickling, and dries, without distinctive heat or cooling. The sweet concocts, relaxes, rarefies. The oil-like moistens, softens, relaxes. It is now easy, judging by what has been said, to discover which of the flavours are contrary in their mixtures and which in their actions. For my part, it would be a fitting moment, once I have defined the orders of the mixtures and powers in drugs, to bring the discussion to a close here. The well-proportioned drug, being of a mixture like that of the thing to which it is applied, in that it neither dries nor moistens, neither cools nor heats, ought to be called neither dry nor moist, neither cold nor hot.

But that which is either drier or moister, or hotter [787] or colder, is named from the predominating power. And it suffices, for practical purposes, to establish four orders for each predominance: naming hot in the first order whatever heats us, not however manifestly, but such that some rational demonstration is additionally required. So also with cold and moist and dry: whatever needs demonstration, not yet possessing a strong or manifest activity. Those things, however, whose nature is already plainly to heat or to cool or to dry or to moisten will be said to be of the second order. Those that do so already vehemently, yet not to the extreme, of the third. And those whose nature is to heat in such a way as to produce an eschar and to burn, of the fourth. So too those whose nature is to cool more vehemently, so as already to deaden, these also are of the fourth. But it is not possible to find anything drying of the fourth order without its burning; for whatever dries to the extreme certainly also burns.

Of the third order of drying things, however, there can be something that does not also burn, as is the case with all things that are strongly astringent, [788] among which are omphakion, sumach, alum, balaustion, and the unripe oak-gall. Among these very things, some are close to the burning ones, such as flake of copper and burnt copper, so that they lie somewhere in the indistinct region between the third and the fourth order. Others are in the middle, such as burnt copper if it has been washed, and others at the beginning, such as hypocistis. In the same way, in the second and in the fourth order too, it is possible to make threefold distinctions. For the cautery-iron surely does not dry in the same way as mustard, although both belong to the fourth order. Concerning all these things, distinctions will be drawn in what follows for each simple drug individually.

Since, however, a drug is also said to be softening and relaxing, rarefying and condensing, clogging and dispersing, and very many other things similar to these, it would be better to go through such things too. Together with them, or even still before them, I should also treat the [620] substance and at the same time the power of all the flavours (χυμοί). Something was said about this in the first of these commentaries too, at the end, when I also quoted the passage of Plato from the Timaeus. But there it was for the sake of recalling the perceptible affections which the tongue is naturally disposed to undergo in respect of each of them, whereas here my discourse will be about their substance and power. For the other parts of the animal are, of course, also affected in a way similar to the tongue, yet they do not perceive the affections precisely. The tongue, however, besides being affected, also possesses precision of sensation, and so it is capable of discerning the nature of all these things. For it is not the case that what is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist is naturally disposed to cool, or heat, or dry, or moisten the tongue, but not each of the other parts as well. Rather, just as it disposes and alters the tongue, so it also disposes and alters the other parts, the difference arising in them according to the more and the less, not according to being affected or not being affected.

For it is plain to everyone that the tongue is by nature [621] able to discern a dry and a moist, a hot and a cold body no less than all the other parts of the animal; but bitterness and sweetness, saltiness and sourness, harshness, acerbity and pungency it alone is believed to distinguish, although one can find the similarity of the affections in all the other parts as well, and especially in those that are ulcerated. For the hardness and density of the skin shuts out and fights off, and prevents from passing through to the flesh, the powers of the things that fall upon it from outside. For it is in this sense that Hippocrates also made that statement: 'to ulcers cold is biting', although to the skin before it was ulcerated it was not biting. And to the eyes too, and to the nostrils, and to the parts of the animal in the mouth, cold is biting.

and not least to the inner parts of the stomach and intestines, so that it is often difficult to distinguish whether someone has been chilled or is being bitten through the pungency of a humour. These things happen with good reason. For since the cold draws together the substance of whatever it touches, and condenses and constricts it, it is necessary, first, that in this process the thin fluids are excreted, [622] as tears from the eyes and coryza from the nostrils; and then it also appears biting to these parts, though in a different manner from the hot. For it is not by eating through what is continuous, but by tearing it apart, that the cold is at once painful and biting; hence it does not appear such to hard bodies either. For when soft things are drawn together and compressed, it happens both that their fluid is squeezed out and that their parts are torn apart: the fluid, as in a sponge drawn together and compressed by our hands; the tearing apart, as in things that are divided and torn apart, whether by us pulling with our hands or by something else. For something of this sort must also be suffered by rare and soft bodies under the action of the cold, since their rarity readily admits the chilling within, and the soft parts in the depth are still more readily congealed by it.

Entering, then, through each of the pores in rare bodies (such as are all ulcerated parts, and the eyes, the nostrils, the mouth and the parts about the stomach), the cold lays hold of all the parts of the bodies being cooled and, as it were with many [623] grips all round, gathering them together and compressing them, tears them away from the parts continuous with them. In this affection, then, not a few empty spaces must come to be, not only because the thin fluids are pressed and excreted, but also because the soft substance is drawn together into a smaller place. But an empty space cannot arise in continuous bodies while their continuity is preserved. If, then, one does arise, it is clear that this continuity is destroyed and the continuous body is torn apart; and in this the affection of sensation that is at once distressing and biting presents itself. Yet the quality of both is not the same, of the things that bite by cooling and of those that bite by heating. In the former we at once also have a perception of the substance being drawn together and constricted; in the latter, a perception of its being dissolved and diffused. Moreover, the speed is not alike in the two affections: with cooling things the biting is somehow slower, whereas with heating things it passes through most swiftly.

Since, then, the matter has now been adequately distinguished, both by the very nature of the things and by our perception of them, and it has been stated clearly [624] in what way the hot, and in what way the cold, appears biting, one ought surely to reason out, even before hearing it from us, that of the biting drugs some must be hot in their powers and others cold. One can also learn from us in addition their precise distinctions, once we have first recalled that we call both a drink and a bath 'hot' when they are well-tempered, sometimes using the term loosely. For they ought rather to be called well-tempered and moderate than hot. Things hot in this way, then, are gentle and congenial. For what is compacted and congealed in our bodies is diffused, and it is chiefly in this affection that pleasure lies for animals. But if prolonged, these too gradually become distressing. For the diffusion passes over into such immoderation that our substance is dispersed, dissolved and scattered. Yet even in this case they cause distress without biting, producing fainting and collapse of strength, so that even death follows.

But things still hotter than these cut, divide and separate the substance, so that of necessity they appear biting, as [625] do boiling water and fire itself. And in the same way, of cold things, those that draw together but do not yet tear apart the continuity of the body they come near are only cold, and not yet in any way biting. But those that tear apart in addition to drawing together appear biting; all such things evidently employ their compression violently. To draw together and to congeal the underlying matter is therefore always peculiar to the cold, and to diffuse and to melt is peculiar to the hot; but biting is common to both when they have increased beyond measure. Now those things that are cold and hot in the strict sense lay hold even of our skin, in addition to all the other rare and soft members of which we spoke earlier. I remember once journeying through snow so deep that no part of the ground appeared bare. The air appeared perfectly clear, and a breeze blew off the snow, so very cold that it bit not only the eyes, or the nostrils as well, but the whole face too. And if one also put a hand out, it laid hold of this likewise.

But whatever falls short of extreme coldness or heat does not bite the [626] skin. The cooling ones are neither able to tear apart any of its continuity, on account of its hardness, nor do they succeed in penetrating into the depth, because of the condensation of the surface. The heating ones do not bite it because they do not eat through it but only diffuse, and because they sometimes pass readily through the pores. What contributes most to such affections is whether the substance of the drugs is coarse-particled or fine-particled. For among the cooling drugs the fine-particled reach further into the depth, and for this reason bite more vehemently; among the heating drugs the coarse-particled ulcerate more, and for this reason distress more violently. Now air is more fine-particled and earth more coarse-particled, and water lies between both. But air, when set on fire, becomes flame, and earth becomes live coal. Water admits a strong warmth, yet it becomes neither flame nor live coal, on account of its innate moisture. For flame and live coal are kinds of fire.

All fire is hot and dry, but it is not possible for water to become dry, and for this reason it does not receive the quality of fire precisely, as earth and air do. Now no drug [627] is as hot as flame or live coal or boiling water; even if it is very hot, it surely falls very far short of these at any rate. Their heat does, however, advance as far as burning when it is contained in a coarse-particled substance. Those whose heat is in fine-particled substances sometimes do not bite at all, but only heat. At other times the drug is biting, but does not yet also burn. One must remember the conception of fine-particled and coarse-particled things: those that are quickly dissolved into fine parts we call fine-particled, and those that cannot undergo this we call coarse-particled. What dissolves them is the heat in the body of the animal, in whatever way they happen to be applied on each occasion. Their being broken up into fine or coarse parts, however, they have from their own nature. So also among the cooling drugs, those that are coarse-particled cannot bite, since they do not succeed in getting through the outer surface of the skin.

But those that are fine-particled both slip through easily and penetrate into the [628] depth, and bite the soft parts of the animal; and still more do those bite which are at once fine-particled and anomalous in their mixtures. It has been shown in what precedes that nearly all things are anomalous. For it is either impossible or very difficult to discover any substance whatsoever that is exactly homoeomerous. Wine, at any rate, we said has within itself, first, one coarse-particled residue, from which, as it is separated out and carried down in the course of time, the lees are formed; second, another, which is called the 'flower', floating on the surface during the time of boiling, but later carried down into the lees; and a third, watery, mixed through the whole of the wine, to which the boiling belongs first and most of all. Fourth, in addition to these, is the wine itself, that which is truly wine. It has been shown too that in oil and milk and all the other juices there is a similar nature of residues, and still more so in all mined substances taken as wholes.

Having recalled these things, we must now examine all drugs, and first guard against suffering what most of those who have investigated such matters [629] have suffered. For they frame their argument as though all things were homoeomerous, not granting that either wine or oil or any of the other things is composed of parts differing in their powers; and still more than at these, in the case of vinegar they are astonished if we dare to say of it that it has lost the innate heat of the wine and has instead heat from putrefaction, which is indeed the view of both Aristotle and Theophrastus. For the vinous parts of the wine are cooled off in the change into vinegar, while the watery residue, putrefying, takes on a certain acquired heat, just as all other things that have putrefied do. And so vinegar becomes something compounded of parts most opposite in their powers, some cooled off, others hot, as are all the ashes of burnt wood. For in these too a sort of ember is scattered about in small particles, and this is quite hot, while all the rest is earthy and cold.

And for this reason, whenever ash moistened with water is strained in due measure through certain rare bodies, the hot and [630] pungent parts are carried off along with it in this process, while what remains is no longer hot, having deposited its fiery parts in the water. People call such water lye (κονία), analogous to sea-water and brine in respect of disposition, of generation and of power. For those are composed of water and salt, whereas the water that washes round the ash, having become composite out of itself and of the parts it carried along with it, has in this way produced what is named lye. Had we not known beforehand that this lye came into being out of water and the sooty parts of the ash, we might perhaps have supposed it to be a simple and uncompounded body.

For we have experienced something of this sort in the case of vinegar too: being unable to see its generation through sense-perception, we disbelieve the argument. But, if nothing else, once we have considered at least its difference from the unripe grape, we shall be right to believe that not a sour flavour only, but also some other, pungent flavour is mixed into it. For this reason the juice of the unripe grape cools completely, so that it is also supremely suited to causus, when applied over the mouth of the stomach or over the whole of the hypochondria, and to anything whatever that we may wish to cool, [631] but vinegar does not do so in like manner. For it is not strictly one thing, nor sour only, but also pungent. Now whatever is sour only is in every case cold, whether a pear, or an apple, or sumach, or the fruit from brambles, or that from the mulberry, or that from the pomegranate, or any other whatever, be it fruit, or juice, or plant, such as oxylapathon and oxalis, which they also call oxys. For if, when you taste it, the sourness in it shows itself strong and distinct, while nothing of pungency appears in it, you will find this flavour cooling in every case, and you may use it with confidence, whether you wish to use it for causus, applying it over the hypochondria, or for erysipelas, or for any other hot affection. In the same way you will also clearly find all the cold diseases harmed by it. But when the quality appears to you mixed, then with pungency one must also suspect heat, and with astringency some other kind of coldness. For sour coldness is fine-particled, astringent coldness coarse-particled.

[632] But we shall state the proofs of these things a little later. What must first be advised to those who examine such matters without sophistical imposture, for the sake of the truth itself, it is now time for me to say: that one must not be trained in reason alone, through the logical methods which I am always urging and which I set out in the commentaries On Demonstration, but must also diligently train the gustatory sense on flavours, beginning from those that possess one single quality, whichever it may be, in the most evident form.

If you wish to apprehend pungency clearly, do so with garlic and onion and things similar to them, tasting them repeatedly and chewing them for as long as possible, and trying to lay up accurately in your memory the sensation of the affection that arises; if astringency, with oak-gall and sumach and things similar; if bitterness, by tasting nitre and bile; if sweetness, boiled-down must and honey. And further, in addition to these, whether you wish to regard it as without quality or as intermediate in quality with respect to taste, I ask that you taste [633] water too and hold it accurately in your memory, and above all water that displays none of the qualities I have just named, neither sweetness nor pungency nor sourness nor bitterness, and in addition to these is neither notably hot nor excessively cold. For setting out from this you will arrive more readily at the discernment of all the other faint flavours, and at that of those which I call sweet but certain others call watery, such as the flavour of green reeds and of agrostis-grass, and moreover of wheat and barley and zeia and many others, which Theophrastus also mentions when he inquires whether several species of sweet flavours are to be posited, or whether they are to be supposed to differ from one another by the more and the less. But concerning these I shall draw distinctions later.

Whatever sensation the water that is most devoid of quality affords you, when you find such a sensation in one of the dry substances, such a substance is evidently outside all manifest heat and coldness, having a state as nearly intermediate as possible [634], or else one inclining slightly towards the cold. But if, being so disposed as regards the difference of heat and coldness, it is dry in consistency, it must necessarily be earthy and dry without biting. All such drugs are called by the physicians clogging, as are most of those that have been thoroughly washed: starch, pompholyx, white lead, lime, cadmia, Cretan earth, Cimolian earth, groats, Samian star and fullers' earth belong to the clogging drugs. Some of them are not only earthy but also watery in nature, and some even contain no small amount of air within them; all these, however, are viscous, and for this reason clogging. For the nature of clogging substances is twofold: the one exactly earthy and dry, the other wholly viscous, but mixed of water and earth and in most cases also of air, as is sweet olive oil too. I have said earlier what I mean by sweet.

This, then, is mixed from airy and at the same time earthy and watery substance; the white of the egg [635] is in a way from the same, but it is more earthy than oil. And indeed the cheesy part of milk is also clogging, as is the fat of the pig. For the fat of the bull and of the he-goat has much pungency, and that fiery; that of the ox and the goat has less, but in some measure the suet of these too is already pungent. For indeed the fat of such animals is also called 'suet' (stear) on account of its thickness. For, further, it is not only hotter but also more earthy than that of pigs. The fat of the goose and of the cock is both hotter and drier than that of pigs, but it is also fine-particled and least earthy. So too is that of all birds, because the substance of their body also has no small share of the airy. But about these there is another discussion. Such fats, then, as do not yet have any pungency are clogging of the pores, and more so the drier and more earthy ones. Of this kind too is washed wax; for it also puts off the pungency derived from the honey. It is plain that these things are not said of wax that is bitter by nature, such as the Pontic is.

For that wax gets its bitterness from wormwood [636], and even if you were to wash it ten thousand times, you would not completely wash out the bitterness. One must also beware of wax from pungent, thyme-flavoured honey whenever you wish to prepare a drug that is strictly non-biting. The wax suited to washing, then, is that from a more watery and least pungent honey. Such, then, are the clogging drugs. I return now to the astringent and the sour. The astringent are earthy and coarse-particled in the consistencies of their masses, and cold in quality. The sour are fine-particled in their bodies, but cold in the same way as the astringent. The proof concerning both is twofold: in respect of perception, by apagōgē; in respect of reason, from their substance. The first of the proofs to be stated will be the one that is clearer to most people, but weaker as regards scientific demonstration.

All the fruits of trees which appear sweet to us when ripened are, when just being formed, acerbic and dry in consistency, each in accordance with the nature of the [637] tree that produces it, as Theophrastus too said somewhere: olives, grapes, apples, pomegranates, mulberries, dates, pears. As time goes on they become moister and take on sourness in addition to their acerbity, and then, putting this off little by little, they become sweet in turn as they are brought to completion. Some, however, do not do so even on the trees, but recover their sweetness after a time once they have been picked. And certain others do not pass through sourness as an intermediate stage, but go directly from acerbity to sweetness, as does the fruit of the olive. And indeed that they are all concocted by the hot is plain; and that this hot is twofold, the one proper and innate in each, the other coming from outside, from the sun, yet congenital and akin to them, we surely know clearly, if we remember the elements always laid down by us as foundations. But if they are more acerbic at the beginning and become sweet as they ripen, then their sweetness has come about from warmth, and their sourness and acerbity from cooling.

Since, moreover, [638] at the beginning, while still woody, as Theophrastus also said, they are at once dry and acerbic, and it is the quantity of the moisture flowing in upon them that makes them sour, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is more earthy and the sour one moister. Hence Plato too, in defining them, rightly said: all such earthy particles as are carried along in the juices, melting down and contracting and drying out the moist parts of the sensory parts of the tongue, appear acerbic when they are rougher, and harsh when they roughen less. And we in addition to these points shall rightly say that such a flavour is also cold in its mixture. For if it were only earthy, it would be clogging, not acerbic; and in a way the argument, having now passed over to the very substance of the flavours, lays hold of scientific demonstration.

For if the acerbic juice clearly has the property of contracting, drying and roughening the tongue, and it was shown in the preceding discussions that bodies are contracted, constricted and compacted by cold alone, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is altogether cold. And since it also dries unevenly [639] (for this was what roughens), it would also be altogether earthy. For the watery passes evenly through everything, since it belongs to it inseparably to unite again, even if it is torn apart; whereas the earthy body carried along in the juices is already subject to being torn apart, and it is also its property no longer to come together easily. Moreover, the sensation proper to each of the two affections, once you recall it, will bear witness to the same conclusions. For the passage of sour flavours through the sentient bodies is seen to take place quickly, and that of acerbic flavours slowly. And sour things are seen to act more in depth, acerbic things on the surface. All these things, then, indicate that acerbic bodies are coarse-particled and that sour ones are fine-particled.

These things, then, agree sufficiently with one another: both what has been said on the basis of the very substance of the things, and what has been said through induction from what has been found by perception. But it would be no worse to add the following as well, remembering here too, once again, the usage of the names: both the harsh and the acerbic are said to be astringent, but they differ in the more [640] and the less. Moreover, that drugs possess many qualities, not only different but also conflicting with one another, and sometimes even wholly contrary, has been shown sufficiently earlier; but it is necessary to begin from this point now as well. For if on tasting it the same thing should appear to you at once acerbic and biting, I shall bid you leave this drug aside and go on to the acerbic one that is without biting. And if it should appear neither sour, nor sweet, nor bitter, but, as far as is possible, to have one unmixed quality, that of astringency, then you should at once test it by trial in the manner I have often proposed to you before. For if it has at the same time both being astringent and biting, or some other evident quality and power mixed in with the astringency, it is superfluous and vain to bring such a drug to trial when you are assessing the action of astringency. For it is unclear whether it acted in this particular way upon the body near it because of the astringency, or because of one of the qualities mixed in with it, or because of both.

Chalcitis, then, and misy [641] and chalcanthus and copper scale and sory, being at once astringent and biting, act according to both qualities upon each of the bodies they come into contact with, but they cannot teach us clearly whether they have their burning through the astringency or through the pungency. It is better, then, to leave these aside and to taste many others in succession, looking for an astringency that is pure, by itself and on its own as far as possible; and when you find such, then at last judge the drug by the methods you have often heard of before. For instance, if on tasting it balaustion, or oak-gall, or cytinus, or hypocistis, or strychnos, or glaucium, or acacia, or the juice of sumach, or some other such thing appears to you to be precisely acerbic and to have no other evident quality, then examine on such things, and test precisely, the action of astringency. And let the examination, as has been said many times, be made by you both on bodies in the best constitution that are perfectly healthy and on the simple affections, whether hot, or cold, or dry, or moist.

For if it should clearly appear both to cool the healthy [642] body itself and to suit hot affections, and to impart the cold quality manifestly to the patient himself as well, then one may venture to make some declaration about astringency as cooling. But if it should be found to behave in the opposite way, healthy bodies being heated by it, hot diseases exacerbated and cold ones benefited, one must consider such a drug not to cool but to heat. In the same way one should also test the pungent things by themselves, going to onion, garlic, pepper, pellitory, ginger and struthion, as well as elecampane and lime. For just as one who has mixed pepper with the juice of nightshade is able to test neither of them, so neither is one who tests things mixed by nature. In the same manner I require you also to examine the sour quality, the bitter and the sweet, bringing them to the test intense and alone as far as possible, and discovering their powers by experience.

But to submit to experience anything whatever that is acerbic, or harsh, or bitter, as though one were going to obtain from it a test either of acerbity, or of harshness, [643] or of bitterness, is terribly absurd. For if it partakes of one single quality, you will have the same experience of the drug as of the quality; but if of several, then the drug will clearly exert an activity mixed from all of them, so that the activity of the one quality being judged still remains unclear. If, then, one must judge as has been said before, those were not right in their supposition who thought that it was not possible at all to declare anything about the power of the flavours, nor were those who made the judgement in a different way. For it is both possible to declare something about them, and it is fitting to make the judgement in no other way than as has now been said. Now if they had said that there is no need whatever of the investigation concerning the flavours when we examine the powers of drugs (for it is possible even without these to find out their power by experience), I would praise them rather than blame them. But since they treat it as something necessary, yet unknowable, it is just to blame the men on two counts: because they supposed what is not necessary to be necessary, and because they despaired in advance of discovering it.

For indeed the judgement of the [644] power of each of the drugs is found sufficiently, without the discernment of the flavours, by experience alone, when it is tested in the manner I have already stated countless times. And I too have now come to the account of the flavours, not because it is impossible to discover what is sought in another way, but both for the sake of consistency with the principles, so that I might show that everything follows the reasonings about the elements and that nothing anywhere conflicts with them, and so that I might refute those who said that all astringent things heat. And some use of it might also be found for the present treatise of ours. But these things I shall try to show later; for now I return to the matter proposed, and I urge those who long for the truth to taste all the astringent things themselves, as we did, and when they find astringency precisely in some body, as unmixed as possible with the other qualities, then to examine through experience whether such a body is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist. This, then, each person, if he is sensible, will do by himself.

For me, however, it is perhaps necessary [645] to declare something about my own experience: in general terms in the present discourse, and in particular through the books that follow. The general account, covering all of them, would be this. Every astringent body, at least one that is pure of the other qualities as far as perception goes, I have always found, on testing, to be cold. And some even of those mixed with other qualities, namely the moderately sweet, bitter and pungent, were clearly found to cool, evidently because in them the power of astringing and cooling prevails, so that the others are obscured. By the same reasoning all sour things too, both those that are simply sour, such as sorrel (ὀξαλίς) and sour dock (ὀξυλάπαθον), and some of those mixed with other qualities, whether sweet, pungent or bitter, are found to cool no less: pomegranates, apples, plums, grapes, figs, mulberries, cherries, and vinegar itself. But vinegar, as was said before, has a certain pungency mixed into it, while the fruits have sweetnesses and acerbities, and some of them faint bitternesses as well.

And indeed [646] all things that are at once astringent and sour in their qualities, these too I found on testing to be clearly cooling; whereas all things that are sweet only I found to partake of heat directly in proportion to the quantity of their sweetness, so that none of the very sweet things is cold. Something moderately sweet might, however, be cold, when the greater part of the substance of its body is watery; yet not so cold as what is strongly acerbic or sour, but in the way that was said somewhere earlier about the things that partake of a lukewarm warmth. And all bitter things are hot, such as bile, nitre, very old wines, and countless seeds. For the seed of rue, and especially that of the wild rue, and that of tordylon, and that of spondylion, and that of melanthion, and lupins, and the wild ones more so, and bitter vetches, and of these too the wild ones more so, and the so-called pelekinos (it is found among the wheat), and certain almonds, which for this very reason are called bitter, and some seeds of sikya, and that of the Median apple, and besides these countless others, appear bitter to those who taste them.

[647] But concerning bitter things more will be said in what follows. Let us now take up again the account of astringent and sour things and give it its fitting conclusion. That the harsh is a slackened acerbic, one need only be reminded of what sensation tells us. How it comes into being will now be stated. Since the acerbic body was earthy and cold, it will of necessity be slackened in three ways: either by being heated, or by being moistened, or by undergoing both together at the same time. If, then, it is only heated, it does not become either moister or softer, but, remaining hard, it will acquire sweetness, as do the acorns of oaks, and especially those named chestnuts. But if it is only moistened, then if the moisture is coarse-particled and watery, it will be rendered harsh, for watery moisture blunts the power of every flavour; but if the moisture is fine-particled and airy, it makes it sour. For it has been shown that the fine-particled cold produces a sour quality.

But if it is both moistened and heated at the same time, then with watery moisture it will undergo the change into sweetness, and with airy moisture [648] into oiliness. And it has now become evident how fruits, which are acerbic at the beginning, as time goes on in some cases become exactly sweet, in others sour, in others harsh, while some remain acerbic always and some end up oily; and indeed, according to the admixtures of the qualities mentioned, they show a very great variety. Acerbic to the end, then, is the fruit of the prinos (holm oak) and of the komaros (strawberry tree) and of the phēgos (oak) and of the cornel, because it stays cold and dry, just as it was from the beginning, only increasing in size but acquiring no other great alteration. For these very trees themselves are also denser and at the same time drier and colder. Acerbic and at the same time sweet are the fruit of the myrtle, that of the wild pear and that of the oak, and more sweet than acerbic is the fruit called the chestnut. Harsh only are both the fruit and the wine of the Aminaean vines, and all that are similar to these. Harsh and at the same time sweet are the fruit of the date palm and, among wines, the Surrentine, the Sabine and the one called Albatan, and all others of this kind.

Sweet only are the Theraean [wine] [649] and the Scybellites and boiled-down must, and whatever else resembles these. Oily in fruit and juice at once, in the strict sense, is that of the olive, and indeed also all the others from which oil is prepared, such as that of the castor-oil plant and that of the radish, as well as sesame seeds themselves, nuts and almonds. For all such things, as they grow old, become completely oily: the watery and superfluous moisture in them breathes off, while their proper moisture is worked up by the innate heat and exactly concocted. Now those fruits that become only oil-like are edible and sweet. But those to which some bitterness is added in the course of the change become inedible. For everything bitter is inedible, and it comes about through an excess of warmth, as we shall demonstrate next.

But everything sweet is hot, and does not immoderately exceed the heat in us. Rather, it is like hot water, which we take pleasure in touching, especially when we have been chilled: so long as it warms us only to the point of diffusing the parts of the body congealed by the cold [650], and does not dissolve them or cut and separate their continuity, it is most pleasant and most beneficial. So too every sweet food is certainly hot, yet it does not reach a degree of heat that causes distress; it remains within the limits of what diffuses, smooths and softens. Here too recall once more what we have often said before: some things act and are acted upon by one another according to one or two qualities, others according to their whole substances, and among the latter we said there are not a few drugs and all foods. Their kind seems to be twofold, as Theophrastus also indicated. For some are oily, like fat, and others are more or less sweet, such as all the fruits we eat and the flesh of animals, and also many herbs, roots, flowers and shoots. For even if one of these is acerbic, like wild pears and cornels,

it too certainly partakes of sweetness, provided at least that such things are not precisely acerbic, as oak-gall and sumach are; nevertheless, for these very reasons their use is already rather [651] that of drugs than of food. At any rate, women suffering from the craving of pregnancy (kitta), those who are replete, and those whose stomach is slack are seen to desire to taste such things, whereas those who are hungry, on the contrary, turn away from both acerbic and sour things, but take to sweet and oily things and long to be filled with these. Now the oily itself is, of course, also sweet, and everything that nourishes belongs to the genus of sweet things. And this holds of them with good reason, and in accordance with the very substance, so to speak, of food. For nutrition is the replenishment of what has been evacuated. But what was evacuated was proper [to the body], so that what nourishes must also be proper. And if it is proper, it must necessarily be pleasant and friendly, and at the same time also commensurately warm in relation to what is being nourished. But in this there is no small degree of more and less, because we do not come to our food in a precisely natural condition.

For the body of those who need nourishment must only have been emptied, if they are to be exact and fair judges [652] of the quality proper to them. But if, in addition to this, they have become hotter than they ought, or colder, whether in the whole body or in the regions about the tongue or the stomach, they will need not only things that will nourish but also things that either cool or heat. For this reason too, among foodstuffs, now one and now another appears more pleasant to such people. For the pleasant is twofold in kind. One kind refills what has been emptied, and this was nourishment. The other kind heals what has been altered, and this is already a drug. So it happens to foods, when they are given not only to bodies that have been emptied but also to bodies that have been changed in quality, that they now give pleasure in a twofold way, as nourishment and drugs at once. Now as drugs, certain things that cool, heat, dry and moisten will, in due proportion, both gratify and benefit at the same time. As nourishment, however, only those things will do so that are akin and proper to the whole substances of the things being nourished. These, evidently, are by that very fact commensurately hot relative to the things being nourished.

And for this reason there is not one kind of foods [653] or of drugs for all animals. For each of them, according to its own proper substance and at the same time its disposition, is both pleased and benefited by both; but if these things are so, the less sweet of foods will also be less hot, and the sweeter will be hotter by just as much as it is also sweeter. But if it should fall into an immoderation of heat, such a thing is no longer sweet but already appears bitter, as honey does when it grows old and is boiled down, and each of the other sweet things. For just as sweetness arises in each body in a twofold way from a due proportion of heat (some being sweet by their proper and innate heat, others by acquired heat), in the same way bitter things too undergo this: some by being immoderately heated by themselves in the course of the changes over time, and some by being fired by acquired warmth. About bitter things, then, we shall speak next.

All sweet things come close in heat to the bodies to which they appear sweet, but, as has been said, they become [654] such in a twofold manner: some by their own heat, as honey, others by acquired heat, as all things prepared by means of fire. And for this very reason, so long as they are hot, to that extent they also appear more pleasant to those in need of renourishment. And it seems that a certain must, too, appears sweet not through its own warmth alone but also through acquired warmth. For, as both Theophrastus and Aristotle said, there is present in grapes and in the other fruits much of what comes from the sun's warmth, as it were a sort of ember, by which the watery element in them, still as it were half-concocted, is brought to concoction and worked up, being assimilated to what changes it; so that, if you press out the juice of any fruit whatsoever, you will find it at once seething just like must, but its seething differing by more and less to the extent that one fruit differs from another in heat. And once the watery and half-concocted element has been changed and worked up, and the warmth that produces the seething has been breathed out, the proper qualities of the juices appear unmixed, so that it is then that we also discern what sort the wines are according to their own nature.

And at this point [655] I ask you above all to attend to the fact that all harsh wines gradually cease to be such. For as they grow ever older they acquire a certain pungency and sweetness, and in time they lose the astringency that was formerly present in them. Now in some wines, after the boiling, there is an unmixed sweetness, at once pleasant and proper to the nature of the juice itself, not, like the earlier sweetness, a mixed one arising both from the proper sweetness and from the boiling of the half-concocted and watery residue. So that, if it is agreed that all wines become hotter as they age, and it happens that the harsh among them, in growing old, first take on a certain sweetness and pungency as they lay aside their astringency, next increase in pungency and gradually lose their sweetness, and then again, over a longer time, become quite pungent and take on ever more bitterness, and finally, when they thicken, become completely bitter, it is also plain that the sweet is hotter than the acerbic, and the bitter hotter than the sweet.

But if sweetness is produced by [656] a due proportion of heat, it is clear that acerbity will be brought about by the cold when it prevails. That sourness too is fashioned by chilling has indeed been shown by us earlier as well. But since in the present discussion we have explained the change of wines over time that is according to nature, let us also say something about the change that is contrary to nature. Just as, then, the acerbic wine over time is rendered first sweeter, and next more pungent and more bitter, and in the end becomes thoroughly bitter, so in the same manner the wine that has been chilled becomes sourer at once, and if it should be completely chilled it becomes completely sour; and the wine that, rain having set in right at the gathering of the fruit, has been filled with extraneous moisture, and the wine that has otherwise taken on water: all such wines readily turn out sour upon slight occasions. Conversely to them, wines that are brought near fire become ever more sweet, both immediately and afterwards.

But when they pass into a very long time, these too change no less than the others into bitterness, [657] and this seems somehow to be consistent with itself also according to natural reasoning. For if the unripe grape is sour, but the ripe grape is sweet, and ripening comes about in all fruits from the heat of the sun, it is quite clear that what is less complete and colder is sour, and what is more complete and warmer is sweet. Whenever, then, wine turns sour again in being cooled, it is evident that it returns again to the same juice from which it came into being. The juice of the unripe grape, however, differs in power from vinegar to this extent: to vinegar there is added a certain pungency arising from a putrefactive heat. And for this reason Aristotle rightly said of it that the wine's own heat has become cold, while the acquired heat is hot. But the juice of the unripe grape does not have this heat, and for this reason does not have the pungency either. There is, then, a further difference between them, arising from the more and the less in the fine-particled character of their substance. For vinegar is more fine-particled than the juice of the unripe grape, and indeed perception too bears witness to the reasoning. For the cooling from vinegar differs from that from the juice of unripe grapes in its intensity and in its mixed character.

[658] For the cooling from the unripe grape is weaker, yet it does not partake of alien heat, not even a little; that from vinegar, on the other hand, is stronger to the same degree that it is also more fine-particled. And it also has a share of a heating pungency, which is not sufficient to overcome the cooling that comes from the sourness, but which assists the speed of its passage through. For to the degree that the hot is more penetrating than the cold, to that degree the pungent flavour also passes through the pores of the sentient bodies more readily than the sour one, so that the one, arriving first, as it were opens the way, and the other follows not far behind. In this way the mixed and hard-to-express character of the sensation is produced: the sensation can declare vinegar neither simply cold, for it perceives in it a certain fiery pungency, nor simply hot. For the cooling from the sourness that follows continually overtakes the warming from the pungency that leads the way, and at once dims and extinguishes it. And for this reason the sensation and the condition arising from the cooling are much greater than those arising from the heat.

[659] If you mix a little vinegar with a larger amount of honey, you will at once clearly perceive cooling and heat. For if you blend a little honey with much vinegar, the mixture will appear to you cold in greater measure than hot; but if a little vinegar with much honey, more heating than cold. And even if you mix them equal in bulk, you will find that the vinegar still prevails, at least in power. But if, as has been said, the honey is much the greater, you will find, conversely, that in such a blend the cooling is equal to the heat. For the vinegar has departed from the moderately hot things towards cooling by some many times greater amount than the honey has towards heat. It has at any rate been shown before as well that violent heat cannot coexist with sweetness. And it was well said long ago that all true things agree with one another. And indeed, for burning hypochondria the juice of the unripe grape is better than vinegar itself, because its cooling is neither violent and smiting nor admixed with biting heat.

Those so affected need to be soothed without violence, as has been said, and not to acquire from outside any [660] biting heat or pungency. These matters, then, already in some way touch upon the therapeutic method, which in many places shares common ground with the present treatise; and for this reason let us leave them and return again to the matter at hand. Now the juice of the unripe grape is not only sour but also acerbic. For, as was also said before, nearly all the fruits of trees in their first growth, as Theophrastus too used to say, are acerbic to those who taste them; then, when they are filled with moisture, they take on sourness and lose some of their acerbity. But neither what is added nor what is taken away is equal in all fruits, neither in respect of their species nor in respect of their genus in any way. For instance, of unripe grapes some partake more of acerbity, some more of sourness, and some of both in equal measure. But for cooling burning fevers (kausoi) they are all reasonably suitable. For not only is the sour cold, but also the acerbic, as we were saying before. Here again, then, the discussion is drifting away towards the therapeutic method.

Let us therefore bring it back once more to the matter proposed. [661] What was proposed from the beginning in this book, I believe, was to go through all the flavours. Most of them have in fact pretty much been discussed already, since through the interconnection of the argument we were compelled to touch upon the others as well. For it is not only the acerbic, the harsh and the sour that have been discussed, but also, often already, the sweet, the bitter and the pungent. But it is necessary to add what is lacking for the completeness of the whole account. In the case of astringent things nothing great or noteworthy is lacking that will not also become clear from what has already been said. But in the case of sour things something might perhaps seem to someone to be lacking, a matter that has deceived even some of the reputable physicians. Weak wines change and turn sour in spring and summer, but in winter are preserved in their proper qualities. Because of this it has seemed to some that sourness is generated by heat. Their supposition is reinforced both by wine that has been agitated rather violently and by wine that has been transported rather far in ships.

For all such wines, when they are weak, [662] turn sour very quickly. Moreover, some of those who have written on agriculture recommend that the storage jars be buried in houses facing north, on the grounds that cold preserves their quality whereas heat changes it. And indeed this is seen to happen in many places, having been tested by experience itself. For some wines readily turn sour when they are stored in southerly and sunny places; and it seems to me that the beginning of the solution of what has been said should be made from this point. For the fact that neither do all wines turn sour when heated, but only those that are colder right from the outset, nor does this happen to any of those that have been aged, will find for us the road to the truth. For the argument will seek the cause on account of which the wine that is by nature cold and weak is exposed by the external heat; and yet this very word, 'is exposed' (ἐξελέγχεται), once spoken, resolves all the difficulties mentioned. For something closely similar happens to those wines that are by nature colder and more watery, such as also happens to small and weak flames.

For if you set these too in strong sun, [663] you will see them become entirely faint, or even extinguished altogether. So too a burning lamp, if you place it beside some other flame that is vehement and large, or set it in strong sun, you will at once see withering and being dispersed. And indeed, if you fan a weak and small flame strongly, you will sooner extinguish it than increase it. For a weak nature endures neither strong motion nor strong warmth, but is dispersed by it rather than increased; since indeed in many places they deliberately move and transport wines, just as they also expose them to the sun and warm them, so that some of them become unpleasant, taking on the quality that comes from the smoke. And among us in Asia, when the summer season comes, almost all of them are poured into flagons and set upon the roof-tiles of the houses, and after this they take them down and store them in upper rooms beneath which, in the ground-floor rooms, a great flame is to be burned; and in general they always turn their storerooms toward the south and toward the sun, by which means it will more quickly concoct them and make them drinkable.

For what comes about for the others in a long time, [664] this comes about in a very short time for those that have been heated in this way. It is no wonder that some of those who have written on agriculture made pronouncements too rashly about all wines on the basis of the experience gained in their own regions. But Theophrastus and Aristotle and their circle, having extended their experience further and, through their training in natural philosophy, having articulated everything more precisely, taught us many other such things and also, concerning wines, that they undergo something similar to our own bodies. For do we not see that these too, according to how they stand in respect of weakness or strength, are benefited and harmed by the same things? For vigorous exercises and the sun make hot and robust bodies stronger, but they lay low, disperse and chill those that are not such. And of wines, those that are hot by nature are ripened more quickly by motion that fans them, by sun that heats them thoroughly, and by flames burning nearby.

But all such things expose those wines that are colder and more watery, and compel them to suffer sooner what they would have suffered a little [665] later. For each of the things that exist is preserved in its proper nature by its proper heat, but is destroyed by excess coming from outside, either by an alien heat or by a preponderance of cold. And what is brought about by both is one, but the manner of its coming-to-be is not one. Hence this manner of the difference is not equally easy to detect for all laymen. When the heat of each individual existing thing is overcome by the cold, this is quite clear even to anyone at all. But when it is dispersed by a more vehement heat surrounding it from outside, it escapes the notice of those untrained in the study of nature, who do not know that moderate heat is beneficial to all things, while immoderate heat is no less harmful than cold. But in general it is good to know this: sourness in the humours seems most of all to come about when they are being changed by the heat but are not completely mastered by it.

One might infer this not least from sour belchings as well: these do not follow upon foods that are not changed at all in the stomach, just as they do not follow upon those that have been precisely concocted, [666] but only upon those that are half-concocted, as one might put it. I call half-concocted those foods which, having received the alteration produced by the heat in the stomach, were not afterwards mastered by it to the end. In the same way milk, the juice of barley-gruel and all other such things turn sour more quickly in the summer season than in winter, and require cold storerooms in which they are to be laid up so that they keep for a longer time. From all of this it is clear that the coming-into-being of the sour quality lies in being changed by the heat without yet having been completely mastered by it. For this reason sourness is also present in most fruits before they ripen. And in a way this too seems to agree with what was said at the beginning about sour flavours. For if they have been affected in a way similar to northerly conditions of the weather, so as to be at once fine-particled and cold, it is evident that their coming-into-being is not without heat, just as it is not for the air either.

And for this reason the things that chill us completely and deaden us, such as hemlock and poppy juice, henbane and mandrake, are least of all [667] sour. All sour flavours are indeed cold, yet they do not chill to such a degree as to kill. For they would not be fine-particled either if they were extremely cold. So it has now become apparent not only that the sour flavour is cold, but also to what degree it is cold. One should test what sort of thing it is in its nature on oxylapathon (sorrel) and oxalis, which they also call oxys. This is a wild potherb. For in these it has appeared to me most nearly unmixed and alone, partaking of no acerbity, as the fruits of trees do. These fruits plainly have their sourness admixed with a certain acerbity, just as vinegar has its sourness admixed with pungency. Now what is properly called sour among the flavours is perceptible to the tongue alone, as is the pungent as well; but what is common to both, the biting, is perceptible to touch also. The tongue is able to discern both kinds: the common ones as one of the sentient bodies like any other, and the proper ones as the organ of taste. And this, it seems to me, is its special prerogative, in respect of the affinity and the foreignness of whole substances.

For it has already been stated and demonstrated many times, [668] but it will nonetheless be stated once again, what it is to act or to be acted upon in respect of whole substances. And it seems I must recall it now as well, so far as suffices for the present matters, starting from somewhere about here. The generations of all individual bodies come from the four elements, and they are unequal and differ in their mixtures. For some have more fire than of the other elements, some more water, others, as it may happen, more earth, and some more air. From such inequality, then, the particular characters of the individual bodies were brought about: those of plants from the elements themselves, and those of animals from the plants, as has been shown in the discussions on the elements. Some things change into one another directly, others through other intermediate things. For example, earth changes into wheat and barley and the other things of that kind, and each of these in turn into human flesh; but it is not possible for the earth itself to become flesh by passing over the change that lies in between.

And indeed, of the things that change into one another, some have a ready and quick alteration, others a difficult and protracted [669] one. Those that are near in their similarities have a quick alteration, those that are further off a slower one. It was necessary, therefore, I think, that some organ should be produced by nature for animals that discriminates the similarity and dissimilarity of substances, so that, recognising their natures, it would choose what is proper and flee what is alien. This, then, is the tongue: by the exceptional degree of its sensation it has discernment not only of cold or hot or dry or moist things, but also of things proper and not proper. For into this part alone six nerves are implanted, whereas each of the other parts has received a share of either one or two, and not even these so large. And since some things are more proper to the nature of our body and others less, and some are in this pairing of the mixture and others in that, of necessity the gustatory qualities came to be more numerous.

But common to all things that nourish is the sweet; for everything that nourishes is sweet to a greater or a lesser degree. Common to the things that do not nourish is what is named by negation of the sweet, or privatively, [670] such as 'not sweet' and 'salty'. The particular differences, however, have reasonably become more numerous, because what is proper to each existing thing is one, since its own nature is also one, whereas the things alien to it are very many, some more removed from its substance and others less. So all things that are strictly sour and acerbic and bitter, and in short that have any other quality besides the sweet, are all non-nourishing, just as all things that are only sweet are all nourishing. Of the things that are admixed in their qualities, those that are at once sweet and acerbic are more coarse-particled in their substances and cold in their mixtures, as we also showed a little earlier; those that are at once sour and sweet are more fine-particled than the acerbic ones, but they too in turn cool. And further, the bitter ones are hot, and the pungent ones are hotter still than these. All such things, then, nourish together with their sweetness; but none of the things mentioned is by itself capable of nourishing.

Things become mixed in two ways: either being anhomoeomerous in their substances and having qualities that differ in their parts [671], or being simple and homoeomerous but having come to be so in the course of the change into one another of things that differ greatly. For honey does not become bitter suddenly; whether it is boiled for a longer time or grows old, it changes into bitterness, undergoing this little by little. Nor do those fruits that turn out sweet, such as some of the cucumbers and the melons (mēlopepones), cast off their original quality all at once. For in all things altered by nature the changes take place little by little, and especially when their alteration and transition into qualities that differ greatly, or are even wholly contrary, is brought to completion. Just as, then, the strictly sweet is nourishing and the purely bitter is non-nourishing, so what is intermediate nourishes, but less than the sweet. And it is the same with the other qualities: all of them except the sweet are non-nourishing. And indeed the elements themselves are much more non-nourishing and without quality to the taste.

And for this reason earth and water too — for these as well are both without quality to the taste and non-nourishing, just as air and fire are — so that through the admixture [672] of the qualities the quality of sweet things is often weakened: watery substance predominates in the fruits of almost all plants that grow on the ground. For wheat, barley, broad beans, chickpeas and all other such things, which on account of their moisture are at first nearly without quality to the taste, become sweeter in time as they ripen and dry. Earthy and dry substance predominates in chaff, hay, couch-grass, dry reeds and wood. Some of these, before they have dried out, are sweet to us and sometimes give nourishment to the body: for instance the 'brain' of the date-palm (for so they name its topmost part), the soft roots of couch-grass and of reeds, especially those in Egypt, and also the shoots of most trees. For what nourishes always appears sweet by its likeness to what is nourished, and not sweet by its unlikeness.

And since the dissimilarities are many, it is necessary that in this case the qualities that are not sweet also come to be many. These it is impossible to express in words, but it is possible to call them to mind, since all human beings know precisely that the sensation and condition arising in the tongue from acerbic things [673] is one thing and that from sour things another, and that the one from salty things is different again, and the one from bitter things different again. Just as, then, those foods that are most similar to the natures of the things being nourished both display sweetness and need no preparation besides, in the same way those that are further removed in their mixture need, some of them, seasonings, and others both together. And it is not at all surprising that the seasonings themselves, although none of them is edible, contribute to the pleasantness of what has been prepared by means of them. For when two immoderate things come together, it is possible for what is mixed from both to be rendered moderate, and for this reason to appear sweet, although the immoderate things were not such. And indeed when the preparation of foods takes place through boiling or roasting, or in general by some heat, it is neither puzzling nor irrational that things which before were not pleasant now become most pleasant.

For the nature of the hot is seen to alter quickly whatever it comes into contact with, and to change it [674] into another form, so that this too is no longer puzzling: that some things become more pleasant and others more unpleasant when brought near the fire, and that some need to be boiled for a very short time and others for a very long time. For the things most like the mixtures of the bodies that are nourished appear sweet already, without boiling and preparation, whereas the unlike ones are all unpleasant before they have been prepared. The excessively hot need to be checked by the cold, and those that are considerably cold need both admixtures of hot foods and fire. In the same way, things that are earthy and dry need moisture, and those that are more watery and moist than is fitting need dryness. Dryness, then, is corrected by admixtures of moist things, and moisture by admixtures of dry things and by fire. The greatest proof of what is said is the change that takes place in the mouth. At any rate, in those who have gone without food for rather a long time the saliva appears salty, and if for a very long time, not only salty but by then bitter as well.
