In this way the whole body also becomes bilious; and if the whole of it were capable of perception in the same way as the tongue, it would, I think, easily perceive the saltiness [675] in it and the bitterness, and besides this also the sweetness itself, which is always present in blood that is in its natural state. But as it is, whenever, a vessel having either ruptured or had its mouth opened, blood is poured out onto the tongue in quantity and hot, it appears very sweet, when, as has been said, it is in its natural state. For blood that has become diseased is bitter or salty, or displays some other such quality; but what is in the whole body of the animal escapes notice, as do the biles and the phlegm. And yet of the biles the one always appears bitter, even if it touches the tongue with a small portion, while the black is sour. And of phlegm also, when it comes into contact with the tongue, one kind has often clearly appeared sweet, another sour, another salty, although this too is imperceptible throughout the whole animal. There is nothing remarkable, then, either as to why honey, the sweetest of all things, generates the most bitter humour, or as to why it does so especially in those who are in their prime, those who are hot by nature, and those who are fevered.

For just as outside the body too, when it has been in contact for a longer time with [676] fire, it is rendered bitter, in the same way in the bodies of animals also, whenever it comes near unmixed heat, it generates the bilious humour. But in colder mixtures, whether on account of age, or on account of the nature of the body, or on account of disease, it changes readily into good and well-proportioned blood. For in such bodies it is not overheated, nor altered to a greater degree; rather, undergoing something like what has been moderately boiled undergoes, it is completely assimilated to them and preserves its sweetness. And what is surprising in honey departing from its original sweetness under the more vehement heat in animals, or under more prolonged boiling, when even without these it is rendered bitter, over a longer time, by the heat within itself? For the difference lies only in the speed of the change, not in its undergoing a different affection from a different cause.

For since there is both the affection itself and the cause that changes [the honey], the affection being bitterness and the cause the immoderateness of heat, and since the immoderateness that leads to alteration is twofold in genus, [namely] strength of what approaches it, [677] or length of time, honey receives the one from us and from fire, and the other from itself. And it is fitting that it undergoes this [alteration] that comes from itself over a longer time, because what changes it is also weaker. What, then, is surprising if that which comes about from a lesser cause over a longer time comes about from a greater one in a shorter time? Milk, however, although it is sweet to the taste, never becomes bitter of itself. For in it the hot is overcome by the cold rather than overcoming it, and for this reason it turns sour when it is left standing. For it is composed of three substances that differ in their qualities, as I also said earlier: first the thick substance, from which cheese is made; second the oily, from which butter is made; and third the watery, which we call whey. Of these, the oily is the most well-tempered, and the thick falls a little short of it. The whey-like residue is cold and moist, so that milk taken as a whole falls considerably short of a body moderate in heat, and for this reason it changes of itself into sourness rather than into bitterness.

[678] And if it were possible to taste it once it has been concocted both in the stomach and in the veins, it would be found, I think, sweeter than honey. For what honey has both from outside and from itself, this milk acquires in being concocted. And indeed, when the body of the animal is sufficiently hot, milk gains as much sweetness as honey loses. And this happens with good reason. For what is extremely sweet, and for this reason no longer admits any addition of sweetness, must change into the next quality in order; but to what is deficient, completion accrues from concoction. This, then, is why milk, when it remains unconcocted in the stomach, also undergoes twofold alterations: in the colder belly it turns sour, while in the hotter one it is rendered nidorous and bitter. Honey, however, never undergoes the change into sourness in being concocted; for it is too hot to be overpowered and turned sour. For both are biting to the tongue, the sour and the bitter, yet the sense of the tongue does not possess this as its own proper object.

For indeed, if you apply them to any other flesh whatsoever that is bare of skin, they bite [679] that too; from which it is clear that the biting is a perceptible proper to touch, not to taste. And moreover, the things called pungent, such as pellitory and garlic and onion, also have the property of biting not the tongue alone but all the rest of our flesh as well. And so this biting is common to three flavours, the sour, the bitter and the pungent; but it belongs to the sour as being at once cold and fine-particled (for this was shown earlier), and to the bitter and the pungent as being hot. That the bitter flavour is hot, then, has just now been shown by me. But concerning what is properly called pungent there is no need of demonstration at all. For the evidence (ἐνέργεια, perhaps for ἐνάργεια) that comes from sense-perception anticipates the conviction that comes from reason, so that no one has ever disputed about it. Rather, Plato declares it to be the hottest of all, and so do Aristotle and Theophrastus, and there is no one among the physicians, either of the ancients or of the more recent, who holds any other view.

For heating belongs to it by the very account of its substance, so that if you were to ask any layman whatsoever what he calls a pungent [680] food, he would say, I think, that it is what heats strongly in the tasting, as pepper does, and pellitory, cress, garlic, onions and all things of this kind. And it seems to me that this genus of flavours alone, lacking a name of its own, has made use of the common name by way of pre-eminence. For although the bitter flavour and the sour are both pungent, in whatever body we find the pungency to be intense, even if it is neither bitter nor sour, we are accustomed to call it pungent, and this although such bodies are many in species. For some of them are edible, others not. The edible ones, then, of necessity have some faint sweet quality mixed in. For this reason we use many of them as a relish, and many only as a seasoning; but none of them as food, on account of the intensity of their power. Of those that are not eaten, some are deadly, others simply drugs; all of them, however, when applied to our skin, readily produce an ulcer.

Some of these too [681] exhibit a bitter quality, just as not a few of the edible things exhibit a sweet one; yet they are not called bitter, because this quality is slight and weak in them, whereas that of pungency is strong. Some of them we do not even dare to taste, for instance thapsia, or cantharides, or any other of those that kill by erosion or putrefaction; but even of these one can infer that their taste is pungent from the effects they produce on the body as a whole. Many, moreover, are strange in their very smells from the outset and clearly indicate their contrariety to man, as are these very ones mentioned before, as well as the juice of hemlock and that of poppy, and further the juice of mandrake and of henbane. Indeed, only lately we saw the juice of a plant which a certain centurion brought from the barbarian country bordering on Egypt. It was so heavy and unpleasant in smell that we did not even dare to taste it, but conjectured that it was deadly; he used it for arthritic pains at their peak, and it clearly seemed, even to the patients themselves, to have a cooling power.

It is yellowish in colour, and as heavy in smell as [682] hemlock, except insofar as it gives off a slight, aromatic sort of fragrance. He said that the name of the plant from which the juice comes was lykopersion. But concerning deleterious drugs we shall speak another time. All pungent flavours, for it was about these that the discussion was, one must recognise as being extremely hot; next after them come the bitter, and then, next after these, the sweet. And since in all of them there is a considerable range, the one that is more pungent, or bitter, or sweet is evidently also more hot, while the one that is less so falls short of heat to the same degree as it falls short of the exact quality in taste.

The defining mark of the bitter flavour is to cleanse, of the pungent to burn, of the sweet to nourish, at least when each of them is in a perfect state according to its own nature, that is, when they are as far as possible unmixed with other qualities. For example, the bitter is in every case hot; but that which has only just come into being from a change of the sweet is both less bitter and less hot, while that which has been changed to the greatest extent is extremely bitter [683] and already comes close to the pungent, so that it no longer only cleanses but also corrodes and bites. Thus birthwort, iris and panax do only this very thing: they cleanse away and make ulcers clean. But wild stavesacre is no less pungent than these, unless indeed it is even more bitter; for it is already pungent, and very much so, and vehemently hot, whence it not only removes the filth of ulcers but is by nature apt to melt away the flesh itself. And all bitter flavours, when taken inside the body, are by nature apt to do something of the same kind as they do in the case of ulcers: for they cleanse and thoroughly clean them, and they cut the thickness of the humours in the veins, whence they both provoke the menses and assist in the bringing up of pus from the chest and lung; and in general, whether it be thick phlegm contained in them, or pus, or some other such thing, they thoroughly clean it out, and in this way they help in epilepsies, at least those of them that are not deleterious in nature; for those are contrary to nature in their whole kind. And in the same way they are apt to harm those who spit blood.

[684] For those people need things that are astringent and viscid, not things that cut and divide. These matters, however, already in some way touch upon the therapeutic method. Having now defined the power of the bitter flavours, and having said that they are cutting, thinning and cleansing, and clearly hot to such a degree that they do not yet burn, let us in our account go on once more to the pungent ones. And first let us say that they are strictly hot, then that they are corrosive, caustic, eschar-forming and colliquative: all such are so when applied to the skin. When taken inside the body, however, those that are most opposite in their whole substances to certain animals are all putrefying and deleterious to those animals. Those that are so only through the immoderation of their heat are ulcerating to the inner parts if they are coarse-particled and earthy. If they are fine-particled, they are diuretic and sudorific, and, to put it simply, cutting and dispersing.

Some of them also assist both expectorations from the chest [685] and the flows of the menses; but when, how, and by what method one should use them, it is not the business of the present treatise to set out. For all such matters will be discussed in the Method of Healing, so that I shall now stop writing at greater length about the nature of the pungent flavours as well. It is enough only to add to them, further, more precise distinctions, by which they differ from the bitter. For not only are they by nature such as to differ from them in strong heat, but also in this: all the bitter are not only hot but also dry in power, as one might most clearly compare them, like ash; whereas in the pungent, at least those that are not bitter, much moisture is sometimes mixed in, and it is for this reason that we eat not a few bodies of this kind. That every bitter flavour is not only hot but also dry in its mixture is taught first and foremost by qualified experience, of which I have spoken many times before; and, in addition to experience, it turns out the same way for those who examine the matter by reason.

At any rate, when sweet things are heated to a greater extent, whether [686] by fire or by the innate heat, the generation of bitter bodies was shown to result. And these at once appear drier in their consistency as well; and since their moisture is continually being consumed and flowing away, evaporated by the heat, what is left must necessarily turn out more earthy and drier. For the sweet itself, besides being hot to a greater or lesser degree, is of necessity, surely, also moist to a greater or lesser degree. If indeed it is most akin to the nature of our body, and this nature was well-tempered, moist and hot, then what comes into being when the sweet is, as it were, over-roasted, being similar to lime and ash, is of necessity rendered dry and hot. And indeed for this very reason it is by nature cleansing, and apt to break up and cut viscous and thick humours, as ash and nitre are. For their consistency is neither airy nor fine-particled, nor yet watery, but, as was said a little before, more earthy, thoroughly worked up by the heat, their substance having been, as it were, over-roasted.

So, compared with astringent drugs, bitter drugs would be finer-particled by no small amount, but compared with pungent ones, [687] more coarse-particled. For this reason they neither pass easily through viscous and thick humours, as do the things that are finer-particled in their substances, nor are they unable to cut them, as the coarse-particled ones are. What is to cut must be placed in the middle between each of the two excesses, so that it neither passes through readily, as flame itself does, nor, by lingering and being slow, is unable to divide. But these matters will be discussed in the following book as well, the fifth. For now it is enough to know this much at least: every bitter quality belongs to substances that are at once hot and dry, and, in addition to these, fine-particled and earthy. One must take in the whole of what is said, joining both together into one, and not read each separately.

For taken in that way the fine-particled would seem to conflict with the earthy. But I say that the bitter is not simply fine-particled; rather, it is fine-particled as in an earthy consistency, such as lime and ash and everything that has been thoroughly roasted and has become cinders. Or perhaps it might more truly be likened to a kind of smoky soot and to the soot [688] of flame, which also appears bitter to those who taste it. Iron and stone, then, are a coarse-particled earthy body, whereas soot and ash are fine-particled. Red-hot stone or iron, however, is more coarse-particled than lime and ash, and much more so than soot, and in addition to these things it is also hotter. But the drugs that kill by corrosion resemble red-hot iron and stone, being brought to this state, evidently, by the warmth in the body itself, as chalcitis, misy and sory do, and in addition arsenikon, quicksilver, litharge and countless others. For all such things are coarse-particled and hot in potency. For this reason, becoming fiery in time through the change they undergo in the animal, they ulcerate and burn the parts about the stomach just as red-hot stones or iron do, being unable even to be distributed on account of their weight.

Still more fine-particled than these, although earthy in their consistencies, are lime, cantharis and the sea hare. Of these, some ascend as far as the regions about the liver, and others even as far as the bladder and the thorax, acquiring their fiery quality over so great a distance [689] of travel. Aristolochia and iris are more fine-particled even than these. For they partake more than these do of moist and of airy substance. This is clear from their being neither so dry and brittle nor so heavy, and for this reason they have escaped the class of deleterious drugs. Indeed, cantharis too, when taken at times in a small amount and mixed with the things it ought to be mixed with, not only does no harm to the bladder but also thoroughly cleanses the kidneys. And the more active of the diuretic drugs contain some cantharis as well. But concerning such matters there is another discussion. That the bitter flavour coexists with bodies that are dry in their mixture one may infer also from this: bitter things are, of all things, the most resistant to putrefaction. They are also least apt to generate worms and certain other animals, such as naturally arise in roots, herbs and fruits when these putrefy. For it is above all in moist bodies that we see both worms and putrefactions arising.

But things that are exactly bitter (and I call so whatever has no share in any other perceptible quality) are inedible to almost all [690] animals, not to humans alone, because every animal is moist, to a greater or lesser degree, while bitter things are dry, closely resembling ash and lye. So no animal eats ash or lye or soot or lime, nor any of the things that are exactly bitter. For wormwood is not only bitter but also acerbic, and the sea is briny rather than bitter, and has a very large share of drinkable water, as Aristotle long ago adequately demonstrated. But the water of the lake in Palestinian Syria, which some name the Dead Sea and others the Asphalt Lake, is, to those who taste it, not only salty but also bitter. The salts generated from it are likewise somewhat bitter. To the sight too it appears at once whiter and thicker than any sea, resembling saturated brine, in which salts will no longer dissolve even if you throw them in, for it already contains a very great quantity of them.

And if someone dives down into it and then comes up again, he would at once have a crust of salt (ἄχνην ἁλῶν) all round his whole body. For this reason that water is heavier than the rest of the sea [691] by as much as sea-water is heavier than rivers. So even if you wanted to let yourself down into the depth and be carried downwards, you would not be able to; so strongly does the water lift and buoy one up. This is not because it is light by nature, as one of the ancient sophists once said, but, as Aristotle said, because through its heaviness it carries lighter things, as mud does. And for this very reason, if you bind a man's two hands and two feet and let him go into the water of that lake, he will not go down. Moreover, just as in the sea ships carry greater loads than in lakes and rivers without being sunk, in the same way in the Dead Lake they carry many times the loads they carry in the sea. For the water in it is heavier than sea-water by as much as sea-water is heavier than lake-water and river-water, since the substance of the salts, earthy and heavy, is added to it. You yourself can also produce sea-water by dissolving salt in potable water, and so learn how much heavier such water turns out than sweet water.

Indeed, people have even established a measure of the [692] brine's being well tempered for salting: if an egg is seen floating on it. For while the egg still sinks and does not yet swim about at the surface of the brine, the brine is more watery and sweet. It becomes extremely salty when so much salt has been thrown in that what is added further can no longer dissolve in it. And if you weigh this water, it will be found heavier than all other waters. So I once showed the ambition of the rich man to be vain, who had brought so much water from the Dead Sea to Italy as to fill a basin. For I readily produced the same thing by throwing a great quantity of salt into drinking water. You could make such water heavier still if, after dissolving as much salt as possible at the rising of the Dog Star, when the heat is at its most intense, you let it be thoroughly baked, just like the water of the Asphalt Lake. For in this way this water too will be as heavy as that. And if you bind a man, or throw any other animal whatever into it, it will ride upon the water just as ships do.

And indeed such water will at once also be more bitter [693], just as if you chose to boil it down over a fire; for whatever salty thing you heat more thoroughly will become bitter for you. Thus, for instance, the very water of the Asphaltite lake, enclosed as it is in a hollow and hot place and thoroughly baked by the sun, becomes bitter. For this very reason it is more bitter in summer than in winter. And if you draw off some of it and set it down in a hollow vessel in a sunny place, as we too did in the summer season, it will very soon appear to you to have become more bitter than it was. But all these things bear sufficient witness to what was said a little earlier about the generation of the bitter. Yet the purpose for which the discussion turned aside to the Asphaltite lake has not yet been fully stated by me. For it is evident that in that water neither any animal nor any plant comes into being; moreover, although both the rivers that empty into it contain very large and very numerous fish, and especially the one near Jericho, which they call the Jordan, not a single one of the fish passes beyond the mouths of the rivers.

And if someone were to catch them and throw them into the lake, he will see them quickly perishing. So hostile to all things, both animals and plants, is what is exactly bitter, being parched and dry and in its nature like soot produced by roasting. And yet not even the water of that lake is exactly bitter, since not even the salts themselves are; they call them Sodomene, from the mountains surrounding the lake, which are called Sodom, and many of those who live round about use them for all the purposes for which we use the other salts. Their power is not only drying to a greater degree than that of the other salts, but also thinning, because they have been roasted more thoroughly than the others. For all salts possess something faintly astringent as well, by which they bind and compact meats that are being pickled, and especially when they are coarse-grained and hard to break. Such, most exactly, are most of the mined salts; less so than these are those from the sea and those produced in many places on earth from light waters that have dried up. Third after these are the mined salts, which are by nature disposed to cleanse rather than to be astringent and draw together.

Close to these in power are the Sodomene salts, [695] which are coarse-grained like the sea salts, but because of the bitterness mixed into them are more cleansing and more dispersing than those from the sea. In the same way nitre itself, its foam, and what is called by a compound name aphronitre are by nature still more cleansing than the others, inasmuch as they are least astringent and thoroughly bitter. For the salty flavour is close to the bitter, since both are earthy and hot. Nevertheless they differ by no obscure difference, in that the bitter has been thinned and worked up more by dry heat. In the same way, among the salts themselves, those that are harder, denser and more earthy (and almost all the mined salts are of this kind) are less hot and less fine-particled, whereas those that are easily crumbled and porous are at once more fine-particled and hotter in power, and some of them are slightly bitter, standing in a way between the hard salts and aphronitre. Now even among the aphronitres themselves there are some that are hard and coarse-particled, and they do not even dissolve readily in water.

But [696] my discussion now is not about the poor-quality ones, but about those which, in accordance with the name, are foamy in their substance by nature, such as is the foam of nitre itself. For this is the most fine-particled of all those mentioned, just as is also the flower of the Asian stone. For this too is sufficiently fine-particled, but less hot than aphronitre. Hence it also melts away overgrown flesh more painlessly, whereas the flower of nitre already bites it, and aphronitre bites it too, and no less does nitre itself, even though it is less hot than those. But it has also been said earlier that coarse-particled substance corrodes more, provided, that is, that it partakes of some heat. For no part of it passes through painlessly and quickly, as happens with fine-particled substance; instead, being held back, always remaining and lingering, and staying for a longer time at one place in our body, it reasonably becomes distressing, like a stake fixed in the flesh. Since what is fitting has been said about all the flavours, it would remain still to speak also about vapours.

For [697] it is for this genus of sensible objects that nature fashioned the sensation of odour. Most of them affect us in the same way as the flavours themselves. For all sour things, and before these vinegar itself, move the sense of smell and the taste alike; and pungent things, such as garlic and onions, these too, no less than they do the taste, distress and bite the sense of smell. So too in each of the others the sensation of odour is nearly similar to that of taste, so that of some bodies, such as dung, we know the quality without ever having tasted them, and for this reason we do not even attempt to taste them in the first place, because we trust the sense of smell very strongly indeed. Moreover, of fragrant foods, those that have putrefied and distress us by their odour we likewise throw away at once, not even attempting to taste them; and in nearly all cases smell and taste agree with one another. In the case of the most pleasant things, however, such as roses, they differ and stand very far apart.

For not only are they not pleasant to those who taste them, but they also display no small amount [698] of bitterness. And yet the bitter was never fragrant, nor pleasant to us either as a drug or as a food. What, then, is the cause of this disagreement? Theophrastus too inquired into it, but it is perhaps better that we also say what we know about it. The generation of the bitter flavour was shown to come about from sweet things thinned by heat, and bitter things are evidently hotter and more fine-particled in their mixture than sweet things. Moreover, the sensation of smell takes place in the very ventricles of the brain, as I have demonstrated about these matters elsewhere, and the substance of the objects of smell is vaporous. For the things that flow off from bodies, mixing with the surrounding air and then being carried into the brain by inhalation through the nostrils, move the sense. Reasonably, then, all things that are odorous are also hot, for an abundance of vapours depends on heat. Yet it does not follow at once that everything odorous is also pleasant, because not everything is akin to the pneuma in the ventricles of the brain.

For just as, of the flavours that fall upon the [699] tongue, the most proper were sweet, while those that were not proper possessed many differences, so too of the vapours, those proper to the pneuma in the brain are friendly and pleasant, while those that are not proper differ from one another by not a few differences, yet names have not been laid down for all of these, as they have in the case of the flavours. For we do say that this or that thing has a sour and pungent smell, but we no longer speak of a harsh or acerbic or salty or bitter one; rather, we reduce most objects of smell to these two designations, calling them fragrant and malodorous: fragrant by analogy with the things that are sweet to the tongue, malodorous by analogy with those that are not sweet. For, so far as the flavours are concerned, the class of these latter has no name expressed by a single appellation. It seems that from bodies that are not odorous either altogether little flows off, or what flows off is incommensurate in its particles, as in the case of things that are strictly salty and acerbic. And whenever I say that something is strictly of this or that kind, I mean that it is pure and unmixed with another quality, so far as that is possible.

For the substance of both is coarse-particled, and in addition that of the acerbic ones is cold, [700] so that it is likely that what flows off from them is small in quantity, thick, and as it were earthy in its corpuscles, and for this reason does not even enter the brain in respiration. Hence it is not safe to infer the mixture of perceptible things from smell, as it is from taste. For odourless things are coarse-particled in their substances, but it is not yet clear how they stand with respect to heat and cold; odorous things, by contrast, are in some way fine-particled and hot. The amount of their fine-particledness or of their heat, however, is not further indicated. But the greatest reason why none of the odorous things indicates anything clear about the mixture is the unevenness of their substance. I have already spoken of this many times, showing that most bodies are anhomoeomerous in their constitutions. For the sake of clarity, one example will be given now as well.

The rose, then, is anhomoeomerous not only in this respect, that one part in it is containing and another contained, the containing part being the hard and earthy, and contained within this [701] a certain moist juice. It is also anhomoeomerous because the juice itself must necessarily have three residues, as we also showed earlier. One is earthy, like the lees in wines. Another is airy, and this too is analogous to the flower in wines. The third is watery, which we said produces the boiling in all of them, and also their corruption, whenever it is not mastered nor completely altered during the time of the boiling. It is on account of such a residue that some people boil the juices before storing them, and others first dry them in strong sun. For on account of the earthy and the airy residues they are not much afraid that the juices will spoil, since they see that these both separate out and are hard to putrefy in their substances, because they are also dry in their mixtures. But enough has been said about these matters earlier.

In the nature of the rose there is, to those who taste it, one component that is acerbic, which must necessarily be earthy, coarse-particled and cold; another that is bitter, which is fine-particled and hot; and a third besides these, the watery, which is of necessity cold, but in the opposition between fine-particled and coarse-particled [702] lies somehow midway between the extremes. Because this is mixed in, neither the acerbic nor the bitter is in the extreme degree what it is called, for the admixture of the watery weakens all the qualities. This watery component itself, then, seems somehow to have already been worked up, thinned and heated, and for this reason to be readily brought into vapours; and it is in this way that the rose is both odorous and dries out very quickly. All these things about it can be inferred through taste, but not through smell, because neither do all its parts give off vapour alike nor do they move the sense alike. In taste, by contrast, all the parts of tastable bodies alike fall upon the tongue, and each of them moves the sense according to its own nature. So it is not safe, as has been said, to infer the whole power of drugs from smell, for only such things as have just now been stated can be discerned by it. Still less is it possible to conjecture anything about the power of drugs from their colours.

For in every colour there are found things hot and cold and dry and moist, as has been demonstrated by me in the first books [703] of this treatise. Within each kind, however, whether of seed or of root or of juice, it is possible to obtain from the colour as well some indication of the mixture. For example, onions and squill and wine: the whiter they are, the less hot they are, while the yellowish and tawny ones are hotter. Wheat, millet, ochroi, phaseloi, chickpeas, the root of the iris, that of the asphodel and those of many other plants are affected in a similar way. For in each kind, on the whole, those that are tawny, yellow and red are hotter than the white ones. So if anything can be inferred from this source too about the power of drugs, let it be added to the account. Best of all, however, as has been said and stated many times, is to discover the powers from qualified experience, for you would not go wrong even in this case. Before recognising the power by experience, however, taste reveals most things, with smell, as has been said, also bearing some slight additional witness.

[704] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK V. Having undertaken this fifth discourse on the power of simple drugs, I shall first recall those things I demonstrated in the preceding books that are useful for the present matters, making my beginning from the elements, water and fire, air and earth, which some people, naming them derivatively from the qualities, say are the moist and the dry and the hot and the cold.

If anyone is annoyed at the length of the discussions, he ought not to blame us, but the physicians who wrote things [541] that are plausible but not true. For I, for my part, am even now still afraid that, because of the haste of my refutation of them, some of the sophisms may lead astray the young men who keep company with them. For if they came to the reading of the books trained in the logical methods and knowing how sophisms must be resolved, neither those who commit some fallacy in their demonstrations would escape their notice, nor would we, who concisely teach the truth itself. But since most of the physicians themselves are untrained in these matters, and some, in addition to this, are also by nature rather sluggish in reasoning, these men, unless they obtain help from us refuting the sophisms, will easily be persuaded by the sophists; so that, as far as these men are concerned, the treatise might even seem to be lacking something.

But since it is not possible to aim at all those who read [these books], since they are unlike not only in their natures but also in their ages and conditions, in the two books before this one I adopted that form [542] of discourse which seemed likely to be most useful to the majority: in the first I examined the power of vinegar and water, and in the second I went through mostly matters concerning oil, adding a few things about rose oil as well. In this third book I shall give the discourse the form I had resolved from the very beginning to undertake. I shall first distinguish the meanings of each of the names; next I shall go through what are, as it were, the elements of the whole treatise; and then I shall come in this way to what are, as it were, the syllables, from which the very end of the treatise, towards which we are hastening, will readily follow. Now the division of the names teaches nothing further than what was said in the third book On Mixtures and in the first of these books, but I shall remind you of it now as well. Each body is both said and seen to be either hot, or cold, or dry, or wet: sometimes it is so according to its own nature, sometimes because it has taken on some acquired quality.

It is our custom to say that what is such according to its own nature is, and appears, such primarily, per se and through itself, [543] in potentiality; but that what has taken on the acquired quality is, and appears, such by some accident. And of those things themselves which are said to be hot, or cold, or dry, or moist according to their proper nature, some are such in actuality, others in potentiality. This 'in potentiality' now spoken of differs from the one mentioned a little before: for that one was distinguished as the opposite of 'by accident', whereas this one is distinguished as the opposite of 'in actuality'. And of those things themselves which are such in actuality, one is called hot, or cold, or moist, or dry simply, as are the elements; another by predominance, as a man, a horse, an ox, a dog, and animals generally; another in relation to the well-proportioned of the same genus or of the same species, as, for instance, a lion compared with a man, and a man in his prime compared with a child; and another in relation to any chance thing whatever, as Dion in relation to Theon.

Moreover, of the bodies said to be potentially of this or that kind, we stated that each must necessarily be spoken of as referred to what is so in actuality: the one, because it is readily set on fire, in relation to what is simply hot in [544] actuality; the other, because it heats animals, in relation to what is so by predominance. So too, what heats a human being is potentially hot in relation to a human being, and what heats an ox or a horse is so in relation to an ox or a horse. Likewise also, one thing is so for this particular human being, while another is hot or cold or moist when compared with the nature of that one alone. From this distinction of the terms we were helped towards the recognition of their mixture. For if something should be said to be hot, or cold, or dry, or moist in relation to a human being, we held that one should leave aside all the other animals and make the trial and the test on the human being himself alone; and if something is so said in relation to an ox, or a horse, or a deer, or some one of the other animals, that the trial in turn be made on that animal alone. In these discussions we also censured those who attempt to discover the powers of drugs from the consistency, or colour, or weight, or lightness, or the quality of each of the drugs with respect to taste or smell.

All these things, then, evidently followed from the correct division of the names. [545] And the elements, as it were, of the present inquiry we showed to lie in the knowledge of the primary qualities, which we demonstrated in the work On the Elements according to Hippocrates: moistness and dryness, heat and coldness. Indeed, our discovery of these too came about almost entirely from correctly distinguishing the meanings of the names. For having distinguished drug from food by this, that the one alters according to quality while the other is assimilated to the substance of the body, we were guided from there by reasoning to the discovery of the qualities that alter us. Alterations are twofold in genus. Some are form-producing, and these are properly and primarily named alterations. Others break up and draw together the parts of our body, and people call these alterations by a misuse of the term rather than by naming them properly. Since this is so, we say that the powers of drugs are contained in the first kind.

For nothing, we say, can change from one form to another without being heated and cooled and dried and [546] moistened. I mean 'from form to form' when from bread and barley-gruel and lentils there come to be blood and phlegm and bile, both yellow and black, and from these in turn bone and fat and nerve and flesh, artery and vein, and each of the other parts of the animal. But if something that cuts us, as glass or a sword does, or that crushes, like stone and lead, or that draws together the parts that have been anointed, as bandaging does, alters these parts in some way, these are not drugs; for such an alteration does not displace any existing thing from its proper nature. For whether you break bread into many pieces and cut it up, or gather it from many small pieces into one, it does not depart from its proper form. Bread does not become flesh by being broken up, nor bone if it should happen to be gathered together in this way. But when, in being concocted in the stomach and the veins, it changes into blood and phlegm, and then from these into bone and flesh and the other parts of the body, it is altered in its whole substance and departs from its original nature, passing over into another form.

Yet it has been shown that all the affections of the body receive their alterations and changes of substance into another form from nothing other than the hot, the cold, the dry [547] and the wet. And on this account we said that the primary and elemental form-producing qualities are four: wetness, dryness, heat, coldness; and we inquire, of each of the drugs, which of these it possesses as predominant in its mixture. Straightaway, then, on this very first point most of those who have inquired into them seem to me to have gone wrong, in examining the predominant quality absolutely, as certain natural philosophers do; and indeed many of them seem to reason fallaciously, reading the treatises of Theophrastus and Aristotle without method. And yet it makes a very great difference whether one draws distinctions about hot, cold, dry and wet with an eye to nature as a whole, or with reference to human beings alone. For to those who look to nature as a whole, each of these is spoken of in two ways: in one sense absolutely, in the other by predominance.

each of the elements simply, but man and [548] horse and ox by predominance. But when the examination is conducted in the category of relation, one must consider only that in relation to which the thing is said. What we are seeking is not whether, in sea-water, the moist is simply greater than the dry, for this we see plainly, but whether it is so in relation to man. Nor indeed do we seek it in relation to him when he is compared simply in this offhand way, as if you were to compare a lion with him as well; for even taken thus sea-water is moister than man. How, then, do we still inquire whether sea-water is dry in power? How otherwise than as equivalent to its being drying of the human body? To this alone, then, one must look, leaving the other things aside. But most physicians do the opposite, for they look to all the other things rather than to this. How, then, by turning to man and withdrawing from the rest, shall we come to know how sea-water stands in respect of activity towards him?

Is it not, clearly, by applying it to the body and making trial of what happens, both in bathing in the sea and in drenching with it or pouring it over the body, and also, as is often done, in laying on the parts wool and sponges soaked in sea-water, and in mixing it into plasters and cerates, [549] and in all these cases distinguishing what is brought about in accordance with the proper power of the drug itself from what sometimes results incidentally? For in this lies the whole decisive authority of the discovery, and this alone almost none of them touches. Rather, the pronouncements of the philosophers deceive them, since they are unable to perceive the homonymy. For, as was said just now, they do not only speak of one thing as being so simply and of another as being so by predominance (for fire is hot simply, but a human being by predominance). They also hold that 'by predominance' is itself said in two ways. One is according to the bulks of the substance, as we too distinguished in the commentaries On Mixtures, as if you were to mix two choes of extremely boiling water with one chous of altogether cold water. The other is according to the activity of the qualities. This second sense they state as something that already depends on doctrine, no longer taking it from what is evidently apparent.

For, having laid down as a hypothesis that the cold draws together and compresses and renders the substance motionless, while the hot rarefies and diffuses and concocts and [550] moves, they reasonably declare that in all plants the hot prevails. For neither, they say, would the distribution of the nourishment from the earth to a very great distance come about otherwise, nor its alteration nor its concoction, nor indeed the growth of plants at all, or their sprouting, or the generation of their fruits, unless the hot prevailed; and so in this way they go on to declare, among the plants themselves in turn, one hotter and another colder. On this hypothesis, then, depends also the argument about roses themselves, that they are hot: for the hot prevails in them to a greater extent than in certain other plants. And from yet another hypothesis, again, comes the argument about oil and fat: for because they blaze up very quickly, for this reason they say that they are hot in power. And in yet another way, again, whatever things are sweet: for because they are most akin and most similar to our mixtures, which are by nature hot, for this reason they say that these too are hot.

For the philosophers, then, inasmuch as they are making pronouncements about nature as a whole, such matters are rightly investigated and stated; but for physicians, who have a different [551] aim, not rightly. For neither because the hot predominates in the activities in roses, nor, more generally, because the rose belongs to the genus of plant, is it on that account hot by reason of either of these. For we were not investigating the hot in this sense, but in relation to man, since, if it is a matter of the hot predominating in the activities, every plant will be hot, and all animals still more so. Let them then say that poppy and mandrake and hemlock and salamander are hot. But they do not say so; rather, all of them, as if from one mouth, declare all these things to be cold. And yet the salamander is an animal, one that is surely nourished and grows and moves, which are things they say come about when the hot predominates in the mixture. How, then, is it that in these cases they look to the relation to man, but in others to nature as a whole, or to the activities of the primary qualities? I, for my part, say that one ought to declare not only the salamander or hemlock to be cold in their powers, in relation to man, but also to judge all other things in the same way.

For hemlock not only does not chill starlings nor kill [552] them, as it does us, but actually nourishes them and plainly heats them; for everything that nourishes a hot substance surely increases and preserves its heat. And the substance of the body of starlings is hot, not only inasmuch as they are animals but also inasmuch as they are blooded. Now I have shown many times already, in many treatises, that there are certain affinities and conflicts of qualities in all existing things, and that what is akin is readily assimilated, whereas what is contrary sometimes changes both plants and animals to destruction. And indeed I have also stated and demonstrated many times that their affinities arise in accordance with the particular character of the whole substance. But these people are unable to perceive this, and for this reason they make pronouncements about most drugs that are at once careless and false. For in these matters there is only one secure criterion: experience with respect to the human being, provided that in it we distinguish what is accidental from what is per se.

And if one attends to this, one will call neither vinegar nor rose oil hot; for both cool us primarily and of themselves, the vinegar strongly, [553] the rose oil to a slight degree. What this 'to a slight degree' amounts to, I shall explain; for together with it the account of the middle mixture of all drugs will also come into view, of which I made mention in the book before this one as well, when discussing olive oil. Now, if any of the bodies or drugs that come into contact with us is in actuality hot in the same way as we are, or, on being brought near us, becomes hot in like manner to us, such a thing is of the middle mixture, as compared with us; since, taken of itself, it could be called hot by predominance, just as we too are. But if something neither is already hot in the way we are nor becomes such on being brought near us, this is colder than the mixture of a human being, even if the hot predominates in it to whatever degree. And indeed, on being brought near us, it will take away something from the heat present in us and diminish it.

For just as, if of two waters both are hot, but the one more so and the other less, and you mix the less hot into the more hot, you will slacken its warmth, so, if into the heat from rose oil, [554] which is lukewarm even relative to the mixture of a human being, you mix human heat, you will certainly take away something of it and cool it down. One should not wonder, then, if one of the things that are hot individually and in themselves, when applied to another, hotter thing, is able to cool it. For this nature is common to all bodies capable of alteration: when they come near one another they act and are acted upon in ways not apparent (εἰς ἄδηλα), the less hot being made hotter by the more hot, and the more hot being affected in the opposite way by the less hot. You may learn this plainly through touch itself. For the same things often appear to it at one time hot, at another cold: cold when it has become hotter, hot when it has become colder. And someone recently put the question to us why we pass urine that is cold in the baths but hot outside, not following that the urine itself is equally lukewarm both in the baths and outside, whereas we are not in the same condition as regards the surface of the body while bathing and before it.

For while bathing we have it hotter [555] than the urine is, but outside colder; so that, reasonably, to it the urine too appears hot outside the bath but cold inside. For of what is less hot than itself it has the sensation as of something cooling it down, and of what is hotter than itself as of something heating it through. And you may, to test what has been said, when you have already been sufficiently heated, while bathing order a small tub (kadiskos) of moderately lukewarm water to be brought in, and put your hands or feet into it. For the water will appear to you not lukewarm but considerably cold. But if immediately upon entering the bath you touch the water in the tub, it will appear less cold to you. For always, to whatever degree you have been previously heated, to that degree it will appear cold. And there is nothing surprising in this, since most well waters too, those that have deep sources, when touched in winter appear lukewarm. But if after bathing you touch them with hot hands, they would not appear lukewarm to you, and much less so if you are still bathing.

Since, then, we take touch as our criterion in the discernment of hot and cold things, and refer [556] our judgements about them to its condition, it is reasonable that we are often misled, so as to call what is not cold in itself cold, and what is not hot in itself hot. For this reason, when bathing we think the urine cold, and when we have been chilled in frost we think well-water hot. And if we were to forget the conditions we were in when we touched each of them, remembering only the sensation that arose in us, we might perhaps at some time declare the water to be hot simply and the urine cold. But neither is either hot or cold simply; each is so relative to us. And again, it is not even relative to us simply, but relative to us when we are in some particular state. What each of them is simply relative to us would be stated when it is examined against our middle and best mixture; just as, if it were being tested against man simply, the examination would surely be made against the well-mixed man. All these errors, then, depend on the division of names, which almost everyone despises.

[557] For since 'cold' and 'hot' are said in one sense simply, in another by predominance, in another by comparison with what is well-proportioned of the same genus, and in another in relation to anything whatever that happens to be at hand, it is reasonable that we often go wrong among the homonymies, forgetting what sort of 'hot' we are judging and passing over to another. But it has already been said countless times, and will be said again, that one must examine the power of drugs according to the fourth and last of the meanings just mentioned. For neither is each of them hot simply, as fire is (that would indeed be impossible), nor is the proposed inquiry whether it is hot by predominance, as blood is; nor yet whether it is called hot in relation to what is well-proportioned of the same genus or of the same species, as a lion is among animals, and, in each of the species, what is in its prime relative to what has grown old. Rather, the inquiry is whether each of the drugs is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist in relation to a human being.

And not even in relation to him in the way that what is compared falls under the category of relation, but whether it is so potentially; that [558] is, whether, when brought near to him, it renders the part that it touches hotter, or colder, or moister, or drier. So that both the matter of judgement and the matter of discernment will lie in experience. Most physicians abandon this and instead examine whether the rose is red or fragrant. When they have been scorched by heat on the head, they neglect to place upon it garlands of roses, or their juice, or rose oil, and so to learn by experience what happens. For if they are heated through, it would be rather hot; but if they are cooled, cold. Here 'cold' is equivalent to being cooling of the nature of man, for one must always remember this. Yet although I keep saying it countless times, most people mishear it, and one must forgive them, perverted as they have been by the sophists who drivel at length. The matters of experience, then, are this easy, both concerning the power of roses and concerning all the other drugs.

For it is surely possible both to crown oneself with roses, and at some time, having pounded them, to apply them as a poultice to the mouth of the stomach of a person suffering from burning fever, and, [559] having squeezed out their juice, to sip it down, and, having mixed it with water or oil, to rub some one of the parts of the body with it. And yet why do I speak of these things, when some people, mixing juice of roses with balsam sap, rub down their bodies during the heats under the Dog-star for the sake of cooling, having learned by experience itself that they cool sufficiently? But out of excessive cleverness Herodotus the physician does not even admit that rose oil with vinegar, which they call specifically oxyrhodinon, cools us. Then, remembering at least this much, that he himself uses it at the beginnings of phrenitic diseases, and perceiving the contradiction (for it is agreed by nearly all physicians, down even to the followers of the most insensate Thessalus, that at the beginning one must repel and cool rather than heat and relax), he says that it does not cool but is astringent. And yet there would have been no difficulty, when he too had at some time been overheated (for he was a man subject to the same affections as we are), in moistening his head with oxyrhodinon and learning by experience the action of the drug.

[560] And it would have been very easy, I think, for him also to use it at some time when he had been chilled, pouring it over the head, dropping it into the ears, pouring it into the nostrils and rubbing it over the whole forehead, just as we use marjoram oil and iris oil and the other warming unguents. For indeed, by his account, oxyrhodinum heats in no merely moderate degree, being compounded of two very hot drugs. But if Herodotus did not dare to use it, it is right, I think, for those now living to test the power of the drug on themselves, whenever they have been either chilled or overheated, as I have often tested it on myself and on not a few others who were overheated, moistening the head with it. For it is better that they themselves first test the things they speak of, and only then advise us and record them in their books. But somehow, I know not how, although I was guarding against taking up controversy, I have been compelled to it by their shamelessness.

So I return once again to what I proposed at the outset: that the powers of drugs [561] must be judged by experience, using them irreproachably on those who are healthy, and on those who are sick with diseases as simple as possible, either hot, or cold, or dry, or moist. For if you judge in this way, oil will be said to be neither hot nor cold in relation to a well-tempered human being, while rose oil is already somewhat colder, yet not strongly cold, but, as I am accustomed to name it, of the first distance and order of cooling things. For just as with water, say, one is exactly well-tempered while another is either warmer or colder, yet not such that one could already call it hot or cold absolutely, so too among drugs oil is of the middle mixture, whereas the juice of roses is of the colder, though not by any great amount, being, as I have also said before, of lukewarm warmth. Of the same order as it is what is called linseed, so far as the lukewarm quality of its warmth is concerned, but by being coarse-particled it differs from it by no small amount.

For the juice of roses is precisely fine-particled, as is shown [562] by its drying easily, by its having no share of viscidity, and by its dispelling the odours of the other perfumes. For it is evident that it does this too by nothing other than by being first to fill the olfactory passages: for when the others are about to pass through and slip into them, it occupies them beforehand and fills them. Chamomile too, as far as fineness of particles goes, is close to the rose, but as far as heat goes, it is rather of the power of oil, a power that is proper to the animal and well-proportioned. For this reason it is a help against fatigue if anything else is, and soothing of pains; it relaxes and loosens what is tensed, softens what is moderately hard, and rarefies what has been condensed. And it is resolvent of fevers, of as many as trouble the patient without inflammation of a viscus, and most of all of those that arise from bilious humours or from condensation of the skin. It is for this very reason that among the Egyptians the wisest have consecrated it to the sun and have held it to be a remedy for all fevers. But in this they are not right. For it is a remedy only for the fevers I have mentioned, and for these only when they are already being concocted.

It does, however, also benefit well all the [563] other fevers, both those that are melancholic and those that are phlegmatic and those that are the offspring of inflammation of an internal organ. For chamomile is a most excellent (γενναιότατον) remedy for these too, when it is administered to them when they are already being concocted; and for this reason it is also kindly to the hypochondria, if anything else is. Linseed, at any rate, the old account (ὁ παλαιὸς λόγος) states to be of this kind as well. And indeed that too really is kindly to the internal organs in the region of the hypochondria, but less so than chamomile. For it is both less hot, as has been said, and in addition to this it is coarse-particled. The rose, however, does not come near them for these purposes. And yet, as far as the lukewarm character of its heat and its fine-particled nature are concerned, it too would be quite useful for inflammations in the region of the hypochondria; but the astringency present in it does harm in many ways. It does so especially in those things in which chamomile is highly esteemed: either rarefying the condensed parts of bodies, or softening those that have been hardened, or relaxing those that are stretched tight. For astringency is hostile to all such things.

For the ascents and increases of inflammations, however, and especially [564] of those near the surface, rose oil is better than chamomile, because these call for both a lukewarm warmth and a slight astringency. For at the beginning, things that cool and are astringent are serviceable; during the progressions, those that are lukewarm and moderately astringent; and at the peaks of the inflammations, those that rather warm in due measure and disperse strongly. All these matters will be discussed at greater length in the books of the Therapeutic Method; but now I return once more to the subject in hand. For drugs of the middle mixture, and those that deviate slightly to either side, might seem at one time to warm and at another, again, to cool, and sometimes neither to warm nor to cool but to preserve the bodies in the condition in which they received them. And this happens to them with good reason, since lukewarm water and urine appear cold in the baths, but warm to those who have been chilled.

If, then, it is evident that the agent which affects, too, does not act in the same way according to the condition of the things being affected, it is clear that neither the rose nor olive oil nor chamomile [565] nor linseed, nor yet dill nor fenugreek meal, nor yet wheaten meal nor countless others, both those exactly intermediate in their mixtures and those that deviate slightly, will display the same activity in every case. For neither are we all mixed alike when healthy, nor do we suffer from the same diseases. Rose oil, for instance, is mixed with a mixture intermediate between olive oil and the juice of roses: for it is less hot than the former and hotter than the latter. It cools again those who are overheated, evidently by the lukewarm character of its heat, and it also warms to some small degree those who are chilled. This too is the work of lukewarm warmth, just as the baths both warm those who are shivering and cool again those who are overheated. And for this reason, if you mix rose oil into drugs that are naturally disposed to cool or to warm, you will do no great harm, just as you will do no noteworthy good either. For lukewarm warmth is not capable of harming things that have been chilled, yet it cannot cure them.

For everything that is [566] being treated, inasmuch as it is being brought from some immoderation into due proportion, needs not the mixture of the moderate itself but that of the opposite immoderation. So if you should wish to make cold water well-tempered, you must not mix in water that is already well-tempered, for in that way the mixture made from both will be lukewarm. Rather one ought to go to boiling water and mix this with the cold. And what is mixed with the cold must be hotter than the moderate by just as much as the cold itself was colder than the moderate. For neither will what is slightly colder than the moderate recover the middle mixture through what is much hotter, nor what is much colder through what is slightly hotter. But if what needs treatment is much colder, then what is to treat it must necessarily also be much hotter; and if it is a little colder, then what treats it must also be a little hotter. In a word, what is to treat must stand as far from the middle as does what is to be treated, the departure of each evidently lying in opposite directions.

For what is, to a comparable degree, [567] removed in the same direction, being similar in mixture to what is being treated, is capable of bringing about no alteration, so that it will neither harm anything that has been affected (τι παθὸν) nor benefit it. What is less removed will benefit, yet it will certainly not cure. If, then, the affection is cold and the heat of the drug lukewarm, it will certainly confer some additional benefit on the affection, yet it will certainly not bring it back to the natural due proportion, so that it will cure it completely in no respect. Again, if the affection is small, so as to have shifted from the moderate natural warmth to a sort of lukewarm one, and the drug is cold, the affection must necessarily be further chilled and harmed by the cold. The same holds if the affection is hotter than due proportion: by drugs similar to it, it will be kept in the same state, and it will be harmed by those less hot than themselves (ἧττον ἑαυτῶν θερμῶν, so the text), yet it will certainly not be thoroughly cured. Here too, then, there arises again a certain homonymy, extended over the whole of life and causing error in many places.

For we sometimes call what is mixed in due proportion [568] 'hot': so, for example, we call such a bath hot, and such a drink, and also whatever falls short of it by not much, and, besides these, everything that is hotter still. But if we used names precisely, we would call what is in due proportion not 'hot' but 'well-tempered'. Whatever departs further from due proportion than this, we would call 'hot' to a lesser or greater degree when it is immoderate toward the hotter, and 'cold' to a lesser or greater degree when it is immoderate toward the colder. In the same way, I think, if we named drugs precisely, we would have called a drug 'well-tempered' and 'intermediate', as olive oil is. If a drug were hotter than this, we would have called it 'hot', as fenugreek is. If it were colder than this, we would have called it 'cold', as the rose is. But the reason we do not use names in this way is that not all bodies are cooled by such drugs, of which rose oil too is one. For of the bodies that are as cold as it and those that are colder, it does not alter the former at all, and it even heats the latter.

It might seem, then, to be unreasonable if, while agreeing that something heats, we then call it cold, [569] just as if someone were to call cold the well-water in winter, which appears lukewarm to chilled hands. From these reasons, then, the use of names, having been thrown into confusion, also throws into confusion the knowledge of the things themselves. In the same way, too, with regard to dry and moist, once the names had been confused, the knowledge of the things was confused as well. And yet, although it seems a small matter to distinguish well the meanings of names, it is found to have the greatest force for the knowledge of things. But concerning moist and dry we shall speak shortly, once we have brought to a conclusion the discussion of hot and cold. For not much of the distinctions belonging to it seems still to be lacking, now that it has once been clearly shown that it is nothing surprising if, by one drug, different bodies are in some cases heated, in others cooled, and in others undergo neither of these.

For in the relative sense it is very easy, when one comes to particulars, to say that rose oil, when applied to a body of such a kind, is naturally apt to preserve it in the mixture in which it found it, while when applied to some other body of a certain kind it heats [570], and to another it cools. But to pronounce universally about its power is difficult without first distinguishing the names and agreeing upon them. The distinction and the convention would be of the following kind. Since the bodies of human beings differ very greatly, both in their original mixtures and in those that accrue to them according to their ages and according to the habits of their life, it is surely necessary that they are altered differently by the same drugs. At any rate, if you compare a young man who is hot by nature and a labourer in his way of life with an old woman who is also colder by nature, you would find the excess to be no less than that of one of the strongly heating drugs over the cooling ones. Conceive for me, then, someone midway between these, who is well-mixed in nature right from the start and who preserves this good mixture by suitable habits.

And, having set these three side by side in your mind as standards, as it were, of mixture, consider the drug that is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist without qualification: looking to which of these mixtures [571] is it better to give it that name? Is it to the best-tempered, which is indeed one single mixture and the mean of all the others, or to the immoderate, ill-tempered and indeterminate ones, which are almost infinite in number? To me the two members of this division do not even seem comparable, nor does the question seem to need any examination; rather, it appears plainly, to anyone with even a little sense, that one should lay down the rightly constituted body, which is simple and single, as a kind of rule and standard, direct oneself by it, and so judge the other things by reference to it. Let such a body, then, be laid down by us as the rule for the power of drugs. Let what kindles a warmth similar to this body's mixture be called well-tempered, even if it seems very manifestly to warm an old man who has been chilled. But of what either warms or cools such a body, let that which warms be called hot, and that which cools cold.

For the sake of clear instruction, let there be established a series of ranks of these deviations themselves. Towards the cold, the first, in which one might place rose oil; the second, in which the rose itself will be; and a third after this one, and a fourth, until in our account we arrive at the [572] coldest things: hemlock, poppy juice, mandrake and henbane. Towards the hot, in turn, dill and fenugreek first; second, next in order, whatever things appear to be second; and so third and fourth, until we arrive at the things that burn. In the same way also with the moistening drugs, starting again from the moderate, let us make ranks in sequence up to the extremes. For the use of such knowledge for the therapeutic method is not small. Or rather, if one must speak the truth, unless one makes distinctions in this way, one will harm rather than benefit one's readers. For as things now stand, in addition to the other errors that most physicians commit when they expound the powers of simple drugs, one can also find this one, the more harmful: among the heating drugs there is written, as it may happen, dill and fenugreek and misy and lime, and among the cooling drugs rose oil and mandrake and hemlock, as though fenugreek were close to lime, or rose oil to hemlock, and they were not separated by many intermediate ranks of drugs.

But [573] we at least shall try, as far as we are able, to bring so great and difficult a task into some kind of order, and to write down both the things that are near to one another in their powers and those that are far apart. And let us do this not by entrusting the judgement of them to plausible arguments, but to qualified experience, as has also been said many times in what precedes. It is surely evident that such a judgement is secure, but at the same time long and involving much labour for us who are to reach through it the end of what has been proposed; for those, however, who wish to read through these writings, it alone is able to make them skilled in the art and to furnish, as it were, a kind of eye capable of discerning the truth. Accordingly, after adding in this book whatever is still lacking for the complete elementary exposition, in the fourth we shall speak about the power of flavours, since this too seemed right to our companions; and in the fifth about the secondary and compound powers in all simple drugs in general; and then we shall pass on in this way to the particulars in the treatises that follow.

[574] What remains, then, is first the point which the account has often been compelled to mention before, but has not gone through completely. It is this: nearly all drugs, even if they appear simple to perception, are at any rate composite in their nature, and often indeed they contain within themselves the most opposite powers, such as an expelling and a checking power, a thickening and a thinning, a rarefying and a condensing, a clogging and a cleansing, a tightening and a relaxing, and all the other oppositions, as we shall show in the account after this. And it is no wonder if, in the case of such powers, one and the same drug should appear both heating and cooling, or drying and moistening, fine-particled and coarse-particled. For if the first and most active powers did not have such an interweaving, neither would those that come after them have been interwoven in the same way.

But if we ourselves mix, as it may happen, pomegranate juice with honey, we grant that what is mixed from both has not only an astringent but also a cleansing power, and is not only retentive [575] of the belly but also evacuative. That in milk, however, the two powers are contained, the excretory and at the same time the restraining power of the belly, we no longer likewise grant. And yet milk is both easily separated into whey and cheese, and it is agreed by all that the one moves the belly downward, while the other holds it back. This, again, we no longer readily grant in the case of cabbage either. For when we squeeze out its juice and gulp it down, either by itself or with honey, we see that it is purgative; but since we are not able to eat the remainder, we disbelieve that it is restraining. But if someone, having boiled the cabbage whole, pours off the first water, into which it has deposited its juice, and then puts it again into other, clean water, and having boiled it once more pours this off too, he will find that the juice purges, while the cabbage itself holds back the belly; and much more so if one pours off the water not twice but three or four times.

For the more thoroughly it deposits its juice in it, the more purgative it will make that water, while it will show the remaining substance of the cabbage, the flesh, as it were, of the vegetable, to be binding [576]. So it is also with beets and with nearly all the others whose juice is either pungent or nitrous or salty, since even lentils, although they have considerable astringency to the taste, nevertheless have something of this kind. For their decoction too is laxative of the belly; but this juice is plainly admixed in taste, as if you were to mix something nitrous with something harsh. The juice of small sea shellfish, however, and of all the other testaceans, is simply salty and laxative. Yet their flesh itself checks the belly, and you will find by trial that what is said is true if you prepare them in the same way as cabbages. For indeed the broth of older cocks also moves the belly, although the flesh is binding. In flake of copper too there is a twofold power, just as there is also a twofold quality, for it is both astringent and biting. For this reason, by being astringent it cicatrises the dry parts of ulcerated flesh, and by biting it melts down the flabby parts.

But if it is taken inside the body [577], it purges, but does not check the belly. For the astringent power is overcome by the pungent and purgative one, just as if you were to mix the juice of sumach with scammony. For what is made from both will be purgative, not checking the belly, even though to the taste the harsh juice will prevail more. In the same way, not a few purgative drugs, when given with the flesh of the quince, escape the notice of the taste and become apparent only through their action. Some are also given in the flesh of the date, and others in myrtle berries or with Chian mastic, or with some other of the things that are good for the stomach and astringent, so as both to escape the taste and to upset the stomach less. But even if the astringent things prevail over the purgative ones in the quality perceived by the taste, they are at any rate overcome in the other power. For often the tongue is overcome according to the preponderant part of the substance, whereas the action comes about according to the strength of the power.

When, therefore, a small substance having a vehement power, mixed with another substance that is abundant and has a weak power, arrives inside the body, it escapes the notice of the taste, but it accomplishes its work [578] more effectively than that other substance. These things too are marvelled at by the many, and they consider it a matter without explanation if some astringent body is naturally such as to purge, for example aloe, flake of copper and burnt copper; for, they say, these ought on the contrary rather to check the belly, not to urge it on. But that the apple, as it may happen, which is astringent, purges when taken with scammony, at this nobody marvels; and yet, starting from this, it would have been very easy, I think, to infer in the case of aloe too that there is some mixed power. And if it were possible to separate in it what purges from what does not purge, as we do in the case of milk and cabbage and a great many others, it would no longer be marvelled at. And indeed it is in some way possible to do this. For aloe that has been carefully washed moves the belly altogether weakly, or not at all. This same thing happens also to flake of copper and to burnt copper itself, as we too have found by trial, having washed them thoroughly: they purge only faintly. But in any case the drug-like character of the quality too, immediately upon tasting, shows the mixed nature of the power.

[579] For if there were always a single quality in each of the drugs that are astringent to the taste, it would never be the case that some of them are edible and others drug-like; rather, they would differ from one another only in being more or less astringent. But as it is, this is not so. For one astringency appears pleasant and mild, another unpleasant and drug-like: that of pear, apple and pomegranate is pleasant, while that of copper scale and aloe is unpleasant and drug-like. And yet copper scale is less astringent than quince, so that one could not attribute the strangeness of its quality to the intensity of its astringency either. Similarly, other edible things too are more astringent than aloe, copper scale, and burnt copper itself. In such cases, then, the mixed nature of the substance is plainly apparent; in others, even if it is not apparent, one must infer it by reasoning, and not suppose that one thing produces the astringency in aloe and another in the apple. For it is reasonable that a single thing produces, in all cases and according to its own nature, not astringency alone but each of the other qualities as well.

But because nothing is found that is precisely pure and unmixed [580] with other qualities, the differences of the activities are different in each of the astringent [drugs]. For the effect of medlar is one thing, that of the flake [sc. of copper] another, that of aloe another, and that of mulberries different again, or, as it may happen, of oak-gall, or of pomegranate rinds, or of alum, or of sumac. And it would have been better if those who ventured to make any pronouncement about the activity of astringent drugs had spoken in general about astringency itself rather than about the astringent [drugs]. For the astringent [drug] is not only astringent: in addition to being astringent it is either pungent, or oily, or sweet, or bitter, or salty, or sour. Astringency, on the other hand, is always this one thing only, that which it is, just as sweetness and saltiness and each of the other qualities are. If, just as astringency is one, the astringent [drug] were also one, its effect would always be one. But since, in addition to being astringent, it has been shown [to possess] not a few other qualities as well, it will always act according to all of them, but manifestly now according to one, now according to another, whichever prevails, relative to the condition of the body it comes into contact with.

At any rate, milk, lentils and cabbage are seen to loosen the bowel in some people and to bind it in others. [581] The cause why any one quality and power of the drug, whichever it may be, does not act manifestly always and in each of the bodies, I shall state in the following book. For now my only aim is to recall what happens, so that no one may disbelieve that in most drugs there are opposite qualities and powers.
