Yet this very point also calls for much investigation and not a few distinctions, even if it has seemed easy to everyone to find out the qualities and powers that are opposite to one another. At any rate, nearly everyone readily posits that being astringent is opposite to cleansing. But it is in no way opposite, as I shall demonstrate as the discussion proceeds. For the present, however, my argument has been brought to completion more than sufficiently, since I have shown that even if someone posits them to be opposites, nothing absurd follows, it being possible for the most opposite qualities and powers sometimes to come together into a single substance.

In the case of juices, at any rate, it was said earlier too [582] that the heaviest part in them is one thing, the lightest another, and a third something else again, mixed through the whole juice. And it is nothing surprising if in the juice of the rose as well there is a heaviest part, analogous to amurca and lees, and a lightest part, this too analogous to the flowers that ride on the surface of each of the juices; and a third, such as the fermenting part in must; and besides these a fourth, the most unmixed and purest part itself, of which these three are the residues. It happens, however, that all the other juices turn sour and putrefy as they spoil, and that only oil, honey and wine hold out for a long time. So that it is not possible, through the fermentation and separation of the other juices, to discover clearly the form of each of the residues; rather, right from the beginning they require some boiling and mixing with some other one of the juices that keep. Thus, then, we also store the juice of the rose, by mixing it with honey, or by boiling it together with oil, or by steeping the whole roses in them.

But that in this too it is plausible that the four kinds are present, both the [583] proper [part] of the juice itself and the three residues, is plain to see, and above all because the matter of their quality is not simple. Rather, the rose will seem to you to have some astringency as well, if you should wish to chew it thoroughly; and it also has a certain sweetness and, as it were, a slight biting. Yet even if none of these were apparent to those tasting it, it would have been enough to conceive of the admixtures of the other juices from the fact that it is not completely astringent. For if the harsh [juice] were alone, it would be extreme; so that, if it is not extreme, neither is it alone. For whatever origin of astringency you may suppose, if you conceive of it alone, without the others, coming to be present, this must necessarily be rendered extreme; just as, if heat alone were to come to be present in some body, such a thing will be completely fire. For the admixtures of contraries break down the extremes.

In homoeomerous bodies, then, it is heat and cold, wetness and dryness that produce all the particular differences; in anhomoeomerous bodies it is pungencies and sournesses, harshnesses [584] and acerbities, sweetnesses and oilinesses. Each of the homoeomerous bodies, taken in its parts themselves, therefore has not many qualities but one, while the anhomoeomerous whole has very many. For if, as it may happen, a thousand homoeomerous bodies are contained in a cyathus of some particular juice, it is possible that a hundred of them are astringent, sixty biting, six hundred sweet, two hundred bitter and forty salty, and that all these are mixed with one another, so that no perceptible part can be taken so small as not to share in all of them.

so that, in touching the tongue, all of them act, each of them on whatever different part of it it happens to come into contact with, while the affection is transmitted from the part first affected to the whole tongue; just as, when in severe cold we plunge one finger suddenly into cold water, we shiver over the whole hand, and often over the entire body as well. For in sensitive bodies the transmission from the part first affected to the whole animal takes place quickly, so that the whole is heated together with what is being heated, cooled together with what is being cooled, dried [585] together with what is being dried, and moistened together with what is being moistened, and often the whole suffers contrary things at one and the same time. But in order that you may arrive more fully at a conception of what is being said, it is perhaps better to turn your mind to another example as well. You have seen, I suppose, at some time, when a stone was thrown into still water, the water beginning to move from it and extending its movement in a circle, the thing that struck it being, as it were, the centre. Now when, at one and the same time, two stones thrown into different places of still water generate two circles that travel through one another, you will see contrary movements in every part of the water; whence this phenomenon has also caused perplexity to the natural philosophers themselves, whether different parts are moved for each of the two movements, or the same parts are moved by both. For that the one circle does not stop the other circle, nor prevent it from travelling onward, is plainly seen. Conceive, I ask you, the same thing as this when at one and the same time we plunge the feet into cold water and the hands into hot. For the movement of each of the two affections passes through the whole body, and they meet one another as contraries.

[586] And perhaps it makes no difference even if the motions do not travel in opposite directions, but approach one another, the one having taken its start from one of the feet and the other from the other. For in that case it is not possible to say either that the whole body is affected in no way, or that it is affected by only one of the two. For it is plainly affected, and affected by both, being heated and cooled at the same time, just as, I think, also happens in the leipyriae and in the epialoi fevers; except that in those cases it is not from outside, but from the body itself, that both the condition of cooling and that of heat take their start. But if someone does not follow what is being said even now, then from what is about to be said it is very easy for him to put it to the test. For it is not far removed from the matters under investigation, but belongs to the very affections of the tongue. For if, having mixed precisely equal bulks of wormwood and honey, you place it on the tongue, the mixture of the two will appear to you bittersweet, as the poets call love; the tongue does not perceive the honey at one time and the wormwood at another, nor only one of them, but perceives both throughout, mixed in a certain unaccustomed mixture.

Something of this sort [587] happens also when a harsh and a nitrous power come together into a single flavour, whether nature itself has mixed them or some physician has compounded them. For the tongue perceives the quality of each of the two flavours at one and the same time; and if it perceives them, it is clearly also disposed according to their proper powers. Each of the other parts of the body must likewise be affected in the same way, even if it does not perceive the qualities. For one must not suppose that the tongue differs from the other parts in being affected or not being affected, but in that none of its own affections escapes it, owing to the precision of its perceptive faculty. Its looseness of texture also contributes to this. For the juices, descending more easily into its depth and acting upon its soft parts, produce a strong condition, and also a more evident perception of that condition. But the greater capacity lies rather in the precision of the perception, not in the strength of the condition. For the strength of the condition arises no less in ulcerated parts as well; yet because precision of perception is absent there, the qualities of the juices go unnoticed.

[588] It is possible, however, both in those cases and even before them, while the skin is not yet ulcerated, to infer the mixed action that arises from contrary powers, coming about at the same time in the bodies. For if you apply the juice of strychnos to an inflamed part, you will see it being condensed and compacted, and its transpirations being checked. So that, if you do this for a longer time, you will no longer even keep the part red, but will make it either livid or black, which is just the sort of thing that most physicians continually do in erysipelases as well. For these too they blacken and harden in the course of time, by cooling them immoderately. If, then, you apply not strychnos but anthemis to the inflamed part, you will see it undergoing everything contrary. For it will be rare and diffused and soft and slack, and much of the superfluity in it will be transpired, and it will never be livid or black, even if you use the chamomile for many days in succession; for this is by nature such as to diffuse and to disperse, not to draw together, nor to condense, nor to shut in the transpirations.

That camomile, then, is of a power contrary to strychnos is [589] clear from these things. That if you should mix both, you will clearly observe the powers of each, I tell you having made trial of it myself; but I would rather that you too should arrive at knowledge of what happens through experience itself than put your trust in me as I relate it. This, I know, everyone will do who is a lover of truth. But I must carry through the argument that follows as though this had already been shown. For if, when strychnos and anthemis are applied together, the part is seen to take on neither so dense and hard and tightly stretched and livid a condition as if one had used strychnos alone, nor so rare and soft and lax and red a condition as if one had used camomile alone, but the condition intermediate between each of those mentioned, it is reasonable that both drugs acted according to their own power. For if neither had acted, but both had remained at rest, the part would have kept its original condition, as if we had applied nothing at all; and if one of them had acted while the other was completely overcome, the part would have suffered not the intermediate condition but one or other of the extremes.

And indeed, if each [590] acted, and these were contrary in their powers, then the body was undergoing contraries at the same time. For they certainly did not act by dividing the times between them, so that, for instance, when both had been applied for a whole day, one of the drugs acted during the first six hours and the other during the remaining six. For this hypothesis is nonsensical, and devoid not only of all demonstration but even of plausibility. Therefore the underlying substance was not diffused and drawn together in the way it is for those who have washed in a bath and afterwards stepped into cold water, but rather as if you were to sprinkle cold water on someone while he is bathing. For in this way he will undergo the contraries not at different times but at one and the same time. Just as, then, in the case of compound drugs there is nothing surprising in contrary conditions arising in bodies at the same time, so neither is there in the case of simple drugs, when these too appear simple to perception and diagnosis in other respects, but are compound with respect to their nature itself.

Moreover, just as with the things that we ourselves compound and mix, putting in, as it may happen, sometimes more of the [591] astringent juice, sometimes more of the sweet, or bitter, or salty, or pungent, or some other of the opposites, and sometimes both in equal amounts, so too it is possible for nature, in trees and shrubs and herbs and animals and in the earth itself, to mix the opposite flavours, either in their bulks or in their powers. And sometimes she also makes the one more predominant, so that their activities too are similar in the equal mixtures but differ in the unequal ones. Let no one, then, as has also been said before, suppose that it is the same thing to discourse about an astringent juice and about astringency itself. For astringency is conceived as one simple thing, whereas the astringent body is twofold, just as the heating body is: the one simple and extreme, such as fire, the other by predominance of heat, such as blood.

And so too with the astringent: one kind is extreme, such as, for instance, alum, melanteria, oak-gall and sumach; the other is astringent by partaking to some degree of the astringent quality, such as pear, wine, apple [592] and rose. For in the rose a very small amount of the astringent is mixed with a many times greater amount of what is not such, so that the effects of its astringency are, reasonably enough, slight. They go only so far as to keep the tone of the bodies in contact with it from being dissolved by the relaxing power in the rose. It is therefore no wonder that it is a remedy for inflammations, especially in their progression and increase, or rather even while they are still beginning. Nor is it any wonder that rose oil, being intermediate in nature between olive oil and rose, is the best drug in the increases of inflammations. For olive oil itself is useful at the peaks of inflammations, as experience shows; and in the books of the Therapeutic Method we shall state the cause. But rose oil is intermediate between the simples from whose blending it came to be, and so it displays its benefit at the intermediate time.

For at the beginnings one must rather repel and check the influxes, at the peaks disperse without biting, and in the advances both repel and disperse at the same time; which someone hearing it without the reasonings stated before might perhaps [593] disbelieve. But now I do not know whether anyone is so dull as not yet to have been persuaded by the argument. For indeed the indications in the ascents of inflammations must necessarily be contrary. For to pass all at once from things that are astringent and that draw the substance together to things that relax and diffuse it is absurd; and in the interval between the peak and the beginning, while the diseases are still increasing, it is right neither simply to repel, as at the beginnings, nor already to disperse, as at the peaks; but just as the condition of the affection is intermediate between the contraries, so the cure too must be intermediate, neither astringent, as at the beginnings, nor dispersing, as at the peaks. And indeed every intermediate is mixed from the contraries, either with these blended with one another through and through, or in small particles of the things lying side by side, which escape perception. Whether, then, you would have rose oil blended from the contraries in this way or in that, it makes no difference to me; for the proposition is demonstrated either way.

I know, however, that if you become more fully conversant with all the reasonings on these matters, both those which Theophrastus [594] wrote and those which we set out throughout this whole treatise, you will find that it is the second mode of mixture. Moreover, rose oil also has the property of sinking down into the depth, and of moistening the dry among bodies more than olive oil does. And I think you have often seen people rubbing the dense kinds of leather cloaks with rose oil. For olive oil and hydrelaeon (oil-and-water) do not soak them well, since they are too coarse-grained to be able to sink inward; but in rose oil it happens that, in addition to the other properties it has, its astringency too, being slight, contributes not a little to this. For things that are intensely harsh and acerbic, by condensing the outer surface immediately as they come into contact with it, prevent the moistures from being carried inward. But those that are astringent only to a slight degree, while containing for the most part a substance at once fine-particled and lukewarm, not only are not prevented by the astringency from descending into the depth of the bodies they approach, but are actually assisted, being pushed onward by it.

For whatever things are simply fine-particled and hot rather disperse [595] the moistures out of the bodies they come near, and do not add others. Those that are at once coarse-particled and cold are not naturally fitted to introduce any moisture at all in the first place. But as for things in which there is a moisture at once lukewarm and fine-particled, nothing prevents these, being readily moved on account of the fine-particled and lukewarm nature of their substance, from passing through the pores of the bodies being moved. That they do not heat sufficiently is clear from the fact that they do not disperse the moisture present in them. And if, besides being of this kind, they also share in some slight astringency, such as both to push onward toward the depth whatever fine-particled matter has already penetrated into the pores, and in some way to constrict and condense the outer surface, these are the most effective of all moistening agents. For astringency, by closing off the pores before anything else and by drawing together into itself and compacting the substance that comes near it, stands in the way of the things naturally fitted to moisten.

But astringency that is so weak, as in rose oil, where it is overcome rather than overcoming, is not able to get ahead of the [596] fine-particled and fine parts of the rose oil; rather, once those have sunk into the depth, it begins to act on the outer surface, compressing, drawing together and condensing as far as it is able. From this it necessarily follows that the small-particled bodies which got ahead and entered the pores are pushed further inward, and are prevented from running back outward, since the pores have been closed off. And in operations of this kind the innate heat of our bodies also cooperates to no small degree. For it both draws inward to itself and thins by breaking up; in this way even drugs that are cold by nature, those called deleterious (hemlock and poppy and henbane seed and mandrake and all others of that kind), act faster and more strongly in hot natures. And this too, though it might be supposed to be one of the insoluble problems, will readily have its solution for you, if you do not attend carelessly to what is said.

For if it is impossible for such drugs to kill unless they also chill the heart itself, then surely they must travel inward [597], being broken down and thinned. But this they do not have from their own nature, for they are coarse-grained and hard to move, and would never of themselves achieve division into fine pieces and forward movement; so they need some acquired heat, which cuts, thins and breaks them down into small pieces and, as it were, guides them on their way and leads them along into the fine pores of all the parts. So long, then, as the drug lacks such heat, it lingers and is slow, being held back in the large pores and, as it were, swimming about in the veins and arteries; and in the course of time, through its long wandering, it is perhaps also acted upon in some degree in return by the humours in them.

For it has already been shown many times that all the qualities act upon one another in some respect, and that a stone has been affected by the continual striking of a drip of water, and that a sword has been blunted by cutting wax. It has also been demonstrated that the activities in animals come about through the solid bodies in them; so long as these have not yet been chilled by the chilling drugs, it is necessary [598] that the animal survive. And they are not chilled before the drugs have entered into their proper passages. This the coarse-grained and cold drugs do not possess of themselves, unless they meet with something to guide them on their way. What guides them, as the first cause, is the attraction of the arteries, for they were shown to draw everything that is near them when they dilate; and, as the second and material cause, the fine-particledness of the substance, which the colder and more coarse-particled drugs do not have of themselves, and so they require things that will supply it. Now all bodies that are cold in their mixtures have the attraction of the arteries weaker than hot bodies have (for this too was shown), and they are unable to break up the substances of the drugs quickly into small pieces. As a consequence, the drug lingers and is likely in time to be itself affected as well, so that sometimes it is even concocted, as is the juice of lettuce too: for this too is concocted in time; but if it reaches the heart first while still unaltered, it kills in much the same way as hemlock. All the other strongly chilling juices also undergo this.

For if [599] they are unable to destroy quickly, from that point on they become altogether ineffective. But those that kill by erosion and putrefaction may become strong by lingering. For everything putrefies in time, and still more so in a moist and warm place. Fittingly, then, for those whose harm comes from cooling, the speed of their action contributes to destruction. For, being warmed in the course of time, they lose the power by which they had the capacity to act. But for those whose acting comes from putrefying, time increases their activity, because it also increases the putrefaction. For no animal can perish without the heart ceasing from its activity, and the heart cannot cease without some very great bad mixture. For it will certainly not stop moving simply by becoming hotter than it should to some chance degree, or colder. In the same way, neither will it if it becomes moderately dry or moist. For it will act worse because of such bad mixtures, but it will not be motionless until it has taken on some extraordinary warmth, or cooling, or some other of the active qualities.

Something similar happens to the drugs that kill by cooling [600] whenever they are slow in coming to the heart, similar to what often happens with moist and green wood. For these too, when many are put on the fire all at once, quickly put it out; but when they are all set around it in a circle and dried and heated beforehand, and then put on little by little, they not only do not put it out but even become nourishment of the fire. In the same way, then, hemlock kills a human being, because of the width of the pores, the abundance of the heat, and the strength of the attraction of the arteries, since it arrives at the heart while still strong. But it does not kill starlings, since for the opposite causes it is held back and slowed, and has time to be concocted beforehand and prepared beforehand, being warmed beforehand by the heart as by a kind of hearth, as the wood is outside. So this too is neither surprising nor puzzling, but is just like what happens with lettuces as well. For these nourish human beings when eaten in moderation.

But if someone should squeeze out their juice and gulp down a copious amount, he will die in the same manner as those who have taken hemlock [601] or poppy juice. Just as, then, lettuce kills if it has first chilled the heart, but becomes nourishment for the animal once it has been concocted, so in the same manner, I think, hemlock too kills a human being by getting there first, but nourishes starlings by being slow. Yet it will not kill even a human being if taken in a small amount. This was shown by the Attic old woman, whom everyone mentions: she began with a very small amount of hemlock and advanced without harm to a considerable quantity. For at the beginning the small amount was overcome because of its very smallness, and through habituation it became connatural. This is not the time to give the cause of habits having the greatest power and being acquired natures, as the ancients said they are. For in that case the side-issue would become greater than the main task, besides the fact that I have written about it separately. But we must join together and bring to an end the present discussion.

Of the drugs, then, that kill by chilling, none is deleterious in its kind, but [602] only in its quantity. With those that corrode, putrefy and heat, however, the case is not the same; but of these we shall speak a little later. Those that kill by chilling will not kill when taken in a small amount, just as a great flame will not be put out if you pour a little water on it, or lay on it a single piece of wood that is moist and green. For just as the drug cannot kill unless it meets with abundant warmth that breaks it up and conducts it as far as the heart, so, if that which breaks it up and conducts it is much the stronger, it will completely overcome the drug, transform it, and make it nourishment for itself. Right here, then, we must also remember that the ancients were right to call even the drugs that are cold by nature 'potentially cold'. For in a certain way these too take their chilling from us, just as the hot ones take their heating. It makes no difference if the hot ones do this in one way and these in another. For what is universal and common to both is the same: the starting point of the alteration passes from the body that is to be affected to the drug that is to act.

Drugs are altered, [603] those that are hot in potency only by being heated by us, but those that are cold by nature by being broken down and by acquiring an adventitious motion. Since, then, it is not possible for them to act as cold things without the body that is acted upon, they have rightly been called potentially cold. For they do not possess the cooling of us in actuality entirely from themselves; rather, they first need to be acted upon by us in order to cool. For both being broken down into small parts and acquiring an adventitious motion are affections of the drugs. To anyone, however, who wishes to call such things cold in actuality as well, the point must be conceded, since the disagreement will henceforth lie in a name, provided the matter itself is agreed upon. For all such things, as has just been shown by me, need a hot body in order to act. And for this reason both meconium and hemlock, when mixed with wine, naturally kill more quickly, but not in every proportion. For when very small amounts are mixed with a very great quantity of wine, they might be completely overcome; but when large amounts are mixed with little wine, they are guided to the heart, yet cannot be overcome.

But if someone has already drunk juice of the poppy, which is by nature capable of killing, and is still alive, it is reasonable that [604] old wine, drunk in quantity, cures this man too, and the more so if it is one of the noble wines; for these also heat more. That the heart has not yet been violently chilled is clear from the fact that the person is still alive. That, in the slowness of its journey, the drug has in any case already been somewhat altered beforehand by the body, just like green wood when it lies near the fire, this too is not unclear. A hot wine, then, drunk in this situation is the best remedy, and we ourselves have before now saved with Lesbian wine someone who had been chilled to the utmost degree. Falernian and Surrentine, Ariusian and the harsh Tmolite, and all the other hot and truly vinous wines, could display the same action as the Lesbian. For in general, whichever wine is thin and translucent in consistency, tawny or yellow in colour, fragrant in smell, and in being mixed requires a very great quantity of water, is by nature capable of heating strongly and of being carried readily to every part of the body.

Such a wine, then, of this kind by nature and old in age, when mixed rather undiluted [605], cures not only those already chilled by poppy juice or by some other of the cooling drugs of this kind, but also those who in diseases suffer syncope, whether of the stomachic or of the cardiac sort. But the wine that is drunk together with the cooling drugs themselves in order to kill more quickly is neither much nor of a noble kind; it is only as much as serves to break them up and to convey them to the heart by the impetus of the distribution. And let this suffice about these matters. Since I also promised to speak about the drugs that kill by way of putrefaction and erosion, explaining how they become worse with time and are by their kind destructive of our nature, and not, like the cooling drugs, by their quantity alone, it would now be time for me to speak about these as well. For the account of them is in a way also connected with the account of the drugs that heat in potentiality.

For it is likely that most such drugs are already hot in actuality as well, but that this escapes us, [606] either because we ourselves partake of more warmth, or because their substance is coarse-particled. Let us again recall the same examples: in the bath our urine appears cold to us. Let us recall too how, sometimes unable to get down into a hot basin, we first got down into another less hot than it, and then used without distress the one that until then had seemed unbearable. And spring water in winter appears lukewarm to those whose hands are cold, but to others it does not appear so. For in general, as was also said before, each body perceives the things that come near it according to its own condition. Thus, if your hand is cold and you put it into a heap of wheat, you will clearly perceive heat, but if your hand is hot, you will not. Into a heap of pigeons' dung, however, and especially that of wild pigeons, you will perceive distinct warmth even if the hand you put in is hot. In the same way misy and chalcitis, verdigris and lime, and countless other such substances will at once appear hot to you if you thrust your hand into them while they lie heaped up.

If, however, you take some lump of one of them, whose outer [607] surface has been chilled by the external and surrounding air, you will reasonably perceive no heat at all. For you are touching those parts of it that have been chilled, and doing so before breaking it up into fine pieces. In the same way, in winter, well water, or spring water of some other kind, has often appeared warm to those touching it; but if someone touches it after first warming his hands, it will appear cold. And it is possible to recall countless other such things, from which no one would doubt that those drugs which are hot in potentiality relative to us are hot in actuality for another kind of animal. Let this, then, be said as a kind of digression by the way. But those things which, on coming into contact with us, kill either by erosion or by putrefaction (for it was about these that the discussion was) are reasonably supposed to be deleterious to the human constitution in their kind, and not, like cooling things, in quantity only.

For these are sometimes even overcome and become nourishment for the animal, whereas things that putrefy, even if they are taken in the very smallest bulk, are in every case corrupted, since all things capable of putrefaction putrefy [608] when they are heated and moistened, and the blood is hot and moist. Putrefactive drugs, therefore, can never cease from putrefying and from causing putrefaction in turn. And for this reason some of them kill a very long time after they have been taken, and especially those that are coarse-particled and earthy in their substances. For these settle in our bodies, and then, putrefying in the course of time, they eat through the neighbouring parts of the animal and corrupt them along with themselves. For the more fine-particled ones may even be excreted at times together with the residues; and it is for roughly these two causes that some of the drugs that kill by putrefaction and erosion have on occasion not killed. One is the cause I have just finished stating: when they happen to have been excreted together with the residues before harming the body. The other is when the person who took them is somehow fortunate enough to make use of foods, or of things that would in other ways have benefited him, or of some physician supervising him, if it so happened.

For when the harm from them is great, it is not possible [609] for [the person] to be restored [even] by regimen and the use of potent drugs and the help of a physician. But if the poison should be altogether small in amount, it is possible that this too accomplishes nothing, through its being excreted with the residues and through the person's following the proper regimen; for example, if it were a hundredth part of a drachm of cantharis. For this will be excreted together with the urine before it harms the animal. Indeed, cantharis is even mixed into diuretic drugs, just as a great many other deadly substances are also mixed into antidotes. And such compound drugs, when they are suitably mixed, become most efficacious, as is also the diuretic made with cantharis. For cantharides do in any case, in a certain way, have an impulse towards the bladder by way of the urine; at any rate, it is in this way that they ulcerate it, eating it away. But when a small amount of them is mixed with many beneficial [ingredients], it guides those along, but is not able to corrode.

For everything that is going to act, I think, even if it be most powerful, requires some definite amount of magnitude, since even fire, if it be altogether very small, [610] besides not burning, cannot even heat. At any rate, the hundredth part of a spark is imperceptible to us. From all of which it is quite clear that those things which destroy by cooling could, when taken in small quantities, nourish the body, as the juice of lettuce does, whereas those which destroy by corroding or putrefying are not capable of nourishing, even if, owing to their smallness, they should pass through the body without harm. For such things are in their kind contrary to the constitution of man. Just as we said earlier about the juices (χυλῶν), that hardly any of them is unmixed with a foreign quality, but whether in trees, in herbs or in fruits they are mixed with things of other kinds, so one must understand that in drugs too the substances of many things of other kinds are mixed together. For you would find, if you reasoned it out, that the Cnidian berry differs from cnicus in partaking of a very large share of heat. For you can learn the similarity of the substances of both through touch and through sight, and thirdly, in addition to these, from the fact that both are agents for drawing off phlegm.

For it has been shown [611] by us in the commentaries on the natural faculties that attractions are accomplished through affinity of the qualities in the substances. For a considerable heat has been mixed into the berry, and in this it differs from cnicus. And for this reason some of the purgative drugs, when they fail to purge, in some cases, besides doing the body no harm, even become nourishment for the animal, while others turn aside into what is destructive and deleterious. For the purging drug certainly has some likeness to at least one of the humours in us; but it is not in every case that some deleterious power has been mixed in with it, so that it will not in every case do harm when it has not purged. Rather, it will be digested and will generate a humour of the same kind as the one it was drawing. I am not unaware that it is not possible to follow such arguments adequately for those who have not been trained beforehand in the commentaries on the natural faculties.

For it was shown in those [commentaries] that most attractions come about in an affinity of qualities, and that for this reason each of the parts of the animal too [612] draws its proper nourishment to itself. And it follows from this doctrine that purgative drugs are akin to the humours that are attracted, but that the things which attract are in some way more active, just as the Magnesian stone is in relation to iron. For it too is iron-like, is found in iron mines, and closely resembles iron in appearance, but it is somehow stronger, so as to attract rather than be attracted. And indeed one should not despair of cnicus being phlegmatic, as it shows in its colour, but through its heat it is stronger than phlegm, so as to attract rather than be attracted. In the same way also the Cnidian berry. But if ever it should be overcome by our body (and this happens continually with cnicus, but hardly at all with the berry, on account of its strength), then instead of purging it becomes nourishment, just as hellebore always does for quails. And since I have come to this argument, I wish also to recall a certain logical theorem, demonstrated also in my commentaries On Demonstrations, which is useful for the present matters. The theorem is as follows.

Of demonstrations, [613] some conclude that this belongs to that of necessity, others that it may belong. Of these latter, some pass over into belonging of necessity when they follow upon necessary principles, as is the case with this very thing which has just been demonstrated by us. For in the berry and in the safflower it is not possible to show evidently the phlegmatic humour contained in them; but the possible, the likely and the contingent belong to the argument. But since we have shown that attractions too come about through the similarities of substances (for it has been shown many times that in purgations there is an attraction of what is proper to the purging drugs, not an alteration of all the humours together), it is necessary that some similarity belong to both substances, that of the purging thing and that of the thing purged. Since, then, what is purged is phlegm, it is surely altogether necessary that what attracts be phlegmatic as well. I said that what attracts must be phlegmatic, not that it is outright phlegm itself. For we said that a similarity belongs to the substances, not an identity.

For it is wholly the contrary: neither does iron attract iron nor does [614] flesh attract flesh; rather, the iron-stone (sideritis) attracts iron, and flesh attracts blood. For the same and the similar differ, I think. Phlegm is the same as phlegm, and cnicus as cnicus, but cnicus is similar to phlegm, not, however, the same. Nor, indeed, when we speak of certain foods as bilious or phlegmatic do we give them these names as though they already contained bile or phlegm. For the absurdity of this opinion too has been shown, both in the commentaries On the Natural Faculties and in many other places. These matters, then, and all such, must be passed over; but that other point must be taken up again: of the purging drugs themselves, some already possess the similarity suitable for attraction, while some do not yet have it completely,

but acquire it in the body of the animal, in the same way as the caustic drugs; so that in these too the similarity is twofold, the one in actuality, the other in potentiality, just as in all other cases; and moreover that mixed with the similar humours in [615] each are other, dissimilar ones, some of them drug-like, others not. And thus, in the failures of purgations, some of the purging drugs do us some harm, while others become harmless nourishment. Since I have once arrived at the discussion of purging drugs, it is perhaps not amiss to say something also about the so-called hyperpurgations. These, then, occur when the purgative drug, having prevailed sufficiently, produces at the mouths of the vessels that reach down to the stomach both biting and at the same time a greater opening of their mouths, and, continually irritating and tearing their bodies, dissolves the faculty in the vessels. For just what is seen to happen in the case of the stomach, when its faculty collapses into extreme weakness, such a thing one must consider to occur in the veins too. What, then, is it that happens in the case of the stomach? Vomitings of everything swallowed, when the weakness befalls its upper parts, and lienteries, when it befalls the lower.

These matters too are demonstrated [616] at greater length in the [treatise on the] Causes of What Is Evacuated. One must suppose that some such affection befalls the veins in excessive purgations. While at the beginning both the opening of the orifices and the weakness are still moderate, what is thinnest and less proper is excreted; but when both have advanced further, then the thick things too, and those most proper to the animal, are evacuated. For this reason, then, yellow bile is excreted first, phlegm second, black bile third, and last of all these in excessive purgations the blood: this as the humour most proper to the nature, while before it the thinnest is first and the thickest last. Now the order of their evacuation has also been stated by Hippocrates in the book On the Nature of Man, but it will be stated now as well, so that nothing may be lacking to the account. For if you give a drug that is an evacuant of phlegm, in excessive purgations the yellow [bile] is evacuated first, the black second, and the blood last. But if the drug should be an evacuant of yellow bile, the phlegm will follow, the black [bile] third, and the blood fourth.

Moreover [617], if it should be purgative of black bile, it will evacuate that first, after it the yellow, then in this way the phlegm, and last of all the blood will follow, flowing out as if from vessels already lifeless, since great weakness has seized them and their mouths have reached the utmost distension. From this it is clear that in excessive purgations the humour most proper to human beings is evacuated last, and each of the others according to the degree of thinness or thickness it happens to have. The cause of the humours that are not proper to the purging drug being excreted at all lies in these three things: the weakness of the vessels, the width of their mouths, and the biting of the purgative. For when the vessels are no longer able to hold the humours within themselves, and their mouths are opened wide, and the drug continues to irritate but no longer has its proper humour to draw, it is altogether necessary that the others be excreted in the order stated.

For perhaps the biting alone, if it persisted, would have sufficed to rouse the organs to excretion, but much more so when [618] opening of the mouths and weakness of the vessels concur together. The opening of the mouths comes about, as has been said, through the strength of the drug, the same strength through which the biting also comes about; the weakness of the vessels comes about both through the violent fatigue which they undergo in being bitten and, as it were, sucked by the purging drug, and further through the bad mixture that seizes them in excessive purgations. For whichever of the humours you evacuate entirely, a bad mixture must of necessity follow. These, then, are the causes of the evacuation even of the humours foreign to the purging drug. Of their evacuation in the order stated before, the cause is the thinness and thickness of the evacuated humours themselves, and in addition the greater or lesser affinity of each of the humours to the constitution of the animal.

[619] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 4. In what way, then, a drug is said to be cold, or hot, or dry, or moist in power, and by what method one must test it, has been set out in detail earlier.

And most of them do this while being ignorant not only of natural theory [460] but also of the logical methods which anyone who demonstrates anything whatsoever must necessarily use; so that, knowing neither what has been rightly discovered by the natural philosophers nor the very points about which these men have reasonably been in doubt, they often dare to declare the opposite in both cases. Come now, by the gods: suppose I now began to speak in some such way as this: that, there being four elements, air and earth and water and fire, the white and bright colour is innate in nothing else except light and fire. Suppose that I then called Empedocles and certain others of the natural philosophers as witnesses to the argument, and declared that all bright bodies partake of fire in the greatest measure, having neglected to look at snow and white lead and ice and countless other things that are at once brightest and coldest. Suppose further that, when someone put these forward, I ran away from the refutation that comes from sensation and demanded that we proceed to reason, and by it examine the nature of things, rather than entrust everything to the irrational senses. Would I not seem to those who have sense to be mad, not knowing even the things from which I begin my argument?

For it is from sensation [461], I think, and through sensation that we have learned all such axioms as these: that the sun is bright, that flames are yellowish, and that most live coals are yellow. If, then, we must abandon the senses, we shall have no demonstration, neither we of the things we have just stated, nor Empedocles when he writes thus: 'Behold the sun, hot and bright everywhere.' But if these things are true, it is clear that sensation must be trustworthy long before them. 'But,' they say, 'it is necessary for us, being human, to begin from the senses; yet it is not fitting to remain with sensation forever, but rather to proceed to what is more divine, reason. For we share sensation even with irrational animals, but reason only with the gods.' And beginning from this point they draw the argument out to great length. And some of them even call upon Anaxagoras as a witness, since he declared of snow that it was not white.

This man, then, they say, being a natural philosopher, is above the senses and despises [462] their appearances; he ascends instead to reason, and by it hunts down the nature of the things that are. But if I must say what occurs to me, as one of free and liberal spirit who has pursued truth throughout his whole life, I consider that those who talk such nonsense have gone beyond melancholy. For if they overturn what appears clearly through the senses, they will have no point from which to begin their demonstrations. But if they begin from these as from things worthy of trust, how will they afterwards reasonably withdraw their trust? For the starting-points of demonstrations are more trustworthy than the things demonstrated, which need to be made credible from other things. And the starting-points of demonstrations are trustworthy not only in and by themselves, but also for the discovery of the things sought. For my part, I would pray that all things fell clearly under our senses and that nothing escaped them, since in this way nothing would be either insoluble or disputed.

But since some things do escape them, one must try to bring reason to bear on them, though neither from afar, as those people do, nor by drawing inconclusive syllogisms, but first [463] by precisely distinguishing the meanings of the names, so that no deception arises in what follows through homonymy; and second, by separating off that which acts in some way per se from that which acts per accidens. Both of these have been discussed precisely in what precedes, and the meanings of things said to be potentially hot, or cold, or dry, or moist, or to be anything else whatever, have been distinguished. And how one might discover the proper power of each drug, separating it off from what is per accidens, we have gone through in general terms in the third book On Mixtures, and in the present treatise we go through it by way of particulars, as we already did in the first book in the case of water and vinegar; and here again we shall do so in the case of oil and rose oil, having first shown how greatly those physicians err who begin their demonstrations from afar. For why should one examine the colour of oil, or of roses, when one is able to use the things themselves in many ways, not only on healthy bodies but also on diseased ones?

For it is possible to take roses themselves, on their own, and their juice, and apply them [464] to the body, both when it is healthy and when it is suffering from a simple disease, as was said earlier; and also, mixing them with sweet oil, to apply them to bodies that have been strongly chilled or heated, rubbing them in, pouring them over (?) and soaking the parts; and to take them into the inside of the body, either from above through the mouth or from below through the anus; and then to observe what happens with each use. Indeed, it is for this reason too that we investigate the power of all drugs: so that we may have the ones we must use when the hypochondria and the head are burning, or have been chilled, or are ulcerated, or are inflamed, or suffer some other such affection, both these parts themselves and all the other members of the body. Then, when we thus have a road to what we are seeking that is at once evident and short, shall we still examine the colours, or smells, or consistencies, or sounds of each of the drugs? In doing so we would be acting much like those who wish to recognise some man from an image, whether sculpted or painted, when it is possible to look at the very man who is to be recognised.

[465] In this respect, then, they seem to me to err in no small way, and still more in those matters in which they babble inconclusive and undemonstrated things, being ignorant of demonstrative method. For let fire be supposed to be either yellow or red, or however they wish, for it makes no difference to me. What, then, has this to do with everything red being hot? For every fire, if it should so happen, must be said to be red. But to say that everything red is fire is ridiculous, and still more so if one were to say that everything red is hot. If it had been assumed from the beginning in the argument that everything hot is red, it would perhaps have been possible, by twisting the proposition round, to declare everything red hot, though erring plainly even in this. For it is propositions that convert (antistrephontes) with one another, not those that are reversed (anastrephontes), that are true together; but nevertheless the paralogism would, I think, have been a near one. But since not even this itself has been assumed at the outset, I mean that everything hot is red, it is not possible, even by reversing it, to say that everything red is hot.

Those who assert that roses are hot in their mixture, [466] because they are also red, therefore err in three ways in their argument. First, because, without having shown that all fire is red, they try to make another proposition convert with it, namely that everything red is fire, as though it were true. Second, because they do not know that it is the propositions that convert, not those that are inverted, which are themselves true along with true propositions. And third, because even if they do convert, what will be concluded from the conversion is not that everything red in colour is hot, but some other proposition of this kind, different from it: that everything red is fire. That such a proposition is not only useless for the present purposes but also manifestly false is clear to everyone. For what we need to have demonstrated is not whether everything red is fire, but that it is hot. Indeed, if everything red is fire, then evidently the rose too will be fire for us. But physicians who do not know the logical methods, I think, go most gravely wrong first of all in this very thing: in overstepping their own proper boundaries.

For experience together with brief inferences is sufficient to discover the powers of drugs; and then they also err in their arguments, like boys newly instructed [467] in logical theory. The same fault is committed by all who infer something about the power of drugs from their odours. For neither is everything fragrant hot, as some say (being ignorant of how one ought to understand what Aristotle and Theophrastus said on these matters, which we shall define in the fourth book of these commentaries), nor is everything hot fragrant; nor indeed is everything malodorous hot, nor, if something is hot, is it malodorous. So too, if someone were to say that everything malodorous is cold, or that what is cold is malodorous, he does not speak the truth. For of hot things countless are fragrant, others malodorous, others neither; and likewise of cold things. And yet why do I say cold and hot, when we ought to say heating and cooling, which is exactly what we are investigating? For what is now proposed for examination is not what is hot simply, or what is assessed in relation to this, but what heats the human body. And likewise not cold simply, but whatever cools a human being.

Here again, then, by not distinguishing the things signified by the names, [468] they are misled through the homonymy, just as if someone discoursing about the land dog were to pass over in his argument to the sea dog, supposing that, as the name of both animals is one, so too their nature is one. But it has been shown clearly by us in the commentaries On Mixtures, which we said right at the beginning should precede this treatise, that what is hot in potentiality is one thing, and what is hot in actuality another. And of this hot in actuality, one is called hot simply, another by predominance, another in relation to the well-proportioned thing of the same kind, and another in relation to any chance thing whatever. And indeed we said that man is hot not simply, as fire is, but hot by predominance; for there is in him a greater portion of the hot than of the cold. And so whatever things are said in relation to these [πρὸς τούτων; perhaps to be read πρὸς τοῦτον, 'in relation to him'] to be hot in potentiality will be so called by virtue of heating him. And the judgement of them is very easy, and will be tested through experience, requiring, as has been said before as well, brief inferences.

Passing over these, then, the sophists both waste the time [469] of the young men and, leading astray with sophisms people untrained in the solution of sophisms, fill them up with false doctrines. For they ought to have mentioned neither colour nor smell, nor indeed consistency, or smoothness, or roughness, or any other such thing. For what does it matter that oil is viscous, or that it is smooth, or that it glistens, or is liquid, or pale yellow, or oily, or slippery, or slow to dry when smeared on bodies? For from none of such things is it possible to infer whether it is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist in power. For of viscous and smooth and glistening things, some evidently heat us, others cool us, and some dry, others moisten. And with respect to each of the accidents, not in oil alone but in all other things as well, it is impossible to find anything fixed or constant, so as to establish on it some universal premise.

For I pass over the fact that in all such matters the sophists do not even use scientific arguments [470] for finding the lemmas, but argue from induction. Worst of all, they have never once examined the nature of induction, and they do not dare to follow even if someone challenges them to it; they even censure those who devote some labour to demonstration. Still worse, they draw their conclusions not from induction alone but sometimes from examples, as the rhetors do. For the man who says that oil is cold because it is viscous, as phlegm also is, reasons through an example. He offers a demonstration of equal force with that of the man who says it is hot because it is viscous, like birdlime. Likewise, the man who says it is hot because it easily bursts into flame, like bitumen, offers a demonstration of equal force with that of the man who says it is cold because it easily congeals, like water.

For establishing something from an example, or from examples, differs from establishing it through induction in this: the one who establishes from examples cites one or two of the things of the same kind, or in any case a few, leaving out the greater number, whereas the one who argues from induction tries to take in all the things known through experience, and [471] to leave out, so far as possible, nothing: not [only] what is evident and plain to the many, but [also] what is hidden and known to few. Hence induction through all the things known from experience is both compelling and strongly persuasive, and its imposture becomes detectable only to those trained in demonstrative methods. For this reason we went through it at greater length in the commentaries On Demonstration; and perhaps at some time we may also compose a single work about it separately, on its own. Yet even now the nature of induction itself will be no less apparent, and much more so that of the example. For I have resolved to go through, under main headings, everything that has been said by the physicians about the power of oil, plausibly in appearance, but certainly not truly. And first, what was stated by Diocles in the Archidamus: that Archidamus supposed that the skin becomes hardened and scorched in those who are rubbed in oil, and for this reason preferred dry rubbing.

For he thought, he says, that the oil, being heated by the rubbing, becomes fiery along with [the body] and scorches, [472] and in this way draws out the moisture and dries considerably, just as, among things being roasted, those that are anointed do. For these too become harder than if one were to roast them without oil. But perhaps it is better to copy out the whole statement of Diocles itself. It runs thus: 'Rubbing with oil he did not approve of in the same way. For in the first place he thought that such rubbing turns out uneven, because the hands slip and cannot take hold of the flesh evenly on account of the fat. Further, he said that the skin is also hardened and scorched in those rubbed in this way more than in those rubbed dry. For the oil, heated by the rubbing, becomes fiery along with it and scorches, just as, among things being roasted, those that are anointed, being heated as the oil becomes fiery and having their moisture drawn out excessively, become harder than those not anointed. Likewise things boiled in oil also become brittle and crisp for the same cause. In addition to these, just as wood and hides and the other things rubbed with oil let the oil pass through inwards along with them, so, he thought, do bodies also.'

And when this happens, [473] many of the things that are accustomed to flow through the flesh together with the pneuma and to pass out are, he thought, shut in; just as through strainers and linen cloths and wool, and through all the things through which something poured on or smeared on is strained, liquids cannot flow in the same way. And when such excretion is intercepted, some of it flows back inward, and, collecting, fills up the pores, being interwoven with one another and enveloped by the oil, because the oil has something viscid about it, just as in other cases the oily is seen to catch up dust, bits of chaff and other such things. And as the pores are continually and little by little obstructed, it is necessary that many of the things accustomed to take place according to nature be accomplished worse. He also supposed that it has something biting in it, on account of which it makes the eyes shed tears, makes the throat rough, scrapes the belly and, when drunk, produces bloody evacuations.

So when people are anointed without rubbing, [he says,] it does them no harm at all, for its biting is too weak to produce any sensation; but with rubbing, [474] as it sinks into the flesh, it does more mischief through its biting, just as many drugs, when merely smeared on, have less strength, but when pressed in and sinking inward act more. And indeed nettles and many other things do not trouble at all those who touch them gently, but they hurt those who strike them and press against them. This, then, is what Diocles says in the Archidamus. One may examine at the same time what is plausible in these statements and what is faulty. For that anything whatsoever boiled in oil loses its proper moisture and quickly becomes friable and brittle, whereas it undergoes nothing of the kind in water, we have been taught by experience, so that in this respect Archidamus said nothing false. But Aristotle and Theophrastus, and certain other philosophical men, propose and solve problems of this kind in their inquiries into nature. He too, if he really wished to seek the causes of all things that come about, ought to have proposed and solved them in the same way as they do. And if he is evidently not doing this, it is in this above all, it seems to me, that he goes wrong.

For what appears evidently must always [475] be laid down first, and only afterwards, if one so wishes, should its cause be examined, by composing physical problems in the following way. Why does oil make the things boiled down in it dry, friable and brittle, whereas water makes them moist and soft? Or why are things boiled in oil dried out, while things otherwise steeped in it keep their proper moisture better than if they had not been steeped at all? And why does it heal the bitings from squill and nettle? And why is it curative of these, yet itself bites the eyes? Why does it not bite all the rest of the body, but bites the eyes? Why does it roughen the pharynx, yet soothe ulcers? Why does it draw down the belly? Why is it remedial of fatigues? Why does it keep those who are to be anointed free from chilling? Why is it destructive of insects? Why is it softening of thongs and hides, but hardening of almost all the things boiled in it? This is for you one kind of problems, befitting the natural philosopher alone. The other, which is now common also to those who come from the arts, is of this sort.

For what reason do cooks, when they roast fish and meat, first anoint [476] them with oil? Why do trainers rub athletes with oil? And why do the masters of the palaestra (paidotribai) do so to boys as well? For it is possible to give an empirical cause for each of such problems: the cooks would say that they anoint the fish and the meat for this reason, that their outer parts become dry and scorched all round when they are roasted without the fat; the trainers would say that they rub the athletes in oil because it both dissolves the fatigues already present and soothes those that are to come, and renders the rubbing itself even and perfectly gentle, and prepares the body for the movements that are to follow. And for these same reasons the masters of the palaestra too will say that they anoint the boys both before the exercises and after the exercises. Why, however, oil is a remedy for fatigues, this neither trainer nor master of the palaestra nor Empiricist physician knows any further. Yet neither do they, because they do not know it, abandon what is evidently apparent.

For although they do not know why white hellebore purges upwards and black hellebore downwards, [477] nor why cnicus is an evacuant of phlegm and epithymum of black [humours], they nevertheless use the drugs for those purposes which experience has taught, and they treat those in need, and they trust what is plainly apparent, and they laugh at those who construct the contrary by reasoning. But Archidamus, besides despising in many matters what is plainly apparent, seems to me to deserve blame in this respect as well. For he says that dry rubbing is better than rubbing with oil, because [oil] renders the body harder and drier in those who are anointed, whereas in those who are rubbed dry it becomes softer. Yet, going on a little further in this very argument, he no less says that pieces of wood and hides and the other things rubbed with oil let it pass through to their very depth, and that this is the greatest testimony that in our bodies too it passes inwards, blocks up the pores, and prevents the outflows of the fluids. And I, for my part, do not know how these statements agree.

For if oil prevents the outflows of the fluids, it could surely not be said to dry; so that [478] it is in vain that it is avoided in rubbings as something drying. He also seems to me to err in thinking that those rubbed with it are affected in much the same way as things boiled in oil. For surely, he says (?), hot, or cold, or well-tempered, or lukewarm, or boiling oil does not produce these same effects, just as water itself does not either. For this too, if it is applied cold, evidently condenses, compacts, contracts and constricts what is being excreted, just as, if it is extremely boiling, it burns; but if it is applied well-tempered and moderately hot, it relaxes, rarefies, diffuses and disperses. And if it is neither markedly cold nor hot, but such as what most people call spring-water, it then does none of the things mentioned, but displays its own proper power. So, then, if anyone wishes to examine oil as well, let him first make it free of all acquired cooling and heat, and in that state carry out the test.

For what is extremely cold will act upon the things that come near it no longer according to its own power alone, but also through the predominance of the foreign quality; [479] and so too what is sufficiently hot. But if you wish to test it after placing it outside both of these, only in this way would you discover the proper power of oil. So, when someone is rubbed with oil in the customary way, as all who practise gymnastics are, he is rubbed with oil alone, every quality from outside being absent from the start. But when someone uses it after having made it either boiling or sufficiently hot, or else extremely cold, then the action must necessarily be compound, arising both from the proper power of oil and from the acquired quality. And often, indeed, the proper power of each of the drugs must be completely concealed, when it takes on a very strong quality from outside. What likeness, then, is there between boiling herbs in boiling oil and rubbing down the bodies of those who exercise? For above all, as has also been shown before, one must avoid proofs drawn from external things, at least when one is able to apply to each thing the test proper to it. But if someone should after all wish to do this too, let him at least try to compare like with like, as he did in the case of the hides and the straps.

For no one warms the oil beforehand or [480] chills it beforehand in snow; each takes whatever comes to hand and rubs down straps and hides with it. In the same way, I think, the masters of the palaestra (paidotribai) rub down the boys with whatever oil comes to hand, neither warming it beforehand over a fire nor chilling it beforehand on snow. Indeed, we ourselves have not infrequently cooled a burning head by pouring very cold oil over it. And if the oil has no salt in it either, it will cool still more; and if it is also pressed from unripe olives (ōmotribes), very much more still. We prepare this too in a similar way to water: having first heated it, we then set it in unmixed cold water. And if there is also a jet of water above it dashing down upon it, the vessel containing the oil having of course first been made watertight, it would in this way be made colder still. It also becomes sufficiently cold when, after first being heated, it is hung in a well touching the water. For it becomes cold even when it does not touch the water, but less so. Such preparations, then, render the oil cold, and the opposite ones render it hot.

We also use the latter, in the case of chilled bodies, [481] placing into a tank of hot oil those who have become numbed in some part, or are tremulous, or spasmodic, or palpitating, or immobile, or without sensation, or with impaired sensation, or suffering some other such thing. If, then, someone were to pronounce on the power of drugs on the basis of every use, he would straightaway think that oil is both heating and cooling for us, and both moistening and drying, just as Diocles' Archidamus does, even if he does not follow through the contradictions. For when he says that the things boiled in oil are dried and become brittle, he shows a certain drying and dispersing power in it; but when he says that it sinks into hides, plugs our pores and prevents the natural outflows of the fluids, from these he again shows its power to be, surely, most opposite to things that disperse and dry. In these matters, however, while he at least still states the phenomena, he does not reason correctly about them. But in his account of its biting he does not even go through all of them.

For its biting the eyes, making the throat rough [482], scraping the belly and bringing on bloody evacuations are sufficient testimonies that it possesses a biting power. But that it is also painless to ulcers, and that, poured on and injected, it in every case heals the bitings of the belly and soothes the irritations arising from itchings, which are themselves in turn no small signs of its opposite power, has been omitted altogether. And if, both having been stated one after the other, someone should wish to draw a conclusion, it will be one of two things: either, as an Empiric, he will say that he knows from experience the power of each of the drugs in relation to something, but is ignorant of its proper nature in and of itself; or, as a Rationalist, that opposite powers, biting and soothing, belong to the same drug; and then, I think, he will be in the greatest difficulty when he gives the cause why sometimes the one of them acts perceptibly and sometimes the other, the other having either perished or at any rate not being clearly apparent.

The solutions of all such difficulties, if they were put forward as problems of natural philosophy, are extremely hard; but if they were referred to the use of the art, they require much experience [483], and inferences that are not many but precise and properly distinguished. For first, whether all oil is biting to the eyes or not is better determined by experience, not by improvising, like rhetors arguing on either side. Then next, whether all oil is likewise roughening, or a purgative of the belly, or scrapes it so as sometimes to set bloody excretions in motion; or whether one of the oils does these things and another does not, and one does so more and another less. By differences of oil I do not now mean, as one might suppose, those of a different kind, such as castor oil, radish oil, nut oil, balanos oil and the like. The physician must indeed know the powers of these too, but it is not fitting to mention them at present. For it suffices, I think, at the outset at least, to examine that which is oil in the most proper sense and is above all so named by all men. For the fruit from which this comes is, alone among the others, called olive, and the tree is also called olive.

And this [484] is called oil simply and in the primary sense, while all the others are so called by a kind of transference and catachresis. I say, then, that of the oil properly so called itself, about which we are conducting the whole discussion at present, there are several differences. According to age: when it is either fresh and, as it were, must, or at its prime, or old. According to the manner of preparation: when it is either plain, simple and alone, or made with salt. According to the difference in the fruit itself: when the fruit is either ripe or unripe. According to the alteration produced by artificial treatment: when it is either kept just as it happened to be prepared from the beginning, or has been whitened. Not a few others have written about its whitening, and it will be discussed by us too in what follows. I myself have taken pains to test the power of all these oils, and what I detected in each case I shall relate later. For now, I wish first to bring to completion what I set out to do.

For most physicians do not, it seems, [485] go about correctly either testing drugs or reasoning about their power. One must test only those that are unmixed and free of every acquired quality: first on the best constitution of the body, next also on ill-tempered bodies, and then likewise on simple diseases, as has been set out both in the preceding book and in the third book On Mixtures. And one must reason while always distinguishing what is incidental from what is primary and per se. Some physicians go wrong not only in these matters but also in their opinions about the affections. Take oil, for instance: almost everyone agrees that it is a remedy for fatigues, but they no longer agree about what sort of affection fatigue is. One says that it is a dryness of the joints, which have been drained of their moisture in the movements; another adds the dryness of the muscles as well; and yet another, contrary to these, says it is a great moistness together with tension and warmth, because a flux has come upon the parts that were violently moved.

Another blames not a quantity of fluids but [486] a quality alone, saying that in the more immoderate movements certain colliquations take place of fat together with soft flesh, of which one part is dispersed outwards by transpiration, while another part is retained in the body, and this, being pungent and biting, produces the, as it were, oil-like condition. So that, even if it is agreed that lassitudes are treated by oil, the fact that the condition of the body is disputed allows nothing firm to be inferred about the power of oil. And this has happened not only in the case of lassitude, but also whenever we give oil to drink on account of pain, or biting, or inflammation, or inject it through the anus, or pour it over the part. For in the case of inflamed ulcers we pour it on not by itself but with moderately hot water, just as in lassitudes together with baths of sweet waters. Yet not even in the case of inflammation is it agreed what sort of condition it is. And when we inject it through the anus or give it to drink, not even then do we know clearly to what sort of body we are applying it, whether one full of phlegm, or of bile, or of some other residues.

For it is clear that it will not [487] dispose the person in the same way when it finds the whole intestine together with the stomach full of viscous phlegm, and when it finds it full of bilious residues, or of some other pungent humours, or of much faeces; or when it finds none of these, but meets with the whole stomach and the intestines perfectly clean; or when, besides being clean, this is also roughened. Most physicians, then, reason about all these matters very carelessly and indolently, not stating in what condition the person is to whom the oil is given, nor even of what kind the oil itself is. And then they assert, some that it in every case bites and scrapes the internal parts, others that, if there should be some biting already present beforehand, it soothes this too. For surely it makes no small difference whether one puts oil that is called, and truly is, entirely unsalted into a phlegmatic belly, or oil that has a very large share of salt into a clean one. For both will loosen the belly, but by different powers.

For the unsalted [oil] will loosen a phlegmatic [belly] through its slipperiness, in the same way as [488] mallows, blites and mulberries; the salted [oil] will loosen a clean [belly] through its pungency, similarly to brine and sea-water. And indeed the latter will scrape, while the other will not scrape. Let us therefore say neither that oil simply scrapes the inner parts in every case, or produces bloody evacuations, nor that it soothes bitings. Let us say rather that the salty [oil] scrapes in a clean [belly], and that the unsalted [oil] in a phlegmatic [belly] does not scrape. Sometimes, however, the briny [oil] might heal bitings incidentally, just as honey-water, brine and whey of milk also do. For these sometimes carry out along with themselves the humour that produces the biting, and so become remedies for biting, like all the other things that wash away and cleanse. But after the injection such drugs not only fail to stop the biting at once; they even aggravate it. For they effect the cure by way of evacuation, not by way of tempering. A cerate made with rose oil and suet or fat, however, when injected, has often healed bitings on the spot by way of tempering.

And indeed oil [489] by itself alone, when it is very sweet, has often done this, just as goat's suet has too, or juice of groats (chondros), or a cerate made with sweet oil. We, moreover, by injecting hot oil into those who suffer pain internally through some chilling, have often made them free of pain at once. And if we conjecture the chilling to be greater, we add dill as well, heating the oil, and if greater still, rue and asphalt too. All such things, then, [are unknown, the verb is not expressed in the Greek] to the majority of physicians, who know neither how to distinguish pain that arises from bad mixture from pain that arises from bad humours, nor that, of the drugs injected on account of pain, one cures by heating the chilled part, another by evacuating the biting humour, and another by tempering it.

Often, too, mixed conditions arise from bad mixture and biting together; in these we are accustomed to pour in oil of dill or oil of rue, having first melted goose fat into it; if this is not at hand, then [490] at any rate fowl's fat; and if not even this, one of the others. When none of these is available, we mix in some unbiting wax (I call so the washed wax), or indeed, by Zeus, the oil itself, the whitened kind, poured in. For this too is analogous to unbiting wax. Rash, then, and undiscriminating is both the pronouncement of those who have declared all oil biting on every occasion and that of those who have declared it soothing. For the briny oil is biting, while the unsalted and sweet oil is soothing, so far as lies in itself. For this too might sometimes seem, depending on the conditions to which it is applied, to be no longer of this character. For each of the tempering drugs, when it becomes stronger than the biting humours, blunts their biting. But if it is mixed in, in small quantity, with stronger powers, or with many, it is corrupted along with them and nourishes the bad humours; hence those who are exacerbated by the tempering remedies must also be evacuated at once, as being filled with much corruption that is hard to move.

[491] In the same way, then, milk too often, as soon as it has been administered, turns sour in some people and becomes nidorous in others, before, having been well concocted, it can temper the corruption. In these cases one must first evacuate the bulk of the bad humours, and only then administer groats and ptisan and milk and the other things which, when well concocted, contribute to good humours. One must not, however, suppose that all these, so far as depends on themselves, possess either the worse or the contrary powers, nor in one's account deliberately pass over one of the two sets of things that happen, as Archidamus did in the case of oil. He mentioned the eyes that are bitten, the rasping throat and the scraped belly, but he no longer mentioned that sweet oil, when drunk, has often at once healed even a stomach that was strongly bitten, that when injected it has soothed the bitings throughout the whole belly, and that when smeared on it has stopped those arising on the skin from thapsia, nettle and squill.

I myself neither dispute nor disbelieve those who say that in almost all existing things many and differing powers are contained; on the contrary, I even undertake to demonstrate [492] this in the discussion that follows. Not, however, on this account do I say that the power which prevails in each thing is also unknowable. But if you distinguish what is so in itself from what is so by accident, everything will be clearly recognised.
