For consider each of the two in some such way as this, by means of examples, setting up as an illustration in the argument two men who suffer biting alike at the mouth of the stomach, and who take the juice of ptisane, or groats (chondros), or washed bread; then in the one the biting ceases, while in the other it increases. Is, then, the juice of ptisane, or the groats, or the bread, biting so far as lies in itself, but by some accident, in the case of the other of the two men, not only did not increase the biting but actually soothed it? Or did it soothe so far as lies in itself, but by some accident, in the case of the other, exacerbate it? I for my part say that the juice of ptisane, or the groats, or the bread, or, by Zeus, the milk, is tempering by its own nature, and that the biting is exacerbated in the other of the two men because the food has first been overcome by the corruption.

Thus too, I know, almost all the [493] ancient physicians understood it, as do the best of the more recent ones as well, though there may perhaps be someone who escapes my notice. For nothing is too audacious for some of the more recent physicians, so that they declare that groats, or bread, or ptisane increases the corruptions by its own nature, yet in some people soothes them by some accident. But whoever says this has no demonstration to offer for his pronouncement. We, however, say that if ptisane were by nature productive of bad humours, it would never soothe bitings. Yet in fact it is seen, whether taken from above or injected through the anus, often soothing, from which it is clear that in its own nature it is productive of good humours; but when it is sometimes corrupted together with the humours that produce the bitings, it increases the symptom. Perhaps, then, someone might ask us whether none of the things productive of bad humours has ever cured a biting. For my part I know that this happens not infrequently; but I say that such drugs cure the bitings not by tempering them, but by carrying out along with themselves what is biting.

And for this reason they bite the person both at once and until [494] they have been evacuated, and they leave behind a certain rough sensation in the parts, which requires another drug; this is not so, however, with the drugs of good juice and of sweet juice. For these both soothe at once, and do so without producing an evacuation, and they bring on no rough sensation; quite the contrary, they are themselves remedial for rough sensations. At any rate, in such conditions we give groats (chondros), milk and ptisane both to be eaten and to be injected through the seat, once we have washed away what is troubling, either by means of honey or by some other such thing. At this time suet also becomes useful to us, and sweet cerate, and sweet oil. Take me, both now and in the account that follows, to call 'sweet' all things that are prepared without salt, and those that have been washed. Since, then, you are able to distinguish by four signs what is soothing of itself from what is soothing by accident, you will easily discover the power of each such drug. These four signs are as follows.

First, whether it soothes at once or not; second, whether the troublesome matters are evacuated together with it or not; [495] third, whether it leaves behind some roughness about the bodies or not; and fourth, whether it should fail to appear wholesome to those who are in this condition. For that which neither soothes the bitings at once, but is excreted with greater violence, nor heals by remaining within, and which leaves behind about the bodies a distressing roughness and aggravates it if it is applied a second time, is erosive and biting by nature, but by accident sometimes heals bitings. That which is soothing at once and provokes no excretion, does not roughen while it remains, and becomes a remedy for what has been roughened, is itself wholesome by nature, but sometimes becomes biting through the bad humours that alter and corrupt it.

These things have been said by me, and the argument has at once taught the right moment or the manner of use of each of the two kinds of drugs, and at once the discovery of the power. It has also shown that the juice of ptisane, chondros, tragos, milk and washed bread belong among the things of good juice, and indeed that fat and suet, sweet oil [496] and sweet wax are of the nature of soothing things. Sweet wax would be both that which is such by nature, since some waxes are bitter to those who taste them, and that which, besides being such, has also been washed in good water. One must wash not only wax but also pitch and resin, oil, and anything else of this kind that does not mix with water. First warm it moderately, then pour it into a broad, large vessel holding a quantity of water that is at once purest and most free of quality. For into this the thing being washed, whatever it may be, deposits its own pungency. One must also rub it, beat it, squeeze it and knead it with the hands sufficiently, so that every part of the drug being washed comes into contact with the water. Having done this, one must pour off the first water, and, warming the thing being washed again, throw it into other water that is likewise clean, and one must beat it up again for as long as possible, until it deposits its own quality in the water.

You can also discern this by tasting. Then do this a third and a [497] fourth time, and many times in succession, until the water no longer receives any quality from the drug being washed. In this way, then, one should wash everything that can be heated and made to flow. But if something is stony and hard, such as cadmia, flake of copper and burnt copper, one should break these up thoroughly into fine pieces and grind them for a very long time in spring water that is as pure as possible, often pouring off the earlier water, until nothing any longer forms on the surface when the water has settled, and the water becomes without quality from the drug being ground. As long as either something of its quality is apparent to those who taste it, or something forms on the surface, for so long one should keep grinding and pouring off. For if one washes in this way anything that is capable of being washed, it becomes free of biting. And indeed oil, too, is seen in this process to become not only free of biting but also whiter. One must not, however, beat it vigorously in the same way as pitch, wax and resin, so that its mixture with the water may not become hard to separate. Rather, once one has let it stand still, it is easy to take it off as it floats on top.

There are also other methods of whitening oil, set out by those who have written both the [498] books on preparations and those on materia medica, such as those in Dioscorides too, in the first [book]. But most of those methods, by using up the watery and the tawny part of the oil, render the remainder white, whereas the method by washing does so by, as it were, cleansing it of dirt and wiping it clean. Concerning the condition of drugs that can be washed and whitened, more will be said later. But I return to the matter at hand. If oil is neither the so-called omphacine (for this is astringent), nor prepared with salt, nor fresh and, as it were, still seething, and if, in addition to all these, it has been carefully washed, it will produce no biting, whether drunk or injected. And if it is roughening to the throat, this would contribute nothing toward its being biting. For everything that bites and is pungent is also roughening, but not everything roughening is biting and pungent. For only in this way would oil have been shown to be biting, if it had been agreed that everything roughening is biting.

Here, then, there comes in once again [499] the error arising from the conversion of the conditional, a small and paltry sort of error. For it is agreed that everything that bites is roughening, and it is agreed too that oil is roughening. But from these assumptions it is not concluded that oil is biting, whether we make the premises categorical or hypothetical, because nothing is concluded from two universal affirmatives in the second figure, and the conditional is not necessarily true. In the categorical syllogism the two premises will be these: everything that bites is roughening; all oil is roughening. When these are granted, nothing will be concluded from them. And the hypothetical premise, which Chrysippus and his school call a conditional proposition, we cannot take as true either from perception or from logical consequence.

For it is not [?] through perception, or from perception, or however one may wish to name it, that propositions of this kind have been obtained: 'everything biting is also roughening', and 'if something is biting, this is also roughening'. Yet neither, if everything biting is roughening, does it follow that everything roughening [500] is thereby biting; nor from 'everything, if it is biting, is also roughening' does there follow 'everything, if it is roughening, is also biting'. Rather, 'if it is not roughening, neither is it biting' is true, for it converts by contraposition (ἀντιστρέφει); but not 'if something is roughening, it is straightway also biting', for this is a mere reversal (ἀναστρέφει). It has been shown in the logical methods that statements which are contrapositives of true statements are true, whereas those which are reversals are no longer true in every case. If, then, it is not of necessity true that if something is roughening it is straightway also biting, neither could oil be shown to be biting from its being roughening. For only if it had been agreed that everything roughening is biting would a conditional of this sort have been found true, 'if oil is roughening, it is also biting'. Then, when an additional assumption (πρόσληψις) of this kind is made to this statement, 'but oil is roughening', the conclusion follows, according to the first undemonstrated [argument], as follows: 'therefore oil is biting'.

But in fact they ought not to have argued in this way, [501] that if something is biting, it is at once also roughening, but rather that only biting things are roughening; for in that way all roughening things would be biting. Yet this very claim, that only biting things appear roughening, is made contrary to perception (for oily things too appear roughening), and the point at issue has been readily assumed, confirmed neither from perception nor from demonstration. And further, besides these things, it is characteristic of people who do not know what sort of condition being roughened is, which it is perhaps better to explain to them. Being roughened occurs when some unevenness forms in the throat contrary to nature. For the pneuma, being accustomed always to travel through a clean and smooth passage, whenever it strikes against certain projections in it, produces a kind of agitation and, as it were, an uneven shaking in the throat, and in this way the animal is provoked to cough. For just as nature has wrought into animals many other innate affections for the sake of their preservation, in the same way she has also wrought sneezing and cough.

sneezing for the sake of thrusting out the things in the [502] nostrils that irritate and distress them, and coughing for the sake of thrusting out those in the throat. Such a condition is twofold: either the membrane along the artery is itself being dried up and roughened, or some uneven body is being carried in it, whether liquid or solid in nature. For this reason, if some small particle of bread or of some other food ever slips, against our will, into the passage of the breath, we are compelled to cough; and if, while we are drinking, some of the drink flows aside in a mass, it is likewise irritated and calls forth a cough. For some of what is drunk always filters through the rough artery into the lung, but so little that it is at once snatched up by the organs and readily distributed in every direction. It does not, however, stand apart in a mass anywhere in the passages of the breath, nor is the animal provoked to coughing. But whenever either this in a larger quantity, or some other such liquid, or a solid body is carried into the rough artery, it is from then on necessary to cough, until what is causing the distress is thrown out by the violence of the breath.

Something analogous to this also happens when the breath strikes against the membrane itself on the inside of the windpipe (ἀρτηρία) after it has been roughened [503]; this condition, however, is different from the one described before. For in this one something is taken away and scraped off from the membrane of the windpipe, whereas in the former condition something falls upon it on the inside. What is common to both is the unevenness of the passage of the breath. These matters have been discussed more fully in the [books on the] Causes of Symptoms. But for the present it is enough to know that all biting things produce the unevenness and the hoarseness (κέρχνος) by roughening the throat, while oil-like and oily things do so by being plastered around it. For whatever falls upon the coat of the windpipe contrary to nature, and is plastered onto it so as to be hard to detach, becomes unaccustomed to the organs and to the breath carried through them, and distressing to the animal. And I do not say this now as though most oils were not also biting in their quality.

For those that contain salt, and those that are quite new, are altogether biting. This is not because of their own proper substance, but because in all the juices from plants a twofold residue is carried along, as Theophrastus has sufficiently shown and as we too shall show in what follows: the one thicker [504] and, as it were, more earthy, the other thinner and more watery. Both of these are present in oil too, and they require time for concoction and separation; but in time the one settles and the other is consumed. First the earthy and thicker one settles, the so-called amurca (ἀμόργη). The other, the thinner and, as it were, more watery one, is itself in a way also compound, made up of a certain airy substance and a thin whey-like one. This whey-like part is tawny in colour, and it has taken on the impress of the quality of the settling, thick and earthy part. But the oil itself is non-biting and white in its own nature. Hence, once this thin residue has been separated off, it becomes whiter and sweeter than it was. It is separated off in many ways. Either they set a wide-mouthed vessel full of oil in the hot sun, take it up with shells and repeatedly dash it down from above, or they put hot ash under the vessels containing the oil, imitating as closely as possible the sun-like warmth.

[505] For they guard against the greater heat, which alters it in quality and readily makes it smell burnt; or they set olive stones or grain in a circle around it, or they also throw certain drugs into the vessels themselves. In a word, they draw off and consume the watery part, and preserve the rest. If, then, you take oil made sweet and white in this way, oil which from the beginning did not contain salt, and further also wash it, as was said earlier, this is for you the least biting of all drugs. And indeed we have often given such oil to certain persons to drink, and have taken it ourselves for the sake of trial, and it was entirely non-biting in the intestine and least of all roughening to the throat; and when poured into the eyes it produced only a slight sensation, troubling them by its mere strangeness and unfamiliarity rather than by any pungency. Such oil, then, being oil in the strict sense, moistens and softens all things, when it is applied neither extremely cold, as has been said, nor hot.

But oil that also has a share of salt necessarily has something of biting as well. Yet I should be surprised if anyone [506] throws in so much salt that it becomes stronger than the oil-like and oily substance, so that one might accept Archidamus when he says that the skin is burned in those who are rubbed down in oil. For I know that this too is often done, both for certain other purposes and for podagra and arthritis. Some people rub the affected parts with finely ground salt together with a little oil, in the intervals, obviously, and not in the paroxysms, in order to dry and disperse all the superfluity and to instil a certain good condition and strength in the weak parts. But in this preparation the salt prevails, whereas in oil it is prevailed over. And one ought to compare the person who is anointed and rubbed down to things that are soaked in oil rather than to things that are boiled, since we are not going to boil the man down in seething oil, but to anoint him with well-tempered oil. For it would have been better, as I have often said before as well, to look at what actually happens, since it is perceptible and entirely clear. Surely there is no need of external examples in matters that can be known in this way.

But if [507] ever the thing under investigation should be unclear, so as to need proof from other things, not even then should one set down the most remote and most dissimilar testimonies to the power of the thing under investigation, passing over what lies close at hand. It is surely evident and clear to all that rubbing with oil is much less fatiguing than dry rubbing, and that it softens bodies, holding together and shutting in, rather than dispersing and drying, whatever naturally flows off from us to the outside. Diocles himself also agreed with this, declaring that oil is clogging of the pores, retentive of what flows off, and softening of hides. But if what appears was not sufficient for him, and for this reason he thought it better to bring some external proof into the argument, he ought to have mentioned things soaked through in cold oil, not things boiled down in boiling oil. Just as in such matters he passes over what appears, so too in asserting that rubbing in oil becomes uneven, as the hands slip.

For we all clearly perceive the very opposite: rubbing with [508] oil is even, and dry rubbing is uneven. For in dry rubbings the hands draw the skin along with them and, as it were, double it and fold it over upon itself, firmly and contrary to nature. Then, when the earlier doubling, as one may call it, can no longer follow the hands as they glide along past it, this doubling runs back and is drawn back to the continuous skin, while the hands pass all at once to another part of the skin, passing over the lower part of the doubling. For this reason we perceive such rubbing as hard, uneven and fatiguing: hard because the skin is forcibly stretched and bruised, and fatiguing for the same reasons; uneven because the rubbing hands do not fall upon every part of the skin but always pass over the lower part of the doubling. This happens both because of the natural roughnesses of the skin, especially in bodies past their prime, and because the skin is slack in almost all others, most of all in the lean and the old.

For if the skin were smooth, evenly so throughout, and precisely stretched, it would not readily fold over [509], nor would it make the movements of the hands upon it uneven. Rather, I think, the hands would run easily forward, slipping readily from the first parts on to others, because no part of the skin is drawn along together with them. But since the skin is lax and rough, it needs some drug from outside that will fill up its wrinkles and provide a gliding for the rubbing hands. For these purposes you would find nothing more suitable than oil. One might well wonder at Archidamus, who neither respected what is plainly apparent nor found out the reasoning about it, but declared the opposite in both respects. For dry rubbing appears uneven and rubbing with oil even, and reason bears witness to these things, not least by explaining the cause. But about Archidamus and Diocles, enough for the present at least. For since I have once come to showing the faulty method of the discovery of powers, using oil as an example, I wish to go through the whole argument as quickly as possible.

So, when the philosophers say that oil is hot [510] and put forward as no small proof of this, as they think, the speed of its change into flame, some, contradicting them, say that this does indeed belong to it, but because it is fine and airy; whereas from its congealing quickly in winter it clearly indicates its coldness. For it is overcome by the cold more readily not only than wine and vinegar but even than water itself. Others, contradicting these, concede that it is airy, and say that this is plainly apparent from its lightness, but they do not agree that it is also cold in its power. For all air, they say, is hot in its nature, as its generation also shows: water, when thinned and dissolved by heat, becomes air. And it is clear that from this point a very great question succeeds to them, one disputed even among the most renowned philosophers, Aristotle and those under him supposing air to be hot, and those from the Stoa supposing it to be cold.

But concerning oil's congealing quickly, too, which was the view of those who declare it cold, those who assert that it is hot counter-propose that it does not congeal vigorously, as water does. [511] For they say that what happens in its case is not even congelation at all, if we examine it precisely, but a sort of consolidation and thickening; and they say this occurs because it is thick and viscous, not because it is cold. So here too, once again, the argument arrives at an impasse from both sides: the one party establishes the contrary from the fact that oil is overcome by cooling more quickly than water, the other from the fact that water congeals more than oil. In addition, then, to the dispute on these points, not even all agree that it is airy. For its lightness, they say, is a token of this, but its thickness is no small proof that it is earthy. Some, combining both, say that it is at once airy and earthy. But there are those who laugh at these people, on the grounds that in their account they entirely take away moistness, which is what most belongs to oil. Furthermore, from its being viscous, some demonstrate that it is cold, some that it is hot, and some that it is dry, others that it is moist.

For if its parts had not been drawn together and condensed and did not hold tightly to one another, it would not have become viscous; [512] and all these, they say, are works of the cold. For it is the nature of the hot to diffuse, loosen, thin, and separate the parts from one another. Others, on the contrary, say that nothing at all would become viscous without heat prevailing, as is shown also in the boiling of all juices, both those pressed out of herbs and those pressed out of fruits. For being watery at first, thin in their consistency and running freely, once they are boiled they become thick and viscous. And indeed, from particular examples as well, each side plausibly establishes the opposite conclusion: the one side putting forward birdlime, honey, liquid pitch and resin, and other such things that are agreed to be at once viscous and hot; the other side mentioning the juice of hemlock, fleawort, orache and blite, and, in addition to these, bringing forward phlegm as a kind of finishing stroke to the argument; for this seems to them plainly to be both viscous and cold. But also from the fact that oil dripped onto those being phlebotomised makes the blood flow freely, one can see each side establishing opposite conclusions.

For the one party say that it produces the free flow as liquefying [the blood] by its heat, the others as [513] furnishing slipperiness by its coldness, in the manner of ice. And then, turning aside from this point, they hold discourse about the nature of all slippery things, ascending in their argument to the very extremity of learned disputation. Others, condemning the wandering of these men, as they say, put forward fat for the argument, since it is very close to oil in nature, yet can be clearly discovered as to what sort it is in its mixture; for since it is formed within us ourselves, it could not escape notice. For instance, they say that much fat is generated in healthy and well-nourished bodies, which not even a madman would call cold. For such things come about when nature is strong, and nature all the natural philosophers have agreed to be a hot thing. But some, contradicting these, say that fat is generated in colder mixtures, as women and those who live idly make plain.

Further, regarding peoples, they say that where cold prevails men become fat, but where heat prevails, lean; and they put forward as an example for the argument the Celts, Thracians, [514] Bithynians, Pontians and Galatians, who are at once inhabitants of a cold country and also, as a rule, fat; and the Arabs, Libyans, Egyptians and Ethiopians, and all others who inhabit a hot land, all lean and dry. There are also those who, even apart from particular examples, dispute with one another over the general argument itself: some say that the oily humour would not even come into being in us unless the foods were properly worked up by nature; others say that it is contained in the foods, but is consumed by the warmth in us, as oil is by the flame, and that when this warmth becomes weak, it collects in the body. Some of them also adduce animals for the argument: those that are colder by nature are all fattier, such as bears, sheep and pigs, whereas those that are hotter are drier and without fat, such as lions, leopards and dogs. Moreover, from the fact that bees, flies, wasps and ants are destroyed when wetted with oil, some try to show that oil is cold, others that it is hot, and some that it is moist, others that it is dry.

For since the animals mentioned are bloodless and for this reason cold, [515] some say that they are readily chilled by the oil and die because of this; but others say that, being heated through, they cannot bear the change to the opposite. And indeed others say that, being dried immoderately, they are harmed by reason of the immoderation, because they have already been dried beforehand by nature; and still others that, being moistened, they are harmed by the contrariety to their nature. Now that these men argue in opposite directions to one another in the case of the insects (ἔντομα ζῷα) would perhaps be nothing surprising; but that they argue for either side even from what happens to us ourselves, this is now worth wondering at. For of those who assert that one sweats more, and of those who assert that one sweats less, if one anoints oneself while bathing, neither do those who said 'more' agree with one another about the general power, nor do those who said 'less'.

But of those who say that we sweat more, some people refer the cause to heat, others to viscosity. The former say that what is hot is by nature provocative of sweats. The latter say that the viscous becomes apt to catch and collect what until then was flowing off quickly and for that reason escaping perception, and so makes the [516] quantity of the sweats evident. Those who say that people who have anointed themselves in baths and gymnasia sweat less ascribe to it (sc. the oil), some a clogging power, others a cooling one. Moreover, from the phenomena too, some say that it dries and others that it moistens: all those who suppose that the anointed sweat more say that it moistens, and still others that it dries. And further, as to its keeping those who have anointed themselves unchilled, some say that by its thickness and viscosity it shuts out the cold like some garment or screen, others that by its natural heat it also heats along with itself whatever is near it. Further, from the fact that it neither damages nor erases what is written in ink in books, although all the other liquids do erase it, some say that its nature is dry and, as it were, without moisture, like sand and ashes; some say that it is rather coarse-particled and unworked. So too its not mixing with the other liquids some refer to lightness and fine-particledness, others to viscosity and thickness, since it does mix with juices of like kind, as, for example, with the decoction of mallows.

The same holds also [517] concerning the fact that earth is not readily moistened by oil, although it is soaked by the other liquids, such as water, wine and vinegar. Here too some blame the dryness of its substance, some its fine-particled character, and there are those who blame its coarse-particled character. Those who blame its fine-particledness say that it passes through the pores of the earth without touching them, and those who blame its coarse-particledness say that it does not even enter them in the first place. It is possible to refute neither party, since some things can fail to mix with what is near them for either of the two causes, if indeed some of the natural philosophers hold that the commensurability of the pores is the cause of mixing. I am now going through these matters under main headings, recalling only the starting-points of the arguments. But if anyone wished to extend each of them and to argue the case on either side, he would, I think, fill not merely one book in this way but very many. It is already possible to see that such a wandering of the arguments is not only long, which would be tolerable, but also reaches up into the highest natural philosophy, and is at times also hard to decide.

But if one should further know that it is also entirely [518] useless to physicians, one will, I think, shun such a path of argument all the more. For we do not inquire simply whether each of the drugs is hot or cold or dry or moist, nor whether it is moistening or drying or heating or cooling for ants or wasps or bees or any other of the animals, but how it stands in relation to the human body. Since, then, it is possible to carry out the test on human beings, they do not do well to turn aside to other things. The correct test is, first, that on well-tempered bodies; next, that on ill-tempered ones; then, as we have often said before as well, that on hot, cold, dry and moist diseases. In these we thought it right to pay attention also to how one is to distinguish what does something of itself from what does so by accident.

This, we held, would be achieved, first, if the drug were applied to affections as simple as possible; second, if we note whether it shows its own power perceptibly at once, from the very beginning, or after a time, or even only once it has been entirely removed, as cold water does, which brings about a recall of warmth [519]; and further, besides these, if it is unmixed with any other quality, so far as it is possible to make such a thing so. How one might make oil of this kind has been stated before. How one might apply it to a simple disease will be stated now, once we have first recalled this much: as was shown in the Differences of Diseases, some bodies have been turned towards the hotter without any bad humours or inflammation of the chest or of a viscus, as usually happens in violent sun-scorchings, and others towards the colder, as in what all people now customarily call chills. In conditions of this kind, then, if you apply oil, you will find out clearly whether it is its nature to heat us or rather to cool us. It must, of course, be free of every strong acquired quality, for this must always be borne in mind in the case of every drug. That is the sum of the argument. What actually happens is shown by experience. Those scorched by the sun, besides not being relieved of their heat, become still more distressed and, as time goes on, hotter.

[520] But for those who have been chilled, no benefit or harm clearly results from anointing with oil. From this it is also clear that, even if it is of a nature to heat us, it at any rate no longer does so vehemently or manifestly, as resin and pitch and asphalt do. Here you must understand by these neither dry resin nor dry pitch nor dry asphalt, for no one would anoint himself with them. Nor do I mean those that have been melted in the sun, for such a thing would no longer be a simple or naturally occurring drug. By resin I mean either the one called 'self-flowing', or the terebinth resin and the mastic resin while still liquid and fresh, or, of the pine resin, the oil-like part that stands on top in the earthenware jars. Of pitch I mean the liquid kind, and still more the oil-like part that floats on it, which they call pissanthos ['pitch-flower'], for it truly is, as it were, a sort of flower of pitch. In the same way I mean the liquid asphalt, further the one from Media.

For all these are oily and have very much of the oleaginous nature, yet they heat manifestly; just as stacte myrrh, and pine oil, or juniper oil, or cedar oil and laurel oil, and other such things, clearly heat thoroughly those who have been chilled, [521] but distress to the utmost those who have been scorched. These, then, are agreed on both counts to heat. Oil, however, on neither count strongly either heats thoroughly those who are chilled or harms those who are scorched. Yet, not obscurely either, it does become a cause of some discomfort in those who have become feverish from scorching, and it is seen to increase the heat, as also in genuine erysipelata. These, of course, are bilious fluxes; for clearly, of course, in these very cases too it is seen to increase the warmth, even if you apply it extremely cold. For in cases of scorching, if it is without salt and has moreover been whitened, it gives some relief when poured over cold; but in erysipelata, however cold it may be, it does no good, but is even apt to do harm: to all those that arise purely from a bilious flux, very great harm; to those from a flux with blood mixed in it, smaller harm, though not ordinary harm either. Less than these, but still manifestly, it also aggravates seething inflammations. Inferring from all these things, it seemed to me that it kindles a heat similar to that of whatever it happens to come into contact with.

It appears, [522] at any rate, that when applied to bodies that are moderately hot it heats them moderately, but in those that are strongly hot it kindles a strong warmth. Now it has already been said in the third book On Mixtures, and it will be said now as well, that each of the drugs applied to the body which we have said are hot in their powers, taking the beginning of their being heated from us, in some cases heat us in return to the same degree, and in other cases more vehemently. Among those that heat in return to an equal degree olive oil appeared to me to belong, when I examined its particular powers. For I always found it producing a lukewarm heat in moderately hot bodies, but a seething heat in seething ones. And for this reason it appeared to me neither to benefit to any noteworthy extent, nor to harm, spasms and tremors, and losses of sensation and impairments of sensation.

For it could not help, because it does not heat strongly, and it was not capable of harming, because it did not cool at all; but once it has taken on a strong acquired heat, it [appeared] to help sufficiently: whenever we set those so affected into tubs [523] of hot oil that have certain roots, or heating herbs, boiled in them. Hence, with good reason, it is as it were a kind of material for the other drugs. For if you mix cold things with it, the mixture will be cold, and if hot things, hot. For whatever is of the middle mixture serves each of the two extremes, so that, if it should be mixed with something hot, it is not able to render cold what is mixed from both, since it is not itself cold either; nor, if [mixed] with something cold, [to render it] hot, for neither is it hot. And on this account, with good reason, some declare that it heats us, others that it does not heat. For it would seem to heat in that it arrives at a warmth equal to that of the body that heats it; at any rate in this respect it is able to heat in return. But in that it does not further increase the heat which it found, it would not seem to heat. For it is not the preserving of the heat that it found, but the increasing of it, that is the work of what heats.

There are three sources of a dispute of this kind: failing to distinguish the classes of the things said to heat [524] us, using homonymies confusedly, and leaving no mean. Now, the things said to heat us are both those hot in actuality, like fire itself, and those hot in potentiality; and of the things hot in potentiality some heat as foods, some as drugs, and some as coverings. And 'hot' itself is the name we are accustomed to give both to what is already such in actuality and to what is such in potentiality, as has often been said before as well. But the hot in actuality includes what is hot simply, such as fire; what is hot by predominance, such as the animal; what is called hot when compared with the well-proportioned member of the same genus; and what is called hot when compared with any chance thing whatever. The hot in potentiality is, first, distinguished in opposition to the hot by accident, and then, next, it has as many differences of meaning as the hot in actuality has. For since it is, as it were, a material suited to what is hot in actuality, one thing would be the proper material for the things called hot simply, another for those hot by predominance, and yet another for those called hot when compared with the well-proportioned member of the same genus or of the same species, or with any chance thing whatever.

That is why we thought it right that those who examine matters in relation to man [525] should withdraw from all the others. In all these things, then, those who have investigated the power of drugs go wrong, and besides these they also pass over the mean states, both in our natural mixtures, as we showed in the commentaries On Mixtures, and in the examinations of drugs. For they frame their arguments as though the drug under test must of necessity be either hot, or dry, or moist, or cold, as if it were not possible for something to be ranked in between the things that heat and cool us, and something else in between the things that dry and moisten us. And some are so foolish that they cannot follow the truth even when they have heard it. At any rate, I know some who even attempt to argue that nothing is intermediate in its mixture. But to these people what is appropriate has been said in the work On Mixtures, and it will be said no less in what follows.

Hastening to bring the present [526] discussion to an end, I return once more to olive oil. For it belongs to it, as a nutriment, perhaps to heat us when it is taken into the interior of the body; for it seems to some physicians and philosophers of no mean repute that an addition to the body comes about from oil, just as it does from foods. It belongs to it also, as a drug, to be in a way intermediate between the things that heat us and those that cool us. And it belongs to it as well to heat us as a covering, and indeed the most proper image of its nature seems to me to be something of this kind. For just as each of our garments, being heated by us ourselves, naturally heats us in return, so too does oil. But just as none of those garments becomes hotter than the very body that heats it, so neither does oil.

You would understand the whole matter well, and it will be useful not only for present purposes but for everything to come, if you were to recall the very air that surrounds us. Sometimes it becomes colder than the heat in us, to such a degree that we need certain shields and coverings against it. At other times, again, it becomes hotter, to such a degree that we cannot bear it but take refuge in [527] some shelter and shade. And there are times when it is so moderately disposed that we desire neither things that will warm us nor things that will cool us, and our contact with it is painless and imperceptible. This third mixture, the one just described, I call moderate, and I say that it is intermediate between the others and neither warms nor cools our body; of the other two, the one warms us and the other cools us. And I say that the warmth arising from garments and that arising from oil resemble the intermediate and moderate mixture of the air surrounding us. If even so what I wish to make clear is not plain, I think you would understand it better in the following way. Imagine for me two human beings whose bodies are similarly mixed, touching each other either with the chest and belly only, or also with the hands and the legs. Now if the air surrounding these two human beings had the same mixture as they, so that the warmth in the three bodies were equal, nothing would be said, in this case at least, to be warmed by anything.

For bodies alike in every respect, at one another's hands, [528] undergo no alteration. But if the surrounding air is cold, the men would be said to warm one another, although they are not in fact warming but keeping off the cold. The many, then, being accustomed to misuse names, call what prevents being chilled 'warming', and not correctly. We must, then, allow them to name things as they wish; but we must by no means go on to allow them to signify the same thing by the verb 'to warm' in each of the two expressions. For it is surely not the same thing to supply warmth to something from oneself and to prevent the cold. This being so, whatever things fall upon us from outside having the same warmth as the body, whether they have taken it from themselves, or from others, or even from us ourselves, these must, by the strict account, be said neither to warm us nor to cool us. But if anyone wishes to use the terms loosely, it must be allowed, provided only that in the expression he keeps in mind the difference between the meanings. For the warmer air is said to warm us in one way, and the moderate air in another.

Pellitory, mustard and [529] pepper stand in a relation analogous to the hotter air, and fat and oil to the moderate air. For the airs are hot in actuality, but the drugs are hot in potentiality. We ourselves do not make the air hot; rather, we are affected because we come close to air of that kind. But the drugs, as I also showed in the third book On Mixtures, take from us the starting-point of their change towards being heated. Some of them are then naturally disposed to heat us in return to an equal degree, others more, others less. Among those that heat in return to an equal degree is oil. Because it is viscous, hard to flow off, and obstructive of the pores, it also has the property of increasing, in a twofold way, so it seems, the warmth. By being plastered round the body like a garment or a protective screen, and by obstructing the pores, it prevents the greater part of the vaporous heat from flowing away from within. For these reasons, then, it does not allow our bodies to be dried either, unless it is applied hot and for a longer time. And all men, having learned this power of it by experience—

Those whom they wish to sweat more copiously, whether bathed or unbathed, they do not apply oil to straight away at the outset. [530] Instead, in the case of those who have been ill, once they have begun to sweat, they warm the oil and pour it over them; in the case of the sick, once they have sweated sufficiently. In the case of the healthy, those who come from a long journey on foot and from rather much exercise, or whose body has been dried out in any other way whatever, these they allow to be anointed even before sweating. But those who have failed to digest, or who have a plethoric body, these they do not permit to use oil even when they bathe. And it seems to me that here too oil is midway between the things that moisten us and those that dry us, just as a little earlier it was shown to be midway between those that heat and those that cool. For water moistens, whereas laurel oil and cedar oil dry.

So, at any rate, oil applied simply in this way, without being warmed beforehand or cooled by us ourselves through artificial treatment (for this must always be borne in mind in every case), preserves our mixture just as it received it, shutting in as far as possible and preventing all the vaporous transpirations from being evacuated from the body. But if you rub the [531] limbs with oil at greater length, you will generate a certain acquired heat from the rubbing, and in this you will benefit those who are fatigued: on the one hand because the fat sinks inward into the body, into the fine pores, so as to soften what has become hardened; on the other because by its heat it disperses whatever pungent and thin fluid, generated in fatigues from colliquation, was being held in by the skin. For sweats are seen flowing off outwardly in those who exercise, and not a few residues are seen flowing together inwardly into the belly, as it were colliquated matter. From these things one must reason, even if it is not apparent, that many such things requiring evacuation are also left behind throughout the whole body. For a twofold condition arises in fatigues, as has been shown elsewhere: the homoeomerous parts of the animal are dried, while the empty spaces are moistened, not with a wholesome and natural moisture (for that was plethora), but with a thin, pungent and biting one; and for this reason they also need twofold remedies, those that soak the dryness and those that evacuate the pungent moisture.

And for this reason, for both these purposes, baths of sweet waters prove to be most useful, correcting the dryness of the organs by their moisture, and by their heat, in turn, dispersing the thin [fluid] as well. And if the water were able to remain on the bodies and not run off easily, it alone would be sufficient. But since what is poured over from outside runs off easily, and what sinks into the pores of the body flows out again, having no grip, for this very purpose oil is usefully mixed in, and all the more so if one is rubbed down at length with both, which the ancients called chytlousthai (being anointed with oil and water), and they contrasted it with xeraleiphein (dry anointing). This too is, in a way, by itself curative of fatigues, but it falls very far short of chytlosis. For among other things, when the water is beaten up and rubbed together with oil, it has a mixture that is quite hard to dissolve, so that on whatever bodies the oil is spread and plastered round, the water too is compelled to remain in contact with them for longer. Here too, then, the oil is, as it were, a kind of matter for moistening and drying agents, just as it was shown earlier to be for heating and cooling agents.

For if it is mixed with something drying [533], it renders the whole drying; and if with something moistening, it makes this too moistening, and often the mixture of both turns out even more moistening than the primarily moistening thing itself, as is the case with water. For this moistens primarily, but, because it does not remain for long, its activity is of short duration and it benefits only weakly. The oil, then, becoming a bond for it and compelling it to remain in contact for a very long time with those who need the help it gives, has turned out to be the best of all remedies for bodies that are dried out and parched. In the same way, if you mix a drying drug with oil, such as chalcitis, or pellitory, or oak-gall, or struthion, the mixture of both will be drying. Since, then, oil serves all the things mixed with it, it is with good reason a kind of matter for all of them. It necessarily diminishes their proper activity, but not their benefit; on the contrary, it sometimes even increases it. For it is not the same thing, even if it will seem so to some, to increase the activity of something and to increase its benefit.

For the activity is in accordance with the proper power of each thing, whereas the benefit [534] sometimes arises also by accident. More will be said at greater length in what follows about benefit by accident; but it will be stated now as well, to the extent that the present matter requires. For water beaten up with oil, so as to produce what is called hydrelaeon, helps those suffering from fatigue more than if it were on its own, not because its proper power is intensified, but because it remains for a long time upon those who need it. That, if the binding agent were not intermediate in its mixture, it would often oppose the activities of the things that primarily help those in need, this you can learn both in general from the very nature of drugs and from the record of drugs according to their species. From the general consideration, because what is mixed in, if it draws the power of the drug blended with it towards the contrary, can at times even overcome it and change the mixture of both completely into another kind.

For that which has the role (logos) of matter must display no distinctive quality (idea) or power [535] in the mixture. From experience of the particulars you would learn as follows that what has the role of matter must neither heat nor cool nor dry nor moisten, if you first recall what I mentioned a little earlier concerning liquid pitch, resin and myrrh, asphalt, cedar oil and laurel oil, and all the other things that heat. For all of these, when rubbed up with water in the same way as oil, heat rather than cool and dry rather than moisten; for this reason they are not at all naturally suited to relieve sensations of fatigue. For such a substance is neither of the same power as water, so as to cooperate with it somewhat rather than counteract it, nor of the power intermediate between the extremes, so as to serve as a kind of matter for what acts primarily. For it rather dries and heats, and does not moisten and cool as water does. But if you mix water into one of the things that dry and heat strongly, you will see not only that none of the things it naturally does takes place, but that it is completely obscured, as if it had not been mixed in at all.

Thus chalcitis, sandarach and misy [536] and all the other things that heat and dry us violently still preserve their own power strong when mixed with water. From every side, then, it is clear that whatever is going to serve both extremes, like a kind of matter, must be intermediate in its mixture (krasis); and in placing oil too in this position you would not err. For all the particular effects will agree with you, and for the length of the discussions you will blame not us, but those who overstep the right road and turn aside onto roads that are both bad and long. This is why I too was compelled to lengthen this account, since the truth itself is found most quickly, inasmuch as it starts out from the very things that appear evidently. Yet I have not lengthened the account as far as is possible for one who has chosen both to write out everything that has been wrongly said by them and to teach in full the causes of their errors. And yet it is perhaps necessary to state the causes, so that one may both guard against the paralogisms arising from them in the whole judgement of individual drugs and hold to the true teaching more scientifically.

[537] For our convictions about things are strengthened when we not only know the truth itself but also learn thoroughly the causes of all the paralogisms. This, then, we shall do in what follows. For now, after adding a few words about rose oil to what was said at the beginning, I shall bring the discussion to an end here. It has been said, then, that it is not reasonable to direct one's attention either to odours or to colours or to any other of the accidents in the examinations of powers, but rather to what is evidently apparent in healthy and diseased bodies. It has also been demonstrated that oil, when it is unsalted and perfectly pure, is of the middle matter. So the rose oil too, the exact, simple and genuine rose oil, must be prepared from this oil and must contain nothing more drug-like in itself, as the perfumers are accustomed to prepare it: to make it lasting and more fragrant, they first astringe the oil with aromatics before putting in the roses.

But it is perhaps better to distinguish them by their names as well, [538] just as I know the ancients also did. For they name as rose oil that which has been prepared without the aromatics; but that into which some of these too has been added they no longer call oil but now call an unguent. So, since oil is, as it were, a kind of matter for heating and cooling drugs, being of the middle mixture, and rose oil is compounded of oil and the juices of roses, it is surely itself of the same mixture as the juice of the roses is. And it is surely very easy to make the test of its power, not only of the juice of roses itself on its own, but also, having compounded rose oil, on both healthy and sick bodies, as has already been said many times. You will find, then, that those who are still burnt are cooled by it and at once perceive some benefit, while all those who have been chilled are manifestly harmed, so that from both sides you clearly understand that its power cools rather than heats.

Yet the cooling produced by rose oil will not appear strong to you; rather, it will seem to be in some way very close [539] to the middle mixture. For the sake of clear teaching I name such drugs as being of the first nature and order of the cooling drugs, just as, conversely, I name those that have departed a little from the middle mixture towards the hotter as being of the first remove and order of the heating drugs. This, then, is what one must know about rose oil for the present. For it will be necessary for me in the following discourse as well to mention this drug again and to add what is lacking from what we have said.

[540] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 3. That I had resolved to write in this present treatise only what is itself useful for cures, I have as my first and chief witnesses the divine powers, and then also the companions who urged me to make mention, so far as is possible, of those who have pronounced incorrectly about the power of simple drugs.

[379] Galen, On the Mixture and Power of Simple Drugs, Book 1. How great a benefit it is to know precisely the powers of simple drugs, both for the compounding of complex drugs and for the timely use of those already discovered, I do not need to show now. For the former will be demonstrated in the books On the Composition of Drugs, the latter in the writings of the Therapeutic Method.

But what follows next after the treatise On Mixtures, that is what will be stated here, [380] once we have first distinguished the meanings of the expressions and of the names that we shall use in this discourse. We call a drug, then, everything whatever that is capable of altering our nature, just as, I think, we call food whatever is capable of increasing our substance; for both belong to the category of relation. The simple drug has itself been so named by way of its contrast with the compound, and it is that which holds unmixedly to its own nature. A power is a certain active cause. Of this, one kind exists in actuality, the other in prospect. In actuality there is the power of heating in fire and that of cooling in ice. In prospect there is the power of heating in pellitory and castoreum and the like, and that of cooling in henbane and mandrake and similar things. That there is some power, then, hardly anyone will dispute: in purgative drugs a purgative power, in emetic drugs an emetic power, in sternutatory drugs a sternutatory power, and in cough drugs a cough power, and so for each of the other effects a power named paronymously after what comes about through them.

But what the substance of this power is, [381] some have supposed to be unknowable, as for instance the Sceptic philosophers and, among the physicians, those called Empiricists. Those who declare it to be knowable have also disagreed with one another. For some refer it to the sizes, shapes and positions of the corpuscles and pores, and others to heat, coldness, moisture and dryness, each party according to its own doctrine of the elements. So we too, since we have shown in the treatises On the Elements according to Hippocrates that both the bodies of all other things and those of animals have come into being from hot, cold, dry and moist, shall posit these as the substances of the active powers, both in all other things and in drugs. For this had been shown in this way also in the third book On Mixtures. Whoever wishes to follow what is now being said must have been trained in that treatise, for indeed everything that one must know about drugs in general has been stated in that work. Now we shall say nothing newer in the whole genus; but whatever has been written there generically, this we shall work out specifically in these commentaries.

[382] First, then, and above all, one must make the test of the power being judged from the very thing with reference to which it is said. For if hemlock is cooling to a human being, it does not follow that it is so to a starling as well; nor, if it is nourishing to the starling, does it follow that it is so to a human being as well. In the same way, if hellebore is purgative, it does not follow that it is purgative of quails as well; nor, if it is nourishing to them, does it follow that it is so to human beings as well. Next, one must distinguish what is so by accident from what is so primarily and in itself. For cold water sometimes brings about a recall of heat by cooling the skin and contracting and condensing it, since a recall of heat follows upon this, as was shown in the third book On Mixtures. The hot, in turn, often cools by dispersing the heating humour. For if someone, having made these distinctions with precision, were to come to the examination of the power under inquiry, he would not, it seems to me, easily go wrong.

Now, to make the judgement from nothing else than from that with reference to which [the power] is spoken of is in fact quite easy: we must not consider whether oil is destructive of insects, nor whether it is [383] oily or viscous or light, when we are inquiring whether it is of a nature to heat, or to cool, or to dry, or to moisten the human body. In the same way, we must not consider whether the rose is red in colour, nor whether white lead is white. For neither is what is red necessarily hot, nor what is white necessarily cold. Rather, if, when applied to our bodies, they heat thoroughly primarily and of themselves, and this is neither through some other intermediary nor accidental, then, in this way at least, they would be hot in power, just as, if they cool, they would be cold. For otherwise, by the gods, on what ground can we say whether white pepper, the Cnidian berry, cnicus, lime and white hellebore are hot in power? Or on what ground can we say that Samian star, Selinusian earth, white lead, snow and milk are cold? For all the things mentioned are white in colour, yet in their powers they are most opposite. Snow and lime are most alike in colour, but in their powers they are most opposite; and it is perception that judges this opposition.

For when snow is applied, we perceive it as cold at once, at the [384] first application, and for as long as it is in contact with us it cools ever more and more. We see, too, that it neither endures any longer nor is preserved if it meets with even a little heat. Lime, on the other hand, does not appear to cool even at the first application, and for as long as it is near us it clearly heats ever more and more. From this it is also plain that the proper power of a drug will be judged by its doing one and the same thing throughout, for as long as the drug is in contact with us. For what heats ever more and more from beginning to end, so long as it is in contact, is such not by some accident but according to its own nature. In the same way, what cools from beginning to end is cold according to its own power, not by accident. But if you examine its power neither after waiting for a time nor later, after the washing, you will be deceived in many ways. And perhaps you will even at times call cold water not only cold in power but also hot.

cold, when it appears cooling throughout, as long as it is close to us; hot, when, as often happens, it has brought on a recall of heat [385]. One must not, then, leave these matters undistinguished. And each of the drugs under judgement, as was also said in the work On Mixture, should partake of no acquired cooling or heat, so that the acquired quality may not adulterate its natural power. Further, in addition to these, as was also said there, let food be distinguished by you from drug. Let it be remembered that both are spoken of relatively, but in many cases are found together in one substance, in the way in which we also demonstrated this. No less should it be remembered that some things act on and are affected by one another with their whole substances, others according to one or two qualities. In addition, some are fine-particled, others coarse-particled: fine-particled are those that are easily broken down into fine pieces, coarse-particled the opposite. To put it simply, one must remember all the distinctions stated in the third book On Mixtures, so that the power of drugs of every kind may be examined in accordance with them.

Let water, then, first be set before us for examination, since it is both the thing most common to all human beings, [386] healthy and sick alike, and the most necessary for life. And first let it be applied to a well-tempered body, being neither notably cold nor hot. Next, let it be applied to those that are ill-tempered by nature, and thirdly to those that are so through an affection. For in this way we would examine precisely, in every case, its proper power. When applied, then, to the well-tempered body over a longer time, it will in every case cool it. In the ill-tempered body it will cool the colder one more quickly and the hotter one more slowly. And it will always cool all of them, even if one uses it not on many successive days but on one day, or for several hours. For water of this kind will not produce a recall of heat in any of them. For it is unmixed cold that, when it consorts for a short time with a well-fleshed and young nature of body, calls back warmth; but when people use it otherwise, it will always cool.

Moreover, even if such water be applied to those suffering from some simple disease, either hot or cold in its mixture, it will clearly cool these too; for the affection must be simple, as had also been distinguished in the third book On Mixtures, in order that what is applied may cool not incidentally, [387] but through its own nature. For often, when the condition is compound, one thing is brought about primarily by the drug and another incidentally, as in inflammations. For the affection is the offspring of a hot and copious flux. But those drugs that warm moderately, by evacuating the superfluity, at once, I think, also make the affected part colder. But when the condition is simple and single, the incidental effect cannot occur in it. Thus, at any rate, to you who examine it from every side, potable water will appear cold. The other, naturally occurring waters, however, those that are sulphurous, bituminous and nitrous in their qualities, do not have the same power; for none of them, when it is applied separated from acquired heat or coldness, appears to cool. And indeed the sea itself too, before it takes on an acquired unmixed coldness, does not appear to cool very much at all.

For in the case of potable water, if someone were to swim in it throughout a whole day, even when it is not very cold but lukewarm, as from the sun, he will of necessity [388] be chilled. But the sea a great many of the young have borne without harm, not only throughout a whole day but sometimes also through the night. From this it is clear that water, at any rate potable and sweet water, is always cold in its own nature, whereas the sea is not likewise. And if at some point in the discussion we should not add 'potable', but should say simply that water, in so far as depends on itself, is cold, one ought not to cavil at us as having spoken defectively or without drawing a distinction. For whatever is precisely and purely water, unmixed with any other substance, that is of necessity cold in respect of its own power. But if, filtering through asphaltic, or sulphurous, or nitrous, or alum-bearing ground, it should scour off something of the substance of that ground and carry it along with itself, such water is already mixed and not precisely water. It is just as if you yourself should wish to mix a good quantity of salt, or alum, or some other such thing with potable water, as indeed we often do when, being without sea-water, we wish to prepare brine.

For in that case we throw some salt into the water, and so great [389] then is the difference in power that the water itself, the sweet water that is, being neither manifestly cold nor hot but like what is called 'sun-warmed', if you apply it to an erysipelas, will do no harm to the body of the human being. But if you apply sea-water or brine or some such admixed water, asphaltic or sulphurous, you would harm the human being so much as to burn the part. Water, then, in and of itself is cold in power. But if, having attached an acquired heat to it, you should wish to pour it over a human body, you will perhaps think that you have applied something simple and natural, whereas it is in fact in some way compound, having taken on either some portion of the substance of fire or, at any rate and in every case, its quality. For just as, if you had also mixed some salt into it, it would admittedly be compound, so too, and still more, since you have mixed in fire, whether its quality or its substance, you have now also made it in some way compound. And of course muddy water too is compound, such as that of the Nile and that throughout Egypt; but when filtered through earthenware vessels it becomes perfectly pure.

One must filter it not once, however, but [390] twice or three times, although even so it is perhaps impossible to make it exactly pure; but when the silt carried in the waters escapes all perception, it suffices, at least for a use of this kind, to call such waters pure and unmixed. These are judged by three senses: taste, sight and smell. Pure to taste, if it has taken on no quality but appears exactly without quality; pure to sight, when it is unmixed and exactly translucent. So too with respect to smell it must display no quality, in the way that some of the utterly bad waters strike the sense with sourness, or pungency, or brine, or putrefaction, or some other indescribable foulness. Water, then, that is free of all these is not itself exactly unmixed with respect to its nature, just as no other of the four perceptible elements is either; it is, however, unmixed as far as perception and use are concerned.

Water of this sort, at any rate, is also cold, as has been said, in its own nature; for if you were to heat strongly not only water, [391] but also mandrake, henbane, hemlock and poppy juice, then on applying them you would not only heat a human body through but even burn it. Let all the drugs being tested, then, not water alone, be free of every acquired and intense heat and cooling. That all sweet water clearly cools you may learn from the following as well. If you soften a liquid cerate with cold water, work it through carefully, and apply it to some hot affection, you will cool that affection at once. One must mix in as much of the water as possible, and the mixing would be done best roughly as follows. One should melt the purest possible wax with oil to make a liquid cerate; then, having cooled it and scraped it, soften it with the hands in a mortar, pouring cold water in alongside, as much as the cerate can take up, and so that the water does not run off around it.

This also cools those who are burning in fever, if it is applied over the hypochondria, and every inflammation, and likewise herpētes and anthrakes, erysipelata and phygethla and, to put it simply, all the [392] hot diseases. If, then, instead of sweet water you mix sea water or brine into it and use it on whichever one of the aforesaid you wish, you will at once observe no small difference: the drug so produced not only no longer cools any of the aforesaid conditions, but even inflames them further. So great, then, is the difference between potable waters and brine and sea water. And no less than brine and sea water, the sulphurous and bituminous waters, the nitrous ones, and those that reveal to the taste chalkanthon, misy and chalkitis, or, in short, any of the drugs that are hot by nature, are all hostile to the hot conditions of our body. By which it is clear that all these are hot in their powers, while potable water alone is cold. That this alone of the waters mentioned is also strictly moist you will recognise by the same method.

For if you moisten with this ulcers that are squalid and dry beyond what is due, you will very quickly make them moist and flabby, whereas all the other waters dry ulcers: those of fishermen [393] appear dry and pickled, while those of bath-attendants appear moist and flabby. And if you should wish to soak lint and apply it to the ulcers, you will find them becoming moist from the potable water, but dry from brine and sea-water. The aluminous waters, however, such as those in Italy called Albula, are suitable for the other ulcers as well, and they readily dry all the fluxional ones. Thus none of the other waters is by nature such as to moisten, because none is water in the strict sense, but admixed and spurious, having taken in either alum and chalcitis, or salts, or some other such thing. Hence some of them, namely those that are sufficiently pungent and biting, are exacerbating to ulcers.

Moreover, for one who is thirsty water is a soothing remedy, whereas all the other [waters] exacerbate [the thirst]; and for dropsical patients sweet water, both as drink and as bath, is most contrary, whereas the briny, nitrous, sulphurous and bituminous [waters] are all beneficial. And you could imitate, just as [394] sea water, so also each of the others, by admixture of the substance that appears to predominate in each. For by putting sulphur into sweet water you will make sulphurous water, and by putting in alum, aluminous water, and likewise each of the others. The proper nature of water itself, then, is moist and cold. But when it takes on acquired heat, it heats and moistens the things that come near it; yet it is not naturally disposed to do both alike at the same time. Rather, it moistens to the highest degree, whether it is lukewarm, or temperate, or even rather hot, but it does not heat to the highest degree, at least if it is not boiling to the utmost. Let the argument be examined first in the case of the well-tempered nature. If, then, you apply to this nature moderately hot water, whether in bathing it or in pouring it over some part or other, you will render it moister than it was and hotter during the very time of the affusion.

But if, after this, you were to stop without having drawn together, compressed and condensed the body by the use of cold, a little later you will find that it has become colder than it was; for a body that is rarefied becomes colder, since the innate [395] warmth is dispersed more immoderately. The use of the hot does not, however, render the body drier afterwards in the way that it renders it colder afterwards. And yet this too might seem to happen, because of the rarefaction of the pores, the softness of the body and the diffusion of its substance; for in such conditions it must necessarily give off more vapour, and vapour is moisture that has been thinned. But the truth is not so. For the softness that bodies acquire after hot baths is a sign peculiar to and inseparable from moisture alone in the body of an animal, as we showed in the work on mixtures; and the flesh in ulcerated parts clearly displays this, being rendered flabby and fungous by these affusions of hot water. The body is, however, emptied in such conditions, so that it now holds less moisture within itself than before. And one might pardon those who think that the body is dried by hot baths and by affusions of the moderately hot.

For they err in much the same way as those who suppose that old men [396] are moister than young men. For the moist superfluities are more abundant in old men, but the natural and organic parts themselves are moister in young men, as has been shown also in the second book On Mixtures. So it is too with affusions and baths and, in a word, with all wetting by means of hot water. For the moistures in the vessels and in the other empty spaces are all evacuated, but the bodies of the vessels themselves and the whole fleshy kind become moister than they were before. And this power alone, it seems, sweet water (that is to say) never loses. For not even when, boiling, it burns bodies, do the burnt parts become dry, as happens in those roasted by fire. In the same way, not even when, having become extremely cold, it is poured over some part for a whole day or for a still longer time, does it render this part drier, although the part does appear wrinkled and very small.

But these things happen to it because the moisture from the vessels and from the other spaces has been evacuated, whereas the naturally constituted parts themselves become in no respect drier than they were; and one must [397] remember this too, and keep it always in view throughout the whole account: that the power of each drug is to be inferred from what is evidently apparent, and that one must always test it against that in relation to which it is said to be hot or cold or moist or dry. If someone wishes, by way of supplement, to adduce proofs from external things, I do not forbid this either, but I advise him to attend to it with precision. For it involves many paralogisms; these, however, I shall discuss in what follows. The only thing one might take from external things as evidence of whether the drug under judgement heats or cools is what concerns its contact with fire. For it is not unreasonable to suppose that what readily catches fire is hot in potentiality. For we remember, I think, all the senses of 'in potentiality' that were distinguished in the third book On Mixtures. One of them, then, was also the sense in which, by virtue of the proper matter of the thing spoken of, something is such-and-such in potentiality. And if something readily changes into fire, this is fire in potentiality, not, of course, in actuality.

For this [398] 'potentially' is set in opposition to 'in actuality', whereas the other, 'in itself', is set in opposition to 'by accident'. It is in this mode of judgement, then, that one ought to examine and to draw distinctions. One who wishes to pass safely from external things to the bodies of animals must consider, first, whether the drug being tested is fine-particled or coarse-particled, and second, whether it is continuous with itself and dense throughout, or has interstices and is rare. And for this reason one must give a fuller account of this matter too, for it seems itself to be a kind of principle and, as it were, an element requiring very extensive theoretical study. Now, none of the things agreed to be hot in their powers is seen to heat us before it has been broken down into fine pieces. Thus, if someone sprinkles coarse-grained pepper on the skin, he would perceive no heat at all. And likewise if he places it on the tongue, or swallows it, or uses it coarse-grained in any other way whatever, without having ground it precisely, sifted it, and ground it very thoroughly so that it becomes like fine dust.

For when it is as fine as [399] powder and sprinkled on the skin, it heats, and does so the more if you rub it in; and likewise when it is put on the tongue and when it is swallowed down into the stomach. But when it is applied whole and coarse-grained, it neither heats the skin, and it brings to the tongue and to the stomach only a slight sensation of heat. Since, then, that is called fine-particled which is easily broken down into fine pieces, and coarse-grained the opposite, and since it belongs to hard and viscous things to be broken down into fine pieces either barely and with difficulty or not at all, whereas it belongs to brittle things, and to soft things without viscosity, to be readily resolved into the finest pieces, it is plain from this, I think, that many things are hot in potentiality and are easily set on fire, yet do not easily heat us.

For fire, being of all things at once the most fine-particled and the hottest, both penetrates easily into the depth and breaks up, thins, changes, overcomes and transposes into its own nature whatever is near it, consorting with it on every side and mastering it. Our warmth, on the other hand, besides being coarse-particled and vaporous, is also weak, so that it does not easily [400] change what is near it. It was shown in the third book On Mixtures, without which it is impossible to follow what is said in this one, that none of the things that appear to heat us is of a nature to heat as fire does, but rather as readily kindled matter. For, taking the beginning of their change from the heat in us, as dry reeds do from fire, they heat us in return and become, as it were, certain parts of the innate warmth, just as those reeds become parts of the fire. For what was previously reed now becomes fire, so that it even increases the whole substance of the fire that changes it. It was also shown that some things, after receiving a slight change from outside, then advance by their own nature to a very great degree of alteration. So it is nothing remarkable if one of the drugs takes the beginning of its first change from the warmth in us, and from there advances further even than the very thing that changes it. For the particular character of each body, being in one case naturally apt and in another naturally unapt for warmth, does not, from equal beginnings, have an equal increase following upon them.

[401] And indeed, the fact that a very small body is easily altered and changed by what is near it, while a larger one undergoes its alteration only in time and barely perceptibly, has not only been demonstrated by natural philosophers but is also believed by all men from the very experience of what happens, and it bears sufficient witness to what is now being said. For if the particles of pepper need to receive some beginning of change from us, and receive it more easily the smaller they are, it is nothing surprising if we perceive them heating more quickly the more carefully we crush them into the smallest pieces. Moreover, no one disputes that the outer limit of the skin is callous, hard and cold, while the whole depth beneath it is hotter in proportion as we proceed inward. If you add to this account two further principles, which have been demonstrated by us in other treatises, you will then be able to reason out the whole by syllogism.

One of the principles for the demonstration (or lemmas, or [402] axioms, or premises, or however you wish to name them) has been demonstrated in the commentaries On Mixtures: that the whole skin is continuous with itself in its original generation, but in the course of time becomes perforated and has a great many pores, like sieves. The other of the premises useful for the syllogism is that the whole body breathes out and breathes in, as Hippocrates said.
