This premise too has been discussed at greater length in On the Use of Pulses, where we showed that when the arteries, as they dilate, draw into themselves from every side and attract through all the pores, they draw not only air or vapour but also everything that, being easily drawn and fine-particled, readily follows the impetus of the pneumatic substance. This being so, many veins and arteries open with their mouths both into the pores of the skin and onto its inner surface, and one must suppose that not a few mouths of arteries and veins reach into the perforations of the pores, and no less toward the outer surface, so that they terminate there with their mouths.

But whatever part of the pepper has become precisely a fine dust [403] the arteries draw in together with the surrounding air. Straightaway this too is changed by the innate heat, both because of its smallness and because of its connatural suitability for alteration by warmth. For being hot in potency was for it nothing other than being naturally apt to be heated readily. And once this belongs to it, it is nothing surprising that, being carried in the course of time everywhere through the body, it heats the body in return. On this account the parts that first touched such drugs are heated by them first and most of all, and secondly the parts continuous with these. And so in succession third and fourth parts, according to the proximity of their position, are heated along with what was first heated. These things have a scientific demonstration, yet not one credible to those who are untrained in the first principles. For one must have been trained both in the reasonings about the elements and in the treatises on mixtures and on the use of pulses, and, before all these, must have been exercised in the demonstrative methods. Few, however, are those able to go through them all.

[404] Nevertheless, even for these it will suffice, in my judgement at least, to occupy themselves with the evident things themselves, applying brief inferences. They should then consider that the cause on account of which coarse-particled things, when applied, do not heat the bodies of human beings, even if they are hot in their nature, has been stated only for those who are able to follow it, while they themselves should be content with what appears evidently through the senses. And it appears evidently that none of the coarse-particled things, before it has been exactly broken up and thinned, either itself suffers anything from our body or is able to act upon it in return. For this holds not only for pepper, or mustard, or kachrys, or all the other things that heat us, but likewise also for those that are cold in their powers. The bark of the mandrake root, at any rate, if one breaks it into large pieces and lays it upon the skin, or spreads it on as a plaster, or swallows it, will achieve nothing at all; but when it has been sufficiently finely worked, it is of a nature to cool.

So too the seed of the poppy and that of hemlock (although this latter is the most powerful of cooling things), before it has been thoroughly broken up, is altogether weak when it comes close to [405] our skin. Do not be surprised, then, if dry reeds and hairs, though easily set alight, nevertheless do not heat us when they come close to us. For to begin with, they are not even altered by the warmth in us so as to heat in return, because they cannot be broken up into a downy powder; since the reed from India, which they also call 'aromatic', is evidently seen, by being pounded and sifted and, in general, by being broken up, to heat more than the reed of our own country, as all the physicians older than ourselves have agreed. One must examine, as has been said, not only whether the substance of the drugs under examination is coarse-particled or fine-particled, but also whether it is rare or dense. I call rare that substance whose parts are separated by empty spaces, we knowing, of course, and always remembering in what sense 'empty space' is spoken of by those who assert that substance is unified: namely, that it is not as Epicurus and Asclepiades hold, but in all rare bodies the empty space is full of air.

Whenever, then, the body is interspersed with many such [406] open spaces, it is more readily set on fire than dense bodies, even if it has a mixture, as regards hot and cold, similar to theirs. For the air in the open spaces, being most easily affected, itself bursts into flame immediately at the first onset of the fire, and along with itself it burns up the whole body as well, laying hold of each of its parts from every side. If, then, small bodies catch fire readily when flame surrounds them in a circle (for this is plainly seen), it is reasonable that the rare body is quickly set on fire, since the flame touches all of its parts that lie in the depth. So too, then, fire burns dry reeds quickly, even if they are less hot than another substance, on account of the multitude of their pores, which air previously occupied, but over which, once the fire has touched them, the flame spreads. For air, when set on fire, is flame, and earth, when set on fire, is a live coal. That the dry reed has a great many airy pores, the greatest proof is its lightness.

For a body that is dry by nature cannot otherwise [407] become light, unless it has emptiness. In the same way pumice and a dry sponge, and all things that are cavernous and full of empty spaces, are light in weight. So too the reed, not only by being dry but also by partaking of a very great amount of air, readily bursts into flame; but for our body it is hard to heat, because of the coarse-particled character of its substance. Whenever, therefore, inferring the mixture of one of the drugs from its contact with fire, we wish to discover whether it also appears such in relation to us, we must look to the constitution of its substance. For if it is fine-particled and continuous with itself, it will display towards us the very same nature that it displays towards fire. But if it is rare and coarse-particled, it may be readily altered by fire, yet not by the warmth in us, and for this reason it may not heat us in return either. Now that these matters have been thus distinguished, let us return once more to the account of water. That it is fine-particled one may infer from its flowing most readily through both locks of hair and woven fabrics.

For because of its moisture [408] and softness and its having nothing viscous, it has parts that are easily broken up, even down to the very smallest, being readily divided. Yet, though it is of this kind, it neither heats us by its own nature nor is it a proper nourishment of fire; quite the contrary, it stands against it, is at strife with it and extinguishes it, as being most opposite to it. And it is nothing to wonder at if water, being cold and moist, is ranged against fire, which is by nature hottest and driest. One conjectures, then, as has been said, also from the contact with fire, how each of the drugs stands in respect of heat or coldness. Yet one should not at once suppose that it also appears such to us, unless it is fine-particled and dense as well. Thus, for instance, oil too, although it is readily set ablaze, does not heat us at all quickly or manifestly, because of the viscous and coarse-particled character of its substance, adhering, hard to detach, to whatever it first comes into contact with. And for this reason it remains for a very long time on everything onto which it is smeared, being able neither to be thinned and dispersed readily by the surrounding [air], nor even to be readily taken over into the interior of the body.

Water [409], on the contrary, being resolved very quickly into vapours, is readily dispersed. And for this reason, even if you boil oil with water, putting them into the same vessel, the water is dispersed and used up first. So too, if you mix litharge, or white lead, or anything else whatever thoroughly, and wish to boil both, you will see the water being dispersed first. Not, therefore, is it simply the case that whatever is set on fire more quickly at once also appears hotter in relation to us. For it was shown earlier too that, of the things that heat in actuality, one was hot simply, as fire is, another hot by predominance, as that in us is. So too, of the things potentially hot, one is such in relation to what is first and simply hot, another in relation to what is called hot by predominance. Consequently one ought not to pass over to ourselves simply from the relation to fire of the drugs being judged, but only after having drawn the distinction that has been stated.

This same distinction is necessary also whenever we infer, from the fact that something congeals easily, that it is cold [410]. For of things that are alike as regards the fine-particled or coarse-particled character of their consistency, the one congealed more quickly by the cold is colder in its mixture. But if the one should be more fine-particled, as wine for instance, and the other more coarse-particled, as oil, it is not necessary that the colder congeal more quickly or more. Rather, if by as much as the one is colder, by so much the other should be more coarse-particled, both will congeal at the same time, but the more coarse-particled would seem to have congealed more, by reason of the hardness of its consistency. For it is reasonable, I think, that of things congealed to a like degree the more coarse-particled also becomes harder. But if either the one should be colder by more than the remaining one is more coarse-particled, or, conversely, the one of them should be colder by less, while the remaining one is more coarse-particled, it is no longer possible for these to congeal in an equal time. Rather, the one that is colder by more than the other is more coarse-particled will congeal in less time, and the one that is colder by less than the remaining one is more coarse-particled, in more.

So too the fact that either of them appears more or less [411] hard must necessarily turn out in proportion to the magnitude of the excess. One must therefore remember these things, and also that being cooled is not the same as being congealed, even if congealing comes about above all through being cooled. For to be cooled is to receive a cold quality, whereas to be congealed is to be hardened through cooling. Accordingly, all bodies that are fine-particled, because they are easily affected, are readily heated and cooled, but are no longer readily congealed, as is the case with air and fire. For fire is not congealed at all, and air not in the same way as glass, pitch, wax, resin and bitumen; and yet bitumen is extremely hot, but its coarse-particled and earthy character contributes to the thickness of its congelation. And if you touch it, you would find it still hot when it has already completely congealed, just as, I think, lead and tin likewise are congealed while still boiling hot. So it is, too, that Hippocrates said of water that the water which is quickly heated and quickly cooled is always the lightest. For the more fine-particled it is, the more easily it is affected.

[412] And that which has the least share of earthy silt is more fine-particled. One must therefore not infer the power of a material in relation to us from its affections in relation to fire without qualification or haphazardly, but with the distinctions that have been stated. Hence the judgement of its power in relation to ourselves is not equally safe either. And a transition that goes still further beyond this one is altogether hazardous; and yet a great many physicians make use of it, some saying that everything viscous is hot, others everything astringent, others everything sweet, others again the harsh or the acerbic. Some lay down the opposite in the case of each of these. About the errors in these matters I shall speak in what follows. For now I wish to complete the present account [the text reads ἐνεστῶταστρυφνὸν, apparently a corruption]: if one wishes to judge a material from its relation to fire as well, it is not proper to judge without qualification or indeterminately, nor to suppose that each of the things being judged stands in the same way towards both man and fire. Now water is most opposite to fire, being cold and moist in its power.

[413] But brine and sea-water and bituminous water and sulphurous water are no longer in the same condition, for all such waters have departed from water towards the hotter. But concerning the naturally occurring waters, even these remarks are sufficient; for when we treat of each of the drugs whose qualities the water itself has taken up, we shall add whatever has now been said about them too obscurely or too incompletely. Let us now pass on to the remaining liquid drugs, among which there has been dispute above all about vinegar: some say that it is cold, others that it is hot, and some grant it a certain heat but take away a certain other heat. Such are those who say that vinegar is dead wine and a corpse. For these say that it has lost the heat proper to wine, but has taken on a certain putrefactive heat.

And I for my part would have praised their judgement, readily accepted it, and shared the risk of both the pronouncement and the opinion, if I had been able to find some means of separating the contrary parts here too, as in milk. But as it is, that milk as a whole is not homoeomerous, nor everywhere the same as itself, is clearly shown [414] by its splitting, since many ways have been discovered by men for separating the cheesy parts from the wheyey ones. In the case of vinegar, however, nothing of this kind has been discovered. Nor is it possible to demonstrate clearly that whatever of it is exactly thin and liquid cools, while what is carried along in it in the substance of the lees, as also in wines, heats. For only in this way could one clearly show that it is composed of parts contrary in their powers, as milk is. Now in all liquids produced from pressed fruits something coarse-particled is carried along, which in time settles to the bottom; it is called lees in the case of wines and amurca in the case of oil. And in all the others too there is analogously a sort of lees in them, even if it has not obtained names of its own. There is, then, something of this kind in vinegar too; and perhaps this is what shares in heat, while what shares in cooling is the thin part.

And perhaps within the thin part itself [415] there is also carried something small, distributed in a large amount, of a nature other than that of the whole. For that it is cold in the greater portion rather than hot is, I think, clearly apparent to those who examine its power truthfully. And I wonder how some have declared vinegar to be hot to such a degree that it resembles a cautery. It is in this way, at any rate, that they say it also checks haemorrhages. For in the first place so great a heat would not have escaped our perception. And then, on the analogy of those hot things themselves, if it were of such a kind it would surely somewhere have produced an eschar, in the same way as the hot drugs. For we clearly see in the case of these, whenever we wish to check blood by means of them, that an eschar of no small size is formed, so that if you do not produce an eschar, you do not check the blood either. For this eschar becomes as it were a kind of covering over the bleeding bodies. And for this reason we also apply to them cautery-irons that have been thoroughly heated in the fire, knowing, I think, that those which are not such, besides accomplishing nothing, also do harm and aggravate the haemorrhages.

For it is not, [416] indeed, by its own proper nature, nor by heating, that fire stops them; rather, by burning up whatever it falls upon, it makes what is, as it were, the residue of the burning into a lid for the underlying parts, which the Greeks are accustomed to call an eschar. But vinegar stops haemorrhages not in the same way as any of the eschar-forming drugs, but rather as the astringent drugs do, without an eschar; so that in this respect it would be supposed not to heat to an extreme degree, but to cool. It is better, however, as has also been said before, to withdraw from indications of this kind. For such reasoning does not refer the judgement back to sense-perception, nor does it reason from what lies at hand or from close by, but from far off and through long premises. And I shall show its absurdity more fully in the discourses that follow. We, then, following the method laid down from the beginning, shall make trial of its power first on those who are in faultless health, and then next on the ill-tempered, and after that also on the sick.

Having soaked a sponge or wool in vinegar, then, we shall apply it to any part whatever of healthy bodies, and then [417], as has been said before, we shall immediately ask laymen (for they will judge such things impartially, because they are not slaves to a doctrine) whether they perceive cooling or warmth. It is clear that we shall apply it neither extremely cold nor hot, for this too has already been discussed before. If, then, the vinegar applied is of this kind, and especially if it is not very old nor extremely pungent, they will perceive a distinct cooling, immediately and after one hour, and two, and three, and four; later, however, they will also have some impression of a certain warmth now arising little by little in the part. But when the vinegar is strongly pungent, at the beginning they will say that in this case too they are cooled, yet they will quickly perceive the returning warmth, and not after a long time, as with the newer and not very pungent vinegar.

From which it is clear that it is cold in every respect, but already also has a share of some slight warmth, which, by reason of its pungency, warms bodies moderately in the course of time, [418] by some accident; and it does not naturally do even this always, but only in some cases. Thus those swellings that are lax and painless have no sensation of warmth when vinegar is used, either immediately or later. Itching does, however, arise in them, and because of it a thin redness often also spreads over those who use it to the extreme. So it would seem not to warm primarily, nor according to its proper order, but to irritate by the biting of its pungency. And since we have once passed over from healthy bodies to affections, let us recall what it naturally does in the hottest and the coldest conditions. When, then, someone is burning all through from thapsia smeared on him, vinegar quenches the burning heat.

And anyone who wishes may learn this by experience, just as we ourselves did on our own persons in order to obtain an exact test of the drug's power. We smeared our shins with it in many places, and when, after four or five hours, they began to burn and to become inflamed, we sprinkled some vinegar on one place and some water on another; one place we anointed with oil, another with rose oil, and another with some other one of the things believed either to blunt pungencies [419] or to cool heats. Of them all, vinegar was found to be the most effective. It is clear, then, that it acts not by blunting pungencies and bitings, in the manner of oil and rose oil (for it too is by nature such as to produce these things), but by cooling. For if it cannot cure the inflammations arising from thapsia in any other way than either by cooling or by blunting the bitings and pungencies, and the second of these does not belong to it, then it must necessarily cure by the remaining one. And it is cooling for all the other hot affections as well, for some more, for others less: inflammations, herpetes, phygethla, erysipelases, carbuncles. So that, were it not that the vehemence and roughness of its power is troublesome, we would use nothing else for cooling. And yet some posit this very thing as the greatest sign of its heat. For it would not, they say, be pungent or biting or corrosive or roughening unless it had an abundant share of heat.

For just as contracting and condensing is proper to the cold, so [420] cutting and dividing is proper to the hot, and this, they say, belongs not least to vinegar. For it cuts and eats through not only the bodies of animals but also clots, tufa, stones, earthenware, bronze, iron and lead; and, almost as with fire, so for it too all things are passable and pervious, since no substance withstands it, nor is able to stand against it or hold out against the violence of its passage through. For it is indeed also fine-particled, much as fire is; and of this the touch too is no small testimony, and moreover it appears such to those who taste it, and it filters through the finest woven fabrics more readily than water, and eats through everything, as was said a little before. Indeed, what else than fire do they declare vinegar to be by their argument? Just so, of course, do those too who assert that it dissolves clots by its cooling, through pressing, compacting and constricting everything from all sides, just as if someone were to take hold of them and crush them with his own fingers. But these in their turn also overshoot so far as to declare it colder even than snow.

But it is just to censure both parties for their [421] lack of measure. For neither, if it is cold, does it follow that one should at once declare it colder even than snow; nor, if it is hot, that it is hottest. For there would not even be any dispute about its power were it not ranked somewhere near the middle and far removed from each of the two extremes. For no one has ever disputed about the power of hemlock or of mandrake, nor about cardamom and cachrys; rather, the former are agreed by all physicians to be cold, the latter hot. In the same way henbane and poppy juice are cold, and pepper and mustard hot. And besides these, countless others, some hot in power, some cold, are agreed upon by all physicians. But vinegar, just as rose oil too, is neither extremely cold nor extremely hot, and this is plain from the very fact that it is disputed. And each of them must in some way be neutral.

Now since things are called 'neutral' in three ways, as Herophilus too distinguished them, some by sharing equally in both the extremes, others by sharing in neither, others by sharing now in this one and now in that one, these too [vinegar and rose oil] are surely in every case, according to one or another of these senses, of the nature of the neutrals. [422] To me, indeed, it seems rather that they are so by sharing in each of the extremes, and by seeming now to heat perceptibly and again to cool. In this way, then, both vinegar and rose oil might be called neutral. But if someone should also attempt to show them to be neutral by their sharing in neither of the extremes, he too will perhaps be well supplied with some persuasive arguments, though not with demonstrative and scientific ones. This I believe I know precisely, and especially in the case of vinegar. For the fact that both parties are well supplied with persuasive arguments, both those who prove it to be coldest and those who prove it to be hottest, is no small proof that it shares in both. It is difficult, however, to establish adequately by argument its participation in the contraries, since we are unable to resolve and split its substance, as we do in the case of milk and a great many other things, all of which the account will show as it proceeds. And for this reason we long to lay hold of a more evident and less hazardous starting point.

But that starting-point, as it appears to me, is to be hunted for in the fine-particled [423] and coarse-particled nature. I have indeed spoken about this before, but it is better now too to go through it at greater length, since Plato also says that the most discussions must be had about first principles. Now, there is no one who has not called air fine-particled, evidently because it is easily broken up into fine pieces and passes readily through the densest bodies. Or, if they apply the name 'fine-particled' to it on account of something else, let them teach us this clearly. For we at any rate shall not say that air is composed of fine corpuscles (ὄγκων), as the leaders of the other sect would say. For it is continuous and one whole, nowhere containing any void within itself. In a bodily nature of this kind, fine-particledness is conceived solely in terms of the speed of its division into small parts. But if it is for this reason that air is fine-particled, then not all fire will be fine-particled. For bronze and iron and stone and wood, and everything that has been turned into live coal, is surely fire, yet it is not more fine-particled now than before.

Flames, however, [424] which are another kind of fire, are truly fine-particled. So neither is all fire fine-particled, nor is everything fine-particled fire. For since the live coal is fire but not fine-particled, while air is fine-particled but not fire, why ever is it that almost all physicians and philosophers alike take up all the premises without examination, both the one declaring that all fire is fine-particled and the one declaring that everything fine-particled is fiery? For if one were to consider the matter precisely and apply one's mind to the things themselves, one would not say that the live coal is finer-particled than air. Let us recall the clearness of the air surrounding us in severe cold and a northerly condition of the weather, and let us compare it, if you like, with red-hot iron; for we shall recognise from such examples that there is something that is both cold and strictly fine-particled, and something that is both hot and coarse-particled.

So whenever some people reason, on the ground that vinegar is biting, that it is fine-particled and hot, [425] one must not concede this to them. For not everything fine-particled is hot; and perhaps not even everything biting is fine-particled. But for the present let this be conceded, although we could say that snow, the north wind and cold water are biting not only to the eyes but also to ulcers and to all rare bodies, just as Hippocrates too said: 'the cold is biting'. But even if, as I said, one were to concede this, that everything biting is also fine-particled, he will not straightaway concede that it is also hot. Vinegar, then, is not also hot on this account, because it is biting; rather it is fine-particled, like the northern air, but not hot. Whence, then, do some people get a perception of faint heat? Perhaps, as I said before as well, it is composed of opposite powers, like milk; perhaps also because it brings about a recall of heat. And that which has a rough and distressing passage could also produce pain and draw a hot flux to the place. For this too is evident, that something flows into parts that are in pain.

But [426] not much would flow in, because the vinegar is cold and repels what is being carried towards the part. Whatever is exactly thin, however, escapes the grip of the drug, slips in alongside, and becomes fixed in the part, no longer running back again as the thicker matter does. And indeed an exactly thin redness is seen blooming on the parts that have been irritated by vinegar. Perhaps, though, there is also some other cause which cannot be known. It was for this very reason that I tried to prevent the examination of the powers from being begun from far back: one is then necessarily drawn into problems of natural philosophy, which involve no small difficulties. Our task now, however, is not, as it is for natural philosophers, to discover the causes of all things. It is to recognise the powers of the drugs, so that we may both use them skilfully and become good makers of compound drugs.

For that it is not possible either to compound a drug well oneself or to use one compounded by another before knowing the powers of the simple drugs is sufficiently demonstrated both in the Therapeutic Method and in the work on [427] the composition of drugs. Since, then, the present treatise has this aim, as soon as we have first found what is useful from them, we must withdraw from natural problems, which contain many difficulties. For by what mixture, speaking in general, are sourness and sweetness and bitterness, saltiness and harshness and pungency, and each of the other qualities naturally produced? Even to the natural philosophers themselves, as they inquire, very great and very numerous difficulties come to light in their arguments. These, then, I advise that we guard against as against a precipice, since we have a highway by which it is possible to judge drugs. First, as I have already said a little earlier, we should reckon that no power of the strongly heating or cooling drugs is disputed, but that those drugs about which such dispute has arisen possess neither power. Next, we should reckon that many of the simples are, as far as perception goes, compounded of contrary powers.

For not only milk, but also the sulphurous, the bituminous and the nitrous, and all such as are of this kind among the naturally occurring [428] waters, came into being from an admixture of the opposite powers, if indeed water is cold and moist according to its own nature, while bitumen and sulphur and misy and chalcitis and the other things of this kind are hot. One must also remember that many of the hot things are coarse-particled, and many of the cold things fine-particled, and on these principles pronounce with security about the power of drugs. For instance, it suffices to say that vinegar is fine-particled, and cooling and drying, leaving aside the more physical reasonings about it. For from knowing these things one will know how one ought to mix it with the other drugs.

These things, then, I find fault with in those who have prattled at length about its [sc. vinegar's] power, and still more than in these, in almost all the physicians: that they did not distinguish all the simple drugs according to the more and the less, but it sufficed them to say that these, as it may be, heat and those cool, and these dry and those moisten. For this, known simply in this way, is not useful, [429] but rather to what degree fleawort cools, and to what degree nightshade or chervil or white lead, and purslane and lettuce; and to what degree cassia heats, and to what degree cinnamon, or amomum or marjoram. So too with drugs that dry and moisten in their powers, one must know not only the general fact, but which has first departed from what is well-proportioned and intermediate between the contraries in their powers, and which comes next after that one; and thus to distinguish also a third and a fourth and a fifth remove, if possible, defining them by clear boundaries. For in such a recognition of the powers lies our ability both to use the simples themselves according to art and to be able to compound them methodically, and in addition to this also to use them correctly once they have been compounded.

This, then, is a most difficult matter, and one requiring much precision and practice. For in all such matters it is necessary to begin from experience, as has already been said, and to reason securely, taking care not to [430] entangle oneself in insoluble questions. For which reason one might well be astonished at those who have investigated such things, seeing them come to grief at their own hands in most of what they investigate and write, as Herodotus does. For, beginning from the whole of the most ancient record of compound drugs, they proceed to the examination of the simples contained in them. Since, say, vinegar has been mixed into these or those warming drugs, they thereupon declare it too to be hot. But it is not clear whether it has been rightly mixed in, before one has discovered its power on its own. Nor, even if this were granted, do we yet know the method of the composition of drugs, by whose judgement we shall discover for what reason a single cooling drug has been mixed with many warming drugs, or indeed a warming one with chilling drugs.

And when they also mention non-evident conditions for which [the drug] seems to be suitable, and then attach further paralogisms to dogmatic assumptions, deducing things under inquiry from things under inquiry and non-evident things from non-evident [431] things by means of one another, then indeed one can most of all recognise their idle chatter. For in speaking thus they also furnish the Empiricists with an occasion for counter-argument, since they readily trust all compound remedies, as though it were not possible that many of them have been made in error and badly compounded. For the Empiricists will say, I think, just as they in fact do say, that we inquire in vain into the primary and active powers of each of the drugs, since experience already possesses a countless multitude of simple and compound drugs, which are trusted even by those very people who inquire in vain into the primary powers. For if all their particular uses are known and agreed upon by everyone, while the causes by which [each] acts have not yet been agreed upon, it is plain that neither the compounding nor the use of drugs has been discovered from knowledge of the primary powers; rather, experience put these together, and reason advances only as far as the plausible.

These things, then, and many other things of the kind, the physicians who proceed from experience will seem [432] to say rightly against those who trust all the drugs written down in any way whatsoever, and who choose to fit plausible causes to the claims made for them.

But I for my part would add to these this further point: that Herodotus, who holds all the other sects to be bad except the Pneumatic, and Metrodorus all except that of Asclepiades, and Zeno all except that of Herophilus, and Hermogenes all except that of Erasistratus, and each of the others all except his own, these men, in the matter of compound drugs alone, believe without scrutiny all the writings, whether of those who share their doctrine or of anyone who happens along, and often they even try to supply plausible causes for very badly composed drugs. And what is more remarkable than this: that, having no experience of the things they praise, but having trusted others... Thus someone recently was going through many great praises of a drug for gout. While he was still speaking, a certain gouty man came up, affected only moderately, so that he was able to walk, and we bade him make trial of it first on that man [433]. He applied the drug to the foot, and the man was sleepless the whole night, and on the following day he was able not only not to walk as before, but not even to be carried. So without scrutiny and so rashly do some trust others, while others deliberately deceive others. But even if all the compositions of the drugs that they record were sound, they nevertheless overturn, by what they do, the usefulness of the theoretical study of them. For they say that it is for the sake of the preparation and use of compound drugs that they investigate the powers of the simples, and as witnesses to this they call upon nearly all the ancients: Erasistratus, Herophilus, Philotimus, Diocles, Praxagoras, and Hippocrates himself. But when they come to the examination of them, they argue as though we already knew all the compound powers.

"And how are you not seeking in vain the [powers] of the simples," someone might say, I think, to [434] them, "if you already know those of the compound drugs? For if you already know those for the sake of which you undertook the inquiry into the simples, it is superfluous to seek the former." Even if someone were to concede this point to them, yet as for what has already been said before, I do not know how anyone could tolerate it, when they attempt to establish, out of long arguments, things contrary to what is evidently apparent. For I have already had experience of someone who had come to such a pitch of senselessness that he thought fit to despise the senses. Someone straightaway asked him whether white pepper seemed to him to be hot. He, as was to be expected, agreed; then, being asked in turn, "Whence do you know this?", and saying that it appears such, he was deservedly laughed at by those present, not understanding what he was uttering. For this very 'appearing' declared sensation trustworthy for him, which a little before he had condemned as untrustworthy. For whence, by the gods, do we know that fire is hot, having learned it from what syllogism?

[435] Or by what kind of demonstration did we confirm it? And from what source other than sensation did we learn that ice is cold? Then someone, having set this aside, fills his books with problems of natural philosophy. Or is not this, too, one of them: for what cause vinegar makes the earth ferment? For it is open to us, I think, to say that we do not know, as with many other problems of this kind. But if someone readily assumes that it is because it is hot, or because it is cold (for they say both), he throws himself into disputed and obscure arguments. For my part, I would be content if I could discover with precision even the things lying next to what appears through the senses, defining and distinguishing among them what is so in itself from what is so by accident. For example, some people who drink oxycrate in the summer season are clearly cooled and remain free from thirst. But it is not yet clear whether this is because of the vinegar, for they mix a little of it with a great deal of water, and they take it not hot but as cold as possible.

Perhaps, then, someone might say that, because water is slower and remains for a very long time in the hypochondria, [436] being neither passed downward nor distributed, the vinegar is mixed with it for this reason, to become as it were a vehicle for its conveyance in every direction. In the same way, if water is drunk with wine, it leaves one less thirsty than water by itself, since the wine guides it toward distribution. Thus the cooling and the cure of thirst come about from the water, which is cold and moist in its nature. The wine and the vinegar, on the other hand, become an aid to it and, as it were, wings for its conveyance into all the parts of the animal, without themselves cooling and moistening. For otherwise they would be given alone rather than with water, since by their thinness they are readily distributed and pass away from the hypochondria. But since we have once arrived at this argument, it is not amiss to go through the whole of it precisely. That it is possible both for the vinegar to guide the water without itself cooling, and for it not merely to guide but also to cool, is plainly evident. But which of the two is true requires investigation.

This very point could be settled in the following way, if one were to give [437] someone both wine and vinegar, each separately by itself. For the person is evidently always made thirstier by wine, whereas after drinking vinegar he is sometimes thirstier and sometimes less thirsty. This is because thirst itself also arises in two ways, the one from a deficiency of moisture, the other from an excess of heat. So it is no wonder if vinegar does not cure the former but does cure the other, for it cannot moisten, but it cools not ignobly. Therefore vinegar when drunk could never cure either the thirst arising from a dry condition or that arising from a hot and dry one. But if moisture should ever concur with heat in the same body, vinegar will be the best remedy for such thirst. Such a condition is indeed rare. It occurs sometimes in dropsical effusions, when a quantity of briny fluid has collected in the stomach, and in those in whom salty phlegm has become plastered onto it.

But for those who are thirsty in the other way, in burning fevers (kausoi), in all the intensely burning [fevers], and in those who are so in summer and in fierce heat, [438] the condition is compound, of heat and dryness, so that for them the remedy too is reasonably compound: vinegar, which cools not feebly and passes easily in every direction, and water, which besides cooling is also the moistest of all things, for nothing is moister than water. Therefore, just as reasoning that is remote from the perception of the drug under test is not secure, so neither is the use of it when it has been mixed with another. For the thing being judged must be examined by itself alone, both in healthy bodies, well-tempered and ill-tempered alike, and in the sick. In well-tempered bodies, then, as has also been said before; in ill-tempered ones, as Hippocrates said, vinegar is most beneficial to bitter-bilious natures, and is most contrary to those who are melancholic in their mixture. And again, in the sick, if a simple [drug] were examined in a simple condition.

But if it should ever be mixed with something else, what is mixed with it must be intermediate in its mixture, as the earlier [439] argument demonstrated in the case of water and cerate. For it is reasonable, I think, that what has been combined with something that is neither of the extremes in its mixture, but as far as possible intermediate, should itself become the cause of the effects produced. Thus cold water, mixed with simple cerate, which neither heats nor cools, cooled because it was cold in its mixture. But if you had mixed one of the heating things with such a cerate, the drug would have become heating for you, just as we have often added euphorbium or castoreum in many conditions. In the same way, then, if you mix vinegar with a cerate that is strictly simple, you will make the drug much colder than the cerate, since what has been mixed in is cold. And this will be a good drug for you against erysipelata and inflammations, herpetes and anthraces. But if you examine the mixed drug as though it were simple, as indeed they also do, you will err most gravely.

For one ought not to call vinegar agglutinating of wounds, but oxycrate, which is something by far different in nature [440] from vinegar. For just as verdigris is not flesh-forming of wounds, but rather the cerate that has taken up a small portion of verdigris, in the same way vinegar is not agglutinating either, but rather water that has taken up a very small amount of vinegar; vinegar itself, on its own, alone and unmixed, considerably exacerbates those wounds that require agglutination, since by its fine-particledness it is corrosive and painful. Neither, then, do they speak properly about such things, nor when they join unknown things to unknown things. For without having demonstrated anything specifically about wounds that are to be agglutinated, or filled with flesh, or cicatrised, they reason by induction, asserting that all astringent things are agglutinating of wounds. But such things must be grasped in universal form not by induction but through demonstration, as we shall do in the commentaries on the Therapeutic Method; stated simply in this way, any one of such claims is not only undemonstrated but also false.

For neither chalcitis, nor oak-gall, nor the very rinds of pomegranates, [441] nor omphacium, nor alum, and still much less burnt copper, nor scale, nor misy, is of a nature to agglutinate wounds, and countless others among the astringent things are unable to agglutinate. But if, then, someone should say not this, but rather that all agglutinating things are astringent, it will be shown in this case too that many things agglutinate without being astringent. Neither statement, then, is true when it is said simply and without distinction: neither when they assert that all astringent things agglutinate a wound, nor when they assert that all things that are agglutinated are agglutinated by means of astringent things. And things still much more absurd and false than these they now say even concerning sensation itself, when they say that the biting, the pungent, the bitter and the salty things, and in addition to these even the things that are softest and most pleasant in their qualities, are astringent, as though the astringent were not something perceptible to taste, but something taken from their own legislation. For the pomegranate, and the apple, as it may be, and the medlar, and certain kinds of pears, and myrtle berries, and sorbs, and Aminaean and Marsian wine evidently have an astringent effect on us.

But wheat, zeia and millet were perhaps astringent to Herodotus [442], though to no other human being. For I inquired of countless people both about these and, much more still, about starch, since Herodotus says that this too is astringent, as indeed he says of pepper as well, which is itself astringent to none of the other people who examine the qualities purely and impartially. Herodotus, however, confounded everything into one and the same thing, both the things most pungent in their powers and the extremely corrosive ones, and the softest and the most gentle. He said that all are astringent, as though victory lay in bearing false witness against the senses in certain cases. Yet this very thing will not be the greatest proof of the badness of his arguments. For, as if wishing to outdo him in falsehoods against the senses, the Asclepiadean Metrodorus does not admit, among other things, that resin and asphalt heat us, and he says that all astringent things also cool, even though, if nothing else, chalcitis, chalcanthe and misy are sufficiently astringent and yet reach such a degree of heat as to burn us.

It is therefore no longer at all surprising if [443] these men talk a great deal of nonsense and mislead themselves by false reasoning, since they do not dare to admit the truth even about things that are evidently apparent. Then some of them, such as Herodotus and Dioscorides, infer from the fact that certain drugs benefit diarrhoeas and dysenteries that these drugs are astringent, although they do not share in even the least astringency. Quite the contrary: in their powers they are more rarefying and relaxing than the astringents, which draw together, compress, condense and bind tight the bodies. For having once despised sense-perception, they have overturned everything and have confounded the things that can clearly be discerned by perception, trying to establish these by faulty reasoning. Goat's fat, at any rate, is most opposite to all astringents both in taste and in power, just as wheat flour is, and starch, and countless other things among those that plaster over, soothe and blunt pungencies, and in this way help those who pass biting and pungent evacuations.

And if it is astringent for these reasons, then let olive oil too be counted by us among the astringents, [444] since it too has often benefited, when injected, those suffering violent biting. And wax will be astringent too, and pig's fat, fowl's fat and goose fat, and the juice of groats and of tragos. For we inject these too, and sometimes a cerate, into those suffering strong biting, just as we do goat's fat. But goat's fat displays a more evident benefit, because it readily congeals, is smeared over the intestines, and remains there for a very long time. Whether it congeals quickly because of its thickness or for some other cause, I have no need to inquire into these things now, since the fact is plainly evident. But just as the fact that it congeals very quickly and blunts the bitings of the intestines is rendered more credible by its being apparent, so too is the fact that it has no share in any cooling or astringency. These men, then, reason from things non-evident about things apparent; or rather, if the truth must be told, they deceive themselves by false reasoning. We, however, ought all the more to go back to sense-perception and to attend to it carefully at all times, in proportion as all the sophists tell not a few lies against it.

Having therefore reminded [445] them once again that what is evident to laymen was evident to them too, at a time when they did not yet, out of love of contention, look down on the senses, but was afterwards lost through excessive cleverness, I shall pass on to the continuation of the argument. Each nature among the sensibles is subject to a sense proper to it: heat and coldness and hardness and softness to touch; whiteness and blackness and yellowness, redness and, to put it summarily, the whole genus of colours to sight; bitterness and sweetness, harshness and acerbity, sourness and saltiness and pungency to taste. And anyone will plainly seem to be mad who should attempt either to judge colours by taste or flavours by sight. In the same way one must understand concerning touch and the other senses as well, that tangible differences are to be judged by touch, audible ones by hearing, and those in vapours by smell. These things being so, let us hear, if you wish, Plato too, as he expounds the differences of tastes. One must not, however, direct one's attention to his natural philosophy.

For it would not be opportune for me now [446] to make mention of it, nor do I call the man as a witness for this, but only for the purpose of showing to what thing it is the custom among the Greeks to apply each of the names. Hear, then, Plato saying: 'For whatever earthy particles, entering about the small veins, which are as it were the testers of the tongue, stretched towards the heart, and falling upon the moist and soft parts of the flesh, are melted down and contract the small veins and dry them out, these, when they are rougher, are called acerbic, and when they roughen less, harsh. Those of them that are cleansing and wash off everything about the tongue, if they do this beyond the moderate and lay hold of it besides, so as to melt away something of its very nature, as the power of nitres does, are all thus named bitter. But those that fall short of the nitrous condition and employ cleansing in moderation appear to us salty, without rough bitterness, and rather more agreeable.'

Those, again, which share in the heat of the mouth and are smoothed by it, which are set on fire along with it and in their turn burn back that which heated them, and which are also carried upward by their lightness towards the senses of the head [447], cutting everything they fall upon: on account of these powers all such things have been called pungent. When the same things, having first been thinned by putrefaction, enter the narrow veins, and have a commensurateness with the earthy parts present there and with whatever parts of air are there, so that they set them moving about one another and cause them to be stirred up, they, being stirred up, fall around one another and, entering into one another, produce other hollows, stretching themselves around the things that enter. When moisture, hollow, is stretched around air, sometimes earthy moisture and sometimes also pure, these become moist vessels of air, hollow and round waters. Those of pure moisture stand around as transparent vessels, which are called by name bubbles. Those of earthy moisture, which is moved and raised at the same time, are called by the names boiling and fermentation. The cause of these affections is called sour.

To all the things that have been said about these there is an opposite affection, arising from an opposite cause, whenever the composition of what enters, in liquids, being by nature akin to the condition of the tongue, smooths by anointing the parts that have been roughened, and of the parts that are contrary to nature either compacted or diffused, the ones it [448] draws together, the others it relaxes, and settles all of them as far as possible according to nature: every such thing, becoming a remedy of the violent affections and being pleasant and agreeable to everyone, has been called sweet. Through this whole passage Plato explained which things it is customary to name harsh and which acerbic, which salty and nitrous and which bitter, and which pungent, which sour and which sweet; evidently calling 'harsh' what we call astringent, for so it was named among the ancient Greeks. He does not, however, confound everything into the same thing, as these people do, who say that pepper is astringent, although it belongs to the nature of the pungent, and vinegar, although it belongs to that of the sour, and who are not ashamed to assign even some of the sweetest things to the astringents. Since, then, everything is confounded by them, right at the outset not even powers can be discovered. For the starting-points of all discovery and demonstration are the things that are evident to perception and to understanding.

These men throw both of these into confusion and confound everything together, both the functions and the affections of the senses and, much more still, those of intellection, [449] inasmuch as they are not trained in logical theory. So it is a task to guard against their idle chatter and not to get some share of their so abundant and vain nonsense. And it is no small task, too, to re-teach and change those who have been perverted by them to such a degree that they despise the senses, are untrained in logical theory, and have not even heard of the reasonings about nature which the philosophers investigate. For surely they would at least have recognised this much: that one must fear and guard against the difficulties (aporiai) in those reasonings, and must trust the senses rather than counterfeit arguments about the power of simple drugs. But it is not possible to re-teach such people. For the sake of the others, who are able to be benefited, we must take up again and define precisely the account concerning the sense-objects proper to the tongue.

Now by Theophrastus, Aristotle and Mnesitheus the physician, and those of their school, the gustatory power is named chymos, with the letter m beginning the [450] second syllable; but the consistency arising from moist and dry, when these have been concocted by heat, is named chylos, with l beginning the second syllable. Among their older predecessors, however, not only the Attic writers but also the Ionians, both are written with m. For it is found so in Plato the philosopher, in Hippocrates, and in the old comic poets. In the present treatise at any rate, for the sake of clear instruction, let us say that the gustatory power, or quality, or however one may wish to name it, is chymos, with the letter m, while the thickened moisture in animals and plants is chylos, with l beginning the second syllable. It must be understood, then, that the chymoi found in each plant and animal, and indeed also those found in the earth, are very numerous and not easily counted in their kinds (ἰδέαις). The gustatory differences among them, however, have seemed to some to be eight in number, to others seven, and to others even fewer than these.

Plato, then, in the Timaeus, in the passage quoted above, first mentions two flavours that are of the same kind but differ by more and less [451]. He calls one of them harsh, the other acerbic. The harsh would correspond to the one we call astringent, while the acerbic arises from an intensification of it, just as Plato himself also made clear. These, then, must be counted as a single kind. Another kind is that of their opposites, the nitrous, the salty and the bitter. Among these too, the bitter arises from an intensification of the nitrous, while the salty is either weaker than the nitrous or else also takes on something of astringency. Next, Plato names the pungent, after it the sour, and last the sweet. Theophrastus also adds the oily. Plato omitted it in his account of the sensibles proper to the tongue, but had written of it shortly before, among the juices of plants, where he distinguished the wine-like from the oil-like and the honey-like. In that account, besides the three I have just named, he posited a fourth genus of juice, comprehending it under a single appellation and calling it 'sap' (opos). But where he passed on to the things perceptible to taste, he at once mentioned the sweet among them.

For it surely makes no difference whether one says 'sweet' or [452] 'honey-like', just as it makes none whether one says 'oily' or 'olive-oil-like'. But he has left out the oily as having nothing to do with taste. To express it precisely is not possible, since neither can any other of the perceptible affections be so expressed; but it is possible to remind someone who has shared in the same sensation. If anyone has ever tasted quinces, or apples, or myrtle-berries, or medlars, he knows clearly that the sensation arising in us on the tongue from these is one thing, and that from astringent bodies another. For astringent or cooling things appear to press the part of us that touches them inward evenly from every side, as if pushing, compressing and drawing it together; whereas harsh things seem both to penetrate into the depth and to bring on a rough and uneven sensation, as if drying up and grazing away all the moisture of the sensing bodies. So the particular character of the affections produced in us by astringent bodies and by harsh flavours is different, and it cannot even be stated clearly.

But any man who has sense knows [453] what I mean. When the body that comes into contact with the tongue dries it vehemently, draws it together and roughens it to a greater depth, as unripe wild pears and cornels do, everything of this kind is called acerbic, differing from the harsh by intensity. What we call astringent, however, is scarcely to be found mentioned by Theophrastus and his school. It seems either to signify the same thing as the harsh, or to be a genus common to this and to the acerbic. Those things which, in touching the tongue, do not draw it together, nor constrict it as astringents do, but appear to do entirely the opposite, cleansing and washing away even whatever of the astringents may be lying upon it, all these we call salty. Those that cleanse still more than these, to the point of roughening it painfully, are called bitter. Those that are biting and corroding with strong heat are called pungent. Those that are biting without it are called sour, and to these belongs also the property of leavening.

Those things which, as it were, smear over, fill up and restore the roughened and, as it were, eaten-through parts of the [454] tongue are called sweet when they touch it with manifest pleasure, and oily when they do so without it. I, then, have attempted to set out in words, as far as I possibly could, matters that are hard to express. But I am astonished at those who readily call everything astringent: the pungent, the bitter, the sweet, the oily and the sour. For different names have been assigned to these things from ancient times, and the difference among the perceptible affections is no small one for us. It would perhaps have been better, if they wished to study nature, not to overturn the phenomena and confound the appellations, but to seek of what mixture or condition or constitution of body (or however they may wish to name it) astringency is the offspring, and of what saltiness and bitterness, sourness and pungency, sweetness and oiliness are the offspring. These are the very things that Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus attempted to define.

For it is clear that, if all things have been mixed from hot, cold, dry and moist coming together, each of the qualities mentioned also arises from the mixture [455] of these. If, then, they were to attempt to explain how each of the flavours mentioned comes about, I would gladly listen to them and would feel no small gratitude towards them. But if they do not even do this, and moreover confound all the perceptible differences into one and the same thing, so that they run the risk of calling all bodies astringent, I would not wish to listen to them, and I would pray that they too might cease from their vain contentiousness. But we, in what follows, shall try to show of what mixture each of the flavours is the offspring. For the present I wish only to accustom the learners, as they come to the test of experience, first to pick out just that which is useful for the art, whenever they wish to judge how each of the drugs disposes us. For we are certainly not examining what sort of thing it is in itself and in relation to nature as a whole. For it is clear that in this way neither vinegar nor sea-water could be said to dry us, or to be dry in power.

For each of them is moist in actuality; but if it appears to dry us, [456] it will be called dry, evidently in relation to us and to our nature, equivalent to 'drying'. And indeed, in the same way, things will be called hot, cold and moist when they heat, cool and moisten us: in relation to us, not in relation to the whole of substance, nor in themselves. And indeed, if we keep this alone in mind, experience alone will be the most secure criterion of all, so that those who abandon it and argue from elsewhere not only speak falsely but also overturn what is useful in the inquiry. For our task is not to investigate what each of the drugs is in its own nature, but what it is naturally disposed to do to us. So let my first book end here. In the next, the second, taking oil and rose oil as an example for the discussion, I shall show here too the faulty paths of argument. Most physicians use these paths and so mislead first themselves, and then, along with themselves, many others as well.

And when this has been brought to completion, I shall pass on to the third of these commentaries and try to go through all the logical questions [457] that precede the whole exposition concerning simple drugs, so that in the fourth I may at last define the powers themselves of all of them. I would have taken these up straight from the beginning, had not almost all the books of the more recent physicians been full of paralogisms. These, then, must first be cleansed out and cleared away from the soul of the learner, so that they may in no way obstruct the truths. For as Hippocrates says, so Plato too used to say: not only with bodies that are not pure, the more you nourish them, the more you will harm them; but also to impure souls, if you offer nourishing discourses, not only would you benefit them in nothing, but you will also harm them in no small degree.

For these very reasons, then, and because many of my companions wished the paralogisms of the more recent physicians to be refuted not only in the meetings which we hold on each occasion when spending time with them, but also through these commentaries, I was compelled to linger at greater length over the first two books. My purpose was that in the third, having by then a hearer pure in soul and able to follow true arguments, I might go through everything that one must know about the principles of the theory set before us [458], and after that might go over all the powers of each of the drugs. This will be done, as I think, in eleven books in all, each of very much the same size as this one also is, the first of them all. And since this book already has its due measure, I place this very statement upon it as its ending.

[459] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK II. The sophists who overstep their proper bounds make our account of the power of simple drugs a long one. For by beginning from far back and slighting sense-perception, and by throwing themselves into questions that remain unresolved even among the philosophers, they ruin, along with the things they do not know, the things that are clearly known as well.

[11.1.1] [1. On the flesh of the viper.] Not all the fleshes of animals nourish a human being. Those of some are even deadly, no less than the drug-like substances which they call dēlētēria. Of the fleshes that do nourish us, some are foods and only that, while others, besides nourishing, also have the power as of a drug, since they alter the body by drying or moistening and by heating or cooling. At any rate, one can see plainly that the fleshes of vipers heat and dry when they are dressed as eels are, with oil, salts, dill, leek, and of course water in due measure. That they cleanse the whole body through the skin you may learn also from what I experienced when I was still young, in our Asia; I shall now go through each of these cases in order. A man ill with the affection called elephas for a time shared the same regimen with his household. But when, from association and intercourse with him, some of them came to share the affection, and he himself was by now foul-smelling and loathsome to look upon, they built a hut for him near the village on a low hill beside a spring and settled the man in it, bringing him each day as much food as was sufficient to live on. About the rising of the Dog Star, some wine was brought in an earthenware jar to reapers who were reaping near him; it was very fragrant. The man who brought it set it down near the reapers and went away. When the time for drinking came, their custom was to pour the wine out into a mixing-bowl and mix it with a moderate amount of water. But when a young man took up the jar and was drawing the wine out into the mixing-bowl, a dead viper fell out along with it. The reapers, fearing that they might suffer some harm from the drink, drank water themselves. As they were leaving, they made a present of the whole wine, ostensibly out of humanity, to the man ill with elephas, judging that it was better for him to be dead than to live in such a state. He, drinking from it, became healthy in a wonderful manner. For the whole lumpy part of his skin fell off like the covering of the soft-shelled animals, and what remained appeared quite soft, like that of crayfish and crabs when the shell around them has fallen off. Another such case arose from a similar chance occurrence in Asian Mysia, not far from our city. A man suffering from elephas set out to use naturally hot waters in the hope of benefit. He had a concubine, a slave, young and beautiful and with many lovers. To her the sick man entrusted various other affairs of the household, and in particular those of the storeroom. While he was using the waters they lodged in a house that had next to it a dry, squalid plot full of vipers. One of the vipers fell into a jar of wine that had been carelessly left lying and died in it. The concubine, considering this chance event a windfall, offered her master his drink from that jar. He, drinking it, was healed in the same way as the man in the hut. These two lessons you now have from the experience of chance occurrence; and besides them a third, from our imitation. For a man ill with this disease, more philosophical than the many, was terribly vexed by it and kept saying that it was better to be dead than to live. Since he was in so wretched a condition, I disclosed to him the two chance occurrences just related. He was himself experienced in bird-omens and had a friend wonderfully successful in this learning. Taking his seat with that friend to observe the birds, he was urged on to imitate what had been learned through experience, and by drinking wine drugged in this way he became leprous. Some time later we cured his lepra too with the usual drugs. A fourth man after this, who had made it his craft to catch live vipers, was at the beginning of that affection, and our purpose was that he should be cured as quickly as possible. So, having cut his vein and purged him with a drug that evacuates black bile, we advised him to make use of the vipers he caught, preparing them in a lopas as one does eels. This man, then, was treated in this way, the affection being breathed out of him through transpiration. Another man, a rich one, was not of our country but came from the middle of Thrace, a dream having urged him to Pergamum. The god then commanded him in a dream to drink each day of the drug made from vipers and to anoint his body from outside. Not many days later the affection changed into lepra, and this disease too was cured in its turn with the drugs the god ordered. So great a degree of drying power, then, does the flesh of vipers attain. But some of those who ate it were seized by a most violent thirst, and for this reason they call the vipers dipsades. There are also some who say that those bitten by them, though they drink, are not filled, but burst before they cease to thirst. For this reason I inquired of those in Rome who hunt vipers, whom they call Marsi, whether they had any sign to teach me that distinguishes the two kinds of vipers. They said that there is no kind of dipsas vipers at all. Rather, those that live by the sea and in places with much saline earth (halmyris) have briny flesh, and for this reason many such occur in Libya, but there are none in Italy because of the moistness of the land. These things, then, I heard the Marsi say, but I cannot state with certainty whether they speak the truth in everything or are also lying in some respect. That in the places they named some vipers occur which have salty flesh seems to me most plausible, for I know that the fleshes of animals change along with their foods. But I cannot declare that there is no kind of dipsas vipers. The safest course, then, is to take care not to hunt vipers in such places, whether for eating or for the preparation of a drug, such as this celebrated one which nearly all physicians call theriac. Now it is our custom, when we prepare the so-called theriac pastilles (artiskoi), to remove not only their head but also the tail. I have often reflected that the whole head is perhaps reasonably removed, on account of the venom contained in the mouth, but the tail unreasonably. Nor can one say that it must be done so on account of the residues of the food, both the moist and the dry. For having killed them, then flayed them and laid them open, we take out and throw away all the inner parts, so that only the substance of the fleshes is left, together with the arteries and veins that grow through it. These have a very small bulk relative to the whole flesh and are not even visible unless one inspects very carefully. The pastilles, then, which they also name theriac pastilles, we prepare thus. Taking the vipers cleaned, we boil them in water until they seem to us to be exactly boiled. We put dill into the water along with them right from the start. After the boiling we separate the spines from the fleshes, and then mix the flesh with ground bread. This bread we do not take at random, but the purest possible, well baked in an oven (klibanos), with a moderate amount of salt and leaven. We dry it beforehand in a dry room without moisture, until it becomes dry enough to be pounded in a mortar. Yet we do not mix it in by pounding it, but by soaking it in the water in which we boiled the vipers. The flesh itself, before mixing it with the bread, we triturate in a cooks' mortar until it becomes exactly smooth. After this, having moulded small thin pastilles, we dry them in a warm and dry room and keep them, storing them again in such a room. These we prepare at the onset of summer, when the flesh of vipers is at its very best. Later we use them by pounding and sifting them, then triturating them again and mixing them with salts prepared for pleasantness of taste; we also put them into the theriac. At the same season the salts made from roasted vipers are also prepared. We throw the vipers alive into a new pot together with the drugs strewn underneath and laid around them, all of which it is not the business of the present treatise to state now. Indeed, someone might perhaps reasonably reproach us even over the preparation of the pastilles, as having gone through it out of place. But since these things have already been said, let them stand, even if they seem not altogether proper to the present treatise. What follows, let it be said in fitting measure. It is fitting to recall, concerning the general power of the flesh of vipers, that it is drying and strongly dispersing, while heating moderately. Its power, it seems, presses towards the skin, and through the skin it moves the residues in the body. So a not inconsiderable multitude of lice is generated in those who have abundant kakochymia in their bodies. Also, the so-called epidermis separates from the skin and falls off like a husk; it is in the epidermis that the thick and earthy humours, among those carried to the skin, are more held back, and by these psōrai, leprai and elephantes arise. This, then, is what I had to tell you about the fleshes of the viper; next I shall take up the account again. The fleshes of animals that are hotter by nature not only nourish us but also heat, while those of colder animals cool. In the same way, those of drier animals dry, and those of moister animals moisten. Remember, then, what you learned in the work On Mixtures. When you recognise that some animal is drier in mixture, as for instance the wild boar than the domestic pig, know that its flesh too is more drying. The same holds for the other differences of mixtures: for example, the sheep is drier than the pig, the goat than the sheep, the ox than the goat, and the lion than the ox. So too in respect of heat, the lion is hotter than the dog, the dog than the bull, and the bull than the ox whose testicles have been cut out. In proportion, then, to their excess in mixture over the other animals, their fleshes will also differ. For this reason, when you wish to dry the body, you will give the flesh of animals drier in mixture; when you want to heat it, that of hotter ones; when you undertake to make it colder, that of colder ones; and when moister, that of moister ones. No small difference among the fleshes lies also in some of them having been salted. For they differ altogether, so that often the salted flesh of an animal most moist in mixture is far more drying than the unsalted flesh of one dry by nature. And the roasted flesh is drier than that boiled in water. Some have also written that the fleshes of other animals benefit when eaten and when applied to the affected parts. One example is the flesh of the land hedgehog, dried, if it is drunk by those with elephantiasis, cachectics, those subject to spasms and nephritics, and further by those who have the dropsy called anasarca. If it is of a nature to do these things, its power would be strongly dispersing and drying, as is that of the dried weasel, which indeed benefits epileptics when drunk. They say that the flesh of salted cats, ground and applied, draws out splinters, evidently as having a drawing power. They also say that the flesh of mussels (myakes) suits ulcers caused by a biting dog. I, however, find no special power that ulcers of this kind require, as those produced by the bite of a rabid dog do. The flesh of snails too, first pounded in a mortar and afterwards triturated, becomes the most drying of all for parts having superfluous moisture, so that it suits the dropsical as well. The moisture from them, taken alone by itself without the flesh, is called by most people snail's mucus. Mixed with frankincense or aloe or myrrh, or some or all of these, until it has the thickness of a cerate, it becomes a glue-like drug and dries the purulent mucous discharges of the ears well. Applied on the forehead, it is also a drying adhesive application (anakollēma) against fluxes into the eyes. Some also use the snails for splinters, triturating them whole with their shells, and there are some who use them for checking the menses. The fleshes alone I myself once triturated and applied, in the country, to a wound that had occurred together with a wounding and crushing of a nerve. The wound was glued together well and the nerve did not become inflamed. The man was tough and rustic; I mixed with the fleshes, as they were being triturated, fine flour-dust, taking it from the wall next to the mill. Some of the physicians before us have written that one ought to mix myrrh or frankincense with them for such a use, but I had neither of these, being outside the city on the country estate. One could also mix in ground roasted resin, if it is to hand. Whenever you wish to obtain much of the snails' mucus by itself, prick their flesh with a stylus. One must not catch them many days beforehand, for they dry out over time. When fresh they have much of the viscous moisture, which they emit when pricked with the stylus. This moisture also serves to glue back the hairs in the eyelids that are contrary to nature.

[11.1.2] [2. On fat and suet.] Fat (pimelē) and suet (stear). These too are among the commonest of the parts in animals. For all well-nourished animals have fat or suet, whereas lean and ill-nourished ones often appear to have none at all, and often have so little, and that so dry, that it is hard to use. Suet differs from fat in thickness; for this reason suet arises in animals whose whole nature is more earthy, just as fat does in those whose nature is more moist. For this very reason, then, fat melts easily under fire, but once melted does not easily congeal; suet, by contrast, does not melt easily, and if it is melted it congeals very quickly and appears much harder than fat. The pig, then, when well nourished, has a very great deal of fat on account of the natural moistness of its mixture, whereas oxen and goats and all other horned animals produce suet in greatest quantity on account of their dryness. You may, if you wish, call the whole oleaginous and oily substance in animals suet, as most physicians do; and you may also name this whole kind fat. You may not, however, if you wish not to speak falsely, say that the suet of goats is moister than that of pigs. For the latter is the moistest of nearly all the others, and for this reason in its action it is close to oil in power, though it is more softening than oil and more concoctive. And for this reason it is mixed into the poultices suited to inflammations. But for those who are bitten in the region of the rectum or the colon we inject goat's rather than pig's suet, not because it is more blunting of pungency (for, so far as its nature goes, pig's suet blunts more, and for this reason it is also mixed into drugs that treat ulcers, such as the one called parygron), but because goat's suet congeals easily on account of its thickness, whereas pig's flows away just like oil; for this reason we inject the former rather in dysenteric and tenesmic patients, when we wish to soothe their biting. Some things also blunt pungencies more on account of fineness of particles, when what is giving pain lies in the depth of the bodies that are being bitten. For the coarse-particled passes less, and the fine-particled more, through whole bodies, and mixes itself with all the biting ichors. In this respect, at any rate, goose suet blunts more effectively what bites in the depth of bodies. It is also hotter than pig's. Between them lies that of cocks; and that of male animals is always hotter and drier. Among these themselves, that of those whose testicles are excised is less hot and dry; for the castrated male always comes to resemble the females of the same kind. The general heading of the account, which must be remembered, is this: that the differences of the fat or suet in animals (or however you wish to name this whole kind of oleaginous and oily body in animals) always arise according to the mixture of the animals. Since, then, the pig falls short in heat and dryness of nearly all four-footed animals, for this reason it also has fat that is both less hot and more moist. Now the power of all fat is moistening and heating of human bodies; for this must be remembered throughout, having been stated at the beginning of this treatise; and the differences in each of them are matters of more and less.
