For the fat of the pig, relative to us, has moistening in abundance, but heating not in the same way as oil; rather, the fat (lipos) of pigs is on a level with the heat in us. That of bulls is much hotter and drier than that of pigs, we again remembering here too that the male is always drier and hotter than the female, and that the castrated male resembles the female, as indeed does everything young; and that among the young themselves the female is moister and less hot than the male. Thus calf's suet falls short of that of bulls in heat and dryness, and that of kids of that of goats, and that of goats falls short of that of he-goats, and again that of bulls in turn falls short of that of lions; for that is the most dispersing of nearly all those in quadrupeds. For it is also the hottest of them and the most fine-particled, so that if you mix it into the drugs suited to ulcers and inflammations, you will not only do no good but will even do harm, having made the drug more pungent than is fitting. But for chronic hardened swellings, contractures (ankylai) of sinews, and in short whatever is scirrhous, it is most suitable, in cases in which that of pigs appears most ineffective. That of bulls stands roughly equally distant from each, being as much hotter and drier than that of pigs as it falls short of that of lions. As being placed in the middle, then, it is reasonably mixed into each kind of drug, both those that treat scirrhous conditions and those that concoct inflamed parts, such as the one called tetrapharmakon, composed of wax, resin, pitch and suet. For into this, whether you put bull's or calf's or he-goat's or goat's or pig's, you will make a suppurative and concoctive drug. But pig's, when put in, suits children and women and, in a word, the soft-fleshed, while bull's is useful for diggers, reapers and all who have hard flesh, whether through their natural mixture or through the kind of life they lead. All suet, as it ages, becomes hotter and more fine-particled than it was, and so also more dispersing. This holds for nearly all things that age, at least those that do not rot first. For wine, honey, vinegar, cheese, butter and oesypum, and every oil, whether mastic oil or castor oil or radish oil or the very oil from olives, become thinner and more fine-particled as they age, and for this reason appear more pungent to those who taste them and more dispersing to those who use them, in all hardened and hard-to-resolve affections. I, then, have said that they appear more pungent to those who taste them. But some of those who corrupt the meanings of words call all such things not pungent but astringent, even down to pepper, as if it made no difference whether one says astringent or pungent. And if you ask them in turn about oak-galls, myrtles, medlars, pomegranate rinds, omphakion and sumach, they say that these too are astringent, although the perception we have from them is the most opposite to that which arises in us from pepper, pyrethron, mustard, euphorbium, onion, garlic and adarce. If, then, just as they apply the name of astringency in common to both of the affections arising in us in taste, so too they think that the affections themselves have a single nature, they must be considered anything rather than human beings, as alone possessing senses peculiar to themselves. But if they agree that unripe grape, sumach, oak-gall, balaustion and hypocistis draw together and constrict our substance, while pepper, mustard and pyrethron separate, bite and pass through it, then they improperly name the biting and heating things astringent, but they have not erred in their knowledge of the drugs themselves. If one must say by conjecture whether they err in the names or in the things, I for my part would say that these men have erred rather in the names, and especially those unaccustomed to the Greek tongue, such as Dioscorides of Anazarbus, who has said many things well among the matters recorded concerning medical material, but is ignorant of the meanings of Greek words. When this man, then, says that the suet of goats is more astringent than that of pigs, if by 'more astringent' he wishes to indicate 'more pungent', we shall accept the statement as true; but if he means what has the kind of quality and power that sumach and rhēon, hypocistis and balaustion have, we shall say that the statement is not true. Since they also say that the suet of vipers, when someone plucks out the hairs in the armpits by the roots and anoints the place, prevents these from growing again, I thought it better to test this too, and having done as they bade I found them to be lying, as also in the claim that it cures the beginnings of hypochyses. That the suet of bears suits alopecias they wrote truly, but we have more approved drugs than it for the affection. As for that of foxes, however, when they say that it treats earaches without distinguishing what sort of earaches they mean, as men who do not even know articulately what they are saying, one should not pay any attention to them at all. Others praise the suet of fishes, as being for hypochyses or whatever affection they wish to name. Others again write not simply of fishes, but of river fishes, and others rather of sea fishes, so that they may seem to know something more than the many.

[11.1.3] [3. On marrow.] Marrow is of a power softening of bodies that are hardened and becoming scirrhous, whether muscles or tendons or ligaments suffer this, or also viscera. I have always found by experience that the marrow of deer is the best, and next after it that of young cattle, whom they also call calves (moschoi), and for this reason they name their marrow too 'calf's marrow' (moscheios). That of he-goats and of bulls is more pungent than these and more drying, so that it cannot dissolve scirrhous hardnesses, if we remember anything of what was said about these matters in the fifth book. From calf's and deer's marrow, at any rate, softening pessaries are compounded for conditions in the uterus, and drugs prepared with marrow, having a softening power, are applied over the uterus itself from outside. Not only is the marrow from the bones taken, which is indeed marrow in the true sense, but also that from the spine, which they too name spinal marrow, being harder and more parched than the other. For the former is softer and more oily, and for this reason I store the marrow from the spine separately on its own, apart from the other. I take care that neither of the two marrows should rot or become mouldy. So first I take them in winter, just as I do the suet, then, drying them in an upper room free of moisture, I put them away with dry bay leaves. For moist and fresh leaves impart much of their own quality, so that the marrows become more pungent. And if ever you should wish to put away marrows or suet when the surrounding air is hot and humid, let a room be prepared for you that is neither hot, as are especially those facing south, for it rots in such rooms, nor underground and damp, for it grows mouldy in such rooms, but upper and facing north, having small windows open so as to receive the northern winds by day and by night.

[11.1.4] [4. On the heads of maenides.] Someone used to burn the heads of salted maenides and use them for fissures in the seat, and this same man also used them for a uvula that had been scirrhous for a long time. Their power, then, seems to be a kind of drying one, not very pungent. For this is the case with some of the substances that have been burnt, just as drying, at any rate, is common to them all.

[11.1.5] [5. On the head of hares.] Another man used to burn the whole head of a hare and use it for alopeciae, with bear's fat. [11.1.6] [6. On the head of lizards.] Some people write that the head of the lizard, ground smooth, draws out splinters and also myrmeciae, acrochordones and clavi.

[11.1.7] [7. On the brain of a hare.] We have learned that the brain of a hare, both rubbed on and eaten, is beneficial in the case of teething children, the whole head of course having first been boiled, as I am accustomed [to do]. Its power, however, is not exceptional, but similar to honey and butter and the other things that are suitable for little children whose teeth are growing in. And some have also written that this brain, when eaten, helps against fears.

[11.1.8] [8. On the horns of deer and of goats.] People use the horns of deer and of goat chiefly when burnt, just as we too have often used them, both for brightening the teeth and for contracting gums that are flabby. Some of those who have written on such matters especially praise that of the deer, [saying] that, if after being burnt it is washed, it thoroughly cures dysentery and spitting of blood, and furthermore the so-called coeliac conditions, and that when given to those with jaundice it is beneficial; and in all these cases they direct that two spoonfuls be given. Some have also mixed it, burnt and washed as has been said, into the collyria that dry up the fluxes in the eyes. For the power of all such things is evidently drying, just as has also been said.

[11.1.9] [9. On the lung of the lamb, of the pig, and of the fox.] Lamb's lung and pig's lung are believed to heal the abrasions caused by shoes. That of the fox, if it is dried and drunk, benefits the asthmatic.

[11.1.10] [10. On the liver of a rabid dog.] The liver of a rabid dog, some have written, if it is roasted and eaten, becomes a remedy for those who have been bitten by it. And indeed I know of some of those who took it who are alive, but not through that alone: they had also used, in succession, the other drugs of which we have experience in the case of those bitten by rabid animals. But I have heard that some who put their trust in it alone afterwards died.

[11.1.11] [11. On the liver of the she-goat and of the he-goat.] Some people roast the liver of the she-goat, then take the ichor that runs off it and use it for nyctalopes, and they also bid them receive its vapour, while it is being boiled, into their eyes held open. Moreover, they say that eaten roasted it is also suited to these affections, and that it exposes epileptics, if it is eaten. And the he-goat's liver has the same power.

[11.1.12] [12. On the liver of the lizard.] Some have written that the liver of a lizard, placed into decayed teeth, produces freedom from pain. [11.1.13] [13. On the stomach of the aithyia.] Some praise the stomach of the aithyia as a concoctive drug, if one takes it either boiled immediately or dried and then administers it. But we, having made trial of it, found the promise vain, just as also that of the inner coat of hens, which some people likewise dry and say benefits those with stomach complaints, if it is drunk.

[11.1.14] [14. On the liver of the wolf.] The liver of the wolf I often used to put into the hepatic drug made with eupatorium; I did not, however, find any noteworthy superiority from it when I compared with it the drug prepared without this ingredient.

[11.1.15] [15. On castoreum.] The testicles of the beaver they call castoreum. It is a celebrated drug with many uses, so much so that Archigenes wrote a whole book on the use of castoreum. He went through its particular powers one by one. I, as with the other drugs, so with this one too, shall state its general power; by looking to this, one will be able to discover the particular ones for oneself. That it heats is quite evident. For if you grind it exactly smooth, moisten it with oil, and then anoint and rub some part with it, you will clearly perceive the part being heated. All things that heat, by dispersing some of the substance that lies near them, at once also dry it. The exception is something moist by nature, such as oil and water, which takes on an acquired hot quality and not a power, as these very things do when brought near fire or the summer sun. Castoreum, then, since its consistency is dry and it has also acquired the capacity to heat, reasonably dries. This it has in common with very many other drugs. But it is sufficiently fine-particled, and in this respect it is more powerful than other drugs that heat and dry to the same degree as it does. For fine-particled drugs are more active than coarse-particled ones, even if they have an equal power, because they pass through and go into the depth of the bodies they come into contact with, especially when these are dense, as the sinewy ones are. At any rate, such parts are clearly greatly benefited by castoreum for the stated cause. Most physicians, however, are ignorant of this. In using castoreum they attend only to the fact that some part trembles or is convulsed, or is insensible or motionless, or has impaired sensation or impaired motion. They do not know that such symptoms follow unlike conditions of the body. But you have learnt from Hippocrates that convulsion arises both from repletion and from evacuation. Where it is necessary to evacuate what is contained in the nerves contrary to nature, give castoreum to drink and also apply it externally upon the skin. But where convulsion arises through excessive dryness, know that this drug is most contrary. By the same reasoning it is most beneficial to those who tremble through plethos, but most contrary to those who fall into such an affection through evacuation. Analogously to the affections mentioned, I found and distinguished the condition of the hiccup that arises in the stomach. If the patients suffer this from plethos, proceed to the use of castoreum; but if it arises through dryness and evacuation, or through the biting of pungent fluids, avoid the drug. Now someone attending to its smell and taste might suspect that it has a substance most alien to the human body. In use, however, it appears to do none of the things that such substances do, some of them harming the stomach, others the belly, others the head, others some other part. This drug, by contrast, displays great benefit and inflicts no harm whatever on any part. This holds whether you apply it to a moist body needing dryness, or to a cold one needing heat, or to a moist and cold one requiring heat and dryness. It holds especially when the person is without fever. It holds also for those who are feverish, but not very hotly, having rather what one might call a lukewarm fever, such as occurs above all in kataphorai and lethargies. We have given castoreum to very many people, together with white pepper, a spoonful's quantity of each, given to drink in honey-water, and no one was harmed in any way. When the menses were retained, I first evacuated moderately from the ankle, then gave castoreum with pennyroyal or kalaminthē. I always found that the drug set purgation in motion, without the woman being harmed at all. It also expels retained afterbirths. All these things, then, it accomplishes when drunk in honey-water. Some people are intractably inflated in the belly, or suffer gripes, or hiccup, from cold and viscid humours or from thick and flatulent pneuma. These it benefits when drunk in oxycrate. Whatever it benefits when taken into the body, it also benefits when applied upon the skin together with Sicyonian or old oil. Conditions needing more heat should also be rubbed with it on its own. It also benefits if one burns it as a fumigation on coals and draws it in by inhalation, especially for the moist and cold affections of the lung and brain. All lethargic and kataphoric affections accompanied by fevers, however, are better treated not by moistening it with one of the oils mentioned, but rather by applying it with rose oil to the head and the neck.

[11.1.16] [16. On the kidneys of skinks.] The parts around the kidneys of skinks are drunk as tensive of the genitals, and lettuce seed drunk with water is thought to be especially counteractive to them. Some people also say that the decoction of lentils, drunk with honey, stops the tensions.

[11.1.17] [17. On the hooves of goats and of asses.] Some people burn the hooves of goats, then moisten the ash with vinegar and smear it on alopeciae, so that such ash too would be of thinning power. Some people say that the hooves of asses, burnt, cure epileptics if they are drunk continually, and that, kneaded with oil, they disperse choirades; and that the same ash, sprinkled on dry, heals chilblains (chimethla).

[11.1.18] [18. On burnt bones.] Burnt bones are of a quite strongly dispersing and drying power, and some people say that human bones above all have this capacity. They have said that the astragalus of a pig, burnt and then drunk, cures inflations and gripings. And I have known some people of our time who gave burnt bones to drink, without those drinking knowing what they were drinking, so that they would not be disgusted, and who had thoroughly cured many people of epilepsy and arthritis.

[11.1.19] [19. On the slough of a snake.] Some have written that the slough of a snake, boiled up in vinegar, heals toothaches. [11.1.20] [20. On the skin of a sheep.] The skin of a sheep freshly flayed, wrapped around those who have been flogged in any way whatsoever, manifestly benefits them more than all other remedies, so as to heal them in one day and night; for it both concocts and disperses the blood-suffused parts.

[11.1.21] [21. On the leichenes of horses.] Some have written that the leichenes of horses, ground fine with vinegar, cure epilepsies, and some people also advise using them against the bite of any venomous creature. [11.1.22] [22. On the spider's web.] Some write that a spider's web keeps superficial ulcers free of inflammation.

[11.1.23] [23. On old leathers.] Old leathers, those from shoe-soles, when burnt, are recorded as suitable for the chafings (ekthlimmata) caused by shoes, as though, forsooth, they did this by some antipathy. While the chafings are inflamed, then, they are not benefited; but once the inflammation has ceased, they are with good reason benefited by being dried, for such ash is drying. I myself also once used it in the country for an ulcer of this kind arising from a chafe (paratrimma). Such ash also, with good reason, heals the burns among ulcers and the so-called chafes (paratrimmata) that occur on the thighs.

[11.1.24] [24. On ostreia.] Some people call ostreia all the creatures that were named ostracoderms ('shell-skinned') by Aristotle. The one that most people call ostreon, pronounced without the iota in the second syllable, they set down as one particular species of the ostreia, and in the genus as a whole they include trumpet-shells (kērykes), purple-shells (porphyrai), clams (chēmai) and pinnas (pinai), and all the similar creatures, which I shall discuss next.

[11.1.25] [25. On trumpet-shells and purple-shells.] The shell of trumpet-shells (kērykes) and purple-shells (porphyrai), since it is extremely hard, I have never used without burning. Burnt, however, it is of a drying power; but it must be ground precisely, so that it becomes downy-fine, having of course first pounded and sifted it. Let this be a rule common to all things that have a stony or shell-like substance. For if it is not ground precisely, it is much like grains of sand. And the meal produced when they are ground, used by itself, is suited to malignant ulcers. This very property is also common to all things that dry strongly without conspicuously biting; for those that bite, by irritating, become causes of fluxes. And there is something else common to all such things: with oxycrate or vinegar or honeyed wine [oinomeli] or oxymel they become serviceable for putrefactive ulcers. For this reason all the stones too, when brought to such a use, are beneficial, some more, some less, but all of them nonetheless.

[11.1.26] [26. On oysters.] The shell of oysters, when burnt, is of a power similar to that of the shell of whelks, and still more fine-particled, or, to put it more safely, less coarse-particled. For all things which have an earthy and hard consistency and solidity of body are quite coarse-particled, which is why it is proper to grind them carefully. So whenever we say that one of these is more fine-particled than another, the expression must be understood in the same way as if we were to say that Odysseus is bigger than Thersites, though both are small, or that Ajax is smaller than Achilles, though both of these are big. As has also been said before, all such things have in themselves something of the contracting power, on account of which, their substance having been compacted, they have also become hard and earthy; and having cast this off through burning, they acquire the opposite power, which we call dispersing. If you wash them and burn them, all of what is, as it were, the fiery residue is deposited in the water, and this acts by heating in a fine-particled way, so as at times even to cause putrefaction. The remainder becomes earthy and non-biting, which is especially useful on moist ulcers, for filling them up and bringing them to close with a scar. I use the burnt shell of those that are properly called oysters for the chronic cavities that arise from fluxes and are hard to fill with flesh, those that are fistulous and deep, applying it on the outside with old pig's fat; this is called axungia by most people. And into the sinus itself I put one of the things that fill such places with flesh, such as burnt diphryges, which they call spekarion. The shells of the other testaceans too, when burnt, are of a power similar in kind, but especially, as I said, that of oysters, and next that of whelks and purple-shells. Such ash, then, is mixed into clogging dispersing drugs, and with any fat it disperses. Because old fat is more dispersing, it is mixed rather with that. The drug becomes more pungent than is proper if you mix with it one of the pungent fats, about which I made distinctions earlier. But the ash of all such things also brightens the teeth, not only by the cleansing quality of its power but also by the roughness of its substance, just as pumice and oven-potsherd do. Now in this kind of use it is not necessary to grind very thoroughly the things burnt in this way, but for malignant ulcers you will in all cases grind them precisely beforehand. They also moderately reduce and repress excess flesh. Moreover, all such things burnt with salt make the tooth-cleansing powder more effective, so as to dry the flabby parts of the gums, and they also benefit putrefying ulcers.

[11.1.27] [27. On the cuttlefish.] The shell of the cuttlefish is quite porous, not stony like those of oysters. Cleansing, then, it has in common with them, as do the other shells of the testaceans, just as it also has drying. But the fine-particled nature of its substance belongs to it as a special property beyond the others; for this reason we also use it burnt for alphoi, ephelis, phakoi (lentil-spots) and psorai. Moreover, mixed with mined salt, it melts away the pterygia that arise on the eyes. And even before it is burnt, when roasted and ground smooth, it brightens the teeth and dries ulcers. We are also accustomed to use the moderate degree of its roughness against the great roughnesses in the eyes which they call sykōseis: we carve out of it something resembling a collyrium in shape and rub them with it so as to draw blood. For when this has been done, the reducing collyria also act better upon them.

[11.1.28] [28. On the lids of purple-shells.] Some have written that the lids of purple-shells, drunk in vinegar, cure swollen spleens, and that, used as a fumigation, they benefit women who are suffocated hysterically, that is, from the womb, and expel retained afterbirths.

[11.1.29] [29. On oesypous wool.] Wool that is still dirty, and for this reason called by some 'oesypous', usefully takes up the embrocations applied to parts that have been bruised or struck in any way whatever, and it contributes to the benefit derived from them on account of its oesypum. Wool that has been washed and no longer has its oesypum becomes a suitable material for taking up the liquids poured over it. When burnt, it has a power that is pungent and hot, together with a fine-particled nature, so that it very quickly melts away even flabby flesh in ulcers. It is also put into a drying drug. Burn it as you burn most other things: fill a new pot, then close it with a lid that has several holes.

[11.1.30] [30. On burnt hairs.] Burnt hairs, like burnt wool, are of a fairly strong heating and drying power. [11.1.31] [31. On the power of eggs.] It would be fitting, as a sequel to the teaching about the parts, to speak also about eggs, for I have nowhere else to mention them. Eggs, then, are not parts of animals, just as fruit is not a part of trees, nor embryos of pregnant females; but they are analogous to outgrowths. Of outgrowths, some appear to be wholly proper to the natures of the plants or animals, others not wholly such: for example the mistletoe that grows on oaks, or, in general, anything of a different kind that grows on trees, whether tree or shrub or fruit or herb or in general some shoot, as mushrooms do. Among the proper ones, then, are the wool on sheep and the hairs on the other animals; and the horns that fall off and grow again, as in male deer, are also of this kind. Things conceived are analogous to fruits, being produced by nature for the sake of the succession of the kind. One of these is the egg, which has come into being for the sake of the preservation of the kind. It is also useful as food, but it is not now proposed to speak about food. Whatever, then, it effects as a drug will be stated in this discussion, as we discover its power from a few particular uses, both in respect of its parts and of its whole substance; for we have learned how, once the universal power of each existing thing has been found, we are able to extend it to many particular uses. And we have also learned beforehand how it is possible, from one or a second trial, to reason about the universal power. The white and thin part of eggs, which we also use for ophthalmias, is among the least biting of drugs, nor did they have any failure arising from such a dyscrasia as milk often has, as we showed earlier in the case of animals that have suffered indigestion, or have been excessively hungry or excessively thirsty, or have used bad foods, things which indeed tend to happen more in women because of error in regimen. Eggs admit only one defect, that from age, which is very easily guarded against by one who uses fresh ones. The most customary for us and the most easily obtained is that of hens, and for this reason we use it, having no need of the others, although they have the same nature. In its mixture it is colder than the well-balanced. One should therefore use the white of eggs not only for the eyes but also in all other cases that require the least biting drugs, such as all malignant ulcers at the seat and the genitals. It is also usefully mixed with the drugs that check haemorrhages from the meninges, which are those that plaster on without biting and are astringent. And for malignant ulcers it is mixed with those that by nature dry them without biting, of which kind of drug are washed pompholyx and some of the metallic substances when washed, about which it has been said before in the discussion proper to them. The yolk of eggs too is of a similar nature, and for this reason it is mixed into non-biting cerates, the eggs having been boiled or roasted. It is evident that these will differ from one another by a slight difference, because roasting makes them slightly more drying, and as much of this power as they have acquired, so much of the soothing they lose. It is also mixed into anti-inflammatory poultices, as at the seat into those made with melilot. We use the raw whole egg, mixing in rose oil, for inflammations at the eyelids, ears and breasts, whether they arise from these parts having been struck or otherwise, and also on sinewy bodies, such as the elbow and the tendons at the fingers, or the joints in the feet and hands. If an egg boiled in vinegar is eaten, it dries fluxes in the belly. And if you mix with it one of the things suited to dysentery or to the coeliac condition, and then fry it over a smokeless and moderate fire, such as that from coals, and give it to eat, you will benefit the patients not least. Most suitable for such a mixture are omphacium and sumach, the kind sprinkled on relishes, called red, and its juice, and oak-gall, and pomegranate rind, and the ash of whole roasted snails. Suitable also are grape-pips, myrtle berries, medlars and cornels. More drug-like than these are balaustion, hypocistis and cytini. For burns too, applied raw at once, it is beneficial, whether one takes up the white alone in soft wool, or moistens the whole together with the yolk and applies it. For it cools moderately and dries without biting. Since it is such, we use it also for the so-called anacollemata applied to the forehead, and we glue back the hairs of the eyelids, mixing in some suitable substance, such as frankincense, especially when it is oily and not old and dry. But in such cases it is the viscosity of the white of eggs that is useful, not its mixture, unless one were to say that the latter is useful insofar as it in no way opposes the drug applied. For some viscous things are opposed, as birdlime, being pungent and hot, is for things that do not need to be heated. And it has been said many times that drugs having no strong power are mixed with those having such powers as a matter, and for this reason they are of many uses, serving those that act strongly. The egg, being of this kind, and at the same time acquiring in addition no small difference according to the amount of boiling or roasting, becomes of many uses. For with drugs that dry up moistures it is mixed boiled, roasted and fried; but with those that cut the matters in the chest and lung, the so-called sippable egg, which should be boiled in water only so long as to become hot. According to the same nature it is employed for those whose throat has been roughened through shouting or through the pungency of a humour, being plastered around the affected parts and remaining there like a poultice, and through the non-biting quality of its substance at once soothing and healing them. By the same reasoning it also cures roughnesses in the stomach, belly, intestines and bladder.

[11.1.32] [32. On burnt echinoi.] Of both echinoi, the sea one and the terrestrial one, the whole body, when burnt, yields an ash of cleansing, dispersing and reducing power. Some people, at any rate, have used it both for parts that have grown excess flesh and for foul ulcers.

[11.1.33] [33. On snails.] Whole snails, burnt together with their shells, with omphacitis gall and white pepper mixed in with them, are of great benefit in dysenteries, in those cases where the ulcers are not yet putrefying. There should be one part of the pepper, two of the gall, and four of the ash of the snails. Having made these thoroughly smooth, sprinkle them on the cooked dishes and give them to drink in water or in wine that is white and harsh. Apart from being mixed with gall, the ash of snails is of a sufficiently drying power, which also has something of heat on account of the burning. Unburnt snails, ground smooth together with their shells, are applied both over the whole belly in the dropsical and over the swellings in the joints in the arthritic. Their application becomes hard to remove, but it dries sufficiently. And indeed it is proper to let them remain applied the whole time, until they fall off of their own accord. This is to be done also in the case of swellings from a blow that are hard to resolve, and with a contusion that has occurred in the ears. For they sufficiently dry all of these, even if a viscous and thick fluid is contained in the depth.

[11.1.34] [34. On burnt crabs.] The ash of river crabs is drying, like the things mentioned before, but by a property of its whole substance it acts wonderfully in those bitten by a rabid animal, both on its own and, much more, together with gentian and frankincense. There should be one part of the frankincense, five of the gentian and ten of the crabs. On occasion, and rarely, we have used them burnt in other ways, but for the most part in the way that Aeschrion the Empiricist used them, an old man most experienced in drugs, our fellow citizen and teacher. It was a dish of red copper, on which he placed the crabs alive and burned them until they were reduced to ash, so that they could easily be ground fine. This Aeschrion always had the drug prepared and ready in his house, burning the crabs in the summer season, after the rising of the Dog Star, when the sun was in Leo and the moon was in its eighteenth day. He gave this drug to drink every day to those bitten by a rabid animal, up to the fortieth day, sprinkling a good-sized spoonful into water. But if he took charge of the bitten person not from the beginning but some days after the bite, he sprinkled in two spoonfuls each day. On the wound itself he also used the plaster drug made with Bruttian pitch, opopanax and vinegar, which takes one litra of pitch, one Italian xestes of the most pungent vinegar, and three ounces of opopanax. Although these things do not belong to the present treatise, I have written them because of my confidence in the drug, since no one of those who used it in the way described has ever died. I shall also compose separately another treatise on the things that act by a property of the whole substance, among which are all things of this kind. One must therefore pardon the untimeliness of the writing, both now and in other places of this treatise where it sometimes occurs, on account of the benefit from what is said, which is very great, and which I wish to be preserved for the people after us, even if death intervening should prevent me from writing the next parts of this treatise. Our teacher Pelops, wishing to state the causes of all such things, said that the crab, being an aquatic animal, reasonably benefits those bitten by a rabid animal, who are in fear of being seized by lytta, a most dry affection, which is why they also fear water. He said that river crabs, not sea crabs, are suitable, since because of the admixture of salts, which are most drying, sea animals would not preserve an exact contrariety to lytta. And when someone said to him, 'Why then do not all the animals in drinkable water benefit similarly to the crabs?', 'Because,' he said, 'they cannot receive a preparation similar to that of the crabs. For when these are burnt, their ash, becoming drying, both consumes and at the same time disperses the venom of the biting dogs.' These, then, were the things Pelops said, professing and priding himself on knowing the causes of them all. But I, unless I first persuade myself that I know something exactly, do not attempt to persuade my neighbours. Accordingly I did not accept Pelops' argument as true either, since it is open to many objections, but I hold that the crabs too benefit by the property of the whole substance. But because none of those who used them has died, I wished this to have been made clear by me already, with the whole bodies at any rate, even if it is not proper to the present treatise. For this was not what was proposed.

[11.1.35] [35. On burnt swallows.] Not only in the case of the animals I have mentioned: many have also used swallows, burning them and mixing honey with the ash, then anointing those suffering from synanche with it; and in general all the affections that occur in the pharynx and the uvula accompanied by swellings. Some people also use this ash for sharpness of sight. Others, drying them out [σκελετεύοντες, literally 'desiccating', 'mummifying'], give them to drink in the quantity of a drachm.

[11.1.36] [36. On cicadas.] Some also use dried cicadas in colic conditions, together with grains of pepper equal to them in number, and they give either three or five or seven, both during the intermissions and during the paroxysms. Others roast them and give them to eat to those affected in the bladder.

[11.1.37] [37. On crested larks.] The crested lark, this small winged creature that we often see along the roads, benefits colic sufferers when it is boiled in broth. One must eat it continually and often, together with the broth. This creature has on its head something like a crest of naturally occurring hairs, and it was on account of this crest that the fable which Aristophanes the comic poet wrote was invented. He speaks of it in this way: 'For you are by nature ignorant and a busybody, and you have not learned your Aesop, who used to say that the crested lark came into being first of all birds, before the earth, and that then her father died of a disease, but there was no earth, and he lay out for five days, and she, at a loss and having no other means, buried her father in her head.' They say that Theocritus too alludes to this when he says, 'Nor are the tomb-crested larks roaming about.' For they say he means those that have the tomb on their head. I have added these things to the account because I wish to show clearly what kind of raising of the hairs on its head the creature, the crested lark, has. I have tested its benefit for colic sufferers, and I wish to make it properly known to those who do not know it, since it resembles the birds called pyrgētoi, but it is distinguished by its crest and is a little larger than it. Indeed the herb called korydalis is also suitable for colic sufferers themselves. Let this too be known to you, by the way.

[11.1.38] [38. On hens.] The plain broth of hens has a tempering power, just as that of old cocks has a laxative one. One must boil them with salt for a very long time. But of these things we ourselves have experience.

[11.1.39] [39. On the weasel.] The weasel we have never burnt. Of it they have written that its ash, smeared on with vinegar, benefits those suffering from podagra and from arthritis, since it is by nature capable of dispersing powerfully; and that, when dried and drunk, it benefits epileptics, evidently by virtue of the same power. Some people also say that it is in every way an antidote against a venomous creature, and especially its belly.

[11.1.40] [40. On burnt frogs.] The ash of burnt frogs, they say, is a remedy for haemorrhage when sprinkled on, and it cures alopecias when applied with liquid pitch. [11.1.41] [41. On the hippocampus.] Some have also written that the hippocampus, the sea animal, burnt whole, benefits alopecias, and that it too, or rather its ash, is evidently of a drying and fine-particled power. Some mix this ash with amaracine (marjoram) unguent, some with liquid pitch, and some with old swine's fat.

[11.1.42] [42. On salted tellins.] They say also that salted tellins, when burnt, produce an ash so caustic that, mixed with cedar-resin and dropped into the spot when we have pulled the hairs of the eyelids out from their roots, it prevents them from growing again. On earthworms. Some of the physicians have made trial, or have written as though they had made trial, of whole animals applied to the affected parts, or taken into the body, without burning or boiling: that earthworms (literally 'intestines of the earth'), ground smooth and applied to severed nerves, help at once in a wonderful way, and that these same things, all of them, drunk with sweet wine, are a diuretic drug.

[11.1.43] [43. On bugs.] They have also written about bugs, that, if they are drunk with vinegar, they expel leeches that have been swallowed. But we, since we always expel these by the eating of garlic, have had no need of bugs.

[11.1.44] [44. On cantharides.] Of cantharides, at any rate, we have ample experience in the case of psoric nails: applied to these together with suitable cerates or plasters, they draw the nails out, so that they fall off entire. We have also mixed them into the compositions (δυνάμεσι) suited to psorai and leprai, and into some of the putrefying drugs, and sometimes also into those that expel the so-called corns. One of our teachers used to put a little of them into a diuretic drug. Some people put in only the wings and the feet, which they also say are a remedy for those who have drunk their bodies (τὰ τώματα); others do the reverse; but we put them in whole. More suitable for the purposes for which I said I had tested cantharides are those from the wheat that have transverse yellow bands on their wings; and they are more so if you put them into a new earthenware vessel, then place some piece of loose-woven linen over the mouth of the vessel, and hold the vessel in such a way that the linen is turned downwards, receiving the vapour of the vinegar that rises up, until the cantharides die.
[11.1.45] [45. On the buprestis.] In the same way it is fitting to lay up the buprestes as well. These too are a certain kind of animal, closely resembling the cantharides in form and in power.

[11.1.46] [46. On the pine-caterpillar.] Moreover, the caterpillars on pine trees too, which are fittingly called pine-caterpillars (pityokampai), are of such a power. [11.1.47] [47. On the salamander.] Some people also mix the ash of the burnt salamander into putrefying, lepric and psoric preparations.

[11.1.48] [48. On the torpedo.] Some people have also written that the torpedo as a whole (I mean, of course, the sea animal) cures headaches when applied to the head, and turns back in a prolapsed (everted) anus. But I tested it in both respects and found that it accomplished neither. Then I conceived the idea of applying it, while still alive, to someone suffering pain in the head, reasoning that it could be an anodyne drug, like the other things that numb sensation, and I found that this was so. I think that the first person who used it was also led to use it by some such notion.

[11.1.49] [49. On the sea dragon and the red mullet.] Some have written that the following animals, split open alive and applied at once to the affected parts, are beneficial: the sea dragon placed upon its own sting, and likewise the red mullet upon that of the sea dragon; house mice upon that of the scorpion, as also the lizard; the shrew-mouse upon its own bite, and the Chalcidian lizard, which they also give to drink in wine, as healing its own bite. They have written too that the scorpion thoroughly heals its own sting when applied ground smooth, and likewise when eaten roasted. They say that it is also suited to those bitten by a viper, and the gecko to those stung by a scorpion. They say also that in the districts of Egypt the so-called aseirakos, dried, is given to those stung by a scorpion, and that the so-called kybion is usefully employed for the bite of a dog, applied over the wound; and many other such things, about which we shall speak at greater length in the discussion of things that act by a peculiarity of the whole substance. Some of the physicians of our time have used the oil in which whole animals have been boiled. Some of the earlier ones, for stripping off hairs, used pine-caterpillars, sea nettles, the sea hare and the sea scolopendra; and for earache, silphai boiled in the oil, and the so-called oniskoi. These are animals that become ball-shaped by drawing themselves together upon themselves, which some among us call ‘beans’, since, when they have rolled themselves into a ball, they are very like edible beans, being dusky in colour. In the country one may see very many of them breeding under the water-jars in which the country people carry water from the springs and which they set down near the hearth; and I have seen some of those who practise medicine in the country always using the oil made from them for all pains of the ears, without distinguishing in what condition the pain has arisen; whence, naturally, they sometimes succeed and sometimes also do harm. And what wonder is it, when even some of the reputable physicians have written about such things without distinction? Such, at any rate, are also the books of Apollonius on readily procured drugs. This man, then, has also written that earthworms boiled down in oil soothe pains of the ears; and some think it right to mix them with goose fat and use them thus.

[11.1.50] [50. On foxes and hyenas.] Concerning foxes boiled whole in oil (for some treat arthritics in this way, some throwing the foxes alive into a very large cauldron, others dead), it is necessary to speak at greater length. They seemed at first to have freed many people from the affection, but after no long time to have only benefited them. For the affection returned in them, though not so violent as it had been before. Now what comes from foxes is in no way more dispersing than what comes from the hyena; when it is likewise boiled in oil, the oil becomes most dispersing. It has been said many times that drugs of this kind have the property of drawing to the surface what is contained in the depth of the body, and in this way sometimes of stopping pains. For this does not follow from them in every case. Only those pains are stopped by such drugs in which a humour productive of pain is contained in the depth, whether because of the thickness of its substance, or because of coldness or violent pungency, or else a flatulent pneuma that has no outlet. Those, then, who used the foxes likewise made the oil dispersing. Then, filling tubs with it, they set the arthritics in them whole, bidding them remain in them for a long time. From this it came about that not only the swellings about their joints but also the whole body was evacuated. Since, then, the whole body was previously in a plethoric condition, it was no wonder that benefit arose from the evacuation, with nothing flowing onto the affected parts, because the whole body was being evacuated and the humours contained in those parts were being dispersed. But just as formerly, when their body was free of the affection, the bad regimen produced the affection, in the same way, or even more so, it was likely that through a similar regimen they would again be similarly disposed in the joints that had suffered.

[11.2.1] [1. On the things generated in the sea and in salty waters.] These things alone, which are still lacking to the whole treatise, have this as their fitting occasion. For the animals generated in the sea and in water were discussed in the preceding account concerning animals; but those things that are generated in waters or from waters, yet are not animals, will now be discussed.

[11.2.2] [2. On adarcium.] Adarcium, which some people call in the masculine adarcos and others in the feminine adarce, is in its substance like a sort of congealed foam of salty water, congealing around litter and reeds. It is extremely pungent and extremely heating. For this reason it is useless on its own, but it is mixed with things that blunt its power, and in this way it becomes of many uses, applied externally, in conditions that need to be heated. For it is not possible to take it inside the body, because of the vehemence of its power.

[11.2.3] [3. On alkyonia.] All alkyonia are cleansing and dispersing, having a pungent quality and a hot power. But the more and the less among them is not slight, both in the very respects I have mentioned and, further, in how fine-particled their whole substance is. One of them is dense and heavy and foul in smell, for it smells of rotten fish, and in shape it resembles a sponge. A second is more elongated in shape, light and porous, with a smell like that of seaweeds. A third is close in shape to a worm, is purplish in colour and soft in consistency; they call it Milesian. Besides these there is a fourth, which is light and porous like the second one mentioned, but resembles greasy unwashed wool. The fifth is bounded on the outside by a smooth surface but has a rough substance within. It has no smell at all but is perceived as pungent to the taste; for it is, of course, also the hottest of all the alkyonia, so that it can burn off hair. Therefore, while the first two benefit leichenes and alphoi, and indeed also psorai and leprai, and moreover make the skin bright because of the moderateness of their power, this last-mentioned one is able to do the same. For it does not merely cleanse those conditions off, as it would the outer surface, but it flays and strips off the skin, penetrating into the depth of the skin so as to produce ulcers. The third mentioned is the most fine-particled of all. Therefore, when burnt, it also heals alopekiai when smeared on with wine that is tawny in colour and thin in consistency. The fourth of them is of the same kind as these in its power, but weaker to no small degree.

[11.2.4] [4. On salts.] Salts, both the dug and the sea salts, are of the same power in kind. They differ in that the substance of the salts from the earth is more compacted, which is why the coarse-particled and the astringent are present to a greater degree in these. Sea salts, then, dissolve at once when water is poured around them, whereas those from the earth do not undergo this. Of the same kind as the sea salts are also those produced in summer in certain lakes that contain brine, when the water is baked out of them, as, for instance, the Tragasian salts near Sminthium. For there, from the naturally arising waters, which are quite hot, an abundant water collects, standing as a pool over no large area, and in summer this is entirely used up, being dried by the sun; and since the place has brine inherent in it, all that is left of the water becomes salts, which take their name from the place and from the waters. For the naturally arising waters of that place are themselves called Tragasian, being of a most drying power, and the physicians of that place do indeed use them for this purpose. The Sodomene salts, produced in what is called the Dead Sea, have also been discussed in the fourth book, and if anyone has read that book carefully, he will now need only to be reminded, so that, once the quality perceived by taste has been stated, he will know the power of the drug. Since, then, the salty quality both disperses and at the same time draws together the substance it comes near, what is called aphronitron differs in this respect, inasmuch as in it one can clearly see only one prevailing flavour, which they call bitter, having a dispersing power but not having a drawing-together power, as salts do. For salts consume all the moisture that is in bodies, while the remainder of the solid substance they draw together by their astringency; for this reason they also pickle, and keep unputrefied, the bodies of things that putrefy, which have residual moisture that is undissipated and a substance that is not tightly bound. Those bodies, then, in which there is no superfluous moisture at all, as in the finest honey, and whose solid body is compacted, as in stones, cannot putrefy; for this reason the use of salts is not esteemed in their case, but in those in which putrefaction is to be suspected.

[11.2.5] [5. On burnt salt.] Burnt salt has the dispersing [property] to a greater degree than unburnt salt, in proportion as its body becomes more fine-particled, taking on a power from the fire, as was shown to happen also in the case of the other burnt [substances]; it is not, however, still able to draw together and compact the solid substance in the same way as unburnt salt.

[11.2.6] [6. On nitron.] Nitron. This drug too has been shown to have a power intermediate between that of salt and that of aphronitron. [11.2.7] [7. On flower of salt.] Flower of salt: some people call it halosanthon, as a single word, while others divide it and call it 'flower of salt' (halos anthos). This drug is liquid, more fine-particled even than burnt salt, pungent in quality and considerably dispersing in power.

[11.2.8] [8. On froth of salt.] Froth of salt (halos achnē) is a foamy efflorescence of salts, being of a much more fine-particled nature than the salts themselves, so that it is able both to thin and to disperse much more than they are; but it is not able, as salts are, to draw together the remainder of the substance.

[11.2.9] [9. On asphalt.] Asphalt. This too is one of the things generated in sea-water and in any other water similar to the sea. Thus at Apollonia in Epirus and in other such places this drug is found riding like foam upon many naturally occurring waters. It is soft while it floats on the surface, but afterwards it dries, so that it becomes harder than dry pitch.

[11.2.10] [10. On the asphalt produced in the Dead Sea.] The finest asphalt is produced in the sea called 'Dead'. This is a salt lake in Coele Syria. The power of the drug is drying and heating, somewhere about the second order. Reasonably, then, it is used for the agglutination of fresh bleeding wounds, [and] for the other things that need drying together with moderate heating.

[11.2.11] [11. On sponge.] Sponge, when burnt, is of a pungent and dispersing power. One of our teachers also used it against the haemorrhages that occur in surgical operations. He kept it ready, dry and without moisture, but soaked, preferably in asphalt, or in pitch if asphalt was not available. He applied it, still burning, to the haemorrhaging places, so that the part was at the same moment turned into an eschar and received the very body of the burnt sponge as a kind of lid. A new sponge by itself is not, like wool or plucked lint, merely material for the liquids with which it is moistened; it also clearly dries. You will know this if you use it on its own on a wound, with water or oxycrate or wine according to the differences of the bodies, as was said before. For it will agglutinate them in a way similar to the drugs called enhaemous. But if it is not new but has been used, you will clearly recognise how far it falls short of the new one when it is applied to wounds, whether soaked in water, in wine or in oxycrate. And it is nothing surprising that, in the case of a new sponge, while the power that it had from the sea is still preserved, the bodies are moderately dried. It is able to do this when it still preserves the smell from the sea. For in the course of time, even if it has not yet been put to use, it loses its smell and is not able to dry in the same way.

[11.2.12] [12. On garum.] Garum is of a considerably hot and dry power, and for this reason some physicians have used it for the putrefactive among ulcers, and they also inject it into dysenterics and ischiadics.

[11.2.13] [13. On brine.] The brine of salted fish, like garum, is suitable both for putrefactions and, when injected, for cases of ischias and dysentery. By its pungency it draws out the humours that trouble the hip and evacuates them through the intestines, while the putrefactive ulcers in dysentery it washes around and dries. Some physicians have used especially the brine of salted siluri and the brine of maenides for such conditions, and we too have used it in the case of putrefactive ulcers in the mouth.

[10.2.1] On the fluids in animals. [1. On blood.] Blood: one must of course understand in addition 'of an animal in its natural state', for this is what is truly blood. Melancholic, bitter-bilious, phlegmatic, serous or putrefactive blood is mixed, composed of blood in the true sense and of the humour and ichor that have been mixed with it. And of natural blood itself, in each animal some is moister and some drier, and some more and some less hot; for no blood is cold.

[10.2.2] [2. On pig's blood.] Pig's blood, then, is moist and less hot, and most closely resembles human blood in its mixture, since the flesh of pigs too resembles that of humans. Indeed, we already know of many innkeepers and cooks who were caught selling human flesh as pork, and yet none of those who ate it perceived any difference. Moreover, I heard trustworthy people relate that in a certain inn they had eaten abundant broth with most delicious meat, and when they had already eaten their fill, they found in it the front part of a finger, at the nail itself. Fearing that the people in the inn might eat them too, as being accustomed to the practice, they left at once, vomited up what they had eaten, and continued their journey. They also said that not long afterwards the people at the inn were caught for the human beings they used to slaughter. So one might reasonably suppose that the blood of pigs too is most similar to that of humans. For it is from such blood that the flesh has both its first generation and its nourishment thereafter. Hence whoever says that human blood is useful against some disease, let him first demonstrate in pig's blood, if not the same action, at least a similar one. For even if it should fall short of human blood in some respect of its power, it will at any rate do something comparable, and once this is known we shall expect the benefit from human blood to be more complete. But if it appears to preserve not even a little of what is promised, there is no reason to make trial of human blood either. For we have found by experience that similar things are productive of similar effects. At any rate, among us in Pergamum, and indeed throughout almost the whole of Asia, those who have trepanned fractured bones of the head are accustomed to pour dove's blood onto the thick membrane [κατασχεῖν, probably to be read καταχεῖν]. Then someone who happened to have a wood-pigeon but not a dove used the wood-pigeon's blood, and the man was nevertheless saved. And another, using the blood of a turtle-dove on another patient, did the man no harm. For to use similar things for the same affections when those tested beforehand are not available is one of the things agreed upon and attested by experience. And indeed most of human life is carried on in this way.

[10.2.3] [3. On the blood of the pigeon.] Since I have mentioned the blood of pigeons by way of example, it would be no bad thing to take this up now in the discussion as well. For some people also use it for hyposphagmata occurring in the eyes, taking, clearly, what flows out of the animal at once as it is being slaughtered. One man, pouring it warm onto the hyposphagmata, would cut the veins at the origin of the wings, so that the animal itself might suffice for many applications. Another, plucking the feathers of tender nestlings (these are soft and have their quills full of fluid), squeezed out this very fluid and instilled it into the eyes. Among other physicians a dispute arose whether one ought to drip onto the meninx the blood of a nestling or of a full-grown pigeon, and whether of a male or a female. But I know countless people in Rome whose skull bones had been trepanned and who were not harmed at all by the use of rose oil without pigeon's blood; but it must be warm, just as the pigeon's blood is. And perhaps it is beneficial by the moderateness of its warmth to the touch, not by some special and unknown power. A good mixture in respect of power also belongs to it, but what of that? For rose oil too has this, together with partaking of a slight astringency, so that, at least in the case of a trepanned head, you will have nothing more if you use good rose oil. I have shown earlier how the faultless rose oil must be prepared. There are also a great many collyria healing of hyposphagmata, especially those containing much myrrh, such as the one called the diasmyrnon of Democrates. Next after these come those made with much frankincense, and after these those made with saffron; and the juice of fenugreek is better than pigeon's blood for such purposes. What need would there be, then, to wait for pigeons or wood-pigeons or turtle-doves, when we have fenugreek, the most easily procured remedy of all, and the collyria mentioned ready to hand? In the same way we shall not need the blood of an owl for those suffering from dyspnoea either. Some, indeed, do not give the blood to drink, but boil the bird itself and bid them eat it in plain broth. As for the blood, some give it dripped into water, others into wine; and someone was praising this blood extravagantly in the case of a woman continually suffering from dyspnoea, but when I asked him what kind of dyspnoea he knew to have been cured by it, he did not even know that there are several kinds.

And so he used it on the woman, but it did her no good at all, [10.2.4] [4. On the blood of the bat, and of the hare, and of hens, and of goats, lambs and kids, and of bears, bulls and he-goats.] just as neither does that of the bat, which some have written keeps the breasts of maidens drawn in for a very long time when smeared on them. This too is a falsehood, as indeed is the claim that hairs do not grow in the armpits, which Xenocrates rightly discredited as untrue. He himself recommends, after the use of that blood, sprinkling on either chalcanthum or hemlock seed. And he says that when people do this the hairs either do not grow at all or grow downy, as though in applying the hemlock seed he were applying some trifling drug, and one not capable by itself of vigorously chilling whatever parts it is placed on. Some also smear the bat's blood on the genitals of boys, thinking that by this they will keep the parts without pubic hair for a very long time. And yet they ought to think not 'for a very long time', but that the parts will remain so permanently, just as they suppose of the armpits too. Now it is reasonable that something of this sort should come about from the part's being strongly chilled; but the bat's blood is not cold in potency to such a degree, for no blood at all is cold. As food, however, many people often use the blood of the hare, of hens and of goats: the blood of the hare and of hens not a few even of those in the cities, and that of goats those in the countryside, who fill the goats' stomachs with it together with the fat, as Homer said of the suitors. But our present discussion is not about things administered in the role of food, but about those administered as drugs. Some things, as was also said earlier, are at once foods and drugs, and of these we speak in this treatise insofar as they are drugs, not insofar as they are foods. For those who have given goat's blood with honey to dropsical patients administer it as a drug, not as a food, and so too those who have used it roasted for dysentery or for a flux of the belly. And it seems to me that someone arrived at this use having supposed that its coarse-particled and earthy nature, together with heat, is drying. For haemorrhages of the meninges I found the blood of the cock and of the hen written up by them, yet I neither expected it to accomplish anything great, and as for judging it by trial, on the one hand I was ashamed, lest I should seem meddlesome or foolish if, passing over so many and such well-approved drugs, I were to hope that the blood of these birds would accomplish more; and on the other hand, since such a haemorrhage is dangerous, it did not seem right to me to resort to anything untried. For such an experiment is hazardous in this way, and is reasonably undertaken only by kings, on wicked men. I condemned in advance also the blood of lambs, which some say cures epilepsy when drunk; accordingly I was not going to judge this by trial either. But if anyone wishes to make the trial, I know clearly that he will find himself condemning the very people who wrote such things. For all drugs that benefit epileptics when drunk are of the cutting power, and the blood of lambs is least of all of this kind. As for what Xenocrates said about the blood of kids, since I thought it possible that it accomplishes something on account of the admixture of vinegar, I handed it over to be carried out by one of those who live in the country, a man devoted to farming, but who had received the elementary education; and he says that, having used it on two people who had spat blood, he found by trial some benefit. It seemed to me, however, from what he related, that neither of them had spat it either from the windpipe or from the larynx or lung. At any rate Xenocrates, in the first book On the Benefit Derived from Animals, where he discusses kids, writes word for word as follows: 'Very beneficial for those who spit blood. One should mix about half a kotylē of it, while not yet congealed, with an equal amount of pungent vinegar, then, having boiled it up, divide it into three and give one portion each day to be gulped down.' So it is open to you, when you are in the country at some time and at a loss for other remedies, to use this too, since the trial of it carries no danger. The blood of the bear, applied warm on abscesses, can ripen them. I shall add to the account also that of the goat, of the he-goat and of the bull. And it is open to you, if you wish, passing over countless easily procured drugs with which we ripen abscesses, to sacrifice bears and bulls and he-goats, evidently for each single application. For surely no one, having applied it once to the affected part, will demand from it what the drug promises; nor indeed will one apply it once it has already become cold so as to have congealed.

[10.2.5] [5. On the blood of green frogs.] When someone firmly asserted that the blood of the small green frogs, which some call *brexantes*, if you smear it on after plucking out the hairs of the eyelids, the hairs no longer grow back, I put it to the test and found it false. Afterwards I also found it written by certain authors, as was also that of the ticks, which the ancients rather call *kynoraistai*. But this too, when brought to the test, did not make good its promise.

[10.2.6] [6. On the blood of the crocodile and the rest.] If the blood of the terrestrial crocodile is productive of sharpness of sight, I was not even going to test it, since I had approved sight-sharpening drugs; just as I was not going to test whether the blood of stallions that are covering mares is eschar-forming and putrefying, nor whether that of house mice makes acrochordons fall off. For I had many other remedies even for this affection, as also for the one more difficult to cure than it, the so-called myrmecia. I was also on my guard against acquiring a reputation for sorcery, since the envious physicians were already saying that I made my predictions in the case of the sick from some divinatory, not medical, theory.

[10.2.7] [7. On milk.] Milk. This has a twofold use, the one as a food, the other as a drug. Now what it is able to do as a food has been shown both through the Therapeutic Method and in the other works. Its power as a drug I shall now state, having first reminded you in this case too, as a little earlier in the case of blood, that what is going to be said must be understood not of diseased milk but of the milk that is in its natural state in each of the animals. The most healthy milk, then, like the blood too, is pure and unmixed, partaking neither of bitterness nor of sourness nor of pungency nor of saltiness nor of foul odour, but, as one might say, fragrant or odourless, or, if indeed it partakes of any fragrance, of a slight one. It is evident that to the taste too it is pleasant, having a slight sweetness, just as the healthy blood does, from which the generation of milk also comes about. Such milk is most beneficial against pungent and biting fluxes, not only washing them off the troubled parts (for this it has in common with water too), but also being plastered around the bodies, so that what flows in does not fall upon them bare. And it is superior to water not only in this respect but also in washing it around, because it contains within itself a cleansing fluid called whey, which is washed off first and washes off the bodies as well. With all the rest of it, which is thick and oily, it is plastered around them in the same manner as lard and suet, the white of egg, and the cerate made from washed wax and oil; for these too soothe the bitings from pungent ichors, through being plastered around the bodies, since they have a non-biting nature. But since all milk is very easily altered, and especially when the ambient air is hot, it loses much of the aforementioned power, unless one uses it immediately, warm, as it is poured out from the breasts. Above all, then, one should use the milk of a woman who is in good condition and following a good regimen, for this is most proper to the human body; and second, that of the other animals, as many as are not far separated from the nature of man. You will know this easily from the smell of their flesh, which is unpleasant in those that stand far apart in their mixtures, such as the dog, wolf, lion, leopard, fox, hyena, bear and the like, but not unpleasant in those that are not far apart, such as the pig, goat, horse, ox, ass, sheep. And accordingly all men, taught by experience, use goat's and sheep's and cow's and ass's milk, and they also make cheeses from them, except from the ass's. For this is very thin and full of whey-like fluid, just as cow's milk is thick. Goat's milk is intermediate in consistency, while the pig has milk that is unconcocted and watery. All milk is composed of three substances, cheesy, whey-like and oily; this last cow's milk appears to have in the greatest quantity, and from it they also make what is called butter, which is of a concocting and relaxing power; for this reason they use it especially for parotid swellings and buboes.

[10.2.8] [8. On the whey of milk.] Whey, as has been said, has a cleansing power. It is taken for the purpose of evacuating the belly and is injected by clysters, cleansing and washing away, without biting, the pungencies in the intestines. And one would do best to wash out ulcers that have pungent ichors with whey instead of water. And all the drugs that are dispersing of ecchymoses and melasmata are also better washed off with whey, not with water. So too we use it for bruises and hyposphagmata, mixing it with the drugs appropriate to these. The cheesy and thick part of the milk forms more of a plaster-like coating, and in this way blunts pungencies. When it takes on some other drying power, it becomes an excellent drug for dysenteric patients and for all pungent fluxes in the belly. It takes this on through red-hot stones, boiled beforehand, that are cast into it. These should be the ones they call kachlēkes [pebbles], and the milk should be boiled until most of its wheyey moisture has been consumed. We, however, also produce the same or even a better power by casting red-hot iron cylinders into it. For iron, as has been said, shares in astringent power, and for this reason I myself had several cylinders made, fixed on the ends of spits, so that one may easily lift the heated iron by the handle. As with cauteries, so with these too I wrap the handles in rags. Whole milk is useful for pungent fluxes of the eyes, both on its own and with the simple collyria, and further for hyposphagmata and bruises. Moreover, applied on the eyelids from outside, together with rose oil and egg, when those suffering from ophthalmia are about to sleep, it concocts their inflammations; but let this milk be a woman's, dripped fresh from the teats. We also inject it into ulcerated wombs, both on its own and mixed with the drugs that treat without biting, with which it mixes; and also when we soothe ulcers at the seat that are painful because of pungent ichors or inflammations or swollen (?) folds. In the same way we use it also for those at the genitals, and simply for everything that needs soothing because of inflammation or biting or malignancy. For this reason, then, it is also applied to cancerous ulcers, mixed with anodyne drugs, such as above all those made with pompholyx. And what need is there to say that as a rinse and as a mouth-hold for inflamed parts in the mouth, when gargled, it is most anodyne? It also considerably soothes inflamed paristhmia at the uvula and the antiades, and for this reason synanchē as well; and, to speak simply, as I said, it is a soothing drug, having a non-biting nature even in its whole substance, but much more so when by moderate boiling we consume the greater part of its wheyey moisture. It is thus, at any rate, that the physicians seem to me to have been led to give milk also against the deadly drugs that kill by erosion, as the sea hare kills and the cantharis. Some also give it to those who have taken aconite or thapsia. But these things they devised reasonably; other things they have plainly falsified, such as the claim about bitch's milk, that it prevents hair from growing up from the eyelids if, after the hairs have been pulled out, it is smeared on the place from which the roots of the hairs were drawn out. And on the same reasoning those who have written that it keeps the hairs from growing out quickly on the genitals if smeared round them before puberty, and that it expels dead embryos when drunk, do not tell the truth. And they write other things savouring of sorcery about this milk and the milk of certain other animals, which I myself refused from the very beginning to speak of, even if I had had experience of them as truly stated.

[10.2.9] [9. On cheese.] Cheese. It is fitting to add an account of cheese to the account of milk, because cheese is curdled milk. Not, however, that the whole substance of the milk is curdled in cheeses: only the thick part is, while the thin and whey-like part is separated off and parted from it. It was said that milk also has within itself a certain oily and, as it were, oil-like nature, and I said that this is present in greatest quantity in cow's milk. When this oily part is separated from the rest of the milk and comes to be by itself, it is called butter. But when it is curdled together with the whole of the milk (the whey-like moisture, that is, having been separated in the curdling), they make the cheese oily. And some cow's cheeses become so oily that something oil-like flows out of them. With time both these and all the others will appear more pungent to you when you taste and smell them. Once, judging from its smell that a cow's cheese brought to me was pungent, I threw it away, and I thought it had been used up by the servants. But the one accustomed to keep such things brought it out of the storeroom after a long time and asked what I wished to be done with it. Since it proved inedible because of its pungency, it became a problem, half in jest, how one might dispose of it usefully. At that moment an arthritic man who had concretions (pōroi) in his joints was brought to me on a chair. It occurred to me to take a salted leg of pork, which was in the house, boil it, moisten the cheese with the decoction, unite it well in a mortar, and apply it over the concretions. And so the arthritic man was benefited very greatly by this remedy. For the skin broke open spontaneously, without incision, and every day parts of the concretions flowed out painlessly. When the cheese I had was entirely used up, the arthritic man procured another of the same kind for himself and kept it for a later time. Afterwards he used it again when it had grown old, and since on that occasion too I experienced [sic; perhaps 'he experienced'] the same benefit, he continued thereafter to use it often, and he taught it to some other friends who suffered in the same way. This, then, came to be known from our own idea, confirmed by experience. Fresh cheese, which is of a mixture contrary to that of old cheese, I once applied, having first ground it smooth of course, to a man in the countryside who had a wound of moderate size. Over it, on the outside, I placed dock leaves. If these are not to hand, leaves of vine, plane tree, beet and lettuce could also be laid on. The cheese itself, being somewhat soft, agglutinated the wound. Another cheese, the one called oxygalaktinos ('sour-milk cheese') in Pergamum, where I come from, and in upper Asia, agglutinated a large wound that a peasant had when it was applied in the same way. For soft and newly curdled cheese has a repelling power, cooling gently. The sour-milk cheese acquires, in addition to these, a slight dispersing power as well.

[10.2.10] [10. On butter.] Boutyros or boutyron, whichever you wish to call it, in the masculine or in the neuter. It is produced, then, from the oiliest part of milk, as has been said before. I wonder how Dioscorides says that it has its origin from sheep's milk and goat's milk [αὐγείου]. For I know this drug as produced from cow's milk, and for this reason I think it is also called boutyron. It is of a concocting power, having a little of the dispersing power, in bodies intermediate in softness and hardness. For one must always remember that pronouncements that are simple, and made without addition and without any qualification, are stated of bodies intermediate in mixture. In completely hard bodies this drug is unable to disperse the swellings contrary to nature, but soft parts that are inflamed it both concocts and disperses easily. So we have completely healed with it alone parotid swellings, buboes, inflammations in the mouth and countless others, when the bodies of children and of women were affected. Moreover, in children who are growing teeth, when it is smeared on continually it thins, no less than honey, the gums through which the teeth make their way out. And all the other inflammatory affections in the mouth it both disperses and concocts, after what flows in has ceased. For this reason it is also mixed into the poultices applied externally, on parotid swellings, on the hypochondria and on buboes. And moreover, when swallowed into the stomach and distributed through it, it contributes greatly to expectorations from the lung in pleuritic and peripneumonic affections, while also concocting them. Licked up by itself, then, it concocts more but brings up less; with honey and bitter almonds it brings up more but concocts less.

[10.2.10] [11. On rennet.] All rennet is of a pungent and dispersing power, and evidently also of a drying one, for this follows of necessity from what has been said. But that of hares, they have written, treats epileptics if it is drunk with vinegar, cures the female flux, and dissolves milk that has clotted in the belly. We too have tested this, not with hare's rennet alone but also with the rennet of the other animals; better than all of them, however, is that of the hare. Drunk in the same way, it also dissolves blood clotting in the belly: the hare's perhaps more than the others, but certainly not alone, as some have written; rather, this too is common to all rennet. Some people say that hare's rennet, when drunk, checks spittings of blood from the chest; but I have neither seen anyone else use it, nor have I myself dared to use a pungent drug against an affection that requires astringency. Horse rennet, they have written, is especially suited to dysenterics and coeliacs.

[10.2.12] [12. On the rennet of the seal.] That of the seal they praise as exceptionally suitable, as having the power of castoreum. But as for the effects which they have written that each of the rennets produces through the specific property of its whole substance, now is not the time to speak of them.

[10.2.13] [13. On bile.] This humour has been shown to be the hottest of the humours in each animal. Just as animals have blood and flesh that are unlike in their mixture, so by the same reasoning they also have unlike bile. For in the hottest animals the bile too must necessarily exceed the biles of the other animals, while in those less hot than these this humour too falls short in proportion, by as much as it falls short in the other things as well. For you have learned that all the humours in each of the blooded animals are four: blood, phlegm, and yellow and black bile.
