You have also learned that it is the custom not only of physicians but of all the Greeks to call yellow bile simply 'bile', on the understanding that the hearers will supply the name of the colour, but not to call black bile simply 'bile'; instead, with this whole addition, they call it 'black bile'. You also know that they sometimes call yellow bile 'pale yellow', and that in the bladder on the liver we see it in the dissections of animals sometimes pale yellow and sometimes yellow. You have also heard that yellow bile is hotter than pale yellow bile by as much as it is also thicker. For when a serous moisture is mixed with yellow bile, the pale yellow comes to be, just as the pale yellow, when heated further, is rendered thick in consistency and yellow in colour. And indeed in animals too it appears yellow in those that are hotter and pale yellow in those that are less so. And whenever hot animals happen to have gone hungry and thirsty, it turns towards the dark colour: sometimes this is verdigris-like, sometimes dark blue, and sometimes that of woad, which is duskier than that of cabbage. Pay attention, then, you too, to the colour of the biles whenever you prepare a drug in which some bile is also contained. Into the so-called kykliskoi and trochiskoi, such as that of Andron, of Polyeides, of Pasion and that of Bitinus, they mix the bile of the bull. When they prepare drugs useful for the eyes, they use that of the hyena, the cock, the partridge and certain other animals. The bull's bile is evidently hotter and more drying than that of castrated oxen. For the castrated animal always comes to resemble the female and the young. Just as these exceed the mature in moisture but fall short in heat, in the same way the castrated ox falls short of bulls. And I have seen the bile of some bulls dark blue, the yellow having been over-roasted; I did not think fit to put it into the drug being prepared, but chose the moderately yellow bile of another bull. For that bull had been exhausted by excessive toil, being dragged with violent bonds, so that it is quite clear that, having also been enraged in this work, it had a hotter mixture. It was likely too that it had been thirsty and hungry while being dragged violently. To speak in summary: just as urine appears moderately pale yellow with moderate drinking, yellow in those who have been thirsty, have gone without food and have toiled much, and white in those who have been filled and become drunk, so bile too changes its colours, towards the yellower in exercises, fasting and thirst, and towards the whiter in the opposite conditions. Know then that if you put markedly yellow bile into the drug being prepared, you will make it hotter; if pale yellow bile, moderately hot; and if bile that is slack and watery, falling short of the appropriate mixture by as much as the bile has turned towards the whiter. In this way, then, for those who open closed haemorrhoids by means of bull's bile, it has sometimes appeared weak and sometimes pungent beyond what is appropriate. Some difference also arises from the body that uses the bile, according as it is sensitive or insensitive, readily affected or not readily affected. But from the bile itself, as I said, the variation is not small. At any rate the same person is bitten more by yellow bile and less by pale yellow. It is possible, then, to see clearly how pungent this humour is from its opening haemorrhoids; but it also appears biting to those who use it, and for this reason we take care not to use yellow bile by itself alone for any other disease or symptom. For the kykliskoi mentioned take little of the bile; and of the drugs compounded for sharpness of sight, some take hyena's bile, others that of the partridge or the cock or some other animal, and they contain honey mixed in and fennel juice or opobalsam. The bile of certain animals has been especially praised by physicians as at once sharpening the sight and dispersing the beginnings of suffusions, such as that of the fish they call kallionymos, and that of the hyena, of the sea scorpion, of the hen and of the partridge. Weakest is that of swine, to such a degree that it is not even intolerable to ulcers; it appears the most watery of all biles, except that of wild swine that live in the mountains. For just as their whole flesh is hotter and drier, so too is their bile. Some use the bile of domestic swine for ulcers in the ears, a drug not without repute, and you too should use it when no other of the compound drugs is available, for there are countless of them. According to the magnitude of the condition, the bile of some other animal could also be suitable. For when the ulcer is chronic and has much ichor and pus, it will tolerate the more drying biles as well, such as that of sheep, which is slightly more pungent than that of swine, and, more so than this, that of goats, to which that of bears and of oxen is somewhat similar. That of bulls is stronger than these, but falls short of that of hyenas. This in turn falls short of that of the kallionymos, the sea scorpion and the sea turtle. Some have written that the bile of the wild goat benefits those suffering from nyctalopia. The biles of winged animals are all more pungent and more drying than those in quadrupeds, and among the winged animals themselves those of hens and partridges are better for medical use. Those of hawks and eagles are markedly pungent and are also erosive; for this reason they also appear verdigris-like in colour, and sometimes even black. Knowing, then, these differences among them, and knowing also which affections need to be dried more and which less, if you have tested any one bile whatsoever by its effects, you will be able to pass from these to the others by method, so as always to employ the one that suits the affection. For since the intensity of each power lies in conjecture, you must pass from some defined starting-point to the untested material, having learned the degrees of excess among them from what has been tested beforehand. And I have also gone through for you clear signs taken from the colour of the biles and the mixture of the animals.

[10.2.14] [14. On sweat.] Sweat. This too is one of the fluids generated in the body of the animal, and it has the same material and the same manner of generation as the urine. For both are generated from the fluid that is drunk, which is heated in the body and at the same time takes on some bilious substance. Sweat, however, has been worked up to a greater degree, having passed through all the intervening parts as far as the skin. Necessarily, though, both sweats and urines differ from one another according to the mixtures of the animals, which vary from one another both by nature and according to the ages, and not slightly also according to the preceding regimen. It is clear too, even if it is sometimes left unsaid, that the factor of the seasons of the year and of the present state [of the air], and further of the regions, produces no small difference in the bodies of animals. But for the sake of brevity in the account I am accustomed to comprise all such things under one heading, saying that they vary according to the mixture of the air that surrounds us. For this comprises the differences among the regions with respect to heat and cold, just as it does the seasons of the year and the present or the preceding state. Whenever, then, the account concerns urines or sweats or blood or fat or suet or any other of the things in the body, as we distinguish the differences among animals, one must understand the account as referring to healthy bodies, which are in the middle state of their own proper mixture. So too with sweat: that it shares in the quality called salty and briny, taste bears witness. For sweat, often running down into the mouth of people against their will, displays the said quality, and often it also displays along with it a distinct bitterness. Its colour too shows its nature. For just as natural urine is moderately pale yellow, so also is sweat. You will recognise this easily in those who bathe, when they are scraped down with the strigil without oil. For it collects in the hollow of the strigil, displaying the colour I have described and the taste, having the salty distinctly, but the bitter faintly. Now about urine the physicians have written even more than is fitting, because it collects in abundance every day for all people, both privately and publicly. About sweats, however, they have written either nothing or rather some over-curious things which belong to sorcery. And apart from such things some have recorded superfluous things which can be accomplished by means of other medical material. In the palaestras the sweat of those exercising is mixed with the dirt (pátos), and some of those who Atticise over-curiously call it konisalos; it contributes something to the plain dirt towards the dispersing of swellings contrary to nature. For the plain dirt has more of the repelling [power], but the dispersing quite faint; but after it receives the sweat of those exercising, it acquires much of the dispersing power. At any rate, for inflammations of the breasts such dirt applied by itself is a rather efficacious remedy. If it seems to you rather drier, anoint with henna oil, and if it is very dry indeed, soften it also with the henna oil. It is better, however, to choose not the dry but the soft. If henna oil is not at hand, it suffices to mix in good rose oil. This drug is also quite useful for women after childbirth who choose to quench the milk, when it has become, as it were, curdled in the breasts. Starting out from it you can also use it for other similar affections. I at any rate once used it also on a bubo and saw the swelling quickly subside.

[10.2.15] [15. On urine.] Urine. Its whole nature has already been discussed in the account of sweats. But it will be stated now as well that as great as the difference of the biles is among animals, so great is the difference also of the urines. All are hot in their powers, but that of the hotter animals more so, and that of the colder less. On human urine. Human urine is almost the weakest of all the other urines, except that of domestic pigs whose testicles they cut out. For the mixture of their whole body is similar to that of humans, and their urine is likewise weak. Strong, on the other hand, is that of the boars in the mountains, as is evident from its smell too, which is most pungent. And in all the other animals as well you can recognise its power by the smell. For tasting those urines is most loathsome, given that even the urine of boys a certain man notable in character and way of life could not bring himself to drink when he fell ill with the pestilential disease in Syria, during which many, having drunk urine, some of boys and some of men, were thought to have been saved by it. Human urine, then, is of cleansing power if anything else is, as many show, and the fullers among them, who clean out and wash off for us the dirty garments with it. Physicians too, having observed this power of it, scour off psora and lepra with it, and pour it over those ulcers that are full of much moisture, filth and impurity, and much more so when they have something putrefactive. They also inject urine into the private parts when these are so affected, and into ears that discharge pus. And they treat achores and pityra with it, pouring it over the head. We, however, have rather felt disgust at doing these things, being well supplied with other drugs for them. But ulcers on the toes, especially those from stubbing, once they have become free of inflammation, I myself have often healed with urine in slaves and country people setting off on a journey without a physician. For, placing a lint plug on the ulcer for them, then wrapping it round on the outside with a linen bandage and tying it, I told them, whenever they wished to urinate, to let the urine run down onto the toe and not to undo it until it was completely healed. For I also allowed it if I learned of anyone else in the countryside without a physician pouring urine over ulcers, when they are in the parts below the thorax down to the tips of the feet; but ulcers that arise about the head or on the face, these I was disgusted to let anyone pour urine over. The drug prepared with a boy's urine, however, which some call chrysocolla, since they use it for the soldering of gold, I declare to be the finest for ulcers that are hard to cure. It is made when a mortar has been constructed in the shape of a phiale out of red copper, having a pestle of the same material; into this the boy urinates and the pestle is turned round many times, so as to throw off something not only from the mortar but also from itself; and this is done over several days, until the urine acquires a honey-like consistency. This must be done in the sun; for it is rubbed off the copper more easily in such air; or, if there is no sun, the room should be warm in some other way. This drug, mixed with suitable ingredients, we use for the healing of malignant ulcers, as I said, as the best. For it has none of the loathsomeness belonging to urine poured down over the head and about certain other parts. As for actually drinking urine, what could one even say? Some physicians, indeed, have written about the thick and white matter that settles in urine, saying that it treats cases of erysipelas. Now those that are still fiery and truly erysipelas no drug among the hot and pungent ones can benefit. But those already cooled down by cooling agents both this and many other dispersing drugs can help. It may be used, then, when the erysipelas has formed not about the face or near it, but either on one of the limbs or on the back or the belly. To drink a boy's urine for the so-called orthopnoea is not necessary, since there are other drugs too which help this affection. And indeed someone who drank it was not rid of the affection, so that it does not have anything special beyond the others.

[10.2.16] [16. On saliva.] Saliva: whether one wishes to call it sielon, or sialon, or ptyelon, makes no difference to me. One must know, however, that its power differs both among the kinds of animals and, within each of them, according as the animal is healthy or sick, has eaten or drunk, or is without drink and fasting. For as with urine, the biles and sweat, so too spittle is weak in those who have eaten, but strong and pungent in those who have been excessively thirsty and excessively hungry. Midway between the two is that of those who have digested well but have not yet eaten or drunk. Accordingly, it is with this saliva that children's nurses too cure leichenes: they wet the little finger and then rub the affected skin. They do this often, so that the power derived from the saliva is preserved in the leichen during the time between applications. Many country people, too, chew wheat grains and apply them to boils, for it disperses them and concocts them quickly. And yet if the grains were moistened with water, they would not help in the same way. It is quite clear, then, that the saliva itself supplies the strength of the benefit. On soft bodies and those of children, however, they apply not wheat but bread, which they have chewed. All things chewed in this way disperse both bruises and the other ecchymoses, and more so when the bread has been chewed together with a little radish. By its whole substance spittle is most contrary to the beasts that kill human beings, as Nicander the poet also says somewhere. Someone who had promised to show me an incantation that kills scorpions spoke it once and spat upon the scorpion; next he spoke it a second time and spat again; then, when he had spoken it a third time and spat down upon it, the scorpion died. Later I myself saw, without the incantation, the scorpion die from the saliva alone, and suffer this very thing quickly with the spittle of people who were hungry and thirsty, slowly with that of people filled with foods and drinks, and proportionally with that of the others.

[10.2.17] [17. On the things generated in the body.] Other things contrary to nature are also generated in the body, which it is not seemly to mention. The stone in the bladder is generated there too, and some have written about it to the effect that it breaks up the stones in the bladder. This, then, has been judged false by experience. Whether it breaks up the stones in the kidneys at all, I have not even tried, since I have other approved drugs for this symptom. As for pus and all such things, I leave the discussion of them to those who are clever at such matters, together with certain sorceries. Dung, however, is one of the things generated in the body while the animals are in their natural condition, as is also the dirt in the ears; I shall therefore go through each of the two in turn.

[10.2.18] [18. On dung.] Dung: whether you choose to call it 'dung' (kopros) or 'excrement' (apopatēma) will make no difference. Know that this substance has a most dispersing power. That of human beings is loathsome on account of its foul smell. But that of oxen, goats and terrestrial crocodiles, and that of dogs when they have eaten bones, is not ill-smelling, and it has afforded sufficient experience not to us alone but also to the others among the earlier physicians. Asclepiades, for instance, who was surnamed Pharmakion, collected all the other compound drugs as well, so as to fill many books. He also often uses dung for many affections, mixing it not only into drugs applied externally but also into those taken in by the mouth.

[10.2.19] [19. On dog's dung.] I myself, at any rate, know it, having experienced the wonderful power both of human dung and of dog's dung. I shall tell you first about the dog's, which one of our teachers used continually. He gave a dog nothing but bones to eat for two days in succession, as a result of which the dung becomes hard and white and least ill-smelling. Taking this, then, he dried it, so that later, whenever he wished to use it, it could easily be ground fine. He used it for synanchai, for dysenteries and for the most chronic of ulcers. For synanchai he mixed it with the drugs that are suited to this affection in any case. In the case of dysenteric patients he mixed it with boiled milk into which the so-called pebbles (kachlēkes), red-hot, had been thrown, or, as I later came to do with iron because it is easy to procure, throwing this red-hot into milk that had first been well boiled. Some of the physicians, I do not know why, call such milk 'split' (schiston). For this ought not to be called so; rather, the name belongs to the cases in which we separate and split the whey from the cheesy part. But the physician ground some dry dog's dung and threw it, without its being noticed, into the milk that had the pebbles quenched in it, and he taught this to his most genuine pupils alone. Of these two uses of dog's dung, then, I have a very great deal of experience, as of a wonderful drug, just as I have of its use for the most malignant ulcers. For in those cases too he mixed a little dog's dung with the approved drugs, and the drug clearly became stronger than it had been by itself. And wherever there was need to disperse and dry something, he mixed it into those drugs as well.

[10.2.20] [20. On human dung.] Of human dung I have experience of the following kind. A certain man was repeatedly and severely troubled by inflammations in the region of the pharynx, so that he was in danger of being choked, and indeed he was compelled to undergo venesection because of this danger. Someone who met him promised to give him a trial of a drug, and asked to be called before the venesection whenever some one of the parts in the region of his pharynx should again become inflamed. And so, having been called, he then anointed the parts thoroughly with the drug and quickly cured the man. When it had worked once more, not only in his case but also in others similarly affected, the man who was repeatedly in danger of choking asked to learn the drug, offering a fee. He was both wealthy and liberal in the expenditure of money. When they had come to an agreement about the fee, the one selling the prescription said that the drug had its benefit through a certain antipathy, and that the antipathy consisted in the person being treated not knowing what it is compounded of. He therefore bade him send another to learn it in his stead, whoever seemed to him most trustworthy, and that this man, wishing [to learn it], should swear to give the prescription of the drug to no one so long as the seller himself lived. In this way, then, after the death of the one who had shown it, the man who had learned it cures not only his own man but others as well; and to me, though I did not even ask for it, he willingly gave the prescription of the drug. It was the dry dung of a child, ground smooth with Attic honey. The child whose dung they were going to take was fed, as the one who gave me the drug himself showed, on a diet of lupins, these being the kind commonly eaten, together with well-baked oven bread containing moderate amounts of salt and leaven. He also gave it old wine to drink. All these were moderate in quantity, so that the child might digest them perfectly. Having used such a regimen on the first day, he did not yet take up the dung on the following day; but on that day, having again fed it in the same way, he took what was excreted on the third day, and, drying it, used it in a manner similar to the dog's dung, as has been said before. He said that the man who had taught him chose the lupins because he avoided the foul smell [produced] by the other foods, but that he himself, for the sake of trial, had often fed it fowl's flesh and partridge's flesh well boiled in water or in plain broth, and the drug had worked no less. These, then, are the things I have to tell you about dog's and human dung.

[10.2.21] [21. On wolf dung.] Someone used to give the dung of wolves to drink to those suffering from colic, not only during the paroxysms but also in the intervals, at least to those who suffered without inflammation. I saw some of them no longer seized by the affection, and those who were seized never again afterwards suffering severely, nor even after a short time. He too preferred to take the whiter dung of wolves, which is excreted when they have eaten bones. I marvelled at it, that even when hung on as an amulet it often gave clear benefit. This man used to take dung that had not even fallen onto the ground, and this is not difficult to do. For that animal has by nature, like the dog, the habit of raising one of its hind legs to urinate and to defecate against something projecting from the ground. Wolf dung is therefore often found in the summer season on thorny plants, on certain shrubs, on barriers (κλείθροις) and on well-grown plants. In their dung there is also found some part of the very bones of the devoured animal which has escaped digestion just as it escaped chewing; this too he pounded and ground fine and gave to colic sufferers to drink. And if the person was a fastidious one (καθαρότητος), he mixed in salt and pepper or something of that kind. He gave it for the most part in a wine thin in consistency, but sometimes also in water. As for the portion of the dung hung around the flanks of the patient, he directed that it should have a suspensory cord, preferably made of wool not from any chance sheep. For he said that the wool of a sheep torn apart by the wolf is much better as regards being suited to such a use. If such wool were not to hand, he directed that the strap wound round the flanks, and also the very thing that is to enclose the dung, be made of deerskin. We too, putting some of the dung into a little pot as large as the largest bean, hung it on some people for the sake of trial, and we marvelled on seeing most of them manifestly benefited. We made on the little pot two things like ears, through which the strap was passed. This, then, I say by the way, in case anyone is going to put trust also in things hung on in this manner; and I mean this in the sense that what is hung on is a substance, not barbarous names, as some of the sorcerers are accustomed to use, since I have also made trial of other substances acting in a similar way upon other affections. But this is not the time to speak about them; let us therefore return to the matter in hand.

[10.2.22] [22. On goat's dung.] I have mentioned human, dog's and wolf's dung, but not yet the others, although several more still remain besides those already discussed, some of which have a very frequent use and others a rarer one. The dung we use most frequently is that of goats; these droppings are specifically called spyrathoi. They are of a pungent and dispersing power, so that they are suitable for indurated (scirrhous) swellings not only of the spleen, for which many physicians use such dung most frequently, but also of other parts. I myself used it on a knee that had a chronic swelling, hard to resolve: I ordered it to be applied as a poultice with oxycrate, barley meal being added to the dung, and the man was wonderfully benefited. The man on whom this was done was one of the rustics. Another rustic too has since been benefited in the same way, using it similarly for similar swellings, not only on the knee but also on other parts. For the drug is too pungent to treat town women or children, or soft-fleshed people in general. But the particular use of all drugs will be discussed in the work on their composition. We also use goat's dung in many ways in the case of the dropsical and the splenic. Moreover, when burnt it becomes more fine-particled, though not clearly more pungent. Hence it is suitable for alopeciai and for all the conditions that require cleansing drugs, such as leprai, psorai and leichenes, and the others of this kind. It is also mixed into dispersing poultices, such as those for parotids and for buboes that have become chronic. For its power, both unburnt and burnt, is cleansing and dispersing, and its dispersing quality is not slight. At any rate, a certain physician of those who practise in the fields and villages used it with vinegar against the bites of vipers, and still more against those of the other venomous beasts, and saved a great many. This same physician also gave spyrathoi in wine to the jaundiced to drink, and used them against female flux, applying them together with frankincense. The best physician must know all such things, but must select the better ones, especially in the case of town-dwelling and distinguished men, for whom I would never have used such a drug, having an abundance of very many better ones. Nevertheless the need for such things does sometimes arise on journeys, at hunts and during a stay in the country, when none of the better remedies is at hand, or when the person is a hard-fleshed rustic, like an ass. For many such people in the countryside are fit to drink spyrathoi. And what was said in the preceding sections about urines, biles and salivas, remember now too: the general and common power is the same in all kinds of dung, but it varies according to the mixtures of the animals. For the dung of animals drier in mixture is also more drying, just as that of hotter animals is more heating; but none cools, just as none moistens. There would also be a great difference arising from the nature of what they have eaten, and for this reason the difference is greater in humans than in the other animals, because this animal uses the most varied food. For what likeness is there between those who have eaten garlic and onions and those who have eaten gourd, if it so happened? The spyrathoi of a goat, by contrast, would differ a little from one another according to the pastures, but not nearly as much as human dung does.

[10.2.23] [23. On cow dung.] In the same way the dungs of oxen also show little difference among themselves, these too being of a drying power. They also have the drawing power, as they show by benefiting the stings of bees and wasps. These, however, may possibly also be benefited in virtue of the peculiarity of the whole substance. A certain physician in Mysia on the Hellespont, one experienced in drugs, used to smear the dropsical with cow dung and lay them down in the sun. This same man also applied it to the inflamed parts of country people, taking it moist in spring, when the oxen graze on the grass. It is quite clear that this is much more moderate in power than the other. By the other I mean that which follows the eating of chaff. For this is intermediate between the one mentioned and that which follows the feeding on bitter vetch. It is evident, then, that just as the dung from grassy pasture is suited to inflammations, so this one is suited to the dropsical. One must know, however, that all such drugs suit the hard bodies of country people, diggers and reapers and those who perform similarly strenuous work; and on this basis the physician in Mysia also used it for choirades and for all scirrhous swellings, applying it as a poultice with vinegar.

[10.2.24] [24. On sheep's dung.] This same man also used sheep's dung, moistening it with vinegar, against acrochordons, myrmeciae, thymi, and the hard boils called 'corns'. He also brought burns to a scar by mixing this dung with rose-oil cerate. And indeed he treated people who had been burned in the same way also by means of goats' dung, mixing a very small quantity of this too with a bulk of the cerate many times greater. And in general it was his particular study to treat everything by means of the remedies easily procured in the countryside, among which, evidently, are herbs and shrubs, and, of trees, the shoots, the sprouts, the soft leaves, the fruits and the barks; about these more will be said in the work on easily procured remedies.

[10.2.25] [25. On pigeon dung.] The dung, then, of grazing pigeons (for so some people call them, distinguishing them from the domestic ones) I myself also use very frequently, as a heating drug, for many purposes. Pounded and sifted dry together with cress seed, I apply it instead of mustard in those who need reddening. It is quite clear that by this I mean all those who have become chronic in such affections as sciatica, hemicrania, darkenings of vision and vertigos with darkening, chronic headaches, and chronic pains in the sides or shoulder blades or the tendon or the loins; and besides these, nephritic and coeliac conditions and podagric arthritides, at least when there is not yet any formation of calluses in their joints. Now this dung has nothing ill-smelling about it, especially when dried. For this reason we also use it in the cities in many ways, mixing it now with one drug, now with another.

[10.2.26] [26. On hen's dung.] Having seen the man in Mysia using the dung of hens in the case of those choking from eating mushrooms, I myself also used it in the case of some people in the city, administering it in every case ground smooth in three or four cyathi of oxycrate and oxymel, and it plainly gave benefit, and quickly. For a little later those who were choking vomited a phlegmatic, very thick humour, upon which they were completely relieved of the symptom. This dung is less hot than that of pigeons. And the doctor in Mysia also gave hens' dung to chronic colic sufferers to drink in honeyed wine [oinomeli]; if this was not to hand, in vinegar or in wine mixed with water. You must remember the general account concerning all animals: that both in respect of what is contained in their bodies, fluid and solid, and in respect of their parts, there is a very great difference between those called mountain animals and those of the plains, marshes and lakes, and those of the house. For animals that exercise are always drier than those that do not exercise, and those that use drier and hotter foods are drier than those that use moister and colder ones. In the case of pigeons, at any rate, through constantly using their dung I have always found that of the pigeons reared about houses falling very far short of that of the mountain foraging pigeons. And I have found that of hens, too, to be much weaker in the case of those shut in and fed on bran, and not a little stronger in the case of those that forage in the country, in the farmyards and outside them.

[10.2.27] [27. On the dung of geese and storks.] The dung of geese is useless on account of its great pungency. I reckon that of hawks and eagles to be so too. Moreover, the difficulty of procuring all material of this kind is a reason to avoid it. Taking this very difficulty as their starting point, some attest strong powers to such materials, in the belief that they will not easily be refuted; such are those who have written that the dung of storks cures epileptics. And yet this dung, although it is much easier to procure than many of the other things they write about, is nevertheless superfluous, besides the fact that what has been written about it is not even true. At any rate someone who was persuaded by those who write such things drank this dung and was in no way benefited. Indeed, even before any trial, those who write these things reveal the worthlessness of what they promise. For while people suffer from dyspnoea in many ways, they add in their account neither what suits all of them nor what suits these particular people or this particular person. Some of those who have written go further and say that such things are remedies not simply for dyspnoeas but for orthopnoeas: stork dung, the blood of an owl, human urine, and other things more absurd than these. They do not know that a phlegmatic and viscous humour obstructing the bronchia of the lung is the cause of this affection; that the cure consists in evacuating it; that its evacuation takes place when it is brought up with coughing; and that this cannot happen unless a more pungent drug is drunk many times. But these people are such triflers, or charlatans, or I know not what to call them, that they claim each of these absurd potions, drunk once, rids the patients of their dyspnoea. Yet this would not be accomplished in a single attempt even if someone could let a probe down into the lung and remove the impacted humour with it. It would have been better, then, for them to say not that this particular blood or urine cures dyspnoea if it is drunk once, but if it is drunk repeatedly. And better still to say not that it will cure in every case and by all means, even if drunk continually, but that it has cured many, and has benefited many others without fully ridding them of the disease. But let us now leave these people and go on to what follows in the account. Since all dung has the pungent and dispersing quality, and one has such a power to a greater or lesser degree than another, the particular differences arise among them, and for this reason some treat this affection better and others that one.

[10.2.28] [28. On the dung of mice.] Thus, at any rate, they have also written that the droppings of mice treat alopeciae, and there was a certain physician who used the compounded drug prepared with mouse dung for this affection. And someone else ordered the members of the household to apply to a child who needed it a suppository prepared with mouse dung. At this all who heard it laughed: when there are so many things which, applied to the seat, rouse the intestine to excretion, he passed over them all and came to the dung of mice. For one ought truly to be ashamed of such things, and of bringing them to trial, when everyone condemns as a meddler and a charlatan whoever does and says these things. Concerning the dung of mice, then, this too is sufficient.

[10.2.29] [29. On the dung of land crocodiles and of starlings.] The dung of land crocodiles, those small ones that creep low along the ground, has been made a thing of value by luxury-loving women. It will not suffice them to make the skin of the face bright and taut with the other drugs, numerous as these are, but they add to them the crocodiles' dung as well. Similar to it is also the dung of starlings, when they eat rice alone. It is quite clear, then, that such dungs have a cleansing and a drying power, each of them moderate, and that the dungs of the starlings are much more moderate and fainter. The dung of the crocodiles, however, just as it is naturally apt to remove ephelis from the face, so it is also apt to take away alphoi and leichenes.

[10.2.30] [30. On the dirt of human beings.] Dirt is generated not only over the whole skin of the body but also in the ears. Because there is so little of it, however, it is hard to procure, and for this reason nothing has been written about it, except that the dirt from the ear is suitable for paronychiae; and this is the only kind that can be obtained by itself. For the dirt that accumulates on the whole skin is cleansed off in the baths and the palaestrae, and it too contributes something to what is called patos, which has been discussed earlier. Its generation also shows its nature. For if dirt comes to be as the coarse-particled and earthy residue of what is evacuated through imperceptible transpiration, it is of a drying power, and has something of heat as well. The dirt that accumulates on the fleeces of sheep, however, from which they make what is called oesypum, is of a concocting power, similar to butter; and it also has a slight dispersing [power]. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK XI. Preface. Most of the parts in animals are common to all of them, yet none is so common as flesh. For every animal has it. It has blood in man, in all quadrupeds and birds, in snakes, lizards, tortoises and other such animals. It is without blood in all the shellfish and in not a few of the aquatic animals, as also in those that live in the earth itself. Flesh is also chiefly what is eaten of animals. For indeed the greatest bulk of the viscera too consists of the flesh in them. Some physicians call the flesh in these parenchyma, because, as they suppose, the blood poured out of the veins congeals around all the vessels, and they give the name flesh only to that in the muscles. Now one ought not to quarrel about names, as we always say, but one must cultivate knowledge of the things themselves. Laying claim to this knowledge throughout, we shall next set out in order all that we know about the parts, particular and common, in each animal, having learned some things from experience and others from reason. We shall make our beginning from what is properly called flesh.

[9.1.1] On earths. [1. On the differences of earth.] Since two things are signified by the name 'earth', it is necessary first to distinguish them, for the sake of clarity in what is to be said. One of them is familiar to all the Greeks. For when they sow wheat or barley or any other of the seeds that are called 'Demetrian', they say that the earth must be moderately moist; and when they plant vines or fig trees or olives or any other trees, they bid one guard against earth that is extremely without moisture and dry, and against earth that is moist and muddy. For indeed they call earth kneaded with liquid 'mud', and those who have written on agriculture, in treating the differences of lands, speak of black-earth, clayey and sandy lands as distinguished from one another. They also call 'oily' the earth from which the mud becomes viscous, and another, disposed in the contrary way to this, non-oily, producing a mud that is, as one might say, friable. This, then, is one meaning of the name 'earth', familiar to all. The other is familiar only to the philosophers, since they say that the elements of bodies are earth, water, air and fire. For they call the extremely dry and cold body 'earth'. According to these men, then, none of these composite bodies is elemental earth, yet they say that they contain a very great deal of earth, as for example adamant and rocks; and the harder they are in body, the more earthy they say they are, the opposite of the farmers. For the latter do not call the harder consistency of bodies more earthy; rather, they call such things stones and rocks, most unsuitable for farming, and they say that the most exact earth is that which is furthest in consistency from rock, inasmuch as they find fault even with the clayey and the sandy for most purposes. According to the meaning current among the philosophers, then, the differences of earth will be defined by three genera. For one kind of it is stone, another is a mined body, and the third is the farmed earth, there having arisen disagreement among them concerning the mined bodies that are fused, such as copper, tin and lead. For some people say that these contain more not of earth but of water. All other men, however, call 'earth' only that substance which, kneaded with liquid, becomes mud. It is of this that I too have now decided to state the differences, adding only this further point: that the aforementioned division of earthy bodies into stones, mined things and farmed earth was stated without the bodies that are properly called 'natural'. When these are added, all woods too, and many parts of fruits, as also of animals, will be said to be earthy in substance: parts of fruits, olive stones, grape pips, and the husks of nuts and of pine cones, and many others of this kind; of animals, the bones, the horns and the teeth. But concerning the parts in plants that are earthy and hard, something has been said somewhere before, and something may also be said now; concerning those in animals it will be said next in order, after I have first gone through the kinds of earth. For you are at liberty to call them differences, or kinds, or genera. By these I mean stones, mined bodies, and the earth that dissolves into mud. And first I shall state the differences of the earth so named by all the Greeks, which has this in common: on coming near water it dissolves at once and becomes mud. For what is so called among the philosophers has a meaning not common to all, but familiar to them alone.

[9.1.2] [2. On the differences of what is customarily called earth.] I said that it is customary among all Greeks to call earth that which, when thrown into liquid, at once dissolves and becomes mud. Of this, then, one kind is that which men cultivate, and it has certain differences according to its own proper account: one kind is oily and viscid, and this is in every case also black in colour; the other is more friable and non-oily, which they call clay, and this too is somewhat whiter. These differences are the most opposed; the others lie between them, either approaching one of the two more than the other, while some even seem to be exactly in the middle, standing at an equal distance from both. Other differences of earth arise from the admixture of bodies of another kind, in so far as earths are stony and sandy. People separate the admixed substance from such earths by soaking them and kneading them up with much water until they make the whole liquid. For when this settles, everything of the stony and sandy kind that was borne along in it sinks to the bottom, and the pure earth floats on top. Something of this sort is done with the Lemnian earth, which some call Lemnian red ochre and certain others Lemnian seal, because of the seal sacred to Artemis that is impressed upon it. The priestess takes this earth with a certain local rite, in which no animals are sacrificed but wheat and barley are given to the place in return, and brings it to the city. She kneads it up with water, makes a liquid mud, and stirs this vigorously; then, having let it settle, she first removes the water on the surface. Next she takes the oily part of the earth beneath it, leaving behind only the stony and sandy sediment, which is also useless, and dries the oily mud until it reaches the consistency of soft wax. Taking small portions of this, she impresses on them the sacred seal of Artemis, and then dries them again in the shade until they are made completely free of moisture. So is produced the drug known to all physicians, the Lemnian seal. For, as I said, some call it so because of the seal impressed upon it, just as some, because of its colour, call it Lemnian red ochre. It has the same colour as red ochre, but differs from it in not staining when touched, as that does. And [it is found] on the hill in Lemnos which is entirely tawny in colour, on which there is neither tree nor rock nor plant, but only earth of this sort. Three differences of it are found: one is the aforementioned sacred earth, which no one touches except the priestess; the second is another, that of true red ochre, which carpenters use most of all; the third is that of the cleansing earth, which those who wash linens and garments use if they wish. Having read in Dioscorides and certain others that goat's blood is mixed with the Lemnian earth, and that from the mud produced by this mixture the priestess moulds and seals what they call Lemnian seals, I myself was eager to inquire into the proportion of the mixture. So, just as I travelled to Cyprus for the sake of its mines, and to Coele Syria, which is part of Palestine, for the sake of asphalt and certain other things there worth inquiring into, so too I did not hesitate to sail to Lemnos, to see how much of the blood is mixed with the earth. On the second occasion, when I was to reach Rome from Asia travelling on foot through Thrace and Macedonia, I first sailed from Alexandria Troas to Lemnos, having found a ship putting out for Thessalonica, the ship-master having agreed to put in at Lemnos first. He did put in, but not at the city where he should have. For I did not even know at first that there were two cities on the island; I supposed that Lemnos, like Samos, Chios, Cos, Andros, Tenos and all the islands of the Aegean, had a single city bearing the same name as the whole island. When I left the ship, I learned that the city was called Myrina, and that neither the place associated with Philoctetes nor the hill sacred to Hephaestus lay in the territory of that city, but in that of the other, called Hephaestias, and that that city was not even near Myrina. As the ship-master could not wait for me, I put off seeing Hephaestias until another time, when I should come from Rome to Asia. And this was accomplished for me just as I had hoped and intended. For when I had crossed from Italy into Macedonia and, having travelled through almost the whole of it on foot, arrived at Philippi, which is a city bordering on Thrace, I went down from there to the nearby sea, a hundred and twenty stades distant, and sailed first to Thasos, about two hundred stades, and from there to Lemnos, seven hundred, and then again from Lemnos the same seven hundred to Alexandria Troas. I have written about the voyage and the stades on purpose, so that if anyone wishes, like me, to see Hephaestias for himself, he may know its position and prepare himself accordingly for the voyage. For on the whole island of Lemnos, Hephaestias lies in the part towards the east, and Myrina in the part towards the west. And as for what the poet says of Hephaestus, 'he fell in Lemnos', the myth seems to me to rest on the nature of the hill. For it appears very like something burnt, both in its colour and because nothing grows on it. To this hill, then, the priestess came at the very time when I landed on the island; she cast a certain number of wheat and barley grains onto the earth, performed certain other things according to the local worship, and filled a whole wagon with the earth. Having brought it to the city, she prepared, as I said just now, the much-celebrated Lemnian seals. It seemed good to me, then, to inquire whether they had received any account of he-goat's or goat's blood having ever formerly been mixed with this earth. At this question all who heard it laughed, and they were not ordinary men, but very well educated, both in other matters and in the whole local history. Indeed I also received a book from one of them, written formerly by one of the local men, in which he taught the entire use of the Lemnian earth; whence I too did not hesitate to make trial of the drug, taking twenty thousand seals. The man who gave me the book, who was counted among the foremost of Hephaestias, himself used the drug for many purposes. He used the seal for wounds, both old and hard to cicatrise, for viper bites and bites of venomous animals generally, and for deadly drugs, not only giving it beforehand but also afterwards. He said too that he had experience of the drug made with juniper berries, into which the Lemnian earth is also put, which provokes vomiting if someone drinks the remedy against it while the deadly drug is still in the belly. We ourselves have experience of this in the case of the sea-hare and cantharides: persons who suspected that they had taken something of the sort vomited everything at once on taking the drug made with the Lemnian seal, and afterwards suffered none of the symptoms that follow the sea-hare and cantharides, although the administration of the deadly drugs had been established. Whether the drug made with juniper berries and the Lemnian earth has the same power against the other deadly drugs too, those called poisons, is unclear to me. But the man from Hephaestias went so far as to declare that it heals even the bite of a rabid dog, when drunk in diluted wine and applied to the ulcer in very pungent vinegar. He said also that in vinegar it heals the bites of the other venomous animals, with the leaves of herbs laid on externally, herbs which we have learnt act contrary to putrefactions; he praised most of all skordion, then the slender centaury, then prasion. Moreover, whenever I used the Lemnian earth on malignant and putrefactive ulcers, it helped greatly. The use is made according to the degree of the ulcer's badness. For the foul-smelling, very flabby and dirty ulcer tolerates the Lemnian earth dissolved in the most pungent vinegar to a muddy consistency, in the same way as the troches, of which different people use different ones, I mean those of Polyeidus, Pasion and Andron, and this one now mentioned, which is called the Betinus. For all these, drying strongly, benefit malignant ulcers, being diluted sometimes with sweet wine, sometimes with siraion, sometimes with honeyed wine [oinomeli], sometimes with some of the white wines or the tawny or yellow ones, as need requires; for these matters will be determined elsewhere. Likewise they are sometimes diluted with vinegar, and with wine or water or oxymel, or oxycrate and melikraton. And the Lemnian earth too, diluted with each of the substances mentioned, is a drug suited both to the agglutination of fresh wounds and to the healing of chronic, hard-to-cicatrise or malignant ones. So likewise is all other medicinal earth. For it will be necessary to distinguish, just as earlier we separated from the elemental earth, in which the stones were also included, the earth that dissolves into mud, so now to separate from the cultivated earth the medicinal. There is no harm in so naming the earth that we use for treatments, although of the cultivated earth too the oily kind is useful for the treatment of all parts that need to be dried; whence in Alexandria and Egypt many use it, many by their own choice, many as a result of dreams. I saw, at any rate, in Alexandria, some dropsical persons and some suffering from the spleen using the mud of the Egyptian earth. And many, anointing their shins, thighs, forearms, upper arms, backs, sides and chests with the mud of this earth, were clearly benefited. In the same way this mud helps old inflammations and lax swellings, so that I know some who had become swollen in their whole habit from immoderate evacuation through haemorrhoids to have been evidently benefited. And some have completely cured chronic pains fixed in some part with this mud; for all earth has a drying power. For its body is by nature dry, and when it is entirely unmixed with fiery substance it dries with the least biting; and its having been washed contributes to this.

[9.1.3] [3. On the washing of earth.] Every earth is washed in the same manner as was stated before concerning the Lemnian. First it is kneaded up with water that shows no trace of any medicinal quality. Then, when the mud has settled and the water has been removed from the top, the [layer] beneath it is next separated from the stony and sandy matter that settles to the bottom. And if you also have a trained gustatory sense, you will yourself be an exact judge of which earth must be washed and which not. For some do not need washing, while others need to be washed twice or three times. The Lemnian, then, you receive ready, washed once already by the priestess, and not needing to be washed a second time.

[9.1.4] [4. On Samian earth.] Samian earth does not even need to be washed. Of its two kinds we use the one which they also call the ‘Samian star’ more, for spittings of blood from whatever source they happen to arise, just as we also use the Lemnian seal. By the same power these also benefit haemorrhages from the womb and the so-called female flux, and indeed also dysenteric ulcerations before the ulcers have become putrefactive. Physicians are accustomed to call such conditions ‘nomai’ (spreading sores), from the putrefaction's spreading (nemesthai) to the adjoining parts and destroying them together with the part first damaged. I have sometimes used Lemnian earth in such cases too, and it clearly helped, both injected through the anus and drunk, the ulcers having first been washed out, as we are accustomed to do, first with rather undiluted honey-water (melikraton) and second with brine. It was injected in plantain juice and drunk in watery oxycrate. Lemnian earth appears to have a power more active than the Samian by no small amount. Hence parts that are already inflamed do not tolerate its power, but are clearly roughened, especially when the person is soft-fleshed. By Samian earth, however, not only is none of the parts in that state exacerbated, but they are even soothed, especially the warmer and looser parts, such as the breasts, the testicles and the glands. In such cases you would suitably use this earth after levigating it with water, mixing in as much good rose oil as will keep the drug from drying out once it is mixed in. What is prepared in this way is also good for the other inflammations that are hot, for incipient buboes, for gouty fluxes, and in general wherever we wish to cool moderately while also soothing. It thus plainly appears that the power of Samian earth is moderately cooling. Its substance is also somewhat airier when compared with the Lemnian, as its lightness shows. From these signs, then, test every other medicinal earth too. By signs I mean lightness and heaviness in consistency, roughness and smoothness in taste, and in addition the glutinous and the cleansing. For the Samian star is glue-like and viscid, and the Lemnian seal also has a little of this quality. Selinusian earth and Chian have a cleansing power, and a moderate one; this is why some women use them on the face. It was shown in the third book of the Therapeutic Method that everything slightly cleansing is suitable for the fleshing of ulcers, and, if it also dries, good for cicatrization as well. Most suitable of these for superficial ulcers and for burns are those which, besides drying without biting, neither clearly heat nor cool. Hence Selinusian and Chian earth are excellent drugs for burn ulcers. For these need drugs that cleanse most moderately, without evident heating or cooling, and this belongs to Selinusian, to Chian and to Samian earth. It has been said that there is also a kind of this last, called the star, which exceeds the other earth in having something viscid and glutinous. Hence, both for other ulcers and for burns, it is no match for the others, that is, for those which have nothing glutinous. For the glutinous makes the substance more clogging, so that it does not cleanse, provided, of course, that no other pungency is present in the viscid and glutinous body, as there is in birdlimes (ixoi). Chian and Selinusian earth, however, fall short of Samian for incipient inflammations around the breasts, the testicles and buboes. Nevertheless they are not unfitting when none of the other drugs that act to the highest degree is at hand. Kimolian earth, being of mixed power, has something cooling and also something slightly dispersing. Hence when washed it lays the latter aside, while without washing it acts with both its powers, just as many of the compound drugs both disperse and repel. In accordance with the nature of the liquids mixed with it, it plainly displays each of its powers. For mixed with repelling and cooling substances, it makes the mud formed from it and them cooling and repelling, and mixed with dispersing substances it makes the mud dispersing too. Thus it is also fitting for burns, and some laymen smear it on, kneading it with vinegar on the spot. In such use the vinegar must not be too pungent; if it is, it is better to mix water with it. Remember that this is common to all light earth: all of them benefit burns when smeared on immediately with vinegar or oxycrate, preventing blistering. In this matter, look also at the nature of the body being treated, whether it is soft or hard, knowing always as a universal rule that soft bodies do not bear the power of strong drugs, while hard ones do. These matters, however, do not belong to the present treatise; they will be discussed more fully in the works On the Composition of Drugs and On Readily Procured Remedies. The present exposition has from the beginning been concerned to find the universal powers of drugs. Whoever attends to these will have very great resource for their use in particular cases, having of course also learned the method of using them. So it is no longer fitting to be lengthy, but only to recall now too what was said before: earth itself, unmixed with any other heterogeneous substance, is of a power drying without biting. Since it is impossible to find any body that is precisely unmixed, one should further consider the mixture of the attributes that accompany it, according to the differences in lightness and heaviness and those in taste. If it gives an indication of some astringency, it has taken on as much cooling as it has astringency. If something of pungency appears, it has as much heat as it has pungency. Likewise one should consider the light and the heavy earth. The light earth becomes such when it partakes of abundant airy substance in its mixture throughout itself. The heavy earth, the more it is such, the purer is the earth it consists of. It is proper to earth not to melt when it comes near fire, as lead and tin, silver and gold do. So when you hear of argyritis or chrysitis or sideritis earth (for some so name the earths taken from mines), do not suppose that the silver or the gold or the iron is blended with the earth throughout. Rather, small particles mixed in lie alongside small particles of the earth: of gold in chrysitis, of silver in argyritis, of iron in sideritis. In the furnaces these are melted by the fire and come together with one another. In the same way the earth containing glass is sandy, for small flakes of such substance are often found chiefly in sand. Those experienced in these matters, on seeing such sands, know how much glass they can gather from them. Many small flakes of gold are also found in certain sands. But those occupied with these things do not extract the gold and the glass from every sand. They select, of course, those that yield the most at little expense, since spending much in the furnaces to obtain little of the collected substance seems unprofitable to them. For this reason, although many sands contain flakes of gold and glass, the experts in these matters do not resort to all of them. By the same reasoning they do not extract copper or silver or iron or tin or lead from every earth either. Nor, when they have separated each of the metals mentioned from the earth mixed with it, is what remains like the other earths. These, as I said, are customarily so named by all Greeks, and they have as their common sign that they are soaked and readily dissolve into mud. For the residue of the earth in mines becomes stony, both unmeltable and unsoakable. By ‘being soaked’ (tengesthai) I mean becoming moist through the whole substance, and by ‘being wetted’ (brechesthai) becoming moist on the outer surface only, the moisture not penetrating into the depth. In this way mined cadmia too is produced, being stony and unsoakable. But about such bodies we shall speak next. Now I shall return to medicinal earth. Because it readily dissolves into mud when soaked in water, it is called earth; and because we have need of it as of other drugs, it might reasonably be called pharmakitis. Yet some call only the earth named ampelitis pharmakitis, either as being the only earth of this sort or as having the more active medicinal power, which is in fact true. It is called ampelitis not because it is better to plant vines (ampeloi) in it, but because, smeared around the vines, it destroys the worms that are generated on them, which our vine-dressers call sknipes. These are generated at the onset of spring, when the vines bud, together with that swelling part of them from which the shoot grows, which they call the ‘eye’. By gnawing through these eyes the sknipes do the vines no small harm, which is why the experts in these matters smear around the bases of these eyes. It is on this account that such earth is called ampelitis and pharmakitis, and by destroying the sknipes it shows how much medicinal power it possesses. It stands far apart from the other kinds of earth which we use for cures, coming already close to the stony. Hence you will find it mixed into the recipes of drugs where it is fitting to dry and disperse something. For it does not have the non-biting, moderate and soothing character that Chian, Samian and Selinusian earth have. It has also been said before about Kimolian earth that it is a little stronger than these, but is itself still non-biting, especially if it is washed. Cretan earth is also somewhat similar to these, but it is quite weak, having much of the airy. It does, however, have the cleansing quality, which is why people brighten dirty silverware with it. So you may use this one too for the purposes for which we said earlier that the other non-bitingly cleansing earths are suitable. Lemnian earth has a stronger power than all of these, for some astringency also belongs to it. Eretrian earth is stronger still than Lemnian, though not so strong as to bite. If it is washed, it becomes quite moderate, like those mentioned before. This earth can be washed not once only but also twice or three times, as Kimolian can. Moreover, some burn it, thereby making it more fine-particled and more pungent, so that it passes over to the dispersing power. If it is washed after being burnt, it leaves its pungency behind in the water while keeping the fine-particled quality from the roasting, and so becomes more drying. Hence, since by the general account all unburnt earth is useful for ulcers, the earth washed after burning is still more useful, and serves also for ulcers that are hard to flesh and hard to cicatrize. Of its two kinds, the one ash-coloured in hue is better than the very white one. There is also another earth called pnigitis, resembling Kimolian in its whole power but differing in colour. For it is black like ampelitis, and it has the viscid and glutinous quality no less than Samian earth, and sometimes even more. During this great plague there was also given to us another earth, from the Armenia that borders Cappadocia, more drying and pale yellow in colour. The man who gave it called it a stone, not an earth, and it is very easily levigated, like quicklime (titanos); by this name I mean, of course, burnt rock. And just as nothing sandy is carried in quicklime, so nothing sandy is carried in the Armenian earth either. After it has been crushed with the pestle in the mortar, it is as smooth and free of stone as quicklime and the Samian star, though not as light as the star. Hence it is also more condensed than the star and less airy, and for this reason it gives those who look at it carelessly the impression of being a stone. For present purposes it makes no difference whether we call it stone or earth, so long as we know that it dries to the highest degree. For it is most fitting for dysenteries and fluxes of the belly, for spitting of blood and catarrh, and in addition for the putrefactive ulcers in the mouth. It also greatly benefits those who have a flux from the head to the chest, so that it strongly helps those who are continually short of breath from such a cause. It also benefits those who suffer from phthoē, for it dries their ulcer so that they no longer cough. This holds unless they err considerably in their regimen, or the ambient air suddenly changes to a bad mixture. We have often observed fistulas, not only in other parts but also at the anus, being drawn together and closed by the drying drug alone, without inserting a collyrium to remove the filth or the callus of the fistula. It seems to me that the same thing happens with the ulcer in the lung. For this too appears to be helped in the same way by drying drugs, when it is moderate and not very large. As a result, some of those who had such ulcers seemed to be completely rid of them. Of those who travelled from Rome to Libya for this reason, some were fully convinced that they were healthy and lived without complaint for some years. Then at some later time, when they lived more carelessly, a relapse of the disease occurred. These people, as I said, the Armenian clod (bōlos) plainly helped, even though they were living in Rome, and it helped still more those continually short of breath. In this great plague, similar in form to the one that occurred in Thucydides' time, all who drank this drug were quickly cured. All whom it did not help died, nor were they helped by anything else, which also makes it clear that it failed to help only those who were incurable. It is drunk with wine of thin consistency, mixed moderately if the person is entirely without fever or only slightly feverish, but very watery if he is more feverish. Plague fevers, however, are not vehement in their heat. As for ulcers that need drying, what need is there even to say how great a power this Armenian clod has? As I said, you may call it a stone, as the man who gave it named it, or an earth, as I would say, since it is soaked by liquids.

[9.2.1] On stones. [1. On the stones that act by their qualities.] Among naturally occurring bodies are also the stones (hai lithoi, feminine), which differ from what is customarily called earth in not being soaked through. They have powers, some according to the specific property of their whole substance, others according to their active qualities. How these differ from one another has been stated before. Now, then, let our discussion be about those that act according to their active qualities, in which the method of their use itself also lies. For it was shown that the powers according to the specific property of the whole substance are without method and without reason, and are known by experience alone. For why this particular stone, when it touches a bleeding wound, checks the flow, we do not know; but why they put the stone called haematites into ophthalmic preparations we do know, for such a thing is a discovery of reason. At any rate, if you rub it down with water on an ophthalmic whetstone to the thickness of honey and choose to taste it, you will perceive an astringent power. And you have learned that inflammations that are still increasing, especially in sinewy parts, must be repelled with astringent drugs; and that when the blood no longer flows into the part, one must mix discutient drugs with the astringent ones, and pass over gradually to these alone. About such powers in stones, then, we shall speak, having first recalled what we went through at very great length in the work against those who censure people who commit solecisms in speech. For some of these do not permit one to say lithos in the masculine; but if you say 'throw the stone (ton lithon) at the dog', they cry out as though they themselves had been struck on the head with a stone; just as, if someone says ton dryn ('the oak', in the masculine), they shout as though they had been struck with a piece of wood. If, then, someone persuaded by them should remodel the names customary among physicians, saying hē lithos haimatitis, pyritis, galaktitis and schistē, he will be condemned as over-fastidious and counterfeit, since all, from what is by now an old custom, name their varieties in the masculine: haematites, pyrites, galactites, melitites, gagates, schistos, Phrygian, Arabian, Memphite. Conversely, they say petra in the feminine, not petros in the masculine. Thus they speak of the 'Asian petra', not the 'Asian petros', while the stone (ton lithon) they call 'Asian' in the masculine. So also 'flower of Asian rock (petra)'; and they say that quicklime comes from burnt rock (petra). Heraclides of Tarentum, however, and certain others say that quicklime comes not from every stone but only from petra, using this name by pre-eminence for the single hardest of the stones. I, at any rate, am in the habit of deliberately varying the names and saying in both ways all such things about which some people quarrel uselessly, showing in practice that the clarity of the expression is in no way harmed, whichever way one says it. It is no wonder that those who do not know that clarity must be set down either as the one and only virtue of natural expression, or at least as the first and best of all the others, are diverted into such nonsense. First, then, I shall speak about those stones which, when rubbed on mortars or whetstones, dissolve into a juice.

[9.2.2] [2. On haematites, galactites and melitites.] One of such stones is also the so-called haematites, named thus from its likeness in colour, just as galactites is too, since it also, when dissolved into a juice, appears like milk. Melitites, which produces a juice close to the latter's in colour, has been so named from its likeness in taste. It has been shown in the fourth of these commentaries that every sweet juice becomes such through moderate warmth, and the astringent juice through cooling. Accordingly the haematites stone will have as much of cooling as of astringency, melitites a moderate heat, and galactites a mixture intermediate between both. With good reason, then, the physicians have ventured to mix the haematites stone into ophthalmic preparations. You could also use it alone when the eyelids have become rough: if they have become so together with inflammation, making the dilution with egg, or better still with a decoction of fenugreek; if without inflammation, with water. Always begin by instilling it moderately fluid with the probe, and when you see that the part bears its power, make it ever thicker and thicker. And in the end you will make it so thick as to smear it on with the knob of the probe, by placing it under the eyelid or by everting the eyelid. This same stone, rubbed down in the same way on a whetstone, is suited to spittings of blood and to all ulcers. Ground dry so as to become fine as down, it represses fleshy overgrowths. Now no one uses it alone by itself; but I used it in the cases I have mentioned, having discovered its power from its quality in taste, and then wishing to test by experience whether I had inferred correctly. And by itself alone it also cicatrises the ulcers in the eyes themselves, being rubbed down, as I said a little before, and either instilled or smeared on. For I tested this too by experience.

[9.2.3] [3. On schistos and many other stones.] A power similar to that of this stone, but weaker, is possessed by the stone called schistos, and after it by galaktites. Melitites, as I said, has already taken on something of heat as well. Each of them, then, departing little by little from the power of haematites, is likewise brought into use for the eyes, but is milder. Milder drugs are always gentler for parts that are still inflamed, but weaker for bringing to complete health parts that have ceased to be inflamed. Drying is common to all stones. Those of them which, whether dissolved into a juice or pounded fine in some other way, have at first no quality perceptible to the taste must be considered the weakest, the gentlest and the least biting. Those which appear to display some clear quality to the taste have a strength proportionate to that quality. If they are astringent, their strength is for repressing, constricting, compacting and drawing together. If they are biting, it is for heating, dispersing and melting. Intermediate between them are those that are only cleansing, without being astringent or biting. Now haematites and schistos, galaktites and melitites dissolve into a juice when rubbed, as I said, on whetstones and in mortars. There are also other stones that dissolve into a juice, such as the one produced in Egypt, which people use to glaze linen cloths. This stone is more devoid of quality than those already mentioned, displaying neither astringency nor cleansing nor biting. Hence this very thing alone belongs to this stone, namely drying. For this reason they mix it with cerate and use it for the cicatrization of ulcers in soft bodies. Such stones are also mixed into ophthalmic preparations, in the same way as those mentioned before. By as much as it is more softening than they are, through having no active quality, by so much it is more moderate and produces less sensation. Some people call this stone moroxos, others graphis.

[9.2.4] [4. On the thyites of Dioscorides.] Stronger in power than all the stones mentioned is the one brought from Ethiopia, somewhat greenish, named as a kind of jasper. When this stone is dissolved, it yields a juice milky in colour and biting to those who taste it. For this reason no one has mixed it into ophthalmic preparations, neither those repelling fluxes nor those healing of ulcers. It is used only to purify and cleanse the things that, without inflammation, darken the pupils, among which are also the fresh scars, which it is of a nature to thin. It also cleanses away those pterygia that are not very hard.

[9.2.5] [5. On the Jewish stone.] There is also another stone, stronger in power, which occurs in Palestinian Syria. It is white in colour, well-proportioned in shape, and has lines as if made by a lathe. They name it 'Jewish' after the country in which it is naturally produced, and they use it against stones in the bladder, rubbing it down on a whetstone and giving it to drink in warm water, three cyathi. But in the cases in which we tested it, it achieved nothing as regards stones in the bladder; in the case of those forming in the kidneys, however, it is efficacious.

[9.2.6] [6. On pyrites.] One of those that have a strong power is also the stone named pyrites, which we use by mixing it into a dispersing plaster. The schistos is also added to it. By this drug often pus, but also a clotted (thrombus-like) consistency formed in the spaces between the muscles, has been dispersed. All the stones, when they are brought into use, must be pounded and ground very smooth indeed, in the same way as those mixed into ophthalmic preparations. For unless they are made as fine as down, so as to sink into the depth of the bodies to which they are applied, they will remain like these sea and river sands, which themselves also have the common power of all stones. At any rate they dry flesh that is somewhat swollen and dropsical, when the patients lie down in them after they have been heated. We do not, however, use them for anything else, as we use the stones mentioned before for ophthalmic preparations and preparations that check blood and the female flux, and further for what is agglutinating of ulcers, scarring and flesh-forming. For all of them that are not pungent are useful for these purposes, just as the pungent ones, which I mentioned later, are useful for cleansing, scouring off and removing, thinning, dispersing, drying vigorously and melting.

[9.2.7] [7. On Phrygian stone.] The stone called Phrygian also possesses this power. I have always used it burnt, and for putrefactive ulcers either by itself on its own or with vinegar or with honeyed wine [oinomeli] or with oxycrate. For the eyes, I make a dry drug from it, which many people have already received from me and now possess. I also mix certain other things with it. This will be discussed in the treatise On the Composition of Drugs. For now it suffices to have set out its general power. For it dries strongly, having something of astringency and at the same time of biting. And I have also said in what precedes that all mixed drugs which contain within themselves the two powers, the repelling and the dispersing, are excellent and of many uses.

[9.2.8] [8. On agēratos.] There is also the stone called agēratos, which we see shoemakers using. It is of a mixed power, astringent and dispersing, but we must consider only the astringent one. It manifestly benefits inflamed uvulas, yet to those who taste it it does not appear to have a clear astringency or pungency.

[9.2.9] [9. On the Assian stone.] There is also another stone, produced in Assos, which for this very reason they call Assian. It is not hard as rocks are, for it is like poros-stone both in colour and in consistency, and it is friable and loose. Upon it there grows something closely resembling the finest flour, namely the flour that settles on the walls of the places in mills where flour is sifted. They call this drug 'flower of the Asian rock'. It is fine-particled, so that it melts down flabby flesh without biting. The rock on which it is produced has a power similar to it but falls short in the vehemence of its activity. For the flower surpasses it not only in melting down, dispersing and curing (as by salting) to a greater degree, but also in doing these things strongly without biting. This flower of the Asian rock also has something salty in the taste, so that one may conjecture that it gets its origin from some dew from the sea settling on the rock and then being dried by the sun.

[9.2.10] [10. On gagates and the Thracian (stone).] There is also another stone, black in colour, which, when it comes into contact with fire, gives off a smell closely resembling that of asphalt. Dioscorides and certain others say that it is found in Lycia, along the river named Gagates, from which we say the stone itself also takes its name. I, however, did not see that river, although I sailed along the whole of Lycia in a small boat for the sake of investigating the things in it. But I brought back from Coele Syria many plate-like black stones which, if they were placed on a fire, produced a weak flame. They are produced on the hill that surrounds the sea called the Dead Sea, in its eastern parts, where asphalt also occurs. The smell of the stones was closely similar to asphalt. I used them for chronic emphysemata occurring at the knee that are hard to cure, mixing them with the compound remedies (δυνάμεσιν) that have been tested against this symptom, and it clearly seemed to us to have made their power more evident.
