I also mixed it into the (plaster) called Barbara, and the drug clearly became more drying, so that it even drew sinuses together, and did not only agglutinate bloody wounds, for which it is above all believed to be suited. There is also another stone, which Nicander too mentions, writing thus: 'Or do you burn the Thracian (stone) exceedingly (λίαν) in fire; then, sprinkled with water, it is driven (ἐλάσεται), and it (sc. the fire?) quenched it (αὐτὴν) a little, when it smells oil sprinkled upon it; (the stone) which herdsmen bring from the Thracian river, which they call Pontus.' But not even Nicander writes of any benefit from it for medicine, apart from its foul smell, which, when burnt as a fumigation (θυμιώμενα), drives away wild creatures.
[9.2.11] [11. On the magnetis and the Heraclean stone.] One of the stones is also the one called both magnetis and Heraclean, which has a power similar to that of haematites.

[9.2.12] [12. On the Arabian stone.] The stone called Arabian, which resembles ivory, is of a drying and cleansing power. [9.2.13] [13. On alabastrites.] The onyx called alabastrites, too, comes into medical use when burnt. Some people also give it to those with stomach complaints to drink.

[9.2.14] [14. On smyris.] And as for the so-called smyris, that it is of a strongly cleansing power is clear also from the ring-engravers who use it for this kind of purpose; but that it also makes the teeth clean is something we have found by experience.

[9.2.15] [15. On pumice.] If pumice too is to be counted among the stones, it also is of the same power as far as cleansing is concerned, as indeed is the potsherd from roof-tiles, and still more than this the potsherd from ovens. But emery has something pungent, and for this reason some mix it into caustic and drying medicines and into those that treat flabby gums. Pumice, when burnt, falls no way short of emery for the same uses.

[9.2.16] [16. On the stones in sponges.] The stones found in sponges are also of a power capable of breaking up stones. It is not, however, so strong as to break up the stones in the bladder: those who wrote this were lying. But they do break up those that are in the kidneys, as do also the stones from Cappadocia, which they say are generated on the Argaeus. These dissolve into a juice milky in colour, so that it is quite clear that they are of a thinning power without heating manifestly.

[9.2.17] [17. On ostracites.] I hear some people praising the stone called ostracites as having a sufficiently drying power, compounded from astringency and pungency mixed in, just as indeed they praise the so-called earthy stone too, saying that it cleanses the pupils and heals inflammations of the breasts and testicles when put into water (ἐνιέμενοι, so the text). The scrapings of the Naxian whetstone, at any rate, prevent maidens' breasts from swelling up as they come to their prime (πρὸς ὥρας), and boys' testicles likewise, evidently because it also partakes of a cooling power.

[9.2.18] [18. On ophites.] The stone called ophites, too, when burnt, has a cleansing power and one capable of breaking up, just as glass does. For glass too, drunk with white, thin wine, quite effectively breaks up the stones in the bladder; but no one would count it among the stones.

[9.2.19] [18. On green jasper, and omphatites, and hierakites, and the Indian stone.] Some attest to certain stones a specific property of the kind that green jasper truly does possess: it benefits the stomach and the mouth of the belly when worn as an amulet. Some also set it in a ring and engrave on it the serpent that has the rays, just as King Nechepsos also wrote in his fourteenth book. Of this stone I too have adequate experience. Indeed, having made a string of such small stones, I hung it from the neck at such a suitable length that the stones touched the mouth of the belly. And they appeared to be no less beneficial than if they did not have the engraving which Nechepsos wrote of. A man truly worthy of credence said that the omphatites stone, worn as an amulet, benefits those bitten by vipers. But such powers lie outside use according to method, just as does also that of hierakites and of the Indian stone, which stops the blood from haemorrhoids.

[9.2.20] [20. On sapphire.] For indeed the sapphire too is believed, when drunk, to benefit those who have been struck by a scorpion. [9.2.21] [21. On aphroselinus.] And the stone called aphroselinus is believed to benefit epileptics as well; we, however, have not tested it. There are also certain other stones that are hung on as amulets by some people, and some of them also have certain characters and letters engraved on them, just as the hieracites, which is suited to haemorrhoids, does; this one we too have tested. But now is not the time to speak about such things, which have their credibility from experience alone and have not been brought into use according to some rational method. There will, then, be another time and place for these. For now let us go back again to what was set before us from the beginning in the whole treatise.

[9.3.1] On metallic drugs. [1. On the general accounts, concretions and powers of metals.] It is customary among physicians to call 'metallic drugs' those whose generation takes place in the mines, whether it is self-grown or comes about by means of a furnace. And third, in addition to these, are all those that people in turn prepare from these very things in whatever manner, such as white lead (psimmythion), psorikon, sandyx and phykos. Next, then, all of them will be discussed in the order of the letters with which each of their names begins, once we have first said in advance something common to all of them, as we did a little before in the case of the stones, and, earlier than these, concerning medicinal earth. For just as those, so in the same way all metallic drugs too have drying in common. For their substance is earthy, as I am now using the name in the sense of the elemental earth. But just as storage jars, roof-tiles, cooking-pots and the other things of this kind are made by us from potter's earth, being hardened by fire once its moisture has been roasted out, in the same way, in the earth, when a long-lasting warmth unites and blends the substance mixed from earth and water, and sometimes also air, and then dries it, the concretions of the metallic drugs come into being. And the nature of the places in which these concrete, according as they are more or less cold, congeals some more and others less. Just as, then, in the varieties of earth the substance of the elemental earth is very great and that of the airy is small, so in mined substances much of the fiery has been mixed in. Between them are the stones; and for this reason most of the metallic drugs, when washed, some once or twice, others more often, become useful for powers that dry without biting. Such, then, are the general accounts which it is necessary to know beforehand about all of them; next will be stated the account proper to each, in the order of the letters with which the names of the drugs begin.

[9.3.2] [2. On salts.] Salts. Some of these too come from the sea, in the so-called salt-pans, which we shall also mention among the marine drugs. But there are also the so-called dug salts, which are included in the class of the metallic drugs. All of them, both the dug ones and those from the sea, have a power similar to one another. They were discussed earlier, in the fourth book, in the account where we distinguished the salty and briny flavour from the bitter. It will be said now as well that the flavour in aphronitre is bitter and cleansing, while that in salts falls as far short in cleansing as it exceeds in astringency. For it is mixed from two qualities, a cleansing and an astringent one. That both of them dry considerably had also been shown before. In the middle between both is the flavour of litron.

[9.3.3] [3. On Armenian.] Armenian has a cleansing power together with a slight pungency and a very slight astringency. Accordingly, being of this kind, it is mixed into ophthalmic preparations as well; and people also grind it by itself, make it into a fine, down-like powder, and use it dry for the growth of the hairs on the eyelids, when, because of the pungency of humours, some of these hairs fall out and others become without growth and without nourishment. For by using up these pungencies it brings the part back to its natural good condition, to which belongs, among other things, the producing, increasing and strengthening of the hairs of the eyelids. For some of the effects of drugs are direct, others come about through the mediation of the nature that governs the bodies of animals, as is the case with those among these very drugs that they call kalliblephara ['eyelid-beautifiers']: for these themselves moderately dry the moderately damaged parts, using up the moisture that destroys the hairs; and once this has been done away with, nature proceeds to its proper activities, since the things that until then were hindering it are no longer present.

[9.3.4] [4. On arrhenikon.] Arrhenikē or arrhenikon (for it is named in both ways) is of a caustic power, both unburnt and burnt. It is quite clear that it also becomes more fine-particled when burnt. They use it also for the stripping of hairs, since it burns them off; if, at any rate, it stays on for a long time, it attacks the skin itself as well.

[9.3.5] [5. On aphrolitron.] Aphrolitron differs from aphronitron. For the foam of nitron is a drying drug, similar in appearance to wheaten flour. Indeed it is also white, and not ash-coloured like the flower of the Asian stone. Aphronitron, on the other hand, is neither floury nor loose, but solidified and compact; it is what all those who are dirty use daily in the baths, since it has a cleansing power, so that it not only wipes off the dirt but also cures itching, because the ichors that produce the itching are dispersed by it. Reasonably, then, physicians prepare many of the dispersing drugs with it. The foam of nitron is of the same nature and power as nitron, but it has a more fine-particled substance. It was said a little earlier that aphrolitron is intermediate in power between aphronitron and salts. For aphrolitron possesses the cleansing power alone, whereas salts have the astringent power as well, though the cleansing is much greater.

[9.3.6] [6. On gypsum.] Gypsum too, in addition to the power common to all earthy and stony bodies, by which it was said to dry, has further acquired this as well: it is of a clogging power. For it unites with itself, congeals and turns to stone when wetted. Therefore it is also usefully mixed into the dry drugs suited to haemorrhage. For by itself alone it becomes stony and hard as it congeals, and for this reason I devised moistening it with the thin and white part of egg, the kind useful for ophthalmias, mixing in the most downy part of wheaten flour, which settles on the walls in the mills. What has been kneaded in this way should be taken up with soft hare's hairs, or with some others that are similarly soft.

[9.3.7] [7. On burnt gypsum.] Gypsum, when burnt, does not have the clogging property in the same way, but it becomes more fine-particled and more drying, and indeed also repelling, and especially when it is moistened with oxycrate.

[9.3.8] [8. On diphryges.] Diphryges is of mixed quality and power. For it has in itself something moderately astringent and moderately pungent, and so it is also a good drug for malignant ulcers. I brought back a large quantity of this drug too from Soli in Cyprus, where the mine is, about thirty stades from the city. For it had been thrown away in the space between the building that stands in front at the mine and the village that lies below it. The overseer in charge of the mine said that this material, which is found after the cadmia, was useless, and that this was why it was thrown away, like the ash of burnt wood in the hearths. But this drug proved very serviceable to me against the putrefactive ulcers in the mouth, both by itself and with skimmed honey, and also against synanchē, once the inflowing matter has already been checked by astringent drugs. And when I had excised the uvula, I used it alone, both immediately and until the wound closed with a scar, since it often produced a precisely sealed scar both in this part and in all ulcerated parts. So too against all ulcers on the genitals and at the seat. The manner of use is similar to that for ulcers in the mouth. For parts that are similarly warm and moist in some way take kindly to the same drugs. But an account of this kind already touches on the treatise on the composition of drugs. So let us leave it aside and go on to the matter before us, stating the general power itself of each drug, as we have also done for diphryges. I shall, however, add to the account of it something that is useful to know not about diphryges only, but also about the Lemnian seal, pompholyx, opobalsam and Indian lykion. For while still a youth I learned preparations of these, by which I made the prepared product indistinguishable from the genuine ones. The man who taught me, for a large fee, was a most elaborate practitioner of such curious arts, not only in these but in other similar things too. For this reason, then, I took pains to travel to Lemnos, to Cyprus and to Palestinian Syria and to lay up a large quantity of each of these drugs for my whole life; and I was also fortunate enough to obtain Indian lykion that had just been brought into Phoenicia together with Indian aloe, at the time when I was returning by the road from Palestine. I was persuaded that it was Indian both by the very fact that it had been brought by camel together with the whole cargo, and by the fact that the adulterated kind could not be known to those who carried it, since the material from which it is prepared does not grow in those regions. It seemed better to me not to write down the compositions of the counterfeits at all, since wicked men regard learning such things as a windfall. Nor is it necessary, along with the means of recognising the true and genuine drugs, to know the compositions of the counterfeits, since they contribute nothing at all to recognising them. Indeed, if it had been possible for me, I would have wished also to erase the preparations of counterfeited drugs that are found in the writers older than me.

[9.3.9] [9. On sulphur.] All sulphur is of a drawing power: it is hot in its mixture and fine-particled in its substance, so that it also resists many of the venomous creatures. I, at any rate, have often used it for the sea stingray and the weever, and, having taught some fishermen, I heard after a time that they praised the drug greatly. It is used both by sprinkling the drug dry upon the puncture and mixed with saliva. For this too I devised, and found it attested by experience; and I also conceived that it would work when moistened with urine. For I was teaching fishermen drugs that are wholly easily procured, and I told them that they would also do well to use it with old oil, with honey, and with terebinth resin. And indeed experience has made the judgement on all these. And I have not infrequently cured psorai, leichenes and leprai with this drug, together with terebinth resin. For it cleanses away all such affections without repelling them into the depth, whereas many other drugs that cure them have a mixed power, so as both to disperse and to repel.

[9.3.10] [10. On verdigris.] Verdigris has a pungent quality to those who taste it, and it is dispersing, reducing and colliquative not only of soft but also of hard flesh. It was said in what went before that some people call many drugs of this kind scarring, because, having ground it fine and made it downy, they touch ulcers with overgrown flesh with the bulb of a probe. Then on the following day they find them shrunk down, although they know that if they were to apply a little more, they will find the ulcer not reduced but actually being eaten away; for it melts and disperses the flesh, whereas scarring drugs draw it together, compact it, constrict it and make it callous. Verdigris is biting to the taste as well, not only to ulcers. But if one mixes a little of it with much cerate, the mixture made from both becomes cleansing without biting. It was said earlier concerning the nature of such drugs, and how some people misreason themselves on the basis of such compositions, attaching either a flesh-forming or a scarring power to drugs to which they ought not, drugs which are not by nature such as to do this themselves, but which contribute to the compounds composed of them.

[9.3.11] [11. On cadmia.] Cadmia is produced in the furnaces during the generation of copper: all that earth from which the copper is generated in the smelting sends up on high something like a soot or smut, or *aithalē* and *asbolē*, whichever one wishes to call it. If you would rather call it not an earth but a stone, which in being separated in the furnaces becomes partly copper, partly cadmia, partly diphryges, let it make no difference. It is also produced in the silver mines by a similar separation, or generation, or whatever you wish to name it. Cadmia is also produced when pyrites stone is smelted. And cadmia is found in Cyprus without a furnace too, and one would rightly name such cadmia a stone. In Soli, at any rate, there was still very little of the cadmia generated in the smelting-works at the time I stayed on the island. But I received from the man in charge of the mines stones found in the mountains and the watercourses. When I brought these to Asia and Italy, my friends thought they were receiving a very great gift, since that cadmia was better than the other cadmia. Such cadmia, then, one might reasonably name stony cadmia. Of the smelted cadmia, physicians call one kind botryitis and another placitis. Botryitis is the cadmia that collects in the higher parts of the chambers during the smelting, and placitis the cadmia that collects in the lower parts. It is evident that botryitis is more fine-particled and placitis more coarse-particled. Both are of a drying power, as are the other mined, stony and earthy substances as well. Besides the drying power, cadmia also has a moderately cleansing one. Cadmia from the furnaces, however, of necessity also has something of the power of fire. Reasonably, then, by washing it they make a drug that dries and cleanses moderately without biting, useful for ulcers that need filling, both in the eyes and in the whole body. As for ulcers that are very moist or putrefactive, in very soft bodies, such as those of eunuchs, children and women, such cadmia is beneficial. In hard and taut bodies, however, there is need of drugs that dry more vigorously. One must therefore always remember that, in everything stated simply, the account is referred to the well-tempered nature, intermediate between the excesses. For instance, this holds when we say that a drug is filling of ulcers or scarring, or that it does anything else whatever. Referring to this standard, we too now say that the power of cadmia is drying and slightly cleansing. In the difference of heat and cold it is in some way balanced, producing neither conspicuously.

[9.3.12] [12. On cinnabar.] Cinnabar is of a moderately pungent power, and it also has something of astringency. [9.3.13] [13. On pumice.] Pumice: if you class it among the mined substances, the fault-finders will find fault; and if among the stones, they will not allow that it is a stone, and much less that it is earth, or any of the things from the sea. And yet one must at some point speak about it, since it is put into flesh-forming drugs and into cleansing preparations for the teeth: into the one unburnt, into the other burnt, at which time it also becomes more fine-particled, in the same way as all the other burnt things; but in the burning it takes on something pungent, and it lays this aside again when it is washed. It would seem to brighten the teeth not by its power alone but also by its roughness, just as if you were to grind emery or potsherd or something of that sort and apply it; these too perhaps brighten in both respects, both because they have something cleansing and by their roughness. By the same reasoning burnt horns too are brighteners of the teeth.

[9.3.14] [14. On lye made from ash.] Lye. Lye comes into being when ash has been washed; and the Greeks call 'ash' the residue of burnt bodies, whether these be stony in nature or parts of trees or of animals. The lye, then, also comes to be according to the nature of what is washed: from that which has a most pungent fiery quality acquired in burning, it is most pungent; from that which is not of this kind, it is more moderate. For this reason it is also mixed into the so-called putrefying preparations, since it has a caustic heat, burning painlessly through the fine-particled character of its substance.

[9.3.15] [15. On kyanos.] Kyanos, whether you wish to name this drug in the masculine or in the feminine, is of a pungent power, both reducing and dispersing to a greater degree than cinnabar; and it also has a share of astringency.

[9.3.16] [16. On the scale from copper, from iron and from steel.] One scale is of copper, a drug of many uses; another is of iron and of steel. Some also name a scale 'helitis'. All of them, then, dry strongly, but they differ from one another in the drying itself, less and more, in being of a more coarse-particled or more fine-particled substance, and in partaking of astringency less and more. The helitis, then, is first in drying. For it is also more fine-particled than the others, having taken on some verdigris as well. The scale of iron, however, partakes of more astringency, and that of steel still more so; and for this reason they are better than that of copper for malignant ulcers. That of copper, on the other hand, reduces and melts flesh more, and the helitis still more than it. All scales are biting to no slight degree, from which it is also clear that the consistency of their substance is not at all fine-particled, but rather coarse-particled. For among things that have the same power, the more fine-particled is always less biting, as was shown in the earlier discussions.

[9.3.17] [17. On litharge.] Litharge dries, as do all the other metallic, earthy and stony drugs, but it does this in a most moderate way. In respect of its other qualities and powers, too, it stands somehow in the middle: it neither heats nor cools perceptibly, and it partakes moderately of being astringent and of cleansing away. For this reason it falls short of the flesh-forming drugs, which were shown to be moderately cleansing, and also of those that draw together and are astringent. But for abrasions on the thighs it is a useful drug, since it partakes slightly of both the powers mentioned. Among the metallic substances, then, it would reasonably be considered to belong to the middle rank. For this reason we also often use it as a material, mixing it with those that have a strong power, whether biting or astringent or doing anything else, just as in melted preparations we use wax as a kind of material for most drugs, because wax too is placed somehow in the middle in relation to those that have a strong power.

[9.3.18] [18. On nitron.] Nitron has been said earlier as well to be of a power intermediate between that of aphronitron and that of salts; when burnt, it comes nearer to aphronitron, being rendered more fine-particled by the burning. It therefore dries and disperses and, if taken inside the body, cuts and thins thick and viscid humours much more than salts do. Aphronitron, on the other hand, no one even swallows unless there is great necessity, since it is bad for the stomach; for it is indeed more cutting than nitron. At any rate, in cases of choking mushrooms a certain countryman used it and was successful every time. We too use nitron in such cases, both burnt and unburnt, and still more its foam.

[9.3.19] [19. On melanteria.] Melanteria is one of the considerably astringent drugs, and besides this it is also fine-particled, very nearly the most so of all the astringents. [9.3.20] [20. On writing ink.] The ink with which we write: this too dries considerably when dissolved in water. It also benefits those ulcers that are burns when smeared on immediately. And if it also contains vinegar, it does so much more.

[9.3.21] [21. On misy.] Misy. At the mine in Cyprus mentioned earlier, in the mountains of Soli, there was a large building. In its right-hand wall (left, as regards us who were entering) there was an entrance into the mine itself, in which I saw three bands, as it were, extending over a very great length one upon another: the lowest that of sory, upon it that of chalcitis, then that of misy. The overseer of the mine at that time, showing me these, said: "Just as you have come now when we are in poverty of the cadmia that is smelted in furnaces, so you see these three established in wonderful abundance." And accordingly I took a very great quantity of it and carried it first to Asia, and from there to Rome, and I have kept it until now, about thirty years having passed in between. And by a certain chance the present treatise advanced as far as the eighth book, about twenty years ago, without this ninth one being added to it, because I had not yet seen some of the stones, and moreover also because of the occupations that intervened on account of other matters. But now, as I was adding this ninth book, there occurred in the meantime by chance a most beautiful sight, such as one might have contrived on purpose oneself. For, needing misy for a certain drug that was being prepared, I took up a lump about a handful in size, although misy does not at all usually have such a consistency, but breaks up into small aggregates. Wondering, then, at its unaccustomed compactness, I crushed the lump and found misy on the surface all round, like a kind of efflorescence of what was inside; and next to it, between chalcitis and misy, a sort of half-way change, as it were, from chalcitis into misy. For the lump had originally been a lump of chalcitis. And as much of it as lay in the depth was pure chalcitis, having as yet undergone no alteration. Having seen this, and having reflected that in the mine too misy is generated upon chalcitis in this way, just as verdigris is upon copper, I examined the sory that is still preserved in my possession, to see whether it was undergoing any change into chalcitis; and a slight indication appeared, which perhaps would itself also be able in a long time to undergo the change into chalcitis. So it is nothing surprising that the three drugs, I mean sory, chalcitis and misy, are of a homogeneous power, differing in fineness of particles and coarseness of particles. For the most coarse-particled among them is sory, the most fine-particled is misy, and chalcitis has a power intermediate between the two. All three burn and produce what are called eschars; yet, although they burn, they do share in astringency. Misy, when applied to hard flesh, is less biting than chalcitis, although it is not less hot than it; it has this from the fine-particled character of its substance. And whereas both are fusible in boilings, chalcitis more so than misy, sory does not melt, because it has a more stony and more vehement solidification; just as, again, misy, from having been worked upon by its innate heat, being drier than chalcitis, is reasonably also harder to melt.

[9.3.22] [22. On molybdaena.] Molybdaena has a power closely resembling that of litharge, departing a little from the middle mixture towards the colder side, but it does not even share in a cleansing power. Both drugs are fusible, and not infusible like the stones, cadmia and sand. They melt most quickly when the oil has had vinegar added to it. They do melt, however, even if you mix in water and boil them for a very long time. Just as in Cyprus I took the cadmia that is generated in the mountains and in the stream-beds, which is, as I said, a kind of stone, in the same way I also saw molybdaena lying scattered together with very many other stones along the road that leads from Pergamum to Ergasteria. Ergasteria is the name of a village, in which there are also mines, between Pergamum and Cyzicus, four hundred and forty stades distant from Pergamum.

[9.3.23] [23. On lead.] Lead is of a cooling power. For it has not only much moist substance congealed by cold, but also airy substance, while it partakes of little earthy substance. That it has a very great amount of moist substance congealed by cold, let the melting and flowing that comes about in it quickly whenever it meets fire be your proof. That it also has airy substance, this is a sign: lead alone (μόνος μόνος, sic) of the things we know increases both in bulk and in weight when it is stored in underground chambers that have turbid air, such that the things lying in them are quickly filled with mould; and the leads that bind the feet of statues to their stones have often been seen to have grown. Some have even risen to so great a bulk that they hang down from the stones like ice. These, then, are plausible indications, prior to experience, of its moistness and coldness. But what is scientific and secure is known through experience. If, then, having prepared a mortar of lead, you put into it, together with a pestle of lead, whatever liquid you wish, and grind it so that the pestle and the lead give off some juice, you will find that what is produced from both is far colder in power than the liquid was. You may put in water, thin watery wine, oil and anything at all of that kind. If you wish to make the juice still more refrigerant, let the oil be omphacine oil, rose oil, quince oil or myrtle oil. Using the juice so produced for inflammations arising in the seat with ulcers or folds, and for those in the genitals, testicles and breasts, you will have an excellent drug. Likewise also against all the other fluxes when they are beginning, such as settle into buboes, the feet or the other joints, and moreover also for malignant ulcers, so that, using it for cancerous ones too, you will marvel at the drug. If you wish to collect a great deal of the juice of lead quickly, try grinding in the sun or in air that has become warm in any way whatever. The drug will be of many uses to you if you also grind it with some of the cooling juices thrown in, such as of houseleek, navelwort, chicory, lettuce, chondrilla, psyllium, unripe grape and purslane. Those of these that do not readily give off juice, as purslane, mix with some of the other liquids, such as that of the unripe grape, which, put by itself alone into the aforementioned mortar, also produces a most excellent refrigerant drug. But lead too, flattened out, without any of the others, by itself alone, becomes an underlay for the loins of athletes in training when they have nocturnal emissions, evidently cooling them. And on one occasion a thin sheet made of lead, properly bound on over a ganglion, made it disappear completely. Anyone will bind it on properly who has learned from Hippocrates to press more on the lesion than on either side. It is therefore no wonder that burnt lead too, when it has been washed, becomes of cooling power, while before it is washed it is clearly of mixed power. And this very drug, burnt lead, is good for ulcers that are turning malignant; but when it has been washed it becomes a far better drug, an excellent one, for both their filling-up and their cicatrization. It is suitable also for the so-called Chironian ulcers and for all cancerous ones, both by itself and mixed with some of the cicatrizing drugs, such as the one made with cadmia. One must undo the dressing at the beginning every day, if the ichor is copious; if not, every third or even every fourth day. Let a sponge from cold water lie on the outside, and whenever it dries, let it be moistened. These things, then, have been said at greater length than the present treatise requires, since I was led on by the affinity of the discussion. It is now time to pass to what follows.

[9.3.24] [24. On potsherd.] Potsherd is of a drying and cleansing power, especially that from the ovens (klibanoi), because it has been thoroughly baked. For this reason, among the plasters, the one they call hephaestias, when prepared with this, becomes a most excellent scarring drug.

[9.3.25] [25. On pompholyx and spodium.] Pompholyx is produced in the smelting of copper, as cadmia also is. But it is also produced when cadmia itself is smelted. In Cyprus, for instance, since the overseer did not have the equipment for smelting copper, he ordered pompholyx to be prepared from the cadmia itself, in my presence and while I watched. The cadmia was thrown onto the fire in small fragments, and the fire evidently had something of a smithing nature applied to it. There was a closed roof that received the soot carried upward as the cadmia was smelted, and by gathering this I obtained pompholyx. What is carried back down and falls onto the floor is what is called spodos; a greater amount of it is collected in the smelting of copper. Some people call it spodium, in the neuter, and the so-called antispodium seems to have a power similar to it. I myself have never used it, because one always has pompholyx in abundance. For anyone who has this would not use spodium, still less antispodium. Pompholyx, if it is washed, is almost the most excellent drug of all those whose nature is to dry without biting. Hence it is suitable for cancerous ulcers and for all the other malignant ones. Accordingly it is mixed into the collyria compounded for fluxes in the eyes and for those that treat the phlyctaenae or ulcers in them, and into remedies for ulcers at the seat and the genitals. And it is a most excellent drug, drying, as I said, without biting. But to dwell on these matters does not belong to the present treatise.

[9.3.26] [26. On sandarakē.] Sandarakē is of a caustic power, as is the substance named arrhenikon. Reasonably, then, they mix it into dispersing compositions and into cleansing ones. [9.3.27] [27. On sandyx.] Of what power sandyx is will be stated in the account of psimmythion.

[9.3.28] [28. On slag.] All slag is a considerably drying drug, but that of iron most of all. And indeed, grinding it very fine in the most pungent vinegar and after this boiling it, I use it for ears that discharge pus chronically as a most drying drug, so that those who saw it being prepared were amazed and distrusted it before the trial, as to whether the ears could tolerate such a drug. The slag of silver they call by the special name helkysma, and it is also mixed into certain plasters which are, evidently, of drying power.

[9.3.29] [29. On stimmi.] Stimmi. In addition to its drying power, this drug also has astringency; for this reason it is also mixed into ophthalmic drugs, both those that are moulded into what are called collyria and the dry ones, which they call dry collyria.

[9.3.30] [30. On split, round and liquid alum.] Alum (styptēria). The very name of this drug is derived from astringency (stypsis), for it has astringency in the highest degree. But although the drug is coarse-particled, the alum called 'split' is somewhat more fine-particled than the other alums. After it comes the round, knucklebone-shaped alum. The liquid alum, and those named plate alum and brick alum, are quite coarse-particled.

[9.3.31] [31. On lime (titanos).] Lime: unslaked lime burns violently, so as to produce an eschar; slaked lime likewise forms an eschar immediately, but after one or two days it burns less and forms less of an eschar, and after a time it does not produce eschars at all. It still heats, however, and melts down the flesh. If it is washed, it deposits its biting in the water and makes what is called lye, while it itself dries without biting. And if it is washed twice or three times or more often, it becomes completely non-biting and dries vigorously without biting.

[9.3.32] [32. On quicksilver.] Quicksilver is not one of the naturally occurring drugs but one of those that are prepared, like white lead, verdigris, psōrikon and litharge. I have no experience of it at all, either of its killing when swallowed or of its being applied externally.

[9.3.33] [33. On phykos.] What power phykos has will be stated in the discussion of white lead. [9.3.34] [34. On chalcanthum.] Chalcanthum. I have also made an inquiry concerning chalcanthum, which by chance was changing into chalcitis. For I brought this drug too from Cyprus in great quantity. All of its outer part, after about twenty years, became chalcitis, while what was inside was still chalcanthum. For this reason I still keep, even now, what is changing in this way, watching whether the change advances into the depth each year, as with the change of chalcitis into misy, as has been said before. One may wonder at how, in this drug, a not ignoble heat is mixed with a most powerful astringency. It is clear, then, that it is able beyond all others to pickle moist flesh, consuming the moisture by its heat and, by its astringency, drawing together and compacting the substance. For in this action it squeezes out besides some of the moisture itself, and it binds, dries and draws together towards itself the substance of the whole flesh. Now in Cyprus, at the time when I was there, I saw this drug being collected in the following manner. There was a building, large but not high, lying in front of the entrance to the mine. And in the left wall of this building, which was on the right hand for those entering, a passage had been hewn out into the adjoining hill, in breadth such that three men would touch one another, in height such that the tallest man could walk upright. This passage sloped downward, though not steeply or precipitously. At its end, the passage being about a stade long, there was a pit full of green, thick, lukewarm water. Throughout the whole descent there was a warmth similar to that in the first rooms of the baths, which they are accustomed to call promalaktēria. The water collected each day amounted to about eight Roman amphorae, coming down in small drops over the twenty-four hours of the whole day and night from the bored-through hill. Certain fettered convicts carried this water up and poured it into square tubs in the building in front, made of earthenware, in which, solidifying in a few days, it became chalcanthum. When I went down to the end of the excavation, where the lukewarm and green water collected, the odour of the air appeared to me stifling and hard to bear, smelling of chalcitis and of verdigris. The water itself, when tasted, also had such a quality. For this reason the fettered convicts carried up the amphorae naked and in haste, and did not endure to linger longer, but ran quickly back up, lamps burning on either side in the walls of the excavation at moderate intervals; and these themselves did not last a long time either, but went out very quickly. I heard from them that this excavation had been dug little by little over many years. For they said: this green water which you now see coming down from the hill into the pit is accustomed to become less than it was, little by little, and when it is near to stopping, the fettered convicts again dig under the adjoining part of the hill. And once before, the part being dug through fell in all at once, so as to kill all of them and to destroy the whole way. So whenever this happens, they make another opening and dig through, until the water responds. These things I had to tell you about chalcanthum; perhaps they are not necessary, yet it is better that they be known than unknown. Remember that I said the mine of sory, chalcitis and misy was seen by me on the left hand of those entering, so that from these facts I was able to conceive that the rain water percolating in the hill washes around and rinses all that earth from which there came into being naturally sory, misy and chalcitis, and, when smelted, copper, cadmia, pompholyx, and spodium and diphryges.

[9.3.35] [35. On chalcitis.] Chalcitis: it has been discussed in the account of misy, so for now it will suffice to say this much, that it has the astringent and the pungent power mixed together. The pungent prevails, being so vehement as to burn the flesh and produce what is called an eschar. When burnt, this drug bites less but dries no less, and it also lays aside not a little of its astringency, so that burnt chalcitis is in every respect better than unburnt: it becomes more fine-particled, as other burnt things also do, but it does not take on pungency, as many others do. You have also learned that all burnt things, when washed, become more moderate and less biting.

[9.3.36] [36. On burnt copper.] Burnt copper has something pungent as well, and it also partakes of astringency; and for this reason, if it is washed, it is a most excellent drug for bringing wounds to close with a scar. It is able to accomplish this even before it has been washed, and especially in the case of harder flesh; but for tender flesh the washed copper is more useful.

[9.3.37] [37. On flower of copper.] Flower of copper: this is of a more fine-particled power than both burnt copper and the scale. Fittingly, therefore, by preparing collyria with it they cleanse and remove the large roughnesses of the eyelids, which they call sykōseis.

[9.3.38] [38. On chrysocolla.] Chrysocolla. This drug too is among those that melt down flesh; it does not, however, bite strongly, but it is sufficiently dispersing and drying. Now some people give this name only to the mined kind, while others give it to the kind prepared in a copper mortar with a copper pestle by means of a boy's urine, which some count among the varieties of verdigris. It is better to prepare it in summer, or at any rate in hot air, grinding the urine in the mortar. It is better too that the copper from which you make both the mortar itself and the pestle be red. For more is rubbed off as the pestle is turned round when the copper is softer. This drug is most suitable for malignant ulcers, both on its own and mixed with others, as will be said in the works on the composition of drugs. For now it is enough to know that, by as much as it dries more and bites less than the mined chrysocolla, by so much does it surpass it in fineness of particles. And indeed, if you burn that chrysocolla itself, you will make it much more fine-particled.

[9.3.39] [39. On white lead.] White lead (psimmythion). This drug too bears witness to the power stated just before this one. At any rate, although it comes from being dissolved by pungent vinegar, when tasted it is nevertheless neither pungent nor biting nor dispersing, but clogging and cooling, being of a power most contrary to verdigris (ios). And yet verdigris too comes about when vinegar dissolves copper. White lead, when burnt, changing into what is called sandyx, becomes a drug more fine-particled than itself, but not yet, at any rate, heating. Phykos, however, preserving the cooling quality of white lead, has taken on fineness of particles, so that through it its power is able to sink down into the depth of the bodies with which it comes into contact.

[9.3.40] [40. On psoricum.] Psoricum. The drug is made from litharge mixed with twice as much chalcitis. Both are first ground in the most pungent vinegar and then put into a new pot, which you will bury in dung for forty days in midsummer. This drug becomes both more drying and at the same time less biting than chalcitis, and evidently also more fine-particled. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 10. None of the things now about to be said will bring great benefit to those who are ignorant of what was said at the beginning of the treatise in the first five books. Perhaps it will even harm a person who uses the drugs written about in it without having a method. I shall therefore address you as one who has learned those things, after recalling the main point of the whole treatise. It was shown that drugs act according to the so-called active qualities, heat and coldness and dryness and moisture. Through the mixture of these they become acerbic and harsh and briny and salty and bitter and pungent and sweet. Some become cleansing, others repelling, others drawing, others softening, others caustic, others putrefying, others eschar-forming. In addition to these, according to other more specific actions, they become flesh-forming and cicatrizing and agglutinating of fistulas or ulcers, or reducing of overgrowing flesh. It was also shown that the universal power would be discovered indicatively from a single trial. This is not just any trial, but one carried out with the distinctions that were stated. Once the universal power has been discovered, there is no longer any need of trial for the particular actions, except solely for confirmation of what reason has discovered. In this way, then, let us now too make our judgement of the material before us, and this is the material from animals. For in the three books that follow the fifth in sequence, the sixth, seventh and eighth, we went through the material concerning plants. We did not, evidently, go through all of it throughout the whole inhabited world, but only as much as we have experience of. In the book before this one, the ninth of the whole treatise, we went through the material concerning earthy and stony bodies. It remains for us still to go through the material concerning animals. After that there still remains what is generated in the sea and lakes, or generally in water, things which are neither plants nor earth nor stone nor animal. Such things are altogether very few, and they will be written of last, after we have gone through what concerns the bodies of animals. The order of instruction for these too will follow the order of the first letters in their names. In the material of plants I also gave an account of the juices that come from them. So now too the instruction about power will concern not only the solid parts in animals but also what is contained in them: phlegm, bile, blood, urine, dung and the like. In what was said earlier, not many of the particular items in the materia medica written by the physicians remained unknown to me. I myself took pains to know their powers through experience. If there was something I did not know, I did not write about it at all, since I did not think it right to trust others about even one such thing, because I had learned that some people tell many lies. With the material now before us, however, it is not so. I confess that there are very many of the parts and fluids contained in the bodies of animals of which I myself have had no such experience as some have written about. For some of them are licentious and disgusting, and some are even forbidden by the laws. About these I do not know how Xenocrates came to write. He was a man who lived not long ago but in the time of our grandfathers, when the Roman empire had forbidden men to eat human beings. Yet he, at any rate, writes quite credibly, as one who had himself made trial of them. He records which affections the brain or flesh or liver of a human being naturally cures when eaten, and which the bones of the head or shin or fingers cure when drunk, some burnt and others unburnt, and which blood itself cures. These things, then, even if contrary to the laws, are at least not licentious. But the drinking of sweat and urine and a woman's menses is licentious and disgusting. No less so than these is dung. Xenocrates wrote what it can do when smeared on the parts in the mouth and pharynx and when swallowed into the stomach. He has also written about ear-wax when swallowed. I, for my part, would not have consented to swallow even this, even on condition of never falling ill. And I consider dung far more disgusting than it. Indeed, it is a greater reproach for a temperate man to be called a dung-eater than a doer of obscene acts or a catamite. But even among those who do obscene acts we loathe the 'phoenicizers' more than the 'lesbianizers', and the one who drinks menses seems to me to suffer something similar to the former. No man in his natural condition, then, would consent to make trial of these things. Nor would he consent to make trial of those that are more moderate than these but still licentious, such as smearing some part of the body with dung for the sake of the affection in it, or with human semen. Xenocrates is accustomed to call it 'gonos'. He distinguishes with all care which conditions the gonos itself, by itself, naturally benefits when smeared on, and which it benefits after the intercourse of man and woman, when it falls out of the female bosom. For there must be some great poverty of remedies for anyone to treat chilblains [ὑπερεχούσας?] with a man's semen that has not stayed inside but has flowed out of the woman after intercourse. This kind of material too is plentiful in what he has written about the benefit from animals. For he recounts not only, evidently, for man, what power urine has when drunk, or dung when swallowed and when smeared on the parts in the mouth. He recounts this also for each of the other animals, and much else that is hard to procure, as when he mentions the elephant or the Nile horse. The beast called the basilisk I have never even seen, and if what is said about it is true, it is dangerous even to come near this animal. Certain others too wrote things similar to Xenocrates about animals, and from them Xenocrates himself copied out most of what he wrote. For whence would he have had the means to make trial himself of so many and such things? Our own former king Attalus, at any rate, appears to write of fewer, although he was most ambitious in the testing of such things. Someone who praised the treatise of Ateuristus on the same subject also gave it to me to go through. As it seems to me, it had been composed without any personal autopsy on the part of the man who wrote it. I, then, shall mention neither basilisks nor elephants nor Nile horses, nor anything else of which I myself have no experience. As for the so-called philtres, attraction-charms, dream-senders and hate-charms, I deliberately use their own very names for them. I would not have mentioned these in writing at all, not even if I had sufficient experience of them. In the same way I do not mention the deadly drugs, or those which they themselves call 'affection-producing'. Some of these are even ridiculous, such as binding one's legal opponents so that they cannot utter anything in court, or causing a pregnant woman to miscarry, or making her never conceive, and other such things. Most of these are, even by the test of experience, impossible. Some, even if possible, are at any rate harmful to the life of men, so that I, by the gods, wonder with what intention certain people came to write them. Things that bring disrepute even to the living once they are known, how did they hope these would bring them good repute after death? Now if they had been kings and had made trial of these things on men condemned to death, they would have done nothing terrible. But they were private persons who had no such authority in their whole life, and yet they came to write these things. So it is one of two things. Either they write, without having made trial themselves, about what they do not know. Or, if they did make trial, they are the most impious of all men, having given deadly drugs for the sake of trial to those who had done no wrong, and sometimes even to fine and good men. Someone, at any rate, saw two physicians standing by the dealers in petty wares and brought them honey, supposedly to sell it. They tasted it and discussed the price, and as they offered little, he hurriedly went off [ἐχωρήθη], and neither of the physicians survived. All such things, then, deserve to be hated in those who wrote them no less than in those who did them, indeed even more. For it is a lesser wrong to do some evil alone than to do it along with many [ὅσῳ ... μετὰ πολλῶν]. The experience of evil precepts died together with the one who did the deed. But the experience of all those who wrote is immortal, furnishing the wicked with weapons of malefaction. Let us, then, now speak about the things useful to men, of which we have experience.

[8.13.1] [1. On the spike of nard.] The spike of nard heats in the third degree, and dries in the second degree, at its completion. It is composed of a substance that is adequately astringent, of a pungent and hot one that is not abundant, and of a certain slightly bitter one in small amount. The root, being composed of such powers, is with good reason suited both to the liver and to the stomach. Both when drunk and when applied externally it moves urine, heals bitings of the stomach, and dries the fluxes in the belly and the intestines, and in addition to these also those in the head and the chest. Stronger is the kind called Indian, which is blacker than the one called Syrian.

[8.13.2] [2. On Celtic nard.] Celtic nard is somewhat similar in the kind of its power to the aforementioned [nards], but weaker in every respect except as regards urine. For it is hotter than those, but is less astringent.

[8.13.3] [3. On mountain nard.] Mountain nard, which is also called thylakitis and pyritis, grows in greatest abundance in Cilicia, and it is weaker than those mentioned before. [8.13.4] [4. On narthex.] Of the narthex, the seed heats and thins, while the inner part when still green, the so-called pith (enteriōnē), shares in a certain astringent quality, on account of which it is suitable for those who spit blood and for coeliacs.

[8.13.5] [5. On mustard.] Mustard heats and dries in the fourth rank. [8.13.6] [6. On narcissus.] The root of narcissus is of a drying power to such a degree as to conglutinate the very largest wounds, even as far as severances of the tendons. It also has something cleansing and attractive.

[8.13.7] [7. On neuras.] Neuras, which some call poterion, is of a drying power that does not bite, so that it is even believed to unite severed nerves. Its roots are especially of this kind. And indeed some also give the decoction of them to those who have suffered an affection of the nerves.

[8.13.8] [8. On nērion.] Nērion, or rhododaphnē, is a shrub familiar to everyone. If it is applied as a cataplasm on the outside of the body, it is of a dispersing power; but taken internally it is deadly and deleterious not to human beings only, but also to most grazing animals.

[8.13.9] [9. On nymphaea.] Both the root and the seed of nymphaea have a drying, non-biting power. Accordingly, they check fluxes of the belly, and also semen that is discharged in dream-emissions or otherwise too immoderately; and they also benefit dysenterics. The nymphaea that has the white root is of a more vehement power, so that it heals female flux. Both this one and the one that has the black root are drunk in dark, harsh wine. They also share to some degree in a cleansing power, so that they heal both alphoi and alopeciae. For the alphoi they are moistened with water, and for the alopeciae with liquid pitch. For these purposes the one that has the black root is better, just as the one with the white root is better for the other purposes.

[8.14.1] [1. On xanthion.] Xanthion. It is also called phasganion; its fruit is of a dispersing power. [8.14.2] [2. On xyris.] Xyris (some call it xyrida) is of a fine-particled, drawing and dispersing, and clearly also drying power, both the root and, much more than it, the fruit, which is also diuretic and healing of spleens that are becoming scirrhous.

[8.14.3] [3. On xiphion.] The root of xiphion, and especially the other one, the upper one, is of a drawing and dispersing and, evidently, also drying power. [8.15.1] [1. On oē.] Oē, the tree whose fruit is called oa, but by most people oua, with the upsilon, partakes of an astringent quality, but one much weaker than that of the medlar. For this reason it is also pleasant when eaten, and less binding of the belly than the medlar is.

[8.15.2] [2. On wine.] Wine belongs to the second order of heating things, but wine that is sufficiently old belongs to the third, just as what is called must belongs to the first order. And its drynesses are proportionate to its heats.

[8.15.3] [3. On olynthoi.] Olynthoi (unripe figs) are of a pungent and dispersing power, because of the juice contained in them, which is common to the whole tree. Boiled, then, they disperse hard swellings; raw, they also remove myrmeciae and thymi.

[8.15.4] [4. On holostion.] Holostion is of a drying power together with being astringent, whence they also give it to drink for ruptures. [8.15.5] [5. On olyra.] Olyra is of a nature intermediate between wheat and barley, both as a food and as a drug. So reason about it too on the basis of those.

[8.15.6] [6. On onagra.] Onagra, or onothēra, or onothouris. The root of this, when dried, smells somewhat of wine; and in its power too it is most of all like wine. [8.15.7] [7. On onosma.] Onosma, or osmas, or phlonitis, or onōnis, is composed of a pungent and bitter substance. For this reason it is also believed both to kill and to expel embryos, when its leaves are drunk with wine.

[8.15.8] [8. On onobrychis.] Onobrychis is of a rarefying and dispersing power. For this reason its leaves, when fresh, applied as a poultice, disperse phymata; when dry, drunk with wine, they cure strangury. And moreover, it also provokes sweats when rubbed on with oil.

[8.15.9] [9. On ononis.] Ononis has a root that is heating, already somewhere about the third order. Its bark is especially useful, since it has something both cleansing and cutting; hence it is not only diuretic but also capable of breaking up stones. By the same power it also quickly detaches eschars. People also use it for pains of the teeth, boiling it down in oxycrate and bidding the patient rinse the mouth with it.

[8.15.10] [10. On vinegar.] Vinegar has been shown in the first of these commentaries to be of a mixed substance, cold and hot, both of them fine-particled; and the cold predominates over the hot. The drug is considerably drying, so as to be of the third order, already being completed, whenever it is strong.

[8.15.11] [11. On oxyakanthos.] Oxyakanthos. For this tree is close to the wild pear in its form, and close to it in its power as well. And indeed the fruits too: that of the wild pear is simply acerbic, whereas that of the oxyakantha is both fine-particled and has a little of the cutting [quality]. Yet the fruit of the tree does not resemble that of the wild pear; it is like myrtle berries, being red and loose-textured. It also has stones. Not only when eaten but also when drunk, it is checking of all fluxional affections.

[8.15.12] [12. On sap.] Sap: the Cyrenaic is the hottest and most fine-particled of all, and for this reason also the most dispersing. Nevertheless the others too are considerably hot and windy, for the greater part in them is of airy and fiery substance. There are very many saps, for when any root whatever or stem has been cut, what flows from the cut, thick and viscous, is sap. But more specifically, as by a kind of pre-eminence, they give this name to the Cyrenaic, the Median and the Syrian.

[8.15.13] [13. On origanum.] Of origanum, the Heracleotic is more active than the onitis, and more active than both is the wild one, which some call Heracleian panaces and others konylē. All of them are of a cutting, thinning and heating power, possessing these qualities in the third degree. The one called tragoriganos has also acquired some astringency.

[8.15.14] [14. On orobos.] Orobos (bitter vetch) dries in the second distance, at its intensified level, and heats in the first; and to the extent that it has a share of bitterness, to that extent it cuts, is cleansing, and clears obstructions. Taken in larger quantity, it brings blood out through the urine.
[8.15.15] [15. On orobanche.] Orobanche is of a dry and cold mixture in the first order. [8.15.16] [16. On rice.] Rice has something astringent; for this reason it also moderately checks the belly.

[8.15.17] [17. On dog's orchis.] Orchis. The same plant is also called dog's orchis (kynos orchis). The power of its root, which is bulbous and double, is moist and hot; hence it also appears rather sweet to those who taste it. But the larger root seems to contain much moisture, both residual and flatulent; for this reason, when drunk, it also incites to sexual activity. The other, smaller one, conversely, is sufficiently worked up (concocted), so that its mixture inclines towards the hotter and drier; whence this root not only does not incite the impulses towards sexual intercourse, but, quite the contrary, actually checks and suppresses them. They are eaten roasted, in the manner of bulbs.

[8.15.18] [18. On the orchis [called] serapias.] Orchis, which they also call serapias, is of a drier power than the former, so that it is not equally suitable for sexual matters. But applied as a cataplasm it disperses oedemas, cleanses foul ulcers and heals herpētes. When dried, it dries still very much more, so that it heals even the putrefactive and the malignant among ulcers. For it also has something slightly astringent, and for this reason, drunk with wine, it checks the belly.
[8.15.19] [19. On osyris.] Of the herb osyris, from which brooms are also made, the quality is bitter and the power unblocking; hence it also benefits obstructions in the liver.

[8.16.1] [1. On pancratium.] Pancratium. Its root resembles squill both in taste and in power, so that some people even use it when squill is not available. For it effects all the same things in the same way as far as kind goes, but is far weaker.

[8.16.2] [2. On paliurus.] The leaves and the root of paliurus share not indistinctly in an astringent power, so as even to check a flowing belly, and in a dispersing one to such a degree as even to treat phymata, at least those that are not exceedingly inflammatory and hot. The fruit shares in a cutting power to so great a degree as even to break up stones in the bladder and to help expectorations from the chest and lung.

[8.16.3] [3. On papyrus.] Papyrus by itself, on its own, does not even come into medical use; but when soaked or burnt it becomes useful. Soaked, then, in oxycrate or wine, it agglutinates fresh wounds, especially when laid round them in a circle. But in this case it is, as it were, a kind of material receptive of the healing drugs. Once it has been burnt, however, it then becomes a drying drug, just as the ash of burnt paper also is, except in so far as that of papyrus is weaker.

[8.16.4] [4. On Heracleian panax.] Heracleian panakes: from this also comes what is called opopanax, when its roots and stalks are cut into. Opopanax itself is of very many uses, being heating, softening and dispersing. One might place it, as regards heating, in the third order, and as regards drying, in the second. The bark of the root is a drug that is at once drying and heating, but less so than the juice. It also has something cleansing about it. For this reason we use it both for bones that are laid bare and for ulcers that are becoming malignant. For it is quite capable of filling such things with flesh, in that it at once cleanses and dries and does not heat very vehemently, all of which is required of whatever is to fill with flesh, as we demonstrate in the books of the Therapeutic Method. Its fruit, being itself also hot, is a drug that is a promoter of the menses. But, I do not know how, it has now become customary with almost everyone to call this herb not panakes but panax (πάνακα).

[8.16.5] [5. On Asclepian panax.] Asclepian panax. This is less hot than the panax written of before; hence people use both its flowers and its fruit, mixing them with honey, for ulcers, phymata and phagedaenae.

[8.16.6] [6. On Chironian panax.] Chironian panax. This too is of a power similar to the one written above. [8.16.7] [7. On paronychia.] Paronychia has been named from its action, for it heals paronychiae; and, as Dioscorides says, ceria as well. Its power is fine-particled, drying, and does not bite. For such must the drugs for paronychia also be. And it is clear that such a thing is also capable of dispersing all the affections that require to be dispersed. For such are those which belong to the third order both in heating and in drying, just as this one too is of fine-particled substance.

[8.16.8] [8. On cinquefoil.] Cinquefoil. Its root dries strongly, but is very little pungent. For this reason it is also of many uses, just as are all the other things which, being fine-particled, dry without biting. For this root too is drying, from somewhere already in the third order, while having very little share in manifest heat.

[8.16.9] [9. On peplos.] Peplos, which some call 'foamy' poppy (mēkōn aphrōdēs). This shrublet too has a juice like that of the spurges (tithymalloi), both in other respects and in that it purges, as they do.

[8.16.10] [10. On peplion.] Peplion. This shrublet too has a juice, as the tithymalli also do, and it grows for the most part by the sea, having a useless root, just as the peplos also does. Its juice is strong, but this too is not of much use; the seed, however, is useful and flatulent, purging in the same way as the seed of the peplos.

[8.16.11] [11. On pepper.] The root of pepper most resembles costus in its power. Of the fruit, that of the plant when it is just sprouting is long pepper, which is why it is also moister than the ripe fruit. A sign of its moisture is both that, when stored, it is readily pierced, and that it does not bite at once, but begins to do so after a short while and persists for a longer time. The fruit that is like an unripe grape is white pepper, which is more pungent than the black. For the black is, as it were, already over-roasted and over-dried. Both heat and dry strongly.

[8.16.12] [12. On persea.] The leaves of persea partake in a moderate degree of an astringent power, so that they can sometimes be applied with benefit even to parts that are haemorrhaging. [8.16.13] [13. On periclymenum.] Both the fruit and the leaves of periclymenum are useful, being of a cutting and at the same time heating power, to such an extent that they even make the urine bloody when they are drunk for a longer time. At the beginning, however, it is only diuretic; and applied externally, rubbed on together with oil, it heats. It also benefits the splenic and the dyspnoeic. The due measure of the draught is a quantity of one drachm with wine. It also dries up the seed, and some say that if it is drunk for a longer time, those who drink it become wholly infertile. Some also define a fixed term of days for such drinking, as does Dioscorides too, saying that they are reported to be thirty-seven. He also says that the urine becomes bloody from the sixth of the days onward.

[8.16.14] [14. On peristereon.] Peristereon has been named from the fact that doves spend their time in it. Its drying power is so great that it glues wounds together. [8.16.15] [15. On petasites.] Petasites belongs to the third order of drying things; for this reason they use it on malignant and phagedaenic ulcers.

[8.16.16] [16. On parsley.] Of parsley it is the seed that is most useful, while the whole herb together with the roots is of a similar but weaker power. And just as it is pungent with bitterness in taste, so also in its effects it is hot together with cutting, and for these reasons it promotes the menses and urine copiously. It is also free of flatulence. It would therefore itself also belong to the third order of things that heat and dry. The people in Cilicia call 'parsley' only the plant that grows on the Amanus. It is, however, smyrnion rather than parsley, yet it certainly does not differ much from the power of parsley.

[8.16.17] [17. On peucedanum.] Of peucedanum we use the root above all, but we also use the sap and the juice. All of these are of the same power in kind, but the sap is the strongest of them, heating and dispersing considerably; for this reason it is also believed to be suited to all affections of the nerves, and to the diseases of the lung and thorax that arise from thickness or viscosity of the humours. It is beneficial not only when taken inside the body, but also when smelled. By thinning and cutting it has sometimes immediately stopped the pains of perforated teeth when placed in the carious cavity, because it is fine-particled and heating. Moreover, it also benefits indurated (scirrhous) spleens by cutting, dispersing and thinning the thick humours. The root may be used for these purposes as well. It also detaches scales of bone very quickly, because it dries vehemently, while heating less than the sap does. And for malignant ulcers it is an excellent drug when plastered on dry. For it cleanses, fills with flesh and leads on to cicatrisation, heating in the second order where this is by now somewhere near completion, and drying in the third at its beginning.

[8.16.18] [18. On rue.] Rue: the wild kind already belongs to the fourth order of heating things, the cultivated kind to the third. To the taste it is not only pungent but also bitter, and by virtue of this it also has the property of cutting and dispersing thick and viscid humours. Through this same power it also provokes evacuation by way of the urine. Moreover, it is also fine-particled and free of flatulence, and for this reason it is suited to inflations, checks the desires for sexual intercourse, and disperses and dries vigorously; for it is one of the strongly drying drugs. And that which in the earlier discussions we said is called moly and besasa would itself also be wild rue.

[8.16.19] [19. On pitch.] Dry pitch dries and heats in the second remove from the moderate, and it is of a nature to dry more than to heat. Liquid pitch, conversely, heats more than it dries. It also has something fine-particled, by which it benefits the asthmatic and those with empyema. As for quantity, it is enough to take a cyathus, mixing it with honey [lit. 'a cyathus of honey']. But they also have something cleansing, concocting and dispersing, just as they are also somewhat bitter and pungent to the taste. Thus, mixed with wax, they remove leprous nails and cleanse away leichenes. They also concoct all hard and unconcocted swellings when added to poultices, and for all such purposes the liquid is stronger. Dry pitch is inferior for these purposes, but more suitable for the gluing together of wounds. It is clear from this, then, that an abundant quantity of hot moisture is mixed into liquid pitch.

[8.16.20] [20. On pitch-oil.] Pitch-oil (pisselaion) is made from liquid pitch; it is similar to it in kind, but more fine-particled in substance. [8.16.21] [21. On the pistachio.] Pistachio. This plant grows most abundantly in Syria. Its fruit is of a somewhat more fine-particled substance, one that has something somewhat bitter and aromatic about it. Accordingly it clears obstructions and thoroughly cleanses above all the parts about the liver, but also those about the thorax and lung.

[8.16.22] [22. On pityides.] Pityides. This is the name given to the fruit of the pine (pitys); but some, using the term loosely, call that of the pitch-pine (peukē) by the same name as well. They are of mixed power, inasmuch as they are both astringent and possess a certain pungency together with bitterness. Hence they also assist expectorations from the chest and lung.

[8.16.23] [23. On the pine (pitys).] The bark of the pine has the astringent power predominant to such a degree that, applied as a plaster, it heals chafings excellently, and it checks the belly if drunk. It also cicatrizes burns. The bark of the peukē-pine is similar to it, but more moderate in its power. In the leaves of both trees, inasmuch as they are much moister than the bark, there is a power agglutinating wounds. In the cone, however, even if the power is close to these, it is nevertheless stronger than in the bark and the leaves, so that it can no longer do any of the aforementioned things well, but already has something biting and distressing. The soot from the aforesaid is useful for eyelids that have lost their lashes, and for canthi that are dank, eroded round about, and watering.

[8.16.24] [24. On pityousa.] Pityousa. Some consider this too to be a kind of spurge (tithymallos), because it has juice just as those do, and because it purges in a similar way to them, and in all other respects it resembles them in its power.

[8.16.25] [25. On the plane tree.] The plane tree is of a moister and colder substance than the moderate ones, though not by very much. For this reason its green leaves, pounded smooth and applied as a poultice, benefit inflammations in the process of forming, and not obscurely. Its bark and its little balls are already of a more drying power, so that the bark, boiled down in vinegar, is employed for pains of the teeth, and the little balls, with fat, for ulcers caused by burning. There are some who also burn the bark and make of it a drying and cleansing drug, so that with water it heals leprai, and applied by itself as a plaster it heals ulcers that are old and foul through much moisture. One must beware of the down on the leaves of the tree: for when breathed in it harms the windpipe, drying and roughening it violently, and it damages the voice, just as it also damages sight and hearing when it falls into the eyes and ears.

[8.16.26] [26. On polygonon.] Polygonon has something astringent as well, but the watery cold predominates in it, so that it stands in the second order among cooling drugs, or perhaps even somewhere at the beginning of the third. At any rate, applied cold externally as a poultice, it benefits those who suffer burning in the stomach, as it also benefits erysipelas and hot inflammations. Being of such a kind, it also repels fluxes, and in this respect it seems to be drying. For this reason it is also a good drug for herpes, and for ulcers, both the others and, most evidently, those that are inflamed and fluxional. It is also agglutinating of bloody wounds. It also benefits ulcers in the ears, even if there is a good deal of pus in them, and this too it dries. Through the same powers it also stops female flux, dysentery, the bringing up of blood, and immoderate discharges from any other place whatever. Dioscorides also says that it provokes urine when given to those suffering from strangury; he does not, however, distinguish precisely the condition in which it ought to be given. For all the things mentioned the male is stronger than the female.

[8.16.27] [27. On polygala.] Polygala has moderately harsh leaves. When drunk, they are thought to generate milk, so that the hot and the moist would predominate in it. [8.16.28] [28. On polygonatum.] Polygonatum is of mixed power and quality. For it has something of astringency, of pungency and of bitterness, and of a certain indescribable unpleasantness. For this reason it is not of many uses either, except only that some apply the root as a plaster to wounds. And there are those who cleanse away spots on the face by means of it.

[8.16.29] [29. On polemonion.] Polemonion (others call it philetairion, and some, as the Cappadocians do, chiliodynamis) is of a fine-particled and drying power. For this reason some give its root to drink with wine for cases of ischias and dysentery and for a spleen that is becoming scirrhous.

[8.16.30] [30. On polion.] Polion is bitter to those who taste it, and moderately pungent. Accordingly it clears obstructions from all the viscera and moves urine and menses; and while it is still green it agglutinates large wounds, its shrubby kind most of all. When it has become dry it heals malignant ulcers when sprinkled on, and the smaller kind does this more.

[8.16.31] [31. On the small polion.] The small polion is the one we also use in antidotes; for it is both more pungent and more bitter than the larger, so that it belongs to the third order of drying things and to the completed second order of heating things.

[8.16.32] [32. On polyknēmon.] Polyknēmon dries and heats in the second remove, so that for this reason too it is agglutinating of wounds. [8.16.33] [33. On potamogeiton.] Potamogeiton is astringent and cools much as polygonon does; but its substance is more coarse-particled than that of polygonon.

[8.16.34] [34. On polypody.] Polypody has the sweet and at the same time harsh quality predominating, so that it is of a drying power that is quite free from biting. [8.16.35] [35. On horehound.] Horehound, just as it is bitter to the taste, so also for those who use it has an activity in agreement with such a flavour: it clears obstructions of both liver and spleen, thoroughly clears out the parts in the thorax and the lung, and promotes the menses. Moreover, applied as a poultice, it is both cleansing and dispersing. One might place it, as regards heat, somewhere in the second order, already being completed, and as regards dryness in the third, either at its middle and being completed. Its juice they use with honey for sharpness of sight; moreover, they also purge jaundices through the nostrils with it, and they employ it for pains of the ears that have already become chronic, insofar as there is need to clear obstructions from and thoroughly clear out both the passage itself and the offshoots of the meninges.

[8.16.36] [36. On propolis.] Propolis is of a cleansing power that is not strong, but of a drawing power that is quite strong; for it is fine-particled in its substance. It heats at the second remove, already being completed, and at the beginning of the third.

[8.16.37] [37. On ptarmikē.] The flowers of ptarmikē are of a sternutatory power, which is indeed why the herb has its name. The whole shrublet disperses bruises beneath the eyes (hypōpia) and the other ecchymoses. For its mixture is hot and dry: while it is still green, in the second order, but if it has been dried, in the third.

[8.16.38] [38. On elm.] With the leaves of the elm we once agglutinated a fresh wound, confident in the fact that they carry an astringent and at the same time cleansing power. The bark is even more both somewhat bitter and astringent, so that with vinegar it even heals lepra; and while it is still green and fresh, if it is wound around wounds as a bandage, it is able to agglutinate them. The roots too are of the same power, so that some people also bathe with the decoction those fractures that require the formation of callus.

[8.16.39] [39. On fern and female fern.] Fern has a root that is especially useful. For it kills the broad worm, if one takes a weight of four drachms of it in honey-water. And in the same way it is no wonder that it destroys embryos that are living and expels those that are dead. For it is bitter, partaking of a little astringency. For this reason, when it is applied to ulcers too, it is of a strongly drying power, yet not biting. And the so-called female fern also has a power similar to it.

[8.16.40] [40. On pyknokomon.] Of pyknokomon the root, the fruit and the leaves are all of a dispersing and drawing power, being also pungent to the taste.
