The leaves, then, disperse phymata and boils, while the fruit is stronger, and it is naturally able to accomplish these things when mixed with some one of the dispersing poultices, such as is also the one made with barley [meal]; and it also draws splinters and all such things out towards the outer surface. The root, however, is inferior and weaker for the purposes mentioned before, but it is purgative of yellow bile.

[8.16.41] [41. On pyrethron.] Of pyrethron we use chiefly the root, which has a caustic power. By this power it soothes the pains of chilled teeth, and, rubbed on with oil before the periodic rigors, it benefits those who are numb and those who are paralysed.

[8.16.42] [42. On wheat.] Of what nature wheat is as a food is not a matter for the present treatise; but as a drug applied externally it belongs to the first order of heating things, though it is not of a nature either to dry or to moisten perceptibly. It also has something viscid and obstructive. The starch prepared from it becomes both colder and more drying than it. And the poultice made from bread is of a more dispersing power than that made from wheat grains, since the bread has previously taken up both salt and leaven. For leaven is of a power both attractive and dispersing of things from the depth.

[8.17.1] [1. On rhamnos.] Rhamnos dries and is dispersing in the second degree, and cools in the first degree at its completion, or in the second at its beginning. For this reason it also heals herpētes and erysipelas that are not very hot. One should use its tender leaves for these purposes.

[8.17.2] [2. On radish.] Radish heats in the third remove and dries in the second. The wild radish is more efficacious in both respects; and indeed the seed is also more efficacious than the plant itself. The power in it is dispersing, so that, owing to this kind of power, they have also proved beneficial for bruises and other livid marks.

[8.17.3] [3. On rhēon.] Rhēon, which some call rha, is of a mixed mixture and power. For it has something earthy and cold, as its astringency shows; but a certain heat is also present in it, for when chewed for a longer time it appears somewhat pungent. And indeed, that it partakes of a fine-particled, airy substance is shown both by its loose texture and its lightness, but not least also by its effects. For precisely because of this, although it is astringent, it nevertheless benefits not only strains (spasmata) but also ruptures and orthopnoea. So too it heals livid marks and leichenes when smeared on with vinegar. That the effects of its astringency are also vigorous may be learned from the benefit it gives to those who spit blood, to coeliacs and to dysenterics. For the fine-particled airy part does not work against the earthy cold part; rather, what guides it on its way and leads it into the depth becomes the cause of a stronger action.

[8.17.4] [4. On resins.] All resins dry and heat. They differ from one another in having more or less of what is pungent in taste and heating in power; in some of them being less fine-particled and others more; and in some partaking of astringency and others not. Of them all, the resin of the schinos is with good reason given first place; they call it mastic. For besides partaking of a little astringency, so that it suits atonies and inflammations of the stomach, the belly and the liver, it also has the property of drying without causing distress. For it is the least pungent and the most fine-particled. Of the others, the terebinth resin holds first place. It does not have an astringency as evident as that of mastic, but it possesses a certain bitterness, through which it also disperses more than mastic does. Through this same quality it also has a cleansing property to such a degree that it even heals psōrai. Moreover it draws out what lies in the depth more than the other resins do, because it is also more fine-particled than they are. The peukē resin, and still more than this the strobilos resin, are more pungent than it, yet they neither disperse more nor draw more. Intermediate between them are the pitys resin and the fir resin, being more pungent than the terebinth resin but less pungent than the peukē and strobilos resins. The terebinth resin also has something softening. Second in softening is the schinos resin, just as the cypress resin is pungent.

[8.17.5] [5. On Roses.] The power of roses has been stated at some length in the foregoing: it is composed of a warm watery substance mixed with two other qualities, the astringent and the bitter. Moreover, what each of the two is like in its nature, both the bitter and the astringent, I have stated in the fourth of these commentaries. Their flower is still more astringent than the roses themselves, and for this reason, evidently, drying.

[8.17.6] [6. On rhodia root.] Rhodia root, the kind that grows in Macedonia, is of a fine-particled and dispersing power. In heating, one should place it somewhere in the second remove, or else at the beginning of the third.

[8.17.7] [7. On rhododaphne.] Rhododaphne is, by its whole substance, deleterious not only to human beings but also to most grazing animals; in its mixture, however, it belongs to the beginning of the third mixture of heating things, and to the first of drying things.

[8.17.8] [8. On pomegranates.] Every pomegranate shares in the astringent quality, though that quality does not predominate in all of them. For some of them are sour, and some are sweet rather than harsh. And indeed the benefits of each of them must come about according to the predominant quality. In the fourth of these commentaries an account was given of the sweet, the harsh and the sour flavour, so that from what was said there you can also work out the difference among pomegranates. The seeds are more astringent and more drying than the juice, and the rinds, which are called sidia, are still more so than the seeds. The flower-cups (kytinoi) are of a power similar to these.

[8.17.9] [9. On rhus.] Rhus, the shrubby plant, is astringent and drying, just as tanners also use the plant to dry and astringe hides; and for this reason the physicians call it 'tanners' rhus' (byrsodepsikē). Its fruit above all, and its juice, come into use, being of a considerably harsh quality. And all its use in particular cases agrees with the perception by taste. So this drug too would be drying of the third order, and cooling of the second.

[8.17.10] [10. On rhypos.] The rhypos from the statues in the gymnasia, on which abundant oil lies, is both dispersing and softening. That in the palaestrae differs from it to the extent that it has taken up dust; this rhypos they call patos. The former, then, is dispersing of unconcocted phymata, while the second is an excellent remedy for phlegmone of the breasts. For it quenches their fiery heat, checks what flows in, and disperses what is contained there; for it is composed of dust, oil, human rhypos and sweat. Now the dust is emplastic, cooling and repelling; the oil is softening; and the sweat and the rhypos are dispersing. The rhypos from the statues, since it has no dust and has also taken up some verdigris (ios) from the bronze, is reasonably more pungent. We have mentioned it here too because the greater part of it consists of oil-like substance, which has its origin from a plant. But it will be necessary to mention it also among the drugs from animals, on account of the sweat.

[8.18.1] [1. On sagapenum.] Sagapenum is a sap, hot and fine-particled, like the other saps. It also has something cleansing, by which it both cleans away and thins the scars in the eyes. Moreover, it is also a good drug for suffusions and for amblyopias that arise through thickness of the fluids. The plant itself from which it comes, which resembles giant fennel, is weak and useless; and it is evidently that plant which is called sagapenum in the first instance. For its sap is so named by those who use the word loosely, just as we also name many other things, by an abuse of terms, with an elliptical expression. For it would have been more complete to call it not 'sagapenum' but 'sap of sagapenum'.

[8.18.2] [2. On sampsuchon.] Sampsuchon is of a fine-particled and dispersing power, for it both dries and heats in the third order. [8.18.3] [3. On the rottenness of woods.] The rottenness of woods, and especially of those that partake of astringency together with cleansing, as the elm also does, cleans and fills up the moist ones among ulcers.

[8.18.4] [4. On sarcocolla.] Sarcocolla is the tear of a Persian tree. It has a mixed power, made up of a certain clogging substance and a slight bitter one; hence it dries without biting, and for this reason it is able to glue wounds together.

[8.18.5] [5. On satyrion.] Satyrion, or trifolium, is moist and hot in its mixture, and this is why it also appears sweet when tasted. It possesses, however, a residual and flatulent moisture, and for this reason it incites to sexual intercourse. The root of the plant is also naturally disposed to do these same things. And, as some write, it also cures opisthotonus when drunk with black harsh wine.

[8.18.6] [6. On celery.] Celery is hot to such a degree as to provoke both urine and menses. It is also free of flatulence, and the seed more so than the herb. The power of mountain celery and of horse celery is also similar. Horse celery is weaker, just as mountain celery is stronger.

[8.18.7] [7. On seris.] Seris is a somewhat bitter pot-herb, and the wild kind more so; for this very reason some call it picris, while others name it kichorion. It is of a dry and cold mixture, having both at the first remove. The cultivated kind cools more than the wild, but through the admixture of much extraneous moisture it loses its drying. Both share in the astringent quality, as does chondrilla too; for it is also a kind of seris.

[8.18.8] [8. On seriphon.] Seriphon. This has been discussed in the sixth book, in the account of wormwood. For it is similar to wormwood in appearance and in taste, but it nonetheless differs from it: in taste, in that it is not astringent to the same degree as that plant, and in that it heats more and is more bitter, with a certain saltiness; and in its power, in that it is bad for the stomach and kills worms more than wormwood does, both when applied externally and when taken inside the body. Furthermore, it must be classed as heating in the second order, at its intensified end, and as drying in the third.

[8.18.9] [9. On seseli.] Seseli. Both its root and, further, its fruit belong to the warming drugs to such a degree that it is a markedly diuretic drug. It is also fine-particled, so that it is suitable also for epilepsies and orthopnoeas.

[8.18.10] [10. On sesame.] Sesame has in itself no small amount of the viscous and oily, whence it is clogging and at the same time softening, and moderately warm. The oil made from it is also of the same power. And the decoction of the herb, too, is of a similar power.

[8.18.11] [11. On sesamoides.] The great sesamoides, which has also been named Anticyran hellebore because its seed purges in a manner similar to hellebore. This plant is similar to hellebore in its other power as well. And indeed in cleansing, heating and drying too it is like that drug in its power.

[8.18.12] [12. On the white sesamoides.] The seed of the white sesamoides has some share of a pungent quality as well, but it is considerably bitter. Accordingly, it heats, ruptures, and is cleansing.

[8.18.13] [13. On sideritis.] Sideritis has something cleansing too, but the greater part of it is moist and moderately cold, and it has a share of a slight astringency; hence it is both preventive of inflammation and agglutinating. Some also call the Achilleios sideritis; it resembles the aforementioned in its power, at least as regards what has now been said, but it exceeds it in astringency. For this reason it is suited also to haemorrhages, dysentery and female fluxes.

[8.18.14] [14. On the edible cucumber.] Of the edible cucumber, the one that is already ripe is of a more fine-particled substance, while the one that is not so is of a more coarse-particled substance. Nevertheless, they also have a share in a cleansing and cutting power, whence they are both diuretic and make the body bright, and more so if one dries the seed, and then pounds and sifts it and uses it as a detergent. In them a moist and cold mixture prevails, not strongly, however, but such that it is placed somewhere in the second order. If, however, one dries the seed or the root, it is no longer of a moist nature either, but already of a drying one, somewhere in the first order, or even at the beginning of the second. And the cleansing quality is also greater in these than in the flesh of the fruit.

[8.18.15] [15. On the wild cucumber.] Of the wild cucumber, both the juice of the fruit, which they call elaterium, and, not least, that of the root and of the leaves, are suitable for treatments. Elaterium, then, provokes the menses and destroys what is being carried in the womb when applied as a pessary, as do the other substances that are at once bitter and fine-particled, especially if they also partake of some heat, as indeed elaterium does. For it is extremely bitter, but hot only to a slight degree, so as to belong to the second order in respect of heat. And such a substance is at once also of dispersing power; thus some anoint those suffering from synanche with it, together with honey or old oil. It is good also for those with jaundice when poured into the nostrils with milk. And used in this way it also cures headaches. Such, then, is elaterium. The juice of the root, as also that of the leaves, is similar to elaterium in power, but weaker. And the root itself is also of a closely similar power. For it cleanses, disperses and softens; but its bark is more drying than it.

[8.18.16] [16. On silphium.] Of silphium the sap is the hottest, but nevertheless the leaves, the stalk and the root also heat vigorously. All of them, however, are of a rather flatulent substance, and for this reason hard to digest. Applied externally to the body, though, they are more efficacious, and the sap most of all, since it is of a considerably drawing power. Moreover it also has something reducing and colliquative about it, on account of its aforementioned mixture.
[8.18.17] [17. On sison.] Sison is hot and somewhat bitter in taste. Hence it is both diuretic and concoctive, and provocative of the menses, and unblocking of all obstructions in the viscera.

[8.18.18] [18. On sion.] Sion, to the extent that it is somewhat aromatic in taste, to that same extent it also partakes of a somewhat heating power. It is dispersing and diuretic, breaks up stones in the kidneys, and is a promoter of the menses.

[8.18.19] [19. On the root of skirret.] The root of skirret, when boiled, is good for the stomach and diuretic, heating in the second order, and it also has something of bitterness and something of a slight astringency.

[8.18.20] [20. On sisymbrion.] Sisymbrion is of a fine-particled, dispersing power and mixture, heating and drying in the third order. Its seed too is fine-particled and hot, whence some give it with wine to those who hiccup and to those suffering from gripings.

[8.18.21] [21. On sisymbrion.] Sisymbrion, which some call kardaminē, since it has something resembling kardamōmon in taste, when it is dry, belongs to the third order of things that both dry and at the same time heat; but when it is moist and green, to the second.

[8.18.22] [22. On skandix.] Skandix is one of the wild pot-herbs, somewhat acrid and bitter, so that in drying and in heating it belongs either to the second order at its intensified end or to the third order at its beginning. It is considerably diuretic and unblocking of the viscera, being composed of the aforementioned qualities.

[8.18.23] [23. On squill] Squill is of a considerably cutting power, though not strongly hot; in this respect, at any rate, one might place it in the second rank of heating things. It is better to take it after roasting or boiling it, for in this way the violence of its power is dissipated.

[8.18.24] [24. On the root of scolymus.] The root of scolymus brings out a quantity of foul-smelling urine, if one boils it down in wine and drinks it. And for this reason it also cures the foul smells both of the armpits and of the whole body. This, then, belongs to the drug, as being purgative of a humour of this kind, by virtue of its whole substance. But its activity according to the qualities shows the drug to be hot in the second order, when this is already being completed, or at the beginning of the third, and dry in the second.

[8.18.25] [25. On skordion.] Skordion. This is composed of manifold flavours and powers. For it has something bitter, acerbic and pungent, and its pungency resembles garlic most of all, whence, I think, it also took its name. Accordingly, it at the same time thoroughly cleanses and warms the viscera, and provokes the menses and urine; and when drunk it heals sprains and ruptures, and pains of the sides arising from obstruction and chilling. Applied green as a plaster it agglutinates large wounds, and sprinkled on dry it cleans out foul ones and brings malignant ones to a scar.

[8.18.26] [26. On garlic.] Garlic dries and heats in the fourth degree. The so-called ophioskorodon ('snake-garlic') is a wild garlic, stronger than the cultivated, just as the other wild plants are too.
[8.18.27] [27. On skordoprason.] Skordoprason, just as in taste and in smell it possesses a quality mixed of garlic and leek, so in the same manner it does also in its power.
[8.18.28] [28. On scorpioides.] Scorpioides heats in the third order and dries in the second. [8.18.29] [29. On smilax.] Smilax, or taxos, is a tree of deleterious power.

[8.18.30] [30. On myrrh.] Myrrh belongs to the second order of things that heat and dry. At any rate, when applied as a plaster to wounds in the head, it is able to conglutinate them. It also partakes of no small bitterness, on account of which it both kills and expels embryos and worms. Its cleansing property also comes to it from this source. Thus, at any rate, it is also mixed into those ophthalmic preparations that are compounded for ulcers and thick scars. And for the same reason it is mixed into the drugs given for chronic cough and asthma. Yet it does not roughen the windpipe, as some of the cleansing drugs do; rather, its cleansing is so moderate that some even mix it into the drugs called arteriac, as a drug that heats and dries sufficiently, and they are not at all wary of the cleansing that comes from its bitterness.

[8.18.31] [31. On 'ox' myrrh.] 'Ox' myrrh has a heating, diffusing, softening power. [8.18.32] [32. On smyrnion.] Smyrnion, which some call wild horse-celery, is also of the same genus as celery and parsley. It would be stronger than celery but weaker than parsley. So it promotes the menses, is diuretic, and is hot and dry in the third order. The people in Cilicia give the name parsley to the plant that grows on Amanus. This too, however, is a smyrnion, but it is less pungent than parsley and smyrnion, and for this reason it can also be applied to wounds, because it dries without causing pain. It is also dispersing of hardened swellings. Its other power is similar to that of celery and parsley, and for this reason we also use its seed for the menses, urine and asthma.

[8.18.33] [33. On sonchos.] Sonchos, once it has reached maturity, is one of the thorny plants, but while still green and tender it is eaten in the same way as the other wild vegetables. Its mixture is in a certain way mixed, for it is composed of a watery and an earthy substance, both of them mildly cold. For it partakes of some astringency and clearly cools, whether applied as a poultice or eaten. But when it has been completely dried, its mixture becomes earthy, possessing a moderate heat.

[8.18.34] [34. On sparganion.] Sparganion is also of a drying power. [8.18.35] [35. On spartē.] Spartē, with which the vines are bound in our country: both its fruit and the juice of its rods are of a drawing power, and not feebly so.

[8.18.36] [36. On staphylinos.] Of staphylinos, the cultivated kind is weaker and the wild kind stronger in all respects. It moves urine and promotes the menses; the whole herb does this, but above all the seed and the root. It also has something cleansing in it, and for this reason some people plaster phagedaenic ulcers with its leaves, while green, together with honey, in order to make them clean.

[8.18.37] [37. On stachys.] Stachys, the shrub that resembles prasion, is pungent and bitter when tasted, and belongs to the third order of heating things. It is therefore reasonable that it not only moves the menses but is also an abortifacient drug, and it expels afterbirths.

[8.18.38] [38. On stoibē.] Of stoibē the fruit and the leaves are especially useful, having an astringent power that does not bite. It is also manifestly drying, at about the beginning of the third order. Hence their decoction is both injected for dysenterics and into suppurating ears, and it is agglutinating of large wounds. It does these things more manifestly with dark, harsh wine, for it strongly dries all moistures contrary to nature. Further, the leaves, applied green as a poultice, have a power checking haemorrhages; and applied as a poultice it also benefits the confusions of the eyes resulting from a blow.

[8.18.39] [39. On stoechas.] The quality of stoechas as regards taste is bitter and mildly astringent, to a moderate degree. Its mixture is composite: a small amount of cold earthy substance, from which it is astringent, and a larger amount of another earthy substance that has been thinned, from which it is bitter. Through the conjunction of both it is naturally apt to clear obstructions, to thin, to cleanse, and to strengthen all the viscera and the condition of the whole animal. For it was shown in the preceding books that all drugs composed of such substances perform the actions stated.

[8.18.40] [40. On stratiotes.] Of stratiotes, the aquatic kind is moist and cold in power, while the terrestrial kind also has some astringency, so that for this reason it is able to conglutinate wounds and is useful for ulcers. Some people also use it for haemorrhage and for fistulae.

[8.18.41] [41. On strouthion.] Of strouthion we use chiefly the root, which is pungent to the taste, and hot and dry in its mixture, presumably of the fourth order. It is also cleansing and irritating, and for this reason it provokes sneezes, in the same way as the other things that are pungent when tasted and hot in their mixtures.

[8.18.42] [42. On storax.] Storax heats, softens and concocts; for this reason it is also beneficial for coughs, catarrhs, coryzas and hoarsenesses, and it promotes the menses both when drunk and when applied as a pessary. The soot of it, when it is burnt, is in some way similar to that of frankincense.

[8.18.43] [43. On figs.] Of figs, the dry ones are hot in power, somewhere about the first order when it is already being completed, or the second when it is beginning; and they also have something fine-particled. From both of these [properties] they are capable of concocting hard swellings, and they also disperse them straightaway. So when applied as a poultice by themselves they are of such a power; and their decoction is also of a similar nature. Where you wish rather to concoct, you should mix in wheaten meal, and where you wish to disperse, barley [meal]. Bread is intermediate between these. But such matters belong more properly to the composition of drugs and to the therapeutic method. For the present purpose it is enough to know these things about dried figs. One should also know that the dirtier ones are more apt to concoct, while those that are more pungent to the taste are naturally disposed to be cleansing and dispersing; and what results from them when they are boiled in water for a very long time is like honey, not only in consistency but also in power. Fresh figs, when eaten, are of weaker power because of the admixture of moisture; both, however, the moist and the dry alike, move the bowel. The figs of the wild fig trees are of pungent and dispersing power. So too are the unripe figs of the cultivated trees, for they still share in the sap of the fig tree.

[8.18.44] [44. On the fig tree.] The fig tree is of a hot and fine-particled mixture, as both its sap and the juice of its leaves show. For each of them is strongly hot, so that it not only bites or cleanses vehemently, but also ulcerates, opens the mouths of vessels and removes myrmeciae. It is also purgative. The sap and juice of the wild fig tree, which they call erineos, are stronger in every respect than those of the cultivated. And their branches are so hot and fine-particled in mixture that, when thrown in with tough beef that is being boiled, they make it tender.

[8.18.45] [45. On rock symphyton.] Rock symphyton is composed of opposite powers. For it has something cutting, by which it is also naturally able to clear out the pus contained in the thorax and lung. It also has something that draws together, by which it also gives help against the bringing-up of blood. And, third, besides these, it has a certain moisture that is warm in no immoderate degree, on account of which it also appears sweet to those who taste it and pleasant to the sense of smell. When chewed it allays thirst, and it heals roughnesses in the windpipe (arteria). In accordance with the mixture of all the powers mentioned, it is able at the same time both to disperse and to draw together and to constrict bodies. For this reason it is both applied to enteroceles and drunk with oxymel for strains and ruptures. Those who give it, boiled in wine, for dysentery and red flux use it as something that dries and draws together; and those who give it for nephritis use it as something that clears out and cuts.

[8.18.46] [46. On the great symphyton.] The other symphyton, the great one, is of a power closely similar to the one previously described; it does not, however, appear sweet to those who taste it, nor fragrant to those who smell it; in these respects, then, it has departed from the one written about before. But in so far as it has something viscid and biting, it is closely similar to squill. People use it for the same things as the one previously described.

[8.18.47] [47. On sphondylion.] The fruit of sphondylion is of a pungent and cutting power, so that it is a good drug both for asthma and for epilepsy. It also benefits those with jaundice. The root too, being of a similar power, is suitable in the same cases; in addition, it also removes the callosities of fistulae. One must scrape it all round and insert it. The juice of the flower is also laid by in store, being suitable for the more chronic ulcers in the ears.

[8.18.48] [48. On mastic.] Mastic: this shrub is composed of a watery substance gently hot in power and of an earthy, cold substance, not in great quantity, on account of which it is also moderately astringent. It dries, then, in the second order when this is already being completed, or at the beginning of the third. In the distinction according to heat and cold it is in some way intermediate and well-balanced. It has a similar astringency in all its parts: in the roots, in the branches, in the shoots, in the sprouts, in the leaves, and further in the fruit and the bark. And if you squeeze out juice from its leaves while green, this too is of a similar order, being moderately astringent; hence it is drunk both on its own and together with the other drugs that cure dysentery and coeliac affections. And indeed it is also suitable for spittings of blood, haemorrhages from the uterus, and prolapses of the seat and of the womb, being somewhat close to hypocistis.

[8.18.49] [49. On the flower of mastic.] The flower of mastic heats moderately and is moderately astringent; moreover, it has not been deprived of its fine-particled nature. Accordingly, for these reasons the drug is both diuretic and a promoter of the menses, when employed in fomentations and in potions. It also benefits inflammations in the liver, the stomach and the belly. Its root is more astringent, while the so-called flower is hotter. In all its parts, more in some and less in others, something of astringency shows itself on tasting, and on account of this it is also mixed into the drugs given to those who spit blood.

[8.18.50] [50. On smooth rush, oxyschoenus and holoschoenus.] Of rush (schoinos) one kind is called smooth, another oxyschoinos, and another holoschoinos. The oxyschoinos is slenderer and harder, while the holoschoinos is thicker and more porous. The fruit of the holoschoinos is sleep-inducing. Of the oxyschoinos there are two kinds: the one fruitless, which has no use for cures, the other fruit-bearing. The fruit of this one too is soporific, but less so than that of the holoschoinos. This fruit is, however, also productive of headache. Both, if they are roasted and drunk with wine, dry the fluxions in the belly and check the red flux. From this it is clear that their mixture is compounded of an earthy substance that is mildly cold and a watery one that is mildly hot, so that they are able both to dry the parts below and to send up to the head mildly cold vapours, by which they also prove soporific.

[8.19.1] [1. On terebinth.] Of the terebinth, the bark, the leaves and the fruit all have something astringent. But they also heat in the second order, so that it is already clear that they also dry: moderately while they are still fresh and moist, but in the second order once they have been dried. The dry fruit is close even to the third order of drying things. For it is so hot that its heat becomes quite clear at once even to those who chew it. Accordingly these are both diuretic and beneficial to spleens.

[8.19.2] [2. On beet.] Beet has a share of a certain nitrous power, by which it both cleanses and disperses and purges through the nostrils. When boiled, it lays aside all that is nitrous and pungent, and becomes of a power free from inflammation and gently dispersing. The white beet is stronger both for cleansing and for dispersing, since the black at any rate also has something of astringency, and more so in the root than in the other parts.

[8.19.3] [3. On teucrium.] Teucrium is of a cutting and fine-particled power, whence it also heals spleens. And one might place it in the third order of drying things, but in the second of heating things.

[8.19.4] [4. On ash.] Ash. The residue of burnt wood is called by this name; it is compounded of contrary substances and qualities. For it has in itself on the one hand something earthy, and on the other something as it were sooty or fuliginous, or however one may wish to call it. These parts, then, are fine-particled, and when the ash is wetted with water and strained they are carried off along with it. But whatever earthy part is left behind becomes weak and non-biting, having deposited its hot power in the lye. Not all ash has exactly the same mixture; rather, it varies according to the difference of the material burnt. Dioscorides, I do not know how, says that it has an astringent power. Yet the ash of fig-wood is free of every such quality, because the tree itself, unlike oak, holm-oak, arbutus, phēgos-oak, mastic and ivy, and all the others of this kind, does not display the acerbic quality in any part of itself, but is wholly full of a strong, hot and pungent juice. From acerbic woods, then, the ash has no little astringency, and I myself know that I once stopped haemorrhages by means of it, when no other drug was at hand. But no one would ever use fig-wood ash for this purpose, for it has much of the pungent and the caustic mixed with the cleansing, and in both respects it differs from the ash of oak woods: both because the sooty part in it is much more pungent, and because the as it were earthy part, which in those is in some way mildly astringent, is in this one cleansing, as in the ash of spurges (tithymalloi). Quicklime (titanos) too is a kind of ash, being more fine-particled than the ash from woods, inasmuch as the stones need to be more thoroughly roasted in order to become ash; nevertheless it too has much of what one might call fiery residue. And for this reason, when washed, it becomes a drug that is drying without biting, and the more so if it is washed twice or even three times. It becomes sufficiently dispersing when washed with sea water. It will be spoken of also when our account comes to the mined substances.

[8.19.5] [5. On telephion.] Telephion is of a drying and cleansing power, though not manifestly hot; rather, in this respect one might perhaps place it in the first order. It dries, however, in the second order at its intensified end, or at the beginning of the third. And for this reason it is suitable for the putrefactive among ulcers, and with vinegar it heals leukai and alphoi.

[8.19.6] [6. On fenugreek.] Fenugreek is hot from the second order, and dry from the first; and for this reason it exacerbates boiling inflammations, but those that are less hot, and those that are more scirrhous, it treats by dispersing them.

[8.19.7] [7. On spurges.] All spurges (tithymalloi) have the pungent and hot power predominant, and there is also bitterness in them. The strongest of it is the juice (opos); next come both the fruit and the leaves. The root too shares in the powers mentioned, but not equally. The root, then, boiled with vinegar, cures pains of the teeth, and especially those that arise when the teeth are eaten away. The juices, having a more vehement power, are put into the hole of the teeth; but if they touch the other parts of the body they at once burn them and ulcerate them, which is why wax is moulded around them on the outside. For they belong to the fourth order of heating things, which, as we said, is that of the caustic things. In this way the juice also removes the hairs when smeared around. But since it is more vehement, it is mixed with oil; and if this is done often, the roots of the hairs are completely destroyed by being burnt, and the body becomes bare of them. By the same power they remove acrochordones, myrmeciae, pterygia and thymi. They also cleanse away leichenes and psorai, because they also share in the cleansing power on account of their bitterness. And they are naturally apt to benefit phagedaenic ulcers, carbuncular ones and gangrenous ones, because they both heat vehemently and cleanse, provided one uses them at the right time and in the right measure. And indeed by the same power they also remove the callosities of fistulae (syringes). All these effects the leaves and the fruit are naturally apt to produce in the same way as to kind, but more weakly. People are also accustomed to use these against the fish in standing waters; for the fish, very quickly stunned by them and made half-dead, are carried up to the surface of the water. There being seven of them, the strongest are the one named characias, which some people also call the male, the female one called myrsinites, and the tree-like one that grows on rocks; next the one resembling mullein (phlomos), and the cyparissias; after these the coastal one, then the helioscopos. In proportion to their stated power are the ash and the lye made from it.

[8.19.8] [8. On tragacanth.] Tragacanth has a power similar to gum, a clogging one, with a somewhat blunter pungency. It also dries in a similar way to gum. [8.19.9] [9. On tragion.] Of tragion, the leaves, the fruit and the tear are all of a drawing and dispersing power. It is also fine-particled and hot in power, belonging already, it seems, to the third order, at its beginning. It draws out splinters, breaks up stones, and moves the menses when drunk in the weight of a drachm. This tragion grows in Crete alone and resembles mastic. The other tragion, which is smaller than this one and whose leaves resemble skolopendrion, appears in many places; it shares in no small astringent power, so that it is also suited to fluxional affections.

[8.19.10] [10. On tragoriganum.] Tragoriganum: it has been spoken of earlier, in the account of origanum. [8.19.11] [11. On caltrop.] Caltrop is composed of a moist substance that is moderately cold and of a dry substance, this too cold, and not moderately so. In the land caltrop the cold earthy element predominates, which we have also shown to be astringent; in the aquatic one the watery element predominates. For this reason both are suited to the onsets of inflammations and, in general, to all influxes. The fruit of the land caltrop, being fine-particled, breaks up the stones in the kidneys when drunk.

[8.19.12] [12. On tripolium.] Tripolium. Its root is pungent to the taste, and hot in power in the third remove. [8.19.13] [13. On trifolium.] Trifolium, which others call asphaltion, others oxyphyllon, some people minyanthes, and there are those who name it knikion. The first three names come from the attributes of the shrub; where the remaining two come from I do not know. The power of the plant is hot and dry, like asphalt, which it closely resembles in smell, and it is of the third order in both respects. For this reason, when drunk, it benefits pains of the sides that arise from obstructions, and it moves urine and menses.

[8.19.14] [14. On trichomanes.] Trichomanes has all the same powers as adiantum. [8.19.15] [15. On trychnon or strychnon.] Trychnon, which some people call strychnon, with the sigma. Everyone knows the edible kind that grows in gardens, and people use it for whatever needs cooling and astringent action, for it has both these powers in the second order. Of the other kinds, which are not edible, one is called halicacabum. It has a reddish fruit resembling a grape berry in shape and size, and people also use it for garlands. The second is the shrubby one, the soporific, and third after these is the manic one. Halicacabum is similar in the power of its leaves to the garden trychnon, but its fruit is diuretic. For this reason it is also mixed into many of the compound drugs that are suited to the liver or bladder or kidneys. Of the soporific strychnon, the bark of the root drunk with wine is soporific when taken in the weight of a drachm. In other respects too it is similar to the juice of the poppy, but weaker to such an extent that it belongs to the third order of cooling things, whereas that is ranked in the fourth. The seed of this trychnon has a diuretic power, but it causes madness when more than twelve clusters are drunk. The remaining one of the trychna mentioned is of no use for the treatment of internal parts. For if four drachms of them are taken, they bring on death, and if fewer, madness. One drachm is harmless, but it too has nothing useful. Applied as a plaster externally to the body, it treats malignant and spreading ulcers. Best for this purpose is the bark of the root, which dries in about the second order, where that order is already being completed and the third is beginning, and cools in the beginning of the second order.

[8.20.1] [1. On hyacinth.] The root of hyacinth, being bulbous, is of the first order in drying, and of the second in cooling, the second being by now about completed, or even of the third at its beginning. At any rate, when applied as a plaster in wine, it is believed to keep boys without pubic hair for a very long time. The fruit is gently cleansing and astringent, and for this reason it too is given in wine to those with jaundice. It dries by now somewhere in the third order, but stands midway between heat and cold.

[8.20.2] [2. On truffle.] Truffles, which are familiar to everyone, possess in their consistency a predominating, rather earthy substance, with a small amount of the fine-particled mixed in with it. [8.20.3] [3. On water-pepper.] Water-pepper is so called from the places in which it grows and from its similarity in taste to pepper. It is hot, but not to the degree that pepper is; and moreover the little herb, while still green, applied as a poultice together with its fruit, disperses hypopia (livid bruises under the eye) and swellings that are becoming scirrhous.

[8.20.4] [4. On henbane.] Henbane: the kind that has the black seed is productive of madness and stupefying. Close to it in power is also the kind whose seed is moderately yellow, and one should avoid both as useless and deleterious. Most suitable for cures is the kind whose seed and flower are both white, belonging somewhere to the third order of cooling drugs. The flower of the kind that has the black seed is moderately purplish, while that of the yellowish kind is faintly quince-yellow.

[8.20.5] [5. On hypericum.] Hypericum heats and dries, being of fine-particled substance, so that it provokes both the menses and urine. For these purposes one must take the whole fruit, not the seed alone; but applied green as a plaster together with the leaves, it is able to bring to a scar both other [lesions] and burns. And if you dry them, pound them and sprinkle them on, you will heal the flabby and putrefactive among ulcers. Some people also give it to sciatics to drink.

[8.20.6] [6. On hypecoum.] Hypecoum is of a cooling power, somewhere in the third order of cooling things, so that it falls a little short of poppy. [8.20.7] [7. On hypoglosson.] Hypoglosson is so named because it produces outgrowths of little tongues beneath the tips of its clusters. The root and the juice of the shrublet are of a softening power.

[8.20.8] [8. On hyssop.] Hyssop heats and dries in the third order, and it is also fine-particled. [8.21.1] [1. On lentils.] Lentils are strongly astringent, but they stand in the middle between heat and cold. Moreover, they also dry in the second order. Their body itself, then, dries and stops the belly, whereas the decoction stimulates it; this is why the first water is poured off whenever they are taken for the sake of retention.

[8.21.2] [2. On the lentil.] The lentil that grows on stagnant pools is of a moist and cold mixture, belonging somewhere about the second order in both respects. [8.21.3] [3. On phalaris.] Of the herb phalaris, the juice, the seed and the leaves, when drunk, are believed to help with pains of the bladder, since the herb has something fine-particled and hot.

[8.21.4] [4. On phalangitēs.] Phalangitēs. It has been so named from its helping those bitten by phalangia. It is of a fine-particled drying power, whence it is also thought to help those suffering from griping.

[8.21.5] [5. On mullein (phlomos).] Phlomos: some people both write and pronounce it with a π. One kind is white in its leaves, the other black. Of the white, one is male, whose leaves are narrower, the other female, whose leaves are larger. Besides these there is another phlomos called wild, which is gold-like and yellowish (μηλίζουσα) in its flowers. And besides these there is yet another, which they call specifically phlomis and thryallis. Now the root of the first two, being acerbic to the taste, helps fluxional affections. Some also rinse the mouth with it for pains of the teeth. The leaves, however, are of a dispersing power. So too are the leaves of the others, and especially of the one that is golden in its flowers, with which they also dye the hair blond. For the leaves of all of them are of a drying and moderately cleansing power.

[8.21.6] [6. On the date palm.] The date palm, the tree, has a share of astringent power in all of its parts. Now the juice of the branches is harsh, being composed of a lukewarm watery substance and a cold earthy one. Of a nature similar to this is also the so-called 'brain', which is edible. Its fruit, and especially the sweet kind, has taken on no small heat. Being edible, it comes into wide use. It is not only applied externally, where we need to tone, dry, draw together, compact and condense something, but it is also taken as food, both together with other things and by itself. What they call elatē, the tender shoot of the palm, has the same power as the brain within it. Its so-to-speak wrapping also possesses an astringent quality, but it dries more than all the things mentioned, since it is drier than they are in the consistency of its substance as well and has the least share of moisture. So they rightly use it for putrefactive ulcers. They also mix it into the drugs that draw together the relaxed parts of the joints, and into hepatic and stomachic remedies, both external and internal. The root of the plant, too, is of a drying power without biting, and it also has something of astringency itself.

[8.21.7] [7. On phorbion.] The seed of phorbion they use with honey for leucomata, and moreover it is believed to draw out splinters. The herb too seems to be able to do the same as this; from which it is clear that it partakes of a fine-particled, drawing and cleansing power.

[8.21.8] [8. On phou.] Phou. The root of this herb is somewhat aromatic, similar in power to nard, but inferior to it in most respects; it provokes urine, however, more than Indian and Syrian nard, and to the same degree as the Celtic.
[8.21.9] [9. On seaweed.] Seaweed (phykos), taken out of the sea while still moist and green, both cools and dries in the second order; for it also has something moderately acerbic.

[8.21.10] [10. On phyllitis.] Phyllitis, being of an acerbic quality, is, not unreasonably, beneficial for diarrhoeas and dysenteries when drunk. [8.21.11] [11. On the leaf of malabathrum.] The leaf of malabathrum is close to nard in its power.

[8.22.1] [1. On galbanum.] Galbanum is the sap of a plant resembling giant fennel, and is of a softening and dispersing power. And in heating it would be somewhere at the beginning of the third order or at the completion of the second, and in drying at the beginning of the second.

[8.22.2] [2. On chamaedrys.] Chamaedrys has the bitter quality predominating, but it is also somewhat pungent. From these [qualities], evidently, it fittingly melts the spleen, provokes urine and menses, cuts thickness of humours, and clears out the obstructions in the viscera. One might place it in the third order with respect to drying and heating, and indeed more with respect to drying than to heating.

[8.22.3] [3. On chamaecissus.] The flower of chamaecissus, being considerably bitter, clears the obstructions of the parts in the liver. And some people also give it to ischiadics. [8.22.4] [4. On chamelaea.] Chamelaea has the bitter quality predominating. For this reason, with honey, it is able to cleanse thoroughly even very foul ulcers and those that have very large eschars.

[8.22.5] [5. On chamaeleuce.] Chamaeleuce is hot in its power somewhere about the third order, and dry in the first. [8.22.6] [6. On chamaeleon.] The root of the black chamaeleon has something poisonous in it, so its use is external, for psorai and leichenes and alphoi and in general whatever needs cleansing; and it is mixed into softening and dispersing drugs. Applied as a poultice, it also heals the phagedaenic ones among ulcers. For it is dry already somewhere about the third order, and in heating it is of the second order at its completion. The root of the white chamaeleon is given for flat worms, in the amount of an oxybaphon, with harsh wine. They also administer it to the dropsical, since it too is close in its mixture to the root of the black, except in so far as it is more bitter than that one.

[8.22.7] [7. On chamaepitys.] Chamaepitys, in taste, has the bitter flavour stronger than the pungent; in its activity, however, it purges and cleanses the viscera more than it heats. For this reason it is a good drug for the icteric and, in general, for those whose liver is easily obstructed. It also brings on the menses, both when drunk and when applied with honey. It is also a diuretic drug. Some people also give it to sciatics, boiling it down in honey-water. The herb when green is able to conglutinate even large wounds, heals putrefactive ulcers, and disperses hardnesses in the breasts. For it is of the third order in drying, and of the second in heating.

[8.22.8] [8. On chamaesyce.] Chamaesyce has a power at once cleansing and pungent, so that its shoots, applied as a plaster, and the sap from them remove both acrochordons and myrmeciae. With honey they also cleanse away the thick scars in the eyes. They also benefit amblyopias due to thickness, as indeed they do the beginnings of suffusions.

[8.22.9] [9. On chelidonium.] Chelidonium is of a strongly cleansing and hot power; and indeed its juice too is useful for sharpness of sight in those in whom something thick collects at the pupil that needs to be dispersed. Some people have also used the root for those who are icteric from obstruction of the liver, giving it to drink in white wine with anise. Chewed, it is useful for pains of the teeth. The smaller chelidonium, being more pungent than the larger, quickly ulcerates the skin when applied as a plaster, and it casts off leprous nails. Its juice, being strongly pungent, purges through the nostrils, so that this herb too would belong somewhere to the fourth order, the order being by now brought to completion, both in heating and in drying.

[8.22.10] [10. On chondrilla.] Chondrilla. Some people call this too seris. For it is in some way of the same power as that [plant], except in so far as it has more of the somewhat bitter in its taste, and for this reason it is drier in its power.

[8.22.11] [11. On groats.] Groats (chondros) are, of course, also a most excellent food, as wheat is too; but it is not the business of the present treatise to draw distinctions about food. As a drug, groats are of the clogging power. In their mixture they are close to wheat, having more of the viscous than it does, and by this they are also more nourishing than it, and they become a kind of material suitable for the reception of vinegar, sea-water and brine, and of such other things as dry strongly. For this reason some have thought that this seed too is among those that dry considerably. But groats themselves are rather among the things able to assist concoction, as wheat is too, and these dry least of all. Because of the admixture of drying drugs, however, the compound made from them becomes drying and deceives most physicians, so that they attribute the cause of the drying to the groats themselves and disregard the things mixed in.

[8.22.12] [12. On chrysocome.] Chrysocome, which is also called chrysites: its root has as its predominant qualities the pungent and at the same time the astringent, and for this reason it is not of many uses. Its use, however, when it has been boiled down in honey-water, is in peripneumoniae and in hepatic diseases. It also has something that promotes the purgation of the menses.

[8.23.1] [1. On pseudodittany.] Pseudodittany has the power of a weak dittany. [8.23.2] [2. On psyllium.] Of psyllium it is the seed that is most useful, being of the second order of cooling things; with respect to the pairing concerned with drying and moistening, it is in some way intermediate and well-proportioned.

[8.24.1] [1. On basil.] Basil belongs to the second order of heating [drugs], but it has a residual moisture. Hence it is not useful when taken inside the body, but applied externally as a poultice it is useful for dispersing and concocting.

[8.24.2] [2. On ōkimoeides.] Ōkimoeides: some call it philetairion. Its root is useless, but its seed is of a fine-particled and drying power, without biting. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK X. Preface. Those drugs that are parts of plants, and fruits, and juices, and saps, have been discussed before. It is now proposed to go through the remaining drugs: those that are mined, and those that are kinds of earth itself. After this something will also be said about the parts in animals that we use as drugs for cures. It seems better to me, however, to set first a common account about all of them, for the sake both of clarity and of hearing what is said in an articulated way. For if someone were to follow in everything those who have written treatises either on drugs, or on materia, or on their preparation, he will err very greatly in many things and will mishear what I say with distinctions. The common account about to be given has two heads. The one is whether the burnt among the self-grown drugs should be considered hotter or colder. The other concerns the astringent drugs, of which the harsh and the acerbic were shown earlier to be species. These matters have already been discussed in the fourth of these books, but it is better to recall now too that the quality and power of the astringent drugs appears to be most contrary to that of the pungent ones. For acacia and balaustion are astringent, as are hypocistis and kytinoi and oak-gall and rhēon and sumach, omphakion and medlars, and cornels and pomegranate rinds and myrtle-berries. Pungent are euphorbium and garlic and onions and leeks and mustard and pepper and ginger and smyrnion, oregano and pennyroyal, and calamint and thyme. We need, then, only to recall what kind of sensation we have of each of the things mentioned. For the difference of their quality will follow at once, which I went through in the fourth book together with all the other differences of taste. Astringents draw together, constrict and compress our substance. For this reason, when applied externally to whatever limb you please, they at once render it wrinkled and contracted. Conversely, pungents applied to the skin plainly heat it and raise it into a swelling with a red colour, and if they remain long, they ulcerate it. These things plainly appear to be cutting and heating, and for this reason to draw to themselves the blood from the neighbouring parts. Astringents, by contrast, are by nature such as to repel what is contained in the parts, by cooling, drawing together and compressing. So the power of astringents is most contrary to that of pungents, and their quality in taste has nothing similar. How, then, some say that pepper and garlic and all the pungents are astringent, it is not even possible to conceive. Suppose that, just as they call these astringent, they likewise called sumach and balaustion and omphakion and medlar and the other such things pungent, altering the usage of the Greeks in names. In that case we would suppose them ignorant of the words of the Greeks together with what is signified by them, but not insensible in their gustatory or olfactory faculty. But since they call by one name two things which have a nature most contrary to one another, both to the sense of smell and to that of taste, and in what they are seen to do, it is fitting to wonder at these people, either for their insensibility, or for their folly, or for both at once. For they do something very like a man who says that snow produces the same sensation as fire. And indeed someone, from habituation to so outlandish a use of names, once told me that nothing prevents saying that snow has the same quality and power as fire, for snow too has often been seen to burn off the feet of those who walk through it for a long time. Men of this kind need no small time to cleanse the filth from their soul. There are others who have not been so unfortunate as to live out their lives in complete ignorance, and who have previously read the fourth of these commentaries. For them what has been said so far suffices by way of reminder, for the sake of hearing in an articulated way the names applied to each of their proper things, as all Greeks are accustomed to use them. I shall now pass to the second inquiry, which is no longer about a name and what is signified by it, but about the nature of a thing. Most people think that all things burnt become colder than they themselves were. Some, conversely, think that the heat of all burnt things is increased. Both err. For some will plainly appear to become hotter, in taste and touch and in the power observed in use, as I said earlier in the case of the pungent and the astringent things. Others, conversely, appear less hot after being burnt; and this we discern clearly both by sense and by use. By use I mean, as I said in the earlier cases, when, applied to the skin, some make it redder and hotter, others bloodless and cold, and some raise it into a swelling, while others contract it. The pungents, then, lose much of their heat when burnt, while those that are not such gain heat; but nothing burnt is completely cold. For there is left in them, as it were, a certain empyreuma (for Aristotle called it so), and this is what is washed away in washings. It is the most fine-particled part of the substance of burnt things. When it has gone off together with the water, the rest of the burnt thing is earthy substance. For burning consumes all the moisture, and what remains is earthy, together with what Aristotle called empyreuma. When, then, someone removes this and separates it by washing, the water in which the drug was washed has acquired a hot, fine-particled power, while the remainder becomes earthy and cold, able to dry without biting. I have spoken about these matters before as well, but it is no worse to recall them now too, so that someone who has the recollection of them fresh may follow more precisely what will be said.

[7.10.1] [1. On kalaminthē.] Kalaminthē is fine-particled in its substance and hot and dry in its mixture, somewhere in the third order in respect of both qualities. The signs of these are clear: both those that appear to the taste and those that are known through experience. For to the taste it is plainly pungent and hot, and it has something, altogether slight, that is somewhat bitter. When one tests it and applies it to the body, first, placed on the outside, it heats strongly, bites and scratches the skin, and in the end produces an ulcer. Taken inside the body, whether by itself dry or in melikraton, it plainly heats, provokes sweats, and disperses and dries the whole body. For this reason, at any rate, some have used it also for periodic rigors: externally, boiling it in oil and anointing the whole body with vigorous rubbing, and internally, taking it as has been said. Moreover, some apply it as a poultice over the hips in sciatic ailments as a powerful remedy; for it draws what lies in the depth to the outer surface and heats the whole joint, and it plainly burns the skin; and, drunk and applied as a pessary, it calls forth the menses very effectively. It is also a good drug for those suffering from elephantiasis, not only by vigorously dispersing the thin humours but also by strongly thinning and cutting the thick ones, of which kind are those that generate such a disease; and in the same way it also brightens black scars and disperses bruises. In such cases it is better to apply it as a poultice green, boiled in wine, rather than dry; for when dried it becomes stronger and readier to burn. Because it is of this kind it is also employed for the bites of venomous beasts, just like cauteries and those drugs that are hot, pungent and fine-particled and easily draw to themselves from the depth all the adjacent moisture. The bitterness present in it is altogether slight; but in some respects it does what the strongest bitterness does, because it is joined with a vehement heat together with a fine-particled substance. Thus, at any rate, its juice, injected and drunk, is by nature able to kill ascarides and helminths; and by the same reasoning also the worms in the ears, or if such a condition should arise anywhere else in the body, upon a putrefying ulcer. Thus too, drunk and applied as a pessary, it destroys and expels the foetus. Its cutting power, then, is due to its heat, its fine-particled nature and its bitterness, while its cleansing power is due to the bitterness alone. And accordingly it benefits the asthmatic through all the properties stated, and the jaundiced chiefly through its bitterness, just as almost all the other bitter things do, by cleansing and purging the obstructions in the liver. For all the purposes stated the mountain kind is more effective.

[7.10.2] [2. On aromatic reed.] Aromatic reed has a share both of a slight astringency and of a very small pungency. The greater part of it, however, is of earthy and airy substance, well-tempered in the conjugation of hotness and coldness. Hence it is moderately diuretic, and it is mixed into the powers that are applied to the liver and the stomach; it is also usefully mixed into the fomentations of the uterus that are employed on account of inflammation or for the provocation of the menses. Let it therefore be placed in the second order of things that heat and dry, and indeed of things that dry more strongly than they heat. It also has something fine-particled, as do all the other aromatics as well. But in most of those the fine-particled is present in very great amount, whereas in the reed it is not much.

[7.10.3] [3. On the fence reed (kalamos phragmitēs).] Some have written that the root of the fence reed, together with bulbs, draws out barbs and splinters from deep within, on the grounds that it possesses some drawing power. We ourselves, however, have not tested this. But so far as one can judge by taste, it has a share of a cleansing power to no small degree, and is very little pungent. The green leaves, however, cool moderately, and these too have a share of the cleansing power. Its rind, when burnt, comes to have a fairly fine-particled and dispersing power, with something cleansing in it as well, so that it both dries and heats somewhere about the third order, and dries more than it heats. One should beware of its so-called anthēlē (plume). For when it falls into the ears it sticks fast so that it cannot be dislodged and damages the hearing, so that it often produces deafness.

[7.10.4] [4. On kankanon.] The root of kankanon is of a power that does not bite and is moderately drying, but of a coarse-particled, clogging substance. Hence, when steeped in wine, like tragacanth, and licked up, it heals the roughnesses of the windpipe; and no less, if one should also chew it, the juice that flows down from it benefits the windpipe, just as that of liquorice does.

[7.10.5] [5. On hemp.] The fruit of hemp is free from flatulence and drying to such a degree that, if more of it is eaten, it dries up the semen. Some, expressing its juice while it is green, use it for pains of the ears that arise, as it seems to me, by way of obstruction.

[7.10.6] [6. On kapnion.] Kapnios, which others call kapnos, partakes of a quality at once pungent and bitter, but is not entirely free of the acerbic either. Hence it promotes copious bilious urine and cures obstructions and atonies in the liver. Its juice, too, is sight-sharpening and draws out no small quantity of tears, as smoke does, and from this it also has its name. A certain layman also used it as strengthening the stomach while at the same time loosening the belly. For he first dried the herb and stored it away, and then sprinkled it on: for the sake of evacuation, in honey-water, but when he wished to strengthen the stomach, in mixed wine [evidently].

[7.10.7] [7. On caper.] Of the caper, the bark of the root has the bitter quality predominating, the pungent second, and after this the acerbic. From this it is also clear that it is composed of different and conflicting powers. For it is able to cleanse, to purge thoroughly and to cut by the bitterness that accompanies it, to heat, cut and disperse by its pungency, and to draw together, condense and constrict by its acerbity. And for this reason this drug too, if anything else does, benefits scirrhous spleens, when mixed externally with suitable poultices, and when taken inside the body, either boiled down in vinegar and oxymel and the like, or dry, pounded and mixed with them. For indeed, taken in this way, it also evidently evacuates the viscid and thick humours, not only through the urine but also through the belly. And often they also pass bloody matter, upon which both the spleens are benefited and the pains at the hip. Moreover it also moves the menses, draws off phlegm, and helps ruptures and sprains. With what drink one should mix it in each of the affections is not the business of the present treatise, but either of the one on the composition of drugs or of the therapeutic method. And the bark of the root, applied as a poultice to malignant ulcers, is a good drug, as being able both to cleanse them and to dry strongly; and it benefits pains of the teeth by virtue of the qualities mentioned before, sometimes boiled together with vinegar, sometimes with wine, and often itself alone held between the teeth. Nor is it the business of the present treatise to define the proper occasions for these. For this is not what is now proposed, but rather to take from each of its particular effects some indication of its powers, bringing the account back to the principles laid down from the beginning. It is evident, then, from what has been said, that there is in it a certain cutting power, as well as a cleansing, a dispersing and a contracting one. For indeed it also removes alphoi with vinegar, and disperses choirades and hard swellings when mixed with the drugs suitable for these. The fruit has a power analogous to the bark of the root, except insofar as it is weaker in all respects. Moreover the leaves and their stem are also of similar power, and I myself know that I once dispersed a scrofulous hardness with the leaves in a few days. We mix with them, of course, something of the things that blunt the vehemence of the power. And it is nothing surprising if the juice also kills the worms in the ears because of its bitterness. The caper that grows in very hot regions, as also that in Arabia, is much more pungent than ours, so that it also partakes to a greater degree of the caustic power.

[7.10.8] [8. On cress.] The seed of cress shares in a caustic power, as does mustard, and for this reason people thoroughly heat with it cases of sciatica, headaches, and anything else among the conditions that require rubefaction, just as they do with mustard. It is also mixed into the drugs given to the asthmatic, evidently as being able to cut the thick humours strongly, as mustard also does; for it resembles that in all respects. The herb, too, when it has become dry, is of a power close to that of the seed. But while it is still moist and green, it falls very far short because of the admixture of watery moisture, and in this state it is so moderate in its biting that one can even use it with bread as a relish.

[7.10.9] [9. On cardamom.] Cardamom too is, to be sure, of a sufficiently hot power, though not so strongly as cress; but by as much as it is more pleasant and more aromatic than cress, by so much has it also partaken of a weaker hot power. It is not, however, capable of ulcerating, even when applied by itself as a plaster. But it also has some bitterness borne along within it, on account of which it both destroys worms and strongly cleanses away psōrai, also together with vinegar.

[7.10.10] [10. On caraway.] The seed of caraway heats and dries in about the third order, having a moderately pungent quality. For this reason it is free of flatulence and diuretic, not the seed alone but the plant as well.

[7.10.11] [11. On cassia.] Cassia dries and heats in about the third order. It is also sufficiently fine-particled, and in taste the pungent quality is very great in it, but there is also something slightly astringent, so that through all these it both cuts and at the same time disperses the superfluities in the body, and in addition to these it further imparts strength to the organs. It is also suitable for retentions of the menses, when they are prevented from being sufficiently evacuated by both the quantity and at the same time the thickness of the residues.

[7.10.12] [12. On nuts.] Nuts. The tree has something astringent both in its shoots and in its leaves, but it is evident and most abundant in the husk of the nut, both fresh and dry. It is for this reason, at any rate, that dyers also use it. We, for our part, squeezing them and boiling the juice with honey in the same way as that of mulberries and brambles, use it as a drug for the mouth, and also for all the other things for which the juices mentioned above are suitable. Of the nut itself, the edible part is oily and fine-particled, so that for this reason it both yields its juice easily and becomes more of this kind the longer it lies in storage. At any rate, it is possible to press oil out of it when it grows old. At that time it also becomes considerably dispersing, so that some even heal gangrainai, anthrakes and aigilōpes with it, and some also use it for wounds of the nerves. When it is fresh, it also has something of the astringent quality. That which is still unripe and not yet dry, like the other fruits that are green, is full of half-concocted moisture. Its dry shell, however, when burnt, becomes a fine-particled, drying and non-biting drug. There is also another kind of smaller nuts, which are called Pontic, which partakes more of the cold earthy substance, so that to one tasting them the plant itself, the fruit and the bark appear harsher; in other respects it is similar to the large nut, called by some 'royal'. This small nut is called by most people leptokaryon.

[7.10.13] [13. On kaukalis.] Kaukalis. Some call this wild daukos, for it is similar to it both in taste and in power. For it heats as that does, and dries, and is diuretic; and it is also pickled for keeping in store.

[7.10.14] [14. On karpēsion.] Karpēsion is similar to what is called phou both in taste and in power, but it is fine-particled to a greater degree. For this reason it also cleanses the obstructions of the viscera more than that does, promotes urine, and clears out kidneys that are forming stones. Yet it is not so fine-particled that one may use it in place of cinnamon when that is not available, as Quintus used to do. The Pontic karpēsion is better than the Laertic; yet even it is not close to cinnamon in power, and it falls short by no small amount even of the best cassia. Each is named after certain mountains of Pamphylia, in which it grows; and you could obtain a very great quantity of them in Syria.

[7.10.15] [15. On millet.] Millet (kenchros) cools in the first order, and dries either in the third order slackened or in the second intensified. It is also somewhat fine-particled, to a slight degree. From such a consistency and mixture, then, when it is eaten as a food it is the least nourishing of practically all the cereal foods. Moreover it also dries the belly. Applied externally by means of bags, it is a suitable fomentation for those who need to be dried without biting; and applied as a poultice it is likewise naturally drying, although the poultice made from it becomes quite crumbly and for this reason awkward to use.

[7.10.16] [16. On cedar.] Cedar is twofold in kind: the one is shrubby, like the junipers, the other a tree of no small size. Both are of a hot and dry mixture, belonging somewhere to the third order in both respects. The cedar oil, however (for so the oil from the cedar is called), would seem to reach already into the fourth order, being both sufficiently hot and at the same time fine-particled. It therefore putrefies soft flesh both readily and painlessly, as do the other things that are of the same order in heating and are fine-particled in their substances; but on hard flesh it acts over a longer time and with difficulty. All such drugs, then, are called putrefying and putrefactive. They differ from one another by more and less. And among these drugs themselves cedar oil belongs to the first and weakest order, for most of them are sufficiently active. Such drugs, then, also destroy the flesh of dead bodies; cedar oil, however, dries dead bodies and preserves them unputrefied, consuming their superfluous moistures while not touching the solid bodies. In the living, the heat in the bodies, augmenting the power of the cedar oil, becomes the cause of soft flesh being burned through by it. It is no wonder if, being of such power, it naturally destroys lice, nits, ascarides and the worms in the ears, and, applied as a pessary, kills living embryos and expels dead ones; so too the very semen of intercourse, when it is smeared around the genitals. And for this reason it is a contraceptive drug second to none for those who use it in this way, and it effects many other such things in particular cases. A proof, at any rate, of its heating strongly is, for instance, when it is dripped into the cavities of the teeth: for it soothes the pain, but shatters the teeth. It also thins the scars of the eyes and heals the amblyopias due to thickness of humours. The oiliest and most exactly oil-like part of it, which is collected by means of wool suspended above it while it is boiled, becomes more fine-particled than the whole cedar oil, and less pungent, yet no less heating. For it stands, relative to the coarser-particled residue of the cedar oil, in the same ratio as olive oil to amurca. Hence that residue, being coarse-particled, is biting and anastomotic, and for this reason irritating to ulcers and at the same time productive of inflammation. But the oil-like cedar oil is so mild in power that laymen, having learned by experience, treat the wounds inflicted by the shears on sheep being shorn by smearing it on, as they also do liquid pitch. They also use it for the psora of sheep and for ticks. The kedrides (for so they name the fruit of the cedar) have a more moderate power, so that they can even be eaten. Yet if someone takes too many of these as well, he suffers pain in the head, is heated, and is bitten in the stomach.

[7.10.17] [17. On the great centaury.] The root of the great centaury, just as it displays contrary qualities in taste, so too in use it displays contrary activities. In taste, then, it appears pungent and at the same time astringent, with a certain slight sweetness. In its activities, the pungency displays the works of heat, provoking the menses, drawing down dead embryos, and destroying and expelling living ones. The astringency displays the works of coarse-particled and earthy coldness, both in conglutinating wounds and in benefiting those who spit blood. Two drachms are given to these: to the fevered with water, to the afebrile with wine. And by virtue of the activity arising from all its qualities together it is suited also to ruptures, strains, dyspnoea and chronic coughs. For in these cases one must not only evacuate what is contrary to nature, but also strengthen and give tone to the parts that have been cleansed. For evacuating, then, pungency is useful, when it is neither alone nor unmixed, but is either mixed with some sweetness, or at any rate not altogether with bitterness. For in this way it will not have its strength and violence, since some well-tempered substance is mixed with it; for such is the sweet. For strengthening and drawing together the parts that have been evacuated, there is need of astringency. Its juice does the same things as the root, and some use the drug in place of lycium.

[7.10.18] [18. On the small centaury.] Of the small centaury the root is entirely inactive, but the shoots, and still more the leaves on them and the flowers, are most useful. In them the bitter quality predominates, with a small share of astringency as well, and because of such a mixture the drug is strongly drying, without biting. That all such things are more useful has been said before as well, and now no less it is the right moment to recall it, once we have gone through all its particular activities. Large wounds are agglutinated when it is applied as a plaster, the herb itself while still fresh; and the old and hard-to-cicatrize ulcers are cicatrized when it is used in the same way; and when dried it is mixed into the agglutinating and drying remedies that by nature heal sinuses and fistulas, soften old indurations and heal malignant ulcers. It is mixed into those that heal fluxional conditions, for which the best drugs are those that dry strongly together with some astringency and have no biting. Some inject the decoction of the herb in sciatics, as drawing off bilious and thick matters; for it does purge such matters, and indeed when it acts vehemently, so as to evacuate bloody matter, it benefits all the more. Its juice, being of a close power, that is, the drying and cleansing one, by nature performs well both the other things mentioned before, and it is smeared on the eyes with honey, and when applied as a pessary it draws down the menses and embryos. Some also give it to drink to those affected in the nerves, as evacuating and drying without distress what has become impacted in them. And indeed it is also an excellent drug for obstructions in the liver, and good too for a spleen becoming scirrhous, both when applied from outside and no less if one wishes to drink it.

[7.10.19] [19. On the cherry.] The cherry tree bears a fruit that does not have an equal share of astringency in all the individual plants. For in these too, as also in pomegranates and apples, in some the harsh quality prevails, in some the sweet, and in some the sour. Moreover, among the sweet ones themselves, those that are not yet ripe turn out in some cases to be quite acerbic and in others sour, in the same way as mulberries. But in unripe mulberries the sour quality prevails over the acerbic, whereas in cherries it does not always do so. Now the sweeter ones move down the contents of the intestine more, but are less good for the stomach; the harsh ones do the reverse. The sour ones suit phlegmatic and residual stomachs, for they dry more than the harsh ones and also have something cutting. The gum of the tree has, on the one hand, a certain power common to all drugs that are at once viscous and non-biting, which also suits roughened windpipes; on the other hand, it has a peculiar power, if what some write is true, that drunk with wine it benefits those suffering from stone. For in that case at least some fine-particled power would belong to it.

[7.10.20] [20. On the carob tree.] The carob tree is of a drying and astringent power, as is also its fruit, the so-called keratia, which evidently also partakes of a certain sweetness. These too are affected in a way somewhat similar to cherries: when moist they rather loosen the belly, but when dry they rather stop it, since they have exhaled their moisture and retain the more earthy part of their substance as a residue.

[7.10.21] [21. On kestron.] Kestron, or psychotrophon, in the Roman tongue betonica, has a cutting power, as the taste shows. For the herb is rather bitter and somewhat acrid, as its particular actions also show. For it breaks up stones in the kidneys, purges and scours the lung, thorax and liver, provokes the menses, benefits epileptics and heals ruptures and sprains. Applied as a plaster to the wound, it helps in all bites of wild animals, and taken as a drink it benefits those suffering from sour belching and ischiadics.

[7.10.22] [22. On the oak-gall.] The oak-gall that is called omphacitis is a quite acerbic drug, partaking for the most part of a cold earthy substance, on account of which it dries, repels fluxes, draws together and constricts slack and weak parts, and vigorously resists all fluxional affections. Let it be placed in the third order in drying and in the second order in cooling.
