The other oak-gall, the yellow, loose and large one, also dries, but less to the same degree as it has also partaken less of the acerbic quality. Accordingly, when it is boiled by itself and then ground smooth, it is a not ignoble poultice for inflammations and prolapses in the seat. One must boil it in water when one needs moderate astringency, and in wine when one needs stronger; and if one should need to increase the astringency still further, let your wine also be harsher. The country-people among us call this oinokēkis ('wine-gall'). When burnt, oak-galls become of a blood-staunching power, and evidently take on heat and pungency from the burning, and they are more fine-particled than the unburnt ones and more drying. When you wish to make them blood-staunching, you must make them red-hot over coals and quench them in wine or vinegar.

[7.10.23] [23. On wax.] Wax is in a way intermediate between things that heat and things that cool, and between things that moisten and things that dry. It also has something coarse-particled and clogging, and for this reason it might perhaps seem not only not to dry, but even incidentally to moisten, by obstructing the transpirations. Hence it is also the material for the other drugs, both those that heat and those that cool, while by itself it would be among the weak concoctive drugs: not among those taken into the body, but among those applied from outside. For it has a slight share of a dispersing and hot power, of which honey has received a very large amount.

[7.10.24] [24. On kiki.] The fruit of kiki, just as it both purges and has a cleansing and dispersing power, so too does the leaf, but it is weaker in every respect. The oil made from the fruit, at any rate, is hotter and more fine-particled than common oil, and for this reason it is also dispersing.

[7.10.25] [25. On cinnamon.] Cinnamon is extremely fine-particled, though not extremely hot, but of the third order; and none of the things that heat to the same degree as it dries so much, on account of the fine-particled character of its substance. Kinnamōmis, however, is as it were a weak cinnamon, and some call it pseudo-cinnamon.

[7.10.26] [26. On kirkaia.] Of the herb kirkaia, Dioscorides says that the root, drunk with sweet wine, cleanses the uterus, being fragrant and heating, and that the fruit, given in a gruel, assists in the generation of milk.

[7.10.27] [27. On kistos.] Kistos, or kistharos, is a shrub that is astringent both to the taste and in all its particular effects. Its leaves, however, and its small shoots, when pounded smooth, dry and astringe to such a degree as to conglutinate wounds. The flowers are more efficacious, so that, drunk with wine, they cure dysenteries, atonies of the belly, and fluxes and moistures. Applied as a plaster, they benefit the putrefactive ones among ulcers, for their power is drying in no feeble way, roughly at about the second remove, counting from things of moderate mixture, [that remove] being by now somewhere near completion. The shrub is cold only to such an extent as to share in a lukewarm heat. The so-called hypokistis is very much more astringent even than the leaves, a quite efficacious drug for all fluxional affections, such as bringings-up of blood, women's fluxes, and coeliac and dysenteric conditions. Moreover, if you should wish to strengthen some part that has become slack through excessive moisture, it imparts tone to it in no feeble way. Thus it is also mixed into stomachic and hepatic applications, and is put into the antidote made from vipers for the sake of strengthening and tone of the body.

[7.10.28] [28. On kisthos.] Kisthos, or ladanon. This kisthos, when it grows in hotter regions, though it is not different in kind from the one found among us, has acquired on account of the region a peculiar heat of its own, and a dispersing one, and it has come to differ from ours in both respects: by having put off the coldness and by having taken on heat. The other parts of this kisthos, then, are similar to those of ours, but the so-called ladanon that comes from it is a drug hot in the first order, which is by now somewhere near completion, so that it also touches on the second, and it also partakes of a slight astringency. It is also fine-particled in substance, and for these reasons it is moderately softening, dispersing likewise, and evidently also concocting. It is no wonder, then, that it is especially suited to the affections of the uterus, because in addition to what has been said it also has something slightly astringent; for this reason it also strengthens hair that is falling out. For it consumes whatever bad moistures are at their roots, and by its astringency it draws together and binds tight the pores in which they are fixed. But it is unable to cure alopeciae and ophiases, since these are affections that require a more dispersing power than that in ladanon. For these arise through bad humours, viscid and thick, which cutting and dispersing drugs above all draw out and evacuate. Such drugs must be of a fine-particled power and least of all astringent, yet not so fine-particled and drying as to overdry, and to consume, together with the humours collected there contrary to nature, the natural moisture that makes the hairs grow. For in that way it will not cure alopeciae so much as produce baldness. But these matters belong by now to the therapeutic method.

[7.10.29] [29. On ivy.] Ivy is composed of opposite powers. For it has something of an astringent substance, which we showed to be earthy and cold, and it also has something of a pungent substance, which taste too attests to be hot; and in addition to these it partakes of a third, watery and lukewarm substance, at least the green ivy does. For in the course of being dried this substance must necessarily be dispersed first, while the more earthy one is left behind, both the cold and astringent and the hot and pungent. But the green ivy, when its leaves are boiled with wine, is agglutinating even of large wounds and healing of those that are turning malignant. It also cicatrizes ulcerations from fire. Boiled with vinegar, the leaves benefit splenic patients. Its flowers are somewhat stronger, so that, ground smooth with a cerate, they are suitable for burns. The juice is an errhine drug, and it also heals chronic fluxes of the ears and old ulcers in the ears and the nostrils. But since it appears rather pungent, it is mixed with rose oil or with sweet olive oil. Its tear kills lice and strips away hairs, being of a hot power to such a degree as to burn faintly. For it is, as it were, a kind of watery sap, like other tears too.

[7.10.30] [30. On klinopodion.] Klinopodion is of a heating power, but not yet caustic. It is also fine-particled in its substance, and one might place it in the third order both in heating and in drying.

[7.10.31] [31. On klēmatis.] The leaves of klēmatis are of a pungent and caustic power, so that they even strip off leprai. It would therefore belong to the fourth order of heating things, at its beginning. But the daphnoeides ('laurel-like') is also called klēmatis, which some call myrsinoeides ('myrtle-like') and others polygonoeides ('knotgrass-like'). This, however, is neither ulcerating nor pungent, as the one previously mentioned is; rather, drunk with wine it benefits diarrhoea and dysenteries. Chewed, it soothes pains of the teeth, and applied in a pessary it benefits pains of the womb; so far does it fall short of burning or ulcerating, as the former does. But the most admirable Pamphilus, just as he talks nonsense about everything else, writing about things he does not know, so too he has confused both of these together into one and the same. Dioscorides, however, mentions both in his fourth book: the one simply called klēmatoeides ('vine-like') at the end of the book, the other at the beginning. Hence I too need not describe the forms of the two any further, just as I did not do for the others either.
[7.10.32] [32. On cnicus.] We use the seed of cnicus only for purgations; for it belongs to the third order of heating agents, if one should wish to use it externally.

[7.10.33] [33. On the Cnidian berry.] The Cnidian berry (kokkos Knidios) also purges, but it is of a pungent and caustic power. [7.10.34] [34. On the dyer's berry.] The dyer's berry (kokkos baphikos) has a quality that is astringent and at the same time bitter, and by both of these it dries without biting; for this reason it is suited both to large wounds and to woundings of the nerves. Some grind it smooth with vinegar at such a time (?τηνικαῦτα), others with oxymel.

[7.10.35] [35. On the plum tree.] The fruit of the plum tree loosens the belly, more so when it is fresh, less when it has been dried. Dioscorides, I do not know how, says that the Damascene plums, when dried, check [ὑπέχειν, text uncertain; perhaps for ἐπέχειν] the belly. For these too plainly loosen it, but less than those from Iberia. The Damascene ones are more astringent, those from Iberia sweeter; and indeed the trees too correspond to their fruits: those in Iberia are less astringent, those around Damascus more so. To put it simply, those in whose leaves or shoots some clear astringency shows itself, these, when boiled down, make a mouth-rinse for inflammations about the uvula and the paristhmia. The fruit of the wild ones is manifestly astringent and checks the belly. This plant is called prumnon in Asia. Some say that the gum of the tree, drunk with wine, breaks up stones, and with vinegar heals the lichens of children; and if it does this, it is clear that it partakes of a cutting and fine-particled power.
[7.10.36] [36. On glue.] Glue, which they prepare for books from semidalis-flour and fine meal, is of a clogging and concoctive power for whatever parts it is applied to as a poultice.

[7.10.37] [37. On the gourd.] The gourd is of a moist and cold mixture, in the second order in both respects; hence the juice of its scrapings is also suitable for earaches that arise from inflammation, for those who use it with rose oil. In the same way, applied whole as a cataplasm, it moderately cools hot inflammations. And when eaten it is also watery and allays thirst.

[7.10.38] [38. On colocynth.] Colocynth is bitter in taste, but whatever effects of bitterness belong to a drug that is drunk, these it cannot manifestly produce, because of the purgative power, a strong one, that it possesses in itself: it is excreted through the belly first, together with what it purges. The juice of the green colocynth, rubbed in, benefits cases of ischias.

[7.10.39] [39. On komaros.] Komaros [strawberry tree]. The tree, together with its fruit, is acerbic in quality; they call it [i.e. the fruit] memekylon. This is also bad for the stomach and productive of headache. [7.10.40] [40. On gum.] Gum is a tear that congeals upon the trunks of the trees that produce it, just as resin also does on those of many trees, namely all those whose nature it is to produce resin. It is of a drying and clogging power, and is clearly also healing of roughnesses.

[7.10.41] [41. On lye.] Lye (konia). What is, as it were, the rinsing of ash is called by this name. Most cleansing and most drying of all is the lye made from fig-wood ash and from the ash of the spurges (tithymalloi); it is already very nearly of the so-called putrefying power, the nature of which I set out in the fifth book.

[7.10.42] [42. On konyza.] Konyza, both the greater and the small, are of similar mixture and power. To the taste they appear pungent and bitter, and they heat quite clearly, if one pounds the leaves together with the tender sprigs (for the plant is shrubby) and applies them as a plaster to some part, and also if one boils them in oil and uses this. At any rate such an oil is thought to be a remedy against periodic rigors. Their flowers too are of similar power, so that some people pound these together with the leaves and give them to drink with wine in order to move the menses forcibly and to expel embryos. There is also a third kind of konyza, which grows in moister places; it is more ill-smelling and weaker than both of them. But those mentioned first belong to the third order in drying and heating.

[7.10.43] [43. On coriander.] Coriander (koriannon), or korion, or however you wish to name it: for the ancient Greeks call it koriannon, while the more recent physicians all name it korion, as does Dioscorides, who says, incorrectly, that the herb is cooling. For it is composed of contrary powers. It has much bitter substance, which was shown to be fine-particled and earthy, and not a little watery moisture, lukewarm in power, and it also has something of a slight astringency. From all of these it brings about, in varied ways, the effects that Dioscorides wrote of, but certainly not by cooling alone. But I shall set out the cause of each of its particular actions, even though my intention in the present account was to go through my own judgement only. Perhaps, though, nothing will prevent this; rather, if one must speak the truth, what is said in this manner about a few drugs will be of some benefit and will serve as a reminder of the methods set out earlier. First, then, not Dioscorides alone but also many other physicians make pronouncements about diseases without drawing distinctions, just as, indeed, even among present-day physicians one can find not a few who are well regarded in other respects but who err very greatly in this. For sometimes, when the part that has had the erysipelas has become black, livid and cold, and no longer needs cooling drugs as before, but now needs those that evacuate the humour unnaturally impacted in the region, these people still cool it. At other times they pass on to dispersing drugs, yet they say that they are curing erysipelas. And indeed they also prescribe some drugs while the cases of erysipelas are still beginning and increasing, and others when they are declining. But this is not how things are. For neither should it still be called erysipelas once its fiery, seething and bilious character has gone, nor should the remedies for such conditions be thought cold in their powers. Suppose that right at the start, whether from a blow or in any other way, a livid or black swelling had arisen in some part: it would have been thought to be a cold affection and to need dispersing and heating drugs. In the same way, if a hot condition should at some point change into a cold one, it is right to forget the former and to name the second by another name. Or, if you would not wish to change the name, but, as some do, write some remedies for the beginning and others for the decline, then at least you should not think that the drugs of the decline are also cold. One must grant that someone may call such a condition erysipelas if he wishes, but one must not grant that he still call it hot, once it has been chilled. Let us therefore not think either that what helps it at that time is cooling, as Dioscorides thinks coriander is, because, as he himself says, when applied as a poultice with bread or barley-groats it cures erysipelas. For an exact erysipelas, which is fiery and yellow, coriander with bread would never cure; it cures only one that is already cooling off. For this reason, in the earlier books, when we required that the power of each drug be tested by qualified experience, we advised choosing an affection as simple as possible. But most physicians do not know even that most diseases attack as compound right from the beginning. Nor do they know that exact erysipelas is one affection, and that which is now customarily called by all of us, or at any rate by the ancients, phlegmone is another. In between there are very many others: some one might call phlegmonous cases of erysipelas, others, as it were, certain erysipelatous phlegmonai. You may sometimes also find neither prevailing, but the two exactly balanced. Indeed, erysipelas sometimes appears to become oedematous, as another becomes scirrhous, so that a not inconsiderable multitude of compound diseases is also gathered. About these things more has been said both in certain other works and in the books of the Therapeutic Method, and something will be said now as well. At least this much of them it is necessary to recall: the aforementioned poultice would never cure exact erysipelas. I call it exact when the part has been filled by a bilious flux. That coriander is far from cooling you can learn even from what Dioscorides himself wrote. He says, at any rate, that together with crushed pulse (eregmos) it resolves choirades. That none of the cooling drugs is capable of resolving choirades, not even Dioscorides himself, I think, will dispute. He recorded countless drugs that cure choirades, all of which are agreed to be hot in their mixtures and dispersing in their actions.

[7.10.44] [44. On coronopus.] The root of coronopus is believed to benefit coeliacs when eaten. [7.10.45] [45. On costus.] Costus has a very small share of the bitter quality and power, but a very large share of the pungent and hot, so that it is already even ulcerating. For this reason they rub the body with it, together with oil, before the onset [of the paroxysm] in those who suffer rigors periodically. In the same way they also turn to costus in cases of sciatics and the paralysed, and generally in those cases where the aim is either to heat some part or to draw some humour from the depth to the surface. For the same reason it is also diuretic and brings on the menses, and it is suitable for ruptures and sprains and pains of the sides. Because of the bitterness present in it, it also kills flat worms; on account of this same bitterness they also use it for ephelides, with water or honey. There is also present in its mixture a certain flatulent moisture, on account of which it also stimulates to sexual intercourse when taken with honeyed wine [oinomeli].

[7.10.46] [46. On kotyledon.] Kotyledon is of a mixed power: a moist, somewhat cold one, and a certain one that is faintly somewhat astringent, and with it a slight bitter one; hence it cools, repels, cleanses and disperses. It therefore treats erysipelatous inflammations and inflammatory erysipelas, and it is a quite useful plaster especially when the stomach is burning. The leaves, eaten together with the root, are believed both to break up stones and to provoke urine.

[7.10.47] [47. On the cornel (krania).] Of the cornel tree, the fruit too is quite acerbic, although it is edible, so that it is no wonder that it draws and strongly holds back the belly, just as medlars also do. The leaves and the shoots too are acerbic to the taste and dry strongly, so that they are able to agglutinate even the largest wounds, and especially those of hard bodies. But to small wounds or soft bodies they are rather contrary, for they draw these tight, drying them to a greater degree than is needed.

[7.10.48] [48. On krambē.] Edible krambē is of a drying power, both when eaten and when applied externally. It is not, however, in any way yet considerably pungent, but only to the extent that it unites wounds and heals the malignant among ulcers, and inflammations that are already becoming scirrhous and hard to resolve, and the like among erysipelata. By the same power it heals epinyktides and herpētes. It also has something cleansing in it, in virtue of which it also treats leprai. Its seed, when drunk, destroys worms, and especially the seed of the Egyptian krambē, inasmuch as this is also drier in its mixture; and evidently the seed partakes of a bitter quality, as do all the other drugs suited against worms. By the same power it benefits ephēlides and phakoi and whatever else requires moderate cleansing. And the stalks of krambē, when burnt, produce a strongly drying ash, so that it already partakes somewhat of the caustic power as well. On this account, then, they also mix old fat with it and use it for chronic pains of the sides, and wherever there may be any other such thing. For the drug is rendered strongly dispersing.

[7.10.49] [49. On wild cabbage.] Wild cabbage is hotter and drier in its mixture than the cultivated, just as nearly all the other wild plants are stronger in both powers than the cultivated ones of the same kind. Hence it is not taken inside the body without harm either, since it has departed further from the human mixture. For this very reason it is also more bitter to those who taste it than the cultivated. For the cultivated too has something somewhat bitter and pungent in it, but the wild has each of these strongly; hence it also disperses and cleanses away more vigorously than the cultivated.

[7.10.50] [50. On sea cabbage.] Sea cabbage, [suitable] for evacuating the belly, being slightly salty and somewhat bitter in taste, would also be suitable for uses external to the body, for all those things for which such qualities are fitting.

[7.10.51] [51. On krataiogonon.] The fruit of the herb krataiogonon is pungent to those who taste it, and strongly so to those who use it, being similar to millet. [7.10.52] [52. On krēthmon.] Krēthmon is somewhat salty to those who taste it, together with a slight bitterness; for this reason its power too is at once cleansing and drying. But it is weaker in both respects than the bitter drugs.

[7.10.53] [53. On barley.] Barley is of the first order in drying and cooling, and it also has a slight cleansing quality. It is a little more drying than bean meal without the husk; in all other respects the two are similar when used externally. When eaten, however, barley has this advantage over beans: it lays aside its flatulent quality, whereas in the bean, however it is boiled, the flatulent quality remains. For the bean is of a more coarse-particled substance than barley, and for this reason it is also more nourishing than barley. And since both have departed only a little from the mean, for this reason they are of many uses. For such drugs are often mixed with others, as a kind of base material, and for this reason wax and oil too are combined with not a few drugs. Barley groats are much more drying even than barley itself.

[7.10.54] [54. On krimnon.] Krimnon. This is the name given to the coarse-particled part both of wheaten flour and of the flour made from zeia. It is more nourishing than barley-groats, but harder to digest. The gruel made from it is called poltos, and the one from zeia is gently binding to the belly, and more so if the krimnon has been parched.

[7.10.55] [55. On the lily.] The flower of the lily is, in its mixture, compounded of a certain fine-particled and earthy substance, from which it also has its bitterness in taste, and of a certain well-tempered watery substance. Hence the oil made from it and the perfume are likewise of a non-biting, dispersing and softening power, and on account of these they are also most suitable for hardnesses in the uterus. The root and the leaves, ground smooth by themselves, dry, cleanse and disperse moderately. In this way, at any rate, they are suited also to burns, for these too require a power that is moderately drying and at the same time cleansing. So they roast the root, then grind it smooth together with rose oil and apply it to burns until they close with a scar. For it is in other respects too a good drug for bringing all ulcers to cicatrization. Not only this, but it also softens wombs and calls forth the menses. The leaves they boil lightly and apply them too, until they have scarred over, not only to burns but also to other ulcers. Some also preserve them in vinegar and use them as wound remedies. There is more of the cleansing power in the root than in the leaves, yet not much even in it, as was said before; for they belong to the first order of cleansing drugs. Hence, whenever we wish to cleanse away alphoi or psora or lepra or achores or anything of that kind, we mix with it some other of the stronger drugs, such as honey is. This, mixed with it in due proportion, suits both severings of the nerves and all other things that need to be dried strongly without biting. We once also stored up the juice of the leaves, having boiled it with vinegar and honey. The juice was fivefold the amount of each, and the drug was highly esteemed for all things that need to be dried strongly without being bitten, such as wounds that are large, and especially those occurring at the heads of the muscles, and those ulcers that are flabby, chronic and hard to cicatrize. These matters, however, already belong to the treatise on the composition of drugs, from which I try to abstain as far as possible for the present; yet the nature of the subject often compels me to touch upon it, and one must quickly withdraw from these matters again and return to what is now before us.

[7.10.56] [56. On krokodeilion.] The seed of krokodeilion is pungent and aromatic, and diuretic and stimulating of the menses, so that it would also be of a hot power, and a dispersing and drying one. The juice too, both of the stem and of the seed, being of a similar power, benefits nephritics. The root strongly assists expectorations from the chest, being less pungent than the seed, but no less bitter. It also draws blood through the nostrils.

[7.10.57] [57. On saffron.] Saffron has something astringent in it too, though only a little, and this was shown to be earthy and cold. But a heating quality and power prevails in it, so that its whole substance belongs to the second order of heating things and to the first of drying things. For this reason it also has something concoctive about it, the slight astringency also helping towards this. For in drugs that do not heat vigorously, if a little astringency is present, they have the same power as the substances called clogging, which, when they coexist with heat, we showed to be not very concoctive.

[7.10.58] [58. On onion.] Onion belongs to the fourth order of heating things. Its substance is rather coarse-particled; hence, applied as a suppository, it opens haemorrhoids; smeared on with vinegar in the sun it cleanses away alphoi; and rubbed on alopeciae it stimulates the hairs more quickly than alcyonium. If one separates the juice from it, what remains is abundantly of an earthy, hot substance, while the juice itself is of a watery and airy heat. So, then, when anointed on, it [the juice] also benefits those suffering from suffusion and those with dim sight owing to thickness of humours. From the mixture of this [juice], the onion as a whole is flatulent when eaten; and for this reason those that are drier in mixture are less flatulent.

[7.10.59] [59. On the bean.] The bean is, on each side, of the middle mixture, lying very close to it as regards drying and as regards cooling. Its flesh also shares, to a small degree, in a certain cleansing power, just as the husk shares in the astringent one; and for this reason some physicians have boiled the whole bean with oxycrate and given it to dysenteric patients, to coeliacs and to those prone to vomiting. As a food it is flatulent and hard to concoct, if anything else is, yet it is suitable for expectorations from the chest and lung. As a drug applied externally it dries without causing distress. For gouty patients, however, we have often used it, boiling it in water and then mixing in pig's fat. For contusions and ulcers in the region of the nerves we have applied the meal with oxymel, and for parts already inflamed from a blow, with barley groats. It is also a good poultice for the testicles and the breasts, for these parts, when inflamed, are disposed to be cooled moderately, and especially when the breasts are inflamed from milk curdled in them. Accordingly the milk too is quenched by such a poultice, just as the pubes of boys, when plastered with bean meal, remains hairless for longer.

[7.10.60] [60. On cyclamen.] Cyclamen is varied in its power: for it cleanses, cuts, opens the mouths of vessels, draws, and disperses. This is clear from its particular effects. Its juice, applied on a flock of wool, opens the mouths of haemorrhoids and forcibly provokes to stool. In the same way it is also mixed into the powers that disperse tumours (phymata), scrofulous swellings (choirades) and all other hardnesses. Smeared on with honey, it is suited to those suffering from cataract (hypochysis), and in addition to these it also purges through the nostrils. Its power is so vehement that even when the epigastrium is anointed with it, it moves the bowels and destroys embryos; for it is in any case a strong abortifacient when applied in a pessary. The whole root is weaker than the juice, but it too is vehement. For it moves the menses when drunk and when applied, and it benefits the jaundiced, not only by thoroughly purging the viscus but also by excreting the bile in the whole body through sweats. Hence, upon the drinking of it, one must assist the generation of sweats in every way. The amount of it drunk should be up to three drachms, with either sweet wine or melikraton. It also cleanses the skin, both in other respects and in treating alopecias, ephelides and all eruptions. It also benefits hard spleens when applied as a plaster, whether fresh or dry. Some also give the dry root to the asthmatic. The other cyclamen, which some call kissanthemon because it resembles ivy in its flower, has a useless root but a sufficiently active fruit, so that when drunk with white wine, in an amount of two cyathi, for several days, it heals spleens, moving the urine and loosening the bowels; it also expels the afterbirths and helps the asthmatic. Its quality to one who tastes it is pungent and somewhat viscid.

[7.10.61] [61. On cumin.] Of cumin we use chiefly the seed, as we do of anise, lovage, caraway and parsley. It is also of a heating power, as each of those is too, and of a diuretic and wind-dispelling power, belonging to the third order of heating things.

[7.10.62] [62. On kynosbatos.] Kynosbatos (dog-rose). The fruit of this shrub is quite considerably astringent, the leaves moderately so, so that their use in particular cases is also evident. But one should beware of the woolly matter in the fruit, as being injurious to the windpipe (artēria).

[7.10.63] [63. On cypress.] The leaves of the cypress, its shoots, and its young, soft little balls are agglutinating of large wounds in hard bodies. From this it is clear that it is of a drying power, one that has nothing conspicuously pungent and hot, as indeed the taste also testifies. For in the taste the pungent appears to be slight, the bitter very great, and the acerbic much greater still throughout the whole plant. The pungent and the hot in it are only so much as to guide the acerbity into the depth, but not to produce any heat or biting in bodies. For this reason it feeds upon and consumes the moistures in the depth in flabby and putrefactive conditions, both painlessly and safely at once, whereas the heating and drying powers use up the moistures contained there but draw in others by their pungency and heat. In this way it also benefits those suffering from enterocele. For it both dries and imparts tone to bodies that are slack through moisture, since the astringency sinks down into the depth by being guided by the heat mixed with it, which reaches such a measure that it is able to guide but not yet able to bite. Some also use it for carbuncles and herpes, mixing it with barley-meal, on the ground that it uses up, without heating, the moistures that produce such diseases. Some also use it for erysipelas, mixing it with barley-meal together with water or watery oxycrate.

[7.10.64] [64. On cyperus.] Of cyperus the roots are the most useful part, heating and drying without biting. Hence they are wonderfully beneficial to ulcers that are hard to cicatrize on account of much moisture. For they also have something astringent, and for this reason they are also suited to ulcers in the mouth; and indeed a certain cutting power must also be attested of them, by which they are both fitting for those suffering from stone and move the urine and the menses.

[7.10.65] [65. On kypros.] Kypros. Of this tree the leaves and the shoots come into use, being above all of a mixed power and mixture. For it has something dispersing, from a watery substance that is moderately hot, and it has something astringent, from its earthy cooling; hence people boil them down and pour the water over burns. They also use them against fiery inflammations and carbuncles, for they are drying without causing distress and without biting. Moreover, when chewed it is suited to the ulcers that arise spontaneously in the mouth, and above all to the aphthous ones and to the aphthae of children themselves.

[7.10.66] [66. On kytisos.] The leaves of kytisos are of a dispersing power, mixed with a lukewarm watery one, just as those of mallow also are. [7.10.67] [67. On hemlock.] That hemlock is of an extremely cooling power, everyone knows.

[7.10.68] [68. On the pine cone.] The fruit of the pine cone (κῶνος), which they also call kokalos and strobilos, taken whole while green, has something bitter and pungent together with moistness, and for this reason it is suitable for the empyematous, and for any others who need to cough up and spit up easily what is in the chest and lung. The edible fruit that comes out of it is a nourishment both hard to digest and strong, but it is also suitable as a drug for smoothing roughnesses, especially when, steeped in water, it gives off into the water all the pungency it has. For all that remains becomes less biting and more clogging, being placed in the middle between hot and cold quality, mixed from a watery and an earthy substance, and having very little share of airy substance.

[7.11.1] [1. On lagopous.] Lagopous (hare's-foot) is of a drying power, so that it dries up the fluxes in the belly well. [7.11.2] [2. On lathyris.] Lathyris. This too some say is a kind of tithymallus, both because it has a juice similar to theirs and because it purges in the same manner as they do; and it is similar to them in its whole power, except insofar as the seed appears sweet to those who taste it, and it is this, indeed, that has the purgative power most of all.

[7.11.3] [3. On lampsane.] Lampsane, when eaten, is productive of bad humours, but when applied as a poultice it has something cleansing and dispersing. [7.11.4] [4. On docks.] Dock is of a moderately dispersing power, and oxylapathon (sharp dock) of a mixed one; for together with the dispersing power it also partakes of something repelling. Their seed clearly has something astringent as well, so that it cures dysenteries and diarrhoea, and especially that of oxylapathon. Hippolapathon (horse dock) grows for the most part in marshes; it is of the same power as those already mentioned, but of a weaker one.

[7.11.5] [5. On leimonion.] The fruit of leimonion, which is harsh, they give with wine to coeliacs, to dysenteric patients and to those who spit blood. It also benefits the female flux. An oxybaphon's quantity is enough.

[7.11.6] [6. On leichen.] The leichen that grows on rocks is like a kind of bryon, but it would rightly be named as belonging to the class of plants. It seems to have been so named because it treats leichenes. It is of a cleansing and at the same time moderately cooling power, but drying in both respects. It takes its cleansing and drying quality from the rock, and its cooling quality from the watery component. For it grows on moist and dewy rocks. It is nothing surprising that what is composed of such substances is preventive of inflammation. But whether it also stops haemorrhages, as Dioscorides says, I am not able to say.

[7.11.7] [7. On leontopetalon.] Of leontopetalon we use chiefly the root, which is dispersing, drying and heating in the third order. [7.11.8] [8. On lepidion.] Lepidion belongs to the fourth order of heating things; it is similar to cress in smell, taste and power, but it dries less than cress.

[7.11.9] [9. On leukas.] Leukas is of a pungent quality, which predominates, and of a hot and dry mixture, somewhere about the third order. [7.11.10] [10. On leukakanthos.] Leukakanthos, which some call polygonaton and others ischias: its root is bitter, and for this reason it cuts and dries in the third order; but in heating it is of the first order.

[7.11.11] [11. On leukoion.] Of leukoion the whole shrub is of a cleansing and fine-particled power, but the flowers share in it to a greater degree, and of these the drier more than the fresh, so that they even thin the thick scars on the eyes, and their decoction promotes the menses and draws out afterbirths and dead embryos, and if it is drunk, it is an abortifacient drug. For indeed it is also bitter, if anything else is, and if one should soften the vehemence of its power by mixing in much water, or something of that kind, one will have a good drug also for inflammation. Thus, at any rate, its decoction too, if it is not undiluted, heals inflammations in the womb when poured over them, and especially those that have become chronic in a scirrhous manner. And thus also, with a cerate, it treats ulcers that are hard to cicatrize. Some also use it with honey for aphthae. The fruit, being of the same power, is most suitable when drunk in an amount of two drachms or applied as a pessary with honey; it is believed both to move the menses and to destroy living embryos and expel dead ones. The roots, being of a similar power, except insofar as they are more coarse-particled and more earthy, heal indurated (scirrhous) spleens with vinegar. And some also heal indurating (scirrhous) inflammations by means of it.

[7.11.12] [12. On white poplar.] The white poplar, the tree, is in a way mixed in its mixture, from a lukewarm watery substance and an attenuated earthy one; hence it also has a share in the cleansing power.

[7.11.13] [13. On frankincense.] Frankincense is heating in the second order and drying in the first. It also has something slightly astringent, though the astringency is least evident in the kind that is white in colour. Its bark, however, plainly possesses the astringent power, and for this reason it also dries vigorously, being among the drying things at the completion of the second order. It is also more coarse-particled than the frankincense and partakes of pungency very little. Because of these qualities and powers of it, physicians make considerable use of it for those who spit blood, stomachic, coeliac and dysenteric patients, mixing it not only into things applied externally but also into things taken inside the body. Its shoot is of a drier and hotter power than frankincense itself, so as to reach the third remove. It also has something cleansing, so that for this reason it is thought both to clean out and to fill up ulcers in the eyes, as do also that from myrrh and that from storax.

[7.11.14] [14. On the libanotides.] There are three libanotides: one is fruitless, while the other two bear fruit, and all are of a similar power, softening and dispersing. The juice, both that of the root and that of the herb, mixed with honey, treats amblyopias, those that arise from thickness of fluids. Of the libanotis that is useful for garlands, which the Romans call rusmarinum, the decoction, when drunk, benefits the icteric. For all the libanotides share in a cleansing and cutting power.

[7.11.15] [15. On soot.] All soot is drying, and for this reason it is also of earthy substance. It retains some remnant of the fire that burnt up the material, but only a little. Its whole nature is earthy and fine-particled. The differences in kind within it arise according to the material that was burnt: from more pungent and hotter material the soot also turns out of that kind, and from sweeter material the soot here too becomes similar. For instance, they use the soot of frankincense, mixing it into the ophthalmic remedies, even those suited to eyes that are still inflamed, suffering from flux, and having ulcers. For these are both cleaned out and filled with flesh by them. Further, they also use it in the remedies called kalliblephara. The soot of terebinth and that of myrrh are non-irritating, much like that of frankincense. That of storax is stronger than these, that of liquid pitch still more so, and that of cedar still more than this. They use the more pungent kinds for the eyelids called ptila, for eroded canthi, and for moist eyes without inflammation. They use the milder kinds for these too, but also for the conditions for which, as was said a little earlier, the soot of frankincense is suitable.

[7.11.16] [16. On lovage.] Both the root and the seed of lovage belong to the heating [drugs] to such a degree as to move the menses and to promote urine; and moreover they are also free of flatulence.

[7.11.17] [17. On linseed.] Linseed, when eaten, is flatulent even if it has been roasted; so full, then, is it of residual moisture. It is also hot, somewhere in the first order, and with respect to moisture and dryness it is ranked somewhere in the middle.

[7.11.18] [18. On linozostis.] Everyone uses linozostis only for purgings of the belly. Nevertheless, if anyone should also wish to make trial of it by applying it as a cataplasm, he will find it to be of a considerably dispersing power.

[7.11.19] [19. On lonchitis.] Of lonchitis, the kind that has its seed triangular, resembling a lance-head in shape, happens to have a root very closely similar to that of daukos, and for this reason it is also a diuretic drug. Of the kind similar to skolopendrion, the leaves are suitable, when green, for the conglutination of a wound; when dry, drunk with vinegar, they heal spleens that are becoming scirrhous.

[7.11.20] [20. On lycium.] Lycium, or pyxacanthus, is a thorny tree from which the so-called lycium is also made. This, then, is the liquid drug which they use for bruises below the eyes, and for inflammations and ulcerations in the anus and the mouth, and for herpes, putrefactions, malignant ulcers, ears running with pus, abrasions and paronychias. For it is of drying power, composed of substances of different kinds: the one fine-particled, dispersing and hot, the other earthy and cold, from which it has its astringency. But this quality itself is present in the drug only in a very small amount, whereas its dispersing and drying are not small, but are in the second remove; in heat it is ranked somewhere about the middle and the moderate. For this reason they also use the drug for differing affections: as cleansing, for things that darken the pupils; as contracting, administering it to coeliac and dysenteric patients and for female flux. This lycium, then, is produced in greatest quantity in Lycia and Cappadocia. The other kind, the Indian, is stronger in every respect.

[7.11.21] [21. On lysimachion.] Lysimachios has the astringent quality predominating, on account of which it both glues wounds together and stops haemorrhages from the nostrils when applied as a plaster; and it is also a blood-stanching drug for the other haemorrhages, both the plant itself and its juice; and still more, when it is also drunk, it heals dysenteries, the bringing up of blood, and the female flux.
[7.11.22] [22. On lychnis.] The seed of the lychnis that is used for garlands is hot somewhere in the second order, or even already in the third, and it is also dry in the same way.

[7.11.23] [23. On the cultivated lotus.] The cultivated lotus, which some call trifolium, is of a moderately concoctive power, and likewise of a drying one. In the conjugation of heat and cold it is in some way intermediate and well-tempered. The wild lotus grows most abundantly in Libya. Its seed belongs to the second order of heating things, and it also has something cleansing. The seed of the Egyptian lotus is even made into bread.

[7.11.24] [24. On the lotus, the tree.] The lotus tree has no great share of astringent quality, but it is also fine-particled and drying. At any rate the filings (ῥινήματα) of its wood are suitable both for female flux and for dysenteries and coeliac conditions. They are boiled sometimes in water, sometimes in wine, as the need may direct, and they are not only injected but also drunk. Moreover, the fact that it checks falling hair is no small sign that it is of a somewhat astringent power together with drying moderately. For it was said also in the account of ladanon that whatever is going to check falling hair must be of such a power.

[7.12.1] [1. On macer.] Macer is a bark brought from India. To the taste it is quite acerbic, with a slight aromatic pungency, and to the smell it is pleasant, like most of the Indian aromatics. It seems, then, that it too is composed of a mixed substance, the greatest part of which is earthy and cold, and a small part hot and fine-particled. Hence it is strongly drying and astringent, and for this reason it is mixed into the compound remedies (dynameis) for coeliac and dysenteric conditions. It belongs to the third order of drying things, but in the distinction according to heat and coldness it produces neither manifestly.

[7.12.2] [2. On malabathrum.] The leaf of malabathrum is close in power to the spike of nard. [7.12.3] [3. On mallow and althaea.] Mallow, the wild kind, shares in a power that is gently dispersing and, to a slight degree, softening. The garden kind, in so far as it has taken on a share of watery moisture, is to that extent also weaker in power. Its fruit is stronger to the same degree as it is also drier. The so-called tree-mallow also belongs to this genus, but it is the most dispersing of those mentioned. It is also called althaea.

[7.12.4] [4. On mandrake.] Mandrake has a predominating cooling power, such that it belongs to the third order of things that cool. Nevertheless it also shares in a certain heat and, at least in its apples, also in moisture; hence these are also comatose (sleep-inducing) in their power. The bark of the root, being the strongest part, not only cools but also dries, whereas the rest, the inner part, is weak.

[7.12.5] [5. On fennel] Fennel heats strongly, so that it may already belong to the third order; but it does not dry to the same degree, and in this respect one would place it in the first order. For this reason it is generative of milk, which it would not generate if it dried strongly; and on the same principle it helps those suffering from suffusion. It is also diuretic and a promoter of the menses. There is also another, wild fennel, which they call hippomarathron ('horse-fennel') on account of its size, whose root and seed are of a more drying power than in the cultivated kind; so that they seem to me also to check the belly on this account, for they certainly have no evident astringency. Of this plant, then, not only the root but much more the seed is similar to kachrys, and it is able to break up stones, to cure those affected with jaundice, to move the menses and to promote urination, but not to gather milk as the former does. There is another hippomarathron, whose seed is round and pungent, similar to that of koriannon; it is like the seed of hippomarathron in power, but weaker.

[7.12.6] [6. On mastic.] Mastic: the white kind, usually called Chian, is in a way compounded of contrary powers, astringent and softening. For this reason it is suited to inflammations of the stomach, belly, intestines and liver, warming and drying at the second remove. The black kind, called Egyptian, dries more than the former and has less share in the astringent power; hence it is in a way better suited to conditions that require a stronger dispersal. For this reason, at any rate, it is also a good drug for boils. The mastic oil and the mastic unguent, however, are prepared from the Chian kind, and hardly at all from the Egyptian. This too is evidently of a power similar to that of mastic.

[7.12.7] [7. On melanthion.] Melanthion heats and dries in the third order. It also seems to be fine-particled; at any rate it is in this way that it heals catarrhs, when applied warm in a linen cloth so that it is smelled continually. Moreover, it is also least productive of wind (ἀφυσότατον) when taken into the body, from which it is clear that it is of a substance that is fine-particled and thoroughly worked up by heat. It is for this very reason that it is also bitter. It was shown in the fourth of these commentaries that the bitter quality is generated when the earthy substance reaches the utmost fineness and elaboration. It is therefore no wonder if it is naturally able to destroy worms, not only when eaten but also when applied externally over the belly, for it was shown that the bitter flavour (χυμός) is naturally able to do this as well. Nor, to anyone who remembers what was said earlier, is it a wonder that it removes leprai, corns and myrmeciae. In this way it also benefits orthopnoea and promotes the menses that have been held back through thickness or viscosity of the humours; and in general, wherever we need to cut, cleanse, dry and heat, the drug is most useful.
[7.12.8] [8. On melilot.] Melilot is of a mixed power. For it has something astringent too, but it also disperses and concocts. For there is more of the hot substance in it than of the cold.

[7.12.9] [9. On honey.] Honey both dries and heats in the second order. It is of as simple a power and mixture as can be, belonging to the class of drugs that we customarily call cleansing. When boiled, it becomes less pungent and cleansing, which is why people use it for the conglutination of sinuses. If some honey is bitter, as is the honey in Sardinia, it is evident that this too is of mixed power, as if one of us had mixed wormwood with it. What is called sakchar [sugar], which is brought from India and from Arabia Felix, congeals, so they say, on reeds, and it too is a kind of honey. It is less sweet than ours, but similar to it in power, inasmuch as it cleanses away, dries and disperses; inasmuch as it is neither bad for the stomach, as ours is, nor productive of thirst, [these qualities] have departed from its substance.

[7.12.10] [10. On melissophyllon.] Melissophyllon is similar to horehound in its power, but falls very far short of it. For this reason no one even uses it; for it is superfluous to use melissophyllon when horehound is present so abundantly in every part of the earth. If, however, horehound should at some time not be available, it is possible to use [melissophyllon] for all the purposes for which [one uses] that [plant], provided one recognises the deficiency of its activity.

[7.12.11] [11. On the medlar.] The medlar is sometimes called 'tricoccum' (three-pipped), because it has three pips in all inside it. Each of them is a seed of the tree, just as the seeds found in apples are seeds of the apple-tree, the grape-stones of the vine, and the kenchramides of the fig-tree. The fruit of the tree is quite acerbic and scarcely edible, and it is strongly checking of the belly. In its shoots and in its leaves, too, the acerbic quality is present to no small degree.

[7.12.12] [12. On medion.] It happens that the root of medion is of a mixture contrary to that of its fruit. For the root is harsh and checking of fluxes, both of the others and indeed of the so-called female flux; whereas the seed is so far from doing anything of this kind that it even stimulates the menses, being of a fine-particled and cutting power.

[7.12.13] [13. On the poppy.] Of the poppy (mēkōn), one kind is called rhoias, because its flower falls off (aporrhei) quickly; another is called the cultivated, since it is grown in gardens. And indeed, besides these there are two other, wild poppies: the one having its head (kōdya) as it were seated within, the other having it more elongated than this one, and the plant as a whole more luxuriant [? auxanestera] and more parched. From this poppy the juice (opos) flows off, which is why some also call it rhoias. The power of all of them is cooling. But of the garden kind, which they also call thylakitis, the seed, white to look at, is moderately soporific. This is why they also sprinkle these [seeds] on their loaves and eat them moistened with honey. Of the first-named kind, whose flower we say falls off quickly, the seed cools more strongly, so that one could not use it on its own without harm, as one does that of the garden kind, mixing it with honey. Taken in this way it is quite soporific; but they sprinkle it in small quantity on honey cakes, on itria and on loaves. Of the third-named kind the seed, being black, is already drug-like (pharmakōdes), cooling considerably. The fourth-named is the most drug-like of all, in its seed, in its heads, in its leaves and in its juice; for it cools strongly, bringing on torpor (narkē) and mortification (nekrōsis). Hence it is the physician's task to use it well, mixing it with drugs that blunt the strength of its cooling. For it belongs to the fourth and last rank of cooling things. How one might best make the mixture methodically is not proper to the present treatise, but to the one on the composition of drugs, which we are writing next after this one.

[7.12.14] [14. On the horned poppy.] The horned poppy (mēkōn keratitis) has been named from its fruit, which has a short curvature, as fenugreek also has, so that it resembles the horn of an ox. It is called by some 'seaside poppy', since for the most part it grows near the sea. It has a cutting and cleansing power, so that the root of the herb, boiled down in water to half, benefits hepatic conditions. The leaves and the flowers help those ulcers that are very foul and malignant. But one must desist from them once the ulcers have become clean. For it is by nature cleansing to such a degree that it melts away something even of the clean flesh itself. Indeed, because of this strength it removes from ulcers not only the foulness but also the eschars.
[7.12.15] [15. On Heracleian poppy.] Heracleian poppy is also called 'foamy' (aphrōdēs), because it is wholly white and foamy, being small. Its seed is purgative of phlegm.

[7.12.16] [16. On the apple tree.] The apple tree is not all of one nature, just as its fruit is not either. For some apples are sweet, some harsh, some acerbic, some sour, and some completely insipid and watery. And indeed in these last the watery predominates, so that their mixture is moister and colder; in the acerbic ones the cold earthy predominates, and in the harsh ones both this and the cold watery, just as in the sweet ones the well-tempered watery predominates. In the same way the leaves, the juices and the barks of the trees also differ from one another, so that with the harsher and sourer ones you can agglutinate wounds, check what flows in to inflammations that are in the process of forming, and strengthen a slack stomach and the belly; and with the more watery ones you can relax moderate inflammations, both those beginning and those increasing. But these matters belong already to the therapeutic method, and for this reason they must be left aside quickly. That a very great residual and cold moisture is carried in all apples is clear also from the fact that the juice of none of them keeps, but all of them turn sour and spoil. For only the juice of quinces and strouthia, which on account of their predominant astringency are less moist than the others, is able to keep when boiled with honey; by itself, however, it is not lasting even so.

[7.12.17] [17. On the Persian apple-tree.] The Persian apple-tree is now customarily called by everyone simply 'Persian', since they leave out precisely this word, 'apple'. The tree has the bitter quality predominating in both its shoots and its leaves, and for this reason its leaves, when ground smooth and applied over the navel, kill worms. In other respects too it is a dispersing drug. Its fruit, which is the edible 'Persian', is moister and colder in its mixture.

[7.12.18] [18. On the Armenian apple-tree.] The Armenian apple-tree. The old name of this tree has fallen out of use, for everyone calls both the fruit and the tree prekokkion. The fruit is moist and cold, having been affected in both respects most probably somewhere around the second remove.

[7.12.19] [19. On the Median apple-tree.] Median apple-tree. The fruit of this is no longer called 'Median apple' but is named *kitrion* by everyone. In its seed it has a sour quality and a drying power predominating, so as to be of the third order among things that dry and cool. In its rind it has here too a share of a drying mixture, but one that has no small amount of the pungent; for which reason this too dries in the second remove. It is not, however, cold, but either balanced or a little lower. Its flesh is of thick humours, phlegmatic and cold; for it is eaten, just as the rind is. But the seed is entirely inedible: both the moist and sourish part, which I discussed first, and the kernel found within it, which is truly the seed. This is bitter, and evidently dispersing and drying, standing off from the balanced things somewhere about the second order. And the leaves too are of a drying and dispersing power.

[7.12.20] [20. On meum.] Meum. Its roots are useful, being hot in the third remove and dry in the second. For this reason, at any rate, those who wish to promote urine and to call forth the menses make use of this drug. It is productive of headache when taken in larger quantity, inasmuch as it is hot to a greater degree than it is dry. For the heat in it, carrying up to the head a moisture that is still rather undigested and rather flatulent, in this way harms the head.

[7.12.21] [21. On rough smilax.] Rough smilax is vine-like (klêmatôdês), so that it winds itself about the trees in many ways, upwards and downwards. Its leaves, when tasted, have something pungent, and when used in other ways they heat.

[7.12.22] [22. On smooth milax.] Smooth milax is somewhat similar in power to the one previously described. [7.12.23] [23. On the mulberry tree.] Of the mulberry tree, the ripe fruit moves the belly downwards, while the unripe fruit, when dried, becomes a sufficiently binding drug, so that it is suitable both for dysenteries and for coeliac conditions and for the other conditions that involve a flux. It is pounded and mixed into dishes, just as the fruit of sumac is, or, if one wishes, it is drunk in water or wine. That the juice of the ripe fruit is useful for drugs for the mouth on account of the astringency present in it, nobody is unaware. And clearly it is also suitable for many other particular conditions, those that require a moderate astringency. The unripe fruits, in addition to their acerbity, also have a share of sourness. And the whole tree, in all its parts, seems to have a mixed power composed of a checking and a purging power. In the bark of the root the purging power predominates, along with a certain bitterness, so that it even kills the broad worm; in the other parts the checking power predominates. In the leaves and the shoots the mixture is somehow intermediate between both.

[7.12.24] [24. On myagros.] The seed of myagros is oily, so that, if it is crushed, it gives off something oil-like that is of a clogging power. [7.12.25] [25. On mushrooms.] The mushroom is a plant that is quite cold and moist, and for this reason it comes close to a deleterious power. Indeed some of them even kill, especially those that have a nature mixed with a certain putrefactive quality.

[7.12.26] [26. On myle.] The root of myle, being similar to a small bulb, is of a contracting power, so that Dioscorides says that, applied together with darnel flour, it heals a womb whose mouth has been opened.

[7.12.27] [27. On mouse's ear.] Mouse's ear (myos ōtis); some call it mouse's ears. It dries in the second order, but possesses no evident heat. [7.12.28] [28. On tamarisk.] Tamarisk is of a cleansing and cutting power, without drying evidently, but it also has some astringency. Because of these qualities and powers it benefits greatly a spleen that has become scirrhous, when its roots, or its twigs, or its leaves are boiled down with vinegar or wine. It also heals toothaches. The fruit and the bark have taken on no slight astringency, so that they come close even to the omphacitis gall, except insofar as the acerbity is clear in the gall, whereas in the fruit of the tamarisk the mixture is uneven. For much that is cleansing and fine-particled is mixed into its nature, which the gall does not have. One can, however, use it, when gall is not to hand, for all the purposes for which that is used, and the bark likewise. The ash of tamarisk, when it has been burned, also becomes of a strongly drying power, one that has a very great deal of the cleansing and cutting, but little of the astringent.

[7.12.29] [29. On myriophyllon.] Myriophyllon is of a drying power to such a degree as to conglutinate wounds. [7.12.30] [30. On myrrhis.] Myrrhis, which some call myrrha, has a fragrant and sweet root; it is promotive of the menses and clears out [matter] from the chest and lung, so that it would belong to the second order of heating things, having also something fine-particled.

[7.12.31] [31. On myrtle.] Myrtle. This plant too is composed of contrary substances. Nevertheless, an earthy cold [substance] predominates in it, but it also has a fine-particled hot [substance], whence it dries strongly. The leaves, the shoots, the fruit and the juice do not differ from one another to any great degree in astringency. The knobby outgrowth on the trunk and on the branches themselves, however, which some call myrtas: by as much as it is drier than the aforementioned, by so much does it both dry and astringe more vehemently. Some store it by pounding it, and then taking it up in wine and moulding it into pastilles. The dry leaves are also more drying than the green ones, for evidently a certain moisture is mixed in the green ones. The juice is pressed out not only from the green leaves but also from the fruit. All of these are of a binding power, both when applied to the outside of the body and when taken internally, because they have no poisonous or purgative substance already mixed in.

[7.12.32] [32. On moly.] Moly. Some call this wild rue, others harmala, and the Syrians besasa, just as the Cappadocians too call it moly, because it is black in its root but has a milk-white flower. Its power is fine-particled and hot in the third remove, whence it also cuts thick and viscid humours, disperses, and promotes urination. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 9. Preface. As much, then, as remains of the power found in plants will be stated in this book, and not even all of that, but only the activities of the active qualities; for the works of the whole substance of plants we shall go through later, on their own. So, having once again reminded those who have read the preceding books of these points: that for each simple power we made the division according to the more and the less into four ranks; that we delimited the breadth of each rank by clear boundaries and taught a certain method for the very discovery of the powers; and that we made demonstrations of all these things and laid down aims and criteria, both particular and common, for each power. Having done so, we shall now add what remains. We urge anyone who has not engaged with the preceding books either to keep away from these too altogether, or, if he is industrious, first to read through the treatise from the beginning. For everything that is going to be said will appear to him both unclear and undemonstrated until he has exercised himself in those books.

[6.1.1] [1. On southernwood and wormwood and the species of each.] Of southernwood, this herb, one need not describe the form, after so many men of such quality, nor its particular actions, since those men set them out, if not with precise distinctions, at least clearly. More will also be said by us about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs and in that on easily procured remedies, and sometimes also in the writings of the Therapeutic Method, when need calls. Only what was proposed from the beginning, to examine the universal powers of all drugs, follows in the case of the others too, and it must now already be done here. It must be said that southernwood is hot and dry in power, ranked somewhere in the third order and remove beyond the balanced state, and has a certain dispersing and cutting power. Of the same power also is its rubbing (?) having taken [it] (τρίψις … εἰληφυῖα), as also the flesh-forming and the biting. That such an order is assessed relative to the well-tempered nature has often been said before. We found out its mixture not least by judging also from taste, for it is quite bitter. Such a flavour was shown to be earthy in its substance and to be thinned by abundant heat, so as both to heat and to dry not feebly. Moreover, having tested it accurately also by the qualified experience, about which it has often been said before, we found this drug to be of the same mixture. For if you pound the foliage together with the flowers (for the rest of it, the dry stalk, is useless) and sprinkle it on a clean ulcer, it appears biting and irritant; and if you steep it in oil and choose to pour it over either the head or the belly, it will be found to heat strongly. And indeed those who are seized by rigors at periods, if you rub them down with it before the onset, shiver less; nor does it escape perception, immediately as it is applied, that it heats. That it is likely to destroy worms, being bitter, is clear even before experience, if we remember anything of what was said in the fourth of these commentaries about the nature of the bitter flavour. You will know at once that it also has a certain dispersing and cutting power. And that this must belong to it more than to wormwood you will be able to infer, first from the taste. For southernwood partakes of a very small acerbity, but wormwood of not a little; and then also from the fact that southernwood is bad for the stomach, as is seriphon too, whereas wormwood is good for the stomach. For it was shown earlier about these things too that the bitter by itself is wholly bad for the stomach, whereas the harsh or acerbic or, in general, the astringent is good for the stomach; and when the qualities are mixed with one another, the stronger would prevail. This, then, is enough for you to know in this treatise. For it will be shown in the writings of the Therapeutic Method how one may best use such a drug. And for this reason do not seek any longer to hear either that, applied as a poultice with boiled quince or with bread, it heals inflammations of the eyes, or that, boiled smooth with ōmēlysis, it disperses phymata. For neither of these nor any of the others is proper to the present treatise; rather, for those who give an empirical teaching it is written in the easily procured drugs, while those who wish to practise the art rationally have need of the Therapeutic Method. For, among other things, one would be harmed rather than benefited by such a report. Now Hippocrates, writing in the Aphorisms, 'pains of the eyes are resolved by drinking of unmixed wine, or a bath, or a vapour-bath, or venesection, or purging', yet not adding what kind of pains drinking of unmixed wine resolves, what kind a bath, which a vapour-bath, which venesection, which purging, one would pardon, I think, for three reasons. For he was giving an aphoristic teaching, in which, because of brevity, many things are allowed to be stated in this way; and he wrote down all the remedies of the pains, even if he did not distinguish which of them suits which kind of pain; or else in many places of his other writings he has given us starting-points for the distinctions in what was stated in this way. But those who have written about such aphorisms neither in other books nor in a detailed and long treatise, but write aphoristically and briefly, and besides this (εἴτε τὸ πρὸς τούτοις) indicate one thing out of many, harm us in more cases than they help. For since there are many differentiae among ophthalmias, and one of them requires the aforementioned poultice while the others are harmed by it, he who uses it on all of them without distinction will harm many more than he helps. In this manner, then, we must write not about southernwood alone but about all the others as well, the powers relating to heating and cooling or moistening or drying being found (εὑρίσκουσιν) by the methods I have often spoken of, but whatever is effected by the peculiarity of the whole substance by experience alone. It has been shown about such things too that they are deleterious, and protective against deleterious things, and purgative. For of these it is not possible to make a rational discovery; rather, it is only possible to find in some cases a certain plausible conjecture, and not indeed in all, just as this very point has been made clear in what precedes. But about the powers found in this way I shall give an account separately in what follows, once I have first gone through, for each species of drug, what concerns heating and cooling, moistening and drying, and whatever follows on these. Having added this much more about southernwood, however, I shall end the discussion: that the most admirable Pamphilus, although writing of this as his first herb, and having perhaps wished, if of none of the following, at least of this one to become an eyewitness, nevertheless erred most greatly, believing that the plant is called santonicum by the Romans. For southernwood differs from santonicum, as Dioscorides too wrote most accurately in the third book On Materials, and all physicians and dealers in small wares (ῥωποπῶλαι) know this at least. For of southernwood there are two species, one considered male, the other female, as this too has been distinguished by Dioscorides and Pamphilus and countless others. Different from it is wormwood, of which again one must posit species, and these threefold: of which one is called wormwood, homonymously with the genus, of which kind especially is the Pontic, another seriphon, another santonicum. But if one should say that wormwood is one thing, seriphon another, and santonicum another, it makes no difference for present purposes. For we have not come to divide a name, but are concerned with the things themselves. Since, then, these are clearly different from one another in form, in taste and in powers, let anyone, if he wishes, name them all by a single appellation, but let him teach their powers accurately. We said, then, that the forms have been described adequately by Dioscorides and not a few others, so that one need not write again what was correctly said by our predecessors. But if those men left anything undistinguished in the powers of this one, for the sake of which indeed I have come to this exposition (ἔξοδον), I shall try to add it. Wormwood is less hot than those mentioned, inasmuch as it partakes of the most astringency. And if it is also less fine-particled than those, it is then in the same way also less thinning than those, yet not less drying. Of the others, santonicum, which has its appellation from the Santonian country in which it grows, is nearest in power to seriphon, falling short by a little in thinning, heating and drying. Seriphon itself is less hot than southernwood but hotter than wormwood, and quite bad for the stomach, as presenting a certain saltiness together with bitterness, and it further partakes a little of acerbity. So too southernwood and santonicum are quite bad for the stomach. For among them wormwood alone, and especially the Pontic, is good for the stomach, because it partakes of the most astringency. Burnt southernwood is hot and dry in power, even more so than burnt dry gourd and dill root. For those suit ulcers that are moist and at the same time calloused without inflammation, and for this reason they seem to be especially in accord with those on the prepuce of the genitals. But the ash of southernwood is biting to all ulcers. And for this reason it suits alopeciae, with a fine-particled oil, namely castor oil or radish oil or Sicyonian or old oil, and especially the Sabine. It also calls forth beards that are slow to come up, with any one of the oils mentioned, and no less than with those when moistened with mastic oil. For it is rarefying, besides being fine-particled, biting and hot; and these are the powers of it that one must especially know, and needs nothing further of the particulars in this treatise.

[6.1.2] [2. On agnos or lygos.] Agnos or lygos, the shrubby plant, is hot and drying in about the third remove, and considerably fine-particled; and to the taste the agnos, or lygos, is pungent and at the same time astringent. Its withies (lygoi) themselves it has as useless for medical treatment, but the leaves and the seed are dry and hot in power and fine-particled in substance. For so they appear to those who use them, and to those who taste them the leaf, the flower and the fruit are pungent and at the same time slightly astringent. The fruit is also edible, and it plainly heats, while also being productive of headache. But if it is roasted (for it is eaten in this way too, along with dessert-nibbles), it affects the head less. And it is free of wind in the belly: the unroasted fruit is so, but the roasted still more. Both the roasted and the unroasted fruit also check the impulses towards sexual intercourse, and the leaves and the flowers of the shrub are able to do this same thing, so that they are believed to contribute to chastity not only when eaten and drunk, but also when strewn beneath one. This is why at the Thesmophoria in Athens the women strew the whole shrub beneath themselves, and from this too comes its name. From all of this it is clear, if we remember what was said in the preceding treatises, that agnos heats and at the same time dries, and is most free of wind. That its power is precisely fine-particled, there is evidence. For its affecting the head is reasonably ascribed not to a quantity of vaporous pneuma generated by it, but rather to heat and fineness of particles. For if it were productive of windy pneuma, it would both have inflated the belly and have roused the impulses towards sexual intercourse, as rocket does. But since it not only does not rouse them but is by nature such as to suppress them, it would be most nearly of the power of rue in heating and drying, though it is not equal to it; for it falls a little short in both respects, rue being both more heating and more drying than it. It differs also in the admixture of quality and power. For the seed and the shoots of agnos bring in, besides, a certain moderate astringency. Rue, on the other hand, when it is dry, is exactly bitter and pungent, and when it is moist, somewhat bitter. No harsh or acerbic quality, however, belongs to it; or if it should seem to anyone to belong to it, I know that it will seem altogether faint, and in no way equal to that of agnos. This is why for the liver and the spleen, when they are hardened and obstructed, the seed of agnos is more suitable than rue. But these matters already belong to the therapeutic method: it is impossible, when declaring the power of drugs, not to touch upon it at all, but to leave it quickly and return again to the matter proposed would be the work of a sensible man. Still more in the case of the drugs that follow I shall try to do this very thing, I mean, having inferred the general power from a few evident facts, to withdraw from the particular activities. For for present purposes it suffices to know only this: that agnos is hot and dry in power, not moderately, but in about the third of the removes, and considerably fine-particled. For whoever knows these things, and then learns in addition the therapeutic method, will himself discover how to move the menses by means of it, how to disperse hardened parts, and how to prepare an anti-fatigue (akopon) or heating unguent by means of it.

[6.1.3] [3. On agrōstis.] Of agrōstis, the root is moderately cold and dry, having a small degree of something biting and fine-particled. The herb cools at the first remove, but is moderate as regards moistness and dryness. The seed of the other kind is weak, but that of the kind on Parnassus is drying, fine-particled and slightly acerbic. Agrōstis has an edible root, as long as it is soft: it is sweet [and] watery, but has something pungent and a little slightly acerbic. The herb itself is entirely watery to those who taste it. From which it is clear that the root is moderately cold and dry, and for this reason is agglutinating of bloody wounds. The herb itself, applied as a poultice, cools, but not strongly, and stands in the middle between moistness and dryness. The biting and fine-particled element in the root is slight, but it is nonetheless sometimes wont also to break up stones, if one boils it down and drinks it. The seed of the other kind is weak, but that of the kind on Parnassus is diuretic and dries fluxes of the belly and stomach. For its power is drying, fine-particled and slightly acerbic.

[6.1.4] [4. On anchousa, and the four anchousai.] Of anchousa there are four kinds. Of these, onokleia has a root that cools and dries considerably, and is at once astringent and somewhat bitter, able to thin and to cleanse away the bilious humours and to condense bodies. Its leaves are weaker than the root, but they too are astringent and drying. The one called lykopsis also cools and dries, but has a root more astringent than that of onokleia. Onocheilos is hotter and more drug-like, for it has more of the pungent, which is evident to the taste at once. Hotter still than this is the one that is small, more bitter and more drug-like still. The anchousai are not all of the same power. The one called onokleia has a root at once astringent and somewhat bitter, able to condense bodies and moderately to thin, cleanse away and wash out the bilious and salty humours. For it was said earlier that the acerbic quality, mixed with the bitter, naturally produces these effects. In this way it is beneficial to those with jaundice, to splenetics and to nephritics. It is also able to cool, and applied as a poultice with barley-groats it helps erysipelas. It cleanses not only when drunk but also when applied externally, and for this reason it heals alphoi and leprai with vinegar. These are the effects of the root, and the powers behind those effects are those stated. The leaves of the plant are weaker than the root, but they are not without drying and astringency, so that, drunk with wine, they also heal diarrhoea. The one called lykopsis is likewise suited to cases of erysipelas, and has a root more astringent than that of onokleia. The power of onocheilos, also called Alkibiadeios, is more drug-like. At any rate it has more of the pungent, evident to the taste at once, and it is well suited to people bitten by vipers, whether applied as a poultice, hung on as an amulet or eaten. The remaining fourth, which is small and almost alone among them without a name, is close to the Alkibiadeios, but more bitter and still more drug-like. For this reason it is useful against flat worms, drunk in the quantity of an oxybaphon with hyssop and cress.

[6.1.5] [5. On the root of agaric.] The root of agaric, that is, the growth upon a tree-trunk, appears at the first taste somewhat sweet, but a little later somewhat bitter, and in time it brings on an impression of a certain pungency and of slight astringency. It is also loose in its consistency.
