From all of this it is quite clear, if we remember what was said in the preceding treatises, that the drug is compounded of an airy and earthy substance thinned by heat, and has very little share in the watery substance. It therefore has a dispersing and heating power, and one that is cutting of thickness; it clears out the obstructions in the viscera, and for this reason it heals those suffering from jaundice, that is, those who are ill in this way from obstruction of the parts about the liver. By the same power it also benefits epileptics, and it heals periodic rigors as well, those that are the offspring of thick or viscid juices. It also helps those bitten or stung by wild creatures that do harm by chilling, both when it is applied externally on the affected part and when it is taken into the body in the weight of one drachm with mixed wine. It is also purgative.

[6.1.6] [6. On agēraton.] Agēraton is of a power that is dispersing and also, in a gentle sort of way, anti-inflammatory. [6.1.7] [7. On adiantum.] Adiantum is moderate as regards heat and cold, but it dries, thins and disperses. For it makes alopeciae grow hair again, disperses choirades and abscessions, breaks up stones when drunk, contributes not a little to the bringing up of viscous and thick humours from the chest and lung, and stops a flux of the belly. Yet it does not impart any manifest heat, just as it does not impart any manifest cooling either. Rather, one might place it in the middle rank with respect to the opposition and mixture of these qualities.

[6.1.8] [8. On aeizoon.] Each kind of aeizoon, both the small and the large, dries to a slight degree, because it is also moderately astringent, while being free of every other strong quality, so that in it the watery substance rather predominates; but it cools to no moderate degree. For it belongs to the third remove and order of cooling things. For this reason it is suitable for erysipelas, and also for herpēs and for the inflammations that arise from fluxes.

[6.1.9] [9. On aigilops.] Aigilops has a dispersing power. This is clear from the taste, for it is in some way gently pungent. It is clear not only from that, however, but also from its healing inflammations that are becoming hard, and aigilopes.

[6.1.10] [10. On darnel (aira).] Darnel dries and heats effectively, so that it is close to the pungent [drugs], and more so to iris. It is not, however, as fine-particled as that [drug], but falls short of it by a good deal in this respect; and one might place it at the beginning of the third order of heating [drugs], but at the end of the second [order] of drying [drugs].

[6.1.11] [11. On the black poplar.] The flowers of the black poplar are hot in power, at the first remove from the well-tempered; and in the distinction concerning drying and moistening they have departed a little from the well-tempered and median things towards the drier. It is also fine-particled rather than coarse-particled. And its leaves are in some way similar to the flowers, except that they are altogether weaker and less efficacious; and its resin too is similar to the flowers in power, and hotter still. The seed is more fine-particled and more drying than the resin and the flowers, but not very much hotter.

[6.1.12] [12. On acacia.] Of acacia, both the plant itself is acerbic, and so are the fruit and the juice; the juice, when washed, becomes at the same time weaker and less biting, as though it laid aside some pungency in the washing. And if it is smeared on some healthy part, it at once renders this drier and drawn tight, and it never produces any sensation of heating, but a cooling that is not very strong. It is clear, then, that the drug is cold and earthy, with some watery substance also mixed into it. One might conjecture that it is not even uniform in its parts, but has certain particles dispersed through it that are fine-particled and hot, and that these depart in the washing. And let this drug too be placed in the third order of drying things and in the second of cooling things once it has been washed, and the unwashed in the first.

[6.1.13] [13. On nettle.] Nettle. Of this herb too both the fruit and the leaves (for it is these that chiefly come into use) are of a sufficiently dispersing power, so that they heal both phymata and parotid swellings. It also has something flatulent, by which it also stirs up urges to sexual intercourse, and especially when the seed is drunk with sweet wine. That it does not heat strongly, but is sufficiently fine-particled, is attested both by the bringing up of the thick and viscous humours in the thorax and lung and by the itching of those parts of the body which it touches. The windy quality, in which it has been said to share, is generated when it is digested; for it is not windy in actuality, but in potentiality. It moves the bowel moderately solely by cleansing and, as it were, tickling, not by purging. And it fittingly heals gangrenous and cancerous lesions and in general whatever needs to be dried without being bitten, being fine-particled and dry in its mixture, yet not sharing in heat to such a degree as already to bite.
[6.1.14] [14. On acanthus.] Acanthus. Some call it melamphyllon, others paiderōs. Its leaves have a moderately dispersing power, while the root is drying and gently cutting, and fine-particled.

[6.1.15] [15. On akanthion.] Akanthion. Its root and its leaves are of a fine-particled and hot power, so that they also help those who suffer spasms. [6.1.16] [16. On the white thorn.] White thorn. Some call this leukakanthos. Its root is drying and moderately astringent, which is why it benefits coeliacs and stomachics, checks discharges of blood, and, applied as a plaster, contracts oedemas; it also benefits aching teeth, if the mouth is rinsed with the decoction. The seed is of a fine-particled and hot power, so that, when drunk, it is also suitable for those who suffer spasms.

[6.1.17] [17. On the Egyptian acanthus.] Egyptian acanthus: some call it Arabian. It also resembles the white acanthus found in our parts, but it is more astringent and more drying in its power, so that its root even benefits female flux. And for all the other things for which ours is used, both the root and its fruit help more powerfully. This [fruit] also [helps] the swellings (ἐμφυσώμενα) at the uvula and at the seat, and it brings ulcers to a scar, since it has a moderate and not unpleasant astringency.

[6.1.18] [18. On akoron.] Akoron. We use its root, which is pungent and moderately bitterish to the taste, but not unpleasant in smell. From this it is clear that it is hot in its power and fine-particled in its consistency. Its provoking urine and benefiting scirrhous spleens also agree with this, as does its cleansing and thinning the thickenings of the horn-like coat [of the eye]. Its juice is better for this purpose. It is clear that it is certainly drying. So let it be placed in the third order in both respects, in heating and in drying.

[6.1.19] [19. On aconite or pardalianches.] Aconite or pardalianches. This is of a putrefying and deleterious power, whence one must beware of taking it in food or in drink. For causing something to putrefy away from the body, however, or at the seat, it is suitable. The root of the herb is useful for these purposes.

[6.1.20] [20. On aconite or lykoktonon.] Aconite or lykoktonon ('wolf-killer'). This too is of a power similar to the other, but more particularly it is by nature apt to destroy wolves, just as that one destroys leopards. [6.1.21] [21. On elder and dwarf elder.] Elder (aktē), both the large and tree-like kind and the more herbaceous one, which they also call chamaiaktē ('dwarf elder'): both are of a drying power, agglutinating and moderately dispersing.

[6.1.22] [22. On halimon.] Halimon. This plant is a shrub, growing in greatest abundance above all in Cilicia, where people also eat its shoots, both fresh and laying them up in store for keeping. The plant is also generative of seed and of milk, and to the taste it is salty and has a slight astringency. From all of which it is clear that it is of dissimilar parts, but that the greater part of its substance is temperately warm, together with a moisture that is unconcocted and gently flatulent.

[6.1.23] [23. On aloe.] Aloe. This herb does not grow much at all in our country, and the kind that grows in Great Syria is more watery and weaker in its power. Nevertheless it is naturally so drying that it agglutinates wounds. In the hotter regions, among which are Coele Syria and Arabia, it is much better. Best of all is the one in India, whose juice is this drug brought here and called aloe, which is of very great use because it dries without biting. It is not of a simple nature. As the taste also testifies, it is at once astringent and bitter: it is moderately astringent, but strongly bitter. It also loosens the bowel, being one of the drugs called eccoprotic. So from what has been said it is clear, if we remember anything of what was shown in the fourth book, that among drying drugs it is of the third order, and among heating drugs either of the first order intensified or of the second relaxed. Its particular effects also bear witness to the mixed character of its power. For the drug is good for the stomach, if anything is, and agglutinating of sinuses. It heals ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, especially those at the seat and the genitals. Dissolved in water, it also benefits their inflammations, and it agglutinates wounds in the same way. It is likewise suitable, for one who uses it in the same manner, against inflammations in the mouth, nose and eyes. In general it is naturally both repelling and dispersing at once, and also cleansing to a slight degree, so far as is harmless to clean ulcers.

[6.1.24] [24. On alysson.] Alysson. The herb has been named alysson because it wonderfully benefits those who have been bitten by a rabid dog. Indeed, when given even to someone already rabid, it has often cured him completely. This it is able to do from the similarity of its whole substance; and it has been said before that such a power is grasped from experience alone and is entirely without method. But if one should also use it for many purposes, one will recognise that it is of a moderately drying and dispersing power, in addition to having something cleansing as well. It is in this way, at any rate, that it also clears away alphoi and ephelis.

[6.1.25] [25. On alsine.] Alsine, or mouse's ears. This plant too has a power similar to that of helxine, cooling and moistening. For it is of a watery, cold substance, and therefore it cools even without astringency. Accordingly it is suited to seething inflammations and to moderate erysipelas.
[6.1.26] [26. On amarakon.] Amarakon heats not feebly, but dries not vehemently. Rather, in its heat it is of the third order, and in drying of the second.

[6.1.27] [27. On ambrosia.] Ambrosia, applied as a plaster, has an astringent and repelling power. [6.1.28] [28. On ammi.] Ammi. Of the herb which they call ammi, the seed is the most useful part; it is of a heating, drying and fine-particled power. To those who taste it, it is also somewhat bitter and pungent, and it is clear that it is also diuretic and dispersing. It would follow that it both heats and dries in the third order, at its intensified end.

[6.1.29] [29. On amaranth.] Amaranth is of a cutting and thinning power. Accordingly its head [kómē], drunk with wine, brings on the menses, and it is believed to dissolve clots of blood themselves, not only those in the belly but also those in the bladder. In that case, however, one should rather drink it with honeyed wine [oinomeli]. And, when drunk, it is simply drying of all fluxes, though it is bad for the stomach.

[6.1.30] [30. On amurca.] Amurca is of an earthy, hot substance, yet it does not partake of heat to such a degree as to bite perceptibly. And if it is also boiled, it becomes still much more coarse-particled and dry. And it would belong to the second order of things that heat and dry, somewhat intensified. Thus indeed it heals the ulcers of bodies that are dry in their mixture, but in all others it exacerbates them. For it is tightening, like resin, dry pitch and asphalt, which themselves too are agglutinating for very hard bodies that have either a wound or sinuses, but all other bodies they both tighten and exacerbate.

[6.1.31] [31. On ampeloprason.] Ampeloprason: if you were to conceive of something intermediate between garlic and leek, you would find the power of ampeloprason. For it is, as one might say, a wild leek, whence it is also more pungent and drier than it, just as all other wild plants are than the cultivated ones; and for this reason it is both worse for the stomach and more cutting of thick and viscous humours, and more unblocking of obstructed organs. In this way, indeed, it has often set in motion both urine and menses, when they are held back by a thick and viscous humour. It is so hot that, applied as a poultice, it can already ulcerate. It was said earlier that all things which are hot in this way belong to the last order.

[6.1.32] [32. On the wild vine.] The clusters of the wild vine are of a cleansing power, so that they treat ephelides and spots and all such things as arise on the surface of the skin. They also have something astringent, both they themselves and the shoots, which are in fact pickled.

[6.1.33] [33. On the cultivated vine.] The power of the cultivated vine is similar to that of the wild vine, but weaker in every respect. [6.1.34] [34. On the white vine.] Of the white vine, which they call bryōnia and psilōthron, the first shoots are customarily eaten by everyone in spring as a food good for the stomach because they are astringent; their astringency is also somewhat bitter and mildly pungent, and for this reason they also provoke urination moderately. The root has a cleansing, drying and fine-particled power, and is moderately hot. For this reason it also melts down spleens that are becoming scirrhous; and, both when drunk and when applied externally with figs, it also heals psora and lepra. Its fruit, which grows in grape-like clusters, is useful to tanners.

[6.1.35] [35. On the black vine.] Black vine. This is the one properly called bryōnia; it is similar in all respects to the one mentioned before, except that it is weaker. [6.1.36] [36. On almonds.] Almonds. The bitter ones are manifestly of an entirely thinning power, both to one who infers from their quality and to one who judges by experience. Now, the bitter quality has been discussed in the fourth of these commentaries. Of the evidence from experience, it is enough to bring forward these two instances and to learn from these very things about their power. They clean away freckles, and they contribute considerably to the bringing up, from the thorax and lung, of viscid and thick humours. These effects were shown by us to belong, by genus, to the thinning power, and, by species, to the cleansing power. Moreover, that they would also be of an unblocking power, by accident, has likewise been demonstrated earlier. But experience bears witness too: at any rate they thoroughly clear out the impactions of thick and viscid humours at the extremities of the vessels in the liver. Moreover, they also cure pains of the sides that arise from a cause of this kind, and those in the spleen, colon and kidneys. The whole tree itself has a similar power, so that people also clean away freckles by sprinkling on its roots, boiled. As for the sweet almonds, these too share in a slight bitterness, but because the sweetness prevails it is hidden, and it becomes plainly evident when they have been kept a long time. It has been demonstrated earlier that the sweet quality is moderately hot.

[6.1.37] [37. On ammoniakon.] Ammoniakon is the sap of a certain narthex. It is of an intensified softening power, so that it both dissolves the pōroi (callous concretions) around the joints, heals spleens that have become scirrhous, and disperses choirades.

[6.1.38] [38. On amomon.] Amomon resembles akoron in its power, except that akoron is drier, while amomon is more concocting. [6.1.39] [39. On anagallis.] Both kinds of anagallis, the one with the dark-blue flower and the one with the crimson, are of a markedly cleansing power, and they also have something somewhat warm and drawing, so that they even draw out splinters. Their juice purges through the nostrils for the same reason. To speak generally, they have a drying power that does not bite, and for this reason they also agglutinate wounds and help putrefying parts.

[6.1.40] [40. On anagyros.] Anagyros is a shrub, ill-smelling and pungent, of a dispersing and heating power. But the green leaves, being less pungent because of the admixture of moisture, are repressive of swellings, whereas when dried they are of a strongly cutting and drying power. The bark of their root is also of a somewhat similar nature. The seed is of a still more fine-particled [power], but it is also emetic.

[6.1.41] [41. On androsaemon.] Androsaemon is a shrubby plant of twofold nature: the one kind is named ascyron or ascyroides, being a species of hypericum; the other is the one named by some dionysias. Their fruit is purgative, while the power of the leaves is drying and moderately cleansing, so that they are also believed to heal burns. Boiled down in harsh wine, they render the wine agglutinating of large wounds.
[6.1.42] [42. On androsaces.] Androsaces is a bitter and pungent herb. When dried and drunk, both it and its fruit are able to provoke urine powerfully, and evidently also to disperse and to dry.

[6.1.43] [43. On purslane.] Purslane is cold and watery in its mixture, but it partakes of a small amount of something harsh. For this reason it both repels fluxes, especially bilious and hot ones, and, besides changing them and altering them in their quality, it cools sufficiently. It would be, in the power of cooling, of the third remove from the well-proportioned and median, and in that of moistening, of the second. For these reasons it benefits those suffering from ardent fever as much as anything else, when applied over the mouth of the stomach and the whole of the hypochondria, and especially in hectic fevers. It is also a remedy for teeth set on edge (haimōdia), itself swiftly smoothing and filling up [the parts] dried out by contact with the acid juices, because it has a viscous moisture. Its juice likewise, so that it cools not only when applied externally but also when drunk. This indeed also belongs to the plant itself when eaten whole. Because it is slightly astringent it is also a suitable food for dysenterics, and for the female flux and for bringings-up of blood. For these purposes, however, the juice is much more efficacious than the herb itself.

[6.1.44] [44. On anemone.] All anemones are of a pungent and cleansing power, and also of an attractive and anastomotic one. Hence the root, when chewed, calls forth phlegm, and the juice purges through the nostrils and thins scars in the eyes. The anemones also cleanse the foul among ulcers and remove leprai, and when applied as a pessary they call forth the menses, and they draw up milk.

[6.1.45] [45. On dill.] Dill heats to such a degree that one may take it to be either of the second order at its intensified end or of the third at its relaxed end. Among drying agents it is of the second order at its beginning, or of the first at its intensified end, so that, as one would expect, when boiled in oil it is dispersing, anodyne, sleep-inducing, and concoctive of raw and unconcocted swellings. For the oil made from it comes close in mixture to the drugs called pus-producing and concoctive, except that it is slightly hotter than these and fine-particled, and for this reason also dispersing. When burnt, it becomes of the third order of heating and drying agents, and for this reason, applied as a plaster, it benefits flabby ulcers, and especially those on the genitals. And the chronic ones on the prepuce it also cicatrises well. The dill that is still green and full of juice is, clearly, moister and less hot, so that it will be more concoctive and more sleep-inducing than the dry, but less dispersing. For this reason, it seems to me, the ancients too used garlands made of it at symposia.

[6.1.46] [46. On anthyllis.] Anthyllis is twofold, and both kinds dry moderately, so as even to agglutinate wounds. One of them, the one resembling chamaepitys, is somewhat more fine-particled than the other, so that it is also suited to epileptics. It is also more cleansing than the other.

[6.1.47] [47. On anthemis.] Anthemis, or chamomile. This herb has already been discussed at greater length in the third book; but it will now also be stated in summary that it dries and heats in the first order. It is also fine-particled, and for these reasons it is dispersing, rarefying and relaxing in its power.

[6.1.48] [48. On anise.] Of anise it is the seed that is chiefly useful. It is pungent and somewhat bitter, so that in heat it comes close to the caustic drugs. In drying it is of the third remove, just as it is also in heating. For this reason it is both diuretic and dispersing, and it settles inflations in the belly.

[6.1.49] [49. On antirrhinon.] Antirrhion (sic) or anarrhinon has its fruit like the nostrils of a calf; it is useless for cures. The plant itself is of a power closely similar to that of bubonion, but much weaker, so that from what was said about that you will learn about this one as well.

[6.1.50] [50. On aparine.] Aparine, which some call philanthrōpon and others omphakokarpon, is moderately cleansing and drying. It also has something fine-particled about it. [6.1.51] [51. On the pear.] Of the pear tree the leaves and the shoots are harsh, while the fruit also has something of a watery sweetness. From these it is clear that its mixture too is uneven in its parts: in one part it has something earthy, in another something watery, and in each of these, partly something cold and partly something well-tempered. For this reason, when eaten, they are good for the stomach and allay thirst; and when applied as a plaster they both dry and moderately cool, as I myself know, having agglutinated a wound with them when no other drug was at hand.

[6.1.52] [52. On wild pears.] The so-called wild pears (achrades) are both more astringent than the other pears and more drying; and for this reason, evidently, they also agglutinate larger wounds and turn back fluxes.

[6.1.53] [53. On apocynon.] Apocynon, or cynocrambe. Some also call it cynomoron, because it kills dogs very quickly, just as lycoctonon kills wolves. It is also a poison to human beings, a quite ill-smelling herb; for this reason it is certainly hot, and to no small degree, though not, however, correspondingly dry. On this account, then, when applied as a cataplasm it is of a strongly dispersing power.

[6.1.54] [54. On argemone.] Argemone. The power of this herb too is cleansing and dispersing. [6.1.55] [55. On arisaron.] Arisaron. This is both much smaller than aron, and has a root the size of an olive. But it is much more pungent than it.

[6.1.56] [56. On aristolochia.] The root of aristolochia is most useful for cures, being bitter and somewhat pungent. Of its kinds, the round one is more fine-particled and in every respect more active. Of the other two, the clematitis is more fragrant, so that the perfumers even use it for their perfumes, but it is weaker for cures. The long one is less fine-particled than the round, yet it is not itself inactive either: it is of a cleansing and heating power. It cleanses and disperses less than the round, but it heats no less, and perhaps even more. Hence in cases where there is need of moderate cleansing the long one is more useful, as in the filling-up of ulcers with flesh and in fomentations of the womb. But in cases where a thick humour must be thinned more strongly, there is need of the round one. For this reason the round one also treats better the pains that arise from obstruction or from some thickness of unconcocted pneumata. It draws out splinters, heals putrefactions, cleans foul ulcers, and brightens the teeth and gums. Drunk with water, it also helps the asthmatic and those with hiccups, epileptics and gouty patients; and it is suited to ruptures and strains if any other drug is.

[6.1.57] [57. On juniper.] Juniper is hot and dry, of the third order in both respects. Its fruit is hot to the same degree, but it does not dry to the same degree; rather, in this respect it would be of the first order.

[6.1.58] [58. On arktion.] Arktion — the one resembling phlomos, which has a tender, white and sweet root, a long and soft stem, and a fruit like cumin — is of a quite fine-particled power, and for this very reason drying, and also moderately cleansing. Hence both its root and its fruit, decocted with wine, somewhat soothe pains of the teeth. And for burns and chilblains not only the decoction of these, poured over, but also the shoots are remedies.

[6.1.59] [59. On the other arktion.] The other arktion, which they also call prosōpis, whose leaves are very closely similar to those of the gourd, except in so far as they are larger and harder, is dispersing and drying. It also has something astringent in moderate degree; for this reason its leaves too are healing of old ulcers.

[6.1.60] [60. On plantain.] Plantain (arnoglosson). This too is of a mixed mixture. For it has something watery and cold, and it also has something harsh, which is earthy, dry and cold. So it cools and dries at the same time, and in both respects it is of the second remove from the median. All drugs that are dry together with cooling are suited to malignant ulcers, to fluxes and to putrefactions. On this account they are also suited to dysenteries, for they stop haemorrhages and, if anything is burning hot, they cool it; and they are agglutinating of sinuses and of the other ulcers, fresh and old alike. In nearly all such drugs plantain is either first or second to none in the due proportion of its mixture. For it partakes of a dryness that does not bite and of a coldness not yet numbing. Its fruit and its roots are also of a similar power, except that their power is drier and less cold. But the fruit is more fine-particled, and the roots more coarse-particled. The leaves of the herb themselves, when dried, also come to be of a more fine-particled and less cold power, since the watery residue has breathed out of them and been dispersed. For this reason people use the roots against toothaches as well, chewed and boiled in their mouthwashes. Against obstructions in the liver and kidneys they use these too, but also the leaves, and much more still the fruit. For all of these partake of a certain cleansing power, which is likely to be present in the green herb as well, but to be overcome by the quantity of its moisture.

[6.1.61] [61. On aron.] Aron. This too is composed of an earthy, hot substance, and for this reason it is of a cleansing power, though not a strong one, as dracontium is. It is therefore, in drying and in heating, of the first order in both respects. Its roots are the most useful part. And indeed, when eaten, they cut the thickness of humours moderately, so that they are also suitable for expectorations from the thorax. But dracontium is more suitable for these purposes.

[6.1.62] [62. On artemisia.] Artemisia. The herb artemisia too is twofold. Both kinds heat and dry moderately, and let them be placed, in heating, at the second remove, and in drying either at the intensified first or the beginning of the second. They are also moderately fine-particled, so that they are moderately suited both against stones in the kidneys and for fomentations of the uterus.

[6.1.63] [63. On asaron.] Asaron. The roots of this herb are useful, being close to those of akoron in their power, but more intense, so that from what has been said before about that one, one must also recognise the facts about this one.

[6.1.64] [64. On asklēpias.] Asklēpias. Dioscorides wrote about this herb in his third [book]. We, however, have as yet had no experience of it. [6.1.65] [65. On aspalathos.] Aspalathos is both pungent and at the same time astringent in taste, and in its power it is evidently composed of dissimilar parts (ἐξ ἀνομοιομερῶν), heating by those of its parts that are pungent and cooling by its other parts, the harsh ones, so that it dries in both respects and cools; and for this reason it is useful against putrefactions and fluxes.

[6.1.66] [66. On asparagus.] Asparagus, the rock kind or the mouse-thorn kind, is of a cleansing power; it does not, however, perceptibly either heat or cool. For this reason it is also unblocking of the kidneys and the liver, and especially the roots of the plant and its seed. And indeed it also heals toothaches by drying, which is precisely what the teeth most need. The Athenians say it with a phi: aspharagos.

[6.1.67] [67. On asplenon.] Asplenon. The herb is fine-particled, but certainly not hot in power. For this reason it both breaks up stones and melts away spleens. [6.1.68] [68. On astragalus.] Astragalus is a small shrublet having astringent roots, and therefore it is also among the drying drugs to no mean degree. At any rate it cicatrises old ulcers and stops a belly suffering from flux, if one boils the root down in wine and drinks it. The shrub grows in greatest abundance at Pheneus in Arcadia.

[6.1.69] [69. On the Attic aster.] Attic aster. Some call it bubonion, because it is believed to heal buboes not only when applied as a plaster but also when hung around the body as an amulet. It has something dispersing about it, but no less something cooling and repelling as well, so that it is of a mixed power, as is the rose too; this one, however, is not astringent.

[6.1.70] [70. On astaphis.] Astaphis: the cultivated kind shares at once in a concoctive, an astringent and a gently dispersing power. The wild kind shares strongly in a pungent one, so as both to draw off phlegm and to cleanse vigorously, so that it is also suitable for psora. It also shares in a certain caustic power.

[6.1.71] [71. On asphodel.] Asphodel. Of this too the root is useful, as with aron, asaron and dracontium, being of a cleansing and dispersing power. When it is burned, its ash becomes hotter, more drying, more fine-particled and more dispersing, and for this reason it also heals alopeciae.

[6.1.72] [72. On atractylis.] Atractylis, or wild cnicus, is one of the thorny plants. This plant is of a drying and moderately hot power. [6.1.73] [73. On atraphaxis.] Atraphaxis is moist and cold in its mixture: moist in the second order from the middle ones, and cold in the first, which we said is indeed a lukewarm warmth, such as also belongs to roses, except that it does not share in astringency. Rather, it is watery and least of all earthy, like the mallow, and indeed it also passes quickly through the belly, as that one does, on account of its viscosity. It has some quite small dispersing element. The cultivated mallows and atraphaxeis are much moister and colder than the wild ones. For this reason, for inflammations and phygethla that are beginning and increasing, and are still soft and as it were boiling, the cultivated ones are more suitable, but for those at their peak and declining and becoming hard, the wild ones. Its fruit is of a cleansing power, and so it is also useful for jaundices that follow upon obstructions of the liver.

[6.1.74] [74. On aphakē.] Aphakē is of an astringent power, just as the lentil also is. Moreover, it is eaten in the same way as lentils. It is harder to digest than they are, but it dries more strongly, and it partakes of a moderate heat.

[6.1.75] [75. On wormwood.] Wormwood possesses an astringent, a bitter and a pungent quality at once, and it is at the same time heating, cleansing, toning and drying. For this reason it both draws off the bilious humours in the stomach towards evacuation below and empties them through the urine. Still more does it purge out through the urine what is bilious in the veins. For these reasons too, when administered, it is of no benefit for phlegms contained in the stomach, and likewise if they should happen to be in the thorax and lung. For the astringent power in it is stronger than the bitter. But because it also has a share of a certain pungency, it is hot in greater measure than cold. If one should need, comprehending its mixture in general terms, to define it according to the primary powers, even though it is non-uniform (anhomoiomerous), we would say that it is hot of the first remove and dry of the third. Its juice is much hotter than the herb.

[6.2.1] [1. On the perfumers' balanos.] The perfumers' balanos is brought from the barbarian country, and the perfumers use the juice of its flesh, which is hot in power. The remaining pressed residue (apothlimma), which is earthy and hard, has the bitter quality predominant. But something of astringency is also mixed in it, and for this reason it has an activity that is at once cleansing and cutting, and also contracting and condensing, so that it is suited to ionthoi, phakoi, ephelis and itching, and indeed also to psora and lepra; moreover it also melts spleens and a liver that is becoming scirrhous. If someone drinks a drachm's weight of the flesh itself with melikraton, he will experience the drug as an emetic. Often it also purges copiously through the lower belly. Hence, when we use the drug for the purpose of thoroughly cleansing one of the viscera, and especially the liver or the spleen, we give it with oxykraton. For its other, external activities too it does best with vinegar. For in this way it becomes so active as to cleanse away psora and lepra, and much more still the lesser of these conditions: phakoi, alphoi, ionthoi, ephelis, achores, and all eruptions that are ulcerous and of thick humours. It also brightens scars. That, when applying it as a cataplasm to the spleen, it is better to mix in some one of the drying meals, such as bitter-vetch meal and darnel meal, would belong rather to the treatise on the composition of drugs, not to the present one; but it will also be stated in the work on easily procured remedies. For the present it is enough to have said that the power of the aforementioned drug is cleansing and cutting together with a certain astringency, and to pass on to another. Its bark, however, is very astringent, so that one could use this too for all those purposes for which there is need of strong astringency.

[6.2.2] [2. On balsam.] Balsam dries and heats in the second remove. It is also fine-particled, so as to be aromatic. Its sap is of a more fine-particled power than even the plant itself, yet it is not hot to so great an extent as some suppose, deceived by its fine-particledness. Its fruit is of a power similar in kind, but falls far short in fine-particledness.

[6.2.3] [3. On balaustion.] Balaustion is the flower of the wild pomegranate, just as the kytinos is the flower of the cultivated ones. It is strongly astringent to the taste. And indeed it is of a drying and astringent power, and clearly also coarse-particled, if we remember anything of what was said in the fourth of these commentaries, when we showed that everything astringent is earthy and cold. It gives no indication of any other quality, and for this reason one might posit that it dries and cools to no mean degree, if indeed it was not wrongly shown by us in the fourth of these commentaries that the astringent quality belongs to earthy cold bodies. Moreover, the phenomena also bear witness. For if you sprinkle it on abrasions and on other ulcers, you would see them going very quickly to a scar. For this reason, too, in the case of dysenterics who bring up blood, and further in fluxes of the belly and the womb, there is no one among the physicians who have written therapeutic treatises who does not use this drug.

[6.2.4] [4. On bramble.] The leaves of the bramble, and likewise its shoots, flower, fruit and root, partake of an astringent quality, and not indistinctly. But they differ from one another in this: the leaves, especially the soft and young ones, partake of a very large amount of water and are slightly astringent. By the same reasoning the shoots are too, so that when chewed they heal aphthae and the other ulcers in the mouth, and they are also able to conglutinate other wounds. For their mixture is made of a cold earthy substance and a lukewarm watery one. The fruit, if it is ripe, also partakes in no small measure of a moderately warm juice, which is sweet, as we have shown. So on account of this and of its moderate astringency it is not unpleasant to eat. The unripe fruit is dominated by cold earthy substance, and for this reason it is acerbic and strongly drying. Indeed each of the two is also stored away dried, being more drying than the fresh. The flower too is of the same power as the unripe fruit: they are drugs suitable for dysenteries, fluxes of the belly, atonies, and spittings of blood. The root, besides being astringent, has also received no small amount of fine-particled substance, and because of this it also breaks up the stones in the kidneys.

[6.2.5] [5. On batrachion.] Batrachion has four differences according to species. All of them are of a strongly pungent power, so as to ulcerate with pain. For this reason, when one uses it in due measure, it strips off psorai and leprai, detaches leprous nails, disperses tattoo-marks, and removes acrochordones and myrmeciae. Moreover, it also benefits alopeciae when applied for a short time; for if it is left on for a long time, the skin is not only flayed but also forms an eschar. All these, then, are the works of the stem and the leaves applied green as a plaster. The root, when dried, is a sternutatory drug, like all the other things that dry strongly. It also benefits pains of the teeth, though at the same time it shatters them, evidently by drying strongly. And, to put it briefly, both the root and the whole herb are vehemently hot and dry.

[6.2.6] [6. On bdellium.] Of bdellium, the kind called Scythian, which is blacker and more resinous, is of a quite softening and active power. The other, the Arabian, which is more translucent, dries more than the softening [drugs] do. Whatever of it is fresh is also moist and softens easily when pounded, and it is suitable for all the same purposes as the Scythian. But whatever is older, quite bitter to the taste, pungent and dry, has already fallen away from the due proportion (symmetria) of the [drugs] that soften parts becoming scirrhous. Some people use them, and especially the Arabian, for bronchoceles and hydroceles, moistening them with fasting spittle so that they have a plaster-like consistency. The Arabian, when drunk, also seems to break up stones in the kidneys, to promote urine, to cure the coursings of unconcocted pneumata, and pains of the sides and ruptures.

[6.2.7] [7. On bēchion.] Bēchion has been so named from its being believed to benefit coughs and orthopnoeas, if one takes either the leaves dry, or the root, burns it as a fumigation over coals, and inhales the sooty smoke that rises. It is moderately pungent, so that it is even believed to rupture painlessly all the abscessions in the thorax. The green leaves, applied externally as a poultice, also benefit inflamed parts that are slow to concoct, on account of the admixture of watery moisture, in which all green and tender things share, some more, some less. For the leaves of bēchion that are already dry are of a more pungent power than suits inflamed parts.

[6.2.8] [8. On blite.] Blite is an edible vegetable, moist and cold in its mixture, at most in the second remove from the well-mixed. [6.2.9] [9. On the cultivated bulb.] The bulb, when eaten, is colder and thicker, and generative of viscid humour. For it is hard to digest, flatulent and aphrodisiac. When applied as a plaster, however, because it partakes of bitterness and astringency at the same time, it becomes astringent and agglutinating, and evidently drying. For it was shown that bitterness is found in cleansing substances and astringency in agglutinating ones, while dryness has accompanied both.

[6.2.10] [10. On the emetic bulb.] The emetic bulb is much hotter than the mixture of the bulb mentioned before. [6.2.11] [11. On bubonion.] Bubonion, or Attic aster, has been named from its being believed to heal buboes when applied as a plaster and when tied on as an amulet. It is of a moderately dispersing power, since it is both moderately hot and dries not vehemently nor intensely, and especially when it is still soft and young.

[6.2.12] [12. On bugloss.] Bugloss is moist and hot in its mixture; hence it is also believed, when put into wines, to be a cause of good cheer. It is also suitable, boiled down in honey-water, for those who cough on account of roughness of the pharynx.

[6.2.13] [13. On bunion.] Bunion, which some call arktikon, is among the warming drugs, to such a degree that it is both diuretic and a promoter of the menses. And pseudobunion too is warm in a manner closely similar to it.

[6.2.14] [14. On bouphthalmon.] Bouphthalmon is so named from its flowers, which seem to resemble an ox's eye in shape; and moreover in colour they are very closely similar to those of anthemis. But they are larger than these by a good deal, and more pungent, and for this reason also more dispersing, to the point that, mixed with a cerate, they even heal indurations.

[6.2.15] [15. On brathy.] Brathy is one of the things that dry strongly, at least with respect to the three qualities which it also makes evident to the taste, much like cypress, except that it is more pungent than cypress and, as one might say, more aromatic. It therefore shares in this very quality I have just named, the pungent, which arises from a hot mixture, and further in bitterness and in an astringency fainter than that in cypress. For in so far as it exceeds cypress in pungency, it is for this reason also more dispersing. It cannot, then, glue [wounds] together, because of the strength of its dryness and heat. For it has partaken of both of these to such an extent as already to be tightening and fiery. For putrefactions, however, it is suited in the same way as cypress, and especially for those that are more malignant and more chronic, for these bear the strength of the drug without distress. And so, with honey, it also cleans out things that have become blackened and those that are very foul, and it detaches carbuncles. Because of its fineness of particles it is a promoter of the menses, if anything else is, and it moves blood through the urine, and it destroys living embryos and expels dead ones. Let this drug too, then, be placed in the third of the removes with respect to both heating and drying, being among the most fine-particled things. That is why it is both mixed into unguents, especially the gleucinum, and put into a great many antidotes. Some also put it in, in double quantity, in place of cinnamon, for it is of a thinning and dispersing power, should one want this.

[6.2.16] [16. On britannikē.] The leaves of the herb britannikē are astringent and agglutinating of wounds; they are like those of the wild docks, except in so far as they appear darker and more hairy. The juice from them is likewise astringent, so that some people even boil it down and store it as the most efficacious of the drugs for the mouth. For it seems to heal even things that are already putrefying.

[6.2.17] [17. On bromos (oats).] Bromos is one of the pulses, but as a drug it has a power similar to barley. For when applied as a poultice it dries and disperses, both moderately and without biting. It is also slightly colder in its mixture, and has something of astringency as well, so that it also benefits diarrhoeas of the belly.

[6.2.18] [18. On bryon.] Sea bryon is composed of an earthy and at the same time a watery substance, both of them cold. For it is astringent when tasted, and when applied as a poultice it manifestly cools and benefits all things that are hot.

[6.2.19] [19. On bryon, or also splanchnon.] Bryon, which some call splanchnon. It is found on oaks, pines and white poplars. It also has an astringent power, though not a strong one. For it is not sufficiently cold either, but is somehow close to the intermediate ones, since it also partakes of a dispersing and softening power, and especially that which is found on cedar wood.

[6.3.1] [1. On galion.] Galion has been named from its curdling (πηγνύναι) milk (γάλα). It is similar to aparinē, having a drying and somewhat acrid power. Its flower is thought to be suitable for haemorrhages and to heal burns. It is fragrant and quince-yellow in colour.

[6.3.2] [2. On gentian.] Gentian. The root of this herb is quite efficacious wherever there is need to thin, to cleanse thoroughly, to wash away and to clear obstructions; and it is nothing to wonder at that it can do these things, since it is exceedingly bitter.

[6.3.3] [3. On grape-stones.] Grape-stones are dry in the second order and cold in the first. Their substance is coarse-particled and earthy, as is shown by the taste, for they appear acerbic; and experience teaches it too, for they are well suited to all the fluxional affections of the belly.

[6.3.4] [4. On gingidion.] Gingidion, just as in taste it partakes of both bitterness and astringency, so also in its mixture it partakes of both heat and cold. It is drying in respect of both qualities, and moreover good for the stomach, because it has a share of no small astringency. Warmth, then, it does not possess in any very evident degree; but it dries in the second remove.

[6.3.5] [5. On glaucium.] Glaucium is astringent, with a certain unpleasantness, but it also cools so distinctly that on its own it often cures erysipelas, at least such cases as are not severe. And its mixture is compounded of a watery and an earthy substance, both of them cold, though not extremely so, but in the way that spring water is.
[6.3.6] [6. On glaux.] Glaux, the herb: this too is thought to be generative of milk. And if this is so, it would be in some way hot and moist in its mixture.

[6.3.7] [7. On pennyroyal.] Pennyroyal. This herb too, being pungent and somewhat bitter, heats and thins strongly. A sufficient sign of its heating is that, when applied as a plaster, it reddens, and, if it stays on longer, it ulcerates; and of its thinning, that it makes the thick and viscous fluids from the thorax and lung easy to cough up, and it stimulates the menses.

[6.3.8] [8. On gloios.] Gloios is also moderately softening. [6.3.9] [9. On glykyrrhiza.] Glykyrrhiza. Of this shrub the juice of the roots is the most useful part. Like its roots it is sweet, together with a certain slight astringency. For this reason it is by nature apt to smooth roughnesses, not only in the windpipe [artēria] but also in a psoric bladder, by the moderateness of its mixture. Its nature, then, would be akin to our own mixture, for such the sweet was shown to be. But since some astringency is also present, its whole mixture, so far as heat and astringency are concerned, would lie most of all at a lukewarm warmth, very close to the well-balanced one. And since what is moderately sweet is also moist in its mixture, the drug is fittingly thirst-quenching, being at once moderately moist and colder than the nature of man. Dioscorides says that the root, dried and ground fine, becomes a suitable sprinkling drug for pterygia.

[6.3.10] [10. On glykysidē.] Glykysidē, which they also call pentorobos and paeonia, has a root that is gently astringent with some sweetness, and, when chewed for longer, also with a somewhat bitter pungency. For this reason it provokes the menses, when drunk in the amount of an almond with melicrat; one must, evidently, pound it and sift it and so sprinkle it on. It also cleanses out an obstructed liver and the kidneys. But these things it is naturally disposed to effect inasmuch as it is pungent and somewhat bitter; inasmuch as it also has something astringent, it stops the fluxes of the belly. In that case one must boil it down in one of the harsh wines and drink it. On the whole it is strongly drying in its power, so that I would not despair that it is with good reason believed to cure the epilepsies of children even when hung around them. And indeed I know of a little child who for eight months had no seizure at all from the time he wore some of the root; but when the amulet somehow fell off his neck, he was at once seized, and when another was hung around him again he was once more faultlessly well. It seemed better to me to remove it yet again for the sake of a trial, and having done so, when he was again convulsed, we hung a large and fresh piece of the root from his neck, and from then on for the rest of the time the boy became entirely healthy and was no longer seized. It was reasonable, then, either that certain particles flowing off from the root, and then drawn in through inhalation, heal in this way the affected places, or else that the air itself is turned and altered by the root. For so too the Cyrenaic juice benefits an inflamed uvula, and roasted melanthion manifestly dries catarrhs and coryzas, if one ties it while hot in a loose-woven linen cloth and continually draws in the heat from it through inhalation by the nostrils. And indeed, if you put several threads, especially ones dyed with sea purple, around the neck of a viper and strangle the viper with them, and then hang each of the threads around the neck, it wonderfully benefits paristhmia and whatever sprouts up about the neck. About such matters, then, I might perhaps go through them separately at some time. But one must know that the mixture of paeonia is fine-particled and drying, yet not manifestly hot, but either well-balanced or a little hotter.

[6.3.11] [11. On gnaphalion.] Gnaphalion. It is so named because its leaves, which are soft, are used in place of gnaphala (flocks of wool for stuffing). They are white and moderately astringent, and for this reason some give it to dysenterics with one of the harsh wines.

[6.3.12] [12. On the turnip (gongylis).] The seed of the turnip stimulates to sexual intercourse, being generative of flatulent pneuma. In the same way the root too is hard to digest and flatulent and generative of semen.

[6.4.1] [1. On damasonium.] Damasonium, or also alisma. About this herb Dioscorides says in the third [book] that its root, if drunk, heals dysenteries, checks the belly, and soothes oedemas. We, however, have not tested these things; but we have found by testing that the water in which it happens to have been boiled, when drunk, breaks up the stones that form in the kidneys. It is clear, then, that it has a certain cleansing power.

[6.4.2] [2. On daukos.] Daukos, which some indeed call staphylinos. The wild kind is less edible than the cultivated, but more vehement in every respect; the cultivated is edible, but weaker. It is of a pungent and heating power, and for this reason also of a thinning one. The root, then, in addition to what has been said, also possesses something flatulent and aphrodisiac. As for the seed, that of the cultivated kind itself also has something that provokes to sexual intercourse, while that of the wild kind is entirely free of flatulence, and for this reason it is both diuretic and promotes the menses.

[6.4.3] [3. On the seed of Daukos.] The seed of the herb Daukos is heating to a considerable degree, so that it is a diuretic drug among the most efficacious, and provocative of the menses. It is also considerably dispersing when applied externally. And its herb too is of a similar power, but weaker than that of the seed, because of the admixture of watery moisture. Nevertheless this too is hot in its mixture.

[6.4.4] [4. On the laurel tree.] Both the leaves and the fruit of the laurel tree dry and heat strongly, and its fruit does so more than the leaves. The bark of the root is less pungent and hot, but more bitter, and it also has some astringency. This, then, is why it both breaks up stones and benefits the liver. It is drunk with fragrant wine, in the weight of three obols.

[6.4.5] [5. On the laurel that is a herb.] The mixture of the laurel that is a herb, which they also call Alexandrian, is evidently hot. To those who taste it, it is pungent and somewhat bitter, and when drunk it provokes both the menses and the urine. Of the chamaedaphne, the tender shoots are also eaten. This plant too is similar in its power to the Alexandrian laurel, as is also the plant called daphnoides.
[6.4.6] [6. On dittany.] Dittany is of a more fine-particled substance than pennyroyal. In other respects it is similar to it; but the so-called pseudo-dittany is weaker than dittany in all respects.

[6.4.7] [7. On dipsacus] The root of dipsacus, the thorny plant, is drying in the second order, and it also has something cleansing. [6.4.8] [8. On dorycnidium.] Dorycnidium is similar in mixture to poppy and mandragora and to the drugs that are cooling in this way, being dominated by a watery coldness that is very active. For taken in a small quantity it induces torpor, but taken in a larger quantity it kills.

[6.4.9] [9. On dracontium.] Dracontium has something similar to arum in both its leaves and its root. But it is more pungent than it and more bitter, and for this reason both more heating and more fine-particled. It also has a slight astringency, and when this combines with the two qualities mentioned before, the pungent and the bitter, the drug becomes one of the most effective. For the root thoroughly clears all the viscera, thinning above all the thick and viscid humours, and it is an excellent drug for malignant ulcers; and it generally clears away and cleanses off both everything else that requires cleansing and, with vinegar, alphoi. The leaves, having a similar power, are suitable for ulcers and for freshly inflicted wounds, and the less dry they are, the more they conglutinate. For the drier ones are more pungent in their power than befits wounds. It is also believed to keep moist cheese free from putrefaction when placed around it on the outside, on account of the dryness of its mixture. The fruit is stronger not only than the leaves but also than the root, so that it is believed to melt away even cancers and polyps. And its juice clears away the things in the eyes.

[6.4.10] [10. On dryopteris.] Dryopteris is, to one who tastes it, of a mixed quality: sweet, pungent, slightly bitter, and in the root also acerbic. It has a putrefying power, which is why it also strips away hair.

[6.4.11] [11. On the oak.] All the parts of the oak share in an astringent quality, but to a greater degree the membranous part in the bark of the trunk, and that which lies under the shell of the acorn, upon the flesh of the fruit. For this reason it is also believed to be useful against female flux, spittings of blood, dysenteries and chronic fluxes of the belly; and people use it chiefly by boiling it down. The phēgos and the prinos are still more vehemently astringent, whether one wishes to call them species of oak or to hold that they differ in their whole genus. Moreover, the tender leaves of these plants, applied as a poultice, are by nature able to dry not ignobly, but those of the other oak less so, in proportion as they also partake less of astringency. I myself, at any rate, know that I once agglutinated a wound made by a sickle with the leaves of the oak, when no other drug at all was at hand. I ground them on a smooth stone and plastered them over the wound together with the whole surrounding region. The fruit of the oak is also of the same power as the leaves. And some physicians have in fact used it for inflammations that are still beginning and increasing; for those that are already intense do not require astringents. But such matters belong to the therapeutic treatise rather than to the present one. For present purposes it suffices to know that the oak partakes of an astringent power to the extent stated, and for this reason of a drying and astringent one, and that it is hot to a slight degree, below the middle ones, among those which, as one might put it, are lukewarm.

[6.5.1] [1. On hibiscus.] Hibiscus, or althaea. It is the wild mallow: dispersing, relaxing, anti-inflammatory, soothing, concoctive of tumours that are hard to concoct. Its root and its seed act in other respects like the green herb, but they show a power more fine-particled than it, more drying and, besides, more cleansing, so that they even cleanse away alphoi, and the seed breaks up stones in the kidneys. The decoction of the root is also beneficial for dysentery and diarrhoea and for the bringing up of blood, since the root has a certain astringent power.

[6.5.2] [2. On ebony.] Ebony is one of the woods that dissolve into a juice if rubbed down with water, as some of the stones do. Its power is heating, cleansing and fine-particled, which is why it is also believed to cleanse the things that darken the pupils. It is also mixed into the other ophthalmic preparations, those suited to old ulcers, fluxes and phlyctaenae.

[6.5.3] [3. On the olive.] The young shoots of the olive share in cold to the same degree as they share in astringency. Of the fruit, that which is fully ripe is moderately hot, while the unripe is more astringent and colder.

[6.5.4] [4. On oil.] Of oil, the kind that comes from the olive, which we also call oil in the most proper sense, what sort of thing it is in its mixture has been determined in the preceding discussions: it was shown to be moistening and moderately warm. Such is the sweetest oil, produced above all from fruit that has fallen ripe from the tree (drupetēs). The oil called 'raw-pressed' (ōmotribes) and omphacine partakes of cooling to the same extent that it has taken a share of astringency. As for old oil, that which arises from sweet oil growing old is warmer and more dispersing. That which arises from raw-pressed oil is of mixed power so long as it preserves some of its astringency, but when it loses this completely it becomes like the other. Moreover, those who add olive shoots during the preparation also produce an oil similar to omphacine oil. One should not enquire how it has been prepared, but taste it oneself. If it shows some astringency, one should suppose that it shares in cooling to the same extent that it partakes of astringency, as is the case with the oil brought from Iberia, which they call Spanish. But if on tasting it appears not to be astringent at all, and is exactly sweet, one should consider it moderately warm. And if it also appears fine-particled, one should consider it the finest and the one possessing above all the excellence of oil, such as the Sabine is. Fine-particled oil is that which looks pure and translucent, and which, when a small amount is taken, is spread over a very large part of the body, remains continuous with itself, and is drunk up by the skin. That washed oil is the least biting has also been said before. How one might best wash it I shall tell in the following treatise, the one on the composition of drugs; there I shall also speak about Sicyonian oil and any other such oil. For now I am going through the simple drugs, and I shall next add the account of the other oils. There is also an oil called kikinon, produced mostly in Egypt from the fruit of the kiki, and there are radish oil and sesame oil, almond oil and nut oil, and further mustard oil, lentisk oil, laurel oil, melanthium oil, terebinth oil, mastic oil, myrtle oil, balanos oil, henbane oil, and not a few others besides these, all pressed out of fruits. These differ from one another by the same differences as the fruits do. Kikinon oil is more fine-particled and more dispersing, very similar to the old oil from the olive. Therefore, wherever kikinon oil is written in some composition of a drug and it is not available, one should use common oil, especially if it is Sabine. Radish oil is similar to this in other respects but warmer, and mustard oil is still more so than this. Similar to it is the oil from melanthium. Opposite to these are myrtle oil and sesame oil, the former because it is astringent, the latter because it is coarse-particled. Lentisk oil, terebinth oil and mastic oil are of mixed power, for they do not only soften but are also astringent. Almond oil has bitterness predominating, but it also partakes of some astringency. Nut oil does not; it is above all of a simple power, the dispersing one. Laurel oil is warmer and more dispersing than it, and cedar oil is still more so than this. Close to it is the torch-wood oil (dadinon) from liquid pitch, which is less warm than laurel oil but dries more. Henbane oil is of mixed power, at once softening and cooling. Kikinon oil loosens the belly. The oil from the Cnidian berry does so still more than this, and more by as much as the berry is more purgative than the kiki itself. The oil from the wild olive is also not of a simple mixture, but at once cleansing and astringent. For an oil, this one is rather dry (auchmēroteron), and after it comes the Istrian. Next to these comes the Spanish. The most oily are the Libyan and the Cilician, while the Sabine is at once oily and fine-particled. In the middle of all those mentioned is the oil of the Cyclades islands, of Greece and of Asia. Oily oil is judged by its viscidity. Fine-particled oil is judged by its translucency and purity, by a very large part of the body being anointed by a very small amount, and by its being readily drunk up by the skin. From what has been said you are now able to know also about the other oils that are called by the same names as the perfumes, I mean rose oil, quince oil, lily oil, and all such as are made by steeping fruits, flowers, shoots or leaves in oil. For each of these, when prepared together with aromatics, is made into a perfume. More will be said about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs. Having said what is useful for the present purpose, I shall finish. The oil will be altered according to the nature of each of the things put into it. You learn in general about each of these ingredients throughout this whole account, and from this you will be able to know also about the oil of each of them individually.

[6.5.5] [5. On elatine.] Elatine is moderately cooling and astringent. [6.5.6] [6. On elaphoboscum.] Elaphoboscum is of a hot and fine-particled power, and for this reason also of a drying one, at about the second of the removes, more or less.

[6.5.7] [7. On helenium.] Of the herb helenium it is the root that is most useful. It does not heat immediately at the first application, and for this reason it must be said to be not strictly hot and dry, as black and white pepper are, but hot and dry together with a residual moisture. For this reason too it is suitably mixed into the linctuses used for the bringing up of the viscid and thick humours in the chest and lung, and with it they redden the parts troubled by cold and chronic affections, such as certain cases of ischias, hemicranias, and continual dislocations of certain joints owing to moisture.

[6.5.8] [8. On elelisphakos.] Elelisphakos is of a clearly heating mixture, one that is gently somewhat astringent. [6.5.9] [9. On hellebore.] Each hellebore, both the white and the black, is of a power at once cleansing and heating. For this reason they are suitable for alphoi, leichenes, psorai and leprai. Moreover, the black, inserted into a callused fistula, detaches its callus in some two or three days. Used as a mouth-rinse with vinegar, it also benefits the teeth. Let them be placed in the third order of things that heat and dry. In taste the black is hotter, while the white is somewhat bitter.

[6.5.10] [10. On helxine.] Helxine: some call it perdikion, others parthenion, others sideritis, and there are those who call it Herakleia. Its power is cleansing and gently astringent, together with a slightly cold moisture. Hence it heals all inflammations at their beginning and during their increase up to the peak, and especially the hot ones. Moreover, it is also applied as a plaster to phygethla when they are beginning. And its juice, with rose oil, is moderately suited to inflammatory pains of the ears. Some also gargle with it for paristhmia, and some of the physicians have given it to those who cough chronically. Of its cleansing it gives clear proof in the case of glass vessels too.

[6.5.11] [11. On black helxine.] Helxine, which is also called kissampelos, is of a dispersing power. [6.5.12] [12. On elymos.] Elymos is also called meline. It is one of the pulses, similar to millet both in form and in power, of little nourishment and drying. It also somewhat stops the fluxes in the belly, just as millet does too. And if it is applied externally as a plaster, it both dries and cools.

[6.5.13] [13. On empetron.] Empetron seems to be useful for purgations only, drawing off phlegm and bile. It is salty to the taste, so that one might also use it for other purposes, those for which we showed the salty substance too to be effective. It is also called prasoeides ('leek-like').

[6.5.14] [14. On epithymon.] Epithymon is stronger than the power of thyme, which dries and heats in all respects in the third distance. [6.5.15] [15. On epimedium.] The power of epimedium is moderately cooling, with a watery moistness. At any rate it has no notable quality, but when applied as a plaster it is able to keep the breasts upright, and they say that it also prevents conception when drunk.

[6.5.16] [16. On epimēlis.] Epimēlis: this plant is acerbic and is, as one might say, a wild apple-tree. It is called unedōn by the country-people in Italy, and it grows most abundantly in Calabria. Its fruit is acerbic, yet bad for the stomach and productive of headache, for a certain strange quality is mixed in with it.

[6.5.17] [17. On chickpea.] Chickpea: a flatulent pulse, nourishing, good for the bowels, diuretic, generative of milk and of semen; it also promotes the menses. Those called 'rams' (krioi) are more diuretic than the others, and their decoction breaks up the stones in the kidneys. The other kind of chickpeas are called orobiai, and they are of the same power: drawing, dispersing, cutting, cleansing. For they are hot and moderately dry, and they also have some share of bitterness. On account of this they purge spleen, liver and kidneys, cleanse away psorai and leichenes, disperse parotides and testicles that are becoming scirrhous, and with honey they also heal malignant ulcers.

[6.5.18] [18. On wild chickpea.] Wild chickpea is stronger in every respect than the cultivated, that is, it is both hotter and more drying, to the same degree that it is also more pungent and more bitter.

[6.5.19] [19. On heath.] Heath is of a dispersing power. One should use above all its flower and its leaves. [6.5.20] [20. On tufted thyme.] Tufted thyme is of a heating power to such a degree as to move both the menses and urine. It is also sufficiently pungent to the taste.

[6.5.21] [21. On erysimum.] The seed of erysimum appears similar to cress in taste, and in the same way it is fiery and heating in its power. Whenever one needs to use it in a linctus, it is better to steep it in water beforehand and parch it, or else to tie it up in a linen cloth, then wrap it round with dough and roast it. With linctuses it is useful for the expectoration of viscous and thick humours from the chest and lung. It also benefits parotides that are becoming scirrhous, and old indurations in the breasts and testicles. Dioscorides says that, applied as a plaster with water or honey, it helps hidden cancers.

[6.5.22] [22. On erythrodanon.] Erythrodanon. This is the red root of the dyers, acerbic and bitter to the taste. Hence all the effects that were said in the preceding book to be produced by such powers when they come together with one another, you will clearly observe in this root. For it thoroughly cleanses both spleen and liver; it evacuates thick and copious urine, sometimes even bloody urine; and it also promotes the menses, and cleanses in due measure whatever stands in need of cleansing. So, for instance, it benefits white alphoi when smeared on with vinegar. Some also give it to sciatics and to the paralysed to drink with melikraton.

[6.5.23] [23. On eupatorium.] Eupatorium, the herb, is of a fine-particled, cutting and cleansing power, without manifest heat; hence it also clears out the obstructions in the liver. It also partakes of a slight astringency, on account of which it also imparts tone to the viscus.

[6.5.24] [24. On euphorbium.] Euphorbium is of a caustic and fine-particled power, like the other saps. [6.5.25] [25. On ephemeron.] Ephemeron: not the poisonous one, which they also name Colchicum, but the other, which is also called wild iris. It has leaves and a stalk like the lily, but a long root, not a round one as Colchicum has. It is about a finger in thickness, and it is astringent and fragrant. From these things it is clear that it is of a mixed power and mixture, both repelling and dispersing. Its particular effects also bear witness to this. For the root at least is a not ineffective mouth-rinse for toothache, and the leaves are suited to the rising stages and the peaks of phymata. One must boil them in wine and apply them as a plaster before suppuration takes place.
[6.5.26] [26. On echinus.] The fruit of the herb echinus is acerbic, and for this reason repelling and drying. People use it both for the fluxes of the eyes and for the ears.

[6.6.1] [1. On zeia.] Zeia is, in its whole power, somewhere between wheat and barley, so let it be known from those. [6.6.2] [2. On ginger.] The root of ginger is the useful part; it is this that they bring to us from the barbarian country. It heats strongly, but not at the first contact, as pepper does. For this very reason one must suppose that it is less fine-particled than pepper. For otherwise it would be dissolved into fine particles and would quickly become hot in actuality, as that does. It appears, at any rate, to contain a substance that is still somewhat unconcocted and more coarse-particled, and this not dry and earthy, but rather moist and watery. It is for this reason too that it is readily worm-eaten, because it contains residual moisture. None of those things that are either exactly dry, or moist but possessing a concocted and proper moisture, suffers this. Long pepper is affected in the same way, and for this reason the heat from ginger and long pepper persists longer than that from white and black pepper. For just as the flame from dry reeds catches all at once and very quickly spreads in every direction, so too does the heat from drugs that are dry in power. That from the moister ones, analogously to green wood, both kindles more slowly and persists longer; hence the use of each kind of drug is also different. For when we wish to heat the whole body quickly, we must give those things which heat quickly on coming into contact with the animal's heat, and which are quickly carried in every direction. But when we wish to heat some chilled part, we must do the opposite: those things which, being heated slowly, persist for a very long time are the ones applied. Ginger and long pepper, then, even if they differ from black pepper in this respect, do so only slightly. But cress, mustard, thapsia and the dung of wild pigeons both become fully fiery over a longer time and persist for a very long time.

[6.6.3] [3. On zythos.] Zythos is more pungent than barley by no small margin, and productive of bad humours, inasmuch as it has come into being from putrefaction. It is also flatulent, and has some part that is pungent and heating, but its greatest part is cold, watery and sour.

[6.6.4] [4. On leaven.] Leaven is fine-particled and moderately hot. For this reason, then, it both draws out what lies in the depth and at the same time disperses it, without pain and without biting. This too is mixed from opposite powers, as many other things also are. For it partakes of a cold sourness and of a putrefactive heat, and in addition of the [power] that comes from the salt and of the [power] that belongs by nature to the flour.

[6.7.1] [1. On hēdyosmon.] Hēdyosmon, which some call mint (minthē). For there is a certain other mint, not fragrant, which they also call kalaminthē. Both are pungent to those who taste them, and hot in power, somewhere in the third order of heating things. The fragrant mint, however, is weaker than kalaminthē and less heating. For, to speak generally, the latter is a sort of wild plant and the former a cultivated one, so that, on account of the moisture present in it from being grown in gardens, it also moderately incites to sexual intercourse. This is common to all things that have a share of a half-concocted and flatulent moisture. On account of such a mixture of the herb, some also apply it with barley-meal to abscesses, which kalaminthē cannot do, because it heats and dries more vehemently than such [conditions require]. It also has something bitter and acerbic in itself, and by the bitter it destroys worms, while by the acerbic, when drunk with oxycrate, it checks recent bringings-up of blood. And it is fine-particled in its substance, if any other herb is.

[6.7.2] [2. On hedysaron.] Hedysaron, or pelekinos. The seed of this shrub is tawny in colour, and two-edged like axes; it appears bitter and slightly acerbic, and so it is good for the stomach when drunk, and it clears out the obstructions in the viscera. The twigs of the whole shrub act in the same way.

[6.7.3] [3. On hemerocallis.] The root of hemerocallis, being similar to that of the lily both in form and in power, benefits burns in a similar way to it. For it is of a gently dispersing power, while also having something repelling.

[6.7.4] [4. On hēmionitis.] Hēmionitis partakes of astringency together with bitterness; for this reason it also benefits those suffering in the spleen when drunk with vinegar. [6.7.5] [5. On ērigerōn.] Ērigerōn has a mixed power, at once cooling and moderately dispersing.

[6.7.6] [6. On eryngium.] Eryngium exceeds the moderate in heat either slightly or not at all, but it has no small share of a fine-particled dryness. [6.8.1] [1. On thalictrum.] Thalictrum has leaves resembling coriander, and a stem of the thickness of that of rue. Its power is drying without biting; at any rate it cicatrizes the chronic among ulcers.

[6.8.2] [2. On thapsia.] Thapsia is of a pungent and strongly heating power, together with moisture. For it draws forcibly from the depth, and disperses what has been drawn. But it accomplishes these things over a longer time, because it is filled with abundant residual moisture, on account of which it also quickly spoils.

[6.8.3] [3. On the lupine.] The lupine is eaten when it has been boiled and has, over many days, deposited its bitterness in water; it then becomes a food of thick humours. As a drug, the lupine so treated belongs among the clogging drugs, whereas the one that keeps its innate bitterness is cleansing and dispersing. It also kills worms, whether applied as a plaster, licked up with honey, or drunk with oxycrate. Its decoction, too, is by nature able to expel worms. Moreover, poured over the body from outside, it benefits alphoi, achores, exanthemata, psorai, gangrainai and malignant ulcers, some by cleansing, others by dispersing and drying without biting. It also thoroughly purges liver and spleen when taken with rue and pepper for the sake of pleasantness. It also draws out the menses and embryos when applied with myrrh and honey. The meal of lupines is also dispersing without biting. For it treats not only livid marks but also choirades and hard phymata. In that case one must boil it in vinegar, or oxymel, or oxycrate, finding out what is required evidently according to the mixtures of the patients and the difference of the affection. But it is not the business of the treatise now before us to distinguish such matters. It also disperses livid marks; and all the other things that the decoction was said above to do, the meal too is by nature able to effect. Some also apply it as a cataplasm to sufferers from sciatica.

[6.8.4] [4. On wild lupin.] Wild lupin is more bitter than the cultivated and stronger in all respects, being of the same power as it in kind. [6.8.5] [5. On thlaspi.] Seed of thlaspi. This too is pungent in its power, so that when given to drink it ruptures internal abscessions, sets the menses in motion and kills embryos, and when injected through the anus it benefits cases of ischias by evacuating bloody matter. For it is also otherwise purgative of bilious matter both upward and downward, when drunk in the quantity of an oxybaphon.

[6.8.6] [6. On lettuce.] Lettuce is a moist and cold vegetable, though not extremely so, for then it would not be edible. Rather, it has, so to speak, chiefly the power, or coldness, of spring waters. For this reason it is suited to hot inflammations and to the small and mild among the cases of erysipelas, but it is not able to cope with the larger ones. It is also a thirst-allaying food. Its seed, when drunk, checks seminal flux, and so it is also given to those who have wet dreams. So too does the seed of the wild lettuce, whose juice people also collect; smeared on with woman's milk, it cleans away argema and achlys, and it serves for epicaumata.

[6.8.7] [7. On thyme.] Thyme cuts and heats manifestly; for this reason it also provokes urine and menses, draws down embryos, and thoroughly cleanses the viscera when drunk, and it assists the bringing up of matter from the thorax and lung. Accordingly, both in drying and in heating it must be placed in the third order.

[6.9.1] [1. On the Idaean root.] The Idaean root is both very acerbic when tasted and, to one who tests it by its effects, displays the same power, treating haemorrhages, fluxes of the belly, dysenteries, the female flux, and all other such conditions, both when drunk and when applied externally.

[6.9.2] [2. On birdlime.] Birdlime (ixos) is composed of a very large amount of airy and watery substance, which is hot, and a very small amount of earthy substance. At any rate, the pungent in it is greater than the bitter, and accordingly its effects too correspond to its substance. For it powerfully draws moistures out of the depth, not only the thin ones but also the thicker ones, and it both diffuses and disperses them. It is one of those drugs that do not heat at once, after the first application, but require time, like thapsia. This was also said earlier: it is a property of drugs that are hot in power when they contain abundant residual moisture.

[6.9.3] [3. On ion (violet).] The leaves of ion possess a predominating substance that is watery and somewhat cold, and for this reason, applied as a plaster both by themselves and with barley-groats, they soothe hot inflammations. They are also applied over the mouth of the stomach when it is burning, and over the eyes.

[6.9.4] [4. On hippuris.] Hippuris has an astringent quality together with bitterness, and for this reason it is drying, both strongly and at the same time without biting. So when applied as a plaster it agglutinates the very greatest wounds, even if sinews happen to have been cut through, and also the so-called enteroceles.
